What matters is how you feel, your usual level of activity and any health advice specific to you. One person may enjoy their normal session while another needs a slower day. Hormones change over the cycle; estrogen and progesterone are generally low around the beginning of a natural menstrual period, not throughout the whole cycle. That does not predict everyone’s energy or performance. Cramps, disrupted sleep, bleeding, stress and how well you have eaten can all affect the experience of a workout. Rest is a reasonable choice when you need it. You do not have to prove that exercise helps by pushing through symptoms, and a missed session is not a failure. Equally, feeling well during your period does not oblige you to reduce a routine that is already suitable for you. Which benefits are realistic? Regular activity may help with premenstrual symptoms, including feeling tense or low, and can be one part of a broader routine that includes sleep and adequate food. PMS describes symptoms before a period, so the aim is a sustainable habit across the month rather than a special workout once bleeding starts. Movement can also feel refreshing or lift your mood. Endorphins are often mentioned as one possible explanation for feeling better after activity, but this is not a promise that a session will switch off cramps. Some people find that light movement eases back discomfort or tension; others find rest more helpful. Headaches, fatigue and breast tenderness do not respond identically in everyone. For primary dysmenorrhoea (period pain without an identified underlying condition) a 2019 Cochrane review found that regular exercise may reduce pain, but the evidence was low quality. The studies generally used activity across the month, and some excluded exercise on bleeding days. They do not establish that a single walk will immediately relieve pain, or that exercise can replace a treatment that works for you. Choose a session that fits how you feel today The first days can be the most uncomfortable, especially when bleeding or cramps are heavier. If you want to move, choose something familiar and easy to adjust. For example, a short walk near home is easier to shorten than a long route with no convenient way back. Start gently and see whether you feel the same, better or worse. If your normal session feels unusually difficult, changing one part may be enough: take more breaks, shorten the session, reduce the load or choose a less intense activity. You can also stop. A useful plan leaves room for that decision instead of setting a target you must finish regardless of symptoms. Walking, cardio and swimming Light walking, relaxed cycling or an easy swim are options when you want movement without a demanding session. A shorter version of your usual aerobic activity may be more comfortable. If you feel well and have no relevant restriction, menstruation by itself does not rule out a harder session you are accustomed to. There is no established rule that everyone should save aerobic exercise for the end of their period because their lungs will work better then. Breathing difficulty deserves attention on its own terms. Do not explain new or disproportionate breathlessness away as a normal cycle effect. Practical comfort matters too. Choose a menstrual product that suits the activity and follow its changing or emptying instructions. Allow access to a bathroom and spare supplies if you need them. You do not need to tolerate leakage worries or uncomfortable clothing to make a workout count. Strength work, yoga and Pilates Strength training can remain part of your routine. On a less comfortable day, fewer sets, lighter weights or longer rests may help you maintain control and enjoy the session. On a comfortable day, there is no automatic requirement to make every exercise easier. Avoid using a predicted “strong phase” as a reason to attempt unfamiliar maximum lifts. Yoga, stretching or Pilates may appeal when you want slower movement and a chance to relax. Choose positions that feel comfortable and modify or stop movements that increase pain. They can be options before a period as well as during it; there is no exclusive two- or three-day window when they must be done. These choices are alternatives, not a hierarchy. A gentle class is not guaranteed to treat breast tenderness, headache or fatigue, and a more intense class is not automatically better because it combines strength and cardio. Your response matters more than the class label. You do not need a rigid cycle-based exercise schedule Claims that everyone becomes stronger in the first two weeks, must reduce all training during bleeding, or should avoid skill and precision work are too broad. A 2020 systematic review found small average differences and substantial variation between studies; the evidence did not support a universal phase-by-phase performance plan. You may still notice a pattern of your own. A simple record of symptoms, bleeding, sleep and how a session felt can help you discuss adjustments with a coach or clinician. Record good days as well as difficult ones. A calendar estimate cannot tell you in advance how capable you will feel. Hormonal contraception can change bleeding patterns and hormone exposure, so advice based on a natural cycle may not apply. Irregular cycles also make calendar predictions less useful. You do not need hormone testing or a paid cycle programme simply to choose a comfortable walk, workout or rest day. When to pause exercise and get checked Pain that repeatedly keeps you away from work, school or normal activities deserves assessment. So do increasingly painful or irregular periods, bleeding between periods, or pain with sex, urination or bowel movements. These symptoms should not be treated as a fitness problem or solved only by trying a different workout. Heavy bleeding can contribute to iron deficiency or anaemia. Mention flooding through clothing, frequent product changes, prolonged bleeding, marked tiredness or unusual breathlessness to a clinician. Treatment can address the bleeding and any deficiency; do not assume you need high-dose iron without advice. Stop if you become faint, develop chest pain, have severe new pain or struggle to breathe. Seek urgent help for severe or worsening pelvic pain that is not settling, particularly if pregnancy is possible. Heavy bleeding with faintness or significant weakness also needs urgent assessment rather than waiting for the next training day. If training is followed by missed periods Periods becoming infrequent or stopping during increased training are not proof that you are getting fitter. One possible contributor is insufficient energy intake for your activity and everyday needs, sometimes part of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs). Pregnancy and other medical causes also need consideration. Discuss a new or persistent change with a clinician rather than trying to diagnose it from an app. Adequate meals, recovery and appropriate training are important, and a sports dietitian may help when under-fuelling is suspected. Contraceptive bleeding patterns can complicate interpretation; tell the clinician what you use. Build a flexible routine you can return to Keep a few options available: your usual session, a shorter or gentler version, and rest. That makes it easier to respond to the day without abandoning a routine for an entire week or feeling pressured to complete it unchanged. Eat regularly, drink according to your needs and make recovery part of the plan. If gentle movement helps, it can sit alongside other appropriate comfort measures or prescribed treatment. If symptoms repeatedly require major changes, bring that pattern to a health appointment. The goal is to stay active in a way that supports you, while taking pain and bleeding seriously. Menstruation alone does not require stopping your normal exercise. Walking, cardio, strength work, yoga and Pilates can be adjusted to comfort; rest is also valid. There is no reliable universal rule for a stronger week or a forbidden type of exercise. Heavy bleeding, limiting pain or missed periods should prompt care, not pressure to train harder. Can I exercise on the first day of my period? Usually, if you feel well. You may prefer a shorter walk, a gentler session or rest if that day is uncomfortable. There is no requirement to push through cramps or reduce every workout simply because bleeding has started. Will a workout stop period cramps? It may help you feel more comfortable, but immediate relief is not guaranteed. Evidence about regular exercise across the month should not be read as proof that one session treats today’s pain. Do I need to avoid lifting weights? Not just because of menstruation. Keep to loads and movements you can control comfortably, and reduce or stop if symptoms interfere. Your period is not a reason to attempt a new maximum either. Are yoga and Pilates only useful before a period? No. You can choose them whenever they feel comfortable. They may offer gentle movement or relaxation, but there is no special timing window and no guarantee they will relieve every symptom. Can I swim while menstruating? Menstruation alone does not prevent swimming. Use a suitable menstrual product if needed, follow its instructions and choose a session that matches how you feel. Should I avoid sport that requires skill or concentration? There is no blanket ban. If pain, fatigue or dizziness makes an activity unsafe for you that day, change the activity or stop. That is different from assuming everyone loses skill during a period. Is rest a bad choice? No. Rest can be the right response to discomfort or poor recovery. A flexible routine includes easier days, and you do not need to earn rest by trying a workout first. What if I am unusually tired or breathless during my period? Pause the session and consider medical advice, especially with heavy bleeding. Persistent fatigue or breathlessness can need investigation; sudden severe breathlessness, chest pain or fainting needs urgent help. Is it normal for periods to stop when I train more? It should not be treated as a desirable training result. Arrange assessment for a new or persistent change. Under-fuelling is one possible cause, but pregnancy, contraception and other medical conditions also matter.

title: Why is my period lasting longer than usual?
description: Explore prolonged bleeding, medicines, contraception, ovulation and uterine causes, plus urgent signs and what an assessment may involve.
body: A period that lasts longer than expected can be unsettling. Several treatable causes are possible, but the amount of bleeding, associated symptoms and chance of pregnancy matter as much as the number of days. Separate the length of a period from the length of a cycle A period is the time you bleed. A menstrual cycle is counted from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. A longer cycle and a longer bleed are different changes, even though they can happen together. Many periods last about two to seven days. Adult cycle intervals are often described as roughly 21 to 35 days, with variation by age and individual pattern. Twenty-eight days is an average, not a requirement. The early years after periods begin and the years approaching menopause may be less predictable. Bleeding for more than a week, a substantial change from your usual pattern or bleeding that disrupts daily life deserves attention. Duration alone cannot tell you whether ovulation occurred. A cycle outside a typical interval may prompt assessment, but it does not prove that an egg was released too early or not at all. Check whether the bleeding needs urgent attention Seek urgent medical advice for very heavy ongoing bleeding, particularly if you are soaking a pad or tampon about every hour. Do not wait to reach a fixed number if you feel unwell. Emergency help is needed if heavy bleeding comes with fainting, marked dizziness, shortness of breath, chest pain or severe weakness. ACOG specifically advises emergency care when products need changing hourly for more than two hours and there is lightheadedness, dizziness, breathlessness or chest pain. This is an example of a concerning pattern, not a rule that other symptoms must wait. If pregnancy is possible, unusual bleeding with abdominal or pelvic pain needs prompt assessment. Severe or one-sided pain, shoulder-tip pain, faintness or collapse can signal an emergency such as ectopic pregnancy. Bleeding does not reliably exclude pregnancy. Some non-hormonal medicines change bleeding Aspirin reduces platelet activity and can make bleeding heavier. It is an antiplatelet medicine, whereas anticoagulants work through other parts of the clotting system; both can be relevant to prolonged menstrual bleeding. Tell the clinician why the medicine was prescribed and when you started it. Other anti-inflammatory medicines, including ibuprofen and naproxen, can reduce menstrual blood loss and cramps in appropriate patients. Their effect is different from aspirin’s, but they are not suitable for everyone. Do not add them without advice if you take a blood thinner, have relevant stomach or kidney problems, or could be pregnant. Some antidepressants and medicines used for epilepsy may affect bleeding, hormones or contraceptive effectiveness. Effects depend on the particular drug and combination. Do not assume every medicine in a class does this, that symptoms must settle in three months, or that you should wait that long for help. Never stop an essential medicine abruptly to test the theory. Contraception can alter the pattern Combined pills, progestogen-only pills, implants, vaginal rings, patches, injections and hormonal intrauterine systems can change when and how much you bleed. Some methods are also used to treat heavy periods. Spotting or breakthrough bleeding is not necessarily a normal ovulatory period. A hormonal intrauterine system often makes bleeding lighter over time, although irregular bleeding can occur initially. A copper IUD can make periods heavier or longer. Contraceptive injections may produce irregular or prolonged bleeding in some people and little or no bleeding in others. When a pattern changes, note the method, start date, missed doses, other medicines and any pain or discharge. A clinician can assess whether the change fits the method or whether pregnancy, infection or another cause needs checking. New persistent bleeding after a previously stable pattern should not automatically be attributed to contraception. Delayed or absent ovulation is one possible cause Hormonal changes can alter when an ovary releases an egg, or a cycle may occur without ovulation. The uterine lining can then shed unpredictably, sometimes after a longer gap and sometimes with prolonged or heavy bleeding. Ovulation does not always happen exactly halfway through a cycle. Stress, thyroid disease, polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, breastfeeding and some medicines can be relevant. Changes in basal body temperature, cervical mucus or lower abdominal sensations may help someone notice a pattern, but they do not confirm the cause of delayed ovulation on their own. Track the dates and symptoms if it helps, but do not use an app’s prediction as a diagnosis or assume a prolonged bleed means you cannot become pregnant. Persistent irregularity, very long gaps or difficulty conceiving can justify a discussion about hormonal and reproductive assessment. Emergency contraception may affect the next bleed Emergency contraceptive pills work mainly by delaying or preventing ovulation. The next period may arrive earlier or later than expected, and the amount or duration of bleeding can differ. Spotting and cramps can also occur. These changes do not show whether the method worked. Take a pregnancy test from the first day of a missed period, or at least 21 days after the most recent unprotected sex if you are unsure when a period is due. Sex after taking an emergency pill can create a new pregnancy risk, so follow the advice given about ongoing contraception. Do not assume every later episode of prolonged bleeding is an after-effect of one emergency pill. Seek advice if the change persists, bleeding is heavy or pain develops. A negative test taken too early may need repeating at the appropriate time. Bleeding after pregnancy loss or abortion is not the next period Bleeding immediately after miscarriage or abortion is related to the pregnancy ending and the uterus recovering. It is different from the next menstrual period. Its amount and duration vary with the pregnancy, treatment and individual recovery, so follow the instructions from the care team. The first later period may differ from your usual one, and hormones can take time to settle. There is no reliable rule that a procedure produces a short first period while medicine produces a long one. Bloating, headache, breast tenderness, mood changes or tiredness are also not enough to decide whether recovery is complete. After miscarriage, a period can take up to eight weeks to return; after abortion, timing also depends on recovery and any contraception started. Ask your service if a period has not returned when expected, and follow its pregnancy-test plan. Ovulation and a new pregnancy can occur before the next period. Worsening pain, fever, offensive discharge, persistent pregnancy symptoms or heavy bleeding needs earlier help rather than waiting eight weeks. Fibroids and polyps can cause prolonged bleeding Fibroids are non-cancerous growths of muscle and fibrous tissue in or around the uterus. Polyps are growths arising from the uterine lining. Either may contribute to heavy, prolonged or irregular bleeding, sometimes with clots. They are not limited to people aged 35 to 50. Fibroids can also cause pelvic pressure, frequent or difficult urination, constipation and back discomfort. Some people describe pain spreading towards a leg, but this is not specific to fibroids and needs assessment. Polyps may cause bleeding between periods or after menopause and can sometimes affect fertility. Ultrasound can help assess fibroids. A hysteroscopy uses a narrow camera to inspect the uterine cavity and can help identify or remove a polyp or certain fibroids. Treatment depends on symptoms, size, position and reproductive plans. Medicines or targeted procedures may be appropriate; removing the uterus is not the automatic next step. Thyroid symptoms provide useful clues An underactive thyroid can be associated with heavier or irregular periods. Other possible symptoms include feeling unusually cold, fatigue, constipation, weight gain, dry skin or hair, brittle nails and low mood. Appetite changes may occur too, but none of these symptoms alone confirms thyroid disease. The pattern often develops gradually rather than as a sudden, unmistakable change. Mention symptoms beyond bleeding so the clinician can decide whether thyroid testing is appropriate. A thyroid test is not automatically required for every heavy period when there are no other suggestive features. If thyroid disease is found, treatment should address it alongside the effect of blood loss, including possible anaemia. Do not start thyroid supplements or change a prescription based only on a period-tracking result. PCOS, now also called PMOS, may cause long gaps and irregular bleeding The condition traditionally called polycystic ovary syndrome, or PCOS, is now called polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, or PMOS, in current NHS guidance. It involves hormone and metabolic patterns that can affect ovulation, periods, skin and hair. Both names may still appear in medical records and patient information. Periods may be infrequent, absent, light or irregular, and bleeding after a long gap can sometimes be heavy or prolonged. Acne, increased facial or body hair, scalp hair thinning, weight changes and darkened thick skin around the neck, armpits or other folds may be clues. People do not all have the same symptoms or body size. The condition is more complex than simply having too much of a male hormone. Androgens are present in everyone, and assessment considers the overall pattern and other possible causes. Long gaps between bleeds may require a plan to protect the uterine lining, even when the lack of periods is convenient. Endometriosis needs assessment even after a normal scan Endometriosis involves tissue similar to the uterine lining growing outside the uterus. It can cause painful periods, pelvic or lower-back pain, pain during or after sex, bowel or bladder symptoms, fatigue and difficulty conceiving. Some people also have heavy bleeding. Bowel symptoms can include constipation, diarrhoea or painful bowel movements; urinary symptoms can include pain or altered frequency. These symptoms have other possible causes too, so noting whether they change with the cycle can help the consultation without proving the diagnosis. Ultrasound can identify some forms of endometriosis and other pelvic problems, but a normal ultrasound does not exclude it. Persistent symptoms may need specialist assessment, further imaging or consideration of laparoscopy. It is incorrect to assume most cases are ruled in or out by a routine scan alone. Adenomyosis is a different uterine condition Adenomyosis involves endometrial tissue within the muscular wall of the uterus. It differs from endometriosis outside the uterus, although the two can coexist. Some people have no noticeable symptoms; others have heavy bleeding, severe cramps or ongoing pelvic discomfort. A feeling of pelvic fullness, bloating or pain with sex may occur. Examination and imaging, usually ultrasound and sometimes MRI, can help assess the problem and distinguish it from other causes. Symptoms alone are not enough to know which condition is present. Treatment may include medicines to reduce bleeding or pain and hormonal options. The best choice depends on severity, other conditions and whether future pregnancy is a priority. Surgery is considered individually if simpler approaches are unsuitable or ineffective. Perimenopause can change periods but does not explain every bleed During the transition towards menopause, hormone fluctuations can make periods closer together or further apart, lighter or heavier. Hot flushes, night sweats, sleep difficulty, vaginal dryness, urinary symptoms and changes in sexual comfort may occur at the same time. Menopause often occurs between ages 45 and 55, but the transition begins at different times and age alone does not establish its cause. A new heavy or prolonged pattern, bleeding between periods or bleeding after sex still needs assessment. It should not simply be dismissed as an expected stage. Once someone has gone 12 months without a natural period and reached menopause, any new vaginal bleeding needs checking, even a small amount once. Hormonal contraception and some treatments can complicate interpretation, so tell the clinician what you use. What a clinician may check Bring a record of bleeding days, flow, clots, pain and any dizziness or tiredness. Include pregnancy possibility, contraception, medicines, previous pregnancies and whether heavy bleeding has been present since your first periods. A personal or family history of easy bruising or abnormal bleeding may suggest a clotting disorder. Assessment may include a pregnancy test, an examination with your consent and a full blood count to look for anaemia. Other tests depend on the history. For example, coagulation testing may be appropriate for longstanding heavy bleeding with a suggestive history, while thyroid testing is more useful when other thyroid symptoms are present. Ultrasound, hysteroscopy or a sample of the uterine lining may be recommended for particular findings or risk factors. The aim is to identify causes such as fibroids, polyps or endometrial changes, including uncommon serious causes, rather than give everyone the same test panel. Treatment should fit the cause and your plans Options may include tranexamic acid, an appropriate anti-inflammatory medicine, hormonal treatment or a hormonal intrauterine system. Iron treatment may be needed if blood loss has caused iron deficiency. Suitability depends on pregnancy possibility, clotting risk, other medicines and medical history. A polyp, fibroid or other identified condition may need a specific procedure. Discuss whether you want to become pregnant, because some procedures affect fertility permanently. A treatment that improves bleeding is useful only if its other effects also fit your priorities. Contact a clinician when bleeding lasts more than a week, repeatedly differs from your usual pattern or disrupts daily life. You do not need to wait several months to ask. Seek help sooner for pain, pregnancy possibility or signs of significant blood loss, and agree when the response to treatment will be reviewed. A period and a menstrual cycle are different measurements. Bleeding over a week or a major pattern change is worth discussing. Do not stop prescribed medicine without advice. Pregnancy and postmenopausal bleeding require specific assessment. Treatment depends on the cause, severity and reproductive plans. Does a period lasting over seven days mean I did not ovulate? No. Prolonged bleeding has several possible causes. Duration alone cannot confirm whether ovulation occurred, although the pattern may help a clinician decide what to investigate. Should I wait three months before asking about a medicine? No. Ask sooner if bleeding is heavy, persistent, painful or concerning. Effects vary by medicine, and an essential prescription should not be stopped abruptly without advice. Can an IUD make a period longer? A copper IUD can increase bleeding or duration. A hormonal intrauterine system often reduces bleeding over time, though irregular bleeding can happen initially. New symptoms still deserve assessment. Does bleeding after an emergency pill mean I am not pregnant? No. Bleeding is not a reliable pregnancy test. Test from a missed period, or at least 21 days after the most recent unprotected sex when timing is uncertain, and seek care for concerning pain or bleeding. Is bleeding after miscarriage or abortion my next period? Usually the immediate bleeding relates to the pregnancy ending and recovery, not the next menstrual cycle. Follow the care team’s instructions and testing plan; heavy bleeding, fever or worsening pain needs earlier help. Does a normal ultrasound rule out endometriosis? No. A normal ultrasound does not exclude endometriosis. Persistent pain or other suggestive symptoms may still need specialist assessment. Are PCOS and PMOS different conditions? PMOS is the newer name now used in NHS guidance for the condition traditionally called PCOS. Both terms may appear while terminology changes; care should address the individual hormonal and metabolic pattern. Is heavier bleeding always normal near menopause? No. Hormonal changes can affect periods, but new heavy or prolonged bleeding still needs assessment. Any bleeding after menopause should be checked, even if it happens only once. Will fibroids or polyps always need a hysterectomy? No. Depending on the cause and symptoms, medicines or targeted procedures may be options. Future pregnancy plans should be discussed before choosing treatment. When should I seek emergency help? Seek emergency help for heavy bleeding with fainting, marked dizziness, chest pain, breathlessness or severe weakness. Severe abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain or collapse when pregnancy is possible is also an emergency.

title: Stringy period blood and clots: what matters
description: Texture and colour can vary during a period. The amount of bleeding, pain, pregnancy possibility and changes from your usual pattern matter more.
body: Menstrual fluid is not only blood. It also contains material from the uterine lining and normal genital secretions, so it may look thin, sticky, stringy or jelly-like. An occasional small clot or strand can occur during an otherwise ordinary period. Appearance alone cannot tell you whether there is a medical problem. Why the texture can change Blood can clot as it collects before leaving the uterus, and mucus can make menstrual fluid look stretchy or slippery. Small clots are often noticed during heavier flow. The mixture can change between days and between cycles. A strand does not prove that the uterine lining has become unusually thick, and a jelly-like piece does not identify a particular hormone condition. Try to assess the overall bleeding pattern rather than one isolated appearance. Flow is often heaviest in the first day or two, but this varies. Clots can occur whenever flow is heavy enough for blood to pool; they are not restricted to the last days of a period. The material includes blood and shed uterine lining mixed with normal vaginal and cervical fluid. Colour is not a diagnosis Fresh menstrual blood may look bright red, while blood that takes longer to leave can become dark red or brown. A small amount mixed with other fluid can look paler or thinner. Bright red or watery bleeding does not, on its own, diagnose an injury or miscarriage. Likewise, dark blood does not prove that everything is fine. The timing, volume and accompanying symptoms are more useful than matching the colour to an online chart. New discharge with an unpleasant smell, irritation or pelvic pain needs advice. Do not diagnose infection from a shade alone or try to treat it with internal washes. When clots are part of a heavy-bleeding problem Arrange a review if you repeatedly pass large clots, especially around 2.5 centimetres or larger, or if clots are a new feature of much heavier bleeding. That size is a useful prompt for assessment, not a precise boundary between safe and unsafe. Other reasons to seek care include bleeding longer than seven days, flooding onto clothes or bedding, frequent product changes, increasing period pain, or bleeding between periods or after sex. Persistent fatigue or breathlessness may indicate anaemia from blood loss. Easy bruising or frequent nosebleeds can suggest a separate bleeding tendency. Mention these, particularly if heavy periods have been present since menstruation began. Bruising is not simply another name for iron-deficiency anaemia. Know when to get urgent help If blood is soaking through a pad or tampon about every hour, continues heavily or becomes difficult to manage, seek urgent advice. Heavy bleeding with fainting, substantial dizziness, chest pain, breathlessness or severe weakness needs emergency care. Act on how you feel as well as the amount of blood. Do not wait to photograph another clot, measure every piece or reach a set number of hours if you are becoming unwell. If pregnancy is possible, treat bleeding differently Bleeding and clots can occur with an early pregnancy complication, but they cannot confirm a miscarriage by sight. A pregnancy test and sometimes an ultrasound or blood tests are needed to understand what is happening. Severe or one-sided abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain or faintness can indicate an ectopic pregnancy and needs immediate assessment, even if a home pregnancy test has not yet been positive. If you know you are pregnant, contact your maternity or early-pregnancy service about bleeding. Bleeding after birth, miscarriage or an abortion has its own expected course and warning signs. Follow your aftercare instructions rather than treating it as an ordinary period. What a clinician may look for Heavy or changing bleeding can have several explanations, including fibroids, polyps, adenomyosis, ovulation changes, some medicines, contraception or a bleeding disorder. Less commonly, changes in the uterine lining need investigation. The appearance of a clot cannot distinguish among these. A clinician may review your medicines, check for pregnancy and anaemia, and decide whether an examination, ultrasound or another investigation is appropriate. Any bleeding after menopause needs review, even without large clots. Record the dates, product changes, pain and impact on daily life. A rough description of clot size is enough to start the conversation. Do not stop prescribed medicines or start vitamin K, aspirin or a supposed blood-cleansing remedy on your own. Treatment should address the cause and your preferences, including future pregnancy plans. Fibroids are usually benign growths in the uterine muscle; polyps grow from the lining. Adenomyosis involves lining-like tissue within the uterine muscle, while endometriosis involves tissue outside the uterus and may contribute to painful periods. Ovulation disorders, including the condition previously called PCOS, can change how regularly the lining sheds; bleeding is not simply caused by ovarian cysts bursting. Thyroid disease can also alter periods. A copper IUD may increase bleeding, particularly at first, whereas some hormonal IUDs are used to reduce heavy periods. Anticoagulants and inherited bleeding disorders can also contribute. Endometrial hyperplasia or cancer is a less common explanation, especially requiring consideration with bleeding after menopause or other concerning changes. Vitamin K deficiency is an unusual medical cause of impaired clotting, not a diagnosis made from menstrual texture or a reason to self-prescribe supplements. Menstrual texture naturally varies because blood mixes with tissue and secretions. Colour or stringiness cannot diagnose miscarriage, infection or a hormone disorder. Repeated large clots and heavy or prolonged bleeding deserve assessment. Heavy bleeding with feeling faint or short of breath needs urgent help. Is every stringy piece a blood clot? No. Mucus and shed tissue can also affect texture. You cannot reliably identify the exact material from appearance alone. Does bright red watery blood mean miscarriage? No. It is not diagnostic. If pregnancy is possible, use appropriate testing and seek advice, especially with pain or heavy bleeding. Should I bring a photograph to an appointment? It may help describe a change if you are comfortable doing so, but it is optional and should never delay urgent care. The bleeding pattern and symptoms remain important.

title: Why periods happen: and what your cycle can tell you
description: A period is the shedding of the uterine lining. Learn how to count a cycle, interpret bleeding changes and discuss lighter or less frequent periods.
body: A period is part of the hormonal cycle that can prepare the body for pregnancy. When pregnancy does not occur, changes in hormone levels lead the lining of the uterus to shed. Menstruation is common, but disabling pain or bleeding that disrupts daily life is not something you simply have to accept. What happens during the cycle Hormonal signals involving the brain and ovaries help coordinate the menstrual cycle. The uterine lining develops, and in an ovulatory cycle an egg is released from an ovary. After ovulation, progesterone helps support the lining. If pregnancy does not develop, estrogen and progesterone levels fall, and part of the lining leaves the body through the cervix and vagina. Menstrual fluid contains blood as well as tissue and other fluid. Bleeding alone does not prove that ovulation occurred normally. Bleeding associated with hormonal contraception, for example, may follow a different pattern from a natural ovulatory cycle. The hypothalamus and pituitary in the brain send signals to the ovaries, which then affect the uterine lining. Ovulation, fertilisation and implantation are distinct steps: sperm fertilises an egg, and a resulting embryo may later implant in the lining. When the hormonal support for the lining falls without an ongoing pregnancy, bleeding begins and the cycle can start again. Count from one starting day to the next Cycle length is measured from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. It is not the interval from the end of bleeding to the next start. A 28-day cycle is an average, not a requirement. Cycle length and the number of bleeding days vary between people and across life stages. Early teenage cycles, breastfeeding, perimenopause and hormonal contraception can change the pattern. Record the start and end of bleeding and any symptoms that matter to you. A persistent change from your usual pattern may be more informative than comparing yourself with another person. An app’s predicted date is an estimate, not proof of when ovulation happens. Periods commonly begin in the early teens, but the age varies; a first period by age 15 is an assessment threshold rather than a requirement to start between 11 and 14. Menopause most often occurs between 45 and 55, with an average around 51 in the UK. These are population patterns, not deadlines for every person. How much blood is typical? A commonly quoted average is roughly two to three tablespoons of blood over the whole period: not each day. The total fluid you see is not all blood, and the appearance of a pad, tampon or toilet bowl cannot measure it precisely. You do not need to calculate an exact volume before asking for help. Bleeding that requires very frequent changes, leaks through clothes or bedding, lasts more than seven days or limits ordinary activities is worth discussing with a clinician. Heavy bleeding can lead to iron-deficiency anaemia. Unusual tiredness, breathlessness or reduced exercise tolerance should be mentioned as well. The impact on your life matters, even if you cannot describe the amount in millilitres. Pain deserves attention too Mild cramps can accompany the uterus contracting, but pain that repeatedly stops you sleeping, going to school or working deserves assessment. Conditions such as endometriosis, adenomyosis or fibroids may be involved, although symptoms alone cannot establish a diagnosis. Heat and appropriate pain relief may help. Ask a pharmacist or clinician which medicine is suitable if pregnancy is possible, you have another medical condition or you take other medicines. Seek urgent advice if the pain is severe or worse than usual and usual measures are not helping. Periods can be reduced or sometimes stopped with treatment You can discuss menstrual suppression if you want fewer bleeding days or relief from heavy or painful periods. Options include certain hormonal pills, patches or rings used in an extended pattern, progestin-only methods, injections and a hormonal intrauterine system. Some people stop bleeding with a chosen method; others have lighter or less frequent bleeding, and spotting can occur. There is no single success percentage for every pill, implant or hormonal intrauterine device. The formulation, dose, duration and individual response matter. A monthly withdrawal bleed is not required for health when using an appropriate hormonal regimen. The lining does not need a monthly “clean-out.” However, the best method depends on your health history, preferences and pregnancy plans, and some menstrual treatments are not contraceptives. The contraceptive injection can delay the return of fertility after it is stopped; this is not the same as permanent infertility. If you hope to conceive soon, discuss the timing before choosing a method. Do not change a prescribed regimen without checking its instructions. A missed period is not always a disorder Pregnancy, breastfeeding, menopause, hormonal medicines, stress and changes in energy intake or exercise can affect bleeding. A missed period can also have a medical cause. If pregnancy is possible, take a pregnancy test at the appropriate time. Arrange review for repeatedly missed periods, a substantial unexplained change, or other symptoms such as unusual hair growth or marked weight change. A lack of bleeding while using contraception does not by itself prove that pregnancy is impossible. A period is not a test of femininity, health or fertility on its own. Some healthy people do not menstruate because of treatment or their life stage, and some people with regular bleeding still need help with symptoms or conception. When to seek urgent help Get urgent medical advice for rapidly heavy bleeding. Call emergency services if heavy bleeding is accompanied by fainting, severe weakness, chest pain or difficulty breathing. Do not wait to measure the total blood loss. If pregnancy is possible, bleeding with severe or one-sided pelvic pain, shoulder-tip pain or faintness needs urgent assessment for causes including ectopic pregnancy. Bleeding after menopause also needs review, even if it is light. A cycle is counted from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. The usual blood-loss estimate refers to the whole period, not each day. Pain and bleeding that disrupt life deserve care. Suitable hormonal treatment can reduce or stop bleeding, but results vary. Does everyone need a 28-day cycle? No. Cycle lengths vary. Track your own pattern and ask about persistent or unexplained changes. Is it unhealthy to skip the monthly bleed on hormonal contraception? A monthly withdrawal bleed is not medically necessary with a suitable regimen. Check which schedule is appropriate for the specific product and your health history. Does having a period guarantee that I can get pregnant? No. Bleeding alone does not establish normal ovulation or evaluate every factor involved in fertility.

title: Heavy periods: recognising the problem and choosing treatment
description: Understand signs of heavy menstrual bleeding, urgent warning symptoms, possible causes, tests and treatment choices that fit your health and pregnancy plans.
body: Periods vary, but bleeding that disrupts your life or leaves you exhausted deserves attention. You do not need to measure an exact amount before asking for help, and treatment can address both the bleeding and its effects. Heavy bleeding is about its effect on your life Heavy menstrual bleeding, sometimes called menorrhagia, means periods that cause problems because of the amount or duration of bleeding. You do not need to prove an exact volume before asking for help. Missing work, avoiding activities, disturbed sleep or constantly planning around leaks are important symptoms in their own right. Research has often used more than eighty millilitres of blood per cycle as a threshold. Eighty millilitres is not an upper limit on how much someone can lose. Commonly quoted average volumes, such as thirty to forty millilitres, are not a practical home target, because menstrual fluid and product absorbency vary. Useful signs include soaking products every one to two hours, using extra protection, bleeding through clothing or bedding, passing clots larger than about 2.5 centimetres or bleeding for more than seven days. The number of pads alone is imperfect: changing for comfort is different from completely soaking one. Know when you need help immediately Bleeding that soaks a pad or tampon about every hour for several hours needs prompt medical advice. If heavy bleeding is accompanied by fainting, marked dizziness, chest pain, shortness of breath, collapse or feeling seriously unwell, seek emergency care. Do not wait to reach a precise product count or two-hour threshold if you already have severe symptoms. Severe abdominal or pelvic pain also changes the urgency, especially if pregnancy is possible. Use the local emergency number or urgent-care service rather than waiting for a routine menstrual appointment. Have someone help you travel if you feel faint; do not drive yourself. For a stable but persistently heavy pattern, arrange an appointment rather than accepting it indefinitely. Severe cramps, bleeding between periods or after sex, and pain with sex, urination or bowel movements deserve discussion. You can ask for treatment while the cause and any effects of blood loss are assessed. Bleeding related to pregnancy is not an ordinary period A miscarriage can sometimes look like an unusually heavy or late period. An ectopic pregnancy, in which a pregnancy develops outside the uterus, can cause bleeding and pain and may become life-threatening. The amount of vaginal bleeding does not reliably show how much bleeding is happening internally. If pregnancy is possible, tell the clinician and consider a pregnancy test, but do not delay urgent care to obtain one. One-sided lower abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain, severe dizziness or fainting needs urgent assessment even without a previous positive result. Symptoms, examination, ultrasound and blood tests may all contribute to the diagnosis. Bleeding after giving birth is also different from menstruation. Heavy or increasing postpartum bleeding, large clots, fever, faintness or feeling unwell needs prompt maternity advice. Later returning periods may differ from before pregnancy, but “you recently had a baby” is not enough to dismiss severe bleeding. Hormonal changes can alter the pattern Ovulation and the changing effects of oestrogen and progesterone influence how the uterine lining builds and sheds. When ovulation is irregular, the lining may shed unpredictably and sometimes heavily. This is more complex than diagnosing “too much oestrogen” from the appearance of a period. Cycles can change when periods first begin, around the transition to menopause, after pregnancy or after starting or stopping hormonal contraception. Conditions affecting ovulation, including polycystic ovary syndrome, can also contribute. An underactive thyroid is another possible cause when the overall symptoms suggest thyroid disease. A heavier first day or one unusually heavy month does not identify a particular cause. Likewise, repeated heavy cycles do not prove a single hormonal problem. Describe the pattern and relevant changes in medicines, contraception or health rather than assigning causes according to which day is heaviest. Structural conditions and pelvic pain need consideration Polyps are growths from the uterine lining that can contribute to bleeding. Fibroids are non-cancerous growths of uterine muscle. Their size and location matter: a fibroid affecting the cavity may cause different problems from one growing mainly toward the outside of the uterus. Adenomyosis involves endometrial-type tissue within the muscle of the uterine wall and can be associated with heavy, painful periods. Endometriosis involves tissue similar to the uterine lining outside the uterus and commonly causes period-related pelvic pain; some people also report heavy bleeding or lower-back pain. These conditions can coexist, and symptoms alone may not distinguish them. A painful period does not automatically mean endometriosis, and finding a small fibroid does not establish that it explains everything. The clinician considers the examination, symptoms and appropriate investigations together before choosing treatment. Medicines, contraception and bleeding disorders matter A copper IUD can make periods heavier, particularly after insertion. A hormonal intrauterine system is different and may be used to reduce heavy bleeding. If bleeding is new or troublesome with either device, ask for assessment rather than removing it yourself or assuming every IUD has the same effect. Anticoagulants and some other medicines can increase bleeding. Bring a full medicine list, including aspirin, supplements and recent changes. Do not stop a prescribed anticoagulant independently; the prescriber can help balance bleeding control against the reason the medicine is needed. A bleeding disorder such as von Willebrand disease may make it harder for bleeding to stop. Mention heavy periods since they first began, easy bruising, frequent nosebleeds, prolonged bleeding after dental work or surgery and relevant family history. Testing is guided by that history; a single prevalence figure does not predict whether you have a disorder. Cancer is an uncommon cause, but certain changes must be checked Most heavy periods are not caused by cancer. Nevertheless, abnormal bleeding can be associated with disease of the uterine lining or cervix, including cancer. It is not useful to present uterine, cervical and ovarian cancers as equally likely explanations for a heavy period. Bleeding between periods, after sex or after menopause should be reported. Once menopause has occurred, even a small amount of bleeding on one occasion needs assessment. Do not label it a returning period without medical advice. Age, the bleeding pattern, medicines and other risk factors help determine which investigations are appropriate. The aim is neither automatic cancer testing for every person nor reassurance based only on a common life stage. Ask what possible causes the assessment is intended to rule out and when results should arrive. Prepare for a focused assessment A useful record includes cycle dates, duration, fully soaked products, leaks, clot size, pain and the effect on daily activities. Tell the clinician whether pregnancy is possible, whether you want future pregnancy and what treatment outcomes matter most to you. You do not have to wait several cycles to begin this conversation. A full blood count checks for anaemia and is routinely recommended for heavy menstrual bleeding. Other testing depends on the history. Clotting tests may be appropriate when a bleeding disorder is suspected; thyroid testing is generally reserved for additional suggestive symptoms, and a broad hormone panel is not routinely needed. An examination, ultrasound, hysteroscopy to look inside the uterus or a sample of the lining may be recommended for particular findings or risks. Not everyone needs every test. Ask what each procedure can show, how discomfort will be managed and whether treatment can start while you wait for investigation. Medicines can reduce bleeding and treat its effects Options include a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system, combined hormonal contraception or selected progestogen treatments. These have different effects on bleeding, contraception and side effects. A treatment used for bleeding control may also prevent pregnancy while you use it, which should be part of the choice. Non-hormonal options include tranexamic acid and suitable anti-inflammatory medicines, such as certain NSAIDs. NSAIDs can reduce menstrual bleeding and cramps for some people but are unsuitable in some circumstances, including particular bleeding, stomach or kidney problems. Do not combine painkillers or use someone else’s prescription. Tranexamic acid also requires a suitability check, especially with a history of blood clots, kidney problems, irregular unexplained bleeding or pregnancy possibility. Iron treatment may be needed for iron deficiency or anaemia, but iron alone does not control the cause of bleeding. Ask when treatment should help and how response will be reviewed. Procedures and follow-up should fit your priorities Removing a polyp or treating a fibroid may reduce bleeding when it is responsible. Options depend on location, size and symptoms. More extensive treatments, including endometrial ablation or hysterectomy, have important consequences and should follow a discussion of alternatives, risks and future pregnancy plans. Endometrial ablation is not suitable if you want a future pregnancy, and contraception is still needed afterward because pregnancy can occur and be dangerous. Hysterectomy removes the uterus and permanently ends the ability to carry a pregnancy. These are not interchangeable with procedures intended to preserve the uterus. Review both the bleeding and how you feel: energy, pain, daily activity and any anaemia matter. If treatment is ineffective, poorly tolerated or no longer fits your plans, return to discuss another approach. Heavy periods are a valid reason to seek care, and a clear follow-up plan is part of treatment rather than an optional extra. Eighty millilitres is not a maximum blood loss or a home test you must complete. An hourly soaked product pattern needs prompt advice. Copper and hormonal intrauterine devices have different effects. Do not stop prescribed blood thinners without advice. Treatment choices should include their effects on future pregnancy. Must I measure eighty millilitres before seeking help? No. The effect on your life, bleeding pattern and symptoms are enough to start an assessment. Does a heavy first day identify the cause? No. Timing alone cannot distinguish hormones, structural conditions, medicines or other causes. Could a heavy period actually be pregnancy bleeding? Yes. Miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy can resemble a period. Possible pregnancy with pain or faintness needs urgent assessment. Are heavy periods after birth always normal? No. Postpartum bleeding and later returning periods need to be distinguished, and severe or worsening bleeding should not be dismissed. Do all IUDs make periods heavier? No. Copper IUDs can increase bleeding, while a hormonal intrauterine system may reduce it. Should I stop my anticoagulant? Do not stop it independently. Ask the prescriber for a plan that addresses bleeding and the condition being treated. Does everyone need thyroid and hormone tests? No. A full blood count is routine, while thyroid, clotting and other tests are selected for the clinical history. Can NSAIDs reduce menstrual bleeding? They can help some people, but suitability depends on medicines and health conditions. Ask before using them if you have bleeding, stomach or kidney problems. Does endometrial ablation prevent pregnancy? No. It is not contraception; pregnancy afterward can be dangerous, and it is unsuitable when future pregnancy is desired. Is one small bleed after menopause worth checking? Yes. Even a small amount or a single episode of postmenopausal bleeding needs medical assessment.

title: Bowel changes around your period
description: Periods can coincide with looser stools, constipation or a change in smell. Track the pattern, manage mild symptoms and know what needs assessment.
body: Bowel movements may change before or during a period. Some people notice urgency or looser stools; others feel constipated or more bloated. A change in smell can happen too, but smell alone cannot tell you whether hormones, food or a digestive condition is responsible. Mild, brief changes are different from ongoing pain, bleeding or illness. Why the bowel and period can feel connected The menstrual cycle can affect bowel habits and abdominal sensations. Prostaglandins, chemical messengers involved in menstrual cramping, may also affect intestinal movement. Changes in hormone levels, food intake and existing digestive conditions can contribute. This does not mean that a particular stool proves you have too much of one hormone. Research has documented cycle-related bowel symptoms, but individual responses vary. Constipation before a period and looser stools during it are possible patterns, not rules everyone follows. People with irritable bowel syndrome or inflammatory bowel disease may notice symptoms around menstruation. If you have a diagnosed condition, follow your care plan and report a significant change rather than assuming every flare is hormonal. Prostaglandins help the uterus contract and shed its lining; bowel activity can change at the same time. Progesterone-related slowing before a period may contribute to constipation in some people, but a symptom cannot measure either chemical. Pressure may be felt in the pelvis, lower back or buttocks, making cramps and the urge to pass stool hard to distinguish. A stronger smell is not a diagnosis Stool normally has an odour, and food changes can alter it. Changes in stool consistency or how quickly food moves through the bowel may occur at the same time. It is not accurate to blame every change on eating chocolate or on a lack of willpower. A short diary of food, medicines, bleeding days, stool consistency and pain may identify a pattern without requiring a restrictive diet. Arrange assessment for an unusually foul smell that persists, especially with greasy stools, weight loss, fever, ongoing diarrhoea or pain. Infection, malabsorption and other digestive problems can cause abnormal stool, so the menstrual timing should not close off other explanations. If stools are loose Drink regularly and consider an oral rehydration solution if repeated watery stools are causing fluid loss. A pharmacist can help choose one. Signs such as very little urine, dark urine, dizziness or inability to keep fluids down need medical advice. If coffee reliably triggers urgency, try reducing it and see whether that helps. Decaffeinated coffee can still stimulate bowel activity in some people. You do not need to stop every food that has ever been blamed for digestive symptoms. Do not automatically take an antidiarrhoeal medicine for bloody diarrhoea, fever or severe pain. Ask a pharmacist or clinician about suitability, particularly if pregnant or if you have another bowel condition. If you are constipated Regular fluids, gradual increases in suitable fibre and gentle activity may help. Respond to the urge to use the toilet and avoid prolonged straining. A small footstool can make the position more comfortable. If simple changes are insufficient, a pharmacist can recommend an appropriate laxative. There is no single product that is right for everyone, and constipation with severe pain, vomiting or inability to pass gas needs assessment rather than repeated self-treatment. Recurring constipation deserves review if it is new, troublesome or accompanied by bleeding, unexplained weight loss or a persistent change in bowel habits. Painful bowel movements are worth discussing Hard stool can cause pain, and diarrhoea can irritate the anal area. Haemorrhoids or a small anal tear are other possibilities. Pelvic cramping can also make it hard to tell exactly where discomfort is coming from. Pain with bowel movements that repeatedly worsens around menstruation can be a symptom of endometriosis. It does not establish the diagnosis, and bowel symptoms may have another cause. Record the timing and discuss it, particularly if periods or sex are also painful. Do not dismiss rectal bleeding as part of menstruation. If you are unsure whether blood is coming from the vagina or bowel, tell the clinician rather than guessing. A normal basic scan does not settle every possible cause of cyclical pelvic pain. Fibroids or an ovarian cyst can sometimes contribute to pelvic pressure or pain, while irritable bowel syndrome is a separate bowel condition. A diagnosis affecting ovulation does not by itself explain painful or foul-smelling stools. Persistent mucus, heavy periods, recurrent pain or symptoms between periods are reasons to seek assessment. Using a tampon when you have a bowel movement The vagina and rectum are separate passages, so you can usually pass stool while a tampon is in place. It is not true that most people inevitably push a tampon out every time. Keep the string away from stool and wipe from front to back. Replace a tampon if it becomes contaminated, moves partly out or is uncomfortable. Do not push a soiled tampon back in. Wash your hands before and after handling menstrual products. Otherwise, follow the product’s usual timing: FDA guidance is to change tampons every four to eight hours and never leave one in longer than eight hours. Use the lowest absorbency that meets your needs. If a tampon repeatedly slips out, seek advice about fit and symptoms rather than assuming a menstrual cup will necessarily solve it. When not to wait for the period to end Seek urgent help for severe or worsening abdominal pain, black tarry stool, substantial rectal bleeding, fainting or significant dehydration. Iron tablets and some medicines can darken stool, but do not use that explanation to dismiss tarry stool or feeling unwell. Get clinical advice for blood in stool, symptoms that persist between periods, unexplained weight loss or repeated pain that limits normal life. A predictable monthly pattern is useful information, not a reason to accept symptoms without care. Mild bowel changes can occur around menstruation, but they vary. Stool smell alone cannot identify a hormone problem. Painful bowel movements or rectal bleeding deserve assessment. A bowel movement does not automatically require a tampon change, but contamination and usual wear-time limits do. Is diarrhoea always normal during a period? No. A brief familiar change may be cycle-related, but fever, blood, dehydration, severe pain or persistent symptoms need assessment. Can endometriosis cause bowel symptoms? Yes, including pain when passing stool, sometimes with a cyclical pattern. Other conditions can produce similar symptoms, so clinical assessment matters. Do I have to change my diet completely? Usually not. Start by observing your own triggers and maintaining adequate food and fluids. Persistent symptoms deserve advice before major dietary restrictions.

title: How often should you have sex when trying to conceive?
description: Sex every two to three days is a practical approach. If you track ovulation, aim for every one to two days during the fertile window without pressure.
body: You do not need a perfect timetable to try for pregnancy. Having vaginal sex without contraception every two to three days throughout the cycle is a practical starting point. If you prefer to track ovulation, sex every one to two days during the fertile window can help. Choose a pattern that is comfortable for both of you. Understand the fertile window The fertile window is usually described as the five days before ovulation plus the day of ovulation. Sperm can remain available while waiting for an egg, so sex before ovulation matters; waiting only for the day you believe the egg is released can miss useful days. These dates are estimates in real life. Ovulation can shift even when periods seem regular. A calendar label should not be treated as proof that pregnancy is impossible on another day, and conception-focused tracking is not the same as a reliable contraceptive plan. Day 14 is not a rule Ovulation does not invariably occur on cycle day 14, even in someone who often has 28-day cycles. Cycle length and the time between ovulation and the next period both vary. A predicted date in an app cannot confirm that an egg has actually been released. Tracking cervical mucus or using an ovulation-prediction kit may help identify a likely window if you find it useful. If tracking makes sex feel pressured, regular intercourse across the cycle is a reasonable alternative. Having sex only once a week may miss the fertile window. Daily sex does not usually use up fertility You do not have to leave a day between encounters so sperm can mature. Daily ejaculation generally does not reduce fertility in someone with normal semen quality. Every-other-day intercourse is a convenient option, not a biological requirement. More than once a day is not necessary. There is no obligation to keep going when either partner is tired, uncomfortable or not interested. If a fertility clinic gives different instructions for a semen sample or procedure, follow those specific instructions; they are not a universal rule for intercourse at home. One encounter can be enough, but timing is not everything Pregnancy can follow a single encounter in the fertile window, but it is not guaranteed. Repeated opportunities across that window reduce the chance of missing ovulation. A cycle without pregnancy does not prove that you timed sex incorrectly. Ovulation, sperm function, age and other reproductive factors all influence the chance of conception. No position, post-sex routine or frequency can guarantee pregnancy. Avoid judging either partner’s effort by whether a test is positive that month. If intercourse is painful or ejaculation is difficult, ask for help. You do not need to repeatedly push through pain or distress to qualify for fertility advice. Know when to ask for support A commonly used threshold for fertility evaluation is 12 months of trying when the person providing the eggs is under 35, or six months from age 35. Over 40, an earlier discussion is appropriate. Local pathways differ, and these waiting periods are not a reason to postpone care for a known concern. Seek advice sooner for absent or very irregular periods, known reproductive conditions, previous cancer treatment, a suspected sperm problem or difficulty having intercourse. An evaluation should consider both partners where relevant, rather than assuming the problem lies with one person. A preconception appointment is useful even before those thresholds. Review medical conditions and medicines, and ask about recommended vaccinations and folic acid. For most people who could become pregnant, 400 micrograms of folic acid daily is recommended; some need a different prescribed dose because of their history. Every two to three days across the cycle is a practical approach. When tracking, every one to two days in the fertile window is reasonable. Daily ejaculation usually does not require a recovery day for fertility. Seek earlier advice for irregular cycles, pain or a known reproductive concern. Must we have sex exactly on ovulation day? No. The days before ovulation are important too, and the exact day is not always predictable. Should we save sperm by abstaining for a week? Usually not when trying naturally. Follow a clinic’s separate instructions if preparing for a semen test or fertility procedure. Can we conceive from one time? Yes, if sperm and an egg meet at the right time, but no single encounter guarantees a pregnancy.

title: Spotting, a period or early pregnancy: how to check
description: Colour, cramps and timing cannot reliably identify implantation bleeding. A correctly timed pregnancy test and attention to warning symptoms are more useful.
body: A small amount of bleeding while you are waiting to test can raise hopes, worries or both. It may be the start of a period, bleeding in early pregnancy or something unrelated to pregnancy. You cannot reliably tell the cause from a pink or brown stain, how mild the cramps feel or how many days the spotting lasts. Why a spotting checklist cannot give an answer People often use the term implantation bleeding for light bleeding around the time a pregnancy might begin. However, it is not a diagnosis that can be confirmed from its appearance. Research has not established a dependable bleeding pattern caused by implantation. A period can start lightly, be brown or pink and stop and start. Early-pregnancy bleeding can also vary in colour and amount. Comparing these features cannot confirm a pregnancy or show that it is developing normally. Clots do not prove that you are simply having a period. Bleeding with clots can occur in a pregnancy loss, and some pregnancy complications cause only light bleeding. Breast tenderness, tiredness, nausea, backache and mood changes can overlap with premenstrual symptoms. They may be worth noting, but they are not substitutes for a pregnancy test. Use a test at an appropriate time Most home urine tests can be used from the first day of a missed period. If you do not know when your period is due, test at least 21 days after the most recent unprotected sex that could have caused pregnancy. Follow the instructions for the specific test, including when to read the result. An early negative result may occur before there is enough pregnancy hormone, hCG, to detect. If the result is negative but you still think you may be pregnant, repeat after a few days or at the appropriate testing point. Seek advice if repeated tests are negative and your period has not arrived. A positive test is usually reliable when used correctly, but it does not establish where the pregnancy is located or whether it is continuing normally. Bleeding after a positive result is a reason to contact your pregnancy-care service. A clinician may use a blood hCG test when appropriate. Neither a single blood result nor a urine test can provide every answer, and there is no universal day after conception on which every pregnancy is detectable. Calendar estimates have limits Ovulation does not occur on day fourteen for everyone, and even usually regular cycles can vary. The date predicted by an app is an estimate, not confirmation of the day an egg was released. For this reason, spotting before the expected period is not automatically more likely to be implantation. The timing of ovulation, fertilisation and hormone detection cannot be reconstructed precisely from bleeding alone. Record the first day of your last period, usual cycle pattern, relevant test dates and when the bleeding began. These details help a clinician interpret the situation, but you do not need to solve it perfectly before asking for help. The fertile window spans several days because sperm can survive for up to about five days, while an egg remains available for roughly a day after ovulation. These are approximate biological limits, not a way to date a pregnancy from spotting or to guarantee a safe day for unprotected sex. What early-pregnancy bleeding may mean Light bleeding can come from changes in the cervix, sometimes after sex or an examination. An infection or a collection of blood near the pregnancy, called a subchorionic haematoma, can also be involved. Bleeding can be a sign of miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy, where the pregnancy is outside the womb. A molar pregnancy is a less common condition involving abnormal placental tissue that also needs specialist assessment. The amount or colour alone cannot separate these possibilities. Many people who have bleeding in early pregnancy go on to have a healthy pregnancy. That reassurance should sit alongside an appropriate assessment, rather than an assumption that every light bleed is harmless. Depending on symptoms and timing, you may be offered an examination, ultrasound and repeat blood tests. Very early scans can be inconclusive. If the pregnancy’s location is not yet clear, follow-up and instructions about worsening symptoms are important. Symptoms that should not wait for another test Seek emergency assessment for severe abdominal or pelvic pain, shoulder-tip pain, fainting, marked dizziness, collapse or heavy bleeding. A dangerous ectopic pregnancy can involve internal bleeding without a large amount of vaginal blood. If pregnancy is possible and you have one-sided pain or bleeding that concerns you, obtain medical advice promptly, even without a positive home test. Do not wait a week just to see whether a test changes. Fever, worsening pain or feeling very unwell also needs prompt assessment. Let the service know if you have had an ectopic pregnancy before or have other relevant pregnancy history. While arranging advice, a sanitary pad can help you observe the amount of bleeding. Note pain and other symptoms rather than judging safety by whether the blood is brown instead of red. Make the waiting period more manageable Choose a sensible date to test rather than checking every physical sensation for proof. If the first result is too early to settle the question, decide when to repeat it. You can ask for support when waiting is distressing, especially after a previous loss. A symptom that turns out to be a period does not mean you misread your body, and a pregnancy complication is not caused by noticing or worrying about spotting. The useful next step is usually clear: test at the right time, contact a clinician about bleeding in a known or possible pregnancy, and act immediately on serious symptoms. Spotting colour and duration cannot confirm implantation. Clots do not rule out pregnancy or pregnancy loss. Test from a missed period, or 21 days after relevant unprotected sex if timing is unclear. Severe pain, shoulder-tip pain, faintness or heavy bleeding needs urgent help. Does brown spotting mean implantation has happened? No. Brown blood can occur in several situations, including a period. It does not confirm the cause or safety of a bleed. Can I be pregnant if I pass clots? Yes. Clots are not proof of a period; bleeding in pregnancy needs appropriate assessment. Should I wait for a positive test before seeking help for severe pain? No. Severe pain, fainting or other warning symptoms need immediate assessment even if a home test is negative or has not been taken.

title: Spotting instead of a period: eleven possible explanations
description: Understand light spotting, pregnancy checks, infections, hormonal changes and contraception, with clear advice on when to seek care.
body: A few spots when you expected a period can be confusing. The amount and timing provide clues, but they cannot identify the cause on their own. Consider pregnancy possibility, other symptoms, medicines and your usual cycle before deciding what to do next. Spotting describes a small amount, not a diagnosis Spotting usually means a few marks of blood on underwear or toilet tissue, or bleeding light enough that a liner may be sufficient. A usual period often has a changing flow over several days and may require a pad, tampon or menstrual cup. The amount matters more than the product you choose. Both spotting and a period can look pink, red or brown. Brown blood is not a reliable sign of pregnancy or a particular illness. Spotting can happen at any point in the month and last for different lengths of time, so colour and timing alone cannot establish its cause. Periods commonly last several days, with lighter and heavier days, but individual patterns vary. Acne, bloating, fatigue, sore breasts, bowel changes, mood changes, sleep difficulty, poor concentration, anxiety or a change in sexual interest may accompany a period. Similar symptoms can occur in other situations; they cannot reliably distinguish a light period from early pregnancy. 1. Pregnancy should be considered first when possible A lighter-than-usual bleed around the expected period can occur in early pregnancy. People often call this implantation bleeding, but spotting cannot tell you that implantation has happened or identify a precise day after ovulation. Early pregnancy bleeding has several possible causes, some of which need urgent care. Breast tenderness, nausea, vomiting, tiredness and needing to urinate more often may occur in pregnancy, but they are not confirmation. A home pregnancy test is more useful than comparing symptoms or blood colour with an online picture. Most tests can be used from the first day of a missed period. If your cycle timing is uncertain, test at least 21 days after the last unprotected sex. You do not routinely need to wait a whole extra week. Follow the instructions and repeat an early negative result when appropriate if a normal period does not arrive. 2. Sexually transmitted infections can cause unexpected bleeding Chlamydia and gonorrhoea can cause bleeding between periods or after sex, sometimes without other obvious symptoms. They can be transmitted through vaginal, anal or oral sexual contact. A person does not need to look or feel unwell to have an infection. Possible symptoms include burning when urinating, pain during sex and changed vaginal discharge. Rectal infection may cause pain, discharge or bleeding. Yellow or green discharge, odour or itching needs assessment, but none identifies the organism by itself. Fever, nausea or pelvic pain may indicate a more significant problem. Testing and appropriate antibiotics can treat these infections. Recent partners may also need assessment and treatment to reduce reinfection. Follow the sexual-health service’s advice about avoiding sexual contact until treatment requirements are met; do not rely only on whether symptoms have stopped. 3. Pelvic inflammatory disease needs prompt treatment Pelvic inflammatory disease, or PID, affects the upper reproductive tract, such as the uterus and fallopian tubes. It can follow an STI, but not every case is caused by an STI or a known infection that has been present for a long time. Spotting can occur with lower abdominal or pelvic pain, pain during sex, unusual discharge, bleeding after sex or between periods, and sometimes fever or chills. Urinary discomfort can overlap with other conditions. Some cases are mild, so the absence of dramatic symptoms does not rule it out. Prompt antibiotic treatment helps reduce complications. The clinician will discuss partner testing when relevant and when sexual contact can resume. Severe pain, fever, vomiting, faintness or pregnancy possibility requires urgent assessment rather than waiting for the next period. 4. Age and reproductive stage can change the pattern Cycles are often less predictable in the first years after periods begin. The first period commonly occurs in the early teenage years, but timing varies. Bleeds may be closer together, further apart, light or heavy as the hormonal pattern develops. Perimenopause can also bring unpredictable intervals and changing flow before periods stop. This may explain a pattern, but age should not be used to dismiss new bleeding, pain or possible pregnancy. Adolescents also need care for significant bleeding or long gaps rather than assuming every change is normal. After menopause, new spotting is different: it should be assessed even if it happens only once. If you have gone 12 months without a natural period, tell the clinician about any new vaginal blood and any hormones or contraception you use. 5. Low energy availability can disrupt periods Not having enough energy available for the body’s needs can suppress the signals involved in ovulation. It may follow restrictive eating, weight loss or a demanding training programme. This can happen at different body sizes, so appearance alone cannot confirm or exclude it. The female athlete triad describes related concerns involving low energy availability, menstrual disruption and reduced bone strength. Disordered eating may be present, but is not required. Persistent energy deficiency can affect fertility and bone health, and severe nutritional illness can also affect circulation and heart function. Hair loss, headaches, acne or milky nipple discharge should not all be labelled symptoms of being underweight. They may point to other hormonal or medical causes and deserve individual assessment. Care may involve improving nutrition, adjusting exercise and support for an eating problem, rather than simply prescribing more relaxation. 6. Bleeding does not always mean ovulation occurred Ovulation is the release of an egg from an ovary. After ovulation, progesterone helps prepare the uterine lining; when pregnancy does not occur, falling hormones contribute to a period. Day 14 is an example for some cycles, not a universal timetable. If ovulation is delayed or absent, the lining may shed irregularly. This can produce spotting or light bleeding, but sometimes a heavier or prolonged bleed. An isolated change may accompany illness or stress; a repeated pattern can indicate an underlying hormonal condition. A tracking app can record bleeding but cannot prove ovulation from dates alone. Repeatedly missing periods or having only unpredictable spotting is a reason to discuss assessment, even if pregnancy is not currently a goal. 7. PCOS or PMOS can cause irregular cycles The condition traditionally called polycystic ovary syndrome, or PCOS, is now described as polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, or PMOS, in current NHS guidance. Hormonal and metabolic changes can interfere with regular ovulation and produce long gaps, absent periods or irregular bleeding. Acne, increased facial or body hair, scalp hair thinning, weight changes and difficulty conceiving may occur, but the pattern differs between people. Pelvic pain is not a defining diagnostic sign and may have another cause. Neither spotting nor an ultrasound appearance alone establishes the condition. Treatment depends on the person’s symptoms, metabolic health and pregnancy plans.
