A raised result does not identify a specific organism, prove an STI or establish a structural or immune diagnosis. Is yellow semen the main symptom? No. Colour does not measure white cells, and the finding may occur without symptoms. Persistent colour change, pain, urinary symptoms or discharge merits assessment. Blood in semen should be checked; suspected blood in urine needs urgent advice. Is genital infection always the commonest explanation? An infection needs to be considered, but one laboratory result cannot establish it or rank the cause in an individual. Nonbacterial inflammation exists. Avoid assuming that antibiotics or partner treatment are necessary before assessment. What does one million cells per millilitre mean? WHO uses at least one million peroxidase-positive cells per millilitre as an abnormal consensus threshold; EAU describes leukocytospermia as more than one million white cells per millilitre. The assay and cell identification matter. Round cells are not all leukocytes, and neither threshold is a pregnancy prediction. Will antibiotics, supplements or an anti-inflammatory cure it? Not automatically. Antibiotics are selected for an infection or a clinically justified presumptive diagnosis; white cells alone do not establish benefit. Supplements and NSAIDs are not proven universal fertility treatments. Treating the cause or improving a result does not guarantee conception. Can we still try for a pregnancy? A raised count does not by itself make natural conception impossible. If infection or an STI is suspected, ask the clinic about sex, testing and partner care first; follow any advised abstinence period. Otherwise the full fertility assessment, not one white-cell result, guides the plan. Which symptoms need emergency care? Sudden severe testicular pain, pain with nausea/vomiting or abdominal pain, pain lasting over an hour or at rest, inability to urinate or severe abdominal pain needs emergency care. So does serious illness with sudden confusion, abnormal speech, blue/grey/pale/blotchy colour, a non-fading rash or severe breathing difficulty. Do not wait for all signs, a repeat semen test or an app check; arrange another driver or an ambulance.

title: Antidepressants and fertility: evidence and planning for both partners
description: Understand sexual side effects, sperm and conception studies, and how both partners can plan treatment safely while trying for pregnancy.
body: Taking an antidepressant does not mean you are infertile. Some medicines can affect sexual function, and research has raised questions about sperm measures and the time it takes to conceive. Those questions need to be weighed alongside the illness being treated and the risks of changing effective care. A useful plan protects mental health while investigating fertility concerns in both partners. Three different questions about fertility Sexual desire, erections, lubrication, orgasm and ejaculation can affect whether sex is comfortable and whether semen reaches the vagina. A change in one of these functions is not the same as a diagnosis of infertility. Depression itself can also affect sexual interest, so timing and the person’s symptoms matter when a new problem appears. Laboratory sperm results and the chance of pregnancy are different outcomes again. A study showing a change in sperm DNA does not directly measure how many couples conceive or have a baby. Likewise, a lower average chance of conception per cycle in a study is not a prediction that a particular person cannot become pregnant. Why separating illness from treatment is difficult People prescribed antidepressants differ from people who are not taking them. The severity and duration of depression, anxiety, sexual activity, other medicines and health circumstances can influence the comparison. Difficulty conceiving can itself affect mental health. Researchers try to account for these factors, but an observed association does not automatically show that the drug caused infertility. Depression is not evidence that someone has an unhealthy lifestyle or is responsible for delayed conception. Sleep, nutrition, substance use and relationship pressures can be discussed without blame. Neither an assumed cortisol imbalance nor a medication name should replace assessment of other possible causes when pregnancy is taking longer than expected. Sexual side effects in either partner Antidepressants, including some selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), can cause reduced desire, difficulty reaching orgasm or erection problems; vaginal dryness and ejaculation difficulties can also matter. Tell the prescriber what changed, when it began and whether it followed starting treatment or a dose change. Symptoms may have more than one cause and deserve attention even if mood has improved. Do not assume that every sexual side effect is temporary or will disappear promptly after stopping. In October 2026, the UK MHRA announced clearer communication of known persistent sexual-dysfunction risks with some antidepressants. This does not tell an individual how likely persistence is, but it supports taking symptoms seriously and discussing them rather than silently abandoning treatment. What sperm studies can (and cannot) show A small prospective study published in 2010 followed 35 healthy men taking paroxetine for several weeks. It found increased sperm DNA fragmentation, while conventional semen measurements did not significantly change. Fragmentation was present before treatment too: it is incorrect to say sperm DNA damage only happens in men who have taken antidepressants. The study did not establish a pregnancy or live-birth rate. Different medicines cannot be treated as interchangeable. A 2021 placebo-controlled trial in 68 healthy men found no clinically meaningful adverse effect of short-term duloxetine on semen measures or sperm DNA integrity. Its selected participants and brief follow-up do not prove long-term reproductive safety, or make duloxetine the right substitute for every patient. Neither study justifies choosing or stopping a drug without the treating clinician. Does paternal antidepressant use delay conception? A prospective North American study of 2,398 couples examined male depression, psychotropic medication and time to pregnancy. Some estimates suggested slightly lower conception chances among users of particular medication groups, but the estimates were imprecise and compatible with chance. The researchers could not fully separate treatment from the reasons it was prescribed. This evidence is more directly about conception than a semen test, but it still cannot diagnose the cause of one couple’s difficulty. If erections or ejaculation prevent intercourse or sperm delivery, seek help early. If fertility testing is indicated, the clinician can assess semen and relevant history alongside the other partner’s evaluation; antidepressant use alone does not establish a need for a particular specialist sperm test. What studies in women have found The findings are mixed. In a prospective cohort of 2,146 women trying to conceive, more severe depressive symptoms were associated with a lower chance of conception in a cycle (fecundability), while psychotropic medication use did not show a clear overall harmful association. Estimates changed with the way medication use was classified. This was not proof that every antidepressant has no effect. Another study measured urinary SSRI exposure in 1,228 women with a history of pregnancy loss. SSRI exposure was associated with lower odds of conception in a cycle, but medication use was not randomized and depression itself was not directly measured. The selected population and remaining confounding limit application to everyone trying for pregnancy. These studies do not establish that stopping treatment improves fertility. No universal monthly risk or safest drug ranking It is too strong to say an antidepressant definitely reduces a woman’s chance of pregnancy that month, or that SSRIs have almost no effect on female fertility. The evidence cannot supply one reliable percentage for every drug, diagnosis and person. A percentage describing a relative association in a study is also different from a percentage-point reduction in someone’s own chance. For example, MotherToBaby describes uncertainty about whether sertraline itself makes conception harder, because the underlying condition may contribute. This is a drug-specific discussion, not a recommendation to switch to sertraline or a guarantee for all SSRIs. Fertility, pregnancy-exposure safety and symptom control are separate questions that need to be considered together. Prepare a treatment review before trying Arrange a discussion with the prescribing clinician before changing treatment. Bring the medicine name, dose, duration, reason for treatment, benefit, side effects and all other medicines or supplements. Explain whether you will carry the pregnancy or provide sperm, how long you have been trying, and any menstrual or sexual-function problems. If both partners take medication, each needs an individual review. Describe previous severe episodes, relapse after stopping, treatments that failed or helped, and relevant personal or family mental-health history. Ask who will coordinate with fertility or maternity care and when progress will be reviewed. A family history can inform clinical assessment and support planning; it cannot by itself predict that a future child will develop depression or decide which medicine is suitable. Possible adjustments need a shared plan Depending on the problem, the clinician may discuss monitoring symptoms, psychological treatment, an individualized medication adjustment or a different medicine. A change must balance the likely benefit for sexual function or other side effects against withdrawal, interactions and loss of mental-health stability. There is no single replacement that is best for everyone planning a baby. Do not skip doses around the fertile window or try a self-directed “drug holiday”. NICE notes that missed doses and abrupt or partial stopping can cause withdrawal. If stopping is appropriate, agree an individualized reduction and follow-up plan with the prescriber. A fixed online schedule cannot account for your medicine, treatment history and response. Therapy and everyday support have a role Evidence-based psychological treatments, such as cognitive behavioural therapy, can be part of care. NICE recommends matching treatment to clinical needs and preferences: psychological approaches may be appropriate for less severe depression, while combined therapy and medication is one option for more severe illness. Access and previous response matter, not only a wish to avoid medicines. Sleep routines, enjoyable activity, practical support and help with relationship or sexual difficulties can complement treatment. Yoga, diet changes or family support should not be presented as guaranteed ways to replace an effective antidepressant or restore fertility. Ask what support is available while waiting for therapy, and how worsening symptoms will be managed. Where sildenafil may fit Sildenafil treats erection difficulties; it is not a general medicine to increase desire, repair sperm or improve pregnancy rates. An older randomized trial in men with depression in remission and antidepressant-associated sexual dysfunction found that 54.5% of the sildenafil group versus 4.4% of the placebo group were rated much or very much improved. That is a proportion of participants responding, not a 55% increase in sexual function or fertility. A clinician must assess whether it is suitable and check interactions. Sildenafil must not be combined with nitrates or nitrites, including nitrate medicines or “poppers”, or with riociguat; cardiovascular circumstances can also make it unsuitable. Do not borrow it or add it as a fertility supplement. An erection lasting more than four hours needs immediate medical help; if you develop sudden vision loss or a sudden decrease or loss of hearing, stop taking sildenafil and seek medical attention promptly. If a pregnancy test becomes positive Contact the prescriber and maternity team to review the actual medicine and your mental-health history. A positive test is not an instruction to stop abruptly. ACOG advises against withholding or discontinuing mental-health medication solely because of pregnancy or lactation; the discussion must consider the individual benefits and risks of treatment and untreated illness. Some pregnancy studies cannot fully separate medicine effects from the underlying condition. Sertraline information, for example, discusses generally reassuring birth-defect findings alongside uncertainty about some other outcomes and possible temporary newborn symptoms. These details cannot be generalized to every antidepressant. Ask about your specific medicine, any monitoring and a plan for pregnancy, after birth and feeding. When to seek a fertility assessment A fertility review commonly starts after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse when the partner providing eggs is under 35, or after 6 months at 35 or older. Over 40, earlier assessment may be appropriate. Seek advice sooner for irregular or absent periods, known fertility risks, or sexual dysfunction that is interfering with attempts. These are clinical assessment thresholds, not a reason to postpone help with distressing side effects. Both partners should be considered in parallel where applicable. Take a clear timeline of medication changes, symptoms, menstrual cycles and attempts to conceive. A clinician may recommend appropriate investigations rather than assuming the antidepressant explains everything. The aim is to avoid both unnecessary treatment changes and delayed investigation of another cause. Mental-health safety comes first Seek urgent clinical help for new or worsening suicidal thoughts or thoughts of self-harm, particularly after starting an antidepressant or changing the dose. If you have harmed yourself, are in immediate danger or cannot keep yourself or someone else safe, use local emergency services or attend emergency care immediately. Do not wait for a routine fertility appointment. Keep the agreed contact details and follow-up plan accessible. Tell a trusted person how to help if you want their support, and contact the treating team if mood or functioning deteriorates. Protecting mental health and planning pregnancy are compatible goals; treatment decisions should support both rather than treating a theoretical fertility concern as a reason to manage a serious illness alone. Antidepressant use does not itself diagnose infertility; sexual function, sperm measures and pregnancy outcomes are different questions. Studies in both sexes have important limits, including confounding by the illness being treated; no universal fertility percentage applies. Sexual side effects deserve review and may sometimes persist after treatment stops. Plan changes with the prescriber; do not skip doses, abruptly stop or self-prescribe sildenafil. Investigate fertility concerns in both partners while maintaining mental-health support and a clear urgent-care plan. Do antidepressants make men infertile? Not necessarily. Some small studies found changes in sperm measures, and sexual side effects can interfere with attempts, but these findings do not prove that every man taking treatment becomes infertile. Drug-specific evidence and the couple’s actual circumstances matter. Do they reduce a woman’s chance of pregnancy every month? There is no definite effect or universal percentage for every woman. Some observational studies found lower conception chances, while other findings depended on symptoms and medication definitions. Illness and other factors can be difficult to separate from treatment. I take an antidepressant and want a baby. What should I do first? Arrange a medication and mental-health review before making changes. Bring your treatment history, current medicines, side effects and fertility timeline. Agree a plan for symptom control, any treatment changes and follow-up rather than stopping because of a study headline. Can therapy, exercise or diet replace my medicine? Sometimes a psychological treatment may be appropriate, alone or alongside medication, but the decision depends on severity, history and preference. Lifestyle support is useful care, not a guaranteed substitute for treatment of a serious illness. Should I skip tablets during the fertile window? No self-directed dose skipping or drug holidays. Missed doses can cause withdrawal, and stopping treatment can lead to relapse. If a change is appropriate, the prescriber should agree an individualized plan and monitor the response. Will sexual side effects always disappear after stopping? No. Some people report persistent sexual dysfunction after treatment ends. Discuss symptoms with the prescriber; do not assume stopping will promptly resolve them or that continuing symptoms must be ignored. Does sildenafil improve fertility by 55%? No. The older trial reported the proportion of men whose sexual dysfunction improved, not a 55% fertility gain. Sildenafil may help selected erection problems after clinical assessment, but it has important contraindications and is not a sperm or conception treatment. Should I stop as soon as I find out I am pregnant? Do not stop abruptly. Contact the prescriber and maternity team for a medicine-specific benefit–risk review and mental-health plan. If you develop suicidal thoughts seek urgent help; immediate danger or inability to keep yourself or others safe needs emergency care.

title: Understanding a semen analysis: numbers, movement, shape and next steps
description: Read the main semen-analysis measures, understand reference values and collection limits, and learn how repeat testing and a full fertility assessment guide care.
body: A semen report contains several observations about the fluid and the sperm it carries. A flag beside one number can be unsettling, but it is not a verdict on whether you can have a child. The useful question is how the whole pattern, the way the sample was collected and both partners’ circumstances fit together. This guide explains the main entries and the decisions to discuss with your clinician. Reference values are a guide, not a fertility score The World Health Organization’s 2021 reference data describe a group of men whose partners conceived within 12 months. A lower fifth-centile value marks the lower end of that group’s distribution; it does not separate everyone who can conceive from everyone who cannot. Results need the laboratory’s methods and clinical context. A result above every reference value cannot guarantee pregnancy, and one below a value does not rule it out. NICE’s 2026 guidance uses these lower reference values: volume 1.4 mL; total sperm number 39 million per ejaculate; concentration 16 million per mL; total motility 42%; progressive motility 30%; vitality 54%; and normal forms on morphology assessment 4%. These are different measurements with different units. Older reports and websites may show earlier values, so ask which methods and references your laboratory uses rather than mixing tables. Check the collection details before interpreting the numbers Follow your laboratory’s instructions for abstinence, the collection container and delivery. A commonly used abstinence interval is two to seven days. Collect the entire ejaculate and tell the laboratory if any was missed, especially the first portion. Report the collection time, recent fever or illness, medicines and any difficulty producing the sample. A collection problem is useful information, not something to hide. Ordinary condoms, saliva and unapproved lubricants can interfere with testing. Ask the laboratory about approved alternatives if needed. Do not collect spilled material back into the pot. Home collection may be possible, but timing and transport conditions belong to the receiving laboratory’s instructions. A home sperm-count kit does not necessarily assess the full set of measures discussed here. Volume: how much fluid was collected Volume is the amount of semen, measured in millilitres. Semen includes sperm from the testes and fluid from reproductive glands, especially the seminal vesicles and prostate. More fluid does not necessarily mean more sperm: a sample can have a large volume but a low concentration, or contain no sperm despite visible ejaculation. A low volume may reflect an incomplete sample, some semen passing backwards into the bladder, a duct problem or a hormone problem. The clinician looks at the other findings before deciding what to investigate. Do not use the old 1.5–6 mL range as a universal fertility test, or assume that a high volume proves inflammation. Appearance and quantity alone cannot establish the cause. Concentration and total number: read the units Concentration means how many sperm are present in one millilitre. Total sperm number describes the whole ejaculate. For example, a 3 mL sample with 20 million sperm per mL contains about 60 million sperm in total. A report may write millions as 10⁶. Confusing per-millilitre with per-ejaculate values can make the same result seem much better or worse than it is. A low concentration is often called oligozoospermia. Azoospermia means that no sperm are found after the appropriate laboratory assessment; it does not mean that sperm merely move slowly. Very low or absent sperm needs confirmation and specialist assessment, including consideration of production and blockage problems. Do not choose treatment from a single count or assume that no sperm in one sample means that none can ever be found. Motility: moving is not the same as moving forward Total motility includes sperm moving forward and sperm moving without effective forward progress. Progressive motility concerns forward movement, including movement in a broad circular path. Reports may separate faster and slower progression or use abbreviations such as PR for progressive and NP for non-progressive movement. Read the laboratory’s key rather than adding percentages from different categories twice. The current reference values are 42% for total movement and 30% for progressive movement. A low movement result is described as reduced motility, sometimes called asthenozoospermia. Collection and transport, illness and other reproductive factors can affect the finding. The result does not by itself establish which factor caused it, and low motility is not the same condition as absent sperm. Vitality: living sperm may be immotile Vitality estimates the proportion of sperm that are alive. It answers a different question from motility: a sperm that is not moving may still be alive. Laboratories use special tests to make that distinction, particularly when many sperm are immotile. The current lower reference value is 54% living sperm. Reduced vitality does not necessarily mean every sperm is dead. Ask whether the result could have been affected by collection materials, delay or handling, and whether confirmation is needed. Do not infer sperm survival from the appearance of semen or try to change a laboratory result with a lubricant or supplement. The team interprets vitality alongside movement, number and the rest of the assessment. Morphology: what the shape percentage means Morphology is a microscopic assessment of the head, middle section and tail using defined criteria. Under strict methods, only a small proportion may meet every normal-form criterion. The 4% reference value is a proportion of sperm shapes, not a 4% chance of pregnancy and not a measure of the percentage of genetically healthy sperm. An isolated low morphology result cannot tell you that natural conception is impossible. Equally, normal count and movement do not prove fertility when shape is abnormal. Ask about the method, whether there is a particular severe pattern and how repeat results compare. Morphology helps inform the whole assessment; it does not automatically dictate IVF or ICSI. Liquefaction and viscosity describe different properties Fresh semen can be gel-like and then become more fluid. Liquefaction describes that change over time; viscosity describes how thick or resistant to flow the sample remains. These should not be treated as interchangeable entries. Laboratories assess them under controlled conditions, and a report may note delayed or incomplete liquefaction rather than a single pass–fail number. ASRM laboratory guidance describes allowing 30–60 minutes for liquefaction. Use the laboratory’s actual method and comment rather than diagnosing a gland problem from a home observation. A thick sample is not proof of blockage or infertility. The older suggestion to resolve the question with a postcoital cervical-mucus test is not routine current care: NICE advises against that test for predicting pregnancy. pH: acidity is interpreted with the rest of the sample The pH describes how acidic or alkaline the semen is. NICE uses 7.2 or above as a reference. This is a separate type of observation from sperm count or movement, and a pH result does not provide a personal probability of conception. Ask the clinician to explain the laboratory comment rather than trying to alter semen pH yourself. An acidic sample together with low volume and absent sperm can raise concern about a duct or gland-related problem. That pattern may lead to selected investigations; low pH alone is not enough to diagnose an obstruction. Imaging is chosen for the findings, not automatically ordered for everyone with an out-of-range result. White cells and round cells need clarification A report may mention white blood cells, also called leukocytes, or the broader category of round cells. Round cells can include immature germ cells as well as white cells, so further laboratory assessment may be needed. Around one million white cells per mL is an important threshold used in interpretation; the cell type and testing method matter. Increased white cells can indicate inflammation but do not by themselves prove bacterial infection. Symptoms and further tests guide whether infection treatment is appropriate. Antibiotics are not a way to correct every white-cell flag, and treating white cells alone has not been shown to improve conception. The report cannot establish that a dental problem caused the finding. What happens after an abnormal result? Semen measures vary, and one sample may not represent your usual pattern. Ask whether the laboratory recommends confirmation, whether collection conditions should change and when the clinician wants to review you. Bring the complete report rather than only the flagged number. A repeat test is an opportunity to clarify the result, not proof that the first test was useless. Timing depends on the finding and guidance used. WHO’s 2025 guideline conditionally suggests at least 11 weeks before repeating abnormal parameters, with very low certainty of evidence. NICE recommends about three months ideally, but earlier confirmation for absent sperm or a severe deficiency. Do not postpone an indicated specialist assessment simply to complete a standard waiting interval. If every value is in range, the clinical history can still require investigation. The assessment looks for causes in the whole clinical picture Possible contributors include problems with sperm production, reproductive ducts or ejaculation, hormonal or genetic conditions, varicocele, infection, previous treatment and some medicines. Recent illness and sample conditions also matter. Sometimes no single cause is found. A result alone cannot distinguish all of these or tell you that a particular habit is responsible. A clinician reviews reproductive and medical history and examines you, then chooses tests that could change care. Hormone tests, genetic tests and imaging have specific indications; not everyone needs every test. When relevant, the other partner’s assessment proceeds alongside yours because age, ovulation, tubes and other factors influence the options and timing. An abnormal report should not become a reason to blame either person. Treat a cause where possible and support general health Care may involve treating an identified infection or hormone disorder, reviewing a medicine, or considering repair of a suitable varicocele or obstruction. Hormone treatment is selected for a diagnosis, not prescribed to everyone with a low count. Testosterone taken from outside the body can reduce or stop sperm production; do not use it as a fertility booster or stop a prescription without discussing a supervised plan. Stopping smoking, avoiding recreational drugs and anabolic steroids, moderating alcohol, managing health conditions and reviewing heat or workplace exposures are reasonable topics for the consultation. Improvement is not guaranteed. Supplements marketed for fertility have uncertain benefit and should not postpone assessment. Ask what change is justified, what benefit is realistic and how progress will be assessed. IUI, IVF and ICSI have different roles In IUI, a clinic prepares sperm and places the selected sample into the uterus; fertilisation still needs to happen inside the body. Suitability depends on both partners’ findings, and a persistently low number of moving sperm can reduce the chance of success. In IVF, eggs are collected and fertilisation takes place in the laboratory before an embryo is transferred. ICSI is a technique within IVF in which an embryologist injects one sperm into an egg. It may be useful for particular sperm problems or previous fertilisation failure, but it is not automatically the only option for every low count or poor shape result. It adds procedures and can damage an egg. Discuss the reason for recommending it, alternatives and the prospects for a live birth; successful fertilisation is not a pregnancy guarantee. Sperm retrieval and donor treatment are individual choices If suitable sperm cannot be obtained in an ejaculate, a specialist may consider retrieval from the epididymis or testis. The method depends on whether sperm are blocked or poorly produced and on other findings. Some methods use a needle; others involve tissue sampling or microsurgery. A low count or ejaculation difficulty does not automatically require an operation, and retrieval may find no usable sperm. Retrieved sperm generally need an assisted treatment such as ICSI. Discuss surgical risks, storage plans and what happens if the procedure is unsuccessful before proceeding. Donor sperm may be another option when appropriate, with counselling and local consent, screening and legal requirements. People can also choose to pause or stop treatment. The best plan reflects preferences and the whole assessment, not simply the aim of making every report value normal. Prepare questions and know when not to wait For the next appointment, ask which findings are most significant, whether the sample was complete, when to repeat it and which further tests would change the plan. Write down the agreed follow-up date and seek emotional support if the uncertainty is difficult. Do not wait for a repeat semen test to report a new testicular lump, swelling, change in shape or concerning discomfort; obtain urgent medical advice. Sudden severe testicle pain, pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or pain lasting more than an hour or continuing at rest needs emergency assessment. Do not drive yourself; arrange a safe driver or an ambulance through local emergency services. A semen report, even a reassuring one, cannot rule out an urgent cause of symptoms. Read the whole report with collection details and the clinician’s assessment. Reference values do not divide everyone into fertile and infertile groups. Concentration, total number, movement, vitality and shape answer different questions. White cells do not automatically prove infection, and delayed liquefaction is not the same as viscosity. Repeat timing and treatment depend on the findings; severe results and urgent symptoms should not wait for a routine timetable. How many sperm should there be in the whole sample? The current lower reference value is 39 million per ejaculate. This is the total number, not the concentration per millilitre, and it is not a pregnancy guarantee or an absolute infertility boundary. The clinician considers the rest of the report and both partners’ circumstances. What concentration is used as a reference? NICE’s 2026 guidance uses 16 million sperm per mL with the relevant WHO methods. Older tables may show 15 million. Check the report’s units and laboratory methods; a small difference around a reference value should not determine treatment by itself. How much movement is expected? The current lower reference values are 42% total motility and 30% progressive motility. Total movement includes non-progressive movement; progressive movement describes travel forward. A low movement result is not azoospermia, which means no sperm are found after appropriate assessment. What does sperm morphology measure? It assesses shape under defined laboratory criteria. A 4% normal-forms result is not a 4% chance of pregnancy and does not reveal which sperm are genetically healthy. Shape must be considered with the complete semen analysis and clinical assessment. If sperm do not move, are they all dead? No. Vitality testing distinguishes living immotile sperm from dead sperm. A low vitality percentage also does not necessarily mean that every sperm is dead. Ask whether the sample needs confirmation and whether collection or handling affected it. Do white cells or thick semen mean I need antibiotics? Not automatically. White cells may reflect inflammation without infection, and round cells are not always white cells. Liquefaction and viscosity are separate observations. Symptoms and appropriate tests guide care; do not start antibiotics or another treatment to correct a flag yourself. Should I always wait three months for another test? No. Guidance commonly allows time for a new sperm-production cycle, but absent sperm or severe deficiencies can need earlier confirmation and assessment. Agree the timing with the clinician. New symptoms need their own assessment rather than waiting for the next semen sample. Does an abnormal report mean IVF or surgery is unavoidable? No. Confirmation, the cause, other reproductive factors and your preferences guide the plan. Options may include treating an identified problem, selected fertility treatment or donor sperm. ICSI and surgical retrieval have specific roles and cannot guarantee a baby; discuss why any proposed procedure is appropriate.

title: Preparing a semen sample: collection, transport and questions before the test
description: How to prepare for a diagnostic semen analysis, arrange private collection, handle medicines and recent illness, and deliver a sample the laboratory can assess.
body: A semen analysis examines more than sperm count. How the sample is collected and delivered helps the laboratory interpret its findings. Start with the instructions from the laboratory that will receive it, because appointment, container, abstinence and transport requirements differ. Needing help to provide a sample is a practical concern the team can discuss without judging you. Understand why the test is part of assessment Fertility difficulties can involve either partner, both partners or factors that remain unexplained after assessment. A known condition in one partner does not establish that the other partner’s fertility is normal. Semen testing can contribute to a coordinated evaluation and treatment plan; it is not a test of masculinity, sexual performance or personal worth. Tell the clinician why the test was requested. A diagnostic fertility assessment, a sample for treatment and a post-vasectomy check can have different instructions and interpretations. This guide concerns diagnostic collection. Do not use a general article or a home sperm-count result to decide whether contraception can be stopped after a vasectomy. Arrange the appointment and collection location first Contact the receiving laboratory before collecting anything. Confirm the referral, appointment, identification documents, approved container and how the sample will be handed over. Ask whether there is a private collection room at your chosen site. Different branches of the same service may have different facilities; do not assume that an unbooked sample can be accepted. If you prefer home collection, ask whether it is allowed and whether your journey meets the laboratory’s delivery window. Discuss privacy, accessibility, language support and any assistance you need in advance. Obtain the written instructions and a contact number so that a delay or collection problem can be resolved before you travel. Count abstinence from ejaculation For a standard diagnostic sample, the WHO manual commonly uses two to seven days without ejaculation. This includes ejaculation during masturbation as well as intercourse. Your laboratory may request a narrower interval, so follow its exact instruction and record how long you actually abstained. More days is not automatically a better way to prepare. If you ejaculated within the requested interval, had an involuntary ejaculation or cannot meet the timing, tell the laboratory and ask whether to keep the appointment. Do not give an inaccurate date to make the sample seem acceptable. Treatment-related collections may have different requirements; instructions for one test should not be transferred automatically to another. Report fever, illness and substantial heat exposure A recent fever or illness can temporarily affect semen findings. Tell the team when it happened, how unwell you were and whether you are still recovering. The clinician may decide to test now, repeat later or change the appointment according to the clinical question. Do not assume that every illness requires the same waiting period or that an abnormal result after fever proves a permanent problem. Also mention repeated hot-tub or sauna use and significant occupational heat exposure. Sensible longer-term health changes are different from trying to alter a result in a few days. Ask whether your circumstances require a change in exposure or test timing. Discuss smoking, alcohol, caffeine intake and recreational drugs honestly; a one-week detox cannot guarantee a normal sample. Bring a complete medicine and supplement list Include prescription medicines, non-prescription products, vitamins, herbal or bodybuilding supplements, doses, routes and recent changes. Mention medicines used for hair loss, urinary symptoms, blood pressure, inflammation, infection or cancer, as well as testosterone. An effect on ejaculation, sexual function or a semen measurement does not necessarily show an effect on the chance of pregnancy. Do not stop, skip or switch prescribed treatment to improve the test. The prescriber may want a sample while treatment continues, may review a possible contribution or may arrange follow-up after a supervised change. The underlying illness can also affect the findings. A laboratory result and a medicine name alone cannot establish the cause. Hair-loss and prostate medicines are not one uniform group Finasteride and dutasteride are 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors. Their product information describes different semen findings and reports, with uncertainty about what they mean for individual fertility. Dose, indication and the person studied matter. Information from a 5 mg finasteride study should not be treated as proof that everyone taking a different dose will become infertile. Alpha blockers such as silodosin, tamsulosin and alfuzosin also differ. Some can reduce or alter ejaculation, and a dry or smaller ejaculate is not the same as proven failure to produce sperm. Short studies of semen measurements cannot establish a class-wide effect on conception. Report the exact product and symptoms rather than changing treatment yourself. Other named medicines need specific interpretation Sulfasalazine has been associated with low sperm counts and male infertility that may improve after withdrawal, but the disease still needs treatment and recovery is not guaranteed on a fixed schedule. Colchicine has rare reports of potentially reversible fertility problems; the illness it treats can itself be relevant. Oral ketoconazole can affect testosterone and sperm-related measures. That does not establish the same risk for a topical cream or shampoo. Spironolactone’s antiandrogenic and sexual effects warrant an individual review. Nifedipine information describes limited reports involving sperm function in IVF, not proof that it lowers everyone’s sperm count. Cimetidine’s product label reports no effect in human studies on sperm production, count, movement or shape; taking it does not establish that it caused an abnormal semen result. Sexual side effects are a separate question. Distinguish infection treatment, steroids and cancer care Antibiotics are not a single category that can be said to lower sperm count. The infection, associated fever, exact drug and clinical situation all matter. Prescribed corticosteroids also differ from anabolic steroids used for bodybuilding; the evidence does not support treating every steroid preparation as equivalent. In particular, do not abruptly stop prescribed corticosteroids. Exogenous testosterone can suppress sperm production and is not a fertility booster; discuss conception plans with its prescriber. Cancer and cancer-directed treatment may affect fertility in different ways. If treatment is planned, ask the oncology team promptly about fertility preservation, ideally before treatment begins. Some people may need specialist help if they cannot provide an ejaculated sample. Do not delay or stop cancer treatment on your own, assume every regimen causes permanent infertility, or rely on a universal recovery interval. Use the supplied container and collect the whole sample Use the container supplied or specifically approved by the laboratory. Follow the laboratory’s instructions for washing your hands and penis, rinsing away soap and drying as directed. Avoid touching the inside of the pot or lid. The usual method is masturbation directly into the container, collecting the whole ejaculate rather than trying to produce a particular volume. The pot does not need to be filled. Close the lid securely and complete the required identifiers, collection time and other paperwork. Tell the laboratory if any portion was missed, especially the first portion. Do not scoop spilled semen back into the pot, add water or another substance, or hide a problem. The team can decide whether the sample is interpretable or should be repeated. Ask before using lubricant or a collection condom Do not use saliva, an ordinary lubricant or a consumer condom unless the laboratory has specifically approved it for this collection. Materials and additives can interfere with the sample. A product described as non-spermicidal or fertility-friendly is not automatically validated for diagnostic testing. If lubrication is needed, ask for an approved option before the appointment. When masturbation is not suitable, some laboratories can arrange a specially approved collection condom for intercourse. This needs discussion and specific handling instructions; sample loss and contamination remain possible. Do not improvise with withdrawal or an ordinary condom. Ask whether transfer to the laboratory container is required and exactly how to deliver the sample. Protect the sample during transport For approved home collection, establish the maximum time to delivery and the temperature instructions before starting. Semen examination is time-sensitive. A statement that delivery should take at least two hours is wrong; waiting that long may make a sample unsuitable. Different laboratories specify different shorter windows, so use the receiving service’s instructions rather than choosing the longest allowance found online. Record the collection time, secure the container in the supplied packaging and avoid overheating or chilling it. Do not refrigerate, freeze, place on a radiator or use a heating pad unless the laboratory has given a specific instruction for a different type of test. If traffic, a spill or another delay disrupts the plan, call the laboratory and report what happened instead of guessing whether the sample is still usable. If anxiety or difficulty producing the sample gets in the way An unfamiliar room, time pressure, pain, disability, personal beliefs or worries about results can make collection difficult. Tell the team which part is a problem. Depending on the service and clinical circumstances, they may discuss another appointment, a more suitable setting, approved home collection or an alternative collection method. These options must be arranged, rather than assumed to be available everywhere. You do not need to conceal a failed attempt or force yourself to continue in distress. Ask how to contact staff privately and how your information and results will be handled. A sample problem does not define your fertility or your relationship. If reluctance is delaying assessment, discuss the concern with the clinician so that support and an acceptable plan can be considered. Know what is being measured Semen includes sperm made in the testes and fluid from glands, particularly the seminal vesicles and prostate. The amount of fluid is not the same as the number of sperm. A visible ejaculate can contain few or no sperm, and appearance cannot establish fertility. A fixed percentage of semen described as sperm is not a useful personal test. The report may assess volume, concentration, total sperm number, movement, shape and other features. Its reference values describe measurements in a particular context; they are not a simple fertile-versus-infertile boundary. Ask the clinician to interpret the full pattern with the collection details and both partners’ history. Home kits may measure only part of what a laboratory analysis assesses. Agree when a repeat sample is useful There is no universal rule that everyone needs two samples exactly one month apart. A repeat may clarify an abnormal finding, assess a collection problem or help answer a treatment question. NICE’s current fertility guidance recommends confirming an abnormal initial result, ideally around three months later, but repeating as soon as possible when no sperm or a severe reduction is found. WHO’s 2025 infertility guideline suggests a repeat after at least eleven weeks when one or more parameters are outside its reference ranges, with very low certainty of evidence; it does not suggest routine repetition when all are within range in that assessment context. These recommendations need clinical interpretation. Ask why your interval was chosen, and do not postpone assessment of a severe result simply to meet a general waiting rule. Keep symptoms separate from the routine test appointment A semen test does not replace assessment of a new lump, swelling or worrying testicular discomfort. Arrange urgent clinical advice for these changes rather than waiting for a laboratory result. Mention pain, ejaculation changes, medicines and recent illness to the clinician; the next investigation should address the actual concern. Seek emergency care for sudden severe testicular pain, pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or testicular pain lasting more than an hour or continuing at rest. Do not drive yourself to emergency care; ask another person to take you or call for an ambulance. Do not delay urgent help to finish an abstinence interval or produce a sample. Leave with a clear follow-up plan Before leaving, confirm that the laboratory has the collection details and knows about any lost sample, delay, fever or medicine change. Ask when results are expected, who will explain them and how to follow up if they do not arrive. Keep the test instructions and the actual collection details together so that a repeat can be compared fairly. The aim is a reliable assessment that helps guide care, not a perfect-looking result. An abnormal finding does not automatically mean that pregnancy is impossible, and a reassuring report does not explain every fertility difficulty. Follow the agreed review plan and discuss any treatment decision with the responsible clinician. Arrange the appointment, approved container, collection location and delivery plan before producing a sample. Follow the laboratory’s abstinence interval, counted from ejaculation, and report what actually happened. Disclose recent fever, medicines and collection problems; do not stop prescribed treatment to change a result. Use only laboratory-approved collection materials and tell staff about sample loss or transport delays. Agree how results and any repeat test will be interpreted, and seek urgent help for concerning symptoms independently of the test. Can a fever affect a semen test? Yes, recent fever or illness can temporarily affect findings. Tell the team when it occurred and whether you have recovered. The clinician can decide whether to test now or change the timing; there is no single waiting period for every illness. Can I use lubricant or saliva to collect the sample? Avoid saliva and unapproved lubricants. Ask the receiving laboratory for a validated option if needed. A consumer product labelled fertility-friendly is not automatically suitable for diagnostic collection. How far apart should two semen tests be? The interval depends on the result and purpose. NICE advises confirmation of an abnormal result ideally around three months later, but as soon as possible for absent or severely reduced sperm. WHO’s conditional eleven-week suggestion has a defined context and very low-certainty evidence. Do not assume everyone must wait the same interval. How long should I avoid ejaculation before the test? Two to seven days is a common diagnostic standard, but laboratories may specify a narrower window. Count ejaculation during masturbation as well as intercourse, follow your service’s instructions and report the actual interval. Can I collect at home or during intercourse? Sometimes, after arranging it with the laboratory. Home collection must meet its transport requirements. Intercourse collection requires a specially approved method and supplies; do not use an ordinary condom or withdrawal as a substitute. What if I spill part of the sample or cannot produce one? Tell the laboratory, including whether the first portion was lost. Do not put spilled material back into the container. If collection is difficult, ask for support or another arrangement; a failed attempt is not a fertility diagnosis. Should I stop medicines before testing? No, not on your own. Bring a complete list and discuss the exact product, dose, route and symptoms. Medicines can affect different endpoints, and the illness itself may matter. The clinician may want to assess the sample while treatment continues or plan a supervised review. Does an abnormal result mean pregnancy is impossible? No. The whole report, collection quality and both partners’ circumstances need interpretation. Some people conceive naturally despite an abnormal measurement; others need further assessment or treatment. New lumps or swelling need urgent advice, and emergency testicular-pain symptoms should not wait for test results.

title: Diabetes, fertility and pregnancy: a plan for both partners
description: How established diabetes can affect fertility in either partner, what sperm studies can and cannot show, and how to prepare for pregnancy and newborn care.
body: Diabetes does not automatically prevent pregnancy. It can affect sexual function, sperm, ovulation and pregnancy health, but those are different questions with different investigations. A useful plan considers both partners, the type of diabetes, current treatment and other possible fertility factors. Improving health can reduce some risks without guaranteeing conception or a particular pregnancy outcome. Start with both partners, not a verdict from one diagnosis Many people with diabetes become parents. If pregnancy is taking longer than expected, do not assume that diabetes explains everything or that the partner without diabetes needs no assessment. Age, ovulation, sperm delivery and production, the fallopian tubes and other conditions can all matter. A blood glucose result can help assess diabetes; it cannot identify the precise cause of a couple’s fertility difficulty. Ask your diabetes clinician about family plans before trying to conceive, and raise sexual symptoms without embarrassment. Bring both partners’ relevant history, medicines and previous results to a fertility appointment. There is no established “fertility cleanse” that removes diabetes-related reproductive risk. Avoid replacing necessary care with a supplement, restrictive diet or an online promise of a quick cure. Type 1, type 2 and gestational diabetes are not interchangeable Type 1 diabetes usually involves an immune attack on the insulin-producing cells. Insulin treatment is essential; it is not a condition that can be managed by simply avoiding sugar. Type 2 diabetes involves reduced responsiveness to insulin and insufficient insulin production for the body’s needs. It can require medicines or insulin as well as practical nutrition and activity support, and is not necessarily mild. Gestational diabetes is diagnosed during pregnancy in someone who did not previously have established diabetes. It is a separate situation from entering pregnancy with type 1 or type 2 diabetes. Neither stress nor body weight alone explains every diagnosis. Avoid ranking one type as universally the most dangerous: treatment, complications, glucose patterns and the individual pregnancy determine the care needed. Erections, ejaculation and sperm delivery Diabetes-related nerve or blood-vessel damage can contribute to erection difficulties. Medicines, hormones, other illnesses, pain, emotional strain and relationship factors may also contribute. Delayed ejaculation, inability to ejaculate or retrograde ejaculation can reduce the chance of sperm reaching the vagina even when sperm are being produced. Little or no outward semen after orgasm, or cloudy urine afterwards, can prompt assessment for retrograde ejaculation, in which semen travels into the bladder. A clinician can review the history, examination and relevant tests rather than treating every problem as low sperm count. Selected cases need a urine sample after ejaculation or a fertility/urology referral. Treatment may address sexual function or sperm delivery, and specialists can discuss assisted conception when appropriate. Do not start testosterone as a fertility booster: external testosterone can suppress sperm production, even if it improves some symptoms of low testosterone. What the often-quoted sperm-DNA study actually found A small 2007 study compared 27 men with diabetes with 29 men without diabetes who were undergoing infertility investigations. Average semen volume was 2.6 versus 3.3 mL; the other conventional semen measures did not differ significantly. Nuclear sperm-DNA fragmentation averaged 53% versus 32%, and the median number of mitochondrial DNA deletions was four versus three. Those are laboratory findings in a particular study, not a fertility prediction for every man with diabetes. The fragmentation difference was 21 percentage points, not “20% more DNA.” The study did not measure an individual’s miscarriage, birth-defect or live-birth probability. A specialist should interpret actual semen results and the couple’s circumstances; this paper alone does not justify routine DNA-fragmentation testing for everyone with diabetes. Paternal diabetes and pregnancy outcomes: what remains uncertain Damage measured in a sperm test is not the same as proving harm to a future baby. A Danish assisted-reproduction cohort published online in 2024 did not find a statistically significant reduction in pregnancy or live-birth outcomes with paternal diabetes, but estimates were imprecise and the findings concern people receiving that treatment. A separate US claims study associated a father’s metabolic health problems with pregnancy loss; this observational association cannot establish that diabetes caused a loss. A 2026 Danish study found that the assessed outcomes with paternal type 1 diabetes were broadly comparable with the general population after adjustment, whereas maternal type 1 diabetes carried greater risks. It examined outcomes such as prematurity and birth size, not every possible outcome or congenital abnormality. Together these studies support an honest discussion of uncertainty, not a blanket claim that paternal diabetes either causes fetal malformations or has no possible reproductive effects. Female fertility, cycles and other conditions Diabetes can coexist with irregular ovulation, sexual discomfort and other conditions affecting conception. Higher body weight and insulin resistance may overlap with polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, or PMOS, previously called polycystic ovary syndrome or PCOS. Having diabetes does not itself establish that diagnosis. Pain, vaginal dryness or reduced desire can also make intercourse difficult and deserve care rather than blame. A Swedish register study of women with type 2 diabetes found more recorded infertility and miscarriage and fewer births than in its comparison group. It was observational and cannot provide an individual loss percentage or prove the mechanism. It does not support claims that someone becomes pregnant every month but cannot implant an embryo, or that all people with diabetes face a 30–60% miscarriage rate. Irregular or absent periods warrant an individualized investigation. Choose tests for the question being asked Fertility evaluation usually starts with both partners’ histories, assessment of ovulation and a semen analysis when relevant. Examination, tubal assessment, hormone tests or other investigations follow the findings. AUA/ASRM guidance does not recommend sperm-DNA fragmentation as a routine initial test. It can have a selected role, for example in some recurrent pregnancy-loss or assisted-treatment assessments; diabetes alone is not a universal indication. Type 1 diabetes and other autoimmune conditions can coexist, but this does not prove thyroid disease, premature ovarian insufficiency or early menopause in a particular person. Diabetes-specific preconception care can include thyroid testing. In a general fertility assessment, thyroid and reproductive hormone tests should follow the clinical context: FSH and estradiol may help investigate absent periods, for example. An automatic TSH/FSH panel cannot settle every fertility question or replace interpreting symptoms and results together. When to arrange fertility assessment Arrange preconception diabetes care before trying, regardless of how long you have been trying to conceive. For fertility investigation, ASRM generally advises assessment after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse when the egg-producing partner is under 35, or after six months at 35 or older. Over 40, an earlier assessment may be appropriate. Local referral arrangements and individual circumstances can differ. Do not wait for those intervals if there are irregular or absent periods, known reproductive problems, concerning semen results or sexual difficulties that prevent conception. Evaluate both partners in parallel where applicable. A fertility referral need not mean that IVF is required; the next step depends on the identified problem, age, preferences and the time available. Ask for a plan that coordinates the fertility and diabetes teams. Before conception, agree safe glucose goals Glucose control before conception matters because early development occurs before many people know they are pregnant. NICE and ADA use an HbA1c goal below 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) before conception when this can be achieved safely, without problematic hypoglycaemia. HbA1c reflects longer-term glucose exposure; it is not the same measurement as a current finger-prick glucose reading. The team should help set realistic targets, monitoring and treatment changes. A very high HbA1c needs prompt specialist planning; NICE advises avoiding conception while HbA1c is above 10% (86 mmol/mol) until it is lowered. Discuss contraception if you wish to defer pregnancy while improving control, without treating a target as a judgement about you. Any improvement may help, and a result below target cannot guarantee a complication-free pregnancy. Review medicines and folic acid before trying Do not stop essential insulin or change diabetes treatment on your own. Some glucose, blood-pressure and cholesterol medicines need replacement or a planned pause before pregnancy; others may remain appropriate. The team must arrange effective treatment while making changes. US ADA guidance prefers insulin for type 2 diabetes in pregnancy, while UK NICE permits selected metformin use when benefits outweigh potential harm. Your actual prescription, including any combination tablet, needs an individual review. Ask which folic acid recommendation applies where you receive care. UK NICE recommends prescribed 5 mg daily for women with diabetes planning pregnancy until 12 weeks; US ADA preconception guidance describes prenatal folic acid of 400–800 micrograms daily. These are different guideline approaches, not instructions to combine products or choose the highest dose yourself. Bring supplements and all medicine packaging, including weight-management treatments, to the review. Check complications and make the plan workable Preconception assessment includes eye and kidney health, blood pressure and other relevant conditions. Retinal assessment is particularly important before rapidly improving glucose control when retinopathy may be present. Kidney function and urine protein findings can influence pregnancy monitoring and medicines. Ask which checks are due, what any abnormal result means and whether a specialist review is needed before conception. A sustainable plan also covers food access, activity, tobacco or alcohol concerns, sleep, emotional wellbeing and the cost of medicines or monitoring supplies. Seek individualized nutrition advice rather than a crash diet or blame about weight. Agree whom to contact outside clinic hours and how fertility treatment, pregnancy care and diabetes follow-up will communicate. Write down the next appointment and what information to bring. After a positive test, contact the team promptly An unexpected pregnancy is a reason for prompt diabetes and maternity advice, not panic or self-directed treatment withdrawal. Provide the test date, current medicines, glucose information and any symptoms. Poorly controlled maternal diabetes can increase miscarriage and congenital-abnormality risks, especially around conception, and can affect fetal growth and later pregnancy. Care aims to lower these risks while preventing severe low glucose. The monitoring plan may include review of eye or kidney disease, fetal assessment and growth monitoring, and individualized decisions about birth and newborn care. A normal scan does not answer every question, and diabetes does not mean that loss or malformation is inevitable. Ask which risks apply to your circumstances rather than relying on a single internet percentage. The medication and monitoring plan may need adjustment as pregnancy progresses. The baby’s glucose exposure is different from inherited susceptibility When the pregnant person has diabetes, high glucose reaching the fetus can stimulate fetal insulin production and contribute to a larger baby. After birth, that insulin effect can cause low newborn glucose. Some babies also develop jaundice, a high red-cell count or breathing problems; growth restriction can occur in other circumstances. These are reasons for an individualized newborn feeding and monitoring plan, not outcomes that every baby will develop. A father’s diabetes does not expose the fetus to high maternal blood glucose by the same pathway. Either parent can contribute inherited susceptibility to diabetes, but genes are not the whole explanation and a child is not certain to develop it. Newborn low glucose is not proof that the baby has inherited diabetes. Ask the team to separate family-history questions from pregnancy exposure and the baby’s immediate clinical needs. High glucose, illness and ketoacidosis need a clear response Ask for written sick-day and ketone instructions, especially with type 1 diabetes, and do not simply omit insulin because you are eating less. Contact the team urgently for high readings that are not responding to your agreed treatment, concerning ketones or difficulty managing illness. Pregnancy can bring diabetic ketoacidosis at lower glucose levels than usual, so a glucose reading that is not extremely high cannot rule it out. Suspected ketoacidosis needs emergency assessment. Possible symptoms include vomiting, abdominal pain, deep breathing, fruity-smelling breath, unusual drowsiness or confusion; thirst and frequent urination can also occur. Do not wait for every sign or extremely high glucose. Seek emergency help directly and do not drive yourself. Prepare for low glucose and keep support available Insulin and some other diabetes medicines can cause low glucose. If you are awake and able to swallow safely, follow your agreed plan for fast-acting carbohydrate and rechecking; the NHS general advice is to recheck after 10–15 minutes. Repeated episodes need a treatment review. Tell someone close to you how to recognize a low and where your supplies are kept, particularly while preparing for or going through pregnancy. If a person is unconscious or cannot swallow safely, give nothing by mouth. Call for emergency help when they are not responding normally or are unconscious, place a breathing person in the recovery position, and use prescribed glucagon only if available and you know how. Do not leave them alone. Once an episode is resolved, review its cause and prevention with the diabetes team rather than stopping insulin or abandoning pregnancy plans without advice. Turn the next appointment into a shared plan Bring your diabetes type, treatment list, recent glucose or HbA1c results, cycle or sexual symptoms, previous pregnancies and how long you have been trying. Ask what needs attention before conception, whether both partners need fertility investigations, what changes after a positive test and how to obtain urgent advice. If a suggested test or treatment is costly, ask what question it answers and how its result would change care. Managing diabetes and fertility together can be tiring. Support for anxiety, sexual concerns, grief after loss or practical access difficulties is part of care. BeMama can help keep your questions and clinician-issued plans together; it cannot diagnose infertility or estimate an individual baby’s risk from a sperm or glucose result. A clear follow-up date and named contact are more useful than a promise that perfect control guarantees a baby. Diabetes can affect fertility in either partner, but does not automatically make pregnancy impossible. Semen laboratory findings, paternal pregnancy outcomes and maternal glucose exposure are different kinds of evidence. Investigate both partners as appropriate; do not assume one diagnosis explains every fertility difficulty. Arrange preconception glucose, medicine, folate, eye and kidney planning without stopping necessary treatment yourself. A positive pregnancy test needs prompt team contact, and suspected ketoacidosis or severe hypoglycaemia needs emergency care. Can a couple conceive if one partner has diabetes? Yes, many do. Diabetes may affect sexual function, sperm, ovulation or pregnancy health, but is not an automatic infertility diagnosis. Preconception diabetes care and, when needed, assessment of both partners help identify the relevant issues. A single glucose test cannot explain every difficulty conceiving. How can diabetes affect male fertility? Nerve and blood-vessel effects can contribute to erections or ejaculation difficulties; some people also have abnormal semen findings. Other conditions and medicines may matter. Little outward semen or cloudy urine after orgasm can prompt assessment for retrograde ejaculation. Do not take testosterone to improve fertility, because it can suppress sperm production. Does diabetes always damage sperm DNA? No. A small 2007 study found higher average DNA fragmentation in its diabetes group, but this does not describe every person or measure a future baby’s outcome. Semen analysis and clinical history usually come first; DNA-fragmentation testing is selected, not routine for everyone with diabetes. Does a father’s diabetes cause miscarriage or birth defects? It is not justified to make that blanket claim. Some observational paternal-health studies find associations, while other studies of particular treatment or pregnancy outcomes are reassuring. They examine different populations and cannot guarantee every outcome. Sperm-DNA findings alone do not establish that paternal diabetes caused a loss or malformation. Do all women with diabetes need thyroid and FSH tests? Testing depends on the question. Diabetes-specific preconception care can include thyroid assessment, while general fertility testing is guided by symptoms, cycle history and findings. FSH and other hormones can help investigate absent periods but are not a universal fertility screen. Diabetes does not automatically mean PMOS/PCOS or premature ovarian insufficiency. What should I do before trying or after a positive test? Arrange a diabetes/preconception review before trying, or contact the team promptly after a positive test. Discuss safe glucose targets, medicines, folic acid, eyes, kidneys and pregnancy monitoring. Guidelines differ on some medicine and folate choices; do not select a regimen online or stop insulin while waiting for an appointment. Will the baby inherit diabetes? Parental diabetes can contribute to susceptibility, but inheritance is not certain and other factors matter. This differs from effects of high maternal glucose during pregnancy. A newborn’s low glucose, jaundice or need for monitoring does not by itself mean the baby has inherited diabetes. Which diabetes symptoms cannot wait? Suspected ketoacidosis needs emergency care, with possible symptoms such as vomiting, abdominal pain, deep breathing, fruity breath, unusual drowsiness or confusion; do not wait for every sign or extremely high glucose. For an unresponsive or unconscious person with suspected low glucose, summon emergency help and give nothing by mouth; use prescribed glucagon only if available and you know how. Follow the sick-day plan and do not simply stop insulin.

title: Trying for a baby while COVID-19 is circulating
description: How to weigh readiness, care access, health history and COVID-19 protection when deciding whether to try for pregnancy, with practical preparation and emotional support.
body: Wanting a baby and feeling uncertain about COVID-19 can happen at the same time. A useful decision brings together your own health, the care you can access and the support available to you. This guide explains how to prepare, what to do if illness occurs while trying, and when physical or emotional symptoms need help. Deciding whether to start trying now Choosing a time to try for a baby can feel difficult when infection news, work pressures and uncertainty compete with your hopes. COVID-19 remains one consideration, but a headline cannot decide whether starting now or waiting is right for you. Think about your health, reproductive history, access to care, support and wishes together. Neither a blanket instruction to wait until COVID-19 disappears nor a promise that infection carries no pregnancy risk is a useful personal plan. A short pause may help you arrange treatment, recover from illness or put practical support in place. For someone else, an open-ended delay could conflict with age-related fertility concerns or an existing treatment plan. Discuss what a delay would actually achieve and agree when to review it. You do not need a perfectly calm life to ask for preconception advice, and seeking advice does not commit you to trying immediately. Understanding the risk without assuming the worst Pregnancy and the weeks after it increase the risk of severe COVID-19 compared with not being pregnant. Age and other health conditions can add to that risk. Infection during pregnancy has also been associated with preterm birth and stillbirth, and some evidence links it with pre-eclampsia. Many people recover without serious complications, but that is different from saying that pregnancy, the placenta or the baby cannot be affected. Evidence about early miscarriage and birth defects is more reassuring than some frightening online claims suggest. MotherToBaby’s December 2024 review reports that the studies it assessed did not find an increased miscarriage risk or a clear pattern of birth defects from COVID-19. These findings do not guarantee an individual outcome or cancel concerns about later pregnancy complications and fetal growth. Discuss your own illness and history rather than applying an old risk estimate to every variant, vaccination status and stage of pregnancy. Review previous pregnancies, conditions and medicines Arrange a preconception discussion if you have a long-term condition, take regular medicines, have had a complicated pregnancy or have questions about your health. Bring the names and doses of prescribed medicines, over-the-counter products, supplements and any fertility treatment. Ask whether your condition is adequately managed, whether anything needs changing before conception, and who will coordinate care if you become pregnant. Do not stop essential treatment because you are worried about either COVID-19 or pregnancy. A medicine change may require a supervised plan, and untreated illness can also matter. Include the health of a partner who will contribute sperm. If a previous experience of loss or difficult care affects your decision, ask for time to discuss it rather than assuming that the same outcome will happen again. Check how you will obtain care Service availability differs between places and changes over time. Ask your local practice or maternity service how to arrange preconception advice, how to book after a positive pregnancy test, which visits need to be in person and whom to contact outside normal hours. Check transport, costs, interpreting needs and whether someone can help with childcare or accompany you when allowed. These are practical questions to resolve, not evidence that every service is currently disrupted. Once pregnant, do not simply skip recommended appointments or scans to avoid exposure. If you develop symptoms before a visit, call the service: it can decide whether to alter the time, use a remote consultation or arrange an appropriate in-person assessment. A telephone or video appointment can be useful, but it cannot replace every examination, blood test or scan. Urgent concerns need the urgent route, even when a routine appointment is delayed. Vaccination is part of preparation, not the whole decision Check your current local COVID-19 vaccine advice and discuss the product, eligibility and timing with a clinician or vaccination service. As checked in November 2026, ACOG recommends vaccination for people contemplating or trying for pregnancy, and Canadian public-health advice also recommends vaccination when planning pregnancy. The evidence reviewed by these bodies does not show that COVID-19 vaccination causes infertility. Recommendations and access rules can differ between countries and services. ACOG does not require delaying pregnancy after a COVID-19 vaccine series or booster; Canada similarly advises no delay after an mRNA vaccine. This answers the vaccine-timing question, not every medical or practical reason someone might choose to wait. Do not postpone a useful discussion while waiting for an unspecified future vaccine. Tell the service about a recent infection, previous reactions and other vaccines, because advice for a particular product or a different vaccine may be different. Reduce exposure in ways you can sustain Use several realistic precautions rather than expecting one measure to remove all risk. Cleaner indoor air, a well-fitting mask when appropriate, and avoiding close contact with people who are ill can complement vaccination. Discuss situations that matter in your own life, such as a crowded workplace, caring for a vulnerable relative or frequent healthcare visits. Household members can share the responsibility for reducing exposure. If you develop respiratory symptoms, stay away from others as far as practical and follow current local advice about testing, staying home and returning to activities. The CDC’s public advice uses overall improvement and resolution of fever, followed by additional precautions; healthcare settings may have separate rules. A public-health return-to-activity rule is not a fertility clearance test. Continue needed care by contacting the service for instructions. Prepare food, drink and daily habits Start with ordinary preparation: a varied diet, support to stop smoking, avoidance of recreational drugs, and no alcohol while trying for pregnancy. Ask for help if changing a habit is difficult. Discuss weight and nutritional needs without crash dieting or treating a body-size target as a moral test. Both partners can benefit from practical changes, and health support should remain accessible while those changes are underway. Because pregnancy may begin before a test becomes positive, it is practical to become familiar with pregnancy food-safety advice now. Wash produce, store chilled food properly and follow local cooking advice. NHS pregnancy advice limits total caffeine to 200 mg a day; count coffee, tea, cola, energy drinks and other sources together. Avoid liver and liver products in pregnancy because of their high vitamin A content. A special “immune-boosting” diet cannot guarantee protection from infection or conception success. Use supplements for the right purpose Folic acid helps prevent neural tube defects; it is not a COVID-19 treatment. NHS advice is 400 micrograms daily while trying, ideally starting before conception, and through the first 12 weeks of pregnancy. Some people need a prescribed higher dose because of particular conditions, medicines or a personal or family history. Ask which dose applies to you instead of combining several prenatal products. Vitamin D advice depends on local guidance and individual circumstances. For example, NHS pregnancy advice recommends 10 micrograms daily from October to March, with year-round use considered or advised for some people with limited sunlight exposure or darker skin. This is UK seasonal advice, not a worldwide schedule. Check labels and avoid pregnancy supplements containing retinol or cod liver oil. More is not necessarily better; bring all supplements to your medication review. Keep movement manageable at home or outside Choose activity you can maintain, such as walking, gentle dancing, gardening or an appropriate class. Short periods of movement can be useful when time, weather or access to facilities is limited. An online class is an option, not a requirement, and it should suit your health and experience. If you are inactive, start gradually rather than making an abrupt change to intense training. Once pregnant, adapt activity to how you feel and to any clinical advice.
