The placenta is developing alongside all of this and will gradually take over hormone production. Because early growth follows such a predictable pace, an ultrasound measurement in these weeks gives one of the most reliable estimates of your due date. How you might feel, week by week At week 4, many people feel nothing beyond a missed period, and that is completely normal. Symptoms follow hormone levels, and hormones are only starting to climb. Through weeks 5 and 6, fatigue is often the first thing to arrive, and it can feel heavier than ordinary tiredness. Your breasts may feel sore, swollen, or tingly. You may need to pee more often, and certain smells, like coffee or cooking meat, can suddenly turn your stomach. None of this is required, though. Plenty of healthy pregnancies begin with barely a symptom, so a quiet start is not a warning sign on its own. Nausea often starts around week 6, and despite the name morning sickness, it can show up at any hour. Relief options deserve their own space, and they have a separate guide on this site, so the short version is this: nausea is common, it tends to ease by the second trimester, and having none does not mean anything is wrong. Mood swings are normal too, as are symptoms that come and go. A day with less nausea or softer breasts does not mean trouble. Early symptoms naturally fluctuate, and each pregnancy sets its own pattern. Your first prenatal appointment Call your clinic or midwife as soon as you have a positive test, because first appointments are typically scheduled for around 8 weeks. Some clinics see you earlier if you have a health condition, take regular medication, or have had complications before, so mention those when you call. Before the visit, note the first day of your last period, since dating starts from there. Pull together a list of your medications and supplements, your own health history, and any family history of conditions on either side. Ten minutes of preparation makes the appointment far more useful. The visit itself usually covers three things. First, a detailed history: your health, past pregnancies, medications, and lifestyle. Second, baseline tests, often including blood type, a blood count, immunity and infection screening, and a urine sample. Third, many clinics do a dating ultrasound to confirm how far along you are and check the heartbeat, though some schedule the scan separately. Bring questions. Keep a running list of dates, symptoms, and things you want to ask in BeMama or a notebook, because questions have a way of vanishing the moment someone asks if you have any. Small steps that matter right now Take 400 micrograms of folic acid every day if you are not already. ACOG and the CDC recommend it because the neural tube closes by about week 6, often before a first appointment, and folic acid lowers the risk of defects in that closure. Most prenatal vitamins contain at least this amount, so one daily prenatal usually covers it. Beyond that, eat what you can manage. Small, frequent meals are easier on an uneasy stomach than three large ones, and no single day of eating makes or breaks early pregnancy. Drink water steadily and rest when your body asks for it. Stop alcohol; no amount is known to be safe in pregnancy. If you smoke or vape, tell your clinician and ask for help quitting rather than trying to white-knuckle it alone. Keep caffeine under 200 mg a day, which is roughly one 12-ounce cup of coffee. Most importantly, do not stop a prescribed medication on your own. Many treatments are safe to continue, and stopping some of them abruptly is riskier than the medicine itself. Call the prescriber or a pharmacist, say you are pregnant, and ask what to do. That one phone call is often the most valuable step of the whole first trimester. When to call your clinician Some discomfort is expected. Mild cramping that feels like a light period, brief twinges on either side, and even light spotting can happen in a normal early pregnancy, especially around the time implantation finishes. Call your clinician the same day for bleeding that is more than light spotting or cramping that feels stronger than a period. Seek emergency care right away for heavy bleeding that soaks a pad in an hour, severe pain, pain that sits on one side, shoulder-tip pain, or dizziness and fainting. These can signal an ectopic pregnancy, which needs immediate assessment. Calling does not commit you to anything. It simply gets an experienced person looking at your specific situation early, which is exactly what early care is for. Also call if you cannot keep fluids down for around 24 hours, if you feel faint or notice much darker urine, or if you have a fever or burning when you pee. Persistent vomiting has effective treatments, and dehydration is worth catching early. Finally, remember what an article can and cannot do. This guide describes what is typical; it cannot see your history or examine you. If something feels wrong to you, that feeling alone is a good enough reason to call. Clinics expect these calls from newly pregnant patients and would far rather hear from you early than late. 5 weeks pregnant: dates and first steps A late period may be your first clue, while tiredness or breast tenderness may also occur. Symptoms vary. Around this stage the embryo is approximately 2 mm long in the NHS illustration; a size comparison describes development, not the health of an individual pregnancy. Start a short appointment note: the first day of the last period if known, test dates, current medicines and the questions you want answered. Contact your local maternity service to arrange care. If your dates are uncertain, say so; keep your record separate from the estimated due date. 6 weeks pregnant: symptoms and useful notes Nausea can happen throughout the day. Limb buds are developing; the NHS gives an approximate embryo length of 6 mm. Symptoms or their absence do not replace clinical assessment. If nausea is affecting you, note when it occurs, whether you can keep fluids down and what you want to ask about support. Contact your clinician if food or fluids will not stay down. Do not wait for the next weekly article when you need care, and do not stop prescribed medicine without advice. 8 weeks pregnant: prepare for the first appointments The NHS describes an embryo around 16 mm long at this stage. Energy, mood and symptoms can change. A fruit-size image is an educational comparison, not a measurement of your pregnancy. Prepare your medical and pregnancy history, medicine list and practical questions. Ask what appointments and tests are offered locally, how results are explained and whom to contact between visits. Tell the team about ongoing low mood or anxiety so support can begin early. Continue with these practical guides By 8 weeks your baby has grown from poppy seed size to about 1.5 cm, roughly a kidney bean. Fatigue, breast tenderness, and nausea often start around week 6 and vary from day to day. The first prenatal visit usually happens around 8 weeks and includes history, baseline labs, and often a dating ultrasound. Take 400 mcg of folic acid daily and review medications with a clinician before changing anything. Seek emergency care for heavy bleeding or severe one-sided pain, and call your clinic if you cannot keep fluids down for 24 hours. What happens at 6 weeks pregnant? At 6 weeks, the neural tube that becomes the brain and spinal cord is closing, and cardiac activity can often be seen on a transvaginal ultrasound. The embryo is around the size of a lentil. For you, this is also when fatigue, breast tenderness, and nausea most commonly begin. How big is baby at 8 weeks? At 8 weeks, your baby measures about 1.5 cm, roughly the size of a kidney bean. Arm and leg buds are lengthening, facial features are forming, and the embryo is already moving, although you will not feel movement for several more months. Is cramping at 6 weeks pregnant normal? Mild cramping at 6 weeks is common and usually normal as your uterus grows and stretches. It often feels like a light period. Seek emergency care right away if cramping is severe or sits on one side, or if it comes with heavy bleeding, dizziness, or shoulder-tip pain, since those signs can mean an ectopic pregnancy and need immediate assessment. When is the first prenatal appointment? The first prenatal appointment usually happens around 8 weeks of pregnancy. Call your clinic as soon as you have a positive test, because schedules fill up, and mention any health conditions or regular medications, since those may mean you are seen earlier. Why did my estimated pregnancy week change? The starting dates may have been uncertain, or your care team may have revised the dating after assessment. Keep the original observations and the clinician-confirmed date clearly distinguished. Can symptom strength tell me whether development is normal? Symptoms alone cannot establish this. Contact your maternity service about worrying changes. Severe pain, fainting or heavy bleeding needs urgent assessment.

title: 9 to 12 Weeks Pregnant: Symptoms, Screening, Baby Growth
description: What happens between 9 and 12 weeks pregnant: how your baby grows from grape to lime size, why nausea peaks then fades, and when NIPT and the nuchal scan happen.
body: At 12 weeks pregnant, your baby measures about 5 to 6 cm from crown to rump, roughly the size of a lime, and every major organ has formed and is now busy growing. The stretch from week 9 to week 12 also covers the official shift from embryo to fetus, the usual peak of nausea, and the first big screening decisions, with NIPT possible from 10 weeks and the nuchal translucency scan at about 11 to 13 weeks. Here is what is happening, how you might feel, and what is worth doing before these windows close. From embryo to fetus: what changes in weeks 9 to 12 Around week 10, your baby graduates from embryo to fetus. The new name marks a real milestone: every major organ and body system has formed, and the work from here is growth and maturing rather than building from scratch. The size change across these weeks is striking. At week 9, your baby is about the size of a grape. By week 12, the crown to rump measurement is roughly 5 to 6 cm, about the size of a lime. The head still looks large compared with the body, which is normal at this stage, and the proportions slowly even out over the months ahead. A lot is happening in the details. Fingers and toes have separated, and tiny nails are starting to form. The intestines, which developed partly inside the umbilical cord, are moving into the abdomen. The kidneys begin producing urine, and the baby swallows small amounts of amniotic fluid. There is real movement too: stretching, flexing, even hiccup-like motions, although the baby is far too small for you to feel any of it yet. Near the end of this stretch, the placenta takes over most hormone production from the ovary, one reason many early symptoms begin to ease as you approach the second trimester. How you might feel right now For many people, nausea peaks somewhere around weeks 9 to 10 and then slowly loosens its grip between weeks 12 and 14. That timing is an average, not a promise. Some feel better sooner, some carry queasiness into the second trimester, and some never had it at all, which is also normal. Fatigue can be heavy through these weeks, the kind that makes an early bedtime feel non-negotiable. Food aversions and a sharp sense of smell are common, and bloating can make your waistband tight long before there is a true bump. If you want practical relief ideas, our guide to easing pregnancy nausea covers them in depth. You may also notice sore breasts, more saliva than usual, constipation, mild headaches, and mood swings that arrive without warning. Hormone levels are still climbing, and carrying a big secret while feeling unwell is genuinely tiring, so be patient with yourself. One quiet worry deserves a mention: some people panic when symptoms fade around week 11 or 12, but easing nausea at this stage usually reflects the normal hormonal shift, not a problem. Symptoms are a rough signal at best. If something feels wrong to you, or if vomiting is so constant that fluids will not stay down, contact your clinic rather than waiting it out. Screening decisions: NIPT and the nuchal scan Weeks 9 to 12 open the main first-trimester screening window, and the timing matters. Cell-free DNA screening, usually called NIPT, is a blood draw available from 10 weeks onward that screens for the most common chromosomal conditions. The nuchal translucency scan, an ultrasound that measures fluid at the back of the baby's neck, is done at about 11 to 13 weeks and is often combined with blood work as first-trimester combined screening. These are screening tests: they estimate chance, they do not give a diagnosis. What each test measures and how to read the results are covered in our guide to pregnancy blood tests and screening. Screening is a choice, not a requirement. Some people want as much information as early as possible, others prefer to skip optional tests, and both are reasonable. It helps to decide before the window arrives, because the nuchal scan cannot be done accurately after about 13 to 14 weeks. Useful questions for your clinic: which screens do you offer, what do they cost or does insurance cover them, how long do results take, and what would the next step be after a higher-chance result. Talk it through with your partner or a support person if the decision feels heavy. There is no single right answer, only the one that fits you. Hearing the heartbeat At a prenatal visit, a handheld doppler can often pick up the heartbeat somewhere around 10 to 12 weeks. Often is the honest word. Whether it works at a given visit depends on the position of the uterus and placenta, your body build, and how far along you actually are, since dating can be off by several days. Not finding the heartbeat with a doppler at this stage is common and is not, by itself, a sign that something is wrong. When a clinician cannot find it and wants reassurance, an ultrasound gives a much clearer answer, and many clinics move straight to one rather than searching for long. Home dopplers deserve a careful word. They are easy to buy and hard to use well. Untrained ears often mistake the mother's own pulse or blood flow through the placenta for the baby's heartbeat, which can give false reassurance when something needs attention, or false alarm when everything is fine. Most maternity guidance suggests leaving doppler checks to trained clinicians for exactly this reason. If you are worried between appointments, especially about bleeding, pain, or a sudden change in how you feel, call your clinic and describe the symptoms. A short phone conversation with someone qualified is worth more than an hour of anxious searching with a device at home. Your to-do list, and when to call A few tasks are genuinely time-sensitive right now. If you want the nuchal translucency scan, book it early, because the measurement window closes at about 13 to 14 weeks and appointment slots fill. Decide whether you want NIPT, and if so, arrange the blood draw any time from 10 weeks. If you have not had a first prenatal visit, schedule one. This is also when many people plan how to share the news. Waiting until after 12 weeks or the first scan is common, but there is no rule; a good test is to tell the people you would want support from if anything changed. Jot dates, symptoms, and questions in BeMama or a notebook so nothing gets lost. Some symptoms need a same-day call to your clinic, whatever the hour: bleeding heavier than light spotting, cramping that keeps getting worse, a fever of 38 C (100.4 F) or higher, or burning when you urinate. So does vomiting that will not let fluids stay down, especially with signs of dehydration like dark urine or lightheadedness, since treatment can help and nobody should simply endure it. A smaller set of symptoms means emergency care right away rather than waiting for a callback: severe or one-sided belly pain, pain with dizziness, fainting, or shoulder-tip pain, or bleeding that soaks a pad within an hour, because these can signal internal bleeding that must be checked immediately. Light spotting on its own is common in early pregnancy and often harmless, but mention it at your next visit; when you are unsure which category you are in, call, because triage nurses answer exactly these questions all day. Continue with these practical guides Around week 10 your baby officially becomes a fetus, and by week 12 measures about 5 to 6 cm, the size of a lime. Nausea often peaks near weeks 9 to 10 and eases for many people between weeks 12 and 14. NIPT is possible from 10 weeks, and the nuchal translucency scan happens at about 11 to 13 weeks. A doppler often finds the heartbeat around 10 to 12 weeks, but not always, and that alone is not alarming. Call your clinic the same day for heavy bleeding, worsening cramps, fever, or vomiting that keeps fluids from staying down; severe one-sided pain with dizziness or shoulder pain means emergency care. When can you get NIPT testing? NIPT, the cell-free DNA blood test, can be done any time from 10 weeks of pregnancy onward. There is no late cutoff, so you can also choose it after the first trimester if you decide later. It is a screening test that estimates the chance of common chromosomal conditions, not a diagnosis, so a higher-chance result would be followed by confirmatory testing. When does morning sickness peak? Nausea most often peaks around weeks 9 to 10 and starts easing between weeks 12 and 14. The pattern varies a lot from person to person, and some people stay queasy well into the second trimester. Contact your clinician if vomiting keeps you from holding down fluids, because effective treatment exists and you do not have to wait it out. What week is the nuchal translucency scan done? The nuchal translucency scan is done at about 11 to 13 weeks of pregnancy. The measurement is only accurate inside that window, so it helps to book early once your clinic offers it. It is often paired with a blood test as first-trimester combined screening, and like all screening it is optional. When can you hear the heartbeat with a doppler? A clinician can often find the heartbeat with a handheld doppler around 10 to 12 weeks, though sometimes not until a little later. The position of the uterus and placenta, body build, and dating that is off by a few days all affect it. Not hearing it at this stage is common and not by itself a warning sign; an ultrasound can confirm quickly if reassurance is needed.

title: 13 to 16 Weeks Pregnant: Second Trimester Start Guide
description: What to expect from 13 to 16 weeks pregnant: how your baby grows, which symptoms ease or begin, the tests offered in this window, and when to call your clinician.
body: At 16 weeks pregnant, your baby is about the size of an avocado, and many parents notice more energy, less nausea, and the first round ligament twinges as the uterus rises out of the pelvis. Weeks 13 to 16 are the opening stretch of the second trimester, a window when appointments settle into a rhythm and a few optional tests come up. This guide walks through what is growing, how you might feel, and what is worth doing now. Your baby, from a lemon to an avocado At 13 weeks, your baby is about the size of a lemon, roughly 7 centimeters from head to bottom. Over the next few weeks that length nearly doubles. At 14 weeks the kidneys are producing urine, the neck is lengthening, and facial muscles are starting to work, so your baby can squint and grimace. Fine, soft hair called lanugo begins to cover the skin, and the arms grow to a length that better matches the body. None of this is visible from the outside yet, which can feel strange. Growth in this window is fast, steady, and mostly quiet. By 15 to 16 weeks, your baby is about the size of an avocado, around 11 to 12 centimeters from crown to rump. Sucking motions begin, a rehearsal for feeding later. The ears have moved close to their final position, and the eyes have begun to make slow movements even though the eyelids stay fused. On an ultrasound around this time, the sex may be visible, although position and image quality decide whether the sonographer can say anything with confidence. Some parents feel the first faint flutters near 16 weeks, but many feel nothing until 18 to 22 weeks, especially in a first pregnancy. Both are normal. How you might feel from week 13 to 16 For many people, this stretch is when pregnancy finally starts to feel easier. Nausea fades for a large share of parents somewhere between 13 and 16 weeks, appetite comes back, and energy often returns as first trimester exhaustion lifts. The shift is real but not universal. Some people stay queasy into the second trimester, and a smaller group deals with nausea for much longer. If you are still vomiting often, cannot keep fluids down, or are losing weight, tell your clinician rather than waiting for it to pass. There is treatment for persistent nausea, and asking for it is not a failure. New sensations arrive as your uterus rises up and out of the pelvis. Round ligament pain often starts in this window: quick, sharp twinges low in the belly or groin when you stand, cough, sneeze, or roll over in bed. It is common and usually brief, and our round ligament pain guide covers relief in detail. You may also notice a firmer lower belly, nasal stuffiness, gum tenderness, and mild lightheadedness when you get up quickly, all tied to extra blood flow. A visible bump follows its own schedule, which our guide on when you start showing explains, so try not to compare yourself with others. Appointments and tests in this window Prenatal visits usually settle into a rhythm of roughly every four weeks through the middle of pregnancy, as long as things are going smoothly. Expect the basics at each visit: blood pressure, weight, urine checks, and listening to the fetal heartbeat with a handheld Doppler. These weeks sit just after the first trimester screening window, so if you had that testing, this is often when results are discussed. Because the second trimester officially begins around this point, a topic our trimesters guide covers, many clinics also use these visits to plan the rest of your testing calendar. Bring questions written down; short visits go faster than expected. Two tests belong to this stretch. The quad screen, a blood test that estimates the chance of neural tube defects and certain chromosomal conditions, including Down syndrome, is offered between about 15 and 22 weeks, and many clinics aim for 16 to 18 weeks. It is optional, and it is a screening test, not a diagnosis. Amniocentesis, when it is indicated by screening results, family history, or your own preference after counseling, is usually performed between about 15 and 20 weeks. If either test is on your mind, raise it at your next visit so the calendar does not decide for you. Good things to do between 13 and 16 weeks Book the anatomy scan now if your clinic has not already scheduled it. This detailed ultrasound usually happens between 18 and 22 weeks, and appointment slots can fill early, especially if you want a particular day or time. It is also a sensible moment to plan travel. Many people find the middle weeks of pregnancy the most comfortable for a trip: nausea has often faded, the bump is still small, and energy is better. Check your travel insurance, pack a copy of your prenatal records, and ask your clinician about anything specific to the destination, such as long flights, altitude, or food and water safety. If energy is returning, put some of it into gentle movement such as walking, swimming, or prenatal yoga; our safe exercise guide covers what to choose and what to skip. This is also a good window for unglamorous logistics: check parental leave paperwork deadlines, start a short list of questions for the anatomy scan, and note symptoms or dates somewhere you will actually find them later, whether that is a notebook or the BeMama app. Small habits started now, like a consistent bedtime and a water bottle you refill all day, tend to matter more in the third trimester than any single burst of preparation. When to call your clinician Call promptly for bleeding that is more than light spotting, fluid leaking from the vagina, a fever of 38 C (100.4 F) or higher, severe or one-sided abdominal pain, pain or burning when you urinate, or vomiting that keeps you from holding down fluids. These signs do not automatically mean something is wrong, but each one deserves a same-day conversation rather than a search engine. Heavy bleeding that soaks a pad in an hour, severe pain that does not ease, fainting, or trouble breathing calls for emergency care right away, not a message and a wait. If you notice spotting after sex or a pelvic exam, mention that too; it is often harmless, and your clinician can tell you what to watch for. Save the office number and the after-hours line in your phone now, before you need them. Mood deserves the same attention as physical symptoms. Relief and excitement often grow in these weeks, but anxiety, low mood, or intrusive worry can grow too, and pregnancy hormones are not a reason to dismiss them. Tell your clinician if sadness or worry fills most of the day for more than two weeks, disturbs your sleep beyond ordinary discomfort, or makes it hard to eat or function. Support ranges from talk therapy to medication that can be used in pregnancy, and any thoughts of harming yourself deserve immediate help from a crisis line or your care team, not a wait for the next appointment. This guide is general education, not a diagnosis; your own care team knows your history and is the right place for personal answers. Continue with these practical guides Your baby grows from about a lemon to an avocado between 13 and 16 weeks. Energy often returns and nausea fades for many people, but not for everyone. Round ligament twinges commonly begin as the uterus rises out of the pelvis. The quad screen is offered at about 15 to 22 weeks, and the anatomy scan should be booked for 18 to 22 weeks. Call your clinician the same day for bleeding, leaking fluid, or fever. How big is baby at 16 weeks? At 16 weeks, a baby is about the size of an avocado, roughly 11 to 12 centimeters from crown to rump and around 100 grams. Ultrasound measurements normally vary a little from these averages. A steady growth pattern over time matters more than any single number on a report. What weeks is the quad screen done? The quad screen is offered between about 15 and 22 weeks of pregnancy, and many clinics aim for 16 to 18 weeks. It is an optional blood test that estimates the chance of certain conditions rather than diagnosing them. If a result is flagged, your clinician will walk you through follow-up options such as detailed ultrasound or amniocentesis. When does round ligament pain start? Round ligament pain most often starts in the early second trimester, around 13 to 16 weeks, as the uterus rises out of the pelvis and its supporting ligaments stretch. The twinges are typically sharp, brief, and set off by sudden movement like standing, coughing, or rolling over. Pain that is severe, constant, or paired with bleeding or fever is not typical round ligament pain, so call your clinician. Do you feel better in the second trimester? Many people do feel better in the second trimester, with nausea fading, energy returning, and appetite improving, often somewhere between 13 and 16 weeks. The change is gradual rather than a switch flipping on a set day. If you still feel rough at 16 weeks, that is common too, and persistent vomiting or exhaustion is worth raising at your next visit.

title: 17 to 20 Weeks Pregnant: Movement and the Anatomy Scan
description: A calm guide to being 20 weeks pregnant and the weeks around it: how your baby grows from week 17 to 20, first movements, the anatomy scan, and what to do next.
body: At 20 weeks pregnant you are roughly halfway through a 40 week pregnancy, and your baby now measures about 25 cm from crown to heel and weighs around 300 g. The stretch from week 17 to week 20 brings two milestones most parents remember: the first flutters of movement and the anatomy scan. This guide walks through what is developing, how you might feel, and the short list of things worth doing now. How your baby grows from week 17 to 20 Between weeks 17 and 20, your baby roughly doubles in weight. By week 20, most babies measure about 25 cm from crown to heel, around 10 inches, and weigh close to 300 g, a little over 10 ounces. Part of the jump you see on growth charts is a change in how babies are measured: before 20 weeks, length is usually given from crown to rump, and after that from crown to heel, so the legs suddenly count. Underneath the numbers, steady work is happening. Fat is beginning to form under the skin, muscles are getting stronger, and the movements that once looked random on ultrasound are becoming smoother and more coordinated. Two protective layers now cover your baby's skin. Vernix is a creamy white coating that shields the skin from the surrounding amniotic fluid, and lanugo is a layer of fine, soft hair that helps hold the vernix in place. Both are normal, and most of each disappears before birth. Hearing is developing quickly in this window too. The inner ear structures are maturing, and many babies begin responding to muffled sounds from your body and, a little later, to voices from outside. Your baby also swallows small amounts of amniotic fluid, which is early practice for feeding, and cycles through sleep and wake periods that may not match yours at all. How you might feel right now Somewhere in this stretch, many people feel movement for the first time. Most notice it between 16 and 22 weeks, and it often comes later in a first pregnancy simply because the sensation is easy to miss. Early movement rarely feels like a kick. It is closer to flutters, bubbles, or light tapping that comes and goes, and it is easiest to catch when you are lying down quietly. An anterior placenta, one that sits at the front of the uterus, can cushion the feeling for a few more weeks. If you have felt nothing yet, that is common at this stage and not a sign that something is wrong. Your body is changing visibly now. The top of the uterus reaches about the level of your belly button around week 20, so the bump is usually hard to hide. Common symptoms in this window include backache as your posture shifts, brief sharp twinges low in the belly when you stand or twist, known as round ligament pain, a stuffy nose, leg cramps at night, and skin changes such as a dark line down the belly or darker patches on the face. Appetite often picks up, and many people have more energy than they did in the first trimester. Comfortable shoes, regular snacks, and side sleeping with a pillow between your knees all start earning their keep. The anatomy scan, this window's headline appointment The headline appointment in this window is the anatomy scan, sometimes called the mid-pregnancy ultrasound or the 20 week scan. It is usually done between 18 and 22 weeks. A sonographer takes a long, careful look at how your baby is growing and checks the major organs and structures, from the brain and heart to the spine and limbs, in more detail than earlier scans could. The scan also looks at what surrounds your baby, including where the placenta is attached and how much amniotic fluid is present. It is a screening scan, which means it looks for anything that deserves a closer look. It is not a final verdict on your baby's health. For many parents this is also the moment they can learn their baby's sex, if the position cooperates and if they want to know. Tell the sonographer at the start if you would rather keep it a surprise. Plan for the appointment to take a while, often 30 to 45 minutes, and follow your clinic's instructions about arriving with a full bladder. Babies do not always pose helpfully, so being asked to walk around, or to return another day for repeat views, is common and usually means nothing more than an awkward angle. Your clinic will talk you through the findings and arrange any follow-up that is needed. Is 20 weeks really the halfway point? Twenty weeks is the halfway point in the way pregnancy is usually counted: 40 weeks from the first day of your last period. It is a fair milestone, but hold it loosely. Term is a window rather than a single date, and most babies arrive sometime between 37 and 42 weeks, so your second half may run a little shorter or longer than the first. If your due date was adjusted after an early ultrasound, use your clinic's dating rather than your own calendar math. However you count it, this is a natural moment to look up from week by week symptoms and start thinking about the months ahead. A short list beats a long one. First, book the anatomy scan if it is not already scheduled, because the 18 to 22 week window passes quickly. Second, start a low-effort movement habit: simply notice when your baby tends to be active, such as after meals or in the evening. There is no need to count anything yet, since formal kick counting belongs to the third trimester. Third, look into childbirth classes now, because popular ones fill up and many run across several weeks. This is also a reasonable time to ask about maternity or parental leave paperwork at work, while there is no urgency behind the question. Comfort, self-care, and when to call Small comforts matter more as the bump grows. Side sleeping with a pillow between your knees eases back strain, and rolling to your side before getting up from bed protects the round ligaments. Keep water nearby, keep snacks simple and regular, and use an unscented moisturizer if the skin over your belly feels itchy as it stretches. Gentle exercise such as walking or swimming is encouraged for most people; check with your clinician if you have been told to limit activity. It also helps to keep a running list of questions for the scan appointment. A notebook works well, or you can note dates, symptoms, and questions in the BeMama app so they are ready when you need them. At this stage, no one expects you to monitor movement formally, and a quiet day is not yet something clinicians ask you to track. Some symptoms should be reported promptly at any stage, though. Call your maternity team right away, rather than waiting for your next appointment, for vaginal bleeding, a gush or steady trickle of fluid, a severe or persistent headache, changes in your vision, a fever, pain or burning when you pass urine, or strong cramping that does not settle with rest. None of these automatically means something is wrong, but each deserves a real conversation rather than a search engine, and your team would much rather hear about a symptom early than have you wait and worry. Continue with these practical guides By week 20 your baby measures about 25 cm from crown to heel and weighs around 300 g. First movements are usually felt between 16 and 22 weeks, and often later in a first pregnancy. The anatomy scan happens between 18 and 22 weeks and checks growth, organs, and placenta position. Twenty weeks is roughly halfway through a standard 40 week pregnancy, so it is a good moment to book classes and plan ahead. Report bleeding, leaking fluid, severe headache, vision changes, or fever to your clinician promptly at any stage. When do you first feel the baby kick? Most people first feel movement between 16 and 22 weeks of pregnancy. In a first pregnancy it often comes later in that window, because the early flutters are easy to mistake for gas or muscle twitches. An anterior placenta can also cushion the sensation for a few extra weeks. Feeling nothing yet at 17 to 20 weeks is common and usually normal. What week is the anatomy scan done? The anatomy scan is usually done between 18 and 22 weeks of pregnancy, most often around week 20. It is a detailed ultrasound that checks your baby's growth and major organs, along with the placenta's position and the amount of amniotic fluid. If yours is not booked yet, contact your clinic soon, because the window is fairly narrow. Is 20 weeks halfway through pregnancy? Yes, 20 weeks is roughly the halfway point, because pregnancy is usually counted as 40 weeks from the first day of your last period. In practice the second half varies, since most babies arrive somewhere between 37 and 42 weeks. Treat it as a milestone rather than an exact countdown. What happens at 18 weeks pregnant? At 18 weeks your baby is about 14 cm from crown to rump and weighs around 200 g, the ears are settling into position, and hearing is developing. Many people feel the first flutters of movement around this week, though feeling them later is still normal. It is also the earliest week many clinics book the anatomy scan.

title: 21 to 24 Weeks Pregnant: Baby Growth and Viability
description: What to expect from 21 to 24 weeks pregnant: how your baby grows to viability, common symptoms like Braxton Hicks, and the appointments and to-dos for this window.
body: At 24 weeks pregnant, your baby is about 30 cm long, weighs around 600 g, just over a pound, and has reached the milestone many clinicians call viability. Weeks 21 to 24 bring stronger daily kicks, possibly your first Braxton Hicks contractions, and a few new items for the calendar, including the glucose screen. This guide walks through what is developing, what you may feel, and what is worth doing now. How your baby grows from week 21 to 24 Between weeks 21 and 24, your baby puts on weight quickly, gaining more than half again what they weighed at the start of this window. At 21 weeks, most babies weigh around 350 to 400 g and measure about 26 to 27 cm from head to heel. By 24 weeks, typical estimates are close to 600 g, just over a pound, and about 30 cm, roughly the length of an ear of corn. Fat is starting to build under the skin, which still looks thin and wrinkled. Movements are more coordinated now: stretching, kicking, turning, even grabbing the umbilical cord. Many parents begin to notice a loose pattern of active and quiet periods across the day. Two developments in this window matter a great deal. The lungs begin producing the early building blocks of surfactant, the substance that will eventually let the air sacs stay open after birth. That process continues for many weeks, which is one reason every extra week of pregnancy helps. Hearing also matures noticeably. Your baby can pick up your voice, your heartbeat, and louder sounds from outside, and may respond to them with a kick or a wriggle. Talking, reading, or singing is not required homework, but if it feels natural, this is the stage where your baby genuinely starts to listen. What viability at 24 weeks actually means You will often see 24 weeks described as the threshold of viability. In plain terms, it is the point where, if a baby were born extremely early, hospitals with a neonatal intensive care unit can usually offer full support, and survival becomes a realistic possibility. Chances improve meaningfully with every additional week after that. Exact outcomes vary by country, by hospital, and by the baby's own condition, so no single number applies to everyone. Some hospitals also consider active care slightly earlier in specific situations, a decision made case by case together with the family. It helps to hold this milestone lightly. The vast majority of pregnancies continue far beyond 24 weeks, and reaching this point is not a hint that anything is about to go wrong. Think of it as quiet reassurance in the background rather than a deadline you were racing toward. The practical use of the information is simple: know which nearby hospital has newborn intensive care, keep your maternity notes easy to find, and learn the signs of preterm labor covered below so you could act quickly in the unlikely event you ever needed to. How your body may feel in these weeks Kicks change character in this stretch. What felt like flutters becomes unmistakable thumps, and by 24 weeks many parents feel movement every day, often strongest in the evening or after meals. You do not need to count anything formally yet; just get familiar with what a normal day of movement feels like for your baby. You may also meet Braxton Hicks contractions for the first time. These are practice tightenings of the uterus: the bump goes hard for perhaps 30 to 60 seconds, then relaxes. They are irregular, usually painless, and often triggered by activity, a full bladder, or dehydration. Other common companions include leg cramps that strike at night, mild swelling in the ankles and feet by the end of the day, a heartier appetite, backache, and round ligament twinges when you stand up or roll over quickly. Gentle calf stretches before bed, steady water intake, putting your feet up, and supportive shoes take the edge off most of it. Swelling that is sudden, severe, or involves your face and hands is different: that deserves a same-day call to your clinician, because it can occasionally signal a blood pressure problem rather than ordinary pregnancy puffiness. Appointments and checks in this window From about 24 weeks, prenatal visits usually add a simple new measurement: fundal height. Your clinician or midwife runs a tape measure from the top of the pubic bone to the top of the uterus. In centimeters, the number roughly matches your week of pregnancy, give or take a couple of centimeters. It is a quick, low-tech way to confirm that growth is tracking as expected between ultrasounds. If the measurement runs noticeably ahead of or behind your dates, the usual next step is a growth ultrasound, which most of the time simply confirms that everything is fine. This is also the moment to get your glucose screen on the calendar. Most clinics order it for the 24 to 28 week window, so if no one has mentioned it yet, ask at your next visit and book a slot that suits your schedule. Some people also have follow-up imaging if the anatomy scan could not see everything, which is common and rarely a cause for worry. Between appointments, jot down questions in BeMama or on paper as they occur to you: sleep positions, travel plans, workplace adjustments. A short written list makes a fifteen-minute visit far more useful. Useful things to do before the third trimester Energy is often decent in this stretch, which makes it a good season for practical projects. Start or finish the baby registry, sketch out the nursery or sleeping arrangement, and compare parental leave dates with your partner or employer. None of it has to be finished this month, but spreading the work out beats a third-trimester scramble. Keep paying casual attention to movement, too. If your baby seems clearly quieter than usual for a day, lie down on your side and pay close attention for a while; if you are still not reassured, call your clinic the same day rather than waiting. Learn the signs of preterm labor now, while everything is calm. Call your clinic or maternity unit promptly if you notice contractions that come regularly and keep coming, perhaps four or more in an hour, a constant low backache that is new, strong pelvic or vaginal pressure, period-like cramping, a gush or steady trickle of fluid, or any bleeding. Do not wait overnight to see whether it settles, and do not worry about being wrong. Preterm labor can often be slowed or treated when it is caught early, and maternity staff would much rather check a false alarm than miss a real one. Continue with these practical guides By 24 weeks your baby is about 30 cm long and just over a pound, with lungs and hearing developing fast. Viability at 24 weeks is background reassurance, not a deadline; most pregnancies continue far beyond it. Braxton Hicks are irregular, usually painless practice tightenings that pass with rest and water. Ask at your next visit to book the glucose screen for the 24 to 28 week window. Call your clinic promptly for regular tightening, pelvic pressure, leaking fluid, or bleeding. What symptoms are normal at 24 weeks pregnant? Strong daily kicks, Braxton Hicks tightenings, leg cramps, mild ankle swelling, backache, and a bigger appetite are all common at 24 weeks. Most ease with water, movement breaks, calf stretches, and putting your feet up. Sudden severe swelling, regular painful contractions, bleeding, or leaking fluid are not routine symptoms and deserve a same-day call to your clinician. Is a baby viable at 24 weeks? Yes, 24 weeks is the point most often cited as viability, meaning a baby born this early has a realistic chance of survival with neonatal intensive care. Outcomes vary with the baby's condition and the hospital's resources, and chances improve substantially with each further week. Birth this early is uncommon, so treat the milestone as reassurance rather than a prediction. When do Braxton Hicks contractions start? Many people first notice Braxton Hicks contractions in the second trimester, often somewhere around weeks 20 to 24, though some feel them earlier and some never notice them at all. They are irregular, usually painless tightenings that pass with rest, a drink of water, or a change of position. Contractions that become regular, painful, or persistent before 37 weeks should be reported to your clinic promptly. How big is a baby at 24 weeks? At 24 weeks a baby typically measures about 30 cm from head to heel and weighs around 600 g, a little over a pound, roughly the size of an ear of corn. Ultrasound estimates carry a margin of error, and healthy babies come in a range of sizes at every week. Your clinician watches the trend over time rather than any single number.

title: 25 to 28 Weeks Pregnant: Glucose Test and Third Trimester
description: What to expect from 25 to 28 weeks pregnant: how big your baby is at 28 weeks, the glucose test window, the Tdap and RhoGAM shots, and when to call.
body: At 28 weeks pregnant you are entering the third trimester: your baby weighs about 1 kilogram, roughly 2 to 2.5 pounds, measures around 35 to 37 centimeters, and their eyes have recently opened. Weeks 25 to 28 are the busiest testing stretch of pregnancy, with the glucose screen due, the Tdap window opening at 27 weeks, and a RhoGAM shot around week 28 for Rh negative parents. Visits also move to every two weeks from here. If you want a refresher on how trimesters are counted, our trimester guide covers that; this one sticks to what these four weeks feel like and what to get done. How your baby grows from week 25 to 28 Between weeks 25 and 28, your baby's eyes open for the first time, usually around week 26 to 28, and the eyelids begin to blink. The brain is growing quickly, and its surface starts to fold, packing in more surface area for everything it will do later. The lungs are maturing too. They produce a substance called surfactant that will help the air sacs stay open after birth, and your baby practices breathing movements with amniotic fluid. By week 28, most babies measure roughly 35 to 37 centimeters from head to heel and weigh about 1 kilogram, which is around 2 to 2.5 pounds. You may start to notice a rhythm to all this growing. Many babies develop clearer sleep and wake cycles in this stretch, so quiet spells and busy spells become easier to recognize. Hiccups can show up as small rhythmic taps that go on for a few minutes, and they are completely normal. Fat is slowly building under the skin, which smooths it out and will help with temperature control after birth. Your baby still has plenty of room to move, so do not worry about position yet. Many babies flip repeatedly for weeks before settling head down closer to the end. How you might feel right now Heartburn is one of the most common complaints in this stretch. Pregnancy hormones relax the valve at the top of the stomach while the growing uterus presses upward, so acid escapes more easily. Smaller meals, eating slowly, and staying upright for a while after food often help, and you can ask your clinician about antacids that are considered safe in pregnancy. Backache is common too, because your center of gravity shifts forward and ligaments loosen. Gentle stretching, supportive shoes, a warm shower, and a pillow between your knees at night can each take some of the pressure off. Sleep often gets harder before it gets better. Side sleeping with a pillow under your bump and another between your knees is a comfortable, commonly recommended setup. Kicks are vivid now, and you will probably notice active periods, often after meals or when you lie down at night. Some people also feel practice contractions called Braxton Hicks: irregular tightenings that ease with rest, a position change, or a glass of water. Leg cramps and mild ankle swelling at the end of the day are common as well. Sudden or severe swelling is different, and it is covered further down. Three tests share this window The glucose screen is due now if you have not had it yet. It is usually done between 24 and 28 weeks, and it checks how your body handles sugar during pregnancy, because gestational diabetes often causes no symptoms at all. If your clinic has not mentioned it by your next visit, ask about it directly. Our separate glucose test guide walks through the drink, the difference between the one hour and three hour versions, and what the results mean, so here the message is simple: get it on the calendar. It is one of the most useful routine checks in the whole pregnancy. Two shots may also come up. If your blood type is Rh negative, most clinicians recommend an injection of Rh immune globulin, often called RhoGAM, around 28 weeks. It stops your immune system from making antibodies against your baby's blood cells, which protects this pregnancy and future ones. Separately, the Tdap vaccine window opens at 27 weeks. The CDC recommends Tdap between 27 and 36 weeks of every pregnancy so your baby is born with some early protection against whooping cough. Our vaccine guide covers the details. For now, simply ask about both at your next appointment. Visits move to every two weeks From around week 28, prenatal visits typically move from once a month to every two weeks. Each visit is usually short: blood pressure, your baby's heartbeat, a belly measurement called fundal height, and time for your questions. The new rhythm can feel sudden, so it helps to book several appointments ahead while convenient time slots are still open. Write questions down as they occur to you during the week, because they have a way of vanishing in the exam room. No question is too small at this stage, including anything about symptoms, work, travel, or early thoughts on birth plans. This is also when daily movement starts to matter more. From about week 28, get to know your baby's normal: when the active periods happen, what they feel like, and roughly how busy a typical day is. There is no single magic number of kicks. The useful signal is a change from your own baby's usual pattern. Some clinicians suggest formal kick counting sessions, so it is worth asking whether they want you to do that and how. A quick note of active times in BeMama or a notebook makes it easier to spot a real change instead of guessing from memory. When to call your clinician Call right away if your baby's movements slow down or stop once you know their pattern. Do not wait until morning, and do not talk yourself out of it. Clinics expect these calls, checking is quick, and most calls end in reassurance. The same urgency applies to a severe headache that does not ease, vision changes such as blurring or flashing spots, sudden swelling of your face or hands, or pain high in your belly. These can signal a blood pressure problem, and our blood pressure and preeclampsia guide explains what clinicians look for in more depth. Call right away as well for regular painful tightenings before 37 weeks, a gush or steady trickle of fluid, or any bleeding. Fever, or pain and burning when you pee, deserve a same day call. None of these automatically means something is wrong, but each one is worth a professional opinion rather than a night of worrying. Save your clinic's daytime and after hours numbers in your phone now, before you need them. Your care team knows your history and would rather hear from you early. When in doubt, make the call. That is exactly what they are there for. Continue with these practical guides By 28 weeks your baby weighs about 1 kilogram and measures roughly 35 to 37 centimeters. The glucose screen is usually done between 24 and 28 weeks, so book it if you have not already. The Tdap window opens at 27 weeks, and Rh negative parents usually get RhoGAM around week 28. Prenatal visits typically move to every two weeks starting around week 28. Call your clinician right away for decreased movement, severe headache, vision changes, or sudden swelling. What are common symptoms at 28 weeks pregnant? Common symptoms at 28 weeks include heartburn, backache, trouble sleeping, leg cramps, mild ankle swelling, and strong kicks with recognizable active periods. Irregular practice contractions called Braxton Hicks are also common and ease with rest or a change of position. Sudden severe swelling, a headache that will not ease, or vision changes are different: call your clinician right away for those. How big is a baby at 28 weeks? At 28 weeks, most babies weigh about 1 kilogram, roughly 2 to 2.5 pounds, and measure around 35 to 37 centimeters from head to heel. Healthy babies vary, so your own measurements may sit a little above or below these ranges. Your clinician tracks growth over time rather than judging any single number. What week is the glucose test in pregnancy? The glucose screen is usually done between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy. Some people are screened earlier if they have risk factors, and your clinic will tell you if that applies to you. Our separate glucose test guide explains the drink, the one hour and three hour versions, and what the results mean. When do you get the Tdap shot in pregnancy? The CDC recommends the Tdap vaccine between 27 and 36 weeks in every pregnancy, and earlier in that window gives your baby more time to receive protective antibodies before birth. The goal is early protection against whooping cough for your newborn. Ask about it at your next prenatal visit, and see our vaccine guide for more detail.

title: 29 to 32 Weeks Pregnant: Kick Counts and Rapid Growth
description: What to expect at 29 to 32 weeks pregnant: your baby's fastest growth stretch, common symptoms like breathlessness and heartburn, daily kick counts, and the appointments that matter now.
body: At 32 weeks pregnant, your baby usually weighs about 1.7 to 2 kg, close to 4 pounds, measures around 40 to 42 cm from head to heel, and is often settling head down. Weeks 29 to 32 are one of the fastest growth stretches of pregnancy, and you will likely feel it in your ribs, your bladder, and your sleep. Here is what is changing, what is normal to feel, and what to do about it. Your baby's fastest growth stretch Weeks 29 to 32 are the fastest weight-gain stretch of pregnancy. Your baby adds roughly 200 grams or more each week, moving from around 1.2 kg at week 29 to about 1.7 to 2 kg, close to 4 pounds, by week 32. Length reaches roughly 40 to 42 cm from head to heel. Much of the new weight is fat under the skin, which smooths out wrinkles and will help your baby hold a steady temperature after birth. You may notice the growth yourself: your bump rises higher, kicks land harder, and your appetite may swing between hungry and full after a few bites as space gets tight. Inside, the pace matches the scale. Bones are hardening, though the skull stays soft and flexible so the head can mold during birth. The lungs are maturing, and your baby practices breathing movements with amniotic fluid. The brain is growing quickly, and sleep cycles are becoming more organized, which is why you may notice active and quiet stretches at predictable times of day. Many babies begin settling head down during these weeks. If yours is still breech or lying sideways, there is no need to worry yet; most babies turn on their own before the final weeks, and your provider will keep checking position at each visit. How you might feel right now Feeling short of breath around 30 weeks is common and usually harmless. The top of your uterus now sits high enough to crowd your diaphragm, so your lungs have less room to expand even though you and your baby are getting plenty of oxygen. Slowing your pace, sitting tall, sleeping propped on pillows, and lifting your arms overhead for a moment can all ease it. Many people get relief later on, when the baby drops lower into the pelvis. Breathlessness that comes on suddenly, feels severe, or arrives with chest pain, a racing heart, or dizziness is different: seek emergency care right away, because these can be signs of a blood clot in the lung, which is rare but serious in pregnancy. Heartburn often flares in this stretch because the uterus presses on your stomach and pregnancy hormones relax the valve at the top of it. Smaller meals, staying upright after eating, and asking your provider about safe antacids can help. Pelvic pressure and a heavier feeling low in the belly are typical as the baby gains weight. You may also notice Braxton Hicks contractions: irregular tightenings that fade when you change position, walk, rest, or drink water. Sleep tends to fragment now between bathroom trips, a busy baby, and finding a comfortable position. Short daytime rests and an earlier wind-down help more than trying to force one long perfect night. Kick counts become part of the day From around week 28, many providers suggest a daily kick count, and weeks 29 to 32 are when the habit is worth locking in. A common method is simple: pick the same hour each day, ideally when your baby is usually active, such as after a meal. Settle on your side, start a timer, and note how long it takes to feel 10 movements. Kicks, rolls, swishes, and stretches all count; hiccups do not. Your provider may teach a slightly different method, and theirs is the one to follow. Jot the time in BeMama or on paper so a pattern builds; the record matters more than any single day. The point of counting is to learn your baby's normal, because every baby has its own rhythm. Some are busiest at night, others after breakfast. A change from that usual pattern matters more than any comparison with someone else's pregnancy. If movement seems reduced, slower, or different, contact your maternity unit or provider right away, even in the middle of the night. Do not wait until tomorrow, and do not rely on cold drinks or sugary snacks to wake the baby before calling; a prompt check is the reliable answer. Our separate guide to baby movement patterns covers counting methods and what changes can mean in more detail. Appointments, position checks, and the Tdap window Prenatal visits usually run every two weeks through this stretch. Expect the familiar basics: blood pressure, urine, your baby's heartbeat, and a fundal height measurement to track growth. Around now, providers also start feeling your belly to check which way the baby is lying, and they will keep doing this at every visit until birth. Bring your questions written down, because two-week gaps go fast. Good ones for this window: When should I call about contractions? What does your office want me to do about reduced movement after hours? When will we talk through my birth preferences? Short visits work better when you arrive with a short list. If you have not had the Tdap vaccine yet this pregnancy, this is the window: it is recommended between 27 and 36 weeks, and earlier in that range gives your body more time to pass protective antibodies to your baby before birth. Those antibodies help shield a newborn from whooping cough during the first months, before the baby's own vaccines begin. Ask at your next visit if it has not come up. This is also a good moment to ask which other seasonal vaccines, such as flu or RSV protection, are recommended where you live, since guidance depends on the season and your situation. Small to-dos, and when to call A few low-effort tasks now save stress later. Settle into sleeping on your side if you have not already; from the third trimester it is the position providers recommend, and our sleep positions guide covers the details. Tour your birth location, whether hospital or birth center, and learn where to park, which entrance is open at night, and where to check in. If you have older children or pets, sketch a plan for who covers them when labor starts, including a backup. Keep water and snacks within reach at your desk and bedside. None of this needs to be finished this week; one small task per weekend is enough. Keep the call-now list somewhere easy to find. Contact your provider or maternity unit right away, at any hour, for reduced or changed fetal movement. Call promptly for a headache that will not ease, especially with vision changes such as flashing lights or blurring, or sudden swelling of your face or hands; these can be signs of a blood pressure problem that needs checking. Also call for regular painful tightenings before 37 weeks, a gush or steady trickle of fluid, bleeding, fever, or pain when you pee. This guide is general education, not a diagnosis, and your care team would rather hear from you early than have you wait and worry at home. Continue with these practical guides By week 32, most babies weigh about 1.7 to 2 kg and many are settling head down. Breathlessness, heartburn, pelvic pressure, and Braxton Hicks are all common in these weeks. Start a daily kick count at the same hour each day, and call right away if movement drops. Visits move to every two weeks, and Tdap belongs in the 27 to 36 week window. A headache with vision changes or sudden swelling of your face or hands needs a prompt call. How big is my baby at 32 weeks? At 32 weeks, babies typically weigh about 1.7 to 2 kg, close to 4 pounds, and measure roughly 40 to 42 cm from head to heel. Growth is fast right now, at roughly 200 grams or more per week, and much of it is the fat that helps newborns stay warm after birth. Your provider tracks this with fundal height measurements and, when needed, an ultrasound. When should I start counting kicks? Most providers suggest starting daily kick counts around week 28, so weeks 29 to 32 are the time to make it routine if you have not begun. Pick the same hour each day, rest on your side, and time how long it takes to feel 10 movements. Follow your own provider's method if they teach a different one, and call right away, even at night, if movement seems reduced. Is shortness of breath normal at 30 weeks pregnant? Yes, mild breathlessness around 30 weeks is common because the growing uterus crowds the diaphragm and leaves the lungs less room to expand. Slowing down, sitting tall, and sleeping propped up usually help, and many people breathe easier once the baby drops lower into the pelvis. Sudden or severe shortness of breath, or breathlessness with chest pain, a racing heart, or dizziness, is different: seek emergency care right away. Should my baby be head down at 32 weeks? Many babies settle head down by around 32 weeks, but plenty are still breech or sideways at this point, and most turn on their own in the following weeks. Position is not fixed yet, so a breech finding now is information, not a problem to solve today. Your provider will keep checking at each visit and will discuss options only if the baby stays breech closer to term.

title: 33 to 36 Weeks Pregnant: GBS Test and Getting Ready
description: What to expect from 33 to 36 weeks pregnant: your baby's growth, common symptoms, the group B strep test, weekly prenatal visits, and a calm get-ready checklist.
body: At 36 weeks pregnant, your baby is roughly 47 cm long and weighs about 2.5 to 3 kg, prenatal visits usually move to a weekly schedule, and the group B strep swab is done between 36 and 37 weeks. The month from week 33 to week 36 is the getting-ready stretch: your baby's lungs near maturity, your body starts rehearsing, and the practical to-do list finally gets short enough to finish. This guide walks through what changes, which appointments anchor these weeks, and what deserves a call to your clinician. How your baby grows from week 33 to 36 Between weeks 33 and 36, your baby moves from busy practice to near readiness. At 33 weeks, many babies measure around 43 cm from head to heel and weigh close to 2 kg. By 36 weeks, that has often grown to roughly 47 cm and 2.5 to 3 kg, about 5.5 to 6.5 pounds. The lungs are close to mature, and most babies born after this window breathe well, though some still need short-term support. Fat is building under the skin, which smooths out wrinkles and helps with temperature control after birth. The skull stays soft and flexible on purpose, ready to mold during birth. Most babies settle head down during this stretch, and your clinician will start checking position at each visit. Sometime in these weeks, or later, the baby may drop lower into your pelvis. This is called lightening. In first pregnancies it often happens a few weeks before labor; in later pregnancies it may wait until labor starts. Movements feel different now, more rolls and stretches than sharp kicks, because space is tight. The frequency should not fall, though. If you notice fewer movements than usual for your baby, call your clinician or maternity unit right away, not tomorrow. What weeks 33 to 36 can feel like Braxton Hicks contractions often get stronger and more noticeable now. They are usually irregular and tend to settle when you change position, rest, or drink water. Pelvic pressure, lower backache, heartburn, and swollen feet and ankles are common too, and sleep can get harder just when you need it most. If the baby has dropped, you may breathe a little easier because there is less pressure on your diaphragm. The trade is that the bathroom trips of early pregnancy come back, since the baby's head now rests closer to your bladder. Short walks, a supportive pillow, and smaller meals can each help a little. Fatigue and bursts of nesting energy often show up together. It is normal to want to wash tiny clothes at nine in the evening and then feel wiped out by a trip to the store. Let the energy work for you in short sessions: twenty minutes of sorting, then a rest. Skip ladders, heavy lifting, and marathon cleaning days, and ask for help with anything that involves reaching or climbing. Keep drinking water through the day, because dehydration can make tightenings more frequent. If contractions start coming at regular intervals and keep building before 37 weeks, stop and call your clinic rather than pushing through the to-do list. Appointments from here to the finish From around week 36, prenatal visits usually move to a weekly schedule. Each visit is short but useful: blood pressure, urine, your baby's heartbeat, the size of your bump, and the baby's position. This is also when the group B strep test happens. Guidance from groups like ACOG places the swab between 36 and 37 weeks. It is a quick swab of the vagina and rectum, done in seconds. Group B strep is a common bacterium that many healthy adults carry without symptoms. If your result is positive, your care team will explain the plan for labor, and our blood tests and screening guide walks through what that means. Position checks matter more each week. If your baby is still breech around 36 to 37 weeks, your clinician will talk through options. One is external cephalic version, a procedure typically offered around 37 weeks in which a clinician presses on your belly to encourage the baby to turn head down. It does not work for everyone and it is not right for every pregnancy, so ask what makes sense in your situation. Good questions for these visits: How is the baby lying? Is my blood pressure where you want it? When should I call, and when should I come in? Write the answers down while they are fresh. A short get-ready list that builds momentum A short list done steadily beats a long list done in a panic. Install the car seat now and read the manual twice; many communities offer free checks by a certified technician through hospitals, fire stations, or public health programs. Pack the hospital bag; our hospital bag guide has the full checklist so you do not have to invent one. If you want a birth plan, finish a simple one page version; our birth plan guide covers how. Choose and confirm a pediatrician who can see the baby in the first week. Then drive the route to your birth location once, including where to park and which entrance is open at night. Round out the list with the quiet logistics. Pre-register at the hospital or birth center if that is offered, and keep your health card and insurance details in the bag. Line up care for older children and pets, with a backup person. Put a few easy meals in the freezer and keep the car fueled. Save the clinic's daytime and after-hours numbers in your phone. Jot dates, questions, and symptoms in the BeMama app or a small notebook so nothing rides on memory at 3 a.m. None of this needs to happen in one weekend. One item a day from now until week 37 gets it all done. When to call your clinician Before 37 weeks, contractions that come at regular intervals and keep getting stronger deserve a call, even if you are not sure they are the real thing. Do the same for a low, dull backache that will not ease, period-like cramping, a feeling of the baby pushing down hard, or a clear change in discharge. Leaking fluid, whether a slow trickle or a sudden gush, and any bright red bleeding are reasons to call right away, day or night. If bleeding is heavy or comes with severe, constant belly pain, go straight to emergency care instead of waiting for a call back. Clinics expect these calls in late pregnancy. Nobody will think you are overreacting, and an early call is far better than a late one. Keep paying attention to movement. By now you know your baby's usual rhythm, and that rhythm should continue right up to birth. Babies do not run out of room enough to go quiet. If movements slow, weaken, or stop, contact your clinician or maternity unit right away, even at night, and ask to be checked; do not rely on a home doppler for reassurance. Call right away, too, about a severe headache that will not ease, changes in your vision, sudden swelling of your face or hands, or pain high in your belly, since these can signal blood pressure problems that need prompt treatment. Your own team knows your history, so their instructions come first. Continue with these practical guides From week 33 to week 36, babies typically grow from about 43 cm and 2 kg to roughly 47 cm and 2.5 to 3 kg. The group B strep swab is usually done between 36 and 37 weeks. Prenatal visits typically move to a weekly schedule from around week 36. Lightening, when the baby drops into the pelvis, can ease breathing while adding pelvic pressure. Call your clinician about regular tightenings before 37 weeks, leaking fluid, bleeding, or reduced movement. What week is the group B strep test done? The group B strep test is usually done between 36 and 37 weeks of pregnancy, in line with ACOG guidance. It is a quick swab of the vagina and rectum taken during a routine visit. Many healthy adults carry this bacterium, so a positive result is common and manageable. If yours is positive, your care team will explain the plan for labor, and our blood tests and screening guide covers the details. When does the baby drop? In first pregnancies, the baby often drops into the pelvis, called lightening, in the last few weeks before labor, sometimes around weeks 34 to 38. In later pregnancies it may not happen until labor begins. The timing varies a lot and is not a reliable predictor of when labor will start. You may notice easier breathing along with more pelvic pressure and more frequent bathroom trips. How big is my baby at 36 weeks? At 36 weeks, many babies measure roughly 47 cm from head to heel and weigh about 2.5 to 3 kg, which is around 5.5 to 6.5 pounds. Healthy babies vary, so your clinician's growth checks matter more than any average. From here, most babies keep gaining steadily until birth. When do prenatal visits become weekly? Prenatal visits usually become weekly starting around 36 weeks in a typical pregnancy. Before that, most schedules run every two weeks from about week 28 to week 36. Your clinician may see you more often if blood pressure, growth, or anything else needs a closer eye.

title: 37 to 40 Weeks Pregnant: Full Term and Signs of Labor
description: What to expect from 37 to 40 weeks pregnant: full term definitions, how big your baby is now, late pregnancy symptoms, weekly checkups, and the signs that mean it is time to go in.
body: At 40 weeks pregnant you have reached your due date: your baby is full term, fully developed, and most people go into labor within a week or two of this point. The stretch from 37 to 40 weeks is a mix of finishing touches for your baby and waiting, watching, and weekly checkups for you. This guide covers what the term labels actually mean, how you might feel, what appointments look like now, and the clear signs that it is time to call or go in. Early term, full term, and why the labels matter For years, anything past 37 weeks was casually called full term. The definitions used by ACOG are now more precise, because those extra days matter. Early term runs from 37 weeks 0 days to 38 weeks 6 days. Full term runs from 39 weeks 0 days to 40 weeks 6 days. Late term covers the week after your due date, and post term begins at 42 weeks. Babies born at 39 weeks or later tend to have an easier start with breathing and feeding than babies born in the early term window, which is why elective deliveries are usually not scheduled before 39 weeks without a medical reason. These labels also shape what happens if your due date passes. Going a few days past 40 weeks is common and, on its own, not an emergency. Most clinicians start talking about closer monitoring and about induction around 41 weeks, and a separate guide on this site walks through that conversation in detail. For now, the useful takeaway is simple: your due date is the middle of a window, not a deadline. A first baby in particular often arrives after the date on the calendar, and that alone says nothing about how labor will go. How big your baby is now By 40 weeks, most babies measure about 48 to 52 cm from head to heel and weigh somewhere between 3 and 3.6 kg, roughly 6.5 to 8 pounds. Those are averages, and healthy newborns land on both sides of them. In these final weeks your baby is mostly gaining fat, which smooths the skin, helps regulate temperature after birth, and adds those newborn rolls. The fine hair called lanugo has largely disappeared, and the waxy coating called vernix is shedding into the amniotic fluid, though some babies still arrive with patches of it. The lungs and brain keep maturing right up to birth, which is part of why the 39 week mark matters. Your baby has also settled into a birth position, usually head down, and has less room to move, but movement should not become weak or infrequent. You should keep feeling the same pattern of rolls, stretches, and pushes you know, right through labor itself. If movements slow down or feel different from your baby's usual pattern, do not wait for the next appointment or until morning. Call your maternity unit or clinician right away, at any hour, because a fresh check is quick and reassuring. How you might feel from 37 weeks on Many people feel the baby drop lower into the pelvis in these weeks, especially with a first pregnancy. Breathing may get easier while walking, sleeping, and bathroom trips get harder. Pelvic pressure, hip ache, swollen feet, and sharp little zings in the cervix, sometimes called lightning pain, are all common. You may lose the mucus plug, a thick glob of discharge that can be clear, pink, or streaked with blood. That is a sign the cervix is changing, but labor can still be hours or weeks away. Practice contractions may also get stronger and more frequent without settling into a pattern. Sleep often falls apart at exactly the moment everyone tells you to rest up. Try a pillow between your knees and one under your bump, small evening meals to calm heartburn, and permission to nap in fragments instead of chasing one long night. The impatience is real too, and worth naming kindly. Watching your due date approach, fielding daily is the baby here yet messages, and inspecting every twinge with suspicion is genuinely tiring. It can help to plan one small pleasant thing per day, mute the check-in texts for a while, and remind yourself that your body does not owe anyone a schedule. What appointments look like now From around 36 or 37 weeks, prenatal visits usually move to once a week. Expect the routine basics: blood pressure, a urine check, your baby's heartbeat, and a measure or feel of your belly to confirm growth and position. Your clinician may offer a vaginal exam to see whether the cervix has started to soften, thin, or open. These checks are optional in a routine pregnancy and do not predict when labor will start, so it is fine to accept them or to decline. If you have not yet reviewed your group B strep result and what it means for labor, this is a good week to ask. Near or past your due date, your clinician may mention a membrane sweep. During a vaginal exam, they sweep a finger around the inside of the cervix to separate the membranes from its edge, which releases natural prostaglandins and can nudge labor to start within a few days. It is uncomfortable rather than dangerous for most people, can cause spotting and cramping afterward, and is always your choice. If you pass 40 to 41 weeks, expect a plan for extra monitoring, often a nonstress test to watch the heartbeat and an ultrasound to check fluid levels, along with a conversation about next steps. Waiting well, and when to go in There is no proven, reliably safe home method to start labor, which is worth knowing before you buy anything. Walking, staying gently active, and sex when your water has not broken are reasonable and pleasant, even though the evidence for all of them is mixed. Skip castor oil and unverified herbal preparations unless your clinician specifically recommends them, since they can cause strong cramping and dehydration. Spend the energy on rest instead: sleep when you can, keep meals simple, install the car seat, pack the bag, and confirm exactly who you will call first when contractions start, day or night. Call your maternity unit or go in if your water breaks, if you have bright red bleeding, if contractions become regular and strong following the pattern your provider gave you, often about five minutes apart and lasting a minute each for an hour with a first baby, or if your baby's movements decrease. A severe headache that will not ease, vision changes, or sudden swelling of your face and hands need an immediate call, whatever the hour, because they can signal preeclampsia. Our signs of labor guide covers true versus false labor in more detail. Jotting contraction times and questions in BeMama or on paper keeps the details handy for that first phone call, and once the bag is packed, a simple postpartum plan is the natural next thing to sketch. Continue with these practical guides Full term begins at 39 weeks 0 days; 37 to 38 weeks 6 days counts as early term. Most babies arrive around 48 to 52 cm long and 3 to 3.6 kg, and are mainly gaining fat now. Weekly visits continue, and cervical checks and membrane sweeps are optional choices, not requirements.
