Agree on thresholds with your care team before you start: which numbers are fine, which mean call within a day, and which mean be seen now. As a general guide, repeated readings of 140/90 or higher are worth reporting promptly, and 160/110 or higher that persists after a few minutes of rest needs urgent attention. Keep a simple log of the date, time, and both numbers. The notes in BeMama work well for this, and so does paper. Bring the log to every visit. Home readings add information between appointments, but they do not replace prenatal checks, where urine and other signs are also reviewed. Treatment, delivery, and the weeks after birth Delivery is the definitive treatment for preeclampsia, because the placenta drives the condition, though blood pressure can take days to weeks to settle after birth. Everything before that point is management: more frequent visits, lab tests, blood pressure medicines that are considered safe in pregnancy, and extra monitoring of the baby's growth and wellbeing. If an early birth looks likely, you may be offered steroid injections to help the baby's lungs mature, and in severe cases magnesium sulfate is given around delivery to prevent seizures. The timing of birth is a balance between how far along you are and how severe things look. Many people with milder preeclampsia are supported to around 37 weeks before delivery is recommended. Preeclampsia can also begin after birth. Postpartum preeclampsia most often appears within the first week, but it can show up any time in the first six weeks, including in people whose blood pressure was normal for the whole pregnancy. The warning signs are the same: severe headache, vision changes, pain under the right ribs, trouble breathing, or new swelling. New parents often blame headaches on exhaustion, so be deliberate about this one. A severe headache after birth deserves a same-day call, and if it comes with vision changes or trouble breathing, emergency care. Treated promptly, postpartum preeclampsia responds well to blood pressure medicines and monitoring. High blood pressure in pregnancy means 140/90 or higher after 20 weeks, confirmed on two checks. A reading of 160/110 or higher that persists after a few minutes of rest needs urgent care right away. Severe headache, vision changes, right-rib pain, or sudden face and hand swelling are call-now signs. Preeclampsia is often silent, so keep every prenatal appointment even when you feel well. Watch for the same warning signs for six weeks after birth, and take postpartum headaches seriously. What is preeclampsia? Preeclampsia is a pregnancy condition defined by new high blood pressure after 20 weeks plus protein in the urine or signs of strain on organs such as the liver, kidneys, or brain. It affects roughly 1 in 25 pregnancies in the United States and ranges from mild to severe. It is treatable, and routine prenatal checks exist largely to catch it early. What blood pressure is too high in pregnancy? A reading of 140/90 or higher, confirmed on a second check at least four hours later, is considered high in pregnancy. A reading of 160/110 or higher is severely high, and if it persists after a few minutes of rest it needs urgent evaluation right away. If a home reading looks high, rest for a few minutes, recheck, and report persistent high numbers to your care team promptly. When does preeclampsia start? Preeclampsia starts after 20 weeks of pregnancy, most often in the third trimester, and it can also begin after birth. Cases that start before 34 weeks are less common and tend to be watched more closely. Postpartum preeclampsia usually appears within the first week after delivery but can occur up to about six weeks out. What are the symptoms of postpartum preeclampsia? Postpartum preeclampsia symptoms include severe headache, vision changes, pain under the right ribs, shortness of breath, new swelling, and high blood pressure readings in the first six weeks after birth. It can occur even if your blood pressure was normal during pregnancy. Treat a severe headache after delivery as a same-day medical call, and seek emergency care if vision changes or breathing trouble come with it.

title: Vaccines During Pregnancy: Which Shots and When
description: Which vaccines during pregnancy protect you and your baby, when to get the Tdap, flu, COVID-19, and RSV shots, and which vaccines wait until after delivery.
body: Most pregnant people are advised to get up to four vaccines during pregnancy: Tdap between 27 and 36 weeks, a flu shot in any trimester during flu season, COVID-19 vaccination at any point, and the RSV vaccine at 32 to 36 weeks during RSV season. Tdap and the RSV shot exist mainly for your baby, because the antibodies you build cross the placenta and protect your newborn before their own vaccines begin. The flu and COVID-19 shots protect you first, since pregnancy makes both illnesses more likely to turn severe, and they pass some protection to your baby as well. Live vaccines such as MMR and chickenpox are the ones that wait until after delivery. Here is how each shot works and how to map the timing onto your own calendar. Why vaccines in pregnancy protect your baby Your baby is born with almost no immune protection of their own, and most of their vaccines cannot start right away. Vaccines during pregnancy work around that gap. After each shot, your body builds antibodies, and those antibodies cross the placenta in the following weeks. Your baby arrives with borrowed protection that covers the earliest, most vulnerable months, exactly when infections like whooping cough and RSV are most dangerous to them. The timing of each shot is chosen so that antibody transfer peaks before birth. Your baby's own vaccine schedule begins later and is a separate topic; this guide covers only the shots you receive while pregnant. The vaccines recommended in pregnancy are inactivated or protein-based. None of them contain live virus, and none of them can cause the illness they protect against. Flu and Tdap shots have been given to pregnant people for many years, and safety monitoring continues for every vaccine in the lineup. The most common side effects are a sore arm, tiredness, and sometimes a low fever for a day or two. Your own clinician knows your history, your allergies, and your due date, so treat every timing window here as the starting point for that conversation. Tdap between 27 and 36 weeks, in every pregnancy Tdap protects against tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis, better known as whooping cough. Whooping cough can be severe in newborns, who may struggle to breathe during coughing spells and often need hospital care if they catch it in the first weeks of life. ACOG and the CDC recommend one Tdap dose in every pregnancy, given between 27 and 36 weeks. Many clinicians aim for the earlier part of that window, because antibodies take about two weeks to build and transfer, and an earlier dose gives more time before birth. If your baby is likely to arrive early, ask whether to schedule the shot sooner within the window. You need the shot again in each pregnancy, even if your last dose was recent, because antibody levels fall over time and each baby needs a fresh supply. If the window passes without a dose and you have never had Tdap before, you can still receive it right after delivery. That protects you from catching and passing on whooping cough, although your baby gets less direct benefit than from a dose during pregnancy. It also helps to ask partners, grandparents, and other close caregivers to check that their own pertussis vaccination is current. The people who will hold your newborn the most are also the most likely sources of infection. The flu shot and the COVID vaccine while pregnant The inactivated flu shot is recommended in any trimester and is considered safe throughout pregnancy. Pregnancy changes your heart, lungs, and immune system in ways that make flu more likely to become severe, so the shot protects you first. It also passes antibodies to your baby, which matters because infants under six months are too young for their own flu vaccine. If you are pregnant during flu season, usually fall and winter, get the shot when it becomes available rather than waiting for a particular week. One version to skip: the nasal spray flu vaccine is a live vaccine and is not used in pregnancy. COVID-19 vaccination during pregnancy is recommended by ACOG and other major maternal health groups, and it can be given at any point. Pregnancy raises the risk of severe COVID-19 illness, and vaccination lowers that risk for you while passing some protection to your baby for the early months. Guidance on updated doses changes from season to season, so ask your clinician which formulation applies to you and when to get it. It is fine to receive the COVID-19 vaccine at the same visit as other pregnancy shots. If you had COVID-19 recently, mention that too, since your clinician may suggest a short wait before the next dose. The RSV vaccine at 32 to 36 weeks RSV is a common respiratory virus that usually causes a cold in adults but can cause serious breathing problems in young babies, and it is a leading reason infants are admitted to hospital. The maternal RSV vaccine is given once, between 32 and 36 weeks, and only during RSV season, which the CDC defines as roughly September through January in most of the continental United States. Local timing varies, so your clinic will follow the season in your region. The shot prompts your body to make antibodies that cross the placenta and protect your baby through their first RSV season, when the risk is highest. There is an alternative pathway. Instead of the vaccine during pregnancy, your baby can receive an antibody injection, often called nirsevimab, shortly after birth or before their first RSV season. In most cases a baby needs one form of protection or the other, not both. Which one fits better depends on your due date, the local season, and availability, so this is a genuine conversation to have with your clinician rather than a fixed rule. One timing detail worth knowing: the maternal vaccine needs about two weeks before birth to transfer enough antibody, so if your baby arrives sooner than that, the infant antibody shot usually steps in. Which vaccines are not safe during pregnancy Live vaccines wait until after delivery. That includes MMR, which covers measles, mumps, and rubella, the varicella vaccine for chickenpox, and the nasal spray flu vaccine. These use weakened live viruses, and although harm from accidental doses appears to be very rare, waiting is the standard precaution. If early pregnancy bloodwork shows you are not immune to rubella or chickenpox, the usual plan is to vaccinate right after delivery, and these shots are considered compatible with breastfeeding. Ideally that catch-up is handled before pregnancy at a preconception visit. If you received a live vaccine before you knew you were pregnant, tell your clinician rather than assuming the worst. A little preparation makes the vaccine conversation quick. Bring your vaccination record if you have one, or ask a previous clinic or pharmacy to send it. Mention any travel plans, since travel vaccines need an individual decision that weighs the destination against your stage of pregnancy. Flag allergies and any past reaction to a vaccine. It helps to note shot dates, side effects, and questions in the BeMama app or on paper so nothing gets lost between visits. Afterward, a sore arm and a tired day are normal. Call your clinician for a fever that stays high or redness that keeps spreading, and call emergency services for signs of a serious allergic reaction, such as trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or hives spreading over the body, which usually appear within minutes to hours of the shot. Tdap is recommended in every pregnancy, between 27 and 36 weeks. The inactivated flu shot is safe in any trimester and is worth getting early in flu season. ACOG recommends COVID-19 vaccination, which can be given at any point in pregnancy. The RSV vaccine is given at 32 to 36 weeks during RSV season, or your baby can get an antibody shot after birth instead. Live vaccines such as MMR and chickenpox wait until after delivery. What vaccines do you need when pregnant? Most pregnant people need up to four: Tdap between 27 and 36 weeks, a flu shot in any trimester during flu season, COVID-19 vaccination at any point, and the RSV vaccine at 32 to 36 weeks in season. Your clinician may adjust the list for allergies, travel, or timing. Everything else, including live vaccines like MMR, usually waits until after delivery. What week of pregnancy do you get the Tdap vaccine? Tdap is given between 27 and 36 weeks, and earlier in that window is often preferred so antibodies have time to build and cross the placenta before birth. You need a dose in every pregnancy, even if your last one was recent. If the window passes and you have never had Tdap, you can still receive it right after delivery. Is the flu shot safe during pregnancy? Yes, the inactivated flu shot is recommended in any trimester and has a long record of use in pregnancy. It protects you from severe flu and passes antibodies to your baby for their first months. The nasal spray version is a live vaccine and is not used in pregnancy. When is the RSV vaccine given during pregnancy? The maternal RSV vaccine is given once, between 32 and 36 weeks, and only during RSV season, roughly September through January in most of the continental United States. If the timing does not line up, your baby can receive an RSV antibody injection after birth instead. Ask your clinician which pathway fits your due date and local season.

title: What Medicine Can You Take While Pregnant? A Safety Guide
description: What medicine can you take while pregnant? A calm, symptom-by-symptom guide to pain relievers, cold and allergy medicines, prescriptions, and supplements, with clear check-first flags and questions for your pharmacist.
body: You can usually take acetaminophen (Tylenol) for pain or fever and certain antihistamines such as loratadine for allergies during pregnancy, while ibuprofen and most multi-symptom cold medicines are best avoided unless a clinician says otherwise. Every pregnancy is different, so run any medicine, even an over-the-counter one, past your provider or pharmacist before you take it. This guide walks through the common situations calmly, one symptom at a time. How medicine safety is judged now For decades, medicines carried letter grades for pregnancy: A, B, C, D, and X. The FDA retired that system in 2015 because a single letter hid too much. Labels now describe what is actually known: the studies that exist, the experience gathered from pregnancy registries, and the points in pregnancy where a concern applies. That change explains why you rarely hear a flat yes or no. Very few medicines are formally tested in pregnant people, so guidance is built from years of real-world use. When a medicine has been taken by many pregnant people over many years without a pattern of harm, clinicians gain confidence in it, even without a perfect trial. In practice, the question is never just is this safe. It is whether the benefit of treating your symptom outweighs any known concern, at this dose, at this point in pregnancy. That is why the same medicine can be reasonable at 10 weeks and discouraged at 30. Two habits make this easy to live with. First, use the lowest dose that works, for the shortest time that works. Second, make the pharmacist your first call for over-the-counter questions. They can check a product in minutes, at no cost, and tell you whether it needs a conversation with your provider. Keep a simple list of what you take and when, so nobody has to guess later. Pain and fever: what usually gets a yes Acetaminophen, sold as Tylenol and known as paracetamol in many countries, is the usual first choice for pain and fever in pregnancy. Mainstream guidance supports using it when you need it, at the lowest effective dose, for the shortest time that does the job. Untreated high fever and severe pain carry risks of their own, so suffering through is not the safer path. Do watch the total daily amount, because acetaminophen hides in many combination products for colds, flu, and sleep. Read every label, count every source, and ask a pharmacist what your daily limit should be. If you find yourself needing pain relief most days, that pattern itself is worth a call to your provider. Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin at regular pain-relief doses belong in the check-first column, and for much of pregnancy the answer is no. These are NSAIDs, and the FDA advises avoiding them at 20 weeks and beyond because they can affect the baby's kidneys and lower the level of amniotic fluid. Many clinicians suggest skipping them earlier in pregnancy too unless there is a specific reason. Low-dose aspirin is a separate story: some people are prescribed it for particular conditions, and that plan should be followed exactly as written. If you took an NSAID before you knew you were pregnant, do not panic. Mention it at your next appointment and switch going forward. Colds and allergies without the guesswork Start with the drug-free options, because they help more than you might expect: saline nasal spray or rinse, a humidifier, warm fluids, honey for a cough, and rest whenever you can get it. When you need more, antihistamines have some of the best track records of any over-the-counter medicines in pregnancy. Loratadine (Claritin) and cetirizine (Zyrtec) are widely used and commonly recommended for allergies. Chlorpheniramine, an older antihistamine, is another long-standing option, though it can make you drowsy. Steroid nasal sprays for allergy symptoms are often considered reasonable as well. Confirm your specific product with a pharmacist, since one brand name can cover several different formulas. Decongestants are the main check-first flag in the cold aisle. Oral decongestants such as pseudoephedrine and phenylephrine are often discouraged in the first trimester, and people with high blood pressure are usually told to avoid them at any stage. Cough ingredients like dextromethorphan and guaifenesin are commonly used in pregnancy, but confirm the exact product before you buy. The bigger trap is the multi-symptom box: one package can bundle a pain reliever, a decongestant, an antihistamine, and sometimes alcohol. Buy single-ingredient products so you treat only the symptom you actually have. Call your provider if a cold comes with a fever of 100.4 F (38 C) or higher or symptoms lasting more than about ten days, and get medical care right away for trouble breathing, chest pain, or a fever that will not come down. Prescription medicines: never stop without a plan If you take a prescription medicine for depression, anxiety, thyroid disease, seizures, asthma, diabetes, or blood pressure, the rule is simple: do not stop on your own. Untreated illness carries real risks for you and the pregnancy, and stopping some medicines abruptly can cause withdrawal or a dangerous flare. Antidepressants deserve a special mention because so many people quietly quit them after a positive test. For many people, staying on treatment is the safer choice, and several options have long track records in pregnancy. Call your prescriber as soon as you know you are pregnant, keep taking the medicine until you have talked, and make the plan together. Some prescriptions genuinely do need to change in pregnancy. Isotretinoin for acne, warfarin in most situations, certain blood pressure medicines, and a few seizure medicines are on the list clinicians act on quickly. The key word is supervised: your prescriber will move you to a better-studied option and tell you exactly how to make the change, sometimes with a taper or overlapping doses. This is also why telling every clinician you see that you are pregnant, including your dentist and any walk-in clinic, is worth the repetition. Whenever a new medicine is prescribed, one short question protects you: is this okay in pregnancy, and is there a better-studied alternative? Supplements, herbs, and the pharmacist script Herbal products deserve the same caution as medicines, and often more, because they are studied less. Natural does not mean safe in pregnancy: some herbs can affect hormones, the uterus, or bleeding, and doses vary between brands and even between batches. Teas, gummies, tinctures, and wellness blends all count. Tell your provider or pharmacist about every one, and be wary of anything marketed for detox or rapid results. Your prenatal vitamin, plus any specific supplement your clinician recommends, is usually enough. Stacking extra products risks duplicate ingredients and doses of certain vitamins, such as vitamin A, that can be too high for pregnancy. When you are standing in the pharmacy aisle, a short script gets you a reliable answer fast. Try: I am 16 weeks pregnant. Is this product okay for me, is there a better-studied choice, what dose should I use, and for how long? Then note what you took and when, in the BeMama app or wherever you keep pregnancy notes, so you can answer confidently at your next appointment. Contact your provider promptly if a symptom is severe, getting worse, or paired with fever, bleeding, or reduced movement later in pregnancy, or if something simply feels wrong. Medicine questions are exactly what your care team expects, so ask early and often. Acetaminophen is the usual first choice for pain and fever, at the lowest dose that works. Avoid ibuprofen and other NSAIDs, especially at 20 weeks and beyond, unless a clinician prescribes them. Never stop antidepressants, thyroid, seizure, or asthma medicines without a plan from your prescriber. Choose single-ingredient cold products and check decongestants with a pharmacist first. Treat herbal supplements as real medicines and mention every one to your care team. Is Tylenol safe during pregnancy? Yes, acetaminophen (Tylenol) is generally considered the first-choice pain and fever medicine in pregnancy when used at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time needed. Watch combination cold and flu products, which often contain acetaminophen too, so doses do not add up without you noticing. If you need it most days, tell your provider so the underlying cause gets attention. Can I take ibuprofen while pregnant? No, ibuprofen is generally not recommended in pregnancy unless a clinician specifically prescribes it. The FDA advises avoiding NSAIDs at 20 weeks and beyond because they can affect the baby's kidneys and amniotic fluid, and many providers suggest skipping them earlier as well. Acetaminophen is the usual alternative for everyday pain, and one accidental dose before you knew is not a reason to panic. What allergy medicine is safe during pregnancy? Loratadine (Claritin) and cetirizine (Zyrtec) are widely used in pregnancy and are commonly recommended first for allergy symptoms. Chlorpheniramine is another long-standing option, though it can cause drowsiness, and steroid nasal sprays are often considered reasonable too. Confirm your exact product with a pharmacist, because one brand name can cover several formulas, some of which add a decongestant. Can I keep taking my antidepressant while pregnant? Often yes, and you should never stop an antidepressant suddenly on your own. Untreated depression and anxiety carry real risks in pregnancy, and many antidepressants have long track records of use. Call your prescriber as soon as you know you are pregnant, keep taking your medicine until you have talked, and decide together whether to continue, adjust, or switch.

title: Best Sleeping Position During Pregnancy by Trimester
description: The best sleeping position during pregnancy is on your side, especially from 28 weeks. Here is what changes each trimester, why back sleeping matters, and how to get comfortable.
body: The best sleeping position during pregnancy is on your side, and it matters most from 28 weeks onward. Before that, in the first and second trimesters, any position that feels comfortable is fine, including your back and your stomach. If you wake up on your back later in pregnancy, do not panic: the position you fall asleep in is the one that counts, so simply roll onto your side and settle back to sleep. This guide walks through what changes each trimester and how to stay comfortable on your side. Why side sleeping matters from 28 weeks From around 28 weeks, the advice becomes specific: go to sleep on your side. When you lie flat on your back in later pregnancy, the weight of the uterus can press on the large blood vessels that run behind it, which can reduce blood flow to you and to the baby. UK guidance from the NHS links falling asleep on the back in the third trimester with a higher risk of stillbirth. That sounds frightening, so keep it in proportion: the overall risk is small, and settling onto your side at bedtime and after night wakings is a simple, concrete way to lower it further. The reason guidance focuses on the position you fall asleep in is practical: it is the position you hold longest, and it is the only one you can actually control. Everyone moves during sleep, and pregnant bodies are no exception. If you wake up on your back, this is not an emergency and it does not mean you have harmed your baby. Roll onto your side, get comfortable, and go back to sleep. Many people find their body starts waking them naturally when they end up flat, with a vague ache or a restless feeling. Treat that as a helpful nudge, not a warning sign. Early pregnancy: sleep in whatever position works In the first trimester, sleep position is genuinely a non-issue. The uterus is still small and sits low in the pelvis, protected by bone, so your back, your stomach, and either side are all fine. If you are exhausted and queasy in early pregnancy, permission to sleep however you can is worth having in writing: comfort wins. Stomach sleeping does not squash the baby. The muscular wall of the uterus and the amniotic fluid around the baby provide real cushioning, so you can stay a front sleeper for as long as it feels good, usually well into the second trimester. Most people give up stomach sleeping somewhere in the second trimester, not because it becomes dangerous but because sleeping on a growing bump feels like sleeping on a ball. That transition is a useful moment to start practicing side sleeping, even though the 28 week advice has not kicked in yet. Habits formed at 20 weeks make the third trimester easier. Some people also notice that lying flat on the back starts to feel unpleasant earlier, with dizziness or a faint feeling. That sensation is the same blood vessel pressure at work, and shifting onto your side usually settles it within a minute or two. Left side, right side, and what actually matters The left side is often suggested first because the largest vein returning blood to your heart runs slightly to the right of your spine, so lying on the left keeps the uterus off it most completely. Some clinicians also mention that left side lying may support blood flow to the placenta and the kidneys. That said, mainstream guidance treats side sleeping as the goal, not left side sleeping specifically. Falling asleep on your right side is acceptable, and current guidance treats either side as safe for going to sleep. If your left hip aches or your left shoulder complains, switch. A comfortable right side beats a miserable left side. You also do not need to hold a rigid position all night, and you could not even if you tried. Switching sides when a hip gets sore is normal and fine. You do not have to be perfectly perpendicular to the mattress either: a relaxed position where your body is tilted toward one side, supported by a pillow behind your back, still counts as side sleeping. What you are avoiding is lying flat on your back for long stretches in late pregnancy. Think of it as a direction to lean, not a pose to perform, and let comfort settle the details night by night. A pillow setup that keeps you on your side You can build a solid setup with three ordinary pillows. Place one between your knees, with your knees bent, to line up your hips and ease pressure on your lower back. Tuck a second under the side of your bump so its weight is carried by the pillow instead of pulling on your skin and back muscles. Wedge the third behind your back, snug against you, so rolling flat feels blocked rather than easy. If nighttime heartburn bothers you, raising your head and shoulders a little on an extra pillow can take the edge off. That is the whole system: knees, bump, back. A full length pregnancy pillow does the same job in one piece. With a U shaped pillow, rest your head at the curve, hug one arm of the U, slide it between your knees, and let the other arm support your back. With a C shape, face into the opening so the curve supports your head, bump, and knees, or flip it so the spine of the C blocks your back. Give any new pillow a week before judging it. If you still drift onto your back, a firm wedge behind your lower back tips you toward your side, so you land tilted rather than flat. When sleep belongs on your prenatal visit list Accidentally sleeping on your back does not need reporting, treatment, or a night of worry. It is one of the most common anxieties of the third trimester, and the honest answer is reassuring: roll over and carry on. Guidance focuses on the going to sleep position precisely because it is the part you can control. Save your energy for the things that do warrant a conversation. If you cannot find any comfortable position for several nights running, if lying down regularly makes you feel faint or dizzy, or if new loud snoring appears, those are reasonable things to raise at your next appointment. One thing is different and more urgent: your baby's movements. If you notice your baby moving less than usual, or the pattern changes, contact your midwife or maternity unit right away rather than waiting for a scheduled visit, whatever position you slept in. For everything else, a short note helps the appointment go further. Jot down which positions you have tried, how many nights sleep has been rough, and any question you keep meaning to ask; the BeMama app is a handy place to keep those notes with dates attached. Your midwife or doctor knows your pregnancy and can tailor position advice to you. From 28 weeks, go to sleep on your side; the position you fall asleep in is the one that counts. In the first trimester, any position that feels comfortable is fine, including your back and your stomach. The left side is often suggested, but falling asleep on your right side is acceptable too. Pillows between your knees, under your bump, and behind your back make side sleeping stick. Waking on your back is normal, just roll over; contact your maternity team promptly if your baby's movements change. When should I stop sleeping on my back while pregnant? Aim to stop falling asleep on your back from 28 weeks, the start of the third trimester. From that point, guidance links going to sleep on your back with reduced blood flow and a higher risk of stillbirth, and side sleeping avoids that pressure. If lying on your back already feels dizzy or unpleasant earlier, switch sooner. What matters is the position you settle into, not where you drift during the night. Is it OK to sleep on my right side while pregnant? Yes, sleeping on your right side is fine. The left side is often suggested first because it keeps the uterus off a large vein that sits slightly to the right of your spine, but guidance treats either side as safe for falling asleep. Switch sides whenever a hip or shoulder gets sore. A comfortable position you can hold beats a perfect one you cannot. What happens if I accidentally sleep on my back while pregnant? Nothing that needs fixing: just roll onto your side and go back to sleep. The advice is about the position you fall asleep in, because no one can control where they move overnight, and waking up on your back is common. Many people find their body wakes them with discomfort when they end up flat. If your baby's movements ever seem reduced or changed, contact your maternity team promptly, whatever position you slept in. Can I sleep on my stomach while pregnant? Yes, you can sleep on your stomach for as long as it feels comfortable, which is often well into the second trimester. The muscular wall of the uterus and the amniotic fluid cushion the baby, so front sleeping does not cause harm in early pregnancy. Most people give it up naturally as the bump grows. Use that transition to start practicing side sleeping before the 28 week advice begins.

title: Flying While Pregnant: Travel Safety Through 36 Weeks
description: Flying while pregnant is generally safe in an uncomplicated pregnancy through about 36 weeks. Here is when to travel, airline cutoffs, seatbelt positioning, clot prevention, and how to screen a destination.
body: Flying while pregnant is generally safe in an uncomplicated pregnancy, and most airlines allow it until around 36 weeks for domestic flights, often earlier for international ones. The most comfortable window for travel of any kind is mid pregnancy, roughly 14 to 28 weeks. This guide covers the decisions that actually come up: airline cutoffs, clot prevention on long trips, seatbelt position in the car, and how to vet a destination. Bring your specific plans to your prenatal care team so they can tailor the advice to your pregnancy. The best window: roughly 14 to 28 weeks For most people, the easiest stretch to travel is mid pregnancy, roughly 14 to 28 weeks. Guidance from groups like ACOG points to this window because early nausea and fatigue have usually eased, energy is often back, and the middle months tend to carry the lowest risk of complications that would cut a trip short. You are also still comfortable in a standard seat, and walking through an airport or a rest stop feels manageable rather than exhausting. If you can schedule a trip freely, such as a babymoon or a family visit, aim for this window. It will not guarantee a smooth trip, but it stacks the odds in your favor. Travel outside that window is not forbidden, it just takes more planning. In the first trimester, the main obstacles are nausea, exhaustion, and a frequent need for bathrooms, so build in rest days and easy food. In the third trimester, the practical concern is distance from your own care team as your due date approaches, plus airline cutoffs that arrive sooner than many people expect. Whatever the timing, mention the trip at a prenatal visit. Your clinician can flag anything in your history that changes the advice and can tell you what to do if symptoms start away from home. Airline rules and the letter you may need In an uncomplicated pregnancy, flying itself is considered safe, and cabin pressure and airport security scanners are not a concern at any stage. The limits come from airlines, not from your body. Most carriers stop pregnant passengers around 36 weeks for domestic flights, and many set an earlier cutoff for international routes, sometimes 28 to 35 weeks. Past a certain point, often around 28 weeks, some airlines also ask for a letter from your clinician confirming your due date and fitness to fly. Policies vary widely, so check your specific airline's written rules before you book, and again before you fly, since gate agents can ask for proof. A few habits make the flight easier. Book an aisle seat so you can get up without climbing over anyone. Keep the seatbelt fastened low, under your bump, whenever you are seated, because sudden turbulence is the main injury risk during a flight. Drink water steadily, since cabin air is dry, and resist the urge to restrict fluids just to avoid the bathroom. Gas expands at altitude, so go easy on fizzy drinks before boarding. If you are prone to swelling, wear loose shoes you can slip off and back on. None of this requires special gear, just a little planning at booking time. Long trips: move, drink, and consider compression stockings Pregnancy makes blood clot more easily, and sitting still for hours adds to that risk. On any flight or drive longer than about four hours, get up and walk for a few minutes every hour or two. When you cannot walk, pump your ankles and flex your calves in your seat, and avoid crossing your legs for long stretches. Drink water regularly. Graduated compression stockings are a reasonable extra step for long trips, especially if you have had a clot before or your clinician has flagged a higher risk. Put them on before you board, not after your legs have already swollen. Know the travel signs that need attention. Swelling, pain, or warmth in one calf, especially when one leg looks different from the other, can signal a clot and deserves prompt medical care. Sudden chest pain or trouble breathing is an emergency wherever you are. The same goes for pregnancy warning signs that would send you in at home: bleeding, leaking fluid, regular contractions before term, a severe headache, or a clear drop in your baby's movements later in pregnancy. Do not wait until you are home to be checked. A local urgent care clinic or emergency department is the right call. Car travel: how to wear the seatbelt Wear the lap belt low, under your bump, so it lies across your hips and upper thighs, never across your belly. Route the shoulder belt to the side of your bump and between your breasts, resting on your chest and collarbone. Never tuck the shoulder belt behind your back or under your arm, and never skip the belt because it feels snug. A correctly worn belt protects both you and the baby far better than no belt in a crash. Leave the airbags on, and if you are driving, slide the seat back so there is space between your bump and the wheel while you can still reach the pedals. For road trips, plan stops every hour or two, the same rhythm that protects against clots, and use them for a bathroom break, a snack, and a short walk. Share the driving when you can, and keep water and plain snacks within reach rather than in the trunk. Late in pregnancy, think twice about long solo drives far from your care team. If you are in any collision, even a low-speed bump with no obvious injury, contact your prenatal team the same day. They may want to check on the pregnancy, and it is a call worth making even when you feel completely fine. Vet the destination before you book Check CDC travel health notices for your destination before you pay for anything. Pregnant travelers are generally advised to avoid areas with active Zika risk, because infection during pregnancy can cause serious birth defects, and to postpone travel to malaria regions when possible, since malaria is more dangerous during pregnancy. If a malaria-region trip cannot wait, ask a clinician about prevention well before departure. If the destination calls for travel vaccines, raise it at a prenatal visit well before departure; the details belong in a conversation about your specific trip. Then look at practicalities: how far the nearest hospital with maternity care is, what your travel insurance covers if the pregnancy needs attention abroad, and whether medical evacuation is included for remote destinations. Carry a copy of your prenatal records, on paper or your phone, including your due date, blood type, and any complications, and keep your clinic's number, trip dates, and questions somewhere easy to find, such as a note in the BeMama app. Some pregnancies deserve a clinician conversation before booking at all: a history of preterm birth, placenta previa, preeclampsia, cervical insufficiency, twins or more later in pregnancy, or a chronic condition that is not well controlled. That conversation is not a ban on travel. It is how you find out whether this trip, at this stage, makes sense for this pregnancy. The most comfortable window to travel is usually mid pregnancy, about 14 to 28 weeks. Most airlines stop pregnant passengers around 36 weeks for domestic flights, earlier for international ones, and may ask for a clinician letter. On any trip over a few hours, walk every hour or two, drink water, and consider compression stockings. Wear the lap belt low under your bump and the shoulder belt between your breasts, never behind your back. Check CDC notices for Zika and malaria, and clear a complicated pregnancy with your care team before booking. How many weeks pregnant can you fly? Most airlines allow flying until around 36 weeks for domestic flights, and many set earlier cutoffs of roughly 28 to 35 weeks for international routes. The limit comes from airline policy, not from pregnancy itself, and it varies by carrier. Some airlines require a clinician's letter in the last trimester, so check your airline's written policy before booking. Is it safe to travel during pregnancy? Yes, travel is generally safe in an uncomplicated pregnancy, especially during the middle months. The main cautions are clot prevention on long trips, correct seatbelt use, destination risks such as Zika and malaria, and staying within reach of maternity care late in pregnancy. If you have complications, clear the plan with your prenatal team before booking. Can you travel in the first trimester? Yes, first trimester travel is fine in most pregnancies, and travel itself is not known to raise miscarriage risk. Nausea and deep fatigue can make it less pleasant, so plan lighter days, easy food, and quick bathroom access. If you have bleeding, severe vomiting, or other complications, ask your clinician before you go. How should you wear a seatbelt while pregnant? Place the lap belt low under your bump, across your hips and upper thighs, and run the shoulder belt between your breasts and to the side of your belly. Never put the shoulder belt behind your back or under your arm. Buckle up for every ride, including short ones, because a correctly worn belt protects both of you in a crash.

title: When to Start Maternity Leave and How to Plan for It
description: A trimester by trimester plan for when to start maternity leave, when to tell your employer, how FMLA and short term disability work, and what to finish before 36 weeks.
body: Many people start maternity leave between 38 and 39 weeks of pregnancy or at their due date, though stopping earlier is common and reasonable when a job is physically demanding or a clinician recommends it. There is no fixed rule, so the right answer depends on your health, your role, and how the money works. This guide walks through the decisions by trimester: when to tell your employer, how to piece together FMLA, disability pay, and state programs, and what to finish before 36 weeks. It is general education, not legal or medical advice, so confirm details with HR and your care team. First trimester: decide when to tell your employer There is no rule that forces you to announce a pregnancy at any particular week. Many people wait until after 12 to 13 weeks, when the chance of miscarriage drops and the worst of the nausea and exhaustion often eases. Waiting is reasonable, but earlier can be smarter in some jobs. Tell someone sooner if your work involves heavy lifting, long standing, chemicals, or radiation, if severe symptoms are affecting your performance, or if you need flexibility for frequent appointments. You do not owe anyone the news before you are ready. When you do share it, consider telling HR as well as your manager, and follow up in writing so there is a clear date on record. Once your employer knows, protections begin. In the United States, the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act requires employers with 15 or more employees to provide reasonable accommodations for pregnancy. That can include extra bathroom or rest breaks, a stool or chair, water at your station, lighter lifting limits, and schedule changes for morning sickness or prenatal visits. You usually just need to ask, and a note from your clinician can help even when it is not required. Pregnancy discrimination, such as being demoted or fired because you are pregnant, is illegal under federal law. If a conversation with your manager goes badly, contact HR and write down what was said and when. Second trimester: map the leave math The second trimester is a good time to map the money and the weeks, because the pieces rarely come from one place. In the US, the Family and Medical Leave Act protects up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave, with your health insurance continued and your job, or an equivalent one, waiting when you return. You qualify if you have worked for your employer for at least 12 months, logged at least 1,250 hours in the past year, and the company has 50 or more employees within 75 miles of your worksite. FMLA protects the time, but it does not pay you. Ask HR whether your employer offers separate paid parental leave. Pay usually comes from a mix of sources. Short-term disability insurance, if you have it, often replaces part of your wages while you recover from birth, commonly around six weeks after a vaginal delivery and around eight after a cesarean, though policies vary. A growing number of states run paid family and medical leave programs that can add paid weeks on top, so check your state labor department's website for current rules. Saved vacation and sick time can fill gaps. If you live outside the US, your national or provincial scheme likely works very differently, often with longer paid leave, so start with your government's official parental leave pages. Third trimester: choose your last day of work With an uncomplicated pregnancy, many people work until 38 or 39 weeks, and some work right up to their due date. There is no medal for lasting longer. Consider starting leave earlier if your job is physically demanding, your commute is long, sleep is badly broken, or you simply feel done. One practical detail matters here: find out whether your leave clock starts on your last day of work or on the day of birth. If leave starts when you stop working, every week you work before the birth can preserve a week of recovery and baby time afterward. Weigh that math against how you actually feel. Your body gets a vote, and so does your clinician. Bring a description of your duties to a third-trimester visit and ask whether anything should change. Call your care team right away if you notice regular contractions before 37 weeks, leaking fluid, a severe headache that does not ease, vision changes, sudden swelling of your face or hands, dizziness at work, or a drop in your baby's movements, and go to the emergency room for heavy bleeding or severe abdominal pain. Some conditions, such as blood pressure problems or a risk of preterm labor, can make earlier leave or modified duties the safer path, and your clinician can provide the documentation your employer needs. Starting leave early for medical reasons is not quitting early. It is following the plan. Finish the paperwork and the handover by 36 weeks Try to finish the paperwork by about 36 weeks, because babies do not read calendars. FMLA allows employers to ask for 30 days notice when leave is foreseeable, so submit those forms once your dates firm up. File your short-term disability claim early too, since most insurers need a form signed by your clinician. Apply to your state paid leave program if one exists, because approvals can take weeks. Then ask HR two easy-to-miss questions: how you will pay your share of health insurance premiums during unpaid weeks, and how to add the baby to your plan, which usually must happen within about 30 days of the birth. Then write the handover. Keep it to a few pages: recurring tasks and their deadlines, where files live, the status of open projects, who covers what, and a single contact list. Share account access through your company's proper channels rather than personal notes. Decide your boundaries now, such as whether you want one monthly update or complete silence, and say so plainly before you go. Finally, keep your own dates, forms, symptoms, and questions in one place, whether that is the BeMama app or a paper notebook, so nothing depends on your memory during a sleepless stretch. Set up your return before you go The easiest time to arrange your return is before you leave, while you are still in the building and goodwill is high. Ask whether a phased return, part-time weeks, or remote days are possible for your first month back. If you plan to breastfeed, ask where the lactation space is and how pumping breaks are handled on your team. In the US, the PUMP Act entitles most employees to reasonable break time and a private space that is not a bathroom for up to a year after the birth. Getting these answers now saves you from negotiating logistics while caring for a newborn. Set a tentative return date and treat it as a draft. Recovery timelines vary widely, and a date that looked fine at 30 weeks pregnant can feel very different with a six-week-old at home. Know your options before you commit: whether you can extend with vacation time, unpaid leave, or a schedule change, and how much notice each one requires. If your state paid leave program includes bonding weeks, ask whether you must take them in one block or can spread them out, since that changes what a phased return looks like. Give yourself permission to reassess. A return plan that bends is far more useful than one that looks tidy on paper and breaks in real life. Many people work until 38 to 39 weeks, but earlier is right for demanding jobs or medical reasons. Many wait until after 12 to 13 weeks to tell their employer, and sooner is wise when work has physical risks. FMLA protects up to 12 unpaid weeks if you meet the tenure, hours, and employer-size rules. Pay often comes from short-term disability, state paid leave programs, and saved time off combined. Finish forms and your handover by about 36 weeks, and arrange pumping breaks and space before you go. When should you tell your employer you are pregnant? Many people tell their employer after 12 to 13 weeks, once the first trimester ends and the chance of miscarriage drops. Tell sooner if your job involves lifting, chemicals, or other hazards, or if you need accommodations for symptoms or appointments. There is no legal deadline for the personal announcement, though FMLA paperwork requires 30 days notice when leave is foreseeable. How long is maternity leave in the US? There is no single national paid maternity leave in the US; FMLA protects up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave for eligible employees. Paid time comes separately, from employer policies, short-term disability, or state paid leave programs, so totals range from a few weeks to several months. Check all three sources before assuming your number. How long can you work while pregnant? With an uncomplicated pregnancy, most people can work until 38 to 39 weeks, and some until their due date. Physically demanding work, long shifts, or complications such as blood pressure problems can make an earlier stop safer. Ask your clinician to review your specific duties, and call right away for warning signs like regular contractions before 37 weeks, bleeding, or reduced fetal movement. How does short term disability work for maternity leave? Short-term disability replaces part of your paycheck while you recover from birth, commonly for around six weeks after a vaginal delivery and around eight after a cesarean. You typically need to be enrolled before you become pregnant for the birth to be covered, so check your policy early. File the claim with a form signed by your clinician, and expect processing to take a few weeks.

title: How to Count Baby Kicks and Track Movement Patterns
description: Learn how to count baby kicks from about 28 weeks, what a normal movement pattern looks like, and exactly what to do the same day if your baby is moving less than usual.
body: To count baby kicks, pick a time of day when your baby is usually active, lie on your side, and time how long it takes to feel 10 distinct movements, which commonly happens within two hours. From about 28 weeks, this simple habit teaches you your baby's personal pattern, and that pattern is the benchmark that matters most. This guide walks through the method, the things that muddle it, and exactly what to do if movement drops. Your baby's normal is the benchmark This guide is about the third trimester, when movement stops being a novelty and becomes information. From about 28 weeks, most babies settle into a daily rhythm: stretches of activity, stretches of rest, and times of day when they are reliably busy. That rhythm is worth learning, because it becomes your personal baseline. Earlier in pregnancy, movement is often too erratic to read much into, and a quiet day usually means nothing. Once a pattern is established, though, a real change from it is the single most useful movement signal you have. Spend a few days simply noticing: when is your baby active, and what does a busy stretch feel like? Guidance in the ACOG and NHS tradition deliberately avoids naming one universal kicks-per-hour number, because healthy babies vary enormously. Some are gymnasts, some are gentle rollers, and both can be perfectly well. Comparing your baby to a friend's baby, or to a number from a forum, only creates noise. Compare your baby to your baby. If yours usually wakes you with a flurry after breakfast and rolls all evening, that is the pattern to protect. A quiet baby who has always been quiet is not automatically a concern, and a lively baby who goes unusually still is not reassured by an average. How to count kicks, step by step Pick a time of day when your baby is usually active, often after a meal or in the evening. Lie on your side, left or right, in a quiet spot where you can pay attention. Note the time, then count distinct movements: kicks, jabs, rolls, swishes, and stretches each count as one. Rhythmic hiccups do not count. Keep going until you reach 10 movements, then note how long it took. Many parents get there in well under an hour once they catch an active window. The commonly used benchmark, drawn from the ACOG tradition, is 10 movements within two hours. Do the count at roughly the same time each day if your provider has asked you to count daily, or whenever something feels off. Write the start and finish times somewhere consistent, on paper or in the BeMama app, so you can see your baby's usual speed at a glance. That record turns a vague worry into a clear sentence for your provider: my baby usually reaches 10 movements in 30 minutes and today took two hours. If you hit the two-hour mark without feeling 10 distinct movements, stop counting and call your provider right away, whatever the hour. What can muddle the pattern Babies sleep in the womb, usually in cycles of about 20 to 40 minutes and rarely longer than around 90 minutes. A quiet half hour is very often a nap, which is why the counting method uses a two-hour window rather than a single hour. Your own attention matters too. On busy days when you are on your feet, the motion of walking can rock a baby to sleep and keep you too distracted to notice movement. That is why the method asks you to lie down on your side and focus. Many babies wake up and perform the moment you finally rest. An anterior placenta, one attached to the front wall of the uterus, acts like a cushion between the baby and your belly. It can mute smaller movements, especially in the early third trimester, and you may feel more at the sides and low in the pelvis than in the middle. You can still learn a pattern; it may just be softer and slightly slower to emerge. The same action rule applies: once you know your baby's normal, a real drop from it deserves a same-day call, and an anterior placenta is not a reason for anyone to dismiss your concern. Babies do not slow down before labor It is a persistent myth that babies run out of room and go quiet before labor. What actually changes late in pregnancy is the character of movement: fewer dramatic somersaults, more rolls, presses, stretches, and squirms, because space is tight. The frequency should hold. Babies should keep moving right up to labor and during labor itself. A baby who is genuinely moving less at 38 or 40 weeks is not showing a sign that birth is near. That baby needs to be checked the same day, exactly as at 30 weeks, so do not let the myth talk you out of calling. The myth survives partly because the sensations really do change, and partly because people around you may repeat it kindly and confidently. It helps to decide in advance how you will respond: changed movements that are still frequent are expected, while reduced movements are always worth a call, no matter how close you are to your due date. If you are unsure which one you are feeling, do a side-lying count. Ten distinct movements within two hours, of any type, tells you far more than trying to judge strength from memory ever will. If your baby is moving less than usual Reduced or absent movement is a same-day matter: call your provider, midwife, or the maternity unit as soon as you notice it, day or night, and go in if they ask you to. Do not wait overnight to see whether tomorrow feels better, and do not wait for a scheduled appointment. Monitoring is quick, most visits end in reassurance, and maternity staff expect these calls; checking movement concerns is a normal part of their day. If movements are reduced again on another day, call again. A previous normal check does not cover a new change. Skip the home tests. Sugary drinks, ice water, prodding your belly, and loud music are not reliable ways to confirm wellbeing, and they can delay the call that matters. Home dopplers are the riskiest false comfort of all, because a heartbeat is not the question. A baby can have a heartbeat and still need attention, and untrained listening can mistake your own pulse or the placenta for the baby. The only meaningful test for reduced movement is proper monitoring by people trained to interpret it. Make the call first; everything else can wait. From about 28 weeks, learn your baby's daily movement rhythm and treat it as your baseline. To count kicks, lie on your side and time 10 distinct movements, commonly felt within two hours. Your baby's own normal matters more than any universal kicks-per-hour number. Movements change character before labor, but babies should not move less. Reduced or absent movement means calling your provider the same day, never waiting overnight. How many kicks should I feel in an hour? There is no universal kicks-per-hour number; the widely used benchmark is 10 distinct movements within two hours during one of your baby's active windows. Many babies get there much faster. What matters most is a change from your own baby's usual pattern, so compare today to your baby's normal rather than to an average. When should I start counting kicks? About 28 weeks is the usual starting point, because most babies have settled into a recognizable daily pattern by then. Some providers suggest starting earlier or counting every day in higher-risk pregnancies, so follow the plan you are given. Before the third trimester, movement is often too irregular for counts to mean much. Do babies move less before labor? No, babies should not move less before labor. Movements change in character as space tightens, with more rolls and stretches and fewer big kicks, but the frequency should hold right through labor itself. Treat any real reduction near your due date as reduced movement and call your provider the same day. When should I go to the hospital for reduced fetal movement? The same day you notice it: call your provider or maternity unit right away, at any hour, and go in for monitoring if they ask. Do not wait overnight, and do not test with sugary drinks or a home doppler first. Repeat reductions on later days deserve repeat calls, even if a recent check was normal.

title: How to Prepare for Labor: A Third Trimester Checklist
description: A week by week guide to how to prepare for labor from 28 weeks on: classes, coping skills, gentle exercise, perineal massage, logistics, and the plans that make the day calmer.
body: To prepare for labor, work in three passes from about 28 weeks: take a childbirth class and practice coping skills first, prepare your body and handle logistics between 32 and 36 weeks, then rehearse the details of the day from 36 weeks on. Spreading the work out keeps any single week light. This guide gives you a week-anchored checklist for each pass, so the day feels legible instead of looming. Weeks 28 to 32: book a class and learn how labor works Book a childbirth class now if you have not already. Popular classes fill up, and you want to finish by about 36 to 37 weeks so the information is fresh and the course is done before you reach full term, when labor becomes increasingly likely. Ask your provider, hospital, or local health unit what is available, and pick the format that fits your life: a multi-week evening series, a single weekend day, or a live online course. A good class walks you through the stages of labor, comfort techniques, what your support person can do, and common interventions such as monitoring and epidurals, with time to ask your own questions. Alongside the class, learn the shape of labor at a high level so the day feels familiar instead of mysterious. Early labor is usually the longest part, with contractions that gradually get stronger, longer, and closer together, and with a first baby it can last many hours. Active labor is more intense, then comes pushing, then delivering the placenta. You do not need to memorize details. A rough map is enough to help you rest at home in early labor instead of rushing in too soon. Recognizing when labor has actually started is its own topic, and our guide to the signs of labor covers it. Weeks 28 to 32: practice one or two coping skills Pick one breathing pattern and start practicing it now, weeks before you need it. A simple option is a slow breath in through your nose and a longer, softer breath out through your mouth. Practice during Braxton Hicks tightenings, in the shower, or for two minutes before bed, so the pattern is automatic when a real contraction arrives. Add upright positions to your repertoire: leaning forward over a counter or the back of a chair, kneeling on hands and knees, or sitting and rocking on a birth ball. Many people find that staying upright and moving makes contractions easier to work with than lying flat. Bring your support person into the practice. Counterpressure, which is steady firm pressure on the lower back during a contraction, and a hip squeeze, where they press inward on the sides of your hips, are two techniques a partner can learn in an evening. Rehearse them a few times so nobody is reading instructions between contractions. Keep the whole toolkit small on purpose. One breathing pattern, two positions, and one partner technique that you have actually practiced will serve you better on the day than a long list of ideas you saw once in a video and never tried with your own body. Weeks 32 to 36: prepare your body If your pregnancy is uncomplicated and your clinician agrees, keep moving through the third trimester. Walking, swimming, stationary cycling, and prenatal yoga or stretching all count, and mainstream guidance supports around 150 minutes of moderate activity a week in a healthy pregnancy. The goal is not fitness gains. Labor is physical work, and regular movement supports stamina, sleep, and mood in the weeks before it. Stop and contact your clinician if exercise brings on bleeding, leaking fluid, dizziness, chest pain, or regular contractions. Pelvic floor exercises matter too, and they have their own detailed guide on this site. From about 34 to 35 weeks, you can add perineal massage if you want to. With clean hands and a little unscented oil or water-based lubricant, place one or two thumbs just inside the vaginal opening and press gently downward toward the rectum and out to the sides, holding a mild stretching feeling for a minute or two, a few times a week. Evidence suggests it may reduce the chance of tears that need stitches, particularly in a first vaginal birth. It should stretch, not hurt. Skip it and ask your clinician first if you have an infection, bleeding, placenta previa, or have been told to avoid vaginal contact. Weeks 32 to 36: handle the logistics Between 32 and 36 weeks, clear the practical tasks that are miserable to do in a hurry. Install the car seat and have the installation checked; many hospitals, fire stations, and community programs offer inspections by certified child passenger safety technicians, and it is common for a first installation to need adjusting. Pre-register at your hospital or birth center so the paperwork is done before you arrive in labor, and confirm what identification and insurance or health card details they want. If you have other children or pets, line up two people who could cover them, one primary and one backup, and tell them what a middle-of-the-night call might look like. This is also the window to confirm who will support you in labor. If a partner, friend, or family member is coming, talk through what help you want and make sure they know the coping techniques you have practiced. If you are considering a doula, interview and book one now, since many take a limited number of clients per month. Share your preferences with whoever attends, and if you want them written down, our birth plan guide walks through that document step by step. Packing is covered in our hospital bag checklist. Save your support people's numbers somewhere you can find them half asleep. Weeks 36 and beyond: rehearse the day and settle your mind From 36 weeks, rehearse the day itself. Drive the route to your hospital or birth center at least once, note where to park, and find out which entrance is open at night. Ask your provider for their exact when-to-call rule, since practices vary, and write it down word for word along with the after-hours phone number. Then review pain relief options while you can think clearly: an epidural, nitrous oxide where it is offered, short-acting IV medicines, and unmedicated coping with movement, water, and breathing. You are not committing to anything. You are making sure that decisions during labor are informed rather than improvised, and you can change your mind at any point. Mental preparation is mostly about trading a perfect script for informed flexibility. Labor rarely follows the plan exactly, and people tend to cope better when they expect adjustments rather than treating them as failures. Name your specific fears to someone qualified to answer them, whether that is your provider or your class instructor, because a vague dread usually shrinks when it becomes a concrete question. Keep practicing your breathing for a couple of minutes a day. Jot your questions, practice dates, and the when-to-call rule in BeMama or a notebook. And at any week, call your clinician right away for bleeding, leaking fluid, severe headache, vision changes, or a noticeable drop in your baby's movements, and go straight to emergency care for heavy bleeding or severe, constant abdominal pain. Book a childbirth class around 28 to 32 weeks so it finishes before 37 weeks. Practice one breathing pattern, two upright positions, and one partner technique until they feel automatic. Stay gently active, and consider perineal massage from about 34 to 35 weeks. Install and check the car seat, pre-register, and confirm your support person by 36 weeks. Learn your provider's exact when-to-call rule and review pain relief options before labor starts. When should I take childbirth classes? Most people start a childbirth class between about 28 and 32 weeks, aiming to finish by 36 to 37 weeks. That leaves time to practice what you learn while keeping it fresh. If you are closer to your due date, a condensed one-day or online class still helps, so book whatever fits the time you have left. How do you do perineal massage? With clean hands and unscented oil or water-based lubricant, gently press one or two thumbs just inside the vaginal opening downward and out to the sides, holding a mild stretch for a minute or two, a few times a week from about 34 to 35 weeks. It should feel like stretching, not pain. Ask your clinician first if you have an infection, bleeding, or a condition such as placenta previa. What exercises help prepare your body for birth? Regular moderate activity, such as walking, swimming, and prenatal yoga, is the most useful physical preparation in most healthy pregnancies. Mainstream guidance supports around 150 minutes a week when your clinician agrees. Upright positions and gentle stretching you practice now also double as coping tools during labor. No specific exercise guarantees a shorter or easier birth, so aim for consistency rather than intensity. How can I prepare for labor mentally? Prepare mentally by learning the stages of labor, practicing one or two coping skills until they feel automatic, and reviewing pain relief options before the day arrives. Expect the plan to flex, since labor rarely follows a script exactly. Naming specific fears to your provider or class instructor turns vague dread into questions that can actually be answered.

title: Signs of Labor: How to Tell When It Is Really Starting
description: The most reliable signs of labor are contractions that grow longer, stronger, and closer together, your water breaking, and bloody show. Here is how to read each one calmly.
body: The clearest signs of labor are contractions that become regular, stronger, and closer together, your water breaking, and a blood-tinged discharge called bloody show. In the days before, you may also notice the baby dropping lower, the loss of your mucus plug, loose stools, or a burst of nesting energy. This guide walks through each sign, how to tell practice contractions from the real thing, and when to call your provider or head in. Early clues in the days before labor In the last weeks of pregnancy, your body often sends advance notices. One is lightening, when the baby settles lower into the pelvis. Breathing may feel easier while pelvic pressure and bathroom trips increase. In a first pregnancy this can happen two to four weeks before labor; in later pregnancies it may not happen until labor begins. Many people also notice a low, dull backache, cramps that feel like a period, or looser stools as the body releases hormones that soften the cervix. None of these signs starts a clock. They simply tell you that things are moving in the right direction. You may also lose your mucus plug, the thick discharge that has sealed the cervix. It can come away all at once or in pieces over several days, and it is often tinged pink or brown. That tinge is called bloody show, and it usually means the cervix is softening and beginning to open. Bloody show is one of the better clues that labor is roughly 24 to 48 hours away, especially when it arrives alongside period-like cramps and loose stools, but it carries no guarantee: labor may follow within hours or still be days off, so treat it as a heads-up rather than a starting gun. A sudden burst of energy to clean and organize, often called nesting, is common around this time too. Bright red bleeding is different and deserves a call to your provider. Braxton Hicks or the real thing Braxton Hicks contractions are practice tightenings, and they follow a recognizable pattern of their own. They show up irregularly, do not get closer together, and do not grow stronger over time. Most people feel them only in the front of the belly, as a tightening that is uncomfortable rather than truly painful. The most useful test is to change what you are doing. Walk if you have been resting, lie down on your left side if you have been active, drink a large glass of water, or soak in a warm bath. Braxton Hicks contractions usually fade with one of these changes, especially in the weeks before your due date. True labor contractions keep coming no matter what you do. They settle into a rhythm, arrive at roughly regular intervals, and those intervals gradually shorten. Each contraction also lasts longer and feels stronger than the ones before it. Many people describe a wave that starts in the lower back and wraps around to the front, or a deep menstrual cramp that peaks and then releases. A practical benchmark: when you have to stop walking or talking to breathe through a contraction, it is doing real work. If a warm bath, water, and rest have not slowed the pattern within an hour or so, you are likely watching early labor unfold. What early contractions feel like and how to time them At first, real contractions rarely feel dramatic. Common descriptions include strong period cramps low in the belly, a dull ache in the lower back that comes and goes in waves, or pressure in the pelvis and thighs. In early labor, contractions are often 10 to 20 minutes apart and last around 30 to 45 seconds. Over hours they typically move closer together and stretch toward a minute. Everyone's experience differs; some people feel mostly back pain, and some barely notice early contractions at all. What matters is not how any single contraction feels, but whether the overall pattern is building. Timing removes the guesswork. Measure frequency from the start of one contraction to the start of the next, and duration from the start of a contraction to its end. Time them for about an hour, then rest; there is no need to log every contraction all night. Jot the times in BeMama or on paper so you can read the pattern back to your provider instead of estimating from memory. While you time, keep life gentle: eat something light, sip fluids, empty your bladder, and rest between waves. Early labor can last many hours, and saving energy now is one of the most useful things you can do. If your water breaks Movies suggest labor always begins with a dramatic gush, but only about 1 in 10 labors actually starts with the water breaking. For most people, contractions come first and the water breaks later, sometimes not until well into active labor. When it does happen, it can be a sudden gush or a slow, steady trickle that is easy to mistake for leaking urine. Amniotic fluid is usually clear or pale straw colored, with little or no smell, and it keeps coming even after you empty your bladder. If you are unsure, put on a clean pad and check it again after 30 minutes or so. If you think your water has broken, note four things before you call: the time it happened, the color of the fluid, any odor, and roughly how much there was. Then call your provider even if you feel fine and have no contractions, because once the sac is open the team will want a plan for reducing infection risk. Do not put anything in the vagina, including tampons, and skip baths until you have spoken with someone. Fluid that looks green or brown, or has a foul smell, needs an immediate call, as does any heavy bleeding along with it. When to head in, and when to call right away For a first baby with an uncomplicated pregnancy, many providers suggest the 5-1-1 rule of thumb: call or head in when contractions are about five minutes apart, last about one minute each, and have kept that pattern for one hour. Treat it as a starting point, not a universal rule. Your own provider may set a different threshold, and it is worth asking at a late-pregnancy visit exactly when they want to hear from you. Second and later labors often move faster, so the bar is usually earlier. If you tested positive for group B strep, you may be asked to come in as soon as labor starts or your water breaks. Some signs skip the timing rules entirely. Call your provider or go in right away for bright red bleeding heavier than spotting, regular contractions or leaking fluid before 37 weeks, fluid that is green or brown, a noticeable drop in your baby's movements, constant severe pain, or fever. And call whenever you simply feel that something is wrong; that instinct is a legitimate reason. No article can weigh your history, your exam findings, or your baby's pattern the way your own care team can. Labor triage lines answer these calls all day and night, and no one will mind if the answer turns out to be Braxton Hicks. True labor contractions get longer, stronger, and closer together no matter what you do. Losing your mucus plug or seeing bloody show means labor is near, but it may still be hours or days away. Only about 1 in 10 labors begins with the water breaking; note the time, color, odor, and amount, then call. The 5-1-1 pattern is a common cue to head in, but follow the threshold your own provider gives you. Call right away for bleeding, fluid or regular contractions before 37 weeks, green fluid, or reduced movement. How do I know if I am in labor? You are likely in labor when contractions arrive at regular intervals, get stronger and closer together over an hour or more, and keep going no matter how you rest or move. Braxton Hicks contractions, by contrast, stay irregular and usually fade with a change of position, fluids, or a warm bath. Water breaking or bloody show alongside a building contraction pattern makes labor even more likely. When in doubt, call your provider and describe what you are feeling. What is the difference between Braxton Hicks and real contractions? Braxton Hicks contractions are irregular, stay about the same strength, are felt mostly in the front of the belly, and usually ease with movement, water, or a warm bath. Real labor contractions form a rhythm: they come at shrinking intervals, last longer, feel stronger each time, and continue no matter what you do. Many people feel true contractions start in the back and wrap around to the front. An hour of timing usually makes the difference clear. How do I know if my water broke? Broken water is usually a gush or a continuous trickle of clear or pale straw colored fluid that keeps coming even after you empty your bladder. Urine tends to be yellowish and stops, while amniotic fluid has little or no odor and does not. Put on a clean pad, note the time, color, odor, and amount, then call your provider even if nothing else is happening. Green or brown fluid, or a foul smell, needs an immediate call. When should I go to the hospital for contractions? A common rule of thumb for a first baby is 5-1-1: go in when contractions are about five minutes apart, last about one minute, and have held that pattern for one hour. Your provider may give you a different threshold, and second labors, a long drive, group B strep, or any complication can move it earlier. Go regardless of timing for bleeding, fluid or regular contractions before 37 weeks, green fluid, or reduced movement.

title: What Happens During a C-Section: Step by Step
description: A calm, step by step guide to what happens during a C-section, from the reasons and the spinal to the roughly 45 minute surgery and the recovery that follows.
body: During a C-section, you get a spinal or epidural so you are numb but awake, the surgeon makes a low incision in your abdomen and uterus, and your baby is usually born within the first 10 to 15 minutes of a surgery that takes about 45 minutes. Roughly one in three US births happens this way, according to CDC data, so this is preparation every expecting parent can use, not pessimism. The steps below cover why cesareans happen, how planned and unplanned ones differ, what the operating room is actually like, and how recovery unfolds. Why C-sections happen A cesarean can be recommended for many reasons, and most of them are about positioning, the placenta, or how labor is going.
