If pain is severe, increasing or not relieved by the plan, seek prompt assessment; do not assume you must endure it because a loss has been diagnosed. Severe pain with bleeding, faintness or major illness needs immediate emergency care. 5. Shoulder-tip or one-sided pain Pain at the tip of the shoulder may be a sign of internal bleeding from an ectopic pregnancy, rather than an ordinary part of miscarriage. New shoulder-tip pain or one-sided pelvic pain with possible pregnancy needs urgent assessment now, even without visible bleeding or a positive test. Rectal pressure, painful bowel movements or pelvic discomfort may also occur and should be reported. Sudden or severe abdominal/pelvic pain, shoulder pain with bleeding or faintness, marked dizziness, loss of consciousness or breathing difficulty needs immediate emergency care. Do not wait for a home test or try to settle these symptoms with pain medicine, heat or water. A previously suspected miscarriage does not safely explain every new pain. 6. Weakness, tiredness or headache Physical strain, disrupted sleep and emotional distress can leave you tired, but weakness may also reflect blood loss, anaemia, dehydration or infection. A headache or fatigue is not automatically harmless after a loss. Tell a clinician if symptoms are new, persistent or worsening. Rest, fluids and nourishing food can support recovery after appropriate assessment, but they do not treat dangerous bleeding or infection. Marked dizziness, fainting, breathlessness, racing heartbeat with illness or inability to stand safely needs urgent assessment; loss of consciousness, severe breathlessness or faintness with heavy bleeding is an immediate emergency. Ask whether examination or blood tests are needed. 7. Grief and emotional pain You may feel sadness, shock, anger, guilt, relief, numbness or fear about another pregnancy, sometimes together or at unexpected times. There is no required emotional response, and how far along the pregnancy was does not determine whether support is deserved. Partners and other close people can be affected too. Talking with trusted people, a counsellor, a pregnancy-loss support group or a mental-health professional may help. Grief and depression are not identical, but depression, anxiety or trauma symptoms can follow a loss and are treatable. Estimates from research groups cannot predict your personal risk. Seek care for persistent hopelessness, loss of interest or impaired daily life, and urgent help for self-harm or suicidal thoughts. Immediate danger or inability to stay safe needs local emergency services or an emergency department now. Choosing management after a confirmed loss If no tissue remains and you are well, further treatment may not be needed. Otherwise, options for early miscarriage include expectant management (waiting with a clinical plan) medicines to help tissue pass, or a procedure, often suction aspiration. Surgical management is sometimes called evacuation or D&C; discuss the actual technique and anaesthesia rather than assuming every procedure is the same. Choice depends on symptoms, gestation, scan findings, health, preferences and available services. Heavy bleeding or infection can make urgent hospital treatment necessary. Ask about expected pain and bleeding, side effects, emergency contact arrangements and what happens if the first option is unsuccessful. Waiting is not simply ignoring symptoms, and there is no single pain level or timetable that fits everyone. Bleeding, follow-up and the next period After an early loss, bleeding often gradually lessens over one to two weeks; it can last longer with some management approaches. Do not automatically regard spotting until the next period as normal. Contact the team for persistent, increasing or prolonged bleeding or pain, fever, foul discharge or ongoing pregnancy symptoms; seek emergency care for the warning signs above. Follow the test and review plan: NICE advises a home pregnancy test around three weeks after expectant or medical management, with review if positive. A negative result does not dismiss persistent bleeding, pelvic pain or fever. Repeat ultrasound or other tests may be needed, rather than a scan being mandatory for everyone. Periods often return in four to eight weeks, but timing varies; ask when to contact the team if yours does not return. Ovulation can occur first, so discuss contraception if pregnancy is not wanted. Recovery is individual Some feel physically better in days, while others need weeks or longer depending on the loss, treatment and complications. There is no universal two- or three-week deadline for recovery or a requirement to return to work before you feel ready. Ask for practical help, time off or a review if recovery is not progressing. Emotional recovery may take longer than physical recovery, and support can be requested at any stage. Agree when to seek follow-up and which medicines or activities are suitable. Bring notes if helpful, but symptoms and safety take priority over tracking. You deserve care for both the physical and emotional effects, without needing to prove that the pregnancy was far enough along to matter. Pain or bleeding alone cannot diagnose miscarriage or exclude an ectopic pregnancy. Heavy rapid bleeding, severe pain, shoulder pain with bleeding or faintness, or loss of consciousness needs immediate emergency care; do not wait for a pad-count threshold. Pain relief depends on whether the loss is confirmed, the treatment and your health; heat or hydration must not delay assessment. Fever, foul discharge, increasing pain or persistent bleeding needs review, even after a negative pregnancy test. Recovery and grief vary; support is available for both physical symptoms and emotional distress. What do miscarriage cramps feel like? They may feel like strong period cramps or waves of pain in the lower abdomen or pelvis. Severity varies. Seek advice for pain in possible pregnancy; severe, one-sided or worsening pain or faintness requires urgent or immediate emergency assessment. Are nausea, diarrhoea and vomiting normal? They can occur with hormonal changes or miscarriage medicines, but are not always harmless or caused by a loss. Inability to keep fluids down, reduced urine or worsening illness needs urgent advice; severe pain or loss of consciousness needs emergency care. Is shoulder pain a miscarriage symptom? Shoulder-tip pain can warn of internal bleeding from ectopic pregnancy. Get urgent assessment now with possible pregnancy, even without bleeding or a positive test. Shoulder pain with bleeding, severe pain or faintness needs immediate emergency care. Is weakness or tiredness expected? Tiredness can occur, but weakness may reflect blood loss, dehydration, anaemia or infection. Report persistent or worsening symptoms. Fainting, severe breathlessness, loss of consciousness or heavy bleeding with marked dizziness needs immediate emergency care. How much bleeding means I should get help? Heavy bleeding that quickly soaks a pad, especially with severe pain, dizziness or faintness, needs immediate emergency care. Do not wait for two pads an hour for two hours. Even light bleeding during pregnancy warrants urgent pregnancy-care advice. Can I take ibuprofen for the pain? If pregnancy could still be ongoing, do not self-start it. After a confirmed miscarriage, a team may recommend it if suitable for your treatment and health. Follow your personal plan and avoid duplicate ingredients; uncontrolled pain needs reassessment. What follow-up is needed? Follow the team’s plan for testing and review. A pregnancy test around three weeks after expectant or medical management is commonly advised; a positive result needs review, and negative tests do not dismiss persistent bleeding, pain or fever. When should I seek emotional support? Whenever you want it, including sadness, mixed feelings, anxiety or fear about another pregnancy. Persistent hopelessness or difficulty functioning deserves professional care. Suicidal thoughts need urgent help; immediate danger or inability to stay safe needs emergency services or an emergency department now.

title: Miscarriage risk by week: what the numbers can tell you
description: Understand how miscarriage risk changes with pregnancy dates, age and scan findings, which symptoms need urgent care and when further tests may help.
body: It is understandable to want a reassuring number during early pregnancy, especially after a previous loss. Miscarriage becomes less likely as a pregnancy progresses, but a week alone cannot predict an individual outcome. The meaning of a percentage depends on which pregnancies were studied and what a scan has already shown. What miscarriage figures actually measure Miscarriage means a pregnancy ends before a locally defined gestational limit: many studies use before 20 weeks, while UK guidance uses before 24 weeks. Most losses occur in the first trimester. Estimates also differ according to whether they count all conceptions, pregnancies recognised by a positive test, or pregnancies already shown to be developing on ultrasound. Very early unrecognised losses are often missing from statistics. The proportion of all miscarriages occurring early is different from the chance that an ongoing pregnancy will miscarry from today onward. Neither a general first-trimester estimate nor a later-pregnancy percentage is a personal forecast. There is no medically required week for announcing a pregnancy; you can choose when and with whom to share it according to the support you want. Chromosomes, age and previous pregnancies A typical embryo has 46 chromosomes, with 23 contributed by each parent. Errors involving missing or extra chromosome material can occur as eggs, sperm or the embryo develop. Chromosome abnormalities account for about half of miscarriages and are usually a chance event, even when both parents have normal chromosomes. The chance increases with maternal age, particularly from the mid-30s and more substantially in the 40s; fixed claims of a 75% increase or fivefold risk cannot be applied without their study population and comparison group. One miscarriage does not mean another is inevitable. Previous losses and previous live births both help a clinician assess the next pregnancy alongside age and medical history, but a past live birth is not a guarantee. Recurrent miscarriage definitions and referral thresholds vary: RCOG defines three early losses, including non-consecutive losses, while assessment after two may be appropriate depending on the history and local guidance. Many people have a successful pregnancy even when recurrent loss remains unexplained. Infections: different risks, not a single explanation Infections relevant to pregnancy include Listeria, parvovirus B19, Toxoplasma gondii, rubella, herpes simplex and cytomegalovirus (CMV). These infections can affect pregnancy, but they do not all carry the same miscarriage risk. Listeriosis, toxoplasmosis and rubella can cause pregnancy loss; parvovirus can sometimes cause fetal anaemia and loss, although most exposed or infected pregnancies are not affected. CMV can harm fetal development, and genital herpes is especially important because of infection of the baby around birth; neither should be presented as a routine explanation for every early loss. Contact your maternity team promptly after a concerning exposure, new rash, fever or genital sores. Testing and treatment depend on the infection, symptoms, timing and immunity. Repeated loss alone does not justify indiscriminate infection panels or preventive antibiotics without a specific indication. Food safety, hand hygiene and appropriate vaccination advice help reduce some risks; the live MMR vaccine is not given during pregnancy. Uterine shape, clotting and other medical factors Some differences in the shape of the uterus, or particular fibroids or scar tissue, can affect pregnancy. They do not mean a healthy pregnancy is impossible. Their importance depends on the exact finding, and surgery is not automatically beneficial. Diabetes or thyroid disease may also need review; well-controlled disease does not carry the same risk as poorly controlled disease. Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is an acquired condition associated with pregnancy complications and abnormal clotting. Lupus anticoagulant is one of the antibodies assessed for APS, not a separate diagnosis proved by one blood result. Persistent laboratory findings and the clinical history matter. Inherited thrombophilias are different: routine testing or treatment for them is not recommended for unexplained recurrent early loss. Do not start aspirin, heparin or other treatments yourself; selected patients with confirmed APS may benefit from specialist treatment. Before six weeks: get the dating right Pregnancy weeks are usually counted from the first day of the last menstrual period. In a typical cycle, the first two weeks on that calendar occur before conception. A claim that miscarriage happens in pregnancy week one or two therefore confuses menstrual dating with time since conception. Ovulation varies, and a dating scan may revise the estimate. After conception, a very early loss can occur before someone realises they are pregnant, sometimes around an expected or delayed period. This is one reason risk figures before six weeks are difficult to compare. A single early scan may be too soon to establish viability; follow-up testing or a repeat scan may be needed. Do not use a calendar estimate alone to diagnose loss. Six to twelve weeks: what a heartbeat study showed A 2008 Australian study followed 696 asymptomatic women after an ultrasound showed cardiac activity in a singleton pregnancy at their first visit between 6 weeks 2 days and 11 weeks 6 days. The subsequent miscarriage proportions were 9.4% after a visit at six completed weeks, 4.2% at seven, 1.5% at eight, 0.5% at nine and 0.7% at ten. These were remaining risks of loss before 20 weeks after that visit, not the risk in each individual week or a ten-percentage-point reduction caused by seeing a heartbeat. These older observations describe a selected group with reassuring scan findings and no symptoms; only 11 losses occurred. They are not a universal calculator for bleeding, recurrent miscarriage, multiple pregnancy or every age group. The small rise from nine to ten weeks does not establish a biological increase in risk. Discuss your own scan, dates, symptoms and history with your clinician rather than attaching certainty to a decimal. Thirteen to twenty weeks and beyond Risk generally falls as a pregnancy continues, and later miscarriage is less common than early miscarriage. It does not settle at a universal 5% at twelve weeks or stay above a fixed 5% floor thereafter. Different studies use different gestational limits, populations and starting points; a second-trimester estimate cannot be substituted for the remaining risk after a normal twelve-week scan. A reassuring scan cannot rule out every later complication. Continue antenatal appointments and seek advice about new bleeding, pain, fluid loss or other concerns. Your team may recommend additional monitoring for a particular history or diagnosis. The transition between miscarriage and other forms of pregnancy loss also depends on local definitions, so statistics ending at 20 and 24 weeks should not be treated as equivalent. Bleeding and pain: when to get help Bleeding and cramps in the abdomen, pelvis or lower back can accompany miscarriage, but they can also occur in continuing pregnancies. Some losses cause no obvious symptoms and are found on a scan. Brown or dark-red spotting does not prove that everything is safe, and bright-red blood does not by itself diagnose loss. Get same-day advice from a maternity or early-pregnancy service for any bleeding or spotting during pregnancy, even without pain, or for fluid loss or unusual discharge. Seek immediate emergency care for heavy bleeding that soaks a pad soon after putting it on, severe abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain, marked dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness. One-sided pelvic pain with possible pregnancy needs urgent assessment because of ectopic pregnancy, even without a positive test; severe pain or faintness is an emergency. Ultrasound and sometimes blood tests establish what is happening. An early uncertain result may need follow-up: colour, cramps and a risk chart cannot confirm the diagnosis. Supporting health without blaming yourself Most early losses cannot be prevented by something you do differently. They are not evidence that you failed to rest, think positively or protect the pregnancy. A balanced diet, appropriate regular activity, avoiding smoking, alcohol and recreational drugs, limiting total caffeine to no more than 200 mg daily, and attending antenatal care support health without guaranteeing an outcome. Routine bed rest is not a way to prevent miscarriage; activity advice should be individualised if there is a specific complication. Review existing conditions, medicines, food safety and recommended supplements with your team before pregnancy or as early as possible. Do not stop prescribed medicine or start hormones, blood thinners or unproven supplements on your own. Anxiety after loss deserves support too. You can ask for counselling, practical support and a plan for contact or scans in a future pregnancy, without being promised that extra monitoring prevents every loss. When investigations or genetic counselling may help After repeated loss, assessment starts with the pregnancy, personal and family history. Depending on the situation it may include uterine imaging, APS and thyroid tests, selected diabetes testing, or chromosome testing of pregnancy tissue. Testing one or both parents' chromosomes or arranging genetic counselling may be appropriate after a relevant tissue result or an individual risk assessment; a broad genetic blood panel for every couple is not the default. Ask when referral is appropriate after two or more losses, especially with a later loss, known medical condition or relevant family history. Tests do not always find a cause, and treatment is directed at an established indication rather than a risk percentage alone. A previous loss can remain emotionally significant even when the next pregnancy's outlook is good; support and careful explanations are part of care, not something you have to earn by reaching a particular number of losses. A percentage only makes sense with its population, starting point and definition of loss. Risk generally falls with advancing pregnancy, but there is no fixed 5% floor or universal heartbeat guarantee. Any pregnancy bleeding needs same-day advice; heavy bleeding, severe pain, shoulder pain or faintness need immediate emergency care. Most early losses are beyond personal control; investigations and treatments should follow the history and a clear clinical indication. Which infections can affect miscarriage risk? Listeria, toxoplasma and rubella can cause pregnancy loss, and parvovirus B19 can sometimes cause fetal anaemia and loss. CMV and herpes also matter in pregnancy, but their risks differ and they are not interchangeable explanations for early miscarriage. Ask promptly about symptoms or exposure; do not self-order broad panels or take preventive antibiotics. What is the risk between six and twelve weeks after a heartbeat is seen? It depends on the pregnancy. In the selected asymptomatic singleton group studied in 2008, remaining loss before 20 weeks after a reassuring visit was 9.4% at six completed weeks, then 4.2%, 1.5%, 0.5% and 0.7% at visits at seven, eight, nine and ten weeks. These older figures are not a personal prediction or a ten-point reduction for everyone. Does risk stay at 5% from thirteen to twenty weeks? No. Risk usually decreases as pregnancy progresses, but there is no universal 5% minimum after twelve weeks. A study's starting point, population, scan findings and definition of miscarriage change the estimate. Later symptoms still need assessment. Can I prevent a miscarriage? Most early losses cannot be prevented. Healthy eating, suitable activity, antenatal visits, avoiding smoking, alcohol and recreational drugs, and keeping caffeine at or below 200 mg daily support health. They cannot guarantee prevention, and a miscarriage is not your fault. Can miscarriage happen in the first two pregnancy weeks? With usual last-period dating, those weeks are generally before conception. Very early loss occurs after conception and may pass unrecognised around a period. Menstrual weeks and weeks since conception are different. Are a few brown spots safe to ignore? No. Colour and amount alone cannot show that a pregnancy is safe or diagnose miscarriage. Get same-day advice for any pregnancy spotting or bleeding. Heavy bleeding, severe abdominal or shoulder-tip pain, dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness need immediate emergency care. Does one loss mean I need extensive genetic tests? Usually not. The history guides testing; many early chromosome errors are chance events. Repeated losses, a relevant family history or a pregnancy-tissue finding may lead to selected tests or genetic counselling. Discuss referral rather than assuming a standard panel fits everyone. Will a uterine difference or clotting result prevent a healthy pregnancy? Not necessarily. Many people with uterine differences have healthy pregnancies. An isolated antibody result does not establish APS, and inherited thrombophilia is a separate issue. Assessment and any treatment depend on the exact diagnosis, history and specialist advice.

title: Posterior cervix: position, labour and examinations
description: What a posterior cervix means in pregnancy and outside it, how it relates to the Bishop score, and how to discuss examinations, screening and IUD placement.
body: Hearing that your cervix is posterior can sound worrying, especially near your due date. It usually describes where the cervix lies during an examination, rather than a disease. Position is one piece of information: it cannot tell you exactly when labour will begin or whether your pregnancy is healthy. What posterior and anterior mean The cervix is the lower part of the uterus that opens into the vagina. Posterior means directed towards the back of the pelvis; anterior means towards the front. Posterior does not mean towards the abdomen. A clinician may describe the cervix as posterior, central or anterior, alongside how open, long and firm it feels. Cervical direction and the tilt of the whole uterus are related anatomical observations but are not interchangeable diagnoses. An anteverted uterus tilts forwards; a retroverted uterus tilts backwards. The word posterior applied to the cervix also does not describe the baby's head position, a posterior placenta, a short cervix or cervical insufficiency. Ask which structure the finding refers to. Position during pregnancy and near the due date A posterior cervix can be a normal finding during pregnancy. As the body prepares for labour the cervix may become softer, shorter, more open and more forward-facing, but these changes do not follow an identical timetable in everyone. It is not required to move forwards at 37 or 38 weeks. Being posterior after 38 weeks does not prove that labour is far away, that the body has failed to prepare or that a caesarean birth is needed. Position alone cannot reliably predict a delivery date or rule out labour. Your team considers contractions, cervical change over time, gestation and the wellbeing of you and your baby together. The Bishop score: assessment rather than a countdown Before induction, a clinician may offer a vaginal examination to assess cervical readiness using a Bishop score. Its components include dilation (opening), effacement or length (thinning or shortening), consistency (firmness or softness), position, and the station of the baby's head in relation to the pelvis. A posterior position generally contributes fewer points than an anterior position, but it is only one component. The score helps choose an induction method and discuss likely response; it does not provide a precise time of spontaneous labour or guarantee a particular birth outcome. For example, NICE uses a score of 6 or less versus more than 6 to help select cervical-ripening or other induction approaches. Decisions also depend on your history, any previous caesarean, clinical risks and preferences, not a score you calculate at home. Can the cervix be moved forwards? There is no routine need to manually reposition a posterior cervix simply to start labour. During a necessary clinical procedure a professional may need to access or gently hold the cervix, but that is different from a treatment that permanently turns it forwards. Do not try to pull, push, stretch or repeatedly examine your own cervix to change its position. If induction is appropriate, cervical ripening with a medicine or a mechanical method may be discussed, with benefits, risks, monitoring and consent. A membrane sweep is a separate procedure requiring discussion and consent; it is not merely checking position. None of these should be attempted at home or assumed necessary because the cervix is posterior. How the cervix changes in labour Cervical ripening includes softening and shortening or thinning; opening is called dilation. These changes may begin before established labour and continue during labour. The cervix often becomes more accessible as labour progresses. Full dilation is approximately 10 cm, allowing the baby to pass through the cervix into the birth canal. The order and speed of changes vary, and one examination is a snapshot. Progress is assessed alongside contractions, the baby's descent and position, and maternal and fetal wellbeing. A posterior finding alone is neither evidence of obstructed labour nor a reason to ignore symptoms because labour supposedly cannot be starting. Examinations, discomfort and your consent A cervix that is harder to reach may make an examination more uncomfortable, but pain is not something you must tolerate. Ask why the examination is needed, what it may change in your care and whether another assessment or a later examination is reasonable. Not every antenatal visit needs a cervical check; vaginal examinations should provide useful clinical information. The professional should explain the procedure and obtain informed consent, while protecting privacy, dignity and comfort. You may decline before it starts or ask to stop at any point. Discuss a comfortable position, support person or chaperone and pain-relief options where appropriate. Do not perform home checks to confirm labour, particularly if your waters may have broken: contact the maternity team instead. Outside pregnancy: fertility, screening and IUDs A posterior cervix can also be a normal anatomical variation outside pregnancy. By itself, it is not a diagnosis of infertility and does not mean sperm cannot reach the uterus. A retroverted uterus is a separate finding and usually does not impair fertility either; associated problems such as endometriosis, pain or scarring may warrant assessment. Seek advice for persistent pelvic pain, painful sex, unusual bleeding or difficulty conceiving rather than attributing everything to position. Position may make it harder to see the cervix during cervical screening or to access it for an intrauterine device (IUD), but it does not automatically make either impossible. An experienced professional can assess the anatomy and adapt the approach. For screening, changing position or speculum size may help; you can ask to stop. Before IUD placement, uterine position and the cervix are assessed, and an individual pain-management plan should be discussed. Do not skip recommended screening or assume an IUD is unsuitable from the word posterior alone. When to contact your maternity team Ask your clinician what was found besides position, why an examination was offered and whether the finding changes the plan. If induction is proposed, ask about the reason, options and your preferences. A posterior cervix is not the same as a short or prematurely opening cervix; those findings require their own history-based assessment and sometimes ultrasound or specialist care. Contact maternity services immediately if your waters break, you have vaginal bleeding, your baby moves less than usual, or you suspect labour before 37 weeks; do not wait until the next day. Get emergency help for heavy bleeding, severe persistent abdominal pain, fainting or loss of consciousness, or if birth seems imminent with a strong urge to push. Follow your own team's labour-contact plan even if a recent examination described a posterior cervix. Posterior means towards the back of the pelvis; it is a description of cervical position, not a disease by itself. There is no mandatory forwards shift at 37–38 weeks, and position cannot give a reliable labour countdown. The Bishop score supports induction decisions; do not try to calculate it or move the cervix yourself. Examinations need a clinical purpose and consent. New pregnancy warning signs need assessment regardless of the last cervical finding. Can the cervix be posterior when I am not pregnant? Yes. It can be a normal anatomical variation. The direction of the cervix should not be confused with the tilt of the whole uterus or a diagnosis such as a short cervix. Symptoms or a separate abnormal finding may still need assessment. Does a posterior cervix prevent pregnancy? Position alone is not a diagnosis of infertility and does not mean sperm cannot reach the uterus. If conception is taking longer than expected or you have pain or other symptoms, seek an individual assessment rather than assuming position is the cause. Will cervical screening or an IUD be impossible? Not necessarily. Access may be more difficult, but a clinician can assess the anatomy and adjust the approach or arrange further help. Discuss comfort and pain management, and ask to stop if needed. The position label alone is not a reason to miss screening or rule out an IUD. Is a posterior cervix dangerous in pregnancy? By itself it is often a normal finding, not evidence of a dangerous pregnancy. It is different from shortening or opening too early. Your symptoms, history and the wellbeing of you and your baby determine whether further assessment is needed. Must it move forwards by 38 weeks? No. Cervical changes vary, and there is no required shift at a particular week. A posterior cervix after 38 weeks does not establish that labour is far away or that you need a caesarean. Can I move it or check dilation at home? Do not try to reposition, stretch or repeatedly check it. Home examination cannot reliably determine readiness or diagnose labour. Contact the maternity team for symptoms, especially if your waters may have broken. What does a lower Bishop score mean? It describes the combined findings of opening, thinning or length, softness, position and the baby's head station. It can guide cervical-ripening and induction choices, but does not predict an exact birth time or guarantee an outcome. Can I refuse or stop a vaginal examination? Yes. Ask why it is recommended and how it will affect care. Informed consent, privacy and comfort matter, and you may decline beforehand or ask to stop at any point. The team can discuss alternatives and any implications of delaying the examination.

title: Pregnancy nausea: food, fluids, medicines and when to seek help
description: Practical ways to ease pregnancy sickness, what causes it, how severe vomiting is treated and which symptoms need prompt medical care.
body: Pregnancy nausea can happen all day and can disrupt eating, work and rest. Small changes may help mild symptoms, but you do not have to endure severe sickness or wait for dehydration before asking for treatment. When pregnancy sickness happens Nausea often starts around weeks 4–7, may peak near week 9 and usually improves by weeks 16–20. Some people have symptoms for longer; others never feel sick. Its presence or absence does not reliably measure the health or sex of a baby. Vomiting that first starts after 16 weeks, or comes with abdominal pain, fever or urinary symptoms, needs assessment for other causes. Infection, gastrointestinal illness and other pregnancy conditions should not automatically be labelled morning sickness. Hormones, susceptibility and triggers Research supports an important role for GDF15, produced largely by the fetal–placental unit, and the pregnant person’s sensitivity to it. Genetics and exposure before pregnancy help explain differences in severity. This is not a failure of willpower, and experimental hormone-based approaches are not home treatments. Previous pregnancy sickness, twins or more, family history, migraine or motion sickness can increase susceptibility. Tiredness, an empty stomach, smells or travel may worsen symptoms. Skin colour is not a useful personal prediction, and nausea cannot tell you whether a baby is a girl. No single risk factor determines your experience. Recognising hyperemesis gravidarum Hyperemesis gravidarum (HG) is severe pregnancy sickness that prevents normal eating or drinking and substantially limits daily life. Estimates vary, commonly around 1–3 in 100 pregnancies. You can need treatment before major weight loss or abnormal tests develop. Persistent sickness can cause dehydration, low urine output, weight loss, nutritional or electrolyte problems, weakness, dizziness and a racing pulse. Mild-to-moderate sickness usually does not harm the baby; severe ongoing illness may affect growth and needs follow-up. Emotional distress also deserves support. Abdominal pain requires assessment rather than being assumed to be HG. Small, tolerable meals Try small meals or snacks rather than three large portions. Plain crackers, dry toast, rice, pasta or cereal may be easier to manage; a bedside snack before getting up helps some people. Avoid long gaps if an empty stomach worsens symptoms, and eat slowly. Include protein-containing foods you tolerate, such as yoghurt or well-cooked eggs, alongside other foods. Cold meals may smell less. Reduce rich, greasy or spicy foods only if they trigger you; there is no compulsory menu. Follow pregnancy food-safety guidance, and ask for dietary help if your intake stays restricted. Fluids, rest and practical comfort Sip tolerable drinks little and often rather than forcing a large glass. Some people prefer fluids between meals, but a universal thirty-minute separation is unnecessary: keeping fluids down matters more. If you cannot drink enough, do not rely on crackers or water alone to treat dehydration. Rest and help with meals, childcare or work can reduce strain. Fresh air and ventilation may ease odour triggers; gentle movement is optional when you feel well enough. Sleep or slow breathing can be comforting but does not cure HG. Avoid smoking and second-hand smoke, and ask others to keep your space smoke-free. Supplements, screens and complementary options If a prenatal supplement worsens nausea, ask about changing its timing, formulation or iron component. Bedtime is not best for everyone. Keep essential supplements such as prescribed folic acid on an agreed plan; do not stop essential medicines yourself. Take breaks or adjust screen brightness and text size if scrolling or visual strain triggers symptoms. Ginger-containing foods or drinks may help mild-to-moderate nausea; ask a pharmacist before concentrated supplements. Wrist acupressure may be an additional option. Lemon scent may feel pleasant to some people, but it is not a proven miracle cure, and evidence for aromatherapy is limited. Avoid ingesting essential oils or using unreviewed remedies instead of treatment. Medicines can be offered early Contact your maternity clinician or doctor when symptoms interfere with eating, drinking or daily activities. Pregnancy-appropriate anti-sickness medicines include selected antihistamines or doxylamine with pyridoxine; other medicines may be used if these do not work. Availability and the best choice vary, so discuss benefits, side effects and your previous responses rather than self-prescribing. Metoclopramide or ondansetron may be considered when needed; each has specific risks to discuss, including a very small possible increase in oral clefts with early ondansetron exposure. The risks of untreated severe sickness matter too. If tablets will not stay down, a clinician can arrange another route. Do not increase doses or combine remedies without advice. Assessment, day care and hospital treatment The team asks about intake, urine, weight, symptoms, medicines and daily functioning, and may check vital signs, blood or urine and arrange a scan where indicated. Urine ketones alone do not measure dehydration or determine how ill you are. Treatment can include antiemetics, intravenous fluids and correction of electrolyte problems. Some people improve with outpatient or day-care treatment; others need admission because of dehydration, continuing vomiting, abnormal blood results or inability to take essential medicines. With prolonged vomiting or very poor intake, clinicians provide thiamine (vitamin B1), particularly before intravenous glucose or artificial nutrition, to prevent serious deficiency. Ongoing severe illness may need nutrition, clot-risk and fetal-growth review. When to get urgent help Seek prompt same-day clinical advice if you cannot keep drinks or essential medicines down, are losing weight, have very dark or scant urine, feel weak or dizzy, or have fever, abdominal pain or blood in vomit. No urine for more than 8 hours or inability to retain food or fluids for 24 hours are concerning signs; do not wait for those times if you are worsening. Call emergency services for fainting or loss of consciousness, confusion, severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, severe abdominal pain or substantial bleeding. Blood in vomit with feeling unwell, faintness, abdominal pain or abnormal breathing also needs emergency care. Vomiting with severe headache, vision changes or pain under the ribs later in pregnancy needs immediate maternity assessment. After treatment, follow the medication and review plan; if sickness or dehydration returns, seek reassessment rather than waiting for a routine appointment. Pregnancy sickness can occur at any time; new vomiting after 16 weeks needs consideration of other causes. Small meals, tolerable fluids and trigger adjustments may help, but they do not replace treatment for severe sickness. HG can be treated in the community, day care or hospital according to clinical need; early medicines may help. Poor intake, dehydration signs, pain, fever or bleeding need prompt care; fainting or loss of consciousness or severe symptoms need emergency help. What causes pregnancy nausea? GDF15 from the fetal–placental unit and individual sensitivity play an important role. Previous sickness, multiple pregnancy and other factors can increase susceptibility. Skin colour is not a useful personal predictor of pregnancy sickness. Nausea does not reliably predict a baby’s sex. What complications can severe sickness cause? Dehydration, weight loss, electrolyte or vitamin deficiency and major disruption of daily life can occur. Severe ongoing illness may affect fetal growth. Do not wait for a particular amount of weight loss before seeking help. What can I eat when I feel sick? Try small, frequent portions of tolerable foods such as crackers, toast or rice, with protein foods as tolerated. Cold food may be easier. Ask for treatment and dietary help if you cannot eat or drink adequately. Does ginger or lemon cure pregnancy sickness? Ginger may help milder symptoms, but supplements need advice. Lemon scent is not a proven cure. Neither should delay anti-sickness medicine or assessment for dehydration. Must everyone with HG stay in hospital? No. Some people improve with medicines and day-care fluids; others need admission for ongoing vomiting, dehydration, abnormal tests or other medical risks. The team decides with you based on your condition. Can I take anti-sickness medicine early in pregnancy? Clinicians can offer suitable medicines, including in early pregnancy. The choice depends on benefits, specific risks and your history; untreated severe sickness also has risks. Do not self-prescribe or stop essential medicines. Must I avoid drinking with meals or take every vitamin at night? No universal schedule suits everyone. Choose tolerable fluid timing and ask about supplement timing or formulation. Maintaining hydration and an agreed essential supplement plan is more important than rigid rules. When should I call for help? Seek prompt advice for poor fluid intake, scant dark urine, dizziness, weight loss, fever, pain or blood in vomit. Fainting or loss of consciousness, confusion, severe pain, chest pain, severe breathlessness or substantial bleeding require emergency care.

title: Fetal pleural effusion: assessment, treatment and birth planning
description: Learn what fluid around a fetus’s lungs can mean, how specialists investigate it, when observation or drainage may help, and why delivery and newborn care need a personal plan.
body: Fetal pleural effusion, also called fetal hydrothorax, means fluid in the space around one or both lungs before birth. A scan finding can be frightening, but it does not by itself tell you the cause or your baby’s outcome. A fetal-medicine team can explain the findings, the uncertainty and the next steps. What the fluid can mean Fluid occupies space needed by the developing lungs and, when substantial, can displace the heart and other chest structures. Prolonged compression can limit lung growth. Some babies develop hydrops: abnormal fluid in at least two body areas, not simply a synonym for one pleural effusion. Hydrops can accompany serious circulatory compromise. Possible causes include lymphatic drainage abnormalities, genetic or chromosomal conditions, infection, anaemia, and heart or lung problems. “Primary” describes an effusion without an identified secondary cause after assessment. Some isolated small collections improve or disappear; others enlarge. Neither the amount on one scan nor a reassuring initial test guarantees the course. How it is investigated during pregnancy Ultrasound is the main test. A detailed examination considers one or both sides, fluid size and change, compression, fetal growth, amniotic fluid and signs of hydrops or other abnormalities. It can be found at different pregnancy stages; being before 32 weeks is not a diagnostic requirement. Referral timing follows the findings rather than a universal one-day work-up. Specialists may arrange fetal echocardiography to assess heart structure and function, infection or anaemia investigations, and genetic counselling and testing. Selected complex cases benefit from fetal MRI. Which tests are useful, what they can exclude, their risks and when results return should be discussed; MRI and every genetic test are not automatically necessary for everyone. Observation or treatment before birth A small stable effusion without major compression or hydrops may be monitored rather than drained. Serial scans matter even when intervention is not chosen. The 2026 international expert consensus supports close ultrasound surveillance and emphasizes that management without hydrops remains case-dependent. Ask for your actual scan schedule and a contact for changes. Large or worsening collections, marked chest pressure or hydrops may prompt consideration of fetal drainage in an experienced specialist centre. The team weighs pregnancy stage, underlying cause, fetal and maternal condition, procedural risks and the alternative of delivery when appropriate. Drainage may relieve pressure and allow lung expansion; it cannot guarantee resolution of hydrops, survival or normal long-term health. Needle drainage: thoracocentesis Under ultrasound guidance, a specialist passes a needle to remove fluid from the fetal chest. This can relieve pressure and provide a sample for selected laboratory investigations. Sampling may help identify a cause, but one fluid result does not identify or exclude every genetic condition or infection. The needle is removed after the procedure. Fluid can return, sometimes rapidly. Recurrence does not impose an automatic shunt 24–72 hours later: the amount, compression, hydrops, pregnancy stage and overall assessment guide the next choice. Repeat drainage, a shunt, continued surveillance or birth planning may be discussed. Consent should include possible bleeding, infection, membrane rupture, preterm birth and fetal injury or loss. A thoracoamniotic shunt A shunt is a small tube connecting the fetal pleural space to the amniotic cavity so fluid can drain over time. It is placed with ultrasound guidance using an introducer needle or trocar. The insertion equipment is withdrawn; the shunt, not a large needle through the mother’s abdomen, is intended to remain. Maternal and fetal pain relief or sedation and antibiotics follow the specialist protocol, not a home regimen. A shunt can block, move or stop draining; further procedures may be needed. Monitoring checks fluid, the tube’s position, fetal wellbeing and complications. Discharge that day and a single check one week later are not universal promises. Follow the centre’s written aftercare and ongoing scan plan; the 2026 consensus strongly supports at least weekly ultrasound after intervention, with earlier review when needed. Planning delivery Timing, place and mode of birth should be agreed by fetal-medicine, maternity and neonatal specialists with the family. Larger persistent effusions, hydrops, associated conditions or anticipated immediate treatment usually require a centre with neonatal intensive care and appropriate specialist services. A local hospital may suit a carefully assessed resolved or mild case, but this must be a team decision. The neonatal team must know if a chest shunt remains in place and manage it at birth; parents should not handle or remove it. Planning aims to avoid an unsafe transfer while balancing the risks of prematurity and continuing pregnancy. Neither a routine hospital birth nor a particular delivery week or caesarean is automatically right for every baby. Care after birth and longer-term outlook Some babies need a chest drain, oxygen, intubation or other breathing support. Investigations reassess the underlying cause and whether fluid persists or returns. When lymphatic leakage causes chylothorax, specialized imaging, a nutrition plan and sometimes lymphatic intervention may be considered. These are tailored treatments; families should not change feeds or attempt drainage themselves. Discharge depends on breathing, fluid control, feeding and the care available at home, rather than a fixed number of days. Some infants need home oxygen and specialist follow-up. Outcome and the risk in a later pregnancy depend on the cause, hydrops, lung development, prematurity and response to care. Ask for individual counselling, including what is still unknown and support for difficult decisions. When to contact the team urgently After any fetal procedure, contact the maternity or fetal-treatment service immediately for vaginal fluid leakage or bleeding, fever, worsening abdominal pain, contractions or feeling unwell. Reduced or changed usual fetal movements also need immediate maternity assessment; do not wait for the next scan or use a home device to reassure yourself. Follow the centre’s additional instructions. Heavy bleeding, severe pain, fainting or loss of consciousness or difficulty breathing require emergency care now. Hydrops can also be associated with serious maternal illness, including mirror syndrome; new severe headache, visual disturbance or sudden marked swelling needs immediate maternity assessment. A baby with blue or grey colour, pauses in breathing or severe breathing difficulty needs emergency help immediately. Fluid around the fetal lungs has different causes and courses; one scan cannot predict the outcome. Detailed ultrasound and selective heart, infection, anaemia and genetic investigations guide care. Small stable collections may be observed; severe compression or hydrops may justify specialist drainage. The shunt stays temporarily, while insertion needles are removed; repeat procedures and close surveillance may be needed. Delivery, newborn support and follow-up must be planned for the individual baby. Can it be diagnosed during pregnancy? Yes, usually by ultrasound. It is not limited to diagnosis before 32 weeks. Detailed specialist assessment and repeated scans clarify its extent, associated findings and changes. Does every baby need MRI and chromosome testing? No single test package fits everyone. Genetic testing is often offered after counselling; fetal heart assessment and selected infection or anaemia tests may help. MRI is useful in some complex cases. Discuss each test’s purpose and limits. Is a shunt always the treatment? No. Small stable collections may be monitored. Selected severe or worsening cases may benefit from needle drainage or a shunt. The decision balances expected benefit, risks, pregnancy stage and the underlying cause. Does the insertion needle stay until delivery? No. The needle or trocar is withdrawn after placing the small drainage tube. The shunt may remain, but it can move or block and needs surveillance. Its management at birth belongs to the neonatal team. Does fluid returning mean a shunt within three days? Not automatically. Reassessment considers how much returns, pressure, hydrops and pregnancy stage. The team explains whether another procedure, observation or delivery planning is most appropriate. What problems can occur after birth? A baby may need chest drainage or breathing support. Persistent lymphatic leakage sometimes requires specialized investigations, feeding management or intervention. Others need less treatment; recovery and follow-up vary. Can we deliver at our usual hospital? Ask the specialist team. Severe or persistent disease and likely immediate treatment generally require neonatal intensive care and specialist services at the birth site. A mild or resolved case may have a different plan.

title: Sex and intimacy during pregnancy: safety and comfort
description: Learn when pregnancy sex is usually safe, how desire and comfort may change, when to seek care, and how to approach intimacy after birth.
body: Pregnancy can change how you feel about touch, sex and your body. In an uncomplicated pregnancy, consensual sexual activity usually does not harm the baby. Your own comfort and any advice from your maternity team matter more than a timetable or a partner's expectations. Can penetration harm the baby? A penis, finger or sex toy stays in the vagina; it does not reach the baby inside the uterus. The uterine muscles and amniotic fluid provide protection. Sex does not cause miscarriage in an uncomplicated pregnancy, and it is not a reliable way to start labour. This reassurance is conditional. Bleeding, suspected leaking waters, placenta covering the cervix, early cervical opening or preterm labour can change the advice. A previous premature birth may warrant an individual plan. Ask what a restriction covers: vaginal penetration, orgasm or other activities, and when to review it. Pleasure and orgasm can feel different Some people enjoy greater sensitivity or a different orgasm; others find stimulation uncomfortable or want none. Hormonal changes and increased pelvic blood flow can contribute. Consensual intimacy may feel relaxing or connecting, but orgasm is not a treatment that improves the baby's circulation or development. Brief tightening can occur after orgasm. Stop and contact maternity care promptly for painful, persistent or regular contractions, especially before 37 weeks, or for bleeding or fluid leakage. Do not assume contractions are harmless because they followed sex. If orgasm has been restricted, ask your team for specific advice. Breast sensitivity, discharge and lubrication Breasts and nipples may become fuller and more tender; touch that used to feel pleasant may hurt. Ask before touching and adjust pressure or avoid sensitive areas. Vaginal lubrication can increase or decrease, so increased discharge does not guarantee comfortable penetration. Thin clear or milky discharge without a strong unpleasant smell is common. Itching, soreness, a bad smell, green or yellow discharge or pain passing urine needs assessment. A watery gush or continuing trickle may be leaking waters: contact maternity care promptly and avoid vaginal sex pending advice. Do not douche or treat an assumed infection without pregnancy-specific advice. Comfortable positions and pain Choose a position that lets the pregnant partner control pressure and depth, such as lying on the side, and use pillows or a water-based lubricant if helpful. Change position if dizzy or uncomfortable. Avoid pressure or injury to the abdomen, forceful penetration and restraints that impair breathing or circulation. Pain is a reason to stop, not something to endure for a partner. Persistent or recurrent pain deserves assessment rather than being attributed automatically to pregnancy. Touch, massage, kissing or time together can replace penetration when both people want that; a medical restriction may also limit some alternatives. Bleeding after sex needs advice Pregnancy makes the cervix more prone to contact bleeding, but spotting cannot establish the cause or rule out miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy or a placental problem. Contact your maternity service promptly about any vaginal bleeding, even a small amount without pain, and pause sex until advised. Get emergency help immediately for heavy bleeding that rapidly soaks a pad, severe abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain, marked dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness, particularly with bleeding. Do not wait several days for it to stop. Suspected leaking waters, fever or persistent contractions also require prompt maternity assessment. Desire, body image and consent Desire may rise, fall or vary throughout pregnancy. Nausea, fatigue, tenderness, worry, relationship strain and changes in body image can all matter; the second trimester is not a promised 'golden' phase. A partner's desire can change too. Neither person owes sex, and consent can be withdrawn at any time. Talk about what feels welcome without trying to persuade someone to change their beliefs or perform desire. Comfortable clothing, reassurance or private photographs are optional ways to relate to body changes, never requirements. Seek confidential support for distress, persistent pain, coercion or fear. No particular frequency is necessary to maintain a healthy relationship. Sexual dreams and myths about the baby's sex Sexual dreams and involuntary arousal or orgasm during sleep can occur. A dream does not predict what will happen and does not mean you must change your daytime sexual activity. If sleep-related symptoms cause pain or bleeding, seek the same clinical advice as for symptoms when awake; discuss concerns if orgasm has been restricted. Sex positions during pregnancy cannot change the baby's sex. Neither dream content nor the intensity of orgasm identifies it. There is no need to try a special position or achieve orgasm for the baby's benefit. Preventing sexually transmitted infections Pregnancy does not protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and many have no symptoms. Discuss recommended prenatal testing and any new exposure with your team regardless of how many partners you have. Condoms and dental dams reduce risk during vaginal, anal or oral sex, but do not eliminate every skin-to-skin infection. Avoid sexual contact with active mouth or genital herpes sores, and seek advice about a suspected or diagnosed STI; partners may need testing and treatment too. Follow the clinician's advice about resuming activity. Clean hands and toys, use a new condom for each partner or body site, and do not transfer a body part or toy from anus to vagina without washing and changing its condom. Oral sex, anal sex and toys If activity is otherwise permitted, oral sex or a clean sex toy can be options. Do not blow air into the vagina: forcing air inside can rarely cause a dangerous air embolism. Avoid oral contact with cold sores or genital lesions, and use appropriate barriers for STI protection. Anal sex can be painful with haemorrhoids or cause tears; avoid it if painful or bleeding and do not assume it bypasses a maternity restriction. Lubrication and a new condom help reduce friction and infection risk. Keep anal and vaginal contact separate, clean toys according to their instructions and avoid forceful insertion. Intimacy after birth There is no universal date when everyone is ready, and reaching six weeks is not automatic clearance. Recovery depends on bleeding, tears or stitches, caesarean wounds, complications, pain and personal readiness. Ask your team about healing; restart gradually only when comfortable and wanted, with lubricant if needed. Persistent pain, fever, foul discharge or worsening bleeding needs assessment. Pregnancy can occur from three weeks after birth, before the first period and while breastfeeding. Discuss contraception before resuming sex that could lead to pregnancy: suitable methods and starting times differ. Breastfeeding is not automatically reliable contraception. Affection and nonpenetrative intimacy can continue at a pace that suits both partners without a duty to return to a previous sex life. Sex is usually safe in an uncomplicated pregnancy; specific restrictions need individual advice. Comfort and freely given consent matter throughout pregnancy and after birth. Any pregnancy bleeding or suspected leaking waters needs prompt advice; severe symptoms need emergency care. Protect against infections and plan postpartum contraception before pregnancy becomes possible again. Can penetration touch or injure the baby? In an uncomplicated pregnancy, penetration remains in the vagina and cannot reach the baby in the uterus. This does not override advice to avoid penetration for bleeding, leaking waters or another complication. Does sex or orgasm cause miscarriage? Sex does not cause miscarriage in an uncomplicated pregnancy. Brief tightening may follow orgasm, but persistent pain, contractions, bleeding or leaking fluid needs maternity advice. Follow any individual restriction. Is a little bleeding after sex safe to ignore? No. The cervix can bleed after contact, but the cause cannot be confirmed at home. Contact maternity care promptly for any bleeding. Heavy bleeding, severe pain, shoulder-tip pain, dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness needs immediate emergency help. Is pain during pregnancy sex normal? Stop if it hurts. A different position or lubricant may help discomfort, but persistent or recurring pain needs assessment. You do not have to continue penetration or another activity. Are sexual dreams or sleep orgasms a warning? They can occur without conscious control and are not predictions. Pain, bleeding or leaking fluid still needs clinical advice; ask your team about concerns if orgasm has been restricted. Can a position change the baby's sex? No. Sex positions during an existing pregnancy do not change the baby's sex, and dreams or orgasm strength do not reveal it. What if I do not want sex? You do not have to have it or restore a previous level of desire. Talk about boundaries and any forms of closeness you want. Seek support for pain, distress, pressure or fear. Must we wait exactly six weeks after birth? There is no single restart date. Healing, complications, pain and readiness guide the decision with your care team. Plan contraception: pregnancy is possible from three weeks after birth even without a period and while breastfeeding.

title: Feeling averse to your partner during pregnancy
description: Understanding changes in smell, comfort, desire and feelings during pregnancy, with practical support, consent and signs that need help.
body: You may find a partner’s smell unpleasant, want less touch or feel unusually distant during pregnancy. These experiences deserve understanding, but calling them a pregnancy “craving” does not establish a diagnosis or explain every relationship concern. You can seek comfort and support without forcing affection or dismissing your own feelings. What people mean by partner aversion The phrase may describe nausea around a partner’s smell, irritation, less sexual desire or wanting personal space. These are different experiences and can have different causes; they are not a single established pregnancy diagnosis. A change in desire does not by itself prove that love has ended, and wanting distance does not make you a bad partner. Do not assume every concern is harmless, hormonal or temporary. Difficulties may reflect pregnancy symptoms, unmet support needs, a mental health condition, existing relationship problems or more than one factor. There is no guarantee that feelings will return on a particular timetable. Hormones, physical changes and emotional strain Pregnancy can change mood, appetite and sexual interest. Nausea, fatigue, tender breasts, back discomfort, changes in body shape and worries about pregnancy or the future may make closeness less appealing. These effects vary and are not evidence that your body is unattractive or that you are to blame. Hormones are a possible contributor, not a complete explanation for depression, anxiety or conflict. A partner may not understand how demanding pregnancy feels; dismissing symptoms or leaving all practical work to you can add strain. Neither pregnant people nor partners should be reduced to stereotypes about irrationality, blame or ignorance. When smells trigger nausea A previously acceptable perfume, lotion, shampoo, cooking smell or tobacco smell may now provoke nausea. If it feels safe to discuss, identify the particular trigger and ask for a practical change: fragrance-free products, avoiding that scent nearby, fresh air or some space. Switching to a stronger fragrance to cover a smell may not help. This is not proof that someone is dirty or that the relationship is failing. Keep the home and car smoke-free and support smoking cessation; secondhand smoke is a health concern beyond its smell. Ask your maternity team for help if nausea or vomiting is disrupting eating, drinking or daily life rather than trying to endure it through changes at home alone. Communicating needs without promising a quick fix If the relationship is safe, choose a calm moment and describe what you experience and what would help: “That scent makes me nauseated; could we avoid it?” or “I need rest and help with dinner.” A partner can listen, share tasks, learn about pregnancy and ask before offering touch or advice. You may invite a partner to discuss symptoms with your clinician if you want, but you can also ask to be seen alone. Support can come from friends, family or professionals as well as a partner. Pleasant memories may be comforting if you choose them; they should not be used to persuade you that genuine concerns are imaginary or that you must remain in an unsafe relationship. Affection and sex remain choices You do not owe hugs, kissing, sex or loving words to prevent a partner from feeling rejected. Consent matters every time, and you can change your mind. If both people want it, conversation, shared quiet time or comfortable nonsexual affection may offer closeness; choosing space is also valid. Do not push through pain or distress. Whether sexual activity is medically suitable depends on your pregnancy and any individual restrictions; permission to have sex is never an obligation. Seek clinical advice about pain, bleeding or other pregnancy symptoms rather than treating them as a relationship exercise. When mood or sickness needs professional support Speak with your midwife or clinician if low mood, loss of enjoyment, hopelessness, irritability or anxiety persists or affects daily life. Help is available even without a diagnosis. Assessment can distinguish several overlapping difficulties and lead to talking therapy, practical support or individualized treatment; do not change prescribed mental health medicine on your own. Contact your maternity team promptly if vomiting prevents adequate fluids or food, particularly with very dark or reduced urine, dizziness or weight loss. Blood in vomit, significant abdominal pain or fever needs urgent assessment. Severe pregnancy sickness is not simply a dislike of your partner and may need medical treatment. Safety comes before repairing the relationship Fear, threats, controlling behaviour, humiliation, violence or pressure for unwanted sex should not be explained away as pregnancy hormones. Abuse is not your fault. Seek private support from a clinician or local domestic-abuse service when it is safe to do so; you do not need to confront a partner or attend a joint conversation before getting help. Consider whether a device or message can be seen by someone who may harm you. If you are in immediate danger, or there is an immediate risk of harming yourself or someone else, contact emergency services now. New hallucinations or strongly held beliefs disconnected from reality require urgent medical assessment. An app, waiting for pregnancy to progress or trying harder to be affectionate cannot assess or resolve these emergencies. Changes in smell tolerance, comfort and desire can happen, but partner aversion is not a diagnosis that explains every concern. Ask for practical support and reduced triggers when safe; no one owes affection or sex. Persistent distress, depression, anxiety or poor intake from vomiting deserves clinical help. Take fear, coercion and abuse seriously; immediate danger requires emergency help. What does partner aversion in pregnancy mean? It is an informal description of experiences such as nausea around a partner’s smell, less desire, irritation or needing space. It is not one established diagnosis, and the underlying reasons can differ. Is it all caused by hormones? No. Hormonal and physical changes can contribute, but symptoms, stress, support needs, mental health and relationship circumstances also matter. Do not dismiss distress or unsafe behaviour as hormones. What can I do if my partner’s smell makes me sick? If safe, explain the specific trigger and try fragrance-free products, avoiding the scent nearby, fresh air or space. Keep shared spaces smoke-free and support quitting smoking. Get maternity advice when nausea or vomiting interferes with food, fluids or daily life. Is it normal, and will it definitely pass? Changes in desire and comfort can occur during pregnancy, but not every concern is harmless or temporary. There is no guaranteed recovery timetable. Persistent distress, symptoms or relationship worries deserve support. Should I hug or have sex even when I do not want to? No. Affection and sex require free consent, which can be withdrawn. Choose closeness only if you want it and it feels comfortable; medical permission for sex does not create a duty to have it. When should I speak with a clinician? Ask for help with persistent low mood, loss of enjoyment, hopelessness, anxiety or difficulty coping. Seek prompt help for vomiting with poor intake or dehydration signs, and urgent assessment for vomiting blood, significant pain or fever. Do not change prescribed mental health medicine yourself. What if I am afraid of my partner? Seek confidential support from a clinician or local domestic-abuse service when safe. You do not need a joint discussion or proof that pregnancy caused your feelings. Immediate danger or immediate risk of harm to yourself or others needs emergency services now.

title: Exercise, activity and miscarriage: when pregnancy needs a different plan
description: Ordinary activity and suitable exercise do not cause miscarriage in an uncomplicated pregnancy. Learn about benefits, warning signs and why routine bed rest is not a treatment.
body: It is understandable to question every walk, workout or busy day after a pregnancy loss or a worrying symptom. Most early miscarriages cannot be explained by something a parent did. Suitable activity is usually helpful in an uncomplicated pregnancy; symptoms and particular complications need assessment and an individual plan. Neither exercising harder nor staying completely still can guarantee a pregnancy outcome. Does being active cause miscarriage? For a healthy person with an uncomplicated pregnancy, regular appropriate physical activity does not increase miscarriage risk. Everyday movement is not a reason to blame yourself for a loss. Pregnancy changes balance, stamina and comfort, but does not automatically make the body too fragile for movement. Discuss your usual activities at antenatal visits and adjust them as pregnancy progresses. The phrase ‘too much activity’ has no universal medical cutoff. A familiar workout, a new intense training programme, heavy physical work and exercise despite bleeding are different situations. Your previous fitness, symptoms, medical conditions, surroundings and pregnancy complications matter. Rest when tired and stop for pain or warning signs rather than using exhaustion as a training target. Why miscarriage happens: risk is not an explanation for one loss Many early losses involve a chance chromosome problem in the developing pregnancy; often no individual cause is found. Increasing parental age can affect risk. Loss can be devastating, and a list of possible factors cannot prove why it happened to you. You and your partner can ask for emotional support as well as a medical review. Possible contributors in selected cases include uterine structural differences, some fibroids or scars, poorly controlled diabetes or thyroid disease, hormonal conditions and antiphospholipid syndrome (APS). Well-controlled diabetes or thyroid disease does not carry the same implication. The significance of a fibroid or scar depends on its location and other findings. Recurrent or later losses can need a different investigation pathway. Inherited thrombophilias such as Factor V Leiden are not interchangeable with APS: evidence linking them to recurrent early miscarriage is uncertain, and routine testing or blood-thinning treatment is not a universal solution. Broad claims that the immune system ‘rejects’ the pregnancy are unproven. Lupus or significant heart, kidney or liver disease needs specialist care, rather than a self-diagnosis or a blanket prediction of miscarriage. Illness, medicines and exposures need specific advice Some serious infections, persistent fever, injury and substance exposures can affect pregnancy; this does not mean every cold, food or everyday mishap causes loss. Avoid tobacco, alcohol and recreational drugs, seek support to stop, and follow pregnancy food-safety advice. A fever or significant abdominal injury warrants prompt clinical advice. Do not use a general cause list to conclude that a particular meal or action caused a miscarriage. Check prescribed, non-prescription and herbal products with your clinician or pharmacist; do not stop essential prescribed treatment yourself. Radiation risk depends on the type and dose. Necessary diagnostic imaging is not automatically unsafe or a reason to end a pregnancy: tell the imaging team you are pregnant so they can choose an appropriate test. A suspected unusual exposure needs an individual assessment, not a blanket reassurance or warning. Benefits of suitable activity in a low-risk pregnancy Regular activity can ease constipation and back discomfort, support mood, fitness and healthy weight gain, and help maintain muscle strength and stamina. It may reduce the chance of gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia and caesarean birth. Comfortable movement and strength work can support joints and daily tasks; exercise cannot guarantee an easier birth or prevent depression, miscarriage or every pregnancy complication. Movement also matters when considering circulation and the harms of prolonged immobility. It does not replace an individual blood-clot risk assessment or prescribed clot prevention. A previous clot, new one-sided leg symptoms or a complication needs medical advice, rather than an instruction simply to walk more. Choose activities you enjoy and can sustain without pain or undue strain. How much activity is reasonable? If your care team finds no contraindication, a common goal is at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity a week, spread into manageable sessions. At moderate effort you can still talk comfortably. Walking and swimming are options; suitable strengthening can complement them. If previously inactive, begin with short sessions and build gradually. Some activity is worthwhile even when you cannot reach a target. Someone already accustomed to vigorous exercise may be able to continue an adapted routine after discussion with their clinician. Pregnancy is not the time to suddenly start an unfamiliar intense programme or push through exhaustion. There is no single safe weight, running distance or heart-rate limit for everyone. Heavy work or competitive sport may need occupational or specialist advice, particularly with symptoms or complications. Adapt exercise to the changing body Drink enough, avoid overheating, use comfortable supportive clothing and footwear, warm up and cool down. Adjust for balance, joint discomfort and changing energy needs. Avoid contact sports, activities with a substantial fall or abdominal-impact risk, and scuba diving. Later in pregnancy, avoid prolonged exercise lying flat on your back; change position if dizzy or unwell. Do not exercise through illness, bleeding, persistent pain, painful regular contractions, fluid leakage, faintness, chest symptoms or calf swelling. Stop and obtain the appropriate assessment. A reasonable activity plan can change from one week to another. A qualified pregnancy-exercise professional can help with technique after clinical clearance, but cannot diagnose the cause of a symptom. Complications require a tailored plan, not automatic immobility Bleeding or spotting, pain, contractions, a short or insufficient cervix, a cervical stitch, a previous loss or preterm birth, twins and a subchorionic haematoma all deserve appropriate review. Some conditions mean exercise should pause or change. They do not all mean that complete bed rest prevents miscarriage. A previous loss or twin pregnancy alone is not an instruction to stop all everyday movement. After a cervical stitch, short postoperative recovery advice differs from months of bed rest; RCOG does not routinely recommend ongoing bed rest. A subchorionic haematoma is blood around the pregnancy membranes or placenta and does not inevitably mean loss. Its symptoms, size and location guide follow-up; clinicians may advise temporary limits on strenuous activity or sex, but evidence does not support bed rest as a cure. Follow your own team’s specific instructions and ask when they should be reviewed. Why routine bed rest is generally discouraged SMFM guidance, reaffirmed in 2025 and endorsed by ACOG, advises against routine activity restriction for a short cervix or threatened/arrested preterm labour, and against routine restriction or admission solely to prevent preterm birth in multiple pregnancy. Restriction has not demonstrated the hoped-for benefit in these settings. This does not remove a need for hospital treatment or monitoring when there is another clinical reason. Prolonged bed rest can cause muscle and bone loss, increase clot risk and create emotional, family and financial strain. An individual temporary restriction is different from routine immobility. If advised to restrict activity, ask which movements, work, exercise or sexual activities are limited, why, for how long, what clot-prevention steps are needed and when the plan will be reviewed. Seek prompt clarification rather than independently abandoning an active treatment plan. When to stop and get urgent help Contact your maternity or early-pregnancy team urgently for any vaginal bleeding or spotting, new fluid leakage, persistent abdominal pain or regular painful contractions. Heavy bleeding, severe abdominal or shoulder pain, fainting or collapse needs immediate emergency care; an ectopic pregnancy is one possible cause, including before a pregnancy has been confirmed. Do not lie down and wait for exercise-related symptoms to disappear instead of seeking assessment. Get immediate medical help for chest pain, breathing difficulty, a temperature of 38°C or higher, a severe persistent headache or visual change, or new one-sided leg pain/swelling. These can indicate serious complications, including a blood clot. Once you are aware of the baby’s usual movements, a reduction or stopping needs immediate maternity advice. Stop activity, tell the team you are pregnant and do not delay to track symptoms or reach an exercise target. Suitable exercise in an uncomplicated pregnancy does not increase miscarriage risk; loss is not evidence that you were too active. Choose a gradual, comfortable routine and discuss symptoms, strenuous work or pregnancy complications with your care team. Routine bed rest has no established benefit in several common risk situations and can cause harm; temporary specific limits need a clear reason and review. Bleeding, pain, fluid leakage or maternal warning signs need assessment, with immediate emergency care for severe symptoms. What are the common causes of miscarriage? Many early losses involve chromosome changes or have no identified cause. Selected medical, uterine or hormonal conditions can contribute, but a risk factor cannot explain one person’s loss. Recurrent or later losses may need specialist investigation. What benefits can activity offer during pregnancy? Appropriate activity supports fitness, mood, muscle strength and healthy weight gain, and can ease constipation or back discomfort. It may reduce some pregnancy complications, but cannot guarantee a particular birth or prevent miscarriage. Is vigorous activity always forbidden? No. An experienced exerciser with an uncomplicated pregnancy may continue an adapted routine after discussion. Starting unfamiliar intense exercise, ignoring symptoms or working to exhaustion is different. Individual limits matter more than a vague label of ‘too much’. When should pregnancy activity be limited? Symptoms, some medical conditions and certain obstetric complications may require pausing or changing exercise while assessed. Bleeding, contractions, cervical problems, a stitch or haematoma need a specific plan. Previous loss or twins do not automatically justify complete bed rest. Does staying in bed prevent miscarriage? Routine bed rest is not a proven miscarriage-prevention treatment and can cause physical and emotional harm. Treatment should address the actual condition. Ask for the purpose and duration of any restriction and arrange review rather than changing an active plan yourself. Should I stop prescribed medicines to protect the pregnancy? Do not stop essential prescribed treatment without medical advice. Check all medicines and herbal products with a clinician or pharmacist; untreated illness can also harm pregnancy. Necessary diagnostic imaging should be individually assessed rather than automatically avoided. If bleeding starts after exercise, should I just rest? Stop exercise and obtain urgent maternity or early-pregnancy advice, even for spotting. Seek emergency care immediately for heavy bleeding, severe abdominal or shoulder pain, fainting or collapse.
