Seek prompt medical advice if you are unwell, cannot keep fluids down or symptoms persist; the urgent and emergency signs below should guide how quickly to act. Know when sun exposure needs urgent help Get urgent medical advice for blistered or swollen sunburn, or after sun exposure if you have a very high temperature, feel hot, cold or shivery, feel very tired, dizzy or sick, or develop headache or muscle cramps. During pregnancy, a temperature of 38°C or higher, a headache that does not go away, gets worse or starts suddenly with severe pain, vision changes, vaginal bleeding or fluid leakage, severe abdominal pain, whether sudden, persistent or worsening, contractions before term or reduced fetal movements needs immediate maternity assessment. Do not assume these symptoms are just sunburn. After heat exposure, call emergency services for confusion, poor coordination, a seizure, actual fainting or loss of consciousness, very high temperature, hot skin without sweating, a fast heartbeat, fast breathing or breathlessness. Also call if you remain unwell after 30 minutes of cooling, rest and fluids; do not wait 30 minutes when an emergency sign is already present. Keep cooling while help comes, do not drive yourself, and do not give drinks to someone confused or not fully conscious. You do not need every sign to seek help. Plan shade, clothing and sunscreen together Check local UV and heat forecasts, choose cooler times for outdoor activity and take shade breaks. Use a broad-brimmed hat, UV-protective sunglasses and light, comfortable clothing that covers the skin. Cloud, a breeze or a comfortable air temperature does not guarantee low UV exposure. Protection is still useful after one accidental burn; blame does not help healing. Choose a broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher for exposed, intact skin. Mineral products containing zinc oxide or titanium dioxide may be helpful for sensitive pregnancy skin. This does not mean every other approved sunscreen is proven harmful to the fetus. Ask about a suitable formulation if a product irritates you or you are unsure about its ingredients. Use the product well and review uncertain symptoms Follow the sunscreen label, generally applying before going outside and reapplying at least every 2 hours outdoors and after swimming, sweating or towelling. Cover easy-to-miss areas such as ears, neck and tops of feet. Water resistance is not waterproofing, and SPF is not a number of safe hours. Check expiry and protect the container from excessive heat. Keep burned skin covered from direct sun while it heals; sunscreen cannot treat an existing burn. Bring the product names, exposure time, pregnancy stage, symptoms and medicines used when seeking advice. If the rash is unusual, worsening or not improving, get it examined rather than repeatedly changing home remedies. A clinician can assess both skin care and any pregnancy concern. Leave the sun, cool gently and protect the skin while it heals. Blisters or feeling unwell need advice; heatstroke signs need emergency help. Paracetamol may be appropriate; NSAIDs and numbing products need pregnancy-specific checks. Water and sunscreen do not make tanning safe or guarantee a pregnancy outcome. Use shade, clothing and broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher together. Can I tan safely if I use sunscreen and drink water? No. A UV tan reflects skin damage. Water supports hydration and sunscreen reduces exposure, but neither makes tanning or prolonged heat safe. Choose shade and protection rather than intentional tanning. Does sunburn mean my baby has been harmed? A skin burn alone does not establish fetal harm or measure core temperature. Tell your maternity team about significant heat exposure, illness or a worrying episode so they can assess timing and symptoms. Avoid both automatic reassurance and assuming damage. What can I do for the pain? Use a cool damp cloth or cool bath, gentle moisturising and loose clothing. Paracetamol is generally the preferred painkiller when needed in pregnancy; check the product, dose and your health circumstances. Severe or persistent pain needs assessment. Should I pop a blister? No. Leave it intact, keep it clean and obtain prompt advice about assessment and protection. Follow a specific wound-care plan if it opens, and seek review for worsening pain, swelling, spreading redness, pus or fever. Are aloe and numbing creams automatically safe? No. A suitable aloe-containing moisturiser may soothe intact skin, but raw leaves and oral aloe are not equivalent. Ask before using benzocaine, lidocaine or a medicated mixture on sunburn; the formulation, skin condition, area and pregnancy stage matter. Can I use ibuprofen or my prescribed aspirin? Do not start ibuprofen or another NSAID for sunburn without pregnancy-specific advice, especially from 20 weeks. Low-dose aspirin prescribed for a pregnancy condition is different: keep to the prescribed plan and do not stop or increase it for this burn. When is it an emergency? After heat exposure, confusion, poor coordination, seizures, fainting or loss of consciousness, very high temperature, hot non-sweating skin, a fast heartbeat, rapid breathing or breathlessness needs emergency help. So does remaining unwell after 30 minutes of cooling, rest and fluids. Do not wait for all signs or delay for 30 minutes if one is already present. Which sunscreen should I choose? Use broad-spectrum, water-resistant SPF 30 or higher with shade and clothing. Zinc oxide or titanium dioxide can suit sensitive skin. Follow the label and reapply at least every 2 hours outdoors and after water, sweat or towelling; keep healing burned skin out of direct sun.

title: Melatonin in pregnancy: safety, alternatives and better sleep
description: Understand the limits of melatonin pregnancy evidence, how sleep medicines are assessed, and practical ways to address insomnia and its causes.
body: Sleepless nights can leave you desperate for relief. Melatonin may look like a gentle option, but being a natural hormone does not establish the safety of a supplement in pregnancy. You deserve help with sleep, including a review of the cause and a treatment plan that fits your pregnancy. Start with the sleep problem, not the bottle Tell your midwife or doctor if difficulty falling asleep, repeated waking or early waking is affecting daytime function. You do not need to wait until you have struggled for months before asking for help. Note when the problem began, your sleep schedule, medicines and supplements, and what wakes you. Distinguish lack of an opportunity to sleep from being unable to sleep when you have that opportunity; the practical support needed may differ. Natural melatonin and a supplement are different exposures The body releases melatonin as part of its response to darkness and its daily sleep–wake rhythm. Pregnancy changes this physiology. A tablet, liquid or gummy adds an external dose; its effect cannot be inferred from the fact that your body already makes the hormone. Melatonin is biologically active. Depending on the country and product, it may be a prescription medicine or a dietary supplement. A natural label, easy online purchase or a friend's reassuring experience is not evidence that a particular preparation is suitable for you. What pregnancy research can and cannot tell us Human pregnancy evidence is limited. Small studies have not established a clear major harm signal, but they cannot rule out uncommon effects or answer every question about dose, timing and children's later development. Lack of demonstrated harm is not the same as established safety. Some research concerns specific pregnancy complications rather than treatment of insomnia. Those studies do not demonstrate that melatonin improves pregnancy sleep or should be taken to protect a baby. Current NHS and specialist advice generally discourages routine use during pregnancy because the evidence is insufficient. There is no universal safe dose or trimester A smaller dose, occasional use or being past the first trimester does not create a proven safety threshold. There is no standard melatonin dose that this guide can recommend for pregnancy. Do not copy a general adult dose or an online sleep schedule. If a clinician recommends it for your particular circumstances, ask about the expected benefit, uncertainties, exact product, dose, duration and review date. Follow that individual plan and check before increasing, switching formulations or adding another sleep aid. Already taken it, or already prescribed it? Taking melatonin before realizing you were pregnant does not by itself show that your baby has been harmed. Record the product, ingredients, strength, amount and dates, and contact your maternity clinician, prescriber or pharmacist for an exposure review. If you take it regularly on prescription, discuss continuing or stopping with the prescriber rather than making an unsupported change. The decision should consider why it was prescribed, how severe the sleep problem is, other conditions and available alternatives; reassurance should not be presented as a guarantee. Product quality and other medicines matter In the United States, supplements do not receive FDA approval for safety and effectiveness before sale; this is different from saying they are completely unregulated. In the UK, melatonin is prescription-only. Rules and approved products differ elsewhere, so check locally with a pharmacist. Supplement contents may differ from the label. Review every ingredient, including herbs or other sedating substances, and show all your medicines to the clinician. Interactions matter, including with blood-thinning or epilepsy medicines. Do not use alcohol to help you sleep or combine sedating products on your own; store them away from children. Diphenhydramine and doxylamine are not automatic substitutes These sedating antihistamines have more pregnancy experience than melatonin, but a clinician still needs to decide whether a medicine is needed. Diphenhydramine studies have not shown a consistent birth-defect pattern; excessive or prolonged use is a different situation from occasional recommended use. Diphenhydramine and temazepam should not be used together during pregnancy; discuss any existing combination with your prescriber. Doxylamine is also used with vitamin B6 for pregnancy nausea, with substantial reassuring data for that treatment. This does not prove that every sleep product or dose is appropriate, or that it effectively treats insomnia. Check the active ingredients rather than relying on a brand name. No universal full-tablet or half-tablet schedule is advised here. Build a manageable sleep routine Aim for a reasonably regular waking and bedtime routine, a quiet dark bedroom and a calm wind-down without phone or television use in bed. Gentle breathing or relaxation can help you settle. If you are awake and frustrated, a quiet activity out of bed until sleepy may help, provided you can move safely. Avoid caffeine late in the day and long late naps if they worsen night sleep. Keep suitable daytime activity and use pillows for comfort. After 28 weeks, go to sleep on either side; if you wake on your back, turn onto your side. Adjust habits realistically around work, caring responsibilities and needed rest. Consider structured treatment for persistent insomnia Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, or CBT-I, addresses sleep-related worry and habits through a structured programme. It is an important non-medicine option, rather than simply being told to relax. Ask about a trained practitioner or an appropriate supported remote programme. A clinician can tailor the plan to pregnancy and your health. Do not improvise severe sleep restriction from internet advice. If habits alone have not helped, that is a reason to seek further assessment, not a personal failure or proof that you need a supplement. Treat what is keeping you awake Reflux, nausea, pain, leg cramps or restless legs, frequent urination and discomfort with fetal movement can interrupt sleep. Discuss persistent symptoms so treatment can target the cause. Loud snoring with breathing pauses or waking gasping also deserves assessment for a sleep disorder. Anxiety, low mood and practical stress may be just as important as physical discomfort. Tell your maternity team if worry is hard to manage or you lose interest in things you usually enjoy. Treatment, counselling and practical support can be part of the sleep plan; a sedative alone does not resolve these problems. Recognize medicine side effects and urgent reactions Melatonin may cause daytime sleepiness, headache, nausea or dizziness. Do not drive or use machinery when impaired. Seek urgent medical advice for new vision changes, feeling faint or actually fainting, confusion or spinning dizziness, bleeding that will not stop, unexplained bruising or blood in the urine. After a medicine, call emergency services for sudden lip, mouth, tongue or throat swelling; trouble breathing or swallowing; blue, grey or pale skin or lips; sudden severe confusion, drowsiness or dizziness; or collapse with inability to wake. Any one may be enough: do not wait for all signs or a rash, and do not drive yourself. If you cannot keep yourself safe, seek emergency help too. Agree how you will review the plan Bring your sleep notes and the actual medicine packages to the appointment. Ask what problem each treatment targets, how benefit will be judged, which effects to report and when to reassess. If a medicine is chosen, use only the agreed product and instructions. Review the plan if symptoms continue, daytime safety is affected or a new medicine or pregnancy issue arises. The aim is useful rest and treatment of the underlying problem, with uncertainties discussed openly: not perfect sleep every night or a promise that a product is risk-free. Melatonin pregnancy data are limited; natural does not mean proven safe. No universal dose or post-first-trimester safety threshold has been established. Review previous exposure or a prescription with a clinician rather than assuming harm or safety. Antihistamines require a product-specific decision; nausea-treatment evidence is not proof of insomnia benefit. Sleep habits, CBT-I and treatment of physical or emotional causes all matter. Is melatonin safe during pregnancy? Safety and benefit for pregnancy insomnia are not sufficiently established. Current advice generally discourages routine use; your clinician can consider the particular reason for treatment and alternatives. Why be cautious if it is natural? A supplement adds a dose beyond the body's own production. Pregnancy effects are incompletely studied, and product content and regulation vary. A natural claim does not resolve these uncertainties. My doctor said I can use it occasionally. Is that different? An individualized recommendation can differ from general advice. Confirm the exact product, amount, duration and follow-up, including what to do if it does not help. Occasional use is not a proven universal safety category. What if I took it before knowing I was pregnant? This does not itself demonstrate harm. Keep the package and record how much and when you took it, then ask your clinician or pharmacist to review the exposure and next steps. Can I take diphenhydramine or doxylamine instead? Sometimes a clinician selects an antihistamine, but neither is an automatic replacement. Suitability, ingredients, other medicines, daytime sedation and duration matter. Do not copy a 25 mg or half-tablet recommendation from another person. Does doxylamine with vitamin B6 prove that a sleep aid is safe? That combination has strong pregnancy experience for nausea and vomiting. It does not establish that every doxylamine preparation or sleep regimen is appropriate or effective for insomnia. What can I try without a medicine? A regular routine, less late caffeine, a quiet dark room, comfortable positioning and relaxation can help. Ask about CBT-I and treatment of reflux, nausea, pain, restless legs, breathing problems or anxiety if difficulties persist. When should I ask for more help? Ask when sleep problems affect daily function or persist despite simple measures. Seek urgent advice for concerning medicine effects, and emergency help for serious allergic symptoms, inability to wake after collapse or inability to keep yourself safe.

title: Squats during pregnancy: choosing a comfortable, supported movement
description: How to adapt pregnancy squats with a stable support, comfortable stance and depth, suitable loading, pelvic-pain advice and clear signs to stop.
body: Squats can be part of activity in an uncomplicated pregnancy, but the right version depends on your health, previous training and how you feel today. You do not need to squat deeply, add weights or keep doing a painful movement to prepare for birth. Start with your pregnancy and your starting point Discuss activity at antenatal appointments, especially before starting unfamiliar training. A comfortable bodyweight squat may suit someone who is new to exercise; someone already lifting may need to adapt a familiar routine. Neither pregnancy alone nor a previous workout proves that a particular squat is suitable now. Get an individual plan before exercising if you have a low-lying placenta or placenta praevia, a short or weak cervix, a cervical stitch, bleeding, risk of preterm birth or another pregnancy complication. Significant heart or lung disease, anaemia or uncontrolled illness also needs advice. A past knee, hip or back injury calls for assessment of present symptoms, not an automatic lifelong ban. What squats can (and cannot) offer A squat trains the legs and hips and practises the movement used to sit down and stand up. General pregnancy activity can support fitness, sleep and mood. A squat is one possible part of that activity, not a proven way to prevent every pregnancy discomfort or guarantee an easier vaginal birth. Squatting is also one possible labour position, but practising it does not mean you must use it during birth or that it will start labour. Your comfort, pelvic symptoms, monitoring and maternity advice matter. Squats do not replace specific pelvic-floor exercises: learning to relax those muscles fully matters as well as contracting them. Set up a stable space Choose a clear, non-slip floor and supportive footwear. If you need support, use a fixed rail or another genuinely stable surface that will not slide or tip. A helper can be nearby, but should not pull you through a movement or be your only protection against falling. Start with your feet roughly hip- to shoulder-width apart and adjust only as needed for comfort and room for your bump. Keep weight across both feet with the heels down. A very wide “sumo” stance is optional, not a pregnancy requirement, and may aggravate pelvic girdle pain. Try a small, controlled squat With your chest comfortably lifted and neck and back in a comfortable neutral position, move your hips back and bend your knees slowly, as though beginning to sit. Let your knees follow the direction of your toes rather than collapsing inward. Keep breathing; breathe out as you rise without bearing down or holding your breath. Go only as low as you can control and return from comfortably. A shallow bend is useful; your thighs do not have to reach horizontal. Stop the set when control or balance changes. Avoid bouncing at the bottom, forcing a stretch or chasing a repetition target. Ask a pregnancy-experienced instructor or physiotherapist to check uncertain technique. Choose the version that fits today A supported shallow squat or a slow sit-to-stand from a stable chair may be easier than a deep free-standing squat. A higher chair can reduce the effort needed to rise. Use a chair that will not move, and adjust the movement if it produces pain, pressure or instability. Wall or fitness-ball squats are other options, but a rolling ball adds a balance demand and is not essential. Use appropriate supervision if choosing one. Bodyweight, chair-assisted, wider-stance and deeper squats are alternatives, not a list you must complete. Choose the simplest comfortable version. Adapt through pregnancy, not by a fixed trimester rule There is no trimester in which every person must stop squatting, and no trimester in which every squat is automatically safe. As your bump grows and balance changes, you may prefer more support, a shorter range, a different comfortable stance or fewer repetitions with rests. Pregnancy changes joint and ligament behaviour, but this does not mean your joints are damaged or that you should stretch further. Move smoothly and avoid forcing range. New symptoms or a new complication should prompt reassessment even if the same exercise felt easy last week. A cervical stitch needs the team’s individual activity advice; it does not mean routine bed rest. Weights and effort: experience matters If weights are new to you, ask your maternity team and a suitably trained instructor how to begin. You do not have to postpone every form of resistance exercise until after birth, but pregnancy is not the time to start maximum-effort lifting. Learn a controlled bodyweight movement before considering additional load. If you already lift, review the load and setup as pregnancy progresses. Choose an effort that lets you breathe normally and keep control; avoid straining, breath holding, maximum attempts and weights that could hit your bump. Reduce the load or switch movements if you develop pain, pelvic heaviness or leakage. Pelvic pain or pelvic-floor symptoms need a different plan Pain around the pubic bone, pelvis, hips or back can worsen with wide stances or other movements. Do not push through it to “open the pelvis”. Stop the painful version and ask your midwife or a pelvic-health physiotherapist for a comfortable range, stance or alternative. Difficulty walking, turning in bed or using stairs deserves assessment. Urine leakage, vaginal heaviness or pain during exercise is a reason to seek help, not proof that you simply need more squats or stronger squeezing. A pelvic-floor programme may include both contraction and full release. It should fit your symptoms; constant clenching or bearing down is not the aim. Build a balanced routine and avoid overheating For many uncomplicated pregnancies, guidance aims for about 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly with muscle strengthening on two days. This is an overall activity goal, not 150 minutes of squats or a compulsory daily squat count. Start gradually, use short sessions and keep an intensity at which you can talk. Some activity can still help if you cannot meet the target. Warm up gently, take rests and drink before, during and after activity. Choose a cool environment and avoid exercising when overheated, unwell or on an empty stomach. Dark or scant urine can suggest dehydration, but dizziness or a racing heart should not automatically be dismissed as needing water. Stop and obtain advice for unusual or persistent symptoms. When to stop and contact maternity care Stop exercising and contact your maternity team promptly for vaginal bleeding, leaking fluid, regular painful contractions, abdominal pain, dizziness or feeling faint, a headache, breathlessness before exercise, unusual palpitations, muscle weakness affecting balance, or calf pain or swelling. Contact maternity care immediately if your baby’s usual movements become reduced, weaker or stop; do not wait until the next day. Seek immediate assessment for a severe headache that does not settle, new vision problems, pain below the ribs, sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet, feeling very unwell, heartburn unrelieved by medicine, or vomiting that is concerning in pregnancy. These can be warning signs of pre-eclampsia or another illness. Do not wait for several signs to occur together or assume that exercise caused them. When emergency help is needed Call your local emergency service for severe difficulty breathing, chest pain, collapse or loss of consciousness, severe abdominal pain that persists, sudden severe abdominal pain, or abdominal pain that is getting worse, or heavy bleeding. Calf or leg symptoms together with chest pain or breathlessness also need emergency help. Stop, get assistance and do not drive yourself. Persistent dizziness, repeated vomiting or inability to keep fluids down needs urgent medical assessment too. If you cannot reach the maternity team and symptoms are serious, seek emergency care. Resting or drinking water should not delay help for warning signs; feeling that something is seriously wrong also deserves attention. If squats do not suit you Walking, swimming or appropriate water exercise, a stationary bicycle, or adapted prenatal yoga may be more comfortable. Avoid hot classes and activities with a high risk of falling or a blow to your abdomen. A circuit is only suitable if its individual movements, pace and rest periods fit your pregnancy and experience. Bring specific questions to your clinician or instructor: which movement is comfortable, what support and load to use, which symptoms mean stop, and when to review the plan. Choosing a different activity or resting when unwell is sensible care, not a failure to prepare for birth. Use a comfortable, controlled squat with stable support when needed; depth and width are not targets. Pregnancy complications, current joint pain or pelvic symptoms need individual advice. Begin gently; experienced lifting may continue with adaptation, while maximum-effort attempts and breath holding should be avoided. Squats do not guarantee easier labour or replace specific pelvic-floor contraction and relaxation work. Stop for warning signs and seek the appropriate maternity or emergency assessment without waiting for several symptoms. Can I start squats if I did not exercise before pregnancy? Often a gentle, supported bodyweight version can be considered in an uncomplicated pregnancy. Discuss your starting point and any symptoms with your maternity team, begin gradually and get help with technique. Do not start a demanding weighted routine on your own. When should I avoid squats? Do not exercise through bleeding, leaking fluid, painful contractions, illness or concerning pain. Placenta, cervical or other pregnancy complications need an individual plan before starting or continuing. A previous joint injury is not an automatic ban, but current symptoms need assessment. Are squats safe in every trimester? They may remain suitable, but safety depends on your condition and the version used rather than the trimester alone. Later pregnancy often calls for a shallower movement, more support or a different activity. Reassess when symptoms change. Will squats strengthen my pelvic floor or make labour easier? They can contribute to general leg and hip conditioning. They do not guarantee a stronger pelvic floor, less pain or an easier birth. Specific pelvic-floor work includes full relaxation, and your preferred labour position should be discussed with the maternity team. Do I need a deep or wide squat? No. Choose a depth and stance you can control without pain, pressure or losing balance. A shallow supported squat or chair sit-to-stand can be enough. Wide stances may worsen pelvic girdle pain. Can I use weights? An experienced lifter may continue with appropriate changes. If you are new to weights, seek advice and learn a controlled movement first. Avoid maximum lifts, breath holding and equipment that could hit your bump; there is no universal weight limit suitable for everyone. How many squats should I do each day? There is no pregnancy-wide daily number. Start with a manageable amount, allow rests and stop before technique fails. The weekly activity recommendation covers a mixture of movements; it is not a squat quota. What symptoms mean I should stop? Stop and contact maternity care for bleeding, fluid leakage, regular painful contractions, abdominal pain, dizziness, feeling faint or other warning signs described above; reduced baby movements need immediate contact. Call emergency services for severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or actual fainting, severe abdominal pain that persists, sudden severe abdominal pain, or abdominal pain that is getting worse or heavy bleeding. Do not wait for several signs or drive yourself.

title: Pain medicines in pregnancy: paracetamol, NSAIDs, aspirin and opioids
description: Compare pregnancy pain-relief options, timing-related risks, preventive aspirin and prescribed opioids, and know when pain or a medicine exposure needs care.
body: Pain during pregnancy deserves treatment and an explanation. The best option depends on what is causing it, how severe it is, the week of pregnancy and the exact medicine. An over-the-counter product is not automatically suitable, and a prescription painkiller is not automatically forbidden. Check the active ingredients with your pharmacist or maternity team before starting or changing treatment. Start with the cause and the actual product Headache, backache, dental pain, fever and persistent pain can need different treatment. Tell the clinician how the pain began, what makes it worse, whether you have other symptoms and how it affects sleep or daily activity. A painkiller may ease a symptom without treating its cause. The decision includes the ingredient, dose, route, duration, pregnancy stage, other medicines and conditions such as liver or kidney disease. A familiar brand can contain different ingredients in different countries. Bring the packet, including cold-and-flu remedies, sleep products, gels and supplements; do not judge safety by a brand name or by whether a prescription is required. Paracetamol is usually the first medicine considered Paracetamol and acetaminophen are two names for the same medicine. Current professional guidance generally makes it the first choice when medicine is needed for mild-to-moderate pain or fever during pregnancy. Use it according to your clinician's advice and the product instructions, at the lowest effective dose for the shortest necessary time. Repeated or ineffective treatment needs review. Check every ingredient before combining products: a cold remedy or a prescribed opioid combination may already contain paracetamol. Taking too much can injure the liver. Do not take more than the advised total or add another paracetamol-containing product without checking. Liver disease, other medicines or an uncertain dose are reasons to ask a pharmacist for an individual plan. What about autism and attention-deficit concerns? Some observational studies reported associations between paracetamol exposure in pregnancy and later developmental outcomes. Such studies cannot by themselves show that the medicine caused the outcome: the illness being treated and family or other factors can influence results. An association does not establish an individual child's risk. In its June 2026 statement, the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine reaffirmed paracetamol as first-line treatment when needed and said the evidence does not establish a causal link with autism or ADHD. The FDA's current acetaminophen information also says there is no clear evidence that appropriate use causes developmental problems. This is not a promise of zero risk or a reason for unnecessary use; untreated fever and significant pain also need appropriate care. Ibuprofen and naproxen are not aspirin mixtures Ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac and aspirin belong to the non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug group, or NSAIDs. Ibuprofen and naproxen are separate medicines; they do not contain aspirin just because they belong to that group. Combination products can contain additional ingredients, so the actual label still matters. Do not assume an NSAID is suitable simply because pregnancy is earlier than 20 weeks. A clinician may sometimes choose one for a particular condition, after weighing the alternatives and your medical history. An earlier accidental dose does not by itself mean the baby has been harmed, but the exact exposure should be checked rather than repeated without advice. NSAID restrictions become especially important from 20 weeks From around 20 weeks, systemic NSAIDs can affect the baby's kidneys and reduce amniotic fluid. Avoid self-treatment with them; use after this stage only under specific medical direction. Report use promptly, especially repeated doses. Fluid problems have occasionally developed within 48 hours, but they do not inevitably happen after two days. Improvement after stopping is common, not guaranteed; the team decides whether ultrasound monitoring is needed. Later limits differ by guidance: the US FDA advises avoiding NSAIDs from 30 weeks, and UK guidance contraindicates systemic use from 28 weeks. Earlier medically necessary use still requires the lowest effective dose and shortest duration. Risks include premature closure of a fetal circulation vessel and effects on bleeding or labour. A gel, cream or other route is not automatically exempt: check its pregnancy instructions and get product-specific advice. Preventive low-dose aspirin is a separate decision Do not start aspirin for pain during pregnancy on your own. Its pain-relief doses differ from the low-dose aspirin a maternity clinician may prescribe to reduce pre-eclampsia risk or for another defined medical indication. The preventive prescription has its own dose, start date and stopping plan; these vary with the indication and local guidance. Do not stop prescribed preventive aspirin because you have read a general NSAID warning. Ask your maternity team if the instructions are unclear or if you develop bleeding or other side effects. Conversely, a preventive prescription does not make extra pain-dose aspirin appropriate. If you took aspirin for pain after 20 weeks, contact the team promptly and do not repeat unprescribed doses. What counts as an opioid painkiller? Opioids include codeine, morphine, oxycodone, hydrocodone, fentanyl and pethidine, also called meperidine. Some are derived from opium, some are modified from related compounds and some, such as fentanyl, are synthetic. They are not interchangeable, and their formulations and strengths require individual prescribing. Some products combine an opioid with paracetamol; that paracetamol counts towards the total taken. A long-acting tablet or a patch must not be substituted for another formulation or borrowed from someone else. Tell the prescriber about all other medicines and substances so they can check interactions. The presence of an opioid does not justify changing a prescribed treatment without advice. A prescribed opioid is not automatically forbidden For severe acute pain, a clinician may decide that an opioid's benefit outweighs its risks, using the lowest effective dose for the shortest expected period. Pregnancy should not be a reason to leave severe pain untreated. For ongoing pain, the team usually looks for ways to reduce opioid use where possible while maintaining adequate relief. Pregnancy evidence differs between individual drugs and is often limited. Some studies associate prenatal opioid exposure, particularly in more complex or prolonged-use settings, with poor growth, premature birth and other adverse outcomes. These findings do not mean every short prescription causes those problems, or that all drugs and doses carry the same risk. Your underlying illness and other exposures also matter. Regular opioid use needs a supervised plan If you already take an opioid regularly, contact the prescriber promptly when pregnant or planning pregnancy. Do not stop suddenly or attempt your own taper: withdrawal and poorly controlled pain can create risks. The team can review the indication, dose, alternatives and any gradual change, with specialist help when needed. Physical dependence can occur with ongoing use; it is not by itself the same as opioid use disorder. If use is difficult to control, medication is being obtained outside care or a substance may contain an unknown opioid, ask for confidential, nonjudgmental treatment. Pregnancy care for opioid use disorder often includes medicines such as methadone or buprenorphine rather than an unsupervised withdrawal attempt. Plan ahead for the birth and newborn observation Tell the maternity and newborn teams about opioid use, including the medicine, duration and last dose. Exposure close to delivery can affect the baby's breathing, and longer prenatal exposure can lead to neonatal opioid withdrawal. These are different problems; an opioid given only during delivery does not itself cause the withdrawal syndrome associated with longer exposure. Not every exposed baby develops withdrawal. The care team decides on observation and treatment according to the exposure and the baby's condition. Withdrawal can involve feeding difficulty, tremor, irritability or disturbed sleep. A baby who breathes very fast, has difficulty breathing or pauses in breathing, turns blue, grey or pale, becomes floppy, is difficult to wake or unresponsive, or has a seizure needs emergency medical care; do not wait to decide whether it is withdrawal. If you have already taken a pain medicine Keep the packet and write down the active ingredients, strength, amount, time taken and your pregnancy week. Ask a pharmacist, prescriber or maternity team to assess the actual exposure. A single dose is not proof of fetal harm and does not automatically mean extra scans, but repeated or later-pregnancy NSAID use may need monitoring. If you may have taken too much, or swallowed a harmful or unknown product, obtain emergency medical or poison-service assessment immediately, even if you feel well. Symptoms can be delayed. Bring the packaging and do not make yourself vomit. Loss of consciousness, a seizure or severe breathing difficulty requires emergency help; do not drive yourself. Non-medicine help should fit the pain Depending on the cause, rest, hydration, a supported position, appropriate gentle movement, physiotherapy or a carefully used warm or cool pack may help. These measures can complement treatment; they do not replace assessment for infection, injury or another important cause. Avoid painful exercise and seek advice about any physical treatment you are unsure is suitable in pregnancy. Pain that keeps returning, disrupts sleep, limits eating or drinking, or needs repeated medication deserves a review. Do not keep increasing a dose or cycling through products to mask it. A dentist, physiotherapist, maternity clinician or pain specialist may be the right person to address the cause and make a practical follow-up plan. When pain needs immediate assessment Seek immediate maternity or emergency assessment for a headache that will not go away or is worsening, a sudden severe headache, new vision changes, fever of 38 °C or higher, or abdominal pain that is severe, sudden or worsening. Chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting or loss of consciousness, vaginal bleeding or fluid leakage, or the baby moving less than usual also need immediate care. Do not wait for several signs together or for a painkiller to work. Emergency help is also needed for a severe medicine reaction with breathing difficulty or swelling of the mouth, tongue or throat, or for collapse. Tell the clinician you are pregnant and what you took. A new rash after paracetamol requires stopping it and immediate medical advice; breathing or swelling symptoms make it an emergency. Agree on the next step before leaving the review Ask which ingredient and formulation to use, the total daily limit for you, how long to use it and what to do if it does not help. Check whether it overlaps with another product and whether you need follow-up, a scan or a plan for delivery. A written list makes it easier to share the same information with different clinicians. Keep preventive medicines and long-term treatment on their agreed plan until your own team advises a change. The aim is appropriate relief with the least necessary exposure, while treating the cause and responding promptly to warning signs. A general article cannot choose an individual prescription or replace the product-specific advice you receive. Paracetamol is usually the first medicine considered for pain or fever; check total ingredients and avoid excess dosing. Do not self-treat with NSAIDs from 20 weeks; earlier use also needs an individual decision. Prescribed preventive low-dose aspirin is different from aspirin taken for pain. An opioid may be justified for severe pain; regular use must not be stopped abruptly without a clinical plan. Severe or unusual pain, a possible overdose or a serious reaction needs prompt assessment, not another dose. Can I take ibuprofen or naproxen while pregnant? Do not start either without checking with a pregnancy-informed clinician or pharmacist. They are separate NSAIDs, not aspirin-containing medicines by definition. Earlier use may sometimes be prescribed; from around 20 weeks avoid them unless specifically directed, and later restrictions are stricter. Tell the team if you have already taken them. Does paracetamol cause autism or ADHD? Current evidence does not establish a causal link. Observational associations can be affected by the illness treated and other factors. Current professional guidance still supports paracetamol when needed for pain or fever, using appropriate doses and duration. Discuss repeated use or persistent symptoms instead of assuming either zero risk or proven harm. Why should I not choose aspirin for pain myself? Pain-dose aspirin has pregnancy risks and is generally not recommended without specific prescribing, particularly from 20 weeks. It is different from preventive low-dose aspirin prescribed for pre-eclampsia risk or another indication. Do not stop that preventive prescription or add extra aspirin without asking your maternity team. Are strong painkillers completely banned? No. Severe pain can warrant a prescribed opioid after an individual benefit-risk review. The drug, dose, timing, duration and other medicines all matter. The team may plan extra monitoring or newborn observation. Do not borrow medicines, switch formulations or abruptly stop an opioid you use regularly. Will two days of an NSAID inevitably lower amniotic fluid? No. Cases have occurred as early as 48 hours, but that is not a prediction that every exposure causes harm. Risk depends on the exposure and pregnancy stage. Contact the maternity team about use from 20 weeks, especially repeated doses; they decide whether monitoring is appropriate. What if I took a dose before I knew I was pregnant? Record the product, ingredients, amount and date, and ask for an exposure review. A single dose does not prove the baby was harmed. Do not repeat an unsuitable medicine while waiting. If the amount may have been excessive or the substance harmful or unknown, seek immediate emergency or poison-service advice rather than waiting for symptoms. Can I take a cold remedy with my painkiller? Only after checking every active ingredient. Cold remedies and opioid combination medicines may already contain paracetamol or an NSAID. A pharmacist can check the total dose and interactions. Products with similar names may have different ingredients, and a pregnancy-safe claim on a package does not replace that check. What should I do if pain relief is not working? Contact the appropriate clinician to assess the cause and treatment plan; do not exceed the advised dose. Seek immediate care for the warning signs described above, including severe, sudden or worsening pain, a persistent or worsening headache, fever, breathing problems, fainting, bleeding, fluid leakage or reduced fetal movement. Do not wait for multiple signs together.

title: Ultrasound at 13 weeks: timing, findings and next steps
description: What an ultrasound around 13 weeks can show, how NT and screening windows vary, how to prepare, and what uncertain or unexpected findings mean.
body: An ultrasound around 13 weeks can help date the pregnancy, check cardiac activity and the number of babies, and examine early development. It may also include nuchal translucency (NT) measurement if this fits your chosen screening pathway. Its purpose is wider than a single measurement, and the appointment should leave you with a clear next step. Is a scan at exactly 13 weeks necessary? Many services offer a first-trimester scan within an 11–14-week window rather than on one compulsory day. The offer and timing depend on local care, previous scans, symptoms and the screening you choose. Ask why the scan is recommended and what accepting or declining each part would mean. A separate scan is not automatically needed at 13 weeks if an adequate earlier examination has already answered the questions. Pain, bleeding, an incomplete examination or another concern may justify reassessment. Do not wait for a routine appointment if you develop worrying symptoms. Check the actual screening window The international ISUOG guideline describes the 11+0 to 14+0-week scan. Individual screening programmes use their own dates and size criteria. For example, England’s combined screening uses a crown–rump length (CRL) of 45.0–84.0 mm; this measurement can matter more than a calendar estimate. Contact the booking team promptly if you want screening and are approaching the appointment window. “Before 13 weeks and 6 days” is not a universal rule for every test or service. Ask which examination and blood test are booked, their local deadlines, and what happens if the baby measures outside the eligible range. If you missed the NT appointment Missing one combined-screening window does not mean that all opportunities to assess the baby have disappeared. Depending on gestation, local access and your preferences, options may include cell-free DNA screening (NIPT), a later serum screen, specialist ultrasound or diagnostic testing. These options answer different questions. Later serum programmes differ. England’s current handbook describes a quadruple test at 14+2–20+0 weeks, with Edwards syndrome screening included where that change has been implemented; it does not screen for Patau syndrome. Confirm the actual local offer rather than assuming every later test covers the same conditions. Preparing for the examination Follow the unit’s instructions about a full bladder; it is not required for every type of scan. Bring earlier reports and screening results, and mention IVF dating, previous pregnancies and current symptoms. Comfortable clothing that allows access to the abdomen can help. Ask beforehand about a companion, interpreter or other support. Usually gel is placed on the abdomen and a probe moved across it. A transvaginal scan may be offered when it would clarify the view; the clinician should explain why and obtain your consent. Tell the operator if pressure is uncomfortable. You can ask questions and discuss pausing or declining an examination. How long will it take, and is it safe? A routine appointment often takes around 20–30 minutes, but the baby’s position, the number of babies and the views needed can make it shorter or longer. You may be asked to change position or return for another attempt. A longer appointment or a repeat visit does not by itself mean something is wrong. Ultrasound uses sound waves, not ionising radiation. Medical use by trained staff is considered appropriate when needed, with exposure kept as low and brief as necessary. It is not a reason to seek repeated non-medical reassurance scans. The operator can assess cardiac activity without playing a heartbeat sound; early Doppler audio is not routinely necessary. What the baby may look like At about 13 weeks the baby is roughly 7 cm from head to bottom; this is an illustration, not a personal growth cutoff. Limbs and movements may be seen, and the baby may bring a hand toward the mouth. Not feeling those movements yourself at this stage is expected. A scan shows selected views rather than a complete photograph of every organ. The head, body and limbs change appearance with position and the imaging plane. Ask the sonographer what you are seeing instead of comparing a still image or an approximate weekly size with someone else’s scan. Dating, cardiac activity and more than one baby CRL helps estimate gestational age and the expected date of birth. The team interprets it alongside earlier information; an IVF pregnancy has specific dating information. Cardiac activity and pregnancy location are assessed, while a single measurement cannot promise how the rest of pregnancy will develop. If there are twins or more babies, the team assesses whether they share a placenta and membranes, because this affects follow-up. Dating and identifying the type of multiple pregnancy are important reasons for the scan even when chromosomal screening is declined or has already been done. Early anatomy: useful information with limits The examiner can assess early structures such as the skull and brain, limbs, abdominal wall, stomach, bladder and heart position or activity. A more detailed examination may assess the face, nasal bone, spine, diaphragm and cord vessels. Which views are possible depends on development, position, equipment and expertise. Not all conditions are visible this early, and some develop or become clearer later. A normal early scan does not replace the later anatomy scan. A nasal bone that cannot be clearly seen is not a diagnosis; the quality of the view and the wider screening or specialist assessment matter. Placenta, fluid and fetal sex The scan can describe the placenta and assess the surrounding fluid in the context of this stage. An early low placental position does not automatically predict placenta praevia later. Later-pregnancy placental “age” grades or fluid thresholds should not be imported as a checklist for a 13-week scan. An early suggestion about fetal sex can be wrong and is not the main medical purpose of this appointment. Genital appearance and other small details may not be clear. Do not base medical or major personal decisions on an uncertain early guess or on the orientation of a printed image. What an NT measurement means NT is the ultrasound measurement of fluid beneath the skin at the back of the baby’s neck. In combined screening it is interpreted with blood markers and other information to estimate the chance of certain chromosomal conditions. An enlarged NT may also prompt assessment for structural or other genetic conditions. Neither an enlarged NT nor a higher-chance screening result proves a diagnosis, and a lower-chance result does not exclude every problem. Ask about the actual measurement, the calculated result and the referral plan. In England’s programme, an NT of 3.5 mm or more prompts referral without waiting for the combined result; other services should explain their own pathway. Choosing a screening pathway NIPT analyses cell-free DNA in a blood sample and is a screening test, not a diagnosis. Its result does not replace the medical ultrasound examination. Your team should explain what the chosen test covers, its limitations and what a positive or no-result report would lead to before you decide. A scan solely to obtain NT after a negative NIPT result is not recommended by SMFM. This is different from an ultrasound for dating, multiples, early anatomy or a clinical concern. Discuss the locally recommended combination of examinations rather than booking overlapping tests without a plan. If the scan raises a concern Ask what was actually seen, how certain the finding is, and who will arrange the next appointment. Specialist ultrasound and genetic counselling may help. Further screening can refine a chance estimate but cannot definitively explain every structural finding or rule out all genetic conditions. Diagnostic options may include CVS, which samples the placenta and is usually done at 11–14 weeks, or amniocentesis, which samples fluid and is usually done from 15 weeks. Timing, the tests performed, benefits, limitations and procedure risks need individual discussion. An unexpected result is not an automatic instruction to end a pregnancy; informed decisions and support matter. If cardiac activity is not identified Not hearing a heartbeat during the appointment is different from the clinician finding no cardiac activity on the image. Ask which of these is meant. If activity is genuinely absent at an expected 13 weeks, it needs prompt specialist assessment; it should not be dismissed or interpreted from a home device. Before diagnosing pregnancy loss or choosing treatment, the team checks the images, measurements, previous scans and dates. A second opinion or repeat scan may be needed under conservative diagnostic criteria; the interval depends on the scan type and findings. Do not self-diagnose from a measurement threshold. If loss is confirmed, discuss care choices and emotional support rather than assuming there is only one treatment. Symptoms should not wait for the scan Contact maternity or early-pregnancy care promptly for vaginal bleeding, new or persistent abdominal pain, or other concerning symptoms. Shoulder-tip pain needs immediate medical advice. Fever of 38°C or higher, leaking fluid, repeated vomiting or inability to keep fluids down also needs urgent assessment. A scheduled scan does not replace that assessment. Seek emergency help for heavy bleeding, severe abdominal pain that persists, sudden severe abdominal pain or worsening abdominal pain, actual fainting or collapse, chest pain or severe difficulty breathing. Do not wait for several symptoms together or drive yourself. A scan result cannot make a new emergency symptom safe; ask for help if you feel seriously unwell. The appointment covers dating, cardiac activity, multiples and early anatomy, not only NT. Check local timing and CRL criteria promptly; a missed NT window does not remove all testing options. NT and NIPT estimate chance; neither guarantees health or diagnoses every condition. Normal early views do not replace later anatomy assessment, and unclear findings need a documented follow-up plan. Silence from the machine is not proof of absent cardiac activity; symptoms and suspected loss need proper clinical assessment. Must everyone have a scan at exactly 13 weeks? No. Many services use an 11–14-week window, and previous scans, symptoms and chosen screening affect the plan. The team should explain the recommendation and your choices. A repeat is not automatically required after an adequate earlier scan. Have I lost every testing option after 13 weeks and 6 days? No. Local dates and the baby’s CRL determine eligibility for a particular combined screen. Other screening or diagnostic options may remain available. Contact the team promptly rather than assuming it is too late for any assessment. How long does the scan take? Often around 20–30 minutes, but position, twins and the views needed can change this. Another attempt may be needed. Duration alone is not a sign of a problem. Can the scan show all organs and the baby’s sex? It can assess early structures, but not every condition or detail is visible. Fetal sex may be uncertain. A normal result does not replace the later anatomy scan. Does a high NT mean the baby definitely has Down syndrome? No. NT is one finding and can be associated with different chromosomal, structural or genetic conditions. The team should explain specialist follow-up and any diagnostic options rather than treating the measurement as a diagnosis. Do I still need ultrasound after a low-chance NIPT result? Medical ultrasound still answers dating, multiple-pregnancy and structural questions that NIPT does not. A separate scan solely for NT is a different issue; discuss the local plan to avoid unnecessary duplicate screening. What if I do not hear a heartbeat? Ask whether the clinician saw cardiac activity. Audio may not be used. If activity is truly absent, prompt clinical confirmation, sometimes with a second opinion or repeat scan, is needed before treatment decisions. Do not interpret this yourself from a home monitor. What should I do after an unexpected finding? Ask for the written finding, the next appointment and a contact for questions. Specialist imaging, counselling and selected diagnostic tests may be offered; further screening is not definitive diagnosis. Seek urgent or emergency care for the warning signs above rather than waiting for the next scan.

title: Too-frequent contractions in labour: tachysystole and monitoring
description: Understand excessive contraction frequency, prolonged tightening, possible causes, fetal monitoring and clinical care: and when to call your maternity team urgently.
body: Contractions normally tighten the uterus and then ease. When they come too close together, last unusually long or leave too little recovery, the maternity team needs to assess the pattern and how the baby is coping. Tachysystole describes excessive contraction frequency; it does not by itself mean that every contraction is unusually strong, that the baby has been harmed or that a caesarean is inevitable. What normal contractions and practice tightenings feel like During a contraction the womb tightens, and then relaxes as it ends. Established labour contractions generally become longer, stronger and closer together as labour progresses. Braxton Hicks or practice tightenings are usually shorter, less frequent and do not steadily build in this way. The feeling alone cannot reliably establish whether labour is progressing normally. Pain that does not ease between contractions, an unusually long tightening or a sudden change deserves assessment. Do not assume a very painful episode is simply a stronger practice contraction. If you think labour is starting before 37 weeks, contact your maternity team urgently. Frequency, duration and resting tone are different Frequency describes how often contractions start. Duration is the time from the start to the end of one contraction; the relaxation interval is the gap before the next starts. Strength describes how forcefully the uterus contracts. Resting tone means how relaxed or pressurised the uterus is between contractions, rather than how many seconds the gap lasts. A frequent pattern can occur without unusually strong contractions. A prolonged contraction can also be concerning even when there are not many contractions in ten minutes. Clinicians assess these features together; timing an app or judging the height of an external monitor's peaks cannot measure all of them. Why different guidelines use different numbers ACOG's 2025 clinical guideline defines tachysystole as more than five contractions in ten minutes, averaged over thirty minutes. NICE's induction guideline describes five or more in ten minutes sustained for at least twenty minutes, or a contraction lasting at least two minutes, within its hyperstimulation terminology. These are different clinical frameworks, not interchangeable home diagnostic rules. NICE's fetal-monitoring guidance also calls for assessment and action at five or more contractions in ten minutes, especially when recovery time is reduced. During an oxytocin infusion, its labour-care protocol may require reducing or stopping the infusion above four in ten. A team can therefore act before a formal diagnostic observation period is complete. Do not wait twenty or thirty minutes to ask for help. Why the baby's heart-rate pattern matters Each contraction temporarily changes blood flow through the placenta. The interval between contractions allows recovery; very frequent or sustained activity may reduce that opportunity. How a baby tolerates this depends on more than a count, including placental function, the parent's condition and other events during labour. The baby's heart-rate pattern helps the team judge the response. Excessive activity can occur with or without concerning heart-rate changes. A change on the trace does not automatically prove injury, but a persistent concerning pattern needs prompt action. Conversely, a reassuring moment does not replace continued assessment if excessive activity persists. It can happen with spontaneous or induced labour Oxytocin used to start or strengthen labour, and prostaglandin medicines used for induction, can increase uterine activity. The team balances their intended effect against excessive contractions and monitors the response. Mechanical induction methods are generally less likely than medicines to cause hyperstimulation, although no method removes every labour risk. Tachysystole also occurs in spontaneous labour without these medicines. Studies have found associations with factors such as epidural use and high blood pressure, but an association does not show that either caused an individual episode. Tell the team about all medicines or products used to encourage labour; do not add a labour-stimulating product or change an infusion yourself. How common is it? Read the study numbers carefully Rates depend on the definition, observation period and people studied. A 2013 cohort recorded 7,567 episodes in 5,363 deliveries, rather than 7,567 affected women. In a different cohort of 8,008 labours without prostaglandin or oxytocin, around 11% had tachysystole. These figures describe particular study populations, not your personal probability. An individual can have more than one episode. Studies may count events, deliveries or people, and may observe only part of labour. Induction exposure, medical conditions and how quickly staff respond also differ. A single percentage cannot predict what will happen in a later pregnancy or compare hospitals fairly. Possible consequences: and important uncertainty Some observational studies link tachysystole with heart-rate changes, caesarean birth or neonatal-unit admission; other studies have not found the same newborn outcomes. A 2012 induction study, for example, found more heart-rate decelerations without a clear difference in its adverse-infant-outcome measure. These associations cannot establish that contraction frequency alone caused an outcome. A 2026 review pooling five observational studies found no statistically significant increase in several major adverse outcomes, but uncertainty remained and better-characterised research was needed. That does not prove excessive activity is harmless. Whether contractions were treated, how long they lasted, the baby's response and other risks all affect interpretation. Clinicians respond to the current situation rather than using a pooled average as reassurance. How the maternity team assesses the pattern Assessment includes your symptoms, contraction pattern, medicines, stage of labour, vital signs and the baby's heart rate. Continuous cardiotocography, or CTG, records heart-rate and contraction patterns when indicated. An external contraction sensor mainly shows timing and duration; the height of its trace is not a reliable measurement of contraction strength. Palpation can help assess how the uterus tightens and relaxes. In selected circumstances an internal pressure catheter can provide pressure information after the waters have broken; it is not needed for everyone. Staff also consider other explanations for an abnormal trace or persistent pain, including urgent complications that need a different response. Treatment is adjusted by the clinical team Care depends on the cause, the heart-rate pattern and the overall assessment. Staff may help you change position, reduce or stop oxytocin, withhold further induction medicine, or remove a removable vaginal medicine-delivery system. Some preparations cannot simply be removed. A clinician may give a medicine that relaxes the uterus if excessive activity and concerning fetal findings continue. Fluids, treatment of low blood pressure and other measures are used for specific indications. Oxygen is not routinely recommended solely for an abnormal fetal trace when the parent's oxygen level is normal. The team reassesses the response and decides whether and how to restart treatment. Do not adjust a pump, remove a medicine system or take a contraction-suppressing drug yourself; ask staff to explain what they are doing. Does it mean an urgent caesarean? Not automatically. If activity settles and the baby's assessment is reassuring, labour may continue with appropriate monitoring and a revised plan. The decision includes progress in labour, your preferences where choices remain, and the risks of continuing versus birth. A previous episode does not by itself dictate the mode of birth next time. Persistent serious heart-rate abnormalities or another emergency can require expedited birth. Depending on how far labour has progressed and the clinical circumstances, this might be an assisted vaginal birth or a caesarean. The team should explain the reason and urgency as clearly as the situation allows. Newborn assessment or observation is based on what occurred and the baby's condition, not the label alone. When to call immediately Contact your maternity unit urgently if any contraction lasts more than two minutes, you have six or more in ten minutes, your waters break, there is vaginal bleeding, movements reduce, or labour may be starting before 37 weeks. Call sooner if tightening seems continuous, unusually painful or otherwise worrying; a lower count does not exclude a problem. During outpatient induction follow your return instructions and report excessive activity or a medicine-related concern promptly. In hospital, alert staff immediately. Severe abdominal pain that does not go away, sudden severe pain or pain that is worsening needs immediate assessment. Fainting or loss of consciousness, chest pain, breathing difficulty or a temperature of 38 °C or higher also needs immediate medical care. Call emergency services for collapse, severe breathing difficulty or if the baby seems to be coming now with a strong urge to push. Any one warning can be enough; do not wait for every sign or for an averaging period to finish. Planning after a difficult previous experience If a previous labour involved excessive contractions, ask for a review of the records: which medicines were used, how contractions and the baby's heart rate changed, what staff did and why birth or newborn observation was needed. A difficult experience deserves explanation and support, even when the baby recovered well. For a current or future birth, ask which definition and monitoring plan your unit uses, how excessive activity will be managed, and who to contact during any outpatient induction. Discuss benefits and alternatives before induction where possible. Your history helps tailor care, but neither avoiding all pain relief nor accepting a guaranteed recurrence follows from an observational risk association. Tachysystole concerns contraction frequency; duration, strength and resting tone are separate features. Definitions and treatment thresholds vary, so a home timer cannot make the diagnosis or tell whether the baby is coping. Excessive activity occurs in spontaneous labour as well as during induction or oxytocin augmentation. Management depends on fetal heart-rate findings and the wider situation; harm or caesarean birth is not inevitable. Seek help for concerning symptoms immediately; never change labour medicines or wait for a diagnostic counting period yourself. Is tachysystole the same as very strong contractions? No. It describes excessive frequency. Strength, duration and the uterus's relaxation between contractions are assessed separately. A long contraction or persistent pain can need attention even without a high count. Can it happen without induction medicine? Yes. It occurs in spontaneous labour as well as with oxytocin or prostaglandins. Medicines and other factors can be associated with the pattern, but no single exposure explains every episode. Should I diagnose it by counting five contractions? No. Guidelines use different thresholds and time windows, and clinicians assess fetal heart rate and the whole situation. Call urgently for six or more in ten minutes or any lasting over two minutes, and sooner for other concerns. Do not wait for an average or assume a lower count is safe. Does an epidural cause tachysystole? Some observational studies report an association, which does not prove causation in an individual. Discuss pain relief, blood pressure and monitoring with your team instead of avoiding needed care because of that association. Will my baby definitely be harmed? No. Heart-rate changes and adverse outcomes are not inevitable. Research findings vary, and pooled observational results cannot guarantee safety. Prompt assessment of the actual contraction and fetal heart-rate patterns is what guides care. Can I stop the contractions myself? Do not adjust oxytocin, remove an induction medicine system or take a medicine to suppress contractions yourself. Alert the maternity team promptly. Position changes, medicine changes and any uterine-relaxing treatment are chosen and reassessed by clinicians. Does a previous episode mean I need a caesarean next time? Not by itself. Reviewing the earlier records, cause, fetal response and treatment can help plan monitoring and discuss birth options. Persistent serious fetal concerns in a current labour may require expedited birth, but the route depends on the situation. When should I seek urgent help? Call maternity care immediately for prolonged or very frequent contractions, reduced movements, bleeding, waters breaking or possible labour before 37 weeks. Continuous or severe, sudden or worsening abdominal pain also needs assessment. Fainting, chest pain, breathing difficulty or fever needs immediate care; collapse, severe breathing difficulty or imminent birth with a strong urge to push needs emergency services. One warning is enough.

title: High cholesterol in pregnancy: tests, FH and medicine decisions
description: How to interpret rising cholesterol in pregnancy, plan treatment for familial hypercholesterolemia, and arrange safe medicine, feeding and postpartum follow-up.
body: Cholesterol often rises during pregnancy, but an increased result still needs context. Your previous levels, triglycerides, inherited conditions and cardiovascular history help determine whether you need monitoring, treatment or a specialist plan. Pregnancy and breastfeeding decisions should be agreed with your maternity and prescribing teams. Why cholesterol rises Cholesterol helps build cells and make hormones. Pregnancy changes how the body handles fats to support the placenta and growing baby, so total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol and triglycerides commonly rise. A result flagged against a nonpregnant reference range does not by itself prove disease. However, a normal physiological rise does not make every high result harmless. LDL reflects a different problem from very high triglycerides. Existing cardiovascular disease, familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), diabetes or a marked rise can change the assessment; one number cannot predict whether your baby will be harmed. Testing can still be useful Bring any prepregnancy lipid results to your first maternity appointment. The clinician may review a full lipid profile, repeat it later in pregnancy or arrange closer monitoring if you have a known lipid disorder or other risk factors. Ask whether fasting is needed for the particular test rather than fasting on your own. The assessment may include thyroid function, diabetes, kidney or liver disease, medicines and family history. High cholesterol usually causes no symptoms. Yellowish fatty bumps can occur with severe lipid disorders, but a skin change needs examination rather than self-diagnosis. Do not wait for symptoms before attending planned blood tests. Pregnancy with familial hypercholesterolemia FH causes persistently high LDL from an inherited problem; it can occur despite a healthy diet. Many people with FH can have children and breastfeed, but the plan depends on their own cardiovascular risk. A lipid specialist and maternity team should review previous heart attack, stroke, coronary disease and the duration of treatment interruptions. Rare homozygous FH can carry much greater risk and may involve coronary arteries or the aortic valve. Specialist assessment of these problems is important before pregnancy when possible. Discuss genetic counselling and appropriate family testing; neither an FH diagnosis nor a pregnancy cholesterol result alone determines the baby’s outcome. Plan before trying to conceive List every prescription, supplement and combination tablet, and arrange a review before attempting pregnancy. The plan should specify which medicines to pause, when to do so, whether an alternative is needed and what to do if pregnancy occurs earlier. Do not apply one washout interval to every cholesterol medicine. For people who are not at high cardiovascular risk, the 2026 ACC/AHA guideline recommends stopping a statin one to two months before trying to conceive, or when pregnancy is identified. High-risk exceptions and product-specific restrictions require a different discussion. Follow your own prescriber’s plan rather than changing treatment from a general article. If pregnancy happens while taking treatment Contact the prescriber and maternity team promptly with the medicine name, dose, dates taken and estimated pregnancy stage. Most pregnant patients will be advised to discontinue statins, but the prescriber must identify the uncommon situations where continuing treatment may be appropriate. Seek advice promptly rather than waiting for the next routine visit. An accidental early statin exposure does not establish that the baby has been harmed. The FDA considers unintended early exposure unlikely to harm the developing baby, while acknowledging remaining uncertainty, including about miscarriage. The team can assess the actual medicine and other risks; a blanket prediction of birth defects is not justified. Statins: most pause, some need specialist exceptions The US FDA removed the strongest blanket pregnancy warning in 2021, while still advising that most pregnant patients stop statins. Current ACC/AHA guidance allows an individualized discussion about continuation for selected patients with FH or established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. This is not permission for everyone with a raised LDL to continue. The balance includes the risk of a cardiovascular event without treatment, previous disease and uncertain fetal effects. A specialist may consider the particular statin, including pravastatin in selected circumstances. Statins are not an approved routine treatment to prevent pre-eclampsia, and this article does not provide a self-treatment dose. Bile acid sequestrants need monitoring too Medicines such as colesevelam or cholestyramine stay largely within the gut and can lower LDL without direct systemic drug exposure. They may be considered during pregnancy or breastfeeding, but limited pregnancy data and indirect effects still matter. Constipation, bloating, other medicine absorption and triglyceride levels affect suitability. These medicines can reduce absorption of vitamins A, D, E and K; long-term cholestyramine can also reduce folate. Ordinary prenatal supplements may not be enough. Ask for a nutrition and medicine-spacing plan, including thyroid tablets if used. Do not add high-dose vitamins yourself: the required supplement and timing depend on the exact product and your assessment. Other LDL treatments and apheresis Ezetimibe and newer systemic LDL-lowering agents are generally avoided during pregnancy because suitable safety information is limited or a product has specific fetal risks. A familiar injection or a non-statin tablet is not automatically a safer substitute. A pharmacist can check the exact formulation and local prescribing information. For particularly severe FH, lipoprotein apheresis may be an option during pregnancy or lactation: a specialist service removes LDL-containing particles from the blood. Access and treatment burden vary. The choice is not simply between taking every usual medicine and leaving serious disease untreated. Very high triglycerides are a separate concern Severe fasting triglycerides, from 500 mg/dL (5.7 mmol/L), require active clinical assessment; pancreatitis risk becomes greater at still higher levels, particularly around or above 1,000 mg/dL. The team reviews diabetes and other causes, nutrition and repeat tests. Do not assume an extreme triglyceride result is an ordinary pregnancy change. A specialist may consider prescription omega-3 treatment or a fibrate after the first trimester in selected severe cases. Over-the-counter fish oil is not an equivalent treatment. Bile acid sequestrants can raise triglycerides: the 2026 guideline advises against them at 300 mg/dL or above, while colesevelam’s label also has specific contraindications, including levels above 500 mg/dL or previous triglyceride-induced pancreatitis. Food and activity support the treatment plan Choose a varied pregnancy-appropriate diet with vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans and other suitable protein foods. Replacing some saturated fat with unsaturated oils, nuts or seeds can support LDL management. Keep enough energy and essential nutrients for pregnancy; avoid crash diets or trying to remove all fat. Ask for a dietitian if triglycerides are very high, FH is present or a restrictive diet is proposed. Severe triglyceride management may require a different fat and carbohydrate plan from ordinary LDL advice. Agree suitable physical activity with your maternity team, avoid alcohol in pregnancy and seek help to stop smoking. Food choices do not replace necessary FH treatment. Breastfeeding and medicines: guidance differs Make a feeding and treatment plan before birth. US FDA advice and the 2026 ACC/AHA guideline advise avoiding statins while breastfeeding; if ongoing statin treatment is essential, the FDA recommends an alternative way to feed the baby. Some lower-risk patients can defer restarting treatment, but a prolonged interruption may be unsuitable for high-risk disease. UK NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service guidance updated in July 2026 permits selected statins or ezetimibe cautiously when treatment is needed, with infant feeding, growth and weight monitoring. Its recommendations apply to healthy full-term infants, not automatically to premature or unwell babies. Evidence remains limited. These different approaches require local specialist advice, not an assumption that all medicines are either forbidden or proven safe during breastfeeding. After birth: retest and agree when to restart Lipid levels fall after delivery, but they do not all return to baseline on a fixed day. A check from about six weeks postpartum is often useful, with earlier or further tests when clinically needed. Current ACC guidance supports risk-based testing after six weeks and recognizes that cholesterol may continue settling for several months. Breastfeeding does not make a lipid test useless, and a caesarean birth does not impose a universal three-month delay. Arrange a named follow-up clinician, a repeat-test date and a medicine restart or continuation decision that fits cardiovascular risk and feeding. Do not let a temporary medication pause during pregnancy become an indefinite loss of care. Symptoms that need urgent help Seek urgent assessment for sudden severe abdominal pain that persists or recurs, or for sudden severe abdominal pain with a high temperature or feeling hot, cold or shivery, with or without vomiting. Use emergency services if sudden severe pain spreads to the back, or accompanies abdominal swelling that persists or recurs, a fast heartbeat, breathing difficulty or blue/bruised skin around the abdomen or upper outer thigh.
