New chest pain, sudden breathing difficulty, fainting, a very fast heartbeat or ongoing palpitations that do not settle need emergency assessment; do not wait for iron to help. Why is iron important during pregnancy? Iron supports haemoglobin production as the red-cell mass and the developing pregnancy’s needs increase. Adequate stores also help preserve reserve for blood loss at birth. Plasma expands more than red-cell mass, so some fall in haemoglobin concentration is physiological, but this does not make every low result normal. Testing, appropriate food and prescribed replacement when needed work together; pregnancy does not simply double the person’s blood volume. Can iron-deficiency anaemia affect the baby? Maternal anaemia is associated with outcomes including preterm birth and low birth weight, with particular concern when it is severe. Other maternal and newborn complications are also reported, but the causes and circumstances vary. These associations are not a prediction for one baby, and iron treatment cannot be promised to prevent every complication. Diagnose the cause, treat confirmed deficiency and follow the maternity team’s plan without blame. What should I do before trying to conceive? Ask about assessment if you have symptoms, heavy periods, previous anaemia, a restricted diet or a condition that affects absorption. Treatment should address the cause as well as the iron deficit. Bring previous results and all medicines or supplements. Do not assume that every anaemia is iron deficiency or keep increasing an iron dose without review. Does poor response to tablets mean I need IV iron? Not automatically. The team should review the diagnosis, product, administration, tolerability, absorption, continuing blood loss and other causes, then check the response on an agreed schedule. IV iron may be appropriate if oral treatment cannot be used or has not worked, or if faster correction is needed, generally after the first trimester following a risk–benefit assessment. It needs a suitable monitored service; being in the third trimester alone is not an indication. Will breastfeeding or the end of pregnancy cure the anaemia? No. Blood loss and low stores can leave anaemia after birth, even if periods are absent. Continue the prescribed plan and arrange follow-up rather than stopping because the baby has been born. Oral ferrous sulfate is usually compatible with breastfeeding, but the baby’s iron needs require a separate assessment. Fatigue and mood problems deserve help in their own right; treatment is not a test of parenting or a guaranteed cure for depression. When should I seek urgent or emergency help? Use local emergency services for sudden breathing difficulty, severe breathing trouble, chest or upper-back pain, a tight or heavy chest, pain spreading to the arm, back, neck or jaw, very pale/blue/grey skin or lips, sudden confusion, fainting, a very fast heartbeat, or ongoing palpitations that do not settle. Palpitations with chest pain, breathlessness or faintness also require emergency assessment. Sudden or very heavy postpartum vaginal bleeding needs immediate emergency help. These are independent alternatives; do not wait for all of them. Do not drive yourself; arrange another driver or an ambulance. New or worsening breathlessness, coughing blood, one-sided leg pain or swelling, or postpartum fever with abdominal tenderness or headache with visual changes/vomiting needs immediate clinical advice. Extra iron ingestion needs immediate medical or poison-service advice; suspected poisoning needs emergency assessment without inducing vomiting or giving food or drink while waiting.

title: Umbilical-cord cysts: scan findings, follow-up and your baby’s outlook
description: Understand true cysts and pseudocysts, early resolving versus persistent findings, genetic-test choices, growth checks and individual birth planning.
body: An umbilical-cord cyst is a fluid-filled finding seen along the cord on ultrasound. Hearing the word cyst does not tell you whether your baby has another condition or whether a complication will occur. The useful next step is to clarify where it is, whether it persists and what the rest of the assessment shows. Some early isolated findings resolve; others need specialist investigation and follow-up. What the scan finding means The umbilical cord connects the baby to the placenta and carries vessels involved in the exchange of oxygen, nutrients and waste. A cyst-like area may be found near the baby’s abdomen, near the placenta or along the cord. There may be one or several. A finding beside a vessel is different from a problem inside the vessel, so the exact scan description matters. A cord cyst is not the same as a cyst in placental tissue, an abdominal-wall defect or a knot in the cord. These can require different assessment. Ask the team to explain what they think the structure represents and whether that conclusion is definite or still uncertain. The label alone cannot establish that blood flow is blocked. True cysts and pseudocysts True cysts arise from remnants of early developmental structures, such as the allantoic or urachal connection and the vitelline, also called omphalomesenteric, duct. Pseudocysts are fluid-containing areas associated with changes in Wharton’s jelly, the supporting tissue around the cord vessels. The words describe different tissue origins, rather than two guaranteed levels of danger. Ultrasound may suggest the origin but cannot always establish the tissue lining or exclude a connection that is not visible. Examination after birth may clarify the diagnosis. There is no single size that reliably separates all true cysts from pseudocysts, and an apparently isolated finding does not prove that every associated condition has been ruled out. Location, number and change over time The fetal end of the cord is next to the baby; the placental end attaches to the placenta. They are not interchangeable descriptions. Ask where the finding lies, how it relates to the abdominal wall and bladder, whether there is one cyst or more, and whether the vessels can be assessed clearly. Size is one part of this description. An early cyst that disappears and is followed by otherwise reassuring examinations often has a different outlook from a persistent or later finding with additional abnormalities. Multiple cysts have also been associated with problems in some studies. None of these features alone provides a personal risk percentage: the pregnancy stage, associated findings and quality of follow-up need to be considered together. Detailed ultrasound and specialist review The assessment looks beyond the cyst itself. A detailed scan may review the baby’s anatomy, abdominal wall and bladder, cord insertion and vessels, growth and amniotic fluid. Doppler ultrasound can assess blood-flow patterns when relevant. Repeat imaging helps show whether the finding resolves, enlarges or changes alongside other signs. Additional structural findings or a persistent, unusual or concerning lesion may prompt fetal-medicine review. Ask what the specialist wants to clarify and which result would change the plan. A normal scan is reassuring within its limits; it cannot identify every chromosome, gene or developmental condition. Keep the written report so that later examinations can be compared with the same finding. Genetic counselling and testing are individual decisions Cord cysts can occur with chromosome or other developmental conditions, particularly when other abnormalities are present. An association does not mean that every cyst has a genetic cause or that it caused the other finding. Counselling should consider the whole ultrasound, prior screening, pregnancy stage and your preferences, rather than treating a broad online percentage as your result. Diagnostic testing may be discussed, including sampling and a laboratory test such as chromosomal microarray when appropriate. Screening and diagnostic testing answer different questions. Ask about the procedure, what the selected test can detect, uncertain results and what a normal result cannot exclude. SMFM recommends offering microarray when invasive genetic analysis is undertaken for fetal structural anomalies; this is not a rule that every isolated early cord cyst requires an invasive test. What the small studies can and cannot tell you One study compared 45 pregnancies with first-trimester cord cysts with 85 controls. All the cysts resolved on follow-up, and the investigators found no significant differences in several measured pregnancy outcomes. There were fetal deaths in both groups. The study therefore offers useful context for early resolving findings, but it cannot guarantee an individual outcome or describe every persistent cyst. It did not establish normal long-term child development. A separate report described two pregnancies, one with early cysts that disappeared and one with a later cyst accompanied by additional fluid and growth concerns; both ended in spontaneous births. Two cases are not proof that all cysts are harmless or that a particular delivery route is always safe. Other small studies have found more problems with multiple, persistent or associated findings. Different screening and referral populations also explain why published frequency estimates vary. Growth and blood flow need their own assessment A cyst near a cord insertion does not automatically mean poor growth or reduced oxygen supply. The team considers actual growth measurements, fluid and circulation. A large or changing lesion can sometimes be associated with vessel compression or other complications, but size or location alone does not establish that this is happening. A 2025 case report described a later cord finding followed by reduced movements and abnormal cord blood flow, leading to urgent birth. That shows why new clinical changes matter even after earlier reassuring scans; one case does not predict the course for everyone. Ask how growth and circulation will be followed and which changes should lead to an earlier review. Monitoring is tailored to the findings There is no single scan interval that has been proved appropriate for every cord cyst. The plan may change if a lesion resolves, persists, grows or accompanies a structural, genetic, growth or blood-flow concern. Ask when the next review is due, who will explain results and how to contact the team between visits. Continued monitoring does not mean that a bad outcome is inevitable. Do not try to treat the cyst with a supplement, herbal preparation or a change to prescribed medicines. Care is directed by the actual findings and any associated condition. Even careful surveillance cannot promise to detect or prevent every complication, so a scheduled scan must not become a reason to delay reporting a new concern. Birth planning does not follow one automatic rule A cord-cyst finding alone does not mean that everyone needs a caesarean to prevent rupture. Timing, place and mode of birth depend on the baby’s condition, associated anatomy, circulation, pregnancy stage and ordinary obstetric considerations. Some reported pregnancies have had vaginal births; others have needed caesarean delivery because of specific concerns. Ask what would change the proposed plan, whether additional monitoring during labour is recommended and whether newborn specialists should be present or available. A decision to bring birth forward weighs the reason for concern against the consequences of prematurity. Neither a particular week nor a delivery method can be chosen safely from the cyst label alone. Some babies need assessment after birth The newborn team may examine the cord and abdomen and arrange further assessment according to the prenatal findings. Occasionally a developmental remnant, such as a persistent urachal connection involving the bladder, becomes apparent after birth despite no clear connection on antenatal imaging. Selected babies may need imaging or specialist treatment. This does not mean that every baby with a prenatal cord cyst needs surgery or intensive care. Ask what examination or follow-up is planned even if the cyst has disappeared, and who will explain any cord or placental examination results. If a new umbilical swelling or unusual leakage is noticed after birth, contact the baby’s clinical team for assessment rather than trying to drain or treat it yourself. Movement changes should not wait for the next scan Once you are familiar with your baby’s usual movements, contact your midwife or maternity unit immediately if they become reduced, stop or change from the usual pattern. Call even at night and do not wait until the next day or a booked scan. A home heartbeat device cannot establish that the baby is well. If you have not felt movements by 24 weeks, tell your midwife. These instructions are about assessing the baby’s wellbeing, not diagnosing a cord cyst from symptoms. Follow any additional urgent-contact advice from your own team. If you are unsure whether a new concern needs assessment, contact them; an earlier reassuring result does not replace review of a change. Questions that help you understand the plan Ask: Is the finding isolated? Where is it and has it changed? Is the anatomy otherwise reassuring? What can genetic testing add, and what are its limits? Are growth or blood-flow checks needed? Write down the next appointment, pending results and the contact route for concerns so that the plan is clear. It is reasonable to need more than one conversation about uncertainty. Ask which information is well established and which comes from small studies or individual cases. A useful explanation should avoid both a guarantee that nothing can go wrong and a prediction of loss from one scan label. The aim is a plan based on this pregnancy’s findings and your informed choices. Clarify the cyst’s location, number, persistence and the rest of the scan findings. True cysts and pseudocysts have different origins, but ultrasound cannot always prove the classification. An early resolving isolated finding can be reassuring; it does not guarantee that every risk is absent. Genetic tests, follow-up scans, birth and newborn assessment are chosen for the individual situation. Report reduced, stopped or changed usual fetal movements immediately; do not wait for the next scan. What is an umbilical-cord cyst? It is a fluid-filled or cyst-like finding along the cord on ultrasound. It may be single or multiple and have different tissue origins. The team should distinguish it from vessels, placental lesions and abnormalities at the baby’s abdominal wall. Is it dangerous for the baby? Not necessarily. Some early isolated cysts resolve with reassuring subsequent findings. Persistent, multiple or associated findings may need closer assessment. The whole scan, growth, circulation and any genetic findings matter; the word cyst alone cannot predict the outcome. How is it diagnosed? Ultrasound identifies the finding, and detailed or repeat scans clarify its location, changes and associated anatomy. Doppler may help assess circulation. Ultrasound does not always prove the true-versus-pseudocyst classification or exclude every developmental connection. Can a cord cyst be linked with miscarriage? Some studies report pregnancy loss with cysts, especially alongside other abnormalities or concerning features. That does not show that every cyst causes loss. Early resolving and later associated findings are different populations, so an overall percentage cannot give your individual risk. Does everyone need amniocentesis or microarray? No single testing plan fits every finding. Discuss the ultrasound, prior screening, diagnostic options, procedure risks and your preferences with the fetal-medicine or genetics team. A normal microarray does not exclude every genetic condition, and screening is not the same as diagnosis. Will I need a caesarean? Not automatically. Some reported pregnancies have had vaginal births. The plan depends on fetal wellbeing, anatomy, blood flow and other obstetric factors; a cyst alone does not set the delivery route or week. If the cyst disappears, can follow-up stop? Resolution can be reassuring, but ask the team what further anatomy assessment or follow-up is appropriate. Small early-resolving studies do not guarantee normal outcomes in every situation, and prenatal imaging cannot identify every associated condition. Could my baby need treatment after birth? Some babies need assessment for a cord or abdominal developmental remnant and selected specialist treatment. Many do not need surgery. Ask for the newborn plan and seek assessment of unusual umbilical leakage or a new swelling rather than treating it yourself.

title: Fetal hydrops: causes, assessment, treatment and newborn care
description: What immune and nonimmune fetal hydrops mean, how specialists investigate the cause, which treatments may help, and how maternal safety, birth and newborn care are planned.
body: Fetal hydrops, also called hydrops fetalis, is a serious pattern of abnormal fluid accumulation in a developing baby. It is a finding that can result from different conditions, rather than one disease with one treatment. Prompt fetal-medicine assessment helps identify the cause, consider available treatment and plan care for both the pregnant person and the baby. One scan or a general survival percentage cannot tell a family exactly what will happen. What the scan finding means Classical hydrops means abnormal fluid in at least two fetal compartments. These include the abdomen, the space around the lungs, the space around the heart and generalized swelling beneath the skin. It is not defined simply as fluid in any two organs. Excess amniotic fluid and a thickened or enlarged placenta may occur alongside hydrops, but they are not themselves two of the defining fetal compartments. A single abnormal fetal fluid collection still matters. Current SMFM guidance describes a hydrops spectrum in which one systemic effusion can have many of the same underlying causes as multiple effusions and merit a similar diagnostic assessment. This does not mean that their prognosis or management is identical. Ask which fluid spaces are involved, whether other findings are present and what has changed since the previous scan. Immune hydrops and maternal red-cell antibodies Immune hydrops can develop when relevant maternal antibodies cross the placenta and cause severe fetal anaemia by damaging red blood cells or interfering with their production. The fetal heart has to work harder, and severe anaemia can lead to circulatory failure and fluid accumulation. Anti-D is one important antibody, but anti-c and anti-K can also cause serious fetal or newborn disease. A difference between the parents’ blood groups alone does not diagnose an affected pregnancy. Anti-D immunoglobulin helps prevent eligible people from forming immune anti-D; it does not remove established antibodies, prevent every red-cell antibody or treat nonimmune hydrops. Follow the maternity team’s blood-group, antibody-testing and prevention plan. If a clinically significant antibody is already present, the team assesses whether the fetus carries the relevant antigen and what monitoring or treatment is needed. A missed injection or an antibody result is not by itself a prediction of fetal harm. Nonimmune hydrops has many possible causes Nonimmune hydrops means that red-cell alloimmunization is not the cause. It can occur with structural heart problems, an abnormal heart rhythm, severe anaemia from another cause, infection, chromosome or single-gene conditions, lymphatic abnormalities, lung or chest lesions, liver or metabolic disease, and some placental conditions. Examples include parvovirus infection and inherited blood disorders. Problems that affect circulation, protein balance or lymph drainage can allow fluid to accumulate. Some complications of twins sharing a placenta can also cause hydrops and need their own specialist pathway. More than one finding may have a common genetic or other cause; identifying a heart or lung abnormality does not necessarily complete the investigation. Sometimes the cause remains uncertain even after testing. The label nonimmune does not make the condition mild, nor does uncertainty mean that assessment, monitoring or supportive care has no value. A specialist assessment looks beyond the fluid Ultrasound identifies the fluid pattern and assesses fetal anatomy, growth, the placenta, amniotic fluid and blood flow. A detailed fetal heart scan, or echocardiogram, examines heart structure and function. Doppler assessment of blood flow in a fetal brain artery can help assess the risk of anaemia; it does not by itself replace every confirmatory test. The team also asks about pregnancy history, family history, previous affected pregnancies, infections, relevant exposures and other medical information. Maternal blood tests review the blood group and red-cell antibodies and may investigate infection, a blood disorder or fetal blood loss into the maternal circulation. A previous negative antibody screen does not rule out the need to repeat it when hydrops is investigated. Tests are chosen and interpreted together, including when only one systemic effusion is present. Ask what each result would change, how soon it may return and who will explain it. Genetic tests and different types of sampling Current SMFM guidance recommends diagnostic genetic testing when one or more fetal effusions are detected, usually including chromosomal microarray with or without a karyotype. Selected infection tests may be performed on an appropriate sample. If these tests do not explain the findings, exome or genome sequencing may be offered, with genetic counselling; sometimes tests are considered together. Screening such as cell-free DNA cannot exclude all the genetic conditions that can cause hydrops, and a reassuring screening result is not a complete diagnostic answer. Amniocentesis takes a sample of the fluid surrounding the fetus for selected tests. Fetal blood sampling, sometimes called cordocentesis or PUBS, takes fetal blood, often from the umbilical cord. These are different procedures. Both use ultrasound guidance; fetal blood sampling or transfusion is not guided by amniocentesis. Discuss the purpose, possible results, uncertainty, procedure risks and alternatives before deciding. Test availability, timing, costs and local services vary. Treating selected cases of severe fetal anaemia Severe fetal anaemia can sometimes be treated before birth with an intrauterine transfusion of appropriately matched donor red cells. This may be considered for immune disease and selected nonimmune causes, including some infections, inherited anaemias or fetal blood loss. The specialist may use fetal blood sampling to confirm the problem and give the transfusion during the same procedure when appropriate. This is specialist treatment, not a home intervention or a substitute for establishing the cause. The choice between fetal treatment, continued monitoring and delivery depends on the cause, severity, pregnancy stage, maternal and fetal condition, available expertise and the family’s wishes. More than one transfusion may be needed, and treatment cannot guarantee survival or prevent every later problem. Ask about the expected benefit, procedure-related risks and the next review. Taking extra oral iron yourself does not replace assessment or treatment of fetal anaemia. Other treatments and care when the cause is uncertain Other selected causes require different approaches. Some fetal rhythm problems can be treated with medicines given to the pregnant person under specialist monitoring. A large chest fluid collection may be considered for needle drainage or a temporary shunt to reduce pressure. Particular structural, infectious or genetic conditions have their own management options. An intervention that is useful for one cause should not be assumed to help every baby with hydrops. Not every case has an effective treatment during pregnancy, but an unexplained cause does not automatically mean that only comfort care is possible. The team can continue diagnostic work, reassess the course and plan maternal and newborn support. Discuss all appropriate options, including continuing pregnancy with monitoring or selected treatment, palliative care when relevant, and ending the pregnancy where available within local law and services. Emerging fetal therapies offered in research trials are not the same as established treatment. The pregnant person also needs monitoring Hydrops can be associated with serious maternal illness, including mirror syndrome, a pre-eclampsia-like condition in which maternal illness may accompany fetal fluid accumulation. It can affect blood pressure, breathing, kidney or liver function and blood tests. It does not always produce the complete combination of visible swelling, high blood pressure and protein in the urine. Do not wait to recognize every feature before asking for help. The maternity team may arrange repeated blood-pressure checks, symptom reviews and laboratory tests. Get immediate maternity assessment for a severe persistent headache, visual changes, pain below the ribs, sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet, feeling very unwell, heartburn that does not settle with medicine, or vomiting. New breathlessness or noticeably reduced urine also needs immediate clinical assessment. Mirror syndrome can make continuing pregnancy dangerous; delivery or other pregnancy-management options require urgent individualized counselling rather than routine watchful waiting. Discuss prognosis without treating a percentage as a prediction Hydrops can lead to miscarriage, stillbirth, premature birth or serious newborn illness. Chest fluid or swelling can limit lung growth or interfere with breathing and circulation. The underlying disease may bring additional risks. Outcomes vary with the cause, associated findings, timing, severity, response to treatment and the care the baby needs after birth. Earlier detection can be concerning, but pregnancy week alone does not determine the outcome. Published studies include different diagnoses and populations, and some count only babies who were born alive. A general mortality estimate cannot accurately describe every pregnancy with nonimmune hydrops. Ask the fetal-medicine and neonatal teams what is known about this particular situation, what remains uncertain and which decisions may change as results return. Counselling should respect your priorities and include emotional support, without promising either a cure or an inevitable poor outcome. Plan the timing, place and mode of birth Birth planning involves maternal-fetal medicine, obstetric and neonatal specialists and, when needed, other teams. If immediate intensive treatment is anticipated or the cause remains uncertain, birth at a hospital able to stabilize and treat a critically ill newborn may be needed. Transfer of maternity care before birth may be safer than an unplanned newborn transfer. The plan should record the agreed neonatal resuscitation and treatment goals, including palliative care when chosen. Hydrops does not automatically require caesarean birth or delivery at a fixed week. The team balances the risks of prematurity against maternal illness, labour or membrane rupture, worsening fetal findings and the risks of continuing pregnancy. Caesarean birth is used for appropriate obstetric indications. If preterm birth is expected and neonatal treatment is planned, ask whether antenatal corticosteroids or other preparation is appropriate. Decisions should be revisited when the condition or the family’s goals change. What may happen in the newborn unit A baby with persistent or severe hydrops may be very unwell at birth and need neonatal intensive care. Initial care can include breathing support, sometimes intubation and ventilation, treatment to support circulation, and intravenous medicines or nutrition. Selected fluid collections may need drainage if they impair breathing or circulation. Not every baby needs every procedure, and the care plan should explain why each intervention is being considered. The neonatal team continues the search for the cause and checks how the baby responds. Some babies need surgery or another cause-specific treatment; others need time and supportive care. The degree of swelling alone does not determine the whole treatment plan. Ask who will update you, how you can be involved safely and what the next decision points are. Parents should not manipulate drains, shunts, lines or respiratory equipment themselves. Anaemia, jaundice and glucose after birth If red-cell antibodies caused the illness, the baby may need monitoring and treatment for anaemia or jaundice, including phototherapy or transfusion in selected circumstances. Anaemia can recur in the weeks after birth, including after a fetal transfusion, so follow-up matters even when the baby initially seems better. Ask about planned blood tests and whom to contact for paler colour, unusual sleepiness, poorer feeding or faster breathing. Premature or unwell newborns may also need blood-glucose monitoring and treatment. Severe, persistent or recurrent low glucose can be harmful, but it is not correct to say that every baby with hydrops develops low glucose, seizures or brain injury. Signs such as poor feeding, altered alertness, jitteriness or abnormal movements can have several causes and require clinical assessment and appropriate measurement. Do not try to diagnose or treat them with a home feeding or sugar remedy. Follow-up and support for the family Recovery, feeding support, discharge and longer-term follow-up depend on the underlying condition, prematurity, treatment and the baby’s progress. Some children need ongoing heart, blood, genetic, developmental or other specialist care. Ask for written follow-up and medicine instructions, including any later anaemia testing. There is no standard hospital-stay length or promise that all problems end once the fluid improves. A cause-specific diagnosis can also help explain whether a later pregnancy might be affected and whether testing or early monitoring would be useful. An unexplained result does not mean that every future pregnancy will have the same problem. Genetic counselling, social work, psychological support and palliative-care support can help families with uncertainty and difficult decisions. Needing help or choosing among medically appropriate options is not a failure of parenting. When the pregnant person needs urgent help Contact maternity care immediately for reduced, absent or changed usual fetal movements; do not wait for the next scan or use a home Doppler as reassurance. After amniocentesis or a fetal procedure, follow the centre’s written plan and seek urgent advice for vaginal fluid leakage or bleeding, fever or feeling hot/cold/shivery, contractions, or abdominal pain that does not settle or is worsening. Report the maternal warning symptoms described above immediately, even after birth, rather than waiting for a routine appointment. Use local emergency services for severe breathing difficulty, a tight or heavy chest, pain spreading to an arm, back, neck or jaw, very pale/blue/grey skin or lips, sudden confusion or a first seizure. Severe, worsening or movement/touch-provoked pelvic pain needs emergency assessment; pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or sudden confusion also does. Pregnancy bleeding with severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, nausea, faintness, dizziness or loss of consciousness, or heavy bleeding, is another emergency pathway. These are alternative triggers, not signs that must all occur. The affected person must not drive to emergency care; arrange another driver or an ambulance. When a baby needs urgent help If the baby is in hospital, alert staff immediately about a change in breathing, colour, feeding, alertness or movements. Outside hospital, seek immediate emergency assessment for difficulty breathing or very fast breathing; blue, grey, unusually pale or blotchy colour; cold or damp/clammy skin; difficulty waking or loss of consciousness; a seizure; a weak, high-pitched or continuous cry; no urine for 12 hours; or a temperature of 38°C or more in a baby under 3 months, or below 36°C, or shivering. A baby who is not feeding, is not responding normally or is unusually sleepy also needs immediate emergency assessment. Do not wait for all the signs or for a planned blood test. Jaundice within the first 24 hours needs emergency assessment. In a baby, jaundice with unusual sleepiness or difficult waking, not feeding, floppiness or stiffness, jerking, temperature of 38°C or more or 36°C or less, feeling abnormally hot/cold or shivering, no wet nappies, or breathing difficulty also needs emergency assessment. Later new or worsening jaundice, dark urine or pale stools needs urgent clinical advice even without these emergency signs. Follow the baby’s individual discharge plan too. For emergency transport, ask another adult to drive or arrange an ambulance rather than driving while caring for an acutely unwell baby. Hydrops is a serious fluid-accumulation pattern with different causes; excess amniotic fluid or a large placenta is an associated finding, not a defining fetal compartment. Immune red-cell disease and nonimmune causes need assessment. Anti-D prevention does not treat established antibodies or every cause of hydrops. A single systemic effusion can merit a similar diagnostic work-up. Amniocentesis and fetal blood sampling are different procedures. Selected causes may benefit from fetal treatment, but maternal safety, prognosis, pregnancy choices and birth plans require individualized counselling. Newborn intensive care and later follow-up depend on the cause and response. Maternal illness or a baby’s emergency warning signs must not wait for the next appointment. What are the signs of fetal hydrops? Ultrasound may show abnormal fluid in the abdomen, around the lungs or heart, or generalized swelling under the skin. Classical hydrops involves at least two fetal compartments. Excess amniotic fluid and a thickened placenta may accompany it but are not themselves defining compartments. One abnormal fluid collection can still warrant a comprehensive assessment; it should not automatically be dismissed as harmless. How is fetal hydrops diagnosed and investigated? Ultrasound identifies the fluid pattern, followed by a specialist assessment of anatomy, growth, heart structure/function, blood flow and possible causes. Maternal antibody and selected infection or blood tests help distinguish mechanisms. Diagnostic genetic testing is recommended when one or more fetal effusions are detected, with further sequencing considered if initial testing is unexplained. Amniocentesis samples amniotic fluid; fetal blood sampling samples fetal blood. A screening test or one normal result does not exclude every cause. Can fetal hydrops be treated? Sometimes a specific cause can be treated, for example with an intrauterine transfusion for selected severe fetal anaemia, medicine for certain fetal arrhythmias, or drainage for a significant chest effusion. Treatment choice and risk depend on the diagnosis, severity, pregnancy stage and available expertise. Not every case has an effective prenatal treatment, but an unknown cause does not automatically mean only palliative care. Discuss diagnostic, supportive, treatment and pregnancy-management options without expecting a guaranteed result. What complications can occur? Hydrops can be associated with pregnancy loss, preterm birth, impaired lung growth, breathing or circulatory problems and serious newborn illness. The underlying disorder may add other complications. Maternal mirror syndrome is also a serious risk. Premature or unwell babies may need glucose monitoring, but low glucose, seizures or brain injury are not inevitable consequences of hydrops. Individual counselling is more useful than a universal mortality percentage. Does an anti-D injection prevent or treat all hydrops? No. It helps prevent formation of immune anti-D in eligible circumstances. It does not remove established antibodies, prevent other clinically important red-cell antibodies such as anti-c or anti-K, or treat nonimmune causes. Blood-group differences alone do not show whether a fetus is affected. Follow the team’s antibody-testing, prevention and specialist assessment plan. Is a fetal transfusion the same as amniocentesis? No. Amniocentesis collects amniotic fluid for selected diagnostic tests. Fetal blood sampling and intrauterine transfusion involve the fetal circulation and may be considered for significant fetal anaemia. They use ultrasound guidance, not amniocentesis guidance. The specialist explains whether treatment, monitoring or delivery is appropriate, including risks and alternatives; taking extra oral iron is not a substitute. Will the baby need a caesarean and intensive care? There is no automatic caesarean or fixed delivery week for every case. Maternal health, fetal condition, gestation, appropriate obstetric indications and agreed treatment goals guide the plan. Persistent or severe hydrops may need birth at a centre with neonatal intensive care for breathing, circulation, drainage or cause-specific treatment. The team should discuss likely care before birth while explaining what remains uncertain. Which changes mean we should get help immediately? Contact maternity care immediately for reduced or changed usual fetal movements; postprocedure bleeding, fluid leakage, fever or feeling hot/cold/shivery, contractions or unrelieved/worsening abdominal pain; or severe persistent headache, visual changes, pain below the ribs, sudden face/hand/foot swelling, feeling very unwell, unrelieved heartburn, vomiting, new breathlessness or reduced urine. Use emergency services for severe breathing trouble, a tight/heavy chest, pain spreading to an arm/back/neck/jaw, very pale/blue/grey skin or lips, sudden confusion or a first seizure. Severe, worsening or movement/touch-provoked pelvic pain, or pelvic pain with faintness/dizziness or loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or sudden confusion, also needs emergency help. Pregnancy bleeding with severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, nausea, faintness/dizziness or loss of consciousness, or heavy bleeding, is another emergency. The affected person must not drive; arrange another driver or an ambulance. A baby with breathing difficulty or very fast breathing, blue/grey/unusually pale/blotchy colour, cold or damp skin, difficulty waking, a seizure, a weak/high-pitched/continuous cry, no urine for 12 hours, not feeding or an abnormal response/unusual sleepiness needs emergency assessment. So does a temperature of 38°C or more under 3 months, below 36°C, or shivering. Jaundice before 24 hours, or jaundice with unusual sleepiness/difficult waking, not feeding, floppy/stiff/jerking movements, temperature of 38°C or more or 36°C or less, feeling abnormally hot/cold or shivering, no wet nappies or breathing difficulty also needs emergency assessment. Later new/worsening jaundice, dark urine or pale stools needs urgent clinical advice. These are alternative triggers; do not wait for all of them. Ask another adult to drive or arrange an ambulance rather than driving while caring for an acutely unwell baby.

title: X-rays during pregnancy: dose, timing and decisions
description: Understand necessary or unexpected X-ray exposure in pregnancy, fetal dose, timing, CT and dental imaging, shielding, and when to request an individual assessment.
body: A needed X-ray can help diagnose an injury or illness during pregnancy. An examination performed before you knew you were pregnant does not automatically mean the baby has been harmed. The useful questions are what examination was done, which body area was exposed, the estimated dose reaching the pregnancy and its stage. Most diagnostic examinations use doses well below those associated with developmental harm, but a general reassurance cannot replace assessment of an unusual or substantial exposure. Start with the reason for the examination A fracture, dental infection or serious illness may need imaging so that treatment is not delayed. The clinician weighs the consequences of missing the diagnosis against the exposure involved. Pregnancy is a reason to choose and optimize the examination carefully; it is not an automatic reason to refuse necessary imaging. Tell the referring clinician and radiographer that you are pregnant, might be pregnant or are trying to conceive. Give your estimated pregnancy dates and mention recent related examinations. If an urgent injury or illness is being assessed, tell the team promptly rather than postponing care while you seek an online risk calculation. The body area matters A dental, limb, head or chest examination usually keeps the pregnancy outside the direct X-ray beam. Radiation reaching it is much lower than when the abdomen or pelvis is directly examined. The name of the test alone still cannot establish an individual's dose: the technique, number of images, scan coverage and patient characteristics matter. An abdominal or pelvic examination is not automatically prohibited. It needs a clear clinical reason and a protocol that obtains the necessary information with appropriate exposure. A plain radiograph, a CT scan and a prolonged image-guided procedure can involve very different doses. Do not use the number of appointments as a substitute for the actual examination record. What rad, gray and milligray mean Absorbed dose describes energy deposited in tissue. For this discussion, the relevant quantity is the dose reaching the embryo or fetus, usually expressed in milligray, or mGy. One rad equals 10 mGy: 5 rad is 50 mGy and 10 rad is 100 mGy. These conversions do not tell you how much radiation your baby received. An adult imaging chart may instead show effective dose in millisieverts, or mSv. That is a different measure used to describe overall radiation risk. It cannot simply be substituted for fetal mGy. Likewise, a dose number on a CT report may be a scanner output measure rather than a fetal dose. A radiologist or medical physicist can explain which number you have. Why 5 or 10 rad is not a personal safety rule ACOG describes no reported fetal anomalies, growth restriction or pregnancy loss below 50 mGy. UKTIS states that exposure below this level would not usually itself justify termination or extra fetal monitoring. These statements concern particular outcomes and clinical decisions; they do not promise that every possible risk is zero. Most individual diagnostic studies are below this level. IAEA guidance, drawing on ICRP, says a fetal dose below 100 mGy does not justify termination on radiation grounds alone. This is not permission to aim for that dose, nor does crossing it mean harm is certain or termination is required. Higher or uncertain exposures require specialist assessment of dose, timing and circumstances, with counselling about the available choices. Pregnancy weeks and developmental timing Radiation references may count weeks after conception, whereas maternity records usually date pregnancy from the last menstrual period, roughly two weeks earlier. Mixing the two can place an exposure in the wrong developmental period. The first weeks after conception, organ formation and later brain development have different sensitivities at sufficiently high doses. Statements such as “safe at 3–4 weeks”, “harm above 10 rad at 5–10 weeks” or “brain damage at 11–17 weeks” are too blunt for an individual decision. CDC identifies roughly 8–15 weeks after conception as especially sensitive for intellectual effects from high-dose exposure. Such high-dose observations should not be presented as the expected outcome of a routine dental or limb X-ray. Later pregnancy is not a no-risk window At 18–27 weeks of pregnancy, developmental sensitivity differs from earlier pregnancy, but the exposure and the outcome being considered still matter. After 28 weeks, it is misleading to say that the fetus simply has the same risk as the mother. Some developmental effects become less likely later, while a large exposure can still be important. Cancer risk is a separate question from malformations or effects on brain development. Its size at low diagnostic doses is uncertain, and there is no dependable pregnancy week after which it can be declared absent. This is why neither a gestational-age label nor the absence of a measurable developmental effect proves that an exposure has absolutely no risk. CT, alternatives and whether to wait Ultrasound and MRI do not use ionizing X-rays and may answer the clinical question. They are not interchangeable with every radiograph or CT examination, and availability or speed can matter. If they cannot provide the needed information in time, CT may be the appropriate choice. A necessary scan should not be deferred automatically until 20 weeks or after birth. Ask what the result will change and what could happen if the examination is delayed. The team can decide whether it is genuinely elective or needed now, including after trauma. Contrast material is a separate part of that decision: tell the team about previous contrast reactions and ask why it is required. Iodinated CT contrast crosses the placenta, so its use should have a clinical purpose rather than being treated as identical to a scan without contrast. Dental imaging and treatment A painful tooth or dental infection should be assessed during pregnancy. Necessary dental radiographs can be taken at any stage, and delaying urgent treatment can make the problem more complicated. Tell the dentist about the pregnancy and any maternity concerns so that imaging and treatment can be planned together. Current ADA guidance does not recommend routine abdominal or thyroid shielding for the pregnant dental patient. An absent lead apron therefore does not, by itself, mean unsafe care. Ask the team to explain the indication and its radiation-protection approach; do not avoid needed dental care solely because older advice said every pregnant patient must be shielded. Why routine patient shielding has changed A shield on the abdomen does little to block radiation scattered inside the body from the area being examined. If it moves into the image or affects automatic exposure control, it can hide information, lead to another image or increase exposure. AAPM therefore advises against routine patient gonadal and fetal shielding during diagnostic X-ray imaging. This does not abolish radiation protection. Appropriate examination choice, beam restriction, suitable technique and avoiding unnecessary repeats remain important. Protective barriers and aprons for staff or people assisting during an exposure serve a different purpose. Follow the department's instructions rather than putting a shield in place yourself or assuming every setting uses the same protocol. If imaging happened before you knew Contact your maternity clinician and the imaging department with the examination date, body area, type of test and number of examinations. Include any prolonged procedure or radiation treatment, and the best available pregnancy dates. The team can determine whether ordinary reassurance is enough or whether a medical physicist should estimate fetal exposure from the actual records. An individual calculation is especially useful when substantial abdominal or pelvic exposure is possible, or when several exposures need to be considered together. It is not a sign that damage has already been found. Do not make a pregnancy decision from a generic online dose table. Further monitoring, if indicated, depends on the assessment and any other pregnancy concerns; extra scans are not automatically required after every X-ray. Before conception and after the examination Ordinary X-rays and CT do not leave radioactive material in your body. A past diagnostic examination is therefore different from an ongoing source of radiation. Evidence does not support predicting infertility or harm to a future child from an ordinary diagnostic X-ray, but this reassurance should not be extended to high-dose cancer treatment. If pregnancy may already have begun, disclose that possibility before the examination. Nuclear-medicine tests and radioactive treatments involve different substances and instructions, so ask about the exact procedure rather than using advice about a plain X-ray. Follow any procedure-specific advice about conception; do not invent a universal waiting interval from an online article. Accompanying a child and working around radiation You can tell the department that your child needs support and that you are pregnant or might be. Do not hold the child during an X-ray exposure; ask staff to arrange another helper or appropriate support. Follow instructions about where to wait. If you already helped without realizing you were pregnant, report what happened so the department can assess the circumstances rather than assuming the child's dose was also your dose. If radiation is part of your work, discuss pregnancy with the appropriate supervisor, occupational-health service or radiation safety officer. Review your tasks, monitoring and protective measures under local rules. Continuing work, modifying tasks or changing duties depends on the actual exposure assessment. Patient-dose counselling thresholds are not workplace limits, and advice to stop routine patient shielding does not remove staff protective requirements. Questions to take to the appointment Ask: What diagnosis are we checking? Will the result change treatment? Can ultrasound or MRI answer the same question soon enough? What is the risk of waiting? Will the pregnancy be in the direct beam? Does this examination need a fetal-dose estimate? If you were already exposed, ask who will review the records and when you will receive an explanation. Keep the examination report, dates and the agreed follow-up plan together. If the explanation is unclear or anxiety persists, request a discussion with the radiology or maternity team. Necessary emergency treatment should proceed while the teams coordinate; waiting for a retrospective radiation estimate must not delay assessment of a serious current illness or injury. Necessary imaging can protect health during pregnancy; discuss the clinical question and the consequences of delay. Body area, technique, fetal absorbed dose and developmental timing matter more than the label “X-ray”. Neither 5 or 10 rad nor a particular pregnancy week is a universal zero-risk or certain-harm boundary. Routine patient shielding is different from protective measures for workers and helpers. Unexpected exposure should be assessed from actual records, with specialist counselling when needed. Is an X-ray at 5–10 weeks always dangerous? No. The body area and actual fetal dose matter, as does whether the weeks are counted from the last period or conception. Early development is sensitive to sufficiently high doses, but this does not make an ordinary dental or limb radiograph equivalent to a high-dose exposure. Ask the imaging team to assess the actual examination. Does exposure at 11–17 weeks mean brain damage? No. High-dose research identifies a period of greater brain-development sensitivity, often stated as 8–15 weeks after conception. It cannot predict damage from the pregnancy week alone. A specialist needs the examination details, fetal-dose estimate when indicated and accurate pregnancy dating. Is imaging risk-free at 18–27 weeks or after 28 weeks? No pregnancy week is a blanket zero-risk boundary. Developmental sensitivity changes, but dose and type of effect remain important. Later pregnancy should not be described simply as having the mother's radiation risk, and uncertainty about cancer risk is different from the risk of a developmental abnormality. What determines the risk, and what do 5 and 10 rad mean? The important factors include fetal absorbed dose, body area, technique, exposure pattern and developmental timing. Five rad equals 50 mGy and 10 rad equals 100 mGy. These are not the same as adult effective-dose figures in mSv, and neither is an automatic safe-or-harmful cutoff for an individual pregnancy. Should I cancel a necessary CT or dental X-ray? Discuss the need with the clinical team rather than cancelling because of pregnancy alone. An alternative is useful if it answers the question in time; delaying urgent diagnosis or dental treatment can cause harm. Tell staff about the pregnancy so that they can choose and optimize the examination. What if I had an X-ray before a positive pregnancy test? Give your maternity clinician and the imaging department the date, examination and body area. Most diagnostic exposures are reassuring, but substantial or uncertain exposure may need an individual fetal-dose assessment. Diagnostic exposure alone is not an automatic reason to end a pregnancy or arrange extra monitoring. Does no lead apron mean the baby was unprotected? No. Routine patient fetal shielding is no longer recommended by major medical-physics guidance, and dental guidance also advises against it. An apron does not stop internal scatter and can interfere with imaging. Staff barriers and protective equipment for people assisting during exposure are a different issue. Can I hold my child for an X-ray or keep working in radiology? Do not hold a child during exposure if you are pregnant or might be; tell staff so they can arrange support. Work decisions need an occupational radiation assessment and local precautions, not an automatic ban or a patient-dose threshold. Report any unexpected exposure with its details for advice.

title: When to tell people you are pregnant: timing, privacy and support
description: Decide when and whom to tell about pregnancy, balance early support with privacy, set sharing boundaries and keep care separate from a public announcement.
body: There is no week when you must announce a pregnancy to family and friends. After a positive test, you might want company, time alone with the news, or both. You can tell a few people now and a wider circle later. The useful question is who could support you at this stage, and what you want them to know. Make room for your own reaction Excitement, surprise, worry and uncertainty can coexist. A planned pregnancy does not require an immediately joyful reaction, and an unexpected pregnancy does not require an immediate public explanation. Give yourself space to consider your feelings before planning how to present the news to others. If you are unsure about continuing the pregnancy, seek timely, confidential advice about your options from a qualified service. If anxiety, low mood or distress is affecting you, tell your midwife or doctor. You can ask for professional support while keeping the news private from relatives or social media. Choose people by trust, not a fixed order A partner may be the first person you want to tell, but there is no compulsory sequence of partner, parents, siblings and friends. Think about who listens, respects your decisions and can keep information private. Where it feels comfortable, discuss with your partner how each of you would like to share the news. It can feel easier to start with someone outside the family, such as a trusted friend or a professional. That does not mean you care less about your relatives. You can also choose different formats: a quiet conversation, a phone call or a short message. A surprise announcement is an option, not an obligation. What sharing early can offer Telling a trusted person may make it easier to ask for a lift to an appointment, help with daily tasks or someone to listen. You may enjoy sharing your excitement, or want support while you feel uncertain. Help can be specific: “Could you check in with me after my appointment?” Support is possible, not guaranteed. Consider how someone has responded to private or difficult information before. Suggestions about clinicians or services can be useful starting points, but friends’ pregnancy experiences cannot determine what care you need. Keep medical questions for your own maternity team. What sharing early can make harder Once another person knows, you may receive questions, advice or attention that you did not want. News may travel beyond the people you chose. Before sharing, say whether it is private and whether photographs, messages or online posts are welcome. A clear request helps, although it cannot guarantee confidentiality. You might say, “I am telling you because I would value your support. Please let me tell everyone else myself.” If advice becomes tiring, try, “I have a plan with my clinician; what would help today is some company.” These are examples to adapt, not rules for handling every relationship. What waiting can offer: and what it cannot promise Keeping the news within a small circle can give you time to absorb it and decide what you want to share. It may reduce repeated questions while you wait for an appointment or make personal decisions. You do not need to justify the choice to everyone who asks. Waiting does not have to mean coping alone. You can ask one person for help or use professional support without making a general announcement. Equally, telling someone early does not commit you to regular updates. Review your choice if symptoms, practical needs or your feelings change. Twelve weeks, scans and screening are not announcement rules Some people wait until a first scan around twelve weeks, partly because the risk of miscarriage decreases as pregnancy progresses. That can be a personally meaningful milestone. It is not a deadline, a requirement or a point at which every pregnancy risk disappears. An early announcement does not cause a pregnancy loss. Screening tests estimate the chance of particular conditions; they cannot guarantee that a baby will have no health problems. They are offered at different stages, and you can discuss whether to have them. You do not have to complete screening before telling someone. Ask your clinician what a particular result means, rather than using it as an all-clear for the rest of pregnancy. Think about support if the pregnancy becomes difficult If you have experienced loss, telling people again may feel especially complicated. You may want familiar support or prefer fewer questions. Neither choice measures your hope, attachment or confidence. Scans and reassuring conversations can help some people, but cannot remove all uncertainty about the future. If a loss happens, you can choose whom to tell and how much to explain, even if those people did not know you were pregnant. Someone you trust could pass on a message with your agreement. Support from your care team or a pregnancy-loss service does not depend on having made an announcement. You do not owe everyone the details of your grief. Plan wider sharing with privacy and other people in mind Before posting online, consider whether you are comfortable with the news reaching people outside your intended audience. A private conversation first may suit someone close to you who is experiencing infertility or a loss. Give them room to respond in their own time rather than expecting an immediate celebration. If you have children, consider what they can understand and how they might share the news themselves. A simple explanation and space for questions may work better than asking a young child to manage a complicated secret. You can tell different people at different times; one conversation does not require a public announcement the same day. Arrange care and workplace support separately Contact your local maternity service early after finding out you are pregnant, even if you are waiting to tell friends. If you take medicines or have a long-term condition, arrange timely advice from the relevant clinician. Do not stop prescribed treatment on your own. Privacy about the pregnancy should not delay assessment or care. Workplace notification is a separate practical decision. Check your country’s rules, employment terms and notice requirements for leave or other benefits. If duties may present a pregnancy-related risk or you need adjustments, discuss this promptly with the appropriate workplace contact and your clinician. Ask who needs to know and how confidentiality will be handled; notifying a manager does not have to be an announcement to all colleagues. Use a small plan that you can change Write down three things: who you want to tell now, what help you would welcome, and what should stay private. For example: “My sister can know now, I would like help with appointments, and I do not want messages shared.” Decide when you would like to reconsider, without treating that date as a promise to announce. Medical symptoms need their own response. Seek clinical advice for bleeding or pain in early pregnancy; get urgent help for heavy bleeding, severe pain or feeling very unwell. Severe vomiting or being unable to keep food or fluids down also needs prompt care. Do not wait until your preferred announcement date to ask for help. Choose a disclosure plan around your readiness, privacy and support needs rather than a compulsory week. A small trusted circle can provide support while you keep wider sharing for later. A scan or screening result does not guarantee the rest of pregnancy, and sharing news does not cause a loss. Set clear boundaries about passing on news, photographs and repeated questions. Arrange maternity care and any necessary workplace discussion independently of a public announcement. What are the advantages of telling people early? You may receive emotional or practical support, share excitement and have someone alongside you for difficult decisions or appointments. Choose people you trust and explain the help you want; an early announcement does not guarantee a helpful response. What are the disadvantages of telling people early? You may face unwanted advice, repeated questions or news spreading beyond your intended circle. Set privacy boundaries before sharing. If the pregnancy ends, you still choose how much to explain and can ask someone else to communicate with your agreement. What are the advantages of waiting? Waiting can give you time to process the news, make decisions and limit attention. You can keep wider sharing for later while telling one trusted person or seeking professional support now. Does waiting mean I will have no support? No. A public announcement and access to support are separate. You can speak privately with someone you trust, a maternity professional or a support service, including after a loss that others did not know about. Must I wait until twelve weeks or screening results? No. Some people choose a scan as a milestone, but neither a week of pregnancy nor a screening result guarantees the outcome. Choose when to share on your own terms and discuss test results with your clinician. Should my partner always be the first person I tell? There is no mandatory order. Consider your circumstances and whom you feel comfortable approaching. Where appropriate, discuss a shared plan with your partner, while recognizing your own need for privacy and support. Can I change my mind after telling a few people? Yes. You can widen the circle, postpone further sharing or ask for fewer questions. Explain what you prefer now; sharing once does not require you to provide continuing updates. Can I wait to book maternity care until I announce? Arrange care early, even while keeping the pregnancy private socially. Ask promptly about medicines, existing health conditions or worrying symptoms. Workplace risk and leave-notice discussions may also need to happen before you choose to tell everyone.

title: Viral hepatitis in pregnancy: pregnancy loss, treatment and protecting the baby
description: Compare hepatitis A–E in pregnancy, understand why risk depends on the virus and liver illness, and plan testing, treatment and newborn protection without relying on a fixed risk percentage.
body: Hepatitis means inflammation of the liver. The viruses called hepatitis A, B, C, D and E do not have the same routes of spread, treatments or pregnancy risks. A hepatitis result does not by itself establish that a miscarriage will happen or explain a previous loss. It also should not be dismissed with a blanket promise that pregnancy is unaffected. The useful next step is to identify the virus, assess the pregnant person’s health and make a timely care and newborn-prevention plan. Start with the type and the severity, not a general reassurance A recent infection, a long-standing infection without advanced liver damage and an illness causing liver failure are different situations. The pregnancy stage, other infections, liver function and access to treatment also matter. Miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth and transmission to a baby are different outcomes; a number describing one cannot be used to predict another. Hepatitis E deserves particular attention because symptomatic infection in pregnancy, especially later in pregnancy, can be severe for both the pregnant person and fetus. Hepatitis C has also been associated with preterm birth, reduced fetal growth and other complications in studies, although associations do not prove that the virus caused an individual outcome. Advanced liver disease adds risks whatever the original cause. Ask for an individual assessment rather than assuming either inevitable loss or no danger. How the five viruses differ Hepatitis A is usually spread through contaminated food or water or close contact involving the faecal–oral route. Hepatitis E can spread through contaminated water, and some types through raw or undercooked animal products. Hepatitis B and C are mainly concerns around infected blood; B can also spread through sexual body-fluid exposure. Both can pass from a pregnant person to a baby. Hepatitis D needs hepatitis B to replicate. Acute means a recent, short-term infection; chronic means a persisting infection. A does not become chronic. B and C can, and D can persist with B. E is usually acute but can rarely become chronic, particularly in immunosuppressed people. Symptoms alone cannot reliably tell these viruses apart, and someone with B or C may feel well despite an infection requiring follow-up. Hepatitis A: an acute infection, with prevention available Hepatitis A usually resolves, but it can cause substantial illness and occasionally severe liver failure. It should not be labelled harmless because it does not become chronic. During pregnancy, vomiting, dehydration, jaundice or abdominal pain needs clinical assessment rather than a home diagnosis. Treatment usually supports hydration and recovery; severe illness may require hospital care. A vaccine is available. In US CDC guidance, pregnancy vaccination is recommended when there is a risk of infection or a severe outcome and previous vaccination is absent; local recommendations and the exact product matter. After a possible exposure, contact a clinician promptly because vaccine or immunoglobulin may be appropriate and postexposure prevention is time-sensitive, generally within two weeks. Do not wait for symptoms or arrange injections yourself. Hepatitis B: assess maternal infection and plan prevention A positive hepatitis B surface antigen test, or HBsAg, indicates current infection. The team assesses whether infection is recent or chronic, checks liver health and usually measures HBV DNA to help assess the need for treatment and transmission prevention. Maternal viral activity and prevention measures matter; describing every exposure as a 90% transmission risk is inaccurate. The often-quoted figure of about 90% refers to chronic infection developing among infants who actually acquire HBV, not to every baby of a parent with HBV. Some pregnant people need antiviral treatment for their own liver health, and some with high HBV DNA need it to reduce transmission. Specialist guidance commonly uses tenofovir, with timing determined by the clinical situation and local pathway. Do not start, switch or stop it yourself; stopping can require monitoring for a liver flare. Maternal treatment does not replace the baby’s birth protection. Caesarean birth is not recommended solely to prevent HBV transmission. An HBV-exposed newborn needs an advance birth plan Tell the maternity and newborn teams about a positive HBsAg result before delivery and make sure the result reaches the birth facility. Under US CDC guidance, a baby born to an HBsAg-positive person receives single-antigen hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immunoglobulin, or HBIG, within 12 hours of birth, at different injection sites. The vaccine helps build protection; HBIG supplies immediate antibodies. This applies even if the pregnant person received antivirals. If the maternal result is unknown or undocumented, tell the team immediately: testing and newborn prevention must not wait for a routine appointment. The precise vaccine/HBIG pathway depends on available results, evidence of infection, birth weight and local guidance. If a planned dose was missed, contact the birth team urgently for a catch-up decision rather than assuming it is too late or waiting until the next scheduled vaccine. This is clinical prevention, not a home injection plan. Finish the vaccine course and the baby’s tests Birth protection is the start, not the whole course. In the US CDC pathway, exposed infants complete their vaccine series and have HBsAg and anti-HBs blood tests at 9–12 months, or one to two months after a delayed final dose, but not before nine months. Low birth weight can change the number and timing of doses. A well-looking baby still needs the planned tests; absence of symptoms does not prove that transmission was prevented. Programmes differ. WHO recommends hepatitis B vaccination for all babies as soon as possible after birth, within 24 hours, followed by the course. England’s exposed-baby pathway uses a birth vaccine within 24 hours, HBIG for selected higher-risk babies, further vaccines and infection testing between one year and 18 months. These examples should not be combined into a new schedule. Ask your own team to document the exact birth medicines, later doses, test date and who will review the result, including if you move. Hepatitis C: exposure does not mean infection HCV can pass during pregnancy or birth when the pregnant person has current infection, shown by detectable HCV RNA. An antibody result alone may reflect an infection that has cleared. CDC estimates that roughly 6–7% of perinatally exposed infants acquire infection; this is a population estimate, not a personal prediction. Poorly controlled HIV coinfection raises risk, and effective HIV care is important. There is no hepatitis C vaccine or routine birth immunoglobulin that prevents it. When feasible, cure HCV before pregnancy. During pregnancy, assess liver health and discuss treatment with a specialist: evidence for direct-acting antivirals is still limited, and they are not routinely recommended solely to prevent transmission. Ribavirin has specific pregnancy risks. Do not start or stop a medicine without advice, or infer that every antiviral has the same pregnancy or feeding profile. HCV birth precautions, infant testing and feeding A caesarean is not recommended solely to prevent HCV. Clinicians avoid unnecessary blood-exposing procedures such as internal fetal monitoring and early artificial membrane rupture when possible, while providing appropriate obstetric care. These precautions cannot guarantee prevention. Under the US CDC pathway, an exposed infant has an HCV RNA test at age 2–6 months, with age-based catch-up if missed. A detectable result needs specialist follow-up; local pathways can differ. HCV is not documented to spread through breast milk or ordinary hugging and kissing. Cracked, damaged or bleeding nipples need a temporary feeding plan to avoid blood exposure; HIV coinfection and exact medicines need separate specialist advice. HBV infection also does not automatically prevent breastfeeding when the baby receives the appropriate birth prophylaxis. Keep parental liver follow-up and the child’s testing plan separate, even when both feel well. Hepatitis D depends on B, but can make liver disease more serious HDV cannot replicate without HBV. A person can acquire B and D together, or acquire D after already having chronic B; it is not restricted to people known to have B beforehand. D can accelerate serious liver disease. It is blood-borne and can also spread through sexual exposure; transmission around birth is possible but uncommon. Preventing HBV through vaccination also prevents the B infection that allows D to establish itself in an uninfected person. It does not treat an existing B or D infection. If you have HBV, ask whether D testing is appropriate for your history and local guidance. A positive result needs specialist assessment of liver health, pregnancy and treatment options; do not transfer a B or C treatment plan to D yourself. Hepatitis E can be particularly dangerous in pregnancy HEV infection can cause acute liver failure, pregnancy loss and maternal death, with increased risk described particularly in the second and third trimesters. The risk varies with the setting and infection; a severe-outcome percentage from one group should not be presented as every person’s prediction. Symptomatic pregnant people need urgent assessment, and hospital care may be considered. HEV can also pass from a pregnant person to the baby. New jaundice or feeling unwell must not wait for a routine antenatal visit. It is outdated to say that E never becomes chronic or that no vaccine exists. Chronic infection occurs rarely, especially with immunosuppression. An HEV vaccine is licensed in China and some other countries and has been used in outbreak responses, including campaigns involving pregnant women, but it is not a routinely available pregnancy vaccine everywhere. Ask local public-health or travel clinicians about actual availability and advice. Safe water, sanitation and properly cooked food remain important; do not self-treat hepatitis E with antivirals or liver remedies. Testing and possible exposure need a timely conversation Tell your maternity clinician about a previous hepatitis diagnosis, treatment, vaccine record, relevant travel, possible contaminated food or water, blood exposure and any HIV infection. Testing may include liver blood tests and virus-specific antibody, antigen or RNA tests. Routine antenatal screening does not necessarily test for all five viruses. The US recommends HBV and HCV screening in each pregnancy; available screening and follow-up vary internationally. A needlestick, blood contact, sexual exposure or close contact with hepatitis A can call for prompt assessment even without symptoms. The clinician decides which tests, vaccination or other postexposure measures are appropriate and whether repeat testing is needed. A negative early result may not answer every recent exposure. Do not delay because you are worried about blame, and do not assume that a partner’s diagnosis establishes infection in you or the fetus. Reduce exposure without replacing medical care Use safe drinking water and follow local food-safety advice, including thorough cooking of meat and shellfish. Wash hands, especially after using the toilet and before preparing food. Do not share needles, injection equipment, razors or toothbrushes that may carry blood; use regulated services with appropriate infection control. Discuss sexual protection and whether close contacts need testing or vaccination, without stigma. Avoid alcohol and ask your clinician or pharmacist before using nonprescription medicines, supplements or herbal products when liver disease is suspected or known. A product marketed as a liver detox is not a treatment for viral hepatitis. Keep prescribed treatment and monitoring under review rather than stopping independently. After delivery, continue the parent’s liver care as well as the baby’s vaccines and tests; preventing transmission does not mean the parent’s infection has been cured. When the pregnant or postpartum person needs urgent help Get urgent clinical advice if you think you have hepatitis, develop yellow eyes or skin, dark urine or pale stools, or feel unwell after a possible exposure. Contact maternity care urgently for pregnancy bleeding or pelvic pain, and immediately for reduced or changed usual fetal movements. Do not assume pain, jaundice, itching or vomiting is just a known hepatitis infection; other pregnancy conditions can need treatment. Use emergency services for severe, worsening or movement/touch-provoked pelvic pain, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, passing out, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or sudden confusion. Pregnancy bleeding with severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, nausea, faintness, dizziness or loss of consciousness, or heavy bleeding, is also an emergency. In someone with cirrhosis, vomiting blood, very dark/black stools or sudden confusion/slurred speech need emergency care. These are alternative triggers, not an all-signs checklist. The affected person must not drive; arrange another driver or an ambulance. A newborn’s symptoms do not replace the prevention plan An exposed baby may have no early signs of infection, so keep vaccination and testing appointments. Seek immediate emergency assessment for breathing difficulty or very fast breathing, blue/grey or unusually pale/blotchy colour, cold or damp skin, difficulty waking or loss of consciousness, a seizure, a weak, high-pitched or continuous cry, an abnormal response, not feeding, unusual sleepiness or no urine for 12 hours. A temperature of 38°C or more under three months, below 36°C or shivering also needs immediate emergency assessment. Jaundice in the first 24 hours is an emergency. In a baby, jaundice with unusual sleepiness or difficult waking, not feeding, floppiness, stiffness or jerking, temperature of 38°C or more or 36°C or less, abnormal hot/cold feeling or shivering, no wet nappies or breathing difficulty also needs emergency assessment. Later new or worsening jaundice, dark urine or pale stools needs urgent clinical advice. Do not wait for every sign or the hepatitis test. Ask another adult to drive or arrange an ambulance rather than driving while caring for an acutely unwell baby. A–E are different infections. Pregnancy-loss risk and care depend on the virus, acute or chronic illness, liver health and the individual situation. HBV-exposed newborn prevention must be planned before birth; maternal antivirals do not replace vaccine and any indicated immunoglobulin. Complete the local infant vaccine and testing pathway even when the baby looks well. US and England schedules are not interchangeable. HCV has no vaccine; current infection and infant follow-up matter. D depends on B, and E needs particular pregnancy vigilance. Possible exposure, jaundice, maternal illness or a baby’s emergency warning signs should not wait for a routine appointment. Which hepatitis viruses can pass from a pregnant person to a baby? B and C are important perinatal infections. D can rarely pass around birth in the context of B, and E can also pass to a baby. The route and risk depend on the virus and infection status; a parent’s positive result does not prove that the baby is infected. For HBV, agree birth vaccination and immunoglobulin eligibility in advance, then complete the local vaccine and test plan. Can hepatitis C pass to the baby?
