What an older study can and cannot tell us A 2005 Canadian survey of 316 women at an early postnatal visit found an association between breastfeeding and whether vaginal intercourse had resumed. Babies were around six-and-a-half weeks old on average. Tiredness, lack of interest and concern about pain were among the reasons participants gave for waiting. This study describes one group at one early stage; it does not show that breastfeeding inevitably harms sexual wellbeing or causes relationship difficulties. Resuming intercourse is also not the same measure as feeling close, enjoying affection or being satisfied with a relationship. Its practical message is that feeding, comfort and contraception are worth discussing openly. Hormones affect the body without deciding your feelings Estrogen falls after pregnancy and may remain relatively low during breastfeeding, contributing to vaginal dryness. Prolactin supports milk production, while oxytocin helps release milk through the let-down reflex. These physical processes can overlap with changes in sensation and comfort during intimate contact. They do not mean that feeding a baby replaces a partner or fulfils all your needs for adult closeness. Nor can a single hormone level explain how much sex someone wants. Feeling relaxed after a feed, wanting affection, or wanting some time without being touched are different experiences, and any of them can occur in the same week. Body changes can bring mixed feelings Breast size, shape and sensitivity may change, along with the rest of the body after pregnancy. You may like some changes, feel unfamiliar with others, or have little energy to think about appearance. None of those reactions requires you to present your body in a particular way for someone else. Tell your partner which kinds of touch feel welcome and which do not. Being touched out after hours of feeding or carrying a baby can coexist with affection for a partner. A request for space can be about sensory overload or tiredness, rather than a statement about the relationship. Milk can leak during sexual contact Nipple stimulation or sexual arousal can trigger the milk-release reflex. Milk may drip or spray during intimate activity, including around orgasm. This can be surprising, but leakage on its own does not mean anything is wrong. Some people leak frequently and others hardly at all. Talking about the possibility beforehand can make it less awkward. You can keep a towel nearby, wear a comfortable bra with breast pads, or leave the breasts out of the activity. These are choices for your comfort; there is no need to hide a normal body function if it does not bother you. Manage fullness without creating extra work for yourself Feeding at the baby’s usual time before spending time together may reduce uncomfortable fullness. If a breast remains uncomfortably full, expressing a little for comfort may help. Routine extra pumping solely to prepare for sex is not necessary and can encourage more milk production. Change wet breast pads so the skin does not stay damp, and avoid tight pressure on sore breasts. If fullness, leakage or fast flow is difficult to manage, ask for feeding support rather than repeatedly emptying the breasts. A plan should fit the baby’s needs and your comfort, not create a new obligation around intimacy. Dryness can make penetration uncomfortable Lower estrogen and other changes after birth can make natural lubrication slower or less plentiful. This can happen even when you want sexual contact. Allow time for touch you enjoy and consider a water-based or silicone-based lubricant that is compatible with any condoms or toys being used. If a product stings, stop using it. Oil-based products can weaken latex condoms. A position that avoids pressure on a healing area or allows more control over depth may help, but no position should be used to push through pain. It is fine to choose activities without penetration. Persistent pain needs more than reassurance Scar tenderness, pelvic floor problems, infection, skin irritation and dryness can cause overlapping symptoms. Lubricant may help friction but will not treat every cause. If discomfort persists, arrange an assessment and describe where the pain is, when it occurs and whether it started after a particular event. A clinician may suggest pelvic health physiotherapy, treatment for a diagnosed condition or another approach after discussion. Ask for advice promptly if pain is worsening or accompanied by concerning bleeding, discharge or fever. You can seek treatment to improve everyday comfort without committing to resuming sexual activity. Sore nipples and breast pain deserve attention too If breast or nipple touch hurts, say so and keep that area out of sexual activity. Persistent feeding pain should not be dismissed as the inevitable effect of a baby sucking. Attachment problems, skin damage, pump injury and other causes may need different kinds of support. Ask a midwife, lactation professional or clinician to help if pain continues. A hot, swollen, painful area with fever or flu-like symptoms may need assessment for mastitis. Avoid forceful breast massage or extra pumping as a general solution. Getting comfortable feeding support can benefit wellbeing independently of its effect on sex. Breastfeeding is not automatically contraception Ovulation can return before the first period after birth, so having no periods is not enough to establish protection from pregnancy. Pregnancy can occur from as early as three weeks after birth. Discuss a contraception plan before sexual activity that could lead to pregnancy if another pregnancy is not wanted. There are methods compatible with breastfeeding, including condoms, progestogen-only methods and intrauterine contraception, depending on individual circumstances and timing. Estrogen-containing methods have additional postpartum considerations. A clinician or contraception service can help choose a method that fits your health, preferences and ability to use it consistently. LAM has three conditions that must all remain true The lactational amenorrhea method, or LAM, uses the temporary suppression of ovulation associated with frequent breastfeeding. CDC guidance requires all three conditions: the baby is under six months old; menstrual periods have not returned; and feeding is fully or nearly fully by breastfeeding, with no interval longer than four hours in the day or six hours at night. The protection is time-limited. NHS guidance describes LAM as about 98 percent effective with typical use and more than 99 percent when its instructions are followed correctly; these figures refer to the first six months after birth, not a full year or to all breastfeeding parents. Ask a trained professional to confirm the criteria in your circumstances. Have another plan when feeds or periods change Do not wait for the next period to arrange another method when a LAM condition no longer applies. Longer gaps, stopping night feeds, introducing other feeds or reaching six months should prompt a change in contraception. The effect of expressing milk on LAM is less certain, so exclusive pumping should not be assumed to provide the same protection. Guidance differs in how it describes nearly full versus exclusive breastfeeding; if formula or solids are introduced, or you are unsure about bleeding or feeding intervals, use another method and get advice. LAM does not protect against sexually transmitted infections. If unprotected sex occurs when you may not be protected, ask promptly about emergency contraception suitable for your situation. Make conversations specific and kind Choose a moment outside a sexual encounter to explain how you feel. You might say that you want affection but not breast touch, that you are worried about pain, or that what you need most tonight is uninterrupted rest. Specific requests can be easier to respond to than expecting a partner to infer what has changed. Listen to each other’s feelings while keeping consent clear. Different levels of desire are something to discuss, not a debt one person must repay. If helpful, attend a healthcare appointment together, but you can also speak privately. Repeated pressure, guilt or disregard for a request to stop is not an acceptable solution to a mismatch. Closeness can take several forms Conversation, a shared meal, kissing, cuddling or a gentle massage can provide connection without an expectation that they will progress to intercourse. If both people want sexual activity, options that avoid painful penetration may include mutual touching or other preferred activities. Oral contact or toys still require consent, comfort and attention to infection prevention. Choose activities that respect healing and any advice after birth; a toy should not bypass a restriction on vaginal insertion. Agree that either person can pause or stop. Putting time together in the calendar can be useful if it feels supportive, but it is an invitation to connect rather than a booking that guarantees sex. Shared care and rest are part of support Taking responsibility for household tasks, settling the baby or protecting time for a shower can make daily life more manageable. Partners can share care even when only one person is breastfeeding. Ask for concrete help and review arrangements as feeding and sleep patterns change. Gentle movement, food, rest and time for yourself can support recovery when they are realistic and appropriate to your healing. They are not a guaranteed treatment for low desire, and exercise should not become another performance target. Practical help is part of parenting together; it should never be offered as a transaction that earns sexual contact. Ask for support when the change is distressing A sexual-health professional, pelvic health clinician or qualified counsellor can help when discomfort, communication difficulties or changes in desire are affecting you. You do not need to decide in advance whether the cause is physical, hormonal or emotional. More than one factor may need attention. Persistent low mood, anxiety, hopelessness or loss of enjoyment across everyday life deserves mental-health support too. If you feel at risk of harming yourself or someone else, seek urgent help. Recovery and connection can develop gradually; neither breastfeeding nor the frequency of sex determines your worth as a partner or parent. There is no universal deadline for sex or guaranteed date when desire returns. Hormones, healing, sleep and support can all influence comfort and interest. Milk leakage can be managed with simple choices; routine extra pumping is unnecessary. LAM requires all three criteria, including different day and night feeding intervals. Shared care and affection should remain free from pressure or expectations of sex. Do I have to wait exactly six weeks or resume sex then? No fixed date suits everyone. Follow advice for your own healing and complications, and resume only activities you want and find comfortable. Is lower desire while breastfeeding always a problem? No. Interest can vary. If a change is distressing or accompanied by pain, low mood or other symptoms, ask for support rather than assuming you must tolerate it. Does enjoying breastfeeding mean I no longer need my partner? No. Physical responses during feeding do not replace adult relationships or determine your need for affection. You may also need time without touch. Is milk leakage during sex normal? It can happen when the milk-release reflex is triggered. Pads, a towel or avoiding breast touch may help if it bothers you; leakage alone does not indicate a problem. Should I pump before sex to prevent leaks? Routine extra pumping is not necessary and can encourage oversupply. Feeding at the usual time or expressing a small amount for uncomfortable fullness may be enough. Will lubricant fix painful sex? It may help dryness and friction, but persistent pain can have other causes. Stop if it hurts and seek an assessment rather than repeatedly pushing through. Can I get pregnant before my first period? Yes. Ovulation can return first. Absence of periods alone is not reliable contraception. What are the exact LAM conditions? The baby must be under six months, periods must not have returned, and feeding must be fully or nearly fully by breastfeeding. Under CDC guidance, gaps must be no longer than four hours by day or six hours at night. Ask for advice if any condition is uncertain. Does pumping give the same contraceptive protection? That should not be assumed. Evidence about expressing and LAM is limited. Discuss another method if pumping, longer gaps or mixed feeds make the criteria uncertain. Do I need to wean to improve sexual wellbeing? Not automatically. Start with the discomfort, tiredness, contraception or relationship concern that is affecting you. Feeding decisions should reflect your circumstances and preferences, not pressure to restore a sexual timetable.

title: Should you feed your baby after they vomit?
description: Learn when to offer another milk feed, how to manage small amounts and which vomiting or dehydration signs need urgent care.
body: Often, a baby who is well and hungry after a single vomit can feed again. Start by checking their condition and the vomit’s appearance, then offer milk in small amounts. Repeated vomiting or warning signs need medical advice. Check the baby before deciding about the next feed After an isolated episode, an alert baby who is comfortable, breathing normally and showing hunger cues can usually have another milk feed. Offer a smaller amount or a shorter breastfeed and see how they manage. You do not need to replace an estimated amount of vomit all at once. Milk spread across clothing can look like more than it was. First check for warning signs. Repeated vomiting, difficulty waking, unusual pain, a swollen abdomen or an inability to keep fluids down changes the situation. A newborn or young infant needs a lower threshold for assessment than an older child. Feeding advice for a well baby after one episode should not be used to keep an unwell baby at home. Spit-up and vomiting are not quite the same Spit-up is the relatively effortless return of a little milk, sometimes mixed with saliva, often during or soon after a feed. Vomiting is more forceful, with active stomach and abdominal contractions. The distinction is useful, although parents do not need to name it perfectly before asking for help. The baby’s comfort, hydration, growth and the pattern over time matter more than the label alone. Reflux is common in early infancy because milk can move back from the stomach into the food pipe. It often improves as the baby grows, commonly during the first year. A comfortable baby gaining weight may not need treatment for occasional spit-up. Pain, poor growth, feeding refusal or increasing forcefulness should be assessed rather than assumed to be normal reflux. Several illnesses and triggers can cause vomiting A stomach or intestinal infection may cause vomiting, with or without diarrhoea. Other infections, fever and pain (including an ear infection) can also be relevant. Some medicines or accidentally swallowed substances can trigger vomiting through their effects on the body. An intestinal blockage is less common but important, particularly with green vomit, abdominal swelling or significant pain. Motion or spinning, strong smells and distress can provoke nausea or vomiting in some children. That does not make them a safe explanation for repeated vomiting in a newborn. Similarly, an episode following vaccination does not prove the vaccine is the cause. Note timing and associated symptoms, and let a clinician assess an unwell baby rather than attributing everything to stress, teething or a recent event. Milk allergy and intolerance need a specific assessment Food allergy can occur in infancy; it is not something that starts only after the first birthday. Cow’s-milk protein allergy can resemble reflux in some babies. Food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome, or FPIES, is another possible cause of repeated vomiting after a trigger food and can make a baby very unwell. Timing, repeated patterns and other symptoms help guide assessment. Lactose intolerance concerns difficulty digesting milk sugar and is different from an allergy to milk protein. Primary lactose intolerance is uncommon in young babies. Switching to a lactose-free or “comfort” formula will not necessarily treat a protein allergy. Ask for advice before changing formula or excluding major foods from a breastfeeding parent’s diet. Breathing difficulty, facial swelling, collapse or a rapidly worsening reaction requires emergency help. Offer milk in manageable amounts If there are no warning signs, continue breastfeeding or the baby’s usual formula. Smaller, more frequent feeds may be easier to keep down than a large feed. Let the baby pause, and avoid pressuring them to finish a bottle. If they are actively retching, let the episode settle before offering a little more; there is no universal rule to withhold all milk for an hour after every vomit. Prepare formula at its normal strength with the usual safe preparation method. Do not add extra water to make it “gentler.” If even small feeds repeatedly come back up, or the baby is refusing to drink, seek advice. Persistent vomiting needs a plan based on age, losses and hydration, not repeated attempts to make up a whole missed feed. Know when oral rehydration solution is needed Repeated vomiting or diarrhoea can lead to loss of fluid and salts. A clinician may recommend an age-appropriate oral rehydration solution, or ORS, in small frequent amounts. Mix it exactly as directed. Plain water, juice, sports drinks and homemade mixtures are not interchangeable with ORS. In particular, do not replace a young infant’s milk feeds with plain water. Management differs when a child is clinically dehydrated. A supervised rehydration plan may temporarily prioritise ORS while breastfeeding continues, with other fluids or foods directed by the clinician. After rehydration, full-strength milk and the usual age-appropriate diet can resume. Get advice promptly if the baby refuses ORS, repeatedly vomits it or seems worse; some children need treatment in hospital. Fever, pain and medicines do not create a fixed feeding delay A baby with fever or ear pain may need assessment and relief, but there is no general requirement to wait thirty to sixty minutes after a pain medicine before offering milk. The important questions are whether the baby is well enough to feed, whether they can keep fluids down and whether the medicine is suitable for their age and condition. A baby under three months with a temperature of 38°C or higher needs urgent medical advice. Do not let a medicine trial delay that call. Check age and dose instructions with a professional; some products are unsuitable for very young or dehydrated infants. If a dose is vomited, ask before repeating it because some may already have been absorbed. Do not give anti-vomiting medicine without specific advice. Treat vomiting during travel cautiously Motion sickness usually affects older children more than infants and is uncommon under two years. Recurrent vomiting in a baby during travel therefore should not automatically be labelled car sickness. Consider feeds, illness and other symptoms, and ask for advice when it repeats. Motion-sickness medicines can have important age restrictions and side effects; they are not routine treatment for a vomiting baby. If a baby vomits while travelling, stop somewhere safe before attending to them or offering a feed. Keep them correctly restrained while the vehicle is moving; do not feed or unbuckle them on the road to settle the episode. Once safely stopped and the baby is comfortable, assess for warning signs and offer a small feed if appropriate. Persistent symptoms need medical advice. Watch hydration and seek help early Contact a clinician promptly if there are fewer wet diapers than usual, a dry mouth, sunken eyes or soft spot, worsening sleepiness, persistent distress or refusal to feed. Tears can be difficult to interpret in very young babies, so do not rely on that sign alone. Vomiting with frequent diarrhoea increases fluid losses. The baby’s age and overall condition are more useful than waiting for a fixed number of hours without urine. Do not wait twelve hours simply because an article says vomiting often passes. Seek emergency care for green or yellow-green vomit, blood or material resembling coffee grounds, a markedly swollen or painful abdomen, severe breathing trouble, collapse or a baby who is floppy or not responding normally. New projectile vomiting, blood in the stool or repeated inability to retain fluids also needs urgent assessment. If you are uncertain about vomit colour in a newborn, get urgent advice. Reduce ordinary spit-up without changing safe sleep For a well baby with uncomplicated reflux, review feeding amounts and technique with a health professional. Avoid routinely offering more than the baby wants, pause for burping and keep handling gentle after feeds. Holding the baby upright while you are awake may help comfort. It is not necessary to keep trying to feed until no milk comes back up. For every sleep, place the baby on their back on a firm, flat sleep surface. Do not raise the mattress, use wedges or leave them sleeping propped upright to prevent vomiting. Reflux does not change this advice. If you become sleepy while holding a baby after feeding, move them to their own safe sleep space. Thickened feeds or reflux medicines should be considered only with professional guidance. Return to usual food and keep track of the pattern If the baby already eats solids, there is no universal need to stop all solid food for twenty-four hours after a single vomit. Once comfortable and interested, they can generally return to suitable familiar food, with milk remaining important. During a specific clinical rehydration plan, follow the temporary food instructions and reintroduce normal food afterward. Do not force solids when the baby is nauseated. Make a short note of the time, relation to feeds, colour, force, fever, stools and wet diapers if episodes recur. Tell the clinician about new foods, formula changes, medicines and possible exposures. Keep hands and feeding equipment clean when an infection is possible. The aim is not to prevent every small spit-up; it is to recognise a changing pattern while keeping the baby hydrated and safely fed. Assess the baby before deciding on another feed. Small frequent milk feeds are often appropriate for a well baby. Keep formula at normal strength and do not substitute plain water for milk. Repeated vomiting and dehydration signs need prompt advice. Keep sleep flat and on the back, even with reflux. Can I breastfeed again straight after one vomit? If your baby is alert, comfortable, showing hunger cues and has no warning signs, you can usually offer a shorter feed once retching has settled. Avoid forcing a full replacement feed. Repeated vomiting needs assessment. Should I dilute formula so it stays down? No. Prepare it at the usual strength. Extra water changes the nutrient and salt balance. Smaller, more frequent feeds may be easier to manage, with medical advice if these also keep coming back up. Should I give plain water instead of milk? Do not replace a young infant’s milk with plain water. Repeated fluid losses may require an appropriate oral rehydration solution and an individual feeding plan. Ask a clinician what to use for your baby’s age and condition. Must solids stop for twenty-four hours? No. There is no blanket twenty-four-hour rule. A baby already eating solids can usually resume familiar foods as tolerated. A clinical rehydration plan may temporarily restrict solids, followed by a return to the usual diet. Is green vomit normal after a feed? No. Green or yellow-green vomit needs emergency assessment because it may signal a blockage or another serious problem. Do not wait for another episode or try repeated feeds to see whether it clears. What if my baby has a fever as well? Consider age and overall condition. A baby under three months with a temperature of 38°C or higher needs urgent medical advice. Seek emergency help if they are difficult to wake, have breathing trouble or are not responding normally. Can milk allergy happen before the first birthday? Yes. Milk-protein allergy and other food allergies can occur in infancy. Lactose intolerance is a different condition. Ask for assessment rather than repeatedly changing formula or removing foods without a plan. Should I wait after giving a pain medicine before feeding? There is no universal thirty-to-sixty-minute feeding delay. Check that the medicine is appropriate and the baby can feed safely. If they vomit the dose, ask before repeating it, and do not delay assessment of a sick young infant. Should a baby with reflux sleep on an incline? No. Use a firm, flat sleep surface and place the baby on their back. Do not use a wedge, raise the cot mattress or leave the baby propped upright for sleep. How long can I wait if vomiting keeps happening? There is no single safe waiting period for every baby. Young age, reduced urine, poor feeding, pain or unusual sleepiness justify earlier help. Seek emergency assessment for concerning vomit colour, blood, severe symptoms or reduced responsiveness.

title: Choosing contraception while breastfeeding
description: Compare breastfeeding-compatible contraception, understand when breastfeeding itself can help prevent pregnancy, and plan for missed pills or unprotected sex.
body: Breastfeeding does not automatically prevent another pregnancy. Ovulation can return before the first period, so waiting for bleeding to restart can leave a gap in protection. Several contraceptive methods can be used while breastfeeding, including long-acting devices, progestin-only options and condoms. The best fit depends on your health, how recently you gave birth, feeding circumstances and when you might want another pregnancy. Plan before fertility becomes obvious Pregnancy can become possible from about three weeks after birth, even if you are breastfeeding and have not had a period. The first ovulation may happen before any menstrual warning. If you do not want another pregnancy, discuss a method before resuming vaginal sex. You can make that plan during pregnancy, before leaving the birth setting or at a later appointment. Some methods can start immediately after delivery; others need different timing. There is no universal requirement to wait for the six-week check. Sex should resume when you feel ready and recovery allows. If there were complications, stitches or ongoing pain, ask your maternity team for individual advice. Contraception does not remove the need for comfort, consent and recovery. When breastfeeding can work as contraception The lactational amenorrhoea method, or LAM, relies on breastfeeding suppressing ovulation. All three conditions need to apply: your baby is under six months old, periods have not returned, and breastfeeding is exclusive or nearly exclusive with frequent feeds day and night. Guidance commonly specifies no gap longer than four hours during the day or six hours at night. Regular formula or solid feeds, longer sleep stretches, fewer feeds or the return of periods can mean that LAM no longer provides the expected protection. Expressing milk may not suppress ovulation in the same way as frequent direct feeding, and evidence about pumping-based LAM is limited. If you mainly pump, supplement feeds or are unsure whether the criteria apply, arrange another method. LAM is a temporary method with specific rules, not a promise that any amount of breastfeeding prevents pregnancy. Have a transition plan before six months or an earlier feeding change. It does not protect against sexually transmitted infections. Compare effectiveness using the same kind of measure Perfect use means following every instruction consistently. Typical use includes real-life missed pills, late injections and condom errors. Contraceptive percentages generally describe a year of use, not the chance of pregnancy from one sexual encounter. US CDC estimates put typical-use pregnancy rates below 1 in 100 users per year for IUDs and implants, around 4 in 100 for the injection, 7 in 100 for pills and 13 in 100 for external condoms. Estimates vary between studies and health systems. LAM is assessed over its first-six-month period, so it should not be compared as though it were a year-long method. Effectiveness is only one consideration. Bleeding patterns, daily effort, comfort with a procedure, access, medical eligibility, STI protection and future pregnancy plans also matter. Hormonal and copper IUDs An intrauterine device, or IUD, is a small device placed inside the uterus by a trained clinician. Both copper and hormonal types are long-acting and reversible, and both can be suitable while breastfeeding. Hormonal IUDs release levonorgestrel, a progestin. One important effect is thickening cervical mucus so sperm are less able to pass through. Periods often become lighter, and some users stop having menstrual bleeding. A copper IUD contains no contraceptive hormone and affects sperm function; it may make periods heavier or more crampy. Current US contraceptive approvals differ by product: Mirena and Liletta can be used for up to eight years, Kyleena for five years and Skyla for three years. These durations refer to pregnancy prevention; use for another indication may have a different limit. Confirm the device, local approval and replacement date with the service that fits it. You can ask to have an IUD removed whenever you want. Fertility can return promptly afterward, although no method can guarantee how quickly a particular person will conceive. If you are switching methods, arrange coverage before removal rather than leaving an unintended gap. IUD insertion after birth: timing and risks An IUD can sometimes be fitted immediately after delivery by a trained team. UK guidance describes fitting within 48 hours of birth or, if that window is missed, usually from four weeks onward. Local services and clinical guidance may offer different postpartum arrangements. Immediate postpartum insertion has a higher chance of the device being expelled than insertion later. That needs discussion and follow-up, but it is not the same as saying that all early insertion causes infection. An active postpartum uterine infection is a reason not to insert an IUD at that time. Having more than one sexual partner does not automatically make an IUD unsuitable. The relevant questions are STI risk, screening and whether an infection is currently present. Screening for gonorrhoea or chlamydia can often be performed at the insertion visit; known current infection or purulent cervicitis requires appropriate management before insertion. Discuss pain relief before the procedure. Cramping and spotting can occur afterward, and bleeding patterns may change over the first months. Heavy or persistent bleeding, fever, worsening pelvic pain or possible expulsion need assessment. The rare risk of uterine perforation is also part of informed counselling, particularly around postpartum insertion. An IUD does not prevent STIs. Condoms can be used alongside it when STI protection is needed. The progestin-only pill, or mini pill The mini pill contains a progestin without estrogen and is a common option while breastfeeding. It may be available by prescription or over the counter depending on the formulation and country. Current guidance allows progestin-only pills to start immediately after birth when medically appropriate. You do not routinely need to wait six to eight weeks. Whether backup contraception is needed depends on the particular pill, time since birth and whether all LAM criteria are met. Take your pill according to its instructions each day. Some formulations have a short late-pill window, while others allow more time. Not every pack contains 28 active hormone tablets; some include inactive tablets. Do not apply another person’s schedule or missed-pill advice to your own product. Bleeding may become irregular, lighter, more frequent or absent. No monthly bleed is guaranteed, and having no bleed does not automatically mean pregnancy. If pills were missed or symptoms suggest pregnancy, follow testing advice. Some users report headaches, mood or libido changes, although an individual symptom may have other causes. Functional ovarian cysts can occur and often settle on their own. Report persistent or significant symptoms rather than assuming they are something you must tolerate. Fertility generally returns quickly after stopping the pill. There is no routine requirement to wait several months before trying for pregnancy, but a preconception discussion can help you plan medicines and supplements. Will hormonal contraception reduce milk supply? Estrogen-containing contraception can reduce milk production in some people, particularly while feeding is being established. Progestin-only methods are generally compatible with breastfeeding; available studies have not shown consistent adverse effects on feeding or infant growth, although evidence has limitations. It is therefore misleading to say that every hormonal method commonly reduces milk. If you notice a change after starting a method, consider it alongside feeding frequency, milk transfer, illness and other factors with a clinician or lactation professional. More frequent effective milk removal can be part of an individualized supply plan, but routinely pumping after every feed is not necessary simply because you start a mini pill. It can add a substantial burden and should have a clear purpose. Get feeding support if your baby is not feeding well, has fewer wet nappies than expected or is not gaining weight adequately. If you want to change contraception, arrange another method so that addressing a feeding concern does not create an unplanned gap. Condoms: hormone-free protection and STI prevention External condoms keep semen from entering the vagina. They contain no contraceptive hormones, do not reduce milk supply and can be used whenever you resume sex. They are widely available without a prescription. Correct use means a new condom for every encounter, put on before genital contact and used through withdrawal. Check the packet and expiry date, open it carefully and use a compatible lubricant. Dryness during breastfeeding may make lubrication particularly helpful. Condoms are up to about 98% effective with consistent correct use; typical-use protection is lower because they may be applied late, slip, split or be forgotten. A condom can be combined with an IUD, implant or pill for additional pregnancy protection. Latex and suitable synthetic condoms also reduce the risk of many STIs, although they cannot eliminate every risk, particularly from uncovered skin. Natural-membrane condoms are not a dependable choice for STI prevention. Do not use two condoms at once or an external and internal condom together. Additional spermicide is not needed for ordinary condom use and is not a substitute for correct use. If a condom breaks or slips, seek timely advice about emergency contraception and any STI exposure. The contraceptive implant An implant is a small flexible rod placed under the skin of the upper arm. Nexplanon contains etonogestrel, a progestin that suppresses ovulation and thickens cervical mucus. It is highly effective and does not require a daily action. The US Nexplanon approval was extended to up to five years in 2026. Duration and available implant products vary by country, so use the replacement date given for your actual device. Nexplanon is not the only implant available worldwide. An implant can be placed immediately after birth when appropriate, including during breastfeeding. A trained professional inserts and removes it. You can request removal sooner, and fertility may return quickly afterward. Irregular bleeding is common and may be unpredictable. Contact the service for persistent arm pain, redness or swelling, fever or chills, unusually heavy vaginal bleeding, or if you cannot feel the implant where you were shown. These findings need assessment rather than a promise that complications never occur. The contraceptive injection Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate, or DMPA, is a progestin injection sold under names such as Depo-Provera. Standard repeat dosing is about every three months; CDC guidance specifies 13 weeks. Other injectable products can have different schedules. The injection can be used while breastfeeding, including soon after birth when clinically appropriate. Personal risk factors and local guidance determine timing. Keep a record of the next due date, because protection cannot be assumed indefinitely after a missed appointment. If you are late, contact the service promptly. Whether you need a pregnancy assessment, backup protection or emergency contraception depends on how late the dose is and recent sex. Do not guess from the phrase three months. Possible effects include irregular or absent periods, weight gain, headache and abdominal discomfort. DMPA can reduce bone mineral density during use; the balance of benefits and risks and ongoing suitability should be reviewed with a clinician. Unlike a pill that can be stopped or a device that can be removed, an injection continues working after it has been given. Return of fertility can take months after the last dose and sometimes more than a year. This delay is variable and does not mean permanent infertility, but it matters if another pregnancy is wanted soon. What about the combined pill, patch or ring? Combined hormonal methods contain estrogen as well as a progestin. Estrogen is relevant both to milk supply and to the increased blood-clot risk soon after birth. They are not suitable immediately postpartum. For example, UK guidance usually advises breastfeeding parents to wait at least six weeks before considering them. A clinician must still assess clot risk, medical history and feeding circumstances; reaching six weeks does not automatically make every combined method suitable. It is also too broad to say that estrogen must be avoided for the entire time you breastfeed. Some people can use a combined method later after discussing its risks, benefits and alternatives. Choose the timing with your clinician rather than relying on a general article. Emergency contraception while breastfeeding If a condom breaks, pills are missed or sex happens without adequate contraception, contact a pharmacist or sexual health service promptly. Emergency contraception is time-sensitive. You do not need to wait for a period or prove that pregnancy is likely before asking. The main options are a copper IUD, levonorgestrel emergency pills and ulipristal acetate. Ulipristal acts on progesterone receptors and is not simply another progestin-only mini pill. Older combined estrogen–progestin emergency regimens are less effective and cause more nausea than the dedicated pill options. Oral emergency contraception should be taken as soon as possible, within the relevant product and clinical window. Ulipristal can be used up to five days after sex; levonorgestrel works best earlier and becomes less effective with delay. A copper IUD is the most effective option and may provide ongoing contraception if suitable. NHS specialist breastfeeding guidance allows oral emergency contraception from day 21 after birth and a copper IUD for this purpose from day 28. It prefers copper or levonorgestrel when suitable, while allowing ulipristal after assessment. These postpartum thresholds are separate from the time limit after sex. For a full-term, healthy infant, that specialist guidance does not require breastfeeding interruption after a single dose of levonorgestrel or ulipristal. Evidence is more limited for ulipristal; ask for individualized advice if your baby is premature or unwell, or if local product instructions differ. Ask when to restart your usual contraception. After ulipristal, hormonal contraception is generally delayed for at least five days because taking it too soon can reduce the emergency pill’s effect. After levonorgestrel it can usually restart immediately. Use backup protection as directed and follow pregnancy-testing advice. An emergency pill does not provide reliable protection for later sex in the same cycle. It is useful when needed, while an ongoing method provides more dependable routine coverage. Access, cost and prescription rules vary locally. Choose a method that fits your life A daily pill may suit someone who wants to avoid a procedure and can remember it consistently. An IUD or implant may fit someone who wants longer protection with little daily effort. Condoms offer hormone-free use and STI protection, while an injection avoids daily dosing but may delay return to fertility. Tell the clinician about your feeding pattern, medical conditions, medicines, bleeding preferences and future pregnancy plans. Ask how soon the method works, what backup is needed, which symptoms require help and how to stop or change it. There is no single best method for every breastfeeding parent. A good plan is one you understand, can access and want to use, with a clear way to review it when your circumstances change. Ovulation may return before your first period. Breastfeeding alone is not reliable unless all LAM criteria apply. IUDs, implants and progestin-only options can be suitable during breastfeeding. Check the exact product and current local duration or dosing schedule. Condoms add STI protection that most contraceptives do not provide. Emergency contraception is available during breastfeeding; act promptly. Can I get pregnant before my first period after birth? Yes. Ovulation can occur first, and pregnancy can become possible from about three weeks postpartum. Plan contraception before relying on bleeding as a warning. Does pumping count the same as direct breastfeeding for LAM? That is uncertain. Expressing may not suppress ovulation in the same way. If you mainly pump or do not meet all LAM criteria, choose another contraceptive method. Must I wait six weeks to start the mini pill? Not routinely. Progestin-only pills can usually start immediately after birth when medically appropriate. Backup requirements depend on the pill and circumstances. Does every hormonal method reduce milk supply? No. Progestin-only methods are generally compatible with breastfeeding. If supply or infant growth is concerning, seek an individualized feeding and contraception review. How long do hormonal IUDs last? Current US contraceptive approvals are up to eight years for Mirena and Liletta, five for Kyleena and three for Skyla. Confirm your product, indication and local replacement date. How long does Nexplanon last? The US approval was extended to five years in 2026. Follow the current advice for the actual product and country where you receive it. Which method may delay return to fertility? The DMPA injection can delay fertility for months after the last dose and sometimes over a year. Fertility generally returns more quickly after stopping pills or removing an IUD or implant. Do emergency pills always mean stopping breastfeeding? No. Current NHS specialist guidance does not require an interruption after a single levonorgestrel or ulipristal dose for a full-term, healthy infant. Ask about premature or unwell infants and your local instructions. Can I restart the mini pill immediately after ulipristal? Usually you should wait at least five days before restarting hormonal contraception, then use backup as advised. Ask the pharmacist for instructions specific to your method.

title: Fever after birth: when to get medical help
description: Causes of postpartum fever, symptoms to report, treatment and practical recovery care. A temperature of 38°C or higher needs prompt assessment.
body: Fever after giving birth can come from the uterus, a healing wound, the breasts, the urinary tract or another illness. Some causes are readily treatable, but deciding that it is simply part of recovery can delay important care. Report a temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher immediately, and seek help sooner if you feel seriously unwell. A measured fever deserves prompt care After giving birth, it can be difficult to separate normal recovery from a new illness. Sweating, tiredness and breast fullness can all occur, but a measured temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher is an urgent maternal warning sign. Contact your maternity team or seek medical care immediately. If you cannot reach a clinician promptly, use an urgent or emergency service rather than waiting overnight. You do not need to identify the cause first. Tell the service when you gave birth, whether you had a vaginal or caesarean birth, your temperature and any other symptoms. Significant illness can occur with a lower or even normal temperature, so feeling rapidly worse also matters. A fever-reducing medicine does not establish that an infection has gone away. Know which accompanying symptoms are emergencies Call emergency services for trouble breathing, chest pain, collapse, confusion, a seizure or severe, continuing abdominal pain. Very heavy vaginal bleeding, such as soaking a pad in an hour, or passing very large clots with feeling faint needs urgent assessment. New pain, redness or marked swelling in one leg can indicate a clot and must be assessed promptly. Do not drive yourself if you feel faint or seriously unwell. Ask someone to stay with you and help with the baby. Take your discharge paperwork and medicine list if readily available, but do not delay departure to collect them. Always mention recent pregnancy, including when seeking care outside the maternity service. A caesarean wound can become infected Both planned and unplanned caesarean births leave an incision that needs time to heal. Some discomfort is expected, but increasing pain, spreading redness, swelling, heat, pus or an unpleasant smell needs review. A wound that opens or starts bleeding also requires advice, particularly if you have fever or feel unwell. A sore incision is not the only possible source of fever after surgery. Deep abdominal pain, painful urination or foul-smelling vaginal discharge may point elsewhere, so describe all symptoms rather than assuming the skin wound explains everything. Follow the dressing and cleaning instructions given by your surgical team; do not squeeze the wound or try to close an opening yourself. Endometritis is an infection inside the uterus Postpartum endometritis affects the lining of the uterus. It often begins in the first one to three days after birth, but later symptoms still need attention. Fever or chills, lower-abdominal tenderness, feeling generally ill and unpleasant-smelling discharge are possible signs. Ordinary postpartum bleeding can coexist with infection, so its presence alone does not distinguish normal recovery from illness. Risk is higher after caesarean birth and can also be increased by prolonged labour, a long interval after the waters break, infection during labour, retained or manually removed placental tissue, diabetes and certain bacteria in the genital tract, including group B streptococci. These are reasons for clinical awareness, not proof that someone will develop an infection. Give the team the relevant birth history Mention assisted birth with forceps or vacuum, any infection or unusual fluid during labour, manual placental removal and whether the placenta was thought to be complete. Information about a preterm or overdue birth and gestational diabetes may help the team understand the overall course. None of these details, by itself, establishes the cause of a fever. If pieces of placenta or other pregnancy tissue remain in the uterus, they can contribute to bleeding and infection. The clinician may arrange imaging or other assessment and decide whether treatment beyond antibiotics is needed. Do not wait for a routine postnatal appointment if pain, fever, unusual discharge or bleeding is worsening. Mastitis involves inflammation, sometimes with infection A hot, swollen, painful breast area, a tender lump or wedge-shaped patch can accompany fever, aching, headache and fatigue. Redness may be less obvious on darker skin. Mastitis is inflammation of breast tissue; some cases are bacterial, but inflammation itself can cause systemic symptoms. It can also occur outside breastfeeding and deserves assessment in that situation. Milk production and breast swelling change rapidly in the early days. Do not assume that a fever must be harmless because milk is coming in, or that it will settle within 24 hours. Tell the clinician about breast symptoms when you report the fever. A persistent painful swelling, worsening illness or failure to improve with treatment may require assessment for an abscess. Use gentle breast care while following the treatment plan For most breastfeeding parents with mastitis, continuing normal, responsive feeds is appropriate. If feeding is too painful or milk is not being removed effectively, ask for help with attachment and an expression plan. Avoid forceful massage or repeatedly pumping to empty the breast; these can worsen swelling or oversupply. If you are not breastfeeding but are producing milk, ask how to relieve discomfort without stimulating unnecessary extra production. A cool pack wrapped in cloth can ease discomfort. Cabbage leaves have not been shown to work better than ice, so they are not an essential treatment. Routine nipple scrubbing or washing before and after every feed is unnecessary; seek help for cracked or painful nipples instead. Hand hygiene and appropriate cleaning of feeding equipment still matter. Breast comfort measures should accompany, not delay, assessment of a postpartum fever. A urinary infection may affect the bladder or kidneys Burning when passing urine, an urgent or frequent need to go, passing small amounts, lower-abdominal discomfort or a feeling of incomplete emptying may suggest a urinary problem. Having had a urinary catheter is useful information because catheter use can increase infection risk. A urine sample may help guide treatment. Urine can sting when it touches a healing tear, but persistent or worsening pain should not automatically be called normal after birth. Fever or chills with back or side pain, nausea or marked illness can indicate a kidney infection and needs urgent care. Being unable to empty the bladder also needs prompt assessment; it is not something to manage simply by forcing more fluid. Tears, stitches and other illnesses need consideration too A perineal tear or episiotomy can become infected. Tell the team about increasing soreness, swelling, discharge, a bad smell or a wound that seems to be opening. Inflammation is part of healing, but this does not make a measured fever safe to ignore. The recovery pattern and examination matter more than deciding on your own that the stitches are probably responsible. People who have just given birth can also develop respiratory, gastrointestinal and other illnesses unrelated to the birth wound. Fever with rapidly worsening weakness or confusion can be part of sepsis, a dangerous response to infection. The team may need to look beyond the first obvious symptom when deciding what tests and treatment you need. Treatment is chosen for the cause and severity Assessment may include temperature and other vital signs, examination of the abdomen, wound or breasts, and urine or blood tests. Depending on the findings, imaging or cultures may be needed. Bacterial urinary, uterine, wound or breast infections can require antibiotics. The medicine, route and duration depend on the suspected site, allergy history, local resistance and how unwell you are. More serious infections may need intravenous antibiotics, fluids and hospital monitoring. An abscess or retained tissue can need a procedure as well. Do not take leftover antibiotics or someone else’s prescription. Tell the prescriber if you are breastfeeding and if your baby was premature or has a medical condition, so the treatment plan considers both of you. Prevention supports recovery but cannot prevent every infection Wash your hands before and after wound care, keep the caesarean incision clean and dry as instructed, and change dressings on the schedule your team provides. Clean the perineal area gently with water, change maternity pads regularly and avoid putting products inside the vagina while healing. Sterile water and aggressive washing are not routine requirements for home perineal care. Do not place witch-hazel pads, herbal products or unprescribed creams on an incision without advice. An infection does not mean you were careless. Some risks arise from the birth or the bacteria normally present in the body and cannot be eliminated by additional washing. Antibiotics given around a caesarean are a separate preventive decision made by the surgical team. A major 2016 trial found fewer postoperative infections when azithromycin was added to standard antibiotic prophylaxis for unplanned caesarean births. This does not mean everyone should start azithromycin after going home, or use it to treat an unexplained fever. Relieve discomfort and arrange clear follow-up Paracetamol, also called acetaminophen, and ibuprofen are commonly used after birth and are generally compatible with breastfeeding when appropriate for the individual. Ask a pharmacist or clinician about your health conditions, other medicines and the correct product. Avoid taking several products containing the same ingredient, and follow the prescribed or labelled directions. Rest, regular drinks if you have no fluid restriction, and help with baby care can support recovery. Before leaving an appointment, ask when improvement should begin, how results will be communicated and who to contact if symptoms continue. Get reassessed promptly if you feel worse, cannot keep fluids or medicines down, or develop a new warning sign. Do not wait to finish an antibiotic course before reporting deterioration. A postpartum fever should not be dismissed as milk coming in or stitches healing. Report abdominal, wound, urinary and breast changes together. Treatment may include antibiotics, drainage or other care depending on the cause. Gentle hygiene supports healing; infection is not a personal failure. Fever medicine does not replace assessment or follow-up. Can I wait overnight if the temperature is only 38°C? No. A temperature of 38°C or higher after birth warrants immediate medical advice or assessment, even if you are not sure of the cause. Does a normal temperature rule out a serious complication? No. Severe pain, heavy bleeding, collapse, confusion or breathing difficulty needs urgent care regardless of the thermometer reading. Can milk coming in explain away a fever? No. Breast fullness can occur during normal recovery, but a measured fever needs assessment rather than a promise that it will settle in 24 hours. Is every case of mastitis a bacterial infection? No. Mastitis describes inflammation. Some cases need antibiotics, while others need supportive care and feeding adjustments; your symptoms guide assessment. Should I stop breastfeeding or pump until the breast is empty? Most people can continue normal feeds. Repeated emptying and forceful massage may worsen inflammation. Ask for an individual feeding and expression plan. Is painful urination always normal after a vaginal birth? No. Healing tissue may sting, but persistent pain, frequent urges, fever or side pain needs review for urinary infection or another problem. Can uterine infection occur after a vaginal birth? Yes. Caesarean birth increases risk, but endometritis can occur after either type of birth. Should I take azithromycin left over at home? No. Preventive antibiotics around surgery are different from treating a new postpartum fever. The cause and appropriate prescription need assessment. Do I need sterile water and nipple washing after every feed? Routine home hygiene does not require sterile water for perineal washing or repeated nipple scrubbing. Follow your discharge and feeding-equipment instructions. What if antibiotics or fever medicine are not helping? Contact the care team again. Worsening illness, new symptoms or inability to take treatment needs reassessment; do not wait for the course to end.

title: Why babies rub their eyes
description: Understand tiredness, irritation and other reasons for eye rubbing, with gentle care and clear signs that need an eye assessment.
body: Eye rubbing often goes with tiredness, but the surrounding signs matter. Check whether your baby is comfortable and whether there is redness, watering, discharge, pain or a change in how they look at you. Start with the pattern around the rubbing Babies often bring their hands toward their face, and a brief rub does not by itself mean there is a problem. It may happen with sleepiness, ordinary movement or an uncomfortable eye. Notice whether it affects one eye or both, whether it happens mainly before sleep, and whether the baby settles afterward. Look for redness, watering, discharge or difficulty opening the eye. A baby cannot explain the difference between itching, pain and blurred vision. Persistent or vigorous rubbing therefore deserves attention even if the eye looks normal between episodes. It is not useful to treat the movement as deliberate disobedience or attention-seeking. Comfort and gentle redirection can help while you work out whether there is an underlying cause. Tiredness is common, but sleep needs depend on age Rubbing alongside yawning, looking away and fussiness may be a cue to offer a calm opportunity for sleep. You can reduce stimulation and follow your baby’s usual settling routine. Falling asleep afterward supports tiredness as one possibility, but does not prove that irritation or another concern is absent, particularly if rubbing keeps returning when the baby is rested. The often-quoted twelve to sixteen hours of sleep in twenty-four hours applies to babies aged four to twelve months and includes naps. Newborn patterns differ and sleep is broken around feeding and care. Do not force a fixed schedule or delay necessary feeds to reach a number. For sleep, use a firm, flat surface and place the baby on their back, with their face uncovered. Dust, dryness and allergies can irritate the eyes Dry air, smoke, dust, sand, soap and other irritants can make an eye uncomfortable. Pollen, dust mites, mould or pet dander can trigger allergic symptoms in a susceptible child. Itchiness with watery redness may suggest allergy, but rubbing does not establish it. Allergy is not the default explanation for eye symptoms in a very young infant. Notice whether symptoms follow an exposure, such as a dusty room or a visit with a pet, and remove an obvious irritant where possible. Do not spray cleaning products near the baby to solve the problem. An allergy assessment may be useful for recurrent symptoms, but ask a clinician before using medicated eye drops or antihistamines in a baby. Pain or marked light sensitivity needs a different level of attention. Infection and blocked tear drainage can look similar Conjunctivitis is inflammation of the membrane over the white of the eye and inner eyelids. Viral or bacterial infection can cause redness, watering, discharge or crusted lashes; a recent cold or contact with someone with red eyes may be relevant. Allergy can also inflame this surface. The symptoms overlap, so appearance alone does not reliably determine which medicine is needed. A blocked tear duct can make an infant’s eye watery or sticky because tears do not drain normally. This is different from assuming every discharge is an infection. A professional can check the cause and demonstrate any recommended care. Antibiotics may be appropriate for a particular infection, but do not treat a virus or allergy and do not themselves open a blocked tear duct. Consider vision concerns without diagnosing eye strain A child with a vision problem may rub their eyes, but most rubbing is not enough to diagnose poor vision. Refractive errors affect how the eye focuses; cataracts affect the clarity of the lens. Both are examples of conditions an examination can detect. It is misleading to describe a baby’s eyes simply as overworked muscles or to assume that rubbing will reveal every vision difficulty. Eye screening starts at birth and continues during infancy and childhood. By around three months, most babies can make steady eye contact and follow an object. Frequent inward crossing or outward drifting after about four months should be discussed with a clinician. Concerns at an earlier age also matter. A white or grey appearance in a pupil, a new abnormal eye movement or apparent difficulty seeing needs prompt assessment. Teething should not explain away an eye problem Teething can bring sore gums, increased chewing, drooling and fretfulness. Babies may rub their face or ears during the same period. However, the idea that an upper tooth routinely causes a painful or inflamed eye is not a reliable explanation. Check eye symptoms on their own merits rather than waiting for a tooth to emerge. For gum discomfort, a suitable teething ring cooled in the refrigerator may help; follow its instructions and keep it clean. Do not freeze it or tie it around the neck. If pain medicine is needed, ask about an appropriate product and dose for the baby’s age and weight. Pain relief should not delay assessment of a red, persistently watery or painful eye. Offer gentle care and avoid adding irritation Wash your hands before and after touching the eye area, and keep the baby’s nails short and smooth. While they are awake, try comfort or an age-appropriate toy to redirect rubbing. Loose mittens are not a treatment for an eye condition and should not replace checking the cause; discuss any garment used to prevent scratching with the baby’s care team. For crust on the eyelashes, a clinician may recommend gentle external cleaning with cooled boiled water and a fresh clean pad for each eye. Wipe the lashes without pressing on the eyeball. Do not share towels or washcloths when infection is possible. Avoid tea, breast milk, homemade mixtures, leftover prescriptions or someone else’s eye drops. Use prescribed drops only as directed for this baby. Handle a suspected foreign body or splash safely If loose dust or sand may have entered the eye, clean water can help rinse it away. Do not sweep a cloth, finger or cotton swab across the eyeball or try to dig under a baby’s eyelid. Seek prompt help if you cannot rinse it out, the baby will not open the eye, or watering and distress continue. Do not attempt to remove an object that appears embedded or has pierced the eye. A chemical splash needs immediate action. Start gentle rinsing with plenty of clean, non-hot water and keep rinsing while getting emergency medical advice; NHS guidance recommends at least twenty minutes. Do not delay rinsing to look for a special solution, and do not add another chemical to neutralise it. Take the product container or its details to the medical team if this can be done without delaying care. Know when to get an eye assessment A baby younger than thirty days with red, sticky eyes needs urgent medical assessment. At any age, significant pain, marked swelling, severe redness, light sensitivity, an injury or an apparent change in sight needs urgent care. A baby who is unusually sleepy, feeding poorly or otherwise unwell should also be assessed. Chemical exposure or a penetrating injury is an emergency. For mild rubbing without other symptoms, observe the pattern and offer appropriate rest and comfort. Arrange a visit if it persists, repeatedly affects one eye or worries you. Explain when it started, any exposure and whether feeding, sleep or visual behaviour has changed. You do not need to wait until six months of age, or until obvious discharge develops, to ask for help. Rubbing alone does not identify the cause. Use age-appropriate sleep expectations. Do not dismiss an inflamed eye as teething. Clean lashes gently without wiping across the eyeball. Vision concerns deserve attention at any age. Does every eye rub mean my baby needs a nap? No. Tiredness is one possibility, especially with yawning or fussiness, but irritation and other eye problems can also cause rubbing. Look at the whole pattern and any additional symptoms. Do all babies need twelve to sixteen hours of sleep? That range applies to ages four to twelve months, including naps. Newborn sleep patterns differ. Do not use a single sleep target to delay feeds or ignore persistent eye symptoms. Could my baby have an eye allergy? Possibly, but rubbing does not diagnose one. Itchy, watery eyes and an exposure pattern may help a clinician assess the cause. Do not assume allergy in a very young baby or start medicated drops without advice. Does sticky discharge always mean an infection? No. A blocked tear duct can also cause watering or discharge. A professional can distinguish the possibilities and explain whether cleaning, other care or a medicine is needed. Can teething explain a red or painful eye? It should not be used as that explanation without assessment. Teething commonly affects the gums and chewing behaviour; persistent redness, pain or watering deserves attention as an eye symptom. Should I ignore rubbing as a bad habit? No. A baby is not deliberately misbehaving. Gentle redirection can reduce rubbing, but frequent or forceful rubbing may signal discomfort and should not simply be ignored. Can I wipe a speck from the eyeball with a cloth? Do not wipe across the eyeball or dig for a particle. Gentle rinsing with clean water may remove loose material. An embedded object, injury, persistent distress or inability to open the eye needs urgent help. Do antibiotic drops help every red eye? No. They do not treat viral or allergic conjunctivitis, and they do not open a blocked tear duct. Use a prescribed medicine only for the baby and condition for which it was supplied. When are red, sticky eyes urgent in a newborn? A baby under thirty days with red, sticky eyes needs urgent medical assessment. Do not wait several days for home cleaning to work. Should I wait until six months to mention a vision concern? No. Screening begins earlier, and a concern about sight, eye alignment or pupil appearance should be raised when you notice it. The clinician can decide whether a specialist examination is needed.

title: Fertility and pregnancy spacing after birth
description: Pregnancy can happen before periods return, including during breastfeeding. Planning the next pregnancy involves recovery, contraception and your individual circumstances.
body: The return of fertility after childbirth is unpredictable. It may happen before the first period, so the absence of bleeding does not guarantee protection from pregnancy. If you want to avoid another pregnancy for now, discuss contraception early rather than waiting for a six-week appointment or a familiar cycle. Pregnancy can happen sooner than you expect It is possible to become pregnant from about three weeks after giving birth, including while breastfeeding. This does not mean everyone ovulates at three weeks; it means there is no reliable six-week period of protection to assume. The first ovulation can occur before the first menstrual period. A cycle-tracking app cannot reliably identify that first fertile window from previous period dates alone. Feeding patterns, recovery and individual hormonal changes influence when cycles resume. Another person’s experience, or your experience after an earlier birth, cannot predict this pregnancy’s timeline. Bleeding in the early weeks after delivery is also not necessarily a menstrual period. Illness, stress, sleep disruption, weight changes, smoking and medicines or contraceptive methods can complicate the picture. None provides a dependable rule for predicting the first ovulation, and personal reports of periods returning at six weeks or eight to nine months are examples rather than a timetable. Breastfeeding is contraception only under specific conditions The lactational amenorrhea method, or LAM, can be used only when all its criteria are met: the baby is younger than six months, menstrual periods have not returned, and breastfeeding is fully or nearly fully maintained. CDC guidance includes feeding intervals no longer than about four hours in the day or six hours at night. A daily total of feeding minutes or a fixed number of feeds does not replace those criteria. If longer gaps develop, feeds are replaced or any criterion no longer applies, arrange another contraceptive method promptly. Do not wait for a period to confirm that protection has ended. Ask for individualized advice if expressing milk is the main feeding method or you are unsure whether LAM criteria fit your routine. You do not need to change a suitable infant feeding plan solely to make it function as contraception. Count the interval correctly Pregnancy-spacing guidance usually discusses the interval from the birth of one baby to the conception of the next. That differs from the age gap between children, which includes the duration of the later pregnancy. For example, conceiving 18 months after a birth generally creates a birth-to-birth gap of more than two years if the next pregnancy reaches term. Mixing the two measures can make advice confusing. ACOG advises avoiding a birth-to-conception interval shorter than six months and discussing the risks and benefits of trying before 18 months. WHO’s birth-spacing consultation recommends at least 24 months after a live birth before attempting another pregnancy. Recommendations differ in scope and population; there is no single date that guarantees an uncomplicated outcome. Short intervals are associated with outcomes such as preterm birth in observational research, but the research cannot predict what will happen to an individual family. A shorter interval is a reason for supportive care, not blame. Your history and goals belong in the decision Discuss recovery, anemia or other nutritional concerns, mental health, sleep, support and any complications of the last pregnancy. Age, fertility history and the number of children you hope for may also affect the balance. A previous cesarean deserves a specific discussion about the scar and future birth options. Some research concerns the interval between deliveries, particularly when considering labor after a cesarean, so ask which interval a recommendation refers to. Advice after miscarriage or stillbirth may differ from advice after a live birth. A general spacing article should not become an automatic waiting rule after every pregnancy outcome. If you are already pregnant sooner than intended, arrange antenatal care and a medicine review. An increased statistical risk does not mean that harm is inevitable or that the pregnancy cannot progress well. Very long intervals have also been associated with some adverse outcomes in observational studies. A five-year gap is not a threshold at which harm becomes inevitable; age, health and circumstances may explain part of the association and deserve individual discussion. Choose contraception that fits the postpartum period Several methods can be started soon after birth, including some progestogen-only options and long-acting methods. Timing depends on the method, breastfeeding, clotting risk and medical history. Estrogen-containing contraception needs particular attention in the early postpartum weeks. Ask when the chosen method becomes effective and whether you need temporary backup. If you have unprotected sex after the initial postpartum period or a method fails, contact a pharmacist or sexual-health service promptly about emergency contraception. When you decide to try again, arrange preconception advice, review medicines and discuss folic acid and any condition-specific care. Planning should support your choices while giving you clear information about the available options. Fertility may return before the first postpartum period. LAM requires all its criteria; breastfeeding alone is not a guarantee. Spacing advice usually measures birth to the next conception. Can I become pregnant while breastfeeding and without a period? Yes. Unless all LAM criteria apply or you use another effective method, pregnancy can occur before bleeding returns. Does an 18-month interval mean my children should be 18 months apart? Usually not. Birth-to-conception guidance counts the months before the next pregnancy begins, not the time between the two births.

title: Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis after birth: symptoms, tests and treatment
description: Understand this uncommon infected pelvic-vein clot, why persistent postpartum fever needs assessment, and how antibiotics, scans and blood thinners are used.
body: Fever and abdominal pain after birth deserve attention. One uncommon cause is infection associated with a clot in a pelvic vein. Early assessment helps the team identify this or another treatable cause and choose the right care. What septic pelvic thrombophlebitis means Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis is inflammation and clotting in a pelvic vein associated with infection. “Thrombo” refers to a clot, “phlebitis” to vein inflammation and “septic” to infection. It is an uncommon but important cause of illness after birth, particularly when a fever is not settling with treatment. The condition can involve an ovarian vein or smaller veins around the uterus. Ovarian vein thrombosis is an overlapping diagnosis, but not every ovarian vein clot is infected. This distinction matters because the imaging findings, infection evidence and extent of the clot all influence treatment. When it can happen and how common it is Symptoms often begin in the early days after birth, including the first week, but timing alone cannot rule the condition in or out. It can follow a caesarean or vaginal birth. Pelvic infection or surgery, and occasionally pregnancy loss or termination, can also provide a setting for infected pelvic clots. An often-quoted estimate of about 1 in 3,000 births comes from a 1999 single-centre study. It found 15 cases among 44,922 deliveries, with a higher rate after caesarean than vaginal birth. That historical figure is not a precise estimate for every hospital or person today. Changes in prevention, imaging and diagnostic definitions affect reported rates. Symptoms that need prompt assessment Possible symptoms include fever or repeated chills, persistent lower abdominal pain, pelvic tenderness, pain toward the side or back, nausea and vomiting. Pain may be constant rather than cramping. Some people have only a few of these features, and none is specific enough to diagnose a pelvic clot at home. After birth, a temperature of 38°C or higher, severe or worsening abdominal pain, or feeling significantly unwell warrants urgent contact with a maternity service or emergency care. Serious infection can occur without a fever. Tell the team when you gave birth or had a pregnancy-related procedure and what treatment you have already received. A clinician may rarely feel a tender, cord-like abdominal mass, but most people do not have this finding. Do not try to press deeply on your abdomen to find a clot. Absence of a lump, mild-looking symptoms or a normal temperature at one moment does not establish that you are safe. Why pregnancy, infection and surgery can contribute Three processes can come together: blood is more ready to clot during pregnancy and the postpartum period, blood flow may slow in enlarged pelvic veins, and the vein lining may be injured or inflamed. Birth, an operation or infection spreading from the uterus can contribute to this combination. A uterine infection, called endometritis, is one possible starting point. Bacteria do not have to be detected in a blood sample before clinicians consider an infected pelvic vein. Negative blood cultures therefore do not rule it out, and treatment should not wait for proof of bacteria circulating in the blood when serious infection is suspected. Risk factors are clues, not a prediction Caesarean birth and postpartum uterine infection are important contexts. A long or complicated operation, reduced mobility, obesity and a personal history of blood clots can also affect the broader clot-risk assessment. Prolonged rupture of membranes or other circumstances that increase infection risk may contribute to the overall picture. Pelvic surgery, pelvic infection and recent pregnancy loss should be mentioned during assessment. Having fibroids alone does not establish septic pelvic thrombophlebitis risk; a large mass, an operation or another related complication may be relevant in an individual case. Many people with risk factors never develop the condition, and it can occur without an obvious checklist of risks. How the team investigates persistent postpartum fever The team reviews the birth or procedure, the course of the fever, pain, bleeding or discharge, medicines and previous treatment. Examination may assess the abdomen, uterus, surgical wound and other possible infection sites. Blood tests, blood cultures, urine tests and additional samples may help identify infection and its effects on the body. There is no single blood test that proves septic pelvic thrombophlebitis. Other explanations include a urinary or kidney infection, wound infection, retained infected tissue, a pelvic abscess, an infected collection of blood, appendicitis or a medicine-related fever. More than one problem can be present. In hospital, fever that does not improve as expected after appropriate antibiotics prompts reassessment. That is a clinical observation during treatment, not a recommendation to wait several days at home. Seek help promptly for concerning symptoms, even if you have only just started an antibiotic. What scans can show: and miss CT or MRI can identify a clot in a larger pelvic vein and assess other causes of pain or fever, such as an abscess. Ultrasound, sometimes with Doppler blood-flow assessment, may be used depending on the suspected problem and available expertise. The best first test depends on your condition and local services. Small pelvic-vein clots can be difficult to see, so a negative scan does not always settle the question. At the same time, an unexplained fever is not automatically proof of a hidden clot. Clinicians interpret scans alongside the examination, cultures and response to treatment. A fall in temperature after heparin was historically used as a diagnostic clue. It is not a reliable stand-alone confirmation: fever can improve for other reasons, and the evidence behind this approach is limited. Further assessment may still be needed. Treating infection in hospital Suspected septic pelvic thrombophlebitis usually needs hospital care with antibiotics that cover the likely organisms. Treatment often starts intravenously and is adjusted for allergies, kidney function, cultures, the suspected infection source and response. Older descriptions mention combinations such as clindamycin, gentamicin and a penicillin; this is not a universal prescription for every patient. If sepsis is suspected, treatment and monitoring begin promptly. The team may provide fluids and other support while looking for a source that needs specific treatment, such as drainage of an abscess or removal of infected retained tissue. Tests are useful, but should not cause a substantial delay in urgent antibiotics. The antibiotic course depends on the diagnosis and progress.
