Will lactation cookies or herbal tea fix low supply? They do not guarantee an increase and cannot correct every cause. Food can nourish you without acting as treatment. Herbal products need safety and interaction checks. Does giving additional milk mean breastfeeding has failed? No. Additional milk can protect the baby’s nutrition while the cause of poor intake is addressed. Discuss a feeding plan that fits the baby’s health and your goals.

title: Pelvic-floor recovery after birth: eight things worth knowing
description: Understand leakage, pelvic pain, muscle tension, sex and postpartum pelvic-health appointments, with practical guidance on exercise and when to seek help.
body: Pregnancy and birth can change how your pelvic floor feels and works. Leaking urine, pressure or discomfort may be common, but you do not have to accept them as the permanent price of having a baby. Recovery is individual, and useful treatment starts by identifying the problem. More squeezing is not always the answer: muscles need strength, coordination and the ability to relax. What the pelvic floor does The pelvic floor is a group of muscles and supporting tissues across the base of the pelvis. It extends between the pubic bone, tailbone and sides of the pelvis, helping support the bladder, uterus and bowel. The urethra, vagina and anus pass through this region. These muscles help maintain bladder and bowel control and contribute to sexual function. They need to contract when support is required and relax to allow comfortable emptying. A muscle can be tense without working well, so pelvic health cannot be measured simply by how tightly someone can squeeze. Pregnancy places extra demands on the pelvic floor. Vaginal birth may stretch muscles and nerves or involve a tear, an episiotomy or an assisted delivery. A cesarean birth avoids some vaginal injury but does not remove the effects of pregnancy, possible labour or abdominal surgery. Symptoms deserve attention after either type of birth. 1. Leakage is common, but it is a reason to ask for help Urine may leak with coughing, sneezing, laughing, lifting or a sudden urge to use the toilet. Early recovery can involve changes in muscle support, nerve function, swelling and bladder sensation. Leakage is not proof that a muscle has been permanently torn, and continuing symptoms are not limited to people with a recognised birth injury. There is no single six-week deadline by which every bladder must recover, nor a dependable three-month rule for a particular grade of tear. Some people improve quickly; others need longer and benefit from treatment. The postnatal check is a useful opportunity to talk, but you do not need to wait for it if symptoms are troublesome. Tell your midwife, primary-care clinician or pelvic-health physiotherapist when leakage occurs and how it affects daily life. Mention difficulty passing urine, incomplete emptying or reduced bladder sensation as well. Being unable to urinate needs prompt assessment rather than an exercise plan. Avoid solving leaks by severely restricting drinks, which can add to constipation and discomfort. 2. Weakness and excess tension can both happen The idea that everyone becomes permanently loose after birth is misleading and can create unnecessary shame. Muscles may be weak, overactive, poorly coordinated or affected by a combination of these changes. You cannot tell which problem is present from the appearance of the vulva or from a partner’s opinion. Pain, swelling, a healing tear or an episiotomy can make someone unconsciously brace the area. An episiotomy is a surgical cut, rather than a spontaneous tear. Muscle guarding may make relaxation difficult, including during a bowel movement, an examination or sex. A tense pelvic floor can still lack strength or endurance. Repeated forceful contractions may increase symptoms when relaxation is the missing skill. A physiotherapist can assess how the muscles work and choose strengthening, relaxation or coordination work accordingly. Treatment should respond to your symptoms rather than pursue tightness as a goal. 3. Healing pain should be taken seriously Some perineal soreness is expected after a tear, stitches or an episiotomy, and recovery can take weeks. The amount of pain and its course vary with the birth and the injury. A statement that all pain lasting more than a day is abnormal is too broad, but persistent or worsening pain should not be dismissed as inevitable. Ask about pain relief suitable for you, including if you are breastfeeding. Keep the area clean according to your maternity team’s advice, change pads regularly and avoid irritating products. Comfortable positions and short periods of rest may help. A physiotherapist can contribute to recovery, but first a clinician may need to check wound healing, infection or another cause of pain. Contact your maternity team promptly for increasing pain, fever, a wound that opens, pus or unpleasant-smelling discharge, or difficulty passing urine. Severe pain or feeling very unwell needs urgent care. Do not massage a painful or unhealed wound to try to release tight muscles. 4. Pelvic-floor exercises work best when they suit the problem Pelvic-floor muscle training, often called Kegel exercises, can be helpful. It is not accurate to say that these exercises are always harmful or should never be used on their own. NICE recommends supervised training for at least three months as a first-line approach for stress or mixed urinary incontinence. A useful programme is more than repeatedly clenching as hard as possible. It may develop gentle activation, strength, endurance, quicker responses and complete release between contractions. Your clinician can check technique, adjust the amount of practice and review progress. The three-month treatment period is not a reason to postpone the first assessment. If exercises cause pain, increase pressure or make emptying harder, stop that exercise and ask for an assessment. People with excessive muscle tension may need relaxation and other treatment before or alongside strengthening. If a general online routine has not helped, that is a reason to reconsider the diagnosis and technique, not evidence that you failed. Surgery is not the automatic next step when an unsupervised Kegel routine does not work. Other causes, physiotherapy options, bladder and bowel habits, and sometimes treatments such as a pessary may need discussion. The plan depends on what is actually causing the symptoms. 5. Comfortable intimacy does not follow a fixed calendar There is no universal date when you should feel ready for sex. Healing, fatigue, mood, feeding demands and your own interest all matter. A six-week appointment does not create an obligation to resume penetration, and choosing closeness without penetration is a valid option. Hormonal changes after birth, particularly while breastfeeding, can contribute to vaginal dryness. A suitable lubricant may help; choose a product compatible with any condoms you use. Scar discomfort, infection, pelvic-floor tension and other conditions can also cause pain, so lubrication is not a solution to every problem. If penetration hurts, pause instead of pushing through it. Explain the discomfort to your clinician and ask whether wound healing, dryness or muscle function needs assessment. Persistent pain can need both medical and physiotherapy care. Internal massage, stretching tools or other techniques should not be started simply because an online article recommends them. Sexual pleasure and orgasm depend on many physical and emotional factors. They cannot be predicted by how loose or tight the muscles feel. The aim of recovery is comfort, choice and function, rather than a promise to return to a particular sexual performance. 6. Notice pressure, bowel changes and other quieter symptoms Not every pelvic-floor problem causes obvious leakage. You might feel heaviness, dragging, a bulge at the vaginal opening or a sensation of sitting on something. These can be signs of pelvic organ prolapse, although an examination is needed to understand what is happening. Symptoms can be worth treating even without a large visible bulge. Mention dribbling after urination, trouble starting or finishing a urine stream, difficulty emptying the bladder, constipation, or trouble passing a bowel movement even when the stool is soft. Leaking wind or stool and being unable to defer a bowel movement also deserve attention, especially after a significant tear. These symptoms are not all caused by weak muscles and are not diagnosed solely from a checklist. An infection, wound problem or another bladder or bowel condition may need to be considered. A history of when symptoms began and what makes them worse helps the clinician choose the right assessment. You do not need to wait until symptoms are severe, until six weeks have passed or until they interfere with every activity. If you feel embarrassed, write them down and hand the list to the clinician. Asking specifically about urine, bowel control, pressure and pain can make it easier to discuss the whole picture. 7. You have a choice about an internal examination A pelvic-health appointment usually begins with questions about symptoms, pregnancy and birth, earlier health problems, bladder and bowel habits, activity and your goals. A clinician may also look at breathing, posture, movement and abdominal recovery. You can explain what is most important to you, such as walking comfortably or reducing leaks. An internal vaginal examination may be offered to assess muscle contraction, release, tenderness and healing. It is optional and requires your consent. You may decline, ask for another appointment, request a chaperone or ask the clinician to stop. Tell them about trauma, anxiety or pain so that care can be adapted. When appropriate, an assessment may use a gloved, lubricated finger to feel muscle function. The clinician should explain what they propose and why; do not assume that every appointment uses the same technique. Other examinations or tests, including a rectal assessment for certain bowel problems, require their own explanation and agreement. An internal examination is intimate and should not be described as noninvasive simply to make it sound less significant. If you do not want one, ask what can be learned through discussion and external assessment, and what uncertainty remains. Advice and parts of treatment can often begin without it. Treatment may include education, breathing and relaxation, tailored muscle training, bowel and bladder advice, activity progression or selected hands-on techniques. Internal manual treatment is not compulsory, and no single technique guarantees recovery. Agree on goals and a review point rather than assuming that one appointment must resolve everything. 8. Prevention and access to care matter after every type of birth Information about pelvic health belongs in routine pregnancy and postnatal care. Learning a comfortable contraction and release, discussing constipation and knowing which symptoms to report can help people seek support earlier. Cesarean recovery should not be treated as a reason to exclude pelvic-health questions. Some birth circumstances, such as an assisted delivery or a more significant tear, may lead the maternity team to recommend closer follow-up or supervised training. NICE supports preventive pelvic-floor training during and after pregnancy, with additional supervised support considered for specific risk factors. This does not mean that every person must buy a private internal assessment after birth. Routes to physiotherapy, referral criteria, appointment timing and insurance coverage vary. Ask your maternity service or primary-care clinician what is available and whether there is a self-referral option. If you are told to wait but symptoms are worsening, ask what needs checking now and what should trigger an earlier review. A written plan can make the difference between supported recovery and being left to repeat exercises without knowing whether they are suitable. A gentle starting point for practice and daily activity After an uncomplicated birth, gentle movement and pelvic-floor practice can often begin when you feel able. Follow your own maternity advice after a significant tear, complication or operation. If you have a urinary catheter, wait until it is removed and you are passing urine normally before starting the exercises. In a comfortable supported position, imagine gently closing around the back passage as if holding in wind, then lifting inward around the vagina and urethra. Keep breathing and avoid bearing down or strongly gripping the buttocks. Let the muscles fully soften again. A small comfortable contraction is more useful than a painful maximal effort. Do not repeatedly stop your urine stream as a training exercise. The image of stopping urine can help identify the muscles, but practice should happen away from emptying the bladder. If you cannot feel a lift or release, or are unsure whether you are pushing downward, ask for technique guidance. The number and length of contractions should suit your starting ability. Build gradually using the plan you are given, with rest between efforts. Pairing practice with a familiar daily moment can help, but missing a session during a demanding newborn day does not undo recovery. Return to walking and other activity in manageable stages. Pain, increasing pressure or leakage during an activity are reasons to adjust it and seek advice. Keep stools comfortably soft, avoid straining, and ask about constipation treatment when needed. Recovery involves daily habits and rest as well as exercises. When to seek urgent help Get prompt maternity or medical advice if you cannot pass urine, cannot empty the bladder properly, have worsening perineal pain, fever, a wound problem or new loss of bowel control. These should not be left for a routine physiotherapy appointment. Call emergency services for sudden heavy bleeding with faintness or a racing heart, chest pain, difficulty breathing or collapse. A very severe headache with visual changes after birth also needs urgent assessment. These may be unrelated to the pelvic floor but are important postpartum warning signs. For less urgent symptoms, arrange a review and record what is happening: leaks with particular movements, pain location, pressure, bowel changes and whether symptoms improve or worsen over the day. The purpose is to guide treatment, not to grade how successfully you have recovered. Common postpartum symptoms are still worth discussing and treating. The pelvic floor needs to relax as well as contract; more squeezing is not always better. An internal assessment is optional and requires your consent. Seek help according to symptoms rather than waiting for a fixed recovery deadline. Is leaking urine normal after birth? It is common, but you do not have to accept it indefinitely. Tell your clinician when it happens and whether it is improving. Assessment and an appropriate exercise plan can help, and you do not need to wait for a routine check if it is troubling you. Can my pelvic floor be tight and weak at the same time? Yes. Muscle tension does not necessarily mean useful strength or coordination. Difficulty relaxing can coexist with leakage or poor endurance, so an individual assessment is more helpful than assuming everyone needs stronger contractions. Should everyone do more Kegels? No. Pelvic-floor training is useful for many people, but the technique and amount must suit the problem. Exercises that increase pain, pressure or emptying difficulty should be reviewed rather than intensified. When can I begin gentle exercises? Often when you feel able after an uncomplicated birth, following your maternity advice. Wait until a urinary catheter is removed and you are passing urine normally. Complications, significant injury or pain may require a tailored plan. Should I stop my urine halfway through to practise? No. Repeatedly interrupting urine flow is not recommended training. Use the idea to recognise the muscles, then practise contraction and full release away from the toilet. Do I need an internal examination to get help? No. It may provide useful information, but you can decline, request a chaperone or ask for it to stop. Ask what can be assessed externally and whether a later examination would change the plan. Why can sex hurt even after stitches have healed? Dryness, scar sensitivity, muscle tension and other conditions can contribute. Pause painful penetration and seek advice rather than pushing through. A lubricant may help dryness but does not replace assessment of persistent pain. Do I need pelvic-floor care after a cesarean? Pelvic-health information and symptom assessment are relevant after a cesarean too. Pregnancy and any labour affect the body, and abdominal surgery has its own recovery needs. Treatment depends on your symptoms and circumstances. Does a heavy or bulging feeling mean severe prolapse? Not necessarily. Pressure or a bulge can have different causes and levels of severity. A clinician can assess it and discuss options; symptoms need not become severe before you ask for help. When should I seek help before my postnatal check? Do so for troublesome or worsening symptoms. Inability to urinate, fever with worsening wound pain, a wound opening or new bowel-control problems need prompt assessment. Heavy bleeding with faintness or chest and breathing symptoms require emergency help.

title: When your baby is not feeding well
description: Recognise urgent feeding changes, understand common and less common causes, and build a plan for milk intake, early solids and follow-up.
body: A baby taking much less milk, struggling through feeds or not growing as expected needs attention. Start with how your baby is now, then seek help to understand the cause and keep enough nutrition available. Poor feeding is more than disliking a food A baby may feed poorly because they show little interest, cannot attach or suck effectively, tire before taking enough milk, or struggle with swallowing. The concern is whether they receive and use enough fluid and nutrition for their needs. A sudden reduction from their usual intake matters even before weight changes become apparent. This is different from an older baby rejecting an unfamiliar texture or a toddler preferring certain foods. Feeding difficulty does not automatically mean malnutrition, but sustained low intake can affect hydration, growth and development. It should not be dismissed as something every baby will simply grow out of. Start by checking how your baby is now Get prompt medical advice when a young baby takes much less milk, repeatedly cannot complete feeds or has fewer wet nappies than usual. Unusual sleepiness, persistent vomiting, blood in the stool, a new wheeze or crying that cannot be settled also needs assessment. The urgency depends on the baby’s age, symptoms and general condition, not just a measured volume. A temperature of 38°C or higher in a baby under three months needs urgent assessment. A baby can be seriously ill with a normal temperature or a low one, so do not wait for fever if they look unwell. Record how the temperature was measured, but do not delay help to obtain a perfect reading. Some signs require immediate help Call emergency services if your baby is unresponsive, very difficult to wake, blue or grey, has pauses in breathing or is struggling severely to breathe. Marked chest recession, grunting or exhaustion with breathing is concerning. A baby who cannot breathe or respond normally needs help immediately, not another trial feed. Green or bloody vomit, repeated forceful vomiting, inability to keep feeds down or signs of substantial dehydration needs urgent medical assessment. Small milk possets are different, but a baby vomiting after every feed and becoming less alert or passing much less urine should not be watched indefinitely. You do not need several warning signs to be present together. Premature babies may need extra feeding support Babies born early may not yet coordinate sucking, swallowing and breathing well enough for effective oral feeds. They can tire quickly or need a slower progression while those skills mature. Some need expressed milk and temporary tube feeding as part of their neonatal plan; this is support for their development, not a failure to try. Follow the discharge plan, including any prescribed milk preparation, feeding schedule and weight checks. If feeding remains difficult after going home, contact the neonatal or paediatric team, particularly if it worsens or there is no improvement. Do not assume prematurity explains every new symptom or that extra time alone will be sufficient. Jaundice and infection can interfere with feeding Jaundice is yellowing caused by raised bilirubin. It is common in newborns and should not be grouped simply as a congenital malformation. Poor intake and jaundice can occur together. A jaundiced baby who is difficult to wake or is not feeding needs urgent help rather than being left to sleep through feeds. Infections, including gastroenteritis, may reduce interest in milk or cause vomiting and diarrhoea. Feeding often improves as the illness is treated or resolves, but fluid and nutrition needs continue in the meantime. A very young baby can become dehydrated or unwell quickly, so the plan must include what to offer and when to return. Less common conditions sometimes contribute Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is an uncommon overgrowth condition. In affected infants, a large tongue may interfere with feeding or breathing, and low blood glucose can be another concern. A baby’s size or a single difficult feed cannot diagnose it; assessment is based on the whole clinical pattern. Congenital hypothyroidism means the thyroid gland is not producing enough hormone from birth. Feeding difficulty, unusual sleepiness or constipation can occur, although early signs may be subtle. Newborn screening helps identify the condition where a programme is available, and timely treatment supports development. Babies with Down syndrome may have low muscle tone or a weak suck and benefit from tailored feeding support. These named conditions illustrate possible medical reasons for difficulty; they are not the most likely explanation for every baby who feeds less. A clinician decides whether specific investigation is indicated. Heart conditions may make feeds exhausting Some congenital heart conditions affect a baby’s ability to feed and grow. Hypoplastic left heart syndrome is a serious example in which structures on the left side of the heart are underdeveloped, affecting normal circulation. It requires specialist care and cannot be diagnosed from a feeding pattern alone. A baby with a heart problem may tire during feeds, breathe rapidly or have abnormal colour. Other cardiac conditions can also contribute. Severe breathing difficulty, bluish or grey colour, unusual limpness or rapid deterioration requires emergency help. Feeding adjustments can support nutrition, but they do not replace treatment of an underlying circulation problem. Temporary discomfort still needs careful judgement A blocked nose during a cold, an ear infection or pain in the mouth can make sucking less comfortable. Diarrhoea may reduce appetite while increasing fluid loss. These can be temporary problems, but their effect on a small baby can still be important. Teething can cause sore gums in an older baby, but it should not explain away marked refusal, significant fever, diarrhoea or an unwell appearance. If you are unsure, ask for an assessment. It is safer to describe the symptoms than label them minor before the baby has been checked. A feeding assessment looks at both health and technique Describe when the change began, how milk is offered and what happens during a feed. Mention difficulty attaching, coughing, choking, tiring, falling asleep, pulling away, sweating, vomiting or apparent pain. Keep a short record of feeds and wet nappies if helpful, without postponing urgent care to complete it. A professional may observe a breast or bottle feed and assess positioning, milk transfer, flow and swallowing. Weight and length over time help show the growth pattern; one measurement or the look of a baby is not enough. Examination and any tests should follow the history and findings rather than every baby receiving a broad set of investigations. Treatment depends on the reason and the nutritional need A plan may combine treatment of illness with support for attachment, positioning or bottle flow. Smaller, more frequent feeds may be appropriate for some babies, but that should be a tailored instruction. A sleepy, dehydrated or breathless baby needs assessment before experimenting with schedules at home. If milk allergy or another intolerance is suspected, the clinician can advise whether a specific formula or other change is needed. Repeatedly switching brands without a clear reason can obscure the pattern and delay help. Do not dilute formula, concentrate it or add ingredients without a prescribed plan. Some babies need extra nutrition or a different way of receiving it while the cause is addressed. Agree on what adequate intake should look like, what to monitor and when feeding and weight will be reviewed. Improvement in the original illness does not automatically prove that nutrition has caught up. Breastfeeding support should protect intake and choice If attachment or milk transfer is difficult, an appropriately trained breastfeeding professional can help. Expressed breast milk, formula or a combination may be needed so the baby receives enough. If you want to continue breastfeeding, ask how to support milk production while supplementation is used and how the plan will be reassessed. Needing formula does not mean you have failed or that breastfeeding must end. Some families cannot or do not wish to breastfeed, and they still need respectful, practical feeding support. The priority is a safely fed baby and a workable plan. Tell a pharmacist or clinician that you are breastfeeding before taking a medicine or using a medicated breast product. Many medicines are compatible with breastfeeding; do not stop essential treatment merely because small amounts might enter milk. Products placed where the baby’s mouth contacts the breast need product-specific advice. Avoid unnecessary scented lotions there, but do not treat all prescribed nipple care as forbidden. Make bottle feeds responsive and safe Hold your baby close and watch their sucking and breathing. Allow pauses and stop when they show they have had enough rather than insisting on an empty bottle. Check the flow with a feeding professional if milk spills excessively, the baby coughs or feeds repeatedly become a struggle. Keep equipment clean, prepare formula according to the appropriate instructions and never prop a bottle in the baby’s mouth. Do not add cereal or other food to a bottle as a general answer to poor feeding or short sleep. If a specialist prescribes thickened feeds for a particular condition, the written recipe and follow-up are essential. Introduce complementary foods alongside milk Around six months, when developmentally ready, babies begin complementary foods while continuing breast milk or infant formula. Starting solids does not mean replacing the milk a younger baby needs. Premature babies or those with swallowing or developmental concerns may need individual timing and texture advice. Offer small amounts of safe, soft food suited to the baby’s skills. Mashed vegetables and fruit, appropriately prepared meat or other protein foods, and iron-fortified infant cereals can be options. Vary cereals rather than relying only on rice. A baby does not have to progress through one mandatory food order. A small amount of cereal mixed into food offered by spoon is different from cereal in a bottle, but mixing is not a treatment for a feeding disorder. Begin with manageable opportunities and build up gradually; a fixed two-or-three-meal rule does not resolve poor intake. Avoid pressure and allow repeated exposure. Persistent refusal, choking, difficulty advancing textures or growth concerns merits help. Support the parent and follow the growth pattern Worry is understandable when feeding is difficult. Taking a few slow breaths, having another adult help or making the feeding space calmer can support you. It does not cure a medical feeding problem. Feeling anxious does not mean you spoiled your milk or caused the baby’s difficulty. Sustained inadequate nutrition can affect physical growth and development. WHO’s estimate that nearly half of deaths in children under five are linked to undernutrition describes a global burden, not the chance that an individual baby with a difficult feed will die. It should encourage access to care rather than frighten families with a misleading personal prediction. Ask for a written plan with a review date, warning signs and contact details. Persistent difficulty deserves reassessment even if you have followed every instruction. Feeding problems can improve with the right support, and you should not be left managing uncertainty through willpower alone. Changes in intake and wet nappies matter before weight falls. Prematurity does not explain away new illness. Breast milk, formula or combined feeding may support an individual plan. Parental anxiety is not a reason to blame a caregiver. Is poor feeding the same as being a picky eater? No. The concern is adequate intake, hydration, swallowing and growth, not simply a preference for one food. Must I wait for fever before seeking help? No. A baby can be seriously ill without fever. Reduced responsiveness, breathing problems and markedly poor intake need attention. What temperature is urgent under three months? A temperature of 38°C or higher needs urgent assessment. A low temperature or unwell appearance is also concerning. Can a premature baby just take longer to learn? Some need more time and support, but persistent or worsening difficulty after discharge should be discussed with the neonatal or paediatric team. Does jaundice count as a birth defect? Not generally. It is yellowing caused by bilirubin. A jaundiced baby who is not feeding or is difficult to wake needs urgent help. Should I assume teething explains refusal and diarrhoea? No. Teething should not explain away substantial poor feeding, diarrhoea, fever or an unwell baby. Does supplementation mean breastfeeding must stop? No. Expressed milk, formula or combined feeding may be part of a plan that supports adequate intake and your preferences. Should I stop my medicines while breastfeeding? Not without advice. Many are compatible; a pharmacist or clinician should check the specific medicine and the baby’s circumstances. Can cereal in a bottle fix poor feeding? No. It can increase choking risk. Follow a specialist’s instructions only if a particular thickened-feed treatment has been prescribed. Did my anxiety change my milk and cause this? That is not a justified conclusion. You deserve support, and the baby deserves a feeding assessment rather than blame.

title: Can a baby have too much milk?
description: Use feeding cues and growth checks to guide milk feeds without pressuring a baby or judging their body shape.
body: It is easy to focus on the amount left in a bottle or compare your baby with someone else’s. A better starting point is how your baby feeds, signals fullness and grows over time. A baby’s rounded cheeks or thighs do not tell you whether they are being overfed. Let your baby signal a pause or a finish Young babies may show hunger by turning toward the breast or bottle, bringing hands to the mouth or moving their lips. Crying can come later. During a feed, slowing down, closing the mouth or turning away can mean they need a pause or have had enough. Offer a break and watch what happens next. If your baby continues to show hunger, they may need more. If they are finished, do not repeatedly encourage them to take the last milk simply because it is there. A bottle does not have to be empty for a feed to be successful. Bottle technique matters with either type of milk A bottle can contain expressed breast milk or formula. In either case, a fast flow or pressure to finish can make it harder for a baby to set the pace. Hold your baby close and supported, keep the bottle at an angle that avoids an uncontrolled flow, and allow pauses. Do not prop the bottle or leave your baby to feed alone. Ask for help if your baby repeatedly coughs, gulps, leaks milk or seems distressed during feeds. These signs deserve a check of technique and health rather than simply reducing every feed. Do not change the recipe to influence sleep Prepare infant formula exactly as directed. Extra powder can make a feed unsafe, and extra water can also be harmful. If you are struggling to afford enough formula, ask a health or community service about practical support rather than stretching or concentrating feeds. Do not add juice, cereal or other food to a bottle to keep your baby full for longer. Cereal in a bottle is not a reliable way to improve sleep and can increase choking risk. A clinician-directed thickening plan for a medical problem is different and should have specific instructions. Breast milk or infant formula is the main nutrition during early infancy. Introduce complementary foods at around six months when developmentally ready, while continuing milk feeds. Offer suitable textures and nutrient-rich foods; whole fruit is preferable to juice when age-appropriate, and sweet drinks or sugary packaged foods are not needed. Frequent feeding is not automatically overfeeding Babies’ needs change as they grow, and feeds do not always occur at evenly spaced times. A baby may want several feeds close together. At the breast, responsive feeding is usually appropriate; frequent requests alone do not justify limiting access. Fussiness can also reflect a need for comfort, a diaper change, tiredness or illness. Look at the whole situation rather than assuming every cry means either hunger or too much milk. If you cannot tell what is happening, a feeding review can help. Use growth as a pattern, not a verdict Your clinician follows weight and length over time and interprets them with your baby’s health and feeding history. A single measurement or body shape does not predict an individual child’s future weight. Do not put a baby on a diet or cut milk feeds because they look larger than another baby. Seek advice for persistent vomiting, distress, poor growth or a feeding pattern that worries you. Spitting up alone is not proof of overfeeding. Forceful, green or bloody vomit, dehydration or a baby who seems unwell needs prompt medical assessment. Growth should be followed from infancy, not first checked at the second birthday. For children under two, clinicians use age-appropriate growth measures such as weight relative to length and the pattern across visits. Early feeding does not determine adult body size with certainty. Support makes responsive feeding easier All caregivers can agree to offer feeds calmly, allow pauses and respect fullness. If exhaustion, low mood or financial pressure is making feeding difficult, ask for practical and health support. These circumstances call for help, not assumptions about a parent’s ability or intentions. A baby does not need to finish every bottle. Use responsive technique with expressed milk and formula alike. Assess growth with a clinician; do not restrict milk based on appearance. Does a large baby need less milk? Size alone is not a reason to restrict feeds. Discuss the growth pattern and feeding cues with your baby’s clinician. Will a bigger bedtime feed guarantee better sleep? No. Do not pressure a baby to drink more or add food to a bottle for sleep. Feeding needs and night waking change with development.

title: Mucus in your baby’s stool: look at the whole picture
description: A slimy-looking stool is not a diagnosis. Feeding, hydration, fever, blood, vomiting and your baby’s behaviour help determine the next step.
body: Baby stools vary widely, and a small amount of mucus may occasionally be noticed. Persistent mucus, a sudden change in watery stools or any sign that your baby is unwell deserves advice. A photograph can help a clinician understand the change, but appearance alone cannot identify the cause. Know when to seek help now Get urgent medical assessment for a baby under three months with a temperature of 38°C or higher. Do not assume fever or diarrhea is caused by teething. Seek emergency care for green vomit, a swollen painful abdomen, repeated episodes of severe crying or pain with pallor, marked sleepiness, difficulty waking or signs of shock. Blood mixed with mucus, particularly with vomiting or episodes of pain, can signal a bowel problem such as intussusception. Do not wait for a classic red jelly-like stool; that is a late and uncommon feature. Contact a clinician promptly for blood in the stool, poor feeding, repeated vomiting, fewer wet nappies or a baby who seems unwell. Very young infants need a low threshold for assessment. A dry mouth or fewer tears can add to dehydration concerns, but do not wait for every sign. Mucus has more than one explanation The intestine normally produces mucus. A small isolated amount in an otherwise well baby may not indicate disease, but repeated or increasing mucus should be reviewed. It may look stringy, slippery or jelly-like, rather than like a formed adult stool. Breastfed stools can normally be loose and seedy, and green colour alone does not prove infection. A clear change from the baby’s usual pattern matters more than one colour. An intestinal infection may cause watery stools, fever, vomiting or reduced feeding. Blood or mucus does not reliably tell you whether the cause is bacterial or viral. Teething is not an adequate explanation for diarrhea, blood or an unwell baby. Extra drooling should not be used to dismiss a persistent stool change. Avoid diagnosing milk allergy from a nappy alone Some forms of cow’s milk protein allergy can cause blood-streaked stools with or without mucus, sometimes in an otherwise well young infant. Other causes must still be considered. Mucus alone, fussiness or a single unusual stool does not establish an allergy. Overdiagnosis can lead to unnecessary restrictions and costly formula changes. A clinician may recommend a defined dietary trial and a plan to confirm the diagnosis. If a breastfeeding parent needs to avoid a food, nutritional support helps prevent unnecessary deficiencies. For a formula-fed baby, the appropriate product may be an extensively hydrolyzed or amino-acid formula, depending on the circumstances. Ordinary lactose-free formula, goat’s milk formula and plant drinks are not interchangeable treatments for milk-protein allergy. Do not use commercial food-IgG panels to decide what to remove from the diet. Recognize less common problems without assuming them Cystic fibrosis can affect digestion and growth. Greasy, bulky, unusually foul-smelling stools and poor weight gain may prompt assessment, especially with other symptoms. Visible mucus alone does not diagnose it. The greasy appearance in pancreatic insufficiency relates to poorly digested fat; it should not be described simply as extra mucus passed from other organs. A specialist CF team may prescribe pancreatic enzyme replacement when enzymes are not reaching the intestine adequately, alongside nutrition and growth monitoring. Some children need additional feeding support, including a feeding tube. These are treatments for diagnosed digestive and nutritional problems, not for visible mucus alone. Intussusception occurs when one section of bowel slides into another. It can interfere with blood supply and is an emergency. Hospital treatment may involve an air or fluid enema under imaging, with surgery when needed. An enema for suspected intussusception is a specialist hospital procedure, never a treatment to try at home. Support feeding while following advice For a baby with uncomplicated diarrhea who is being cared for at home, continue breastfeeding or usual correctly prepared formula unless the clinician advises otherwise. Do not dilute formula. Ask about an appropriate oral rehydration solution if fluid losses are significant. Plain water, juice or homemade mixtures should not replace an infant’s feeds or a recommended rehydration plan. Do not give anti-diarrhea medicines or antibiotics unless specifically prescribed. Treatment depends on the cause, and fever medicine should not delay assessment of a young infant. If there are signs of a bowel obstruction or the baby is very unwell, seek emergency care and follow the medical team’s instructions about feeding. Bring useful information to the appointment Record your baby’s age, feeding pattern, wet nappies, temperature, vomiting, stool frequency and whether there is visible blood. Note recent medicines and any formula or food changes. A photo of the nappy can be useful. Bring a sample only if the service asks and explains how to collect it. Ask when improvement is expected and which changes should trigger another call. Persistent symptoms or poor growth need follow-up even if the baby seemed well at the first assessment. Starting solids is not a treatment for mucus and should not be brought forward to make stools look firmer. Assess the baby’s feeding, hydration and behaviour, not just stool appearance. Do not attribute diarrhea or illness to teething. Avoid allergy restrictions or formula changes without a diagnostic plan. Does mucus mean my baby has a milk allergy? No. Allergy is one possibility, but the overall pattern and an appropriate clinical assessment are needed. Should I wait for red jelly-like stool before worrying about intussusception? No. Intermittent severe distress, vomiting, pallor or unusual lethargy may occur earlier and need emergency assessment.

title: Blood clots and bleeding after birth: when to get help
description: A practical guide to lochia, changes during the first six weeks, vaginal clots, urgent warning signs and assessment of abnormal bleeding after birth.
body: After a baby is born, the uterus has healing to do, including at the place where the placenta was attached. Blood, mucus and tissue leave through the vagina as a discharge called lochia. Blood that collects before coming out can form a jelly-like clot. Some bleeding is expected after vaginal birth and after a cesarean, but the amount, the pattern over time and how you feel matter more than a clot’s appearance alone. Know when to get help immediately Seek medical care immediately for bleeding that soaks one or more pads in an hour, a clot bigger than an egg or the passage of tissue. These warnings apply on the first day too. Do not wait until 24 hours have passed, or wait for a second large clot. Smaller clots can also need assessment, especially if bleeding is increasing or you feel unwell. Call emergency services for severe or continuing heavy bleeding, collapse, chest pain or difficulty breathing. A fever of 38°C/100.4°F or above, bad-smelling discharge, severe abdominal pain, persistent dizziness or a severe headache also requires urgent assessment. Tell the service when you gave birth. If you are still in hospital, alert staff immediately. Why bleeding and clots occur The uterus contracts after birth, helping close the vessels that supplied the placenta. Its lining then renews itself. Tears or cuts in the birth canal can add to blood loss after a vaginal birth. The discharge is therefore more than ordinary menstrual blood, and its appearance can change as recovery progresses. A clot may contain mucus or tissue as well as blood, but you cannot reliably identify what it contains by looking at it. Nor can you determine at home whether every part of the placenta has passed. Describe or show a concerning clot to your maternity team when practical; never delay urgent care to collect, measure or photograph it. The first 24 hours Bleeding is usually at its greatest just after birth and may look red or reddish brown. Maternity staff assess the loss, how firmly the uterus is contracting and your general condition. Let them know about a sudden gush, a large clot or feeling faint, even if you have been told to expect a heavier flow than a period. A description such as tomato-sized or golf-ball-sized is not reassurance that a clot is normal. Soaking a pad each hour should not be treated as an expected part of day-one recovery. Heavy loss can need treatment promptly, and the first day is not an exception. Days two to six Across the next few days, the overall amount should decrease. The colour often becomes darker brown or pinkish red. A small clot can sometimes pass, but new, repeated or enlarging clots should be discussed with the maternity team. A change to brown does not prove there is no ongoing bleeding. Watch the trend rather than comparing your pad with a precise stain measurement. Different pads absorb different amounts. If bleeding becomes heavier instead of settling, or pain, fever or an unpleasant smell develops, seek advice promptly. Do not wait for the next scheduled postnatal visit. Days seven to fourteen During days seven to ten, lochia is often lighter in colour and quantity. During days eleven to fourteen it may be lighter again, with some pads barely marked. These stages overlap: everyone does not switch colour on the same date. Activity can briefly make the loss more noticeable. Reduce exertion and follow your recovery advice, but do not explain away a significant increase as merely doing too much. Continuing moderate-to-heavy loss, repeated clots or a return to heavy red bleeding needs assessment. The calendar alone cannot establish that recovery is going well. Weeks three to six and the return of periods By the third and fourth weeks, discharge is often much smaller in amount and may look creamy, pale or lightly blood-stained. In weeks five and six, some people have stopped bleeding, while others still notice occasional pink, brown or yellowish staining. Six weeks is an approximate recovery landmark, not a guaranteed finishing date. Menstrual periods return at different times. Feeding patterns can affect the timing, and a period can restart within the early postpartum weeks. However, fresh bleeding should not automatically be labelled a period if it is heavy, painful or accompanied by illness. Ask for a review when the pattern is not clearly improving or you are uncertain. Why the amount may vary during the day After lying down overnight, blood that has collected can come out when you stand. During a breastfeed, hormones make the uterus contract; you may notice cramps and a temporary change in the flow. A busier day can also make lochia more noticeable. These explanations help describe small variations, but none cancels the warning signs. Tell the team whether a change occurred after feeding, getting up or exercise, and whether it settled. You do not need to stop breastfeeding merely because lochia is present; significant bleeding calls for assessment of you and support with feeding as needed. Other changes that deserve a call A wound or stitches that appear to open, increasing tenderness, worsening pelvic pain or a new offensive smell should be reported. Red blood after day three is not, by itself, a diagnosis of a complication; what matters is whether the loss is heavy, becoming greater or occurring with other symptoms. Keep your maternity contact details accessible after discharge. Explain the number of pads used, whether they were soaked, the size and frequency of any clots and how you feel. Mention medicines, including blood thinners, and any complication during birth. If you cannot reach your usual team and symptoms are urgent, use the local urgent or emergency service. Vaginal clots and clots in blood vessels are different A clot passed through the vagina is not the same as a deep vein thrombosis, or DVT. A DVT forms within a deep vein, often in a leg or the pelvis. Pregnancy and recent birth increase this risk, although these clots remain uncommon. A clot can travel to the lungs and cause a pulmonary embolism. New swelling, warmth or pain affecting one leg needs urgent medical attention. Sudden breathlessness, chest pressure, coughing blood or collapse is an emergency. Sudden one-sided weakness, numbness, loss of balance or a severe new headache also needs emergency assessment for a possible neurological event. These symptoms are not explained by normal lochia; do not wait for vaginal bleeding to occur. How abnormal bleeding is assessed The team first considers how much blood you may be losing and whether you are stable. They may check your pulse and blood pressure, examine the abdomen and birth injuries, take blood samples or use an ultrasound when indicated. Ultrasound can help investigate remaining placental tissue, but it is not automatically needed for every small clot. Possible causes include a uterus that is not contracting effectively, tissue left in the uterus, an injury or infection. Heavy bleeding can happen immediately or develop after discharge. In RCOG terminology, secondary postpartum hemorrhage can occur from 24 hours to 12 weeks after birth, so leaving the hospital or passing the six-week mark does not make abnormal bleeding safe. Treatment depends on the cause and severity If the uterus is not contracting adequately, clinicians may use medicines and other measures to help it contract and control the bleeding. An injury may require repair; infection may need antibiotics. Remaining placental tissue sometimes needs removal under anesthesia. The term dilation and curettage, or D&C, refers to one possible procedure, not the inevitable treatment for any clot. Severe loss may require intravenous fluids, blood transfusion or further procedures to stop bleeding. The team should explain what is happening and why treatment is recommended. Do not try to remove tissue, perform uterine massage or take medicines to stop the bleeding on your own. Pads manage the discharge; they do not treat a hemorrhage. Everyday care while healing Use maternity or period pads and change them regularly. Wash your hands before and after changing a pad or using the toilet, and avoid unnecessary handling of stitches or dressings. Wait until healing has been assessed before returning to internal period products; NHS advice is to avoid tampons until after the six-week postnatal check. You do not need to purchase a particular cooling pad to recover. Ask the maternity team about comfortable perineal care and suitable pain relief if needed. Drink normally, eat a varied diet and ask about constipation treatment if passing stool is difficult. A stool softener or laxative may improve bowel comfort, but does not prevent uterine clots or treat excessive bleeding. Balance rest, movement and prescribed clot prevention Arrange help with lifting and household work so you can rest, then return to movement gradually according to your birth and recovery plan. Complete bed rest is not a routine way to prevent clots. Gentle mobility and avoiding dehydration support recovery, while persistent or increasing bleeding should prompt a call rather than repeated attempts to manage it through rest alone. Compression stockings and blood-thinning injections are recommended for some people after an individual risk assessment. Use the prescribed type and duration; do not start or stop them independently because you see lochia. Raising your legs may help comfort but does not replace assessment of one-sided swelling or prescribed prevention. Measures for vein clots and treatment of uterine bleeding serve different purposes. Follow up after significant blood loss If you needed treatment for a hemorrhage, ask about your blood count, iron replacement, follow-up and what symptoms should trigger another call. Recovery can take time, and practical help with meals, sleep and baby care may be important. Feeling persistently faint or increasingly weak should be assessed rather than attributed automatically to newborn tiredness. It can also help to talk through a frightening birth or emergency treatment with the team. Ask what caused the bleeding, what was done and whether it affects planning for a future pregnancy. A clear discharge plan should tell you whom to contact and how to obtain support while you recover. Lochia should generally diminish, but its colour and duration vary. Large clots, heavy bleeding or feeling unwell need assessment even on the first day. A week-by-week guide cannot establish whether bleeding is safe. Clots inside veins are different from clots passed vaginally and have separate warning signs. Pads, hydration and rest support recovery; they do not treat a postpartum hemorrhage. Can I pass a large clot normally in the first 24 hours? Do not assume it is harmless. Tell the maternity team immediately about a large clot or heavy bleeding, including on the day of birth. What if a clot is smaller than an egg? Size is only one warning sign. Repeated clots, increasing bleeding, pain or feeling unwell can require assessment even when each clot is smaller. Does brown blood mean bleeding has definitely stopped? No. Brown often reflects older blood, but colour alone does not measure the amount being lost or rule out a complication. Should all bleeding stop by six weeks? No exact stopping date applies to everyone. A light, improving discharge can last longer, but worsening or heavy bleeding should be reviewed rather than waiting for a deadline. Why do I notice more blood after getting out of bed? Collected blood may come out on standing. A small temporary change can occur, but a large gush, repeated clots or symptoms of illness should not be dismissed for that reason. Do I bleed vaginally after a cesarean? Yes. The inside of the uterus still heals after the placenta is delivered, even when the baby was born through an abdominal incision. Does a vaginal clot mean I have a clot in my leg? No. They are different processes. One-sided leg swelling or pain needs assessment independently of whether you have vaginal bleeding. Will every clot require a D&C? No. Assessment determines whether treatment is needed and what kind. A procedure may be appropriate for retained tissue, but cannot be decided from clot appearance alone. Can drinking water or using compression stockings stop lochia? No. Normal hydration and prescribed stockings may support recovery or reduce vein-clot risk. They are not treatments for abnormal uterine bleeding. What should I say when I call for help? Give the date and type of birth, explain the bleeding and clots, list other symptoms and mention relevant medicines. Do not delay an emergency call while gathering every detail.

title: A chalazion while breastfeeding: caring for an eyelid lump
description: How a chalazion differs from a stye, gentle home care, breastfeeding treatment questions and when an eyelid lump needs assessment.
body: A new eyelid lump can be uncomfortable, especially when you are also wondering whether treatment could affect your baby. A typical chalazion can often be managed with gentle care, while persistent lumps and eye symptoms deserve a proper examination. What a chalazion is A chalazion is a lump caused by a blocked oil-producing gland in the eyelid. These meibomian glands help supply the oily part of the tear film. When an opening becomes blocked, retained material can cause a local inflammatory lump in either the upper or lower lid. More than one is called chalazia. A typical chalazion is benign, but an unfamiliar eyelid lump should not be diagnosed from a photograph alone. Its position, how quickly it appeared, pain, skin changes and your vision all help a clinician distinguish it from other problems. Breastfeeding does not change the need to assess an unusual or persistent lump. Why it can develop or come back Inflammation around the eyelid glands can make blockage more likely. Blepharitis, which causes inflamed or crusted eyelid edges, and rosacea affecting the face or eyes are relevant examples. Seborrhoeic skin inflammation can coexist with eyelid problems and is worth mentioning at an appointment. A previous stye or recurring lid inflammation may be part of the history. This does not mean you caused the problem through poor hygiene. Ask about an ongoing eyelid-care routine if lumps keep returning, rather than repeatedly treating each one without reviewing the underlying irritation. Tuberculosis is a bacterial disease, not a viral infection. It should not appear in a routine list of common viral causes of chalazion. A clinician investigates unusual causes when the history or examination suggests them; a typical blocked eyelid gland does not by itself suggest tuberculosis. How it differs from a stye A stye is generally an infected eyelash follicle or eyelid gland. It often produces a tender red swelling at the lash line, sometimes with a small pus-filled point, although an internal stye can sit deeper in the lid. The eye may water or feel gritty. A chalazion often becomes a firmer, less tender lump away from the lash edge. However, a newly inflamed chalazion can hurt, so “painful means stye, painless means chalazion” is too simple. The two can be hard to distinguish at home. Marked light sensitivity, pain in the eye itself or altered vision should not be accepted as ordinary features of a harmless lid cyst. Get prompt eye-care advice for these symptoms, even if the lump looks similar to a previous stye. What breastfeeding changes about treatment decisions A blocked eyelid gland is a local problem; the diagnosis alone is not a reason to stop breastfeeding. A clean warm compress and gentle lid care do not expose your baby to a medicine. You can continue normal feeding while arranging assessment when needed. If drops, ointment, tablets or a procedure are proposed, tell the clinician and pharmacist that you are breastfeeding. The exact medicine, dose and your baby’s age and health matter. Ask for a compatible option and practical instructions, rather than assuming all eye medicines are harmless or that all require discarding milk. Do not use leftover antibiotic or steroid eye treatments. A simple chalazion is not automatically an infection, and treatment that suited another eye condition may be inappropriate. Any change to feeding should be based on the particular treatment and professional advice. Using warmth safely Wash your hands, wet a clean soft cloth with comfortably warm water, and place it over the closed eyelid. The warmth should feel soothing, never hot enough to sting or burn. Rewarm the cloth when it cools, checking the temperature again before it touches your skin. A practical starting routine is five to ten minutes several times a day, unless your eye-care professional recommends something different. Published routines vary; longer or more frequent sessions are not a reason to use hotter water. Choose a routine you can safely manage around feeds and rest. Use a clean cloth for each session and avoid sharing it. Keep the baby away from containers of hot water. Warmth may help soften retained oil, but it is not a guarantee that the lump will disappear by a particular date. Gentle massage without squeezing the lump After warming the lid, gentle massage may help move gland contents toward the eyelid edge. Use clean hands, keep the eye closed and ask a clinician to demonstrate if you are unsure about the direction or pressure. Do not press hard on the eyeball, pinch the lump or try to force material through the skin. Never pierce it with a needle or another sharp object. Aggressive manipulation can injure the lid and introduce infection. Stop if the routine causes significant pain or worsening redness. Home care should feel manageable; repeatedly pushing harder because nothing drains is not a useful test of whether it is working. Makeup, contact lenses and everyday hygiene Pause eye makeup while the lid is inflamed, and use glasses instead of contact lenses if your eye is sore or your clinician advises it. Makeup can irritate the area or contaminate an applicator; it is too absolute to say it can never contribute to eyelid trouble. Wash your hands before touching the eye area or handling lenses. Remove makeup before bed, clean reusable tools as instructed and do not share eye products. If an eye infection develops, discard products used during the infection rather than reintroducing contamination. Follow each product’s expiry or after-opening instructions. Mascara is commonly replaced within a few months, but a single three-month deadline is not a universal rule for every eyeliner and powder shadow. Stop a product that causes irritation, and never add saliva to revive dried mascara. How long to watch a lump Many chalazia improve over weeks, while some remain for months. It is reasonable to arrange an eye examination if a lump is not improving after several weeks of gentle care, including around the one-month point. You do not have to wait that long if you are unsure of the diagnosis. Seek review sooner if it grows, repeatedly returns in the same place, causes loss of lashes or changes the surrounding skin. A persistent or recurrent lump sometimes needs closer examination or a small tissue sample to check what it is. That is an assessment step, not a prediction that it is cancer. Keep a brief note of when it began, whether it is getting smaller and which care you have tried. Repeatedly rubbing or measuring it throughout the day can add irritation without giving a clearer answer. When eye symptoms need urgent help Get urgent advice for spreading redness or swelling, increasing pain, fever, significant discharge or an eye that is becoming difficult to open. Changes in vision, marked light sensitivity or pain within the eye also need prompt assessment. Severe eye pain, sudden loss of vision, painful eye movements or rapidly worsening swelling with feeling very unwell requires emergency assessment. These symptoms need a broader examination than a routine home-care plan for a chalazion. Breastfeeding is not a reason to delay necessary treatment. Tell the team about feeding so that they can choose appropriate medicines while treating the eye problem. What an eye specialist may offer If conservative care is unsuccessful, an eye specialist may discuss draining the lump through a small incision, often under local anaesthetic, or a steroid injection in selected cases. These options have different risks and are chosen after confirming the diagnosis. Ask what the procedure involves, whether a sample will be examined, how to care for the lid afterwards and which symptoms should prompt a call. Discuss any prescribed medicine in relation to breastfeeding before leaving. Treatment does not guarantee that another gland will never block. If episodes recur, ongoing care for blepharitis or another associated skin condition may be more helpful than replacing home routines with increasingly forceful massage. A chalazion can be tender when it first develops. Warm means comfortable, not scalding. Do not squeeze, pierce or use leftover eye medicines. Breastfeeding usually continues while the specific treatment is checked. Persistent or recurrent lumps need an eye examination. Is a chalazion the same as a stye? No. A chalazion is a blocked eyelid gland; a stye is usually an infected follicle or gland. Their appearance can overlap. Can a chalazion hurt? Yes. Early inflammation can cause tenderness, although an established lump is often less painful. Do I need to stop breastfeeding because of the lump? No. The diagnosis alone is not a reason to stop. Check any proposed medicine individually with your clinician or pharmacist. How hot should a compress be? Comfortably warm, never hot enough to sting or burn. Check it again whenever you rewarm it. Should I squeeze it after warming? No. Use only gentle care; squeezing or piercing can cause injury and infection. Are antibiotics always needed? No. A simple chalazion is not automatically a bacterial infection. Must every eye cosmetic be replaced after three months? No. Follow the individual product instructions, and discard products contaminated during an eye infection. Will it definitely disappear within a month? No. Resolution varies. Arrange review if it persists or is not improving, and seek help sooner for warning symptoms. Is tuberculosis a common viral cause? No. Tuberculosis is bacterial and does not belong in a routine list of common viral causes of chalazion. Which symptoms should not wait for a routine appointment? Visual changes, significant eye pain, light sensitivity or rapidly spreading swelling need prompt assessment; severe symptoms need emergency care.

title: Reflux in babies: common signs and symptoms that need help
description: Spitting up is often normal, but poor feeding, poor growth and unusual vomiting need assessment. Crying or back arching alone does not diagnose reflux disease.
body: Reflux means stomach contents move back into the food pipe, sometimes reaching the mouth as a small spit-up. It is common in young babies and often improves as they grow. The important question is how your baby is feeding, growing and behaving overall, rather than how many items match an online symptom checklist. Know the warning signs first Green vomit, blood or material resembling coffee grounds in vomit, or repeated forceful projectile vomiting needs urgent medical assessment. These findings should not be labelled ordinary reflux. Seek urgent help if your baby has a swollen or painful abdomen, cannot keep feeds down, is unusually sleepy or has signs of dehydration such as markedly fewer wet nappies. Breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour, unresponsiveness or a choking episode in which the baby cannot breathe requires emergency help. Reflux should not be assumed to explain an episode like this. A young baby with a fever also needs prompt age-appropriate assessment. If you are unsure whether your baby is seriously unwell, seek advice rather than waiting for the next scheduled visit. Ordinary spit-up can happen in a thriving baby Milk can come back up easily while the muscles and feeding system are still maturing. A small amount during or after feeding may look more substantial when it spreads across clothing. Many babies who spit up remain comfortable, feed well and gain weight appropriately. This uncomplicated reflux does not automatically need investigations or medicine. Regurgitation often becomes more noticeable in the first few months and then decreases. Symptoms starting for the first time after about six months or continuing beyond the first birthday deserve review; there is no need to wait until age two. The lower oesophageal sphincter is the ring of muscle at the stomach entrance. It opens for swallowing and normally helps keep stomach contents down. In young babies, a maturing sphincter, frequent liquid feeds and time spent lying down all contribute to regurgitation. Reflux is common and often most noticeable around three to four months, then improves through the first year as feeding and posture change. Crying and arching have several possible explanations Fussiness, hiccups, pulling away from a feed, back arching and interrupted sleep are not specific to acid-related disease. They can occur with normal development, feeding difficulties or other conditions. A baby cannot describe adult-type heartburn. Assuming that every cry means acid pain can lead to unnecessary treatment and delay assessment of the actual problem. Persistent feed refusal, pain with swallowing, poor growth or unusual repeated body posturing should be discussed with a clinician. Describe what you see rather than deciding the diagnosis yourself. Coughing, wheezing or recurrent chest infections also need their own assessment. They are not proof that reflux caused asthma or that milk has entered the lungs. A “wet burp” or hiccup means some milk comes back up at the same time. That can happen without disease. Feed refusal and poor weight gain are more significant when persistent, because a feeding problem or illness may be limiting intake. Rarely, reflux-related irritation is associated with unusual posturing, but repeated arching also has neurological and other explanations that need assessment. Aspiration of feed into the airway can cause lung problems, but coughing or recurrent pneumonia does not establish reflux as the cause. The clinician may need to assess swallowing and other respiratory explanations. Gagging is different from an episode in which a baby cannot breathe; the latter needs immediate help. Ask for a feeding review A clinician or feeding professional can observe a feed, review milk amounts and technique, and check growth and hydration. This is often more useful than immediately changing formula or adding medicine. Support with breastfeeding positioning, bottle flow and pacing may help. Avoid pressuring a baby to finish a bottle or changing the total intake without guidance. Holding your baby upright during and after a feed while you are awake may improve comfort. Keep the airway clear and the head supported. Feed according to your baby’s needs and clinical plan. Do not leave a hungry young baby without milk for a long period before bedtime in an attempt to prevent reflux. Some families are advised to hold a baby upright for roughly twenty to thirty minutes after a feed, while the adult remains awake. The exact duration is not a required treatment dose, and a sleepy caregiver should transfer the baby to the safe flat sleep space. Do not prop the baby up or withhold needed feeds to preserve that interval. Keep sleep flat and on the back Place your baby on their back for every sleep on a firm, flat sleep surface. Reflux is not a reason to use side or tummy sleeping. Do not raise the cot mattress or use wedges, positioners or inclined sleepers. Sitting devices are not a substitute for a safe sleep space. If you become sleepy while holding your baby upright, place them in their own safe sleep space. Arrange help if repeated feeds and crying are leaving you exhausted. Back sleeping remains recommended for babies with reflux; trying to hold milk down does not justify a less safe position. Treatment should have a clear reason Reflux disease is considered when reflux causes troublesome effects or complications, but diagnosis in infants requires care because many symptoms overlap with normal behaviour. Acid-suppressing medicines are not routinely recommended for crying, arching or spitting up in otherwise healthy, growing infants. They do not correct every feeding problem and can cause harms. A clinician may recommend a specific feeding change or treatment when indicated. Thickened feeds or a cow’s-milk-protein elimination trial need a clear plan and review; do not add cereal or switch repeatedly on your own. Keep a brief record of feeds, vomiting, wet nappies and symptoms to support the assessment. Growth measurements and an examination help determine whether your baby needs further investigation. Comfortable spit-up in a growing baby is often uncomplicated reflux. Crying and arching alone do not establish acid disease. Urgent vomiting or breathing warning signs need assessment, and safe sleep remains flat on the back. Does poor sleep prove that my baby has painful reflux? No. Sleep disruption has many causes and should be considered alongside feeding, growth and the examination. Should I tilt the cot to help milk stay down? No. Use a firm, flat surface and place your baby on their back for sleep.

title: When your baby does not want a pacifier
description: Gentle ways to offer a pacifier, feeding and sleep safety, which tricks to avoid, and how to comfort a baby who simply does not want one.
body: A pacifier can seem like the missing answer when you need to settle a baby or take a moment to yourself. Then your baby spits it out, turns away or looks offended by the offer. Some babies enjoy sucking a pacifier, some accept it only occasionally, and some never want one. You can explore the option without turning acceptance into a task your baby has to complete. First check what your baby needs A pacifier offers sucking without milk. That can be comforting after feeding needs are met, but it cannot answer hunger. Before offering one, consider whether your baby needs a feed, a diaper change, a quieter space, a change in temperature or contact with you. Crying is information, even when the reason is hard to work out. Do not use a pacifier to stretch the time between feeds or suppress hunger cues because a schedule says it is too early. A baby who repeatedly refuses milk or seems unwell needs attention to that problem, not more practice with a pacifier. When is a reasonable time to introduce one? For a directly breastfed baby, wait until breastfeeding is established before routine pacifier use. Effective feeding, comfortable attachment, enough milk and appropriate weight gain matter more than a particular birthday. This is often several weeks after birth, but the timing differs between families. If you are not directly breastfeeding, a pacifier can be offered earlier if you wish. A premature baby or a baby with a feeding difficulty may have a specific care plan, so ask their team. No calendar date can guarantee that introducing a pacifier will prevent every feeding problem or a problem described as “nipple confusion.” 1. Give a new object time: but respect a no A pacifier is an unfamiliar object with its own shape, feel and movement. Spitting it out on the first attempt does not tell you whether the baby will ever enjoy it. If they are comfortable, you can leave the possibility open and offer it on another occasion. Patience means allowing time, not repeating the offer until the baby gives in. Turning away, closing the mouth, gagging or becoming more upset are reasons to stop. You do not need a target number of attempts or weeks of persistence. A later offer is optional, and so is deciding you have tried enough. 2. Choose a calm first introduction A baby who is already crying intensely may not be ready to explore something new. Attend to the immediate need and help them settle first. A relaxed, awake moment can make it easier to notice whether they are interested in the pacifier or simply want to look around. Offer it gently without pushing it into a closed or resisting mouth. Watch what happens instead of assuming silence is the only successful result. If the baby loses interest, put it away. You can learn something about their preference even when they never begin to suck. 3. Offer after feeding needs are met When a baby still wants milk, a pacifier is a disappointing substitute. If they seem satisfied after a feed but continue to seek sucking for comfort, that may be a reasonable time to offer one. “After a feed” is an opportunity, not a requirement to introduce a pacifier after every meal. A recent feed does not prove that a baby cannot be hungry again. Continue to notice cues and the wider feeding pattern. If you are unsure about intake, uncomfortable feeding or weight gain, seek feeding support rather than using the pacifier to test whether the baby really needed more milk. 4. Skip milk coatings and sweeteners Dipping a pacifier in breast milk or formula is sometimes suggested to make it more appealing. A coating is not needed to teach a baby what the object is for. Offer a clean, uncoated pacifier; NICHD’s safe-sleep guidance advises against coating it with anything. Never add honey to an infant’s pacifier. Honey can cause infant botulism and should not be given before twelve months. Sugar, syrup and other sweet coatings are not suitable persuasion tools either. Feed milk as part of feeding, and keep an optional comfort object separate from an effort to disguise its taste. 5. Avoid a surprise swap during breastfeeding Quickly substituting a pacifier for the breast before the baby notices may sound convenient, but it does not tell you that feeding is complete or that the baby wants the substitute. Finish responding to the feeding need first, then make a separate, gentle offer if appropriate. Touching the cheek can prompt a young baby to turn and search for a feed. That response is not permission to override resistance or a technique you must practise to secure a pacifier. There is no need to trick your baby. Comfort works best when you can notice and respond to what they are showing you. 6. Try another suitable shape if you want to Pacifiers differ in shape, size and material. A baby may prefer one and reject another. If you choose to try a different model, make sure it is age-appropriate, complies with local safety requirements and is used according to its instructions. A good fit matters more than an impressive marketing description. You do not need a drawer full of products. Trying endless designs can become expensive and tiring without changing the baby’s preference. Do not improvise with a loose bottle nipple or alter a pacifier to make it smaller or softer. A baby who accepts a bottle is not obliged to enjoy a pacifier. 7. Do not turn sucking into a tugging game Pulling lightly on a pacifier while it is in the mouth is sometimes promoted as “reverse psychology,” intended to make a baby suck harder to keep it. A reflex response is not evidence that a reluctant baby now wants the object, and you do not need this manoeuvre to provide comfort. Let the baby suck voluntarily and stop when they release it or resist. Never hold or tape a pacifier in place. Checking a product for loose parts while it is outside the baby’s mouth is a different task from tugging on it during use. Follow the product’s inspection instructions separately. 8. Build a settling routine that works without one You can feed when needed, hold your baby, speak or sing softly, or gently rock them while you are awake. A quieter setting may help when there has been a lot to see and hear. Try to notice which changes seem welcome; doing more and more at once can make it hard to tell. Some babies prefer closeness to sucking an object. That is a preference you can work with. If you need a brief break, put the baby on their back in a safe cot or bassinet, step away for a short time and ask a trusted adult for support if available. Never shake a baby, however overwhelmed you feel. Choose, clean and inspect the product A one-piece pacifier with a suitable shield reduces the risk of parts separating or the whole object going into the mouth. Follow the age range and local product guidance. Keep packaging and small protective caps out of reach, and do not use a bottle teat as a makeshift pacifier. Follow the manufacturer’s cleaning and replacement instructions, using clean hands. Inspect the nipple and other parts regularly, and discard an item that is torn, sticky, damaged or deteriorating. If a cleaning method uses heat, allow the item and any trapped water to cool before offering it. Never repair a damaged pacifier for continued use. Keep the sleep advice in perspective Offering a pacifier at naps and bedtime is part of AAP and NICHD advice for reducing sudden infant death syndrome risk, once feeding is going well. It is still optional if the baby refuses. If it falls out after the baby is asleep, you do not need to keep putting it back. A pacifier does not replace the rest of safe sleep: place the baby on their back on a firm, flat, separate infant sleep surface with a fitted sheet and no loose bedding or soft objects. Do not attach a pacifier to clothing, bedding or toys for sleep, and never put a cord around a baby’s neck.
