Tummy time is play, not a supervised exception for stomach sleeping. Avoid unnecessary stretches of time in car seats or other containers when not needed for travel or safety. Ask for advice if the baby cannot turn comfortably in both directions, strongly dislikes movement or has a flat area that is becoming more pronounced. A persistent head tilt or preference for one side Torticollis describes an abnormal head or neck position. Some babies have a tight neck muscle related to their position before birth; head tilt can also have other causes. It is not accurate to assume that side sleeping by itself caused the condition. You may notice the head consistently tilted one way, difficulty turning fully, a preference for feeding on one side, or the baby following you mainly with the eyes instead of turning the head. A preferred position can contribute to uneven pressure on the skull and make settling or feeding harder. Arrange an assessment rather than waiting for the baby to grow out of a persistent restriction. Treatment may include individualized positioning and physiotherapy. Have a professional show you any recommended exercises; forcing a stretch or using a sleep positioner is not a substitute. Continue back placement for sleep. A new painful tilt, an unwell baby or a sudden loss of normal movement deserves prompt medical advice because not every head-position problem is simple muscular tightness. Temporary colour changes need the right interpretation Some newborns briefly develop a striking difference in skin colour, with one half of the body pink or red and the other paler. This is known as harlequin colour change and may be seen when the baby is lying on one side. It is thought to relate to immature regulation of small blood vessels. In an otherwise well newborn, a clinician may recognize this as a benign, temporary phenomenon. Reports describe episodes lasting from seconds to several minutes, sometimes longer than two minutes. An online description or a percentage quoted for newborns cannot establish that this is what you are seeing. Ask for advice about a new or unexplained colour change, especially if it persists or the baby seems unwell. Blue or grey lips or tongue, difficulty breathing, marked limpness or poor responsiveness is not something to watch at home while waiting for a harmless colour change to fade. Seek emergency help. Do not choose side sleeping to reproduce or test a colour change. Return to the usual safe sleep arrangement and, if the baby is well, describe what you saw to a health professional. A photograph may help explain a brief episode, but taking one must never delay care for an unwell baby. Swaddling: stop when attempts to roll begin Some young babies are soothed by swaddling, but it is optional and is not a way to prevent SIDS. If used before rolling attempts, the wrap should be secure enough not to become loose bedding, allow comfortable breathing and leave room for the hips and knees to move. Always place a swaddled baby on their back. Stop as soon as the baby shows signs of trying to roll. Do not wait until they can complete a roll or reach an expected age. Restriction can make it harder for a baby who turns onto the stomach to change position. Leaving the arms out does not make a restrictive wrap safe once rolling attempts begin. A product that still compresses the chest or body needs the same caution. Do not use weighted swaddles, weighted blankets or objects placed over the baby to keep them still. If you are unsure whether a product is a swaddle or ordinary sleep clothing, look at whether it restricts movement and ask for advice. A product label or marketing claim cannot replace the baby’s developmental signs. Sleep sacks should allow movement, not stop it An appropriately sized, non-weighted sleep sack can provide warmth without a loose blanket. Choose a design that fits securely at the neck and arm openings so the baby cannot slip inside, and allows free movement. Follow the manufacturer’s sizing and use instructions. A sleep sack is not meant to hold a baby on their back or prevent rolling. Designs that compress the arms, chest or body function more like swaddles and should not be used once rolling attempts start. Ordinary, unrestricted sleep clothing is the appropriate distinction, not simply whether the item is called a sack. Keep the rest of the sleep space clear. Using a wearable blanket does not create a need for an additional duvet, cushion or loose cover. Check warmth by the room and the baby’s condition rather than adding layers until movement is limited. Why pillows, positioners and monitors are not a solution It can seem logical to place a folded blanket behind a baby’s back or a cushion beside the head. These objects can move, obstruct the face or create a space where the baby becomes trapped. Avoid wedges, bolsters, nests and products intended to fix a sleeping baby in one position. Padding supplied for a car seat has a different purpose and should not be copied into a cot. Even a device advertised for reflux, head shape or safer sleep may be inappropriate. The FDA has warned about sleep positioners and unsupported claims that products prevent SIDS. A video monitor may help you hear or see the baby from another room, but it does not make unsafe positioning safe. Consumer breathing or heart-rate monitors have not been shown to prevent SIDS and do not replace the recommended sleep environment. Use a medically prescribed monitor as directed for the condition it is intended to address. Keep pillows, stuffed animals, cot bumpers, loose or bulky blankets and excess clothing layers out of the baby’s sleep arrangement. Check the mattress, fitted sheet, product limits and surrounding cords regularly as mobility increases. If a baby rolls, first review these practical safeguards rather than buying something to restrain them. A consistent plan for every caregiver Tell everyone caring for the baby the same essentials: start on the back, use a firm flat clear surface, keep the baby’s own sleep space nearby, and stop swaddling at the first signs of rolling. Explain that independent two-way rolling does not change how an adult initially places the baby. Bring concerns about reflux, head shape, a neck preference or unusual movements to the baby’s clinician. These concerns can be addressed without exchanging safe sleep for side positioning. Ask for a demonstration if instructions are unclear. You do not have to watch every movement all night or achieve a perfectly settled baby to be a caring parent. Build a repeatable sleep setup, share the work where possible and seek practical help when exhaustion makes things difficult. The aim is a safer routine that can be followed for every sleep. Start every sleep on the back throughout the first year. A baby who rolls both ways independently can generally remain in the position they reach. Stop restrictive swaddling when attempts to roll begin. Keep the sleep surface firm, flat, level and free of soft objects. Reflux and flat spots do not justify routine side sleeping. Use awake-time movement and clinical advice for head-shape or neck concerns. Positioners and consumer monitors do not replace safe sleep. At what age can I start putting my baby to sleep on their side? Continue placing the baby on their back for every sleep until age one. Four or six months is not a switch to side placement. Do I need to turn a baby who rolls both ways back all night? Usually not. Start sleep on the back, then allow a baby who independently rolls back-to-stomach and stomach-to-back to remain in the position they reach on a clear, suitable surface. What if the baby only rolls one way? You can return them to their back when you notice them on their stomach. Do not restrain them with a pillow, strap or positioner, and stop swaddling. Does reflux make back sleeping dangerous? Ordinary reflux is not a reason to choose side or stomach sleeping. Use a flat, level surface and seek medical advice for feeding or breathing concerns. Can side sleeping fix a flat spot? It is not the recommended treatment. Maintain back placement and use supervised awake tummy time, varied handling and assessment of any neck preference. Is arms-out swaddling safe after rolling begins? Not if the product still restricts the chest or body. Stop restrictive swaddling at the first attempts to roll, not only after a completed roll. Should a sleep sack stop the baby moving? No. An ordinary non-weighted sleep sack should fit properly and allow movement. It is a substitute for loose bedding, not a restraint. Will a video or breathing monitor prevent SIDS? Consumer monitors have not been shown to prevent SIDS. They do not make side placement, soft bedding or an unsafe surface safe. Is a brief one-sided red colour change always harmless? No online description can confirm the cause. Harlequin colour change can be benign in a well newborn, but unexplained changes need advice and breathing problems or blue/grey lips require emergency help.

title: Necrotising enterocolitis: signs, treatment and recovery
description: NEC is a serious intestinal illness in newborns. Learn which changes need urgent attention and how neonatal teams investigate and treat it.
body: Necrotising enterocolitis, or NEC, causes inflammation and injury in a newborn’s intestine. In severe cases, bowel tissue dies or develops a hole, allowing intestinal contents to leak into the abdomen. It is a medical emergency that needs hospital care, not a feeding problem to manage at home. Which babies are most at risk? NEC mainly affects premature and medically vulnerable newborns. It often develops in the first weeks after birth, but there is no fixed two-week window. Term babies can also be affected, particularly when other illnesses compromise intestinal health or blood flow. There is no single established cause. An immature intestinal barrier, an abnormal inflammatory response, gut bacteria and problems with blood supply can interact. A difficult delivery is not a complete explanation for every case. NEC is not simply an infection caused by bacteria in food. It can occur despite careful neonatal care, and a diagnosis should not be treated as proof that a parent caused it through feeding decisions. Other serious newborn conditions, including those affecting circulation and sometimes an unusually high red-cell concentration, may be considered in the risk assessment. They do not establish the cause of NEC by themselves. Changes that need immediate attention Tell the neonatal team immediately about a newly swollen or discoloured abdomen, vomiting, blood in the stool or a marked change in feeding tolerance. Staff also watch for unusual sleepiness, temperature instability, pauses in breathing and changes in heart rate. At home, a newborn with green vomit, a swollen painful-looking abdomen, blood in the stool or poor feeding together with lethargy needs urgent medical assessment. Do not wait for every symptom to appear or for a routine appointment. Call emergency services if your baby is struggling to breathe, is blue or grey around the lips or tongue, becomes unresponsive or is difficult to wake. These signs can have several causes, all requiring urgent attention. An ordinary episode of wind or spit-up does not diagnose NEC. Equally, a baby does not need a fever to be seriously unwell. Describe what has changed and when it began. Diarrhoea may accompany feeding intolerance, although blood in the stool or a swollen abdomen has other possible causes too. The team considers the combination and progression of signs. How the neonatal team checks for NEC Assessment combines the baby’s condition, abdominal examination, imaging and laboratory tests. Abdominal X-rays can show characteristic gas patterns; ultrasound may provide additional information. Repeated examinations or images may be needed as the illness evolves. Blood tests help assess infection, blood counts, clotting and the effects of illness. Blood in stool can support concern but does not establish NEC on its own. Neither a single high white-cell count nor a low platelet count is a standalone diagnosis. Fluid normally exists within the bowel. Its presence does not prove that there is a hole. The team looks for the overall clinical and imaging evidence of injury or perforation and decides whether surgical assessment is needed. A surgical team may occasionally place a drain into the abdominal cavity in a critically ill baby. This is different from routinely inserting a needle to look for fluid inside the intestine, and is not a standard diagnostic step for every suspected case. Treatment gives the bowel a chance to recover The hospital team usually pauses milk feeds while providing fluids and nutrition through a vein. A tube through the nose or mouth into the stomach can drain fluid and air. Antibiotics treat or help control infection. Breathing support, blood-pressure support and other treatments may be needed according to the baby’s condition. Staff monitor the response closely and involve a neonatal surgeon when appropriate. Do not independently stop feeds for a prolonged period, restart them early or substitute a different milk as treatment. Feeding changes in suspected NEC need prompt clinical supervision and a plan for hydration and nutrition. If you are expressing milk, ask the neonatal team how to maintain your supply and store milk during the treatment period. They will guide its use when feeding can safely resume. Some babies need surgery A perforation, severely damaged bowel or deterioration despite medical treatment can make surgery necessary. The surgeon aims to remove tissue that cannot recover while preserving functioning intestine. Depending on the baby’s stability and findings, treatment may involve a drain, bowel surgery or an ostomy, where bowel is brought to an opening on the abdomen. The exact approach and timing are individual decisions. Ask what the team has found, whether a temporary stoma is expected and how nutrition will be provided. Further operations may be needed, including reconnection of the bowel when appropriate. Recovery and follow-up Many babies recover, but the outlook varies with prematurity, illness severity and how much intestine is affected. It is not possible to promise full recovery from the diagnosis alone. Scar tissue can later narrow the bowel. Babies who lose a substantial length of intestine may have difficulty absorbing nutrients and need specialist nutritional support. Follow-up can include feeding, growth, development and surgical review. After discharge, follow the team’s instructions about vomiting, abdominal swelling, stool changes and feeding difficulties. Keep the neonatal or surgical contact details available and seek urgent help for concerning changes. Human milk can reduce NEC risk in premature babies, but no feeding method guarantees prevention. Do not add an over-the-counter probiotic to a premature baby’s feeds without the neonatal team: products and protocols differ, and live organisms can cause serious infection in vulnerable infants. NEC requires urgent hospital assessment and can progress quickly. Prematurity is a major risk factor, but term babies can also be affected. Diagnosis uses the whole clinical picture, not one symptom or blood result. Recovery may require ongoing feeding, growth and bowel follow-up. Does every baby with NEC need an operation? No. Some improve with bowel rest, intravenous nutrition and antibiotics. Surgery is considered when the findings or response to treatment require it. Is NEC limited to the first two weeks? No. Timing varies, including with gestational age and other medical conditions. Can I prevent NEC with a probiotic? Do not start one yourself. Neonatal units use different evidence-based protocols, and some probiotic products can cause invasive infection in premature infants.

title: Preventing abusive head trauma: safe care when a baby cries
description: Recognise possible abusive head trauma, know when to call emergency services and make a practical plan to keep a baby safe when caregivers feel overwhelmed.
body: Violent shaking or an inflicted blow can cause life-threatening injury to a baby. Suspected injury needs immediate medical help. For everyday care, a simple plan for crying, exhaustion and asking for support can help prevent a dangerous moment. What abusive head trauma means Abusive head trauma is serious injury to an infant or young child caused by violent shaking, an inflicted blow or a combination of these. “Shaken baby syndrome” is a familiar older term, but it does not describe every way the injury can happen. An impact is not required for violent shaking to be dangerous. A baby’s head is relatively large and the neck muscles provide limited support. Violent movement can injure the brain and its blood vessels, leading to bleeding, swelling and impaired brain function. The eyes, neck or spine may also be injured, and other injuries such as fractures can coexist. A brief violent episode can cause severe harm. There is no safe number of shakes or reassuring time threshold. If a baby may have been shaken or struck, seek emergency medical assessment immediately, even when there is no visible bruise or the baby appears to have settled. Young babies are vulnerable, but normal gentle care is different Infants, especially those in their first year, are at greatest risk. Abusive head trauma also occurs in older babies and young children. The first months can be particularly difficult for caregivers because crying and sleep disruption can feel relentless, but a crying peak is not an exact timetable for injury risk. Ordinary gentle rocking, supported cuddling and normal careful handling are different from violent shaking. Support a young baby’s head and neck and keep movements gentle. Do not throw a baby into the air, hit them or deliberately jerk their head to stop crying. This distinction should reassure someone worried about an ordinary cuddle without excusing forceful handling. If an actual injury, fall or violent movement has occurred, describe what happened honestly to a clinician. An online description cannot determine whether a particular child has been injured. Symptoms may be obvious or easy to miss Warning signs can include unusual sleepiness, difficulty waking, poor feeding, repeated vomiting, marked irritability, abnormal movements or seizures. Breathing may become difficult or stop, and the baby may look blue, grey or very pale. Severe injury can cause unresponsiveness or loss of normal movement. There may be no obvious external injury. Some symptoms resemble illness or feeding problems, which is one reason suspected trauma needs assessment rather than home observation. A baby who becomes quiet after being shaken has not necessarily been soothed; reduced responsiveness may be a sign of brain injury. Call the local emergency number for a baby who is unresponsive, has a seizure, is difficult to wake, has abnormal breathing or concerning colour change. Tell the dispatcher about any possible shaking or impact. Do not wait for every symptom to appear or try to prove what happened before obtaining help. Get emergency help and follow current resuscitation guidance If the baby is unresponsive and not breathing normally, including only gasping, call emergency services on speaker and start CPR with dispatcher guidance. A lay rescuer should not delay to search for a pulse. Put the baby on a firm, flat surface and follow the instructions you receive. For infant CPR, 2025 AHA/AAP guidance uses the heel of one hand or two thumbs with the hands encircling the chest; the previous two-finger technique was removed. Compress the breastbone at 100–120 times a minute, about one-third of the chest depth, approximately four centimetres, allowing full recoil. A trained single rescuer uses thirty compressions followed by two breaths, with minimal interruptions. Thirty is a count, not thirty seconds. Breaths are important for infants; if unable to give them, provide compressions rather than doing nothing. Use an AED as soon as available, with paediatric pads or mode if provided, following its prompts. This brief reminder does not replace hands-on training or the dispatcher’s instructions. While help is coming, protect breathing and give a clear history Avoid unnecessary movement when head or neck injury is possible, but keeping the airway open takes priority. Tell the dispatcher if the baby vomits, is breathing but unresponsive, or cannot be kept in a position that allows breathing. Follow guidance about positioning and supporting the head and body together. Do not shake the child to wake them, give food or drink, or put anything in the mouth during a seizure. Keep them away from immediate hazards while waiting for the ambulance. Continue the emergency instructions rather than repeatedly stopping to check whether things have improved. Tell the clinical team when the baby was last behaving normally, what you saw, any possible shaking, blow or fall and when symptoms started. Share what you know without filling gaps with guesses. Fear or embarrassment should not delay treatment; accurate information helps the team choose urgent investigations and protect the child. Diagnosis uses the whole clinical picture Clinicians assess the history, examination and appropriate tests together. They may arrange brain CT or MRI, an eye examination, imaging to look for fractures and blood tests. Different specialists may contribute because brain, eye, bone and other findings require careful interpretation. Some descriptions refer to a “triad” of brain dysfunction, bleeding around the brain and retinal bleeding. These terms need care: encephalopathy means disturbed brain function, not simply swelling, and subdural bleeding is inside the skull rather than ordinary bruising under the skin. No isolated finding or three-item checklist should be used by a reader to diagnose abuse. The team considers alternative explanations where appropriate, such as accidental injury, bleeding disorders, birth-related findings or selected metabolic and genetic conditions. A blood test does not rule out every alternative. A thorough assessment takes the pattern, severity, timing and child’s development into account; it is not a judgement to make from one photograph or scan report. Treatment is tailored to the injuries Emergency treatment may include support for breathing and circulation, treatment of seizures and close monitoring in intensive care. Some children need surgery to treat bleeding or pressure in the head. Eye injuries and other injuries are assessed and managed by the relevant specialists. There is no single medicine that instantly reverses traumatic brain damage, but it is incorrect to say that medicines have no role. They can be essential for complications. Likewise, an operation or a drainage device is used when the particular findings justify it, not automatically for every child. The team should explain the immediate priorities and update the family as information becomes available. At the same time, professionals need to make sure the child will be safe during and after treatment. Medical care and safeguarding assessment can proceed together without waiting for a family to conduct its own investigation. Recovery may require long-term support Outcomes vary with the injuries and the child. Some effects are immediately apparent, while difficulties with learning, movement or behaviour may become clearer as development progresses. Possible consequences include seizures, impaired vision or hearing, developmental disability and cerebral palsy; severe injuries can be fatal. No general article can predict the outcome for an individual child. Ask the treating team what is known now, what remains uncertain and which changes they will monitor. A reassuring early appearance should not be used to cancel recommended follow-up. Rehabilitation and developmental support may involve physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and feeding specialists, hearing or vision services and educational support. Families also need clear appointments and practical help. Keep a shared record of the care plan so new difficulties can be raised promptly with the appropriate service. Make a safe plan for moments of frustration Crying is a normal way for a baby to communicate, and sometimes it continues despite attentive care. Check feeding needs, a wet or dirty nappy, temperature, tiredness and whether the baby seems ill. Gentle holding or soothing may help, but a caregiver cannot always make crying stop immediately. If frustration is rising, place the baby on their back in a safe cot with a firm, flat mattress and no loose soft items. Step into another room briefly to calm down and check back within five to ten minutes. Remain nearby; do not leave the home or hand the baby to someone who is angry, intoxicated or otherwise unsafe. Call a trusted adult for relief. If you think you might hurt the child, put them safely down and get urgent help immediately. This is a protective action, not a failure. Persistent or unusual crying, poor feeding or signs of illness still need medical advice rather than being dismissed as a difficult temperament. Include every caregiver in prevention Agree in advance that no one will shake, strike or throw the baby, including when they are exhausted or trying to wake them. Explain the safe-break plan to partners, relatives, babysitters and anyone else providing care. Leave practical contact details and make it clear that asking for help is welcome. Arrange manageable shifts or specific help with meals, older children and rest when possible. Ongoing anxiety, depression, intrusive thoughts, anger or overwhelming exhaustion deserve professional support. A parent does not need to wait until a crisis to tell a maternity, primary-care or mental-health professional that coping is becoming difficult. If another caregiver’s behaviour makes you fear for a child’s safety, get help from local emergency or child-protection services as appropriate. Do not leave the child in an immediately unsafe situation. Prevention involves dependable support and a clear response to danger, not expecting one person to tolerate unlimited distress alone. Never shake, strike or throw a baby. A baby becoming quiet after violence may be injured. Give clinicians an honest account and seek help promptly. A short nearby break with the baby safely in their cot is protective. All caregivers need support and a shared safety plan. Can a brief episode of shaking cause harm? Yes. There is no safe number of shakes or minimum duration to rely on. Is normal gentle rocking the same as violent shaking? No. Gentle supported care is different. Keep movements gentle, support the head and never throw or jerk a baby. Could a baby be injured without a bruise? Yes. Serious internal injury may occur without an obvious external mark. Should I wait because the baby stopped crying? No. A quiet or less responsive baby after possible shaking may be injured and needs urgent assessment. Is the old two-finger infant CPR technique still in the 2025 AHA guidance? No. The guidance uses one hand or two thumbs encircling the chest. Follow current training and emergency-dispatch instructions. Does a triad of findings automatically diagnose abuse? No. Specialists assess the entire history, examination, tests and appropriate alternative explanations. Is there any treatment for the injury? Yes. Emergency support, medicines for complications, selected surgery and rehabilitation may be needed, although there is no instant reversal of brain injury. May I put a crying baby down to calm myself? Yes. Use a safe cot, place the baby on their back, stay nearby and check back within five to ten minutes while arranging support. What if I am afraid I might hurt the baby? Put the baby safely down and call for urgent help. Do not remain holding them while you feel unable to keep them safe. Who should know the safe-break plan? Every person who cares for the baby, including partners, relatives and babysitters.

title: Choanal atresia: blocked nasal passages in babies and children
description: Learn how one-sided and two-sided choanal atresia differ, which breathing signs are urgent, and how diagnosis, surgery and follow-up work.
body: A persistent blockage at the back of the nose can affect a child’s breathing and feeding. Choanal atresia is present from birth, and its urgency depends especially on whether one or both nasal passages are blocked. What is blocked in choanal atresia? Choanal atresia is a condition present from birth in which the opening at the back of one or both nasal passages is blocked. These openings normally connect the nose to the upper throat. The obstruction may contain bone and soft tissue, rather than being the sort of mucus blockage that clears after a cold. The condition is rare, often described as affecting roughly one baby in several thousand births. Estimates differ between populations and reports. It can occur on its own or alongside differences elsewhere in the body, which is why assessment may involve more than an examination of the nose. Understanding the location helps explain treatment: removing secretions may make an open passage clearer, but it cannot remove a congenital bony barrier. The team needs to establish how much of the airway is affected and whether breathing and feeding are safe before deciding on the next step. One-sided and two-sided blockage behave differently Unilateral choanal atresia affects one side. The other passage may provide enough airflow for the problem to be less obvious at birth. Persistent stuffiness or discharge on the same side can eventually bring it to attention in infancy, childhood or occasionally later. Bilateral choanal atresia affects both sides and can be a breathing emergency in a newborn. Young babies depend heavily on nasal breathing, especially during feeding. They are not literally incapable of mouth breathing until a fixed age, but their ability to compensate can be limited. These are not simply mild and severe labels for the same appointment schedule. A baby struggling to breathe needs immediate support, while a stable child with one open side may have time for a planned assessment. Associated heart, airway or swallowing problems can also change the urgency. Recognise breathing and feeding warning signs With bilateral obstruction, a newborn may have difficult or noisy breathing, chest pulling in, trouble feeding or episodes of blue or grey colour. Breathing may temporarily improve during crying because the mouth opens, then worsen while quiet or feeding. That pattern can suggest nasal obstruction, but it is not a home diagnostic test. Seek emergency help for breathing difficulty, blue or grey lips or tongue, pauses in breathing, collapse or difficulty waking. Do not keep feeding a baby who is struggling to breathe, and do not wait for a routine nose appointment because crying briefly seems to help. One-sided obstruction more often produces ongoing discharge or noisy breathing through the affected side. Repeated symptoms deserve assessment even if growth seems normal. Similar symptoms can have other causes, including inflammation or a nasal foreign body in an older child; the history and examination matter. Why it develops, and why parents should not blame themselves Choanal atresia develops before birth when the normal nasal airway does not form as expected. Several developmental mechanisms have been proposed. In an individual child, there is often no single identifiable explanation and no action a parent could reliably have taken to prevent it. Genetic changes and other developmental factors may contribute. The condition is reported more often in girls and is frequently unilateral, but these patterns cannot predict whether a particular baby has it. The exact mixture of bone and soft tissue is assessed in the child rather than assumed from a population percentage. Carbimazole and methimazole, medicines used for an overactive thyroid, have been associated with a small increase in certain birth differences after early-pregnancy exposure. An association does not establish the cause in one baby. Most exposed babies are healthy, and uncontrolled thyroid disease also carries risks. Do not stop or change prescribed treatment without the treating clinician. Some children need a wider developmental assessment One important association is CHARGE syndrome, which can involve the eyes, heart, nasal openings, growth, genital development and ears. The combination varies considerably. Hearing, balance, feeding and swallowing may also need attention. A child does not need every feature for a specialist to consider the diagnosis. CHARGE is often associated with a change in the CHD7 gene. Many cases result from a new genetic change rather than a condition passed down through several generations. Genetic counselling can explain the actual finding and family implications without assuming that all choanal atresia is inherited. Other craniofacial conditions, including Treacher Collins and Crouzon syndromes, may be considered when the examination suggests them. Rare reports also describe choanal atresia with craniofacial clefts classified using the Tessier system; “Tessier” is not one general syndrome. Eye coloboma or underdevelopment of genital structures may be features of an associated condition, not separate explanations to assign from a checklist. How specialists confirm the diagnosis A clinician assesses nasal airflow and may find that a small catheter cannot pass from the nose into the throat. This is a clinical examination, not something to try at home. A blocked passage has several possible explanations, so an unsuccessful catheter attempt alone does not establish every detail of the diagnosis. An ear, nose and throat specialist may use a small endoscope to inspect the nasal passages. CT imaging helps show the bony anatomy and plan treatment. MRI may be useful for selected questions about other tissues or associated abnormalities, but it is not automatically a replacement for the CT information a surgeon needs. Imaging choices should balance the clinical question, urgency and radiation or sedation considerations. Ask what each test will change in the plan. The team may also arrange hearing, heart, eye, genetic or feeding assessments according to the child’s findings rather than ordering the same set for everyone. Breathing comes first, and repair timing is individual For a newborn with unsafe breathing, the first priority is an open airway. Experienced staff may use an oral airway or place a breathing tube while arranging definitive treatment. Feeding and oxygen support are coordinated with the airway plan; surgery is undertaken when the baby is appropriately stabilised. A child with unilateral atresia who breathes and feeds comfortably may be monitored before repair at an older age. The decision takes account of symptoms, anatomy, growth and associated conditions. It should include a clear follow-up plan, not indefinite reassurance without review. Saline may help clear secretions when recommended by the team, but it does not dissolve bone or open a sealed choana. Do not insert objects, force suction deeply or use unprescribed decongestants to try to make an opening. Ask for the exact home-care method suitable for your child. What an operation aims to do Surgery creates an airway through the obstruction. A transnasal endoscopic approach works through the nose with a viewing instrument and is commonly used. In selected circumstances a different approach, including through the palate, may be considered. The choice depends on the anatomy and the specialist team’s assessment. Some children have a temporary stent placed to help keep the opening clear; others are treated without one. Stents also require care and can cause irritation or blockage. There is no single duration or removal schedule that is right for every operation. Before discharge, ask what was done, whether a stent remains, who will clean or change it and when the opening will be checked. If a tube moves or blocks, use the team’s urgent contact instructions rather than adjusting it yourself. Local surgical protocols can differ while pursuing the same goal of safe breathing and feeding. Recovery includes feeding, growth and repeat checks After repair, the team monitors airflow, oxygen levels when needed, comfort and the ability to feed. Families may receive instructions for saline, prescribed medicines or careful cleaning. Use only the quantities and techniques demonstrated for the particular operation. The new opening can narrow again as it heals. Follow-up allows the specialist to identify this early and decide whether further treatment is needed. Renewed difficulty breathing, worsening feeding or concerning colour changes should not wait until a scheduled review. Children with additional conditions may need more support and a longer recovery. Feeding therapy, hearing care and developmental follow-up address needs beyond the nose itself. Keep these appointments coordinated so that a change in feeding or weight is considered alongside the airway history. What families can expect over time Many children do well after the airway has been opened, although some need further procedures. Prognosis depends on the severity of the obstruction, associated health conditions and healing. A successful operation is an important step, but it does not remove the need to check ongoing symptoms. For a planned visit, bring notes about which side seems blocked, discharge, sleep, feeding and any previous breathing episodes. If you have reports from imaging or other specialists, ask whether the ENT team has received them. A short symptom record can be more useful than repeatedly testing airflow at home. Before leaving, make sure you know the next appointment, the signs that require urgent care and the contact for questions about a stent or cleaning. Ask for a demonstration and written instructions if anything is unclear. Families should have a workable care plan, not be expected to manage a specialised airway device by guesswork. One-sided blockage can be diagnosed later than bilateral blockage. Saline can clear secretions but cannot remove a congenital bony obstruction. Associated findings may need hearing, feeding, genetic or other specialist assessment. Do not stop thyroid medicine because of a suspected association. Follow-up checks for narrowing and feeding or growth difficulties. Is choanal atresia the same as a blocked nose from a cold? No. It is a structural blockage present from birth, although mucus can add to the symptoms. Why might breathing improve when a baby cries? Opening the mouth can temporarily allow another route for air. This pattern needs assessment and is not a reason to delay urgent help. Can it affect only one nostril? Yes. One-sided obstruction may be less obvious at birth and diagnosed later. Can saline open the blockage? No. Saline may help secretions, but it cannot remove the bone or tissue causing the structural blockage. Did a parent cause it? Usually no single cause can be identified. A medicine association does not establish the cause in an individual baby. Does every child have CHARGE syndrome? No. Some have an associated condition and others do not. A specialist assesses the child’s individual findings. Should I try passing a tube through the nose? No. Catheter assessment belongs to trained clinicians and can injure a child if attempted at home. Does every operation need a stent? No. Stent use and duration depend on the procedure, anatomy and treating team. Can the passage narrow again after surgery? Yes. Follow-up checks for recurrent narrowing and any need for further treatment. When is this an emergency? Breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour, collapse or difficulty waking needs emergency help, especially in a newborn.

title: FPIES: recognising a delayed food-allergy reaction
description: Learn the delayed and chronic patterns of FPIES, emergency signs, diagnosis, feeding choices and how tolerance is assessed.
body: A food reaction does not always happen immediately. FPIES can cause repeated vomiting hours after a feed, and sometimes ongoing feeding or growth problems. Recognising the pattern helps families obtain the right assessment and an individual plan. FPIES is a delayed food allergy affecting the gut Food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome, usually shortened to FPIES, is a food allergy that mainly affects the digestive system. It most often begins in infancy or early childhood, sometimes when formula or solid foods are introduced. It differs from the immediate allergy pattern many families recognise because the reaction is usually delayed and does not depend on the same IgE antibody mechanism. A baby can look well immediately after a feed and become unwell later. That gap makes it easy to miss the food connection or mistake the episode for reflux or a stomach infection. FPIES can be serious, so repeated vomiting with marked pallor or lethargy deserves medical assessment rather than a home test with another serving. Acute reactions often begin one to four hours after eating The characteristic acute episode is repeated, sometimes forceful vomiting that usually starts one to four hours after the trigger food. Diarrhoea may follow later. A child may become unusually quiet, pale, cold, weak or floppy, and severe fluid loss can affect blood pressure and circulation. Between separate acute episodes, a child may appear completely well. Not every episode of vomiting after food is FPIES, and not every future episode in a diagnosed child will be caused by the known trigger. Infection and other urgent problems must still be considered, particularly when there has been no plausible exposure. The important pattern is the combination of timing, symptoms and what was eaten. Do not wait for diarrhoea, a rash or a temperature change before seeking help if your child is deteriorating. Chronic exposure can affect weight gain and feeding Chronic FPIES is less common and can occur when an infant regularly receives a trigger, often cow’s-milk or soy protein. Ongoing vomiting or diarrhoea can interfere with intake, hydration and nutrient absorption. Weight may rise slowly, flatten or fall, and the baby may seem persistently unwell rather than having clearly separated attacks. Clinicians may describe poor weight gain as faltering growth or, in some settings, failure to thrive. They review weight, length and sometimes head circumference over time. A single small measurement does not establish FPIES; the overall growth pattern, feeding history and other findings matter. Difficulty rolling, sitting, standing, walking, interacting or learning deserves its own developmental assessment if it is present. FPIES does not automatically cause delay in all these areas. Nutrition and feeding support can help protect development while the cause of poor growth is investigated. Triggers extend beyond milk and soy Cow’s milk and soy are recognised triggers, but grains such as rice, oats and barley can also cause FPIES. Other reported foods include fish, chicken, turkey, squash, green beans and peas. Egg and various other foods can be triggers too, and the most frequent foods differ between regions and age groups. Most affected children react to a limited number of foods, often one, although some react to several. This does not mean a child with one trigger must avoid every food on a published list. A list describes what has happened in other people; it does not identify your child’s allergies. The reaction usually follows the child eating the food directly. FPIES through breast milk is unusual, and exclusive breastfeeding does not follow a predictable timetable for symptom onset. In adults, FPIES is less common and seafood is a recognised trigger; this article’s feeding advice is intended mainly for families with young children. Family allergy history helps the discussion but cannot diagnose FPIES Tell the clinician about eczema, asthma, hay fever and other food allergies in your child or close relatives. These conditions may coexist with FPIES, but family history is neither required nor sufficient for the diagnosis. Reported proportions vary between studies and referral populations. Children of any sex can have FPIES. It is not appropriate to assume girls are at greater risk from a single general statement; published series do not show one consistent female predominance. The actual reaction history is more useful than a demographic label. FPIES is uncommon and may be under-recognised. Estimates of how often it occurs differ with geography and how cases are identified. Greater awareness can increase recorded diagnoses, so a rising case count by itself does not show how much the underlying condition has increased. Immediate allergy and FPIES can exist together Typical FPIES does not cause the hives, lip swelling or wheezing associated with many immediate food allergies. Its gut symptoms can nevertheless lead to severe dehydration or shock. Calling it a gut allergy should not imply that the whole child’s circulation cannot be affected. Some children also have an IgE-mediated allergy, including occasionally to a food that has caused FPIES. Hives, swelling, breathing difficulty or rapid collapse after food should be treated according to the child’s anaphylaxis plan and emergency advice. Do not dismiss these signs because an earlier diagnosis was FPIES. Adrenaline, also called epinephrine, is not the usual treatment for an isolated FPIES reaction. It remains essential when indicated for anaphylaxis. Families with both conditions need clear instructions about which plan to follow; antihistamines should not be relied on to treat shock. Seek emergency help for a severe reaction Call emergency services for vomiting that will not stop, a very sleepy or poorly responsive child, floppiness, fainting, or pale, blue or grey skin. Signs of dehydration, such as markedly reduced urine, dry mouth or absent tears, also require prompt help. A young child can become unwell quickly. Follow the written FPIES plan if one has already been provided, including any prescribed medicine. Do not force drinks or oral medicine into a child who is drowsy or unable to swallow safely. Tell the emergency team what was eaten and when, and bring the plan if possible. If your child has previously had a severe FPIES reaction and eats the known trigger again, follow the plan’s immediate medical-contact instructions rather than assuming it is safe to wait for symptoms. The plan should address this situation before an accidental exposure occurs. Diagnosis relies on the history, not a routine allergy panel Record the food, approximate amount, time eaten, time symptoms began, number of vomiting episodes and what treatment was needed. Include formula changes, new solids, previous similar reactions, growth concerns and foods eaten without difficulty. Photographs of labels or a simple diary can make the consultation more specific. Routine skin-prick or food-specific IgE tests can be negative in FPIES. A normal result therefore does not rule it out. Blood tests during a severe episode can help assess illness and hydration, but there is no single blood result that confirms the diagnosis. The clinician also considers infection, reflux and other digestive or metabolic problems. Improvement after removing a suspected food supports the assessment but does not prove FPIES on its own. An oral food challenge may be used when the history is unclear or later to assess tolerance; it requires an appropriate medical setting and observation. Treatment during a reaction supports hydration and recovery Treatment depends on how unwell the child is. A mild reaction may be managed according to an individual plan, while repeated vomiting or poor circulation can require intravenous fluids and observation in hospital. The immediate aim is to restore hydration and stability. Clinicians may use ondansetron to reduce vomiting when appropriate for the child’s age and circumstances. Corticosteroids are sometimes considered in severe reactions, but evidence proving their benefit in FPIES is limited. A steroid injection should not be presented as the main established treatment or a substitute for fluid resuscitation. Ask the team to explain what happened, which symptoms should trigger another emergency call and whether a take-home medicine is appropriate. Any prescription needs child-specific instructions rather than a dose copied from a general article. Avoid confirmed triggers while keeping the diet as broad as possible Long-term management usually centres on avoiding the identified trigger and supporting nutrition. Removing the cause often resolves ongoing symptoms, but growth and feeding may need follow-up. Do not remove multiple tolerated foods because they appear on an FPIES trigger list. A paediatric allergy dietitian can help replace nutrients, plan new foods and address fear of eating. Feeding therapy may help if repeated illness has made meals distressing or limited accepted textures. Tell childcare and other caregivers exactly which foods are avoided and what to do after a reaction. Keep an up-to-date list of tolerated foods as well as triggers. This makes shopping and meal planning less restrictive and gives the specialist useful information when deciding what to introduce next. Breastfeeding and formula changes need individual advice Breastfeeding can usually continue. If the baby is thriving and symptom-free while breastfed, routine exclusion of the trigger from the breastfeeding parent’s diet is generally unnecessary. Do not stop breastfeeding simply because the baby reacted to a solid food or formula. If symptoms occur during exclusive breastfeeding, seek specialist assessment rather than assuming breast milk itself is unsafe. An advised maternal elimination may occasionally be considered with nutritional support. If feeds must temporarily change, lactation support and expressing milk can help protect supply while the plan is reviewed. When formula is needed, the clinician may recommend an extensively hydrolysed formula or, in some circumstances, an amino-acid formula. A generic hypoallergenic label is not enough to select a product. Soy is not automatically a safe replacement for cow’s milk, and ordinary plant drinks are not a substitute for infant formula. Many children develop tolerance, but reintroduction is planned Many children outgrow FPIES in early childhood, often around the preschool years. The timing varies with the food and the child: some develop tolerance earlier, others remain affected into later childhood or beyond. A third or fourth birthday is not a reliable test that the allergy has ended. The allergy team decides when and where to try the trigger again, often using a supervised oral food challenge with treatment available. Do not give a small amount at home merely to see whether the child has outgrown it. Delayed symptoms mean a brief symptom-free interval does not establish tolerance. With an appropriate diet, growth monitoring and an emergency plan, children can continue learning and enjoying food while the condition is managed. Ask for follow-up dates and practical instructions so avoiding a trigger does not become an indefinite restriction without reassessment. The usual acute delay is one to four hours after food. Chronic exposure can affect feeding and growth. Normal IgE testing does not exclude FPIES. Breastfeeding and tolerated foods usually continue with individual guidance. Tolerance must be assessed rather than assumed from age. Can a food reaction begin hours after my child eats? Yes. Acute FPIES commonly causes repeated vomiting one to four hours after the trigger, sometimes followed by diarrhoea. Timing helps the assessment, but an unwell child still needs evaluation for other causes. Does every child with FPIES have poor growth? No. Children with separate acute reactions may grow normally between episodes. Ongoing trigger exposure or restricted intake can affect growth, so feeding and measurements should be reviewed when concerns arise. Can normal allergy tests rule out FPIES? No. Routine skin-prick and specific-IgE tests do not reliably diagnose this delayed allergy. The clinician uses the history and, when appropriate, a medically supervised food challenge. Which symptoms mean I should call emergency services? Persistent vomiting, floppiness, fainting, poor responsiveness, pale/blue/grey skin or dehydration need urgent help. Follow the child’s written plan and do not wait for a rash. Should I use adrenaline for an FPIES reaction? It is not routine treatment for isolated FPIES. However, if the child has signs of anaphylaxis, use prescribed adrenaline and the anaphylaxis emergency plan. Some children have both types of allergy. Are steroid injections a proven cure? No. Steroids may be considered by clinicians in severe reactions, but their effectiveness in FPIES is not established. They do not replace urgent hydration and circulation support. Do I need to stop breastfeeding? Usually not. If the baby is well while breastfed, routine maternal trigger-food exclusion is generally unnecessary. Symptoms during exclusive breastfeeding need specialist assessment and an individual feeding plan. Should I avoid every food that can trigger FPIES? No. Avoiding tolerated foods unnecessarily can restrict nutrition and feeding development. Work with the allergy team and dietitian to identify actual triggers and plan new foods. Will FPIES definitely be gone by age three? No. Many children improve in early childhood, but timing varies and some remain affected much longer. Age alone does not show that a trigger is now safe. Can I retry the trigger at home in a tiny amount? Do not do this without a specific specialist plan. Reintroduction often requires a supervised challenge, because reactions may be delayed and can need medical treatment.

title: Sore, cracked or crusted nipples: finding the cause
description: Nipple damage may come from feeding, pumping, friction or a skin condition. Early help can reduce pain and identify changes that need examination.
body: A nipple can become sore, cracked or crusted for several reasons. Breastfeeding difficulties are one possibility, but clothing friction, eczema and other skin problems can also damage the area. Persistent pain or bleeding deserves attention rather than being treated as something the skin simply needs to get used to. A scab describes healing, not the original problem A crust may form over a small area of damaged skin, but its presence does not explain why the damage happened. Notice whether the problem began after a feed, pumping session, new skin product, exercise or an injury. Repeated reopening suggests the cause is still present. Avoid picking or scrubbing the area. Hormonal tenderness can occur around a period, but visible cracking, bleeding or an ongoing rash should not automatically be attributed to hormones. When skin breaks, platelets and clotting proteins such as fibrin help seal the injury. Dried blood or fluid can form a crust while tissue repairs underneath. A crust is not proof that infection is absent, and repeated damage can keep reopening it. Get feeding support early If nipples hurt during every feed, look pinched or flattened afterwards, or start to crack or bleed, ask a midwife, lactation professional or other trained breastfeeding supporter to watch a complete feed. Positioning and attachment can make a substantial difference. An assessment can also consider milk transfer and whether the baby needs evaluation for an oral or feeding difficulty. You do not need to wait until damage becomes severe. If direct feeding is too painful, ask for a temporary plan that keeps the baby fed and maintains milk supply, such as comfortable hand expression or carefully adjusted pumping. Simply cutting feeds short without a plan can reduce milk removal. Tongue-tie is one possible contributor, but nipple pain alone does not establish that diagnosis or mean a procedure is needed. Pumping should not injure the nipple Check that the pump’s breast shield fits comfortably and that suction is not causing pinching, rubbing or pulling pain. More suction is not automatically more effective. Stop a painful session and seek advice about fit and settings rather than pushing through bleeding or visible injury. Follow the manufacturer’s cleaning and use instructions. When pumping is part of a feeding plan, a clinician or lactation professional can help adjust the approach while protecting supply and giving damaged skin a chance to recover. Friction and skin irritation need different solutions Repeated rubbing from a shirt or poorly fitting sports bra can make nipples sore during running or other activity. Reduce friction with comfortable clothing and suitable protection, and let damaged skin recover. A bland barrier can help with chafing, but a product intended for sports use is not automatically suitable for a nipple that a baby will put in their mouth. Itching, scaling, weeping or recurring patches may be eczema or contact dermatitis. Triggers can include fragrance, soap, detergent, adhesives and ingredients in creams. Even products marketed as natural or soothing can cause allergy. Avoid a suspected irritant and ask a clinician about a simple skin-care plan. Eczema can recur; changing detergent does not guarantee a permanent cure. Use medicines with clear instructions A clinician may recommend a topical steroid for eczema or treatment for a confirmed infection. Do not repeatedly try antifungal, antibiotic and steroid creams without knowing what is being treated. The location, diagnosis and whether you are breastfeeding affect the choice. For a prescribed steroid on the nipple or areola, NHS medicines guidance recommends applying after feeding and removing it with warm water before the next feed. Ask which preparation, strength and duration are right for you and avoid the baby’s direct contact with treated skin. Seek individual advice for a premature or unwell baby. Know which changes need medical review Seek prompt advice for a hot, swollen, increasingly painful breast, spreading redness, pus, fever or flu-like illness. These can indicate inflammation or infection and may need treatment. Severe illness, fainting, confusion or breathing difficulty needs emergency care. Arrange a medical appointment for a persistent one-sided nipple rash or crust, spontaneous bloody discharge, a new nipple inversion or a breast lump. Most nipple irritation is not cancer, but rare Paget disease of the breast can resemble eczema. It cannot be excluded just by looking at a photograph or trying a cream; examination and sometimes a skin biopsy are needed. Injury and sunburn can also affect nipple skin. Protect the area from further rubbing and sun exposure, and seek care for substantial blistering, worsening pain or a wound that is not healing. Direct friction or injury during sexual activity can also be a trigger. Sun exposure and tanning beds can burn this delicate skin; avoid further exposure and get advice for substantial blistering. Cracking and bleeding are reasons to seek help, not to toughen the nipples. During breastfeeding, an observed feed can identify attachment problems early. Pumping, friction and eczema require attention to their specific causes. Persistent one-sided nipple changes or a new lump need examination. Is painful breastfeeding something I must get used to? No. Some early sensitivity is common, but pain at every feed or damaged skin warrants practical assessment and support. Can nipple eczema be treated while breastfeeding? Often yes. A clinician can choose an appropriate preparation and explain how to use and remove it around feeds. Does a crust on one nipple mean cancer? Usually there are other explanations, but a persistent one-sided change needs medical review. Paget disease can resemble eczema, so do not keep treating an unexplained rash indefinitely.

title: Bumps on the nipple or areola: what they might be
description: Normal glands, irritated skin, milk blebs and infections can look different but overlap. Learn what to leave alone and when to get a lump checked.
body: Small bumps around a nipple are often part of normal anatomy. A new painful spot, a persistent skin change or a lump beneath the skin needs a different response. The location, duration and accompanying symptoms matter more than whether the bump looks like a pimple. Normal glands can look like little pimples The areola is the darker area of skin around the nipple. It contains Montgomery glands, which produce a protective oily secretion. Their visible openings can form small, painless bumps. The number and size vary, and they may become more noticeable in pregnancy or while breastfeeding. These glands are present in people who are not pregnant too, so seeing them is not a reliable pregnancy test. Normal, unchanged bumps do not need squeezing, removal or acne treatment. A gland that becomes blocked may turn swollen or tender; have persistent inflammation assessed rather than trying to pop it. A spot on surrounding skin has several possible causes Hair follicles around the areola can become irritated or inflamed. Friction, sweat, shaving or a skin product may contribute. A small superficial spot is different from a deeper breast lump, but this distinction is not always clear without examination. Itchy, red or flaky skin can also reflect eczema or contact dermatitis. Irritation from a detergent, fragrance, adhesive or nipple cream can resemble infection. Itch alone does not diagnose thrush, and a white bump alone does not establish acne. If symptoms persist, a clinician can decide whether skin treatment, a swab or another test is useful. Hormonal changes around periods can coincide with acne, and prolonged contact with a sweaty sports bra can add friction. That history may help, but a spot on the nipple should not automatically be treated as ordinary acne. During breastfeeding, a white spot may be a milk bleb A small white or yellowish spot on the nipple can be a bleb associated with inflammation at a milk-duct opening. It can be quite painful even when tiny. It is not something to pierce with a needle or scrape open: that can damage tissue and worsen inflammation. Ask a breastfeeding professional or clinician to assess pain, feeding attachment and any breast swelling. Treatment is directed at the cause and may include a prescribed topical medicine. Do not assume that every spot needs an antibiotic or antifungal. A painful swelling may be an abscess An abscess is a collection of pus. It may cause a tender lump, warmth, skin redness, fever or feeling unwell; redness can be less obvious on darker skin. Abscesses can occur during breastfeeding or at other times. A suspected abscess needs prompt clinical assessment. Ultrasound can help identify a collection. Treatment commonly involves drainage with a needle or a small incision, sometimes with antibiotics. Do not try to drain it yourself. If treatment is not helping, or the same problem returns, follow-up is important to reassess the cause. An abscess outside breastfeeding does not automatically mean cancer. A recurrent collection may need a breast specialist to consider whether an affected duct or another underlying problem requires a procedure. Surgery is an individual decision after reassessment. Care for the skin without over-treating it Use gentle cleansing, change out of damp exercise clothing and choose a comfortable bra or shirt that does not rub. Avoid harsh scrubs, repeated disinfecting, squeezing and products that cause stinging or a rash. A normal gland is not a sign of poor hygiene. During breastfeeding, continue responsive feeding when comfortable and seek help if pain interferes. Do not add pumping sessions to try to completely empty the breasts or vigorously massage a lump. Extra milk removal can stimulate oversupply and worsen inflammation. If feeding is too painful or treatment changes how you can feed, arrange an individual expression and feeding plan. If a clinician diagnoses a fungal infection, ask whether the baby also needs assessment or treatment and how to use any cream around feeds. Nipple and deep breast pain have other causes, so repeated treatment for presumed thrush without reassessment can delay useful care. Have persistent or unusual changes examined Arrange assessment for a new breast lump, a bump that enlarges or does not settle, spontaneous bloody discharge, a newly inverted nipple, skin dimpling or a persistent one-sided nipple rash or crust. These signs have several possible explanations, and cancer is uncommon, but they should not be diagnosed from an online picture. Paget disease is a rare breast cancer that can resemble eczema on the nipple. Examination, imaging or biopsy may be needed depending on the findings. The same principle applies to men and anyone with breast tissue: being less likely to develop breast cancer is not a reason to ignore a new lump. Get urgent help for a hot painful breast with a swelling, spreading inflammation, fever or feeling unwell. Rapid deterioration, confusion or fainting requires emergency care. If cancer is diagnosed, treatment is based on its type and extent and may involve breast-conserving surgery or mastectomy, radiotherapy and medicines such as chemotherapy. Those treatments are not prescribed simply because a nipple bump is present. Painless Montgomery-gland bumps are usually normal and need no treatment. Do not squeeze a spot, open a milk bleb or drain a suspected abscess yourself. A painful breast swelling needs assessment, including outside breastfeeding. Persistent nipple changes or a new breast lump should be examined. Should I use an acne cream on a white nipple spot? Not without knowing what it is. A normal gland, milk bleb or dermatitis needs different care, and products applied where a baby feeds need additional consideration. Does an abscess mean breast cancer? No. An abscess is an infection-related collection of pus. A persistent or recurrent problem still needs follow-up so other causes are not missed. Will pumping more prevent nipple bumps and mastitis? No. Pumping beyond the baby’s needs to empty the breasts can increase milk production and inflammation. Get help with a feeding plan suited to your situation.

title: Tingling or burning breasts during feeding: what to notice
description: Understand let-down, latch pain, inflammation, vasospasm and other breast changes, with practical comfort measures and signs that need assessment.
body: Some breast tingling is brief and harmless, but ongoing burning or sharp pain deserves an explanation. The timing, skin changes and feeding pattern help separate a normal milk let-down from problems that need treatment. Notice when the sensation happens A brief prickling sensation as milk starts to flow is different from burning that continues between feeds or wakes you at night. Note whether it is in the nipple, deeper in the breast or on the chest wall, and whether one or both sides are affected. A short symptom record can make the appointment more useful. Look for a relationship to latching, pumping, cold air, a new skin product, your menstrual cycle or a recent operation. Also notice fever, a lump, nipple damage, discharge or a change in skin colour or breast shape. The words “tingling” and “burning” describe a sensation; they do not identify its cause. Pain that makes feeding difficult deserves help even without an obvious lump or rash. Ask a midwife, lactation professional or clinician to watch a feed and, if you express milk, check the pump fit and settings. You do not have to keep feeding through severe pain to demonstrate commitment. Hormonal changes and the milk let-down reflex Breast tissue responds to hormonal changes before a period, during pregnancy and around menopause. In early pregnancy, changes in breast tissue and blood flow can produce fullness, warmth, tenderness or tingling, sometimes before a missed period. These sensations overlap with premenstrual symptoms and cannot confirm pregnancy; use a pregnancy test at the appropriate time. During breastfeeding, oxytocin helps move milk toward the nipple. This milk-ejection response, often called let-down, may feel like a brief tightening or pins and needles as a feed begins. Some people notice it in both breasts, and others do not feel it at all. Neither pattern by itself measures supply. Mild, short-lived let-down sensations may need no treatment. Persistent sharp pain, cracked nipples, repeated burning or feeding distress should not automatically be attributed to hormones. A comfortable latch and effective milk transfer matter more than whether a particular sensation is present. Attachment, fullness and mastitis A shallow latch or poorly fitting pump can compress or injure the nipple. An overfull breast may feel tight and make attachment harder. Skilled observation can distinguish these mechanical problems from inflammation or a skin condition and help you find a more comfortable feeding position. Mastitis means breast inflammation; some cases progress to bacterial infection. It is not restricted to six to eight weeks after birth and is not always caused by bacteria entering a cracked nipple. A hot, tender or swollen area, sometimes with redness, fever, chills or marked fatigue, needs attention. Redness may be less obvious on darker skin. Continue feeding according to your baby’s needs if you can. Avoid forceful massage and extra pumping to “empty” the breast. A cool compress and suitable pain relief may help. Seek care sooner if worsening or very unwell, and if mild symptoms have not improved after 12–24 hours. An abscess or persistent lump needs assessment; antibiotics are used when indicated. Burning does not automatically mean thrush Candida can cause a superficial nipple or skin infection, and antibiotics can increase susceptibility to some yeast infections. Sore, shiny or flaky nipples and a baby with possible oral thrush are reasons for an examination, not proof that yeast is responsible for every painful feed. Dermatitis, latch injury and vasospasm can look or feel similar. The explanation that Candida routinely travels deep into milk ducts and causes stabbing breast pain is disputed: the Academy of Breastfeeding Medicine’s mastitis protocol does not support “Candida mastitis” as an established diagnosis. Do not repeatedly self-treat with antifungals without reassessing persistent pain. If a clinician diagnoses an infection, ask whether the baby also needs assessment and how any prescribed cream should be used around feeds. A painful breast lump should not simply be labelled thrush; it may need a different investigation. Cold-triggered pain and nipple vasospasm Small blood vessels can narrow temporarily, reducing blood flow to the nipple. Vasospasm may cause a white nipple followed by blue, purple or red colour changes, with burning or throbbing during or after a feed. Cold air and nipple compression can be triggers. Raynaud’s phenomenon can affect the nipples as well as fingers and toes. It sometimes accompanies another condition, including an autoimmune disorder, but it is not always an autoimmune disease. Mention other circulation symptoms, medicines and any history of Raynaud’s during an assessment. Keep the nipple comfortably warm after feeds and address any latch or pump pressure. Avoid direct high heat that could burn the skin. Persistent or severe symptoms need a clinician’s review; they may consider treatment after checking other causes. Warmth for vasospasm differs from using a cool compress on an inflamed, swollen breast. Skin irritation and shingles Soaps, fragranced creams, detergents and breast pads can irritate skin or trigger contact allergy. Dermatitis can produce itching, roughness, redness, swelling or burning. Consider what changed before the symptoms began, and pause a suspected nonessential product while seeking advice. Check the suitability of nipple treatments because your baby’s mouth may contact them. Shingles is reactivation of the virus that causes chickenpox. A painful or tingling patch may be followed by grouped blisters, often on one side of the body; fever or feeling unwell can accompany it. A blistering breast rash is not enough to diagnose shingles yourself, but it warrants prompt medical assessment. If shingles lesions are on or near the areola where the baby’s mouth could touch them, CDC advises against feeding from that breast until safe to resume. Express and discard milk from that side as advised, continue on the unaffected side if suitable, and cover other lesions. Contact the baby’s clinician if the baby touches a lesion. The concern is contact with blister fluid, not transmission through breast milk. After breast surgery or with an implant Surgery can alter or injure nerves, leaving numbness, itching, burning or shooting sensations in the breast or chest wall. After mastectomy or lumpectomy, persistent nerve pain can also extend toward the armpit or arm. Tell the surgical team if pain persists, changes or interferes with sleep and movement; it should not be dismissed as something you must simply endure. A silicone implant rupture can sometimes cause tingling, tenderness, numbness, hard areas or changes in breast size and shape. However, many ruptures have no symptoms. Tingling cannot confirm a rupture, and an unchanged appearance cannot rule one out. If you have implants, report a new lump, swelling, asymmetry or altered sensation and follow the recommended implant follow-up plan. A clinician may arrange imaging or refer you to the surgeon. These problems require their own assessment rather than being assumed to be ordinary lactation discomfort. Chest-wall pain, medicines and cycle patterns Pain felt beneath a breast may come from the chest wall. Costochondritis is inflammation around the joints where ribs meet the breastbone. It can cause sharp pain that worsens with movement, coughing, deep breaths or pressure. Muscle strain and shoulder or back problems can also be felt near the breast. Do not use these descriptions to rule out an urgent cause of new chest pain. Cyclical breast pain usually builds before a period, often affects both breasts and feels heavy or aching, then settles as the period ends. Noncyclical pain has no consistent menstrual pattern and may be more localized. Pregnancy, breastfeeding and menopause can change the pattern; there is no promise that starting milk flow will relieve every type of pain. Hormonal contraception, menopausal hormone therapy and some psychiatric medicines can contribute to breast symptoms. Bring a complete medicine list, including the start dates of new products. Do not abruptly stop a prescribed medicine. A symptom diary can help a clinician decide whether the timing suggests a medicine effect or another cause. When breast changes need a closer look Breast pain alone is unlikely to indicate cancer. Even so, a new lump, persistent one-sided change, skin dimpling, a newly inverted nipple, altered breast shape or unexpected nipple discharge should be checked. Bloody discharge or a persistent nipple rash deserves prompt assessment, including during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Paget disease is a rare breast cancer involving the nipple and usually the areola. It can resemble eczema, causing itching, tingling, flaking, crusting or thickened skin, sometimes with flattening of the nipple or yellowish or bloody discharge. Repeatedly applying cream to a persistent unilateral nipple change can delay diagnosis. Most people with these symptoms will have another explanation, but an examination is needed to find it. Depending on the findings, imaging or a skin biopsy may be recommended. Being young or breastfeeding does not make a persistent breast change something to ignore. Choose comfort measures that fit the cause A supportive, well-fitting bra and gentle handling may reduce discomfort. For inflammation or swelling, try a cool compress with a layer protecting the skin. Brief comfortable warmth may help milk flow or cold-related vasospasm, but prolonged heat can worsen inflammation. Avoid deep kneading, squeezing a lump or increasing pump suction through pain. Paracetamol or ibuprofen may be suitable during breastfeeding, but check your own medical conditions, other medicines and pregnancy status with a pharmacist or clinician. Do not put a pain-relief gel or unprescribed cream on an area the baby will lick. A feeding assessment remains important even if painkillers help. Claims for reducing salt or caffeine are not a reliable treatment for everyone. Evidence for vitamin E and evening primrose oil is limited, and supplements may have interactions. Do not let a dietary experiment or supplement replace assessment of persistent pain or an abnormal breast finding. Make a clear plan for follow-up Seek urgent care for breast pain with significant fever, a rapidly spreading hot or swollen area, or feeling markedly unwell. Arrange a prompt examination for a new persistent lump, dimpling, unexplained discharge, nipple inversion or a continuing nipple rash. Tell the service that you are breastfeeding so feeding support can be included. Call emergency services for severe or persistent chest pressure, trouble breathing, fainting, or pain spreading to the arm or jaw. Those symptoms should not be assumed to come from the breast, a milk duct or costochondritis. For symptoms without urgent signs, record the timing and arrange a feeding and medical review if they persist or interfere with feeding. Ask what improvement to expect, when to return if it does not happen, and whether your baby’s milk intake or weight needs checking. Relief should come from addressing the cause, not enduring progressively worse pain. Brief let-down tingling can be normal; persistent pain is a reason for support. Burning alone cannot diagnose thrush, vasospasm or mastitis. Match comfort measures to the cause and avoid forceful massage. Breastfeeding does not remove the need to investigate a new breast change. Is tingling a sign that milk is flowing? It can accompany let-down, but some people do not feel let-down at all. A baby’s swallowing, milk transfer and growth are more useful than the sensation alone. Does breast tingling confirm pregnancy? No. Early pregnancy can cause tenderness or tingling, but premenstrual changes and other causes overlap. Use a pregnancy test when appropriate. Is mastitis always an infection? No. Mastitis can be inflammation without bacterial infection. Assessment and response to initial care help determine whether antibiotics or another treatment are needed. Does burning pain mean I have thrush? No. Latch injury, dermatitis and vasospasm can cause similar pain. A clinician should assess the nipple and consider other causes before repeated antifungal treatment. Why does my nipple turn white after feeding? Compression or vasospasm may temporarily reduce blood flow. Note colour changes, cold triggers and pain, and ask for a latch assessment and clinical advice if it persists. Should I use heat or a cold compress? A cool compress can help inflammation and swelling. Gentle warmth may help vasospasm or milk flow. Avoid prolonged heat, skin burns and forceful massage. Can I breastfeed if I have shingles? It depends on the location of lesions and your health. Do not feed from a breast where lesions could touch the baby’s mouth; seek advice on expressing, discarding milk from that side and resuming safely. Could tingling mean an implant has ruptured?
