Note whether the child is awake and upset, calmly settling or apparently asleep. Behaviour that causes injury or major sleep disruption may be considered a sleep-related movement disorder and needs assessment rather than reassurance alone. Check that the cot or bed is assembled correctly and that nearby hard furniture cannot be struck. Do not add cot bumpers, loose padding, pillows or restraints to an infant sleep space. Maintain an age-appropriate safe sleep arrangement. Ask for advice if there is snoring, unusual breathing, possible seizures or repeated injury; these features may need a different investigation. When to arrange a developmental or medical review Contact your child’s clinician if the behaviour is frequent, increasing, causing bruises or cuts, interfering with family life, or not improving with a calm and consistent approach. You do not have to wait until other symptoms appear. Also mention delayed speech, difficulty hearing, changes in play or interaction, unusual sensory responses or any loss of previously acquired skills. A review may include an examination for pain or illness and questions about development, sleep and communication. Depending on the findings, the clinician may recommend hearing assessment, speech and language support, occupational therapy, developmental assessment or another service. A short record of triggers and responses helps; a video may be useful only if it can be taken without delaying protection or care. Does this mean autism? Head-banging by itself does not diagnose autism, and it does not rule autism out either. Autism assessment considers a broader developmental pattern, including social communication, interaction, repetitive behaviours and sensory differences. Some autistic children head-bang and many do not; some non-autistic children do it too. If you have concerns about communication, response to their name, shared play or other development, discuss them without waiting for a fixed number of signs. Hearing differences and other conditions can also affect these behaviours. Support can address the child’s immediate needs while an assessment is underway, without treating the behaviour as proof of a diagnosis. Know when a head injury needs urgent help After an impact, seek urgent medical advice for vomiting, increasing pain, a concerning wound or a child whose behaviour seems different. Call emergency services for loss of consciousness with failure to wake, a seizure, difficulty staying awake, new weakness or problems with balance, or other signs of a serious injury. The fact that a child caused the impact themselves does not make it harmless. If a clinician advises home observation after a minor injury, follow that plan and know which changes require another call. Separately, ask for support if the repeated behaviour leaves you frightened or exhausted. A trusted caregiver can help you take a break while the child remains supervised. You do not have to manage persistent self-injury alone. Consider pain and unmet needs as well as frustration or sensory experiences. Offer calm protection and connection without rewarding or punishing the hitting. Teach words, gestures and safe actions outside the most upset moment. Ask for help when behaviour persists, causes injury or raises developmental concerns. Is head-banging always a sign of a developmental condition? No. It occurs in children with different developmental profiles. Assessment considers the wider pattern, and the behaviour alone cannot diagnose or exclude autism. Should I ignore it if my child wants attention? Do not ignore injury or distress. Keep your response calm and brief, protect your child and give positive attention when they communicate safely. Should I hold my toddler tightly to stop it? A welcomed comforting hug is different from restraint. Do not pin the child down or use a prolonged squeezing hold. Repeated dangerous episodes need an individualized safety plan. Could an earache or teething be the cause? Pain may contribute, but head-hitting cannot diagnose the source of pain. Seek assessment if your child seems ill, has fever, is eating or drinking less, or has a marked change in behaviour. What can I teach instead of hitting? Choose a simple word, gesture or picture for help or break, and practise a safe action such as squeezing a soft toy or pressing hands together while calm. Match it to your child’s abilities. Does naming feelings mean giving in? No. You can acknowledge disappointment and offer comfort while keeping an appropriate limit. Discuss alternatives once the child has settled. Can I pad the cot to prevent injuries? Do not add cot bumpers, pillows, loose padding or restraints to an infant sleep space. Check the furniture and seek advice about a safe environment if impacts continue. Do I need to wait for other autism signs before calling? No. Persistent head-banging, injury, communication concerns or your own worry are enough to ask for a review. Other signs can help guide assessment but are not a prerequisite for support. What should I note for the clinician? Record when it happens, what came before, the surface involved, whether the child seemed awake or asleep, any injury, and what helped. Include pain, hearing, sleep or developmental concerns. When is a head impact an emergency? Get emergency help for a child who does not wake after losing consciousness, has a seizure, cannot stay awake or develops new weakness or balance problems. Seek urgent advice for vomiting or other concerning changes after an impact.

title: Why your child’s teeth may look yellow
description: Understand normal tooth colour, staining, injury and enamel changes, with safe daily care and a guide to treatments a paediatric dentist may consider.
body: New adult teeth can look noticeably yellow beside remaining baby teeth without being unhealthy. Other colour changes can reflect plaque, a medicine, an injury or a developmental problem. Identifying the cause comes before deciding whether any cosmetic treatment is useful. Adult teeth can look yellower than baby teeth A healthy smile does not have to be bright white. Permanent teeth commonly look more yellow than primary teeth because their structure and the underlying dentin differ. Dentin is the naturally yellowish tissue beneath the translucent outer enamel. Its appearance through the enamel contributes to the colour you see; yellow does not automatically mean a tooth is dirty. The contrast is especially obvious when new adult teeth sit beside whiter baby teeth. Once the remaining baby teeth have been replaced, the difference may be less noticeable. That normal pattern is different from a new patch, a rough area or a single tooth becoming darker. A dental examination can establish which situation applies before anyone tries to whiten the teeth. Notice when and where the colour changed Think about whether the colour was present when the tooth appeared, developed gradually or followed a fall. Look for a change affecting one tooth compared with a similar shade across several teeth. Pain, sensitivity, bleeding gums, a visible hole or a recent medicine change are useful details for the dental team. Photographs taken at different times may help explain the pattern. Do not diagnose a cavity or a dead nerve from colour alone. A smooth yellow tooth, a chalky white patch and a dark mark can have quite different explanations. Scraping at a spot or brushing it harder can injure the surface without identifying the cause. Arrange an assessment for a persistent or new change, even if your child is not complaining of pain. Plaque, food and drinks can leave surface changes When brushing misses areas, plaque can accumulate and change how teeth look. Food and drink pigments may also leave external stains. These sit on the surface rather than changing the whole tooth from within. Improving everyday cleaning or having professional stain removal may help, depending on what is actually present. Decay is another possible cause of a visible change, including white, brown or dark areas. It is not simply a stain to polish away at home. If there is a damaged surface or cavity, the dentist will discuss care for the decay itself. A whitening product cannot repair a hole, and a temporary change in appearance should not delay treatment. A tooth can darken after an injury A knock to the mouth may damage the blood supply or soft tissue inside a tooth. Internal bleeding or later changes in the pulp can alter the colour, sometimes to grey, brown or a darker shade. The change may appear after the initial soreness has settled. Tell the dentist about an earlier fall even if it no longer seems connected. Discolouration does not by itself establish that the nerve has died or that the tooth must be removed. The dentist considers symptoms, the type of tooth, the injury and examination findings, with imaging when appropriate. A tooth that was injured may need follow-up rather than a one-time colour assessment. New swelling, a gum lump or worsening pain should prompt earlier advice. Thin or differently formed enamel can reveal more colour Inherited conditions can affect how enamel develops. If the outer layer is thin or does not form normally, the underlying colour may show more clearly, and the surface may be more vulnerable to damage. Not every yellow tooth has a genetic condition; the pattern across teeth and other examination findings help the dentist distinguish normal variation from a developmental problem. Some colour differences begin inside the tooth while it is forming. They cannot be brushed away, however carefully a child cleans. Treatment may focus first on protecting weak areas and reducing sensitivity or decay risk. A cosmetic change, if needed, comes after the cause and condition of the tooth are understood. Fluorosis reflects exposure while teeth are developing Swallowing too much fluoride over time while enamel is forming can cause dental fluorosis. Mild cases often appear as pale flecks or lines; more pronounced changes can include staining and surface differences. These develop before teeth erupt. Ordinary yellowing in an older child is not evidence that fluoride toothpaste has suddenly created new fluorosis in fully formed enamel. The aim is appropriate fluoride exposure, not avoiding a useful decay-prevention treatment. Ask about the child’s drinking water, supplements and toothpaste amount if there is concern. Do not add fluoride supplements without professional advice, and supervise young children so they do not eat toothpaste. A dentist can distinguish fluorosis from other white or brown enamel changes. Medicines and early illness can have different effects Liquid iron can leave dark external marks on teeth. Needed iron treatment should not be stopped just to avoid staining. Tell the prescriber and dentist what preparation your child uses so they can suggest suitable administration and cleaning advice. A surface iron stain is different from a medicine changing the developing tooth internally. Certain older tetracycline antibiotics can stain teeth when exposure occurs during development, including particular pregnancy or early-childhood exposures. This is not a reason to refuse every related antibiotic. CDC evidence supports short courses of doxycycline for rickettsial infections in children of all ages without the historical tooth-staining concern. Delaying needed treatment for those infections can be dangerous. Some early illnesses can also affect developing teeth. For example, marked bilirubin elevation can sometimes produce unusual yellow or green colour. Yellow teeth alone do not diagnose hepatitis, jaundice or another illness. Share the medical history with the dentist rather than assuming a current liver problem or blaming a medicine from appearance alone. Build a gentle, consistent cleaning routine Brush twice daily for about two minutes, including before bed, using a small soft brush and fluoride toothpaste. Clean all tooth surfaces rather than repeatedly scrubbing a discoloured patch. An adult should help young children and continue supervising until they clean effectively. Where teeth touch, ask the dental team to demonstrate suitable daily interdental cleaning, such as flossing. Use a smear of toothpaste for children under three and a pea-sized amount from three to six, following local dental advice on fluoride strength. Teach children to spit out the excess without swallowing it and without rinsing immediately afterwards. Rinsing then washes away protective fluoride. Improving cleaning can help plaque-related colour, but it does not bleach an internal stain or replace treatment for decay. Food choices support teeth but do not act as a toothbrush Fruit and vegetables can be part of a varied diet, but chewing apples, carrots, celery or pears does not replace brushing. Claims that malic acid or crunchy foods naturally whiten a child’s teeth are not a reason to rub food acids on enamel. Prepare firm foods in forms appropriate to the child’s age and chewing skills so that a dental suggestion does not create a choking hazard. Limit frequent sugary drinks and snacks rather than focusing only on whether a food is brightly coloured. Sticky dried fruit, sweets and starchy snack foods can remain around teeth; timing and repeated exposure matter. Whole fruit does not need to be banned. Offer ordinary water between meals and discuss realistic food habits with the dental team. Separate after-food rinsing from after-toothpaste care Acidic drinks and foods can soften the tooth surface temporarily. Avoid brushing immediately afterwards; ADA advice suggests allowing about an hour after acidic foods so saliva can help restore the surface. A rinse with water after eating or drinking something acidic is reasonable for a child who can rinse and spit safely. That is a different situation from finishing a fluoride-toothpaste brushing session, when spitting without an immediate rinse helps retain fluoride. Repeatedly sipping acidic drinks or holding them around the teeth prolongs contact. Even a sugar-free drink can be acidic. Reducing repeated exposure is more useful than trying to scrub off every trace afterwards. Do not use lemon and baking-soda whitening recipes A homemade lemon-and-baking-soda mixture is not a nearly safe way to whiten a child’s teeth. Acid can erode enamel, while vigorous abrasive scrubbing can remove or damage more of the protective surface. Using a mixture only occasionally does not make an untested recipe appropriate. Loss of enamel may expose more yellow dentin and increase sensitivity. Avoid vinegar, household bleach and other kitchen or cleaning-product whitening experiments too. A formulated toothpaste is different from mixing raw ingredients at home. If a child has pain, irritation or a colour change, ask the dentist what is causing it instead of escalating the strength or duration of a home treatment. Whitening strips and gels need an individual dental decision Shop-bought whitening strips, gels, trays and toothpastes do not all work in the same way. Some remove surface stains; bleaching products change tooth colour chemically. Products can cause tooth sensitivity or gum irritation, and they may produce an uneven result when different kinds of teeth are present. Adult product availability does not establish suitability for a child. The American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry discourages full-arch cosmetic bleaching in primary or mixed dentitions. Selected discolouration in one tooth or an older adolescent may call for another approach under dental supervision. There is no single birthday or completion of adult-tooth eruption that makes every product appropriate. Consider the diagnosis, evidence, expectations and the child’s wishes together. Etch-bleach-seal is a professional technique One technique described for selected developmental stains involves preparing the enamel surface, applying a controlled bleaching treatment and sealing it with resin. It is sometimes called etch-bleach-seal. Although a clinician may use sodium hypochlorite in a controlled dental procedure, that is not permission to put household bleach on teeth at home. Reports of a technique being used successfully in a small number of children do not establish a universal minimum age, guaranteed result or long-term safety for every enamel defect. In particular, a claim that it is simply safe above six should not guide treatment. Ask the paediatric dentist why the proposed procedure fits this tooth and what alternatives preserve more healthy tissue. Microabrasion and resin infiltration treat selected defects Microabrasion combines controlled chemical and mechanical treatment to remove a very thin superficial enamel layer. It may improve a stain that lies near the surface, but it will not solve every deeper or internal discolouration. Because enamel is removed, the choice depends on the depth and nature of the defect, not just a desire for a whiter shade. Resin infiltration is another technique used for selected porous enamel changes, and it is different from covering a tooth with a bonded restoration. A dentist may consider techniques alone or in combination. Neither the number of visits nor the cosmetic result can be guaranteed from a photograph. Ask what change is realistic and how the treated area will be monitored. Bonding and veneers have different trade-offs Composite bonding places tooth-coloured resin onto a tooth to repair or disguise a selected defect. The material is shaped and finished as a restoration; it is not ordinary paint or nail polish. Bonding may help with a chip or persistent colour problem, but it can wear, stain or need repair. Maintenance and changes as a child grows should be part of the discussion. A porcelain veneer covers the front of a tooth and may require removal of healthy enamel. That makes it a substantial and potentially irreversible cosmetic choice, especially for a young person with developing teeth and gums. Veneers are not a first response to normal yellow adult teeth. Ask about observation, protection, less invasive options and the future replacement needs of any restoration. Make habits encouraging and respond to symptoms promptly A two-minute timer, brushing together, a suitable favourite toothbrush or a small reward chart can help a child build a routine. Use toothpaste appropriate to their age and dental advice. Listen if an older child is embarrassed or teased, but avoid teaching them that a natural tooth shade is unattractive. Address bullying and support confidence while obtaining an accurate assessment. Keep check-ups at the interval recommended for your child’s dental risk rather than assuming every child needs exactly the same schedule. Arrange earlier advice for a persistent colour change, sensitivity or injury. Pain with swelling, fever or a suspected abscess needs urgent dental care. Trouble breathing, speaking or swallowing, substantial mouth swelling or an affected eye calls for emergency help. Permanent teeth often look naturally yellower than primary teeth. Have a new or persistent change assessed, especially after injury or with pain. Use suitable amounts of fluoride toothpaste, brush gently and spit without rinsing immediately afterwards. Professional techniques are selected for a diagnosed problem; they are not routine home whitening steps. Does yellow always mean a cavity? No. Normal dentin colour, surface staining and enamel differences are possible. A new patch, damaged surface or painful tooth needs assessment, because colour alone cannot distinguish these from decay. Why do new front teeth look darker than the baby teeth beside them? Permanent teeth have a different structure and often show more of the underlying yellowish dentin. Mixed dentition makes the contrast noticeable. The dentist can confirm whether the appearance is normal. Should I stop liquid iron if it leaves a stain? No. Continue prescribed treatment unless the prescriber changes it. Ask the prescriber and dentist how to administer it and manage any external staining safely. Can my child take doxycycline despite warnings about tetracyclines? Do not reject a prescription based on a blanket warning. Short doxycycline courses used for rickettsial infections have not shown the older tooth-staining risk, and delaying that treatment can be dangerous. Discuss the actual medicine and indication with the prescriber. Can stronger brushing remove an internal stain? No. Brushing removes plaque and some surface material, not every change inside the tooth. Scrubbing harder can damage enamel or gums. Ask the dentist which type of discolouration is present. Is lemon mixed with baking soda safe once a week? No reliable safety rule makes that homemade mixture suitable for a child’s teeth. Acid and abrasive scrubbing can damage the protective enamel. Use ordinary dental care and seek advice about a persistent stain. Should my child rinse after brushing? After fluoride toothpaste, encourage spitting out the excess without rinsing straight away. A water rinse after acidic food is a separate situation. Young children need supervision to avoid swallowing toothpaste. Is there a universal safe age for bleaching? No. The dentist considers the teeth present, cause of the colour, product or technique, evidence and the child’s circumstances. Full-arch cosmetic bleaching is discouraged in primary and mixed dentitions. Is a veneer the same as bonding? No. Composite bonding adds and shapes tooth-coloured resin; a porcelain veneer is a different restoration and may require removing enamel. Both have maintenance needs, and normal tooth colour does not automatically justify either. When does a colour change need urgent help? Seek urgent dental care for significant pain, swelling, fever or a suspected infection. Breathing or swallowing difficulty, substantial mouth swelling or eye involvement requires emergency assessment. A darkened tooth after injury should also be checked even without ongoing pain.

title: When your toddler holds in poo: breaking the constipation cycle
description: Understand stool withholding, support comfortable toileting and learn why early constipation treatment matters more than pressure or bigger rewards.
body: Watching a child hold on despite discomfort can be frustrating and worrying. Often they are trying to avoid pain, not refusing to cooperate. A useful plan treats constipation, reduces fear and makes the next bathroom visit feel achievable. Holding on can begin with one painful poo A toddler may stiffen, cross their legs, squeeze their bottom or hide when they need to pass a stool. These actions can look like straining to poo when the child is actually trying to stop it. One painful hard stool may be enough to make the next urge feel frightening. The longer stool stays in the bowel, the more water can be absorbed from it. It becomes harder to pass, which reinforces the wish to hold on. Breaking this cycle means making stools reliably comfortable as well as helping your child feel secure. Stronger persuasion cannot soften a hard stool. Look for pain, fear and practical obstacles Some children fear the toilet’s size, flushing noise or the feeling of sitting without support. Others dislike a bathroom’s smell, want privacy, prefer the familiarity of a nappy or are too absorbed in play to stop. Pressure to toilet train before they are ready can add another difficulty. Wanting some control is part of toddler development, but withholding is not usefully treated as a contest of wills. Sensory differences can make toileting harder, including for some autistic children; withholding alone does not diagnose autism. Ask what feels difficult, watch what happens and adapt the environment instead of assuming that the child is being deliberately difficult. Constipation can cause more than infrequent stools Hard pellets, very large stools, painful bowel movements, bloating and tummy cramps can all be clues. Appetite may fall when a child is uncomfortable. How the stool feels and how easily it passes matter alongside the number of bowel movements. A build-up of stool, called faecal impaction, can allow softer or liquid stool to leak around it. Soiled pants therefore do not rule out constipation. Bladder symptoms, daytime wetting, bedwetting or urinary infections can also accompany bowel problems. Do not punish accidents or interpret them as proof that your child is ignoring instructions. Other medical causes sometimes need investigation Most childhood constipation is functional: there is no identified structural disease causing it. Less common explanations include coeliac disease, hypothyroidism, Hirschsprung disease, neurological problems or a narrowing or abnormality of the anus or bowel. A clinician considers these when the history, growth, examination or response to treatment raises concern. Slow-transit constipation, sometimes described as colonic inertia, and difficulty coordinating the pelvic floor are specialist considerations in selected cases, not diagnoses to infer from one delayed poo. Faecal impaction is often a consequence of ongoing constipation rather than a separate underlying disease. Tell the clinician about medicines and supplements too; do not stop prescribed treatment without advice. Do not assume every digestive label explains withholding Irritable bowel syndrome can involve repeated abdominal pain with constipation, diarrhoea or both, but it is not an automatic explanation for a toddler holding on during toilet training. The pattern needs clinical assessment. Lactose intolerance more typically causes gas, bloating, abdominal discomfort and diarrhoea after lactose-containing foods. It should not be assumed to explain hard stools. Nor is lactose intolerance the same as a milk-protein allergy. Avoid removing dairy or several food groups on your own; a restricted toddler diet can create new nutritional problems without treating the original one. Get help early, and recognise urgent signs Arrange medical advice when you suspect constipation rather than waiting for every home strategy to fail. Explain pain, withholding, accidents, stool appearance and how long the pattern has lasted. A short bowel diary can help the clinician decide whether a stool build-up needs treatment. Seek urgent assessment for a swollen abdomen with vomiting, persistent severe pain, significant bleeding, weight loss or a child who seems very unwell. Constipation from birth or the first weeks, delayed first meconium, unusual ribbon-like stools or leg weakness needs medical evaluation. A young baby’s symptoms should not be managed by simply applying a toddler’s toilet-training plan. Make the bathroom feel secure Use a stable potty or a child-sized insert on the toilet, with a step that supports the feet. Dangling legs and fear of falling make relaxation harder. Let your child become familiar with the seat while clothed if necessary, and introduce changes gradually. A short book, quiet conversation or a warm bath at another point in the routine may reduce tension. Avoid turning relaxation into a demand to perform immediately. If flushing is frightening, let your child move away first. Stay nearby when helpful, offer age-appropriate privacy and keep the visit brief enough that the toilet does not become a place of prolonged pressure. Build a routine that rewards participation For a child who is ready to sit, offer predictable short opportunities, often after meals, when the bowel may be more active. Do not force sitting or insist on repeated straining. Follow a clinician’s plan if pain or a significant stool build-up is being treated. Praise or a small sticker can recognise a manageable step: taking medicine, coming to the bathroom, sitting comfortably or telling you about an urge. The reward should not depend only on producing a poo. Avoid punishment, public discussion of accidents or an escalating prize that makes the task feel even more important and frightening. Explain the body and slow toilet training if needed Use simple language: the body takes what it needs from food, and the rest comes out as poo. A picture book, toy or doll can make the sequence familiar without making your child watch something they dislike. They do not need a lecture about germs or a demonstration that makes anyone uncomfortable. If a child will only poo in a nappy, suddenly removing that option can intensify withholding. Discuss a gradual transition while treating constipation, rather than making staying clean the immediate goal. You might first work on feeling comfortable in the bathroom and only later change where or how they sit. The pace should reflect readiness and comfort, with the same supportive approach at nursery. Offer fibre without making meals another struggle Include age-appropriate fruit, vegetables, beans and wholegrain foods across ordinary meals and snacks. Adapt texture and size for safe chewing. Food labels can help compare fibre content, but there is no universal requirement that every toddler meal must contain exactly three grams. Bananas do not need to be automatically banned, and all carbohydrates or dairy products should not be removed. If crackers, chicken nuggets or macaroni are familiar foods, add variety alongside them instead of labelling them as bad or abruptly removing most accepted choices. Diet supports treatment; it is often insufficient to clear an established stool build-up. Ask a dietitian for help if intake is very restricted. Make drinks available, without forcing excess Offer water regularly in a cup your child can manage, alongside the milk and other drinks appropriate to their age. Fluids also come from foods such as soup and fruit. Soft, safely prepared cucumber or watermelon can be part of meals; avoid pieces that are hard to chew or easy to choke on. A smoothie or broth is not a necessary constipation treatment, and large amounts can displace food or add unwanted sugar or salt. Aim for adequate intake rather than forcing extra litres. Ask for individual advice if your child drinks very little, has a medical fluid restriction or shows dehydration. Do not dilute infant formula or give an infant a toddler fluid regimen. Keep juice advice appropriate to age Whole fruit usually offers more fibre than juice. Some fruit juices may help soften stools, but a daily large glass is not a universal solution. The American Academy of Pediatrics advises no more than about 120 mL, or four fluid ounces, of juice daily for children aged one to three years; it is a limit, not a target. If juice is used, choose pasteurised 100 percent juice and offer it with a meal rather than for continuous sipping. Diluting it with water does not cancel the sugar in the amount of juice actually used. Routine juice is not recommended below one year; any use for a young baby’s symptoms should follow clinical advice. Excess juice can cause diarrhoea and harm teeth. Medicine can be part of breaking the cycle An assessment may identify the need to clear impacted stool, followed by treatment that keeps new stools soft. Polyethylene glycol, also called macrogol, is commonly used in paediatric plans; the formulation, dose and any additional medicine must fit the child. Do not copy an adult dose or use an enema, suppository or repeated rectal stimulation without professional advice. Most children do not need a scan to diagnose ordinary functional constipation. Examination and history guide testing when another cause is suspected. During treatment, soiling can initially increase. Ask what to expect, how to prepare prescribed medicine correctly, and when to contact the team if the plan is not working. Keep support in place after the first comfortable poo One successful bowel movement does not always mean the cycle has resolved. Maintenance treatment may continue for months while the bowel recovers and the child learns to trust the urge again. Follow the agreed review and gradual reduction plan rather than abruptly stopping medicine after an encouraging day. Daily play, comfortable toilet access and a consistent response from caregivers support recovery. Keep notes simple: stool softness, pain, accidents and prescribed treatment. If symptoms persist or return, ask for review of the plan and possible specialist help. The aim is comfortable, unhurried bowel movements, not winning a battle over the toilet. Pain and withholding can reinforce each other. Soiling can happen around a stool build-up. Support feet, keep routines calm and reward achievable steps. Seek help early and follow treatment beyond the first improvement. Is my child holding on just to be difficult? Do not assume that. Pain, fear, sensory discomfort and interrupted play can all contribute. Does a daily accident mean constipation is impossible? No. Softer stool can leak around an impacted stool mass. A clinician can assess the pattern. Should I wait until all diet changes have failed? No. Seek advice early when constipation is suspected. Diet alone may not clear a stool build-up. How should my child sit on the toilet? Use a secure seat and support the feet on the floor or a step. Avoid long, forced sitting or straining. What should a sticker reward recognise? A manageable step such as sitting comfortably or taking prescribed medicine, rather than only producing a poo. Should I remove nappies immediately? Not if that intensifies withholding. Discuss a gradual transition while making stools comfortable. Do bananas or dairy always need to be avoided? No. Routine blanket exclusions are not recommended. Ask for advice before restricting major food groups. How much juice can a toddler have? For ages one to three, AAP guidance limits juice to about 120 mL a day. It is optional, and more is not necessarily better. Can I stop laxatives after one good poo? Follow the prescribed plan. Maintenance treatment often needs to continue and then be reduced gradually. When is urgent assessment needed? Vomiting with a swollen abdomen, severe persistent pain, significant bleeding, weight loss or a very unwell child needs prompt medical assessment.

title: Tooth decay in children: causes, treatment and prevention
description: Why baby teeth matter, how to recognise possible decay, what dental treatments involve and how brushing, fluoride and food routines can help protect teeth.
body: A cavity in a baby tooth deserves attention even though that tooth will eventually fall out. Decay can affect eating, comfort and the teeth that follow. Knowing the early signs and the range of treatment options can help you seek care before the problem becomes painful or more complicated. Why baby teeth need treatment too Decay can affect both baby and permanent teeth. Baby teeth help a child chew and speak and hold space for the teeth that follow. A painful or infected tooth should not be left untreated simply because it will eventually fall out. Even a child aged one or two may need dental treatment. The word decay covers different stages. Early mineral loss in enamel may be stopped or reversed with appropriate care. Once a hole has formed, that lost tooth structure does not grow back through brushing alone. A dentist can explain whether the aim is to repair a cavity, stop its progression or protect an area before a hole develops. How plaque, food and other factors contribute Plaque is the sticky film that builds up on teeth. Bacteria in it use sugars and starches from food and drink and produce acids. Repeated acid exposure removes minerals from the tooth surface. Fluoride and saliva help protect teeth, but frequent exposure can overwhelm that protection. Sweets, cake, ice cream and sugary drinks are familiar examples, but crackers, chips and other starchy snacks can also contribute. How often a child snacks or sips matters as well as the amount. Foods marketed as natural or healthy are not automatically harmless to teeth. Brushing and cleaning between teeth reduce plaque, but cavities are not proof that a family has been careless. Saliva, fluoride exposure, enamel development, medicines, feeding patterns, access to care and difficulties tolerating brushing can affect risk. Some enamel conditions make teeth more vulnerable; a parent cannot diagnose genetic soft teeth just by looking at a cavity. Signs to notice, even without pain New chalky-white spots, brown or dark areas, a visible hole or sensitivity to cold or sweet foods can indicate a problem. Young children may cry during meals, become unusually irritable, avoid food or chew on one side. A colour change can have another explanation too, so arrange a dental examination rather than diagnosing it from a photograph. Decay may not hurt at first. Regular visits can identify changes before a child can describe them. Book the first visit when teeth appear and by the first birthday; then follow the interval recommended for the child’s risk. Six months is common, but it is not the right fixed interval for every child. Swelling, fever, persistent pain or a child becoming very unwell needs urgent dental assessment. Significant mouth swelling, difficulty breathing, speaking or swallowing, trouble opening the mouth, or swelling around an eye requires emergency care. Do not wait for the next routine check-up or assume unusual lethargy is only a tooth problem. What fillings and other early treatments can do The dentist assesses how deep the decay is, which tooth is involved and whether the child has pain or infection. Early changes may be managed with fluoride and changes to daily care. Sealants can protect suitable grooves in back teeth. A formed cavity may need restoration, but drilling and filling is not the only possible approach in every situation. A filling replaces damaged tooth structure and helps preserve the tooth. Materials may include tooth-coloured restorations or another appropriate material, depending on the tooth, the child’s circumstances and local guidance. The dentist should explain what will be used and why. Restorations can be placed in baby as well as permanent teeth. Silver diamine fluoride is another option for selected decay. It can help arrest a lesion but permanently blackens the decayed area, so families need to understand the appearance and follow-up before agreeing. It is different from routine fluoride varnish and does not restore a tooth’s original shape. When a crown, pulp treatment or extraction is considered A badly damaged baby tooth may need a crown to cover and protect it. Stainless-steel crowns are a familiar silver-coloured option, although the choice depends on the tooth and clinical plan. Decay close to or involving the tooth’s pulp may require additional treatment rather than a small filling. If a tooth cannot be kept safely, removal may be needed. A dentist then considers whether a space maintainer would help preserve room for the permanent tooth. This is an individual decision based on the tooth lost and the stage of development, not an automatic requirement after every extraction. Ask which teeth need prompt care, which can be monitored and what happens if treatment is delayed. A dental infection may need drainage, treatment inside the tooth or extraction. Antibiotics, when indicated, do not by themselves repair the source of the problem. Helping a child feel comfortable during treatment Explanation, familiarisation, breaks and a manageable appointment length can help. Local anaesthetic numbs the treatment area. Nitrous oxide, often called laughing gas, can reduce anxiety while a child usually remains awake; it does not automatically replace local numbing for painful treatment. Some children may need medicine for sedation. Oral medicine is one possible route, but the drug, depth of sedation and monitoring matter more than calling it something to relax the child. Do not give sedatives at home unless the treating team has provided a specific supervised plan. When several teeth need care, staged visits may suit some children. Others may need a different approach to avoid repeated distress or delaying urgent treatment. Ask the team to explain the sequence, how pain will be controlled and what alternatives are available. What general anaesthesia means General anaesthesia makes the child unconscious for treatment and requires a trained anaesthesia team and appropriate monitoring. It differs from lighter sedation or nitrous oxide. Extensive disease, very young age, disability or inability to complete necessary treatment safely may influence the recommendation; difficulty sitting still alone is not a complete risk-benefit assessment. Ask who will provide and monitor the anaesthesia, where care will take place, which teeth will be treated and how recovery will be managed. Discuss medical conditions, medicines and previous reactions. Follow the team’s fasting and medicine instructions exactly, and report a new illness before the procedure. The decision should weigh the risks and benefits of treatment and its alternatives, including the consequences of untreated pain or infection. A plan for preventing new decay is still needed after a successful procedure. A brushing routine that grows with the child Before teeth appear, gently wiping the gums with a clean soft damp cloth can help establish a mouth-care routine. Once the first tooth emerges, begin brushing with fluoride toothpaste. A cloth does not replace brushing teeth. Brush twice daily, including last thing before bed, aiming for about two minutes as the routine develops. Under age three use a tiny smear of toothpaste, about the size of a grain of rice; from three to six use a pea-sized amount. Ask the dental team about the fluoride strength appropriate to local guidance and your child’s risk. An adult should do or closely help with young children’s brushing. Many still need supervision beyond age six or seven; skill and thoroughness matter more than a birthday. Encourage spitting without immediately rinsing, and keep the tube out of reach so toothpaste is not eaten. Help clean between touching teeth daily using the method your dentist demonstrates. Flossing can be difficult for small hands. A predictable routine, a soft age-appropriate brush and small choices can make cooperation easier. Pain, sensory distress or disability may require adaptations from the dental team rather than more pressure on the child. Choose snacks and drinks with teeth and safety in mind Reduce repeated sugary drinks and grazing between meals. Do not leave a baby in bed with a bottle or let milk or juice become an all-night bottle comforter. Discuss normal infant feeding needs and tooth care together with the dental team; feeding advice should account for the baby’s age and needs. Whole fruit, including berries, plain yoghurt, suitable pieces of cheese, soft banana and prepared vegetables can be part of a varied diet. Unsweetened applesauce or other fruit purées may also fit meals, but no snack label guarantees cavity protection. The glycaemic index is not a reliable way to rank foods for tooth safety. Dried fruit, trail mix and granola can contain concentrated or added sugars and may stick to teeth; they are not unlimited substitutes for sweets. Avoid hard frozen banana chunks, whole nuts, hard raw carrot pieces and other choking hazards for young children. Adapt texture and size to the child’s abilities, and supervise eating while the child is seated. Keep follow-up appointments after a filling, crown or other treatment. Repairing one tooth does not remove the causes of decay. Supported cleaning, fluoride, sensible meal and snack routines and regular review can reduce future risk without promising that a child will never have another cavity. Baby teeth support eating, speech and space for permanent teeth. Decay may develop before pain appears. Treatment can include prevention, arresting decay, restoration or extraction, depending on the case. Sedation and general anaesthesia need separate explanations and monitoring plans. Daily prevention and dental follow-up remain important after treatment. Should we wait for a decayed baby tooth to fall out? No. Pain, infection and early tooth loss can affect a child before the normal replacement time. Ask a dentist what the tooth needs. Can my child have decay without pain? Yes. A new spot or visible defect may appear before pain. Regular examinations can find problems a child cannot describe. Does every white spot mean a cavity? No. White areas can have several causes, and early mineral loss may not yet be a hole. A dental assessment is needed. Does every cavity need drilling? Not always. Some lesions can be managed with an arresting treatment or another approach, while others need a filling or crown. The dentist should explain the choice. Why can silver diamine fluoride turn a tooth black? It darkens the decayed tissue it treats. This appearance change should be explained before treatment; it is not the same as a routine fluoride varnish. Is a space maintainer always needed after an extraction? No. The dentist considers the tooth lost, the child’s development and the available space before recommending one. Is laughing gas the same as general anaesthesia? No. With nitrous oxide a child usually remains awake. General anaesthesia involves unconsciousness and a different staffing and monitoring plan. Can a six-year-old brush alone? Some children still need considerable help at that age and beyond. Supervise until they can clean all surfaces effectively, and keep checking the routine. Are dried fruit and granola automatically better for teeth? No. Sugar concentration, stickiness and frequency matter, even without added sugar. Consider age-safe textures and balanced meals rather than a tooth-safe label. Do fillings prevent all future cavities? No. They treat existing damage. Fluoride, supported cleaning, food routines and follow-up are still needed to reduce new decay.

title: Viral gastroenteritis in children: fluids, feeding and warning signs
description: Care for vomiting and diarrhoea with appropriate fluids and food, recognise dehydration, and know when a child needs urgent help.
body: A stomach bug often improves with supportive care, but babies and children can lose fluid quickly. Focus on hydration, feeding and how your child is behaving, while watching for symptoms that need more than home care. “Stomach flu” is not influenza Viral gastroenteritis is an infection of the digestive tract that commonly causes vomiting and watery diarrhoea. The nickname stomach flu can be confusing: influenza is a different infection, mainly affecting the respiratory system. A flu vaccine does not protect against all causes of a vomiting-and-diarrhoea illness. Norovirus, rotavirus and some adenoviruses are among the causes; astrovirus can also cause gastroenteritis. The likely virus varies with age, setting and vaccination history. A population statistic for one country or a particular year cannot tell you which virus your child has. Not every episode is viral. Bacteria, parasites and other problems can cause similar symptoms, and food poisoning can result from viruses as well as bacteria or other contaminants. Severe pain, blood, unusual vomiting or a child who seems very unwell should not be dismissed as a routine stomach bug. Why it spreads quickly through families Very small amounts of infected stool or vomit can contaminate hands, toys, changing surfaces, food or water. Young children often put hands and objects in their mouths and still need help with handwashing, so infections can spread even in a careful household. The interval between exposure and symptoms depends on the virus. Norovirus often starts within twelve to forty-eight hours, while other causes can take longer. There is no fixed rule that every household member will become ill within a week, and some people can spread a virus before symptoms or after they feel better. Avoid blaming a child or caregiver for an infection. The practical response is to support fluids, watch for warning signs and reduce spread. If several people become ill after the same meal or there is a nursery outbreak, tell the clinician because that history can affect advice and testing. Symptoms and recovery times vary Common symptoms include watery loose stools, nausea, vomiting, tummy cramps, reduced appetite and sometimes fever. A child may also have chills, headache, body aches or fatigue. Babies may be fussier than usual or feed less. Fever is not required for the illness to be significant. Vomiting commonly lasts one or two days and usually settles within three; diarrhoea often lasts five to seven days and can take up to two weeks to stop. Some infections are shorter and others longer. These are expected ranges, not a promise that every child will recover within twenty-four to forty-eight hours. Mild tiredness is different from unusual lethargy or difficulty waking. Likewise, a stiff neck, marked body stiffness or severe persistent pain is not something to explain away as a routine symptom. Seek advice earlier whenever the child is worsening; do not wait for the expected duration to pass. Watch hydration more closely than the number of episodes alone Vomiting and diarrhoea cause losses of water and salts. Dehydration is the main immediate concern, especially in babies and young children. Risk also rises if a child cannot drink enough, has repeated losses or has another medical condition. Look for less urine or fewer wet nappies than usual, darker urine, a dry mouth, sunken eyes, fewer tears, increasing sleepiness or unusual irritability. Fast breathing, a fast heartbeat, cold or mottled skin and reduced responsiveness can indicate more serious illness. Do not wait eight to twelve hours without a wet nappy before asking for help if your baby is already feeding poorly or seems unwell. Very little urine, no urine for a prolonged period or a worsening overall picture needs urgent assessment. A short note of drinks, feeds, wet nappies and episodes can help the clinician understand the pattern. Offer oral rehydration little and often Oral rehydration solution, or ORS, contains a balance of water, salts and glucose designed to replace losses. A pharmacist or clinician can advise which product and plan fit your child’s age and condition. Seek early advice for a baby, particularly a young infant, rather than trying to manage significant losses without support. Prepare ORS exactly as the packet directs with the correct amount of safe water. Do not add extra powder, juice, squash or sugar to improve the taste. Offer small, frequent amounts by cup, spoon or an appropriate oral syringe, rather than a large drink at once. Do not force fluid into the mouth of a drowsy child. After vomiting, a brief pause and a slower restart may help, but do not deliberately withhold fluid for a long period or delay it after every loose stool. If the child repeatedly vomits the solution, refuses fluids or cannot keep anything down, obtain medical advice. Some children need supervised rehydration, tube fluids or intravenous treatment. Continue appropriate milk feeds and bring usual food back Continue breastfeeding during the illness, offering feeds as your baby needs them. If a child is not dehydrated, usual milk feeds, including correctly prepared full-strength formula, generally continue. Do not dilute formula or replace a young infant’s milk with plain water, broth or fizzy drinks. If a clinician gives a specific ORS plan to treat dehydration, follow that plan for other drinks and solid food; breastfeeding usually continues. Once rehydrated, return to usual full-strength milk and age-appropriate foods. Prolonged fasting or a strict diet of only toast, rice or bananas is not needed. Offer small portions if the child wants them, without forcing food. Bland familiar options may be comfortable, but hydration is the priority while appetite is low. Juice, ginger ale and other sugary or carbonated drinks are not equivalent to ORS and can worsen diarrhoea. Age-appropriate ORS ice pops may be an option if recommended, but ordinary sweets or ice chips are not an infant rehydration plan. Use medicines for a specific reason, not to “clear the virus” Antibiotics do not treat viral gastroenteritis. A clinician may use them for a diagnosed bacterial or other infection when appropriate, but they are not a routine response to vomiting and diarrhoea. There is also no need to encourage more vomiting or diarrhoea to get rid of a virus. Do not give an adult anti-diarrhoeal or anti-vomiting product to a child on your own. Some are unsuitable for children; a clinician may prescribe an antiemetic in selected circumstances. Medicine does not replace fluid assessment, and blood or severe pain requires evaluation rather than simply suppressing symptoms. For pain or distress, ask about an age- and weight-appropriate medicine and follow the exact product instructions. Avoid ibuprofen when the child is dehydrated. Do not give aspirin to a child under sixteen unless specifically prescribed; it is associated with Reye’s syndrome. Do not use a falling temperature after medicine as proof that a very unwell child is safe. Know when home care is not enough Get emergency help for a child who is difficult to wake, unusually floppy or confused, has serious breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour, a seizure, a non-fading rash or signs of shock. Green vomit, blood in vomit or severe persistent abdominal pain also needs urgent assessment for causes beyond a simple virus. A temperature of 38°C or higher in a baby under three months, or 39°C or higher at three to six months, needs urgent medical assessment. A very low temperature or a baby who seems seriously unwell matters too. Do not rely on a single 38.9°C threshold for every age. Contact a clinician promptly for blood in stool or urine, worsening dehydration, repeated inability to keep fluids down, persistent vomiting or symptoms that are not improving. Blood in urine is not a usual gastroenteritis symptom. Be especially cautious with young infants, children with diabetes or weakened immunity, and whenever your child’s behaviour worries you. Clean hands, surfaces and laundry safely Wash hands with soap and running water for at least twenty seconds after toileting or nappy changes and before preparing or eating food. Help young children wash thoroughly. Hand sanitiser alone does not work well against norovirus, so it is not a substitute for washing. Clean vomit or stool contamination promptly using appropriate gloves and cleaning materials, then disinfect with a product labelled effective against the relevant virus. Follow the label for dilution and wet contact time, ventilate the area and keep children away while cleaning. Never mix bleach with vinegar or other cleaners; a homemade detergent-vinegar mixture is not a validated norovirus disinfectant. Clean frequently touched surfaces and washable toys, handle soiled laundry carefully and avoid sharing towels, bottles, cups or utensils. Wash hands after handling contaminated items. Covering coughs and sneezes is a good general habit, but for these infections the key routes involve stool, vomit, hands, food and contaminated surfaces. Support recovery and reduce the chance of another infection Quiet play, books, comfort and rest can make recovery easier. Keep checking drinking, urine output and alertness even when the vomiting slows. Ask for advice if vomiting continues beyond the usual few days, diarrhoea persists or the child is not returning toward their usual self; seek help sooner for any warning sign. Keep the child out of childcare or school while vomiting or having diarrhoea. Guidance commonly requires at least forty-eight hours after the last episode before returning, with local rules taking priority. UK NICE guidance also advises avoiding swimming pools for two weeks after the last diarrhoea episode. Continued handwashing matters because virus shedding can outlast symptoms. Check that infant rotavirus vaccination is up to date within the local age limits. It reduces the risk of severe rotavirus disease but does not prevent every stomach bug. Repeat infections are possible, so no routine guarantees immunity. Prompt fluids, sensible hygiene and timely medical advice are more useful than assuming every child must have the same illness or recovery course. Offer small frequent fluids rather than delaying them. Mix ORS exactly as directed. Continue breastfeeding and follow any specific rehydration plan. Avoid ibuprofen during dehydration and unprescribed anti-diarrhoeals. Use soap and water and never mix cleaning chemicals. Is stomach flu caused by the influenza virus? No. Viral gastroenteritis involves different viruses. Similar symptoms can also have nonviral causes. Will it always stop within forty-eight hours? No. Vomiting often settles within a few days, while diarrhoea commonly lasts longer. Worsening symptoms need advice regardless of duration. Should I wait after every loose stool before giving a drink? No. Replace losses promptly with small frequent amounts of appropriate fluid. A prolonged fluid delay increases dehydration risk. Can I mix ORS with juice to improve the taste? Prepare it exactly as directed with the correct amount of water. Do not change its concentration or add juice, squash or sugar. Should I stop breastfeeding or dilute formula? Continue breastfeeding. Usual full-strength formula generally continues when the child is not dehydrated; follow a clinician’s specific plan during rehydration. Do not dilute formula yourself. Does my child need only bananas, rice and toast? No. After rehydration, offer usual age-appropriate foods as tolerated. A prolonged restricted diet is not necessary. Should vomiting be encouraged to remove the virus? No. It causes fluid losses. Do not induce it, and ask about treatment if vomiting prevents hydration. Is ibuprofen safe when my child is dehydrated? Avoid it during dehydration. Ask about appropriate pain or fever treatment for the child’s age, weight and symptoms. Can I disinfect with bleach mixed with vinegar? No. Never mix cleaning chemicals. Use a suitable labelled disinfectant and follow its dilution, ventilation and contact-time instructions. When can my child go back to childcare? Usually at least forty-eight hours after the last episode of vomiting or diarrhoea, provided they are well enough and local rules allow it. Continue careful handwashing afterward.

title: When do baby teeth fall out?
description: A complete guide to baby-tooth eruption and loss, adult molars and premolars, loose-tooth care, timing differences and when to see the dentist.
body: Baby teeth usually begin to loosen around age six, but the change to adult teeth takes several years. Knowing the broad sequence can help you support your child without turning the chart into a deadline. Two sets of teeth, with a few years of overlap A first loose tooth can feel like a major milestone. Baby teeth, also called primary teeth, help a child chew and speak and preserve space while the jaws and permanent teeth develop. They need care even though they will eventually be replaced. There are usually twenty primary teeth. They commonly start appearing around six months and are generally all present by about age three. Shedding often begins around six and continues into the early teenage years, with several years when baby and permanent teeth share the mouth. Most children have twenty-eight permanent teeth by the early teens, excluding wisdom teeth. Thirty-two is the total only when all four third molars develop and are included; it is not a number every thirteen-year-old should already have. Why a baby tooth becomes loose As a permanent successor develops and moves toward eruption, the baby tooth’s roots are gradually resorbed. Less root remains to anchor it, and the crown eventually loosens within the surrounding gum. This explains why a naturally shed tooth may look as though it has little or no root. Eruption is the name for a tooth emerging into the mouth; shedding means a primary tooth coming out. The two events are related but do not have to happen on the same day. A gap can remain while the permanent tooth continues to move into place. Children may be excited, cautious or upset about the change. Explain what is happening without promising that it must follow exactly the same timetable as a sibling or classmate. Typical timing for upper baby teeth The following ranges describe when primary teeth usually appear and are lost. They are a guide, not a deadline for each child. Upper central incisors: appear at 8–12 months; shed at 6–7 years. Upper lateral incisors: appear at 9–13 months; shed at 7–8 years. Upper first molars: appear at 13–19 months; shed at 9–11 years. Upper canines: appear at 16–22 months; shed at 10–12 years. Upper second molars: appear at 25–33 months; shed at 10–12 years. Typical timing for lower baby teeth Lower central incisors: appear at 6–10 months; shed at 6–7 years. Lower lateral incisors: appear at 10–16 months; shed at 7–8 years. Lower first molars: appear at 14–18 months; shed at 9–11 years. Lower canines: appear at 17–23 months; shed at 9–12 years. Lower second molars: appear at 23–31 months; shed at 10–12 years. Use these ranges with the dentist’s assessment of the whole mouth. Overlap between ranges means there is not one compulsory order for every tooth. The front teeth usually lead the change The lower central incisors are often the first baby teeth to appear and the first to loosen, around six or seven. The upper central incisors commonly follow. Lateral incisors, the teeth beside the central pair, are often lost around seven or eight. This broadly resembles the early eruption sequence, but it should not be treated as an exact replay. Upper and lower teeth do not always follow the same order in every child. A little tenderness can occur around a very loose tooth. Significant pain, swelling or a child avoiding food deserves dental advice rather than being dismissed as an inevitable part of growing adult teeth. Baby molars are replaced by premolars Primary first molars commonly shed around nine to eleven, while the canines and second primary molars are often lost between about nine and twelve. Their timing overlaps, so a canine may be lost before or after a neighbouring baby molar. The permanent teeth that replace baby molars are called premolars. Permanent molars are additional teeth that emerge farther back as the jaw grows; they do not take the place of baby molars. The first permanent molars often arrive around six or seven, behind the last baby teeth, without any tooth falling out first. Second permanent molars tend to arrive around eleven to thirteen, with upper and lower ranges differing slightly. Watch for these new back teeth when helping with brushing. Let a wobbly tooth progress naturally The AAPD Foundation advises allowing a loose baby tooth to fall out on its own. A child may gently move it with the tongue, but there is no need for a parent to force, twist or attach string to it. If the tooth is painful, remains troublesome or seems to block a permanent tooth, let the dentist examine it. A retained primary tooth sometimes needs professional help, but that decision should follow an assessment. Keeping the child involved can reduce worry. Explain that they can tell you if eating or brushing hurts, and avoid making removal into a test of bravery. Care after a tooth comes out A small amount of bleeding may follow natural shedding. With an adult supervising, a clean folded piece of gauze can be held with gentle, steady pressure at the area. Remove the gauze after bleeding settles; do not leave loose gauze in a child’s mouth during sleep. Avoid poking the gap or repeatedly rinsing and spitting while it is bleeding. A cool damp cloth can offer comfort. Strong or persistent pain, swelling or bleeding that does not settle with pressure warrants advice from a dentist. A salt-water rinse is not a required immediate step after every naturally lost tooth. After a dental extraction, follow the dentist’s specific instructions; postoperative advice commonly avoids vigorous rinsing on the day of the procedure. Only use a rinse when the child can reliably spit it out and the dental team recommends it. An injury is different from normal shedding A baby tooth lost early through decay or an accident may leave space that neighbouring teeth can move into. The dentist may consider a space maintainer, depending on the tooth, age and development of the permanent replacement. It is not needed for every naturally lost tooth. If a tooth is knocked out, seek urgent dental advice. Never put a baby tooth back into its socket, because this can harm the permanent tooth developing beneath it. A knocked-out permanent tooth is a time-sensitive emergency. Handle it by the crown, not the root. If you cannot safely replace it or are unsure which type it is, keep it in milk and contact an emergency dentist immediately. Do not leave it dry while trying to identify it. Wisdom teeth usually come much later Third molars, commonly called wisdom teeth, usually appear in the late teens or early adulthood, if they erupt at all. A commonly used development chart gives seventeen to twenty-one as a typical range, but timing varies. Some people develop fewer than four wisdom teeth or none. Others have teeth that remain within the jaw or only partly emerge. Their familiar name reflects the later age at which they arrive; it does not measure intelligence or maturity. Not all wisdom teeth need removal. The dentist considers position, disease, symptoms and whether the area can be kept clean. Teeth that remain in place still need monitoring. When your child’s timetable looks different Early and late patterns both occur. A child whose first teeth arrived later may also shed them later, but this is not a guarantee about each tooth. A missed birthday target alone cannot diagnose a dental problem. Discuss concerns at regular visits rather than waiting a fixed extra year. Earlier advice is sensible when the two sides develop very differently, a permanent tooth appears behind a baby tooth that is not loosening, a tooth was lost early, or a gap seems unusually prolonged. Pain, swelling, injury or signs of infection should not wait for a timetable comparison. A dentist can decide whether observation or an X-ray is appropriate; images are not automatically needed for every variation. Protect the teeth that are staying and the teeth still to come Arrange the first dental visit when the first tooth appears and no later than the first birthday. Six-monthly check-ups are common, but the dentist should set the interval according to the child’s needs and risk of decay. Brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste. For children under three, use a rice-grain-sized smear; from three to six, use a pea-sized amount. Supervise brushing and help clean where teeth touch. Ask the dentist about the appropriate routine as the child becomes more independent. Limit frequent sugary snacks and drinks, and remember the newly emerging permanent molars at the back. A changing smile still needs consistent care: the aim is comfortable eating and healthy teeth, rather than making every milestone happen on schedule. Twenty baby teeth usually give way during childhood and the early teens. Early teens commonly means twenty-eight permanent teeth, excluding wisdom teeth. The first adult molars may arrive without a tooth falling out. Let a loose tooth come out naturally and keep brushing gently. Routine dental visits matter even when the timetable looks typical. Which baby tooth usually falls out first? Often a lower central incisor, around six or seven, although individual order varies. Do all children lose their first tooth at six? No. Six is a common starting age rather than a deadline. Why does the tooth seem to have no root? Its roots are gradually resorbed as the permanent successor develops, allowing the baby tooth to loosen. Do adult molars replace baby molars? No. Premolars replace baby molars. Adult molars erupt farther back in the mouth. Can an adult tooth appear before any baby tooth falls out? Yes. First permanent molars often arrive behind the baby teeth around six or seven. Should I pull out a loose tooth? Let it fall naturally. If it hurts or causes problems, ask the dentist rather than forcing it. Should I rinse immediately when a tooth falls out? Manage any bleeding gently first and avoid vigorous rinsing or spitting. Follow specific aftercare if the tooth was extracted by a dentist. Should a thirteen-year-old have thirty-two teeth? Not necessarily. Twenty-eight excludes wisdom teeth, which generally appear later and do not develop in everyone. Do I have to wait a year before asking about delayed eruption? No. Raise concerns at a dental visit, and seek earlier advice for pain, swelling, injury or a marked difference between sides. What if a baby tooth is knocked out in a fall? Do not put it back. Contact a dentist urgently for injury assessment and advice about the developing adult tooth.

title: MiraLAX for children: understanding the treatment plan
description: Understand PEG 3350, child-specific prescribing, treatment stages, side effects, reported behaviour changes and the food and toilet routines that support recovery.
body: Painful constipation can turn into a cycle: a child avoids passing stool because it hurts, and holding it in makes the next bowel movement harder. MiraLAX is one brand of a medicine that can help soften stool. Using it for a child means following an individual plan, including the cause of the constipation and how progress will be reviewed. What MiraLAX does MiraLAX contains polyethylene glycol 3350, usually shortened to PEG 3350. It is an osmotic laxative: it keeps water in the bowel so stool becomes softer and easier to pass. It is sold as powder to dissolve in a drink. PEG is also called macrogol, and products with the same broad ingredient family are sold under other names, including GlycoLax and RestoraLAX in some markets. The brand name alone does not tell you whether two products have the same packet size or contain added electrolytes. Check the exact formulation with a pharmacist. PEG has been used in constipation care for many years; describing it as a new treatment does not explain its present evidence or suitability for your child. It is not an immediate rescue medicine. The US MiraLAX label describes a usual bowel movement within one to three days. A child who remains uncomfortable needs the agreed follow-up plan, not repeated extra doses because nothing happened that evening. Why a child’s prescription differs from the package The US over-the-counter directions are for adults and children aged seventeen and older. They describe 17 grams once daily, dissolved in four to eight fluid ounces of a beverage, for no more than seven days without medical advice. The liquid may be cold, warm or at room temperature. These are label details for that age group, not a recommended dose for a younger child. For children aged sixteen or younger, the label says to ask a doctor. Clinicians commonly prescribe PEG for childhood constipation using paediatric evidence and the child’s circumstances. Use outside a product’s licensed age range or duration is called off-label prescribing; that term does not by itself mean the medicine is unsafe or unstudied. A child’s dose depends on factors such as size, symptoms, formulation and the treatment stage. Ask for the product, amount, frequency, mixing instructions, goal and review date in writing. Do not calculate a dose by copying an adult capful, comparing internet recipes or assuming every sachet contains the same quantity. Clean-out and maintenance have different jobs A child may need a planned clean-out to remove a substantial stool build-up, followed by maintenance treatment to prevent another build-up. A clean-out can involve a different amount or schedule. Neither stage should be improvised from the other, and a bowel preparation for a test is another distinct situation. After painful constipation, a child may continue withholding even after the first soft stool. Maintenance may therefore need to continue for longer than a few days under supervision. Stopping too soon can allow pain and withholding to return. Ask when to review the plan and how to reduce treatment rather than treating the first bowel movement as proof that the problem is over. A short record of doses, stool consistency, discomfort and soiling can help the clinician adjust treatment. The aim is comfortable bowel movements. Repeated watery diarrhoea is not a sign that more medicine is needed. Give the prescribed product carefully Use the measurement and drink volume specified by the prescriber or pharmacist and make sure the powder dissolves. If the child refuses the drink, leaves some behind, vomits a dose or misses a dose, ask how to proceed rather than estimating an extra amount. Keep the medicine out of children’s reach. The MiraLAX label warns against mixing with starch-based thickeners used for swallowing problems. A child who needs thickened drinks should have the preparation checked by the pharmacist and feeding team. Also mention kidney disease, fluid or electrolyte problems, other medicines and any previous PEG allergy before treatment. If an excessive amount is taken, contact your local poison service or seek medical advice. Do not wait for symptoms before asking what to do, and have the product container and estimated amount available. Expected side effects and signs that need assessment Bloating, gas, fullness, cramping, abdominal discomfort, nausea and loose stools can occur. Too much laxative can cause diarrhoea rather than comfortable relief. Discuss a response that is too strong or inadequate with the clinician; increasing amounts without a plan can make the situation harder to assess. Vomiting, a progressively swollen abdomen or worsening pain should not simply be accepted as routine side effects. Significant diarrhoea can also lead to dehydration, particularly if the child cannot drink. Poor urination, marked tiredness or a very unwell appearance needs prompt advice. Allergic reactions to PEG are uncommon but possible. Itching, hives, new swelling or unusual symptoms after a dose need assessment. Breathing or swallowing difficulty, tongue or throat swelling, collapse or a rapidly worsening reaction requires emergency help and no further dose while the reaction is assessed. An old count of published cases cannot tell an individual family their current risk. What about reports of behaviour changes? Families have reported anxiety, irritability, changes in mood, anger, aggression and unusual behaviour while a child was taking PEG. Some reports use terms such as paranoia. Those reports are concerns to investigate, not an established list of effects that the medicine is known to cause. Symptoms occurring after a medicine do not prove the medicine caused them. Pain, poor sleep, illness, developmental changes and other medicines can affect behaviour too. Paediatric guidance supports PEG for constipation, while acknowledging that no medicine is completely risk-free and not every individual question has been settled. Take a noticeable change seriously. Record what changed, when it began, the amount taken and any other changes in health or treatment, and contact the prescriber promptly. If you suspect a harmful reaction, seek advice before another dose; severe or rapidly worsening symptoms need urgent care. Families can also report suspected adverse reactions through their local medicine-safety system. A useful discussion should neither dismiss a parent’s observation as a media story nor label the cause as proved without assessment. If you prefer another medicine, ask how to change the plan while continuing to treat the constipation. Look for the reasons constipation keeps returning Withholding is common. A child may fear another painful bowel movement, dislike a school toilet, feel embarrassed, feel rushed or avoid interrupting play. Stool then remains in the bowel longer and can become harder, reinforcing the fear. Soiling in underwear may be leakage around retained stool rather than deliberate misbehaviour. Low fibre intake, too little fluid, limited food choices and changes in routine can contribute. Constipation is not defined only by the number of days between stools: pain, hard stool and difficulty emptying matter as well. Less common causes include hypothyroidism, coeliac disease, disorders of bowel structure or nerve supply, and problems affecting the brain, spinal cord or muscles. Some medicines also contribute. Persistent symptoms, poor growth or constipation beginning early in infancy need clinical assessment rather than an assumption that the child is choosing not to go. Food, drinks and a calmer toilet routine Offer varied, age-appropriate sources of fibre. Examples include prunes, pears, apples, citrus fruit, kiwi, figs, spinach, oats, beans and lentils. Prepare them in textures your child can manage. These are options within a balanced diet, not a requirement to eat every food or a guarantee that one fruit will solve the problem. Provide normal adequate fluids. For a young baby, discuss feeding and stools before adding water, juice or home remedies. Increasing water or fibre far beyond normal needs does not necessarily resolve constipation, and food changes alone may not clear impacted stool. For a toilet-trained child, encourage brief, relaxed sits after meals, with feet supported on a step stool. Praise participation rather than demanding a bowel movement. Forced long sessions, threats and punishment can worsen avoidance. Ask whether school or childcare can provide a private, unhurried opportunity to use the toilet. If PEG is unsuitable or you would prefer another option, the clinician can discuss alternatives such as another osmotic laxative or a different treatment combination. Natural does not automatically mean safer, and untreated painful constipation also affects a child’s wellbeing. When to seek further help Arrange review for persistent or recurring symptoms, treatment that is not working, blood in the stool, poor growth or uncertainty about a dose. A clinician should decide whether examination or further investigation is needed; not every child with constipation needs the same tests. Seek urgent care for severe or constant abdominal pain, a markedly swollen abdomen, repeated vomiting, green vomit, dehydration or a very unwell child. Suspected bowel obstruction needs assessment before laxatives are continued or increased. Bring the treatment record and medicine packaging if possible. Use a written child-specific plan and the exact recommended product. Clean-out and maintenance schedules are different. Do not add extra doses because the effect is not immediate. Discuss symptoms and behaviour changes without assuming their cause. Age-appropriate food, fluids and relaxed toilet habits support medical treatment. Is MiraLAX approved only for adults? The US self-care label covers people aged seventeen and older and directs younger children to a doctor. Clinicians may recommend PEG for children using paediatric evidence and an individual plan. Is the adult capful my child’s dose? Not automatically. The label’s 17-gram adult/adolescent dose is not a default for younger children. Ask the prescriber or pharmacist for the exact amount and product. Does the drink have to be warm? The US label allows cold, hot or room-temperature beverages. Follow the specific child’s prescription and formulation instructions, particularly if drinks must be thickened. Should I give more if nothing happens today? No extra dose should be improvised.
