body: Hydranencephaly is a rare, severe condition present from birth in which almost all of the two cerebral hemispheres are absent and replaced by fluid. A specialist team can explain the diagnosis, plan care around the child’s needs and support the family through uncertain decisions. What the diagnosis means The cerebral hemispheres support thinking, voluntary movement and many sensory functions. In hydranencephaly, much of this tissue has been destroyed or disrupted during development. The skull and some deeper structures, often including the brainstem and cerebellum, remain; it does not mean every part of the forebrain or the entire brain is absent. Cerebrospinal fluid normally cushions the brain and spinal cord. Here it occupies the space left by missing tissue; it is not, by definition, a substance that blocks the brain. Hydranencephaly differs from severe hydrocephalus, where enlarged fluid spaces still surround a remaining layer of cerebral tissue, and from anencephaly. Signs may appear at birth or later Some babies initially have apparently normal reflexes or head size because lower brain structures still function. Others are affected from birth, or develop clearer difficulties over weeks or months. Head size can become unusually large when fluid accumulates, but a large head is not present in every case and cannot establish this diagnosis. Possible problems include seizures or involuntary movements, stiffness or altered muscle tone with limited movement, severe developmental impairment, vision or hearing difficulties, poor feeding and growth, breathing or digestive problems, and difficulty regulating temperature. New symptoms deserve assessment rather than being attributed automatically to the existing condition. Causes and questions about inheritance The exact cause is often uncertain. A leading explanation is interruption of blood flow to the developing cerebral hemispheres, including the internal carotid circulation. Prenatal infections and other vascular events have also been associated with some cases. A suggested exposure or association does not prove what caused an individual child’s condition or establish parental fault. Most cases are sporadic. Rare genetic disorders, including Fowler syndrome, can involve hydranencephaly, so inheritance and recurrence require individual specialist and genetic counseling. A team may consider targeted infection or genetic investigations and imaging in a future pregnancy. There is no proven general measure that guarantees prevention. How specialists confirm it Prenatal ultrasound, sometimes with detailed fetal brain assessment and fetal MRI, may identify the problem. After birth, cranial ultrasound and particularly MRI help show which structures remain. Specialist interpretation distinguishes hydranencephaly from extreme hydrocephalus, holoprosencephaly and other conditions with different anatomy and implications. Passing light through an infant’s skull, called transillumination, is a historical or supplementary observation, not a home test or a substitute for imaging. CT or blood-vessel imaging may be used for selected questions; contrast angiography and radiation-based scans are not automatic tests for every baby. Breathing, movement and everyday comfort Breathing problems need their own assessment, including possible swallowing-related aspiration, infection or impaired neurological control. “Reactive airway disease” is a nonspecific label for asthma-like symptoms before a clear diagnosis; it is neither a synonym for COPD nor an inevitable complication of hydranencephaly. Treatment depends on the actual problem. Severe movement and muscle-tone difficulties may overlap with cerebral palsy patterns. Physiotherapy, positioning, sensory assessment and comfort care should match the child’s needs. Constipation may be worsened by limited mobility, feeding difficulties or medicines; a pediatric bowel plan may include prescribed laxatives. Irritability may signal pain, muscle spasms, digestive discomfort, infection or raised pressure and should not simply be dismissed. Feeding, growth and water-balance problems Feeding can be difficult because of impaired coordination or swallowing. Nutrition and swallowing specialists can assess growth, aspiration risk, suitable feeding methods and whether tube feeding would help. These decisions should reflect safety, comfort and family goals; forcing feeds or changing the diet without advice can create risks. Central diabetes insipidus, also called arginine vasopressin deficiency, has been reported in some affected children. The brain’s hormone signal to conserve water is insufficient; this differs from a primary kidney response problem and from diabetes mellitus. Unusually large amounts of dilute urine, very wet nappies, thirst or dehydration need prompt assessment of fluid balance and sodium. Do not restrict fluids or start hormone treatment yourself; pediatric endocrine care individualizes treatment. Treatment supports needs; a shunt has limits There is no treatment that restores the missing cerebral hemispheres. Care may involve pediatrics, neurology, neurosurgery, rehabilitation, respiratory, nutrition and palliative-care teams. Palliative care can provide symptom relief and family support alongside other treatment, with decisions guided by comfort, expected benefit and the family’s values. If fluid pressure or progressive head enlargement causes problems, selected children may benefit from a shunt that drains fluid, often to the abdomen. This can relieve pressure but does not rebuild brain tissue or guarantee longer life or improved development. Blockage, infection and repeat operations are possible. Other fluid-control procedures are specialist options for selected situations, not universal alternatives or cures. Seizures and medication planning A neurologist can prescribe antiseizure treatment and an individualized emergency plan, including rescue medicine when appropriate and caregiver training. Calming routines may improve comfort but are not seizure treatment. A ketogenic diet is a specialist treatment for selected epilepsies, never a diet to start independently in a child with feeding or fluid-balance problems. Keep a coordinated medicine list and discuss benefits, adverse effects, constipation and interactions with the child’s team. Do not stop antiseizure medicines or add laxatives, sedatives or supplements without advice. Record episodes and their duration when it is safe; during a seizure protect the child from injury, put nothing in the mouth and do not offer food or drink before full recovery. When to get urgent help Seek emergency help immediately for a first seizure, a seizure reaching five minutes or lasting longer than the child’s usual pattern or emergency-plan threshold, repeated seizures without recovery, serious injury, blue or grey coloring, severe breathing difficulty or unresponsiveness. Follow the rescue plan while help is arranged; a first seizure or breathing problem is not a reason to wait five minutes. Contact the child’s team immediately for possible shunt trouble, including new vomiting, marked sleepiness or irritability, fever, redness or tenderness along the shunt, or rapid head change. New poor feeding, a tense or bulging soft spot, unusual temperature or possible dehydration also needs urgent assessment. If the child is very ill, difficult to wake or struggling to breathe, use emergency care. Follow any more specific team instructions promptly. Outlook and support for the family Hydranencephaly is life-limiting and usually causes profound neurological impairment. Death can occur before birth or in infancy, while some children live for years and occasional much longer survival is reported. Limited case reports and selected retrospective cohorts cannot provide a reliable personal deadline or prove that one procedure causes longer survival. Ask the team what is known and uncertain for this child. Families deserve clear conversations about pregnancy or birth planning, ongoing treatment goals, comfort, practical care, respite, psychological support and bereavement support when relevant. Qualified rare-disease organizations may help find peer support and research information, but a listing does not mean a suitable trial is available or a cure is imminent. The child’s comfort, interactions and the family’s priorities remain central. Specialist brain imaging confirms the anatomy; head size or a light test alone cannot diagnose hydranencephaly. Care includes breathing, movement, feeding, bowel, seizure and sometimes hormone needs, individualized for the child. A shunt can relieve selected pressure problems but cannot restore missing brain tissue or promise survival. Use the child’s emergency plan and seek immediate help for seizures, breathing difficulty, unresponsiveness or suspected serious shunt problems. What signs can hydranencephaly cause? Signs include seizures, altered muscle tone and movement, severe developmental difficulties, sensory problems, poor feeding or growth, and breathing, digestion or temperature-control problems. Some emerge later; head size alone does not establish the diagnosis. Is hydranencephaly always inherited? No. Most cases are sporadic and the cause may remain uncertain. Vascular injury is a leading explanation; rare genetic forms exist. Genetic counseling can discuss appropriate investigations and recurrence for the individual family. How is it diagnosed? Specialists use prenatal ultrasound and sometimes fetal MRI, or cranial ultrasound and MRI after birth. They distinguish other severe brain conditions. A flashlight test is not enough, and CT or angiography is reserved for selected questions. Can hydranencephaly be cured? Missing cerebral tissue cannot currently be restored. Treatment aims to relieve symptoms and support safety and comfort. Seizure medicines, feeding support and selected pressure-relieving procedures may help particular needs; none guarantees a cure or a fixed lifespan. Does every child need a shunt? No. Neurosurgeons consider symptoms, pressure, progressive head growth and the goals of care. Shunts can block or become infected, and may need revision. New vomiting, sleepiness, fever or shunt redness needs immediate contact with the care team. Why might a child pass very large amounts of urine? Central diabetes insipidus is one possible cause: too little vasopressin signal allows excessive water loss. It is not diabetes mellitus. Very wet nappies or dehydration require prompt assessment; do not restrict fluids or treat this yourself. When is a seizure an emergency? Get emergency help for a first seizure, one reaching five minutes or exceeding the usual pattern or care-plan threshold, repeated seizures without recovery, injury or breathing problems. Follow the prescribed rescue plan; do not wait five minutes for a first seizure or breathing difficulty. Can anyone predict exactly how long a child will live? No. The condition is severe and life-limiting, but experiences differ and available studies are limited. Some deaths occur before birth or in infancy; longer survival also occurs. The clinical team can discuss individual uncertainties, support and goals.

title: Phimosis: tight foreskin, care and warning signs
description: A foreskin that does not pull back can be normal in childhood. Learn about symptoms, scarring, clinician-led treatments and the emergency signs of paraphimosis.
body: A tight foreskin can mean different things at different ages. In a young child it often reflects normal development; in an older child or adult, pain, scarring or a new loss of retractability may need assessment. The aim is comfortable function and safe care, without forcing the skin or assuming everyone needs surgery. What is phimosis? The foreskin covers the glans, or head, of the penis. Phimosis describes tightness that prevents it from being drawn back over the glans. It is useful to distinguish normal childhood non-retractability from a narrowed, scarred foreskin that is causing a problem. At birth the foreskin is usually attached to the glans and does not retract. It separates and becomes more mobile over time. A child who has no pain and passes urine normally often needs reassurance and ordinary care rather than treatment. There is no universal third-birthday deadline Many foreskins still do not retract at five years, and some take until later childhood or puberty. Lack of retraction at three years alone does not diagnose disease. Children develop at different rates; another child’s experience is not a treatment timetable. Seek advice if the foreskin remains tight at the end of puberty, or if one that previously retracted becomes tight again. Symptoms and signs of scarring matter more than repeatedly testing whether the skin will pull back. Symptoms that deserve attention Arrange assessment for pain, swelling, itching, bleeding, a thick discharge or an unpleasant smell. Pain when passing urine, a weak stream, repeated urinary infections or painful erections are also reasons to seek advice. Skin colour changes may be less obvious on darker skin. The foreskin may balloon during urination in children. Ballooning alone, with a comfortable child and normal urine flow, does not necessarily mean obstruction or a need for circumcision. Persistent ballooning with a very narrow opening, weak flow or other symptoms needs review. An inability to pass urine, a swollen red penis with fever, or blue or black discolouration needs urgent assessment. Do not wait for a routine appointment if the child cannot urinate or tissue looks dark and unhealthy. Scarring, inflammation and skin conditions Forced retraction can cause tears and scarring, making the opening tighter. Inflammation or infection of the glans or foreskin can also contribute. Balanitis means inflammation of the glans; it is not the name for every cause of foreskin tightness. Irritation from soaps or trapped urine, fungal or bacterial infection, and some skin conditions need different approaches. Recurrent problems in an adult may lead a clinician to consider contributing conditions such as diabetes. Symptoms do not prove poor hygiene or a sexually transmitted infection. Lichen sclerosus, sometimes called balanitis xerotica obliterans (BXO), can cause white patches, fragile or itchy skin and scarring. It is a skin condition, not an infection, and is not contagious. White patches, new tightness or skin that repeatedly splits should be examined rather than treated as thrush without assessment. Gentle care without forcing the foreskin Wash the outside gently with warm water and avoid fragranced products or vigorous rubbing. There is no need to clean underneath a young child’s foreskin while it remains attached. Change wet or dirty nappies promptly; do not force the skin back to remove normal smegma. Once the foreskin moves back freely and comfortably, teach gentle cleaning and always return it over the glans afterwards. Stop if movement causes pain. Adults should likewise avoid forcing a tight or inflamed foreskin; ask a clinician about suitable skin care. How a clinician checks the cause The clinician will usually ask about symptoms and previous retractability and examine the penis and foreskin. This can help distinguish normal development, scarring, inflammation or a short frenulum, the band of tissue on the underside. Tests depend on the findings. A urine test, a swab or testing for diabetes may be considered, particularly for recurrent or severe problems. A swab is not automatically needed for every child; samples can be contaminated and results require interpretation. Creams, infection treatment and surgery A clinician may prescribe a topical steroid for selected symptomatic tightness and explain exactly where, how often and how long to apply it. Any movement of the skin should follow their instructions and remain gentle. Do not copy a twice-daily regimen or stretch a scarred foreskin without individual advice. Antibiotics treat appropriate bacterial infections; antifungal treatment may be used for a fungal cause. Neither is a universal phimosis treatment. Irritation or a non-infectious skin condition needs a different plan, and persistent symptoms should be reassessed. Circumcision removes the foreskin and may be recommended for pathological scarring or recurrent problems when other care is unsuitable or unsuccessful. A foreskin-widening procedure may be an option for selected children; it is different from simply removing part of the skin. Discuss benefits, risks, recovery and alternatives with the surgeon. Normal childhood non-retractability alone does not require surgery. Paraphimosis is an emergency Paraphimosis occurs when the foreskin has been pulled back and becomes trapped behind the glans, so it cannot return to cover it. Swelling can worsen the trapping and restrict blood flow. This differs from a foreskin that simply will not retract. Seek emergency care immediately if the retracted foreskin is stuck. Do not wait several hours for pain or colour change, and do not delay care to try lubricants, stretching or online reduction techniques. Clinicians can relieve the trapping, with urgent specialist treatment when needed. Comfort, prevention and follow-up Many children need no intervention, while symptomatic or scarred tightness is often treatable. Follow up if prescribed care does not help, the problem returns or urination remains difficult. A normal developmental variation in one child does not predict the same course in another. For adults, painful erections or intercourse deserve care rather than pushing through pain. Tightness itself does not establish your infection status. Use appropriate safer-sex measures, including condoms to reduce STI risk, and seek sexual-health assessment when relevant. Medical advice should address symptoms without blaming or shaming you. Normal childhood foreskin development is different from pathological scarring. Never force retraction or use age three as an automatic treatment deadline. Pain, recurrent infection, new tightness or changes in urine flow need assessment. Prescribed creams, infection treatment and surgery have different indications. A foreskin trapped behind the glans or inability to urinate requires urgent care. Is a foreskin that will not retract abnormal at three? Not necessarily. Many young children have a normally attached, non-retractable foreskin for years. Do not force it. Symptoms, scarring or persistent tightness beyond puberty are more informative than a third-birthday deadline. What symptoms can phimosis cause? Possible problems include pain, swelling, painful urination or erections, weak urine flow and recurrent inflammation or infection. Ballooning alone can be normal, but ballooning with symptoms needs review. Inability to urinate needs urgent care. What causes a foreskin to become tight? Normal development explains many childhood cases. Tears from forced retraction, inflammation, infection or scarring skin conditions can cause problematic tightness. Lichen sclerosus is a non-contagious skin condition, not an infection. When should we see a clinician? Seek advice for soreness, swelling, discharge, bleeding, urinary difficulty or painful erections. Seek emergency care for a retracted foreskin that is stuck, and urgent assessment for inability to urinate, fever with a swollen red penis or dark tissue. Can I treat it with a steroid cream myself? Use a steroid only with a clinician’s diagnosis and instructions. The product, application site and duration depend on the problem. Do not force stretching or assume that antibiotics, antifungals or an online cream schedule suit every case. Does every child need circumcision? No. Normal non-retractability usually needs no procedure. Surgery may be considered for pathological scarring or recurrent symptoms after assessment. Selected children may have other surgical options; discuss the individual benefits and risks. Can paraphimosis wait until tomorrow? No. A foreskin trapped behind the glans is an emergency because swelling can compromise blood flow. Get emergency care immediately rather than waiting for severe pain or colour change or trying home treatments.

title: Caput succedaneum: newborn scalp swelling and when to seek help
description: Understand birth-related caput swelling, how it differs from other scalp swellings, expected improvement, jaundice checks and urgent warning signs.
body: Caput succedaneum, often called caput, is swelling in the soft tissues of a newborn's scalp after pressure during birth. Once a clinician has confirmed uncomplicated caput in a well baby, it usually settles without treatment. Other causes of swelling can look similar, so a new or changing swelling should not be diagnosed from a photo or treated at home. When a newborn needs help now Tell the birth or neonatal team immediately about new, spreading or increasing scalp swelling. If you are at home, contact maternity or urgent paediatric care now for assessment rather than waiting for a routine appointment. Rapidly enlarging or widespread swelling can represent bleeding beneath the scalp, including subgaleal haemorrhage, which can become life-threatening. A swelling that crosses the skull's suture lines is not proof that it is harmless caput. Seek immediate emergency help if the baby is pale, blue or grey, unusually floppy, difficult to wake, breathing abnormally, having a seizure or otherwise appears seriously unwell. Poor feeding with drowsiness or worsening swelling is especially concerning. Jaundice in the first 24 hours also needs immediate hospital assessment. Do not wait for every warning sign, a head measurement, an app reply or the swelling to settle. For emergency care, do not drive yourself; ask someone to drive you and the baby or call an ambulance. Why caput can happen Pressure on the part of the head presenting through the cervix and birth canal can cause fluid to collect in the superficial scalp tissues. It is more likely after a long or difficult labour and can occur with vacuum- or forceps-assisted birth. This does not mean a parent caused it or that an assisted birth was unnecessary; the team can explain the circumstances of the birth. Early rupture of membranes or reduced amniotic fluid can be associated with swelling developing before delivery, sometimes seen on prenatal ultrasound. That possibility does not make every antenatal scalp swelling caput or prove a simple relationship between fluid amount and injury. Suspected leaking waters during pregnancy needs prompt maternity advice; parents should not try to prevent scalp swelling by managing fluid or labour themselves. What caput may look like Caput is generally noticed at birth or soon afterwards. The swollen area may feel soft or puffy and have bruising or discolouration. It can involve the presenting part of the scalp and extend across suture lines or the midline. These are clinical observations, not instructions to press the baby's head to see whether an indentation remains. Moulding is a different change: the flexible skull plates overlap during birth and can temporarily make the head look elongated or pointed. Moulding and scalp swelling may occur together. The skull's unfused joints allow growth and movement; uncomplicated caput itself is outside the skull and is not brain swelling. This does not rule out a separate injury or another cause of an unusual head shape. Caput, cephalohaematoma and subgaleal bleeding differ A cephalohaematoma is a collection of blood beneath the covering of a skull bone. It is limited by that bone's sutures, may become more noticeable after birth and usually resolves more slowly than caput. Bruising or this blood collection can contribute to jaundice. More than one type of scalp swelling can coexist, and clinical review determines what monitoring is needed. Subgaleal haemorrhage is bleeding in a larger space beneath the scalp's fibrous layer. It can spread across sutures, enlarge and cause substantial blood loss and shock. It is associated particularly with vacuum birth but can occur after other births too. Parents cannot reliably distinguish these conditions by touch, the shape of a lump or whether it crosses a line; suspected bleeding requires urgent specialist assessment. How clinicians assess the swelling A clinician asks about the birth and when the swelling appeared, examines the scalp and head, and checks the baby's colour, activity, feeding, breathing and circulation. A typical uncomplicated caput in a well newborn is often diagnosed on examination, without routine scans. After an assisted delivery or if findings are uncertain, closer observations may be appropriate. If bleeding, anaemia, infection, fracture or another problem is suspected, the team may arrange blood tests and selected imaging and monitor head size and vital signs. Suspected serious bleeding needs stabilisation and hospital treatment, not a delay while parents seek a scan themselves. Ask what diagnosis was made, what improvement is expected, who will review the baby and which changes mean you should return sooner. Usual care and expected improvement Confirmed uncomplicated caput usually starts decreasing soon after birth and often disappears within hours to a few days. The timing varies; it is not a reason to wait two or three weeks before reviewing a swelling that is growing, newly appearing or not improving as expected. Contact the baby's team promptly if the pattern differs from the discharge plan or you are unsure about the diagnosis. Caput generally needs observation rather than drainage or medicine. Do not squeeze, repeatedly press, massage, puncture or try to drain the swelling; these actions can injure the scalp or introduce infection. Handle the baby gently and support the head normally. Keep placing the baby on their back for sleep on a firm, flat, clear sleep surface; do not use a pillow, head-shaping device or side/prone sleeping to treat the swelling. Jaundice needs its own assessment Bruising can increase bilirubin as blood cells break down. Yellow skin or eyes need clinical advice, not a wait of several weeks. For a baby older than 24 hours with suspected, worsening or non-improving jaundice, seek urgent advice, usually the same day. Dark urine or pale, creamy or chalky stools also need urgent review. Colour can be harder to notice on darker skin; appearance alone cannot measure bilirubin. Jaundice before 24 hours, or jaundice with difficulty waking, not feeding, abnormal tone or movements, breathing difficulty, no wet nappies, temperature 38°C or higher or 36°C or lower, requires immediate emergency assessment. Clinicians measure bilirubin and decide about feeding support, repeat tests or phototherapy according to age, gestation and results. Prolonged jaundice also needs investigation, but thresholds such as over 14 days in term babies or over 21 days in preterm babies are not permission to postpone an initial check. For emergency care, do not drive yourself; ask someone to drive you and the baby or call an ambulance. Outlook, follow-up and useful records Uncomplicated caput generally resolves without lasting problems. That reassurance applies to the confirmed diagnosis and a baby progressing as expected, rather than to every large or swollen head. Continue the agreed newborn checks, feeding support and any jaundice monitoring. Seek advice about a persistent unusual head shape or new scalp changes even after the original swelling has improved. BeMama can help record the birth history, feeding and nappies, questions and the follow-up plan. It cannot diagnose caput, distinguish bleeding from fluid, measure bilirubin or confirm that a newborn is safe. A photo, recorded head size or reassuring app entry must not delay clinical care. If the baby is becoming unwell or swelling is increasing, contact care first. Caput is superficial birth-related scalp swelling; a clinician should confirm the cause. Confirmed uncomplicated caput usually improves within hours to a few days, without drainage or massage. Increasing swelling, an unwell newborn or jaundice need timely assessment; crossing sutures does not prove safety. Keep normal safer sleep and follow-up; BeMama can organise records but cannot exclude bleeding or serious illness. What are the symptoms of caput? It is usually a soft, puffy area of scalp visible at birth or soon afterwards, sometimes bruised and crossing the midline or sutures. Those features alone cannot distinguish it from every other swelling. Do not press the scalp as a home test; ask a clinician to assess it. What complications should I watch for? Bruising can contribute to jaundice, which needs its own assessment. A growing swelling or an unwell baby may have another condition, including serious bleeding. Seek immediate help for rapid enlargement, pallor, abnormal breathing, difficulty waking or other emergency signs rather than assuming caput is harmless. How long does caput last? It generally begins to shrink soon after birth and settles within hours to a few days. Follow the individual plan; growing, new or unexpectedly persistent swelling needs prompt review. Do not wait two or three weeks before asking for help about an unexpected change. Does it need treatment? Confirmed uncomplicated caput normally needs observation, not drainage, massage or medicines. A different diagnosis may require tests and treatment. Do not puncture or squeeze the swelling, and do not change to side or front sleeping or use a pillow to reshape the head. Does crossing a suture line mean it is definitely caput? No. Caput can cross sutures, but subgaleal bleeding can too and may be dangerous. Parents should not try to identify suture boundaries or test the lump. New, increasing or spreading swelling needs immediate contact with the neonatal or maternity team. Can I wait for jaundice to disappear? No. Suspected jaundice after 24 hours needs urgent clinical advice; jaundice in the first 24 hours or with an unwell baby needs immediate emergency assessment. Do not wait weeks or rely on a photo. Bilirubin testing and treatment decisions depend on the baby's age and circumstances. For emergency care, do not drive yourself; ask someone to drive you and the baby or call an ambulance. Can BeMama tell me that the swelling is safe? No. It can keep questions and follow-up records, but cannot diagnose the swelling, rule out scalp bleeding or assess bilirubin or the baby's wellbeing. Contact clinical care first for worsening swelling or warning symptoms.

title: When babies recognize their name: signs and when to seek help
description: Learn how babies respond to their name, gentle ways to support communication, how recognition differs from speaking, and when hearing or developmental checks can help.
body: Hearing your baby respond to their name can be a special moment. Recognition develops during the first year, before a child can necessarily say the name. Watch the pattern of communication over time, enjoy playful interaction and share concerns early rather than waiting for a fixed birthday. When name recognition develops Babies may attend to familiar voices and sounds before clearly responding to their own name. Research has observed early sensitivity to name sounds around 4–6 months, but that is not a deadline or proof that every baby understands the word in the same way. CDC lists looking when their name is called as a milestone most babies reach by 9 months. Its checklists describe skills at least 75% of children can do by the stated age; they support discussion, rather than diagnose a delay or autism. Siblings can develop differently. What a response can look like A baby may look toward you, turn, pause their activity, smile or make a sound. Looking at someone who is speaking may begin before name recognition; one reaction alone cannot prove exactly what the baby understands. Notice responses across ordinary, relaxed interactions. Being tired, absorbed in a toy or surrounded by noise can affect attention. Try a quiet moment when your baby is awake and comfortable, then give time to respond. Do not repeatedly test, shout, make loud sounds near the ears or force eye contact. Use their name in everyday conversation Say your baby’s name naturally during feeding, changing and play, such as “Sam, here is your cup.” Pause and respond to their sounds or gestures. Short, warm back-and-forth exchanges are more useful than drilling the name or demanding a particular response. Reduce background television or other distractions and join the activity your baby enjoys. A calm play space can make listening easier, but a response in one quiet trial is not a hearing test and a missed response is not a diagnosis. Play with voices and family pictures Try a gentle sing-song voice or a familiar song containing the name, without raising the volume sharply. Follow your baby’s cues and stop if they turn away, seem tired or become upset. These are enjoyable learning opportunities, not a treatment guaranteed to resolve a delay. Look together at family photos or a picture book and name the people, including your child. Point, describe and wait for their interest; they do not have to identify themselves in a photograph. Supervise awake play and use age-appropriate books or securely held pictures. Recognizing a name differs from saying it Understanding language and producing speech are different skills. A child may respond to their name well before saying it. Speech develops through sounds, gestures, words and conversation; the exact timing and ease of saying a particular name vary. Some toddlers begin saying names in their second year, but 18–24 months is not a universal deadline for saying their own name. CDC’s 3-year checklist includes saying a first name when asked, not a guarantee of a full name by age 2–3. Consider overall communication and seek advice whenever worried. A low-pressure name game for toddlers If your toddler enjoys it, ask “What is your name?” and model the answer gently. Leave a pause so they can join in, accept an approximation and move on when interest fades. Do not withhold something they need until they repeat the answer. A familiar short form may be easier to pronounce than a long name, if your family likes using it; changing the name is not medically necessary. Continue speaking naturally and sharing books, songs and conversation. A speech-language professional can suggest support suited to your child. When to request a hearing or developmental assessment Contact your child’s clinician if they are not responding to their name around the 9-month milestone, respond poorly to sounds, miss other milestones or lose skills. Raise any concern earlier; do not wait until the first birthday or assume every delay will disappear. For babies born early, ask how to use corrected age, commonly until age 2, while still reporting concerns promptly. Assessment considers hearing, understanding, gestures, social communication and overall development. A hearing test may be needed even if newborn screening was passed. Ask about developmental screening, an audiologist, speech-language assessment or local early-intervention services; referral routes vary by country. Does not responding mean autism? No single response or missed response diagnoses autism, and responding to a name does not rule it out. A 2017 study of infant siblings found an association between repeated missed responses and later autism, but its selected sample does not give an individual baby’s probability. Hearing, attention and other developmental differences also need consideration. Keep routine child-health visits and ask for a broader assessment when concerned. Developmental concerns differ from a suddenly unresponsive, seriously ill child: difficulty waking, breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour or a seizure needs immediate emergency help. Do not treat those signs as a name-learning issue. Most babies look when their name is called by 9 months; a checklist is a prompt for discussion, not a diagnosis. Use warm conversation, quieter play, gentle songs and family pictures without repeated testing or forced eye contact. Recognition comes before speaking for many children; the 3-year CDC milestone concerns a first name, not a guaranteed full name. Share hearing concerns, missed milestones or loss of skills promptly; do not wait for a birthday or use a single sign to diagnose autism. At what age do babies recognize their name? Early sensitivity to name sounds can appear around 4–6 months, but CDC’s practical milestone is looking when the name is called by 9 months. Watch the pattern and discuss concerns; an early response or one missed response is not a diagnosis. When will my child say their own name? Speaking is different from recognizing the name. Some toddlers use names in their second year, while CDC lists saying a first name when asked by age 3. There is no universal promise of a full name by 2–3 years, and concerns about communication deserve earlier advice. How can I help if my child does not say their name? Use the name naturally, share pictures and songs, and try a short “What is your name?” game if enjoyable. Model the answer, pause and accept attempts without pressure. Ask for speech-language or developmental advice if worried rather than relying on practice alone. When should I ask for professional help? Ask promptly for concerns about hearing, name response, other milestones or loss of skills. If name response is missing around 9 months, discuss it without waiting until the first birthday. The clinician can arrange hearing and developmental checks or local early support. Does a missed response prove autism? No. Hearing, attention, context and development can affect response. Autism assessment considers a broader pattern; neither one missed response nor one successful response can establish or exclude the diagnosis. Does passing the newborn hearing screen rule out a hearing problem? No. Continue monitoring responses to sound and communication. Discuss concerns with the clinician; an audiology assessment may be appropriate even after normal newborn screening. How does prematurity affect the timeline? Ask the clinical team about corrected age: chronological age minus the weeks born early, commonly used for development until age 2. It helps interpret milestones but is not a reason to dismiss concerns or postpone needed support.

title: Laryngomalacia in babies: noisy breathing, feeding and treatment
description: Learn what laryngomalacia means, how doctors assess noisy breathing, feeding and growth, when surgery helps and which signs need emergency care.
body: Laryngomalacia is floppy tissue above a baby's vocal cords that falls inward during breathing in. It commonly causes a high-pitched sound called stridor. Many affected babies feed and grow well and improve as their airway matures, but some develop serious airway or swallowing problems. A clinician should assess noisy breathing; the sound alone cannot establish the cause or show that a baby is safe. Breathing warning signs need immediate help Seek immediate emergency help if your baby stops breathing, turns blue or grey, becomes floppy or difficult to wake, has difficulty breathing, or has pulling in of the neck or chest. Do not wait for a pause to reach 10 seconds, for repositioning to work or for a routine specialist appointment. Sudden worsening, even in a baby already diagnosed with laryngomalacia, needs assessment rather than assuming it is the usual condition. Repeated choking, taking less milk, tiring during feeds, fewer wet nappies or poor weight gain need prompt clinical review; seek urgent help now if the baby cannot feed, appears dehydrated or unwell. Breathing distress, colour change or reduced responsiveness makes this an emergency. Do not delay care to record a video, time an episode or ask an app. What happens in the voice box and why The soft tissues above the vocal cords partly collapse into the airway during inhalation, creating stridor. This is different from wheezing arising lower in the chest, although parents may describe both as noisy breathing. Laryngomalacia is a common cause of infant stridor; infections, vocal cord movement problems, airway narrowing and other conditions can also cause noise. The precise cause is not fully understood. Development of the airway tissues and their nerve and muscle control may contribute. Symptoms usually become apparent at birth or in the first weeks. Reflux and swallowing problems can coexist, but reflux is not established as the cause of every case. Parents have not caused the condition by normal handling or feeding. Symptoms, severity and expected course The squeak is often louder with crying, agitation or feeding and sometimes when lying on the back. Other findings include regurgitation, coughing or choking during feeds, slow feeding, poor weight gain, chest or neck retractions, breathing pauses and colour changes. Aspiration means milk or food entering the airway; this may need a swallowing assessment rather than being labelled simple reflux. In mild confirmed disease, breathing is noisy but feeding, growth and oxygenation remain satisfactory. Noise may increase during the first months, sometimes around four to eight months, before improving. Many children improve over the first year and outgrow symptoms by about 18 to 24 months, but timing varies. A growth or breathing problem should be reviewed when it occurs, not left until that age. How doctors confirm the diagnosis The clinician asks about onset, breathing during sleep and feeding, colour changes and growth, then examines the baby. A paediatric ear, nose and throat specialist commonly confirms the cause with flexible laryngoscopy, also called nasopharyngolaryngoscopy: a small lighted camera is passed through the nose to view the voice box and its movement during breathing. The examination can also identify other explanations for stridor. It is often performed while the baby is awake in the clinic; the team explains preparation and comfort measures. A recording may help a clinician understand intermittent noise if safely obtained, but cannot replace examination or justify delaying urgent care. Additional tests are chosen for the problem Not every baby needs every test. When symptoms are severe, unusual or suggest another airway disorder, clinicians may select neck or chest X-rays, airway fluoroscopy or microlaryngoscopy and bronchoscopy. The latter examines the voice box and windpipe in an operating room under anaesthesia. The team should explain what question a test answers and its risks. Feeding concerns may lead to a specialist feeding review and a swallow study, such as a videofluoroscopic study or fibreoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES). Selected reflux concerns may warrant pH-impedance monitoring or an upper digestive endoscopy (EGD). These assess different functions; they are not routine requirements for every noisy baby or tests to arrange without the baby's team. Observation, feeding support and safer sleep For a baby with confirmed mild laryngomalacia, care often consists of planned review of breathing, feeds and weight. A feeding specialist may recommend pacing, an appropriate nipple flow, positioning during supervised feeds or a specific thickening plan after assessment. Do not add cereal or a thickener, alter milk concentration or force feeds yourself; the suitable product and method depend on the baby's age and swallowing safety. Even if noise is louder on the back, place the baby on their back for sleep on a firm, flat, clear surface. Do not raise the cot, add pillows or wedges, or use side or tummy sleeping as treatment. Awake, supervised upright holding after feeds is different from a sleep position. If back sleeping causes apparent breathing difficulty, obtain urgent clinical advice rather than improvising a sleep arrangement. Reflux medicines are not an automatic treatment Reflux symptoms deserve assessment, especially with discomfort, feeding problems or poor growth. Some babies with clinically significant reflux disease may benefit from prescribed treatment, but acid-suppressing medicine does not correct floppy airway tissue and should not be given automatically for stridor. Swallowing dysfunction can resemble reflux. Discuss the reason, expected benefit, side effects and review plan for any medicine already prescribed; do not start or change it yourself. Newer evidence questions routine acid suppression. A small randomized trial published online in August 2025, in the January 2026 journal issue, found no additional improvement in airway or reflux symptom scores from famotidine over feeding modifications alone in mild-to-moderate laryngomalacia without substantial reflux disease. Follow-up losses and small numbers limit certainty; it does not settle treatment for severe disease. Earlier observational research also raised concerns, but associations do not prove a medicine caused worse outcomes. When surgery may help A specialist may recommend supraglottoplasty for severe obstruction, significant breathing pauses or blue spells, persistent major retractions, poor growth despite feeding support, an oxygen requirement or heart or lung effects of inadequate oxygen. This is a clinical decision based on the whole baby, not the loudness of a squeak. Emergency symptoms need immediate care before an elective surgery discussion. Under general anaesthesia, the surgeon uses instruments through the mouth to divide or trim selected obstructing tissue above the vocal cords. The operation aims to improve breathing and feeding, but may not remove all noise; some children need further treatment. Hospital monitoring, airway support and recovery are individual. Ask about benefits, bleeding or swelling risks, persistent obstruction and swallowing or aspiration concerns. Swallowing safety should be reassessed after surgery. Follow-up and useful records Follow the team's schedule for weight checks, feeding review and reassessment of breathing, including after surgery. Report new choking, poorer intake, weight loss or worsening effort sooner. Ask whom to contact overnight and what to do during an emergency. Improvement with growth is common, but it is not a guarantee or permission to ignore changes. BeMama can organise feeding and growth records, questions, medicines and appointments. It cannot diagnose laryngomalacia, assess airway obstruction, oxygen levels or swallowing safety, or decide whether a baby needs surgery. A reassuring app entry or recording does not rule out illness. Contact clinical care first for warning symptoms. Laryngomalacia is a common cause of infant stridor, but noisy breathing needs clinical assessment. Many mild cases improve with growth; feeding, weight and breathing still need follow-up. Apnoea, blue or grey colour, breathing difficulty or reduced responsiveness need emergency help without a timed wait. Reflux treatment, feeding modifications and surgery are individual; keep normal safer-sleep practice and never rely on an app for airway safety. What causes laryngomalacia? Floppy tissue above the vocal cords moves inward during inhalation. Its exact developmental cause is uncertain. Reflux or swallowing problems may coexist, but do not explain every case, and ordinary parenting does not cause it. How is it diagnosed? History and examination guide assessment. A paediatric ENT clinician commonly uses a small flexible camera through the nose to watch the voice box. Other tests depend on airway, feeding or reflux concerns; the sound or a video alone is insufficient. Does it go away on its own? Many mild cases improve as the airway matures, often during the first year and by about 18 to 24 months. This is not a fixed deadline or a reason to wait with poor feeding, growth problems or breathing distress. When is surgery needed? Supraglottoplasty may help severe airway obstruction, significant apnoea or blue spells, major retractions, oxygen problems or poor growth despite support. The specialist weighs the whole situation and reviews swallowing safety afterwards. Not every child needs surgery. Should I give reflux medicine? Not automatically. Significant reflux disease may need treatment, but newer evidence does not support routine acid suppression for every mild-to-moderate case. Ask the prescriber about the indication and follow-up; do not start, stop or change treatment yourself. Can my baby sleep on their tummy because the noise is quieter? Do not use tummy or side sleeping, a raised cot or a wedge to treat noise. Use back sleeping on a firm, flat, clear surface. Apparent breathing difficulty in that position needs clinical advice, with immediate emergency care for distress or colour change. Should I wait ten seconds during a breathing pause? No. A baby who stops breathing, turns blue or grey, has difficulty breathing or is floppy or difficult to wake needs immediate emergency help. Do not wait for a timed threshold, a position change or a recording. Can BeMama confirm that my baby's breathing is safe? No. It can organise records and questions, but cannot assess the airway, oxygen or swallowing, or rule out serious illness. Contact the baby's team or emergency care first when warning signs occur.

title: Lissencephaly: diagnosis, development and care
description: What reduced brain folding means, why prenatal scans have limits, and how children with lissencephaly receive individual support for seizures, feeding and development.
body: Lissencephaly describes an uncommon difference in brain development in which the outer brain layer has fewer folds than expected. It is a structural condition present from early development, not a diagnosis made from head shape alone. Its cause, extent and effects vary; a single lifespan or developmental limit cannot describe every child. What a smoother brain surface means Normally, nerve cells move into organised layers as the fetal brain develops, and the cortex forms ridges and grooves. In classic lissencephaly, disrupted development produces absent folds, called agyria, or unusually broad ridges, called pachygyria. Pachygyria does not mean simply thickened grooves. The pattern may involve much of the brain or only part of it. Different causes can affect other brain structures and organs. Imaging terminology and severity descriptions help specialists explain findings, but a grade alone cannot predict a child’s future abilities. Symptoms and development are individual Possible features include delayed head control or movement, learning and communication difficulties, low muscle tone that may later become stiffness, seizures and problems feeding or swallowing. Some children have a small head, either at birth or as they grow; this is not required for the diagnosis. Hand, finger or toe differences can occur with some associated syndromes, rather than in every child. Vision, hearing, growth and motor skills also deserve assessment. Skills and support needs vary with the underlying condition; do not assume that all children stop developing at three to five months. Can it be recognised during pregnancy? Specialist ultrasound may raise concern, with fetal MRI sometimes adding information about the cortex or associated findings. A fetal brain normally has fewer visible folds earlier in pregnancy. A normal early scan therefore cannot exclude lissencephaly, and there is no universal week-20 or week-23 diagnostic rule. MRI is an additional specialist test, not a routine requirement for every pregnancy. Later assessment may show cortical development more clearly, with timing based on the clinical question. A family history or known genetic variant warrants genetic counselling; targeted prenatal testing may be possible, but results and imaging cannot always predict severity. Causes and related conditions need careful distinction Many forms have a genetic cause, including changes affecting PAFAH1B1 or DCX. A change may arise newly or be inherited, depending on the condition. Nerve-cell migration is a complex developmental process, not a single event confined to weeks 12–14 in which every affected cell simply stays still. Lissencephaly can occur on its own or in a syndrome. Miller–Dieker syndrome involves a chromosome deletion and additional features. Walker–Warburg syndrome is a distinct brain, muscle and eye disorder with a cobblestone cortical pattern; it should not be treated as identical to classic lissencephaly. Possible infection or vascular injury requires its own assessment, not an assumed explanation or parental blame. How diagnosis is established after birth A paediatric neurology team combines the child’s history, examination and development with brain imaging, usually MRI to characterise the cortex. Ultrasound or CT may be useful in particular circumstances, but not every child needs all three. EEG assesses suspected seizures; it does not replace structural imaging. Genetic testing is selected with counselling, sometimes including chromosome or broader gene testing. It can clarify the cause and family recurrence risk, although not every test finds an answer. The extent of agyria or pachygyria, associated changes and the clinical course matter more than assuming that most children share one grade or prognosis. Treatment supports health and participation No current treatment restores normal cortical folding, but active care can improve comfort, safety and participation. Seizure treatment is tailored by specialists to the seizure type and response. Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, communication support and help with stiffness or positioning are adapted to the child’s goals. Swallowing assessment, nutrition and respiratory care are important when feeding is difficult or food enters the airway. Some children need temporary tube feeding or a gastrostomy, chosen with the family rather than automatically. Monitor growth, constipation, vision and hearing. Enlarged brain fluid spaces do not by themselves mandate surgery; confirmed hydrocephalus needs specialist assessment and sometimes a drainage procedure. When to seek urgent help Call emergency services for a first suspected seizure, even if it has stopped, a seizure lasting longer than usual or more than five minutes when the usual duration is unknown, repeated seizures without recovery, or three or more seizures in 24 hours. Also get immediate emergency help for breathing difficulty, blue or grey lips or tongue, fainting or loss of consciousness or inability to wake the child. Do not wait five minutes with breathing trouble. For known epilepsy, follow the trained, individual emergency plan. New clusters of brief bending or jerking movements may be infantile spasms and need urgent assessment that day; NICE calls for specialist guidance and referral within 24 hours for suspected spasms under age two. New feeding deterioration, choking, reduced urine, repeated vomiting or a bulging soft spot also needs prompt urgent advice; severe illness or reduced responsiveness is an emergency. Prognosis is not one number Some children have profound disability and difficult-to-control epilepsy; others achieve more motor or communication skills. Aspiration, respiratory illness and severe seizures can shorten life, but a ten-year lifespan or a three-to-five-month developmental ceiling must not be applied to all lissencephaly. Some affected people live into adulthood. A 2026 study found different developmental patterns across genetic groups, but its selected cohort cannot predict an individual child’s outcome. More limited changes can have milder effects without guaranteeing near-normal development. Discuss the child’s own progress and complications with the team, revisiting goals as needs change. Planning care with the family Ask for a coordinated plan covering seizures and rescue treatment, safe feeding, respiratory symptoms, therapies, equipment, follow-up and who to contact outside clinic hours. Families may need practical assistance, respite and emotional support alongside medical care. Comfort-focused support can accompany active treatment. Genetic counselling can explain which tests are informative and whether relatives or a future pregnancy need assessment. Inheritance differs between causes, so a single recurrence percentage is misleading. Decisions should respect the child’s needs and the family’s preferences, without promising a cure or reducing the child to a scan result. Lissencephaly involves reduced cortical folding; its cause and effects vary. Normal early prenatal imaging cannot rule it out, and specialist testing has limits. Seizure, swallowing, nutrition and developmental care are individual and active. Breathing difficulty, inability to wake or concerning seizures need immediate emergency help; suspected infantile spasms need urgent assessment. Neither lifespan nor future abilities can be predicted by one universal number. What causes lissencephaly? Many forms result from genetic changes affecting brain development. Some arise newly and others are inherited. Related syndromes and other suspected causes need specific assessment; it is not evidence that a parent caused the condition. Can a normal pregnancy scan exclude it? No. Brain folds develop with gestation, and an early normal scan may not show a cortical difference. Specialist ultrasound, appropriately timed MRI and selected genetic testing may help, but no single scan or fixed week excludes every form. How is it diagnosed after birth? Clinical assessment and usually brain MRI establish the structural pattern. EEG helps investigate seizures, and selected genetic testing may identify the cause. Not every child needs ultrasound, CT and MRI together. Can treatment reverse the brain changes? Current care cannot restore normal folding, but it can address seizures, swallowing, nutrition, breathing, stiffness and communication. Therapies and feeding support are chosen for the child rather than a universal regimen. Will the child develop or live only ten years? There is no single developmental ceiling or lifespan for every form. Severe conditions may shorten life, while other people live into adulthood and achieve different skills. The cause, extent and complications guide individual counselling. Does every child need a feeding tube or surgery? No. Swallowing safety, growth and family circumstances guide feeding support. Some need a tube or gastrostomy. Hydrocephalus sometimes needs drainage, but enlarged fluid spaces alone do not automatically require surgery. When are seizures an emergency? A first suspected seizure, even if it has stopped, longer-than-usual event, over five minutes if usual duration is unknown, repeated events without recovery or three or more in 24 hours require emergency help. Breathing trouble, blue/grey lips or inability to wake require immediate help without waiting. Follow an established trained care plan for known epilepsy. What about brief repeated jerks in a baby? New clusters of bending or jerking may be infantile spasms, even when each is brief. Seek urgent assessment that day rather than waiting for a routine visit. If breathing, colour or responsiveness is affected, or emergency seizure signs occur, call emergency services immediately.

title: Anorectal malformations: an absent or misplaced anus in a newborn
description: Understand newborn anorectal malformations, urgent signs, associated conditions, genetic counselling, surgery and longer-term bowel and urinary care.
body: An anorectal malformation (ARM) means the anus or the lower end of the bowel did not form normally before birth. An absent anal opening is sometimes called an imperforate anus. Finding this in a newborn can be frightening, but a specialist team can explain the anatomy and plan treatment. A suspected blocked bowel needs urgent newborn assessment, rather than treatment for ordinary constipation at home. When a newborn needs immediate assessment Tell the birth or neonatal team immediately if an anal opening seems absent, the baby has not passed the expected first stool, or stool appears in urine or near the genital opening. Passing some stool through an abnormal opening does not show that the bowel is draining adequately. Do not wait for a routine appointment or try a suppository, enema or instrument to create an opening. Green vomit, an increasingly swollen abdomen, or a baby who is very unwell requires immediate emergency care. Call emergency services for breathing that has stopped or difficulty breathing, blue or grey colour, floppiness or difficulty waking. A bowel obstruction can cause dehydration, perforation and serious infection; an app, a photograph or a home examination cannot rule it out. What the different anatomical forms mean The anus may be missing, covered, too narrow or positioned abnormally. The rectum may end in a closed pouch or connect through a fistula, an abnormal passage. A perineal opening can lie toward the scrotum or the area near the vagina; other fistulas connect the bowel with the urethra, bladder or, less commonly, directly with the vagina. In a persistent cloaca, the bowel, urinary tract and vagina join into a common channel. This needs an experienced specialist team. These differences affect the operation and future bowel and urinary function. Parents cannot identify the exact type reliably from the appearance of the skin, and not every child has a fistula. Symptoms and how the diagnosis is made Many cases are identified during the newborn examination or because meconium, the first dark stool, does not pass normally. Occasionally an opening is present but too narrow or misplaced, and constipation becomes apparent later. A previously reassuring scan or a small amount of stool does not exclude a malformation. The neonatal and paediatric surgical teams examine the baby and decide which imaging is needed. Ultrasound, X-rays and sometimes MRI help define the bowel and surrounding structures. Selected contrast studies can clarify a urinary connection or the bowel before another operation. The tests and timing depend on the anatomy and the baby's condition; every baby does not need every investigation. Causes and genetic counselling For many babies, the cause is unknown and there is no other affected relative. ARM can occur alone or as part of a broader genetic or developmental condition. It is not evidence that a parent caused the problem. A family history or other congenital findings may prompt clinical genetics assessment and, when appropriate, testing. Dominant conditions can result from one altered gene copy; recessive conditions generally involve altered copies inherited from both parents. X-linked conditions have other patterns, and people with two X chromosomes can also have symptoms. These are general models, not a diagnosis of the cause of an isolated ARM. Generic 50% or 25% figures cannot be assigned to every family: recurrence counselling depends on the specific diagnosis, findings and family history. Associated conditions and VACTERL The team checks for associated changes in the kidneys and urinary tract, genital tract, spine and heart. Kidney ultrasound, heart ultrasound and spine assessment may be part of the work-up. An abnormal connection to the urinary system can increase urinary infection risk; any preventive antibiotics or additional tests are individually prescribed. Some children have VACTERL association: a combination involving vertebrae, the anus, the heart, the windpipe and oesophagus, kidneys or limbs. Not all features have to be present, and ARM alone does not establish VACTERL. Clinicians consider the complete pattern and other possible syndromes; most VACTERL cases do not follow a simple inherited pattern. Other causes of a blocked lower bowel Colonic atresia means part of the colon is missing or completely blocked; colonic stenosis is an abnormally narrow segment. These are distinct from an anal malformation and are not all inherited disorders. Narrowing can also develop after injury or inflammation. A visible anal opening therefore does not exclude a blockage farther inside. No stool, abdominal swelling and especially green vomiting in a newborn require immediate assessment. Examination and selected imaging distinguish the cause. Treatment of colonic blockage may remove the affected segment and join healthy bowel, sometimes with a temporary stoma. This is a different surgical plan from simply changing the position of an anal opening. Surgical treatment and a possible temporary stoma A paediatric surgeon plans treatment according to the malformation, associated conditions and the baby's stability. Some children can have a single repair; others need staged surgery. An anorectoplasty creates or repositions the anal opening and brings the rectum into the appropriate muscle area, while closing a fistula when needed. A temporary colostomy diverts stool through an opening on the abdomen into a bag while later repair is planned or heals. Specialist nurses teach stoma care and provide support. Closure is considered when the bowel and repair are ready. The number of operations, age at repair and hospital stay vary; neither one operation nor a fixed three-stage timetable applies to every child. Recovery, dilation and problems to report The team gives a written feeding, pain relief, wound or stoma care and follow-up plan. Some children need prescribed anal dilation to prevent or treat narrowing. This is only done after the surgical team decides it is needed and teaches the family the exact method and schedule. Do not improvise dilation, force an instrument or use constipation treatments to open an unassessed anus. Discuss procedure-specific risks, including bleeding, infection, narrowing, a recurrent fistula, injury to nearby structures, stoma problems or a leak where bowel is joined. Contact the team promptly for fever, worsening pain, wound or stoma changes, poor feeding or reduced output. Green vomiting or a swollen abdomen with an unwell child needs emergency assessment, including after earlier abdominal surgery: a later obstruction remains possible. Longer-term bowel, urinary and family support Repair creates an outlet but does not guarantee effortless continence. Constipation, soiling or difficulties with bowel control can need a personalised bowel programme, medicines or further treatment. Regular review helps families adjust care as a child grows. Toileting support should fit development and the specialist plan, without blame or pressure. Follow-up may also address urinary function, the spine, sexual health and future reproductive concerns, according to the child's anatomy. Families can ask about genetic counselling, emotional support, school care and transition to adult services. BeMama can help organise questions and appointments, but cannot assess a newborn's bowel opening, rule out obstruction or replace surgical follow-up. A suspected absent or abnormal anus needs immediate contact with the newborn team; green vomiting or an unwell, distended baby needs emergency care. The exact anatomy, associated conditions and baby's stability determine treatment; some repairs are staged. Do not use home suppositories, enemas or improvised dilation to open the anus. Prescribed postoperative dilation needs specific training. Genetic risk and future bowel and urinary function are individual; long-term support may be needed even after successful repair. What signs suggest an anorectal malformation? An absent, covered, narrow or misplaced opening, failure to pass the expected first stool, or stool emerging near the genitals or in urine can be clues. Tell the newborn team immediately. Green vomiting, a swollen abdomen or serious illness requires emergency care; some stool passing does not exclude obstruction. Why does it happen? Often the cause is unknown and the case is isolated. Sometimes there are other congenital or genetic findings. A specialist can assess family history and decide whether genetic testing or counselling is useful; a general inheritance percentage is not a personal recurrence estimate. Does it always mean the baby has a syndrome? No. ARM can occur alone. Clinicians check the heart, kidneys, spine and other structures because it can also occur with VACTERL or another condition. One finding alone does not establish the full diagnosis. How is an imperforate anus treated? Specialist surgery creates an appropriate bowel outlet and addresses any fistula. Some children need a temporary colostomy and staged repair, while others have a single operation. Timing and recovery depend on the anatomy and overall health. Can I use a suppository or widen the opening myself? No. Do not insert a suppository, enema or instrument into an unassessed opening. It can cause injury and delay treatment of a blockage. Postoperative dilation is different: use it only if prescribed and personally taught by the surgical team. Will surgery guarantee normal bowel control? No operation can guarantee a particular outcome. Many children do well, but constipation, soiling, urinary problems or other associated conditions may need continuing treatment. A supportive bowel programme and planned review can make a substantial difference. Which symptoms after surgery need urgent help? Contact the surgical team promptly for fever, increasing pain, poor feeding, reduced output or concerning wound or stoma changes. Green vomiting, a swollen abdomen with an unwell child, breathing difficulty or difficulty waking needs immediate emergency care. Do not wait for the next appointment or an app response.

title: Megalencephaly in children: brain growth, assessment and care
description: Learn how enlarged brain tissue differs from a large head, possible causes and symptoms, how children are assessed, and why treatment and outlook are individual.
body: Megalencephaly means an unusually large brain, not simply a large head. Some children have few difficulties, while others need support for seizures, movement or development. The cause, brain structure and the child’s progress matter more than head size alone. Megalencephaly is not the same as a large head Macrocephaly describes a head that is larger than expected for age and sex. Megalencephaly describes increased brain tissue volume. They may occur together, but a large head can also reflect fluid, skull or other differences; appearance cannot establish which is present. Brain overgrowth may be present at birth or become apparent as a child grows. Adult brain-weight cutoffs cannot diagnose an infant. Hydrocephalus means excess cerebrospinal fluid and is a different process, although it can coexist with brain overgrowth. Terms used to describe different forms Clinicians may describe isolated or familial forms with no other identified disorder, or forms associated with a genetic, metabolic or other condition. A family tendency to large heads can be reassuring when growth is stable and development is typical, but should not be assumed to explain new symptoms. Hemimegalencephaly affects one cerebral hemisphere, often with abnormal cortical development. It can cause early seizures, one-sided weakness and developmental difficulties. These descriptions overlap with modern genetic classifications rather than defining three rigid categories with identical outcomes. Possible signs and developmental needs Some children have few or no associated symptoms; brain size alone does not determine intelligence. Others have delays in head control, rolling, sitting, standing or speech; learning difficulties; altered muscle tone; or problems with the pathways controlling movement. Other findings can include body or facial asymmetry, weakness or paralysis, poor coordination, seizures and vision problems. Not every child has every feature. Fainting or unusual episodes should be assessed rather than automatically labelled seizures, and loss of skills deserves prompt medical advice. Why brain overgrowth can occur Some causes involve changes in how developing brain cells grow or divide; others involve abnormal accumulation of substances within brain tissue. Genetic pathways such as PI3K–AKT–mTOR can be involved. A genetic change may be inherited, newly arising or present in only some cells, called mosaicism. It is not evidence of parental fault. Depending on the findings, specialists may consider conditions such as PIK3CA-related overgrowth, Alexander disease, neurofibromatosis type 1, tuberous sclerosis or Sotos syndrome. Broader overgrowth conditions such as Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome may enter the differential assessment, but are not interchangeable causes of enlarged brain tissue. Sometimes the cause remains uncertain. Who is affected and how assessment begins Frequency varies by the underlying condition, and mild cases may be under-recognized. A fixed male-to-female ratio or a percentage involving microcephaly is not a reliable rule for an individual child. Microcephaly means a small head and is distinct from brain overgrowth. The clinician reviews pregnancy, birth, health, development and family history, examines the child and plots accurate serial head measurements on an appropriate growth chart, allowing for prematurity. Parents’ head sizes may help interpret a stable familial pattern. Rapid change, symptoms or developmental concerns require a different assessment. Imaging, blood tests and genetic evaluation Head measurements cannot show brain tissue volume or structure. When indicated, imaging can distinguish tissue overgrowth, fluid and structural abnormalities. MRI provides detailed brain images without ionizing radiation; ultrasound or CT may be appropriate in selected situations. Not every child needs every scan, and urgent imaging should not be delayed when needed. Developmental and neurological assessment guide selected blood, metabolic or genetic tests. Testing depends on the suspected cause; with some mosaic conditions, a normal blood result does not exclude the diagnosis and a specialist may discuss testing affected tissue. Genetic counselling explains the limits, possible results and family implications. Treatment is tailored to the cause and symptoms There is no single treatment that applies to all megalencephaly. Some children need observation, while others need antiseizure medicine, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech-language or feeding support, vision care and an individualized education plan. Associated hydrocephalus or other complications need their own treatment. Selected genetic conditions may have targeted treatment options under specialist care. For example, alpelisib is approved in the US for people aged 2 years or older with severe PIK3CA-related overgrowth requiring systemic therapy. That does not make it a routine treatment for every enlarged brain or a guaranteed reversal of neurological difficulties; benefits, risks and local access require careful review. Hemimegalencephaly, seizures and long-term outlook Difficult-to-control seizures warrant specialist epilepsy assessment and timely consideration of surgical evaluation. Selected children may benefit from disconnecting the affected hemisphere, but an operation is not appropriate for everyone. Teams assess seizure origin, movement, vision, development and the risks; referral does not commit a family to surgery. Outlook depends on the cause, brain abnormalities, seizure control and available support. Hemimegalencephaly can involve substantial disability, but a uniformly poor forecast overlooks individual variation and treatment. A small 2026 surgical series showed possible seizure benefit alongside significant risks; it cannot predict one child’s result. Discuss realistic goals, rehabilitation and continuing family support. Prevention, follow-up and urgent warning signs Many developmental or genetic causes have no known way to prevent them. Genetic counselling can discuss recurrence according to the specific diagnosis, even without a family history; not every genetic condition is inherited or carries the same risk. Keep agreed growth, developmental and condition-specific follow-up. New possible signs of raised pressure, such as a tense or bulging soft spot, repeated unexplained vomiting, abnormal downward-looking eyes, or new headache or unsteadiness, need urgent clinical assessment even if a change in head growth has not been documented. Seek immediate assessment for a rapidly changing head size with a tense soft spot, vomiting, abnormal downward-looking eyes, headache or new unsteadiness. A first seizure, new sudden weakness, difficulty waking, breathing difficulty or blue/grey colour needs immediate emergency care. Do not wait for the next measurement or routine appointment when the child is acutely unwell. For an emergency, call emergency services and ask for an ambulance; do not drive yourself. An enlarged head does not by itself prove enlarged brain tissue; fluid, structure, growth trend and development all matter. Symptoms and causes vary: some children have few difficulties, while others need coordinated neurological and developmental care. Testing and treatment are individualized; selected genetic therapies or epilepsy surgery are options for some children, not universal cures. Keep follow-up and seek immediate care for pressure symptoms, a first seizure, sudden weakness or reduced alertness. What causes megalencephaly? Causes include altered brain-cell growth and some genetic or metabolic conditions. Some genetic changes are mosaic or newly arising rather than inherited. The cause may remain uncertain; a specialist assessment is more useful than assuming one explanation from head size. How is it diagnosed? The team combines accurate head-growth measurements, examination, developmental and family history, and selected brain imaging. Blood, metabolic or genetic tests may help identify a cause. A large head or adult brain-weight threshold cannot establish the diagnosis in a baby. How is it treated? Care targets the cause and the child’s needs, including seizure treatment, movement and communication support, education and associated complications. Some specific diagnoses have targeted options, and selected drug-resistant epilepsy may warrant surgical evaluation. There is no single cure suitable for every child. Can it be prevented? Many causes have no known preventive measure. Genetic counselling can clarify diagnosis-specific recurrence and testing options, including when there is no family history. The condition is not proof that a parent caused it. Is it the same as hydrocephalus? No. Megalencephaly concerns brain tissue overgrowth; hydrocephalus concerns excess cerebrospinal fluid. Either can contribute to a large head, and they can coexist. Examination and appropriate imaging help distinguish them. Will a child necessarily have an intellectual disability? No. Head or brain size alone does not determine intelligence. Some children develop typically, while others have learning, motor, communication or other difficulties. Individual assessment and early support guide care. Does hemimegalencephaly always have the same outcome? No. It can cause serious seizures and developmental or one-sided movement difficulties, but outcomes vary. Specialist seizure care and selected surgery can help some children, with important risks and no guaranteed result. Which symptoms need immediate help? New possible signs of raised pressure, such as a tense or bulging soft spot, repeated unexplained vomiting, abnormal downward-looking eyes, or new headache or unsteadiness, need urgent clinical assessment even if a change in head growth has not been documented. A rapidly changing head size with a tense soft spot, vomiting, abnormal eye position, headache or unsteadiness needs immediate assessment.
