A first seizure, sudden weakness, difficulty waking, breathing trouble or blue/grey colour needs emergency care immediately. For an emergency, call emergency services and ask for an ambulance; do not drive yourself.

title: Osgood–Schlatter knee pain: activity, treatment and recovery
description: Learn why Osgood–Schlatter causes pain below the kneecap, how activity can be adapted, which comfort measures help and when knee pain needs urgent assessment.
body: Osgood–Schlatter disease causes irritation where the patellar tendon attaches to the growing upper shinbone. It often affects children during a growth spurt, especially with repeated running and jumping. Most improve as growth finishes, but a painful knee or limp should not automatically be labelled a growing pain. What happens at the growing shinbone The quadriceps muscles at the front of the thigh pull through the kneecap and patellar tendon onto the tibial tubercle, the bony prominence below the kneecap. Repeated loading can irritate its developing growth area, called an apophysis. This is different from disease inside the knee joint. Growth spurts and sports involving running, jumping or repeated knee loading increase the likelihood. Age varies with development; it is not confined to a fixed 9–14-year range or to boys. Less active children can also be affected. It is not a sign of poor parenting or a child being weak. Typical symptoms and reasons to check another cause Pain, tenderness and sometimes swelling are concentrated over the bump below the kneecap. Running, jumping, stairs, hills, squatting or kneeling may provoke it. One or both knees can hurt; severe pain may cause a limp. A clinician should assess unexplained, persistent or worsening symptoms. Do not assume every knee pain is Osgood–Schlatter. Pain waking a child at night, an unexplained lump, weight loss or ongoing pain at rest need prompt assessment. Hip problems can be felt at the knee. Sudden hip, knee or thigh pain, inability to walk or bear weight, an oddly angled leg or a hot swollen knee with fever or illness need immediate emergency assessment. Absence of fever does not rule out a serious problem. Diagnosis usually starts with history and examination A clinician asks about growth, sport, injury, pain timing and walking, then examines the tender area, movement and relevant muscles. They may examine the hip as well. A typical presentation can usually be diagnosed clinically, without routine scans or blood tests. An X-ray or other investigation is selected when injury, unusual findings or another diagnosis is a concern. A normal X-ray does not exclude every early infection or other cause. Do not delay urgent assessment while arranging a routine scan, and do not diagnose from a photograph or the location alone. Adapt activity instead of following a fixed deadline Reduce activities that trigger troublesome pain. Mild discomfort may be compatible with some activity after assessment, provided movement remains normal and symptoms settle promptly. Stop an activity that causes limping; painkillers should not be used to push through it. More severe symptoms may require a period away from sport under a clinician’s plan. There is no universal return after one or two days. Use symptoms, walking and function during activity and afterwards to guide a gradual return, with the care team if needed. Lower-impact options such as comfortable swimming or cycling may help maintain activity. Reduce the load again if pain or a limp returns, including later that day or the next day. Rehabilitation, footwear and protection A physiotherapist can tailor gradual strengthening and flexibility work, including the quadriceps and hamstrings and, where appropriate, the calf. Warm up and stretch gently as advised; do not force a painful stretch or copy an intense routine. Progress depends on the child’s symptoms and control. Comfortable, well-fitting footwear is sensible. Orthotic inserts are not automatically necessary; ask about a specific foot or footwear concern before buying them. A fitted patellar strap may help selected children, while a pad or sleeve can cushion direct kneeling or contact. Supports do not make painful limping safe or replace rehabilitation. Cold packs, warmth and medicines A towel-wrapped cold pack for a short period, often around 10–15 minutes after activity, may ease discomfort. Follow the product and clinician’s instructions, check the skin and stop if it becomes painful or irritated. Never put ice directly on skin or leave a pack on during sleep. Frequent fixed icing schedules are not essential for every child. Gentle warmth may be comfortable before prescribed rehabilitation, but avoid burns and do not heat a newly hot, red or swollen knee instead of seeking assessment. Paracetamol or ibuprofen may be suitable after checking the child’s age, weight, product and health conditions with a pharmacist or clinician. Follow the label; do not duplicate ingredients, combine NSAIDs or alternate medicines without professional advice. Ibuprofen may be unsuitable with dehydration or some kidney, stomach or allergy problems. Ask for advice if medicine is needed beyond a few days. Recovery varies and a bump may remain Symptoms often fluctuate over months and improve as the growth area matures. There is no guaranteed resolution at a particular birthday, no fixed 14–18-year endpoint and no promise that every symptom is gone when growth stops. A painless prominence may remain; some people find kneeling on it uncomfortable. Most children are managed without surgery. Persistent pain, recurrent limitation or symptoms after growth warrant reassessment rather than simply waiting indefinitely. Surgery is rarely considered for selected persistent problems after appropriate assessment. Recovery and return to sport should be individualized; a visible bump alone does not mean treatment has failed. Know when to seek help Arrange review for unexplained limping, worsening or persistent pain, night pain, a new lump or failure to improve with the agreed plan. Seek immediate emergency assessment for sudden hip, knee or thigh pain, inability to bear weight, deformity, significant injury or a hot swollen joint with fever or an unwell child. A joint infection is an emergency, and not every child has all warning signs. Call emergency services for confusion, breathing difficulty, blue, grey or blotchy skin, fainting or loss of consciousness or difficulty waking. Do not wait for every sign or a specific temperature. Rest, cold packs and medicine should never delay assessment of these symptoms. Osgood–Schlatter usually causes tenderness at the bony bump below the kneecap during growth; one or both knees may hurt. Diagnosis is usually clinical; imaging is selected for a specific concern rather than routine for every child. Adapt activity to symptoms and stop if the child limps. Return gradually rather than after a fixed number of days. Gentle tailored rehabilitation, selected supports and safe short cold-pack use may help; medicines need child-specific advice. Most improve with growth, but persistent pain needs review. Sudden hip, knee or thigh pain, inability to bear weight or an unwell child with a hot swollen joint need immediate emergency assessment. Is Osgood–Schlatter a lifelong disease? Most children improve as the growth area matures. A bump can remain and kneeling may occasionally be uncomfortable. Persistent pain should be reviewed; neither lifelong pain nor complete recovery by a fixed age should be assumed. What symptoms are typical? Tenderness, pain and swelling over the bony bump below the kneecap, often worse with running, jumping, stairs, hills or kneeling. One or both sides can be affected. A limp or an unusual symptom deserves assessment rather than an automatic diagnosis. Does my child need an X-ray? Usually not for a typical presentation after examination. A clinician may request imaging or other tests if injury or another cause is suspected. Do not wait for a scan when hip, knee or thigh pain starts suddenly, the child cannot bear weight or a joint is hot and swollen with illness. Must all sports stop? Not always. Comfortable activity with normal movement may be possible, but stop activity that causes a limp or troublesome pain. More severe symptoms may need a longer break. Swimming or cycling can be options if comfortable; follow the individual plan. Can sport restart after one or two days? There is no universal deadline. Return gradually when symptoms and function allow, monitoring during activity, afterwards and the next day. A returning limp or increased pain means the load needs reducing and sometimes reassessment. Do special insoles, straps or stretches cure it? No single support guarantees recovery. Insoles are not routinely necessary; a selected strap or protective pad may help comfort. A physiotherapist can tailor gentle stretching and strengthening. Do not force exercises through pain or rely on a support to continue limping. How can pain be eased safely? Relative rest and a towel-wrapped cold pack for a short period may help. Never apply ice directly, sleep with a pack or burn the skin with heat. Check child-specific paracetamol or ibuprofen instructions and suitability; do not duplicate, combine or alternate medicines without professional advice, or use them to mask pain during sport. When is knee pain an emergency? Sudden hip, knee or thigh pain, inability to walk or bear weight, deformity, significant injury or a hot swollen joint with fever or illness need immediate emergency assessment. Confusion, breathing difficulty, blue or grey skin, fainting or loss of consciousness or difficulty waking also need emergency help. Do not wait for a specific temperature or every warning sign.

title: Sever’s disease: heel pain in growing children
description: Understand growth-related heel pain, warning signs, diagnosis and a practical plan for activity, footwear, pain relief and returning to sport.
body: Sever’s disease, or calcaneal apophysitis, is a common cause of heel pain while children are growing. It usually settles as the heel matures, but a painful heel or new limp still needs assessment. A tailored plan can keep a child moving without asking them to push through pain. Why the growing heel can hurt The Achilles tendon connects the calf muscles to the heel bone. Its attachment includes a growing area called an apophysis. During growth, this area is more sensitive to repeated impact and tendon pull. Running and jumping can irritate it, particularly during growth spurts. The exact contribution of different factors varies. Sever’s commonly occurs around ages 8–14, although growth timing differs. It can affect girls and boys and sometimes less active children, too. The name does not mean an infection or a progressive destructive disease. Confirmed Sever’s generally stops recurring after the heel growth area has closed. Typical symptoms and reasons to seek help Pain at the back or underside of one or both heels often increases during running or jumping, or afterward, and eases with rest. There may be tenderness, mild swelling, morning stiffness, limping or toe walking to avoid loading the heel. A normal-looking heel does not exclude the condition. Arrange assessment for a new unexplained limp, recurring pain or symptoms limiting usual activities. Seek urgent care if a child cannot walk or bear weight, has severe pain after an injury, or develops fever with a hot, swollen or very painful limb. Serious infection can occur without fever. Pain waking the child at night, pain at rest, persistent swelling, unexplained weight loss or marked tiredness also needs prompt medical review. Do not assume these are ordinary growing pains or wait weeks for them to settle. Training, footwear and other contributors Look for a change in total load: overlapping sports seasons, joining a team with several practices and matches, a tournament with many games, a new sport or a return after a break. Football, netball, running and gymnastics can all stress the heel. New shoes, a low heel, hard or changed surfaces, barefoot sport and poorly supportive sandals may also alter the load. Foot posture, including flatter feet, calf flexibility, height and body mass may contribute, but none alone diagnoses Sever’s or proves why one child hurts. It can occur at different body sizes. Focus on comfortable movement, appropriate footwear and manageable training; avoid blame or making weight loss a condition of receiving care. How clinicians make the diagnosis A clinician asks about the pain, growth, activity changes, injuries and general health, then examines the foot, ankle and gait. They may gently press the heel and assess calf flexibility and nearby joints. A painful heel squeeze can support the assessment but is not a reliable home diagnostic test. Do not repeatedly provoke pain or force a child to hop to prove a diagnosis. X-rays are not usually needed for a typical presentation: the growing heel can look similar in children with and without symptoms. Imaging may be appropriate for injury, unusual features, persistent symptoms or another suspected cause. A normal X-ray does not exclude every problem, particularly early bone infection; reassessment matters if the course does not fit. Keep moving with an adjusted activity plan Start by reducing activities that aggravate pain, rather than automatically stopping all movement. Swimming or cycling may be comfortable alternatives. A child with significant pain or a limp should pause painful running and jumping and obtain advice. Mild symptoms without a limp may allow some sport with an agreed plan; do not use painkillers to force participation. Gradually rebuild activity as comfortable walking and function improve, monitoring symptoms later that day and the next morning. Avoid sudden jumps in training or several full games on return. A short period in a boot or cast is sometimes considered for severe symptoms under supervision. Complete long-term unloading is not the usual goal: appropriate load and conditioning are part of recovery. Shoes, heel supports and exercise Well-fitting supportive shoes, heel cushions or a clinician-selected heel raise may reduce discomfort. Shoe inserts or taping can help selected mechanical problems; they are not guaranteed cures or a requirement for every child. A physiotherapist or podiatrist can assess footwear and foot control and advise whether a support is worth trying. Exercise needs to match the stage of symptoms. During a painful flare, avoid forceful stretching, heel drops over a step and repeated painful hopping or jumping. Once pain improves, gentle calf stretching and progressive strengthening may help; ask for the technique and amount suited to your child. Guidance that supports later stretching does not mean stretching through acute heel pain is helpful. Stop exercises that worsen symptoms and review the plan. Cold packs and medicines for comfort A cold pack wrapped in a towel may soothe the heel for about 10–15 minutes after activity. Protect the skin and do not put ice directly on it. Resting or elevating the leg after a flare can also help. These measures relieve symptoms; they do not replace assessment for warning signs. Ask a pharmacist or clinician about an age-appropriate pain medicine such as paracetamol or ibuprofen, following the product or prescription directions. Ibuprofen is unsuitable for some children, including certain allergy, asthma or kidney situations; seek advice if the child is unwell or at risk of dehydration. Do not combine medicines or NSAIDs without advice, and do not give aspirin under 16 unless specifically prescribed. If pain relief needs to increase or is still needed after a few days, seek review. Recovery, flare-ups and useful records Improvement is variable: some children feel better fairly quickly, while others need weeks or months of changes. There is no guaranteed one-to-two-week cure or fixed two-year countdown. Flare-ups can occur during growth, changes in sport, intensity, shoes or surfaces. The outlook for confirmed Sever’s is usually good, but persistent or changing symptoms should be reconsidered. A simple record of morning pain and stiffness, activity type and duration, limping, footwear changes and growth can help the child and clinician adjust the plan. Agree when to review and how to return to sport; records can reveal patterns but cannot prevent every flare. A limp lasting more than a week deserves reassessment, sooner if it worsens or warning signs appear. Other causes of a painful heel Other possibilities include bursitis, irritation of a fluid-filled cushioning sac from rubbing or overuse; posterior ankle impingement after a sprain or repeated pointed-toe positions; and a stress fracture from repeated loading. A direct fall onto the heel can cause an acute fracture. These need different management and cannot be separated reliably by a symptom checklist. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis can cause ongoing joint pain, swelling and stiffness. Bone or joint infection, and rarely a tumor, must also be considered when symptoms are atypical or the child is unwell. Most heel pain is not caused by a tumor, but a persistent lump, night pain or unexplained systemic symptoms should not be dismissed. A clinician can decide what examination, tests or referral is needed. Sever’s is a common irritation of the growing heel, but not every limp or painful heel is Sever’s. Inability to bear weight, serious injury or signs of infection need urgent assessment. Adjust painful activity and footwear, then rebuild movement gradually; exercises should suit the recovery stage. Recovery and recurrence vary. Seek reassessment for persistent, worsening or unusual symptoms. What is Sever’s disease? It is irritation of the growth area at the back of the heel, also called calcaneal apophysitis. It commonly affects growing children and usually stops recurring once that area has matured. What symptoms are typical? Activity-related heel pain, tenderness, limping, morning stiffness or toe walking may affect one or both feet. An inability to bear weight, severe injury or an unwell child needs urgent evaluation. Do flat feet or body size cause it? Foot posture, growth, body mass, footwear and activity load may contribute together, but no single factor proves the cause. Children of different sizes can be affected; care should focus on comfort and function without blame. How is it diagnosed? Usually through the history and examination. An X-ray is not routinely required for typical Sever’s, but imaging may help investigate an injury or unusual symptoms. A heel squeeze alone is not a diagnosis. Must a child stop every sport? Not necessarily. Reduce painful activities, especially when there is a limp, and agree a suitable plan. Comfortable lower-impact movement may continue. Return to running and jumping gradually rather than pushing through pain. Should we stretch the calf? Gentle stretching may help after the painful flare improves, but forceful stretches or heel drops can aggravate an acutely sore heel. A physiotherapist can advise when and how to exercise. Will it be gone in two weeks? There is no fixed recovery time. Some symptoms improve quickly; others last longer or recur during growth. Arrange review if pain persists, changes or limits walking, and urgently for warning signs. Could the pain be something else? Yes. Injury, bursitis, impingement, stress fracture, arthritis or infection can resemble heel pain attributed to growth; tumors are uncommon. New or unexplained symptoms need clinical assessment rather than self-diagnosis.

title: Klippel–Feil syndrome: fused neck vertebrae, diagnosis and care
description: Understand congenital neck-vertebra fusion, variable signs and genetic causes, associated conditions, selected tests, safe activity, treatment and follow-up into adulthood.
body: Klippel–Feil syndrome (KFS) involves two or more neck vertebrae that joined abnormally during development before birth. It can affect a child with an obvious short or stiff neck, or be discovered much later. Appearance alone cannot establish or exclude the diagnosis. Care depends on the fusion pattern, spinal stability, nerve function and any associated conditions, rather than a single standard operation or a requirement to have every classic sign. What congenital neck fusion means Vertebrae are the bones of the spine; the cervical vertebrae are in the neck. In KFS, some did not separate normally during early development. This is congenital fusion, not the same as a fusion operation or stiffness acquired after an injury. Fusion can involve one pair or several levels, and abnormalities may also occur in the chest or lower spine. A short neck, a low hairline at the back of the head and restricted neck movement are classic features, but fewer than half of affected people have all three. Some have few outward signs or no symptoms. The number and position of fused bones matter more than judging neck length from a photograph, and an ordinary-looking neck does not rule KFS out. When it is found and what causes it The vertebral difference is present from birth even if discovered in an older child or adult. Limited movement, an unusual spinal curve, pain or an incidental scan can lead to assessment; sometimes an injury brings a previously unrecognized problem to attention. Do not wait for an accident to investigate persistent concerns, and do not assume every child with a tilted head has KFS. Some cases involve variants in genes such as GDF6, GDF3 or MEOX1; other genetic causes also exist. Many people have no identified cause or family history. GDF6- or GDF3-related forms may be autosomal dominant, whereas MEOX1-related forms may be autosomal recessive. These patterns are not a personal recurrence estimate without a diagnosis and genetic counselling. A negative genetic result does not exclude the clinical and imaging diagnosis; the condition is not evidence that a parent caused it. Neck, spine and neurological features Possible problems include neck pain, headaches, limited movement, torticollis with the head tilted or turned, scoliosis or kyphosis, rib differences and an elevated underdeveloped shoulder blade called Sprengel deformity. Hand differences can include joined fingers or an underdeveloped thumb. The shoulder blade is positioned abnormally high. Not every person has every feature. Some people have spinal canal narrowing, instability near fused segments or pressure on nerves or the spinal cord. Associated neural tube differences can include spina bifida, involving incomplete closure of the neural tube during pregnancy. Mirror movements, or synkinesia, mean one hand involuntarily copies the other. New weakness, numbness, loss of coordination or walking changes require assessment; a change should not automatically be attributed to a familiar diagnosis. Other body systems may need checking KFS can occur with hearing loss, eye or facial differences, cleft palate, and heart or kidney abnormalities. Breathing difficulties may relate to associated chest, spine, airway or other conditions and need their own assessment. It may also appear as part of another syndrome, including conditions within the Goldenhar or hemifacial microsomia spectrum; the exact combination varies. A team therefore looks beyond the neck and asks about hearing, vision, breathing, heart symptoms, urinary problems and daily function. These are possible associations, not a prediction that a child has every organ problem. Screening and referrals should reflect the examination and specialist plan. Explain symptoms and previous diagnoses without blaming a parent or assuming one cause for every finding. Diagnosis and the choice of tests Assessment begins with medical and family history, an examination of neck movement and alignment, and neurological and functional checks. Spine radiographs can show the fusion and other curves. MRI provides information about the spinal cord, nerves and surrounding tissues; CT can clarify bone anatomy but uses radiation. Specialists select studies for a question, rather than requiring every scan in every child. Genetic testing may use blood or saliva and can help explain a cause or inheritance when appropriate. Kidney ultrasound, cardiac assessment or echocardiography and hearing tests may identify associated conditions. Standing low-dose biplanar imaging such as EOS can help assess spinal alignment where available; it is not essential everywhere. Any movement views of the neck must be clinician-directed: do not force bending at home to test stability. Treatment supports function and treats complications There is no medicine that reverses congenital fusion, but that does not mean nothing can be done. A child without significant symptoms may need monitoring and an activity plan. Pain care, tailored physiotherapy or occupational therapy, selected supports or bracing for a spinal curve, hearing care and management of heart, kidney or other conditions can improve function and comfort. Surgery is considered individually for problems such as instability, spinal cord or nerve compression, a progressive curve or persistent symptoms despite appropriate care. Options may include decompression, stabilization or treatment of a related hand, palate or shoulder abnormality. Growing rods or fusion may be relevant to selected spinal deformities, not every KFS neck. Decisions consider anatomy, severity, age and growth; surgery does not guarantee normal movement or remove all future risks. Activity and procedures need a neck-safety plan Ask the spine team which sports and school activities are suitable. Contact sports, falls, tumbling or extreme neck extension can be unsafe with certain fusion patterns or instability; restrictions depend on individual risk. Encourage appropriate participation rather than assuming every child must avoid all exercise. A physiotherapist should know the diagnosis and imaging findings before prescribing exercises; avoid forceful spinal manipulation or attempts to stretch fused bones apart. Tell dentists, surgeons and anaesthesia staff about KFS before procedures, including any known instability, previous surgery and heart or airway conditions. Positioning and airway management may need special planning. Keep relevant reports and the team's precautions available. Do not use an app, a symptom-free day or a generic exercise video to decide that neck manipulation or a contact sport is safe. Follow-up through growth and adulthood Ongoing review can identify changes in spinal alignment, pain, function or associated conditions as a child grows and later as an adult. The team may include orthopaedics, neurosurgery or neurology, rehabilitation, physiotherapy and occupational therapy, with cardiology, kidney or urinary specialists, respiratory care, audiology, eye care or craniofacial services when needed. Not every person needs every specialist. After surgery, follow the operating team's timetable for wound review, imaging, rehabilitation and activity clearance. Early postoperative checks followed by later reviews and longer-term monitoring are common, but exact one-to-two-week, three-month, six-month or annual schedules are not universal instructions. Bring new symptoms forward rather than waiting for the next routine visit. Arrange transition to adult care and school or work adjustments; prognosis is individual, and many people can function well with appropriate support. Symptoms that should not wait Seek immediate emergency care for sudden weakness or paralysis, new inability to walk, loss of bladder or bowel control with neurological symptoms, or serious difficulty breathing or swallowing. Weakness or numbness after a head, neck or back injury also needs emergency assessment. Significant new neck pain after trauma warrants prompt urgent assessment, especially with known instability; do not test the neck by repeated movement or drive yourself with neurological symptoms. If a spinal injury is suspected, call emergency services and follow the dispatcher's instructions; avoid unnecessary movement or attempts to straighten the neck. Airway and breathing emergencies take priority and require immediate first-aid guidance. New or worsening hand clumsiness, balance change, numbness or limb weakness may signal spinal cord pressure and should be assessed urgently, even without an accident. A symptom diary may help explain a change but must not delay care. KFS is congenital joining of neck vertebrae; the short-neck, low-hairline and restricted-movement triad is not required. Several genetic causes are possible, many remain unexplained, and a negative gene test does not exclude KFS. Family risk needs individual counselling. Care checks spinal stability, nerve function and associated hearing, heart, kidney or other differences; tests and treatments are selected for the person. Use a specialist activity and procedure plan, avoid forceful neck manipulation, and continue appropriate follow-up into adulthood. Sudden weakness, paralysis, major walking change or breathing difficulty, and neurological symptoms after injury require immediate emergency care. How does Klippel–Feil syndrome develop? Some neck vertebrae fail to separate normally before birth. Several genes can be involved, not only GDF6 or GDF3, and many cases have no identified cause. This does not establish parental blame or an individual inheritance risk. When is it diagnosed? It may be recognized at birth, during childhood or much later. Mild outward signs can go unnoticed. Examination and appropriate imaging are important; neck appearance alone cannot confirm or exclude it. What is the main cause? The exact cause is often unknown. Variants in GDF6, GDF3, MEOX1 and other genes explain some cases; genetic counselling interprets testing and family history. A negative result does not rule out the clinical condition. Is there treatment or a cure? No treatment reverses the original congenital fusion, but monitoring, tailored rehabilitation, treatment of associated conditions and selected surgery can help. Surgery is based on instability, nerve pressure, deformity or symptoms, not the diagnosis alone. Must a child have all three classic signs? No. Fewer than half have the full short-neck, low-hairline and limited-movement triad, and some have few symptoms. The diagnosis relies on the whole clinical and imaging assessment. Are MRI, CT and genetic testing always required? No. The team chooses tests to assess fusion, spinal stability, nerves and other systems. CT uses radiation; genetic testing can be helpful but is not a requirement for every diagnosis. Do not force neck movement to reproduce imaging tests at home. Can my child exercise and later receive anaesthesia? Ask for an individual sport and activity plan and avoid forceful spinal manipulation. Tell the anaesthesia and procedure team about KFS in advance so positioning and airway needs can be assessed. Neither all activity nor all procedures are automatically prohibited. Which symptoms require emergency help? Sudden weakness or paralysis, new inability to walk, serious breathing or swallowing difficulty, or bladder or bowel loss with neurological symptoms require immediate emergency care. Neurological symptoms after injury also need emergency assessment. Do not drive yourself or wait for an app record.

title: Mosaic Down syndrome: features, testing and individual support
description: Understand mosaic Down syndrome, why sample percentages cannot predict ability, how screening differs from diagnosis and which health and developmental supports matter.
body: Mosaic Down syndrome means that different cells have different numbers of chromosome 21. It is a chromosome diagnosis, not a percentage measure of a person’s abilities. Learning what the tests show (and their limits) helps families plan health checks, developmental support and informed conversations with specialists. What mosaic Down syndrome means Down syndrome involves extra genetic material from chromosome 21. In mosaic Down syndrome, some cells have three copies of chromosome 21 and others have the usual two. It accounts for about 2% of people with Down syndrome, not 2% of all babies. Most cells with a nucleus usually have 46 chromosomes; eggs and sperm usually have 23 each. At fertilization they combine. A change in chromosome separation during early cell division can create different cell populations. This is not caused by a parent’s ordinary actions, and genetic does not automatically mean inherited. A genetics team can explain the particular chromosome result and future pregnancy implications. Features and development vary Possible features include a flatter facial profile, small ears, upward-slanting eyes, small white iris spots called Brushfield spots, shorter stature and low muscle tone. Some children have fewer visible features; appearance alone cannot confirm or exclude mosaicism or reveal learning ability. Speech, movement and learning may develop differently and need support. Some people with mosaicism have fewer difficulties on average, but others have substantial needs similar to other forms of Down syndrome. A group average or an IQ comparison cannot predict a particular child’s abilities, personality or future independence. Associated health needs still matter Mosaicism can be associated with congenital heart problems, sleep apnea, ear infections and hearing loss, visual problems and immune-related susceptibility to infection. No child necessarily has every problem, but subtle facial features or a low blood percentage are not reasons to omit health checks. Thyroid problems, feeding or swallowing difficulties and iron deficiency also deserve attention. Nutritional deficiencies are assessed from diet, symptoms and appropriate tests; they are not an automatic feature or a reason for unprescribed high-dose vitamins. Ask for a coordinated plan using Down syndrome health-supervision guidance and the child’s actual needs. Prenatal screening is not a diagnosis First- or second-trimester screening may combine maternal blood markers with ultrasound findings such as nuchal translucency. Cell-free DNA screening, often called NIPT, analyzes mainly placental DNA fragments in maternal blood. These estimate a chance; they do not by themselves diagnose mosaic Down syndrome. A higher-chance result needs a discussion of diagnostic options rather than an assumption about the baby. A lower-chance result does not exclude every case, especially all low-level or tissue-specific mosaicism. Screening cannot establish how much support a child will need; a normal ultrasound also cannot settle that question. Testing is a choice, with balanced information and support. Diagnostic testing during pregnancy Chorionic villus sampling, or CVS, tests placental tissue, usually earlier in pregnancy; amniocentesis tests cells in amniotic fluid, usually later. The fetal-medicine and genetics teams explain timing, procedure risks, laboratory methods and what each result can and cannot answer. Placental cells sometimes have a chromosome pattern different from the fetus, called confined placental mosaicism. A mosaic or unexpected CVS result may therefore require additional analysis or amniocentesis. Even diagnostic samples cannot map every fetal tissue or predict the full developmental outcome. Ask the specialist to interpret the complete report before making decisions. Confirming mosaicism after birth Clinicians may suspect Down syndrome from examination, development or associated health findings, but chromosome testing confirms the cause. A blood karyotype examines chromosome number and structure; other methods, such as FISH, may help investigate mosaicism. The appropriate method and number of cells depend on the clinical question and laboratory, not a universal rule requiring exactly 20 cells. If suspicion remains despite a negative blood result, genetics specialists may consider additional cell analysis or another tissue, such as cheek cells. The proportion can differ between blood and other tissues, and detection limits vary. This does not mean everyone needs a biopsy or repeated testing; ask what an additional test would change for care or counseling. What a mosaic percentage can tell you If 15 of 20 cells in a sample have an extra chromosome 21, the observed proportion is 75% in those counted cells. It does not mean the person is “75% affected,” nor that 75% of every organ has that chromosome pattern. The sample, method and uncertainty matter. Cell proportions can vary among tissues and may relate to some features in research, but a blood percentage cannot reliably predict an individual’s intelligence, severity or lifespan. Use the report to guide specialist interpretation, not to rank children or restrict expectations, therapies or health surveillance. Treatment supports health and participation There is no established treatment that removes the chromosome difference throughout the body. Effective care can still address heart disease, hearing or vision problems, sleep-disordered breathing, thyroid disease and feeding difficulties. Treatable illness should not be attributed automatically to Down syndrome. Early speech and language therapy, physiotherapy and occupational therapy can help communication, movement and daily activities. Play, reading, accessible communication and appropriate school support build on individual strengths. Set meaningful goals with the child and family; therapies support progress and participation, not a guaranteed IQ or a promise to erase disability. Planning for the future and getting help Improved healthcare has greatly increased survival, and many people with Down syndrome live into their 60s or beyond. Population figures are not a personal forecast and do not establish a separate guaranteed lifespan for mosaicism. Health conditions, support and access to care matter; continue appropriate follow-up into adult life. Seek emergency help immediately if a baby has difficult or very fast breathing, breathing pauses, blue or grey lips or skin, unusual paleness, blotchy skin, skin that feels abnormally cold or clammy, floppiness, poor responsiveness or difficulty waking, seizures, green vomit or a rash that does not fade when pressed. A temperature of 38°C or higher in a baby under 3 months, or below 36°C in any baby, needs immediate emergency medical assessment. A baby who has had no urine or wet nappy for at least 12 hours also needs emergency help immediately. Do not wait for all warning signs to appear. Poor feeding, fewer wet nappies, choking with feeds, new weakness, loss of skills or a worrying change needs prompt assessment; do not wait for the next routine review. Mosaic Down syndrome includes cells with and without an extra chromosome 21; features and support needs vary widely. A blood percentage describes a sample, not a child’s intelligence, disability level or guaranteed future. Screening estimates a chance; diagnostic testing and possible tissue differences need specialist interpretation. Keep appropriate Down syndrome health surveillance and early support even when features are subtle; respond promptly to concerning illness. What are the signs of mosaic Down syndrome? Features may include low muscle tone, a flatter face, small ears, upward-slanting eyes, white iris spots, shorter stature and speech or learning differences. They vary widely and cannot diagnose the condition or predict ability by appearance. How is it diagnosed? A clinician assesses the person and arranges appropriate chromosome testing, often a blood karyotype with additional analysis if needed. Prenatal screening estimates a chance; it is not a confirmed diagnosis. Can it be diagnosed during pregnancy? CVS or amniocentesis can provide diagnostic chromosome information. A placental mosaic result may need further testing, and specialist interpretation is important. No prenatal test can predict every health or developmental outcome. Is there a cure? No established treatment removes the chromosome difference throughout the body, but medical care, developmental therapies and educational support can make a meaningful difference. Treatment is based on the person’s needs. Does 75% mosaicism mean 75% disability? No. It describes an observed proportion in the tested sample, not a percentage of disability or of all organs. Blood results cannot reliably predict intelligence or severity. Is a negative blood test enough to exclude it? Often blood testing answers the question, but low-level or tissue-specific mosaicism may need further investigation when clinical suspicion remains. A genetics team decides whether another method or tissue is useful. Can fewer visible features mean fewer medical checks? No. People with mosaicism can have the associated medical problems of Down syndrome. Keep an individualized health-supervision plan, including hearing, vision, heart, sleep, thyroid, feeding and nutritional review as appropriate. What should families do after a diagnosis? Ask for genetics counseling, a coordinated pediatric care plan and early developmental support. Obtain understandable copies of results and connect with reliable family support if helpful. New concerning symptoms need assessment rather than waiting for routine care.

title: Pallister–Killian syndrome: mosaicism, diagnosis and lifelong care
description: Understand Pallister–Killian syndrome, its variable features, why blood testing can miss it, prenatal testing limits and individualized developmental and medical support.
body: Pallister–Killian syndrome (PKS) is a rare chromosome condition that can affect development and several organs. A diagnosis describes a broad spectrum, not a fixed future. Clinical genetics and a coordinated care team can help a family understand the findings and plan support around the individual. What the chromosome change means In typical PKS, some cells have an additional isochromosome made of two copies of the short arm of chromosome 12, called 12p. Those cells usually have four copies of 12p rather than two: mosaic tetrasomy 12p. Other cells have the usual chromosome complement. Mosaicism means that these cell populations coexist; it does not mean every cell has 47 chromosomes. The proportion of affected cells can differ between tissues and between samples. Rare, more complex chromosome findings need a geneticist’s interpretation. PKS has been recognized since the 1970s; older counts of published cases are not a current worldwide census. It can affect people of any sex, and milder presentations may go unrecognized. Muscle tone, development and communication Low muscle tone, or hypotonia, is often noticeable early. It may affect sucking, feeding, breathing, sitting and walking. Developmental and intellectual disabilities are common, often substantial, but their extent varies. Some children make slower progress and need extensive assistance; others have milder learning and movement difficulties. Speech may be delayed or limited, so communication support can include gestures, signs, pictures or devices as well as speech therapy. A published walking percentage or one child’s progress cannot predict another child’s abilities. Assessments should identify strengths, access needs and achievable goals rather than set a universal deadline. Physical features and associated health conditions Possible features include sparse hair around the temples, a high forehead, widely spaced eyes or folds at their inner corners, low-set or unusually shaped ears, and a high or cleft palate. Lighter or darker skin patches are pigment differences, not necessarily scars. Extra nipples, limb or skeletal differences, joint stiffness and asymmetry may occur. No appearance alone establishes the diagnosis. Some people have seizures, hearing loss or narrow ear canals, drooping eyelids, squint or other vision problems. Heart differences, congenital diaphragmatic hernia with impaired lung development, and digestive, anal, genital or urinary differences also occur. These are possible associations, not a checklist everyone has. Seizures are episodes of abnormal brain activity and are different from ordinary fainting. Why it happens and whether it is inherited PKS usually arises through a chance error in chromosome division around the formation of reproductive cells and early development. It is generally sporadic rather than passed through a family. It is not caused by parenting, a particular food or something a parent failed to do. A genetic counsellor should explain the actual chromosome result, including whether a rare rearrangement changes advice about parental testing or another pregnancy. A low usual recurrence risk is not a promise of zero risk for every family. Counselling can also address uncertainty, reproductive options and emotional support without blame. Conditions that can look similar Pigmentary mosaicism, sometimes described as hypomelanosis of Ito, can cause streaks or patches of lighter skin and may be associated with neurological, eye or skeletal differences. It is a descriptive clinical pattern with different possible underlying causes, not automatically PKS or a single inherited disorder. Skin changes alone do not establish either diagnosis. Partial trisomy 12p involves an extra copy of part or all of 12p, rather than the typical four-copy pattern in affected PKS cells. Developmental, muscle-tone, facial, palate and hand or finger features can overlap. Clinical genetics uses the examination and appropriate chromosome tests to distinguish these possibilities; resemblance or sex ratios cannot do so. Diagnosis: why a normal blood result may not settle it A clinician reviews development, physical findings, medical history and family history, then arranges chromosome testing. Depending on the question, the laboratory may use a karyotype, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), a chromosome microarray or complementary methods. Blood can miss PKS because the extra chromosome may be absent or present at very low levels in the blood cells tested. If suspicion remains, genetics specialists may recommend another tissue, such as cells from a cheek swab or a skin sample, and an appropriate testing method. Some abnormal cells are lost during laboratory culture. A skin biopsy is not mandatory for every person, and a single sample’s mosaic percentage cannot reliably forecast brain involvement, future abilities or overall severity. What prenatal testing can and cannot tell you Ultrasound may identify findings that prompt further assessment, such as a diaphragmatic hernia, short limb bones or heart differences, but normal ultrasound does not exclude PKS. Diagnostic testing of amniotic-fluid cells or placental tissue from chorionic villus sampling may identify it. Placental and fetal tissues, and cultured and uncultured samples, can give different results because of mosaicism. A fetal-medicine and genetics team should explain the test’s purpose, limitations and procedural risks and whether complementary testing is needed. A small 2021 study of five affected pregnancies illustrates missed or differing results; it does not provide a universal accuracy rate. Routine screening is not a guarantee against PKS, and even a confirmed prenatal diagnosis cannot precisely predict a child’s development. Treatment, practical support and longer-term planning There is no treatment that removes the chromosome change from all cells, but many associated needs can be treated or supported. Care may involve paediatrics, genetics, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, communication and feeding specialists, neurology, hearing and vision services, and education support. Swallowing or breathing concerns need assessment; nutrition, equipment and feeding assistance should be individualized. Selected heart, diaphragm, palate, anal, urinary or skeletal problems may need surgery or other specialist treatment. Seizures require an individual medication and emergency plan; do not start or stop treatment yourself. Mobility aids, accessible learning, family support and transition to adult services matter too. Some people need lifelong extensive support; others have greater independence. Neither a universal life expectancy nor a guaranteed developmental outcome is appropriate. When to seek urgent help Call emergency services for severe breathing difficulty, blue or grey lips or skin, loss of consciousness or difficulty waking, or a child who is suddenly seriously unwell. A first seizure, one lasting longer than usual or more than five minutes when the usual duration is unknown, repeated seizures without recovery, or breathing difficulty after a seizure also needs emergency help. Follow an individualized rescue plan sooner when it instructs you to. Choking that prevents breathing is an emergency: call emergency services immediately. During a convulsive seizure, protect the person from nearby hazards, cushion the head and time the event. Do not restrain them or put anything in their mouth; turn them onto their side once the convulsions stop and do not give food or drink until fully recovered. New feeding difficulty, recurrent coughing or choking during feeds after normal breathing has returned, reduced intake or a change from the child’s usual pattern warrants prompt clinical advice. Do not assume a new problem is simply part of PKS. PKS usually involves four copies of 12p in some cells, with substantial variation between tissues and people. A normal blood chromosome test or ultrasound cannot reliably exclude PKS; genetics selects the tissue and methods. Developmental, communication and medical support should begin according to need, without fixed predictions from case counts or mosaic percentages. It is usually sporadic and is not a parent’s fault; individual genetic counselling explains recurrence and pregnancy testing. Breathing emergencies, impaired consciousness and concerning seizures need immediate help, not an app record or routine appointment. What causes Pallister–Killian syndrome? Usually, an extra isochromosome adds two copies of chromosome 12p in some cells. Other cells have the usual complement. This mosaic chromosome change arises by chance, not from parenting or a particular food. Is PKS inherited or likely to happen again? Most cases are sporadic. A genetic counsellor reviews the specific result and any unusual rearrangement before discussing recurrence, parental tests and options for another pregnancy. Do not treat a generally low risk as a universal zero. Can PKS be diagnosed before birth? Sometimes diagnostic testing of amniotic-fluid or chorionic-villus cells identifies it. Mosaicism, tissue choice and laboratory methods can complicate detection. Ultrasound and routine screening cannot reliably rule it out or predict future abilities. Is there a cure? There is no cure that removes the chromosome change, but developmental therapies, communication aids, seizure care, feeding support and treatment of selected organ problems can improve health and participation. The plan is individualized. Does a normal blood test exclude it? No. Affected cells may be uncommon or absent in the blood sample. If the clinical suspicion remains, a genetics service can consider cheek or skin cells and complementary tests; not everyone needs every test or a biopsy. Does the percentage of affected cells predict severity? Not reliably. The percentage can vary across tissues and with laboratory culture. It does not directly measure the brain or tell you whether a particular child will walk, speak or live independently. Are pale skin patches or similar facial features enough for diagnosis? No. Pigmentary mosaicism and other chromosome conditions, including partial trisomy 12p, can overlap. A clinical examination and appropriate genetic testing distinguish them. When does a seizure need emergency help? A first seizure, a seizure longer than usual or more than five minutes if the usual length is unknown, repeated seizures without recovery, or breathing difficulty needs emergency help. Follow a prescribed rescue plan earlier when directed; never restrain the person or put anything in their mouth.

title: Pulmonary valve stenosis in babies and children: can it be treated?
description: Understand a narrowed pulmonary heart valve, its symptoms and tests, when monitoring or a procedure may help, and which signs in a baby need emergency care.
body: Pulmonary valve stenosis is narrowing of the valve that lets blood leave the right side of the heart for the lungs. Most cases start before birth. Many mild cases need monitoring rather than a procedure; severe or critical narrowing can need early treatment. A paediatric cardiologist assesses the valve, the right ventricle and any other heart differences. A baby becoming blue or struggling to breathe needs immediate emergency care. What the narrowed valve does The pulmonary valve sits between the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery. A usual valve has three flexible leaflets that open to let blood reach the lungs and close to limit backward flow. In congenital stenosis, leaflets may be joined, thickened or poorly formed, or the opening may be small. Narrowing below or above the valve is a different form of obstruction and can need a different approach. The right ventricle must generate more pressure to push blood through the narrowed opening. Its muscle can thicken; substantial obstruction may eventually affect filling or pumping. Mild, moderate and severe describe findings on specialist assessment, not a diagnosis that can be made from symptoms alone. A comfortable-looking child can still need follow-up. Why it happens, and what is different in adults Often the reason the valve formed differently is unknown, and it is not a parent’s fault. Pulmonary stenosis may occur alone or with other congenital heart conditions. It can be associated with Noonan syndrome, sometimes with a thickened or dysplastic valve; family history or other findings may prompt genetic assessment. This does not mean every child has a syndrome or that every case is inherited in the same way. Uncommon acquired narrowing later in life has different causes, including valve damage in carcinoid syndrome or rheumatic fever after certain streptococcal infections. A previously replaced valve may also later narrow or leak. These situations should not be confused with the usual congenital narrowing in a baby; treatment depends on the actual cause and anatomy. Symptoms range from none to a critically unwell newborn Mild stenosis may cause no symptoms and be noticed because of a murmur, an extra sound heard with a stethoscope. A murmur does not by itself show how severe the narrowing is. With more significant obstruction, children may tire easily, become short of breath with activity, have chest pain or faint. New symptoms need assessment rather than being attributed automatically to fitness or anxiety. A severely affected baby may feed poorly, tire or sweat during feeds, gain weight poorly or breathe fast. Critical narrowing can greatly reduce blood reaching the lungs and cause blue or grey lips or tongue. Some newborns depend temporarily on an open ductus arteriosus, a normal fetal blood vessel that usually closes after birth. These babies need urgent specialist hospital treatment, not observation at home. How the heart team makes the diagnosis Examination, oxygen measurement and an echocardiogram with Doppler help assess the valve, blood flow, pressure gradient and right ventricular function, and look for other heart differences. An ECG may show strain but can be normal in mild disease. Some cases are detected on a fetal heart scan; not every defect is identified before birth. MRI, CT or cardiac catheterisation are selected for particular questions; not every child needs all of them. Catheterisation is often used to treat a suitable valve rather than being the first diagnostic test. Ask which type of obstruction is present and what the scan means for your child. A single number or a normal oxygen reading does not replace the cardiologist’s assessment. Monitoring, balloon treatment and surgery Mild stenosis often needs periodic review without an immediate procedure. Infants with more than mild narrowing can need closer checks, especially in the early weeks and months. Monitoring intervals depend on age and findings: mild narrowing is not a promise that it can never change. Treatment decisions consider symptoms, anatomy, obstruction and right ventricular function. Balloon valvuloplasty is commonly used for a suitable narrowed valve: a catheter usually enters through a vein in the groin, and a balloon is inflated across the valve. A very small or dysplastic valve, obstruction elsewhere, other heart defects or an inadequate balloon result may call for surgery, repair or replacement. Critical newborns may first need monitored intravenous prostaglandin to keep the duct open as a temporary bridge. This is intensive hospital care, not a home medicine or definitive cure; procedures have individual risks and do not guarantee a completely normal valve. Possible complications and life after treatment Significant obstruction can strain the right ventricle and contribute to heart failure, with tiredness, breathlessness or swelling of the abdomen or legs. Heart rhythm problems can occur. A new unusually fast or irregular heartbeat, chest pain, breathing difficulty or feeling faint needs immediate emergency help; do not wait for these signs to occur together. After treatment, residual narrowing or a leaking valve may persist or develop, and some people need another procedure later. Infective endocarditis is an uncommon but serious heart infection. Good dental and oral care matter; preventive antibiotics before certain dental procedures are for selected high-risk conditions, such as a prosthetic valve or previous endocarditis, not automatically every isolated mild stenosis. Ask the heart team about your child’s exact advice. Persistent unexplained fever needs medical assessment; do not use leftover antibiotics. Follow-up, activity and growing up Keep cardiology appointments even when a child feels well. The team may repeat scans to check obstruction, leakage and right ventricular function. There is no single follow-up schedule for all ages, and reassuring early results do not remove the need for the agreed plan. Record feeding, growth and exercise changes and bring questions about medicines, procedures and warning signs. Many children with mild or successfully treated disease can be active, but restrictions for severe obstruction, symptoms or competitive sport are individual. Do not impose a blanket exercise ban or push through symptoms. Plan transition to adult congenital heart care when appropriate; pregnancy planning in adulthood may require specialist review, particularly with significant narrowing or other heart problems. When to get urgent or emergency help New poor feeding or deterioration in a newborn needs immediate medical assessment. If no emergency sign is present, seek urgent same-day advice for unusual tiring or sweating with feeds, poor weight gain, or chest discomfort, palpitations, exercise breathlessness or a fainting episode that has stopped and the child has fully recovered. Persistent unexplained fever also needs assessment. Follow the child’s own heart-team plan, but do not wait for a routine appointment if symptoms change. Call emergency services immediately for new blue or grey lips or tongue, difficult breathing or breathing pauses, chest pain, fainting or loss of consciousness, new confusion, unusual drowsiness, dizziness or feeling faint, a new unusually fast or irregular heartbeat, or a floppy, unresponsive or hard-to-wake baby. These are independent warning signs; do not wait for all of them. A baby under three months with a temperature of 38°C or more needs immediate medical help. The unwell person must not drive; follow the emergency dispatcher’s advice about transport. Pulmonary valve stenosis is usually congenital narrowing between the right ventricle and the lungs. Mild disease may need monitoring; critical newborn disease needs immediate specialist treatment. Echocardiography guides assessment; symptoms or a murmur alone do not grade severity. Balloon treatment helps many suitable valves; some children need surgery and ongoing follow-up. New blue or grey lips or tongue, breathing difficulty, reduced responsiveness or fainting require emergency help. Can pulmonary valve stenosis be treated? Yes. Many mild cases need monitoring only, while suitable significant narrowing may be opened with a balloon catheter. Some children need surgery. Critical newborn disease needs immediate hospital care; treatment does not guarantee a completely normal valve or remove follow-up. Does a heart murmur mean severe stenosis? No. A murmur may be the first sign, but does not by itself measure severity. An echocardiogram and specialist assessment check blood flow, the valve and the right ventricle. What symptoms can children have? There may be none in mild disease. Tiredness, activity-related breathlessness, chest pain or fainting can occur. Babies may feed poorly, sweat with feeds, gain weight poorly or breathe fast. New symptoms deserve assessment. Is every case caused by an inherited syndrome? No. Often the cause is unknown. Noonan syndrome and other heart conditions may be associated; genetic assessment is considered when clinical findings or family history suggest it, rather than assuming every child has the same cause. Will every child need a catheter test or surgery? No. Ultrasound of the heart is usually central to diagnosis. Other tests are selected. Balloon valvuloplasty is common for a suitable valve; surgery depends on anatomy, other defects and the result of any previous treatment. Can mild narrowing change or return after treatment? Yes, findings can change, especially in infancy. Residual narrowing or valve leakage may need monitoring after treatment, and some people need further intervention. Keep the individual follow-up plan. Are sport restrictions and dental antibiotics always needed? No. Activity advice depends on severity, symptoms and treatment. Preventive dental antibiotics are for selected high-risk heart conditions, not automatically all pulmonary stenosis; ask the heart team and maintain good oral care. Which symptoms need emergency help? Call emergency services immediately for new blue or grey lips or tongue, difficult breathing or breathing pauses, chest pain, fainting or loss of consciousness, new confusion, unusual drowsiness, dizziness or feeling faint, a new unusually fast or irregular heartbeat, or a floppy, unresponsive or hard-to-wake baby. These are independent warning signs; do not wait for all of them.

title: Aortic valve stenosis in children: severity, treatment and follow-up
description: Understand mild, moderate, severe and critical aortic valve stenosis, how an echocardiogram assesses it, when babies need emergency care and why follow-up continues after treatment.
body: Aortic valve stenosis is narrowing at the valve that lets blood leave the left ventricle for the body. Its effects range from a mild finding needing monitoring to a life-threatening newborn emergency. The valve’s anatomy, blood flow and heart function (not symptoms alone) guide care. What the narrowed valve does to the heart The aortic valve lies between the left ventricle, the main pumping chamber for the body, and the aorta, the main artery carrying blood to the body. It normally opens forward and closes to limit backward flow. A narrowed or stiff valve makes the ventricle work against higher pressure; over time the muscle can thicken, become stiff or pump less effectively. A normal valve usually has three flexible leaflets. A child may be born with one or two leaflets, thickened tissue or partly fused leaflets; the anatomy is not identical in every child. Narrowing below the valve, called subaortic stenosis, or above it, called supravalvular stenosis, is a different location requiring its own assessment. Congenital does not automatically mean inherited, and the cause is often unknown. Mild aortic valve stenosis Mild stenosis causes relatively little obstruction. Many children have no symptoms and can take part in ordinary activities. A murmur or extra click may lead to investigation, but the sound alone cannot determine severity or confirm that the child has no other heart problem. A procedure is often unnecessary at this stage, but regular pediatric cardiology review remains important. Mild narrowing can worsen as a child grows. Ask when the next examination and echocardiogram are due and which changes should trigger earlier contact. Moderate aortic valve stenosis Moderate stenosis creates more obstruction, yet a child may still look well and have no obvious symptoms. A murmur is common, but detection is not guaranteed by a routine examination. Absence of symptoms does not by itself establish that heart pressure or function is normal. Some children can be monitored without an immediate procedure; others need closer assessment or intervention because of measurements, symptoms or changes in the ventricle. The cardiologist decides the follow-up interval and activity advice from the complete findings, rather than the word “moderate” alone. Severe aortic valve stenosis Severe narrowing puts a greater load on the left ventricle and may impair its function. Older children may become unusually tired, short of breath or dizzy with exertion, or have chest pain or fainting. Significant obstruction can need treatment even when a child does not report symptoms. The heart team assesses the need and timing for balloon opening of the valve, surgical repair or, when appropriate, replacement. Do not test a child’s limits with strenuous exercise while awaiting advice. Chest pain, breathing difficulty, fainting or loss of consciousness needs emergency medical assessment, not a routine follow-up appointment. Critical stenosis is a newborn emergency In critical aortic stenosis, the newborn’s heart cannot deliver enough blood to the body. Circulation may depend on the ductus arteriosus, a temporary fetal blood vessel that normally closes after birth. A baby can deteriorate in the first days as it closes, even if the baby initially appeared well. New poor feeding or a sudden decline in a newborn needs immediate medical assessment. Call emergency services immediately for difficult or very fast breathing, blue or grey lips or skin, unusually pale or blotchy skin, skin that feels cold or damp (clammy), chest pain, fainting or loss of consciousness, new confusion, unusual drowsiness or dizziness, a new unusually fast or irregular heartbeat, or a limp, unresponsive or hard-to-wake child. Do not wait for all warning signs to appear. Do not wait to hear a murmur: it may be absent in critical disease. Hospital teams may use intravenous prostaglandin to keep the duct open and support circulation before an urgent valve procedure; this is temporary stabilization, not a cure. How the diagnosis and severity are checked An echocardiogram, or heart ultrasound, is central to identifying the valve anatomy, narrowing, leakage, blood flow and ventricular function. Examination and an ECG add information; catheterization or other imaging is used when needed, not automatically for every child. A murmur is a clue rather than a diagnosis or a reliable measure of severity. Some cases are detected during pregnancy with fetal echocardiography, but a normal prenatal screening scan does not exclude every heart defect. A prenatal diagnosis helps plan delivery and newborn care at an appropriate center. Tell the cardiologist about other heart conditions or a family history of valve disease; assessment of relatives or genetics is individualized. Balloon treatment, repair and replacement Balloon valvuloplasty uses a catheter carrying a balloon across the valve; briefly inflating it can widen the opening. It avoids open-heart surgery in suitable cases, but can leave or increase valve leakage and may not be the right option for every anatomy. Surgery may open or repair a valve when catheter treatment is unsuitable or insufficient. Valve replacement is considered when a useful functioning valve cannot be achieved or maintained, not for every severe or critical case. Options can include a mechanical valve, tissue valve or a Ross procedure using the person’s pulmonary valve and replacing that valve with donor tissue. Growth, future procedures and medicine needs differ; a mechanical valve needs long-term anticoagulation. Ask the specialist about the individual benefits and risks rather than assuming one option is best for every child. Living with the condition after treatment Treatment can improve blood flow and health but does not remove the need for lifelong follow-up. Narrowing may return, leakage may develop or worsen, and some children need further procedures. Follow-up also checks the heart muscle and, when relevant, the aorta. Plan the transition from pediatric to adult congenital-heart care. Activity and sports advice depends on obstruction, leakage and heart function; there is neither a universal exercise ban nor permission for all strenuous activity. Keep good dental care; antibiotics before dental work are for selected high-risk situations, not every child with stenosis. Ask for a written feeding, medicine, follow-up and emergency plan. New feeding difficulties, breathlessness, unusual tiredness or exercise symptoms need prompt contact with the heart team, with emergency help for the warning signs above. Mild, moderate, severe and critical describe different levels of obstruction; appearance or a murmur alone cannot grade it. Critical newborn disease can worsen as the ductus closes and needs immediate hospital care. Balloon treatment, repair and replacement depend on the child’s anatomy and heart function; replacement is not universal. Continue lifelong cardiology follow-up, individualized activity advice and prompt assessment of new symptoms. What is mild aortic valve stenosis? It is relatively limited obstruction, often without symptoms or a need for an immediate procedure. Regular cardiology checks remain necessary because the condition can change; a murmur does not establish the entire diagnosis or prognosis. What is severe aortic valve stenosis? It is substantial obstruction that increases the workload on the left ventricle and can affect its function. Treatment may be necessary even without symptoms. The heart team chooses balloon treatment, repair or replacement according to the findings. What is moderate aortic valve stenosis? It is a level of obstruction between mild and severe. A child may have no obvious symptoms, but echo findings, heart function and changes over time determine monitoring and whether a procedure is needed. What is critical aortic valve stenosis? It is a newborn emergency in which too little blood reaches the body. Temporary duct-dependent circulation may deteriorate as the duct closes. Immediate specialist stabilization and an urgent procedure may be needed; not every baby needs valve replacement. Can a normal examination rule it out? No. A murmur often raises suspicion, but may not be obvious in critical disease. Echocardiography assesses the valve and heart function. A normal prenatal screening scan also cannot exclude every heart defect. Does a balloon procedure permanently cure it? It can relieve obstruction, but the valve may still be abnormal. Leakage or recurrent narrowing can occur, and further procedures may be needed. Keep lifelong cardiology follow-up. Can a child play sports? Many children with little obstruction or leakage can take part in ordinary activities. More significant disease may require restrictions. Ask the cardiologist for individualized advice; chest pain, fainting or breathing difficulty needs emergency assessment. Which symptoms require immediate help? New poor feeding or a sudden decline in a newborn needs immediate medical assessment. Call emergency services immediately for difficult or very fast breathing, blue or grey lips or skin, unusually pale or blotchy skin, skin that feels cold or damp (clammy), chest pain, fainting or loss of consciousness, new confusion, unusual drowsiness or dizziness, a new unusually fast or irregular heartbeat, or a limp, unresponsive or hard-to-wake child. Do not wait for all warning signs to appear. Do not wait for the next heart appointment.

title: Ring chromosome 14 syndrome: genetics, seizures and care
description: Understand ring chromosome 14 syndrome, chromosome testing, variable development, epilepsy care and emergency warning signs for families.
body: Ring chromosome 14 syndrome is a rare chromosome condition associated with developmental disability and epilepsy, often beginning in infancy. Needs vary considerably. A diagnosis should lead to coordinated treatment, communication support and practical help for the family, rather than predictions based on appearance or a chromosome report alone. What a ring chromosome means One copy of chromosome 14 has a circular structure, written r(14). Material may be missing, particularly near the end of its long arm, but rings can have different deletions, duplications or no detectable loss. Ring instability and altered gene activity also matter; deletion size alone cannot predict a child's abilities. Some people have different chromosome patterns in different cells, called mosaicism. The condition is extremely rare, with unknown prevalence. Published case totals are not a current population count, and there is no reliable basis for predicting it from a child's sex. Development and seizures Low muscle tone, slow growth before or after birth, feeding difficulty and delays in movement, learning and speech can occur. Intellectual disability is common and often moderate to severe, but each person's skills, support needs and communication deserve individual assessment. Some also need help with attention, sensory differences or autistic features. Seizures often start in infancy or early childhood and may resist medication. They can involve focal changes in awareness or behavior, sudden muscle jerks, or stiffening followed by rhythmic shaking; loss of consciousness or bladder control can occur. Seizures are not simply fainting. Record changes and discuss any loss of previously acquired skills promptly. Other health features Reported features include a small head, high forehead, longer face, flatter nasal bridge, prominent nasal tip, widely spaced or downward-slanting eyes, thin upper lip, small jaw, high palate or low-set ears. Short neck folds, a single palm crease, widely spaced nipples, lighter skin patches or café-au-lait spots may occur. None diagnoses the condition. Eye issues include retinal pigment changes, squint or cataracts and warrant assessment rather than assuming vision is unaffected. Coordination difficulty, shaking that increases during a purposeful movement, joint contractures and recurrent respiratory infections are possible. Heart defects, including reported aortic or pulmonary artery narrowing, are uncommon; investigations depend on the person's findings. Causes, inheritance and overlapping conditions Most cases arise newly during formation of an egg or sperm or early embryonic development. Parents have not caused this through ordinary activities. Rare parent-to-child transmission is reported, so a geneticist may recommend parental chromosome testing and individualized advice about another pregnancy; recurrence risk is not automatically zero or a fixed percentage. Other chromosome conditions can cause similar developmental or physical features. A terminal deletion of a non-ring chromosome 14 may overlap with ring 14 but is not the same diagnosis or necessarily the same seizure pattern. Chromosome studies, rather than a facial checklist, establish the distinction. Testing after birth A genetics team combines the history and examination with chromosome testing. A karyotype can show the ring structure. Chromosomal microarray can define missing or extra material but may miss a ring without a detectable copy-number change; a normal array does not exclude it. Selected additional cell analysis or FISH may clarify findings and mosaicism. EEG records electrical brain activity to characterize seizures. MRI examines brain structure when indicated; neither confirms the chromosome syndrome. CT uses X-rays and is not an automatic additional test for every child. Hearing, vision, heart and other assessments should be selected and coordinated to address actual needs. Testing during pregnancy Ultrasound may reveal growth or structural concerns but cannot identify a ring chromosome by itself, and a normal scan cannot rule it out. Where appropriate, diagnostic chromosome testing can use amniotic fluid from amniocentesis or placental tissue from chorionic villus sampling. Routine prenatal screening is not a reliable exclusion test for this rare condition. A specialist should explain procedure risks, mosaic or uncertain findings and whether further testing is needed. Even a confirmed chromosome result cannot give a precise forecast of development, seizure severity or lifespan. Genetic counseling can support informed decisions without presenting uncertain outcomes as inevitable. Treating epilepsy and associated needs A pediatric neurologist should create an individualized seizure and emergency plan. Antiseizure medicines, sometimes in combination, require monitoring; difficult-to-control epilepsy merits specialist reassessment. A ketogenic diet or stimulation treatment may be considered in selected cases under specialist supervision. Do not start such treatments or stop prescribed medicines independently. Care may also involve feeding and swallowing assessment, nutrition support, respiratory care, eye and hearing services, and selected cardiology or orthopedic treatment. Physiotherapy and occupational therapy can support movement and contractures. Recurrent infections warrant assessment, sometimes including immunity testing; vaccination and infection plans are individualized, and antibiotics are not automatically appropriate for every illness. Learning, family life and long-term support Early developmental and educational services, speech and language therapy and augmentative communication, including picture cards or devices, can improve access and participation. Support does not depend on a child speaking or reaching a particular milestone. Equipment, social services, respite and psychological support should respond to the child and family's priorities. There is no treatment that reverses the chromosome rearrangement, but many associated problems can be treated. Planning should include adulthood and ongoing epilepsy, breathing, nutrition and communication needs. Available evidence does not establish one lifespan or a guaranteed developmental outcome; review goals and care as the person changes. When urgent help is needed Seek immediate emergency help for a first seizure, a convulsive seizure reaching five minutes, one lasting more than two minutes longer than usual, repeated seizures without recovery, or breathing difficulty after a seizure. Follow a prescribed rescue plan earlier if directed. Severe breathing difficulty, blue or grey lips, inability to wake, loss of consciousness, or choking that prevents breathing also need immediate help. During a seizure, time it, protect the head and remove nearby hazards; do not restrain the person or put anything in their mouth. Once shaking stops, turn them onto their side and give no food or drink until fully recovered.
