Natural sugars matter for carbohydrate planning. Allergy is possible; acne, ulcers and headaches are not guaranteed reactions. Should I eat 10 dates every day for milk supply? No standard dose is established. Ten daily was the intake in one short trial, not a prescription. Date size varies and milk-supply concerns need assessment. Can dates replace iron or calcium treatment? No. Suspected anaemia needs testing and appropriate treatment, and bone health requires adequate overall nutrition. Keep prescribed medicines and discuss supplements with your clinician. Can I eat dates if I have diabetes? Often yes within your individual carbohydrate plan. Consider the portion, date size and other ingredients; natural sugar is still carbohydrate and dates do not cure diabetes. When should feeding concerns be urgent? Seek prompt help for poor feeding, reduced wet nappies or poor growth. Difficulty waking, breathing difficulty or no urine for 12 hours in a baby requires immediate emergency care.

title: Jacobsen syndrome: understanding 11q deletion and care
description: Jacobsen syndrome affects people differently. Learn about genetic diagnosis, bleeding and heart risks, development and an individual care plan.
body: Jacobsen syndrome is a rare chromosome condition caused by missing material from the long arm of chromosome 11, often called an 11q deletion. It can affect growth, development and several organs, but every person has a different combination of needs and strengths. It is different from Jacobs syndrome, another name for 47,XYY. Genetic testing, rather than appearance alone, establishes the diagnosis. Features vary from person to person Growth may be slower before and after birth. Some children have a relatively large head, a pointed forehead, widely spaced eyes, drooping eyelids, low-set ears, a broad nasal bridge, a small lower jaw or a thin upper lip. Not everyone has every feature. A pointed forehead can sometimes reflect early joining of skull bones and needs assessment. Speech, movement, learning and everyday skills may develop more slowly. Attention difficulties, ADHD or autistic characteristics can occur, but these are not universal diagnoses. Hearing, vision, communication and emotional wellbeing deserve assessment alongside learning. A child’s appearance or chromosome report cannot set a fixed ceiling on future abilities. Why the deletion happens Most cases arise as a new chromosome change during formation of an egg or sperm, or early development. They are not caused by a parent’s ordinary actions. Occasionally a parent carries a balanced rearrangement without missing genetic material and can pass on an unbalanced chromosome. Genetic counselling can explain the family’s particular result and recurrence risk. The missing segment and genes vary. Larger deletions can be associated with greater difficulties, but size alone does not determine severity or predict a child’s future. Other genetic findings and individual health matter. Reported population estimates or a greater number of diagnosed girls do not predict an individual child’s course. Diagnosis and prenatal testing A genetics team chooses tests such as chromosomal microarray, which detects missing or extra DNA, and sometimes karyotyping or other targeted tests to clarify chromosome structure. These methods answer different questions; a microarray does not identify every balanced rearrangement. Testing parents may help interpret inheritance. Ask for an explanation of the actual laboratory report. Prenatal cell-free DNA testing, also called NIPT, is screening, not a diagnosis of Jacobsen syndrome. Current ACOG guidance does not recommend routine microdeletion screening for everyone. If a chromosome deletion is a concern, genetic counselling and diagnostic testing using chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis may be offered. Discuss benefits, limitations, procedure risks and your choices before deciding. Bleeding needs its own care plan Many people have Paris–Trousseau platelet abnormalities: the platelet count may be low and platelets may not work normally. Easy bruising, nosebleeds, prolonged bleeding, heavy periods or internal bleeding can occur. A normal count, or a count that improves with age, does not by itself rule out a platelet-function problem. A small recent study supports this important distinction. A haematology team should assess bleeding and plan prevention or treatment for procedures, dental work and injuries. Tell every treating clinician about the condition, even when recent blood counts look reassuring. Treatments depend on the individual; do not assume everyone needs the same transfusion or medicine. Ask before using medicines that could worsen bleeding and keep an accessible written plan. Heart, kidney and digestive health Congenital heart differences can include a hole between the lower heart chambers or more complex problems affecting the left side and blood flow out of the heart. Cardiology assessment and appropriate imaging help determine care. Some need monitoring; others need specialist treatment or surgery. Older study percentages are not a personal prediction. Kidney or urinary-tract differences may include a missing kidney, duplicated drainage tube, cysts or swelling from impaired drainage. Feeding and digestive problems can include narrowing at the stomach outlet, an abnormal anal opening or twisted/abnormally positioned bowel. Examination and selected tests guide treatment; repeated vomiting, poor growth or feeding difficulty should not simply be attributed to development. Vision, hearing, infection and development Eye problems, including cataracts or other vision difficulties, and hearing problems need appropriate checks. Recurrent ear, sinus or respiratory infections may warrant review and, when indicated, immune assessment; not every person has immune deficiency. Follow-up should be tailored to findings, rather than assuming all possible complications will occur. Early support may include speech and communication therapy, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and individual education plans. Assess attention, autistic characteristics, behaviour and mental health when needed. A recent study of 29 people found considerable variation in cognitive and everyday functioning; a small research group cannot forecast one person’s abilities. Support should build skills and participation without making promises about independence. Treatment and family support There is no established treatment that replaces the missing chromosome segment. Care treats the particular health problems and supports development. A paediatrician or other coordinating clinician can bring together genetics, haematology, cardiology and relevant kidney, digestive, eye, hearing and developmental services. The plan should include when checks are needed and who to contact between appointments. Families may benefit from rare-condition organisations, school support, practical services and psychological care. As the child grows, review communication, consent, relationships, daily living and transition to adult services. Ask about goals important to the person and family. No single therapy schedule or operation is appropriate for everyone. What can be said about the future? The outlook varies substantially. Serious heart disease, bleeding and other complications can be life-threatening, particularly early in life. Some people reach adulthood. Life expectancy is not reliably defined for every form of the condition, and older mortality percentages should not be presented as a child’s personal risk or a fixed lifespan. The most useful discussion combines the specific genetic findings with current heart, bleeding, feeding and developmental assessments. Ask what can be treated, what needs surveillance and what uncertainty remains. Progress and support needs can change over time; neither severe disability nor a particular level of independence should be assumed from the diagnosis alone. When to get urgent help Follow the individual bleeding and emergency plan. Contact the treating team urgently for suspected bleeding, a head injury or another significant injury, even without visible bruising. Significant bleeding that does not stop, vomiting blood, black tar-like stool, a sudden severe unusual headache or new neurological symptoms need immediate emergency assessment. Do not wait for a routine blood count. Get emergency help now for breathing difficulty, blue or grey lips or tongue, a seizure, fainting or loss of consciousness, or a child who is difficult to wake. Green vomit in a baby also needs immediate emergency assessment. Poor feeding, recurrent vomiting, new unusual bruising or infections need prompt clinical advice; seek help sooner if the child is deteriorating or you are seriously worried. If a child is unwell and you think something is seriously wrong, get emergency help now even if their signs are not listed here. Do not wait for every warning sign to appear. Jacobsen syndrome is an 11q deletion condition, distinct from 47,XYY. Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis; screening alone does not. Normal platelet numbers do not exclude a bleeding problem. Heart, feeding, growth and development need an individual coordinated plan. There is no fixed lifespan or developmental outcome for every person. What is Jacobsen syndrome? It is a condition caused by missing material from the long arm of chromosome 11. Growth, development, bleeding and several organs may be affected differently in each person. It is not the same as 47,XYY, sometimes called Jacobs syndrome. Which symptoms can occur? Possible features include slower growth, characteristic head or facial differences, learning or communication difficulties, platelet abnormalities and heart, kidney, digestive, eye or hearing problems. A person does not need every feature. Appearance alone does not establish the diagnosis. Does a larger deletion always mean a worse outcome? No. Deletion size and the genes involved can influence the pattern, but do not determine the whole future. Other genetic and health factors matter. Assessment of the individual is more useful than predicting from one chromosome measurement. Is it inherited? Most cases are new changes rather than a condition passed down from an affected parent. In a minority, a parent carries a balanced chromosome rearrangement. A genetics team can advise on parental testing and recurrence risk without blaming anyone. Can a pregnancy blood screening test diagnose it? No. Cell-free DNA/NIPT is screening and can give false positive or false negative results. ACOG does not recommend routine microdeletion screening for everyone. Diagnostic testing through chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis may be discussed with a specialist; the test and its limits need individual counselling. Can the platelet count become normal while bleeding risk remains? Yes. Platelets can still function abnormally despite a normal count. The haematology plan remains important for injuries, surgery, dental procedures and heavy periods. Do not assume a reassuring blood count makes every procedure safe. Can it be cured, and how long will someone live? There is no established way to replace the missing chromosome segment, but individual complications can be treated and development supported. Some people reach adulthood; the outlook depends on their health needs. A fixed lifespan or promise of independence is not reliable. Which symptoms need emergency care? Uncontrolled significant bleeding, vomiting blood, black tar-like stool, a sudden severe unusual headache or new neurological symptoms need immediate assessment. Breathing difficulty, blue or grey lips or tongue, seizures, fainting or loss of consciousness, difficulty waking or green vomiting in a baby also require emergency help. Seek urgent advice after a head injury even without obvious symptoms.

title: Tetralogy of Fallot: diagnosis, treatment and lifelong care
description: Understand the four heart changes in tetralogy of Fallot, variable symptoms, blue-spell emergencies, surgery and follow-up through adulthood.
body: Tetralogy of Fallot, or TOF, is a combination of four heart changes present from birth. They can limit blood flow to the lungs and allow oxygen-poor blood to reach the body. Some babies become blue or grey, while others have little visible colour change at first. The exact anatomy and oxygen levels guide treatment. Surgery can improve circulation, but regular congenital-heart care remains important throughout life. The narrowed lung pathway and the hole in the heart One change is narrowing of the route from the right ventricle, the lower right pumping chamber, to the lungs. It can involve muscle below the pulmonary valve, the valve itself or the pulmonary arteries. In a severe form the valve opening is absent or closed, called pulmonary atresia. This is more than an isolated valve problem. Another change is a ventricular septal defect, or VSD: a hole in the wall between the two lower chambers. Its effect depends on the pressure and resistance in the lung pathway. With substantial obstruction, oxygen-poor blood can cross toward the body’s circulation rather than reaching the lungs to pick up oxygen. Not every person has the same degree of mixing or low oxygen. The overriding aorta and thickened right ventricle The aorta, the main artery carrying blood to the body, sits over the VSD instead of connecting only to the left ventricle. This is called an overriding aorta and allows it to receive blood from both ventricles. Together with the obstructed lung pathway, this can reduce the oxygen in blood reaching the body. The right ventricle’s muscle becomes thicker because it pumps against increased resistance and pressure. This is right ventricular hypertrophy; it is not simply a response to the body wanting more oxygen. Some people also have other features, such as an atrial septal defect, a right-sided aortic arch or differences in the coronary arteries. The cardiology team maps the individual anatomy. Symptoms and blue spells are variable Possible signs include rapid or difficult breathing during feeding or activity, tiring easily, poor weight gain, irritability, prolonged crying and a heart murmur. Low oxygen may cause blue or grey lips, tongue or skin, fainting or seizures. Symptoms depend on blood flow; no blue colour at birth does not rule out TOF, and colour alone cannot diagnose it. Some babies have a sudden drop in oxygen during crying, feeding or other stress. These episodes, called tet spells or hypercyanotic spells, may cause darker blue or grey colour, fast deep breathing, unusual distress and then floppiness or reduced responsiveness. They are not confined to one age window. Dehydration or illness can make a known condition less stable. A blue or unresponsive baby needs emergency help Call emergency services now for sudden blue or grey lips, tongue or face, breathing difficulty, a seizure, fainting or loss of consciousness, marked floppiness or severe difficulty waking. These signs can have several causes and do not prove TOF. Do not delay help while trying to diagnose the colour change or waiting for a heart appointment. For a child with diagnosed TOF, follow the cardiology team’s written spell plan while emergency help is being arranged. The team may have taught a knees-to-chest position and calming measures for that child; these are not a substitute for an ambulance or a general home treatment for an undiagnosed blue baby. Report a first spell or increasing spells promptly, even if the child improves, and follow the team’s instructions about urgent assessment. How it is diagnosed before and after birth A routine pregnancy ultrasound may raise suspicion, and a fetal echocardiogram gives a detailed view of the heart. Some cases are missed before birth; a reassuring routine scan cannot exclude every heart problem. Prenatal diagnosis allows the fetal and cardiac teams to plan delivery location and care after birth according to the baby’s needs. After birth, a murmur, feeding difficulty, colour change or low oxygen can lead to echocardiography. A newborn pulse-oximetry screen can help detect TOF, but a passed screen does not rule out every critical heart defect. Diagnosis is usually made in infancy, although some less obvious cases are identified later. Further tests are selected to clarify anatomy and function, rather than every child needing every test. Causes, genetics and risk without blame TOF develops while the heart forms during pregnancy, and the cause is unknown in many cases. Some children have an associated genetic condition, such as 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, also called DiGeorge syndrome, or trisomy 21/Down syndrome. These are possibilities, not conditions present in everyone with TOF. Ask about appropriate genetic testing and counselling, particularly with other findings or a family history. Research on congenital heart defects links some risks with pre-existing diabetes, certain medicines, smoking or infections such as rubella. Age, nutrition or alcohol exposure cannot establish the cause of an individual child’s TOF, and there is no universal age-40 boundary that diagnoses it. Review health, medicines and vaccinations before pregnancy, avoid alcohol during pregnancy and seek prompt maternity advice after rubella exposure. Do not stop prescriptions yourself or assume a parent is to blame. Treatment may involve one operation or stages TOF usually needs surgical repair. A complete repair closes the VSD with a patch and relieves the blocked route to the lungs; the exact valve and artery work depends on the anatomy. Treatment is commonly planned early in life, but timing is individual. Severe low oxygen or a spell can need urgent hospital treatment rather than waiting for a routine surgery date. Some babies need an initial procedure to improve lung blood flow before full repair, such as a shunt or selected stent procedure. More complex anatomy may need a conduit between the right ventricle and pulmonary artery. The team explains the proposed approach, risks and recovery; no single operation or guaranteed result applies to every baby. Home positioning, supplements or medicines taken without specialist advice cannot repair the structural changes. Follow-up continues after repair Many people do well after treatment, but repair is not the end of care. Pulmonary-valve leakage, recurrent narrowing, heart-rhythm problems or reduced pumping function can appear later. Some people need another catheter procedure, valve intervention, surgery or medicines. Regular paediatric cardiology care should lead into specialist adult congenital-heart care, even when the person feels well. Follow-up tests, including echocardiography and sometimes rhythm monitoring, exercise testing or cardiac MRI, depend on findings. Discuss new fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance or palpitations promptly; fainting, severe breathing difficulty or a new blue spell requires emergency care. Exercise advice is individual: many can enjoy ordinary activity, while significant remaining problems may require restrictions. Ask for a specific plan instead of a lifelong blanket ban on sport. Daily care, dental health and family questions Keep appointments, the treatment history and an accessible emergency plan. Ask for help with feeding, growth, development, school and emotional wellbeing when needed. Before non-heart surgery, invasive procedures or pregnancy planning later in life, discuss the heart condition with the congenital-heart team. A good outlook does not mean every person has identical needs or no future risk. Good dental care matters because some people are at increased risk of infective endocarditis, an infection of the heart lining or valves. Antibiotics before certain dental procedures are for selected high-risk situations, such as unrepaired cyanotic disease, particular prosthetic valves/materials or residual defects; they are not automatic for every person or every procedure. Ask the cardiologist and dentist for the individual recommendation, and do not self-prescribe antibiotics. TOF combines four structural heart changes; its severity varies. Neither the absence of blue colour nor a passed newborn screen fully rules out TOF. Sudden blue or grey colour, breathing difficulty or reduced responsiveness needs emergency help. Repair may be done in one operation or stages according to the baby’s needs. Lifelong follow-up, tailored activity and individual dental advice remain important. What are the four changes in tetralogy of Fallot? They are obstruction of the lung blood-flow pathway, a hole between the ventricles, an aorta overriding that hole and thickening of the right ventricular muscle. The degree and exact anatomy vary, including severe forms with pulmonary atresia. Which symptoms may occur? Rapid or difficult breathing, feeding fatigue, poor growth, irritability, prolonged crying, a murmur and blue or grey colour can occur. Low oxygen can cause fainting or seizures. Not every baby looks blue at birth, and symptoms alone do not establish the diagnosis. Does a baby turning blue prove TOF? No. Heart, lung, airway and other problems can cause low oxygen. Sudden blue or grey lips, tongue or face, breathing difficulty, floppiness, seizures or reduced responsiveness require emergency help now, without waiting to identify the cause. Should I use the knees-to-chest position? Only follow a specific spell plan taught by the cardiac team for a child with diagnosed TOF, while arranging emergency help. It is not a general substitute for assessment of an undiagnosed blue baby. A spell needs urgent attention even if the child seems to recover. What causes it, and did a parent do something wrong? Often no single cause is found. Genetic changes and several other factors can contribute, but a diagnosis does not show that a parent caused it. Genetics and pre-pregnancy counselling can clarify relevant risks; do not change prescription medicines without advice. Can it be detected during pregnancy? Yes, ultrasound may identify it and fetal echocardiography can assess the heart in detail. Some cases are missed, and no scan excludes every problem. A fetal-heart team can plan the place of birth and immediate newborn care when TOF is diagnosed. Will one operation permanently cure it? Repair improves blood flow, but some babies need staged treatment and some people need further procedures later. Valve leakage, narrowing or rhythm problems can develop. Lifelong congenital-heart follow-up remains important even with good health and no symptoms. Are exercise limits and dental antibiotics needed for everyone? No. Activity depends on heart function, residual problems and rhythm. Antibiotics before particular dental procedures are reserved for selected high-risk situations. Ask the cardiology team for your own recommendations instead of avoiding all exercise or taking antibiotics automatically.

title: Childhood tics and Tourette syndrome: choosing support and treatment
description: Understand tic assessment, when treatment can help, CBIT, school and family support, coexisting ADHD or OCD, and safe medicine follow-up.
body: A child with repeated movements or sounds needs understanding rather than pressure to stop. Some tics cause little difficulty; others hurt, interrupt learning or affect confidence. There is no guaranteed cure for Tourette syndrome, but a plan built around the child’s own needs can make everyday life easier. Not every persistent tic is Tourette syndrome Motor tics involve movements, such as blinking or shoulder jerking; vocal tics involve sounds, such as sniffing or throat clearing. Under the DSM-5-TR criteria described by CDC, Tourette syndrome involves at least two motor tics and at least one vocal tic during the illness, starting before age 18 and continuing over at least a year. They need not occur together or without any breaks. Other causes must be considered. Persistent motor or vocal tic disorder involves one type rather than both; provisional tic disorder has lasted less than a year. A diagnosis depends on the pattern and history, not simply a movement continuing or a checklist found online. Tics may change and fluctuate. Their presence is not evidence of poor parenting or deliberate misbehaviour. Start with an appropriate assessment A primary-care clinician or paediatrician can assess the movements, their onset, medicines and impact, and decide whether specialist help is needed. Typical tics are usually diagnosed clinically; a scan, EEG, blood test or genetic test is not automatically necessary. Tests are selected when another condition needs excluding. A new or unusual pattern deserves reassessment, not a label of bad behaviour. Ask for review if tics cause pain, injury, distress, bullying or difficulties with school and daily activities, at any age. Referral may involve neurology, a neurodevelopmental team or mental-health care according to the problem and local pathway. NICE’s UK guidance calls for specialist advice before tic medicines; simple tics that do not trouble the child do not routinely need specialist referral. Treat the difficulties that matter most to the child Discuss reading, writing, speaking, sleep, friendships, sport and music, as well as painful muscle movements or self-injury. A noticeable tic alone is not a reason to prescribe. Supported observation and review can be reasonable when it causes no significant difficulty; it should not mean ignoring the child’s concerns. There is no age below which social or emotional effects can be dismissed. ADHD, obsessive-compulsive disorder, anxiety, low mood and learning difficulties may have a greater effect than the tics. Assess them on their own merits and agree priorities together. School or psychological assessment can identify useful learning support; neither tics nor a learning diagnosis determines intelligence. Anxiety and depression can also affect concentration. Coordinated treatment may address more than one difficulty. Consider CBIT and other tailored behavioural help Comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics, or CBIT, is an evidence-based option to discuss before or alongside medicines. A trained therapist helps the child recognise a tic or preceding urge, practise a suitable competing response and adjust situations that worsen symptoms. The approach is adapted to the person’s understanding, preferences and needs; access to trained practitioners varies. These are skills learned with encouragement, not a test of willpower or a command to hold every tic in. Benefiting from behavioural therapy does not mean the movements are chosen. Parents can support agreed practice without constantly commenting on tics. Therapy for anxiety or OCD, and parent or family support for other behavioural difficulties, may be needed separately. Make home a place of acceptance Let your child know they are valued whether or not the tics improve. Ask what kind of help they want, avoid teasing or reprimands, and help siblings and other relatives understand. Enjoyable interests can support confidence, but a child does not have to excel at sport or music to deserve respect or protection from bullying. Discuss whether, when and how to explain the condition to others, taking the child’s wishes into account. There is no compulsory age or school year for a public announcement, and humour is optional. Peer groups can offer connection without replacing care. Support for a parent’s own distress, or family counselling when useful, is part of helping the family rather than assigning blame for the tics. Plan school support without punishment or exclusion Work with the child, teachers and care team on the actual barriers. Options include comfortable seating, writing or computer adaptations, extra test time and a quieter place for assessments when appropriate. A voluntary break or private space may help; the child should not routinely be sent out or required to suppress tics to stay in class. Educational rights and referral arrangements vary by country. Vocal tics can interrupt lessons and may persist; do not promise they will disappear within a year. Adults should address bullying and explain that tics are involuntary, while protecting privacy. Review accommodations as needs change. The goal is participation and learning, rather than making the child less visible. Support sleep, activity and ordinary routines Regular sleep, enjoyable physical activity and manageable routines can support wellbeing. Stress, excitement and tiredness may change tic frequency, including around happy events. A change does not necessarily mean treatment has failed. Families cannot eliminate every stressor and should not feel responsible for each fluctuation. Offer a varied diet without promises that a particular food, vitamin or herbal supplement will remove tics. Evidence for complementary treatments is limited. Games do not require an automatic ban; agree a balance that protects sleep, school and enjoyable activities. These habits support care and do not replace assessment or an indicated treatment. Medicines are an individual benefit–risk decision When tics remain troublesome, discuss expected improvement, possible adverse effects and alternatives with the specialist. No medicine is best for every child, and complete disappearance is not a realistic requirement for success. Clonidine or guanfacine, medicines that act on alpha-2 receptors, may be considered, particularly when ADHD also needs treatment. They are not universally the first or safest choice. These medicines can cause sleepiness, dizziness, low blood pressure, a slow heart rate or fainting. The prescriber checks pulse and blood pressure and reviews other medicines and relevant heart history; selected risks may require additional cardiac monitoring. Other tic medicines have their own risks. Approvals differ by country and formulation: a US extended-release ADHD indication is not the same as approval to treat every child’s tics. Use a clear prescribing and side-effect plan Ask for written instructions for the exact product, planned changes, missed doses, monitoring and a review date. A tablet, extended-release product or skin patch is not automatically interchangeable. Do not start, increase, reduce or switch medicines using an online schedule. Introducing or changing treatments in a planned way helps identify benefit and adverse effects, but necessary combined treatment is not universally forbidden. Report troublesome sleepiness or other adverse effects; do not assume they must be tolerated for two weeks. Ask the prescriber what to do before the next change, and seek urgent help for concerning symptoms. Clonidine and guanfacine must not be stopped abruptly without medical advice because blood pressure can rise dangerously; any taper needs a supervised plan. If illness or vomiting prevents doses, contact the prescribing team. ADHD medicines do not automatically cause tics Tics and ADHD often coexist, and attention difficulties may be recognised before tics appear. Starting a stimulant around the same time does not prove it caused the movements. Evidence supports appropriate ADHD treatment in children with tics; methylphenidate and selected non-stimulant options can help without a universal worsening of tics. Individual responses differ. If a movement starts or worsens after a change, tell the prescriber about the timing, sleep, stress, other medicines and effect on daily life. They can review the diagnosis and balance of benefits and harms, or consider a different plan. Do not stop a helpful ADHD medicine or adjust its dose independently, and do not assume every new movement is a tic. Review progress without chasing every fluctuation Agree practical goals, such as less pain, easier handwriting or more comfortable participation. Tics naturally wax and wane and often improve as children grow, but some continue into adulthood. Neither a cure nor a fixed recovery deadline can be promised. Review the need for ongoing medicine and the child’s broader wellbeing over time. A brief record of changes and their impact may help; avoid constant counting or repeatedly asking the child to demonstrate. With their agreement, a short recording of a naturally occurring movement can sometimes assist assessment without drawing unnecessary attention. Changing or unfamiliar movements, worsening mood, new learning problems or unexpected adverse effects deserve clinical review. Know when a movement needs urgent help Seek immediate medical assessment for a new movement accompanied by marked unsteadiness, sustained twisting or abnormal posturing, or other new neurological difficulties. A first suspected seizure, loss of consciousness, difficulty breathing, inability to wake normally, serious injury or suspected medicine overdose needs emergency help. Do not treat these as ordinary tics or delay help to record them. Get prompt professional help for self-injury, significant pain, severe distress or thoughts of self-harm. If the child may act on thoughts of harming themselves or anyone is in immediate danger, get emergency help and arrange for a trusted adult to stay with them. A routine appointment, school plan or app entry must not delay urgent care. Different tic disorders have different diagnostic criteria; persistent tics do not automatically mean Tourette syndrome. Base support and treatment on the child’s pain, distress and daily functioning, including ADHD, OCD and learning needs. CBIT, family understanding and individualized school accommodations can help without punishment or forced disclosure. Medicines need product-specific instructions, monitoring and review; do not change doses or stop alpha-2 medicines abruptly yourself. New neurological symptoms, serious medicine effects or immediate danger need urgent or emergency care. Which clinician should assess my child’s tics? Start with a primary-care clinician or paediatrician. They can assess typical tics and arrange neurology, neurodevelopmental or mental-health input when the symptoms, associated conditions or impact warrant it. Local routes differ; medicines need appropriate specialist advice. Are tics always worrying or in need of medicine? No. Mild tics that do not trouble the child may need understanding and review rather than medication. Pain, injury, distress, bullying or functional difficulties deserve attention at any age. A parent’s understandable wish for the tic to disappear is not, by itself, a reason to prescribe. The tics worsened after medicine. What should I do? Contact the prescriber with the timing and any other symptoms. Natural fluctuations and medicine effects both need consideration. Do not start another product, increase doses or abruptly stop clonidine or guanfacine yourself. Severe sleepiness, fainting or other serious symptoms need urgent assessment; unresponsiveness or breathing difficulty is an emergency. What is the best medicine for childhood tics? There is no single best medicine. Clonidine or guanfacine can be useful for selected children, especially with ADHD, but sedation and cardiovascular risks require monitoring. The specialist weighs options alongside CBIT, other conditions and the child’s goals; this article does not provide a dose or taper schedule. Can behavioural therapy cure Tourette syndrome? CBIT can reduce tics or their impact, but it is not a guaranteed cure. It teaches agreed skills with a trained therapist and supportive practice. It does not mean tics are chosen or that a child should be punished for being unable to stop them. Must my child tell the class about the diagnosis? No fixed grade or public disclosure is required. Discuss privacy and what your child wants, while arranging necessary support with appropriate school staff. Adults should address bullying; the child should not have to earn acceptance through achievement or humour. Do stimulant medicines always make tics worse? No. ADHD and tics often occur together, and effective ADHD treatment remains important. Individual changes should be discussed with the prescriber, who can review options without assuming that every tic is caused by the medicine. Do not adjust treatment yourself. Which symptoms should not wait for a routine appointment? New neurological difficulties need immediate medical assessment. A first suspected seizure, loss of consciousness, breathing difficulty, inability to wake normally, serious injury, suspected overdose or immediate risk of self-harm needs emergency help. Significant pain, self-injury or distress also warrants prompt professional care.

title: Multicystic dysplastic kidney in babies: diagnosis and follow-up
description: What MCDK means, how scans assess both kidneys, and why treatment and follow-up depend on the remaining kidney and the baby's overall health.
body: Hearing that a baby's kidney contains many cysts can be frightening. Multicystic dysplastic kidney (MCDK) develops before birth. Many children with one affected kidney and a healthy other kidney grow well; disease affecting both sides needs a different, specialist assessment. What MCDK means In MCDK, a kidney develops abnormally in the womb and much of its normal tissue is replaced by multiple fluid-filled sacs. That kidney has little or no useful function. Kidneys normally remove waste from the blood, regulate fluid and salts, and make urine. MCDK is a severe form of kidney dysplasia. It is different from inherited polycystic kidney disease (PKD), and not every cyst seen in a baby's kidney means MCDK. Ask which diagnosis the scan suggests and how certain it is. One kidney or both: why the distinction matters Most MCDK affects one kidney. If the other kidney is healthy, it can usually provide the function the child needs and may grow larger to compensate. The affected kidney often shrinks over time and can disappear from scans, but this is not guaranteed by a particular age. The outlook depends especially on the other kidney and urinary drainage, not simply the number or size of cysts. An abnormality in the other kidney, obstruction or urine flowing backwards may change the assessment and follow-up plan. Causes, family history and avoiding blame Often no specific cause is identified. MCDK generally occurs sporadically and is not usually caused by something a parent did during pregnancy. There is no established diet or action that reliably prevents it; a diagnosis is not evidence of parental fault. Occasionally a genetic change or a wider syndrome is involved. Tell the team about relatives with kidney problems and any other findings in the baby. Genetic counselling and testing are selected for the circumstances; a family history does not establish the cause or a fixed recurrence risk. Finding MCDK during pregnancy MCDK is often suspected at the mid-pregnancy ultrasound, commonly around 18–22 weeks depending on local screening. Specialists assess both kidneys, the bladder, other organs and the amount of amniotic fluid. Further scans may clarify an uncertain finding and help plan care after birth. Fetal urine contributes to amniotic fluid, which supports lung development. Very low fluid can signal serious kidney problems, particularly when both sides are affected. A prenatal scan cannot always distinguish MCDK from other developmental or drainage problems, so ask what remains uncertain. Confirming the diagnosis after birth A postnatal kidney ultrasound checks the diagnosis and the appearance of the other kidney and urinary tract. Some cases are first discovered after birth or later during a scan for another problem. The team chooses the timing; do not assume a prenatal label removes the need for follow-up. Ultrasound shows structure, growth and drainage clues; it does not directly measure overall filtering function. Blood and urine tests may be needed. A nuclear kidney scan or bladder contrast study is not automatic for every typical, uncomplicated case: specialists select extra tests when they could change care. Who follows the baby, and how often? A paediatric kidney specialist monitors kidney health; a paediatric urologist assesses urinary drainage or surgical concerns. Local services may share care with the child's usual clinician. Ask who reviews results, arranges the next appointment and should be contacted if the baby becomes unwell. Follow-up may include growth, blood pressure, urine protein, kidney-function blood tests and repeat ultrasound. The combination and intervals depend on age, the other kidney and previous results. Not every child needs every test or a scan every six or twelve months; a healthy uncomplicated case can need fewer investigations. Treatment: monitoring is still active care There is no medicine that turns an MCDK kidney into a normally developed kidney. When the other kidney is healthy and the child is well, observation is often appropriate. Surgery to remove the affected kidney is not routine; persistent troublesome complications may justify an individual surgical discussion. Urinary infections or high blood pressure need appropriate treatment if they occur. Preventive antibiotics are not routinely needed in uncomplicated MCDK. Do not start antibiotics, supplements or a restrictive kidney diet yourself; if kidney function is reduced, the team can arrange specific feeding and diet advice. When both kidneys are seriously affected Bilateral MCDK, or MCDK with a severely abnormal other kidney, requires early fetal-medicine, newborn and paediatric kidney expertise. Severe loss of fetal urine can impair lung development, making survival very difficult. The precise findings and lung development matter; a single label cannot give an individual prognosis. Some babies who survive with severe kidney failure need dialysis and later consideration of transplantation. Dialysis replaces some kidney functions; it does not correct underdeveloped lungs or every associated problem. Ask for a clear discussion of available treatment, its limits, comfort care and support for the family. The longer-term outlook Many children with isolated unilateral MCDK and a healthy other kidney have a healthy childhood and ordinary school and play. Continuing the agreed checks matters even when they feel well, because high blood pressure, urine protein or reduced kidney function may be silent. Keep scan reports, test results and the follow-up plan together. Ask when care can be shared locally and how monitoring will continue as the child grows. Report new symptoms rather than waiting for a routine scan; the family's need for practical and emotional support is also part of care. Symptoms that need prompt help Seek prompt medical assessment for possible urine infection, poor feeding, repeated vomiting or noticeably fewer wet nappies. A suspected urinary infection in a baby under three months needs immediate paediatric assessment. Do not wait for several symptoms or the next kidney appointment. Get emergency help for breathing difficulty, blue or grey colouring, a seizure, loss of consciousness or difficulty waking, or no urine for twelve hours. A baby under three months with 38°C or higher, or a young child with a temperature below 36°C, also needs immediate emergency assessment. Seek help sooner if the child seems seriously unwell; do not wait for the twelve-hour mark. MCDK is a developmental kidney condition, distinct from inherited PKD. A healthy other kidney is central to the outlook; one-sided disease is often compatible with normal growth. Prenatal findings need a clear postnatal plan; ultrasound alone does not measure total kidney function. Tests, scan intervals and treatment are individualized; routine removal is usually unnecessary. Serious illness or possible infection needs timely assessment even between planned reviews. What causes MCDK? Often the exact cause is unknown and it occurs sporadically. It is not usually due to something a parent did. Genetic or syndromic causes are possible in selected cases; family history and other findings guide counselling. Do the cysts stop both kidneys working? The MCDK kidney has little or no useful function. When only one side is affected, a healthy other kidney usually provides adequate function and may enlarge. The affected kidney can shrink; its disappearance is not required to prove the other kidney is healthy. How is it diagnosed? It is often suspected on a mid-pregnancy scan and checked after birth with ultrasound. The assessment includes the other kidney and urinary tract. Uncertain findings may need specialist review and selected additional tests. Is there a treatment or cure? There is no medicine to rebuild the affected kidney, but monitoring and treatment of complications are useful care. Many uncomplicated unilateral cases need no operation. Kidney failure affecting both sides requires a separate specialist treatment and prognosis discussion. Does every baby need scans every six months? No single interval suits everyone. Age, the remaining kidney's appearance and growth, blood pressure, infections and previous results help determine follow-up. Ask for the actual schedule and who will review each result. Will a future baby have the same condition? Recurrence is often uncommon in isolated cases, but it is not possible to give one risk for every family. A known genetic cause or associated abnormalities can change the advice. Ask whether genetic counselling is appropriate. Can a child live normally with one working kidney? Many do, with ordinary growth, school and play. Follow the individualized monitoring plan because blood-pressure or kidney-function problems can occur without obvious symptoms. Extra dietary restrictions are not automatically needed. When should I seek urgent help? Possible urine infection, poor feeding, repeated vomiting or fewer wet nappies need prompt assessment; suspected UTI under three months needs immediate paediatric care. Breathing difficulty, blue/grey colour, seizure, loss of consciousness, difficulty waking or no urine for twelve hours are emergencies. Under three months, 38°C or higher is an emergency; a young child's temperature below 36°C also needs immediate emergency assessment. Seek help sooner if seriously unwell.

title: Hepatoblastoma in children: symptoms, treatment and follow-up
description: Understand this childhood liver cancer, the role of AFP and scans, surgery and chemotherapy, selected other treatments, and support during follow-up.
body: Hepatoblastoma is a rare cancer that starts in the liver, most often before age 3. A growing tummy or an unexplained lump needs medical assessment, but does not by itself mean cancer. If hepatoblastoma is diagnosed, a specialist children’s cancer team plans treatment around the tumour and the child’s needs. Changes that deserve assessment A painless lump in the upper abdomen or a gradually enlarging tummy can be the first noticeable change. Other possible symptoms include abdominal or back pain, reduced appetite, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, fever, itching, or yellow skin and eyes. Also report dark urine or newly prominent veins across the abdomen. These changes have several possible causes and do not establish a diagnosis. Arrange prompt medical assessment for an unexplained lump, swelling or persistent changes; jaundice needs urgent advice. Do not wait for pain, every listed symptom or a routine growth check. Sudden illness or severe pain needs the emergency response described below. Risk factors are not a prediction or a parent’s fault Most families cannot identify one cause. Birth very prematurely with very low birth weight is associated with higher risk, as are some predisposition conditions, including Beckwith–Wiedemann spectrum and familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP). Pathogenic changes in the APC tumour-suppressor gene cause FAP; these are connected findings, not two independent explanations. Both girls and boys can be affected. A risk factor does not mean a child will develop cancer, and its absence does not rule cancer out. Discuss a known family or genetic diagnosis with the clinical genetics team. Selected predisposition conditions need planned ultrasound and AFP screening, with the schedule tailored to the condition and regional guidance; this is not routine screening for every premature baby. Examination and blood tests The clinician asks about symptoms, growth, birth and medical history, medicines and family history, and examines the child. Blood tests may include a blood count, liver function and other chemistry tests, alongside alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). AFP can help assess a suspected liver tumour and follow its response to treatment. AFP is normally high in newborns and falls with age. It can also rise with noncancerous conditions or other tumours, and some hepatoblastomas do not produce a high level. Specialists interpret age-adjusted values and trends with imaging and tissue findings. One AFP result or a liver blood test cannot confirm or exclude hepatoblastoma alone. Scans, tissue diagnosis and extent of disease Ultrasound can examine a liver mass and blood vessels. MRI or CT helps map its location and extent; chest imaging, often CT, checks for spread to the lungs. An X-ray may be used for a particular question. The team chooses the necessary tests and explains contrast, radiation and any sedation rather than automatically ordering every scan. A pathologist usually examines tumour tissue, obtained through a team-planned biopsy or an operation that removes the tumour. A separate needle biopsy is not required in every surgical pathway. PRETEXT describes liver involvement before treatment and POSTTEXT after treatment; vessel involvement, several tumour sites and spread outside the liver add information. These findings guide safe treatment rather than size alone. Chemotherapy and surgery form the main treatment pathway The aim is to remove the cancer completely when possible. Many children first receive chemotherapy, commonly including cisplatin, to shrink the tumour before reassessment for surgery. Others can have an operation at diagnosis, depending on anatomy and the treatment protocol. Chemotherapy after surgery is often part of the plan. A partial hepatectomy removes the affected part of the liver. The sequence and amount of treatment depend on extent, tissue type, AFP, age, response and overall health. A small, carefully defined group with completely removed well-differentiated fetal tumours may be monitored without further chemotherapy. This exception does not make observation a substitute for treatment of an unremoved tumour. When a liver transplant may be considered Some tumours cannot be safely removed while leaving an adequate working liver, even after chemotherapy. Early assessment by a team experienced in children’s liver surgery and transplantation is important. A transplant replaces the whole liver with a donor liver; the decision depends on tumour distribution, vessels, treatment response and whether disease outside the liver is controlled, not simply a large measurement. Spread to the lungs may require chemotherapy and sometimes surgery before the liver operation or transplant can proceed. Not every child is eligible for transplantation, and a donor may not be immediately available. After transplant, ongoing specialist care and usually lifelong anti-rejection medicines are needed. Discuss benefits, complications and the plan while waiting. Arterial treatments and ablation are selected options Transarterial radioembolisation (TARE, often using yttrium-90 or Y-90) delivers radioactive microspheres through a catheter into arteries supplying the tumour. Transarterial chemoembolisation (TACE) delivers chemotherapy with material that obstructs tumour blood flow. Experienced centres may consider these approaches to help make selected tumours operable or manage disease that persists or returns. These procedures are not routine first treatment for every child and do not guarantee protection of healthy liver or a cure. Radiofrequency ablation destroys selected tumour deposits with heat and may be considered in recurrent disease or for symptom relief. Freezing is another ablation technique, but it is not an established routine hepatoblastoma treatment. Ask why a proposed procedure fits this child, what evidence supports it and whether it is part of a trial. A coordinated team supports the whole family Care usually involves paediatric oncology and haematology, experienced liver and transplant surgeons, radiologists and selected interventional radiology specialists, pathologists, liver or gastroenterology specialists, genetics professionals, nurses and dietitians. Rehabilitation, psychology, social work and child-life teams can help with development, procedures and everyday coping. Ask for explanations your child can understand and practical help with food, transport, finances, siblings and nursery or school. Nutrition support should follow the team’s advice; supplements or restrictive diets cannot replace cancer treatment. Ask about clinical trials, symptom relief and emotional support at any stage, including when treatment goals change. Outlook depends on more than removing a lump Many children can be cured, particularly when all disease can be removed and responds well to treatment. Outlook also depends on tissue type, extent and spread, blood-vessel involvement, AFP pattern, age and whether the cancer is newly diagnosed or recurrent. Complete surgery is important but cannot promise that cancer will never return or that there will be no lasting effects. Ask the treating team which risk group applies and how response changes the outlook. Published survival percentages describe groups treated in particular settings and periods; they are not an individual forecast or a deadline. A child’s future activities and support needs should be discussed individually, without promising one identical “normal” recovery for everyone. Follow-up checks for recurrence and treatment effects The cancer team sets a written schedule of examinations, AFP measurements when informative and appropriate scans during and after treatment. Early recurrence monitoring can be much more frequent than once a year. Keep the actual dates and ask which changes need earlier contact; a normal AFP alone does not replace the whole follow-up plan. Long-term survivorship care is a separate continuing need. Depending on treatment, checks may address hearing, kidney, heart or liver function, growth, learning and emotional wellbeing. Not every child develops these problems. Keep a treatment summary and survivorship plan, and continue transplant or genetic-condition surveillance when relevant. Know when to seek immediate help During cancer treatment, fever, chills or other signs of infection need immediate contact with the cancer team using its emergency plan, including its temperature threshold. Do not wait for the next visit or give fever-lowering medicine before getting the team’s advice if it could delay assessment or mask illness. Get emergency care immediately for severe or very sudden abdominal pain, pain when the abdomen is touched, breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour, unusual pallor or cold clammy skin, fainting or loss of consciousness, difficulty waking, a seizure, or blood in vomit or stool. These signs do not prove a tumour complication, but need urgent assessment whatever the cause. Do not wait for an app record or a routine appointment. An unexplained abdominal lump or swelling needs assessment; symptoms alone cannot diagnose hepatoblastoma. AFP must be interpreted for age and alongside scans and tissue findings. Chemotherapy, liver surgery and sometimes transplantation are planned by a specialist paediatric team. Arterial treatments and ablation are selected options, not universal substitutes for the main treatment pathway. Keep a written emergency and follow-up plan, including long-term treatment-effect care. What symptoms can hepatoblastoma cause? A painless upper-abdominal lump or swelling, pain, appetite or weight changes, nausea or vomiting can occur. Fever, jaundice, itching and back pain are other possible changes. They have other causes too; arrange assessment and do not wait for every symptom. Which children have higher risk? Very premature birth with very low birth weight and certain predisposition conditions, including Beckwith–Wiedemann spectrum and APC-related FAP, are associated with risk. Most children with a risk factor do not develop hepatoblastoma, and some affected children have no known risk. Can an AFP blood test diagnose it? Not alone. Normal values change with age, and other conditions can raise AFP. Some tumours do not raise it. The team combines age-adjusted results and trends with imaging and, usually, tissue examination. Does every child need chemotherapy and a transplant? No. Chemotherapy and complete tumour removal are common, but the sequence and amount vary. A transplant is considered when suitable complete removal cannot otherwise be achieved. A carefully defined, completely resected fetal-histology group may avoid chemotherapy. Are Y-90, TACE or ablation standard for everyone? No. They may have a role in selected difficult-to-remove, persistent or recurrent disease under experienced specialist care. They are not guaranteed cures or routine replacements for chemotherapy and surgery; ask about the evidence and purpose. Can a child live well after treatment? Many children do well, but outlook depends on tumour features, spread and response, and some need continuing support for treatment effects. Complete surgery does not guarantee no recurrence. Ask for an individual discussion and a survivorship plan. Are yearly checkups enough? Not necessarily. Recurrence checks often need a more frequent, protocol-specific schedule, while long-term survivorship checks address other risks. Follow the treating team’s written plan rather than applying one annual interval to every stage. Which symptoms must not wait? Follow the cancer team’s immediate fever and infection instructions during treatment. Severe or very sudden abdominal pain, abdominal tenderness, breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour, unusual pallor or cold clammy skin, fainting or loss of consciousness, difficulty waking, a seizure or blood in vomit or stool requires immediate emergency care.

title: Hemihyperplasia and lateralized overgrowth: assessment and follow-up
description: Understand one-sided body growth, genetic assessment, individual tumour-surveillance plans, limb-length care and changes that need medical attention.
body: A child's arm, leg or part of the face growing noticeably larger than the other side deserves an assessment. Hemihyperplasia is an older name often used for this pattern; specialists now commonly say lateralized overgrowth. The explanation and the child's particular needs guide care, including whether tumour surveillance is appropriate. What lateralized overgrowth means Lateralized overgrowth describes a substantial difference in the length or thickness of corresponding body parts. It can affect one region or several tissues on one side; it does not have to involve exactly half the body. Older records may use hemihyperplasia or hemihypertrophy. Small differences between the two sides are common and do not automatically indicate a disorder. Sometimes one side is undergrown rather than the other being overgrown. A condition that begins during development before birth may become obvious only later; the pattern reflects differences in tissue growth regulation, and how it changes over time depends on the underlying condition. Signs families may notice One arm or leg may be longer or broader, or the face or trunk may look uneven. Different shoe fit, a limp, toe walking, an uneven standing position or difficulty running may draw attention to a leg-length difference. Some children have few functional difficulties. There is no single reliable frequency estimate for all conditions grouped under this description. Mild differences may be missed, and changing diagnostic terms can mix different causes. Looking at a child lying on a flat surface or comparing photographs cannot establish a diagnosis or measure tumour risk. Genetic changes do not always mean an inherited condition Growth-regulating genetic or epigenetic changes can be involved. In mosaicism, a change is present in some cells rather than every cell. Beckwith–Wiedemann spectrum can involve altered regulation at chromosome region 11p15.5, but this does not explain every child with asymmetric growth. Some changes arise during early development and are not passed down through a family; others can have an inherited component. The specific finding determines recurrence counselling. An unaffected family history does not rule out a genetic cause, and the condition is not evidence that a parent did something wrong. Assessment looks for the whole pattern A paediatrician or clinician experienced in overgrowth, often a clinical geneticist, reviews birth, growth, development and family history. Examination considers limb measurements, gait, skin, other body regions and associated findings. Selected imaging and genetic tests answer particular questions; not every child needs every scan or a biopsy. Beckwith–Wiedemann spectrum may include lateralized overgrowth rather than being a condition that must simply be ruled out first. PIK3CA-related overgrowth, Proteus and Sotos syndromes have different patterns and care needs. Silver–Russell syndrome can cause asymmetry through restricted growth. A normal blood test may miss mosaic changes; specialists may discuss testing another tissue when appropriate. Tumour risk depends on the underlying diagnosis Some overgrowth conditions increase the chance of childhood tumours, particularly Wilms tumour in the kidney and hepatoblastoma in the liver. Other tumours, including adrenal tumours or some soft-tissue sarcomas, occur with particular predisposition conditions. A tumour may be benign or malignant; asymmetric growth itself is not a cancer diagnosis. The risk and the relevant tumour types differ between conditions and molecular findings. Mild visible features do not reliably mean low risk, but not every child with asymmetry has the same increased risk. An individual discussion is more useful than applying a percentage or a long cancer list to every family. Agree on a written surveillance plan When surveillance is indicated, regular tests aim to detect a tumour before symptoms develop. A current North American example for appropriate children is abdominal ultrasound and blood alpha-fetoprotein every three months until the third birthday, followed by kidney ultrasound every three months until the seventh birthday. This is not a universal schedule for every overgrowth diagnosis. Guidance differs by condition and healthcare system and has changed over time. For unexplained isolated overgrowth after a thorough assessment, the affected regions, baseline kidney findings and family preferences can influence the plan. Broader limb or trunk involvement may still warrant surveillance without an identified molecular cause. Ask which current protocol applies; do not stop or reschedule tests independently. How AFP results are interpreted Alpha-fetoprotein, abbreviated AFP, is a blood marker used in selected hepatoblastoma surveillance. It is naturally high in young infants and falls with age; some children with Beckwith–Wiedemann spectrum have a different age-related pattern. The team interprets the trend using appropriate reference values. One high result does not prove cancer, and one reassuring result does not replace the rest of the plan. Unexpected changes may lead to repeat testing or imaging. Ask who will review results and contact you. Home abdominal checks cannot substitute for scheduled clinical examinations, ultrasound or blood tests. Support for limb length and everyday function There is no single treatment that reverses every cause of lateralized overgrowth. Care addresses the diagnosis and its effects. A paediatric orthopaedic team can assess walking, pain, limb lengths and remaining growth, then decide whether observation, a fitted shoe lift, rehabilitation or an operation would help. Treatment is individual: some differences need monitoring only, while selected larger or progressive leg-length differences may benefit from surgery that changes growth or limb length. Timing, benefits and complications need discussion. Do not buy corrective footwear or use a home exercise or measurement routine as a substitute for assessment. Make follow-up workable for the family Keep growth records, relevant previous photographs, test results and questions for visits. Ask for clear dates, the purpose of each test and a contact for missed appointments or new concerns. Genetic counselling can explain what is known, what remains uncertain and whether relatives need evaluation. A child's comfort, mobility, development, school participation and feelings about visible differences also matter. Ask for practical and psychological support when needed. Continue agreed follow-up even when the child feels well; equally, a new symptom needs attention between appointments rather than waiting for the surveillance date. Changes that should not wait Contact the clinical team promptly for a new abdominal lump or swelling, persistent pain, unexplained appetite or weight changes, or a new change in walking. These findings have several causes and do not by themselves prove a tumour. Do not repeatedly press a lump or assume every new symptom is part of the known growth condition. Seek immediate emergency assessment for sudden hip, knee or thigh pain, inability to bear weight, a deformed leg, or a limp with fever and an unwell child. Breathing difficulty, a seizure, difficulty waking or unresponsiveness also needs emergency care. A scheduled scan, app entry or attempt to measure the difference must not delay help. Persistent one-sided growth needs a clinical assessment; ordinary asymmetry and undergrowth are different possibilities. Genetic and mosaic causes vary, and a normal blood test may not answer every question. Tumour surveillance is diagnosis-specific; follow the team's written current plan. AFP is interpreted for age and over time, alongside appropriate scans and examinations. Limb function, development and family support belong alongside tumour-risk care. What causes hemihyperplasia or lateralized overgrowth? Several genetic or epigenetic conditions can affect regional growth, sometimes through mosaic changes present in only some cells. The cause can remain uncertain. It is not always inherited and is not evidence of parental fault. What signs can it cause? A limb may be longer or thicker, or parts of the trunk or face may be uneven. Shoe fit, standing posture or walking can change. Small differences alone do not establish a disorder; persistent or increasing differences deserve assessment. Is it always a chromosome 11 condition? No. Chromosome region 11p15.5 is important in Beckwith–Wiedemann spectrum, but other causes involve different pathways. Family recurrence depends on the diagnosis. Blood testing may miss mosaic findings, so a specialist may discuss other tissue testing. How is it diagnosed? A clinician combines growth and family history with examination, measurements, gait and associated findings. Selected scans and molecular tests can help distinguish overgrowth conditions from ordinary asymmetry or undergrowth. A home flat-surface comparison cannot diagnose it. Does every child need the same cancer screening? No. The diagnosis, molecular findings, distribution of growth, kidney assessment and regional guidance matter. Some children need regular ultrasound and AFP tests; others need a different plan after specialist review. Do not change an existing schedule without the team. Does a high AFP mean cancer? Not necessarily. AFP is naturally high in infancy and must be interpreted using age-related values and trends. The team may repeat a test or arrange imaging. A normal result alone does not replace ultrasound or follow-up when these are indicated. Can the growth difference be treated? Care depends on the cause and functional effect. Observation, a fitted shoe lift, rehabilitation or selected surgery may help a leg-length difference. There is no single cure or operation suitable for everyone, and tumour-risk care remains a separate need. When should we seek help between appointments? Report a new lump, abdominal swelling, persistent pain, unexplained weight or appetite change, or a new limp promptly. Sudden hip, knee or thigh pain, inability to bear weight, a deformed leg, a limp with fever and illness, breathing difficulty, a seizure or reduced responsiveness requires immediate emergency assessment.

title: Cyclopia: prenatal diagnosis, prognosis and family care
description: Understand cyclopia and severe holoprosencephaly, specialist scans and genetic testing, the very poor prognosis, recurrence questions and support for families.
body: Hearing a suspected diagnosis of cyclopia can be overwhelming. It is a rare, very severe developmental condition involving the brain and face, rather than an isolated eye problem. Specialist confirmation, clear explanations and compassionate support can help families understand the findings and make an individual care plan. What cyclopia means Cyclopia describes a single central eye or partly divided eye within one eye socket. The nose may be absent, and a tube-like structure called a proboscis may lie above the eye; it is not always present. These changes develop before birth and are associated with profound abnormalities of the developing forebrain. It occurs at the severe end of holoprosencephaly (HPE), in which the forebrain fails to separate normally into right and left parts. Cyclopia is particularly associated with alobar HPE, the most severe major form. The terms are not interchangeable: not every baby with alobar HPE has cyclopia, and the wider HPE spectrum includes less severe conditions with different outcomes. Causes are varied, and uncertainty is common A chromosome difference, such as an extra chromosome 13, or a change in a gene involved in early brain development can be involved. Some changes arise newly; others can be inherited. A wider genetic syndrome is possible, but a precise cause is not always found. Appearance alone cannot establish which explanation applies. Diabetes in pregnancy is associated with HPE, particularly diabetes present before pregnancy; this does not prove the cause in an individual family. Medicines and other relevant exposures should be reviewed with the specialist, rather than assumed harmless or blamed automatically. A diagnosis is not evidence of parental fault. Do not stop an essential prescription without advice, and do not assume every case is solely genetic or preventable. How the diagnosis is assessed during pregnancy Specialist ultrasound examines the face, forebrain and other organs. Severe alobar HPE can sometimes be identified in the first trimester, but detection depends on gestation, image quality and expertise. The very early developmental event is not the same as a time when a scan can reliably diagnose it; a normal early scan cannot exclude every HPE form. Fetal MRI may add information when expert ultrasound leaves a specific question unanswered. It is not required in every case, and very early MRI often adds little. Ultrasound and MRI do not use ionising radiation; appropriately performed non-contrast fetal MRI has no known adverse fetal effects, but the team still checks indications and safety. Ask what is confirmed, what remains uncertain and whether another specialist review would help. What genetic tests can and cannot answer A fetal-medicine and genetics team may discuss diagnostic sampling, such as chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis, and chromosome or gene tests selected for the findings. Screening blood tests and a scan do not replace every diagnostic test. The team should explain the purpose, limits, timing and risks of any proposed procedure; deciding whether to have testing is personal. Results may clarify a chromosome change, an inherited condition or a new genetic change, but a negative result does not rule out every cause. Parents may be offered testing or examination for subtle related features. If the baby dies, further examination or testing may be discussed with consent. Keep reports and arrange a results appointment even when no definite explanation is found. A very poor prognosis, without a personal clock Cyclopia is associated with extremely severe brain and facial abnormalities. Many affected pregnancies end in miscarriage or stillbirth; babies born alive generally survive only a short time. The outlook is not explained by having one eye alone: severe disruption of brain development and essential functions, and sometimes other organ differences, are central. There is no treatment that reconstructs normal forebrain development or makes this an isolated, correctable eye condition. An individual case report cannot predict another baby’s exact course. Equally, reports of longer survival in other HPE forms must not be presented as reassurance for confirmed cyclopia. Ask specialists to explain the diagnosis-specific prognosis and any remaining uncertainty honestly. Planning pregnancy and newborn care Families should be offered a private discussion with fetal-medicine, newborn and appropriate genetics specialists about available options. These can include continuing the pregnancy with an individual birth and comfort-care plan, and discussion of ending the pregnancy where available. Decisions should be informed and voluntary, with support rather than pressure. There is no single delivery or intervention plan for every family. Perinatal palliative care supports comfort, symptom relief and the family before, during and after birth. A written plan can cover where care will occur, who to contact, newborn assessment, pain and breathing comfort, feeding where appropriate, and time together if wished. The plan may need revision after assessment at birth. Comfort-focused care is active care, although it cannot cure the underlying malformation. Recurrence and a future pregnancy Rarity does not mean that recurrence is impossible, and one affected pregnancy does not prove that a parent carries a genetic change. Risk depends on the cause and the parents’ results. In some inherited forms, relatives can have mild or no obvious features and effects can vary within a family; no single recurrence percentage applies to everyone. Ask for genetic counselling before another pregnancy if possible. Known family findings may allow targeted prenatal or preimplantation genetic testing; these are options to discuss, not guarantees of a particular outcome. The team can advise which relatives might benefit from information or testing, respecting privacy. Review diabetes care, medicines and the future scan plan; no general action guarantees prevention of cyclopia. Support and symptoms that should not wait Grief, shock and guilt can affect both parents and others close to them. Ask for counselling, bereavement and practical support, including follow-up after loss and advice about breast discomfort or milk production when relevant. Seeing or holding the baby and making memories are choices, not obligations. You can ask for explanations again and bring someone you trust to appointments. Continue the agreed maternity plan and seek immediate advice for vaginal bleeding or reduced or changed usual fetal movements; do not wait for an app reminder or the next day. Bleeding with severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, nausea, faintness, dizziness or loss of consciousness, or heavy bleeding needs emergency help. Do not assume symptoms are simply part of the fetal diagnosis. Ask the team for written contact and emergency instructions tailored to your care. Cyclopia is linked to very severe forebrain development differences, not an isolated eye problem. Specialist imaging and selected genetic tests clarify findings but have limits. The prognosis is extremely poor; neither a case report nor another HPE form gives a personal survival prediction. Recurrence advice depends on the actual cause and family results. Individual birth, comfort and family-support plans remain important care. Is cyclopia the same as every form of holoprosencephaly? No. It occurs at the very severe end, particularly with alobar HPE. Other HPE forms and even some alobar cases have different facial findings and outcomes. Specialist interpretation is essential. When can it be diagnosed? Severe findings may be visible on specialist first-trimester ultrasound or later scans. Timing and certainty vary. The condition begins very early, but this does not mean a scan can diagnose it immediately after that developmental event. Will the baby survive? The prognosis for confirmed cyclopia is extremely poor. Many pregnancies end before birth, and live-born babies generally survive briefly. Ask the team about the precise findings and uncertainty; a reported number of hours is not an individual deadline. Can surgery or another treatment cure it? No current treatment restores normal forebrain development. It is not simply an eye problem that an operation can correct. Specialist care can still provide comfort, symptom relief and support for the baby and family. Is it inherited or caused by something a parent did? Chromosome changes, inherited or new gene changes and other factors may be involved; sometimes the cause remains unknown. The diagnosis does not prove parental fault or an inherited change. Tests and counselling address the individual circumstances. Will it happen again in another pregnancy? There is no universal answer. Risk depends on the cause and parental findings, not rarity alone. Genetic counselling can explain testing, relevant family communication and a future pregnancy plan without guaranteeing prevention. Does every family need the same tests or birth plan? No. Imaging findings, genetic questions, procedure risks, available care and the family’s informed preferences matter. Discuss options with the team and ask for a written plan that can be reviewed as new information emerges. When should I contact maternity care urgently? Seek immediate advice for pregnancy bleeding or a reduction or change in usual fetal movements. Bleeding with severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, nausea, faintness, dizziness or loss of consciousness, or heavy bleeding needs emergency help. Follow your individual care plan; do not wait for tracking or a routine visit.

title: Children with one functioning kidney: care, sport and growing up
description: Understand a missing or nonfunctioning kidney, selective testing, lifelong checks and individual sports decisions for children with one functioning kidney.
body: Many children with one healthy functioning kidney grow, attend school and enjoy active lives. The important questions are how that kidney and urinary tract developed, whether they work well, and what follow-up and activity plan fits the child. Having one kidney is not a reason to treat a child as fragile, but normal early results do not remove the need for later checks. One kidney can mean different things Unilateral renal agenesis means one kidney did not develop. A child may instead have two kidneys but only one that works, for example because the other developed abnormally, as in multicystic dysplastic kidney, or was damaged by another condition. These diagnoses share some care needs but are not interchangeable. A pregnancy ultrasound may raise the question; it does not find every case or settle every detail. The team checks the remaining kidney, urine drainage and other development, then usually confirms the anatomy with ultrasound after birth.
