A healthy kidney may enlarge to compensate, but size alone cannot establish that it functions normally. Causes, family history and future pregnancies Often no single cause is identified. Sometimes an absent or abnormal kidney accompanies other urinary, genital or wider developmental differences, including a genetic condition. A finding during pregnancy does not establish that something a parent did caused it. The pregnancy review can include diabetes and medicine exposures, without assuming either explains an individual child's finding. Recurrence depends on the diagnosis, family history and any identified cause; a single reassuring number does not apply to every family. Discuss relatives with kidney problems and associated findings with the team. Genetics advice or testing is selected when useful, rather than required for every otherwise isolated case. Do not stop a prescribed medicine because of a suspected pregnancy association without advice. Which investigations are actually needed? Ultrasound helps assess kidney tissue, growth, position, bladder and urine drainage. Blood tests can estimate kidney function, while urine testing looks for protein or infection. The child's history and examination help decide which tests are needed and when. A voiding cystourethrogram, or VCUG, can investigate urine reflux or an outlet problem; selected nuclear scans can clarify uncertain tissue or drainage. These are not an automatic package for every child with a normal remaining kidney and urinary tract. Abnormal ultrasound findings, infections or concerns about function may change the plan; ask what question an additional test will answer. Blood pressure, urine and long-term follow-up Some children later develop high blood pressure, protein or albumin in urine, or reduced kidney function. Risk is greater when the remaining kidney or urinary tract is also abnormal. A child who feels well can still have changes that are found through checks. Arrange a written follow-up plan. Blood pressure is commonly checked yearly, with urine protein or albumin checks and selected blood tests and repeat imaging according to risk and local practice. Not every child needs every test annually. Growth, puberty, previous results and any urinary infections also matter; nephrology follow-up may be needed for higher-risk findings. Most sport decisions are individual, not a blanket ban Physical activity supports health, confidence and friendships. Most children with one functioning kidney can participate in many sports. Noncontact activities are generally encouraged; contact, collision and activities involving falls need an informed discussion rather than an automatic yes or no. Kidney injuries are uncommon in sport, but an injury to the only functioning kidney could have serious consequences. Research cannot give a reliable personal risk for every activity or child. Consider the child's current health and kidney findings, the activity, playing position, level of competition, maturity and the size and behaviour of other participants. Make participation safer without promising protection Discuss supervision, instruction, suitable equipment and whether rules, position or intensity can be adapted. A coach should understand the agreed plan and know what to do after an injury. Cycling, horse riding, skiing, snowboarding and motorized activities need their own consideration; a simple contact-versus-noncontact label misses some risks. Kidney guards or padding may be considered, but evidence has not established that they prevent serious kidney injury. They do not replace safe practice or individual advice. Review decisions as the child grows or the sport changes, and include the child's preferences. After a significant blow, seek prompt medical advice about pain or blood in urine rather than continuing play or waiting for the next routine visit. Daily life, food, fluids and medicines If kidney function is normal, a special restrictive diet is usually unnecessary. Offer a varied age-appropriate diet, ordinary adequate fluids and healthy growth habits; avoid excessive salt and high-protein supplements. Forcing extra water or cutting a child's protein intake without a professional plan is not a kidney-protection treatment. Tell healthcare professionals about the single functioning kidney before medicines or procedures. Check over-the-counter painkillers and supplements with a clinician or pharmacist, particularly during dehydration or illness; some medicines, including NSAIDs, can stress the kidneys in certain circumstances. A child with reduced function may need specific diet or medicine advice. Do not stop necessary treatment independently. School, independence and adult continuity Keep ordinary well-child care, vaccinations and school participation. Explain the condition in age-appropriate terms and give relevant carers a practical plan, while protecting the child's privacy. Feeling anxious about sport or the future is a reason for support and discussion, not evidence that everyday life must be restricted. Follow-up should continue into adulthood even when childhood tests are reassuring. During transition, make sure the young person knows the diagnosis, current kidney function, monitoring schedule and where to seek help. Adults still need blood-pressure and urine checks with blood tests as advised. Future pregnancy planning can include kidney and blood-pressure review rather than assuming that good childhood health guarantees no later risk. Illness and warning signs: when to get help Seek urgent same-day advice if a child may have a urinary infection, including painful or frequent urination, fever, new wetting, vomiting, poor feeding or pain in the back under the ribs. Blood in urine also needs urgent assessment. Mention the kidney history; a symptom or urine appearance alone cannot diagnose infection. Get emergency help for difficulty breathing, fainting or loss of consciousness, difficulty waking, a seizure, or suspected infection with confusion, unusual drowsiness or speech difficulty. In a child under five, no urine for 12 hours, unusually pale or blue/grey skin, or a baby under three months with a temperature of 38°C or higher also needs emergency assessment. Do not wait for all signs. Do not drive yourself in an emergency; arrange another driver or an ambulance. Confirm why there is one functioning kidney and whether the remaining kidney and urinary tract are healthy. Use a risk-based lifelong plan for blood pressure, urine and other selected tests. Most activities are possible; discuss the actual sport, child, setting and consequences of injury. Padding is not a guarantee, and healthy kidney function usually does not require a restrictive diet. Seek prompt help for suspected urinary infection or injury symptoms; emergency warning signs override routine follow-up. Why was my child born with one kidney? One kidney may not have formed, or one may have developed abnormally and not function. Often a definite cause is not found. Associated findings and family history help determine whether a wider condition should be investigated; the diagnosis does not establish parental fault. Will another child in the family have the same condition? That depends on whether this is an isolated finding or part of a particular genetic or developmental condition. Discuss the exact diagnosis and family history before another pregnancy; genetics counselling is useful when indicated. No single recurrence estimate fits all families. Does a well child still need checks? Yes. Blood pressure and urine protein or albumin can change before symptoms appear. Agree a lifelong plan, commonly including yearly blood pressure, with the frequency of urine, blood and ultrasound checks tailored to risk. A normal early scan does not end follow-up. Do we need to treat our child differently day to day? Support normal school, play and routine healthcare. With normal kidney function, a varied ordinary diet and adequate fluids are generally appropriate. Share the care plan with relevant carers, discuss medicines, and avoid unsupported restrictions or supplements. Are contact sports forbidden? Not automatically. Discuss kidney and general health, the specific sport, playing position, competition level, maturity, other players, coaching and possible adaptations. Evidence does not establish a precise personal risk or guarantee that every activity is suitable. Will a kidney guard make sport safe? A guard may be considered, but protection against serious kidney injury has not been proved. It cannot replace individual advice, suitable supervision, instruction or safe equipment. Revisit the plan if the child or activity changes. Does every child need a VCUG or nuclear scan? No. Ultrasound and the clinical history guide the next steps. Reflux testing or nuclear imaging may be useful for abnormal findings, urinary infections or uncertainty about function or drainage. Ask which question the test would answer and how its result would change care. Which symptoms should not wait? A possible urinary infection, blood in urine or symptoms after a significant impact need urgent advice. Breathing difficulty, fainting or loss of consciousness, difficulty waking, seizures or infection with confusion, unusual drowsiness or speech difficulty need emergency help. Under five, no urine for 12 hours or unusual pallor/blue-grey skin is also an emergency; a baby under three months with 38°C or higher needs emergency assessment. Do not wait for every sign or drive yourself in an emergency.

title: Heart failure in babies and children: symptoms, causes and care
description: Understand pediatric heart failure, feeding and breathing signs, different causes, specialist treatment and nutrition, and which changes need emergency help.
body: Heart failure means that the heart and circulation are not meeting the body’s needs effectively. It does not mean the heart has stopped. In children, an abnormal route of blood flow, an obstruction, a heart-muscle problem or an abnormal rhythm can be responsible. A baby who tires during feeds and an older child who cannot manage usual activity may need different investigations and treatment. What does congestive heart failure mean? The heart normally sends blood to the lungs to receive oxygen and then to the body. Heart failure can develop even when the muscle squeezes reasonably well, if a structural problem makes circulation inefficient. It can also occur when the heart cannot pump or fill effectively. The diagnosis describes a clinical problem, not one specific defect. Congestion means blood and fluid build up where they should not. Problems affecting the left heart can contribute to fluid in the lungs; right-sided problems can cause congestion in the liver and body’s veins. Both sides may be involved. This is different from cardiac arrest, although severe deterioration can be life-threatening. Too much blood going to the lungs Some congenital connections allow oxygen-rich blood to circulate back toward the lungs. Examples include a large ventricular septal defect, an opening between the two lower pumping chambers, and a patent ductus arteriosus, a fetal vessel between the pulmonary artery and aorta that remains open. A large duct can be important in a premature baby. The effect depends on the actual blood flow, not simply the presence of a hole. An aortopulmonary window is an abnormal connection between the great arteries; truncus arteriosus involves a common arterial outlet. They are different defects that can also produce excessive lung blood flow. An isolated atrial septal defect, between the upper chambers, rarely causes heart failure in infancy. The cardiologist explains which anatomy matters for that child. Obstruction, heart-muscle disease and rhythm problems Critical aortic-valve narrowing, coarctation of the aorta or an underdeveloped left heart can obstruct effective blood flow to the body. These are not all the same as a primarily weak heart muscle. Some newborns become seriously ill as fetal connections close, so an apparently comfortable first day does not guarantee safety. Cardiomyopathy affects the heart muscle; myocarditis is inflammation of it. Infections, inherited or other diseases and persistent abnormal rhythms can contribute. Kawasaki disease can affect the heart and coronary arteries. A rhythm that is too fast or too slow may impair pumping. Babies as well as older children can have myocardial or rhythm-related failure, sometimes without an obvious structural defect. Signs in babies: feeding, breathing and growth A baby may tire, sweat or stop early during milk feeds, take less milk or gain weight slowly. Rapid or laboured breathing and a fast heartbeat can increase the effort of feeding. Some babies have less energy or become unusually sleepy; swelling around the eyes, feet or abdomen can occur. A forceful visible heartbeat or a small appearance alone cannot establish the diagnosis. A clinician assesses growth over time, breathing, circulation and signs such as an enlarged liver or unusual heart sounds. Some children need developmental support too. New or worsening feeding fatigue, sweating, reduced intake, swelling or poor growth needs urgent same-day advice from the child’s team. Breathing difficulty, abnormal colour or reduced responsiveness needs emergency help instead. Why symptoms do not always start at birth After birth, blood flow changes as resistance in the lungs falls. A baby with a large left-to-right shunt may initially feed well and develop increasing breathing or feeding difficulty over the following weeks. The timing varies; there is no guaranteed symptom-free first fortnight or fixed week when failure must appear. A severe obstruction or myocardial problem may cause illness much earlier, including in the first days. A normal earlier examination, apparently normal pulses or no obvious murmur cannot exclude later deterioration. Do not wait for a scheduled check or a particular age if the baby becomes unwell. How it may appear in an older child An older child may become breathless or unusually tired with walking, stairs or play they previously managed. Appetite may fall, weight gain may slow or weight may be lost. Conversely, fluid retention can cause swelling and rapid weight gain. Cough, abdominal discomfort or a swollen liver may be part of the picture; a clinician may hear a gallop rhythm. Chest pain, palpitations, dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness also need attention. Compare the child’s abilities with their usual pattern rather than assuming every difference from a friend means disease. Fainting during exercise is an emergency, even if the child then seems better. Stop activity and obtain help; do not test whether the symptoms recur. Which changes need immediate help? Call emergency services for very fast or difficult breathing, blue/grey or unusually pale or blotchy colour, cold or clammy/damp skin, fainting or loss of consciousness, a floppy or hard-to-wake child, a seizure or a weak, high-pitched or continuous cry. In babies under 3 months, a temperature of 38°C or more needs immediate emergency assessment; a temperature below 36°C or no urine for 12 hours in a baby or young child also needs immediate emergency assessment. A child does not need every sign. Chest pain, a new fast or irregular heartbeat, new confusion, drowsiness or dizziness in a child with suspected or known heart disease also warrants immediate emergency help. Fainting during exercise must not wait for a routine appointment. Do not drive the unwell child yourself: arrange another driver or an ambulance as advised. For other new feeding, growth, swelling or exercise concerns, seek urgent same-day clinical advice rather than relying on an app or home monitor. How the team investigates heart failure Assessment starts with the history, feeding and growth pattern, examination and vital signs. Echocardiography shows structure, blood flow and muscle function; an ECG records electrical activity and rhythm. Chest imaging can show heart size and lung congestion. Blood tests may check organ function, body salts and other clues. These findings are interpreted together, not as a home checklist. Some children need cardiac MRI, catheterization to measure pressures or clarify anatomy, selected genetic or infection investigations, or a supervised exercise test when appropriate and stable. Not every child needs every test. The team should explain the suspected cause and the immediate plan; tests must not delay stabilization of an acutely unwell child. Medicines must fit the cause and the child A diuretic such as furosemide helps remove excess fluid through the kidneys. Other selected medicines, including ACE inhibitors or beta blockers, may reduce workload or help particular types of myocardial dysfunction. Digoxin can be useful in selected pumping or rhythm problems. These are examples, not a universal first-line combination: drugs used for muscle failure are not automatically appropriate for every left-to-right shunt. The cardiology team selects the medicine, formulation and dose and monitors effects such as blood pressure, heart rate, kidney function and electrolytes. Check before adding nonprescription or herbal products, and ask what to do after a missed or vomited dose. Do not change doses, stop treatment, double a dose or impose salt or fluid restrictions yourself. A new concerning symptom needs advice rather than assuming it is only a medicine effect. Repairing a defect or treating a rhythm Medicines may control symptoms while a child is assessed for repair; they do not close a structural defect. Some ventricular openings become smaller or close naturally, but waiting for growth is not appropriate for every large symptomatic defect. An aortopulmonary window, truncus arteriosus, critical obstruction or complex left-heart condition may need early intervention, sometimes in stages. Timing follows anatomy and the child’s condition. A slow rhythm may require a pacemaker; some fast rhythms need medicines or a catheter procedure such as ablation. Repair, palliation and rhythm treatment have different goals and risks. Some children recover good function; others need ongoing treatment or further procedures. Ask what the proposed intervention can achieve and what it cannot promise. Nutrition is part of treatment Extra work of breathing and feeding can use energy needed for growth. A dietitian and feeding team may prescribe fortified breast milk, higher-calorie formula or a different feeding schedule. Breastfeeding support can remain valuable. A nasogastric tube carries milk from the nose into the stomach and can reduce feeding effort while delivering the nutrition the child needs; it is not intended to deprive the child of calories. Selected older children also need nutritional or tube-feeding support. The route, amount and any fluid limit are individualized. Do not concentrate or dilute milk, force feeds or give extra water without the team’s instructions. Ask for a written preparation and feeding plan and what to do if intake falls, vomiting occurs or medicines cannot be kept down. Hospital care and advanced support A child who deteriorates may need hospital medicines and breathing or circulatory support. Oxygen is prescribed according to the anatomy and clinical situation: changing lung and body blood flow can matter in some congenital defects. This is not a reason to withhold emergency care or adjust prescribed oxygen at home. Use the cardiac team’s specific targets and response plan. For selected advanced failure, ECMO or a ventricular assist device can support circulation during recovery or while awaiting transplant. Some devices offer longer-term support; a total artificial heart is an option only for selected patients, not every baby or everyone unsuitable for transplant. Body size, anatomy, risks, available expertise and family goals guide decisions. Transplant is one possible pathway, with its own lifelong treatment and follow-up. Activity, outlook and a workable family plan The outlook depends on the cause, severity, response and any remaining disease. Treating a reversible problem or repairing a defect can improve function, but neither a normal life nor progressive decline can be predicted for every child. Cardiomyopathy may improve in some circumstances or progress in others. Keep cardiology follow-up even when symptoms improve, and discuss growth, development, school needs and emotional support. Agree an activity plan with the cardiac team. Some children need limits or supervised rehabilitation; others can enjoy a range of activities. Swimming is not automatically safe for every child with heart failure, and a blanket ban on all play is not an individualized plan. Keep medicine and feeding instructions, contact details and warning thresholds available to caregivers. New symptoms and emergency signs take priority over recording data or waiting for the next visit. Heart failure describes ineffective circulation, not a heart that has stopped; several different childhood mechanisms can cause it. Feeding fatigue, sweating and poor growth in babies, or declining activity in older children, need clinical assessment. Breathing, colour or responsiveness changes and fainting during exercise can require immediate emergency help. Medicines, repair, feeding support and advanced devices are selected for the actual cause; do not alter treatment or milk preparation yourself. Follow-up, activity and outlook are individual, with support for the child and family beyond the next procedure. How is heart failure treated in a baby or child? Treatment follows the cause and severity. It may include selected medicines, nutritional support, repair of a defect or rhythm treatment. Some children need hospital or advanced device/transplant care. Medicines may control symptoms without repairing the anatomy; no single regimen or operation suits everyone. Can a well-squeezing heart still be involved? Yes. An abnormal connection can send excessive blood back to the lungs even when the muscle squeezes well. Obstruction, myocardial disease and rhythm problems are other mechanisms. The team determines which applies rather than diagnosing from the word failure alone. What signs can appear in a baby? Tiring or sweating during feeds, reduced intake, slow growth, fast breathing, less energy or swelling can occur. These signs have other causes too. New feeding or growth changes need urgent advice; difficult breathing, abnormal colour, floppiness or difficulty waking needs emergency help. Can a child lead an active life? Many children improve with treatment, but the outlook depends on the actual condition and response. Some need lifelong medicines, procedures or activity adjustments. Ask for individualized advice about play, school and sport; neither guaranteed recovery nor inevitable decline is accurate for every child. Can symptoms begin after a reassuring newborn check? Yes. Circulation changes after birth, and some shunts cause increasing symptoms over weeks. Severe obstruction or muscle disease may present earlier. A normal previous check is not a reason to ignore new breathing, feeding or responsiveness changes. Does every child need all the heart tests? No. History, examination, echo and ECG often guide care; blood tests, imaging, catheterization, genetics or supervised exercise testing are selected for the findings. A child who is acutely unwell needs stabilization rather than waiting for a complete outpatient test list. Should I add more formula powder or water to help? Do not change milk concentration or fluid intake yourself. The feeding and cardiac teams may prescribe extra calories or tube feeding, but the exact preparation, volume and schedule must fit the child. Ask for written instructions and prompt advice if feeding worsens. When should we get emergency help? Get immediate help for difficult or very fast breathing, blue/grey or unusually pale/blotchy colour, cold or damp skin, fainting or loss of consciousness, floppiness, difficulty waking, seizure or a weak/high-pitched/continuous cry. A baby under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or more needs immediate emergency assessment. A temperature below 36°C or no urine for 12 hours in a baby or young child also needs immediate emergency assessment. Chest pain, new rhythm problems, confusion, drowsiness or dizziness with suspected heart disease, and fainting during exercise, are also emergency warnings. Do not drive the unwell child yourself or wait for all signs.

title: Skeletal dysplasias: signs, diagnosis and lifelong care
description: Understand the varied bone and cartilage conditions called skeletal dysplasias, how they are assessed, and how treatment supports health and daily life.
body: Skeletal dysplasia names a family of conditions, not one diagnosis with one treatment. A child's growth pattern, joints or spine may prompt assessment, but appearance alone cannot identify the condition. Finding the specific cause helps a team plan care around breathing, movement, comfort and participation as well as growth. A diverse family of skeletal conditions Hundreds of genetic disorders affect how bone and cartilage develop, grow or remain healthy. Classification changes as knowledge advances; the broad 2023 genetic skeletal-disorder nosology contained 771 entries. An older estimate of about 400 should not be treated as a fixed current total. Achondroplasia is a common example and the most common cause of disproportionate short stature. It is not a template for every dysplasia. Limb and trunk proportions, height, bone strength and other health effects vary; short stature alone does not establish a skeletal dysplasia or a growth-hormone deficiency. Possible signs are clues, not a checklist Depending on the condition, there may be a spinal curve such as kyphosis, unstable neck vertebrae, narrowing around the spinal cord, bowed legs or knock knees, clubfeet, stiff joints or early arthritis. Some conditions involve fragile bones or teeth, hearing or vision problems, or a cleft palate. No child is expected to have all these features. A larger head or a prominent forehead with shorter limbs occurs in some conditions. A large head alone does not mean hydrocephalus, which involves excess fluid in the brain. Certain dysplasias can compress the spinal cord or brainstem; others have different concerns. Development and learning also need individual assessment rather than assumptions based on body size. Genetics and family questions A causal genetic change may be inherited or arise for the first time in a child. Different disorders have different inheritance patterns, and the absence of a family history does not rule one out. This is not evidence that a parent caused the condition through ordinary daily activity. Genetic counselling can explain what testing may establish, uncertain results and the implications for relatives or future pregnancies. There is no single recurrence percentage for all skeletal dysplasias. Keep a copy of the actual genetic report, since a gene name or an uncertain variant alone may not establish the diagnosis. Recognition and assessment can happen at different ages Some forms are suspected on prenatal ultrasound, others at birth or during childhood, and milder forms may be recognized later. A normal earlier scan does not exclude every condition. Prenatal findings may need specialist imaging, genetic assessment and a plan for birth and newborn care; prognosis depends on the specific disorder and findings. After birth, assessment combines growth and body proportions, family and medical history, examination and appropriately selected imaging. A skeletal survey is a set of X-rays used to recognize patterns when a skeletal disorder is suspected. A specialist may recommend genetic testing and hearing, eye, respiratory or other assessment according to the findings. One test does not answer every question. Imaging follows the clinical question There is no universal rule that every child needs CT, brain ultrasound or MRI only after six months. X-rays help show bone patterns; CT can clarify selected bony questions, while MRI can assess the brain, spinal cord and surrounding tissues. The team chooses the method and timing for the particular concern, sometimes in infancy. MRI does not use ionizing radiation, but remaining still, sedation or anaesthesia and implanted devices require planning. Tell the team about breathing problems, neck or spinal instability, previous operations and implants before any procedure. Ask why imaging is needed and how results will change care; do not try neck movements at home to test stability. Treatment supports the whole person Care may involve a paediatrician, genetics team, orthopaedic or neurosurgical specialists, physiotherapy and occupational therapy, with eye, hearing, dental or respiratory specialists as needed. Observation and planned reviews can be appropriate treatment. Pain management, rehabilitation and suitable equipment can support function without making surgery the default. Agree practical goals such as comfortable sitting, getting around school, hearing lessons or managing fatigue. Activity advice and equipment should fit the diagnosis and the child, not simply height. Some conditions have targeted medicines, but availability, eligibility and benefits are condition-specific; a treatment for achondroplasia is not a treatment for every skeletal dysplasia. Surgery is selected for a defined problem Hydrocephalus may require neurosurgical treatment. When indicated, decompression creates space around compressed nerve tissue, while stabilization or fusion addresses spinal instability. An osteotomy cuts and realigns a bone; joint replacement may be considered for selected severe arthritis. These are different procedures for different problems, not a routine sequence for every child. Limb lengthening is a separate, complex choice, not an obligation or a cure for the underlying condition. Risks can include infection, nerve or vessel injury, joint stiffness and problems with bone healing. Discuss alternatives, rehabilitation, further operations and the child's own goals and participation. Timing depends on the problem, growth and the balance of benefit and risk. Follow-up extends beyond an operation After surgery, follow the individual wound, activity, rehabilitation and review plan. Long-term care is also needed when no operation takes place: symptoms and priorities can change with growth. Ask who coordinates care and how to contact the team between appointments. School adaptations and emotional or peer support can be as important as medical procedures. Plan the move to adult services with the young person, including a named contact, transfer of imaging and genetic results, treatment history and an emergency plan. The pace should reflect readiness and local services rather than an abrupt end to paediatric care. Changes that need prompt help Obtain immediate medical assessment for sudden or rapidly worsening weakness or a new walking abnormality. New loss of bladder or bowel control, particularly with weakness, altered sensation or walking changes, needs urgent assessment. These changes should not be dismissed as part of the child's usual skeletal condition or left until the next routine visit. Call local emergency services for breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour, fainting, difficulty waking or unresponsiveness. A tense or bulging soft spot, persistently downward-looking eyes or repeated unexplained vomiting warrants urgent medical advice, especially with unusual sleepiness, headache or neurological change. Do not wait for all signs to occur or for head growth to be documented; severe deterioration needs emergency help. Prepare for a useful appointment Bring growth records, previous images and reports, genetic results, medicines and a short account of pain, sleep, movement, hearing or vision changes. Describe what the child can do and what has become difficult. Avoid comparing every milestone with children who have a different condition. Ask which diagnosis is confirmed, which questions remain, what monitoring is needed and which symptoms should trigger urgent contact. Agree safe activity and school arrangements in writing when possible. The walking aid in the article image illustrates one possible support; many people with skeletal dysplasias do not need that equipment. Skeletal dysplasias are varied conditions; no single symptom list or height defines them. Recognition may occur before birth, in childhood or later; testing follows the pattern of findings. Imaging, medicines and surgery require a condition-specific plan. Care should include function, school participation and a planned transition to adult services. New neurological changes or breathing and consciousness problems need prompt assessment. What signs can skeletal dysplasia cause? Possible features include different limb or trunk proportions, spinal curves, leg alignment or joint problems. Some disorders also affect hearing, eyes, teeth or other systems. These are possibilities, not features every person will develop. What causes skeletal dysplasia? Many forms result from a genetic change that is inherited or arises for the first time. The exact diagnosis determines inheritance and family implications; there is no universal recurrence risk. How is it diagnosed? Specialists combine history, growth and examination with selected X-rays and genetic testing. Recognition is not limited to the first year, and a normal prenatal scan does not exclude every form. How is skeletal dysplasia treated? Treatment targets the person's actual needs, from monitoring and rehabilitation to selected medicines or operations. Procedures for hydrocephalus, spinal compression, alignment or arthritis are used only when indicated. Does every child need MRI after six months? No. The need and timing depend on the suspected problem. MRI may be needed earlier and is not automatically required for every child; sedation and spinal or breathing precautions need planning. Is increasing height the main goal? Health, comfort, independence and participation matter alongside growth. Medicines and limb lengthening have specific indications and limitations, and the person's preferences are central. What should prompt urgent assessment? Seek immediate assessment for sudden or rapidly worsening weakness or a new walking abnormality. Breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour, fainting or difficulty waking needs emergency help. Do not wait for several symptoms together. Does care stop after childhood? No. Follow-up depends on the condition and continues as needs change. Plan adult care, records and a named contact before leaving paediatric services.

title: Dry eyes in children: symptoms, eye tests and care
description: Understand possible childhood dry-eye symptoms, how an eye examination helps, and care for screen strain, eyelid problems, lenses and other causes.
body: A child who keeps blinking, rubbing their eyes or saying that they feel sandy may have an irritated eye surface. Dry eye is one possibility, but allergy, infection, an injury or a focusing problem can look similar. An assessment can identify what is happening and choose care that fits the child's age, comfort and daily life. Recognize symptoms without assuming the cause Dry eye means the tear film does not keep the eye surface adequately protected. There may be too little tear production, excessive evaporation or problems with how tears spread. Burning, grittiness, redness, watering and vision that comes and goes can occur; an eye that waters is not necessarily well lubricated. Younger children may rub, blink repeatedly, squint or avoid tasks rather than describe dryness. Note when this happens, whether one or both eyes are affected and any crusting or trouble seeing. Persistent symptoms deserve an eye appointment. Do not use the absence of a detailed complaint to decide that a child is comfortable, or label all rubbing as dry eye. Get urgent help for warning signs A very painful red eye or a red eye in a contact-lens wearer needs urgent assessment. A newborn under 28 days with red eyes also needs urgent medical help. A child under two with a red eye should be assessed rather than treated by trial and error. Seek advice sooner if the child is unwell or you are concerned. A red eye with a new change in sight, pain when looking at light, an injury or chemical exposure needs emergency eye care. Severe headache with nausea, a newly unequal pupil or an extremely dark-red eye also needs emergency assessment. These signs should not wait for lubricants or a screen break to work. Arrange appropriate transport; do not drive yourself if your own vision or condition makes it unsafe. Prepare for a child-friendly eye examination Tell the eye-care professional about symptom timing, lenses, screens, allergies, skin or joint problems, other illnesses and all medicines or drops. Bring product names and describe effects on reading, school, sleep or play. The clinician may check sight, eyelids, blinking, the cornea and tear film, looking for causes beyond dryness. Tests are selected for the child's age and ability to cooperate. A slit lamp is a microscope with a narrow bright light for examining the eye and eyelids. A dye may help show the tear film or surface damage; pupil-dilating drops are used when the wider examination calls for them, not because every dry-eye assessment requires the same drops. Ask how to help the child feel comfortable. Understand tear tests and their limits A Schirmer test uses a small paper strip near the lower eyelid to measure how much it becomes wet over several minutes. It can help assess tear production, but discomfort and reflex tearing may affect results. Some children cannot comfortably complete it, and other tests may be more appropriate. It is not a home test or a single answer to every child's symptoms. Tear break-up time, or TBUT, measures how long the tear film remains stable after a blink, sometimes with dye and sometimes using noninvasive equipment. Surface staining can show irritated or damaged areas. Adult cutoffs and questionnaires do not automatically work in children; recent pediatric research still identifies important measurement limits. The clinician interprets the findings together rather than diagnosing from a universal ten-second rule. Review ordinary contact lenses when they are uncomfortable Lenses can contribute to discomfort, but a poorly fitting lens, allergy, surface damage or infection may be responsible. Remove uncomfortable lenses, use glasses and contact the eye-care professional; do not put them back until advised. Redness, worsening pain, light sensitivity, sudden blur or unusual discharge calls for immediate advice, not simply buying a wetter lens. After checking the eye, the clinician may adjust fit, material, wearing time, cleaning or replacement schedule, or recommend a pause. Daily disposables or another material can suit some children, but no type guarantees relief. Follow the prescribed cleaning and wear instructions and use only drops compatible with the particular lenses. Specialist therapeutic lenses are a separate treatment choice. Make screen use easier on the eyes Children often blink less while concentrating on a phone, game or school screen. This can allow tears to evaporate and contribute to discomfort, but a screen history does not establish the diagnosis. Encourage full blinking, comfortable lighting and a screen at a sensible distance, with breaks built into schoolwork and leisure. The 20–20–20 reminder means looking about 20 feet, or six metres, away for 20 seconds every 20 minutes. It is a practical break habit rather than a cure or a test. Balance screen time with other activities and avoid direct fan or air-conditioning flow at the eyes. Persistent pain, headaches, blurred or double vision still needs an eye examination. Treat eyelid inflammation with an individual plan Blepharitis is inflammation around the eyelid margins. Meibomian glands there supply oils that help tears function; when they are inflamed or blocked, crusting, burning, watering or fluctuating blur can accompany dryness. This is more than simply having bacteria on the lashes, and allergy or skin conditions may contribute. The clinician may demonstrate a comfortably warm, never hot, compress and gentle cleaning along the closed lid margins. Ask about the product, pressure and frequency for your child; do not scrub the eyeball or press hard on the lids. Some children need prescribed treatment and follow-up. Office cleaning or heating procedures, including branded treatments, are not automatically appropriate or proven safe for every age. Consider health conditions and medicines when relevant Persistent or severe dryness sometimes accompanies an autoimmune condition such as Sjögren's disease or juvenile idiopathic arthritis, diabetes, or a congenital problem affecting tears, eyelids or corneal sensation. Nutritional deficiency can also affect the eye surface. These are reasons for a careful history and selected assessment, not a reason to assume that every child needs extensive blood tests. Allergy medicines, acne retinoids, some medicines for depression and certain preserved eye drops may contribute. Tell the prescriber about new eye symptoms and when they began. A supervised change may help, but do not stop a prescribed treatment yourself. The pediatric and eye-care teams can coordinate treatment of an underlying condition while protecting the eye surface. Choose lubricants for the child and the diagnosis Artificial tears can improve comfort, and some children need a gel or ointment. Ask an eye-care professional or pharmacist which product and schedule are appropriate, particularly for an infant or a child with other eye disease. Preservative-free preparations may be preferable with frequent use or sensitivity, but the label alone does not make every bottle suitable for every child. Wash hands, keep the dropper tip from touching the eye or skin and follow storage and after-opening expiry instructions. Ask for a demonstration if giving drops is difficult, and how to space different prescribed products. Do not share drops, use homemade mixtures or substitute redness-whitening drops for lubricants. Increasing drops should not conceal persistent pain or a change in sight. Keep food and supplement claims in perspective A varied, age-appropriate diet supports health. A very restricted diet, poor growth, malabsorption or suspected vitamin deficiency deserves pediatric advice, because a genuine deficiency needs proper assessment and treatment. This is different from promising that extra vitamins C or E will prevent tears from evaporating. Omega-3 supplements are sometimes discussed for eyelid or dry-eye problems, but they are not a guaranteed treatment. A large adult dry-eye trial found no benefit over placebo; it does not establish a dose or benefit for children. Discuss any supplement with the child's clinician, including allergies and other medicines, rather than using high-dose vitamins or fish oil in place of eye care. Prescription and office treatments need specialist oversight If lubrication and treatment of the cause are insufficient, an ophthalmologist may consider anti-inflammatory drops or other targeted treatment. The choice depends on the diagnosis, age, local approval and monitoring needs. Antibiotics may be used for selected eyelid problems; they are not a routine cure for every dry eye. Steroid eye drops can raise eye pressure and cause other harm, so they must not be borrowed or started without supervision. An office eyelid procedure should be discussed in terms of the child's ability to cooperate, evidence, discomfort, alternatives and follow-up. Pediatric evidence is less complete than adult evidence, and no branded device should be presented as an inevitable next step. Punctal plugs can retain tears in selected cases Tiny plugs can partly block the drainage openings at the inner eyelid corners, keeping tears on the eye longer. This is different from opening a newborn's blocked tear duct. An eye specialist may consider plugs for persistent, significant dryness after assessing the surface and the response to other care. Small pediatric case series report benefit, but do not guarantee results or safety for every child. Plugs may fall out, symptoms may return and repeat treatment can be needed. Placement may require anaesthesia depending on age and cooperation. Ask why plugs suit this child, what problems to report and how their position and eye health will be checked. Specialist scleral lenses are not permanent implants Severe ocular-surface disease may sometimes be managed with a custom scleral device, including PROSE. A gas-permeable dome rests on the white of the eye and arches over the cornea, holding a fluid reservoir against the surface. It is fitted by a specialist and is different from routinely changing ordinary contact-lens brands. These devices are removable; they are not permanent lenses implanted in the eye. Care involves trained application, removal, cleaning and the prescribed sterile filling solution, usually with removal at bedtime. Selected children with severe disease have benefited, but fitting or daily handling is not feasible for everyone. Evidence from serious conditions such as Stevens–Johnson syndrome cannot promise the same result for ordinary childhood dryness. Plan follow-up around comfort, sight and daily life Agree on how long to try the chosen care, when to return and which changes require earlier help. A simple note about symptoms, drops and school difficulties may be useful. If a routine is painful, takes too much time or is difficult for the child to tolerate, tell the team so it can be adapted rather than silently abandoned. The aim is a comfortable, protected eye surface and clear vision while identifying and managing the cause. Do not keep treating presumed dryness indefinitely when symptoms persist. New pain, light sensitivity or visual change deserves prompt reassessment, and the emergency signs described above should bypass the routine follow-up plan. Rubbing, blinking or watering can have several causes; persistent symptoms need assessment. Tear tests must be interpreted for the child, not through one adult cutoff. Screens, lenses, eyelid inflammation, medicines and other conditions may contribute. Use child-appropriate care and specialist oversight for prescriptions, plugs or therapeutic lenses. Pain, light sensitivity or a new change in sight must not be dismissed as dryness. How is dry eye diagnosed in a child? The clinician combines symptoms, sight and eye-surface examination with selected tear tests. Schirmer testing measures paper wetting, while TBUT assesses tear stability. Age and cooperation affect interpretation; no single test proves every case. Can contact lenses cause a teenager's dry eyes? They can contribute, but infection, allergy or a fit problem may look similar. Remove uncomfortable lenses and obtain advice. Redness, pain, light sensitivity, sudden blur or discharge needs immediate eye-care contact; do not simply switch brands. What signs might a baby or child show? Frequent blinking, rubbing, squinting, grittiness, redness, watering or fluctuating blur may occur. They are not specific to dryness. A newborn with red eyes needs urgent assessment, and pain or apparent difficulty seeing needs prompt help. Can prolonged phone or computer use make eyes dry? Reduced blinking during concentrated screen use can contribute. Regular distance breaks, full blinking and a comfortable setup may help, but persistent symptoms still need examination rather than being blamed automatically on screens. Can I choose any preservative-free eye drop? No. Ask about a suitable lubricant for the child's age and condition and follow its instructions. Preservative-free products can help with frequent use or sensitivity, but do not replace assessment or make every formulation appropriate. Should I give omega-3 or extra vitamins? Do not assume supplements will treat dryness. Discuss a restricted diet or suspected deficiency with the clinician. Benefits of supplements for pediatric dry eye are uncertain, and products can have risks or interactions. Are punctal plugs and PROSE routine treatments? No. They are options for selected cases under specialist care. Plugs retain tears but can be lost or need replacement; custom scleral devices need fitting and daily handling. Neither guarantees a result for every child. When should we seek emergency eye care? A red eye with new sight changes, pain looking at light, injury or chemical exposure needs emergency assessment. Severe headache with nausea or a newly unequal pupil also needs urgent emergency attention. A very painful red eye, a red contact-lens eye or red eyes in a newborn needs urgent medical assessment.

title: When your child does not join other children’s play
description: Understand why a child watches, wanders or avoids peer play, how to offer gentle support at home and preschool, and when to ask for assessment.
body: A child who stays beside you at the park is not necessarily unhappy or unable to make friends. Age, temperament, familiarity and the setting all matter. Look at what happens across everyday situations, then offer support that makes play more comfortable and accessible rather than demanding an immediate performance. Start with age and the kind of play you are seeing Young children may watch, explore alone, play alongside others or join a shared game at different moments. CDC milestones describe playing beside other children and sometimes with them by 30 months, and noticing and joining other children by three years. These describe what most children do, not a requirement to join every group on every outing. A single quiet visit cannot assess development. Notice whether your child enjoys familiar people, communicates interests and sometimes connects in their own way. If an age-related milestone is missing, skills have been lost or you are concerned, discuss it with the child’s clinician; normal variation is not a reason to postpone a concern indefinitely. Why play deserves time Play offers opportunities to move, imagine, solve small problems, communicate and handle feelings. Playing with adults and peers can support relationships and learning. It is useful in its own right, without a promise of higher intelligence, better grades or a particular future personality. Children do not all arrive knowing how to enter an ongoing game or negotiate a turn. Adults can show and support those steps while leaving room for choice. A child who needs help is not failing at childhood, and enjoying solitary play does not make shared play impossible. Observe the situation before choosing a solution Ask what happens before, during and after a difficult playtime. Is the group noisy or unfamiliar? Is your child tired, hungry, uncomfortable, unwell or worried? Are the toys reachable and the activity understandable? Compare the park with home or preschool, and ask the educator what helps there. Describe actions rather than fixed types: watched the blocks, walked between activities, left when shouting began. The same child may show several patterns on different days. Communication, hearing, movement or sensory needs can affect access to play; a label such as lazy, unfriendly or badly behaved does not explain those needs. When a child wanders without starting A busy room with many choices can be hard to enter. Your child may be interested but unsure what to do, unfamiliar with the materials, or unable to tell another child what they want. Start with one or two accessible activities linked to an existing interest and a calm place to watch or try them. You might begin a simple construction beside your child, then pause to see what they choose. Offer a small invitation rather than moving their hands or insisting on a correct result. If wandering is persistent across settings and little seems enjoyable, share that pattern with the educator and clinician instead of assuming the child simply needs more toys. When a child switches activities quickly Brief exploration is common in young children. Rapid switching alone does not establish an attention disorder. Consider whether the activity is too difficult, the room distracting or the child ready for movement or a break. Notice what holds their interest under more comfortable conditions. Try fewer materials and one manageable next step, then allow the child to continue or stop. Join their interest without turning the session into repeated instructions. If difficulty engaging is persistent, causes distress or affects everyday participation, ask for advice; there is no universal number of minutes that proves a child is playing properly. When joining in leads to conflict or exclusion Entering an established game, waiting and explaining an idea take practice. Offer an optional phrase or gesture, demonstrate taking turns, and help children find a role or enough materials. Keep limits clear when someone hits, grabs or hurts another child, while helping everyone settle before discussing what happened. Being left out is not proof that a child lacks empathy or caused the problem. Adults should look for repeated exclusion, teasing, inaccessible activities or unsafe group dynamics and intervene. Work with the preschool to make participation safer and more welcoming; do not tell a child to endure mistreatment as social practice. When worry or unfamiliarity gets in the way Some children need time with an unfamiliar place or person. Predictable routines, a familiar adult nearby and a short meeting with one compatible child may be easier than a crowded group. Explain what will happen and allow a pause, watching or a smaller first step rather than pushing the child into the centre of the game. Listen to what feels hard. Changes at home, stressful experiences and physical discomfort can contribute, but they are not the explanation for every quiet child. Persistent or worsening worry that disrupts play, friendships, sleep or family life deserves professional advice. Thumb sucking, little eye contact or one refusal cannot diagnose anxiety. When a child seems withdrawn or prefers adults A child may prefer familiar adults, quiet activities or being alongside a friend without much conversation. Look for their attempts to connect, including showing an object, a sound, a gesture or shared enjoyment. Join an interest and respond without requiring eye contact, speech or affection as the price of participation. Some children need adjustments for communication, movement or sensory differences. Reduce unnecessary noise, make materials accessible and respect breaks. Little eye contact or different play alone does not diagnose autism; a broader developmental assessment may be useful when there are concerns. Support should help the child communicate and enjoy relationships, not make them hide harmless differences. Make a small, repeatable plan with caregivers Choose one practical change with the educator: a quieter play area, a familiar partner, a clear invitation or an activity the child already likes. Practise a possible way to join through a toy or pretend scene at home, while accepting gestures or other communication. Ask what happened rather than whether the child was good. During play, remain available and supervise for age and safety. Notice concrete efforts, such as offering a block or staying comfortably nearby, without making praise another demand. Review which conditions helped and adjust together. A short enjoyable encounter can be enough; friendship does not require popularity or a large group. Protect free play without removing useful support Leave regular opportunities for children to choose and explore, instead of replacing all play with lessons or adult-set goals. Drawing, building, pretend play and safe movement offer different ways to participate. Free play can include an attentive adult and helpful structure; it does not mean leaving a struggling child unsupported. The balance can differ by child and setting. Predictability or a shared interest may make an open play period more accessible. Play supports development, but there is no basis here for promising academic success or attributing a boys-versus-girls achievement gap to reduced playtime. Follow enjoyment and participation rather than a score. Know when to ask for assessment Talk with the child’s clinician if participation difficulties persist across settings, your child seems distressed, rarely engages in any enjoyable activity, or you have concerns about communication, hearing or development. Seek advice promptly for loss of previously used skills or a marked change; do not wait for school or a fixed trial of play exercises. Bring a few specific observations and the educator’s perspective, including strengths and conditions that help. The clinician can consider health, hearing, development and emotional wellbeing and arrange appropriate support. Developmental checklists are conversation aids, not diagnostic tests. Early-childhood, speech-and-language or other services vary by location; ask how to access them while continuing gentle support. Keep the goal connected to your child The aim is safe, meaningful participation and access to relationships, not making every child outgoing. One child may want help entering a running game; another may enjoy building beside one friend. Ask or observe what your child finds enjoyable and what makes the setting harder. Adults can teach useful skills and change the environment at the same time. Neither a parent nor a child is to blame for needing help. Keep communication open with caregivers, act on persistent concerns and allow progress to look different from another child’s play. Consider age, temperament, access and the setting, not one quiet outing. Describe what happens rather than assigning a fixed type of child. Offer small invitations, shared interests and predictable support without forcing interaction. Address exclusion and environmental barriers as well as teaching useful skills. Discuss persistent difficulties, developmental concerns or lost skills promptly. Why is play important? It gives children opportunities for movement, imagination, communication, problem solving and relationships. It supports development without guaranteeing school results or a particular personality. Why does my child wander instead of choosing a game? Too many choices, unfamiliar materials, discomfort or difficulty communicating can contribute. Offer a simple accessible activity and observe across settings; persistent lack of engagement deserves discussion rather than a fixed label. Does being excluded mean my child lacks social skills? No. Skills may need support, but the group, access barriers and teasing also matter. Adults should protect children from mistreatment and help make play inclusive, rather than blaming the child who is left out. Why might an anxious child avoid play? An unfamiliar or overwhelming setting can feel difficult, and stress or discomfort may contribute. Predictability and small supported steps can help; persistent worry that interferes with everyday life warrants professional advice. Is playing beside other children a problem? Not necessarily. Side-by-side play can be meaningful and is common in early development. Consider age, the wider pattern and concerns; a missed milestone or loss of skills should be discussed with a clinician. Should I insist on eye contact or joining in? No. Offer invitations and accessible ways to communicate, allow breaks and respect comfort. Forced eye contact or performance can make interaction harder; adults can support skills without demanding a particular social style. Does avoiding peers mean autism or ADHD? No single play behaviour diagnoses either condition. Developmental assessment considers a broader pattern and daily needs. Raise concerns or lost skills with the child’s clinician rather than diagnosing from a park visit. When should I ask for help? Ask when difficulties persist, cause distress, affect participation or raise developmental concerns. Seek advice promptly for lost skills or a marked change. You do not need to wait until the child starts school.

title: Mosquito bites in babies and children: relief and prevention
description: How to care for a suspected mosquito bite, choose age-appropriate itch relief, recognize warning signs and reduce further bites safely.
body: An itchy bump after outdoor play may be a mosquito bite, but its appearance cannot reliably identify the insect. Most uncomplicated bites settle with simple care. Your child's age, how they feel, changes in the skin and where exposure happened matter more than naming the bite from a photograph. What a mosquito bite can look and feel like A reaction to mosquito saliva can produce a raised, itchy bump within minutes or a firmer mark later. Some children develop considerable local swelling, small blisters or darker marks. Redness may be less obvious on darker skin; notice warmth, swelling, tenderness and the child's comfort as well as colour. Mosquito bites can be sore, so pain does not prove a bee or another insect was responsible. Conversely, not every itchy bump is a bite: skin irritation, hives and other rashes can look similar. Seek advice if the cause is unclear, the rash persists or your child seems unwell. Clues about fleas, bedbugs, ticks and stings Flea bites often occur around the lower legs, while bedbug marks may appear in groups, lines or scattered areas after sleeping. These are clues, not diagnostic patterns; mosquito, flea and bedbug reactions overlap. Repeated unexplained marks may need assessment of the sleeping environment or professional pest identification, not repeated treatment based on the skin alone. A tick can remain attached. Remove it promptly with clean fine-tipped tweezers close to the skin, pulling steadily without twisting or squeezing its body, then wash the area and hands. Do not apply heat, oil or nail polish to make it detach. Tell a clinician about later fever or an expanding rash and where the tick was acquired. A sting or a bite near the eye needs its own assessment if pain or swelling is significant. A large local reaction is not automatically an infection Children can react strongly around a bite. Rapid swelling and itch often reflect inflammation or allergy rather than bacteria. A large patch alone does not establish infection, and local swelling alone is different from a serious reaction affecting breathing or circulation. Many bites improve over a few days, although itch and discolouration can last longer. Follow the trend rather than expecting a fixed recovery day. Increasing pain, rapidly spreading changes, fever or a child who is becoming unwell need review; do not wait a week simply because some bite reactions last that long. Start with washing and cooling Wash gently with soap and water, then apply a clean cool damp cloth. If using a cold pack, wrap it in cloth and use a short supervised application, checking the skin; never put ice directly on a baby's skin. Comfort and distract your child, and keep nails short to reduce scratching and broken skin. Simple care is usually enough for a mild bite. Avoid squeezing, opening blisters or rubbing harsh substances onto it. Guidance differs about baking-soda paste; it is not necessary for care, and NHS guidance advises against it. Avoid homemade pastes, essential oils and several anti-itch products layered together, especially on an infant. Check before using hydrocortisone or another cream A low-strength steroid may help some itchy local reactions, but a universal 1% hydrocortisone three-times-a-day plan is not appropriate for every baby or child. Ask a pharmacist or clinician whether this particular product suits the child's age, site and skin condition, and confirm frequency and duration. For example, NHS advice requires professional guidance for children under 10; other countries and products have different labels. Do not apply hydrocortisone to broken or infected skin or in or around the eyes. Ask before using it on the face. Use only as directed and do not cover it with a tight dressing or glove to prevent licking unless the clinician specifically instructs you. Keep medicine away from the mouth and wash the applying adult's hands; an area the child sucks needs a safer plan. Oral antihistamines need a medicine-specific plan An oral antihistamine may be considered when itch is troublesome, but evidence for bite relief is limited and products have different age limits, strengths and dosing instructions. Ask a professional before treating an infant or young child. The AAP advises against diphenhydramine, often sold as Benadryl, in children under six unless their pediatrician recommends it; brand ingredients can differ between countries. Do not use an antihistamine to make a child sleep, guess an adult dose or combine products containing the same ingredient. Confirm the medicine, child's weight, concentration and measuring device. Antihistamines do not replace emergency treatment for a severe allergic reaction. A child with mild itch may need no medicine at all. When infection or worsening skin needs attention Seek prompt advice for increasing tenderness, spreading redness or darker colour change, warmth with worsening swelling, pus, red streaks or fever. These signs need assessment together; warmth and swelling alone can occur with an inflammatory reaction. Severe pain out of proportion to the visible mark or rapid deterioration needs urgent care. Do not routinely apply an antibiotic ointment or use leftover oral antibiotics for a bite. Antibiotics treat bacterial infection, not the ordinary saliva reaction, and a clinician should decide if one is needed. Seek advice early for a baby, particularly under one year, or if the child has immune problems, significant swelling near the eye or symptoms that are not improving. Recognize urgent illness and a severe allergic reaction Get emergency help for trouble breathing or swallowing, sudden tongue or throat swelling, collapse, blue or unusually pale skin, or a child who is limp or difficult to wake. Follow a prescribed allergy emergency plan and use prescribed adrenaline/epinephrine as directed; do not wait for an antihistamine to work. Widespread hives with other concerning symptoms also need urgent assessment. Fever, repeated vomiting, poor feeding, fewer wet nappies or unusual lethargy should not simply be blamed on a bite. A baby under three months with a temperature of 38°C or higher needs urgent medical assessment; at three to six months, 39°C or higher also needs urgent advice. Seek help below these thresholds if the child looks ill. Mention recent travel or local mosquito-borne illness when seeking care. Reduce exposure with clothing, screens and netting Use light, loose clothing that covers arms and legs without overheating, and repair window and door screens. Empty and scrub water-holding containers regularly so mosquitoes have fewer breeding sites. Mosquitoes can bite during the day as well as at night; dusk-only precautions are not enough everywhere. A correctly fitted mosquito net can protect a stroller or carrier during supervised use. Keep it clear of the child's face, securely fitted and free of loose cords or gaps; maintain airflow and check temperature. Do not improvise a draped blanket or turn a stroller into a routine sleep space. For a young baby, these barriers are especially useful while you obtain individualized repellent advice. Choose repellent for the child's age and your location DEET and picaridin, also called icaridin, are effective ingredients in registered repellents. Choose a product authorized locally for the child's age and follow its label. Rules differ: the US EPA does not set an age or concentration restriction for DEET, while Health Canada does not recommend DEET or icaridin under six months. AAP guidance urges particular caution for newborn or premature infants. Do not treat a two-month age threshold or a 30% limit as a universal rule. CDC and AAP public advice recommends avoiding oil of lemon eucalyptus (OLE) and PMD under three years. EPA and the CDC Yellow Book describe exceptions for certain registered OLE-only products, so do not assume every similarly named product is interchangeable. For a young child, choose an age-appropriate alternative with professional advice. Pure lemon-eucalyptus essential oil is not the same as a tested registered repellent. Higher concentration often means longer protection, not permission to apply more. Apply repellent carefully An adult should apply it, keeping it off the child's hands, eyes, mouth, broken or irritated skin and skin under clothing. For the face, put a small amount on the adult's hands first and carefully spread it away from eyes and mouth; never spray directly at the child's face. Use sprays in an open area, avoid breathing in the mist and keep it away from food. Reapply only as the label allows. If sunscreen is needed, use separate products and apply sunscreen first, then repellent. Wash treated skin when protection is no longer needed and wash clothing as directed. Stop and wash it off if a reaction develops, and seek advice with the container available. Store products out of reach. Permethrin products intended for clothing or equipment must not be put on skin; local age and product rules also apply. Plan for travel and keep care proportionate The risk of mosquito-borne infection depends on location, season, outbreaks and exposure. Before travel, ask about prevention for the destination and the child's age, including any required malaria prevention or vaccines. A small bite does not tell you whether infection was transmitted, and repellent does not replace other recommended protection. For an otherwise well child with a mild local bump, gentle care and preventing more bites are reasonable. Record when the mark appeared, changes, temperature, products used and travel if you need advice. You have not failed if a bite happens despite precautions; focus on comfort, appropriate prevention and timely help for concerning changes. A bump or bite pattern cannot reliably identify the insect. Wash and cool first; check age, product and site before using medicines. Rapid local swelling is not automatically infection; antibiotics are not routine bite treatment. Breathing difficulty, collapse or abnormal responsiveness need emergency help; fever in a young baby needs urgent assessment. Use barriers and a locally authorized age-appropriate repellent, with careful adult application. What does a mosquito bite look like? Often it is a raised itchy bump that appears quickly or becomes firmer later. Swelling, small blisters or darker marks can occur. Appearance alone cannot distinguish it reliably from other bites or rashes. Are mosquito bites dangerous for babies? Many cause only local itch, but children can have larger reactions, secondary infection or illness related to exposure. Judge the child's overall condition and warning signs, not only the size of the bump. Obtain advice early for an infant. Can I give an antihistamine for the itch? Sometimes, with an age- and product-specific plan. Ask a clinician or pharmacist before treating a young child; do not self-dose diphenhydramine under six or use a sedating medicine to induce sleep. Benefit for insect-bite itch is not certain. How is it different from a flea, bedbug or tick bite? Fleas often affect lower legs; bedbug marks may cluster or form lines, but patterns overlap. An attached tick is a different clue and should be removed promptly. Environmental evidence and clinical assessment are more reliable than diagnosing from a photograph. Should every swollen bite get an antibiotic? No. Rapid itch and swelling often reflect inflammation rather than infection. Increasing pain, spreading changes, pus, fever or worsening general health need assessment; antibiotics are for a diagnosed or suspected bacterial infection. Can I use hydrocortisone on my baby? Only after checking the specific product, age, skin site and instructions with a professional. Do not use a blanket three-times-daily routine, apply it to broken or infected skin or around the eyes, or cover it tightly to prevent licking. Which repellent is safe for a very young baby? Start with clothing, screens and correctly fitted supervised netting, and seek individualized advice. DEET and picaridin labels and age recommendations vary by country; newborn and premature infants need particular care. Do not substitute essential oils for an authorized product. When should I seek urgent help? Immediately for breathing or swallowing difficulty, collapse, severe drowsiness or limpness. Seek urgent assessment for an unwell child, rapidly worsening pain or swelling, or fever in a young baby. Tell the clinician about travel, exposure and medicines already used.

title: Sunburn in babies and children: care, warning signs and prevention
description: Recognise sunburn, know when a baby needs medical advice, soothe injured skin safely and plan shade, clothing and sunscreen for the next outing.
body: A child may look comfortable outdoors and develop sore, hot skin hours later. Sunburn is ultraviolet damage, not simply a sign that the weather felt hot. Move your child out of the sun and assess their age, skin, feeding and behaviour before choosing home care. A baby’s sunburn deserves prompt professional advice even when the area looks small. What sunburn can look and feel like Skin may feel warm, tender or painful, with redness, swelling or later peeling. Severe injury can blister. Colour change can be less obvious on brown or black skin, so look beyond redness to discomfort and the child’s overall condition. Signs often develop several hours after exposure and can worsen over the first day; a normal-looking patch immediately after an outing does not rule out damage. Ultraviolet A and B rays can harm skin and eyes. UVB is strongly associated with burning, while UVA contributes to ageing and other damage; protection should cover both. Babies and young children need particular protection, and darker skin is not immune. A rash or fever after an outing is not automatically sunburn, so seek advice when the cause is unclear. Decide who needs medical help Contact a clinician promptly for any sunburn in a baby, especially under 1 year. NHS guidance also recommends urgent advice for a young child with sunburn. For any age, seek prompt assessment for blisters, a large affected area, substantial swelling, severe or worsening pain, fever, chills, vomiting, headache or a child who seems unwell. Home comfort measures can begin while you arrange advice; they should not postpone it. Call emergency services if your child is difficult to wake, confused, collapses, has a seizure or has serious breathing difficulty, especially after heat exposure. Move them to a cooler place, remove excess layers and follow the dispatcher’s cooling instructions. Do not wait for a particular temperature or a trial of pain medicine. A baby under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or higher needs urgent medical assessment; do not assume the sun explains the fever. Cool gently and make the skin comfortable Go indoors or into reliable shade. A cool, damp cloth or a cool bath can ease soreness; keep the child supervised and avoid making them shiver or too cold. Do not put ice or ice packs directly on sunburn. Pat dry gently, avoid rubbing and choose soft, loose clothing that does not press on sore areas. For intact, mildly burned skin, an unperfumed moisturiser may help. A suitable aloe-containing moisturiser can soothe but cannot undo UV damage; raw leaves, scented gels or a product that stings are poor choices. Stop an irritating product. Ask about suitable products for an infant, and use medicated creams or numbing preparations only if the child’s clinician recommends them. Keep feeds and fluids appropriate for age Offer usual breastfeeds more often if wanted, or correctly prepared formula to an alert baby who can feed normally. Do not dilute formula. Young infants should not be given large amounts of plain water in place of milk. Guidance about small additional water feeds for formula-fed babies under 6 months varies locally, so ask a child-health professional rather than improvising after a burn. From around 6 months, small drinks of water can accompany complementary foods while breast milk or formula remains important; older children can drink water regularly. Poor feeding, fewer wet nappies or less urine, dry mouth, unusual sleepiness or repeated vomiting need prompt advice. Fluids at home do not replace assessment of a sick or dehydrated baby. Check pain medicines before giving them Paracetamol, also called acetaminophen, may be appropriate, but it is not automatically suitable at every infant age or dose. For a baby with sunburn, ask the clinician what to use. US paediatric advice recommends professional guidance before acetaminophen under 2 years; product and age rules differ between countries. Use the child’s weight, the exact product strength and the advised dose, measured with an oral syringe rather than a kitchen spoon. Ibuprofen has age and health restrictions: US guidance says not under 6 months unless a doctor directs it, while some UK products allow younger infants under specified conditions. Do not choose it for a dehydrated child, and check other illnesses or medicines with a pharmacist. Do not give aspirin for a child’s sunburn, double up ingredients or alternate pain medicines without advice. Severe pain despite appropriate relief needs reassessment. Protect blisters and follow healing Do not burst blisters, peel loose skin or scrub the burn. Blistering in a baby or child needs advice about assessment and protection. Recommendations about ointments can differ for intact sunburn and an open blister; use the clinician’s wound-care plan rather than putting petroleum jelly, antibiotics or several household remedies over the whole burn. Do not apply sunscreen into an open wound as a substitute for covering and care. Increasing warmth or swelling, spreading redness, worsening pain, pus or fever can signal a complication and need review. Many mild burns settle over several days, often around a week, but there is no guaranteed healing date. Keep injured skin out of direct sun until healed. If it is not improving or you are unsure whether it is sunburn, seek assessment. Understand the longer-term risk without blame Repeated UV exposure and childhood sunburn increase later skin-cancer risk, including melanoma, and can contribute to premature skin ageing. A past burn does not mean a child will develop cancer. A fixed claim that every blistering burn doubles an individual’s risk, or that sunscreen removes a set percentage of all cancer risk, cannot predict what happens to your child. Protection still matters after a mistake. Make the next outing easier with shade, suitable clothing and the right product available. Some medicines and medical conditions increase sun sensitivity; ask the prescriber or pharmacist when relevant without stopping treatment yourself. Sunscreen supports prevention but does not erase existing damage or make unlimited time in the sun safe. Plan shade and clothing before sunscreen Check the local UV index and heat advice, not only the temperature or whether the sky is blue. UV can be strong through cloud and can reflect from sand, water and snow. Limit exposure around the strongest part of the day; clock times vary with location and season.
