Its hormones thyroxine, or T4, and triiodothyronine, or T3, help regulate energy use and the function of organs including the heart and brain. They also matter for growth and development. The gland also contains C cells that produce calcitonin, a hormone involved in calcium regulation. Calcitonin is not interchangeable with T3 or T4, and a TSH test is not a measurement of calcitonin or a general calcium test. Naming all three thyroid products should not imply that they belong to the same feedback pathway. Understand the usual feedback pattern When circulating thyroid hormone is low, a normally functioning pituitary usually releases more TSH to stimulate the thyroid. If thyroid hormone is high, TSH usually falls. This feedback helps explain why a high TSH can point to an underactive thyroid rather than an overactive one. The relationship has exceptions. A pituitary problem, illness, medicine effect or interference with the laboratory assay can change the pattern. Free T4, and sometimes T3 or other tests, help interpret the result. An isolated number without its reference range and clinical context can be misleading. An underactive thyroid has several possible causes Hypothyroidism means there is too little thyroid hormone for the body’s needs. Fatigue, weakness, difficulty concentrating, cold intolerance, constipation or weight gain can occur, but these symptoms also have other causes. A gradual onset can make the change difficult to notice. Hashimoto’s disease is an autoimmune condition in which immune activity damages the thyroid. It may develop slowly over years before obvious symptoms appear. Other causes include some medicines, thyroid surgery or radiation treatment and, in some settings, insufficient iodine. Finding a high TSH does not distinguish these causes by itself. Thyroid inflammation can have more than one phase Thyroiditis means inflammation of the thyroid. Depending on the type, it may be associated with an autoimmune process, a recent viral illness or another trigger. Damaged cells can release hormone already stored in the gland, temporarily raising blood levels. This leakage is different from the gland actively producing too much new hormone. A later low-hormone phase can occur as stores are depleted or the gland remains damaged. Some people recover and others develop continuing hypothyroidism. The sequence, duration and treatment vary, so a single early test cannot promise that every case will follow the same course. Thyroiditis after birth can resemble ordinary postpartum strain Postpartum thyroiditis can occur during the first year after giving birth. Some people have an early high-hormone phase with palpitations, anxiety, trouble sleeping or weight loss, followed by a low-hormone phase with fatigue, constipation, low mood or weight gain. Not everyone experiences both phases. Symptoms can be mistaken for the demands of caring for a baby, and recovery is not guaranteed in every case. Follow-up testing helps establish whether thyroid function has returned to normal or ongoing treatment is needed. Mention new or persistent symptoms rather than assuming they are an unavoidable part of recovery. An overactive thyroid may arise from Graves’ disease or nodules Hyperthyroidism means the thyroid makes too much hormone. Increased appetite, unintended weight loss, anxiety, heat intolerance, a rapid heartbeat or difficulty sleeping may prompt testing. The gland need not look visibly enlarged for a problem to exist. Graves’ disease is an autoimmune cause of overproduction. Some thyroid nodules also make extra hormone independently. Most nodules are benign and do not produce excess hormone; growth alone does not prove that a nodule has become overactive. A normal TSH does not establish that every lump is harmless, so a new neck lump still needs appropriate assessment. Iodine deficiency and excess can both matter The thyroid needs iodine to make its hormones. Too little can contribute to an underactive gland, but the likelihood depends on diet and local circumstances. More iodine is not automatically better: excess can trigger or worsen thyroid dysfunction in susceptible people. Some heart medicines, certain cough products and supplements contain substantial iodine. Amiodarone can affect the thyroid in more than one way, while seaweed or kelp supplements may supply unpredictable amounts. Do not assume that all cough medicines contain iodine, or start an iodine supplement to correct a TSH result without advice. Share medicines and supplements before the test Give the clinician and laboratory a complete list, including amiodarone, dopamine, lithium, prednisone or other glucocorticoids, potassium iodide and any thyroid treatment. These medicines may affect thyroid function or the interpretation of testing in different ways. They are not all stopped routinely. Biotin, sometimes sold in hair and nail supplements, can interfere with some thyroid blood tests and make results look abnormal when thyroid function is not. Tell the team the product and dose and follow its advice about timing. Do not independently stop a prescribed medicine or use a blanket pause interval for every supplement and laboratory method. Preparation and the blood draw are usually straightforward A TSH test by itself usually does not require fasting. Other tests ordered at the same appointment may have different requirements, so check the instructions. If you take thyroid hormone, ask whether the timing of the sample relative to the dose matters for your particular monitoring plan. A staff member usually cleans the skin, places a band around the upper arm and draws blood from a vein, often near the inner elbow, into a collection tube. The band and needle are then removed, pressure is applied and a small dressing may be placed. The collection usually takes only a few minutes. A brief sting or bruise can occur; mention previous fainting or difficulty with blood draws. Results are reviewed afterward rather than diagnosed at the needle side. Use the range printed on your own report You may see a typical adult TSH range quoted as approximately 0.4 to 4.0 mIU/L, but laboratories and clinical settings use different limits. Some ranges extend higher, and age, pregnancy and the test method affect interpretation. The laboratory’s printed interval is a starting point, not a diagnosis by itself. A treatment target is also individual. A range such as 0.5 to 3.0 is not a universal goal for everyone receiving thyroid medicine. Pregnancy, pituitary disease, age and selected thyroid-cancer treatment can change what the clinician aims for. Compare results with the relevant plan rather than adjusting a dose to match an internet number. Read TSH together with other findings High TSH with low free T4 commonly suggests primary hypothyroidism. Low TSH with high free T4 or T3 commonly suggests excess thyroid hormone. If TSH is abnormal but free hormone levels remain within range, the pattern may be described as subclinical; this does not automatically mean treatment is required. Low or inappropriately normal TSH with low free T4 needs a different explanation, which can include pituitary disease or illness. Depending on the situation, the next step may be repeat testing, thyroid antibodies, a review of medicines or other targeted investigation. Ask what the result means for you, what remains uncertain and when follow-up is due. High TSH often accompanies an underactive thyroid, but there are exceptions. Thyroiditis can cause changing hormone levels over time. Biotin can interfere with laboratory measurements. Fasting is not usually required for TSH alone. A result outside the range does not by itself determine the cause or treatment. Is TSH made by the thyroid? No. It is made by the pituitary gland and signals the thyroid to produce and release thyroid hormones. Does TSH measure calcitonin? No. Calcitonin is produced by thyroid C cells and is involved in calcium regulation; it is assessed separately. Does a high TSH always explain the cause? No. It often suggests an underactive thyroid, but other tests and the clinical history help identify why. Must I fast for a TSH blood test? Usually not for TSH alone. Follow instructions if other tests are being taken at the same time. Should I stop my medicines before testing? Only if your clinician gives specific instructions. Provide the full medicine and supplement list first. Why does the laboratory ask about biotin? Biotin can interfere with some thyroid assays. The team can advise on timing based on the product, dose and test. Is 0.5 to 3.0 the treatment target for everyone? No. Treatment targets depend on the laboratory range and circumstances such as pregnancy, age, pituitary disease or selected thyroid-cancer care. Does postpartum thyroiditis always have two phases? No. Some people have only a high- or low-hormone phase, and some need ongoing treatment. Does a normal TSH prove a thyroid lump is harmless? No. Many nodules do not change hormone levels, and a new lump may need assessment even with normal TSH. Does an abnormal TSH mean I must start medicine immediately? Not necessarily. Free hormone results, symptoms, repeat testing and the cause help determine the next step.

title: Eating well with an overactive thyroid
description: A practical guide to iodine, calcium, vitamin D and everyday foods during hyperthyroidism treatment, without unnecessary restrictions or supplement promises.
body: An overactive thyroid can change your appetite, weight, strength and tolerance of heat. Food helps meet the body’s needs during treatment, but a long list of forbidden ingredients can make recovery harder. Start with the reason your thyroid hormone level is high, then decide with your care team whether any temporary restriction or nutritional support is needed. Understand what an overactive thyroid means The thyroid is a small gland at the front of the neck. Its hormones, principally T4 and T3, help regulate energy use, temperature and the work of many organs. Hyperthyroidism means the gland produces too much hormone. Thyrotoxicosis describes excess thyroid-hormone effects more broadly, including situations where stored hormone leaks from an inflamed gland. Graves’ disease, an autoimmune condition, is a common cause. Overactive nodules, thyroid inflammation and excess thyroid medicine or iodine are other possibilities. Most thyroid nodules are not cancerous. The condition is more common in women, and family history can matter, but neither a food preference nor a symptom checklist establishes the cause. Recognise symptoms without diagnosing yourself from them Weight loss despite eating well, heat intolerance, sweating, shaking hands, weakness and a fast or irregular heartbeat can occur. Some people feel anxious, irritable or unable to sleep even while exhausted. More frequent bowel movements and changes in hair, skin or periods may also appear. A swollen thyroid can enlarge the neck. Graves’ disease can involve eye irritation, swelling or protrusion; less commonly it causes thickened skin over the shins or feet. Symptoms vary and overlap with other illnesses. A clinician uses the history, examination and blood tests, with further tests when needed, rather than prescribing a diet from symptoms alone. Let treatment guide the nutrition plan Untreated excess hormone can affect the heart, muscles and bones. Treatment may involve antithyroid medicine, radioactive iodine or surgery, depending on the cause and circumstances. Medicine to ease a fast heartbeat may also be used. Diet cannot replace these treatments or follow-up blood tests. Tell the team if you are pregnant, breastfeeding or planning pregnancy, because treatment and nutritional decisions change; radioactive iodine is not used during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Appetite and energy needs can change again as hormone levels improve. Continuing the same large portions indefinitely is not automatically necessary, but deliberate restriction during ongoing weight loss can be unhelpful. Distinguish a temporary low-iodine diet from daily eating Iodine is a raw material for thyroid hormones, but aiming for no iodine is not a general treatment plan. A specifically prescribed low-iodine diet may be used before radioactive iodine, particularly in thyroid-cancer treatment. It has a defined purpose and duration rather than becoming a lifelong rule for everyone with hyperthyroidism. If your team recommends it, request its own written start date, end date and food list. Possible ingredients include fresh produce, plain oats or potatoes, egg whites and unsalted nuts, subject to that plan. Bread, cereal, seasonings and prepared foods need ingredient checks. A food described as healthy, organic or low-salt is not automatically suitable for a temporary low-iodine protocol. Watch for excess iodine and hidden exposures Seaweed and kelp products can supply large and unpredictable amounts of iodine. Avoid self-prescribing them or supplements sold as thyroid support. Dairy, egg yolks, seafood and iodized salt also provide iodine, but do not automatically remove all of these ordinary foods without advice. Seaweed-derived ingredients and some bakery ingredients matter when a formal preparation diet requires their exclusion. Iodine can also be present in supplements, some cough remedies, amiodarone and contrast used for imaging. Tell your clinician and imaging team what you take and about your thyroid condition. Do not stop a prescribed medicine on your own. Generic online iodine figures for a spoonful of salt or a gram of seaweed cannot determine your personal intake or treatment target. Build meals that help maintain strength Include a useful protein source, starchy food, fruit or vegetables and suitable fats across the day. Beans, lentils, eggs, poultry, fish, meat and alternatives can all have a place, according to preference and any actual treatment restriction. Smaller meals and snacks may help when a full plate is difficult. Ongoing weight loss, reduced strength or difficulty buying or preparing food deserves practical help. A dietitian can adjust energy and protein intake without relying on a single special food. Keep fluids available if you are sweating more, and ask for individual advice if another condition limits how much you can drink. Keep vegetables in proportion Broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, kale, Brussels sprouts and bok choy are brassica vegetables. They can be part of varied meals. Normal food portions should not be promoted as a way to switch off an overactive thyroid, and eating large amounts is not a substitute for medicine. Cassava is a starchy root, not another brassica vegetable, and it requires proper food preparation. There is no reason to add it as a thyroid remedy. Vary vegetables for taste, fibre and overall nutrition rather than choosing them for a promised hormone-blocking effect. Use iron and zinc foods for nutrition, not a hormone cure Meat, beans, lentils, fortified grains, nuts, seeds and greens can contribute iron, although absorption differs between foods. Zinc is found in foods such as meat, legumes, nuts and seeds. These nutrients support normal body functions; their presence in a food does not establish that it treats Graves’ disease. Do not assume fatigue means you need iron or that every person with hyperthyroidism has a deficiency. Discuss symptoms and dietary limitations, and use tests or supplements when clinically appropriate. Excess supplementation can create side effects and interactions. If thyroid treatment later requires levothyroxine, ask how to separate iron and other mineral supplements from that medicine. Be particularly careful with selenium Fish, meat, eggs, grains, beans and nuts can contribute selenium. Content varies with the food and where it is produced; a list containing mushrooms, tea or rice should not be read as a list of equally rich sources. Brazil nuts may contain especially high amounts, so repeated handfuls plus supplements can supply too much. Extra selenium does not reliably normalise an overactive thyroid. A specialist may consider it in selected people with mild thyroid eye disease, which is a different decision from recommending it to everyone with Graves’ disease. Too much can damage hair and nails and cause other illness. Review the total from combined products before taking it. Give calcium and bone health their own place Excess thyroid hormone over time can weaken bones. Controlling the thyroid disorder matters alongside adequate calcium, vitamin D and appropriate activity. Recovery of bone health varies, so food alone should not be promised to reverse every change. Dairy foods and calcium-fortified alternatives can help meet calcium needs when suitable for your treatment plan. Check plant-drink and cereal labels because fortification differs. Some greens and beans contribute, but spinach is not a dependable substitute for higher-availability calcium sources because much of its calcium is poorly absorbed. Ask about assessment if you have fracture risks or major food restrictions. Choose vitamin D sources realistically Oily fish and some fortified foods provide vitamin D. Fortified milk alternatives, cereals or juices can contribute when the label confirms it. Mushroom content varies, including with ultraviolet exposure. Liver or an unfortified drink should not be assumed to meet your needs. Whether a supplement is appropriate depends on your location, diet and clinical circumstances. Fish may provide vitamin D while being unsuitable during a particular low-iodine preparation period; use the team’s plan to resolve that conflict. Pregnancy adds further food and supplement considerations, including avoiding excessive preformed vitamin A. Use fats and spices for meals, not as thyroid medicines Olive oil, avocado, nuts and seeds can add energy and unsaturated fats to meals. Coconut oil is richer in saturated fat and should not be promoted as a necessary hormone-balancing ingredient. No one oil restores thyroid function simply because it is described as natural. Turmeric and black or green pepper can be used in ordinary cooking if you enjoy them. Claims about antioxidant or anti-inflammatory properties do not demonstrate treatment of an overactive thyroid. Concentrated extracts and mixtures can have different risks from small culinary amounts, so include them in the supplement discussion. Avoid an unnecessary gluten-free diet Gluten occurs in wheat, barley and rye, including related products such as many breads, pastas and malt-containing foods. Coeliac disease requires a gluten-free diet, but hyperthyroidism by itself is not a reason to remove these grains. If coeliac disease is suspected, discuss testing before changing your diet; removing gluten can make diagnosis more difficult. A diet that also excludes dairy, soy and many proteins can become burdensome and nutritionally inadequate. Keep exclusions linked to a confirmed reason rather than an expanding online list. Separate soy advice from medicine timing Tofu, soy milk and other soy foods are not universally forbidden because someone has an overactive thyroid. Instructions may differ during a specific radioactive-iodine preparation protocol, and products may contain other ingredients relevant to that protocol. Soy can affect absorption of levothyroxine, a medicine sometimes needed after thyroid treatment. If you take it, follow the pharmacist’s advice on timing and consistency and mention substantial dietary changes. A medicine interaction is not evidence that ordinary soy foods cause hyperthyroidism in everyone. Adjust caffeine and review supplements Coffee, strong tea, cola, energy drinks and some chocolate contain caffeine. If it makes your heartbeat, anxiety or sleep worse, reducing it may improve comfort. This does not establish that caffeine caused your thyroid disorder. Water or a familiar caffeine-free drink is often a simpler alternative than a marketed thyroid drink. Apple cider vinegar and herbal tea blends are not treatments for excess thyroid hormone. Tell the team about all supplements, including biotin in hair-and-nail products, because it can distort thyroid blood-test results. Ask the laboratory or prescriber whether and when to withhold it; do not choose a universal stopping interval yourself. Make the plan workable and know when to get help Cooking at home can make ingredients easier to check during a prescribed low-iodine period. That does not mean all restaurant or processed food is permanently forbidden. Ask the dietitian for affordable alternatives and a clear return to ordinary eating after a preparation diet. Seek emergency help for a very fast heartbeat with high fever, severe agitation, confusion or collapse; thyroid storm is rare but serious. If taking an antithyroid medicine, follow its urgent instructions for fever or sore throat and contact the treating service promptly. Do not explain new severe symptoms away as something you ate. Treatment comes first; food supports recovery. Use a low-iodine diet only for a defined clinical purpose. Avoid kelp and high-dose thyroid-support supplements. Include protein and consider bone health without blanket exclusions. Ask about medicine timing, pregnancy and blood-test interference. Does everyone with hyperthyroidism need a low-iodine diet? No. It is a specific preparation strategy when prescribed, particularly before radioactive iodine for thyroid cancer, not a universal everyday diet. Should I stop eating all dairy, eggs and fish? Not automatically. Confirm whether your particular treatment requires temporary restrictions and how to replace important nutrients. Can broccoli or cabbage lower hormones enough to replace medicine? Normal portions can be part of meals, but they are not a reliable treatment for hyperthyroidism. Are Brazil nuts a safe selenium prescription? No. Their selenium content varies and can be high. Extra nuts plus supplements may produce excessive intake. Do I need gluten-free foods? Only when there is a separate appropriate reason, such as coeliac disease. Seek testing advice before removing gluten. Is soy always forbidden? No. A preparation protocol or an interaction with levothyroxine may require individual instructions rather than a permanent ban. Can I get calcium from any plant milk? Check the label. Fortification varies, and some drinks provide little calcium unless it has been added. Should I stop amiodarone because it contains iodine? Do not stop it yourself. Tell the prescriber and thyroid team so they can balance the treatment needs. Can biotin affect my thyroid tests? Yes. Share the product and dose with the clinician or laboratory and follow their timing instructions. When is a fast heartbeat an emergency? A racing heartbeat with high fever, confusion, severe agitation or collapse needs emergency assessment. Chest pain, fainting or severe breathlessness also need urgent care.

title: Thyroid storm: recognizing a medical emergency
description: A sudden severe illness involving fever, a very fast heartbeat and confusion needs emergency assessment, especially with known thyroid disease.
body: Thyroid storm is a rare, life-threatening emergency associated with excessive thyroid hormone effects. If someone with possible or known hyperthyroidism becomes severely unwell, particularly with high fever, a very fast heartbeat or confusion, call the local emergency service immediately. Do not wait for an appointment or a home remedy to work. Recognize a severe change Thyroid storm can involve marked agitation, confusion, vomiting, diarrhea, heavy sweating and reduced consciousness. Heart failure or other organ problems may develop. Symptoms are more severe than the everyday discomfort some people experience with an overactive thyroid. Not everyone has every feature, and there is no single heart-rate number a person must reach before getting help. A severely ill person may not be able to explain what is happening or call for care themselves. The absence of a previous thyroid diagnosis does not make the situation safe. A very fast or irregular heartbeat, including atrial fibrillation, can occur. Blood pressure may initially rise, but circulatory failure can also cause low pressure; a normal or low reading must not reassure someone who is severely ill. Heart failure and fluid in the lungs are possible complications. Get help without delaying for a measurement Tell emergency services what has changed and whether thyroid disease or thyroid medicine is involved. Mention pregnancy, recent illness, an operation or a problem taking regular treatment if known. Stay with the person and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Do not let someone who is confused, faint or severely unwell drive. If they become unresponsive, tell the dispatcher immediately so they can guide you. Do not give food, drink or extra medicines to someone who cannot swallow safely. Understand possible triggers without assigning blame Thyroid storm may occur when an overactive thyroid has not yet been diagnosed or is not adequately controlled. Infection, surgery, injury and interruption of treatment can be triggers. Other major illnesses can also contribute. Most people with hyperthyroidism never develop thyroid storm. Its occurrence should not be reduced to a judgement that someone failed to look after themselves. Difficulty obtaining medicine, side effects or an unexpected illness are practical issues the care team needs to understand. The thyroid is a small gland at the front of the lower neck. Its hormones T4 (thyroxine) and T3 (triiodothyronine) help regulate metabolism. Excess hormone effects can speed the pulse and produce tremor or restlessness, but faster speech or an isolated abnormal test does not diagnose thyroid storm. Major triggers can include stroke, diabetic ketoacidosis, heart failure or pulmonary embolism as well as infection, trauma and surgery. Severe emotional or physical stress may contribute in a susceptible person, but storm is not diagnosed simply because someone is distressed. Expect urgent hospital assessment and treatment Clinicians assess the person’s overall condition, take blood tests and look for a trigger. Thyroid hormone results support the assessment, but no hormone level alone separates thyroid storm from every other severe thyroid illness. Treatment may begin before all laboratory results return. Hospital care may include close monitoring, support for circulation and breathing, temperature control and medicines that reduce thyroid hormone production or effects. The combination and sequence depend on the situation. This is not a treatment regimen to reproduce at home. TSH is often suppressed and T3 or T4 elevated, but laboratory reference ranges vary and a universal TSH interval of 0.4–4 does not define the emergency. Clinicians use symptoms and organ dysfunction alongside tests. Hospital medicines may include an antithyroid drug such as propylthiouracil or methimazole, with other treatments chosen and timed by the team. Distinguish hospital iodine treatment from supplements In selected circumstances, clinicians use iodine as part of emergency treatment with careful timing and supervision. That does not mean an iodine supplement or seaweed product is a safe response to symptoms. Extra iodine can be harmful in the wrong setting. Radioactive iodine is a different treatment used in some longer-term thyroid plans; it is not used during pregnancy. Pregnancy does not automatically require thyroid removal, either. Specialists choose appropriate medicines or other care according to the individual condition. Make a continuing plan after recovery After stabilization, the team reviews the cause of hyperthyroidism and the longer-term treatment options. Ask about follow-up tests, medicine supply, side effects and what to do if vomiting or illness prevents usual doses. An agreed plan can reduce avoidable risk, but no article can guarantee prevention. Share warning signs with someone you trust if that would help, and seek urgent care for a severe change even if a previous thyroid test was reassuring. Longer-term options can include antithyroid medicine, radioactive iodine when appropriate, or surgery. Removal or ablation of enough thyroid tissue may require lifelong thyroid-hormone replacement and follow-up. Pregnancy changes which options are suitable; it does not make surgery mandatory. Prompt treatment can be lifesaving, while untreated storm is highly dangerous. A historical estimate that three quarters of untreated patients die is not a dependable individual prediction. Returning hormone levels toward normal is part of recovery, but ongoing organ support and treatment of the trigger may still be needed. Suspected thyroid storm needs emergency care immediately. Do not wait for a particular pulse rate or blood-test result. Hospital treatment and follow-up are individualized; supplements are not emergency treatment. Can a blood test alone diagnose thyroid storm? No. It is a clinical emergency assessed from the overall illness, with laboratory results providing supporting information. Should I take iodine if I think this is happening? No. Call emergency services. Iodine use in hospital is carefully selected and timed; self-treatment may be harmful.

title: Dizziness after standing: understanding postural hypotension
description: Why blood pressure can fall when you stand, how it is assessed, and practical and medical treatments that may help safely.
body: Feeling lightheaded when you stand can reflect a fall in blood pressure, but it is not a diagnosis by itself. Postural hypotension may be temporary or persistent. Understanding the pattern, checking for an underlying cause and preventing falls are more useful than immediately adding salt or stopping a medicine. What happens to circulation when you stand Blood pressure is the force blood exerts on artery walls. When you move upright, gravity shifts blood into the legs and the veins of the abdomen. The body normally responds by tightening blood vessels and adjusting the heart rate, helping maintain enough blood flow to the brain. If this adjustment is too slow or insufficient, blood pressure can fall and you may feel lightheaded. This is called orthostatic, or postural, hypotension. It can happen after rising from bed or a chair, and it is not always caused by moving too quickly. A temporary problem such as dehydration and a longer-term problem with automatic nerve control can produce similar symptoms. Recognise the symptoms without assuming the diagnosis Lightheadedness, blurred or dimmed vision, weakness and unsteadiness are common descriptions. Some people feel nauseated, develop a headache or feel mentally foggy; others describe their legs giving way. Symptoms often ease when they sit or lie down. A brief loss of consciousness is called syncope and may lead to a fall or injury. Neck or shoulder discomfort can occur, particularly with autonomic problems, but a symptom list cannot confirm the cause. Chest pain, an abnormal heartbeat or breathlessness deserves particular attention. Inner-ear disorders, migraine, low blood sugar and other conditions can also cause dizziness, so repeated episodes should be assessed rather than labelled from one symptom alone. Age, illness and the type of blood-pressure fall matter Postural hypotension becomes more common with older age, especially when frailty, medicines or other health conditions affect circulation. Prolonged bed rest or a hospital stay can reduce conditioning. Younger people, including teenagers, can also develop symptoms on standing, but rapid growth alone should not be assumed to explain fainting. Published percentages depend on who was studied and how blood pressure was measured. A 2021 review found an estimated 27.8% prevalence of initial orthostatic hypotension in its older general-population subgroup, with substantial variation between studies. Initial hypotension is a very early, brief drop after standing; this figure should not be treated as the prevalence of every form of persistent postural hypotension or as a personal prediction. Low circulating volume is one possible contributor Not drinking enough, vomiting, diarrhoea, heat exposure or fluid loss can reduce the volume of blood in circulation. Blood loss and anaemia also deserve consideration, particularly after surgery or childbirth. Sometimes more than one factor is present, such as a recent illness, reduced intake and a medicine that lowers blood pressure. After giving birth, ongoing dizziness or fainting should not be dismissed as tiredness or a routine postural episode. Tell the maternity service, especially if there is heavy bleeding, fever, chest pain or breathlessness. If bleeding is severe or you feel close to collapse, obtain emergency help rather than trying to correct the problem only with water or salt. Medicines, heart conditions and nerve control can contribute Some medicines used for high blood pressure, Parkinson’s disease, depression or psychosis can affect blood-vessel tone, circulating volume or the response to standing. Certain chemotherapy treatments may also be relevant through nerve effects, illness or dehydration. Bring a complete list of prescriptions, supplements and non-prescription products, including recent dose changes. Alcohol can make the problem worse. A slow or irregular heart rhythm, heart failure or another problem with the heart’s pumping function may limit compensation. Diabetes and Parkinson’s disease can affect the autonomic nervous system, which manages functions such as blood pressure without conscious effort. Spinal-cord disorders and conditions such as Guillain–Barré syndrome can also involve autonomic regulation. These are possible contexts for assessment, not diagnoses made from dizziness alone. Notice the pattern and act safely when symptoms start Symptoms may be more noticeable in the morning, after a large meal, during hot weather or after standing for a long time. A meal-related fall in blood pressure can occur in the following hours, especially after a large carbohydrate-heavy meal, but it is not identical to every episode triggered by standing. Recording the timing can help distinguish patterns. If you begin to feel faint, sit or lie down promptly in a safe place. Do not try to walk through it or keep carrying a child while unsteady. If you are holding your baby, put them safely in their cot or ask another adult to take them. Avoid driving, ladders or hazardous equipment while symptoms are unexplained or active. Diagnosis starts with properly timed measurements A clinician commonly checks blood pressure and pulse after you have rested lying down and again after standing, often at one and three minutes. A sustained fall of at least 20 mmHg in systolic pressure, the upper number, or 10 mmHg in diastolic pressure, the lower number, within three minutes is a standard criterion for classic orthostatic hypotension. A very early drop can be missed by an ordinary cuff, and some falls occur later than three minutes. A normal single reading therefore does not settle every case. The clinician interprets the results with your symptoms, heart rate, medicines and baseline blood pressure. Do not repeatedly stand unsupported to provoke a faint for a home reading. Further tests depend on what the first assessment suggests A physical examination and history guide the next steps. A complete blood count may look for anaemia; other blood tests may check glucose, kidney function or another suspected contributor. An electrocardiogram, or ECG, records the heart’s electrical activity. Longer rhythm monitoring may be considered if episodes suggest an intermittent rhythm problem. An echocardiogram examines the structure and pumping of the heart. An exercise stress test assesses the response to exertion, and a tilt-table test changes body position under supervision while circulation is monitored. These tests are selected for a reason; everyone with brief dizziness does not need all of them. Postural tachycardia syndrome, often called PoTS, can also cause symptoms upright but involves an excessive rise in heart rate and has different diagnostic criteria. Tests do not simply “rule out Parkinson’s and diabetes” as a group. The aim is to identify the relevant cause or contributing factors and choose the right follow-up. Treat the cause and review medicines with the prescriber Treatment aims to reduce symptoms, prevent falls and improve daily activity. Correcting dehydration, treating anaemia or another illness, and addressing poor conditioning may help. A person with a blood-pressure drop but no symptoms may not need a specific pressure-raising medicine, although the finding and possible causes still deserve review. If a medicine contributes, the prescriber may adjust its dose, timing or choice. Do not stop blood-pressure, Parkinson’s or mental-health treatment on your own. Low pressure when standing can coexist with high pressure when lying down. Improving one at the expense of the other can create problems, so the plan may include readings in different positions and review after each change. Practical changes can make getting up safer Rise in stages: move from lying to sitting, pause, and then stand using a stable support if needed. Seated ankle pumps or gentle leg movements before standing may help. A clinician or physiotherapist can teach appropriate counter-pressure manoeuvres, such as muscle tensing or handgrip using a soft ball or towel. These are prevention tools for selected people, not a reason to remain standing when a faint is developing. Avoid very hot baths and prolonged activity in strong heat if these trigger symptoms. Smaller, more frequent meals may help when large meals are a problem. Keep walkways clear and arrange help for showering or getting out of bed if you have fallen. Ask how to rebuild physical activity safely rather than responding with prolonged bed rest. Fluid, salt and compression advice must fit your health Regular fluids can help when dehydration contributes, and reducing alcohol may reduce episodes. However, someone with heart failure, kidney disease or a prescribed fluid restriction needs an individual target. Adding large amounts of salt without advice can worsen high blood pressure, swelling or another condition. A clinician may suggest compression stockings or an abdominal binder to reduce blood pooling. The fit, pressure and length matter; ordinary tight socks are not equivalent. Ask whether compression is suitable for your circulation, skin and ability to put it on. Combining several measures is sometimes more useful than expecting one change to solve every episode. Prescription treatment is reserved for selected situations Midodrine tightens blood vessels and may be considered when symptoms persist despite other measures. Fludrocortisone promotes salt and water retention but needs careful selection and monitoring, including for swelling, electrolyte changes and high blood pressure. It is unsuitable in heart failure. Depending on the diagnosis and country, a specialist may consider other options, such as droxidopa for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension. These medicines can raise pressure while lying down, so dose timing and monitoring are part of treatment. Erythropoietin, also known through products such as Epogen or Procrit, has been studied in small older trials involving anaemia and autonomic failure. It is not a routine treatment for dizziness or a substitute for finding the cause of anaemia. Specialist assessment is necessary; this list is not a prescribing guide. Follow-up matters even when episodes are brief Fainting and falls can cause injuries, particularly in older adults. Research also finds associations between orthostatic hypotension and cardiovascular illness, but this does not prove that a brief dizzy spell itself causes a stroke. The practical response is to assess repeated symptoms and manage the factors that can be treated. A temporary cause may improve when corrected; a chronic neurological or cardiovascular condition may require a continuing plan. Seek emergency help for chest pain, severe breathlessness, major bleeding, new one-sided weakness or speech difficulty, or a collapse with poor recovery. Otherwise, arrange review for recurrent dizziness, any unexplained faint or symptoms that persist despite the agreed treatment. Symptoms on standing can have several causes. A sustained fall of at least 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within three minutes is one diagnostic criterion. Do not stop prescribed medicines or increase salt without advice. Sit or lie down promptly when faint and reduce fall hazards. Persistent symptoms need follow-up even if episodes are short. Does dizziness after standing always mean low blood pressure? No. Other conditions can feel similar. Repeated episodes need assessment of symptoms, blood pressure, pulse and possible contributors. What do the 20 and 10 mmHg figures mean? They describe a fall from the resting reading: at least 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within three minutes is a standard criterion for classic orthostatic hypotension. Does the 2021 estimate mean 28% of all older people have the same condition? No. That estimate concerned initial orthostatic hypotension in a particular subgroup, with wide variation between studies. Initial and sustained falls are not interchangeable. Can it happen even when my usual blood pressure is high? Yes. Standing hypotension and high pressure while lying down can coexist, which is one reason treatment needs monitoring. Should I stop my blood-pressure medicine? No. Ask the prescriber to review the whole regimen. Stopping treatment automatically can worsen other risks and may not solve the symptoms. Should I add salt and drink as much water as possible? No. Fluid and salt targets depend on your health, especially heart or kidney disease, swelling and high blood pressure. Is PoTS the same as orthostatic hypotension? No. Both can cause symptoms upright, but PoTS focuses on an excessive heart-rate rise and has different diagnostic criteria. Will everyone need a tilt-table or exercise test? No. Additional testing depends on the history, examination and initial measurements. Is erythropoietin a usual treatment for dizzy spells? No. Older small studies concerned selected people with anaemia and autonomic failure. It is not routine treatment for unexplained dizziness. Will the problem go away? A temporary cause may resolve with treatment. Persistent autonomic or heart conditions may need ongoing care; follow-up should focus on symptoms, safety and function.

title: White blood cell counts: understanding a high or low result
description: What a WBC count and differential measure, why results can change, what happens during the test and why treatment depends on the cause.
body: A white blood cell count, often shortened to WBC, measures how many white blood cells are in a sample of blood. These cells are also called leukocytes and form part of the immune system. The result can help a clinician investigate symptoms or monitor treatment, but a number on its own does not identify a disease or prove that the immune system is working normally. Why a clinician may request a WBC count White blood cells develop in the bone marrow and move through the blood and tissues as part of the body’s defence against infection and other threats. A WBC count is commonly included in a complete blood count, or CBC, which also assesses red blood cells and platelets. The test can contribute to an assessment of infection, inflammation, allergy, immune disorders or blood and bone marrow conditions. Sometimes it helps investigate a problem before the cause is obvious, but it is not a test that reliably finds every hidden infection. Counts are also used during treatments such as chemotherapy or radiotherapy to monitor their effects on healthy blood cells. This can help guide treatment timing or infection precautions. It does not, by itself, show how well a cancer treatment is controlling the cancer. A CBC may be requested during a health review, but everyone does not automatically need one every year. The reason for testing, previous results and current symptoms determine how useful it is. What the differential adds The total WBC count combines several kinds of cells. A differential reports their numbers, proportions or both. Looking at the mixture can be more informative than looking only at the total. The five main groups are neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils. Neutrophils are particularly important in defence against bacterial and fungal infection. Lymphocytes include cells involved in antibodies and targeted immune responses. Monocytes help clear germs and damaged material, while eosinophils and basophils have roles in allergy, inflammation and responses to some parasites. These jobs overlap, so the differential cannot identify an organism simply from one high percentage. A clinician may also review a blood smear, where the cells’ appearance is examined, if the pattern needs further explanation. Reference ranges: use the range printed on your report A commonly quoted adult interval is about 4,500 to 11,000 white cells per microlitre, while some laboratories use a lower boundary around 4,000. These are examples, not universal limits. The laboratory’s own interval and the person’s circumstances matter. Results may be written as cells per microlitre, cells per cubic millimetre or ×10⁹/L. One microlitre equals one cubic millimetre; 4,500 cells per microlitre is the same as 4.5 ×10⁹/L. Check the units before comparing results from different reports. Age affects interpretation. Newborns and young children need age-specific ranges, and pregnancy can raise the expected count. Some reference tables also separate adult values by sex. A single simplified range for all children or all adults can therefore be misleading. A result within the reference interval does not prove that every part of immunity is normal. Likewise, a mildly flagged result does not automatically mean serious illness. Previous counts and a person’s usual baseline may help explain the finding. Percentages and absolute counts are not interchangeable An educational adult differential table may show neutrophils around 55–70%, lymphocytes 20–40%, monocytes 2–8%, eosinophils 1–4% and basophils 0.5–1%. These illustrative ranges should not override the laboratory report; proportions differ with age and other factors. A percentage describes a share of the total. If one cell type increases, another type’s percentage can fall even when its actual number has not changed much. This is why clinicians often pay attention to the absolute count, including the absolute neutrophil count, or ANC. An out-of-range percentage is a reason to interpret the whole pattern, not a diagnosis. Ask which actual cell number is abnormal, how large the change is and whether the red cells or platelets are also affected. A low count: leukopenia and possible causes Leukopenia means that the total white cell count is below the relevant reference interval. Possible explanations include reduced production in the marrow, destruction of cells or changes in how cells are distributed or held in organs such as the spleen. Infections, including HIV and some other viral illnesses, can lower counts. Severe bacterial infection can sometimes do so too. Malaria can be associated with a low count in the appropriate exposure setting, but it requires specific testing; WBC alone cannot diagnose or exclude it. Other possibilities include autoimmune conditions such as lupus, bone marrow damage or failure, and cancers that involve the marrow, including some lymphomas. Liver disease or an enlarged, overactive spleen can also be relevant. Chemotherapy, radiotherapy and certain medicines are additional causes. Heavy alcohol use and nutritional deficiencies may contribute in some circumstances. This list describes possibilities rather than their likelihood in a particular person; a clinician uses history, symptoms and other tests to narrow it down. Neutropenia is a specific finding, not another name for every low WBC Neutropenia means a low number of neutrophils. It can account for a low total WBC, but the terms are not interchangeable: other white cell types can be low, and a total alone does not show the neutrophil count. Infection risk depends on how low the ANC is, how long it remains low, the cause and the person’s wider health. A slight isolated reduction does not carry the same risk as profound, prolonged neutropenia during intensive cancer treatment. Some people have a consistently lower baseline count without the same increased infection risk seen with treatment-related neutropenia. This is assessed from the person’s history and laboratory pattern, rather than assuming risk from a demographic label or one result. If your care team says you are at increased risk, ask for a clear plan: which symptoms require an immediate call, what temperature threshold to use, and whom to contact outside office hours. Do not wait for the next routine blood test if you become unwell. A high count: common temporary explanations Leukocytosis means that the total WBC is above the applicable range. Infection is one possible cause, including some serious infections such as sepsis or tuberculosis, but a high count does not establish either diagnosis. Fever is a symptom that provides context rather than a diagnosis in itself. Inflammation and tissue injury can raise counts. Burns, trauma, surgery, a heart attack, significant bleeding or rapid red-cell breakdown may be associated with a reactive increase. Physical or emotional stress can also temporarily change the circulating count. Pregnancy is another context in which counts may be higher without the same meaning as in a nonpregnant adult. Allergic illness or asthma can particularly affect certain cell types. Tell the clinician about a recent vaccination or illness rather than assuming either fully explains a flagged result. Medicines such as corticosteroids or epinephrine can raise the count. A leukemoid reaction is a marked reactive increase that can resemble a blood disorder and needs interpretation; it is not another term for leukemia. When a high count persists Smoking, ongoing inflammatory disease and some conditions associated with obesity can accompany a persistently elevated count. Examples of inflammatory conditions include rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease and vasculitis, which affects blood vessels. Leukemia and other marrow or blood disorders are also among the possibilities. Their presence cannot be confirmed from a high WBC alone. The degree of elevation, which cells are increased, their appearance and changes in other blood cell types all matter. A clinician may repeat the CBC, order a differential or smear, or investigate a suspected infection or inflammatory condition. More specialised testing, including a marrow examination, is reserved for situations where it is needed; it is not the automatic next step for every abnormal result. Symptoms usually come from the underlying problem Low or high white cell counts may cause no obvious symptoms. Body aches, fever, chills and headache can accompany an infection or another illness, but none specifically identifies a low count. You cannot reliably estimate WBC from how you feel. Frequent infections, recurring mouth sores, a sore throat, unexplained tiredness or other persistent changes are worth discussing with a clinician. A high count may be found incidentally, while the condition causing it may produce its own symptoms. During chemotherapy or known significant neutropenia, fever can be the only early sign of a serious infection. Contact your treatment team immediately for a temperature of 38°C/100.4°F or above, or follow their lower threshold if they have given one. Feeling suddenly unwell also deserves urgent advice even without fever. Severe breathlessness, confusion, collapse or rapidly worsening illness needs emergency help. An apparently normal recent count is not a reason to ignore these symptoms. Medicines and preparation for the test An isolated WBC test generally does not require fasting or special preparation. If other blood tests are being done at the same visit, follow the instructions for those tests. Tell the clinic about medicines and supplements rather than changing them yourself. Relevant medicines can include chemotherapy, clozapine, quinidine, some antibiotics including sulfonamides, certain antiseizure medicines and diuretics. Corticosteroids, epinephrine and heparin can also affect the result. Effects differ by drug, dose and individual circumstances. Some histamine-blocking medicines used for stomach acid are associated with blood-count changes; that does not mean every allergy antihistamine has the same effect. Similarly, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs should not be treated as a class that routinely raises WBC. Provide the exact product name so it can be checked. Many medication-related changes are real effects on the cells, rather than an inaccurate laboratory measurement. Do not stop a prescribed treatment to make the number look normal. A prescriber can decide whether a change or additional monitoring is appropriate. What happens when the sample is taken A trained professional usually takes a small blood sample from a vein in the arm, sometimes from the hand. They clean the skin, may place a band around the upper arm to make the vein easier to access, and collect blood through a needle into a tube. After the needle is removed, pressure is applied with gauze and a dressing may be used. The collection itself usually takes only a few minutes. A brief sting or pinch is common; it should not be described as always painless. For a baby or small child, the collection method depends on age, the amount needed and local practice. A heel or finger sample may be suitable for some tests, while a venous sample is needed for others. A WBC count is analysed by the laboratory, not diagnosed by an ordinary home test strip. Results may be provided electronically or on paper. Ask when to expect them and who will explain any abnormal findings, especially if the test is monitoring treatment. Possible discomfort and complications Minor bruising, tenderness or lightheadedness can occur. Finding a vein can be harder in some people and may require another attempt. Tell the person taking the sample if you have fainted before, have a bleeding disorder or take a medicine that affects clotting. If you feel sharp, severe or spreading pain during collection, speak up so the procedure can be reassessed. You do not need to tolerate significant pain because a vein is difficult to locate. Less common problems include prolonged bleeding, a larger collection of blood under the skin called a haematoma, or infection at the puncture site. Follow pressure and dressing advice, and seek help if bleeding will not stop or the area develops increasing redness, warmth, swelling or pain. Follow-up is about the cause and the trend Treatment is directed at the reason for the abnormal count. This might mean treating an infection, reviewing a medicine, managing inflammation or addressing a marrow disorder. Some results need only a planned repeat test; others need prompt investigation. A count that stays abnormal does not automatically mean an illness is getting worse. It may reflect an ongoing treatment effect, a stable baseline or incomplete recovery. A return to the reference range can be reassuring, but it does not by itself prove that the underlying disease has resolved. Keep track of the agreed follow-up date and ask which changes would require earlier review. When comparing results, use the units, reference intervals and dates rather than focusing on whether an app has coloured a number red. Food, supplements and infection precautions Adequate food and protein support normal blood cell production. Vitamin B12 and folate are also needed, and a diagnosed deficiency may require treatment. Correcting a deficiency is different from using supplements to raise every low WBC count. There is no established food combination that reliably corrects low counts from chemotherapy, marrow disease or another cause. Vitamin C, vitamin E, zinc, selenium, garlic and spicy foods should not be promoted as proven WBC boosters. A daily multivitamin is not automatically necessary for everyone with an abnormal result. Discuss supplements with the treating team, particularly during cancer therapy, because some products can interfere with treatment. A dietitian can help if appetite, restrictions or illness make it difficult to meet nutritional needs. If you have clinically important neutropenia, follow the infection-prevention plan your team provides. Hand hygiene, avoiding close contact with sick people and safe food handling are useful measures. Advice about masks, crowds and other exposures should fit your degree of risk rather than being imposed on everyone with a mildly low result. Use your laboratory’s reference interval and check the units. The differential and absolute counts add important information. Leukopenia and neutropenia are not interchangeable. An abnormal count does not automatically mean cancer or infection. Do not change medicines or start supplements to chase a number. Fever during chemotherapy or significant neutropenia needs immediate advice. Does a normal WBC prove that my immune system is healthy? No. It measures cell numbers, not every aspect of immune function, and cannot exclude every illness. Is 4,500 to 11,000 the correct range for everyone? No. It is a common adult example. Use the laboratory’s range and consider age, pregnancy and the clinical context. What is the difference between a total count and a differential? The total combines all white cells. A differential separates the cell types and may report percentages, absolute numbers or both. Does a low total WBC always mean neutropenia? No. Neutropenia refers specifically to low neutrophils. The differential and absolute neutrophil count are needed to identify it. Does a high count mean I have leukemia? No. Infection, inflammation, stress, medicines and other causes can raise it. Further interpretation depends on the whole pattern. Do I need to fast before the test? Usually not for WBC alone. Follow the clinic’s instructions if other tests are being collected at the same time. Should I stop my medicine before a blood count? Do not stop prescribed treatment on your own. Provide an accurate list and ask the prescriber about any specific instructions. Can garlic, vitamins or a special diet raise my white cells? They are not established treatments for an unexplained low count. Adequate nutrition and treatment of a confirmed deficiency can matter, but the underlying cause needs attention. Does an abnormal result that persists mean treatment failed? Not necessarily. Trends must be interpreted alongside the illness, medicines and other tests. Ask what change your team expects. What if I develop a fever during chemotherapy? Contact your treatment team immediately, using their emergency instructions. A temperature of 38°C/100.4°F or above is an urgent warning, and feeling unwell can require help even without fever.

title: Abdominal pain with chills: when to get help
description: Pain and shivering can occur together for several reasons. The severity, other symptoms and your medical circumstances guide the next step.
body: Abdominal pain means discomfort between the chest and pelvis. Chills are a feeling of coldness that may involve shivering, sometimes during a fever. Together, these symptoms can accompany an infection or another illness. They do not identify the cause, and persistent pain with chills deserves prompt medical advice. Notice the pattern, without diagnosing yourself The pain may be constant or come in waves, and it may involve the whole abdomen or one area. Note when it began, whether it is getting worse and whether it moves toward the back or groin. A measured temperature can help, but a normal reading does not rule out a serious problem. Vomiting, diarrhea, urinary discomfort, unusual bleeding and recent travel are useful details to share. Explain whether you are pregnant, recently gave birth, take medicines that suppress immunity or have another significant condition. These circumstances may change how quickly assessment is needed. Shivering involves repeated muscle contractions that generate heat. It can happen during cold exposure or while the body’s temperature setting changes during fever, so chills do not always mean that the surrounding air is cold. Describe cramping, sharp, dull or aching pain as well as its location. Understand the main possibilities An intestinal infection can cause cramps, diarrhea and nausea. A urinary infection involving the kidneys may cause fever or chills, pain in the side or back, and urinary symptoms. Inflammation elsewhere in the abdomen or pelvis can also produce pain and fever. A long list of possible diseases, including rare infections, cannot tell you which condition is likely. Exposure history, examination and selected tests are more useful than matching one symptom to a disease name online. Examples requiring different care include appendicitis, diverticulitis, gallbladder inflammation, pancreatitis and inflammation of the abdominal lining, or peritonitis. Kidney stones may cause severe pain; fever or shaking chills with a suspected stone is especially concerning for associated infection. Foodborne infection, including Salmonella, is another possibility when vomiting or diarrhoea predominates. Urinary or genital causes include kidney infection (pyelonephritis), bladder or urethral infection, prostatitis, epididymitis and pelvic inflammatory disease. Respiratory or other infections, such as pneumonia or infectious mononucleosis, can sometimes be accompanied by abdominal symptoms. A minor cold alone should not be assumed to explain significant abdominal pain. Travel and exposure can change the assessment: malaria, enteric or rickettsial infections, leptospirosis, brucellosis and other uncommon infections are considered when the history fits. A long catalogue of rare diseases does not mean all are equally likely. Tell the clinician about animal contact, unsafe water, insect bites or a new painful rash rather than attempting to choose a diagnosis. Recognize an emergency Get emergency help for sudden severe abdominal pain, collapse, trouble breathing, significant confusion, vomiting blood or black, tar-like stool. Severe pain with a swollen abdomen and inability to pass stool or gas also needs urgent emergency assessment. A person with an infection who becomes rapidly worse, unusually drowsy, confused or very breathless may have sepsis or another emergency. Do not wait for every symptom to appear. Tell emergency services what has changed, and do not drive yourself if you are faint or seriously unwell. Chest pain, pain extending to a shoulder, severe headache with a stiff neck, new neurological or visual changes, or loss of consciousness also needs emergency assessment. Some heart problems can present partly as upper abdominal discomfort. A fever below 38.3°C does not make serious illness impossible, and you should not wait for a particular temperature or twenty-four hours of vomiting before seeking needed help. Seek timely assessment for ongoing symptoms Arrange urgent advice if pain is worsening, chills are marked, you cannot keep fluids down or urine output has fallen substantially. Pain with possible pregnancy, a weakened immune system or recent surgery also needs a lower threshold for assessment. The clinician may check temperature, circulation and the abdomen, then choose urine, blood or imaging tests according to the findings. Antibiotics help particular bacterial infections; they are not a treatment for every episode of chills or abdominal pain. Use simple comfort measures while arranging care Rest and take small drinks if you can swallow safely and are not repeatedly vomiting. Follow any existing fluid restriction. Use comfortable clothing and bedding; forcing yourself into a cold shower or aggressively cooling the skin is not a treatment for the cause and can worsen shivering. Ask a pharmacist or clinician which pain or fever medicine is suitable for you. Pregnancy, kidney disease, stomach problems and other medicines matter. Do not combine products with the same ingredient or use symptom relief as a reason to delay necessary assessment. Paracetamol, also called acetaminophen, may be suitable for some people, while aspirin and ibuprofen are not appropriate for everyone. Aspirin should not be given to a child under sixteen unless specifically prescribed. Follow individual pregnancy and medicine advice, and avoid deliberately chilling yourself with water at a fixed temperature to control shivering. Reduce preventable exposure Regular handwashing, safe food preparation and suitable drinking water reduce some infectious risks. They cannot prevent every cause of abdominal pain. If symptoms follow travel, explain where you went and when you returned rather than assuming it is an ordinary stomach bug. Follow the assessment plan and ask what changes should trigger another call. If you were initially advised to recover at home but become more unwell, seek help again. A previous reassuring assessment does not override a significant change in symptoms. For urinary health, drink an appropriate amount and wipe from front to back after using the toilet, but these measures do not guarantee prevention. Before travel to a malaria-risk area, obtain destination-specific advice about preventive medicine and insect-bite protection. Use an approved repellent according to its label, suitable clothing and bed nets where needed; no single DEET percentage or tablet is appropriate for every journey. Pain with chills needs interpretation in the context of other symptoms. Severe pain, collapse, confusion or breathing difficulty requires emergency help. Treatment depends on the cause; cold showers and routine antibiotics are not universal solutions. Do chills always mean a high fever? No. Shivering can occur at different temperatures, and the overall condition matters more than one reading. Should I wait until symptoms have lasted two days? No fixed waiting period is appropriate. Seek advice sooner for worsening symptoms or any warning sign.

title: Abdominal pain and loss of appetite: understanding the possibilities
description: See how digestive, medical and emotional causes are assessed, which warning signs need urgent care and when gentle home care is reasonable.
body: When your abdomen hurts, it is common not to feel like eating. The important questions are how the symptoms began, what else is happening and whether you can stay hydrated. A useful assessment separates common temporary illness from problems that need prompt treatment. Start with the pattern, not a list of diagnoses Abdominal pain and loss of appetite often occur together. Pain, nausea or early fullness can make food unappealing, while reduced intake can leave you feeling weak or nauseated. The pain may be sharp, dull, burning or cramping. Its location, duration and associated symptoms help determine what to do next. The abdomen contains the stomach and bowel as well as the liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, kidneys and appendix. Pain can also arise from pelvic organs or be felt here because of an illness elsewhere. Two symptoms alone cannot identify which organ is involved. Many episodes are temporary, but a mild-looking episode does not exclude a serious cause if other warning signs appear. Common digestive infections and food-related illness Viral gastroenteritis often causes cramping, vomiting or diarrhoea and temporarily reduces appetite. It is sometimes called stomach flu, although it is not influenza. Food poisoning and bacterial gastroenteritis, including some E. coli infections, can produce similar symptoms. Fever, blood in the stool, dehydration or severe pain changes the urgency of assessment. Giardiasis and hookworm are parasitic infections that may be considered when travel, contaminated water, exposure or persistent symptoms make them relevant. They are not interchangeable with an ordinary short-lived stomach bug. Tell the clinician about sick contacts, food or water concerns and recent travel rather than trying to choose an antibiotic or antiparasitic medicine yourself. Reflux, inflammation and longer-lasting bowel problems Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, gastritis and peptic ulcers can cause upper-abdominal discomfort that interferes with eating. Irritable bowel syndrome can cause recurring pain with changes in bowel habits. Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis are inflammatory bowel diseases and need a different assessment and treatment approach from IBS. Coeliac disease is an immune reaction to gluten that can damage the small bowel. Non-coeliac gluten sensitivity describes a different situation after other causes have been considered. Do not assume they are the same diagnosis or stop gluten before discussing coeliac testing, because dietary restriction can affect test results. Persistent symptoms, bleeding, weight loss or a new pattern deserve review rather than repeated self-diagnosis as food intolerance. Pain may come from the gallbladder, pancreas or appendix Gallstones or an obstructed bile duct can cause substantial abdominal pain and may be accompanied by jaundice. Acute pancreatitis can cause severe persistent pain with vomiting; chronic pancreatitis can produce recurrent pain and problems with digestion. These conditions are not managed by simply waiting for appetite to return. Appendicitis may begin with vague pain and reduced appetite before the pattern becomes clearer. Peritonitis means inflammation of the abdominal lining and can signal a serious infection or another abdominal emergency. Worsening pain, tenderness, fever or a rigid abdomen needs prompt assessment. A clinician uses the whole pattern, examination and selected tests to distinguish these problems. Some infections affect the whole body Hepatitis can affect appetite and cause abdominal symptoms, sometimes with dark urine or yellowing of the skin or eyes. Infectious mononucleosis and chickenpox may also reduce appetite as part of a wider illness. Their usual additional features matter; abdominal pain and poor appetite alone are not enough to diagnose them. Other infections become relevant mainly in a particular exposure or medical setting. Tuberculosis, brucellosis and visceral leishmaniasis can cause prolonged systemic illness. Mention a persistent fever, night sweats, weight loss, animal contact, unpasteurized dairy exposure or travel when they apply. A broad list of possible infections does not mean everyone needs tests for all of them. Travel and exposure clues change which rare illnesses are considered Yellow fever, typhus and West Nile virus infection belong to different infection groups and have distinct exposure patterns. They may involve fever and broader symptoms rather than an isolated appetite change. Typhus is not another name for typhoid fever. A clinician considers where you have been and relevant mosquito, flea or other exposures before choosing investigations. Botulism is a different emergency: a toxin affects the nerves, and foodborne illness may begin with digestive symptoms before problems such as blurred or double vision, difficulty swallowing, weakness or breathing trouble. Get emergency help for these symptoms rather than treating the illness as a routine stomach infection. Bring the exposure history to the care team; do not delay care while trying to identify a particular food. Urinary and pelvic conditions can feel like abdominal illness Pain with urination, discharge or lower-abdominal discomfort may point toward urinary or genital problems. Urethritis is inflammation of the urethra and can have several causes, including sexually transmitted infections such as chlamydia. Chlamydia can also contribute to pelvic inflammatory disease, which affects the upper reproductive tract. These conditions should not be grouped as ordinary digestive infections. Ask for confidential assessment if symptoms or a possible exposure apply. Pelvic pain with fever, worsening illness or pregnancy possibility needs timely care. Testing and treatment depend on the actual diagnosis, and partner-related advice is best discussed with the treating service. Chronic organ disease can reduce appetite Chronic kidney disease, kidney failure and chronic liver disease can affect appetite and nutrition. Advanced liver disease may include cirrhosis or liver failure; alcohol-related liver disease is one possible cause. Abdominal symptoms in someone with an established condition need review in the context of their usual health and treatment. Do not respond to poor intake by forcing large amounts of water if you have been prescribed a fluid restriction for kidney or heart disease. New swelling, confusion, jaundice, vomiting or a marked change in symptoms deserves prompt advice. The care team may need to adjust treatment and arrange nutritional support rather than simply recommending a bland diet. Hormonal and metabolic causes need their own treatment An underactive thyroid can slow the bowel, while hyperparathyroidism can raise blood calcium and affect digestive comfort and appetite. Hypopituitarism involves a shortage of one or more pituitary hormones. These are less common explanations than a short digestive illness and are assessed using other symptoms, history and appropriate blood tests. Adrenal insufficiency, including Addison’s disease, can cause abdominal pain and poor appetite. An adrenal crisis is an emergency. Diabetic ketoacidosis and alcoholic ketoacidosis are also emergencies that may involve abdominal pain, vomiting, dehydration, altered alertness or abnormal breathing. Follow any existing sick-day or emergency plan and seek urgent help; these conditions cannot be corrected with home food choices alone. Inflammatory, blood and cancer conditions are a separate group Sarcoidosis is an inflammatory condition, not a stomach infection. Thalassaemia is an inherited blood disorder; more severe forms can involve the liver or spleen. If either condition is already part of your health history, tell the clinician about a change in appetite or abdominal symptoms rather than assuming it is an unrelated stomach bug. Cancer is one possible explanation for persistent symptoms, but these two symptoms do not make it the most likely one. Pancreatic cancer, stomach adenocarcinoma, ovarian cancer and leukaemia can enter a clinician’s assessment when the wider pattern warrants it. Wilms tumour is a kidney cancer mainly affecting children, not a routine adult diagnosis. A new abdominal lump, persistent swelling, early fullness, unexplained weight loss or ongoing symptoms needs assessment without jumping to a conclusion. Review medicines, including non-prescription products Chemotherapy, some antibiotics and opioid medicines such as codeine or morphine can affect appetite, cause nausea or contribute to constipation. Write down when a medicine began, whether the dose changed and how the symptoms relate to taking it. A pharmacist or prescriber can advise on alternatives, timing or ways to manage side effects. Do not abruptly stop a prescribed medicine because it appears on a possible-cause list. A drug allergy is different from an expected side effect: breathing difficulty, facial or throat swelling or collapse after a medicine requires emergency help. An acetaminophen, also called paracetamol, overdose can seriously damage the liver even when early symptoms are mild. Contact a poison service or emergency care immediately if an overdose may have occurred. Alcohol and other substances deserve a direct, nonjudgmental conversation Alcohol, amphetamines, cocaine and heroin can affect eating, digestion or overall health. A clinician needs an accurate account of what was used, how much and when in order to choose safe care. This information is for treatment, and you can ask how it will be handled confidentially. If alcohol use has become dependent, stopping suddenly without a treatment plan can cause dangerous withdrawal. Ask for medical support rather than attempting an unsupported abrupt stop. Suspected poisoning or swallowing a caustic chemical, which can cause internal chemical burns, requires immediate poison-service or emergency advice. Do not make yourself vomit or try to neutralize the substance with another chemical. Pregnancy, periods and emotional health can change appetite Early pregnancy can bring nausea and altered appetite, and premenstrual symptoms can include cramps and changes in eating. Tell the clinician if pregnancy is possible, even if you have not yet had a positive test. Significant pain should not automatically be attributed to a normal pregnancy or the approaching period; an ectopic pregnancy must be considered when the symptoms fit. Stress, anxiety, grief and depression can also affect appetite and abdominal comfort. That does not make physical symptoms imaginary or mean medical causes should be ignored. Persistent low mood or difficulty eating deserves support alongside any physical assessment. If you might act on thoughts of harming yourself, contact emergency or crisis support now and ask a trusted person to stay with you if possible. Seek emergency care for severe symptoms or sudden deterioration Get urgent emergency help for sudden severe pain, a very tender or rigid abdomen, collapse, vomiting blood, black tar-like stool or heavy bleeding with weakness. Severe chest or back pain extending into the abdomen can occasionally signal an aortic dissection, a tear in the wall of the body’s main artery. Do not drive yourself if you feel faint or seriously unwell. Pregnancy possibility with one-sided pain, shoulder-tip pain or faintness needs emergency assessment for ectopic pregnancy. Sudden testicular pain or swelling, sometimes with abdominal pain or vomiting, may be testicular torsion and needs immediate treatment. Also seek emergency help for suspected poisoning, serious allergic reaction, abnormal breathing or confusion. You do not need to wait two days or reach a particular pain score. Arrange review when symptoms persist, recur or affect nutrition Contact a clinician promptly if pain or appetite loss is worsening, keeps returning or stops you eating and drinking adequately. Repeated vomiting, signs of dehydration, fever, jaundice, prolonged diarrhoea, persistent bloating or unexplained weight loss all matter. Jaundice with fever or significant pain needs urgent assessment. Babies, children, older adults and people with pregnancy, diabetes, immune suppression or established organ disease may need earlier help. Do not wait for a large amount of weight loss before seeking advice. If you are uncertain whether home care is appropriate, describe the symptoms to a local medical advice service and ask what level of assessment is needed. What a clinician may ask and check Be ready to describe when pain began, where it is, what it feels like and whether food, movement, bowel movements or urination change it. Mention vomiting, stool changes, fever, bleeding, weight change, medicines, alcohol or other substances, possible pregnancy, recent travel and anyone else who is ill. A short record of food and fluid intake can help. The clinician may examine the abdomen and check hydration and vital signs. Blood, urine or stool tests, a pregnancy test or imaging such as ultrasound may be selected according to the findings. Not everyone needs every test.
