That does not mean these activities inevitably injure the urethra. Pressure, rubbing, dryness, infection risk and product irritation are different possibilities. Describe a repeated association without assuming which mechanism is responsible. Previous bladder or kidney infection and possible STI exposure affect what needs checking. Sex without barrier protection can increase exposure to some infections, but a pain syndrome is not evidence of an STI, poor hygiene or wrongdoing. Sexual history should be taken respectfully and used to guide appropriate tests. How clinicians work through the diagnosis Assessment starts with the timing and location of pain, urinary and sexual symptoms, previous test results, medicines and relevant medical history. An examination may look for local skin changes, tenderness, pelvic floor problems or other findings. Ask what is being examined and discuss privacy, consent and chaperone preferences. A urine sample may be checked and sent for culture. Separate tests, such as nucleic-acid testing for particular STIs, may be needed depending on symptoms and exposure; a routine urine culture does not test for every infection. The timing of sampling and any antibiotics already taken can also affect interpretation. Blood tests or ultrasound may be useful when the clinician is investigating another condition, but there is no standard procedure called taking a sample of blood from the pelvis for this syndrome. If obstruction, unexplained bleeding or persistent symptoms raise concern, a specialist may consider cystoscopy, using a small camera to examine the urethra and bladder. There is no single test that proves primary urethral pain syndrome. Investigations are selected to answer specific questions and exclude relevant causes. Ask what has been ruled out, what remains uncertain and what would justify further testing rather than repeating the same treatment indefinitely. Practical changes can be individual and reversible Stop a product that repeatedly provokes irritation and use gentle external washing. Avoid douching and stronger cleansers intended to sterilise the area. If a menstrual product or contraceptive product appears to be involved, discuss a comfortable alternative without leaving contraception needs unaddressed. A short diary of pain, urination, drinks, activities and treatment may reveal patterns. Try one reasonable change at a time, such as reducing a drink that consistently worsens urgency or taking breaks from prolonged saddle pressure. There is no need for a broad restrictive diet or permanent ban on exercise without a clear reason. Drink a normal amount appropriate to your health rather than forcing excessive water to flush out an unconfirmed infection. Follow any fluid restrictions given for another condition. If pelvic floor overactivity contributes, a trained physiotherapist may focus on relaxation and coordination; repeatedly tightening the muscles is not automatically the right exercise. Care may also address sleep, stress and the effect of pain on daily life. Psychological support can help with coping and function while medical care continues. It does not mean the symptoms are invented or that distress was their original cause. What medicines can and cannot do Antibiotics treat particular bacterial infections. A clinician may sometimes start treatment while results are pending when infection is likely, but repeated courses are not a default response to persistent pain without supporting findings. CDC guidance for persistent urethritis specifically cautions against retreatment based on symptoms alone without evidence of inflammation. Further assessment is more useful than assuming a longer course must work. Phenazopyridine is a urinary pain-relief medicine, while lidocaine is a local anaesthetic used in selected clinical settings. Neither establishes or cures the underlying cause. The US phenazopyridine label limits use alongside an antibiotic for a UTI to two days and lists renal insufficiency as a contraindication. Ask a pharmacist or clinician before using it, particularly during pregnancy or with kidney disease; it can change urine colour and interfere with some tests. Antispasmodic or antimuscarinic medicines such as hyoscyamine or oxybutynin are sometimes discussed when bladder-spasm or overactive-bladder symptoms overlap. They are not proven universal treatments for primary urethral pain. Dry mouth, constipation and difficulty passing urine are relevant adverse effects, and obstruction or other health conditions may make them unsuitable. Medicines also used as antidepressants, such as amitriptyline or nortriptyline, may be considered for selected persistent pain problems. The intended effect can be pain modulation rather than treatment of depression. Evidence and suitability depend on the diagnosis; sedation, interactions and other adverse effects need review. Do not borrow someone else’s medicine or start a combination from a list. Alpha blockers such as doxazosin relax smooth muscle in the lower urinary tract in conditions for which they are selected. Their urinary effect should not be explained simply as increasing blood flow. Doxazosin and prazosin are not interchangeable routine cures for unexplained urethral pain; low blood pressure and dizziness can be important risks. The European Association of Urology does not identify one specific treatment that can be recommended for all primary urethral pain syndrome. Medication examples are therefore topics for a diagnosis-specific discussion, not a step-by-step regimen. Agree on the intended benefit, trial duration, side effects and follow-up before starting treatment. When a procedure might be appropriate If tests show a true urethral stricture (a narrowed area often involving scar tissue) a urologist may discuss dilation or surgery according to its location, severity and previous treatment. The procedure treats the confirmed structural problem, not every unexplained burning sensation. Dilation or surgery is not a routine next step simply because a urine culture was negative or the first medicine did not help. Ask what finding the procedure is intended to correct, its risks and alternatives, and whether recurrence is possible. Do not attempt self-dilation without a specific specialist plan and training. Reducing recurrence and arranging follow-up Barrier protection and appropriate STI testing and treatment reduce some infection risks. If an STI is diagnosed, follow advice about treatment, partners and when to resume sex. These measures do not prevent every cause of urinary pain, and a noninfectious pain syndrome is not itself something to transmit to a partner. Gentle front-to-back wiping after using the toilet and comfortable clothing are reasonable habits. Cotton underwear or looser trousers may feel better if heat or friction is a trigger. Urinating after sex is commonly suggested in UTI advice, but it cannot be promised to prevent urethral pain syndrome. None of these habits makes persistent pain the person’s fault. Keep a follow-up plan even if the first tests are reassuring. Useful goals include less pain, easier urination, better sleep and returning to activities or comfortable intimacy. Treatment may reduce symptoms without guaranteeing that they never return. New bleeding, discharge, fever, retention or a change in pain should trigger reassessment. A negative first urine test is not a complete diagnosis. Bacteriuria, urethritis and primary urethral pain syndrome mean different things. Treatment should follow the findings, with a review of benefit and side effects. Blood, discharge, fever, retention or acute testicular pain should not be dismissed as routine chronic pain. Is bacteriuria another name for this syndrome? No. Bacteriuria means bacteria in urine. Primary urethral pain syndrome describes ongoing or recurring pain without a proven infection or another obvious local explanation after assessment. Does a normal urine culture exclude an STI? No. Some infections require different tests. The clinician chooses testing according to symptoms and exposure. Will another antibiotic course always help? No. Persistent symptoms need reassessment. Antibiotics are useful for appropriate bacterial diagnoses, but symptoms alone do not justify repeated treatment for persistent urethritis. Can I treat it with phenazopyridine for weeks? Do not use it as a long-term self-treatment plan. It relieves discomfort rather than the cause, has kidney-related restrictions and has a two-day limit in US labelling when used with an antibiotic for a UTI. Why might an antidepressant be discussed for pain? Some of these medicines are used to modify pain signalling. That does not establish that the pain is psychological, and suitability and adverse effects still need review. Does cycling or sex always cause injury? No. Pressure, friction, product irritation or infection may contribute in some situations. Look for your own pattern and seek assessment rather than assuming an activity is inherently harmful. Will dilation cure unexplained urethral pain? Not necessarily. Dilation is considered for a confirmed narrowing, not as a routine cure for pain with normal tests. Can clothing changes or urinating after sex prevent every recurrence? No. Some habits may improve comfort or address particular infection risks, but they cannot guarantee prevention of a persistent pain syndrome.

title: Bladder stones: symptoms, causes, diagnosis and treatment
description: How bladder stones form, why incomplete emptying matters, how they differ from kidney stones and what assessment, treatment and recurrence prevention involve.
body: Bladder stones can cause pain, urinary symptoms or blood in the urine, but the underlying reason for poor emptying is often just as important as the stone itself. Treatment should address both the deposit and the conditions that allowed it to grow. What a bladder stone is Bladder stones are hard deposits that form when substances in urine crystallize and collect together. They may be small or large, and a person may have one stone or several. A stone can irritate the bladder or interfere with urine flow, although some cause few noticeable symptoms. Urine normally contains water and dissolved waste products. When urine remains in the bladder or becomes concentrated, crystals have more opportunity to persist and grow. This does not mean that a single episode of dark urine proves a stone is present. Urine colour also changes with fluid intake, foods, medicines and illness. Brown, cloudy or blood-stained urine needs to be interpreted in context. A diagnosis rests on assessment and appropriate tests, not on matching the colour to a picture online. Why incomplete emptying matters A common issue behind adult bladder stones is urine being left behind after urination. An enlarged prostate can obstruct the outlet, while narrowing of the urethra can make it harder for urine to pass. A bladder that does not contract effectively may also fail to empty. Nerve problems affecting bladder control, injury and changes after urinary tract surgery can contribute. A bladder diverticulum is a pouch in the bladder wall where urine may collect; it is not simply another name for a generally weak bladder. Inflammation, infection or foreign material can also be relevant. Ask whether the team has identified why the stone formed. Removing it can relieve one problem, but a continuing emptying difficulty may allow another to develop. Tell the clinician about previous procedures, recurrent infections, catheter use and changes in your urinary stream, even if those details seem unrelated to the current pain. Who can develop stones, including children Bladder stones are more often encountered in adults with an underlying urinary problem, including older men with prostate enlargement. Age and sex are clues to possible causes, not rules that exclude everyone else. A younger adult or a woman with compatible symptoms still deserves assessment. Children can also develop bladder stones. In some regions, nutritional and hydration problems contribute to a distinct pattern of childhood stones; in other cases, urinary anatomy, infection or other health conditions need investigation. A child’s treatment should be planned by a team familiar with paediatric urinary problems. It is not useful to assume that people in one country develop stones at a particular age because they eat too much fat or sugar. The individual history, access to water and nutrition, bladder function and stone composition provide more meaningful information than a broad stereotype. Symptoms can overlap with other urinary conditions Possible symptoms include discomfort low in the abdomen, pain or burning during urination, frequent trips to the toilet and blood in the urine. Some people notice an interrupted stream, difficulty emptying or leakage. Symptoms may come and go as the stone moves or irritates the bladder. Night-time urination, cloudy urine and urgency can occur for several reasons, including infection or an emptying problem. They do not establish that a stone is the cause. A person can also have a stone and an infection at the same time, so one diagnosis does not necessarily exclude the other. Record what has changed: pain, visible blood, fever, the strength of the stream and whether you feel empty afterwards. Note whether symptoms are continuous or intermittent. This helps the clinician decide what to test rather than relying only on a general description of bladder discomfort. Bladder stones and kidney stones are related but different A kidney stone begins higher in the urinary tract. It may move through a ureter into the bladder. Some small stones then leave in the urine; others can remain and grow, particularly if the bladder is not emptying normally. A stone that forms inside the bladder because of urinary stasis is a different situation from a small stone that has just travelled down from the kidney. This distinction affects whether observation is reasonable and what needs to be investigated. Size alone is not the only consideration. Mention any history of kidney stones, flank pain or previous stone analysis. The team may decide that the upper urinary tract also needs assessment. Advice given for a previous kidney stone should not automatically be reused for a new bladder stone, especially if your ability to pass urine has changed. How clinicians investigate the problem Assessment starts with your symptoms, medical history and an examination. Depending on the circumstances, the clinician may assess the prostate or look for other causes of obstruction. A urine sample can help identify infection, blood and other abnormalities; further tests are chosen according to the findings. Ultrasound is generally the first imaging test for suspected bladder stones. If symptoms persist and ultrasound does not explain them, CT or cystoscopy may be appropriate. Cystoscopy lets a clinician inspect the bladder with a camera. A plain X-ray does not show every stone, and an older intravenous pyelogram is not a routine requirement for everyone. Evaluation may also include urine flow and the amount left after urinating, as well as stone analysis when material is available. Bring a list of medicines and previous urinary procedures. The purpose is both to confirm the stone and to understand the conditions that allowed it to form. When observation or medication may be considered Do not assume that drinking more water will wash out every bladder stone. Selected small stones that have migrated from the upper urinary tract may be observed when they are not causing symptoms and there is no important emptying problem. Stones formed within an abnormal bladder usually need active treatment. The clinician weighs symptoms, obstruction, infection, stone size and the likelihood of passage. Observation should include a clear follow-up plan and instructions about what would require urgent help. It is not the same as ignoring persistent pain or blood in the urine. Certain uric-acid stones may be suitable for medically supervised treatment that changes urine chemistry. That option depends on the stone type and requires monitoring. Do not start alkalinizing products or use a home urine-pH target without a diagnosis and a treatment plan. How stones are broken up or removed A common procedure is cystolitholapaxy: a telescope is passed through the urethra and instruments or laser energy are used to break the stone into pieces that can be removed. The choice of technique and anaesthesia depends on the stone, your health and the service providing care. Some stones or anatomical situations require a different approach. Removal through a small opening above the pubic area or an open operation may be considered, particularly when the stone is very large or access through the urethra is unsuitable. Adult and child procedures should not be treated as identical. Ask whether an underlying outlet problem will be treated at the same time or separately, whether you may need a catheter afterwards and what recovery instructions apply. The aim is not only to make the scan look clear, but to leave you with a practical plan for bladder function and follow-up. Reducing the chance of another stone Prevention depends on why the stone formed. Adequate fluid intake may help avoid very concentrated urine, but an eight-glass rule cannot guarantee prevention. Some people have medical reasons to limit fluids, and extra water does not correct an obstructed outlet or a bladder that cannot empty. Follow the agreed plan for prostate disease, urethral narrowing, infection, bladder dysfunction or catheter care. Do not change catheter routines or try to flush the bladder yourself unless your clinical team has taught you a specific method. Stone analysis may help determine whether further dietary or metabolic advice is useful. At follow-up, ask what was found, whether fragments remain and how recurrence will be checked. Keep a record of the procedure and stone type if known. Repeated symptoms deserve review even when the previous removal initially worked well. Symptoms that should not wait Sudden inability to pass urine, especially with a painful or full lower abdomen, is an emergency. Do not keep forcing fluids and wait for a stone to move. Urinary retention needs prompt assessment and treatment to relieve the problem safely. Fever or chills with urinary symptoms, severe pain or feeling markedly unwell also needs urgent medical attention. Visible blood in the urine should be assessed even if it stops or you believe a previously diagnosed stone explains it. Other conditions can produce similar symptoms. If you are caring for a child, describe changes in urination, pain, fever and behaviour promptly rather than applying an adult stone-passage plan. After treatment, use the discharge instructions and contact details provided. A clear response plan is more helpful than assuming every recurrence can be managed by hydration alone. Incomplete emptying is an important contributor. Adults and children need age-appropriate assessment. Ultrasound, CT and cystoscopy have different roles. Most symptomatic bladder stones need more than extra water. Treat the cause as well as the stone. Does dark urine prove I have a bladder stone? No. Urine colour has several causes; symptoms and appropriate tests are needed. Can an enlarged prostate contribute? Yes. Obstruction can leave urine in the bladder and encourage stone formation. Can children get bladder stones? Yes. They need assessment of the cause and a treatment plan appropriate for children. Are bladder stones always kidney stones that moved down? No. Some migrate from the kidney, while others form within the bladder. Will a plain X-ray show every stone? No. Ultrasound is commonly used first, with other tests selected when necessary. Can I just drink eight glasses of water to cure it? No. Hydration does not reliably remove a stone or correct incomplete emptying. Can any stones be watched rather than removed? Selected small, asymptomatic migratory stones may be observed under a clinical plan when emptying is normal. What does cystolitholapaxy mean? It is a procedure that breaks up bladder stones so the fragments can be removed. Can a stone return after treatment? Yes, particularly when the underlying cause remains. Follow-up and prevention should address that cause. What if I suddenly cannot pass urine? Seek emergency care. Do not wait for fluids to push the stone through.

title: Winter skin care: protect the barrier before adding more products
description: Cold air and indoor heating can leave skin dry. Gentle cleansing, moisturizer and sun protection are practical starting points.
body: Cold outdoor air and dry indoor heat can leave skin tight, flaky or irritated. The answer does not have to be a monthly facial or a complicated collection of serums. A routine that reduces irritation and helps retain moisture is often a more useful place to start. Change the routine when the skin changes Products that felt comfortable in warmer weather may sting or feel insufficient when the air becomes drier. Notice whether the problem is tightness, flaking, itch, redness or cracking rather than treating every change as a need for exfoliation. Wash gently with a fragrance-free cleanser and use warm rather than very hot water. Avoid prolonged hot showers and vigorous rubbing. After washing, pat the skin and apply moisturizer while it is still slightly damp. Choose moisture that suits your skin Creams or ointments may protect very dry areas better than a light lotion. The best option is one you tolerate and can use consistently. A richer product for the hands does not have to be the same product used on an acne-prone face. Ingredients such as glycerin, ceramides or hyaluronic acid may help support hydration. Hyaluronic acid is a moisturizing ingredient, not an exfoliating acid. A high concentration or a long ingredient list is not automatically better. A moisturizer can temporarily soften the appearance of dryness-related lines, but it does not permanently erase wrinkles or reverse all sun damage. If a product burns or causes a persistent rash, stop using it and seek advice rather than assuming the sensation proves it is working. Be cautious with peels and scrubs Dry flakes are not an invitation to scrub harder. Strong exfoliants and frequent acid treatments can worsen irritation, particularly when the skin is already inflamed or cracked. Let comfortable basic care take priority. A professional peel may have a role for a particular skin concern, but winter does not automatically make it suitable or safe. Discuss your skin condition, current medicines and any pregnancy or breastfeeding with a qualified clinician before choosing an active treatment. Do not combine several new exfoliating products at once. A clinician can help adjust acne or other prescribed treatments if winter dryness makes them difficult to tolerate, rather than having you abandon needed treatment or add an aggressive facial. Glycolic acid peels and salicylic acid treatments are examples sometimes offered for dullness, pigment concerns or acne. Their suitability depends on concentration, skin condition and the treatment plan; a cold season does not remove irritation or sun-sensitivity risks. The idea that everyone’s skin-cell turnover slows in winter is too simple to guide treatment. A hydrating mask may be comfortable if well tolerated, but neither masks nor monthly facials are necessary to restore circulation or rebuild the skin. Keep protection in the routine Sun exposure still matters in winter. Use shade, protective clothing and broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher on exposed skin. Cold weather or a cloudy sky does not remove the need for sun protection. Protect hands from cold air and wet work, and reapply moisturizer after washing. A simple lip balm or petrolatum can help dry lips. Soft fabrics may be more comfortable against irritated skin. A humidifier may help in a dry room if it is maintained and cleaned according to its instructions. Drinking normally supports general health, but drinking excessive water is not a substitute for protecting the skin’s outer barrier. Treat product claims as optional, not essential Antioxidant and growth-factor products are marketed with promises about repair, firmness and cell renewal. Their effects depend on the formulation and evidence for the specific product. They are not essential purchases for ordinary winter dryness. If you enjoy a facial, tell the practitioner about sensitive areas and everything you already apply. Avoid a treatment that leaves the skin raw or persistently painful. A relaxing experience and a proven medical treatment are different claims. See a clinician if dryness persists despite gentle care, becomes painful or bleeds, or comes with a spreading or recurrent rash. Eczema, contact allergy and other conditions can need targeted treatment rather than another cosmetic product. Growth factors are signalling molecules involved in biological processes such as repair. That role does not prove that a cosmetic serum delivers clinically meaningful collagen production, firmness or rejuvenation. Similarly, antioxidant activity in a laboratory is not a promise to reverse accumulated pollution or sun damage. Start with gentle cleansing and regular moisturizer. Do not scrub or peel already irritated skin to remove flakes. Keep winter sun protection and seek help for persistent or painful changes. Do I need a professional facial every month in winter? No. Many people manage dryness with a simple home routine. Professional treatment should address a specific need and suit the skin. Does hyaluronic acid exfoliate the skin? No. It is used for hydration. The word acid does not mean every ingredient acts like a peeling treatment.

title: Does testicle size tell you about hormones or fertility?
description: Understand normal variation, puberty, changes in size, hormone and fertility assessment, and symptoms that need urgent help.
body: Testicle size varies naturally, and one may be slightly larger or hang lower. Size can contribute to a medical assessment, but it cannot by itself tell you whether you are fertile, have enough testosterone or will be a caring parent. Normal size varies, and the scrotum is not the testicle The testicles are oval organs that make sperm and testosterone. They usually sit inside the scrotum and are connected to the body by the spermatic cords. The size of the surrounding skin pouch is not the same thing as the size or health of the testicular tissue inside it. An adult testicle is often roughly four centimetres long, with substantial natural variation. A commonly quoted example of dimensions is about four by three by two centimetres, but this is not a pass-or-fail standard. Measurements also depend on the method used; judging by sight or comparing yourself with someone else is not a fertility test. It is common for one testicle to be a little larger or hang lower than the other. A longstanding difference without symptoms is different from a new change. If you are concerned about size, a clinician can examine you respectfully and explain whether any further assessment is useful. Size alone cannot measure fertility or masculinity Testicular volume can be one clue during a clinical assessment because much of the tissue is involved in sperm production. Some conditions associated with smaller testicles can reduce sperm production or hormone output. However, the relationship is not simple enough to diagnose a person from appearance. For fertility concerns, the relevant assessment may include reproductive and medical history, an examination and semen analysis. Semen testing looks at features such as sperm concentration, movement and shape. Results are interpreted together and may need repeating; neither a single measurement nor a normal-looking scrotum guarantees conception. Larger testicles do not automatically mean more testosterone, greater sexual ability or better health. Animal comparisons cannot be used to rank an individual person’s fertility. The useful question is whether there are symptoms or a reproductive concern that merits assessment, not whether you fit an image of masculinity. Low testosterone needs symptoms and proper testing Hypogonadism means the body is not producing enough sex hormones or supporting normal reproductive function because of a problem in the testicles or the signals controlling them. Possible signs include reduced sexual desire, fewer spontaneous erections, loss of muscle or body hair, breast-tissue growth and, in some cases, smaller testicles. These symptoms are not specific. Tiredness or a change in libido can have many causes, and body-hair patterns naturally differ. The Endocrine Society recommends diagnosing testosterone deficiency only when relevant symptoms or signs occur with consistently low blood testosterone, confirmed with repeat morning fasting testing. Further hormone tests can help distinguish a problem in the testicles from one involving the pituitary or hypothalamus. The clinician may also consider medicines, illness and other factors. Do not diagnose yourself from an online size chart or start testosterone simply because a single test result is low. Klinefelter syndrome is one possible cause, not a visual diagnosis Klinefelter syndrome usually involves an additional X chromosome, commonly an XXY pattern. In some people the pattern is present in only some cells. It can affect testicular development, testosterone production and sperm production, but the effects vary widely. Smaller, firm testicles, less facial or body hair, breast-tissue development or fertility difficulties may prompt investigation. Some children have developmental or learning needs, while many people are not diagnosed until adulthood. No one should be labelled from their body shape, appearance or a single physical feature. Diagnosis uses chromosome testing, with hormone assessment and other evaluation as appropriate. Care may involve an endocrinologist, a fertility specialist and support for individual developmental or health needs. Testosterone can help selected hormone-related symptoms, but it does not by itself restore sperm production or reverse infertility. Growth happens through puberty on an individual timetable Testicles are much smaller in childhood than in adulthood. Their enlargement is usually an early sign that puberty has begun, followed by other changes such as growth of the penis and pubic hair. The sequence and pace vary, so a rigid rule that every child’s testicles start growing at eight is not reliable. The Pediatric Endocrine Society describes the usual onset of puberty in boys as between nine and fourteen years. If testicular enlargement has not begun by fourteen, a clinician should assess development. Earlier concerns, including a testicle that cannot be felt in the scrotum or other unusual changes, also deserve advice. A child’s stage of development is best assessed with privacy, consent and age-appropriate explanation. Comparing siblings or classmates is not a substitute. Some young people simply develop later, while others need investigation of hormone signals, testicular function or another health condition. Cold can change position without shrinking the organ In a cold environment or cold water, muscles around the scrotum tighten and the cremaster muscle can pull the testicles closer to the body. The scrotum may look smaller or more drawn up even though the testicular tissue has not suddenly lost volume. This response helps regulate temperature. Testicles normally sit outside the body where the temperature is somewhat lower, which supports sperm production. Warmth can allow the scrotum to relax and hang lower. These short-term changes are different from persistent testicular shrinkage. Do not use a cold-versus-warm comparison to dismiss pain, a lump or a testicle that seems newly out of place. A persistent change warrants an examination. A sudden painful change needs urgent assessment, even if it happened after swimming, exercise or another activity that seems to offer an explanation. Persistent shrinkage or enlargement needs an explanation A lasting reduction in testicular tissue is called atrophy. Hormone levels and testicular function can change with age, but noticeable shrinkage should not automatically be declared harmless ageing. Tell a clinician whether it affects one or both sides and whether there is pain, a lump, a change in sexual function or a fertility concern. Injury, impaired blood supply, hormonal problems and some infections can affect the testicles. Orchitis means inflammation of a testicle; mumps and some bacterial infections, including sexually transmitted infections, are possible causes. Some cases can damage tissue, but size alone cannot identify which infection, if any, is present. Likewise, an enlarging scrotum may reflect fluid, enlarged veins, inflammation or another problem rather than growth of the testicle itself. A new heavy feeling, change in firmness or persistent swelling should be checked. Many causes are benign, but a painless lump can also be a sign of testicular cancer. Sudden pain is an emergency; other new changes still need care Sudden severe testicular pain can be caused by torsion, in which the spermatic cord twists and interrupts blood flow. This is an emergency. Seek emergency care immediately rather than waiting to see whether the testicle becomes more swollen or comparing its size with the other side. Pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or testicular pain that persists at rest, also needs urgent assessment. Do not assume an infection explains it without being examined. A new lump or gradual change without acute pain still needs a prompt appointment, even when you otherwise feel well. A clinician may examine the scrotum and arrange ultrasound or other tests. If cancer is diagnosed, treatment commonly involves removing the affected testicle, sometimes with additional treatment. It is often treatable, but outcomes depend on the condition and stage. Ask about fertility and sperm storage before treatment when appropriate; the other testicle is not protected by a guarantee based only on early detection. Know what is usual for you without repeated anxious checking Public guidance on routine self-examination differs. The NHS advises regular checks, around monthly, while the USPSTF recommends against routine screening of asymptomatic adolescents and adults. This difference concerns screening people without symptoms; it does not mean a new lump or pain should be ignored. If you choose to check, a warm shower can make the scrotum more relaxed. Gently feel one testicle at a time between the thumb and fingers without squeezing. The soft tube behind the testicle is the epididymis and is part of normal anatomy. Ask a clinician to explain anything you cannot confidently distinguish. Avoid measuring or repeatedly pressing the area throughout the day. Seek assessment for a new lump, persistent swelling, unusual firmness, heaviness or pain. If you have a history such as an undescended testicle or previous cancer, ask your clinician what follow-up is appropriate for your individual risk. Treatment should match health and reproductive goals Testosterone therapy can help appropriately diagnosed hormone deficiency, including selected developmental conditions under specialist care. However, taking testosterone from outside the body can suppress sperm production. Tell the prescriber if you want children now or in the future before starting any hormone treatment. Fertility support depends on the cause and may involve a reproductive urologist or fertility team. Do not buy hormone boosters or anabolic steroids to enlarge the testicles or improve conception chances. A treatment that changes a blood hormone level is not automatically a fertility treatment. A small 2013 study reported an association between testicular volume and fathers’ involvement in toddler care. An association cannot establish cause or predict how loving or capable a particular parent will be. Caring behaviour, relationships and health deserve attention on their own terms; testicle size is not a parenting score. A longstanding small difference between sides can be normal. Cold changes scrotal tension and position, not instant organ size. Persistent shrinkage, enlargement or a lump needs assessment. Testosterone treatment can reduce sperm production. Neither masculinity nor parenting ability can be judged from size. Is there one normal adult testicle size? No. Approximate dimensions describe averages, not a personal pass-or-fail test. Examination and clinical context matter more than a ruler. Is it normal for one testicle to hang lower? Yes, a longstanding slight difference is common. A new change in size, position, firmness or discomfort should be checked. Do small testicles always mean infertility? No. Fertility assessment uses history, examination and semen testing when appropriate. Size alone cannot diagnose infertility. Can a single low testosterone result establish a diagnosis? No. Relevant symptoms and consistently low values are needed, usually with repeat morning fasting testing and an assessment of the cause. Can Klinefelter syndrome be diagnosed by appearance? No. Features may prompt assessment, but chromosome testing confirms the diagnosis and effects vary between people. When should delayed puberty be assessed? If testicular enlargement has not begun by fourteen, arrange a clinical assessment. Other concerns can be discussed earlier. Does cold water permanently shrink the testicles? No. It can temporarily tighten the scrotum and pull the testicles closer to the body. Persistent changes are a different issue. Must everyone perform a monthly self-examination? Guidelines differ on routine screening. Learn what is usual for you, discuss individual risk and seek assessment for new symptoms rather than ignoring them. Will testosterone therapy improve sperm production? It can do the opposite: external testosterone can suppress sperm production. Discuss current and future fertility goals before treatment. What pain should make me go to emergency care? Sudden severe testicular pain, pain with nausea or vomiting, or pain persisting at rest needs urgent assessment. Torsion cannot safely wait.

title: White spots on scrotal skin: possible causes and safe next steps
description: An explanation of ingrown hairs, pimples, fungal rashes, cysts, folliculitis, Fordyce spots, genital warts and herpes, with care guided by the actual cause.
body: A pale bump on the scrotum can be worrying, but colour alone cannot tell you what it is. Some bumps are normal oil glands or benign cysts; others involve irritated hair follicles or an infection. A spot does not prove poor hygiene or a sexually transmitted infection. Start by distinguishing a change on the scrotal skin (the pouch around the testicles) from a lump felt inside a testicle, because those need different assessments. Look at the pattern, not only the colour Notice whether the change is a single bump, several similar bumps, a patch of lighter skin, a scaly rash or fluid-filled blisters. Itch, pain, discharge, recent shaving and how quickly the change appeared can help a clinician narrow the possibilities. These clues are useful descriptions, not a reliable home diagnosis. An established cluster of small painless glands can look very different from a new painful cluster of blisters. Likewise, a lump attached to the skin is different from one deeper in the scrotum. If you cannot tell where it is, arrange an examination rather than repeatedly squeezing it. New genital lesions are a reasonable reason to seek care. You do not need to wait until they become painful or reach a certain number. A primary care clinician, dermatologist or sexual health clinic can help, depending on the symptoms and possible exposures. 1. Ingrown hairs After shaving or another form of hair removal, a hair may curve back into the skin rather than grow outward. The resulting bump can be itchy or tender and may develop a pale or pus-filled tip. An ingrown hair can become infected, but inflammation does not always mean that bacteria are involved. Pause hair removal while the area settles. Keep it gently clean and avoid scratching, squeezing or digging for the hair. Trying to release it with a household needle can injure the skin and introduce infection. Advice about exfoliating products, antiseptics or mild steroid creams is not automatically suitable for delicate scrotal skin. Ask a pharmacist or clinician before applying one there, especially if the area is broken, painful or the diagnosis is uncertain. Harsh scrubbing can make irritation worse. A clinician may sometimes release a trapped hair with sterile equipment or prescribe treatment for inflammation or infection. Seek help sooner for increasing pain, warmth, swelling, fever or feeling unwell. There is no need to wait a full week when those symptoms are present. 2. A pimple or blocked pore Oil and dead skin can collect in a pore and create an acne-like bump. A white tip may contain trapped material or pus. Some small bumps settle on their own, but an inflamed one can be painful; painless appearance is not a defining rule. Do not pop it. Squeezing can drive inflammation deeper, damage the surface and leave a scar. Reducing friction and avoiding close shaving over it may help while you arrange advice if it persists or changes. Benzoyl peroxide and salicylic acid are used for acne on suitable skin, but facial acne products should not be applied to the genitals on the assumption that the same treatment fits. They can irritate or burn sensitive tissue. A clinician can determine whether the bump is actually acne, a follicle problem or something else. 3. A fungal groin rash Tinea cruris, often called jock itch, is a fungal infection that usually begins in the groin fold and may spread along the inner thigh. It can be itchy and scaly, with a raised or more active border. Redness may look darker or less obvious on darker skin, and small bumps can occur at the edge. Typical tinea cruris tends to spare the scrotum and penis. Therefore, white scrotal spots alone are not a typical way to identify it. A rash directly involving scrotal skin may have another cause, including a different infection or dermatitis, and should be assessed accordingly. Warmth, moisture, friction and tight clothing can favour fungal growth. Wash gently after sweating, dry the folds carefully and change damp underwear. Breathable clothing may help. The condition is not a verdict on someone’s cleanliness or body size. For a confirmed fungal rash, a clinician or pharmacist may recommend an antifungal such as clotrimazole or terbinafine and explain where and how long to apply it. Do not treat a suspected fungal infection with hydrocortisone alone: a steroid can mask or worsen it. Powders and sprays can also irritate, so choose products suited to the diagnosed condition. Return for review if treatment is not working as expected, the rash spreads or you are unsure of the diagnosis. Simply washing more vigorously is not a reliable cure. 4. A skin cyst A cyst is a sac beneath the surface that can contain keratin, a protein found in skin, hair and nails. An epidermoid cyst can occur on the scrotum and may look like a firm, rounded, skin-coloured, yellowish or pale bump. There may be a small central opening. Pilar, or trichilemmal, cysts are a different type and occur most often on the scalp. Calling every scrotal cyst a pilar cyst is inaccurate. A clinician can assess the type and make sure the lump is in the skin rather than within a testicle. A small uncomplicated cyst may need no treatment. Redness, tenderness or enlargement can occur if it becomes inflamed, ruptures internally or is infected. Do not try to drain it yourself or assume that everything expressed from a cyst is pus. When removal is appropriate, the procedure depends on its size, location and condition. Options can include surgical removal, sometimes through a small incision or punch opening. Removing the lining helps reduce recurrence; simple drainage may not do that. No procedure is guaranteed to avoid scarring, bleeding or damage to nearby skin. An infected or very inflamed cyst may need a different initial plan, such as drainage or medication. Discuss the expected benefit and aftercare rather than choosing a procedure from the appearance alone. 5. Folliculitis Folliculitis means inflammation around a hair follicle. It can produce small red, pale or pus-tipped bumps, with itching, burning or tenderness. Causes include irritation from shaving or regrowing hair as well as bacterial, yeast or other infections. Because the causes differ, one antibacterial or antifungal cream does not treat every case. A clinician may examine the pattern or take a swab when infection is suspected. Mild irritation may improve when the trigger is removed, while a painful boil or spreading infection needs more attention. Treatment can include changes to hair removal, suitable skin care and, when indicated, a prescribed topical or oral medicine. Antibiotics such as cephalexin or doxycycline are options for selected bacterial infections, not default treatment for every white bump. Taking leftover antibiotics or trying several creams can obscure the diagnosis. A larger collection of pus may need professional drainage. Repeated episodes warrant a review of the cause and prevention plan. Laser hair reduction is sometimes considered for recurrent hair-related problems, but it is not a routine first step for unexplained scrotal spots and should be discussed with a qualified practitioner. Seek advice for worsening pain, warmth, swelling, discharge or persistent irritation. Fever or rapidly spreading inflammation should be assessed promptly rather than waiting to see whether another over-the-counter product works. 6. Visible oil glands and Fordyce spots Small pale or yellowish oil-gland bumps in the genital area can be a normal finding. Fordyce spots are visible sebaceous glands rather than an infection. They often become easier to notice from puberty onward, and stretching the skin may make them stand out. Once correctly identified, they are harmless, are not an STI and do not require treatment. They are not something you caught from a partner or a sign that washing has failed. They may remain visible rather than disappearing after a few days. Other lesions can look similar, so have a new or uncertain change assessed before assuming it is a Fordyce spot. Picking or squeezing a normal gland can cause the inflammation you were trying to prevent. If appearance remains a concern after diagnosis, a dermatologist can discuss cosmetic options. Laser treatment, electrosurgery and small surgical techniques such as micro-punch removal have been used in selected cases. Benefit must be weighed against scarring, pigment changes and recurrence; treatment is optional, not medically necessary for normal glands. 7. Genital warts caused by HPV Some types of human papillomavirus, or HPV, cause genital warts. Warts may be skin-coloured, pale, pink or darker, and can be flat, raised or clustered. They can occur on genital skin, including around the scrotum, but white colour is neither required nor diagnostic. HPV spreads through intimate skin contact. Condoms reduce some risk but do not cover every area that can carry the virus. Pills, implants and other pregnancy-prevention methods do not protect against HPV or other STIs. Warts may resolve, persist or grow, and they can recur after treatment. Their persistence does not prove repeated exposure, multiple partners or recent infidelity. The types that usually cause genital warts differ from the types responsible for most HPV-related cancers. Treatment is chosen after diagnosis and may include a prescription cream or solution, freezing with liquid nitrogen, surgical removal or laser treatment. Some prescription products help the immune response; others act on wart tissue. Do not use ordinary hand or foot wart-removal acids on genital skin. Removing visible warts does not guarantee that the virus is gone or that transmission is impossible. A sexual health professional can discuss partner questions and whether HPV vaccination is appropriate. Vaccination helps prevent certain HPV infections but does not treat existing warts. 8. Genital herpes Herpes simplex virus can cause genital blisters or sores. They may begin as small bumps and then break open, with tenderness, burning, itching or fluid from the lesions. Some episodes are mild or atypical, so a photograph or a description of white bumps cannot confirm or exclude herpes. Seek assessment promptly for a first episode or new suspicious sores. A clinician can often take a swab from a fresh lesion, and early treatment can be helpful. Herpes may also be transmitted when visible sores are absent. Oral antiviral medicines used for genital herpes include acyclovir, valacyclovir and famciclovir. They can shorten or reduce symptoms and may be prescribed for episodes or as ongoing suppressive treatment. They do not remove the virus from the body. The choice and schedule depend on the individual situation. A clinician may suggest suitable pain relief, including a particular local anaesthetic preparation in some cases. Do not substitute a cold-sore product or a lidocaine skin patch for a prescribed genital-herpes plan. Formulations and intended sites of use matter. Avoid sexual contact involving the affected area during sores or warning symptoms such as tingling. Condoms and, when indicated, suppressive treatment can reduce transmission risk but do not eliminate it. Discuss these choices without blame; an outbreak cannot reliably establish when the infection was acquired. Everyday care and prevention depend on the cause Gentle washing, careful drying and changing sweaty clothing can reduce irritation. Avoid fragranced genital products and aggressive scrubbing. If shaving triggers bumps, let the skin recover and reconsider close shaving; clean equipment and less friction may help reduce recurrence. Do not pick, squeeze or cut a lesion. Keep personal razors to yourself and avoid sharing treatment creams. An antiseptic, exfoliant, steroid, antifungal and antibiotic are not interchangeable, and using all of them together is more likely to confuse the picture than solve it. For infections passed through sexual contact, discuss appropriate testing, condoms, vaccination and partner advice with a sexual health service. Pregnancy prevention is a separate issue. Avoid contact with unexplained sores while arranging assessment. Normal glands and some benign cysts cannot be prevented through better hygiene. A realistic aim is to reduce avoidable irritation and recognize changes that need advice, not to make genital skin completely uniform. When to seek help Arrange an appointment for a new or unexplained lesion, a bump that persists or changes, a scaly or cracked rash, ongoing itch, bleeding or white or clear discharge. New blisters or ulcers and a possible STI exposure deserve prompt assessment rather than a fixed one-to-two-week wait. There is no useful threshold of twenty bumps before seeking care. One concerning lesion can need assessment, while many stable normal glands may need no treatment. The pattern, symptoms and diagnosis matter more than the number. Seek urgent medical help for severe or rapidly worsening pain, spreading redness, significant swelling, fever or feeling very unwell. Sudden severe pain inside a testicle, especially with nausea, is an emergency because a twisted testicle needs rapid treatment. A lump felt within a testicle or a new change in its size or firmness should be examined even if the skin looks normal. Many causes are treatable, but do not assume a deeper lump is the same as a surface pimple. Tell the clinician exactly where you feel it and when it changed. A white spot is a description, not a diagnosis. Normal glands, cysts, irritation and infections need different care. Scrotal skin bumps are different from lumps inside a testicle. Avoid squeezing and trial-and-error treatment with strong creams. Contraception does not automatically protect against STIs. Seek help based on symptoms, not a fixed number of spots or waiting period. Do white scrotal spots always mean an STI? No. Normal glands, cysts and irritated follicles are among the possibilities. An examination is useful for a new or uncertain change. Are Fordyce spots caused by poor hygiene? No. They are visible oil glands and are not contagious. Once correctly identified, they generally need no treatment. Can I squeeze a pimple or cyst to remove it? Do not squeeze or cut it. This can cause inflammation, infection and scarring, and draining a cyst may leave its lining behind. Is jock itch a common explanation for white spots on the scrotum? Typical tinea cruris affects the groin folds and usually spares the scrotum. A scrotal rash may have another cause, so do not diagnose it by colour alone. Can I use hydrocortisone or acne cream? Ask before using these on genital skin. Steroid alone can worsen a fungal infection, and acne acids or benzoyl peroxide may irritate sensitive tissue. Are all scrotal cysts pilar cysts? No. Epidermoid cysts can occur on the scrotum; pilar cysts are a different type most often found on the scalp. Do condoms completely prevent HPV or herpes? No. They reduce some risk but do not cover all potentially affected skin. Other contraception does not protect against these infections. Does herpes treatment remove the virus permanently? No. Antiviral treatment can control episodes and may reduce transmission risk, but it does not eradicate the virus. Should I wait until I have twenty bumps or symptoms for two weeks? No. Those are not appropriate thresholds. New sores, worsening symptoms or uncertainty can justify earlier assessment. What if the lump feels inside the testicle rather than on the skin? Arrange a medical examination. Sudden severe testicular pain is an emergency, even if the skin looks normal.

title: Testicular injury: bruising, urgent symptoms and recovery
description: Understand the difference between a scrotal bruise and deeper injury, why torsion or rupture needs urgent care and when home comfort measures are appropriate.
body: A visible bruise cannot show whether a testicle is seriously injured. Sudden severe pain or pain that persists at rest needs urgent assessment, even when you know exactly how the impact happened. Severe or persistent pain should not wait A blow to the scrotum may cause a minor bruise, but it can also injure the testicle or interrupt its blood supply. Knowing that you were hit does not make severe pain safe to watch at home. Neither the bruise colour nor its apparent size reliably shows how deep the injury is. Seek emergency assessment for sudden severe testicular pain, pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or pain lasting more than an hour or continuing at rest. Do not wait a week for improvement. A serious condition can need treatment before a bruise has time to change colour. Major swelling, an open wound, ongoing bleeding, a displaced-looking testicle, blood in the urine or difficulty urinating also needs urgent attention. If a child reports pain, take it seriously and help them explain what happened without embarrassment or blame. Bruising can involve skin or deeper structures A bruise forms when small blood vessels are damaged and blood collects under the skin. Scrotal skin bruising is not identical to bruising within a testicle. The scrotum holds the testicles outside the main body cavity, where they can be exposed to a direct impact. Falls, sports collisions, being struck or compressed, and accidents involving furniture or equipment can cause injury. Sexual activity or masturbation can sometimes produce trauma when there is excessive pressure or force. Skin caught in a zip may involve a different injury from a direct blow to the testicle, but trapped or torn tissue still needs appropriate care. Tell the clinician the mechanism and timing as clearly as you can. If you notice bruising without remembering an injury, mention medicines such as blood thinners and any other unusual bleeding. An unexplained change should be assessed rather than automatically labelled a sports bruise or infection. A collection of blood is different from a surface bruise A haematocele is a collection of blood around the testicle within its surrounding coverings. Other bleeding may be described as a haematoma, depending on its location. These terms describe findings that can look similar from the outside but have different implications. Swelling and tenderness can make it difficult to examine the testicle properly. A large collection may conceal an injury underneath, so a clinician may arrange ultrasound and decide whether an operation is needed. Not every collection can safely be managed with ice and rest. Smaller injuries may sometimes be followed without surgery after assessment. If that is the plan, ask what should improve, what worsening would mean and whether repeat examination or imaging is needed. Do not try to drain a collection or press on it to discover whether it is fluid. Testicular rupture needs urgent specialist care Testicular rupture means that the tough protective covering of the testicle, the tunica albuginea, has torn. The tissue inside may also be damaged. It is not simply a skin cut or the whole testicle slipping out through an otherwise minor bruise. Pain and swelling after a forceful impact can raise concern, but a home examination cannot reliably exclude rupture. Clinicians use the history, examination and imaging together. When rupture is suspected or imaging cannot safely rule it out, surgical exploration may be necessary. Treatment aims to preserve viable tissue and repair the damage where possible. More severe injury can sometimes mean that a testicle cannot be saved. Prompt assessment gives the team the best opportunity to protect function; there is no benefit in waiting for a fixed home-treatment period to pass first. Torsion can occur with or without a remembered injury The spermatic cord contains the blood vessels and other structures supplying the testicle. In testicular torsion, the cord twists and can cut off the testicle’s blood supply. The danger is to the testicle itself, not merely to the scrotal skin. Torsion can begin after an injury or without an obvious trigger. Sudden severe pain, often with nausea or vomiting, needs emergency assessment. A known accident should not lead you to assume all the pain is ordinary bruising. Do not try to untwist the testicle yourself or repeatedly squeeze it to check its position. Urgent treatment may be needed to restore blood flow. Even if you are unsure when symptoms began or think too much time has passed, seek help immediately rather than deciding that treatment cannot be useful. Inflammation and infection can also cause pain The epididymis is a coiled tube attached to the testicle where sperm mature and are stored. Inflammation there is called epididymitis. It may be related to an infection or, in some circumstances, injury or another non-infectious cause. Pain and swelling can overlap with symptoms of trauma or torsion. Burning when urinating, discharge from the penis, fever or repeated urges to urinate may help guide testing, but none of these clues should be used to diagnose yourself. Sudden severe pain still needs emergency assessment. Some infections are sexually transmitted, including chlamydia or gonorrhoea, while others are not. Unexplained bruising by itself is not evidence of an STI. Give an honest sexual and urinary history so the clinician can choose appropriate tests and treatment without making assumptions based only on the appearance of the scrotum. A new lump should not be assumed to come from the injury An accident may draw your attention to the area and lead you to notice a lump that was already there. Injury does not prove that a newly discovered lump is a bruise, and it does not establish that an underlying tumour was caused by the accident. Swelling can arise from several conditions, including fluid collections, inflammation and abnormal tissue growth. Not every lump is cancer, but a new testicular lump, a change in shape or a difference in size or firmness needs prompt clinical examination. Avoid repeatedly pressing the lump to decide whether it is dangerous. Explain when you first noticed it, whether it changes and whether pain or urinary symptoms accompany it. The next step should be based on examination and appropriate tests rather than reassurance from the fact that an injury happened recently. What assessment and treatment may involve The clinician will ask how the injury occurred, when pain started and whether there are urinary symptoms or other injuries. Examination may include checking the position of both testicles and the surrounding skin. Mention any testicle that was already absent or not normally located in the scrotum. Ultrasound, including assessment of blood flow when appropriate, can help identify bleeding, tissue injury and other abnormalities. An uncertain scan does not always settle the question. The urgency of surgical assessment depends on the overall concern, particularly for rupture or torsion. Treatment ranges from observation and supportive measures for an assessed minor injury to an operation for significant damage. The team should explain what has been found and what remains uncertain. Blood in the urine, trouble passing urine, fever or discharge may require additional assessment beyond the testicle itself. Home comfort measures are for injuries suitable for home care When a clinician has advised that conservative care is appropriate, rest from movements that worsen pain. Use a comfortable position rather than forcing your knees toward your chest. Supportive underwear can reduce movement, but it should not squeeze painfully or pull the scrotum tightly against the body. A cold pack wrapped in cloth may help discomfort for short periods, with breaks between applications. Do not place ice directly on the skin or apply firm pressure. Follow the advice you were given rather than treating a fixed twenty-minute, four-times-a-day schedule as essential for every injury. Paracetamol or ibuprofen may be suitable for some people, but check your age, medicines and health conditions with a clinician or pharmacist. Pain relief should not delay urgent assessment or be used to hide worsening symptoms. Do not massage, puncture or manipulate the testicle in an attempt to speed recovery. Recovery, sexual activity and longer-term function Minor injuries often improve with appropriate care, but recovery time depends on what was injured. Return to sport, strenuous activity and sex according to comfort and the clinical plan. A general promise that all symptoms disappear in a few days is not a reliable substitute for follow-up. Many minor injuries do not cause lasting problems with fertility, sexual function or sensation. Severe rupture, torsion or repeated injury can have longer-term effects, so ask about follow-up when damage is significant or symptoms persist. An injury does not automatically mean infertility, and the effect cannot be judged from bruising alone. Use suitable protective equipment for sports where direct impacts are possible. Seek reassessment if pain or swelling increases, a new lump appears, the testicle changes size or you develop fever or urinary symptoms. A worsening pattern should not wait until the end of an arbitrary one-week observation period. A known injury does not rule out torsion. Surface bruising and internal bleeding are different findings. Do not squeeze or try to untwist a testicle. Unexplained bruising is not an STI diagnosis. Follow up on persistent pain, swelling or a new lump. Can I wait a week if I know how the injury happened? Not with severe, persistent or concerning symptoms. A known impact does not rule out a serious injury. Does a small bruise prove the testicle is unharmed? No. The appearance of the skin does not reliably show the extent of deeper injury. What is a haematocele? It is a collection of blood around the testicle within its coverings, which may need imaging and specialist assessment. Is rupture the same as a cut in the scrotal skin? No. Rupture involves the protective covering of the testicle and can damage the tissue inside. Can torsion happen without an accident? Yes. It may occur without a remembered injury and still requires emergency care. Should I try to untwist the testicle myself? No. Seek emergency assessment rather than manipulating it. Does unexplained bruising mean chlamydia? No. Bruising alone does not diagnose an STI; symptoms and appropriate testing guide assessment. Can a lump noticed after an injury need its own assessment? Yes. The injury may simply have drawn attention to a pre-existing change. Can I use ice directly on the skin? No. Use a cloth barrier for brief applications if home care is appropriate, and avoid pressure or prolonged cooling. Does every testicular injury cause infertility? No. The effect depends on the type and extent of damage; prompt treatment and follow-up help protect function.

title: Omicron symptoms: what older comparisons can and cannot tell you
description: Cold-like symptoms cannot identify a COVID-19 variant or guarantee mild illness. Testing and individual risk matter more than an old variant label.
body: Early reports about Omicron often described sore throats, runny noses and less loss of smell than in earlier COVID-19 waves. Those reports describe a particular period of the pandemic. They should not be read as a promise about the symptoms, severity or contagiousness of an infection today. Symptoms overlap with other respiratory infections COVID-19 can cause sore throat, cough, fever, congestion, headache, fatigue and muscle aches. Changes in smell or taste can still occur. A person may have only some symptoms, and their absence does not exclude infection. Colds, influenza and other illnesses can look similar. You cannot reliably name the virus, or identify a particular SARS-CoV-2 lineage, from a checklist of symptoms. Feeling as though you have a mild cold does not establish that you cannot pass an infection to someone else. Early reports also described sneezing and a dry or scratchy throat. Fever, dry cough and loss of smell were reported less often in some comparisons, but none of those patterns rules infection in or out. Omicron is not a single unchanging illness The name originally described a variant identified in 2021. Many descendant lineages have emerged since then. Public-health agencies track these changes, so an article comparing the first Omicron wave with Delta is historical information rather than a current ranking. Average severity in a population is influenced by the virus, vaccination, previous infections, age, medical conditions and access to treatment. A statement about an average does not predict what will happen to one person. A fixed numerical comparison with Delta is not a permanent measure of how easily today’s infections spread. Nor should a description of upper-airway symptoms be used to conclude that the lungs cannot be affected. The source’s claim of three times the transmission of Delta reflects an early comparison, not a number that remains true for all later lineages. Even when average severity is lower, many infections can still create a substantial burden of hospital care. Check risk early rather than waiting to become very ill Older adults, people with certain medical conditions and people with weakened immune systems may face greater risk. Pregnancy also increases the risk of severe COVID-19. A history of vaccination or infection does not eliminate the possibility of illness. If you have symptoms and may be at higher risk, contact a healthcare professional promptly about testing and treatment. Some antiviral treatments must begin within a few days of symptom onset. Waiting until breathing becomes difficult can miss that opportunity. The right medicine depends on individual circumstances, including other medicines, kidney function and pregnancy. Do not use another person’s prescription or assume that all COVID-19 treatments are interchangeable. Use tests according to their instructions A rapid antigen test can miss an infection early on. Follow the test’s instructions for repeating a negative result and ask about a molecular test when appropriate. A single negative rapid test is not a guarantee that symptoms are unrelated to COVID-19. For many home antigen tests, repeat testing is recommended after 48 hours. The number of repeats depends on symptoms and the product instructions. People who might benefit from treatment should seek advice promptly rather than completing repeated tests before making contact. Follow current local advice about staying home when ill, masks, ventilation and contact with people at higher risk. An old article’s isolation schedule or reference to a “third dose” may no longer match current recommendations where you live. Recognize illness that needs urgent help Seek emergency care for difficulty breathing, persistent chest pain, new confusion or difficulty staying awake. Concerning symptoms deserve assessment even if a home test is negative or an infection was initially mild. Recovery also varies. Ongoing or new symptoms after the acute illness may need follow-up. Reinfection is possible, so becoming infected should not be treated as a safe strategy for building community immunity. Ask a clinician about the current vaccination recommendation for your age and health circumstances. Protection against severe illness and protection against any infection are different outcomes, and neither should be described as absolute. An old Omicron comparison cannot predict an individual infection today. Cold-like symptoms can still be COVID-19. People at higher risk should ask about treatment early. Does a normal sense of smell rule out COVID-19? No. Many people with COVID-19 do not lose their sense of smell. Can a vaccinated person still become seriously ill? Yes. Vaccination reduces risk but does not remove it, and individual risk factors remain important.

title: Rectal bleeding after sex: causes, care and when to get help
description: Understand tears, haemorrhoids, infections and other causes of bleeding after anal sex, with practical recovery advice and clear urgent-care signs.
body: Bleeding after anal sex may come from a small injury, but it is a reason to stop and find out what happened. The right response depends on the bleeding, pain and other symptoms, not on an assumption that spotting is always harmless. Bleeding is a reason to stop and check A small bright-red mark after anal sex can come from irritated skin or a small tear. It does not always mean a serious injury, but it should not be treated as something you must tolerate or expect. Stop the activity, avoid further penetration and seek advice about the bleeding, particularly if it is new, unexplained or recurring. The amount of blood and any other symptoms help determine urgency. Do not assume that a few drops prove the cause is harmless or that waiting exactly two days is always appropriate. Bleeding may be related to an existing bowel or skin problem that became noticeable during sex. It is also useful to establish whether blood is coming from the anus, vagina or urinary tract. When to get urgent medical help Seek emergency care for bleeding that does not stop, a large amount of blood or clots, faintness, collapse or severe pain. Severe or increasing abdominal pain, abdominal swelling, fever or vomiting after an injury can indicate a deeper problem. A tear through the rectal wall is uncommon but requires urgent treatment. A stuck object needs emergency-department assessment; do not repeatedly try to retrieve it with tools or force. Dark-red or black stools and bloody diarrhoea also need prompt medical advice. The absence of dramatic external bleeding cannot rule out a deeper injury. Tell the clinician what happened so the examination and any imaging can be chosen safely. Small tears and anal fissures Friction, sharp nails or force can damage the delicate tissue around the anus. An anal fissure is a tear near the opening and often causes bright-red bleeding with sharp pain during a bowel movement. Burning or aching may continue afterwards. Hard stool can reopen a healing fissure even when sexual activity has stopped. Not every painful area is a fissure, and a superficial tear is different from a deeper rectal injury. A clinician can examine the area and suggest care to keep stools easy to pass and reduce discomfort. Persistent fissures sometimes need prescription treatment that relaxes the sphincter or other specialist care rather than repeated over-the-counter numbing products. Haemorrhoids can bleed when irritated Haemorrhoids are enlarged or symptomatic vascular cushions in or around the anal canal. They can cause bleeding, itching, pressure or a lump. Internal haemorrhoids may bleed without much pain; external swelling can be more tender, especially when a clot forms. Contact or friction may aggravate symptoms. Having a known haemorrhoid does not prove that it explains every episode of bleeding. Avoid further irritation and have changed or recurrent symptoms checked. Treatment depends on the type and severity, often beginning with bowel-habit measures and short-term symptom relief. Procedures intended for internal haemorrhoids are not treatments to apply to an external lump yourself. Anal warts and other surface lesions HPV-related warts can occur outside the anus or within the anal canal. They may be small and painless, or cause itching, discharge or bleeding when irritated. A new growth should be examined rather than assumed to be a wart, especially if it is ulcerated, firm, changing or bleeding. The treatment depends on the lesion and its exact site. Some external warts can be treated with prescribed creams; others need clinician-applied treatment or a procedure. Internal lesions may need a colorectal specialist. Do not use ordinary wart-removal acids on this sensitive area, and do not continue sexual contact that causes a lesion to bleed. Constipation can contribute to repeated injury Hard stools and straining can worsen haemorrhoids or create a fissure. The same irritated area may then bleed with penetration. A feeling of incomplete emptying, dry stools or difficulty passing them matters even if you still have bowel movements regularly. Constipation is not defined only by a low weekly frequency. Addressing the bowel problem can help recovery, but it should not replace assessment of bleeding. If constipation comes with severe abdominal pain, vomiting or inability to pass gas, seek urgent care. Tell a clinician about a persistent change in bowel habits, unexplained weight loss or tiredness rather than assuming all symptoms are caused by recent sex. Enemas and repeated internal cleaning can cause problems An enema introduces fluid into the rectum, sometimes for a specific medical purpose. It is not automatically harmless because it is used only occasionally. The nozzle, pressure, product and condition of the bowel all affect safety; insertion can injure tissue. Repeated cleaning can also make an already sore area harder to leave undisturbed. Do not use an enema to wash away bleeding, an infection exposure or evidence of an injury. If an enema was prescribed for a medical condition, ask the prescribing team how new pain or bleeding changes the plan. For ordinary external care, gentle cleaning is enough. Avoid introducing soap, disinfectants or unprescribed preparations into the rectum. Herpes and inflammatory infections of the rectum Herpes can cause painful blisters or ulcers around the anus or within the rectum. Irritated sores may bleed. A fresh lesion can be sampled to help identify the cause, and antiviral treatment may be appropriate. Appearance alone cannot distinguish herpes from every other ulcer or skin injury. Proctitis means inflammation of the rectum. Gonorrhoea, chlamydia, herpes and syphilis are among the infections that can cause it after relevant contact. Symptoms can include pain, discharge and a repeated urge to pass stool even when little comes out. Rectal samples may be needed; a urine-only STI test does not necessarily assess the affected site. Lymphogranuloma venereum needs specific treatment Lymphogranuloma venereum, or LGV, is caused by particular strains of chlamydia. It can produce marked rectal inflammation, bloody or mucus-containing discharge, pain, constipation, fever and an uncomfortable urge to empty the bowel. It may resemble inflammatory bowel disease and can cause lasting scarring or other complications if untreated. A clinician considers the symptoms and a chlamydia test from the affected site; specialized strain testing is not always quickly available. Treatment may begin before every result returns if the clinical picture is strongly suggestive. LGV usually needs a longer antibiotic course than uncomplicated chlamydia. Follow the clinic’s treatment, partner-care and repeat-testing plan rather than using leftover antibiotics. A warm bath can soothe, but does not treat every cause A shallow bath in comfortably warm water may ease discomfort from a fissure or haemorrhoids. Keep it warm rather than hot, and gently pat the area dry. Plain water is a reasonable choice. Adding Epsom salts is not necessary, and a bath should not be described as a cure for herpes or a deeper injury. Avoid scrubbing, fragranced products and repeatedly checking the area with a finger. Comfort measures are useful while following an appropriate care plan, but should not delay assessment of continuing bleeding, worsening pain, discharge or fever. If sitting in water makes symptoms worse, stop and ask for advice. Use pain relief and rectal products with a clear purpose A pharmacist can advise on pain relief that fits your medicines and health history. Creams intended for one diagnosed condition may not suit another. Local anaesthetic can be used for selected problems under guidance, but numbing an undiagnosed injury to continue penetration can hide the signal to stop. Do not force a suppository or applicator through a painful or bleeding area. Ask whether a rectal product is appropriate before using it for a new injury. Follow the product or clinician’s duration instructions rather than assuming every medicine has a universal three-day limit. Persistent symptoms call for reassessment, not simply stronger or repeated numbing treatment. Keep stools comfortable to pass Where constipation is contributing, gradually increase suitable fibre foods such as fruit, vegetables and whole grains, and drink an appropriate amount of fluid. Do not ignore the urge to use the toilet, but avoid prolonged pushing. People with a prescribed fluid restriction should follow their individual advice. A clinician or pharmacist may recommend a laxative to soften stool or draw water into the bowel. Choose a preparation suited to the situation instead of assuming a suppository is best for injured tissue. The aim is a comfortable bowel movement, not diarrhoea. Review medicines that may contribute to constipation with a professional; do not stop prescribed treatment on your own. What a medical assessment may involve Expect questions about when the bleeding began, its amount, pain, bowel changes, medicines and the type of contact or object involved.
