With consent, the clinician may inspect the area and perform a gentle examination. Explain if pain is severe or you are worried about an object or deeper injury before anything is inserted. Anoscopy looks at the anal canal with a short instrument. Flexible sigmoidoscopy examines farther into the lower bowel. Swabs, blood tests or imaging may be appropriate depending on the findings. These are not a fixed checklist for everyone, and suspected perforation needs an urgent assessment rather than a routine office scope. You can request privacy, an explanation and a chaperone. Returning to sexual activity after recovery Wait until the cause has been assessed and the tissue has recovered; follow any treatment-specific advice. When you choose to resume, communicate about comfort and stop if pain or bleeding returns. There is no requirement to return to penetration or to the same activity simply because a set number of days has passed. Use enough compatible lubricant to reduce friction. Water-based or suitable silicone-based products can be compatible with latex condoms, whereas oils can damage latex. Check the instructions for any toy because some lubricant materials are incompatible with it. Keep nails smooth and short, remove sharp jewellery and use clean, intact items intended for the purpose. Softness alone does not guarantee safety. Dilators and particular positions are not proven protection Progressively stretching the anus with a dilator should not be treated as routine self-care after bleeding. Dilators have selected medical uses, but need a clear indication and individual instructions. Using a larger device to overcome pain or a feeling of resistance can aggravate an injury. Likewise, no head-down or other specific position guarantees that tearing will not happen. Comfort, control, consent and stopping when symptoms occur are more useful than following a position as a medical prevention rule. Recurrent pain or bleeding should lead to assessment of the cause, not increasingly elaborate attempts to make the same activity possible. Prevent infection and choose the right testing schedule Condoms and other suitable barriers reduce infection exposure but cannot eliminate every risk, particularly infections spread through uncovered skin. Clean hands and toys, and change barriers when moving between body sites. If an infection is diagnosed, follow instructions about treatment for partners and when sexual contact can resume. Screening intervals depend on anatomy, exposures and individual risk. Some people need annual testing and others more frequent checks; symptoms need assessment now rather than waiting for a routine date. If a recent exposure could transmit HIV, seek urgent advice about PEP, which must start within 72 hours. For ongoing risk, ask whether PrEP and recommended vaccinations belong in your prevention plan. Bleeding is a reason to stop and assess, not a necessary part of sexual activity. Tears, haemorrhoids, warts, constipation, cleaning injuries, herpes and LGV are discussed individually. Warm water and comfortable bowel movements may help selected minor conditions; they do not treat every cause. No position or stretching device guarantees protection from injury. Symptoms need appropriate testing now, with routine screening intervals individualized. Is a little bleeding after anal sex always normal? No. A small surface tear is one possibility, but bleeding should not be an expected part of sex. Stop, allow assessment and recovery, and have unexplained or recurrent bleeding checked. Should I wait two days before asking for help? Not if bleeding is heavy or ongoing, pain is severe, you feel faint, or you have abdominal swelling, fever or vomiting. Those symptoms need urgent care. Mild symptoms can also be discussed promptly. Can bright-red blood tell me the exact cause? No. It often comes from near the anal opening, but fissures, haemorrhoids, infection and other problems can overlap. Colour alone does not establish the diagnosis. Will a salt bath heal an STI? No. A warm bath may soothe discomfort but does not replace testing or treatment for herpes, LGV or another infection. Plain water avoids adding unnecessary irritants. Can I use numbing cream to keep having sex? Do not use it to mask pain and continue an activity that caused bleeding. Pain relief for a diagnosed condition is a separate decision to discuss with a pharmacist or clinician. Should I use an enema or suppository to help healing? Not automatically. A painful or bleeding area may be further irritated by insertion. Use a rectal treatment only when it is appropriate for the diagnosed problem and follow the instructions. Does an anal dilator prevent future tears? It is not a routine proven prevention method after bleeding. Use one only for a specific indication with professional guidance; do not stretch through pain. Can a urine STI test check rectal symptoms? A urine test may miss an infection confined to the rectum. Tell the service about the site of contact and symptoms so it can choose rectal swabs and other appropriate tests. How long should I wait before resuming penetration? There is no single safe interval for every cause. Wait for assessment, healing and any required treatment, and follow the clinician’s advice. Stop again if symptoms recur. What if the injury happened without my consent? Medical care and specialist sexual-assault support are available. You can ask about confidentiality, examination choices and time-sensitive infection prevention. Seek urgent care for significant bleeding or pain.

title: Low sexual desire in men: possible causes and ways to get support
description: How hormones, medicines, mood, sleep, illness, stress and habits can affect sexual desire, with careful interpretation of research and treatment matched to the cause.
body: Sexual desire naturally differs between people and can change over time. Wanting sex less often than a partner does not by itself mean that something is wrong. If a change troubles you, persists or comes with other symptoms, it is reasonable to ask for help. Several contributors can overlap, and understanding them is more useful than assuming that low desire always means low testosterone. Start by separating desire from other sexual concerns Libido describes interest in sexual activity. Erectile dysfunction means difficulty getting or keeping an erection firm enough for the sexual activity a person wants. Orgasm, ejaculation and sperm production are different functions again. They can influence one another, but a problem with one does not establish a problem with all the others. For example, someone may want sex but worry about maintaining an erection. Another person may have reliable erections but little interest in sex. Reduced sperm production concerns fertility and cannot be inferred from how much desire someone feels. Notice what changed, whether it happens in every situation and how you feel about it. A longstanding low level of interest that does not distress you is not a failure of masculinity. There is no required number of sexual encounters, and differences between partners never remove the need for consent. Low testosterone: one possibility, not a diagnosis from symptoms alone Testosterone is made mainly in the testicles and contributes to sexual function, muscle and bone health, and the hormonal environment needed for sperm production. A true deficiency can reduce desire, but tiredness or low interest alone is not enough to identify it. The American Urological Association uses total testosterone below 300 ng/dL as a reasonable cutoff supporting a diagnosis. That number is not a universal pass-or-fail test. Diagnosis also requires relevant symptoms and consistently low results, with interpretation suited to the laboratory and clinical circumstances. Testing generally involves at least two early-morning measurements on separate days; Endocrine Society guidance recommends fasting morning confirmation. A clinician may investigate why the level is low and order other hormone tests when appropriate. A single low result should not lead directly to treatment. Prescribed testosterone, including gels or other formulations, may be appropriate for selected people with confirmed deficiency. It needs monitoring and a discussion of benefits and risks. Testosterone taken from outside the body can suppress sperm production, so discuss future fertility before treatment. Online boosters and unsupervised hormones are not a reliable substitute for assessment. Medicines can affect sexual function through different routes Some treatments influence desire, erections, orgasm or hormones. The effect depends on the medicine, dose, individual response and illness being treated. It is misleading to say that every drug associated with a sexual side effect works by lowering testosterone. Blood-pressure medicines are one example: some beta-blockers can contribute to sexual difficulties, while effects differ across drugs and people. ACE inhibitors should not be treated as a class that invariably prevents erections or ejaculation. The underlying high blood pressure can also affect sexual function. Other relevant treatments include chemotherapy or radiotherapy, depending on the treatment and area involved; androgen-deprivation treatment for prostate cancer; long-term systemic corticosteroids; and opioids such as morphine or oxycodone. Their possible effects are not identical, and some may involve hormone suppression or fertility as well as sexual wellbeing. Systemic ketoconazole, an antifungal medicine, and cimetidine, used for acid-related stomach problems, are additional medicines worth mentioning during a review. Antidepressants can also have sexual side effects. Anabolic steroids used for muscle building can disrupt the body’s own hormone production, including after they are stopped. Bring a complete list of prescribed medicines, supplements and non-prescribed substances, along with the timing of symptoms. Do not stop a blood-pressure medicine, antidepressant, steroid or opioid abruptly. A prescriber can consider safer adjustments while preserving treatment for the original condition. Restless legs and the limits of an association Restless legs syndrome involves an urge to move the legs, commonly accompanied by uncomfortable sensations when resting, especially in the evening or at night. Disrupted sleep and discomfort can affect wellbeing, but the condition does not automatically cause low desire. A 2010 observational study of more than 23,000 men found an association between more frequent restless-legs symptoms and erectile dysfunction. It studied erections, not a direct measure of libido, and its estimates varied with symptom frequency. It does not establish that restless legs causes sexual dysfunction or give an individual man a fixed fifty-percent increase in risk. If an urge to move your legs is disturbing sleep, describe that symptom to a clinician rather than treating it as proof of a hormone problem. Assessing the sleep or movement problem and separately discussing sexual symptoms is more useful than assuming one explains everything. Depression and antidepressant treatment Depression can reduce interest and pleasure in many parts of life, including sex. Low energy, anxiety, poor concentration and changes in sleep can contribute. A reduction in desire may therefore be part of the illness, a medication effect, or both. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, including fluoxetine and sertraline, and serotonin–noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors such as duloxetine can cause sexual difficulties. These may involve desire, arousal, delayed orgasm or ejaculation rather than only a change in testosterone. Bupropion has shown fewer sexual adverse effects than some serotonergic antidepressants in comparative research. That does not make it free of side effects or suitable for everyone, and it should not be presented as a guaranteed libido treatment. The choice depends on the person’s mental health, medical history and other medicines. Tell the prescriber when symptoms began and whether depression itself is improving. Options may include waiting for an early side effect to settle, a supervised adjustment or a different treatment, depending on the circumstances. Avoid dose skipping, abrupt withdrawal or switching medicines on your own. Chronic illness, pain and the burden of treatment Persistent pain and serious or long-term illness can leave less energy or attention for sex. Type 2 diabetes, heart disease and cancer are examples; obesity, high blood pressure and high cholesterol may also coexist with conditions affecting sexual health. They are possible contributors, not a judgment about someone’s body or habits. Chronic lung, kidney or liver disease can affect stamina, symptoms, medicines and hormone regulation. Cancer and its treatment may affect body image, sexual function or fertility in different ways. Reduced sperm production should not be used as another name for reduced desire. Discuss pain control, fatigue, breathlessness and practical limits with the treating team. Partners may need to adjust timing, expectations and forms of intimacy. Counselling or a qualified sex therapist can help with communication and adaptation, alongside medical care rather than in place of it. Sleep problems and what the research actually shows Short sleep, disrupted sleep and obstructive sleep apnoea can affect energy and health. Mention loud snoring, witnessed pauses in breathing or marked daytime sleepiness to a clinician. These symptoms deserve attention whether or not desire has changed. A 2017 study examined records from 153 men with sleep apnoea who were not classified as obese. Forty-seven had low testosterone, and most of that group were overweight. This was not evidence that one third of all men with severe sleep apnoea have low testosterone. Weight, age and nighttime oxygen levels were part of the picture. A separate small 2011 experiment involved ten healthy young men. After about a week of restricted sleep with five hours in bed each night, daytime testosterone was roughly ten to fifteen percent lower than after the rested condition, particularly later in the day. The study measured hormones, not whether participants developed low libido. These findings make sleep relevant to assessment, but they do not predict an individual’s hormone level or prove that a set amount of extra sleep will restore desire. Seek help for persistent sleep problems and aim for a sustainable sleep routine instead of buying hormones on the basis of a research percentage. Ageing and changing sexual responses Testosterone is generally highest in youth and may decline gradually with age. That pattern is different from saying that every older man has a hormone disorder. Health conditions, medicines, sleep and life circumstances can be more useful clues than age alone. Arousal may take longer, erections may be less firm and orgasm or ejaculation may feel different. Individual experiences vary; there is no reliable rule that erections will last longer as men age. More time, comfortable stimulation and communication can help people adapt without treating every change as a failure. Persistent erection problems can be assessed and treated, but erection medicines are not a direct cure for lack of interest. Likewise, testosterone is not routinely recommended simply because someone is getting older. The aim is care for a specific concern, not restoring an assumed youthful standard. Stress, major life events and trauma Stress can occupy attention, reduce energy and make sexual situations feel pressured. Nervous-system and hormonal responses may also play a role, but it is too simple to explain every problem as stress narrowing the arteries to the penis. Divorce, bereavement, financial worries, a demanding job, relationship strain or caring for a new baby can all change the context for intimacy. A temporary reduction in desire during an exhausting period does not necessarily mean that attraction or the relationship has disappeared. Research in veterans has linked post-traumatic stress disorder with sexual difficulties. Such findings describe groups in particular settings; they cannot be turned into a universal threefold prediction for every person with trauma. Desire, erections, medicines and other mental-health conditions may all be involved. Therapy, practical support, relaxation exercises, breathing techniques or meditation may help someone manage stress. An eight-week pilot study has explored stress management alongside care for erectile dysfunction, but a small pilot is not proof that these techniques reliably treat low desire. Support should fit the person’s needs and comfort. Self-esteem, body image and performance pressure Feeling unattractive, worrying about body size or expecting to perform in a particular way can make sex feel like a test. Some people avoid intimacy because they anticipate embarrassment or disappointment. That pattern can reinforce anxiety even when desire has not disappeared completely. Low self-esteem may overlap with depression, relationship difficulties or harmful use of alcohol or drugs, but it does not inevitably cause them. It is more useful to explore the actual concern than to assume that one emotional difficulty will lead to a chain of disorders. A therapist can help with body image, self-criticism and performance fears. Partners can discuss affection and closeness without making intercourse, erection or orgasm the only acceptable outcome. Respectful support leaves room for a person to decline sex without guilt. Exercise: both inactivity and inadequate recovery matter Regular physical activity supports general health and can help with mood, sleep and conditions that affect sexual wellbeing. Being inactive may coexist with diabetes, cardiovascular problems or other contributors, but adding exercise is not a guaranteed treatment for low desire. At the other extreme, intense endurance training with insufficient recovery or food can be relevant. A 2017 survey of 1,077 men found an association between heavier endurance-training patterns and lower reported libido. As a cross-sectional survey, it could not prove that exercise caused the change or identify a universal safe training threshold. If symptoms began during a demanding training period, discuss fatigue, nutrition, recovery and other health changes. The answer is not necessarily to stop exercising. A sustainable balance is more useful than assuming that all intense activity is harmful or that a particular evening workout will correct cortisol and libido. Alcohol, smoking and other substances Heavy alcohol use can interfere with sexual function, mood, sleep and relationships. The amount, drinking pattern and individual context matter. A glass, bottle and standard drink are not interchangeable, so conflicting daily and weekly figures should not be turned into a personal drinking prescription. Reducing harmful alcohol use may be one part of a care plan. If reducing drinking is difficult, or you rely on it to manage anxiety or intimacy, ask for professional support rather than treating the issue as a test of willpower. Smoking can damage blood vessels and is relevant to erection difficulties and reproductive health. Opioids can suppress reproductive hormones, including when prescribed for pain. Cannabis and other recreational substances can have varied effects; evidence should not be simplified into a claim that every substance invariably lowers testosterone. Be open about substances and anabolic steroids during assessment. The purpose is to choose safe care, including support for reducing harmful use when needed, rather than to blame someone for their symptoms. Changes to a prescribed opioid should be supervised. Emotional and relationship effects deserve attention too A change in desire may lead to worry about rejection, attractiveness or sexual ability. Anxiety about a previous erection problem can then make the next encounter feel more difficult. This is a possible feedback loop, not proof that low desire inevitably causes erectile dysfunction. Less frequent sex, mismatched expectations and misunderstandings can strain a relationship. Try to describe your experience without assuming what your partner thinks. Saying that you feel exhausted, anxious or less interested is different from assigning blame. Couple counselling or sex therapy may help when both people want that support. It should not be used to pressure someone into sexual activity. The appropriate goal may be clearer communication and more comfortable intimacy, rather than a particular frequency. Assessment and treatment should follow the likely causes A clinician may ask about the onset of symptoms, erections and orgasm, mood, relationship context, sleep, medicines and other illnesses. Examination or blood tests are chosen according to the history. Not everyone needs testosterone treatment or the same set of tests. Treatment may combine management of an illness, a medication review, sleep care and psychological or relationship support. Confirmed hormone deficiency needs its own evaluation and monitoring. Erection medicines are considered for erection problems, while treatment for depression should also protect mental health. Regular activity, adequate nutrition, rest and support with heavy alcohol use can help overall wellbeing. They do not promise an immediate increase in libido. Agree on a follow-up plan and what improvement would mean to you, including comfort, energy, confidence or reduced distress. When to ask for help You can seek advice whenever a change worries you. A persistent or recurring reduction in desire, a sudden unexplained change, sexual side effects from medication or accompanying fatigue, pain or mood symptoms are all reasonable topics for an appointment. There is no required waiting period or sexual-frequency threshold. Compare with your own usual experience rather than a partner’s expectations or an online norm. If you have little sexual interest and that is comfortable for you, it need not be treated as a disorder. If the concern is distress or a change in health, care should focus on that concern. Take low mood seriously in its own right. If you feel at risk of harming yourself or cannot stay safe, seek immediate help through local emergency or crisis services. Otherwise, a primary care or sexual-health appointment is a useful starting point for a calm, private assessment. Desire, erections, ejaculation and fertility are related but different. Health, mood, medicines, sleep and circumstances can contribute together. A study association is not an individual diagnosis or a guaranteed treatment result. Testosterone requires appropriate testing and can suppress sperm production. Review medication effects with the prescriber rather than stopping treatment yourself. Support should respect personal preferences, consent and the concerns that matter to you. Does low desire always mean low testosterone? No. Hormone deficiency is one possible contributor. Diagnosis requires relevant symptoms and consistently low, appropriately timed blood tests. Is a testosterone result below 300 ng/dL enough to start treatment? No. That AUA cutoff supports assessment, but symptoms, repeat early-morning results and the clinical context also matter. Can testosterone treatment affect fertility? Yes. Testosterone taken from outside the body can suppress sperm production. Discuss current and future fertility plans before treatment. Does an erection problem mean I have lost sexual desire? Not necessarily. Someone can want sex and still have difficulty with erections. The two concerns need to be described separately. Should I stop an antidepressant if my sex drive changes? No abrupt change is advisable. Tell the prescriber; the illness and its treatment can both contribute, and supervised options may be available. Is bupropion guaranteed to have no sexual side effects? No. Comparative studies suggest fewer sexual adverse effects than some alternatives, but it is not risk-free or suitable for everyone. Do restless legs or sleep apnoea prove that my libido problem is hormonal? No. The relevant studies describe associations with erections or testosterone in particular groups. They do not diagnose the cause of an individual’s low desire. Will sleeping longer or exercising more definitely restore desire? No. Sleep and sustainable activity support health, but libido has many contributors. Excessive training with inadequate recovery may also deserve discussion. Is it abnormal to want sex less often than my partner? Not by itself. Preferences vary. Discuss the difference respectfully without pressure, and seek support if the change or mismatch is distressing. How long should I wait before asking for help? There is no mandatory waiting period. Ask whenever you are worried, especially if the change is persistent, unexplained, linked to medication or accompanied by other symptoms.

title: Massage for constipation: techniques, evidence and limits
description: Explore gentle abdominal massage, reflexology and perineal pressure, with separate guidance for pregnancy, babies and symptoms needing care.
body: Massage may be a helpful addition to some constipation plans, but it is not a way to clear an obstruction or treat every cause. Before trying a technique, check that it suits your health, use gentle pressure and know when symptoms need assessment. First check whether the problem is constipation Constipation can mean hard or dry stool, difficult or painful passage, straining or a sense that the bowel has not emptied. Fewer than three bowel movements a week is one possible feature, but frequency alone is not a diagnosis. What is usual for you, the stool’s consistency and any new symptoms also matter. Massage is sometimes used alongside a constipation plan. It should not replace an assessment when symptoms are new, persistent or severe. In particular, infant straining with soft stool is not the same problem as an adult’s chronic constipation. The technique and even whether massage is appropriate depend on the person and the cause. Abdominal massage may help, but the evidence has limits Studies in adults suggest that abdominal massage can improve some constipation symptoms, bowel-movement frequency and transit time. It may also ease a feeling of bloating or discomfort. A 2025 review included 23 studies with 1,431 participants, but methods and results varied substantially, and it did not show a clear reduction in laxative use. This supports considering massage as an additional measure for selected people, not promising that it will cure constipation or its underlying cause. Reduced tension may feel helpful for someone with stress-related symptoms, including IBS, without proving that massage treats every aspect of that condition. Do not stop prescribed bowel medicines because you begin massage. Check suitability before pressing on the abdomen Do not massage an abdomen with unexplained severe pain, vomiting, marked swelling or suspected bowel obstruction. An abdominal mass, recent surgery or scarring, inflammatory bowel disease such as Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis, or an unstable spinal injury needs an individualized professional assessment. A hernia also requires advice about whether and how massage could be used. Hospital research on postoperative bowel recovery is not a reason to treat postoperative ileus at home. Ileus is a failure of normal bowel movement that can produce obstruction-like symptoms and needs medical management. If the abdomen becomes painful or distended after surgery, contact the treating team rather than trying to stimulate it with pressure. A gentle abdominal sequence for an adult who has been advised it is suitable Begin in a comfortable lying or supported sitting position, with the knees slightly bent if that helps the abdominal muscles relax. Use the soft pads of your fingers or your palm, keeping pressure light and comfortable. Breathe normally. You should not need to dig into the abdomen, press on pelvic bones or brace against pain. Starting at your own lower right abdomen, make slow gentle circles or strokes upward toward the right rib margin, across the upper abdomen toward the left, then downward along the left side. This follows the broad direction of the colon. Keep movements slow, lift or reposition the hand as needed and repeat only while comfortable. Finish with light broad strokes rather than a forceful upward lift. A clinician or physiotherapist can demonstrate a routine and its duration for your situation. Stop if there is pain, nausea, dizziness or worsening swelling. More pressure and a longer session are not evidence of a better treatment. “Colon massage” is not a way to remove a blockage Some descriptions call the same general approach colon massage, deep abdominal massage or visceral massage. They may use a horseshoe-shaped route: up the right side, across beneath the ribs and down the left. The useful distinction is gentle comfortable movement versus deep force, not a claim that one name reaches hidden waste. Claims that deep massage clears an obstruction, prevents loss of body fluid or broadly detoxifies the digestive system are not established. Do not use fingernails, painful tapping or sustained pressure on a tender spot. A persistent urge to focus on one painful area is a reason to ask about the pain, not to press harder. Suspected impaction or obstruction needs the appropriate clinical assessment. Massage oils are optional, and stronger scents are not stronger treatment A gentle routine can be done without oil, including over light clothing. Castor, argan and coconut oils are sometimes suggested as skin lubricants, but rubbing one on the abdomen has not been established as a treatment that improves constipation beyond the massage itself. They can also irritate or trigger an allergy in some people. Essential oils do not have a proven advantage here and should not be swallowed or applied undiluted. Do not give oils by mouth or use them on a baby to treat constipation. Oral castor oil is a different intervention with its own risks; it should not be confused with optional skin lubrication. If a skin product is needed, ask about a plain suitable product and stop if irritation occurs. Foot massage and reflexology: comfort is different from proof Reflexology maps areas of the feet to other parts of the body. A 2003 observational study enrolled 50 children aged three to fourteen with constipation or soiling; 48 completed six 30-minute sessions over six weeks. Bowel and soiling reports improved, but without a randomized comparison the study cannot establish that the foot technique caused the improvement. One proposed sequence moves gently from the right heel toward the outer ankle and through the centre of the right foot, then along the outer left foot toward the heel and the inner edge. It can be considered a relaxation routine if comfortable, not a validated map for emptying the bowel. Do not press painfully, and seek advice first for wounds, reduced sensation or circulation problems. A child’s constipation or overflow soiling still needs its usual treatment plan. Back or whole-body massage may support relaxation A comfortable back or whole-body massage may help you unwind and reduce a feeling of muscle tension. That can be worthwhile in itself when stress makes symptoms harder to manage. Evidence for a specific constipation effect is less clear than simply noticing that you feel more relaxed afterwards. Tell a massage practitioner about medical conditions, pregnancy, recent procedures and any area that hurts. Choose a qualified practitioner when professional treatment is appropriate. Neither a full-body session nor foot massage should be used to postpone care for bleeding, severe pain or an unexplained change in bowel habit. Perineal self-acupressure has been studied in selected adults The perineum is the external area between the anus and the vaginal opening or scrotum. A 2015 unblinded trial of 100 adults compared standard constipation advice with that advice plus training in external perineal pressure. At four weeks the trained group reported better bowel function and constipation-related quality of life. Pregnant people and those with blood mixed in stool or significant weight loss were excluded. The method involves repeated gentle external pressure before or during the urge to pass stool, rather than inserting fingers or manually removing stool. Descriptions may use two finger pads pressing toward the anus briefly, then releasing. A pelvic-floor clinician should show you whether this is suitable and how to apply it; a generic three-to-five-second instruction does not establish the right force or technique for everyone. Do not try it over a tear, wound, painful haemorrhoid or an area that bleeds, or after a recent birth or operation without advice. Stop if it hurts. Difficulty emptying despite soft stool may need assessment for pelvic-floor coordination or another problem instead of repeated attempts to push externally. For babies, keep touch gentle and assessment early Gentle tummy strokes or slowly moving the legs as if pedalling may comfort a relaxed baby. Calm, responsive touch can also be a pleasant way for a caregiver and baby to connect. Use only light touch, follow the baby’s cues and stop with distress. Avoid massage immediately after a feed or when the baby seems full or uncomfortable. A particular waiting interval is not a guarantee that massage is safe. Do not use an adult pressure routine, deep kneading, oils as laxatives or rectal stimulation. A baby may strain while passing soft stool as coordination develops; hard stool, feeding and growth changes are different concerns. Correct formula preparation matters: never add extra powder or dilute a feed to try to change the stool. Get prompt advice for blood, poor feeding, vomiting, persistent pain or a baby who seems weak or unwell. Green vomit, a swollen painful abdomen or difficulty waking requires emergency assessment. Do not wait a week, or wait for an hour of continuous pain, before seeking help for a concerning infant symptom. Pregnancy needs a separate constipation plan Do not assume abdominal massage becomes safe simply because the first trimester has ended. Cambridge University Hospitals’ bowel-function guidance does not recommend abdominal massage during pregnancy. Ask your midwife or obstetric clinician for an individual plan instead of following a general adult massage routine. Suitable activity, appropriate fluids, gradual dietary fibre and, when needed, a pregnancy-appropriate laxative are more usual parts of care. A prenatal back massage and direct abdominal pressure are different activities. The perineal constipation study also excluded pregnancy; it should not be used to justify this technique during pregnancy or confused with antenatal perineal preparation for birth. Build the everyday bowel routine alongside any massage Drink regularly within any medical fluid limits. A glass of water in the morning can be a useful habit, but it is not a special treatment requirement. Increase fibre gradually through foods such as fruit, vegetables, whole grains and beans, and adjust with advice if fibre worsens symptoms or a particular bowel condition changes what is suitable. Regular walking, cycling, swimming or another activity you can manage may support bowel habits. Make time to use the toilet when the urge comes, and use stable foot support if it improves comfort. Meditation, gentle yoga or other stress-management practices can help with wellbeing, but none guarantees relief. Record stool form, straining, pain, foods and treatments to see what changes over time. Know when the plan needs medical review Three days without a bowel movement is not automatically abnormal for everyone, and a two-week rule is not a reason to ignore warning signs. Seek review for recurring or persistent constipation, a new unexplained change, alternating constipation and loose stool, weight loss or blood. Severe constant pain, vomiting, inability to pass gas or marked swelling needs urgent assessment. Treatment may include reviewing constipating medicines, prescribing a laxative or treating impaction. Do not stop medicines on your own. Pelvic-floor biofeedback or other specialist treatment may help selected evacuation problems, and surgery is reserved for unusual carefully assessed situations. A prescribed bowel clean-out for impaction is different from commercial colon cleansing, which is not a routine answer to constipation. Judge success by comfort and function, not the amount of massage A useful plan makes stools easier to pass and reduces painful straining, bloating or accidents. Keep any agreed follow-up and tell the clinician if massage has no benefit or makes symptoms worse. The aim is a manageable bowel routine, not dependence on ever stronger or more frequent pressure. Mild constipation may improve with everyday changes, while persistent constipation often needs more than one measure. Massage is optional. You have not failed if you need medicine, a physiotherapy assessment or a different diagnosis, and a short symptom diary can make those decisions more informed. Adult studies suggest some benefit, but techniques and results vary. Light comfortable movements are different from deep pressure or attempted blockage removal. Reflexology evidence and perineal-pressure evidence have important limits. Pregnancy and infant care need separate advice. Persistent symptoms may need medicines, pelvic-floor treatment or investigation. Is constipation defined only by fewer than three stools a week? No. Hard stool, straining, discomfort and incomplete emptying also matter, along with your usual pattern. Can massage replace my prescribed laxative? Not automatically. Research has not shown a consistent reduction in laxative use. Review the plan with your prescriber. Which direction does a gentle abdominal routine follow? In an adult for whom it is suitable, it commonly moves from the lower right abdomen upward, across and down the left, following the broad route of the colon. Should I press harder where I feel a painful lump? No. Stop and arrange assessment. Deep pressure is not a treatment for an obstruction or an unexplained mass. Do essential oils make the massage more effective? There is no established advantage for constipation. Avoid undiluted or swallowed oils and do not use oils as infant laxatives. Did the children’s reflexology study prove it works? No. It was a small observational study without a randomized comparison, so improvement cannot reliably be attributed to reflexology. Is perineal pressure the same as inserting a finger to remove stool? No. The studied approach used external pressure taught to selected adults. Manual stool removal is a different procedure and should not be improvised. Can I start abdominal massage in the second trimester? Do not assume the trimester makes it suitable. CUH guidance does not recommend it in pregnancy; ask your maternity clinician for a constipation plan. Should I wait a week before seeking help for a constipated baby? No. Poor feeding, blood, vomiting, significant pain or illness needs prompt advice, with emergency care for green vomit or a swollen painful abdomen. What if massage never helps? It is optional. Persistent constipation needs a review of causes and treatment rather than progressively harder massage.

title: The Norwood scale: stages of male-pattern hair loss
description: Understand stages 1–7 and the class A variant, what the scale cannot diagnose, and the benefits and limits of medicines, devices and procedures.
body: The Norwood scale describes common patterns of recession and crown thinning. It can support a conversation about male-pattern hair loss, but it does not predict an inevitable future or choose a treatment for you. The cause, pace of change and your preferences matter alongside the stage. What the Norwood scale is for The Norwood scale, also called the Hamilton–Norwood scale, describes common patterns of male-pattern hair loss. It gives clinicians and patients a shared way to talk about a receding front hairline and thinning on the crown, the upper area toward the back of the scalp. It is one classification system, not a test of general health or a measure of attractiveness. The scale has seven main stages, along with variants. It can help document the starting pattern and compare photographs over time, but people do not necessarily move through every stage or progress at the same rate. A stage does not predict exactly how much hair you will lose or tell you which treatment you must choose. Other systems describe different hair-loss patterns, including the more diffuse mid-scalp thinning often seen in female-pattern hair loss. A chart intended for male-pattern recession should not be forced onto every scalp. Diagnosis comes before using the number to discuss treatment. Stages 1 to 3: the hairline and early crown changes Stage 1 describes little or no visible recession. Stage 2 describes modest recession at the temples, often referred to as a mature hairline. That label is descriptive: it does not prove that the hairline will remain stable. Comparing a consistent photograph over time is more useful than repeatedly measuring a single corner in a mirror. Stage 3 involves more pronounced recession at both temples, leaving an M-, V- or U-like outline. The receded areas may have very sparse hair or appear bare. This is more than a small change in the shape of the hairline, but assessment should still consider the full pattern and history. The stage 3 vertex variant emphasizes thinning at the crown, sometimes with less marked front recession. “Vertex” means the top or crown, not the low back of the head where donor hair for a transplant is often found. Crown thinning and temple recession can develop at different rates. Stages 4 to 7: larger areas become connected At stage 4, recession at the front and hair loss at the crown are more substantial, with a band of hair still separating them. In stage 5, the two affected areas are larger and the intervening band is narrower and sparser. Lighting and hair length can make that band look different, so staging should not rely on one poorly lit photograph. At stage 6, the front and crown areas of loss join as the separating bridge is lost. Stage 7 describes extensive loss on top, leaving a rim of hair around the sides and back. The density of the remaining rim varies; the stage does not guarantee that enough suitable donor hair is available for a particular transplant plan. A higher stage describes greater visible loss in this pattern. It does not mean that a person needs surgery, that medicines cannot have any role or that choosing no treatment is unreasonable. Treatment goals and the condition of remaining hair are separate from the stage number. The class A pattern is a variant In the class A variant, the front hairline moves backward more continuously, without the usual separate crown patch and intervening island or bridge of hair. The point is the shape of the progression, not that it is a special diagnosis unrelated to androgenetic hair loss. You may also see different labels or versions of a chart used by clinics. Ask which system they are using and what change they are trying to document. An online self-assigned stage should be treated as a starting description, especially when the pattern does not fit neatly into the drawings. Confirm the cause before treating it A clinician usually begins with the pattern, timing, family history, medicines, recent illnesses and an examination of the scalp. They may inspect hairs with magnification or perform a gentle pull test to understand shedding. Laboratory tests or a scalp biopsy are considered when the history or examination points to another cause, rather than being necessary for everyone. Sudden heavy shedding, sharply defined patches, broken hairs, scalp pain, marked itching, inflammation or scarring deserves assessment rather than being labeled a Norwood stage. Infection, alopecia areata, traction, medication effects and shedding after illness are among other possibilities. More than one type of hair loss can occur at once. Unexpected loss at a very young age or a pattern accompanied by other hormonal symptoms also needs an individualized review. A familiar family pattern can be useful information, but it does not rule out a second condition. Bring photographs and a timeline if you have them; do not delay assessment simply to collect a perfect series. Genes, hormones and the hair growth cycle Male-pattern hair loss reflects inherited susceptibility of certain follicles to androgens, especially dihydrotestosterone, or DHT. Genes from either side of the family can contribute. It is not determined only by the maternal grandfather, and relatives may start losing hair at different ages or develop different patterns. Hair normally cycles through growth, transition and rest before shedding and replacement. In susceptible scalp areas, follicles gradually produce finer, shorter hairs through a process called miniaturization, and the growth phase becomes shorter. This is different from all hairs suddenly stopping production at the same moment. The pattern does not necessarily mean that blood testosterone is abnormally high. Nor is there a universal two-year deadline after which every quiet follicle becomes permanently impossible to treat. Earlier discussion can help preserve existing hair, but promises based on an exact inactivity cutoff oversimplify a variable biological process. Topical minoxidil: expectations and routine Topical minoxidil is available without a prescription in many places and can help reduce ongoing loss or improve growth in some people. It is applied to the scalp according to the particular product’s directions. Different formulations and local labels may have different instructions; using more than directed does not guarantee better results. Expect a gradual trial rather than a change within days. A visible response may take several months, and some people do not respond. Full restoration of the original density is unlikely. The benefit generally depends on continued use, so discuss the time, cost and practicality before starting. Scalp irritation, itching or unwanted hair growth can occur. Ask for advice about troublesome reactions and follow the product’s warnings. Oral minoxidil is a different, prescription treatment with systemic risks and should not be substituted for a topical product without medical supervision. A dermatologist may combine treatments when appropriate. Finasteride: benefits and important adverse effects Finasteride is a prescription medicine that reduces formation of DHT and can slow male-pattern loss; some people also gain density. Response varies with the person, outcome measured and length of treatment. A claim that exactly 88% stop losing hair or 66% regrow it should not be treated as an individual guarantee. Several months may be needed to judge benefit, and continued use is usually required to maintain it. Before prescribing, the clinician should review medical history, other medicines and the possible effects on sexual function and mood. Do not obtain an uncertain product online simply because a photograph appears to show dramatic regrowth. UK MHRA warnings include sexual dysfunction, depression and suicidal thoughts; sexual effects have been reported to persist after stopping. If taking finasteride for hair loss and depression or suicidal thoughts develop, stop it and seek medical advice. Immediate danger or an inability to stay safe requires emergency support. Report sexual side effects to the prescriber so the treatment can be reviewed. Laser devices and other advertised treatments Low-level light or laser devices are sold as caps, combs and other home products. Some studies suggest benefit with particular devices, but the quality of evidence, dose schedules and results differ. A marketing clearance or an impressive before-and-after photograph does not establish that every device is effective or that it will work for your pattern. Ask about evidence for the exact product, realistic changes in density, how long treatment must continue, eye/skin precautions and the total cost. A blanket statement that all lasers are proven or all are disproven is less useful than a device-specific discussion. They should not delay diagnosis of painful, inflamed or rapidly changing hair loss. Clinics may also offer injections or combinations of procedures. Ask which parts are established for your diagnosis and which remain uncertain, and how improvement will be measured. Supplements are not a general solution to inherited patterned loss unless there is a relevant deficiency or another specific indication. Transplantation, older operations and camouflage A hair transplant moves suitable donor follicles, usually from the sides or back, into selected areas of loss. It redistributes available hair rather than creating an unlimited new supply. Suitability depends on donor density, the pattern’s stability, scalp health, expectations and the likelihood of further loss. Scarring, complications, cost and possible later procedures belong in the discussion. Older descriptions of treatment may include scalp reduction, in which bald skin is removed and hair-bearing areas are brought closer, or tissue expansion, in which an implanted device stretches skin over time. These are not routine next steps for everyone with advanced male-pattern loss. Their role is specialized, and a source’s fixed three-to-four-week timetable should not be used as a universal surgical plan. Scalp micropigmentation creates small tattooed marks to suggest a closely shaved appearance; it does not grow hair. Wigs, hairpieces, styling changes and cosmetic fibers are other options, depending on the pattern and your preferences. Ask about pigment change, infection, touch-ups or maintenance where relevant. Choosing camouflage or no treatment is a valid decision at any stage. Make the scale useful without letting it define you If you want treatment, agree on a realistic goal: slowing further loss, improving density, changing the hairline’s appearance or feeling more comfortable with your look. Use photographs taken with similar lighting, angle and hair length at sensible intervals to judge progress with the clinician. Daily comparisons can exaggerate normal differences. Review benefits and adverse effects at the agreed time rather than switching products every few weeks. The speed of progression varies, and neither minoxidil nor finasteride guarantees permanent prevention after treatment stops. A long-term plan should account for maintenance as well as the initial result. Hair loss can affect confidence, and those feelings deserve attention. You do not need to minimize distress, but you also do not need to treat a stage number as a measure of age, health or worth. Ask for emotional support if worry is interfering with everyday life, and make treatment choices around your priorities. The scale includes seven main stages and variants; progression is not inevitable. The crown is different from the low back of the scalp. DHT susceptibility can be inherited from either parent. No universal two-year inactivity deadline or fixed success percentage predicts your response. Surgery, camouflage and no treatment are choices, not requirements of a stage. Does stage 2 mean I will eventually reach stage 7? No. Progression and speed vary. The stage describes the current pattern, not a fixed future. What does vertex mean? It means the top or crown of the scalp, rather than the low back of the head. How is the class A pattern different? The front hairline moves backward more continuously, without the usual separate crown patch and intervening bridge of hair. Can the chart diagnose sudden patchy loss? No. Sudden, patchy, painful or inflamed loss needs assessment for other causes rather than a stage assignment. Is male-pattern loss inherited only from my mother? No. Genetic susceptibility can come from either side of the family, and relatives can have different patterns. Do all follicles become untreatable after two years? No. There is no universal two-year cutoff. Earlier treatment may help preserve hair, but response is individual. Will minoxidil restore all my hair? Usually not. It can help some people over several months, and benefit generally depends on continued use. What if finasteride affects my mood? If depression or suicidal thoughts develop during hair-loss treatment, stop it and seek medical advice. If you cannot stay safe, use emergency support immediately. Are all laser devices equally effective? No. Evidence and treatment schedules differ. Ask about the exact device and realistic outcomes before spending money. Does a high stage mean I must have a transplant? No. Suitability and preferences matter. Medicines, camouflage or no treatment may also be reasonable choices.

title: Sexual health for men: consent, communication and care
description: A practical guide to respectful intimacy, masturbation myths, erection difficulties and treatment options, without performance rules or pressure.
body: Sexual wellbeing involves physical health, personal preferences and the freely expressed wishes of anyone you are intimate with. There is no single script for how a man should behave or what a successful encounter must achieve. Honest communication and appropriate medical care can make room for comfort, choice and changing needs. Support general health without promising a performance result Regular activity, suitable food, enough rest and help with stress can support overall and sexual health. Smoking, heavy drinking and some recreational drugs can contribute to erection problems. Changes are worth discussing even when sexual symptoms are not the only concern. These habits do not guarantee confidence, desire or a particular response. Fatigue, illness, relationship circumstances and medicines also matter. A difficulty is not evidence of poor character or insufficient effort, and needing treatment does not mean a healthy lifestyle has failed. Accept a refusal as an answer If a partner says no, accept it. A quick refusal does not mean you chose the wrong words and should try a more persuasive approach. Consent must be freely given, specific to the activity and open to being withdrawn. Previous sex, a relationship, affection or a physical response does not create permission. When someone is unsure, quiet, uncomfortable or no longer participating, stop and check. A person who cannot freely choose or communicate agreement cannot give consent. Neither partner owes an explanation before an activity stops. Let affection and preparation be a shared choice People differ in whether they want touch, closeness or sexual activity at a particular time. What is often called foreplay should be a mutually wanted part of intimacy, not a strategy for changing a refusal into agreement. Someone may want affection without wanting intercourse. Discuss preferences and limits at a calm moment rather than relying on a scene from a film or an assumption about gender. Saying what feels comfortable, what you would prefer and what you do not want can be useful. No list of techniques can replace listening to the person with you. Masturbation is not automatically a relationship problem Some people masturbate while in a relationship and others do not. It can feel relaxing or pleasurable, but it is not a duty or a treatment everyone needs. Private sexual behaviour does not by itself prove dissatisfaction with a partner. Couples may discuss privacy and boundaries without turning the conversation into an inspection of each other. If either person wants to share or discuss an intimate activity, both must freely agree. Watching a partner or disclosing personal preferences is optional, not a required way to learn about each other. Separate masturbation myths from symptoms that need help Masturbation does not ordinarily cause erectile dysfunction or permanently weaken an erection. Friction or rough handling can nevertheless cause sore skin or injury. Stop when there is pain, swelling or bleeding and seek care when symptoms are significant or persist. There is no universal number that defines too much. Consider whether the behaviour feels hard to control, causes injury, interferes with sleep, work or other responsibilities, or creates distress. A sexual-health professional or therapist can help assess the pattern without making shame the treatment. Avoid turning intimacy into an exchange or an exam Giving attention or participating in one activity does not entitle anyone to a return favour. Discussing mutual satisfaction is different from demanding gratitude, a particular sound or an orgasm. A person may express enjoyment quietly and should not need to perform it for reassurance. An unhurried setting and fewer phone or television distractions may help connection when both people want that. Being attentive to the person with you matters more than rigid rules about words or behaviour. It is always acceptable to pause for discomfort, an interruption or a change of mind rather than prioritise a planned outcome. Discuss boundaries before changing the activity Do not introduce rough contact or a more intense activity on the assumption that a partner will object if it is unwanted. Agreeing to one kind of contact does not authorise another. Pain should prompt a stop and a check, not an expectation that someone must endure it. A prearranged signal can be useful, but nobody has to remember a special word for their boundary to count. An ordinary request to stop, withdrawing or uncertainty is enough to pause. Consent is not made permanent by a conversation earlier in the day. Include infection and pregnancy prevention Many sexually transmitted infections have no obvious symptoms. Talk about appropriate testing and which body sites it covers, rather than treating a symptom-free appearance or one past result as a guarantee. Condoms and other barriers reduce several risks but do not prevent every infection involving uncovered skin. Ask about HPV and hepatitis B vaccination and HIV prevention when relevant to your exposure. If pregnancy is possible and not wanted, discuss a contraceptive plan too. A method that prevents pregnancy may provide no protection against an infection. Both people should understand the plan and be able to revisit it. Understand what erectile dysfunction describes Erectile dysfunction means difficulty getting or maintaining an erection sufficient for the sexual activity wanted. Occasional difficulties can happen with stress, tiredness or alcohol. Repeated difficulties may involve blood flow, nerves, diabetes, hormone problems, medicine effects or psychological factors, often in combination. It becomes more common with age, but age does not make assessment pointless. A fixed percentage for every decade cannot describe an individual. Erection difficulties do not automatically mean lack of attraction, low testosterone or a purely psychological problem. Use assessment to identify the relevant causes A clinician may ask about when the problem occurs, other erections, desire, pain, medical history, medicines and relationship stress. Blood pressure and selected checks for diabetes, cholesterol or hormones may be useful. An examination or specialist referral depends on the findings. Bring a list of prescription medicines, over-the-counter products and recreational substances. Do not stop treatment yourself because you suspect a sexual side effect; a safer dose or alternative may be available. Counselling or psychosexual therapy can accompany physical treatment, and partner involvement should be your choice. Erection medicines require an individual safety check Sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil and avanafil are examples of PDE5 inhibitors, which support blood flow involved in an erection. They are not interchangeable with testosterone or guaranteed to solve every cause. Timing, interactions and suitability depend on the medicine and your health. Do not combine these medicines with nitrate treatment for chest pain or recreational nitrites such as poppers; the blood-pressure drop can be dangerous. Tell the prescriber about heart or liver disease and all other products. Use an appropriately regulated prescribing or pharmacy service rather than an unidentified online performance product. Testosterone is for a confirmed deficiency, not routine enhancement Testosterone treatment may be considered when compatible symptoms occur with consistently low measured levels and an appropriate assessment. A clinician usually confirms the result with repeat morning testing and investigates the cause. A single low value or erection difficulty alone is not enough. Gel, patches and injections are among possible forms, depending on local availability and circumstances. They need follow-up for benefit and adverse effects. Tell the clinician about future pregnancy plans before treatment: testosterone supplied from outside the body can suppress sperm production and is not a fertility treatment. Know how injections, vacuum devices and implants differ Specialist medicines can be injected into the penis or, for some products, placed in the urethra. They require a prescription, individual instruction and a plan for adverse effects. They are not automatically safe for every person who cannot take a tablet, and this is not a procedure to learn from a general article. An external vacuum device uses a cylinder and pump to draw blood into the penis, often with a ring to maintain the erection. A penile prosthesis is different: it is implanted surgically and may be inflatable or a bendable device. Most people do not need surgery; discuss alternatives, practical use, complications and long-term expectations with a urologist. Recognise urgent problems and keep follow-up open An erection lasting more than four hours needs emergency assessment, especially after an erection medicine or injection. Sudden loss of vision or hearing after an erection medicine also requires immediate medical advice. Do not take extra doses or wait for the next planned appointment to address these symptoms. Persistent genital pain, sores, discharge or other changes deserve assessment even when they do not seem urgent. Tell the clinician if treatment is not helping or creates new problems. Sexual health can change across life; respectful communication and access to care remain useful at every age, whether or not sexual activity is a priority. A refusal is not an invitation to persuade. There is no required sexual performance or frequency. Masturbation concerns depend on symptoms and daily impact, not an invented quota. Repeated erection problems deserve assessment. Medicine, hormone, device and surgical options have different precautions. Should I ask differently after my partner says no? Accept the answer. Communication should clarify preferences and boundaries, not find a way around a refusal. Does someone need a special word to stop an activity? No. Any request to stop or indication of uncertainty is enough to pause and check. Does masturbation automatically weaken erections? No. It does not ordinarily cause erectile dysfunction, although rough handling can cause soreness or injury. How often is too often? There is no universal number. Consider pain, loss of control, distress and interference with everyday responsibilities. Are erection problems always a sign of low attraction? No. Physical health, medicines, fatigue, stress and other factors can contribute. Can I stop a medicine if it seems to affect erections? Discuss it with the prescriber first. A supervised change may be possible; stopping independently can be unsafe. Can I take sildenafil with a nitrate for chest pain? Do not combine them. Tell the prescriber about nitrates and all other medicines or recreational substances. Will testosterone improve my fertility? Not necessarily; testosterone treatment can suppress sperm production. Discuss current or future pregnancy plans before starting it. Is an external vacuum pump the same as an implant? No. A vacuum device is used outside the body; a prosthesis requires surgery and has different risks and long-term considerations. What if an erection lasts longer than four hours? Seek emergency assessment. Do not wait for it to settle or take another dose of an erection medicine.

title: Contraception, COVID-19 and blood clots: when a plan may need to change
description: Distinguish mild infection from severe illness, understand the limits of early clotting studies, and plan contraception changes with a clinician.
body: A positive COVID-19 test does not automatically mean stopping contraception. Severe illness, reduced mobility and individual clotting risks may change the plan. The important distinction is between different treatments and clinical situations. The concern is real, but the situations differ Severe COVID-19 can disturb the balance between clot formation and the processes that limit it. Oestrogen-containing contraception also increases the risk of a clot in a vein for some users. These facts make a medication review sensible during serious illness; they do not mean that every positive test requires stopping contraception. Your usual method, how unwell you are, whether you can move around and any previous clot or clotting disorder all matter. Age, smoking, body weight, other illnesses and recent surgery may also affect the assessment. A general statement about women, pregnancy and oestrogen cannot substitute for this individual picture. How COVID-19 can contribute to clotting Clotting normally helps stop bleeding after an injury. In severe infection, widespread inflammation, injury to the lining of blood vessels and changes in platelet activity can favour unwanted clot formation. Platelets are small blood components involved in clotting. Reduced movement during illness adds another risk by slowing blood flow. A clot can block the supply of blood to tissue or travel elsewhere. A deep vein thrombosis, often in a leg, can lead to a pulmonary embolism if clot material reaches the lungs. Arterial clots are different and may interrupt blood supply to organs. Reports during severe COVID-19 have included the brain, large arteries, kidney circulation and limbs; these are possible complications, not an expected course for everyone. Why an intensive-care percentage is not your personal risk An early Dutch study followed 184 intensive-care patients with COVID-19 pneumonia and reported an estimated cumulative incidence of thrombotic complications of 31%. It combined several outcomes, including pulmonary embolism and other venous or arterial events. It was not a survey of otherwise well people taking the pill at home. The study helped draw attention to clotting in critical illness. Its setting, observation period, testing practices and early-pandemic treatment context limit what the number can tell a reader today. It should not be reworded as one in three people with COVID-19 developing a clot, or as evidence that contraception caused those events. Early hormone research raised questions rather than settling them A 2020 Endocrinology article discussed possible interactions between COVID-19, oestrogen treatment and pregnancy. It drew on known clotting biology and early observations, including placental vascular findings. A proposed biological explanation is not the same as a trial demonstrating how much risk a particular contraceptive adds during infection. Oestrogen can influence clotting proteins and immune signalling, including pathways involving T cells and ACE2. Those mechanisms do not establish that it either protects an individual from severe COVID-19 or inevitably makes infection worse. Observed differences between women and men have many possible contributors. Findings from selected placental examinations also cannot predict every pregnancy outcome. Descriptions of what had or had not been reported in 2020 belong to that period. They should not be presented as a current claim that no evidence exists or that no clinical guidance is available. Decisions now need the relevant guidance and the person’s health circumstances. Combined contraception is one specific group Combined hormonal contraception contains an oestrogen and a progestogen. It includes combined pills, the contraceptive patch and the vaginal ring. Progestogen-only and non-hormonal methods are separate groups and should not all be assigned the same oestrogen-related risk. Risk varies between formulations and users, and a previous clot or thrombophilia can make a combined method unsuitable. A clot can also occur without a known clotting disorder. The source’s single annual one-in-3,000 estimate and universal three-to-fourfold multiplier are too blunt to guide a personal decision. Ask what the absolute risk means for your own method and circumstances, including starting or restarting it. Menopausal hormone therapy needs a separate assessment Hormone replacement therapy for menopause is not the same treatment as contraception. Oral oestrogen can increase venous clotting risk, while menopausal oestrogen delivered through the skin has a different risk profile. Dose, route, indication and medical history all matter. Do not assume that a contraceptive patch has the same properties as a menopausal oestrogen patch simply because both stick to the skin. If significant illness develops, discuss your particular hormone treatment with the prescribing team. Changing or stopping it should take account of symptoms, benefits and the clinical situation rather than follow a blanket internet rule. Pregnancy and the period after birth also matter Pregnancy changes clotting and circulation, and venous clot risk is increased, especially around the time after birth. This involves more than a higher oestrogen level alone. Severe infection, dehydration, hospitalisation and reduced mobility can add to existing pregnancy-related risks. Tell the maternity team if you have COVID-19 symptoms, especially if you are worsening or struggling to drink or move. They can assess whether treatment or clot prevention is needed. Most pregnant people recover without serious complications, but that is not a reason to dismiss new breathlessness or a swollen painful leg. Clot prevention in pregnancy and after birth must follow maternity advice. Do not use an old six-to-tenfold comparison to calculate your own risk or begin anticoagulants. Likewise, avoiding an unintended pregnancy remains relevant when weighing a change in contraception. Mild COVID-19 usually allows a combined method to continue Society of Family Planning recommendations, reaffirmed in April 2025, allow continuation of combined hormonal contraception with asymptomatic or mild infection. A positive test by itself is not a reason to throw away a pill pack or interrupt protection from pregnancy. Ask for advice if symptoms become more serious or you spend a prolonged time largely immobile. Mention other clotting risks and whether contraception is also treating heavy bleeding or another condition. The plan should cover both pregnancy prevention and any symptoms the method normally controls. Severe illness may require a temporary change Combined hormonal contraception should be suspended during hospitalisation for severe COVID-19, with the treating team coordinating the change. Serious symptoms or prolonged immobility outside hospital also warrant a clinical review. Do not wait for a routine contraceptive appointment if breathing or other symptoms are deteriorating. A suitable progestogen-only or non-hormonal alternative may be offered. Ask when it becomes effective, whether additional protection is needed and what to do if there has already been sex that could lead to pregnancy. Emergency contraception may be relevant after a gap in protection. A temporary change should come with clear instructions, not simply advice to stop. Illness and medicines can affect pill reliability Vomiting or significant diarrhoea can interfere with an oral contraceptive. Follow the instructions for your exact product and seek pharmacy advice if you cannot keep tablets down or do not know whether protection has been interrupted. Instructions differ between pill types. Tell the clinician or pharmacist about contraception before starting an antiviral such as Paxlovid. Product information may advise additional contraception during treatment and for a period afterwards; the current local label and your method should guide the plan. Do not assume that stopping the antiviral immediately ends every interaction precaution. Restarting depends on recovery, mobility and method After severe illness, agree with the clinician when it is appropriate to restart an oestrogen-containing method. A negative COVID-19 test alone does not show that mobility and clotting risk have returned to baseline. Newly diagnosed conditions or a clot may change which method is suitable in the longer term. WHO’s retained pandemic guidance discusses waiting after prolonged immobilisation, but that page is no longer being updated. Use it as context rather than as a substitute for current local advice. Keep the alternative method effective until the switch is complete, and ask whether restarting requires a period of additional protection. Recognise a possible clot promptly New one-sided leg pain, swelling, warmth or colour change needs urgent assessment for a possible deep vein thrombosis. Similar symptoms can occur in an arm. These symptoms are not proof of a clot, but they should not be left until the infection has passed. Sudden breathing difficulty, chest pain, coughing blood, fainting or collapse can indicate a pulmonary embolism and requires immediate medical help. Sudden face or arm weakness, speech difficulty, loss of vision or a severe unexplained headache can signal a stroke. Call emergency services for these symptoms and do not drive yourself. COVID-19, anxiety and a clot can have overlapping symptoms. A reassuring percentage, a previous mild infection or the absence of leg pain cannot safely exclude a pulmonary embolism. Clinical assessment determines whether blood tests or imaging are needed. Practical prevention without self-prescribing Keep gently mobile as your health and the treating team’s advice allow, and avoid unnecessary long periods sitting still. Drink appropriate fluids and seek help with stopping smoking. If you are too unwell to move or keep fluids down, ask for medical advice instead of pushing through exercise. A balanced diet supports general health, but reducing fat or avoiding a particular food does not immediately prevent or treat COVID-related clots. Do not start aspirin or an anticoagulant as a precaution on your own. These medicines can cause bleeding and are prescribed according to an individual benefit-risk assessment. If clot prevention is prescribed, ask how long to take it and what bleeding or other symptoms need help. At discharge or a medication change, request a written plan for contraception, other hormone treatment, follow-up and warning signs. This keeps recovery and pregnancy prevention connected. Mild infection usually does not require stopping a combined method. Severe illness and prolonged immobility need a coordinated review. Contraceptive and menopausal hormone patches are not interchangeable. A change should preserve effective pregnancy prevention. Should I stop my combined pill after any positive test? Usually not for asymptomatic or mild illness. Seek advice if symptoms worsen, mobility is substantially reduced or you have other clotting risks. Does the 31% figure describe everyone with COVID-19? No. It came from an early study of critically ill intensive-care patients and combined several thrombotic outcomes. Do all contraceptive methods contain oestrogen? No. Combined methods, progestogen-only methods and non-hormonal methods have different ingredients and risk profiles. Is an HRT patch the same as a contraceptive patch? No. They use different formulations for different purposes. Advice about menopausal transdermal oestrogen cannot simply be transferred to contraception. Can I have a clot without a known clotting disorder? Yes. Illness, medicines and other factors can contribute, and sometimes there is no obvious explanation. Symptoms need assessment. What if I am pregnant and become unwell? Contact the maternity team for assessment, particularly if symptoms worsen or drinking and mobility are affected. They decide whether any clot-prevention treatment is needed. Can I restart as soon as my test is negative? Not necessarily. Recovery, mobility, new health conditions and the method all matter. Agree on timing and any additional protection. Does an antiviral affect contraception? Some products require interaction precautions. Check the current local leaflet and speak to a pharmacist about the exact medicine, method and duration of backup protection. Should I take aspirin to prevent a clot? Do not start it or an anticoagulant yourself. Prevention is based on clinical risk and bleeding considerations. Can sudden breathlessness wait until my COVID symptoms settle? No. Sudden breathlessness, chest pain, coughing blood, fainting or stroke-like symptoms need immediate medical help.

title: COVID-19 vaccines and Omicron: what the early comparisons showed
description: A dated explanation of Pfizer, Moderna and Janssen findings from the first Omicron wave, and why those figures cannot guide today’s vaccination schedule.
body: When Omicron emerged in late 2021, it changed how well the original COVID-19 vaccines prevented infection. Early studies found that booster doses improved immune responses and protection, especially against serious illness. This article explains those historical Pfizer, Moderna and Johnson & Johnson comparisons, distinguishes laboratory findings from clinical outcomes, and shows why current vaccine decisions need current local guidance. Why the date of a vaccine comparison matters The original Omicron reports were written while the variant was spreading rapidly and researchers were working with incomplete data. They discussed the vaccines, dose schedules and population immunity of late 2021 and early 2022. Those findings remain useful for understanding what happened, but they are not a ranking of the products available now. At that time, two doses of an original mRNA vaccine, or one dose of the original Janssen vaccine, were often described as a completed primary course. The expression fully vaccinated therefore had a different practical meaning from being up to date with a later season’s recommendations. A reported percentage belongs to a particular study. It depends on which outcome was measured, the variant, the participants, previous infection and time since vaccination. There is no single permanent percentage that describes a vaccine against every form of Omicron. Omicron compared with Delta Early Omicron studies found substantially more escape from protection against infection than had been seen with Delta. This helped explain why reinfections and infections in vaccinated people became more common, even when vaccination continued to reduce the risk of severe outcomes. Imperial College London’s December 2021 analysis estimated that the relative risk of reinfection with Omicron was about 5.4 times that with Delta in the data it studied. That comparison was an early population estimate, not a prediction that an individual would be infected a fixed number of times.
