Have the device checked and use another contraceptive method meanwhile. Ask promptly whether emergency contraception is needed after recent sex. Can orgasm cause brief tightenings during pregnancy? Yes, but persistent pain, regular contractions, bleeding or fluid leakage needs maternity advice. Does ovulation mean an egg drops from a tube into the uterus? No. Ovulation is the release of an egg from an ovary. Does urinating after sex guarantee that I will not get a UTI? No. It may be suggested as a preventive step, but it is not guaranteed protection or a treatment. Is PID always the same thing as an STI? No. PID can follow an STI or involve other bacteria and affects the upper reproductive tract. Are ibuprofen and paracetamol muscle relaxants? No. They are pain medicines with different actions and precautions, not a universal treatment for pelvic muscle tension. Should I start several supplements for the pain? No. They are not established treatment for unexplained post-sex pain and may have side effects or interactions. Can I stop an examination if it hurts? Yes. You remain in control and can ask the clinician to pause or stop at any time.

title: Irregular periods: eight home approaches and what the evidence says
description: A detailed guide to yoga, movement, ginger, cinnamon, vitamins, vinegar and pineapple, with clear limits and advice on when irregular bleeding needs care.
body: If your periods have become unpredictable, it is understandable to look for something you can do at home. Begin by checking what has changed and whether there is a cause that needs treatment. Supportive habits can help, but symptom relief and regular ovulation are not the same outcome. First, work out what has changed A menstrual cycle is counted from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. Twenty-eight days is an average, not a target everyone must meet. The US Office on Women’s Health describes a usual adult range of 24–38 days; other guidance uses somewhat different limits. Age, your previous pattern and symptoms matter alongside the number. A few days of variation does not automatically mean disease. Keep a record of starting dates, bleeding duration, flooding, pain and any bleeding between periods. Do not use an app’s predicted ovulation date as proof that you ovulated or as reliable contraception. Irregular timing and heavy bleeding are different problems Periods that arrive unpredictably are different from periods that are unusually heavy or long, although they can happen together. Menorrhagia is an older term for heavy menstrual bleeding; it does not mean every kind of irregular cycle. Repeatedly soaking protection, needing double protection, passing substantial clots or missing ordinary activities deserves attention. Bleeding for more than a week is another reason to arrange an assessment. The impact on your life matters even if you cannot estimate the blood loss in millilitres. Look for a cause before choosing a remedy Pregnancy is one possibility when a period is late. Breastfeeding, puberty, the transition to menopause, stress, changes in weight and insufficient energy intake can also alter cycles. Thyroid disease and an ovulation disorder commonly known as PCOS can require specific treatment. Some current guidance calls PCOS polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, or PMOS. Fibroids, polyps, adenomyosis, endometriosis, pelvic infection and bleeding disorders can contribute to abnormal bleeding or pain. Less commonly, a precancerous or cancerous condition is involved. An explanation such as “too much oestrogen or progesterone” is too simple to identify the cause or select treatment. Medicines and contraception can change the pattern A copper coil can make bleeding heavier or more painful. A hormonal coil often reduces bleeding, although spotting or an unsettled pattern can occur after insertion. Pills, injections and implants can also change bleeding; an absent withdrawal bleed on a contraceptive is not the same situation as unexplained missed natural periods. Blood-thinning medicines may increase bleeding. By contrast, selected anti-inflammatory medicines such as ibuprofen or mefenamic acid are used to reduce period pain and blood loss. They are not suitable for everyone. Do not stop a prescribed medicine or start a new one without checking your individual situation. 1. Yoga may support wellbeing and symptom management Gentle yoga or guided relaxation may be a useful way to manage stress and feel more comfortable. A 2013 randomized study of Yoga Nidra enrolled 150 people with menstrual disorders, with 126 completing the protocol. Its schedule involved 35–40 minutes on five days a week for six months, and it reported changes in several hormone measurements. That result does not establish yoga as a treatment for every cause of irregular periods. Improvements in relaxation, pain or a laboratory value are different from reliably restoring ovulation. Choose a comfortable beginner routine and an appropriately trained instructor if needed; the research schedule is not a prescription you must follow. 2. Support adequate nutrition and a sustainable weight Both substantial weight gain and weight loss can accompany changes in menstruation. Having a higher body weight does not prove that weight is the cause, and ovulation disorders also affect people in smaller bodies. Very restrictive eating can reduce the energy available for normal reproductive function. Discuss recent changes, food access, training demands and any concerns about eating with a clinician or dietitian. If weight management forms part of your care, make the plan individual and realistic. In PCOS, health behaviours can improve wellbeing and metabolic health even when the number on the scale does not change. A crash diet is not a cycle treatment. 3. Choose regular movement without overtraining Walking, swimming, cycling or another enjoyable activity can support general health. Exercise may also ease menstrual cramps for some people. Research on pain relief, including small exercise studies, should not be read as proof that exercise alone corrects irregular ovulation. The balance matters: intensive training combined with inadequate food or recovery can contribute to missed periods. Increasing exercise further is not the answer in that situation. Build activity gradually, allow rest and seek advice if periods stop, fatigue is persistent or you are recovering from an eating disorder. 4. Ginger has more evidence for symptoms than cycle timing Ginger supplements have been studied for cramps, heavy bleeding and premenstrual symptoms. One trial involving 92 young women found less menstrual blood loss over three treatment cycles; a separate small trial reported improvement in PMS symptoms. These are specific outcomes in selected participants, not proof of a general period-regulating effect. NCCIH considers ginger potentially helpful for menstrual cramps, while noting that study quality varies. Research capsule doses and schedules differ and are not interchangeable with ginger tea. Supplements can cause heartburn, diarrhoea or irritation and may interact with medicines. Ask about suitability, particularly with heavy bleeding, pregnancy, breastfeeding or regular medication; do not use ginger to postpone assessment. 5. Cinnamon findings are preliminary A 2014 PCOS trial allocated 45 women to cinnamon or placebo, but only 17 completed all six months. More frequent cycles in the cinnamon group were encouraging, yet the small numbers and loss to follow-up limit confidence. It is not enough evidence to replace established care for an ovulation disorder. Other small studies of painful periods reported differences in cramps, bleeding, nausea and vomiting. Those findings concern symptoms during a period rather than a guarantee of regular future periods. Cinnamon in food is different from concentrated supplements. Cassia cinnamon contains coumarin, which can be a concern with substantial prolonged intake, particularly in liver disease; check any supplement with a professional. 6. Correct deficiencies instead of taking large vitamin doses A 2015 observational study linked lower vitamin D levels with irregular cycles. An association cannot show that low vitamin D caused the irregularity or that taking extra will fix it. Small supplementation studies in people with PCOS and low vitamin D have reported changes in menstrual frequency, but they do not establish a universal treatment. Food sources, fortified products and an appropriate supplement can help meet vitamin D needs. Testing or higher-dose treatment should be based on clinical advice. More is not automatically better: excessive supplemental vitamin D can cause harm. Do not use prolonged unprotected sun exposure as a prescription for cycle regularity. Vitamin B6, calcium and folic acid have different roles Some studies, including a small 2016 calcium-and-B6 trial, have examined premenstrual symptoms. NIH describes the benefit of B6 for PMS as uncertain. Relief of mood changes, breast discomfort or bloating would still not demonstrate that ovulation has become regular. Avoid combining several high-dose products. Excess B6 can damage nerves. Folic acid is important when pregnancy is possible or planned, but is not a medicine to trigger a period. A common recommendation is 400 micrograms daily before conception and through the first 12 weeks; some people need a clinician-prescribed different dose. Check local advice and the contents of any prenatal supplement. 7. Apple cider vinegar is not an established treatment The often-quoted 2013 study included only seven people with PCOS who consumed a vinegar beverage. Ovulatory menstruation was observed in four within 40 days. With such a small uncontrolled study, it is not possible to know whether vinegar caused the change or predict who would benefit. This finding does not establish a safe and effective daily dose for irregular periods or infertility. Adding honey or diluting vinegar does not turn it into a proven hormone treatment. You can use vinegar as a food ingredient if it suits you; do not rely on a vinegar-drinking routine instead of care for missed periods. 8. Pineapple does not reliably bring on a period Pineapple contains bromelain, a group of protein-digesting enzymes. Claims that eating it softens the uterine lining, corrects cycle timing or reliably treats PMS are not supported by good clinical evidence. Findings about inflammation in other settings cannot be assumed to apply to menstruation. Pineapple can be part of an ordinary varied diet if you tolerate it. Bromelain capsules are a different product: they can cause digestive symptoms, may interact with medicines and have limited pregnancy and breastfeeding safety information. Neither food nor a supplement is a dependable way to start a late period. Make a simple plan that you can review Start with a pregnancy test if pregnancy is possible, follow the instructions and get advice if uncertainty remains. Write down when the pattern changed, contraceptive use, medicines, supplements, pain and any major change in eating, exercise or stress. Bring this record to your appointment. Choose supportive habits that fit your life rather than trying all eight approaches at once. If you try an agreed treatment, record the symptom you are trying to improve and when it will be reviewed. Feeling less crampy is useful, but it should not hide persistent missed periods or unusually heavy blood loss. Arrange a medical review for persistent changes Ask for assessment if irregularity continues, periods stop unexpectedly, bleeding is prolonged or symptoms interfere with daily life. Mention new facial hair or acne, marked weight change, unusual nipple discharge, tiredness or difficulty conceiving. These details can help direct pregnancy, blood-count, thyroid or other investigations; not everyone needs every test. Bleeding between periods, after sex or after menopause should be checked. Fever, unusual discharge or significant pelvic pain may need prompt assessment for infection or another cause. Management could involve treating a hormone disorder, reducing heavy bleeding or supporting ovulation, depending on the diagnosis and whether you want pregnancy. Know when bleeding or pain needs urgent care Seek urgent help for very heavy bleeding, severe pain, fainting or feeling seriously unwell. Heavy bleeding with breathlessness, chest pain, dizziness or weakness needs emergency assessment. Do not wait for a supplement to work or for an exact number of hours if you are deteriorating. A missed period followed by unusual bleeding and pelvic or abdominal pain needs urgent advice because an ectopic pregnancy is possible. Severe one-sided pain, shoulder-tip pain or collapse is an emergency. Home remedies cannot safely distinguish these conditions from an ordinary period. Keep timing, duration, pain and blood loss separate in your record. All eight approaches have different evidence and limitations. Ginger and cinnamon symptom studies do not prove reliable cycle regulation. Adequate nutrition matters; overtraining and crash dieting can make matters worse. Persistent changes and urgent symptoms need appropriate medical assessment. Does every healthy cycle need to last 28 days? No. Twenty-eight days is an average. Your age, usual pattern and symptoms matter; persistent changes or concerning bleeding deserve assessment even if an app labels them normal. Can home remedies guarantee regular periods? No. Different causes require different care. Some habits may support wellbeing and some remedies may help symptoms, but none of these eight approaches reliably treats every cause. Does ginger regulate ovulation? The better-known research concerns cramps, heavy bleeding or PMS. That does not establish ginger as a reliable treatment for irregular ovulation. Should I take cinnamon instead of prescribed PCOS treatment? No. The preliminary cycle study was small and had substantial dropout. Discuss any supplement alongside, rather than as a replacement for, your care plan. Is apple cider vinegar proven to restore fertility? No. A seven-person uncontrolled study cannot establish that claim. Do not delay evaluation of irregular ovulation or infertility while trying vinegar. Can pineapple safely bring on a late period? It is not a reliable method. Check for pregnancy when relevant and seek advice about a persistent missed period rather than trying to trigger bleeding with foods or supplements. Will more exercise always help? No. Movement can support health, but excessive exercise with inadequate nutrition can suppress menstruation. A recovery and nutrition plan may be needed instead. Are vitamin supplements harmless because they are vitamins? No. Excess vitamin D can be harmful and high supplemental B6 can damage nerves. Correct a deficiency with appropriate advice and check for overlapping ingredients. Do all coils cause heavy periods? No. A copper coil may increase bleeding; a hormonal coil often reduces it after an initial adjustment period. New heavy bleeding or pain should still be checked. When should I get urgent help? Seek urgent care for severe pain or heavy bleeding, especially with faintness, breathlessness, chest pain or weakness. Possible pregnancy with pain and unusual bleeding also needs prompt assessment.

title: Tampons and pain: cramps, discomfort and safe use
description: Distinguish uterine period cramps from painful tampon use, understand possible causes and learn safe wearing limits and warning signs.
body: A tampon should not be something you have to endure. Period cramps and local insertion pain can happen at the same time, but they may have different causes and need different care. Tampon discomfort and period cramps are different problems If inserting, wearing or removing a tampon hurts, take that discomfort seriously. You do not have to keep using it to prove that you can tolerate it. A tampon can cause local irritation or bring attention to an existing pain problem, even though it is not the usual cause of uterine menstrual cramps. A tampon sits in the vagina, below the cervix. It does not pass into the uterus. Menstrual cramps originate mainly from contractions of the uterus, so cramps beginning on the same day you insert a tampon do not necessarily mean the tampon caused them. Notice whether the discomfort is at the vaginal opening, deeper inside, or across the lower abdomen. Burning with insertion and a familiar period cramp may need different responses. If removing the tampon helps, use an external product and seek advice about recurring pain. Why period cramps often peak early in bleeding Prostaglandins are natural chemicals involved in the contractions that help the uterus shed its lining. Higher levels around the start of a period can contribute to cramping. As the lining is shed and these levels fall, ordinary period pain often eases. Pain may be accompanied by bowel changes, nausea, headache or other period symptoms. Not every symptom during a period is caused by the same chemical, and severe pain should not be dismissed simply because menstruation has begun. Painful periods caused by another condition are sometimes called secondary dysmenorrhoea. They may worsen over time, start before bleeding or last beyond the usual early days. A change from your normal pattern or pain that prevents daily activities deserves assessment. Absorbency, dryness and placement can affect comfort Tampons come in different absorbencies, and some have applicators while others are inserted with a finger. Choose the lowest absorbency that manages the flow. A product intended for heavy flow may feel dry and uncomfortable when bleeding is light, particularly during removal. Read the instructions for the product and do not force insertion against pain. A tampon that sits uncomfortably low may be noticeable, but repeatedly pushing it further is not an answer when insertion is painful. Stop, remove it gently if possible and try an external pad or period underwear instead. Absorbency is not a measure of how mature or experienced you are. There is no requirement to progress to a larger product. If discomfort persists with an appropriate product, seek an explanation rather than assuming you simply need more practice. Urinary or vaginal symptoms need their own assessment A urinary tract infection can cause burning when urinating, urgency, lower abdominal discomfort or changes in urine. People with a shorter urethra are more prone to these infections because bacteria have less distance to travel to the bladder. The urethra and vagina are separate openings. Pelvic discomfort from a UTI may make tampon use uncomfortable, but this does not establish that the tampon caused the infection. Nor does switching products treat it. Urinary symptoms, especially with fever, back pain or pregnancy, need appropriate medical advice. Itching, unusual discharge, soreness or sensitivity to a product may instead suggest a vaginal or skin problem. Tell the clinician about scented products, soaps and anything you have applied. Avoid trying several treatments for presumed infection without knowing what is causing the symptoms. Endometriosis and pelvic pain can coexist with tampon discomfort Endometriosis involves tissue similar to the uterine lining outside the uterus and can be associated with inflammation and pain. Possible symptoms include very painful periods, pain during or after sex and pain with bowel movements or urination. The pattern varies between people. Someone with endometriosis or another pelvic pain condition may find insertion uncomfortable, but tampon pain alone does not diagnose endometriosis. It is also incorrect to assume that every person with the condition will find tampons painful. Describe the wider pattern, including pain on days when you are not using a tampon. Treatment should address the underlying problem and your comfort, rather than focusing only on finding a menstrual product that you can endure. Involuntary tightening is not a failure to relax Vaginismus describes involuntary tightening around the vaginal entrance when insertion is attempted. A tampon, finger, menstrual cup, examination or penetrative sex may trigger discomfort or make insertion difficult. This can occur even when you want the activity and are trying to relax. Forcing an object through pain can make the experience more distressing. Stop and ask for care from a clinician familiar with pelvic-floor or sexual pain. Depending on the cause, treatment may involve pelvic-health physiotherapy, psychological support or other approaches chosen with you. An examination should be explained and carried out with your consent. You can request a chaperone, ask what each step involves and stop at any time. External menstrual products are a valid long-term choice, not merely a temporary step toward using tampons. Use tampons within safe wearing limits Wash your hands before and after handling a tampon, use a fresh one each time and follow the package directions. Tampons are designed for menstrual flow, not for everyday discharge or for practising when you are not bleeding. Do not wash and reuse a single-use product. FDA guidance advises changing a tampon every four to eight hours and never leaving one in longer than eight hours. Use the lowest absorbency you need. If you expect to sleep longer than the safe wearing interval, choose an external product rather than extending the time. If you cannot remove a tampon, think one may have been forgotten or develop unusual discharge or pain, contact a healthcare service promptly. Do not insert another tampon or use sharp instruments to retrieve one. Tell the clinician how long it may have been in place. Know the warning signs of toxic shock syndrome Toxic shock syndrome, or TSS, is a rare but serious illness caused by toxins produced by certain bacteria. Tampon use is one setting in which it can occur, but it can also occur without tampons. It is not accurately explained as a large tampon inevitably scratching bacteria into the bloodstream. Sudden fever, vomiting or diarrhoea, muscle aches, a sunburn-like or rough rash, dizziness or feeling faint during or soon after a period needs urgent attention. Do not wait for every symptom, a particular rash or severe pelvic pain before seeking help. Remove the tampon if you can and seek medical care immediately, telling the team you have been using one. If there is collapse, confusion, difficulty breathing or severe illness, use emergency services. Difficulty removing the tampon should not delay the call for help. Comfort measures for ordinary menstrual cramps For familiar mild cramps, a comfortably warm bath, shower or wrapped heat pack may help. Protect the skin from burns and avoid sleeping on an active heating pad. You do not need cinnamon bark essential oil or other fragranced additives in bathwater; these can irritate sensitive tissue and are not an established cramp treatment. Gentle movement, stretching or exercise may help some people, but adapt it to how you feel. A fixed forty-five-to-sixty-minute session at any intensity is not a requirement, particularly during significant pain. Stop an activity that makes symptoms worse. Ibuprofen or naproxen can reduce prostaglandin-related cramps when suitable for you. Follow the label and check with a clinician or pharmacist if you have health conditions, take other medicines or could be pregnant. Do not combine NSAIDs or use pain relief to continue painful tampon insertion. Longer-term treatment should address the cause Hormonal contraception can help some people with painful or heavy periods, but the choice depends on health history, contraception needs and pregnancy plans. Different methods have different benefits and risks. Discuss these options rather than starting another person’s pill for cramps. Arrange review for severe or worsening period pain, unusually heavy or irregular bleeding, cramps that last longer than your usual pattern, painful insertion or sex, and urinary symptoms. Pain extending beyond the first day or two is worth describing, but a strict day count is not the sole test of whether something is wrong. Seek urgent help for sudden severe pelvic or abdominal pain, especially with faintness, fever, heavy bleeding or possible pregnancy. Keep a brief record of symptoms and which products or treatments you tried. The aim is comfortable menstrual care and an explanation for pain, not persuading you to tolerate it. A tampon sits in the vagina; period cramps arise mainly in the uterus. Painful insertion deserves attention. Tampons are optional. Never wear one longer than eight hours. Do not wait for every TSS symptom before seeking help. Can a tampon reach into the uterus? No. It sits in the vagina below the cervix. Does having cramps while using a tampon prove it caused them? No. Menstrual cramps and tampon use often begin together, but local discomfort may still come from the product or another condition. Should I force insertion if I feel tightness? No. Stop when it hurts and seek advice if the problem recurs. Is higher absorbency always better? No. Use the lowest absorbency that manages your flow; excessive absorbency can feel dry and uncomfortable. Does tampon pain diagnose endometriosis? No. It is one symptom to describe alongside the wider pattern, not a diagnosis on its own. Can vaginismus happen even when I want to use a tampon? Yes. The muscle tightening is involuntary and can be treated with appropriate support. Can I leave a tampon in overnight for ten hours? No. Never leave one in longer than eight hours; use an external product if needed. Should I wait for a rash before seeking help for suspected toxic shock? No. Sudden fever, vomiting, dizziness or serious illness during tampon use needs immediate assessment even without every symptom. Should I add cinnamon essential oil to a bath for cramps? No. It is not an established treatment and may irritate sensitive skin or tissue. Do I have to learn to tolerate tampons? No. Pads or period underwear are valid choices, and pain should be assessed rather than endured.

title: When periods do not start: or stop unexpectedly
description: Missing periods can have several causes. Evaluation depends on age, previous cycles, symptoms and pregnancy possibility, not marital status.
body: Amenorrhea means that menstrual periods are absent. It can describe periods that have never started or periods that stop after previously occurring. The next step is to understand the reason, without making assumptions about someone’s relationships or sexual history. Know when to ask for an assessment Arrange an assessment if a first period has not arrived by age 15, or if breast development has not begun by age 13. A clinician may recommend earlier evaluation based on growth, development, pain or other symptoms. If periods have previously occurred and then stop for around three months without an expected explanation, seek advice. Do not wait for that interval if you have significant symptoms or pregnancy is possible. Cycles can be less predictable in the first years after periods begin, but a very long gap still deserves discussion. It should not be dismissed simply because someone is young. Repeated monthly pelvic pain with little or no bleeding can occasionally signal an obstruction and needs assessment. Consider pregnancy promptly when it is possible Whether a person is married does not determine whether pregnancy is possible. A clinician should ask sensitive questions privately and respectfully. A home pregnancy test can usually be used from the first day of a missed period. If you do not know when the period is due, test at least 21 days after the relevant unprotected sex. A negative result taken too early may need repeating. Severe pelvic pain, faintness, shoulder-tip pain or bleeding with possible pregnancy needs urgent assessment. Do not wait for a later test or a routine amenorrhea appointment. Ovulation can occur before the first returning period after birth or after a period of irregular cycles. Absent bleeding is not automatically reliable contraception. There are several possible explanations Pregnancy, breastfeeding and menopause can explain absent periods in the appropriate circumstances. Some hormonal contraceptives intentionally reduce or stop bleeding. Other possibilities include thyroid disease, raised prolactin, changes in ovarian function and the condition commonly called PCOS, now also called polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome or PMOS. Insufficient energy intake relative to activity, restrictive eating, substantial weight changes, illness and stress may affect the signals that control ovulation. This can happen across different body sizes. Less common explanations include differences in reproductive development, scarring inside the uterus after a procedure, or other structural problems. Hormonal disruption does not usually mean a tumor is present. Some medicines can affect bleeding or prolactin. Bring a complete medicine list, but do not stop a prescription on your own. Examples of less common developmental causes include Turner syndrome and differences in gonadal development such as Swyer syndrome. Intrauterine scar tissue is sometimes called Asherman syndrome. These diagnoses need specialist assessment and are not inferred from a missed period alone. Some antipsychotic or antidepressant medicines can affect prolactin or cycles, while chemotherapy can affect ovarian function. Review blood-pressure medicines and all other prescriptions as well, rather than assuming every drug in a broad class causes amenorrhea. Bleeding can take time to settle after stopping hormonal contraception, but pregnancy testing and review should not be postponed indefinitely. Expect a targeted evaluation The clinician may ask about the timing of puberty, previous periods, weight or eating changes, exercise, headaches, visual changes, nipple discharge and other symptoms. Your answers guide the tests. Depending on the situation, tests may include pregnancy testing and blood tests for thyroid function, prolactin and reproductive hormones. Not everyone needs every hormone measured. Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), luteinising hormone (LH) and estradiol may help distinguish different patterns when indicated. Ultrasound may help assess the uterus and ovaries. If imaging of the pituitary is needed, MRI is usually considered for that specific concern; CT is not a routine next step for everyone with a missed period. An intimate examination should be explained and performed only with your consent. Ask about options if an examination or type of scan is uncomfortable or not appropriate for you. Treatment follows the cause Someone with an expected contraceptive-related bleeding change may need reassurance after relevant checks. Someone with a thyroid disorder or raised prolactin needs care directed at that condition. If low energy availability is contributing, nutrition support and a change in exercise load may be needed. Simply adding a hormone pill does not correct an ongoing energy deficit. Low estrogen can affect bone health, while some patterns of infrequent ovulation require a plan to protect the uterine lining. These are different situations and should not receive the same generic hormone-balancing treatment. Surgery is reserved for particular structural problems. Removing ovarian cysts is not a routine treatment for absent periods, and not every cause can be resolved by making bleeding return. Follow up on the plan Keep a record of bleeding and relevant symptoms, and ask when to return if periods do not resume. Follow-up matters even if pregnancy is not currently a goal. Tell the clinician if you are hoping to conceive, because that changes the discussion of treatment and timing. Seek support if eating, exercise or body-image concerns are involved. The aim is to protect health and understand what your body needs, not to assign blame for a missed period. Marital status is not a medical explanation for absent periods. Investigate a missing first period by age 15 or absent breast development by 13. Do not wait three months to test for a possible pregnancy. Does a missed period always mean a hormone tumor? No. There are many more common explanations. Symptoms and initial tests determine whether specialized imaging is needed. Will any hormone tablet solve the problem? No. Treatment depends on the cause, and producing a withdrawal bleed does not necessarily restore normal ovulation.

title: Abdominal swelling after hysterectomy: recovery and warning signs
description: Some bloating can occur during recovery, but increasing swelling with pain, vomiting or fever needs prompt advice from the surgical team.
body: Your abdomen may feel different after a hysterectomy. Healing tissues, changes in bowel activity and, after keyhole surgery, the gas used during the operation can contribute to discomfort. The direction of the change matters: a steadily improving recovery is different from new or worsening swelling. Check concerning symptoms before trying home remedies Contact the surgical team urgently for increasing abdominal pain or swelling, particularly with fever, repeated vomiting, loss of appetite or difficulty passing urine. A swollen abdomen with inability to pass gas or stool and vomiting needs urgent assessment. Heavy vaginal bleeding, foul-smelling discharge, or a wound that becomes increasingly red, painful or starts draining also needs medical advice. Chest pain, sudden breathlessness, coughing blood or collapse requires emergency help. A newly painful, hot or swollen leg should be assessed promptly for a clot. Do not wait four to six weeks for these symptoms to settle, and do not start strong laxatives or abdominal exercises to try to overcome them. Understand what operation you had A hysterectomy removes the uterus. A total hysterectomy also removes the cervix; removing the ovaries and fallopian tubes is a separate part of the surgical plan. The operation may be performed through the vagina, through small abdominal incisions or through a larger abdominal incision. Robot-assisted surgery is a form of keyhole surgery controlled by the surgeon. The most appropriate approach depends on the diagnosis, anatomy, other procedures needed and individual risks. An open operation is not limited to advanced cancer, and a minimally invasive approach is not suitable for every situation. Check your discharge summary if you are unsure which organs were removed. That information helps explain recovery advice and possible hormonal changes. Reasons can include troublesome fibroids, prolapse, persistent heavy bleeding, adenomyosis, selected cases of endometriosis or chronic pelvic pain, and cancer. Recurrent uterine polyps do not automatically require hysterectomy. For non-cancer conditions, medicines and other procedures should be discussed when suitable; removing the uterus is not a guaranteed cure for every source of pelvic pain. A radical operation for cancer may also remove surrounding tissue, part of the upper vagina or lymph nodes according to the plan. After removal of the uterus, you cannot carry a pregnancy and menstrual bleeding ends, although retaining a cervix can occasionally leave cyclical spotting. Hospital stay depends on the operation and recovery, and some uncomplicated minimally invasive procedures allow same-day discharge. Why bloating can happen The bowel can temporarily slow after an operation. Pain medicines, reduced movement and a changed eating routine may contribute to constipation or trapped wind. After laparoscopy, gas used to create operating space can cause temporary abdominal or shoulder discomfort. This does not explain every later episode of swelling. Healing and tenderness may change how you stand or use your abdominal muscles. Hysterectomy does not normally switch off the deep abdominal muscles or make them permanently nonfunctional. The appearance of the abdomen alone cannot distinguish gas, constipation, healing changes or a complication. Tell the care team if the pattern is worsening or does not match the recovery advice you received. As with other major surgery, possible complications include bleeding, infection, anaesthetic reactions, blood clots and injury to the bladder, ureters, bowel or other nearby structures. Some complications need additional treatment or surgery; new swelling should be judged alongside symptoms rather than automatically labelled normal gas. Support a gradual recovery Take prescribed pain relief and any bowel medicine as directed. Ask for advice if constipation persists or a medicine is making it difficult to eat or move. Once your team has said normal eating is appropriate, regular meals, adequate fluids and suitable fibre can support bowel function. Follow a different plan if you also had bowel surgery or were given specific restrictions. Short, gentle walks and changing position can help recovery. Increase activity gradually within your discharge instructions; strenuous core exercises, heavy lifting and pushing through pain are not shortcuts to healing. Wear comfortable clothing and give yourself permission to rest. A flatter abdomen is not the measure of whether you are recovering correctly. Separate hormonal changes from early swelling If both ovaries are removed before natural menopause, a sudden fall in ovarian hormones can cause menopausal symptoms. If the ovaries remain, immediate surgical menopause is not inevitable, though menopause may occur earlier than otherwise expected. Hot flushes, vaginal dryness, sleep problems or changes in sexual comfort can be discussed with the team. Treatment depends on age, the reason for surgery and individual suitability. Sexual desire can also change, and support should consider comfort, healing, relationships and hormonal factors rather than assuming one inevitable outcome. Early bloating is not automatically weight gain or evidence that menopause has started. Longer-term body changes deserve a separate conversation rather than a restrictive diet during healing. Use follow-up rather than a fixed deadline Recovery after an abdominal hysterectomy often takes several weeks, and the overall timetable differs from keyhole or vaginal surgery. Bloating does not have one guaranteed end date. Ask whom to contact, which symptoms need same-day review and when activity, lifting and vaginal penetration can safely resume. Follow the plan for your operation rather than a generic date online. Persistent swelling, a new localized bulge or symptoms that return after improving should be reviewed. Keep planned follow-up appointments and ask about any tissue-test results. Recovery can also bring relief, grief or changes in how you feel about your body. Support for those feelings is part of postoperative care. Worsening swelling with pain, vomiting or fever needs prompt assessment. Hysterectomy does not routinely disable the abdominal muscles. Recovery and return to activity should follow the individual surgical plan. Should all bloating be gone by six weeks? No fixed deadline applies to everyone. The pattern should be discussed with your team, especially if symptoms worsen or fail to improve. Does a total hysterectomy mean my ovaries were removed? Not necessarily. Total refers to removal of the uterus and cervix. Check whether ovary removal was also part of the operation.

title: Treating cervical stenosis: what a procedure may involve
description: A narrowed cervical canal does not always need treatment. When treatment is needed, the approach depends on symptoms and the reason access is required.
body: Cervical stenosis means that the passage through the cervix is unusually narrow or closed. Some people have no symptoms. Others need treatment because blood or fluid is trapped, pain occurs, or a clinician needs to reach the uterine cavity for a test or fertility procedure. First clarify why treatment is being offered A finding of stenosis does not automatically mean an operation is necessary. Ask whether the aim is to relieve symptoms, investigate abnormal bleeding, obtain a sample or enable another procedure. Possible causes include scarring after cervical treatment, menopausal tissue changes and, less commonly, other disease. Ordinary cervical screening should not be presented as a usual cause of significant scarring. Relevant history includes cone biopsy or other treatment for precancerous cervical changes, endometrial ablation, repeated uterine procedures, pelvic radiation and significant inflammation or infection. Menopausal atrophy may contribute; dryness alone does not diagnose stenosis. Congenital narrowing is uncommon. Cervical or endometrial cancer is a less common but important possibility when symptoms or examination findings raise concern. Painful periods with very little bleeding can occur if blood cannot drain normally. Infection or retained fluid may also need assessment. These findings should not be assumed to be harmless without investigating the cause. Some people have absent or irregular periods, chronic pelvic fullness, difficulty conceiving or a collection of blood or pus in the uterus. Abnormal bleeding, particularly after menopause, may require tissue assessment. Stenosis can make sampling harder, but it is not a reason to abandon necessary investigation. Assessment is more than passing a probe A clinician considers symptoms, previous procedures, examination findings and sometimes ultrasound. Difficulty passing a small instrument can suggest narrowing, but the instrument should never be forced. Narrowing may first be noticed when a cervical screening sample, endometrial sample or fertility catheter is difficult to obtain or pass. A hysteroscope is a thin camera that can help the clinician see the canal and inside the uterus. In a severely narrowed canal, gaining access may itself be the difficult part. Ask what is already known and what remains uncertain. A painful or incomplete office attempt may need a different setting or technique rather than repeated attempts on the same day. Dilation and hysteroscopic treatment are possible approaches Dilation gradually opens the canal using appropriate instruments. Depending on the narrowing and the planned procedure, the clinician may use a small hysteroscope, ultrasound guidance or techniques to release scar tissue under direct vision. When dilators are used, progressively larger instruments may be introduced carefully until the required opening is achieved. Medicines to prepare the cervix may sometimes be considered. Their suitability and timing depend on the person and procedure; they are not a home treatment to try independently. Treatment can sometimes be done in a clinic, while other cases need an operating theatre. Significant stenosis may be technically challenging even for an experienced specialist. Laser is not a universally preferred alternative, and no single method can be promised to prevent the canal narrowing again. Discuss pain relief and the right setting Ask in advance about local anesthetic, sedation or other anesthesia options, and what happens if the procedure is too painful or cannot be completed. Tell the team about previous painful examinations or procedures and any concerns that affect your preferences. You can ask to pause or stop an awake procedure. Possible complications include bleeding, infection, a tear, a false passage or a perforation of the uterus. The clinician should explain the risks of the actual procedure being proposed. Agree on what additional treatment or sampling you are consenting to, rather than assuming every possible intervention will be performed at the same appointment. Keeping the canal open requires an individual plan A temporary stent or another measure may be considered in selected cases. Not everyone needs one, and the type and duration are not the same for every patient. Hormonal intrauterine systems have been reported in particular situations after dilation, but an IUD is not a routine mechanical cure for all cervical stenosis. Its contraceptive effect also matters if you are trying to conceive. Ask what evidence supports the proposed option, when it will be reviewed or removed and what to do if symptoms recur. Do not attempt to check the canal with an instrument yourself. Plan aftercare and follow-up Obtain written instructions about expected discomfort or spotting, pain relief, activity and when to resume vaginal penetration or use internal menstrual products. Advice depends on what was done. Fever, worsening pelvic pain, heavy bleeding, foul-smelling discharge or feeling very unwell after the procedure needs prompt medical advice. Keep the follow-up appointment, particularly if tissue was sent for testing. If periods remain unusually scant or painful, tell the team rather than assuming treatment was successful. If fertility treatment is planned, coordinate timing with that team. Opening the cervix may make access easier, but does not guarantee conception or resolve unrelated fertility factors. Not all cervical stenosis needs treatment. Procedure choice, anesthesia and recurrence prevention should be individualized. An IUD or a fixed stent duration is not standard for everyone. Is treatment always a simple office procedure? No. Some cases are straightforward; severe narrowing can require specialist techniques or a different anesthesia setting. Does dilation guarantee that the canal stays open? No. Recurrence can occur, so follow-up and a plan for returning symptoms are important.

title: Can cervical stenosis cause painful periods?
description: A narrowed cervical canal can sometimes obstruct menstrual flow and cause pain. It is one possible explanation, not the usual conclusion from cramps alone.
body: Severe period pain deserves attention, but it does not identify one particular diagnosis. Cervical stenosis (a narrowing of the passage through the cervix) can sometimes contribute when menstrual blood cannot drain normally. Many other conditions can also cause pain, and some people with stenosis have no symptoms. Understand the possible connection The cervix connects the uterine cavity with the vagina. If its canal becomes substantially narrowed or closed, menstrual blood may collect inside the uterus. That collection is called a hematometra and can cause pelvic pain or cramping. Pain with unexpectedly scant bleeding, or recurring monthly pain without a period, is a pattern to discuss with a clinician. It does not prove that the cervix is blocked. Partial narrowing may still allow drainage. Symptoms vary, so it is inaccurate to say everyone with symptomatic stenosis must have painful periods. Narrowing may also cause unusual bleeding or spotting, make sperm passage or a fertility procedure more difficult, or be found without pain. It does not establish the cause of infertility or predict the success of assisted conception by itself. Consider the history as well as the pain Stenosis can occur after procedures that remove or damage cervical tissue, after some uterine procedures or radiation, and with menopausal tissue changes. Occasionally it is present from birth or associated with other disease. Tell the clinician about previous cervical treatment, uterine surgery, ablation, unusual bleeding and any fertility procedures that were difficult to complete. Do not try to diagnose the problem by feeling the cervix or inserting anything into its opening. The canal cannot be safely assessed at home. Other causes remain important Ordinary period cramps involve uterine contractions and prostaglandins. Pain that becomes more severe, lasts longer or develops after years of manageable periods may have an additional cause. Endometriosis involves tissue similar to the uterine lining outside the uterus. Adenomyosis involves endometrial-type tissue within the muscular uterine wall; it should not be dismissed as an exceptionally rare explanation. Endometriosis can involve ovaries, pelvic surfaces or bowel and may also cause pain with sex, bowel movements or difficulty conceiving. Adenomyosis can cause heavy bleeding as well as pain. Fibroids are growths of uterine muscle and connective tissue, not skin tags. They can contribute to heavy bleeding, pressure or pain depending on their size and location. Pelvic inflammatory disease and other infections can also cause pelvic pain. Symptoms such as fever or unusual discharge change how quickly you need assessment. PID can involve the uterus and fallopian tubes and sometimes surrounding structures; sexually transmitted organisms are common causes, but are not the only possible organisms. Not having given birth is not a reason to accept severe pain, and pregnancy is not a treatment to prescribe for it. Painful periods are associated with factors such as a family history, earlier menarche, heavier or irregular bleeding and smoking, but these do not identify the cause in one person. Having these features is not a reason to dismiss disabling pain or prescribe pregnancy as a solution. Arrange the right assessment A clinician may review a bleeding and pain record, perform an examination with your consent and arrange ultrasound or other tests suited to the symptoms. If pregnancy is possible, testing may be needed even when you think the pain is menstrual. Ultrasound can show retained fluid and assess other pelvic findings. A hysteroscope may help inspect the cervical canal and uterine cavity when appropriate. Tests that pass fluid or a catheter through the cervix are not all routine first-line tests for painful periods. The clinician should explain what each proposed investigation would add. Saline sonography and hysterosalpingography examine different uterine or tubal questions; neither is a universal screening test for cervical stenosis. After menopause, bleeding or a uterine fluid collection may require investigation of the lining or cervix rather than assuming narrowing alone explains it. Treatment depends on what is found Stenosis without symptoms or concerning uterine findings may need no intervention. When blood is trapped or access is needed, a specialist may open the canal with dilation or a guided hysteroscopic procedure. Pain relief and anesthesia options should be discussed in advance. Procedures have risks, including bleeding, infection and injury, and the narrowing can recur. A temporary stent may be considered in selected cases, but it is not required for everyone. Ask how success will be checked and when to report returning symptoms. If you hope to become pregnant, discuss your history of cervical procedures with the team. Risks depend on the original treatment, tissue removed and any injury; a simple statement that all dilation greatly increases miscarriage risk is misleading. Do not wait with urgent symptoms Seek urgent help for sudden severe pelvic pain, fever, vomiting, faintness or feeling very unwell. Severe pain with possible pregnancy, shoulder-tip pain or heavy bleeding needs emergency assessment. For recurring pain without those warning signs, make an appointment and record when the pain occurs, how much you bleed and whether it affects sleep, work or daily activities. A useful plan should address both the cause and symptom relief. If treatment does not help, return for review rather than assuming the diagnosis must have been correct. Cervical narrowing can cause pain if it obstructs menstrual drainage. Cramps alone cannot diagnose stenosis. Investigation and treatment should reflect symptoms, history and future plans. Does severe period pain mean my cervix is too narrow? No. There are several possible causes, including primary cramps, endometriosis, adenomyosis and fibroids. Will everyone with stenosis need dilation? No. Treatment is usually considered for symptoms, concerning findings or a need to access the uterine cavity.

title: Bleeding after sex: causes, checks and treatment
description: Possible causes of spotting or bleeding after sex, what an assessment may involve, and how dryness, infections and other conditions are treated.
body: Bleeding during or after vaginal sex is often called postcoital bleeding. Common explanations include dryness, irritation, infection and changes on the cervix, but the cause cannot be identified from the amount or colour alone. Arrange a medical check even if the bleeding is light or stops quickly. Any bleeding after menopause needs assessment, and heavy bleeding or bleeding with severe pain or faintness may need urgent care. Where the blood may be coming from Blood noticed after sex may come from the vaginal wall, cervix or uterus, or from an injury around the vulva and labia. Occasionally blood from the urinary tract or another nearby area is mistaken for vaginal bleeding. Finding the source helps determine the right tests. The cervix is the opening of the uterus at the top of the vagina. Contact can make a delicate or inflamed area on its surface bleed. After menopause, changes in the vaginal lining and conditions affecting the uterine lining also become important possibilities. Spotting is a small amount of blood, sometimes seen only on tissue or underwear. A larger amount, repeated episodes or bleeding between periods adds useful information, but a small amount does not reliably exclude a condition that needs treatment. You do not need to work out the anatomical source before asking for help. A clinician can review the timing, symptoms and examination findings without assuming that sex itself explains every episode. Infection and inflammation Infection can make tissue more sensitive and likely to bleed when touched. Cervicitis means inflammation of the cervix; vaginitis means inflammation of the vagina. These terms describe the affected area and do not by themselves identify a particular infection. Sexually transmitted infections such as chlamydia can cause bleeding, and pelvic inflammatory disease may also be relevant, especially with pelvic pain or other symptoms. Some infections produce few obvious symptoms, so the absence of a strong smell or itching does not rule them out. Tell the clinician about unusual discharge, pain during sex, burning when passing urine, itching, fever or lower abdominal pain. Questions about partners, barrier use and possible exposure help select tests and treatment. They should be asked respectfully and confidentially. Not every inflamed or sore vagina needs antibiotics. Dryness, irritation and other noninfectious causes can produce similar symptoms. Treatment should follow the diagnosis, and some diagnosed STIs also require partner testing or treatment. Menopause and genitourinary symptoms Lower oestrogen around and after menopause can change the vagina and nearby urinary tissues. The term genitourinary syndrome of menopause, or GSM, includes symptoms such as dryness, irritation, discomfort during sex and some urinary problems. It was previously often described as vaginal atrophy. The vaginal lining may become thinner, less elastic and more easily irritated. Less lubrication and fragile tissue can lead to soreness or small breaks during penetration. Similar hormone-related changes can follow removal of both ovaries or some cancer treatments. These symptoms are treatable and are not something you have to tolerate as the inevitable price of ageing. However, bleeding should be assessed before it is attributed to GSM. A familiar feeling of dryness does not prove that dryness is the only cause. Bleeding after menopause needs a check even if it happened only once, followed sex or appeared as a small pink or brown stain. In this setting, assessment also considers the uterine lining, not only the cervix or vaginal surface. Other reasons for vaginal dryness Dryness can occur before menopause, including after childbirth and during breastfeeding. Some medicines, such as certain antidepressants, hormonal medicines and treatments that reduce oestrogen, may contribute. Chemotherapy, pelvic radiotherapy and surgery can also affect comfort and lubrication. If symptoms began after a medicine change, ask a clinician or pharmacist to review it. Do not stop a prescribed treatment without advice. A general list of cold, asthma or other medicines cannot establish that a particular product is the cause. Arousal-related lubrication varies. Penetration before you feel ready or sufficiently lubricated can increase friction, but pain or dryness should not be framed as a failure to relax. Allowing more time and using suitable lubrication may help while persistent symptoms are assessed. Douching and fragranced intimate washes can irritate the area. Some people are sensitive to detergents or other products. Conditions such as Sjögren’s syndrome can reduce moisture in the body and may contribute to vaginal dryness. Mention symptoms elsewhere or a known diagnosis to your clinician. Polyps and cervical ectropion Polyps are small growths that can occur on the cervix or inside the uterus. Many are benign, but they should not be declared harmless solely from symptoms. Their delicate blood vessels can bleed, including after contact. A clinician may recommend removing a symptomatic polyp or checking tissue, depending on its location and your circumstances. You cannot confirm or treat a polyp at home, and not every episode of spotting comes from one. Another common cause is cervical ectropion, in which delicate glandular cells from inside the cervical canal are visible on its outer surface. It can look red and may bleed after contact or produce more discharge. Ectropion itself is a benign change, not cervical cancer. Before treating troublesome ectropion, clinicians check for infection and other abnormalities. It is important to distinguish this from the idea that an infection has damaged cells that must simply be burned or frozen away. Friction, small tears and injury Friction during penetration can cause small scratches or tears, particularly when tissue is dry or less elastic. Forceful activity can make this more likely. Pain or bleeding is a reason to stop and assess what is happening, not to push through. A small injury may settle, but bleeding after sex should still be discussed with a clinician, especially if it recurs or its source is uncertain. Deep pain, persistent bleeding or an injury that appears significant needs prompt assessment. For future sexual contact, choose a comfortable pace and activity, communicate about discomfort and use an appropriate lubricant if needed. Penetration is optional; it should never be continued because a partner expects it. If the contact was unwanted or forced, you can seek medical care and confidential support. An examination and treatment should respect your choices and need for safety. Could it be cancer? Most bleeding after sex has a noncancerous explanation, but it can be a symptom of cervical or vaginal cancer. Bleeding after menopause can also be associated with cancer of the uterine lining. This possibility is why checking symptoms matters even when the bleeding seems minor. Cervical cancer can occur well before fifty and should not be treated as exclusively a postmenopausal disease. Persistent infection with certain high-risk HPV types is its main cause, and smoking is one of the factors that can increase risk. Endometrial cancer is more common after menopause. Relevant risk factors can include higher body weight, particular hormone exposures and some inherited or family cancer histories. These factors guide assessment; they do not tell you that a current episode is cancer. A normal screening result or a history of HPV vaccination does not replace evaluation of a new symptom. Do not wait until your next routine screening invitation. Early identification of a serious cause can make a meaningful difference to treatment. When to seek care and when it is urgent Book a primary-care, gynaecology or sexual-health appointment for bleeding after sex, including light spotting. Be clear if you have reached menopause, if pregnancy is possible, or if the bleeding has happened more than once. Seek urgent help for heavy or ongoing bleeding, severe abdominal or pelvic pain, faintness, collapse or feeling acutely unwell. Fever with pelvic pain or unusual discharge also needs prompt assessment. The urgency depends on the whole picture, not simply whether the blood looks fresh. A missed period together with unusual bleeding and abdominal pain needs urgent assessment for possible ectopic pregnancy. If you are pregnant, contact your maternity or pregnancy-care service for advice about bleeding rather than assuming sex has made it harmless. Mention associated itching, burning, painful urination, painful sex, lower back pain, nausea or vomiting. These symptoms can help identify infection, injury or another condition, although none points to a single cause on its own. What happens at the appointment The clinician usually asks when the bleeding started, how much there was, whether it happened during or after sex and whether it occurs at other times. Details about periods, menopause, pregnancy possibility, contraception, medicines and previous procedures also help. You may be asked about your sexual history and previous screening or STI tests. These questions are intended to guide care, not to assign blame. Say if a question is unclear or if you need to discuss it privately. An examination may include the vulva and an internal view of the vaginal walls and cervix using a speculum. This can identify a visible tear, polyp, inflamed area or other change. Depending on symptoms, the clinician may also check for tenderness or a possible urinary source. Initial tests may include a pregnancy test, STI testing from a swab or urine sample, and blood tests when the amount or duration of bleeding suggests they would help. Not everyone needs every test, and the sequence depends on the findings. If an examination worries you Tell the service when booking if you are anxious, have experienced pain during an examination or have a history that makes it difficult. You can begin with a conversation about what the clinician recommends and why. Ask for each step to be explained, a suitable chaperone or support person, a pause if needed and adjustments that may improve comfort. You can ask whether a smaller speculum or a different position is suitable. Consent remains yours throughout. Some initial information can be obtained from a discussion, urine testing or, where appropriate and available, a self-collected swab. These options do not always replace an examination when the cervix or vaginal walls need to be seen. It would be misleading to promise that assessment never needs a pelvic examination. The aim is to plan necessary care in a way you can manage, rather than letting fear of one part of the visit prevent you from seeking help at all. Further tests and why a smear is not enough Routine cervical screening is designed to identify HPV-related risk and precancerous changes. It is not a complete diagnostic test for bleeding and does not assess every part of the vagina or uterus. A normal result cannot rule out every relevant disease. A colposcopy uses magnification to examine the cervix more closely and may include a small biopsy. Ultrasound can assess the uterus and other pelvic structures. Hysteroscopy allows a clinician to look inside the uterine cavity, sometimes with tissue sampling. For postmenopausal bleeding, current local pathways determine the initial tests. ACOG’s April 2026 update recommends a combination of transvaginal ultrasound and endometrial tissue sampling for most patients, rather than relying on ultrasound alone. Your specialist can explain how the guidance applies to your situation. Investigation is not always a rigid process of ruling out cancer first and considering everything else afterwards. Several possible causes may be assessed together. If bleeding continues or returns despite reassuring initial results, report it so that the plan can be reconsidered. Lubricants, moisturisers and reducing irritation When dryness contributes to symptoms, a lubricant can reduce friction during sexual activity. A vaginal moisturiser is used regularly according to its instructions to help with ongoing dryness. These products have different purposes and should not be treated as identical. Choose products intended for the area and stop using one that causes irritation. A water-based or suitable silicone-based lubricant may be an option. Follow the instructions for condoms, diaphragms and sex toys, because material compatibility matters. Oil-based products and petroleum jelly can damage latex or polyisoprene condoms and increase the chance of splitting. Do not assume a household cream or oil is safe for use with a barrier method. Avoid douching and perfumed intimate products, and wash the external area gently. These steps can improve comfort but do not replace investigation of bleeding, treat every infection or guarantee that bleeding will never recur. Hormone treatment and other cause-specific care For menopause-related dryness, a clinician may discuss vaginal oestrogen, which is available in forms such as creams, tablets, pessaries or rings. Dosing and replacement intervals depend on the product; a ninety-day schedule applies to some rings, not every treatment. Local treatment and systemic menopausal hormone therapy are different options with different uses and considerations. A systemic regimen is not automatically needed for vaginal symptoms. Discuss your medical history, unexplained bleeding and any history of hormone-sensitive cancer before starting treatment. An identified infection may require antibiotics or another specific medicine. Complete the prescribed course and follow advice about partners and sexual contact if an STI is diagnosed. Antibiotics do not treat all forms of vaginitis, because some are not bacterial infections. Symptomatic polyps may be removed and assessed. Persistent troublesome ectropion may sometimes be treated with silver nitrate, freezing or another procedure after appropriate checks. These are selected treatments for a confirmed condition, not a routine way to remove cells damaged by an untreated infection. If testing identifies a precancerous change or cancer, specialist care is needed. The appropriate plan depends on the finding and its extent. A general article cannot choose the treatment or replace discussion of its benefits and risks. Possible complications and follow-up A few spots of blood do not usually cause anaemia. Repeated, prolonged or heavier bleeding can, however, contribute to iron deficiency. Fatigue, weakness, dizziness, headaches, breathlessness or unusual pallor are reasons to discuss whether blood testing is needed. If iron deficiency is confirmed, care may include iron replacement as well as treating the source of blood loss. Iron-rich food is useful, but diet alone may not correct an established deficiency or explain why bleeding is occurring. Dryness and menopause-related tissue changes can also accompany recurrent urinary symptoms or infections. Burning during urination, frequent urination or repeated suspected UTIs deserve their own assessment rather than being assumed to be caused by a small tear. Many causes of bleeding after sex are treatable. Follow the agreed plan, and return if symptoms persist, worsen or recur. Improvement with lubrication is useful information, but it is not a diagnostic test that rules out other causes. Bleeding after sex often has a treatable cause, but even light bleeding should be checked. Dryness, infection, cervical ectropion, polyps and injury are distinct possibilities with different treatments. Any bleeding after menopause needs assessment; a normal cervical screen does not rule out every cause. An examination can be planned with explanation, consent and adjustments for comfort. Heavy bleeding, severe pain, faintness or possible pregnancy complications need urgent care. Do I need an appointment if it was only a small spot? Yes. Arrange a check even if the bleeding was light or stopped quickly. It is often due to a treatable cause, but the amount alone cannot establish the explanation. Is bleeding after menopause normal if it follows sex? No. It should be assessed even if it happened once or you also have dryness. The clinician may need to examine the vaginal tissues and investigate the uterine lining. Does bleeding after sex usually mean cancer? No. Dryness, infection, ectropion, polyps and injury are other possible causes. Cancer is an important possibility to exclude when appropriate, which is why symptoms should not be dismissed. Can a recent normal smear replace an assessment? No. Routine cervical screening has a different purpose and does not check every possible source of bleeding. Tell a clinician about the symptom rather than waiting for the next screening appointment. What if I am afraid of the pelvic examination? Tell the service in advance. Ask for an explanation, a support person or chaperone, comfort adjustments and the option to pause. Some initial tests can be discussed first, but an examination may still be important for finding the cause. Are a lubricant and a vaginal moisturiser the same thing? No. A lubricant reduces friction during sexual activity, while a vaginal moisturiser is generally used regularly for ongoing dryness. Use products intended for the area and follow their instructions. Can I use petroleum jelly with a condom? Do not use petroleum jelly or other oil-based products with latex or polyisoprene condoms because they can damage the material. Check the barrier product’s instructions and choose a compatible lubricant. Will antibiotics stop the bleeding? Only when an infection that responds to them is the cause. Other explanations require different care. Do not self-treat every episode as an infection. Does ectropion mean that my cervix has cancer or an untreated infection? No. Ectropion is a common benign surface change. Infection and other abnormalities are checked before treatment is considered for persistent symptoms. When should I seek urgent help? Get urgent help for heavy or ongoing bleeding, severe pelvic or abdominal pain, faintness, collapse or feeling very unwell. A missed period with bleeding and abdominal pain could be an ectopic pregnancy and needs urgent assessment.

title: Food cravings before a period: respond without guilt
description: Why appetite may change before a period, how to make food choices comfortably and when cravings or mood symptoms deserve support.
body: Wanting chocolate, crisps or a larger meal before a period is not a failure of self-control. Notice what helps you feel nourished and comfortable, while paying attention to distress, loss-of-control eating or symptoms that disrupt everyday life. Appetite changes can follow a menstrual pattern Feeling hungrier or wanting particular foods before a period is common. Some people notice it in the final seven to ten days before bleeding, while others notice a broader or less predictable pattern in the one or two weeks beforehand. Cravings may ease after bleeding begins. There is no exact timetable that every cycle must follow. Other premenstrual changes can include bloating, headaches, spots, breast tenderness, tiredness and shifts in mood. Bowel habits or gas may also change around this time. Looking at several symptoms together is more informative than treating a single desire for chocolate as a diagnostic sign. Symptoms that continue throughout the month may need another or an additional explanation. Hormones may contribute, but research is not a simple formula Changing ovarian hormones are one possible influence on appetite and cravings. A small 2016 study followed seventeen people with regular menstrual cycles, measuring hormones and asking about foods they craved. It found relationships involving estradiol, sex hormone-binding globulin and leptin, including patterns of stronger sweet and carbohydrate cravings. The findings suggest a biological contribution but do not prove a universal cause. The study does not show that everyone needs a particular food when estrogen or progesterone reaches a certain level. Sleep, stress, familiar foods, access and whether you have eaten enough also affect appetite. Ordinary cravings do not diagnose a hormone imbalance or identify an exact missing nutrient. Testing or supplements should be based on a relevant clinical concern, not a craving alone. Food and mood interact without a guaranteed chemical boost Eating something enjoyable can be comforting, especially when you feel tired, irritable or low. Carbohydrates and brain chemistry, including serotonin pathways, have been studied in relation to mood. However, the claim that a sweet food reliably releases a “happiness chemical” and fixes premenstrual distress is too simple. A short-lived change in how you feel is not treatment for persistent depression or anxiety. You do not need to feel guilty for enjoying food or expect it to meet every emotional need. Notice whether eating helps you feel nourished and satisfied, or whether it has become the only available way to cope. That observation can guide support without labelling foods as good or bad or blaming yourself for wanting relief. Respond to hunger with enough, reasonably regular food Appetite and energy needs can vary across the cycle, but there is no single extra-calorie allowance that every person must add before a period. If you feel hungry, eating a satisfying meal or snack is reasonable. Skipping the next meal to compensate can leave you hungrier and make the cycle more difficult. Include foods you enjoy alongside carbohydrate, protein, fat and fibre across the day. Examples might be rice and beans, toast with eggs, or yogurt with fruit and nuts. If you have a medical meal plan, ask how to accommodate changes in hunger within it. A registered dietitian can help if nutrition advice has become confusing, restrictive or difficult to put into practice. Carbohydrate choices can support comfort and variety Bread, pasta and potatoes are not inherently unsuitable foods before a period. Whole grains and pulses, such as brown rice, oats, beans and lentils, can add fibre and help make a meal satisfying. They are options within ordinary eating, not a guaranteed way to keep serotonin high. You can choose a portion that leaves you comfortable rather than trying to follow a rigid rule. Spaghetti squash can be an enjoyable vegetable in a favourite pasta-style dish, but being lower in calories or carbohydrate does not make it a necessary replacement for pasta. Use it because you like it, and make sure the meal still provides enough nourishment. If large meals or very salty foods seem to worsen bloating, experiment gently with timing or amounts instead of banning an entire food group. Make room for sweet foods and chocolate Sweet snacks can fit into a varied diet. If you want alternatives or additions, possibilities include a smoothie, yogurt and fruit, apple with a little honey, a homemade oat-and-nut snack, or a fruit-and-nut mix. These are choices, not compulsory substitutes for a biscuit or dessert. Pairing a snack with something filling may help if a small sweet item leaves you hungry. Chocolate is a frequently reported craving. Dark chocolate contains cocoa compounds and some minerals, but that does not make it a proven PMS treatment or mean a craving diagnoses magnesium deficiency. You do not have to choose the darkest bar or stop after an arbitrary number of squares. Consider enjoyment, satisfaction and any symptoms you personally notice, without treating a food as a prescription. Broaden the ways you get comfort A walk, a run if you enjoy running, a funny film, a conversation with a friend or time with a pet may help you feel supported or more settled. Consensual intimacy can be enjoyable if you want it, but it is not an obligation or a treatment requirement. Rest can be the more useful choice on a difficult day. These activities should not become a way to earn food or burn off a snack. Their effects cannot be reduced to a guaranteed dose of endorphins, serotonin, oxytocin or dopamine. Choose what feels manageable, and seek support when sadness, anxiety or irritability are strong enough to disrupt your relationships, work, study or ordinary routines. Distinguish cravings, binge eating and PMDD Eating more than usual is not automatically binge eating. Repeated episodes of feeling unable to stop, eating in secrecy, marked distress, or attempts to compensate through vomiting, fasting or excessive exercise deserve professional attention. Support is appropriate at any body size; a significant weight change is not a requirement for care. Restrictive dieting can make loss-of-control eating harder to manage. Premenstrual dysphoric disorder, or PMDD, involves a broader pattern of severe cyclical symptoms, particularly mood symptoms, that interfere with life. Appetite changes may be part of it, but cravings alone do not establish the diagnosis. A clinician may use daily symptom records across at least two cycles. Treatment can include psychological support or medicines; you do not have to manage severe symptoms through food choices alone. Irregular periods and pregnancy need their own consideration Research has found an association between binge eating and menstrual dysfunction. For example, a study of 11,503 Swedish women examined those experiences together. It does not prove that an irregular period causes binge eating, or that a particular percentage applies to everyone. Shared hormonal, metabolic or other factors may contribute. Mention both menstrual changes and distressing eating to a clinician rather than assuming one explains the other. Cravings, nausea, food aversions and breast or nipple changes cannot reliably distinguish pregnancy from PMS. A missed period is a reason to consider a test if pregnancy is possible. Most tests can be used from the first day of a missed period; if you do not know when the next period is due, test at least twenty-one days after unprotected sex. If an early result is negative but concern remains, repeat as instructed or seek advice. Ask for help with persistent distress or non-food cravings Arrange a review if hunger or cravings are new, persist all month, interfere with daily life, cause significant distress or affect recovery from an eating disorder. Also mention ongoing depression, anxiety, major weight changes or other physical symptoms. A brief record of timing, mood, sleep and eating can help; use a gentler approach if tracking makes you more anxious or obsessive. Wanting to eat clay, soil, paper or other non-food substances, or repeatedly craving ice, deserves assessment. This may be pica and can be associated with iron deficiency, particularly with heavy periods, but it is not a diagnosis by itself. Do not eat potentially harmful substances or start high-dose iron on your own. Seek urgent help if you have swallowed something toxic or feel at risk of harming yourself; a symptom diary can wait. Appetite may change without following an exact schedule. A craving is not a hormone or nutrient test. Regular, sufficient eating is more useful than compensation. Comfort can include both food and other enjoyable activities. Distressing eating or severe cyclical mood symptoms deserve care. When do premenstrual cravings usually begin? Some people notice them in the final seven to ten days before bleeding; others have symptoms across the preceding one or two weeks. The pattern varies, and cravings may ease after the period starts. Did the 2016 study prove hormones cause every craving? No. It studied seventeen participants and found associations between hormone-related measures and cravings.
