Vegetables, fruit, legumes, whole grains and unsaturated fats can form part of that pattern. No particular food, caffeinated drink or vitamin supplement has been established as a way to enlarge a healthy adult penis. If erections are persistently difficult, discuss the problem with a healthcare professional. Review your general health, medicines and emotional wellbeing instead of relying on a list of supposed performance foods. The appropriate treatment depends on the cause. Body-image worries also deserve care. A respectful conversation with a partner or a qualified sexual-health therapist can help when comparison or anxiety is affecting intimacy. You do not have to pursue a procedure to make your concern worth taking seriously. Spinach and other folate-rich vegetables, oats and other whole grains can fit into a varied diet. Coffee, tea and vitamin D supplements should not be prescribed as a penis-growth or universal erection treatment. Regular activity, stopping smoking, limiting alcohol and managing stress can support overall and sexual health; supplements are appropriate for an identified need, not a promised size change. When to seek help Arrange medical assessment for persistent soreness, new curvature, a lump, a lasting change in appearance or repeated erection problems. Masturbation can cause irritation when it is rough, but that does not mean every genital symptom should be attributed to friction. An erection lasting about four hours is an emergency, even if you are embarrassed to ask for help. Seek care sooner for a painful erection or if you have sickle cell disease and it lasts more than an hour. Further masturbation is not a treatment for a prolonged erection. There is no universal number of times that defines a problem. If sexual behaviour feels hard to control or regularly interferes with work, relationships or daily responsibilities, confidential professional support can help without shaming you. Masturbation does not permanently shrink or enlarge the penis. Hormone changes around arousal do not mean testosterone has been depleted. Unproven enlargement methods can injure tissue. Persistent symptoms and prolonged erections need appropriate care. Does more frequent masturbation make the penis grow? No. Frequency is not a way to increase its permanent size. Can I treat a suspected hormone problem by abstaining? Abstinence is not a substitute for assessment and treatment of a confirmed hormone disorder. Does a pump’s temporary effect mean enlargement is working? No. Increased blood flow or swelling should not be confused with permanent growth.

title: Can losing your sense of smell or taste mean COVID-19?
description: What smell and taste changes can mean, how to respond to a possible infection, and why recovery estimates and other causes need context.
body: A sudden change in smell or taste can be a symptom of COVID-19, including when your nose does not feel blocked. It is a clue to consider alongside testing and the rest of your health, rather than a diagnosis on its own. Understanding what has changed can help you seek the right care and manage everyday life during recovery. A new change can be an early clue COVID-19 is caused by SARS-CoV-2, a virus that can produce a wide range of symptoms. Some people first notice that a familiar drink has little aroma, or that food seems strangely flavourless. The change may appear before, alongside or after other symptoms. It can happen without a blocked nose, but it does not happen to everyone who has the infection. Colds, flu and sinus inflammation can also temporarily interfere with smell. A new change therefore deserves attention without being treated as a diagnosis. Note when it started, whether it was sudden or gradual, and whether there is congestion, fever or another illness. Being able to smell normally does not rule COVID-19 out. Smell, taste and flavour are related but different Your tongue and other taste-sensitive areas recognise qualities such as sweetness, saltiness, sourness, bitterness and savouriness. Smell adds much of the detail that distinguishes one food from another. Aromas reach the nose both when you sniff and from the back of the mouth while eating. That is why a stuffy nose can make a meal seem dull. A person may still detect that chocolate is sweet while missing its familiar flavour. However, not every taste complaint is simply a smell problem: true changes in taste can occur too. There is no useful rule that a fixed percentage of everyone’s taste loss must come from smell. Describing the two experiences separately helps a clinician assess them. Loss, reduction and distortion can all occur Anosmia means loss of smell; hyposmia means a reduced ability to smell. With parosmia, something familiar smells different, often unpleasant. Phantosmia describes an odour perceived when there is no source. Taste may similarly be reduced, absent or altered, including an unwanted metallic or bitter sensation. These descriptions identify an experience, not its cause. Someone who starts noticing distorted smells during recovery has not necessarily caught COVID-19 again. Conversely, a fresh respiratory illness should not automatically be dismissed as part of an older smell problem. Tell the clinician which changes are new and which have continued since the original illness. What researchers learned about the nose Smell receptors work within a specialised lining high in the nose. The virus uses entry machinery that includes a receptor called ACE2. Early research examined where the relevant genes and proteins were present, to understand why smell could disappear even without the congestion typical of a cold. A 2020 study identified viral-entry-related molecules particularly in non-neuronal supporting cells rather than the smell-sensing neurons themselves. Disruption of those supporting tissues offered a plausible explanation for altered smell. This was evidence about a mechanism, not proof that every patient has the same injury or that a home symptom can reveal which cells are affected. The biology of persistent symptoms is more complex than a single receptor explanation. Why older percentages need context An early review combined twenty-four studies involving 8,438 people with confirmed COVID-19. Its pooled estimates were about 41% for smell disturbance and 38% for taste disturbance. Individual studies differed enormously, reflecting their populations, timing and ways of asking about or measuring symptoms. Those findings describe the early pandemic, not the proportion expected in every outbreak today. That review found lower reported prevalence in studies with an older average age and higher detection when smell was measured rather than only self-reported. It did not find a significant overall difference by sex, although individual studies reported different patterns. None of these observations allows a person to decide whether they have COVID-19 based on age or sex. Circulating variants, immunity and study methods also matter. Smell loss does not predict a mild course Some early observational reports found smell changes more often among people treated outside hospital than among those with severe illness. Such an association does not establish that smell loss protects someone, or that a person who loses smell cannot become seriously unwell. The groups being compared may differ in several other ways. Assess the whole illness. Breathing, alertness, chest symptoms, hydration and relevant medical conditions matter more than whether coffee has an aroma. Do not delay medical help because a symptom list or an old study has described this particular sign as reassuring. Notice everyday changes without unsafe self-testing It can help to explain that you no longer recognise the usual aroma of prepared coffee, garlic in a meal or another familiar food. You may also notice whether a small amount of an ordinary food still seems sweet, salty, sour or bitter. Use only foods you normally tolerate; there is no need to eat something that conflicts with an allergy or dietary restriction. This is an observation for your history, not a COVID-19 test. Do not inhale baby powder or loose spices, put substances inside your nose, sniff solvents or cleaning products, or use a flame to test smell. Strong irritation is a different sensation and does not prove that the smell system is working. Formal smell and taste testing uses controlled methods. Use appropriate infection testing For a new unexplained change, follow local guidance on COVID-19 testing. A rapid antigen test can be negative early in infection. FDA advice for someone with symptoms is to repeat a negative home antigen test after 48 hours, giving at least two tests over three days. Follow the particular kit’s instructions; a clinician may recommend a molecular test. If you have symptoms and a negative result, continue precautions while the cause is uncertain. A negative test does not explain persistent smell loss or exclude another respiratory illness. High-risk people should contact a clinician promptly rather than waiting to complete repeated tests before asking about treatment. Look for the rest of the symptom picture COVID-19 may also cause fever or chills, cough, tiredness, sore throat, a runny or blocked nose, headache, body aches or breathlessness. Nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea can occur. Symptoms can change as the illness develops, and some people have only a few of them. Flu and other infections can look similar. Neither this list nor a smell change reliably distinguishes one virus from another. When contacting a healthcare service, give the symptom start date, test results and any change in breathing or ability to drink. Mention pregnancy, relevant conditions and medicines because they can affect the next steps. Ask early about treatment when risk is higher Older age, a weakened immune system and conditions such as chronic lung or heart disease can increase the chance of severe illness. Diabetes, obesity and pregnancy or recent pregnancy may also be relevant to an individual assessment. A clinician can consider the combination of factors rather than relying on one symptom. Some antiviral options must start within five days of the first symptoms, and another commonly used option within seven. Ask promptly even if the illness seems mild. The prescriber checks suitability and medicine interactions. Treatment for the infection does not guarantee recovery of smell, and an altered taste can sometimes be a medicine side effect. Reduce spread while you are unwell Stay home and reduce close contact when you have a new respiratory illness that is not better explained by another cause. Cleaner indoor air and a well-fitting mask can help when sharing space, particularly with someone at higher risk. The advice that applies depends on where you live and the setting. For general community settings, CDC guidance uses two conditions that have both been met for at least 24 hours: symptoms are improving overall, and there has been no fever without fever-reducing medicine. It then advises five days of extra precautions. If fever returns or you worsen, stay home again. Healthcare and other specific settings have separate rules; persistent smell loss alone cannot measure contagiousness. Know when help is urgent Get emergency help for difficulty breathing, persistent chest pain or pressure, new confusion, or inability to wake or stay awake. Depending on skin tone, lips, nail beds or skin may look unusually pale, grey or blue. Do not wait for a positive test or a change in smell before responding. Seek advice sooner for other severe or worrying symptoms, deterioration or difficulty maintaining fluids. A smell change following a significant head injury also needs assessment in that context. If weakness, trouble speaking or another sudden neurological symptom occurs, treat it as an emergency rather than assuming a respiratory infection. Recovery studies do not set a deadline In an early CDC outpatient study, smell and taste symptoms that had resolved by the follow-up interview had a median resolution time of eight days from the test date. That calculation concerned people whose symptom had ended; it did not mean every participant recovered within eight days. It also was not a promise measured from the first day of illness. A small European report from 2020 described an average smell-loss duration of 8.9 days and recovery within twenty-eight days in 98% of its affected patients. Its size, retrospective reporting and early-pandemic setting limit how broadly that figure can be applied. Some people recover over weeks or months, while others have longer-lasting or incomplete recovery. A cold-related change also has no universal three-to-seven-day deadline. Other causes deserve consideration Nasal allergies, sinus infection and polyps can reduce the arrival of odours at the smell-sensitive area. Smoking, head injury, dental problems and exposure to irritant chemicals or solvents can also be relevant. Mention recent nose, mouth or throat surgery, including sinus or dental procedures, and any head-and-neck radiotherapy. Medicines can contribute, including some antibiotics, antihistamines and blood-pressure treatments. Do not stop prescribed treatment on your own; a pharmacist or prescriber can review the timing and alternatives. Taste changes may relate to oral health as well as to the nose, so an examination may need to consider both. Less common conditions are assessed in context Hormonal and neurological conditions are among the less common explanations. Thyroid problems and conditions such as Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s disease or multiple sclerosis may affect smell. A small study also found smell and taste impairment in people with Cushing’s syndrome. These associations do not make smell loss a screening test for any of those conditions. Rarely, a growth or another structural problem may need investigation. The clinician uses the pattern, examination and accompanying symptoms to decide what is appropriate. A long list of possible causes does not mean that everyone needs a brain scan or an extensive hormone panel. Persistent or progressive symptoms should be assessed rather than assigned to a past infection indefinitely. Get support for persistent changes Arrange a medical review if smell has not returned to normal within a few weeks, or earlier if there are concerning symptoms or trouble eating and drinking. Assessment may include the nose and mouth, medical history, a medicine review and supervised smell or taste tests. Treating an identified sinus or nasal condition may help. Smell training helps some people, although benefit and speed of recovery vary. Ask a clinician or established smell-disorder service for an appropriate method. Do not start steroid treatment, high-dose supplements or concentrated products in the nose without advice. If distorted flavours are limiting meals, a dietitian can help you maintain nutrition; changes in food temperature or texture may be easier to tolerate. Make daily life safer while you recover Check smoke alarms and appropriate gas-safety arrangements rather than trusting your nose to detect a problem. Carbon monoxide has no smell even for someone with normal senses, so a suitable alarm matters independently of smell loss. Follow food-storage instructions and use-by dates; tasting questionable food is not a safe substitute for smelling it. Loss of enjoyment in food, anxiety about safety and feeling disconnected from familiar smells can affect mood and relationships. Explain what has changed to people who support you. Ask for help with poor intake, weight loss or distress. Recovery can be uncertain without making those practical and emotional needs any less important. A new smell or taste change can occur with COVID-19, but normal smell does not exclude infection. Smell-related flavour changes and true taste changes are not identical. Early-pandemic percentages and short recovery averages are not personal guarantees. Use appropriate tests and timely care; do not rely on unsafe kitchen experiments. Persistent symptoms deserve assessment, nutrition support and practical home-safety adjustments. Can smell loss happen before a cough or fever? Yes. It may precede, accompany or follow other symptoms, and sometimes occurs without nasal blockage. Its timing alone does not confirm COVID-19. Does being able to smell exclude COVID-19? No. Many infections occur without smell loss. Testing and the overall clinical picture are more informative. Is bland food always a taste disorder? No. Smell supplies much of flavour, so food can seem bland while basic tastes remain detectable. True taste changes are also possible and deserve separate description. Can I test myself with coffee or cinnamon? Noticing a familiar food’s aroma can help describe the change, but it cannot diagnose infection. Do not inhale powders, irritants or chemicals; use an appropriate COVID-19 test. What if my first rapid test is negative? It may be too early to detect infection. Follow the kit and local guidance; FDA advice for symptomatic people includes another antigen test after 48 hours. Ask promptly about care if you are at higher risk. Does losing smell mean my illness will stay mild? No. It is not protection against severe illness. Seek help according to breathing, chest symptoms, alertness and other warning signs. Should smell return within eight days? There is no such deadline. The early eight-day estimate applied to resolved symptoms in a particular study. Recovery can take weeks or months and may be incomplete. Why do familiar foods suddenly smell unpleasant? This can be parosmia, a distortion of smell that sometimes occurs after infection. Seek support if it affects intake or persists; it does not by itself prove reinfection. Should I stop medicine that might affect taste? No. Ask the prescriber or pharmacist to review it. Stopping treatment without a plan may create a different health problem. When should persistent smell loss be reviewed? Arrange assessment if it has not returned to normal within a few weeks, or sooner for progressive symptoms, an injury, difficulty eating or drinking, or other concerns. Emergency symptoms need immediate help.

title: A purple or bruised penis: when to seek care
description: A new colour change can follow a minor injury, but pain, swelling or a trapped foreskin can signal an emergency. Learn how to get the right assessment.
body: A purple patch on the penis has several possible explanations, from bleeding under the skin to a skin condition or a circulation problem. Colour alone cannot establish the cause. How suddenly it appeared, whether there was an injury and whether you have pain, swelling or urinary symptoms are more useful clues. Check for emergency symptoms first Go to emergency care if an injury to an erect penis causes sudden pain, rapid swelling or bruising, especially with a cracking sound or immediate loss of the erection. This can be a penile fracture: a tear in the covering of the erectile tissue, despite there being no bone. It usually needs urgent surgical treatment. A foreskin trapped behind the head of the penis and unable to move forward is another emergency, called paraphimosis. Swelling and a dark or purple colour can reflect restricted circulation. Do not wait for it to settle or repeatedly force the skin. Seek immediate care for severe pain, rapidly worsening swelling, inability to pass urine, significant bleeding or a penis that becomes dark and numb. An erection lasting about four hours also needs emergency treatment; painful prolonged erections may need help sooner. Embarrassment should not delay assessment. Bruising and collections of blood A bruise forms when small blood vessels leak into nearby tissue. Friction, a knock or a pinch can cause a local mark, which may change colour as it heals. A haematoma is a collection of blood that may produce more noticeable swelling. You cannot reliably judge the depth or seriousness just by whether it feels soft or firm. Avoid further friction or sexual activity if the area is sore, and arrange prompt review if the cause is uncertain, the patch spreads, swelling increases or symptoms persist. A significant injury should be assessed even if pain begins to ease. Do not massage or puncture a swelling. Tell the clinician about blood-thinning medicines and any bruises elsewhere, nosebleeds or blood in urine or stool. Do not stop an anticoagulant on your own. The team may need to assess a bleeding tendency as well as the local injury. A zipper pinch, friction during sex or masturbation, or a sports injury are examples of possible trauma. A small clearly explained bruise may fade gradually, but an enlarging mark, persistent tenderness or a more substantial injury needs review rather than a promise that it will heal within a fixed number of weeks. Purple spots can have other causes Purpura describes bleeding into the skin; it is not one specific disease. It can result from damage to small vessels, inflammation, platelet problems or other conditions. A new unexplained cluster of spots warrants medical assessment, especially with bleeding elsewhere or feeling unwell. Some medication reactions cause a sharply defined red or violet patch that returns in the same place after exposure to the same medicine. This is called a fixed drug eruption and can affect the genitals. Mention all recent medicines, including non-prescription painkillers, but do not deliberately take another dose to test the connection. A widespread painful rash, blistering or peeling, particularly with mouth or eye sores after a new medicine, needs emergency care. These features can occur in a rare serious reaction such as Stevens–Johnson syndrome. Bring your medication list or packaging to the assessment. Nutritional deficiency, medicines or a bleeding or clotting disorder can contribute to unexplained bruising in some people. Mention abdominal or joint pain, fever, new fatigue and bruises beyond the genital area, rather than focusing only on the colour of one patch. Skin disease and infection need different treatments Lichen sclerosus can cause pale or scarred patches, fragile skin, bruising, tearing or a tightening foreskin. It is not a sexually transmitted infection. A dermatologist or urologist can assess it and recommend treatment; stronger steroid ointments require a specific plan, and some people need surgery for complications. Genital ulcers or blisters may also be caused by infections, including herpes or syphilis. Other conditions can look similar, so a visual guess is unreliable. A sexual-health clinic can arrange suitable tests and explain treatment, partner advice and when sexual contact is safe. Do not apply leftover antibiotics, antifungal creams or potent steroids simply because an online photograph looks similar. The wrong treatment may irritate the skin or delay the diagnosis. An ulcer, lump or patch that does not heal also deserves examination. Herpes or syphilis can cause genital sores with pain, itching, burning or urinary discomfort, although syphilis sores may be painless and infections can have few symptoms. Syphilis can be cured with appropriate treatment; herpes can be managed with antiviral treatment but is not eradicated by a short course. What to expect at an appointment The clinician will ask when the change started, whether it is progressing, about recent injury or sexual contact, and about medicines and symptoms elsewhere. They may examine the skin, foreskin and surrounding area and check circulation or urinary function. Depending on the findings, testing may include a swab, blood or urine tests, or imaging for an injury. Not everyone needs an ultrasound. Ask what diagnosis is most likely, how to care for the area and which changes mean you should return sooner. If you are uncomfortable discussing the problem, you can begin with a simple description: a new purple patch, when it appeared and whether it hurts. You can also request a chaperone or ask the service about clinician preferences where available. New discolouration cannot be diagnosed from colour alone. Sudden bruising after an erection injury or a trapped foreskin is an emergency. Unexplained spots, ulcers or persistent changes need medical assessment. Treatment depends on the cause, not on matching an online photograph. Does purple always mean an STI? No. Bruising, circulation problems, skin disease and drug reactions are other possibilities. Can I wait if an injury stops hurting? Not if there was a significant injury, rapid bruising, swelling or loss of an erection. A serious tissue injury can still need urgent care. Should I use steroid cream? Only when a clinician has diagnosed a condition for which that treatment is appropriate and given instructions.

title: What to do if a condom stays in the vagina
description: A gentle removal approach, when to get help, and how to act on pregnancy and STI risks without missing time-sensitive options.
body: A slipped condom can be stressful, but it cannot disappear through the cervix into the abdomen. Remove it gently if it is easy to reach, and get professional help if it is not. Then consider pregnancy and infection risks separately, because removing the condom does not undo the exposure. Remove it promptly and consider the exposure separately A condom that slips off and remains in the vagina should be removed as soon as reasonably possible. If you cannot remove it easily, contact a sexual health clinic, primary-care service or urgent-care service. You do not need to keep trying until you become sore or wait for a regular gynaecology appointment. Removal is only one part of the response. If semen could have reached the vagina and pregnancy is possible, seek emergency-contraception advice promptly. If the exposure may pose an HIV risk, assessment is urgent because preventive treatment must start quickly. These time windows begin at the exposure, not when the condom is finally removed. It cannot disappear into the abdomen The vagina ends around the cervix, the lower part of the uterus. A condom can become folded or sit high in the vaginal canal, but it cannot travel through an intact cervix into the abdomen. Vaginal length and position vary, so not being able to reach it immediately does not mean that something unusual has happened. Take a moment to slow your breathing. Anxiety can make the pelvic-floor muscles tense and reaching uncomfortable. A calm pause is reasonable, but reassurance about the anatomy is not advice to leave the object in place. If you are uncertain whether a condom is still present, a clinician can examine you. A gentle attempt with clean fingers Wash your hands and make sure your fingernails have no sharp edges. In a comfortable position, insert one finger gently to feel for the condom. If needed, use two fingers to catch the material between them and draw it out slowly. Stop if reaching causes pain, bleeding or significant resistance. Squatting or placing one foot on a stable surface may make access easier. A gentle bearing-down action, like starting a bowel movement, can help bring the condom lower. There is no need to strain hard or keep changing position for a long time. If a brief, comfortable attempt does not work, arrange help. What not to put inside Do not use tweezers, scissors, eyelash curlers or another household tool. Even an apparently smooth object can injure delicate tissue, and a small fragment may be pushed farther away. Clinical removal instruments are used with appropriate examination and visualization; they are not a model for an at-home attempt. Do not douche or try to flush the condom out. Washing inside the vagina does not prevent pregnancy or an STI and can cause irritation. Do not insert another object to search for it, and avoid further penetration until the condom has been removed and any pain or injury has been assessed. Comfort, lubricant and asking someone to help If dryness makes a gentle attempt uncomfortable, a small amount of an appropriate water-based intimate lubricant on the finger may help. Do not substitute coconut oil or another kitchen product. A comfortable position and slow breathing are usually more useful than continuing through pain. A warm bath may feel relaxing, but it is not a removal treatment and should not delay getting help. A trusted partner may help only if you want them to and they can follow the same clean-finger, gentle approach. You can stop at any moment. You do not need to accept help from someone if you feel embarrassed, unsafe or pressured; a healthcare professional can assist instead. Check whether the whole condom came out After removal, inspect the condom without pulling it so hard that you tear it yourself. If it seems complete, that is reassuring about the retained material, but it does not prove that no semen escaped. A condom can leak during slippage even if it has not split. If part appears to be missing or you still feel something inside, seek an examination. Do not repeatedly sweep or scrape the vaginal canal looking for a tiny fragment. Let the clinician know whether the condom was intact, torn or difficult to remove, and whether there has been any pain, bleeding, unusual odour or discharge. When professional removal is needed Get prompt help if you cannot reach or remove the condom, are uncertain whether anything remains, or have persistent symptoms. Fever, pelvic or lower abdominal pain, offensive discharge or significant bleeding warrant more urgent assessment. Severe pain, heavy bleeding, fainting or a markedly unwell feeling may require emergency care. There is no universal one- or two-hour safe waiting period that replaces symptom-based advice. A clinician may use a speculum to see the vagina and a suitable instrument to grasp the condom. Ask for an explanation, a chaperone or support person according to local arrangements, and tell the clinician if you need the examination paused. This is a familiar problem for sexual health services. Deciding whether pregnancy is possible Treat condom slippage during penis-in-vagina sex as a possible contraceptive failure if you are relying on that condom. Sperm may have escaped even without a full ejaculation. A condom used only on a clean toy does not create a pregnancy risk by itself, but semen transferred on the toy or hands changes that assessment. A correctly used additional contraceptive method may mean emergency contraception is unnecessary. Tell the pharmacist or clinician about missed pills, a late injection, vomiting, interacting medicines or concerns about an implant or IUD. Infertility does not automatically mean pregnancy is impossible, and irregular or absent periods are not proof of menopause. Confirm uncertainty rather than relying on an exclusion list. Emergency contraception is time-sensitive Contact a pharmacy or sexual health service as soon as possible. Options can include an emergency contraceptive pill or a copper IUD, depending on timing, medical suitability and local availability. A copper IUD can usually be fitted within five days of the exposure and is highly effective; a clinician may assess an additional timing option based on ovulation. Ulipristal acetate can be used within five days. Levonorgestrel is most effective when taken sooner, and local product guidance commonly emphasizes the first three days; clinical guidance may allow use later with lower effectiveness. Do not assume that everything is too late at 72 hours. The best option also depends on medicines, body weight and recent or ongoing hormonal contraception. Plan contraception and a pregnancy test afterwards Tell the service which regular contraception you use. After ulipristal, restarting hormonal contraception too soon can reduce its effect; guidance generally advises waiting at least five days. After levonorgestrel, regular hormonal contraception can usually be resumed immediately. Get written instructions about restarting and how long to use condoms or avoid sex for your particular method. Emergency contraception does not protect against later sex in the same cycle. Plan a pregnancy test around three weeks after the exposure, or follow the service’s advice; a test taken immediately cannot exclude a pregnancy from this incident. If your period does not arrive after a negative test, repeat it and seek advice. Severe abdominal pain or fainting needs urgent assessment, especially if pregnancy is possible. STI assessment depends on the actual exposure A sexual health service can assess whether testing is needed and when to repeat it. Tell them when the incident happened, the types of contact, any symptoms and what is known about each partner’s recent tests or diagnoses. A test performed immediately may provide useful baseline information without ruling out every new infection. If a partner has a diagnosed bacterial STI, you may need prompt assessment and treatment as an exposed partner. That is different from taking a generic preventive antibiotic after every condom slip. The infection, local resistance patterns, pregnancy possibility, allergies and examination findings determine the appropriate plan. Do not take leftover antibiotics or share a partner’s prescription. HIV prevention has a short starting window If the contact could pose a substantial HIV risk, seek urgent assessment for post-exposure prophylaxis, or PEP. Current CDC guidance recommends starting as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours and no later than 72 hours after exposure. When prescribed, the usual course is 28 days. Not every slipped condom requires PEP. The clinician considers the contact, the other person’s HIV status and treatment or viral suppression where known, and your own prevention history. Do not wait for all laboratory results or for the other person to arrange a test before asking. If more than 72 hours have passed, still contact the service for testing and a prevention plan. Herpes and antibiotic prevention are not interchangeable Taking aciclovir or valaciclovir after a single exposure is not an established strategy to prevent genital herpes in a person who does not have it. If blisters, ulcers or other symptoms appear, seek assessment so a lesion can be tested and treatment considered. Management of a partner’s known herpes is a separate discussion. Doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis is recommended for discussion in specific populations with particular STI histories under current CDC guidance. It is not a universal prescription for everyone with a retained vaginal condom, and evidence is insufficient to make the same recommendation for several other populations. Use a sexual health service to decide what is appropriate rather than combining preventive medicines yourself. Reduce the chance of another slip Use a condom that fits, check the expiry date and packet, and store it away from excessive heat. Put it on before genital contact, use the correct orientation and leave space at the tip according to the instructions. Do not use two condoms together. With latex condoms, choose a compatible water- or silicone-based lubricant instead of oil. After ejaculation, withdraw while the penis is still firm enough to keep the condom in place and hold it at the base. Loss of erection, delayed withdrawal, an unsuitable size or excessive lubricant inside can contribute to slipping. Review what happened without blame. Repeated problems are a reason to ask a sexual health professional about fit, technique and additional contraception. Support your partner without taking over A helpful response is practical and non-judgmental. Ask what assistance is wanted, share relevant testing and exposure information honestly, and offer transport or company for a clinic visit. If emergency contraception or care has a cost, discuss sharing it rather than leaving one person to manage the consequences alone. Respect the affected person’s choices about touch, examination and support. A condom slipping does not mean condoms should be abandoned: they remain useful for reducing pregnancy and STI risks. Use the experience to agree a clearer plan for future contraception, testing and what to do if a barrier fails again. A brief, gentle attempt with clean fingers is reasonable; pain or difficulty means stop and get help. Check for missing fragments without assuming an intact condom prevented leakage. Seek emergency-contraception advice promptly; options may remain available up to five days. Possible HIV exposure needs immediate assessment, with PEP started no later than 72 hours when indicated. Can a condom get lost beyond the vagina? It cannot pass through an intact cervix into the abdomen. It may fold or sit high enough to be difficult to reach, in which case a clinician can remove it. Can I use tweezers if my fingers cannot reach? No. Household tools can injure the vaginal tissue or push material farther away. Stop and arrange professional removal. Is there a safe two-hour period to wait? There is no universal waiting rule. Remove it promptly if easy, and get help if you cannot. Symptoms and time-sensitive pregnancy or HIV prevention may require faster action. Can my partner help remove it? Only if you want that help and it can be done gently with clean fingers. Stop for pain or discomfort. You can choose professional assistance instead. What if part of the condom is missing? Seek an examination rather than repeatedly searching with your fingers or a tool. Tell the clinician whether there is pain, bleeding, discharge or odour. Is pregnancy impossible if there was no ejaculation? No. Sperm exposure can be possible without a full ejaculation. If pregnancy is possible and the condom was the main contraceptive method, seek emergency-contraception advice. Is emergency contraception too late after three days? Not necessarily. Ulipristal and a copper IUD may be options within five days, and a clinician can assess timing and suitability. Ask promptly rather than assuming nothing can be done. Should I take herpes medicine just in case? Preventive aciclovir or valaciclovir after exposure is not an established strategy for someone without genital herpes. Ask a sexual health service about symptoms, testing and appropriate care. Do I need an antibiotic after every condom slip? No. Treatment for exposure to a diagnosed STI and doxycycline PEP for selected populations are specific clinical decisions. Do not take leftover antibiotics. When should I take a pregnancy test? Plan a test about three weeks after the exposure or follow the service’s instructions. An immediate negative test cannot rule out pregnancy from this incident; repeat testing or advice may be needed if your period remains absent.

title: Henna for hair: colour, application and safety
description: Understand henna and indigo, realistic benefits, product-based application steps, homemade mix limitations and signs of a dye reaction.
body: Henna can create a lasting warm hair colour, but results and tolerability vary. A clear ingredient list, a strand test and instructions for the actual product are more useful than a universal recipe or a promise of healthier hair. What henna is and what it can change Henna is made from Lawsonia inermis leaves and has a long history of use for hair colour and body decoration in parts of Africa and Asia. Pure henna creates an orange-red to reddish-brown stain. The result depends on the starting colour, previous treatments, hair condition and the formulation, so the same powder will not produce the same shade on every person. Historical medicinal uses are a different matter from hair colouring. Claims about treating illness, digestive problems or reproductive conditions are not reasons to swallow henna or use it as a pregnancy remedy. For hair, the practical question is whether the product can provide a colour you like without an unacceptable reaction or change in texture. Natural origin does not guarantee a suitable result. Colour and texture benefits are different from treating the scalp Some people find their hair looks glossier or feels fuller after henna, while others find it dry or difficult to manage. These experiences can depend on the mix and hair condition. References to tannins, vitamin E, protein or antioxidants do not establish that applying the powder nourishes the follicle or prevents future greying. Covering grey strands changes their appearance; it does not switch natural pigment production back on. Henna is also promoted as an antifungal treatment for dandruff, scalp infection or hair loss. Laboratory activity of a plant ingredient is not proof that a homemade paste treats those problems in people. Persistent flaking, sores, patchy loss or excessive shedding should be assessed so that care targets the cause. A cosmetic dye should not delay that assessment or be applied to an already inflamed scalp. Read past the words natural, neutral and black The ingredient list is more useful than a colour name. Natural henna generally refers to Lawsonia, while products called neutral henna may contain other plants, such as cassia. They do not necessarily behave like pure red henna. A product labelled black henna may be a plant blend or may contain added dyes, including paraphenylenediamine, known as PPD. The label alone cannot tell you which. PPD can cause serious allergy, and a previous black-henna temporary tattoo can increase the risk of a later hair-dye reaction. Choose a clearly labelled product from a traceable supplier and avoid unknown mixtures. This does not mean every henna product contains contaminants or PPD. It means purity and composition should be checked rather than assumed from words such as herbal, organic or chemical-free. Henna and indigo are separate plant dyes Indigofera tinctoria supplies indigo, a different colouring ingredient from Lawsonia. Henna and indigo may be combined, or used in a planned sequence, to create darker brown or black-looking shades. The instructions depend on the particular formulation. Applying indigo after henna is one possible method, not a universal recipe for every product or hair type. Do not assume that henna is always temporary while indigo is always permanent. Colour persistence and later correction depend on the hair and the mixture, and henna colour can be difficult to remove. Neither plant should be treated as a guaranteed hair-growth treatment. Tell a stylist about previous plant dyes before bleaching, perming or applying another colour, especially if you do not know what the earlier product contained. Test and choose the timing before a full application Read all instructions before mixing. Follow the product’s allergy-test directions before each use, even if you used it successfully before. A negative home test does not guarantee that a full application will be reaction-free. If you previously had a dye reaction, get professional advice about the ingredient involved rather than repeatedly testing suspected products on yourself. A strand test serves a different purpose: it helps you see the likely shade and how your hair feels afterward. This is particularly useful with grey, bleached, chemically treated, dry or very porous hair. Do not apply dye to a scratched, sunburned or irritated scalp. Arrange enough time for preparation and rinsing, but do not extend the contact time simply because a recipe promises a stronger result overnight. Set up a clean space and suitable equipment Henna can stain skin, towels and surfaces. Wear gloves and old clothing, protect your shoulders with a towel and cover the work area. Have clips for separating the hair, an applicator brush, a suitable mixing bowl and utensil, water and a timer ready. Use a cap only if the product instructions call for one; keep plastic coverings away from children and the face. Choose equipment compatible with the product. A washable glass or ceramic bowl can be practical, while plastic may stain. A blanket claim that every metal utensil ruins every henna mix is not a substitute for the manufacturer’s directions. Keep dye away from eyes and do not use scalp hair dye on eyelashes or eyebrows. Do not use a hair dryer or sit in strong sun to accelerate processing unless the product specifically directs an appropriate method. Mix according to the formulation, not a universal kitchen recipe Powdered henna is commonly mixed with liquid into a workable paste, but the quantity, water temperature, resting time and storage instructions vary. A one-cup recipe may be far too much or too little for your hair. Use the amounts given for the product and your hair length. Do not assume every paste should stand overnight, or that refrigeration makes any homemade mixture safe to keep indefinitely. Recipes sometimes add lemon juice or apple cider vinegar, or replace water with coffee or black tea for a darker effect. Hibiscus, red tea and beetroot juice are proposed for redder tones. These additions do not guarantee a predictable shade and may irritate skin or alter the formulation. Filtered or distilled water is not universally required either. Avoid improvising acids, drinks or other products when the directions call for a simpler mixture. Apply in sections and monitor how your scalp feels Prepare clean or dry hair as specified by the product; instructions differ. Divide the hair into manageable sections, then apply the paste evenly with gloved hands or the supplied brush. Working methodically from one section to the next, including the crown and roots where appropriate, is more useful than applying extra product indiscriminately. Use clips to keep treated sections separate if needed. Keep the mixture away from your face and eyes and wipe accidental skin contact promptly. Start a timer and follow the stated processing period. Four or five hours, an overnight application and added heat are not universal requirements. Burning, itching or feeling unwell is a reason to stop, not a sign that the colour is working. Remove the product and seek advice if a reaction occurs. Rinse thoroughly and care for the hair afterward At the recommended time, rinse carefully until the paste is removed, following the instructions about water temperature, shampoo and conditioner. Some formulations recommend waiting before the next shampoo, but a fixed twenty-four-hour no-shampoo rule does not apply to every product. If you suspect an allergic reaction, washing the dye out promptly with mild shampoo takes priority over preserving colour. Handle wet hair gently and avoid forceful rubbing or very hot drying. If the hair feels dry, use a suitable conditioner and reassess whether this product suits you before repeating it. Dry or frizzy hair does not automatically rule henna out, but a strand test is particularly valuable. Do not keep reapplying dye to correct a disappointing result without considering the cumulative colour and effect on the hair. Treat food-based masks as optional mixtures, not repair treatments Common homemade additions include egg, yoghurt, shikakai, soaked fenugreek, amla, aloe vera and flaxseed paste. These ingredients have different properties and can introduce allergy, irritation, spoilage or unpredictable colour effects. An elaborate recipe with several cup measures is not evidence that the mixture is suitable for your scalp or able to repair damaged hair. There is no need to combine all of them with henna. In particular, do not leave an egg or dairy mixture warm for hours or overnight and assume a plant powder preserves it. A formulated conditioner with clear directions is often simpler to evaluate. If you choose a hair product containing a botanical ingredient, judge that finished product rather than treating a list of traditional ingredients as a proven treatment. Recognise irritation and allergy A reaction can cause stinging, itch, a rash, swelling or blisters on the scalp, face or neck. Symptoms may develop after a delay, including over the next few days. Severe inflammation can damage skin and contribute to hair loss; it should not be dismissed as normal sensitivity. Stop using the product, wash it off and ask a pharmacist or clinician for advice about a mild reaction. Seek medical help for persistent or worsening symptoms, extensive blistering or marked facial swelling. Trouble breathing, swelling of the lips, mouth or tongue, faintness or collapse requires emergency care. Keep the packaging and ingredient list to help identify the cause. A dermatologist can assess allergy; switching to another product called natural does not necessarily avoid the same ingredient. Using hair colour during pregnancy Available guidance generally finds little exposure from using hair dye correctly on an intact scalp, and henna-based colour can be an option. Pregnancy can still change how the hair responds. Follow precautions such as gloves, ventilation, the shortest instructed contact time and thorough rinsing. Some people choose to wait until after the first twelve weeks, but that is a preference discussed in guidance rather than proof that earlier use necessarily causes harm. Check the complete product rather than relying on the henna name, and ask your maternity clinician if you have a particular concern or a history of reactions. Do not use henna internally or as a medicinal preparation. Whether pregnant or not, you can postpone colouring, choose a different approach or keep your natural colour if the process does not feel right for you. Henna changes colour, not the underlying cause of greying or hair loss. Black henna is a label to investigate, not a single dependable formula. Strand tests and allergy tests answer different questions. Do not assume overnight contact or kitchen additives are required. Will henna stop my hair turning grey? No. It can colour grey strands but has not been shown to restore natural pigment production. Claims about tannins preventing greying should not be treated as established. Is it a treatment for dandruff or hair loss? Not a proven substitute for diagnosis and treatment. Persistent flaking, scalp sores or significant shedding needs assessment rather than repeated dye application. Is black henna always pure indigo? No. Some products contain plant blends and others added dyes such as PPD. Check the full ingredient list and avoid unknown mixtures. Is neutral henna the same plant without the colour? Not necessarily. That name may refer to another plant, such as cassia, or a blend. Read the ingredients and test the effect on a strand. Can a negative patch test guarantee safety? No. It reduces uncertainty but cannot rule out a reaction during full use. Follow the product instructions and seek advice after any previous dye allergy. Must I leave henna on overnight? No. Use the processing time for your product. Longer contact, added heat or sleeping with dye on is not a universal way to improve the result. Should I add lemon juice, coffee or beetroot? Only if the product directions support the addition. These ingredients can change the mixture or irritate skin and do not guarantee a particular shade. Can an egg-and-yoghurt mask prevent dryness? There is no reliable universal recipe. Food mixtures can spoil and cause reactions; a suitable formulated conditioner and strand testing are simpler ways to assess care. Should I avoid shampoo if my scalp starts burning? No. Suspected reaction takes priority over colour. Wash the product out promptly with mild shampoo and seek advice, with emergency help for breathing trouble or mouth swelling. Can I use henna hair colour while pregnant? It can be an option when used correctly, but check every ingredient and follow exposure precautions. Discuss previous reactions or individual concerns with your maternity clinician.

title: Hair around the nipples: what is normal?
description: Why areolar hairs appear, when a changing pattern needs assessment, and how to approach optional hair removal without damaging sensitive skin.
body: A dark or coarse hair around a nipple can be surprising, but a few hairs in the surrounding areola are a normal variation. The useful questions are whether growth is changing quickly, whether other symptoms have appeared and what, if anything, you want to do about it. A few areolar hairs are a normal variation Much of the body has hair follicles, including skin around the breasts. Fine, pale hairs can be easy to miss, while a few darker, longer or coarser hairs stand out. What people call nipple hair usually grows in the areola, the darker skin surrounding the nipple, rather than from the milk-duct opening. The amount and appearance vary between people and can change over time. A few longstanding hairs are not evidence of poor hygiene or an illness, and they do not need to be removed for health reasons. There is no reliable reason to compare yourself with photographs that may show shaved or edited skin. You can choose to leave the hair alone or discuss removal if it bothers you. Hormones matter, but one hair is not a hormone test Body hair can change around puberty, pregnancy and menopause, as well as with ordinary aging. Hormonal shifts can influence the thickness and visibility of hair, but there is no specific age in your twenties or thirties when a new areolar hair automatically means a hormonal imbalance. Androgens, including testosterone, are present in everyone. Higher androgen levels or greater follicle sensitivity to them can produce hirsutism: a broader pattern of coarse, dark hair in areas such as the face, chest, abdomen or back. A few local hairs without other symptoms are different from rapidly increasing hair in several areas. Pay attention to the pattern and pace of change. Increasing facial or body hair with oily skin, acne, irregular or absent periods, or thinning scalp hair is worth discussing with a clinician. Sudden marked growth, a deepening voice or an unexplained increase in muscle bulk needs prompt assessment rather than cosmetic treatment alone. Review medicines before assuming a new disorder Some medicines can alter hair growth, including testosterone or anabolic steroid products, glucocorticoid medicines and particular immune-suppressing treatments such as ciclosporin. Not every medicine in these groups has the same effect, and medicine-related hair growth is not always the same androgen-pattern process as hirsutism. Bring a list of prescriptions, injections, creams and supplements to an appointment, including when they were started or changed. A prescriber can assess whether the timing fits and whether any change is appropriate. Do not abruptly stop steroid medicines or an immunosuppressant because of a cosmetic concern. The condition they are treating and the risks of withdrawal also need consideration. PCOS and Cushing’s syndrome need a broader assessment The condition widely known as polycystic ovary syndrome, or PCOS, is a common cause of androgen-related excess hair. Current NHS information uses the name polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, or PMOS. It can involve irregular ovulation and periods, acne, scalp hair loss and difficulty conceiving. Hair around the nipples by itself cannot diagnose it, and ovarian cysts are not a requirement for every person with the condition. Cushing’s syndrome is a much less common cause of changes in hair and periods. It involves prolonged excess glucocorticoid exposure, from medicines or excess cortisol produced within the body. Features such as easy bruising, wide purple stretch marks, muscle weakness and changes in fat distribution make a broader clinical assessment more useful than focusing on one coarse hair. Pituitary tumors can cause excess ACTH, the signal that tells the adrenal glands to make cortisol; this form is called Cushing’s disease. Adrenal tumors or ACTH-producing tumors elsewhere, including the lungs, are other possible causes. The pituitary must not be excluded from the list. These are explanations a clinician considers when the overall pattern fits, not reasons to assume that ordinary areolar hair indicates a tumor. Choose tests according to the symptoms A clinician will usually ask when the change began, whether periods are regular, whether pregnancy is possible, what medicines you use and whether similar hair patterns run in the family. They may examine the distribution of hair and look for other signs of a hormone condition. You can also explain how much the hair affects your confidence or comfort. Blood tests may be useful for wider hirsutism, menstrual changes or other concerning findings. The Endocrine Society advises against routine androgen testing for isolated local unwanted hair when periods are regular and there is no abnormal hirsutism pattern. More tests do not automatically make a normal variation clearer. If testing is needed, the clinician chooses which hormones, timing and follow-up suit the question. If you want removal, start gently Leaving the hair alone is a valid option. If you prefer to shorten it, careful trimming avoids pulling out the follicle. Use a clean small tool, good lighting and a position in which you can clearly see the skin. Leave a little clearance instead of trying to cut flush with the areola, and stop if you cannot control the tool safely. Trimming removes the visible part, so the hair will grow again and may need repeating. It does not treat a hormone disorder, but it can be enough for a few bothersome hairs. Do not cut into a raised bump or mistake the normal small glands on the areola for ingrown hairs. Seek advice first if the area is sore, cracked or inflamed. Plucking, shaving and waxing can damage sensitive skin Tweezers remove a hair from the follicle, but pulling can cause pain, irritation, ingrown hair or infection. A warm shower may soften skin and hair; it does not literally open pores or make plucking risk-free. Breast-specific NHS advice favors careful trimming over plucking or shaving around the nipple. A razor can nick the nipple or areola, and regrowth may irritate the skin or become ingrown. Waxing or an epilator pulls multiple hairs and may also cause irritation, skin injury or burns from hot wax. A salon appointment does not automatically make those methods suitable for the nipple area. Discuss safer options if the skin is sensitive or you are uncertain. Do not repeatedly squeeze or dig at an ingrown hair. Increasing redness, warmth, swelling, pain or pus can indicate an infection; seek advice, particularly if you feel unwell or have fever. During breastfeeding, avoid creating sore or broken skin where the baby feeds and ask for help if pain interferes with feeding. Creams and home light devices have area restrictions Depilatory creams work by breaking down hair, but can irritate or burn delicate skin. A product suitable for legs, underarms or the bikini line should not be assumed safe on nipples or areolas. Avoid using it there and follow all restrictions rather than trying a stronger product when a gentler one has not worked. The same caution applies to home laser or intense pulsed light devices. Follow the manufacturer’s prohibited-area and skin-tone instructions, including any direction to avoid the nipple and areola. A patch test somewhere else does not establish safety for this pigmented, sensitive area. Do not use a device over a wound or inflamed skin. Professional removal has benefits and limits Laser treatment targets pigment in hair and can reduce growth over a series of sessions. Its suitability depends on the hair, skin tone, treatment area and device. The pigmented areola needs particular care; a dermatologist should assess the exact location rather than assuming a treatment used on the legs is suitable around the nipple. Electrolysis treats individual follicles with electrical energy and can be useful for hairs that do not respond well to laser, including lighter hairs. Both methods can be uncomfortable and require repeated appointments, with costs that add up. Ask about the practitioner’s qualifications, likely number of visits, aftercare and the realistic chance of regrowth. Laser can cause burns, blisters, pigment changes or scarring, particularly in inexperienced hands. Maintenance may be needed even after a successful course. Neither a single session nor a package price guarantees permanent removal of every hair. Tell the clinician if you are pregnant, breastfeeding or taking medicines that affect the skin before booking treatment. Treat an underlying cause when treatment is needed Hormone-related hirsutism may be treated with medicines as well as hair removal. For many people who are not trying to conceive, a combined contraceptive pill is one possible starting option. It contains estrogen and a progestogen, but it is not suitable for everyone. The clinician considers health conditions, clot risk, pregnancy plans and the reason for treatment. An antiandrogen may sometimes be added or selected in appropriate circumstances. These medicines can affect fetal development and require an appropriate pregnancy-prevention plan when pregnancy is possible. An unspecified single-hormone tablet is not interchangeable with a treatment chosen for hirsutism. Do not take someone else’s prescription or self-treat a few hairs with hormones. Hair changes improve gradually, often over several months. Medicines do not instantly remove existing hairs, and a few stable areolar hairs may need no medical treatment at all. Arrange a separate assessment for a new breast lump, unexplained nipple discharge, persistent nipple rash or new inversion; those findings should not be explained away by the presence of hair. A few longstanding areolar hairs are usually normal and removal is optional. The speed and distribution of growth matter more than one hair. Medicines and hormone conditions can contribute, but testing is selective. Careful trimming is a gentler option than pulling at the follicle. Professional and prescription treatments need individualized advice and pregnancy precautions. Is hair around the nipple normal? Yes. Hair follicles can be present in the areola, and a few stable hairs are a normal variation. They do not mean poor hygiene. Does nipple hair prove I have PCOS? No. PCOS, also called PMOS in current NHS guidance, is assessed from a wider pattern of symptoms and findings. One or several local hairs cannot diagnose it. Does everyone need a hormone blood test? No. Isolated local hair with regular periods and no wider concerning pattern often does not need androgen testing. Your clinician selects tests based on the overall picture. Can a medicine make body hair grow more? Yes. Some hormone, steroid and immune-suppressing medicines can do this. Review the medicine with its prescriber instead of stopping it yourself. Can a pituitary problem cause Cushing’s syndrome? Yes. An ACTH-producing pituitary tumor can cause excess cortisol; that form is called Cushing’s disease. Ordinary areolar hair alone is not evidence of it. What is a gentle way to shorten a few hairs? Careful trimming with a clean tool, good lighting and clearance from the skin is an option. Leaving the hair alone is also fine. Does a warm shower make plucking safe? No. Warm water does not open pores or remove the risks of irritation, ingrown hair or infection. Breast-specific guidance favors careful trimming. Can I use a leg-hair removal cream on the areola? Do not assume it is suitable. These products can irritate or burn sensitive skin; avoid application to nipples and areolas and follow the product restrictions. Will one laser session permanently remove the hair? No. Results vary, several sessions may be needed and regrowth can occur. The exact area and skin tone need professional assessment. Can I take antiandrogens while trying to conceive? Do not self-treat. Antiandrogens can affect fetal development and require appropriate pregnancy precautions. Discuss fertility plans before choosing treatment.

title: Naproxen: side effects and precautions
description: Naproxen can relieve pain and inflammation, but it can also affect the stomach, kidneys and heart. Learn the warning signs and when to check before taking it.
body: Naproxen is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, or NSAID. Some products, including certain Aleve tablets, contain naproxen sodium 220 mg, while other strengths and formulations have different directions. Availability without a prescription does not make it suitable for everyone. Check the exact medicine first Read the active ingredients, strength and instructions on your own packet. Naproxen and naproxen sodium labels express strength differently, and tablets with different formulations should not be substituted tablet-for-tablet without advice. Some branded products also contain another medicine. Use the smallest effective dose for the shortest time required. Follow the local product’s maximum dose and self-treatment duration; these are not identical in every country. If pain or fever persists or worsens, seek advice rather than extending treatment yourself. Take the medicine with or after food if the instructions recommend it. Food may help stomach discomfort, but it does not eliminate the possibility of an ulcer or bleeding. Keep medicines out of children’s reach and do not adapt an adult dose for a child. Naproxen reduces production of prostaglandins, chemicals involved in pain, fever and inflammation. These chemicals also help protect the stomach lining and maintain kidney blood flow, so reducing them can produce unwanted effects as well as pain relief. It may be used for muscle or joint pain, headache, period pain, toothache or fever when suitable. Common side effects Naproxen can cause indigestion, nausea, abdominal discomfort, bloating, constipation or diarrhoea. Some people feel dizzy or tired. Ask a pharmacist or clinician for advice if a side effect is troublesome, persistent or worsening. Avoid driving or operating machinery if the medicine makes you dizzy or affects your vision or alertness. Do not add another painkiller without checking the ingredients and whether the combination is suitable. The distinction between short-term and long-term use is not a guarantee of safety. Serious reactions can occur early, although taking higher doses or using the medicine longer can increase certain risks. Recognise bleeding and allergic reactions Stop naproxen and get urgent medical help for vomiting blood, black tar-like stool, significant rectal bleeding, faintness or severe persistent stomach pain. Gastrointestinal bleeding or an ulcer can occur without a long history of indigestion. Call emergency services for difficulty breathing, swelling of the tongue or throat, or collapse. A severe blistering or peeling rash also needs urgent assessment. Do not take another dose while waiting for advice about a suspected serious reaction. Tell the clinician what you took, the strength, dose times and other medicines. Bring the packaging if possible. If you took more than directed, contact a poison-information service or urgent medical service promptly, even if you initially feel well. Ulcers can sometimes perforate, creating a hole in the stomach or intestine. Sudden severe abdominal pain needs emergency assessment. Naproxen can also affect platelet function and bleeding, which is why upcoming surgery and blood-thinning medicines must be discussed. Heart, blood pressure and kidney risks NSAIDs can increase the risk of heart attack and stroke, including during the first weeks of use. They can also worsen high blood pressure or heart failure. Naproxen should not be treated as risk-free because it is available over the counter. Chest pain, sudden one-sided weakness, speech difficulty or severe breathlessness needs emergency help. New leg swelling, rapid unexplained weight gain or a marked reduction in urine needs prompt medical assessment. Kidney problems are more likely in some circumstances, including existing kidney disease or dehydration. If you are vomiting, have significant diarrhoea or cannot drink normally, ask for advice rather than assuming that a usual painkiller remains suitable. Tell the pharmacist about your health and other medicines Check before use if you have had a stomach ulcer or bleeding, kidney or liver disease, heart disease, a stroke, high blood pressure, or an allergic or asthma reaction to aspirin or another NSAID. Also tell the team if you are having surgery. Do not combine naproxen with ibuprofen, another naproxen product or pain-relief doses of aspirin unless specifically instructed. Blood thinners, steroid medicines, some antidepressants, blood-pressure medicines and diuretics can also affect the risk or require monitoring. If you take prescribed low-dose aspirin, do not stop it yourself. Ask whether naproxen is appropriate: the combination can raise bleeding concerns and naproxen may interfere with aspirin’s protective effect. A complete medication list is more useful than checking one pair of drugs at a time. Pregnancy and breastfeeding need a separate check Ask a healthcare professional before taking naproxen during pregnancy or while trying to conceive. From around 20 weeks, NSAIDs can affect fetal kidney function and reduce amniotic fluid. Do not use them at that stage unless specifically directed by a clinician. From around 30 weeks, there is an additional risk to fetal circulation and use should be avoided. If a specialist considers an NSAID necessary between 20 and 30 weeks, the dose, duration and any monitoring need an individual plan. This warning does not mean you should stop clinician-prescribed low-dose aspirin used for a pregnancy indication. During breastfeeding, other options such as ibuprofen are often preferred. A clinician may use naproxen briefly with appropriate caution and infant monitoring, but prolonged self-treatment is unsuitable. Tell the prescriber if the baby is newborn, premature or unwell. Do not stop breastfeeding automatically because you took a dose; seek specific advice. Follow the exact product’s directions; strengths and formulations differ. Serious bleeding or cardiovascular effects are not confined to long-term use. Check for other NSAIDs and medicine interactions. Pregnancy from 20 weeks and breastfeeding require specific advice. Does taking naproxen with food prevent ulcers? It may reduce discomfort but does not remove the risk of an ulcer or bleeding. Can I add ibuprofen if naproxen is not enough? Do not combine them on your own. They are both NSAIDs, and combining them increases risk. Should I stop my prescribed aspirin? No. Ask the prescriber or pharmacist how to manage pain alongside it. Do not alter a prescribed aspirin plan yourself.

title: Acetaminophen: side effects and safer use
description: How to avoid overlapping acetaminophen products, recognise serious reactions and get urgent help after a possible overdose, even without symptoms.
body: Acetaminophen, also known as paracetamol, treats pain and fever and is usually well tolerated when taken correctly. Its familiarity can hide an important risk: several different medicines may contain the same ingredient. Checking every label and keeping a record of doses helps prevent an accidental overdose. Know what you are taking Acetaminophen is available on its own and in combination products for cold symptoms, flu and pain. A different brand name does not necessarily mean a different medicine. Some prescription labels abbreviate it as APAP. Check the active ingredients, the strength of each tablet or liquid, the amount per dose, the minimum time between doses and the limit for 24 hours. Do not combine acetaminophen-containing products unless a clinician has explicitly checked the total and given you a plan. It can ease symptoms while the cause of pain or fever is assessed. It does not treat every cause of those symptoms, so continuing to increase the dose when it is not helping is unsafe. It is used for problems such as headache, toothache, sore throat, muscle aches, period pain and fever. Unlike NSAIDs, it has little anti-inflammatory action. Its exact pain-relieving mechanism is not fully settled, although effects on pain signalling in the nervous system are involved. A maximum is not a target Follow the limit on your own product or the lower limit your clinician gives you. Different formulations and national labels can have different instructions. A general internet number should never override your package directions. The US FDA sets an overall ceiling of 4,000 mg in 24 hours for adults and people aged twelve or older, counting all products together. That is not a recommended daily target or a guarantee that this amount is appropriate for everyone. Some products and individual treatment plans have lower limits. Ask a pharmacist or doctor before use if you have liver or kidney disease, weigh less than 50 kg, drink heavily or take medicines that could interact. If pregnant or breastfeeding, discuss the appropriate product and dose when advice is needed; do not assume another painkiller is automatically safer. Why excess doses can harm the liver The liver processes acetaminophen. Too much can overwhelm its protective mechanisms and cause severe injury. This can follow one large overdose or repeated excessive doses, including unnoticed overlap between products. Warning symptoms can include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion or yellowing of the eyes or skin. However, a person may initially feel well. Symptoms may take time to develop, and early symptoms can look like an ordinary illness. If you or your child may have taken more than directed, contact a poison information service or urgent medical service immediately. Do not wait for pain, jaundice or abnormal behaviour. Have the packages, possible amounts and times available, but do not delay the call while trying to reconstruct everything. Call emergency services if the person collapses, is unconscious or has difficulty breathing. Do not try to make them vomit. A possible overdose needs professional assessment rather than a home remedy or a watch-and-wait experiment. Loss of appetite, unusual tiredness, sweating or pallor can be nonspecific early symptoms; right-upper-abdominal pain, dark urine or unusual bruising may signal serious illness. Black tar-like stool suggests bleeding and also needs urgent assessment, but it is not a specific test for acetaminophen liver injury. Do not wait for any of these signs after a possible overdose. Recognise allergy and serious skin reactions Side effects are uncommon at the correct dose, but a severe allergic reaction is possible. Swelling of the tongue or throat, breathing difficulty or fainting needs emergency help. Stop the medicine. Acetaminophen can also rarely cause serious skin reactions. Stop taking it and seek medical attention promptly if a new rash or skin reaction develops. Blistering, peeling skin or sores affecting the mouth or eyes require urgent assessment. A serious reaction can occur even after previous uneventful use. If a clinician confirms a serious acetaminophen-related skin reaction, avoid acetaminophen-containing products in future and ask about suitable alternatives. Do not deliberately retry it to test the connection. Extra care with children’s medicine Use a children’s preparation and the dose appropriate for your child’s weight, age and the exact concentration on the bottle. An adult dose or a spoonful guessed from memory can be dangerous. Ask a clinician for guidance for a child younger than two, and get prompt medical advice for fever in a baby younger than three months. Measure liquid with the supplied oral syringe or another suitable device recommended by a pharmacist. Kitchen teaspoons are not accurate dosing tools. If you change brands or bottles, check the concentration again before reusing a previous millilitre amount. Write down the medicine, amount and time, and tell other caregivers what has already been given. Do not assume a universal number of daily doses applies to every product or country. Alternating fever medicines can make tracking harder, so use a clear professional plan if advised to do this. Make symptom relief a short, deliberate step Take only the dose needed within the instructions and seek advice when symptoms persist beyond the label’s self-treatment period, worsen or keep returning. Do not use pain medicine simply to make a child sleepy. Keep medicines in their original packaging and out of children’s sight and reach. A pharmacist can review overlapping remedies and help turn confusing instructions into a simple written schedule. Acetaminophen and paracetamol are the same medicine. Count every product containing it and follow the lowest applicable dose limit. A possible overdose needs immediate advice even when the person feels well. Stop and seek help for a new skin reaction; breathing difficulty is an emergency. Is 3,000 mg a universal toxicity threshold? No. Product limits and individual risks vary. Follow your own instructions and seek immediate advice after a possible excess dose rather than judging safety from one number. Can I give the same liquid amount after changing brands? Only after checking the new concentration and dose instructions. Ask a pharmacist if there is any uncertainty. Can liver injury happen before symptoms are obvious? Yes. Feeling well after a possible overdose does not make it safe to wait.

title: Breast tenderness: ten possible causes and ways to find relief
description: Explore breast tenderness from bra fit, muscle strain, hormonal changes, pregnancy, breastfeeding, medicines, fibrocystic changes, mastitis and cysts.
body: Breast tenderness can feel like soreness when touched, fullness, aching, burning or throbbing. It may affect one breast or both, come and go with periods, or start after a change in feeding, activity or medication. Many causes are benign, but persistent pain and new breast changes deserve attention. Understanding the pattern can help you decide what to try and what to discuss with a clinician. Start with the pattern and any new changes Breast pain can happen to anyone with breast tissue. Sometimes the discomfort begins in the breast itself; sometimes a muscle, rib or nearby joint is responsible. The location alone cannot reliably tell you which tissue is causing the pain. Notice when the discomfort began, whether it is on one or both sides, whether movement or pressure triggers it, and whether it changes with your menstrual cycle. A short symptom diary can be useful, particularly if pain repeatedly appears before a period. Breast pain on its own is rarely a sign of cancer. That reassurance does not mean a new lump, nipple change or persistent focal pain should be ignored. There is also no need to endure severe pain simply because a cause is likely to be benign. The ten groups below explain common possibilities and the limits of home care. 1. A bra that presses, rubs or does not support you A bra can contribute to tenderness when its band, straps, seams or cups press into sensitive tissue. Insufficient support may also allow uncomfortable movement during walking or exercise. Breast size and preferred support can change with pregnancy, breastfeeding, weight changes and the menstrual cycle. Check whether the cups cut into breast tissue or gape, the band rides up, straps dig in, or a wire sits on the breast rather than around it. Spilling over a cup or repeatedly adjusting the bra can be a clue that its shape or size is unsuitable. The hook you use, by itself, does not diagnose a poor fit. Try a comfortable supportive fit and reassess during movement, not only while standing still. A fitting service can help, but it is optional. A soft bra at night may be more comfortable for some people; others prefer none. Avoid a garment that squeezes a tender area. 2. Strain in the chest muscles The pectoral muscles lie behind the breasts.
