Straining them during weights, sport, shovelling, lifting bags or repeatedly carrying a child may produce pain that seems to come from the breast. It can be more noticeable on one side and worsen with certain arm or shoulder movements. A more substantial injury may cause bruising, swelling or restricted movement. Temporarily reduce the activity that provokes the pain and return gradually as symptoms improve. Gentle movement within a comfortable range is preferable to forcing a stretch. Yoga or Pilates is not automatically suitable for a fresh injury; avoid any movement that reproduces pain. A wrapped cold pack after an injury or gentle warmth for muscle tightness may help comfort. Ask about suitable pain relief if you need it. Seek assessment for severe pain, significant swelling, weakness or symptoms that are not improving. New chest pressure with breathlessness, sweating or faintness needs emergency care rather than an assumption that you have pulled a muscle. 3. A knock, pressure or other minor injury Breast tissue can become sore after a bump, a heavy bag strap, pressure while carrying a child, or uncomfortable contact during sex. A minor injury may leave a tender or bruised area for several days, although recovery depends on its severity. Reduce pressure on the area and choose clothing or a bra that feels comfortable. A cold pack wrapped in fabric can soothe recent bruising; avoid placing ice directly on skin. Pain relief may be appropriate if it is safe for you. Do not assume that every lump after an injury is simply a bruise. Arrange an examination if a lump persists, swelling increases, the skin changes, or the pain is more severe than expected. Discuss comfortable positioning and touch with a partner rather than continuing contact that hurts. 4. Hormonal changes around a period Changing estrogen and progesterone levels can make breast tissue feel fuller, heavier or more sensitive during the menstrual cycle. Cyclical pain often affects both breasts, especially the outer areas, and may extend towards the armpits or arms. It commonly worsens before a period and settles as the period begins or ends. A supportive bra, a comfortable warm or cool compress, and appropriate pain relief may help. Sleep, rest and relaxation can make persistent discomfort easier to manage; this does not mean the pain is imagined or caused by a failure to relax. Some people notice improvement when they reduce caffeine, but research has not established a consistent benefit. Avoid presenting caffeine restriction or a low-salt diet as a dependable treatment for breast pain. A balanced diet is reasonable without removing multiple foods in search of a cure. If a recurring pattern disrupts daily life, discuss it with a clinician. Hormonal contraception may improve symptoms for some people and cause or worsen tenderness in others. The choice depends on your symptoms, medical history and contraceptive needs. 5. Pregnancy-related tenderness Breasts may become fuller and more sensitive early in pregnancy as hormones change. Nipple sensitivity may also increase. Other possible early symptoms include a missed period, tiredness, nausea with or without vomiting, more frequent urination, constipation, heartburn or changes in taste. These symptoms vary and do not confirm pregnancy. If pregnancy is possible, use a pregnancy test at the appropriate time and seek advice if the result or timing is unclear. Breast tenderness alone cannot tell you whether you are pregnant or whether a pregnancy is progressing normally. A bra with room for changing breast size, soft clothing and reduced friction may help. Soft nipple pads can be useful if fabric rubbing is uncomfortable; keep them clean and change them if damp. An optional soft sleep bra or a gently warm cloth may improve comfort, but avoid heat that burns or increases swelling. New lumps, one-sided redness, fever or unusual discharge still need assessment during pregnancy. Check any medicine with a pharmacist or maternity professional rather than applying ordinary over-the-counter pain advice without considering pregnancy. 6. Breastfeeding, attachment and nipple problems Pain during feeding may relate to shallow attachment, friction, damaged nipple skin, uncomfortable pump fit or breast fullness. Nipples that crack, bleed, become flattened after feeds or hurt throughout each feed are reasons to ask for help early. A breastfeeding specialist can watch a feed and assess both positioning and milk transfer. When a breast is very full, expressing a small amount may soften the area around the nipple enough to help attachment. If direct feeding is too painful, get help with an appropriate expression plan that meets the baby’s needs. Pumping more and more to completely empty the breast can increase supply and aggravate inflammation. Tender lumpy areas are sometimes described as blocked ducts. Avoid trying to force a lump out with deep massage or strong pressure. Cold packs and gentle handling are usually more suitable for inflammation; repeated intense heat can worsen swelling. Change damp breast pads and protect sore skin from friction. Some guidance suggests applying a little expressed milk to cracked nipples, but this is not a substitute for correcting attachment or assessing a wound that is not healing. There is no need to buy a particular pad material as a treatment. Itching, burning or shooting pain needs an assessment rather than an automatic diagnosis of thrush. Nipple skin infection, dermatitis, trauma and blood-vessel spasm can overlap in appearance. If a clinician suspects a fungal infection, they can assess the baby too and advise treatment. Deep breast pain alone does not establish Candida infection. When returning to work, plan feeding or expression around the baby’s usual needs and your comfort. A practical routine and well-fitting pump equipment can help avoid both uncomfortable fullness and unnecessary extra stimulation. 7. Contraception, fertility treatment and other hormonal medicines Hormonal contraception, fertility medicines and menopausal hormone therapy can cause breast tenderness. Some contraceptive pills contain estrogen and a progestogen; others contain only a progestogen. Their effects vary. Headaches, bleeding changes or mood symptoms may occur with some products, but every user does not experience every possible side effect. Tell the prescriber when the pain began and whether it followed a new medicine or dose change. They may suggest waiting for an initial adjustment period, changing the formulation or considering another method. A hormonal intrauterine device does not guarantee freedom from breast tenderness. If contraception is needed, options such as condoms or a copper intrauterine device can be discussed without leaving a gap in pregnancy prevention. Do not stop an essential medicine or fertility treatment without a plan. For menopausal treatment, a change in dose or route may be considered individually. Systemic hormone tablets, patches or gels and local vaginal estrogen preparations have different purposes and are not simply interchangeable. Persistent or new breast changes still require assessment even when a medicine seems a plausible explanation. 8. Fibrocystic breast changes Fibrocystic changes describe tissue that can feel lumpy, thickened or rope-like, sometimes with small cysts. They are common and are not themselves the same as cancer. Some people have no discomfort; others notice tenderness or fullness, particularly in the upper outer breasts. Symptoms often become more noticeable before a period and ease afterwards. The pattern and degree of lumpiness vary between people and across cycles. Comfortable support, a warm or cool compress and suitable pain relief can help. If symptoms remain troublesome, discuss further options with a clinician. A new or persistent lump, a previously assessed lump that enlarges, or a breast change that remains after your period should be checked instead of being labelled fibrocystic at home. 9. Mastitis and breast infection Mastitis involves breast inflammation and may develop into a bacterial infection. It often begins quickly in one breast, with a painful hot area, swelling or a firm region. Redness may be less obvious on darker skin. Fever, chills, aching or feeling generally unwell can accompany the local symptoms. During lactation, continue ordinary responsive feeding if possible, rest and use gentle measures for comfort. Avoid tight pressure, deep massage and expressing extra milk in an effort to clear the breast. A cold compress can help. A feeding specialist can assist if the baby cannot attach or feeding is too painful. Antibiotics are appropriate for bacterial mastitis when clinically indicated; inflammation does not automatically require them. Contact a clinician if symptoms are worsening or have not started improving after twelve to twenty-four hours of home measures. If prescribed antibiotics are not helping within forty-eight hours, seek reassessment. Do not wait for these time points if you feel severely ill. A persistent painful lump or worsening illness can indicate an abscess, which may need imaging and drainage. Mastitis can also occur in people who are not breastfeeding, including men, and should be assessed. Treatment and recovery times depend on the cause; there is no guaranteed one-week course or universal recovery deadline. 10. A breast cyst A cyst is a pocket of fluid within breast tissue. It may feel round or oval, soft or quite firm, and there may be one or several in either breast. Some are painless; others become tender or more noticeable before a period and smaller afterwards. Touch alone cannot reliably distinguish a cyst from a solid lump. A clinician may examine the breast and arrange ultrasound or other investigations according to your age, history and findings. New nipple discharge should be assessed rather than assumed to come from a harmless cyst. A confirmed simple cyst that causes no symptoms may need no treatment. A large or painful cyst can sometimes be drained with a fine needle. Persistent lumps, bloody fluid or a lump that does not disappear after drainage may require further investigation. Cysts can recur. A comfortable bra, a compress and suitable pain relief may ease tenderness. Cutting salt is not an established way to remove cysts, and diet changes do not replace assessment of a new lump. Use pain relief that fits your circumstances Paracetamol, also called acetaminophen, or an anti-inflammatory such as ibuprofen may be suitable for some causes of breast pain. Naproxen is another anti-inflammatory, but these medicines are not appropriate for everyone. Ask about interactions and conditions such as kidney disease, stomach ulcers or previous reactions to anti-inflammatory medicines. Follow the product instructions and avoid combining medicines with the same active ingredient. If a topical pain gel is recommended, check where it can be applied and how to prevent contact with a feeding baby; do not put it on damaged nipples without specific advice. During pregnancy, do not self-treat with ibuprofen, naproxen or other NSAIDs. They should be avoided from twenty weeks unless a clinician specifically advises otherwise. Prescribed low-dose aspirin has a separate role and should not be stopped on the basis of general pain-medicine advice. Breastfeeding also warrants a product-specific check. When to get help and what an assessment can involve Seek prompt medical care for a new lump, skin dimpling or an orange-peel appearance, a change in breast shape, a newly inverted nipple, a persistent nipple rash or unusual discharge, especially blood. A hot swollen breast with fever or chills also needs timely advice. You do not need to have several warning signs together. Call emergency services for severe chest pain with breathing difficulty, collapse, confusion or other signs of a serious acute illness. These symptoms should not be attributed to ordinary breast tenderness. For persistent pain without emergency symptoms, book an appointment if it is worsening, interfering with sleep or activities, or not responding to simple measures. Mention pregnancy or feeding, medicines, prior breast problems and family history. Assessment may involve an examination and, when appropriate, imaging or referral. Finding the cause can take more than one visit. Bring your symptom pattern and questions, and return if a previously assessed problem changes. Relief may be gradual, and the aim is a clear explanation and a workable plan rather than a promise that every cause will resolve within one or two weeks. Breast tenderness has several possible causes, and the pattern is useful information. A comfortable bra and cause-appropriate self-care may help, but new lumps or nipple changes need assessment. Get early feeding support for persistent nipple pain; avoid deep breast massage and extra pumping. Check medicines during pregnancy or breastfeeding rather than using a general pain recommendation. Does breast pain mean breast cancer? Pain alone is rarely a cancer symptom. A new lump, persistent focal pain, skin change, nipple inversion or unusual discharge still needs assessment. A reassuring pattern does not replace checking a new change. Why do both breasts hurt before my period? Hormonal changes can make both breasts fuller and more sensitive before a period. Tracking the pattern may help. Seek advice if symptoms are severe, persistent or accompanied by a new breast change. Can a bra make my breasts sore? Pressure, friction or inadequate support can contribute. Check the cups, band and straps during movement. A comfortable supportive fit may help; wearing a soft bra at night is a personal comfort choice. How can I tell whether pain comes from a muscle? Pain that changes with arm movement or follows lifting may come from the chest wall, but the pattern cannot confirm this. Severe, unexplained or persistent pain needs assessment. Chest pressure with breathlessness or faintness needs emergency care. Does tenderness prove that I am pregnant? No. Period-related changes, medicines and other causes can feel similar. If pregnancy is possible, take a pregnancy test at the appropriate time rather than relying on breast symptoms. Should I massage a painful breast lump while breastfeeding? Avoid deep massage or firm pressure. Inflammation can worsen with forceful handling or extra pumping. Seek feeding support, and arrange assessment for a persistent lump, fever or worsening symptoms. Is shooting breast pain always thrush? No. Attachment problems, trauma, skin conditions and blood-vessel spasm can cause similar pain. A clinician should assess the symptoms and the baby when relevant before recommending antifungal treatment. Should I stop my contraceptive pill or hormone treatment? Discuss a possible medicine-related cause with the prescriber. An alternative may help, but do not stop essential treatment or leave a gap in contraception without a plan. Do breast cysts need to be drained? Not always. A confirmed simple cyst without symptoms may be left alone. A large or painful cyst may benefit from aspiration. New, persistent or changing lumps require assessment before being treated as cysts. Will cutting caffeine or salt cure breast pain? There is limited evidence for dietary changes as treatment. Some people find less caffeine helpful, but it is not a guaranteed cure, and salt restriction has not been established as a cyst or breast-pain treatment.

title: Sinus infection or COVID-19? Symptoms, testing and what to do next
description: Compare overlapping sinus and COVID-19 symptoms, understand testing and recovery, and know when home care, early treatment or urgent assessment is needed.
body: A blocked nose, headache and tiredness do not always reveal which illness you have. Sinus inflammation and COVID-19 can overlap, and sometimes occur together. The useful next step depends on your symptoms, risk factors, test results and how the illness is changing. Sinusitis and COVID-19 describe different things The sinuses are air-filled spaces around the nose, cheeks and forehead. When their lining becomes inflamed, swelling can interfere with mucus drainage and cause pressure or congestion. This is sinusitis. Viruses cause many episodes, although bacteria can sometimes be involved. COVID-19 is the illness caused by SARS-CoV-2. It can affect the upper airways and other parts of the body. A person with COVID-19 can have nasal and sinus symptoms, and another condition can occur at the same time. The labels are not mutually exclusive, and a symptom comparison cannot replace testing or an assessment when needed. The symptoms overlap considerably A runny or blocked nose, headache, sore throat, cough, fever and tiredness can occur in respiratory illnesses, including COVID-19 and an illness associated with sinus inflammation. The absence of fever does not reliably exclude infection. How unwell you feel, your exposure history and the course over several days all matter. Avoid deciding that a familiar-feeling cold must be the same illness you had before. Different infections can feel alike, and repeat COVID-19 infections do not always produce the same symptoms. Until the cause is clearer, take sensible precautions around others, particularly anyone at higher risk of severe illness. Facial pressure can suggest sinus involvement Sinus symptoms may include tenderness around the cheeks, forehead or eyes, pressure when bending forward, mucus dripping down the throat, toothache, bad breath and a reduced sense of smell. Nasal mucus may become thicker or look yellow or green. These features help describe the problem but do not identify the germ. Coloured mucus alone does not prove a bacterial infection or establish that an antibiotic is needed. Severe one-sided pain, worsening illness or eye symptoms deserve assessment rather than a home diagnosis based on the colour of a tissue. Body symptoms and smell changes are not exclusive tests COVID-19 may also cause body aches, breathlessness, nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea. A new loss or change of smell or taste can be a clue, but its frequency varies with the circulating virus and the person’s circumstances. Nasal inflammation and other infections can affect smell too. There is no dependable symptom checklist that makes these conditions completely separate. Nor is there a fixed day on which everyone’s smell returns. If the change persists, ask for advice. Meanwhile, take extra care with smoke or gas alarms and food safety if you cannot rely on your nose. Onset and season provide context, not certainty COVID-19 symptoms can appear in the days after an exposure; public-health guidance describes a possible range of 2–14 days, although timing varies. Some illnesses begin abruptly and others gradually. That difference is not reliable enough to decide whether testing is needed. Sinus inflammation often follows a cold. Allergies to pollen or animal dander, exposure to smoke and other nasal problems can also contribute to congestion or poor drainage. An allergen is not itself an infectious germ. Colds and some respiratory viruses have seasonal peaks, but COVID-19 can circulate throughout the year. Do not use the calendar to rule it out. Recovery times vary more than a simple comparison suggests Acute sinus symptoms commonly improve over a few weeks. Many mild COVID-19 illnesses also improve at home, but a cough, tiredness or other symptoms may last longer than the initial fever. Improvement should be considered alongside your ability to drink, breathe comfortably and manage ordinary activities. A historical US outpatient study from 2020 illustrates the variation. Among 270 people with information about return to usual health, 175 reported recovery, with a median of seven days from testing among that recovered group. The other 95 had not returned to usual health at the interview, conducted roughly two to three weeks after testing. It did not show that everyone recovered in a week, and those early-pandemic findings cannot predict an individual’s recovery now. Test when COVID-19 is possible Testing can help you decide about treatment and precautions. A single negative home antigen test does not rule out infection. For someone with symptoms, current US guidance recommends repeating an antigen test after 48 hours, for at least two tests in total. A clinician may recommend a molecular test or a different local pathway. Follow the instructions for your particular test and tell the clinician when symptoms started. If you are at increased risk of becoming seriously ill, contact care promptly rather than waiting through several days of testing. Treatment assessment may be appropriate before a positive result is available. Ask early about treatment if your risk is higher Age, immune suppression and some long-term conditions can increase the risk of severe COVID-19. Pregnancy and recent pregnancy also matter. Contact your maternity or healthcare team early if you are pregnant or recently gave birth and develop symptoms, even if they seem mild at first. Antiviral treatment for eligible people needs to begin quickly, generally within five to seven days depending on the medicine. Examples include nirmatrelvir with ritonavir and intravenous remdesivir. A clinician checks timing, interactions, kidney or liver considerations and pregnancy suitability. Appropriate treatment should not be withheld solely because someone is pregnant or breastfeeding, but that does not make every antiviral suitable for every pregnancy. Home comfort measures should be simple and safe Rest, drink enough to avoid dehydration and use comfortable food and fluids as tolerated. A warm compress over the face may ease pressure. Saline spray may help nasal discomfort. If you use a sinus-rinsing device, use distilled or sterile water, or water that has been properly boiled and cooled, and follow cleaning instructions. Ordinary unboiled tap water is not suitable for nasal rinsing. Avoid leaning over a bowl of hot water for steam inhalation. Spills can cause serious scalds, especially around children, and there is no strong evidence that this speeds recovery. A comfortable shower may feel soothing, but it is not an antiviral treatment. Ask a pharmacist about pain or fever relief, avoid duplicate ingredients in combination products and check suitability in pregnancy or for a child. Do not share adult cold medicines with children. Antibiotics are not automatically needed for sinus symptoms Most sinus infections do not benefit from antibiotics because a virus is often responsible and the illness may settle on its own. A clinician may suggest observation or a delayed prescription in an appropriate case. Antibiotics do not treat COVID-19 itself, although a separate bacterial infection may sometimes need treatment. Arrange a review for symptoms lasting more than ten days without improvement, worsening after an initial improvement, fever lasting longer than three or four days, or substantial facial pain. Repeated episodes also deserve discussion. The decision about antibiotics depends on the whole assessment rather than a single symptom or a fixed promise that every sinus illness is harmless. Hospital treatment depends on the severity of illness Someone with severe COVID-19 may need oxygen and treatment for complications. Remdesivir is used in selected settings; a steroid such as dexamethasone may be used when COVID-19 causes an oxygen requirement. Steroids are not a routine home remedy for mild COVID-19 without low oxygen. Very severe illness can require intensive care and breathing support, including a ventilator. Older treatment lists also mention anti-SARS-CoV-2 monoclonal antibodies. Their role depends on the product, current variants and local authorization; some earlier treatments lost usefulness as the virus changed. Preventive antibodies offered to selected immunocompromised people are not interchangeable with treatment for an active infection. High-titer convalescent plasma has a specialist role for some immunocompromised patients, rather than being routine treatment for everyone with COVID-19. Recognise symptoms that need emergency assessment Get emergency help for difficulty breathing, persistent chest pain or pressure, new confusion, inability to wake or stay awake, or unusually pale, grey or blue lips, skin or nail beds. The appearance can vary with skin tone. Tell the dispatcher or receiving service that COVID-19 is possible, but do not delay urgent care while trying to confirm a test. Sinus symptoms also need urgent assessment if accompanied by swelling or redness around an eye, double or reduced vision, difficulty moving the eye, severe frontal headache, swelling over the forehead, a stiff neck or new neurological symptoms. These are different from ordinary mild congestion. Seek care whenever the illness is severe or rapidly worsening, even if it does not fit a checklist. Reduce the chance of spreading a respiratory infection While unwell, stay away from others as much as practical, improve ventilation and consider a well-fitting mask when sharing space. A separate sleeping area or bathroom can help if available. Keep hands clean, cover coughs and clean commonly touched surfaces. Let close contacts know if they may have been exposed, so they can follow local advice and protect vulnerable people. Follow the guidance where you live. As an example, current US community guidance allows a return to normal activities once symptoms have been improving overall and fever has been absent without fever-reducing medicine for at least 24 hours. It then advises five days of added precautions. If fever returns or you worsen, stay home again. Healthcare settings and some workplaces have different rules, and feeling better does not instantly mean you cannot transmit infection. Persistent symptoms deserve support Some people have continuing or recurring fatigue, breathlessness, difficulty concentrating or remembering, palpitations, muscle pain or joint pain after COVID-19. These symptoms can affect work, childcare and everyday life. They should not be dismissed simply because the initial infection seemed mild. Discuss persistent symptoms with a clinician and explain how they affect daily activities. Assessment can consider Long COVID as well as other causes that need treatment. You do not need to wait until a formal duration threshold is reached to ask for help. New chest pain, severe breathlessness or other emergency signs require urgent care rather than a routine follow-up. Recovery does not remove the need for future prevention A previous infection does not guarantee lasting protection from another infection. Vaccination decisions should follow current recommendations for your age, health and country. If you have recently recovered, discuss the timing of the next eligible dose with your clinician; a short delay may sometimes be considered according to risk and local guidance. Tell the team if you received antibody treatment or convalescent plasma, but do not assume that an old universal ninety-day vaccine delay still applies. Recommendations have changed since the early pandemic. Keep the dates of symptoms, tests and treatments available, so that future advice is based on your actual course rather than an outdated general rule. Sinusitis describes inflammation; COVID-19 identifies a particular infection. A negative antigen test may need repeating, and higher-risk people should seek advice early. Avoid hot-water steam bowls and use safe water for nasal rinsing. Follow current local precautions rather than an old fixed isolation rule. Does green mucus prove that I need antibiotics? No. Mucus colour alone does not establish bacterial infection. Duration, severity and examination help guide treatment. Can COVID-19 cause sinus-like symptoms? Yes. Nasal congestion and related symptoms overlap, and another sinus condition can coexist. Is loss of smell unique to COVID-19? No. It can occur with nasal inflammation and other infections, and not everyone with COVID-19 loses smell. What if my first home COVID-19 test is negative? A single antigen test can miss infection. With symptoms, current US guidance advises a repeat after 48 hours; follow local and test-specific instructions. Should pregnancy make me wait before seeking treatment? No. Seek early advice. A clinician can select appropriate treatment and should not withhold it solely because of pregnancy or breastfeeding. Did the 2020 study show that everyone recovered in seven days? No. Seven days was the median from testing among those reporting recovery; 35 percent had not returned to usual health when interviewed. Is steam over a bowl of hot water a good remedy? No. It can cause serious scalds and has no strong evidence of speeding recovery. Use safer comfort measures. Can I rinse my nose with ordinary tap water? Use distilled, sterile or properly boiled and cooled water. Follow the device’s cleaning instructions. Do I always need to isolate for ten days? Follow current local rules. Community, healthcare and individual circumstances can differ; old blanket ten-day advice is not a universal current rule. When do sinus or COVID-19 symptoms need emergency help? Breathing difficulty, persistent chest pressure, confusion or inability to stay awake need emergency care. Eye swelling or vision change, severe frontal headache and neurological signs with sinus symptoms also need urgent assessment.

title: COVID tests: what each result can tell you
description: Compare molecular, rapid antigen and antibody tests, understand timing and accuracy, and learn how to use home tests and act on the results.
body: COVID-19 is caused by the virus SARS-CoV-2. Testing can help identify an infection, guide timely treatment and reduce the chance of passing it to someone else. But the different tests do not answer the same question. A swab looking for the virus may help explain a new illness; a blood test for antibodies looks at an immune response. Knowing which test you have, when the sample was taken and what the result cannot show is as important as reading positive or negative. Three test types, two different questions Molecular and antigen tests are viral tests: they look for parts of SARS-CoV-2 in a sample. They are used to investigate a current infection. Molecular testing detects genetic material, whereas antigen testing detects viral proteins. Both can be useful, but they differ in sensitivity, speed and the equipment they require. Antibody testing, also called serology, looks for proteins your immune system has made. It may help answer a selected question about previous infection, but is not the routine way to diagnose today’s cough or fever. A test’s purpose matters more than the place you take it: a pharmacy, clinic or home kit can offer different technologies. How molecular testing works Nucleic acid amplification tests, or NAATs, use laboratory techniques to make small amounts of viral genetic material easier to detect. PCR is one type. You may see RT-PCR, meaning reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction, or RT-LAMP, a different amplification method. Some assays look for more than one viral target. These names describe the technology, rather than a separate illness being tested for. The sample may come from a nasal swab, a throat sample or saliva, depending on the authorized test. Do not substitute one collection method for another. Routine COVID molecular testing is not a blood antibody test. A health professional may collect the sample at a hospital, urgent-care service, clinic or pharmacy; selected products allow collection or testing at home. Molecular results: speed and limitations Some rapid molecular systems can produce a result during a visit, often within an hour. A specimen sent to a laboratory may take one to three days, or longer when services are busy. Ask the provider for its actual turnaround time and how the result will reach you, especially when a treatment decision cannot wait. Molecular tests generally detect smaller amounts of virus than antigen tests. A positive result commonly establishes infection without routine repetition, but recent infection can complicate interpretation. A negative result can still occur if the sample was collected poorly, handling failed or the timing missed detectable virus. Testing immediately after exposure can be too early. There is no fixed day when everyone becomes detectable, and a later positive does not automatically mean someone remains contagious. How rapid antigen tests work Antigen tests use reagents, including antibodies built into the test, to detect particular viral proteins. That does not make them blood antibody tests: the target is material from the virus, not the person’s immune response. Most familiar home kits use a nasal swab and display a result on a small device. Many give results in about 15–30 minutes and are available in pharmacies, clinics, testing services or for home use. Their convenience is valuable, but they are generally more likely than NAATs to miss infection, particularly early on or without symptoms. A positive result should be taken seriously. Unexpected or conflicting findings may need clinical clarification rather than repeated attempts to obtain a preferred answer. What older accuracy percentages actually mean Sensitivity describes how often a test identifies infection among people who truly have it; specificity describes how often it gives a negative result when infection is absent. Neither is a personal guarantee. Test brand, sample quality, symptom timing, the comparison method and the population studied can all change the findings. A Cochrane rapid-test review using evidence through September 2020 reported average detection of 95.1% of infections for the molecular tests studied, and 72% versus 58% for antigen tests in people with and without symptoms. Those historical figures refer to particular studies and products. Many molecular evaluations took place in laboratories rather than real point-of-care use, and some did not follow manufacturer instructions. They should not be quoted as the accuracy of every current PCR or home test. Repeat a negative antigen test at the right interval One negative antigen test does not reliably exclude COVID. Current US FDA advice is to repeat 48 hours after a negative result. If you have symptoms, perform at least two tests in total. If you have no symptoms, perform at least three, with 48 hours between tests. A positive result ends the negative-test sequence and should prompt appropriate precautions and follow-up. Follow the instructions for your particular product and local guidance. Testing again immediately is not equivalent to leaving time for a developing infection to become detectable. A clinician may recommend a molecular test instead, especially when symptoms persist or a rapid answer will affect care. Do not wait through several tests before contacting a clinician if you are at higher risk or becoming more unwell. Antibody tests use a blood sample Serology usually examines blood taken from a vein or, for certain tests, a finger prick. It looks for antibodies against SARS-CoV-2. Depending on the assay, a result may reflect earlier infection, vaccination or both. Antibodies take days to weeks to become detectable, so this approach can miss a recent infection. Access and turnaround depend on the laboratory and the reason for testing. Some services return results the same day; others need several days. Do not assume a blood test marketed online is authorized, useful for your situation or designed for unsupervised home use. Ask what antibody the test measures and what decision its result would change before arranging it. Antibody timing is not an immunity calendar Early research illustrated why serology is unsuitable for an immediate answer. A 2020 Cochrane review found combined IgG/IgM sensitivity of roughly 30% during days 1–7 after symptoms, 72% during days 8–14 and 91% during days 15–21. These were study averages, largely informed by hospitalized patients. Later review estimates changed with the added evidence, and studies from before vaccination do not describe every person’s current immune history. A positive antibody result is not proof that you cannot be reinfected or transmit the virus. A negative result does not prove you never had COVID: the response may be below the test’s detection threshold or may have declined. Research finding antibodies months after infection does not establish a fixed five-to-seven-month period of protection. Antibody tests should not decide whether a vaccine worked or whether a recommended vaccination is needed. When antibody testing can be useful A clinician may use serology to help investigate a particular question about past infection or a suspected complication, such as multisystem inflammatory syndrome. Public-health researchers also use it to estimate exposure across populations. These are different purposes from routine screening before work, travel or a family visit. Interpretation needs the test’s target, vaccination history and timing. Different tests can measure different antibodies, so two results are not necessarily directly comparable. If you are trying to understand a previous illness, discuss whether testing is likely to provide a meaningful answer rather than treating a commercial antibody level as an immunity score. Decide when testing will help Test promptly when new symptoms suggest COVID, regardless of vaccination status. After an exposure without symptoms, testing too soon may miss infection. Current FDA home-testing advice suggests waiting at least five full days after exposure if you remain well; test sooner if symptoms develop. Follow any more specific instructions from your clinician or local public-health service. Testing may also be requested in an outbreak, before a procedure or in a setting caring for vulnerable people. Crowded indoor gatherings, poor ventilation and travel can increase opportunities for exposure, but risk is not confined to unvaccinated people or an exact distance-and-minute threshold. Before travel or attendance at a facility, check the current destination or organization requirements, including the accepted test type and timing. Historical airline rules should not guide a new trip. A recent infection changes the choice of test Tell the clinician when you last tested positive. NAATs can detect residual viral RNA for up to 90 days, while reinfection can also occur within that interval. A positive PCR weeks later therefore cannot, by itself, distinguish a new infection from remaining material or establish how infectious you are. CDC guidance favors antigen testing for new symptoms during the 90 days after a positive result. For people without symptoms, it does not recommend testing for a new infection within the first 30 days; during days 31–90 it recommends antigen testing when testing is undertaken. These are US guidance distinctions, not a claim that recent infection makes someone immune. Individual clinical or setting-specific advice may differ. Home collection and a complete home test are different With a home-collection service, you obtain the specimen yourself and send it to a laboratory. You still have to follow packaging, transport and timing instructions, and the result comes later. With a self-test, you collect the sample, run the device and read the result yourself. Some home products use molecular technology, so the word rapid does not always mean antigen. Choose a product authorized where you live and suitable for the person’s age and symptoms. Some tests require an adult to collect a child’s sample; a younger child may need a different service. Check whether professional supervision is required for any certificate you need. Availability, prescriptions and accepted results differ between locations. Use the kit carefully from start to finish Before starting, read the full instructions, check storage conditions and inspect the expiry date. Certain lots have an officially extended shelf life, but only the regulator’s or manufacturer’s specific information establishes that. Prepare a clean surface and wash your hands. Use only the supplied components and the required sampling site, depth, number of rotations and quantity of liquid. Set a timer and read within the stated window. Do not add a throat sample to a nasal-only procedure or interpret a device hours later. An invalid result, such as a missing control indicator where one is required, is not a negative: repeat as directed with a new kit. Keep liquids and small parts away from children and pets, dispose of used materials appropriately, clean the area and wash your hands. Ask a professional about an unclear result. Plan access, costs and precautions while waiting A local health authority, pharmacy, clinic or your usual healthcare professional can explain nearby testing options. Confirm whether you need an appointment, what samples are accepted, how results are delivered and what to do if no result arrives. If cost is a concern, ask about coverage or available low-cost services before booking. Neither fixed historical prices nor a promise that all tests are free applies everywhere. When you feel ill, stay home and reduce contact with others while clarifying the cause. A negative result does not exclude flu or another respiratory illness. In US community guidance, return to normal activities depends on overall symptom improvement and being fever-free without fever-reducing medicine for at least 24 hours, followed by five days of added precautions. Local rules and healthcare-setting requirements may differ. Cleaner air, appropriate masking and avoiding vulnerable contacts can reduce risk; no test guarantees a risk-free visit. Do not let a test delay treatment or emergency care People at increased risk of severe COVID should seek advice as soon as symptoms begin, even if mild or the first test is negative. Older age, immune suppression and certain medical conditions affect risk. Pregnancy and recent pregnancy also warrant early contact with the care team. Suitable antiviral treatment generally needs to start within five to seven days of symptom onset, depending on the medicine; a clinician considers eligibility, interactions and individual circumstances. Seek emergency help for severe breathing difficulty, persistent chest pain or pressure, new confusion, inability to wake or stay awake, or pale, gray or blue lips or skin. These signs require action regardless of a test result. Testing is a tool to support care, not permission to delay it. Use molecular or antigen testing for suspected current infection; serology has a different purpose. An early or single negative test can miss COVID. Repeat antigen testing at the recommended interval or seek clinical advice. Historical sensitivity percentages are not guarantees for today’s product or your individual result. Recent infection, vaccination history and sample timing change how some results should be interpreted. Check local access and rules, and seek timely care when symptoms or risk factors warrant it. Which test is usually more sensitive, PCR or antigen? Molecular tests such as PCR generally detect lower levels of virus. However, collection quality and timing still matter, and a rapid antigen test can be useful when it gives an actionable result sooner. Is a rapid test always an antigen test? No. Some molecular tests are also rapid. Check the technology, sample requirements and instructions instead of relying on the word rapid. How many times should I repeat a negative home antigen test? FDA advice calls for at least two tests in total if you have symptoms, or three if you have none, spaced 48 hours apart. Follow the product and local instructions, and seek care promptly if you are high risk or worsening. Should I wait five days to test if I already have symptoms? No. The five-full-day advice concerns exposure without symptoms. Test when symptoms develop and arrange appropriate follow-up if the result is negative. Does a positive PCR several weeks later prove I am contagious? No. Residual RNA can remain detectable after the acute illness. Timing, symptoms and your clinical circumstances are needed to interpret the result; a new infection is also possible. Can an antibody test show that my vaccine worked? It should not be used for that decision. Antibody assays measure only part of immune function and differ in what they detect. They cannot provide a personal guarantee against infection or severe disease. Can a negative antibody test prove I never had COVID? No. Antibodies may not yet be detectable, may have declined or may not be the type the assay measures. Discuss the purpose and limits of testing with a clinician. Can I use a kit after the printed expiry date? Only if the relevant authority or manufacturer has officially extended the expiry for that exact product and lot. Do not assume all old kits received an extension. Does a negative COVID result rule out flu or another illness? No. A COVID-only test does not test for every cause of similar symptoms. Some combined products test for additional viruses, but each has its own instructions and limitations. Should I wait for a positive test before asking about treatment? If you are at higher risk, contact a clinician promptly when symptoms start. Treatment windows are short, and care should not be delayed while repeatedly testing at home.

title: What to do if a condom breaks: immediate care and follow-up
description: A practical timeline for emergency contraception, HIV PEP, STI testing, pregnancy testing and safer condom use after a break or slip.
body: A broken condom can feel alarming, but there are useful steps you can take. Act promptly on the options with short deadlines, then arrange testing that matches the exposure and the tests available. Washing and waiting for symptoms cannot replace that plan. Stop, remove the condom and note the time If a condom breaks or slips off, stop intercourse and withdraw carefully. Remove it gently if it is easily reachable; seek help if it is stuck rather than using a sharp object or repeated force. Use a new condom if you choose to continue. Record when the exposure happened, because some preventive options have short time limits. Consider pregnancy prevention and infection prevention as separate questions. Pregnancy is possible when sperm can reach the vagina, while oral, vaginal and anal contact can transmit different infections. The type of contact, existing contraception and what is known about the partner’s health affect the advice. A single exposure is enough to ask for help. Washing or urinating will not undo the exposure You can gently rinse the outside of the genitals with warm water for comfort. Urinating after sex does not wash sperm out of the vagina and does not prevent pregnancy. Squeezing, straining or trying to push fluid out is not an effective substitute for emergency contraception or infection assessment. Do not douche the vagina or rectum or put soap, disinfectant or other chemicals inside. Vaginal douching can disturb the protective environment and increase irritation and infection problems. Cleaning cannot reliably remove an STI exposure. Spend the time contacting care rather than trying to wash the risk away. Make room for support without delaying care Worry, anger, embarrassment or uncertainty are understandable reactions. You do not have to settle every emotion before taking the next practical step. A pharmacist, sexual-health service or urgent-care clinician can help you work out what is needed without assuming that an infection or pregnancy has occurred. If useful, ask someone you trust to help arrange transport or an appointment. If sex was forced, you were unable to consent, or a condom was removed without agreement, specialist sexual-assault support can provide confidential advice and time-sensitive care. Ask the service about its privacy arrangements and the choices available to you. Act now if HIV exposure may have occurred HIV post-exposure prophylaxis, or PEP, is a course of medicine that can reduce the chance of HIV infection after a relevant exposure. It must be started as soon as possible, ideally within hours, and no later than 72 hours. Do not wait for symptoms, a routine test appointment or a partner’s delayed result before seeking assessment. Not every broken condom requires PEP. A clinician assesses the type of exposure, the partner’s HIV status and viral suppression if known, and other circumstances. Contact an emergency department or a service that provides PEP if prompt specialist advice is not otherwise available. After 72 hours, still seek testing and a prevention plan even though starting PEP is generally not recommended. If PEP is prescribed, complete the plan The usual PEP course is 28 days. Take it exactly as prescribed and ask what to do about missed doses, interactions or side effects. An initial HIV test checks your starting status but cannot rule out infection from an exposure that has just happened. When PEP is indicated, laboratory results should not unnecessarily delay the first dose. Follow-up checks confirm that the medicine is accessible and tolerable and arrange later HIV testing. Current US CDC guidance includes early contact and testing follow-up around 4–6 and 12 weeks; the clinic should give you exact dates and test instructions. If exposure may continue, discuss a transition to pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, rather than relying on repeated emergencies. Emergency contraception: do not wait for the morning If pregnancy is possible and not wanted, contact a pharmacist or sexual-health clinician as soon as possible. Emergency contraceptive pills work mainly by preventing or delaying ovulation. A copper IUD is another option. Emergency contraception does not treat an established pregnancy and does not protect against STIs. Tell the clinician when this and any other recent unprotected sex occurred, what contraception you normally use and any medicines or supplements you take. The best option can depend on timing and individual circumstances. Prescription rules, cost and access vary by country, so do not assume every product is available without a prescription. Levonorgestrel: earlier is better Levonorgestrel is the ingredient in products such as Plan B and other brands. Many local product instructions emphasize use within 72 hours. WHO and CDC guidance also discusses use up to 120 hours, but effectiveness falls with delay and other options may be more effective later in that window. Take advice promptly rather than assuming that passing the three-day mark means nothing can be done. A fixed claim such as “95% effective in the first day” is not a personal prediction: effectiveness depends on the timing of ovulation and other factors. Do not delay obtaining an available suitable method while trying to calculate an exact risk. Ulipristal and the copper IUD within five days Ulipristal acetate, sold under names including ella, can be used within 120 hours and is generally more effective than levonorgestrel during days three to five. A pharmacist or clinician should help select it, particularly if you already use hormonal contraception. It also works by delaying ovulation and should be taken promptly. A copper IUD placed within five days is the most effective established emergency contraceptive option, with effectiveness above 99%. A trained clinician checks suitability and inserts it. It can remain as ongoing contraception according to the device’s lifespan. In some circumstances insertion can be possible later based on ovulation timing, so ask rather than self-excluding. Do not deliberately wait until day five. After the emergency pill: symptoms and regular contraception Temporary nausea, headache, cramps or changes in the next bleed can occur. If you vomit soon after taking a pill, contact the pharmacist promptly; whether another dose is needed depends on the product and timing. Emergency pills do not provide continuing protection for later sex in the cycle. After levonorgestrel, regular hormonal contraception can generally be restarted immediately. After ulipristal, restarting progestogen-containing contraception too soon can reduce its effect; CDC guidance generally advises waiting at least five days. Use condoms or avoid sex during the waiting period and until the regular method is effective. Ask for method-specific instructions rather than combining emergency pills yourself. Symptoms mean assessment now, not at a future deadline Seek advice for a new genital or mouth sore, unusual discharge, burning urination, bleeding after sex or between periods, or anal symptoms. A sore throat after oral contact can have many causes, including an infection. Pelvic or testicular pain also needs assessment; severe pain, fever or significant illness should not wait for a home test. Many STIs cause no symptoms. Feeling well does not prove that transmission did not occur, and having symptoms does not identify which infection is present. Tell the clinic about the sites of contact so it can decide whether urine, genital, throat or rectal samples are appropriate. Around two weeks: chlamydia and gonorrhoea testing For an asymptomatic screening sample after a recent exposure, many services recommend waiting about two weeks for chlamydia and gonorrhoea tests. This is a testing window, not a requirement to postpone the first consultation. Symptoms, a diagnosed partner or a clinician’s concern may call for assessment and testing earlier, with a repeat test if necessary. A urine or genital test does not automatically cover the throat or rectum. Ask which sites are being tested. Both infections can be treated with appropriate antibiotics, and partner management helps prevent reinfection. Follow the exact advice about avoiding sex until treatment and the required waiting period are complete for you and relevant partners. Around three weeks: check for pregnancy Most home pregnancy tests can be used from the first day of a missed period. They detect the pregnancy hormone hCG. If you do not know when the period is due, test at least 21 days after the last unprotected sex. Testing too early may give a negative result even when pregnancy has begun. Emergency contraception can shift the timing of bleeding. Follow the kit instructions. If the result is negative but the period still does not arrive or you remain concerned, repeat it and seek advice. A positive result deserves a conversation about pregnancy care and your options. Severe one-sided abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain or fainting with a possible pregnancy needs urgent assessment. HIV testing does not have one three-week deadline The HIV window depends on the test. Without antiretroviral prevention affecting detection, a laboratory antigen/antibody test on blood from a vein usually detects infection within 18–45 days; antibody tests may take 23–90 days. Earlier negative results may need repeating after the relevant window. If you took PEP or use PrEP, follow the clinic’s testing schedule rather than applying those ranges yourself. An early flu-like illness is not a reliable way to diagnose HIV, and absence of symptoms is not reassurance. HIV treatment can control the virus very effectively; confirmatory testing and prompt linkage to care are important after a reactive result. Herpes: a fresh sore can be tested promptly Do not wait three weeks if blisters or ulcers appear. A clinician may take a swab from a fresh lesion before it heals. Routine herpes blood testing is not recommended for everyone without symptoms because false or unclear results can cause harm. Testing decisions should reflect symptoms and the exposure history. When an antibody test is appropriate, it can take much longer than three weeks to detect a new infection. Ask the clinician about timing and interpretation. Antiviral treatment can reduce outbreaks and symptoms, but does not eradicate the virus. A positive result alone usually cannot establish exactly when the infection began. Six weeks and beyond: an individualized syphilis plan Syphilis can cause a painless sore, a rash that may affect palms or soles, or more general symptoms, and it may also go unnoticed. Do not wait for a six-week date if you have symptoms or a partner has been diagnosed. Early blood tests can be negative, and some exposed partners need treatment before a test turns positive. A clinic may repeat testing later to cover the window period; some services use a three-month check after exposure. This differs from follow-up after confirmed syphilis treatment, when blood-test trends are assessed over time. Stage, previous treatment and individual risk affect that schedule. Syphilis is treatable, but delaying appropriate care can allow serious complications. Three-month checks are not the same as a test of cure After treated chlamydia or gonorrhoea, retesting at about three months commonly checks for reinfection. An earlier test of cure is a different decision and is needed in certain circumstances, such as some infections during pregnancy or particular treatment situations. Ask which type of follow-up has been booked and why. You do not need a universal repeat panel for every infection at both three and six months regardless of your results. Similarly, a persistent syphilis antibody result does not by itself prove antibiotic resistance. Keep the clinic’s follow-up plan, tell it about any new exposure and do not interpret a sequence of results without the test type and clinical context. Reduce the chance of another break Use a fresh condom before genital contact, check its expiry and packet, and open it without teeth or sharp objects. Follow the size and application instructions, leaving space at the tip and unrolling it fully. Hold the base during withdrawal so it does not slip off. Use lubricant compatible with the condom: water- or silicone-based products are appropriate for latex, while oil can damage latex. Do not wear two external condoms or combine an external and internal condom. If breakage recurs, ask about fit, lubricant and technique. A practical prevention plan is more helpful than blame. Stop and note the time; washing does not prevent pregnancy or an STI. PEP and emergency contraception have different purposes and deadlines. Ask for advice now even when a later test will be needed. Herpes, HIV and syphilis do not share one testing window. Follow-up depends on the result, treatment and any new exposure. Will urinating or washing stop pregnancy? No. Urinating does not wash sperm from the vagina. Gentle external washing is for comfort; emergency contraception is the relevant preventive option. Should I wait until tomorrow to ask about PEP? No. Seek assessment immediately. PEP works best when started promptly and must begin within 72 hours of a relevant exposure. Does every broken condom require HIV medicine? No. A clinician assesses the exposure and the partner’s HIV and viral-suppression information when available. Do not delay assessment while trying to establish every detail. Is it too late for emergency contraception after three days? Not necessarily. Ulipristal and a copper IUD are options within five days, and local guidance may also consider levonorgestrel. Seek advice as soon as possible. Can I restart my usual pill immediately after ella? Usually you need to wait at least five days after ulipristal before restarting hormonal contraception. Ask for instructions for your method and interim condom use. When should I take a pregnancy test? From a missed period, or at least 21 days after the last unprotected sex if timing is uncertain. Repeat and seek advice if a negative result does not fit the situation. Should I wait two weeks if I have discharge or a sore? No. The window for asymptomatic screening is not a reason to delay assessment of symptoms or a known exposure. Can one HIV test at three weeks rule out infection? Not reliably in every case. Detection depends on the test and whether PEP or PrEP was used. Follow the testing service’s schedule. Does everyone need a herpes blood test? No. Routine testing without symptoms is usually not recommended. Fresh blisters or sores can be swabbed promptly, while selected blood tests have different timing and limitations. Does a positive syphilis antibody result after treatment mean resistance? Not by itself. Some antibodies can remain positive after successful treatment. The clinician interprets the specific test, changing levels and treatment history.

title: Can dry eyes be a sign of COVID?
description: Eye irritation can occur with COVID, but dryness alone cannot identify the cause. Learn what may help and which eye symptoms need urgent care.
body: Gritty, burning or watery eyes can be uncomfortable, especially when you are already unwell. COVID can be associated with eye symptoms, but dry eyes are common for many other reasons. Neither the presence nor the absence of eye irritation can diagnose or rule out the infection. What the research does and does not show Studies during the early pandemic reported redness, watering, irritation and a dry or foreign-body sensation in some people with COVID. A 2021 review found eye symptoms in roughly one in ten participants across its included studies. That figure referred to eye symptoms overall, not to one in ten having dry-eye disease. These studies involved different patient groups and ways of recording symptoms. Their results do not give a reliable personal probability for a new infection today, and an association does not show that the virus directly caused every symptom. Eye findings alone are not a useful substitute for appropriate COVID testing. The early review included 8,219 people. Among reported eye symptoms, a dry or foreign-body sensation accounted for about 16%, redness 13.3%, watering 12.8%, itching 12.6%, pain 9.6% and discharge 8.8%. These percentages describe the review’s symptom reporting, not the chance that each symptom occurs in everyone with COVID. The source’s translation of watering as “tearing” means tears running from the eye, not tissue being torn. The same review reported conjunctivitis, often called pink eye, as the most frequent diagnosis in the small subset with a specified eye disease. Those early findings should not be used to estimate today’s dry-eye prevalence, illness severity or need for intensive care. Dry eye is common even without COVID and becomes more likely with age, particularly after 50. Several factors may affect the surface of the eye A healthy tear film needs enough tears, a suitable composition and normal blinking. Dryness can develop when tears evaporate too quickly or do not cover the surface effectively. It may feel like sand in the eye, and sometimes causes extra watering rather than an obviously dry appearance. Long periods looking at screens, contact lenses, dry indoor air, wind and some medicines can contribute. Eyelid inflammation, allergy and other health conditions may also need consideration. A new symptom during COVID should not automatically be attributed to the infection. Researchers have explored inflammation and direct effects of the virus on the eye. These remain different from proving the mechanism in an individual person. A receptor being present on eye cells is not, by itself, proof that a particular case of dry eye resulted from viral invasion. One proposed explanation involves ACE2, a protein used by SARS-CoV-2 to enter susceptible cells, which has been detected on the ocular surface. Inflammation may also disturb tear function. These are plausible research mechanisms, not a test that establishes the cause of an individual’s symptoms. During screen work, people may blink less often or less completely, allowing more evaporation. If a mask seems to make it worse Air escaping from the top of a poorly fitting mask may travel towards the eyes and increase evaporation. Adjust the nose piece and fit according to the product instructions, keeping the mask snug without interfering with your eyelids. Do not abandon a needed mask because your eyes feel dry. Ask an optometrist or pharmacist about appropriate lubricating drops and fit adjustments. Avoid improvising tape that pulls on the lower eyelid or stops it closing normally. Comfort measures for mild symptoms Take regular breaks from close screen work and blink fully. Reduce direct airflow from a fan or air conditioner, and avoid smoke. If contact lenses are uncomfortable, remove them and use glasses while you seek advice. Artificial tears can help mild dry-eye symptoms. A pharmacist or eye-care professional can advise on the formulation, especially if you need frequent use or normally wear contact lenses. Follow the bottle instructions and do not share drops. Persistent or recurring symptoms deserve an eye examination. The clinician can assess the tear film, eyelids and other causes, then choose treatment. Do not stop a prescribed medicine on your own because you think it may contribute. Know when this needs urgent eye care A painful red eye needs prompt assessment, particularly in a contact-lens wearer. Sudden loss of vision, significant new visual disturbance, pain when looking at light, or a red eye with a severe headache and nausea needs emergency assessment. These are not symptoms to label as simple dryness or wait out until a COVID test becomes negative. Tell the service about any respiratory symptoms before attending so it can advise on infection precautions. When to consider COVID testing If you also have a new respiratory illness, relevant exposure or another reason to suspect COVID, follow current local testing advice. A single negative home antigen test can miss early infection, so repeat it as instructed or ask whether a molecular test is needed. If you are at increased risk of severe COVID, seek treatment advice promptly rather than waiting through repeated tests. Breathing difficulty, persistent chest pain, confusion or difficulty staying awake needs urgent help regardless of eye symptoms or test results. Other possible COVID symptoms include fever or chills, cough, sore throat, congestion or a runny nose, fatigue, body aches, a change in smell or taste, vomiting and diarrhoea. Their frequency varies with circulating variants and prior immunity. Pale, grey or blue lips or skin can also be an emergency sign; colour changes may be harder to notice on darker skin, so do not wait for visible blueness before acting on breathing difficulty or reduced alertness. Dryness alone is not a reliable COVID symptom or diagnostic test. Screens, dry air, contact lenses and mask airflow can contribute. Mild irritation may respond to lubricating drops and environmental changes. Pain, light sensitivity or new vision changes need prompt assessment. Does watery eye mean it cannot be dry eye? No. An irritated eye can produce reflex watering while the tear film still does not work well. Does the one-in-ten research figure mean ten percent develop dry-eye disease? No. The cited early review pooled different eye symptoms, and did not establish that rate of diagnosed dry-eye disease. Should I wait until I recover from COVID before getting eye pain checked? No. Contact an eye-care or urgent-care service promptly and tell them about the infection so they can arrange care appropriately.

title: Bone-density scans: what DXA measures
description: A bone-density scan helps assess fracture risk, but its numbers need to be interpreted alongside age, health and fracture history.
body: A bone-density scan measures the mineral content of selected bones. It can help identify osteoporosis, inform treatment and monitor changes over time. The result is one part of a bone-health assessment, rather than a prediction that a particular bone will definitely break. What happens during the scan The usual test is dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, shortened to DXA or DEXA. A central DXA commonly measures the hip and lower spine while you lie on a padded table and the scanner passes above you. It is generally quick and painless, with a low radiation dose. The scan is different from a nuclear-medicine bone scan and usually does not need an injection. Follow the department's preparation instructions, including any advice about calcium supplements or recent contrast examinations. Tell staff if you are pregnant or could be pregnant before the test. Some devices assess the heel, wrist or another peripheral site. These can provide useful information in particular settings, but they do not automatically replace central hip-and-spine DXA for diagnosis and treatment decisions. Why someone might be offered testing Testing can be considered because of age, menopause, a fracture after relatively minor trauma, a condition affecting bone health, or medicines such as long-term glucocorticoids. A clinician will review the reason for the test rather than assuming everyone needs one. For routine US screening, the USPSTF recommends DXA for women aged 65 or older and for postmenopausal women younger than 65 who have increased fracture risk after assessment. Its evidence statement for routine screening in men remains insufficient; that does not mean men with concerning risk factors should never be assessed. These screening recommendations are separate from investigating a fragility fracture, known osteoporosis or a medical cause of bone loss. Local guidelines may differ. A younger adult should not have symptoms or a low-trauma fracture dismissed simply because they are below the usual screening age. T-scores compare with a young-adult reference For postmenopausal women and men aged 50 or older, a T-score is commonly used to classify bone density. A value of minus 1.0 or above is in the normal range. A value below minus 1.0 but above minus 2.5 is low bone mass, often called osteopenia. Minus 2.5 or lower is in the osteoporosis range at an appropriate diagnostic site. A more negative number indicates lower measured density, but the number alone does not describe the whole severity of the condition. Previous fractures, age, falls and other risks also matter. A fracture can occur in someone whose T-score is not in the osteoporosis range. The score is expressed in standard deviations from the reference average, not a percentage of bone lost. Zero means the measured density matches that young-adult reference average; a positive score is above it and a negative score is below it. The normal range is not capped at plus 1. Younger people are assessed differently Before menopause and in men younger than 50, Z-scores are generally preferred. A Z-score compares bone density with an age-matched reference. A score of minus 2.0 or lower is described as below the expected range for age. Do not apply the older-adult T-score labels to a child or younger adult without specialist interpretation. Low density in these groups calls for a review of clinical history and possible causes; a scan number on its own is not enough to explain the problem. A low result leads to a broader conversation Your clinician may ask about previous fractures, falls, family history, smoking, alcohol, nutrition, menstrual or hormonal changes and medicines. Blood tests or other assessments may be useful when an underlying cause is suspected. Some adults benefit from a fracture-risk calculator that combines clinical factors with or without bone-density information. Such tools have age and population limits and cannot account perfectly for every circumstance. Ask what the estimate means for your own treatment choices. Low bone mass does not inevitably progress to osteoporosis. At the same time, a result that is not extremely low should not be used to dismiss a meaningful fracture history. Inherited differences, low body weight, medical conditions and medicines can all contribute to low bone mass. Finding a cause may change the treatment plan; the scan cannot identify it by itself. Treatment is based on overall risk A plan may include adequate calcium and vitamin D, appropriate strength and weight-bearing activity, balance work and reducing fall hazards. The safest exercise choices depend on your fracture history and physical ability; running or high-impact activity is not automatically suitable for everyone. Medicines may be recommended when fracture risk is high. Different treatments have different benefits, precautions and stopping rules. Do not start, stop or take a break from an osteoporosis medicine solely because a later scan number looks better. A repeat scan should answer a useful clinical question, such as monitoring treatment or reassessing a change in risk. The interval is individual. Whenever possible, comparable scans and consistent equipment help the clinician distinguish a real change from measurement variation. Walking, dancing and, for people for whom it is safe, jogging are examples of weight-bearing activity. Strength training adds a different benefit. Calcium-rich foods and an appropriate vitamin D intake support bone health; supplements or exercise do not replace medication when fracture risk warrants it. Some medicines reduce bone breakdown, while others build bone, and monitoring helps assess response. Questions to bring to your appointment Ask which bones were measured, whether a T-score or Z-score is appropriate, and how the result changes your fracture-risk estimate. It is also useful to ask whether an underlying cause needs investigation and when another scan would actually affect the plan. If you develop new severe back pain after a minor strain, lose noticeable height or sustain a new fracture, contact your clinician rather than waiting for a scheduled follow-up scan. Central DXA usually measures the hip and spine. T-scores and Z-scores apply to different clinical situations. Fracture risk depends on more than a scan number. Treatment and repeat-scan timing should follow an individual plan. Is a heel test the same as a hip-and-spine DXA? No. Peripheral tests can help in selected settings, but results are not automatically interchangeable. Does osteopenia mean I will definitely develop osteoporosis? No. It means low measured bone mass, and your future risk depends on several factors. Does insufficient evidence for screening men mean men do not get osteoporosis? No. Men can have osteoporosis and may need testing based on fractures, medicines or other risks.

title: Why another COVID vaccine dose may be recommended
description: Protection changes over time and the virus evolves. Updated doses aim to reduce serious illness, with schedules based on current guidance and individual risk.
body: Being offered another COVID vaccine dose does not mean an earlier dose was useless. Protection can decline with time, and circulating viruses change. The decision about another dose depends on your age, health, previous vaccination, recent infection and the programme where you live. Protection is not all-or-nothing A vaccine can reduce the chance of severe illness without preventing every infection. Protection against a mild infection and protection against hospitalisation are different outcomes, so one effectiveness percentage cannot describe both. A breakthrough infection does not prove vaccination failed to provide any benefit. At the same time, an old dose does not guarantee lasting protection. Periodic vaccination is particularly relevant for people at higher risk of serious COVID. An updated dose can address changing immunity and variants The term booster is often used for a later dose intended to renew protection. Current programmes may instead describe an updated or seasonal vaccine because the vaccine composition has been adapted to circulating variants. The amount of benefit varies with the product, circulating virus, time since prior immunity and the person receiving it. Percentages from the Delta wave in 2021 should not be used to promise the same effect today. There is also no reliable rule that every person loses exactly the same percentage of protection every two months. Vaccine composition is reviewed as evidence changes. For someone at high risk who is due a dose, waiting indefinitely for a future formulation can leave a gap in protection. Discuss timing with the local vaccination service. The current schedule depends on risk and location Older age, immune suppression and some underlying conditions increase the importance of maintaining protection. Pregnancy is also relevant. National recommendations are not identical, and a schedule from another country may not match local eligibility or available products. For example, Canada's guidance for fall 2026 recommends one dose per year for most populations offered vaccination and a second yearly dose for selected higher-risk groups, including adults aged 80 or older, certain care-home residents, people with moderate or severe immune suppression, and adults aged 65 to 79 with relevant underlying conditions. Canadian programmes may also offer vaccination to other people aged six months or older based on individual assessment or preference. Provinces and territories decide how publicly funded programmes are delivered. This example is not a universal prescription for every reader. Children need age-appropriate products and recommendations. Do not simply apply an adult schedule to a child or assume that everyone needs the same number of additional doses. Pregnancy and breastfeeding are part of the discussion COVID during pregnancy can cause more serious illness and is associated with pregnancy and newborn complications. Current Canadian guidance supports COVID vaccination during pregnancy and breastfeeding. An mRNA dose can be given at any stage of pregnancy when indicated. Large studies have not found increased pregnancy loss, preterm birth or stillbirth after mRNA vaccination. Evidence also does not show that COVID vaccines cause infertility, and there is no need to delay trying to conceive after an mRNA dose. Tell the clinician your pregnancy stage and the dates of your last dose and any recent infection. This helps fit COVID vaccination into your maternity plan alongside other recommended vaccines. Previous infection and previous reactions matter Having had COVID can contribute to immunity, but it does not provide a permanent exemption from future vaccination. The interval after infection depends on current recommendations and individual risk. Bring the approximate infection date rather than guessing that a positive antibody test tells you when another dose is needed. Tell the vaccinator about a severe allergic reaction to a previous dose or ingredient, myocarditis or pericarditis, immune-suppressing treatment and any current significant illness. These details may change product choice, timing or the need for specialist advice. An additional dose used to complete protection in someone with immune suppression is not necessarily the same as routine seasonal revaccination. Ask which purpose applies to your appointment. Understand expected reactions and when to seek help A sore arm, fatigue, headache, muscle aches or a short-lived fever can follow vaccination. Many people have few or no symptoms; the absence of a reaction does not show that the vaccine failed. Follow the product and clinician's advice for comfort measures. Severe allergic reactions are rare and need emergency care. New chest pain, shortness of breath or a racing or irregular heartbeat after vaccination also needs prompt medical assessment. Do not dismiss a serious symptom as an expected reaction. Keep your vaccination record, including the product and date. If you are unsure which dose you need, a pharmacist or vaccination clinic can review the record against the current programme.
