You may not need a period product, although using a liner or pad can help you notice changes. Bleeding that soaks a pad is no longer simply spotting. An episode may last hours, come and go over several days, or recur during different parts of a cycle. Neither a brief duration nor a pink or brown colour proves that it is harmless. The amount, timing, possibility of pregnancy, medicines and accompanying symptoms all matter. Keep a short record of when bleeding started and stopped, its relation to sex or your period, and whether the amount is increasing. Note missed contraceptive doses, a recent method change, pain, discharge or a pregnancy-test result. This gives a clinician more useful information than comparing your experience with someone else’s number of days. Can the duration identify implantation bleeding? People often use the term implantation bleeding for a light bleed near the time a period was expected. Some patient guidance uses that explanation, but bleeding cannot tell you that an embryo has implanted. There is no established hours-to-days rule, colour pattern or cramp pattern that confirms this cause. A prospective study published in 2003 followed women using daily diaries and urine hormone measurements. Among 151 pregnancies lasting at least six weeks from the last period, 14 women recorded bleeding in the first eight weeks. Bleeding rarely coincided with the measured implantation day. This small study does not explain every early bleed, but it does not support diagnosing implantation from spotting. Claims that one third of pregnant people have proven implantation bleeding, that it must occur 10–14 days after fertilisation, or that bleeding for up to seven days can safely be assigned to implantation are too definite. Mild cramps, tiredness, nausea and breast tenderness also overlap with other situations and do not establish the cause. If pregnancy is possible, use a test at the appropriate time. Most home tests are useful from the first day of a missed period; if you do not know when that is, test at least 21 days after the last unprotected sex. An early negative can need repeating. Do not wait to retest if bleeding comes with severe pain, faintness or other urgent symptoms. Spotting in early pregnancy Bleeding is possible during the first trimester, and many pregnancies with a light bleed continue normally. It can also accompany a cervical change, infection, miscarriage or an ectopic pregnancy. A small amount of blood cannot distinguish these possibilities, and there is no single expected duration for all of them. Contact your maternity or early-pregnancy service promptly about bleeding in a known pregnancy, even when it is light or has stopped. The team may use an examination, ultrasound and blood or urine tests. Very early scans can be inconclusive, so ask when repeat testing is needed and which symptoms require immediate help. An ectopic pregnancy develops outside the normal cavity of the womb, most often in a fallopian tube. A rupture can cause dangerous internal bleeding even when little blood is visible vaginally. Severe or one-sided pain, shoulder-tip pain, dizziness or fainting need urgent assessment when pregnancy is possible, even without a positive home test. Treatment is decided by specialists and may involve monitoring in selected cases, medicine or surgery; a suspected rupture is an emergency. How bleeding can change with miscarriage A miscarriage may begin with spotting and progress to heavier bleeding, cramps, clots, fluid or pregnancy tissue. It can also be found on a scan before any bleeding starts. Little or no bleeding does not prove that the pregnancy has been absorbed or that follow-up is unnecessary. Mayo Clinic gives a broad estimate that about 10–20% of known pregnancies end in miscarriage. This is a population-level estimate for recognised pregnancies, not the probability that a particular episode of spotting is a miscarriage. It cannot determine your outcome or replace an assessment. The pattern depends on the stage of pregnancy and whether care involves waiting, medicine or a procedure. NHS information describes bleeding or spotting for up to about two weeks after a miscarriage, while the process and recovery can sometimes take longer. This is a general description after assessment, not permission to watch unexplained or heavy bleeding at home. Follow the discharge and follow-up instructions you receive, including any requested pregnancy test or repeat scan. Ask for help if bleeding increases, you develop fever, worsening pain or feel unwell. A period may take up to eight weeks to return, and cycles may take longer to settle. Physical and emotional recovery do not have to happen on the same timetable. Later pregnancy and bleeding after sex In the second or third trimester, bleeding can arise from changes at the cervix, infection, problems with the placenta or labour. Placental separation and a low-lying placenta are important possibilities. Cervical opening too early can also require assessment. You cannot separate these causes by counting how many hours the spotting lasts. Pregnancy makes the cervix more prone to bleeding, including after sex. Nevertheless, a presumed friction-related bleed should not be dismissed on that basis alone. Tell your maternity team when it happened and whether there is pain, contractions, fluid leakage or reduced movements at a stage when you normally feel your baby. Near birth, a small amount of blood mixed with the mucus plug can be a show. Fresh bleeding, bleeding that is more than a little blood-streaked mucus, or uncertainty about what you are seeing warrants maternity advice. Do not wait until the next appointment because an episode has stopped. Mid-cycle spotting and ovulation Some people notice a brief light bleed around the middle of a natural cycle, sometimes described as lasting a day or two. Hormonal changes around ovulation are one possible explanation, but the timing alone cannot confirm either ovulation or the cause of the bleed. Ovulation does not happen on the same cycle day for everyone or every month. A calendar estimate is particularly uncertain with irregular cycles. Repeated or new bleeding between periods deserves assessment rather than a permanent label of ovulation spotting. Hormonal contraceptives differ in how consistently they suppress ovulation. Many hormonal-coil users continue to ovulate, while other methods act mainly by suppressing it. Spotting while using contraception is not a dependable sign of egg release, contraceptive failure or fertility. Spotting after starting contraception An IUD, implant, injection or contraceptive pill can change bleeding patterns. With a hormonal IUD, spotting or light bleeding is common during the first three to six months and often decreases over time. A copper IUD can initially cause spotting and heavier or longer periods. These are different patterns and should not be given one universal deadline. Implant-related bleeding may settle, continue unpredictably or change later. Injections and pills have their own patterns too. The source’s suggestion that spotting usually stops after two or three months is therefore not a promise that applies to every method. Spotting alone does not mean contraception has stopped working. Missed pills, late injections, interacting medicines, device concerns or pregnancy symptoms need a separate review. A new change after an established pattern, persistent troublesome bleeding, pain or unusual discharge may also call for pregnancy testing or checks for infection or another cause. You can ask for help whenever bleeding is bothersome; you do not have to complete a waiting period first. A clinician can discuss method-specific treatment or a different contraceptive. Avoid adding hormones, taking someone else’s medicine or altering pill-free breaks without suitable advice. Bleeding after sex outside pregnancy Dryness, friction or an injury can cause bleeding during or after sex. Other explanations include infection, a cervical surface change or a polyp; fibroids can contribute to abnormal bleeding as well. Less commonly, bleeding is related to a cervical or other cancer. A small episode may stop quickly, but one or two hours is not a diagnostic or safety threshold. Arrange a check for unexplained bleeding after sex or between periods, especially when it recurs. A clinician may examine the vagina and cervix and recommend a pregnancy test, STI tests or further investigation. Mention pain during sex, burning with urination, itching or changed discharge. These details can guide testing. Being up to date with cervical screening is useful, but a normal previous screening result does not replace an assessment of a new symptom. When to seek help without waiting Get emergency help for bleeding with collapse, faintness, severe abdominal or pelvic pain, or marked weakness. If you could be pregnant, shoulder-tip pain or significant dizziness is especially concerning. Heavy bleeding that rapidly soaks a pad also needs urgent help; do not wait to meet an exact hourly count when you feel unwell. Contact a clinician promptly for fever or chills, worsening pelvic pain, unusual or unpleasant-smelling discharge, painful urination, persistent vomiting, or passing unexpected fluid or tissue. Report any bleeding after menopause, including a single pink or brown stain. Unexpected vaginal bleeding in a child before puberty needs a child-health assessment. A brief small bleed in a newborn’s first week can occur as maternal hormone levels fall, but persistent, heavy or otherwise concerning bleeding still needs advice. Do not use adult menstrual explanations for a child. If a clinician has already assessed a mild episode, follow the agreed plan and return if it recurs or changes. The aim is to understand your pattern and your risks, rather than decide that everybody’s spotting should end on a particular day. Spotting has no single normal or safe duration. Use a pregnancy test when appropriate rather than diagnosing implantation by timing. Contraceptive bleeding patterns vary by method and may persist. Severe symptoms and bleeding after menopause require action regardless of duration. How many days of spotting is normal? There is no single number for every cause. A brief mid-cycle stain, a contraceptive bleeding change and bleeding in pregnancy need different assessments. Timing helps describe the pattern but cannot establish safety. Can seven days of spotting still be implantation bleeding? Seven days is not an established safe or diagnostic limit for implantation. Take a pregnancy test at an appropriate time and seek advice for persistent unexplained bleeding; act urgently for pain, faintness or heavy bleeding. Does brown spotting rule out a miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy? No. Colour cannot rule either out. A clinician may need an ultrasound and blood tests, with follow-up if the pregnancy is too early to assess clearly. Should I wait three months before asking about contraceptive spotting? No. Some methods commonly cause changes over several months, but you can seek help whenever bleeding is troublesome or accompanied by other symptoms. Does spotting mean my contraceptive is not working? Not by itself. Missed doses, late injections, interactions or device concerns affect the assessment and should be discussed separately. Can a miscarriage happen with no bleeding? Yes. A missed miscarriage may be identified on ultrasound before bleeding occurs. Little bleeding does not establish what has happened to the pregnancy or remove the need for care. Can I ignore bleeding after sex if it stops quickly? A short episode still deserves a check when unexplained, particularly if it recurs. In pregnancy, contact your maternity team promptly. What information should I take to an appointment? Record dates, amount, pain, discharge, recent sex, contraception and test results. Bring any previous assessment plan. Seek urgent care first if symptoms are severe rather than waiting to complete a diary.

title: Bleeding with the contraceptive injection: what can help?
description: Spotting, heavy bleeding and absent periods with DMPA, including assessment, short-term treatment, injection timing and decisions about continuing or switching.
body: Bleeding changes are common with the contraceptive injection. You can ask for help before the next dose, whether the concern is heavy bleeding, unpredictable spotting or a method that no longer suits your life. How the injection changes pregnancy risk and bleeding Depo-Provera contains depot medroxyprogesterone acetate, or DMPA, a long-acting progestogen. It is related to the body’s progesterone but is not the same hormone. Its main contraceptive effect is to suppress ovulation; it also alters cervical mucus and the lining of the uterus. The mucus makes sperm passage more difficult, while changes in the uterine lining help explain why bleeding no longer follows the same pattern as an untreated menstrual cycle. A simple story about a fertilised egg being unable to attach is not the best explanation of its principal contraceptive action. Regular injections provide highly effective contraception, but pregnancy risk is not zero. The CDC estimates about four pregnancies per hundred users in the first year with typical use, which includes delays and missed doses. Bleeding is not a test of how well the method is working. Spotting and irregular bleeding are common early on You may notice light spotting, bleeding between expected periods or an unpredictable pattern after the first injection. It can continue for several months. Some people find that it becomes less frequent, while others remain bothered by it. Figures depend on how a study defines bleeding and when it measures it. An often-quoted single percentage for the whole first year should not be treated as a personal prediction. The important question is whether your bleeding is manageable and whether another cause needs checking. There is no guaranteed point at six months, twelve months or after the third or fourth injection when every symptom will stop. Arrange a review if the pattern is affecting your life rather than waiting for a promised adjustment date. Heavier or longer bleeding still deserves attention A longer or heavier episode can occur, but it should not automatically be attributed to DMPA. Tell the service about the amount, duration, clots, pain and any change after a previously stable pattern. Do not wait until fourteen continuous days have passed before asking for help. Earlier assessment is appropriate when bleeding is heavy, painful, persistent or troubling. Unusual tiredness, breathlessness or lightheadedness may prompt a check for anaemia as well as investigation of the bleeding. Very heavy bleeding with faintness, severe abdominal pain, fever or feeling seriously unwell needs urgent care. A possible pregnancy with one-sided pain or shoulder-tip pain also needs prompt assessment. Lighter periods or no periods can be an expected effect Periods often become lighter or stop with continued use. The US prescribing information reports no periods in 55 percent of users at twelve months in its clinical studies. That is a study result, not a guarantee for an individual or a reason to compare yourself with another user. The absence of bleeding, called amenorrhoea, usually does not need treatment while using DMPA. It does not mean menstrual blood is trapped inside the uterus. Pregnancy testing can still be appropriate if an injection was late, symptoms suggest pregnancy or the pattern changes unexpectedly. Do not use either spotting or absent periods as proof of continued contraceptive protection. Other symptoms are worth discussing too Reported symptoms include abdominal discomfort, changes in weight or appetite, headache, nausea, dizziness and breast pain or tenderness. Mood changes, reduced sexual desire, fatigue or weakness may also be reported. Skin and hair concerns can include acne, hair loss or increased facial or body hair. A symptom that appears during use may be related to the medicine, another condition or several factors. Reports in a product leaflet do not establish the cause in your case. It is inaccurate to say that all non-bleeding effects are rare, mild or certain to settle. Describe new or persistent symptoms, including significant mood changes, before deciding whether to continue. Sudden severe headache, weakness, vision loss, chest pain or breathlessness needs urgent assessment. The injection cannot be removed, but symptoms can be treated DMPA is designed to release medicine over time. Once it has been injected, it cannot be taken out in the way an implant can be removed. Stopping means not receiving further doses and planning what happens next. That does not mean you must wait without help. The clinician can assess the bleeding, consider short-term treatment and discuss a different contraceptive method. Avoid attempts to flush out the hormone or reverse it with supplements. Improvement may occur as use continues, but the body does not follow a fixed learning schedule. Your preference matters even if the bleeding is judged medically harmless. Check for other causes before choosing a treatment Bring the date of the last injection, a record of bleeding, pregnancy-test results and a list of medicines and supplements. Mention pelvic pain, discharge, a new sexual-health concern or any late doses. Depending on the findings, assessment may include pregnancy or STI testing, an examination, a blood count or investigation for conditions such as thyroid disease, polyps or fibroids. Not everyone needs every test. Ask whether the proposed treatment is intended to reduce the present bleeding, treat another diagnosis or change contraception. Those are related but different decisions. Short courses of medicine may help For suitable patients, a clinician may consider a short course of a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug, or NSAID, such as an appropriate ibuprofen regimen. CDC guidance describes five to seven days as an option during bleeding. It does not provide a universal self-treatment dose. For heavy or prolonged bleeding, a low-dose combined pill or oestrogen may sometimes be considered for a short course if medically appropriate. Evidence for particular regimens is limited, and bleeding may return after treatment. The advice is more nuanced than either nothing works or extra oestrogen will reliably repair the lining. Kidney disease, stomach ulcers, medicine interactions and other factors can make an NSAID unsuitable. Added oestrogen has separate risks and contraindications. Do not borrow hormone tablets or increase ibuprofen yourself; ask about the intended benefit, duration and follow-up. Keep the next injection date separate from the bleeding pattern Injections are usually scheduled about every twelve to thirteen weeks, depending on the product and local instructions. The CDC uses thirteen weeks for US DMPA guidance, while some product schedules differ. Follow the appointment date given by your service. If you are late, contact the service promptly and use condoms or avoid sex until you have a clear protection and restart plan. Grace periods are not identical everywhere, so an automatic rule that one week late means the same thing for every product is unreliable. Tell the clinician about unprotected sex, particularly in the previous five days, because emergency contraception may be relevant. The choice and timing must fit the restart plan; a pregnancy test taken too soon after sex can miss a pregnancy. The injection does not protect against sexually transmitted infections. Medical history and medicine interactions affect suitability Before the next dose, discuss current or previous breast cancer, unexplained vaginal bleeding, liver disease, clotting history, pregnancy possibility and any other important health condition. The clinician should use the current local product information and eligibility guidance. Bring every medicine and supplement. The UK product information specifically flags aminoglutethimide because it can reduce the amount of DMPA available in the body. This requires a medicine review; do not stop a prescribed treatment on your own. Wanting to conceive soon is a planning issue rather than an automatic medical contraindication. Another method may fit that aim better because return of fertility after DMPA can be delayed. Bone health and meningioma warnings need context DMPA can reduce bone mineral density. A history of fragility fractures, other bone-health risks and planned duration of use should be reviewed. A past fracture alone is not enough for this article to declare that someone can never use the method. The US label advises against long-term use beyond two years unless other options are considered inadequate; local recommendations require an individual discussion of benefits and risks. Do not apply a different country’s label as an unexplained rule for your prescription. Current product information also includes a meningioma warning, particularly relevant to prolonged exposure. A meningioma is a tumour of the membranes around the brain or spinal cord, usually non-cancerous. Tell the prescriber about any current or previous diagnosis and report new progressive neurological symptoms. This information supports a review, not a prediction that an individual will develop a tumour. Plan for continuing, switching or trying for pregnancy Effects on bleeding can last beyond the nominal injection interval and may continue for weeks or months after stopping. Periods and ovulation do not necessarily return together on a fixed date. A delayed return does not by itself mean permanent infertility. If you do not want pregnancy, arrange another method before protection ends. Ongoing spotting or the absence of a period cannot tell you that the previous injection is still preventing ovulation. If you want to continue, discuss the bleeding and any treatment before the next dose. If you want to change methods, say so. Convenience and effectiveness are benefits, but satisfaction is personal and should not be promised simply because you have waited long enough. No bleeding pattern proves that contraception is still effective. There is no guaranteed date when all side effects settle. A given injection cannot be removed, but symptom treatment may be possible. Check the schedule and missed-dose advice for your own product and country. Continuing or switching is a shared decision based on your needs. Does spotting mean Depo-Provera has stopped working? Not by itself. Protection depends on correct use and timing, not the bleeding pattern. Will every user have no periods after a year? No. Many do, but the pattern varies and study percentages do not predict an individual result. Is blood building up if I do not bleed? Usually no; absent bleeding is an expected effect of the changed uterine lining. Pregnancy testing may still be appropriate in some circumstances. Must I wait fourteen days before calling about bleeding? No. Ask earlier if it is heavy, painful, persistent or affecting daily life. Can the injection be removed once it has been given? No, but the clinician can assess symptoms and discuss treatment or future contraception. Can I use a high dose of ibuprofen to stop the bleeding? Do not self-prescribe a bleeding regimen. Suitability, dose and duration need individual advice. Is extra oestrogen suitable for everyone? No. It has separate risks and contraindications, and its benefit may be temporary. What should I do if I am late for an injection? Contact the service promptly, use backup until advised and report recent unprotected sex so emergency contraception and testing can be considered. Does a previous fracture automatically rule out DMPA? No single fact settles suitability. The prescriber should assess the type of fracture, other bone risks and alternatives. Do absent periods after stopping mean I cannot become pregnant? No. Fertility can return unpredictably, and the delay is not proof of permanent infertility or continuing protection.

title: Do vitamins help vaginal dryness?
description: How to interpret supplement claims, the difference between oral and vaginal products, and treatments with a clearer place in care.
body: There is no single best vitamin for vaginal dryness. Some small studies have investigated vitamins and other products, but their results do not make an oral supplement a reliable substitute for assessment and established treatment. The cause of the dryness and the way a product is used both matter. Dryness is not always a nutritional problem Lower oestrogen around menopause can affect vaginal and urinary tissues. Dryness can also occur during breastfeeding, with certain medicines or after cancer treatment. Irritating products, skin conditions and other problems may cause overlapping symptoms. A diet change cannot be assumed to correct all of these causes. Persistent soreness, pain during sex, unusual discharge or urinary symptoms deserve a conversation with a clinician. Tell them about breastfeeding, contraception, medicines and any cancer history. Do not assume that spotting is simply caused by dryness. Bleeding after sex, between periods or after menopause should be checked. Severe pelvic pain, fever or significant bleeding needs more urgent assessment. Vitamin E and vitamin D: promising results are not a prescription Small trials of vaginal vitamin E or vitamin D preparations have reported improvements in some symptoms or measures of vaginal tissue health. These studies generally used a particular formulation for a limited time in selected groups. They do not show that swallowing an ordinary vitamin capsule has the same effect. In an 80-participant trial of oral vitamin D, the treatment group did not improve significantly more than the placebo group on the measured vaginal outcomes. A change within one group alone does not establish a treatment benefit. Treating a confirmed deficiency or taking an appropriate supplement for bone health may still be worthwhile. That is a separate decision from using vitamins as treatment for vaginal dryness. Do not insert oral capsules or cosmetic vitamin oils into the vagina. Vitamin E is a fat-soluble antioxidant, while vitamin D has an established role in bone health. Those general roles do not establish a dryness treatment. Some studies combined vitamins E, A or D with other ingredients, so their findings cannot isolate which component helped. An association between blood vitamin D and tissue moisture likewise does not show that raising the level treats symptoms. Hyaluronic acid: the formulation matters Hyaluronic acid is used in some vaginal moisturisers. It is not a vitamin, and evidence about a product applied inside the vagina cannot be transferred to a swallowed supplement or a facial serum. A small trial involving 42 postmenopausal participants tested vaginal hyaluronic-acid tablets against vaginal estradiol. Both groups improved, with greater improvement on several outcomes in the estradiol group. It was not a trial of oral hyaluronic acid. Other trials have studied vaginal gels, including a more recent pilot comparison with vaginal oestrogen. These findings support discussing a purpose-made vaginal moisturiser as an option; they do not establish that every product containing hyaluronic acid is equivalent. Choose a preparation intended for this use and follow its instructions. A small study of an oral combination containing hyaluronic acid, glucosamine, lipoic acid and vitamins cannot establish that hyaluronic acid itself was responsible for improvement. Cosmetic skin benefits and vaginal benefits also need to be studied separately. Sea buckthorn and fish oil are not established dryness treatments One trial of sea buckthorn oil found a benefit in a measure of vaginal tissue integrity. Some other measures did not show a clear difference from placebo. That is a narrower finding than proving dependable relief from dryness for most people. Fish oil is also marketed for vaginal comfort, but it does not have an established role as a replacement for recommended dryness treatments. Research about skin hydration or hormone levels cannot, by itself, demonstrate that a supplement improves vaginal symptoms. Avoid interpreting an ingredient list as a treatment plan. Supplements can interact with medicines, and a natural label does not establish safety. Bring the exact products and doses to a pharmacist or clinician before combining them. Sea buckthorn oil contains fatty acids, and fish oil supplies omega-3 fatty acids. Laboratory or skin-barrier findings about hydration, healing or collagen are not a substitute for reliable symptom trials in the vagina. Small studies in specific groups, including people treated for breast cancer, do not establish that high supplement doses are safe or effective for everyone. DHEA is a hormone, not a vitamin DHEA, also called prasterone, is converted in the body into other hormones. Prescription vaginal prasterone is used for selected menopause-related symptoms in some countries. It is different from an over-the-counter oral DHEA supplement. The product, route and medical history determine whether it is suitable. Unexplained genital bleeding needs evaluation before treatment. If you have had breast cancer or are receiving hormone-blocking treatment, discuss options with your cancer-care team rather than assuming that DHEA is non-hormonal. Increasing the amount of oestrogen in the bloodstream is not a goal to pursue with self-prescribed supplements. Oral DHEA should not be treated as interchangeable with a prescribed local vaginal preparation. Start with options matched to your symptoms A lubricant helps reduce friction during sexual activity. A vaginal moisturiser is used regularly to relieve ongoing dryness. They have different purposes, and some people use both. Avoid fragranced washes, douching and products that sting. Use a condom-compatible lubricant if you use condoms; oil-based products can damage latex. Stop or change an activity that hurts rather than pushing through pain. For menopause-related symptoms, a clinician may recommend low-dose vaginal oestrogen. It acts mainly locally and can sometimes be used alongside systemic HRT. Other prescription treatments are available when appropriate. A history of breast cancer requires an individual discussion. Non-hormonal moisturisers and lubricants are usually considered first, and persistent symptoms can be reviewed with the relevant specialists. There are options beyond simply enduring the discomfort. Judge progress by comfort and function Keep a brief note of dryness, soreness, pain with sex and urinary symptoms, together with the products you try. Agree on a review if symptoms persist or treatment is uncomfortable. The aim is lasting comfort with a suitable treatment, not a higher vitamin level or an expensive collection of supplements. If one approach does not help, the next step is to reconsider the cause and treatment together. No vitamin is a proven universal remedy for vaginal dryness. Oral supplements and purpose-made vaginal treatments are not interchangeable. DHEA is hormonal and needs appropriate medical advice. Lubricants, moisturisers and local prescription treatments have distinct roles. Unexplained bleeding should be assessed rather than attributed to dryness. Can I put a vitamin capsule inside the vagina? Do not use an oral supplement or cosmetic product this way. Vaginal preparations have specific formulations and instructions. Will treating low vitamin D necessarily stop dryness? No. Correcting a deficiency may benefit health, but dryness can have other causes and may need its own treatment. Is vaginal hyaluronic acid the same as an oral beauty supplement? No. Evidence for a vaginal moisturiser does not establish that a swallowed supplement will relieve vaginal symptoms.

title: Burning or heat in the penis: what needs checking?
description: Possible causes of penile burning, when to get urgent help, and why treatment should follow an assessment rather than a symptom checklist.
body: A burning sensation in the penis can come from irritated skin, the urinary tract or another nearby structure. Noticing whether it happens on the skin, during urination or with ejaculation can help the clinician, but the sensation alone cannot identify the cause. Some symptoms need urgent care Seek emergency care if you cannot pass urine, have sudden severe testicular pain, or have a foreskin that is pulled back and stuck behind the head of the penis. A trapped foreskin can restrict blood flow and should not be left to settle. Fever or shivering with urinary pain, pain in the back below the ribs, vomiting or feeling very unwell needs prompt medical assessment. Confusion, marked drowsiness or difficulty breathing warrants emergency help. Arrange an assessment for persistent burning, a new discharge, sores, swelling or blood in the urine. You do not need to wait for a high fever or several symptoms to appear before seeking help. Irritation and inflammation of the skin Balanitis means inflammation of the head of the penis. It can cause soreness, itching, swelling and changes in skin colour, sometimes with discharge beneath the foreskin. Causes include irritating products, yeast and other infections. Soap, fragranced shower gel, some condoms or lubricants, and friction may aggravate sensitive skin. Gentle washing with water and careful drying can help while you arrange advice. Avoid antiseptics, vigorous scrubbing and applying several creams at once. In adults, only retract the foreskin if it moves comfortably, and return it over the head afterwards. Never force a child’s foreskin back. A clinician may examine the skin, take a swab or check for an underlying problem such as diabetes when appropriate. Treatment might involve an antifungal, an anti-inflammatory cream or another approach, depending on the cause. A steroid or antifungal is not a universal treatment for burning. Thrush is not usually a sexually transmitted infection Yeast can cause irritation around the head of the penis and under the foreskin. It can occur without having sex with someone who has vaginal thrush. Sexual activity may trigger symptoms, but a yeast diagnosis does not establish that a partner passed it on. Antifungal treatment may be appropriate once the cause is clear. Repeated symptoms, a first uncertain episode or treatment that does not help should be reviewed. Do not automatically treat a partner who has no symptoms unless a clinician advises it for a specific reason. An azole antifungal such as clotrimazole or miconazole may be used for confirmed thrush; oral antifungals or a short anti-inflammatory treatment are considered only when appropriate. Imidazole is a drug family, not an additional ingredient everyone needs. Urinary infections and urethritis can feel similar A bladder or urinary-tract infection may cause burning when peeing, urgency, frequent urination and lower abdominal discomfort. A suspected urinary infection in someone with male urinary anatomy should be assessed promptly. The presence or absence of a particular temperature does not reliably establish severity. Urethritis is inflammation of the tube that carries urine out of the body. It can cause burning, irritation at the opening or discharge. Sexually transmitted infections, including chlamydia and gonorrhoea, are possible causes, but there are also non-infectious causes. Urine tests and, depending on symptoms and sexual exposure, samples from other sites can help distinguish the possibilities. Tell the clinic about oral and anal as well as vaginal contact so testing matches the exposure. Many STIs cause no symptoms in one or both partners. Antibiotic treatment needs a current diagnosis and plan The antibiotic needed depends on the infection, test findings, allergies and local resistance guidance. An old combination listed online may no longer be recommended. Do not use leftover antibiotics or copy someone else’s prescription. If an STI is diagnosed, the clinic will explain partner testing or treatment, when it is safe to resume sex and whether a repeat test is needed. Follow that plan even if discomfort improves quickly. Until the cause of unexplained discharge or possible STI symptoms is assessed, avoid sexual contact that could pass an infection on. If symptoms persist after treatment, return for review rather than taking another course on your own. Some urinary pain medicines, such as phenazopyridine where available, reduce discomfort but do not cure an infection. Their use and duration need advice, especially with kidney disease or other medicines. Prostate-related pain is not always a bacterial infection Prostatitis and chronic pelvic pain conditions can cause discomfort in the penis, testicles, lower abdomen or area between the scrotum and anus. Pain with urination or ejaculation and difficulty passing urine can also occur. Acute bacterial prostatitis can make someone suddenly ill and requires prompt treatment. Chronic pelvic pain often does not have a proven bacterial cause, so repeated antibiotics are not a solution for every case. Care may include medicines for pain or urinary symptoms and assessment of pelvic-floor function. The plan should match the findings and be reviewed if symptoms continue. An alpha blocker may sometimes be used to relax muscle near the bladder outlet and ease urinary symptoms. It is a clinician-selected option rather than a cure for every form of prostatitis. Persistent skin changes deserve an examination Penile cancer is uncommon, and burning alone is not a typical way to diagnose it. However, a persistent sore, lump, bleeding, skin thickening or a change that is not healing should be examined. Many such changes have other explanations. An examination and sometimes a small tissue sample help establish the cause. If cancer is found, treatment depends on its location and stage; do not assume that one operation is inevitable. Treatment for confirmed penile cancer may include local treatment or surgery, radiotherapy, and in selected advanced cases chemotherapy. The extent of disease and specialist assessment determine the choices. A separate condition sometimes follows outdoor exposure Summer penile syndrome is an itchy swelling reaction, most often in children, associated with chigger exposure or irritating plants. It is different from informal claims that the penis grows larger in warm weather. A swollen or painful penis should be assessed, especially if urination is difficult. A clinician may recommend an age-appropriate antihistamine or other treatment after checking the cause. Do not assume that all swelling after outdoor play is an allergy. Neither hot weather nor drinking extra water should be used to explain away continuing pain, discharge or a visible abnormality. For an assessed allergic swelling reaction, a cool cloth may help; a clinician may also recommend an antihistamine or a suitable topical steroid. Claims about seasonal size changes from hydration or temperature are not an explanation for painful burning and do not establish a recognised disease. Burning is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Skin irritation, urinary infection and urethritis need different care. Thrush does not usually mean a sexually transmitted infection. Use antibiotics only according to an assessed, current treatment plan. Urinary retention, sudden testicular pain and a trapped foreskin need emergency care. Does burning mean I have an STI? Not necessarily. Irritation and other infections can feel similar, but an STI may need testing even without obvious discharge. Can I use an antifungal cream just in case? It is better to establish the cause, especially with a first episode, sores, urinary symptoms or persistent discomfort. Can prostatitis always be treated with antibiotics? No. Bacterial prostatitis needs antibiotics, but many chronic pelvic pain symptoms have no proven bacterial cause.

title: Mucus or discharge from the anus: when to get help
description: Why anal discharge can occur, how infection differs from other bowel problems, and what an assessment may involve.
body: Mucus, pus or unexpected fluid from the anus can be uncomfortable and worrying. Several conditions can cause it, and the appearance alone cannot tell you which one is responsible. New or persistent discharge deserves assessment, particularly when it comes with pain, bleeding or a change in bowel habits. Notice the pattern without trying to diagnose it Discharge may appear on underwear, on toilet paper or alongside stool. Some people feel a repeated urge to empty the bowel but pass only mucus or a small amount of stool. This sensation is called tenesmus. Describe whether the fluid seems to come from the anus or from a small opening in nearby skin. Note when it started, whether there is blood, pain, a lump, diarrhoea or constipation, and whether you feel unwell. Stool leakage and mucus discharge can coexist but are not exactly the same problem. A colour or smell is not enough to identify an infection. Nor does discharge automatically mean that you have an STI, irritable bowel syndrome or cancer. Recognise symptoms that should not wait Seek emergency help for heavy or nonstop rectal bleeding, large clots, fainting or severe illness. A painful piece of bowel tissue trapped outside the anus also needs urgent emergency assessment. Get urgent advice for severe anal or abdominal pain, a tender swelling with fever, spreading redness, black or dark-red stool, or bloody diarrhoea. An abscess can need treatment even when there is no obvious external lump. Persistent discharge, unexplained weight loss, a new lump or an ongoing change in bowel habits should be reviewed. If you have reduced immunity or diabetes, seek advice promptly when an infection is possible. Infection can inflame the rectum Proctitis means inflammation of the rectum. It can cause pain, mucus or pus, bleeding and the repeated feeling that you need to pass stool. Some cases are caused by infections, while others have different explanations. Gonorrhoea, chlamydia, herpes and syphilis can affect the anal or rectal area. Relevant exposure can include oral, finger or genital contact with the anus, not only penetrative anal intercourse. Tell the clinician about the sites of sexual contact so they can choose the right samples. A urine-only STI test may miss a rectal infection. Testing and treatment should follow local guidance, including advice about partners and when to resume sexual contact. Bowel infections, including some acquired from contaminated food or through faecal contact, can also cause diarrhoea, cramps and mucus. Treatment depends on the organism and severity; not every infection needs antibiotics. Mention travel, recent antibiotics, sick contacts and difficulty keeping fluids down. Examples of bowel infections include Salmonella, norovirus, Campylobacter and Shigella. They may bring nausea, vomiting and cramps as well as diarrhoea. Replace fluid losses with small frequent drinks or an appropriate oral rehydration solution, and ask for advice if you cannot keep up with losses. IBS and inflammatory bowel disease are different Irritable bowel syndrome, or IBS, can include mucus in the stool together with abdominal pain, bloating, constipation or diarrhoea. It involves altered gut function and gut–brain interaction rather than the tissue inflammation seen in inflammatory bowel disease. IBS should not become an explanation for every new symptom. Pus, bleeding, fever or unintentional weight loss needs investigation rather than being dismissed as an IBS flare. Inflammatory bowel disease includes ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease. Either can affect the rectum and cause mucus, blood, urgency or pain. Management may involve medicines and sometimes surgery; diet changes alone should not replace treatment or monitoring. If you already have inflammatory bowel disease, follow your flare plan and contact your team about a new discharge, pain or a possible abscess. With IBS, large meals, particular foods and stress can worsen symptoms for some people. A clinician may discuss meal changes, medicines and psychological therapies; probiotic effects vary by product and person. Crohn’s disease can affect the digestive tract from mouth to anus, whereas ulcerative colitis affects the colon and rectum. Appetite loss, tiredness, fever or weight loss can accompany inflammatory disease and should not be treated as IBS alone. Haemorrhoids, abscesses and fistulas need different care Haemorrhoids can cause itching, bright-red bleeding and mucus leakage, especially when tissue protrudes. However, a previous haemorrhoid diagnosis does not prove that a new episode of bleeding or discharge has the same cause. An anal abscess is a collection of pus. It may cause increasing pain, swelling, fever or feeling unwell and usually needs drainage by a clinician. Antibiotics alone are generally not an adequate substitute. The procedure may take place in a clinic or operating theatre, depending on the abscess. A fistula is a tunnel between the anal canal and nearby skin, often following an abscess. It can repeatedly drain and seem to heal before becoming painful again. A colorectal specialist can assess its course and plan treatment while protecting bowel-control muscles. Many fistulas need a procedure, but those associated with Crohn’s disease require a coordinated medical and surgical approach. Do not squeeze, puncture or probe a draining area yourself. Straining, constipation or repeated diarrhoea can contribute to haemorrhoid symptoms; pregnancy can also increase the risk. Keeping stool comfortable to pass may help, but a new bleed should still be checked. Prolapse and persistent unexplained changes Rectal prolapse occurs when part of the rectum moves down and may come through the anus. It can cause a visible bulge, mucus, bleeding or problems controlling stool. It is not the same as haemorrhoids. An examination is needed to confirm the problem. Adults with full rectal prolapse often need surgery; the choice depends on the findings and overall health. If the protruding tissue becomes trapped and painful, get urgent help. Anal or bowel cancer is another possible cause of persistent symptoms, although many people have a less serious explanation. A new lump, bleeding or a continuing change should be assessed rather than judged using a population-risk statistic. Prolapse is more common in older adults and may be associated with longstanding constipation, although younger people can develop it. Symptoms may initially come and go before worsening. Anal cancer risk is influenced by factors including HPV infection, smoking and age; these factors and a change in stool shape do not diagnose it. What happens at an appointment The clinician may examine the abdomen and skin around the anus and offer a rectal examination. They should explain the examination, ask your consent and discuss a chaperone. You can ask them to pause or stop. Depending on the findings, tests may include stool samples or culture, blood tests and rectal STI swabs. Anoscopy or proctoscopy looks at the anus and rectum; sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy examines more of the bowel. CT or MRI may help with a suspected abscess, fistula or another deeper problem. These tests are chosen for the clinical question, not automatically ordered for every discharge. While waiting, clean the outside gently with water, pat dry and avoid harsh wipes or unprescribed products inside the anus. Keep follow-up appointments and return if symptoms worsen. These are familiar problems in primary care, sexual-health services and colorectal clinics; embarrassment should not keep you from getting help. New or persistent discharge needs a cause-based assessment. Rectal infections may require rectal testing. Do not attribute bleeding, pus or fever to IBS without review. An abscess usually needs drainage; do not try to drain it at home. Heavy bleeding, severe illness or trapped painful prolapse needs urgent care. Does mucus always mean an infection? No. It may occur with IBS, haemorrhoids, prolapse or inflammatory conditions as well as infection. Will a urine STI test rule out a rectal infection? Not reliably. Samples need to match the site of exposure and symptoms. Can a fistula be ignored if it stops draining? No. Temporary closure can be followed by another abscess. Arrange specialist advice if a fistula is suspected.

title: Pink vaginal discharge: possible causes and when to seek care
description: Understand pink discharge around periods, ovulation, pregnancy, birth and menopause, and the symptoms that need medical attention.
body: A pink stain usually means a little blood has mixed with discharge. Its timing and the symptoms alongside it are more useful than the colour alone when deciding what to do next. What gives discharge a pink colour? Pink discharge usually means a small amount of blood has mixed with vaginal fluid or cervical mucus. The blood may come from the uterus, cervix or irritated vaginal tissue. Its diluted colour tells you little about the cause: light pink does not automatically mean harmless, and it does not prove pregnancy. Timing helps make sense of it. Notice whether it appears at the beginning or end of a period, after sex, between periods, after a contraceptive change, during pregnancy or after birth. Pain, odour, itching, fever and how much bleeding there is are at least as important as colour. A new or repeated pattern deserves assessment even if it is only visible when wiping. At the beginning or end of a period When menstrual flow is just starting or finishing, a little blood mixed with ordinary discharge can look pink. A brief episode that follows your familiar period pattern, without other symptoms, often does not need treatment. Period length and cycle length vary between people and can change with age, stress, weight changes or illness. A much lighter bleed than usual is not necessarily a complete period. If pregnancy is possible, use an appropriately timed test rather than counting a day of pink spotting as proof that you are not pregnant. Bleeding between periods or after sex, or a continuing change in your normal pattern, should be checked. Hormonal changes and contraception Changes in estrogen and progesterone influence the uterine lining and can produce irregular bleeding. Low estrogen can also make vaginal tissue drier and more fragile. Hot flushes, sleep problems, mood changes, poor concentration, vaginal dryness and urinary symptoms may occur in some low-estrogen states. Weight change and longer-term bone loss can have many causes; they are not a checklist that diagnoses low estrogen from pink discharge. Starting or changing a hormonal pill, implant, injection or hormonal intrauterine system can alter bleeding. Spotting often improves over the first few months, but some methods cause longer-lasting irregular bleeding. Progestogen-only methods and combined methods can both do this; it is not simply an artificial estrogen imbalance. Check missed doses, vomiting, medication interactions and whether the method is still in date with your pharmacist or clinician. Do not stop contraception or create a hormone-free break on your own. Persistent, new or troublesome bleeding needs a review, including pregnancy or infection testing when relevant, before deciding whether to change the method. Ovulation may cause brief mid-cycle spotting An egg is released from an ovary and then enters the fallopian tube. Some people notice a small amount of bleeding or discharge around this time, sometimes with a brief one-sided ache called ovulation pain or mittelschmerz. Clearer, wetter cervical mucus can make a little blood look pink. Ovulation often occurs roughly two weeks before the next period, but its timing varies. A basal-temperature rise usually happens after ovulation; neither a pink stain nor a temperature change reliably identifies a fertile day by itself. The days before ovulation and the day of ovulation can be fertile. Do not use spotting to decide when unprotected sex is safe, and have severe or recurring pain assessed. Ovarian cysts and pelvic symptoms An ovarian cyst is a fluid-filled structure in or on an ovary. Functional cysts can form when the usual egg-release process changes; many disappear without treatment. Other types include dermoid cysts, cystadenomas and endometriomas associated with endometriosis. They do not all arise from the same hormonal problem. Some cysts are found incidentally. Others can be associated with altered periods, pelvic heaviness, bloating, pain during sex or pressure on the bladder or bowel. Pink discharge alone is not a way to identify a cyst or its type. A clinician may arrange ultrasound if the history and examination suggest one. Monitoring is often appropriate, while persistent, large, concerning or troublesome cysts may need surgery. Sudden severe pelvic pain, especially with nausea or vomiting, needs urgent assessment for complications such as rupture or ovarian torsion. Most untreated cysts do not inevitably twist or destroy an ovary. Early pregnancy: test rather than guessing about implantation Light bleeding can occur in early pregnancy, including around the time a period would have been expected. It is often called implantation bleeding, but appearance and timing cannot establish that implantation caused it. A pink stain is neither confirmation of pregnancy nor reassurance that a pregnancy is developing normally. Breast tenderness, nausea, tiredness and needing to urinate more frequently can occur in pregnancy but also have other explanations. If a period is late or unusually light, take a home pregnancy test from the first day of the missed period. If you cannot predict the next period, test at least 21 days after the last unprotected sex. Repeat an early negative test after a few days if pregnancy remains possible. Contact your maternity or early-pregnancy service about bleeding in a known pregnancy, even if it is light. They may ask about pain and dates, and arrange ultrasound or pregnancy-hormone tests. Very early results sometimes need follow-up because one scan or blood test may not give the answer. Ectopic pregnancy needs prompt attention An ectopic pregnancy develops outside the uterine cavity, most often in a fallopian tube. Bleeding may be light, intermittent, brown or pink, and there may be relatively little visible blood despite internal bleeding. Possible symptoms include one-sided lower abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain, pain or pressure when opening the bowels, dizziness or faintness. Get urgent medical assessment if pregnancy is possible and you have unusual bleeding with abdominal or pelvic pain. Severe pain, shoulder-tip pain, collapse or marked dizziness require emergency care. Do not wait for a positive home test or heavier bleeding. A ruptured ectopic pregnancy can be life-threatening. Depending on the findings, treatment may involve carefully supervised monitoring, methotrexate or surgery. These options need specialist follow-up; they are not interchangeable home treatments. Rupture requires emergency treatment. Miscarriage is another possible cause of pregnancy bleeding A miscarriage can involve spotting, heavier bleeding, cramps, fluid, clots or tissue passing from the vagina. Some pregnancy losses cause few symptoms and are discovered on a scan. Conversely, many pregnancies with early bleeding continue. Discharge colour alone cannot distinguish these situations. A clinician assesses the pregnancy with the history, ultrasound and sometimes blood tests. If a loss is confirmed and you are stable, options may include waiting for it to pass, medication or a procedure using suction to remove remaining pregnancy tissue. Surgery is not automatically necessary. Heavy bleeding, faintness, fever or severe pain changes the urgency and treatment plan. Pink or brown discharge after birth Bleeding and discharge after delivery, called lochia, occur while the uterus heals. It generally starts redder and heavier, then becomes lighter and may appear brown or pink before fading. Recovery varies; an exact change on day four or day ten is not a requirement for normal healing. Use maternity or period pads and follow your maternity team’s advice about internal products while healing. Tell the team about large clots, a bad smell, fever, increasing abdominal tenderness or bleeding that becomes concerning. Sudden heavy blood loss, a racing heart or feeling faint needs emergency help. These symptoms should not be dismissed as an ordinary colour change in lochia. Infection and pelvic inflammatory disease Chlamydia, gonorrhoea and other infections can inflame the cervix and cause spotting or blood-tinged discharge. There may also be bleeding after sex, pain when urinating, a change in discharge, itching or pelvic discomfort. Some infections cause no obvious symptoms, so the absence of smell or pain does not rule them out. Pelvic inflammatory disease, or PID, affects the upper reproductive tract and can cause pelvic pain, fever, painful sex or abnormal bleeding. Untreated PID can contribute to chronic pelvic pain, difficulty conceiving and ectopic pregnancy. Not every episode is caused by a sexually transmitted infection, and pink discharge by itself does not establish PID. Testing and prompt antibiotics are important when infection is suspected. Partners may need testing or treatment, and the clinic will advise when sex can safely resume. Condoms help reduce future infection risk but do not replace completing treatment. Fever with pelvic pain or feeling significantly unwell needs urgent care. Fibroids and other uterine causes Fibroids are non-cancerous growths in or around the uterus. Many cause no symptoms; others lead to heavy or painful periods, bleeding changes, pelvic or lower-back pain, discomfort during sex, or pressure affecting urination and bowel movements. Light bleeding mixed with mucus can be pink, but fibroids are only one possible explanation. An examination and ultrasound may help identify them. Treatment depends on their size and location, symptoms and pregnancy plans. Observation, medicines to control bleeding, and various procedures may be considered. Removing fibroids surgically is not the only option and is not needed for every fibroid. Perimenopause and bleeding after menopause During perimenopause, fluctuating hormones can change the timing and amount of bleeding. Hot flushes, disturbed sleep, vaginal dryness and mood changes may accompany this transition. It usually develops in midlife; a new bleeding pattern in the thirties should not simply be assumed to be menopause. Pregnancy and other causes may still need to be considered. After 12 months without a natural period because of menopause, new bleeding needs medical review, even once, even if it is only pink or brown discharge. Vaginal or uterine-lining thinning is common, but polyps, endometrial changes and cancer are other possibilities. Do not wait for it to become heavy. Treatment follows the diagnosis. Menopausal hormone therapy can help selected symptoms; vaginal estrogen may help local dryness. Non-hormonal treatments can also be useful. Antidepressants treat selected mood or menopausal symptoms, not an estrogen deficiency itself. Unexplained bleeding should be assessed before assuming hormone treatment is the answer. Could it be cervical cancer? Most pink discharge is not caused by cancer. However, cervical cancer can cause bleeding after sex, between periods or after menopause, a persistent change in discharge, and pelvic, back or sexual pain. Early disease may have no symptoms. Discharge does not pass through a dependable white-to-pink colour sequence as cancer develops. Persistent unexplained weight loss, marked fatigue, leg swelling or bladder or bowel changes also need assessment, although many conditions can cause them. Keep up with the cervical-screening programme offered locally, but do not wait for a routine screening appointment to report symptoms. Screening is not a substitute for examining abnormal bleeding. If cancer is diagnosed, care is tailored to its type and stage and may include surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy or other specialist treatments. Pink discharge alone cannot tell you whether any of these treatments is needed. What to record and when to get help Write down the dates, amount, relationship to sex or periods, contraception and medicines, pregnancy-test results and accompanying symptoms. Avoid douching or inserting products intended to change discharge colour. A clinician may offer a pregnancy test, examination, infection swabs or ultrasound depending on what is happening. Arrange a review for unexplained bleeding between periods or after sex, persistent or recurrent discharge changes, or any bleeding after menopause. Seek prompt advice for bleeding in pregnancy or fever with pelvic pain. Severe pain, shoulder-tip pain, collapse, breathlessness or rapidly heavy bleeding needs emergency assessment regardless of the shade of the discharge. A little blood mixed with mucus can look pink. Period or contraceptive-related spotting can occur, but a new pattern deserves attention. A pink stain cannot confirm implantation or rule out ectopic pregnancy. Any postmenopausal bleeding should be checked. Treatment depends on the cause, not the colour. Does pink discharge mean I am pregnant? No. Periods, contraception, ovulation, irritation and infection can also cause it. Take a pregnancy test from a missed period, or at least 21 days after unprotected sex if you do not know when a period is due. Can I identify implantation bleeding by its colour? No. Pink or brown spotting cannot confirm implantation, date a pregnancy or show that it is healthy. Bleeding in a known pregnancy should be discussed with your pregnancy-care team. Is pink discharge at the end of a period normal? A small amount of remaining blood mixed with discharge may look pink. If this is new, continues, occurs between periods or is accompanied by pain, odour or other symptoms, arrange a review. Should I stop my contraceptive pill because of spotting? Do not stop it or take an extra break on your own. A pharmacist or clinician can check missed doses and interactions and help decide whether the bleeding needs investigation or a method change. Can ovulation cause pink spotting? Some people have brief light bleeding around egg release, sometimes with a one-sided ache. Spotting is not an accurate ovulation test, and severe, recurring or pregnancy-associated pain needs assessment. Does an ovarian cyst always need surgery? No. Many functional cysts resolve with observation. Size, ultrasound appearance, symptoms and menopausal status guide care. Sudden severe pain, especially with nausea or vomiting, needs urgent assessment. Can a sexually transmitted infection cause pink discharge without pain? Yes. Cervical infections may cause spotting and can otherwise be symptom-free. A sexual-health service can advise on testing, treatment and partner care. When is pink discharge after birth concerning? Lochia normally becomes lighter over time. A bad smell, fever, worsening abdominal pain or large clots needs maternity advice; sudden heavy bleeding or faintness requires emergency care. Does one episode after menopause need checking? Yes. Even a single small amount of pink or brown discharge after menopause should be assessed. Often the cause is benign, but colour and amount cannot exclude a condition needing treatment. What if the discharge is light but I have severe one-sided pain? Get urgent medical help. If pregnancy is possible, ectopic pregnancy must be considered; severe pain, shoulder-tip pain, marked dizziness or collapse needs emergency care even without a positive test.

title: Grey vaginal discharge: why testing matters
description: Bacterial vaginosis is one possible cause of grey discharge, but symptoms overlap. Learn what to discuss at an appointment and when to seek urgent help.
body: A new grey colour, unusual smell or change in the amount of vaginal discharge is a reason to arrange an assessment. Bacterial vaginosis is a common explanation, but colour cannot confirm it or rule out another condition. The useful next step is a diagnosis, not choosing a treatment from a colour chart. Normal discharge does not need to be washed away Vaginal fluid is normally clear or white and can change in amount and consistency through the menstrual cycle. The vagina has its own microbial environment; it does not need internal washing to remove ordinary discharge. Douching, fragranced products and repeated attempts to disinfect the area can cause irritation or disturb that environment. Gently wash the outside and avoid putting cleansing products inside the vagina. If the discharge is different from your usual pattern, note when it started and whether there is odour, itching, soreness, urinary discomfort or bleeding. These details help the clinician decide what tests are useful. Bacterial vaginosis is a change in the vaginal bacteria Bacterial vaginosis, often shortened to BV, involves a shift in the balance of bacteria in the vagina. It can cause a thin white or grey discharge and a noticeable fishy smell, sometimes more apparent after sex. Some people have no symptoms. Marked itching and soreness are not always present. Frothy discharge or intense irritation should not be used to diagnose BV without considering other causes. More than one condition can occur at the same time. BV does not mean that you are unclean. Sexual activity can influence its occurrence and recurrence, but the diagnosis is not proof that a partner has been unfaithful. Symptomatic BV is usually treated with an appropriate antibiotic, as tablets or a vaginal preparation. The choice depends on circumstances including pregnancy, allergies and previous episodes. Thrush treatments do not treat BV. Other infections can cause overlapping changes Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted infection that may cause unusual discharge, odour, irritation or pain with urination. Its appearance varies, so yellow, green or grey-looking fluid is not enough to identify it. For women, current CDC guidance recommends a multidose oral treatment course rather than presenting a single dose as the standard answer for everyone. The clinic will prescribe the appropriate regimen and explain partner treatment and follow-up. Chlamydia and gonorrhoea can affect the cervix and may cause discharge, bleeding after sex or urinary discomfort. They can also be present without symptoms. Testing is more reliable than trying to distinguish them by colour. An infection cannot usually be dated from the day symptoms appear. Share relevant sexual-contact information privately with the clinician so testing covers the appropriate sites. Chlamydia or gonorrhoea can also cause rectal pain, bleeding or discharge when the rectum is affected. Mention these symptoms so that testing includes the appropriate site; a vaginal or urine sample does not automatically test the rectum. What to expect from an assessment A clinician may ask about symptoms, pregnancy possibility, contraception, recent antibiotics and products used in or around the vagina. Tell them if you have already tried a treatment. They may offer an examination and a vaginal sample. Tests can include vaginal pH, microscopy or laboratory tests for particular infections. A pH result or symptom history on its own is not enough to identify every cause. You can ask what an examination involves, request a chaperone and ask the clinician to stop. In some services, self-collected vaginal swabs are available. Unexplained bleeding, a persistent lump or symptoms that do not improve may need further examination. Vaginal cancer is uncommon and grey discharge is not a specific cancer sign, but continuing changes should not be repeatedly treated as infection without review. Persistent pelvic or lower abdominal pain, a vaginal lump, pain with sex or urination, or new bowel symptoms such as constipation also deserve review. Back pain or leg swelling can have many causes; alongside continuing vaginal symptoms they should be discussed rather than used as a self-test for cancer. Pregnancy and pelvic pain change the urgency If you are pregnant and notice unusual discharge or a new smell, contact your maternity clinician promptly. Symptomatic BV and other infections can be treated during pregnancy with a suitable medicine; do not avoid assessment because you are worried about all antibiotics. Fever, lower abdominal or pelvic pain, pain during sex or feeling unwell can indicate a problem beyond a simple change in discharge, including pelvic inflammatory disease. Seek prompt advice. Severe pain, fainting, heavy bleeding or marked illness needs emergency care. If pregnancy is possible, pelvic pain with bleeding also needs urgent assessment for pregnancy-related causes. Do not diagnose leaking amniotic fluid by colour at home. A persistent watery trickle or gush during pregnancy should be discussed with the maternity service. Follow the treatment and return if it comes back Take or use the prescribed treatment as directed. Ask about sexual contact during treatment and whether the vaginal product affects condoms or diaphragms. The advice depends on the medicine and the diagnosis. Trichomoniasis, chlamydia and gonorrhoea generally require a plan for partners as well as the person with symptoms. Follow the clinic’s instructions about when to resume sex and any repeat testing. Advice about partners in recurrent BV has changed with newer research. Treating an ongoing partner may be discussed in appropriate cases under current local guidance. Do not assume either that partners never need treatment or that everyone should take the same antibiotic. Symptoms may start improving during treatment, but full recovery within exactly one week is not guaranteed. Persistent or recurrent symptoms need reassessment; do not keep alternating antibiotics and thrush remedies without checking the cause. Grey discharge can occur with BV, but appearance is not a diagnosis. Avoid douching and unprescribed internal treatments. Testing can distinguish BV from STIs and other causes. Pregnancy, fever or pelvic pain warrants prompt advice. Partner advice and follow-up depend on the diagnosis and current guidance. Is grey discharge always bacterial vaginosis? No. BV is a common possibility, but other infections and conditions can look similar. Will a thrush medicine help? Not if the cause is BV or an STI. Testing helps avoid treating the wrong condition. Can BV come back after treatment? Yes. Recurrence is common enough to deserve a follow-up plan, including a discussion of partner treatment where appropriate.

title: An itchy penis: gentle care and when to get checked
description: Common causes of genital itching, safer ways to ease irritation, and home remedies that can make sensitive skin worse.
body: Genital itching is not always caused by an infection. Irritating products, skin conditions, parasites and sexually transmitted infections can produce overlapping symptoms. Gentle care can reduce discomfort, but ongoing itching, a new rash or other symptoms needs an assessment rather than a series of home remedies. Begin with simple, gentle care Pause fragranced washes, deodorants, antiseptics and any new product that seems to trigger symptoms. Wash gently with lukewarm water or a suitable soap substitute, then pat dry. Repeated washing and scrubbing can make irritated skin worse. A cool, damp cloth held briefly against the outside skin may ease itching. Do not place ice directly on the penis. Cooling can soothe the sensation but does not treat scabies, a fungal infection or inflammation inside the urethra. Wear comfortable, loose clothing and change out of sweaty clothes. Keep nails short, avoid scratching and pause shaving over irritated or broken skin. Do not pick or squeeze bumps that you think might be ingrown hairs. If the foreskin retracts comfortably, clean gently beneath it and bring it forward again afterwards. Never force a tight foreskin back. Ask a pharmacist or clinician about a bland, fragrance-free emollient suitable for the affected area if the skin is dry. Skip acidic and irritating remedies Do not put apple cider vinegar, lemon juice, essential oils or disinfectant on genital skin. A diluted household product is not automatically safe for this sensitive area and may increase stinging, inflammation or skin injury. Salt baths and homemade oatmeal mixtures should not be treated as proven cures for an unexplained genital rash. A product that is comfortable on an arm or leg may not be suitable for the head of the penis. Avoid ordinary wart-removal liquids or freezing products on genital bumps. These are not designed for genital warts. Likewise, do not borrow a strong steroid cream prescribed for a different body site or another person. Irritation, balanitis and skin conditions Contact dermatitis can follow exposure to a cleanser, lubricant, condom ingredient or another irritant or allergen. Eczema can also affect genital skin; it is not simply an allergy in every case. Balanitis means inflammation of the head of the penis, not inflammation of a gland. It may involve soreness, swelling, itching, discharge beneath the foreskin or discomfort when urinating. The treatment depends on whether irritation, yeast or another cause is present. Psoriasis and lichen planus can occur on the penis. Genital psoriasis may look different from the thick, scaly plaques seen elsewhere. Lichen nitidus can cause tiny bumps and is another condition a clinician may consider. These names cannot reliably be assigned from an online picture. Some normal skin features also look like bumps. A clinician or dermatologist can examine the pattern and, occasionally, arrange a small skin sample if the diagnosis remains uncertain. Infections and parasites need specific treatment Thrush can cause an itchy, sore head of the penis and irritation beneath the foreskin. It is not usually a sexually transmitted infection, and an antifungal will not help if the cause is dermatitis or another condition. Genital herpes may begin with tingling or itching and can cause painful blisters or sores. Warts caused by HPV may itch or bleed, but not every genital bump is a wart. Seek assessment for new sores or bumps rather than trying to remove them yourself. Scabies can cause marked itching, often worse at night, and may affect the penis as well as other areas. Pubic lice live on coarse hair and may cause itching around the pubic region. These require suitable treatment and advice about close contacts, clothing and bedding; soothing the skin alone will not eliminate them. A rash on the groin crease or an inflamed hair follicle may have a different cause from a rash on the penis itself. Tell the clinician exactly where the itching occurs and whether other areas or close contacts are affected. Other groin causes include folliculitis, meaning inflammation around a hair follicle; an ingrown hair after shaving; jock itch, a fungal rash usually affecting the groin folds; and molluscum contagiosum, a viral cause of small bumps. These may be confused with penile conditions and need different treatments. Once irritated skin has healed, avoiding a very close shave and shaving in the direction of hair growth can reduce recurrent ingrown hairs. Get assessed if there are urinary or persistent symptoms Burning during urination, discharge from the urethral opening or pain with sex can indicate urethritis or another infection. A sexual-health clinic can help, whether or not you know of a recent exposure. Arrange a review when itching is severe, affects sleep, keeps returning or does not improve after removing likely irritants. New sores, bleeding, a persistent lump or skin changes that are not healing also need examination. Fever, increasing pain, spreading swelling or feeling unwell calls for prompt advice. Seek emergency care if you cannot urinate, have sudden severe testicular pain or the foreskin is stuck behind the head of the penis. A swab is not a single universal test for every cause. The clinician may use an examination, targeted swabs or urine tests, and sometimes other investigations. Recurrent or severe balanitis may prompt a check for contributing conditions such as diabetes. Use the treatment intended for your diagnosis A diagnosed inflammatory skin condition may need a prescribed steroid or another anti-inflammatory treatment. Genital skin absorbs medicines readily, so the strength, amount and duration should be clear. Stronger treatments sometimes have an appropriate specialist use; they should not be chosen casually for itch. If an STI or a parasite is diagnosed, follow the advice about contacts and when sexual activity can resume. With an unexplained sore or possible STI, avoid contact that could transmit infection while awaiting assessment. If a prescribed treatment burns, worsens the rash or fails to help, contact the prescriber. The goal is to identify and treat the cause while keeping the skin comfortable, not to suppress the symptom indefinitely. Use gentle cleansing and avoid scratching or excessive washing. Do not apply vinegar, household acids or ordinary wart products to genital skin. Skin conditions, infection and parasites require different treatment. New sores, discharge, urinary pain or persistent changes need assessment. Use genital steroid treatments only with a clear diagnosis and instructions. Can a cold cloth cure the cause of itching? No. It may ease discomfort temporarily, but an infection or skin condition may still need treatment. Does genital itching always mean an STI? No. Irritation, eczema and other non-sexually transmitted conditions are also possible. Can I use my usual psoriasis cream on the penis? Check first. Thin genital skin may need a different medicine or schedule from other parts of the body.

title: Urethral swabs and urine tests: what to expect
description: Why a clinician may request a urethral sample, how culture differs from a molecular test, and what your results can tell you.
body: Discharge from the urinary opening, burning when you urinate or a sore tip of the penis can lead a clinician to test for urethritis. Several tests are available. A swab, a urine sample and a culture are not interchangeable terms, and one negative result does not exclude every cause of symptoms. Why testing may be recommended The urethra carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body. Inflammation can result from infection or irritation. A clinician may recommend testing because of symptoms, a partner’s diagnosis or an exposure even when you feel well. Gonorrhoea and chlamydia are possible causes of urethral infection, but they are not the only ones. A sexual-health appointment can also help distinguish urethral discharge from irritation or material beneath the foreskin. Tell the clinician about urinary symptoms, genital sores, recent medicines and any anal or oral exposure. A urine test does not automatically check for an infection in the throat or rectum; those sites may need their own samples. The urethra in a penis also carries semen. Unexpected discharge means fluid other than the usual urine or semen; symptoms prompting assessment include frequent or painful urination, redness at the opening, pus-like fluid and painful or swollen testicles. Gonorrhoea and chlamydia may also affect the rectum, causing pain, blood or discharge, and gonorrhoea can affect the throat. In a partner with a cervix, genital infection can involve abnormal vaginal discharge, pelvic pain or pain during sex and can spread to the uterus and fallopian tubes.
