Culture and molecular testing answer different questions A culture tries to grow an organism from a sample under laboratory conditions. For gonorrhoea, growing the bacteria can allow testing of which antibiotics are likely to work. This is especially important if treatment seems to have failed or antibiotic resistance is suspected. A nucleic acid amplification test, often called a NAAT, looks for genetic material from a particular organism. It is commonly used to detect chlamydia and gonorrhoea and can often be performed on a urine sample from someone with a penis. An ordinary bacterial culture is not a universal chlamydia test. Other infections also require specific tests, and a laboratory only looks for the organisms included in the requested investigation. Ask which infections your sample will be checked for. Follow the instructions for your particular sample The clinic may ask you not to urinate for a period before the appointment or sample collection, often around one to two hours depending on the test. Follow the instructions they give you; if you have already urinated, tell them rather than cancelling or withholding care. For an STI urine test, you will commonly collect the first part of the urine stream. This is different from the midstream sample often requested for a bladder-infection culture. The container instructions matter. Tell the team if you have recently taken an antibiotic, because this can affect interpretation. Do not stop a prescribed medicine or take leftover antibiotics to prepare for a test. If both an STI test and a urine culture are required, ask how the separate samples should be collected. What happens during a swab The clinician should explain the procedure and obtain your agreement. If discharge is visible at the opening, it may be possible to collect it directly without inserting a swab into the urethra. Otherwise, a small swab may be placed briefly inside the opening. This can feel uncomfortable or sting for a few seconds. Let the clinician know if you are anxious, have previously fainted during procedures or need a pause. The exact technique depends on the sample required; not every appointment involves a deep swab. Brief irritation can occur afterwards. Ask for advice if pain or bleeding persists or worsens. Seek prompt care if you develop fever or difficulty urinating. How to understand the result A positive molecular test means the targeted organism was detected. A positive culture means an organism grew, but the clinician still considers the specific organism, symptoms and sample quality when interpreting it. A negative culture means that the organisms sought did not grow under the conditions used. It does not prove that there is no infection anywhere or that the symptoms have no medical cause. Timing, previous antibiotics and the type and site of sample can matter. Ask when results are expected and how you will receive them. Some clinics can provide information quickly, while other results take several days. If treatment is recommended before all results return, that can be appropriate; do not assume you must wait for a positive report. Return if symptoms continue despite treatment or negative tests. Further assessment may look for another organism, reinfection, ongoing inflammation or a non-infectious cause. Repeated antibiotics without reassessment are not the answer to every persistent symptom. Treatment and follow-up are part of testing If an STI is diagnosed, the clinic can help with partner notification, testing and treatment. This is about preventing reinfection and protecting health, not assigning blame. An infection may be present without symptoms. Follow the specific advice on when sexual contact can resume. This commonly involves completing treatment, allowing the required interval and ensuring partners have been treated. Condoms reduce many STI risks but do not replace treatment. A test to confirm cure and a later test for reinfection serve different purposes. Whether and when you need them depends on the organism, infection site and treatment. Keep the follow-up plan provided by your clinic. Do not wait for a routine test appointment if you have sudden severe testicular pain, cannot urinate or are very unwell with fever. These symptoms need urgent assessment. Screening can be worthwhile without symptoms. Recommendations depend on age, sexual practices, exposure and local policy; CDC recommends routine chlamydia and gonorrhoea screening for sexually active women younger than 25 and risk-based screening for others, including at exposed sites for men who have sex with men. Ask the clinic what schedule fits you and your partners. A NAAT detects targeted genetic material; a culture grows organisms. A urine sample can often be used for genital chlamydia and gonorrhoea testing. Follow the clinic’s timing and collection instructions. A negative culture does not exclude every infection or every cause of symptoms. Ask about partner care and any follow-up tests. Will I definitely need a swab inside the penis? No. Many STI tests use urine, and visible discharge may be sampled at the opening. The clinician will explain what is needed. Does a normal urine culture mean I do not have chlamydia? No. Chlamydia usually needs a specifically requested molecular test. Ask what was included in your testing. Can I have an STI without discharge? Yes. Testing may be appropriate after an exposure or a partner’s diagnosis even without symptoms.

title: Can betamethasone help genital itching?
description: Eleven possible causes of penile or groin itch, the limits of home remedies, and when a prescribed steroid or antifungal may be appropriate.
body: Betamethasone can help some diagnosed inflammatory skin conditions, but it is not a general treatment for genital itching. The cause and exact location matter before choosing a cream. Itching is a symptom, not a diagnosis Itching on the penis or surrounding skin can feel awkward to discuss. That embarrassment sometimes leads people to use a familiar cream before finding out what is causing the problem. A clinician or sexual-health service is used to these questions; you do not need to work out the diagnosis before asking for help. Betamethasone is a corticosteroid that reduces inflammation. It can be useful for selected skin conditions, but relief after applying it does not prove that the cause has been treated. An infection, irritation and an inflammatory skin disorder can overlap in appearance. Herpes and genital warts Genital herpes, caused by herpes simplex virus, may produce tingling, itch, pain and small blisters that break into sores. Symptoms can first be noticed months or years after infection. A new outbreak therefore does not, by itself, establish when or from whom the virus was acquired. Genital warts are caused by certain types of human papillomavirus, or HPV. They may occur singly or in groups; grouped growths can resemble a cauliflower, but appearances vary. Many cause no discomfort, while some itch or bleed, including after friction. Neither condition is cured by a steroid cream. New genital blisters, ulcers or growths deserve assessment. Avoid sexual contact while unexplained sores are being assessed, and follow the clinic’s advice about treatment and reducing transmission. Candida and jock itch are different fungal problems Candida, a yeast, can cause irritation at the head of the penis and under the foreskin. Burning, soreness, redness or a whitish discharge may occur. Redness can be less obvious on darker skin. These features suggest possibilities, but do not establish a diagnosis on their own. Jock itch, also called tinea cruris, is caused by a different group of fungi called dermatophytes. It commonly affects the groin folds and nearby skin. It should not be treated as another name for every fungal rash on the penis. The location and diagnosis affect the choice of antifungal. A first suspected episode of genital thrush, a recurring problem or a rash that has not responded to treatment is a reason to seek advice rather than keep changing creams. Lichen planus and psoriasis Lichen planus is an inflammatory condition involving the immune system. Small, shiny, flat-topped purple bumps are one possible appearance; penile lesions can also form rings or patches. Itching may be present, but the condition does not always look or feel the same in every person. Psoriasis can affect genital skin as well as other parts of the body. In this sensitive area it may look smoother and less scaly than psoriasis on an elbow or knee. The absence of thick scales does not rule it out. These conditions may need anti-inflammatory treatment, sometimes including a prescribed steroid. Treatment chosen for another body site should not automatically be transferred to the genitals. Contact dermatitis and atopic eczema Contact dermatitis can follow irritation from a product or an allergic response to an ingredient. Soap, fragrances and substances in clothing or intimate products are possible triggers. Dryness, soreness, itch and a rash may follow; the problem is not necessarily an infection. Atopic eczema also involves an impaired skin barrier and inflammation. It is not simply proof that you have become allergic to one particular substance. Genital or groin symptoms can occur alongside eczema elsewhere. A history of new products, friction or previous eczema can help the clinician. Repeated washing with strong cleansers may aggravate the skin rather than remove the cause. Scabies and ingrown hairs Scabies is caused by tiny mites that burrow into the skin. It can affect the groin and genital area, with intense itching that is often worse at night. Small bumps or narrow burrow-like tracks may be visible, and other body areas or close contacts may also be affected. Scabies requires treatment directed at the mites and advice about close contacts. Reducing the itch with a steroid alone does not clear the infestation. Anyone can get scabies; it is not evidence of poor personal hygiene. An ingrown hair is a different problem. After shaving or waxing, a hair may curl back into hair-bearing skin and produce an itchy or tender bump. This explanation does not fit a bump on the hairless head of the penis. Avoid picking or squeezing a lesion you have not identified. What balanitis tells you: and what it does not Balanitis means inflammation of the head of the penis. Symptoms can include soreness, swelling, itching and discomfort when urinating. The term describes the affected area and inflammation; it does not specify one cause. Irritants, Candida and other infections can contribute. An examination, a swab or, in selected recurrent or severe cases, checks for contributing conditions such as diabetes may be appropriate. Treatment follows the findings, rather than the assumption that all balanitis needs the same cream. Comfort measures while arranging advice Scratching may briefly reduce the sensation but can damage the skin and increase irritation. A clean, cool damp cloth held gently against the external area for a few minutes may feel soothing. Do not apply ice directly, and stop if the skin becomes painful or numb. Wash gently with water and pat dry. Avoid scented soaps, deodorants and vigorous scrubbing. If your foreskin retracts comfortably, clean gently and return it to its normal position; never force a tight foreskin back. Pause shaving or other activities that repeatedly rub the sore area. These measures are for comfort and avoiding further irritation; they do not replace treatment for an infection or persistent skin disease. Coconut oil and baking soda are not established treatments Coconut oil is sometimes suggested because oils can reduce friction or act as a skin barrier. That does not establish that it treats an undiagnosed genital rash, Candida, an STI or scabies. It may also irritate some skin. Oil-based products can damage latex condoms, so check product compatibility rather than assuming a kitchen oil is suitable. A baking-soda paste is also promoted for fungal itch. There is not a sound basis here for recommending that homemade treatment on delicate genital skin, and it may worsen irritation. Guessing that the problem is fungal does not make the paste an appropriate medicine. If a product stings or worsens the rash, stop adding it and seek advice. Bring its name or packaging to the appointment so the clinician can consider contact irritation as well as the original symptoms. Different causes need different medicines Antibiotics treat selected bacterial infections; they are not a remedy for every red or inflamed patch. Antifungal medicines target appropriate fungal infections. Herpes, warts and scabies each need their own assessment and treatment approach. Antihistamines sometimes help certain kinds of itch or an allergic component, but they do not cure an infection simply by reducing symptoms. Hydrocortisone and other topical steroids reduce inflammation and have different strengths and suitable uses. Some products are sold without a prescription in some countries, while others are prescription-only. Availability is not a diagnosis or proof that a medicine is suitable for the penis. Ask a pharmacist or clinician before using an unfamiliar product there. When betamethasone may be prescribed A clinician may choose a steroid for diagnosed eczema, contact dermatitis, psoriasis or lichen planus. The appropriate strength, formulation, amount and duration depend on the condition and exact body site. Betamethasone products are not all interchangeable, and they are prescription-only in the UK. Genital skin is particularly sensitive to treatment. A cream prescribed for thick psoriasis on another area may be unsuitable here. Conversely, a rule that no steroid can ever be used on genital skin would also be wrong: a supervised, site-specific course can be part of appropriate care. Use only the medicine and schedule agreed for this problem. Ask which area to treat and when to return if it is not improving, rather than extending treatment because the tube has not run out. How a steroid can hide a fungal rash A steroid may make an itchy rash temporarily feel calmer while a dermatophyte infection continues to spread. The appearance can change, with less typical scaling or borders. This is known as steroid-modified tinea, or tinea incognito. That is why the CDC advises against using steroid creams for suspected ringworm or an undiagnosed rash that could be ringworm. Improvement in redness is not the same as removal of the fungus. Tell the clinician every cream already used and for how long. They may need to examine or test the rash and change the treatment. Do not repeatedly restart a steroid whenever the itch returns without having the cause reviewed. Clotrimazole with betamethasone is not a universal genital cream A combination product contains both an antifungal and a steroid, but the ingredients do not make it suitable for every fungal or genital complaint. One US prescribing label specifies selected inflammatory tinea infections of the feet, groin or body in people aged seventeen and older. For groin and body tinea, that label describes a short course with reassessment if there is no improvement and a two-week maximum. These are restrictions for a particular prescribed product, not instructions to begin treating an undiagnosed penile rash yourself. The labelled tinea indications do not amount to a general recommendation for penile Candida. The prescriber should establish whether an antifungal alone, a different anti-inflammatory plan or another treatment is appropriate. Side effects and reasons to return for care Prolonged or inappropriate steroid use can cause thinning skin, stretch marks, irritation and other local changes. Burning or redness may reflect a reaction, ongoing disease or an infection rather than a need for a stronger cream. If you have used betamethasone for a long time, ask the prescriber how to reduce or change treatment; abrupt changes can sometimes be followed by rebound or withdrawal symptoms. A short-term plan and a prolonged-use problem should not be managed as though they are identical. Arrange prompt assessment for new sores, blisters, discharge, pain when urinating or symptoms that persist despite treatment. Seek emergency care if a retracted foreskin becomes trapped behind the head of the penis and cannot return to its normal position. Bring all the products you have been using. The eleven possibilities include infections, inflammatory skin disease and local irritation. Balanitis describes inflammation rather than one specific infection. Kitchen remedies are not proven substitutes for diagnosis and treatment. Steroids can disguise and worsen ringworm. A combination antifungal/steroid product has specific indications and limits. Can I use leftover betamethasone on a new genital itch? Do not assume it is suitable. A new rash may have a different cause, and genital skin needs a site-specific plan. Does feeling better after applying it prove that it worked? It may show only that inflammation was suppressed. A fungal infection can continue beneath the changed appearance. Are thrush and jock itch the same? No. Candida is a yeast; tinea cruris is a dermatophyte infection. Their usual sites and appropriate treatment can differ. Does balanitis always require an antibiotic? No. Treatment depends on the cause, which may be irritation, a fungal infection or another problem. Can betamethasone treat herpes, warts or scabies? It does not remove those causes. They need their own assessment and treatment. Can psoriasis be present without thick genital scales? Yes. Genital psoriasis may be smoother and less scaly than psoriasis elsewhere. Are all betamethasone creams the same strength? No. Formulation matters; do not substitute products or body sites without advice. Is clotrimazole with betamethasone automatically suitable for penile thrush? No. The cited US label covers specified inflammatory tinea infections, not a blanket indication for penile Candida. Should I try coconut oil or baking soda first? Neither is an established treatment for an undiagnosed genital itch. Baking soda can irritate, and oil-based products may also be incompatible with latex condoms. Should I abruptly stop a steroid I have used for months? Contact the prescriber for a plan, especially if symptoms are worsening. Prolonged treatment can require a supervised change rather than repeated stopping and restarting.

title: Vaginal discharge around menopause: what changes need checking?
description: Understand normal secretions, dryness, infection and why new or blood-stained discharge deserves assessment.
body: Discharge can continue after menopause, and hormonal changes can alter its amount. The useful question is whether it has changed from your usual pattern or comes with symptoms: not whether every trace of fluid should disappear. Menopause is a transition, not an overnight stop to secretions Natural menopause is usually recognised after twelve months without a period when another cause or hormonal treatment does not explain the absence. It most often happens between forty-five and fifty-five, but can occur earlier. The years leading up to it are called perimenopause, when periods and other symptoms may fluctuate. The transition does not start at the same age or last the same number of years for everyone. A range such as seven to fourteen years is not a timetable each person should expect. Hormonal contraception, hormone therapy and some medical treatments make bleeding patterns harder to use as a marker; ask a clinician if your stage is unclear. Vaginal secretions can continue throughout life. Changes in hormones may alter their amount and feel, but menopause does not mean that every trace of discharge is abnormal. Equally, a new symptom should not automatically be dismissed as a normal consequence of getting older. What usual discharge can look like Discharge is fluid and mucus that helps keep the vagina moist and supports its normal environment. Usual discharge is often clear, white or creamy, without a strong unpleasant smell, itching or pain. It can be thin or more noticeable at some times than others. There is no single correct daily amount. Some people notice little on underwear, while others notice more. What matters is a change from your usual pattern and any accompanying symptoms. New, persistent watery discharge, a marked increase or discharge that repeatedly soaks clothing deserves a review even when the colour looks ordinary. Do not use the need for a liner as the only test of whether something is wrong. A liner can be a practical choice, but sudden heavier discharge should not be explained away by that choice. Describe the amount, duration, colour, smell and associated discomfort when asking for advice. Colour can suggest possibilities but cannot diagnose them Thick white, clumpy discharge with itching may occur with thrush. Thin greyish discharge with a fishy smell can occur with bacterial vaginosis. Yellow-green or frothy discharge may occur with trichomoniasis. These patterns overlap, and none can be diagnosed confidently from colour alone. Low-oestrogen tissue changes or a condition called desquamative inflammatory vaginitis can also cause irritation and abnormal discharge. The latter is an inflammatory condition that needs clinical assessment; yellow discharge is not enough to distinguish it from an infection. Treatment choices differ. Pink, brown or red discharge may contain blood. After menopause, even a small blood-stained episode needs assessment. Persistent odour, soreness, burning, painful urination or pain with sex also deserves attention, regardless of whether the discharge looks white or clear. A new sore, blister or genital rash should be mentioned rather than treated as just another discharge colour. Lower oestrogen can cause dryness and irritation together Lower oestrogen can make vaginal tissue thinner, less elastic and more sensitive. The term genitourinary syndrome of menopause, or GSM, describes a group of changes that may include dryness, burning, discomfort with sex and urinary symptoms. The normal vaginal environment also changes. Dryness and discharge can coexist. Fragile or inflamed tissue may be associated with discharge or spotting, but the body should not be assumed to produce extra fluid simply to compensate for dryness. Irritation from urine, friction, soaps or other products may contribute, and infection can still be present. These symptoms do not reliably disappear at the first anniversary of the last period. They may continue or recur without treatment. You do not need to have penetrative sex to prevent atrophy, and avoiding intercourse does not mean you caused it. Choose activities that feel comfortable and seek help rather than pushing through pain. Hysterectomy and removal of the ovaries have different effects A hysterectomy removes the uterus and stops menstrual bleeding from it, but the ovaries are not always removed. If they remain, hormone production may continue, although menopause can sometimes occur earlier than it otherwise would. The absence of periods after surgery is therefore not, by itself, proof that ovarian menopause began that day. Removing both ovaries before natural menopause causes surgical menopause because ovarian hormone production falls abruptly. The vagina can still produce secretions after hysterectomy. Surgery does not mean that all discharge disappears or that every later discharge is harmless. Tell the clinician whether your uterus, cervix and ovaries were removed and when the operation occurred. If you are unsure, they can check the surgical record. This information changes the assessment of bleeding and discharge and helps avoid investigating a structure that is no longer present or overlooking one that remains. Infections and irritation remain possible after menopause Thrush and bacterial vaginosis can occur after menopause. Sexually transmitted infections, including chlamydia, gonorrhoea and trichomoniasis, are also possible when there has been relevant exposure. Age or the end of fertility does not protect against infection, and condoms can still be useful for prevention. HIV is not usually a direct explanation for a characteristic vaginal discharge. Immune suppression can affect susceptibility to infections such as Candida, but discharge does not identify HIV status. Testing decisions should follow exposure history and routine recommendations rather than a visual guess. Irritants can mimic infection. Fragranced washes, bubble bath, laundry products and repeated use of unnecessary vaginal treatments may worsen sensitive tissue. Avoid repeatedly treating presumed thrush when symptoms are new, recurrent or uncertain. A yeast treatment will not correct every infection, inflammatory condition or source of bleeding. Gentle external care can reduce irritation Wash the vulva, the external genital skin, gently with warm water. A mild unperfumed cleanser may suit some people, but leave it out if it stings or worsens dryness. The vagina is internal and does not need douching. Pat the skin dry rather than scrubbing. Choose comfortable, breathable underwear and change it when damp. If using liners, select unscented ones, change them regularly and stop if they cause irritation. Loose clothing and sleeping without underwear may feel better for some people, but they are optional comfort choices, not treatments required for vaginal health. Avoid scented sprays, vaginal deodorants and harsh bubble-bath products. If laundry products seem to trigger symptoms, use a mild detergent, rinse well and avoid fragranced fabric softeners or dryer sheets. The aim is to reduce exposure to things that irritate you, not to make the genital area sterile or eliminate normal discharge. An examination and targeted tests can clarify the cause At an appointment, describe when the change began, how it differs from usual, associated pain or itching, any blood, sexual exposures, medicines and products you have tried. Mention hormone therapy and any surgery. The clinician may examine the vulva, vagina and cervix if present, with your consent. A vaginal sample may be examined under a microscope or sent for laboratory testing. Acidity, measured as pH, can add information, but menopause itself may change pH, so a home test cannot reliably distinguish all causes. Infection testing is chosen according to symptoms and exposure history. Bleeding after menopause requires a separate assessment rather than assuming that dryness explains it. Tests may include a vaginal ultrasound and sampling the uterine lining if the uterus is present. In its April 2026 update, ACOG recommends both ultrasound and tissue sampling for most initial evaluations. Local pathways and individual circumstances vary; a reassuring scan does not automatically end assessment of persistent or recurrent bleeding. Treatment should match the finding Usual discharge without a concerning change or symptoms does not need medication. If dryness or GSM is the problem, a vaginal moisturiser used regularly may help ongoing discomfort, while a lubricant can reduce friction during wanted sexual activity. Choose products intended for vaginal use rather than ordinary perfumed skin creams. Local vaginal oestrogen is another option for suitable people, including some who already use systemic hormone therapy. It comes in several forms, such as cream, tablets, pessaries or a ring. Symptoms may return after stopping, so follow-up and an ongoing plan may be needed. Discuss unexplained bleeding and a history of breast cancer before deciding on treatment with your clinician. Confirmed yeast infection needs an appropriate antifungal; bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis and other infections need their own treatments and sometimes partner management. The fact that a medicine is sold over the counter does not make it the right diagnosis. If symptoms do not improve, return for review rather than repeating the same product indefinitely. When to arrange a review and when it is urgent Arrange an appointment for a new or persistent change in amount, smell or texture, bothersome itching or burning, painful urination or sex, genital sores, or unexplained pelvic discomfort. You do not need to wait until the discharge turns an unusual colour. Symptoms affecting daily life deserve help. Any vaginal bleeding after menopause, including pink or brown staining and even one small episode, should be checked. Many causes are benign, but assessment matters because bleeding can be a sign of a cancer or precancerous change. If you use hormone therapy, describe the exact regimen and timing so the appropriate bleeding pathway can be followed. Seek urgent care for heavy bleeding with faintness, severe pelvic pain, fever or feeling acutely unwell. For a non-urgent appointment, bring a short symptom record and the names of products or medicines used. A clear description can help the clinician distinguish a normal variation from something that needs treatment. Clear or white discharge can remain normal after menopause. A new persistent watery or heavier pattern also needs review. Dryness, irritation and discharge can occur together. Hysterectomy and removal of both ovaries are different operations. Treatment depends on the cause, and normal discharge does not need to be eliminated. Should vaginal discharge stop completely after menopause? No. Some secretions can continue throughout life. A change from your usual pattern and associated symptoms matter more than the mere presence of discharge. Can I identify an infection by its colour? No. Colour can suggest possibilities, but symptoms overlap. Examination and appropriate tests may be needed. Can dryness occur at the same time as discharge? Yes. Low-oestrogen tissue changes or inflammation can cause both. A new or persistent change should still be assessed. Do I need penetrative sex to prevent vaginal atrophy? No. You do not need to have intercourse to prevent it, and avoiding sex does not mean you caused the condition. Seek treatment for discomfort rather than pushing through pain. Does hysterectomy always cause immediate menopause? No. Removing the uterus stops periods, but retained ovaries may continue producing hormones. Removing both ovaries before natural menopause causes surgical menopause. Will symptoms settle one year after my last period? Not necessarily. Genitourinary symptoms may persist or recur and can benefit from ongoing treatment and review. Is a little brown or pink discharge after menopause worth checking? Yes. It may contain blood, and even a single small episode should be assessed. Many causes are benign, but it should not be ignored. Does a normal ultrasound always rule out the cause of bleeding? No. Further assessment, including tissue sampling, may be needed depending on the circumstances. Persistent or recurrent bleeding deserves follow-up. Should I try repeated over-the-counter thrush treatments? Avoid repeated self-treatment when the cause is uncertain or symptoms recur. Other infections, inflammation and tissue changes need different care. What is the difference between a moisturiser and a lubricant? A vaginal moisturiser helps ongoing dryness when used regularly. A lubricant reduces friction during sexual activity. Use products designed for vaginal use and discuss persistent symptoms.

title: Discharge after your period: usual changes and signs to check
description: Brown spotting or changing cervical mucus can follow a period, but persistent bleeding, pain or an unusual smell needs attention.
body: Vaginal discharge continues between periods. Its amount and texture can change through the menstrual cycle, and a little blood near the end of a period may make it look brown. The colour alone cannot tell you whether a change is harmless or caused by infection. A little brown discharge can be the end of a period Blood becomes darker as it remains exposed to oxygen, so a small amount mixed with discharge can look brown rather than red. This can happen as menstrual flow tapers off. A brief pattern that is usual for you and comes without pain, itching or an unpleasant smell may not need treatment. It does not mean the uterus needs to be cleansed or that blood must be flushed out. If spotting continues, repeatedly occurs between periods or follows sex, arrange a review. A change from your usual pattern is more useful information than whether the amount is enough to need a pad. Cervical mucus changes through the cycle Discharge is often clear or whitish, with no strong unpleasant smell. As ovulation approaches, cervical mucus may become wetter and more slippery. After ovulation it may feel thicker or become less noticeable. The timing varies with cycle length and from one cycle to another. Ovulation is not always on day 14, and a short period does not necessarily mean a short menstrual cycle. Count a cycle from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. Mucus observations can contribute to an established fertility-awareness method, but one day of discharge cannot confirm ovulation or identify a guaranteed pregnancy-free day. If pregnancy is not wanted, use a suitable contraceptive method. Contraception and other factors can change the pattern Hormonal contraception can alter cervical mucus and bleeding. Spotting is possible with several methods, particularly when starting or changing them. Not all pills contain oestrogen, and the effect cannot be reduced to every pill raising both hormone levels. Tell your clinician about your method, any missed doses and new medicines. Persistent or troublesome bleeding may need assessment for pregnancy, infection or another cause as well as a discussion of the contraceptive method. Do not add a pill-free break without method-specific advice. Sexual arousal, semen and vaginal products can also change what you notice in your underwear. Mention these details if you are unsure whether the fluid is new discharge. Infection is possible at any point in the month Thrush can cause itching, soreness and thick white discharge. Bacterial vaginosis often causes thin discharge with a fishy smell and may occur without marked itching. Neither condition can be diagnosed confidently from a colour chart alone. Chlamydia, gonorrhoea and trichomoniasis can cause abnormal discharge, bleeding or discomfort, but an STI can also have few or no symptoms. Normal-looking discharge does not exclude one. A retained tampon is another possible explanation for an unpleasant smell or discharge after a period. If you think one remains and cannot remove it easily, get prompt help. Do not insert tools or keep trying in a way that causes pain. Choose treatment after the cause is clear Ordinary discharge does not require medication. If it helps your comfort, change damp underwear or use an unscented liner briefly, changing it regularly. Stop using a product if it irritates the skin. Wash the external genital area gently. Do not douche, use deodorants inside the vagina or try to remove every natural scent. Repeated washing and fragranced products can worsen irritation. If this is your first suspected thrush infection, symptoms are unusual or treatment has not helped, seek advice rather than repeating products. Thrush needs an appropriate antifungal; household remedies are not a substitute, and recovery is not guaranteed in two or three days. Bacterial vaginosis and STIs require their own treatment plans. In pregnancy, ask before choosing a medicine, including a non-prescription antifungal. A sexual-health service can advise on testing, partner care and follow-up where relevant. When to seek care Arrange a review for a new strong smell, persistent discharge changes, itching, soreness, pain during sex or urination, or recurrent bleeding between periods. Seek more urgent advice for pelvic pain with fever or feeling unwell. If pregnancy is possible and there is unusual bleeding, consider a pregnancy test and contact a clinician. Severe or one-sided abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain, fainting or significant dizziness with possible pregnancy needs emergency assessment. With a retained tampon or recent tampon use, sudden fever, vomiting, a widespread rash, dizziness or rapidly worsening illness needs urgent medical care. Toxic shock syndrome is rare but serious. Persistent spotting can have many causes, including polyps and changes in the cervix or uterus. Occasionally a serious condition is responsible, so do not ignore it simply because the discharge is brown. Any bleeding after menopause also needs assessment. Some brown discharge can occur as a period finishes. Normal mucus changes do not follow an identical calendar in every cycle. Colour alone cannot diagnose infection or confirm fertility. Persistent spotting, pain, itching or a new unpleasant smell should be checked. Avoid douching and repeated treatment without a clear diagnosis. Is all brown discharge old menstrual blood? No. Blood from other causes can also look brown, particularly when the amount is small. Timing, persistence and other symptoms matter. Can I have an STI with clear discharge? Yes. Some STIs cause little or no visible change. Testing is based on symptoms and exposure, not colour alone. Does discharge after a period mean I am pregnant? No. Discharge cannot confirm pregnancy. Use a pregnancy test at the appropriate time if pregnancy is possible.

title: Orange or rust-coloured discharge: what should you do?
description: An orange tint can reflect a little blood mixed with discharge, but colour alone cannot identify an infection or confirm pregnancy.
body: An unfamiliar colour can be worrying, especially when online charts attach a different diagnosis to every shade. Orange or rusty-looking discharge is not a diagnosis. Consider when it started, whether it contains blood and whether you have pain, irritation or an unusual smell. Blood mixed with discharge can change its colour A small amount of blood may make normal vaginal fluid look pink, brown, rusty or orange. This can happen as a period ends or with spotting between periods. The appearance does not tell you where the blood came from. A brief change at the end of your usual period may be less concerning than recurrent bleeding, bleeding after sex or a completely new pattern. Arrange a review if it persists or repeatedly returns rather than assuming the shade proves it is old menstrual blood. After menopause, report any pink, brown or blood-stained discharge promptly, even when the amount is small and you otherwise feel well. An infection is possible, but orange is not a specific sign Bacterial vaginosis changes the balance of vaginal bacteria and often causes thin discharge with a fishy smell. Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted infection that can cause discharge, irritation or burning when urinating. Neither has an exclusive colour that can be recognised reliably at home. Other infections and irritation can produce overlapping symptoms. Many STIs have few or no symptoms, so the absence of a smell or dramatic colour change does not rule one out. If discharge is new, persistent, uncomfortable or associated with a possible STI exposure, contact a clinician or sexual-health service. Assessment may include an examination and a vaginal swab or other targeted test. A home pH reading alone cannot identify the cause. Treatment depends on what is found Symptomatic bacterial vaginosis is usually treated with an appropriate prescription medicine. You do not need to wait for it to recur or become severe before seeking treatment. If symptoms return, ask for reassessment rather than repeatedly using leftover medicine. Trichomoniasis requires specific treatment for the affected person and relevant partners. Complete the prescribed course and follow the advice about avoiding sex until treatment is complete and symptoms have resolved. Treatment does not provide three months of protection against reinfection. The recommendation to retest sexually active women at about three months exists because reinfection is common. Contact the clinic sooner if symptoms persist or return; do not wait for that routine retest. Bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis have different partner-care recommendations. Ask the clinician for advice that fits the diagnosis and your circumstances rather than assuming one rule applies to all vaginal infections. The colour cannot confirm implantation Light bleeding can occur in early pregnancy, but orange or pink discharge cannot tell you that an embryo has implanted. Timing it from sexual intercourse is also unreliable because intercourse and fertilisation do not necessarily happen on the same day. If pregnancy is possible, use a test from the first day of a missed period. If you do not know when the next period is due, test at least 21 days after the last unprotected sex. Follow the kit instructions and repeat or seek advice if the result is negative but the period does not arrive. If you are already pregnant, contact your maternity service about suspected bleeding or a new abnormal discharge. A continuing watery trickle or gush also needs assessment because fluid leakage cannot be identified safely by colour alone. Get help urgently for pain, bleeding or illness Seek urgent assessment for pelvic pain with fever, worsening symptoms or feeling very unwell. Heavy bleeding, fainting or severe abdominal pain needs emergency care. If pregnancy is possible, severe or one-sided abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain or faintness with bleeding can be signs of an ectopic pregnancy. Do not wait for a home test to become positive before seeking help for these symptoms. While arranging advice, avoid douching, internal deodorants and home mixtures. Wash the external area gently, change damp underwear and note any new products or medicines. These details can help the clinician identify irritation or another cause, but hygiene measures do not replace infection treatment. Orange discharge does not point to one specific diagnosis. A little blood can alter the colour of vaginal fluid. Persistent changes, discomfort or a new smell need assessment. STI treatment does not give temporary immunity against reinfection. Use a pregnancy test rather than discharge colour to check for pregnancy. Does orange discharge always mean an infection? No. Blood mixed with normal fluid can change its colour too. Testing and the wider symptom pattern are more useful than the shade. Does it mean implantation has happened? No. Discharge cannot identify implantation or confirm pregnancy. Why is trichomoniasis testing repeated around three months? To look for reinfection after treatment, not because treatment protects you for three months. New symptoms need earlier advice.

title: Athelia: being born without one or both nipples
description: An absent nipple can occur on its own or with other developmental differences. Assessment and support depend on the individual.
body: Athelia means that one or both nipples did not develop before birth. The surrounding darker skin, called the areola, may also be absent. It is uncommon, and its effect on a person’s health depends largely on whether there are other associated differences. An absent nipple is not the same as a flat nipple A flat or inverted nipple is present but has a different shape. Athelia describes absence from birth; a nipple removed through surgery or injured later has a different explanation. The underlying breast tissue may be present, underdeveloped or absent. Absence of the breast is called amastia. Athelia and amastia can occur together, but one word should not automatically be used to mean the other. An examination can clarify the anatomy. Why it can happen Sometimes an absent nipple is part of Poland syndrome, which typically affects development on one side of the chest. Part of a chest muscle may be missing or smaller, and there may be differences in the breast, ribs, arm or hand. Some features become more noticeable during puberty. The exact cause of Poland syndrome is uncertain. A disruption of blood supply during early development is one proposed explanation. Most cases occur without a family history; it is incorrect to describe the condition as routinely caused by a gene passed down by a parent. Ectodermal dysplasias are another possible association. They are a varied group of genetic conditions involving tissues such as skin, hair, teeth, nails and sweat glands. Some affect breast or nipple development. Inheritance and severity differ between types, so they do not all affect males and females in the same way. Scalp-ear-nipple syndrome is a rare example involving changes in the scalp, outer ears and nipples, sometimes with other features. It can result from a new genetic change or an inherited one. A list of rare syndromes cannot establish a diagnosis from appearance alone. In Poland syndrome, the pectoralis major chest muscle may be partly absent, the ribs or forearm bones may be smaller, fingers may be short or joined together, and underarm hair may be sparse. Reported estimates are around one affected newborn in 20,000, with males more often recognized; mild cases may be missed. It is named after Alfred Poland, who described the pattern in the nineteenth century. Depending on the type of ectodermal dysplasia, possible findings include sparse hair, missing or unusually shaped teeth, brittle or abnormal nails, reduced sweating, skin colour changes and underdeveloped breasts. Some syndromes also involve fingers or toes, cleft lip or palate, hearing, vision or breathing. These features vary widely and are not a checklist everyone will have. Ectodermal dysplasias involve development of structures arising from the embryo’s outer layer. A genetic change may be inherited or occur for the first time in a child. The term includes many distinct conditions, so an old fixed count of syndromes cannot guide an individual diagnosis. What an assessment may involve A child’s clinician can review growth, family history and the chest, hands, skin and other relevant findings. Depending on the examination, referral might be made to paediatrics, clinical genetics or another specialist. Tests should answer a specific question rather than being ordered as the same package for every child. The missing nipple itself is not usually an emergency. Associated problems deserve attention, however. For example, some ectodermal dysplasias reduce sweating and can make overheating dangerous. Families need an individual temperature-management plan if this applies. Breathing difficulty or a child who is severely unwell needs urgent care. This is different from assuming that every person with athelia has a serious internal-organ problem. Many people with mild associated chest differences have little or no functional difficulty. Rare severe Poland syndrome can involve a lung or kidney as well as the chest wall. Evaluation follows the child’s findings; missing a nipple alone does not mean those organs are affected. An associated diagnosis, rather than the nipple appearance, determines follow-up and the outlook. Options if someone wants to change the appearance A person does not have to choose cosmetic treatment simply because a nipple is absent. If they want to explore options, a reconstructive specialist can discuss the chest anatomy, development, goals and suitable timing. Possibilities may include creating a nipple shape from skin, medical tattooing, a removable prosthesis or breast reconstruction when breast tissue is also absent. A three-dimensional tattoo creates the visual impression of a nipple; it does not grow a working nipple or milk ducts. Discuss scars, sensation, further procedures and realistic results before deciding. For a child or teenager, their developing preferences and ability to participate in the decision matter. Treatment for a functional problem may follow a different timetable from elective appearance changes. When a whole breast also needs reconstruction, options may include the person’s own tissue from the abdomen, back or buttock, sometimes followed later by nipple and areola work. Suitability depends on anatomy and specialist assessment. A nipple shape can be made from a small skin flap and an areola represented with medical pigment; a three-dimensional tattoo is an optical effect, not a functional breast. Planning infant feeding If pregnancy or breastfeeding is relevant to you, arrange an assessment before birth where possible. The amount of breast tissue, duct development and available nipple openings matter more than the name of the condition alone. Reconstruction of appearance does not necessarily restore feeding function. Feeding from the affected side may not be possible. A normally developed breast on the other side may still provide milk, and a lactation specialist can help create a plan. Some people with ectodermal dysplasia have additional milk-supply difficulties. Monitor the baby’s intake and growth, and use supplementation when needed. Needing another feeding method is not a personal failure. The plan should support both the baby’s nutrition and the parent’s wellbeing. Support is part of care People feel differently about visible body differences. Some are comfortable without treatment; others find them distressing, especially around puberty, intimacy or feeding. Neither response needs to be minimised. A clinician, counsellor or condition-specific support group can help. Genetic counselling may also be useful when an associated diagnosis raises questions about future children. The risk cannot be estimated accurately from an absent nipple alone. Athelia means a nipple was absent from birth. The underlying breast and associated findings need individual assessment. Most Poland syndrome cases are not inherited. Appearance-changing treatment is optional and does not guarantee feeding function. Support can address health, body image and infant-feeding needs. Does athelia always mean the breast is missing? No. Nipple development and underlying breast development need to be assessed separately. Must a child have reconstructive surgery? No. Decisions depend on associated health needs, development and the person’s preferences. Will it be passed on to children? That depends on the cause. A genetics professional can explain inheritance after a specific diagnosis is established.

title: Does the contraceptive pill cause weight gain?
description: What studies show about pills and weight, how injections differ, and how to review symptoms or change contraception while maintaining protection.
body: Research has not shown a major average weight effect from combined contraceptive pills, but a change after starting one still deserves a thoughtful review. The exact method matters, and you have options if it does not suit you. What research says about the combined pill The combined contraceptive pill contains an estrogen and a progestogen. Although weight gain is a common concern, studies have not established that combined pills cause substantial weight gain on average. This is useful reassurance when choosing contraception, but it should not be used to dismiss a change you have noticed. A Cochrane review included forty-nine trials of combined pills or patches. The small group of studies with placebo or no-hormone comparisons did not show a causal effect on weight, and comparisons between formulations generally found no large differences. The reviewers also noted that the evidence was not strong enough to exclude every possible smaller effect. An average result is not a promise that every person’s weight will stay unchanged. It means that starting the pill and later gaining weight do not, by themselves, prove cause and effect. Your symptoms, preferences and the timing of changes still belong in a conversation about whether the method suits you. Why hormones and fluid retention enter the discussion Older contraceptive pills often contained more estrogen than many current formulations. Hormones can influence fluid balance and may affect how a person feels, including bloating or breast fullness. However, a proposed mechanism is not the same as proof of a lasting increase in body fat from modern pills. Current products vary in estrogen type, dose and progestogen. “High dose” and “low dose” are not complete descriptions, and a dose in micrograms cannot be compared across different hormones as though all were identical. Read the active ingredients with a pharmacist rather than relying only on a brand name. For example, one combined formulation contains drospirenone 3 mg and ethinylestradiol 0.03 mg, equivalent to 30 micrograms of ethinylestradiol. Combined pills mainly prevent ovulation and also change cervical mucus. This ingredient combination is not a weight-loss treatment or a guarantee against bloating, and it must still be checked for suitability. The progestogen-only pill is not the same as the injection The progestogen-only pill contains no estrogen. Evidence has not established significant weight gain caused by this pill, although the available research is more limited than many people expect. Results for all progestogen-only methods should not be presented as if they came only from pill users. A 2016 Cochrane review pooled twenty-two studies involving 11,450 participants using several methods, including injections, implants, intrauterine contraception and pills. In most studies, average gain at six or twelve months was less than 2 kg and comparison groups often changed similarly. This was neither a predicted gain for each pill user nor a cutoff above which another cause is certain. Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate, or DMPA, is an injection with a different weight-gain evidence profile. Some users gain weight, and certain adolescent groups may be more susceptible. Advice about that injection should not automatically be applied to combined pills, progestogen-only pills, implants or hormonal coils. Look at the whole pattern without blaming yourself A change in routine can happen around the same time as starting contraception. A more sedentary job, different meal patterns, sleep disruption, stress, illness or another medicine may contribute to weight changes. These are possibilities to explore, not assumptions that you have eaten badly or failed to exercise. Strength training can increase muscle mass, and fluid, bowel contents and time of day can change the number on a scale. Clothes fitting differently, swelling, appetite changes and how quickly the change occurred may provide context. A scale alone does not identify what tissue or fluid has changed. Age and health can affect energy needs over time, but unexplained weight gain does not automatically mean a “slow metabolism.” A clinician can review symptoms and decide whether targeted tests, for example for a suspected thyroid problem, would help. A broad metabolic blood panel is not required solely because you started the pill. Does starting weight predict what will happen? Being in a larger body does not mean the pill will inevitably cause weight gain. Evidence does not support a simple rule that a particular starting weight predicts a pill-related increase. At the same time, limited subgroup studies cannot prove that no individual or group could experience a change. Starting weight may still matter to the safety assessment of some contraceptives. For combined hormonal methods, the prescriber considers clotting risks alongside factors such as age, smoking, blood pressure, migraine and personal or family medical history. That assessment is a different question from whether the pill causes weight gain. If an earlier discussion focused only on your weight, ask to review the full set of options and your priorities. Effective contraception should be chosen through an individual conversation that considers comfort, bleeding patterns, daily routines and health, without pressure to accept a method you dislike. If you notice a change after starting Write down when you started the product, when the change appeared, whether there is swelling or bloating, and any other new symptoms or medicines. If weighing is useful for you, compare occasional measurements under similar conditions. Repeated daily weighing or detailed calorie tracking is not necessary and may be unhelpful for some people. Mild early symptoms may settle over the first few months. That does not mean every increase is water retention or that it will always disappear. If symptoms are troubling, you can ask for advice earlier; you do not have to wait three months to be heard. Persistent or rapid unexplained changes deserve a review. Regular meals, movement you enjoy and adequate rest support health regardless of contraceptive choice. They should not be presented as punishment for starting the pill or a requirement to tolerate unwanted symptoms. Avoid extreme dieting or a promise that a specific exercise routine will reverse a medication effect. Changing methods without losing contraceptive protection If the pill does not feel right, discuss another formulation or a different method. A lower estrogen dose may be suitable for some people, but it is not guaranteed to prevent weight changes and can alter bleeding patterns. The type of progestogen and other risks also matter; choosing the “lowest dose” is not the only goal. Options may include another pill, an implant, an intrauterine method or a nonhormonal approach, depending on your needs. A copper intrauterine device avoids contraceptive hormones, for example, but has its own bleeding and cramping considerations. Ask about effectiveness, expected bleeding and how easy it is to use or discontinue each option. Before stopping or switching, obtain clear instructions on when to start the new method and whether condoms or other backup are needed. Do not halve tablets, skip pills or invent a lower-dose schedule to manage weight. If there has already been a gap and recent sex, ask promptly about emergency contraception and pregnancy testing. Nausea, skin changes and other early effects Some people report nausea, sore breasts, headaches, dizziness or mood changes after starting hormonal contraception. Breakthrough bleeding is also common early on. The timing may suggest a relationship, but nausea alone does not prove that the hormone dose is too high. Taking a pill with food or at a convenient evening time may help some people tolerate it; check the instructions for your product and keep the required timing consistent. Do not reduce the dose yourself. Vomiting or severe diarrhoea can affect protection, so use the product’s missed-pill or illness guidance and ask a pharmacist if unsure. Some combined pills improve acne, while skin may worsen with other formulations or for unrelated reasons. Tell the prescriber what has changed and what matters most to you. A method that helps acne can still be unsuitable for someone with an important estrogen-related risk factor. Headaches and migraine deserve their own review Headache patterns can change with hormonal contraception. Some people improve and others develop new or worse symptoms. Tell the prescriber about any migraine history, including visual disturbances, altered sensation or speech symptoms that have occurred with attacks. Migraine with aura is a contraindication to combined hormonal contraception in CDC guidance because of stroke risk. A progestogen-only or nonhormonal option may be considered instead, with individual advice. Choosing a lower-estrogen combined pill does not remove this restriction. Seek urgent medical advice for new aura or a substantial change in headache pattern. Sudden weakness, trouble speaking, new loss of vision or an abrupt severe headache need emergency assessment, even if you think it might be migraine. Do not wait to see whether a weight-management change resolves neurological symptoms. Know which changes need urgent attention Combined hormonal contraception carries a small increased risk of blood clots. New one-sided leg swelling or pain, chest pain, sudden breathlessness or coughing blood needs urgent medical assessment. Sudden stroke-like symptoms need emergency help. These are not ordinary bloating or a reason to wait for the next routine contraceptive appointment. For a less urgent concern, bring your product pack and symptom notes to the review. Ask whether pregnancy, fluid retention, another medicine or a health condition should be considered, and whether changing contraception makes sense. The clinician should explain the reasoning rather than attributing every change either to the pill or to your habits. You can value effective contraception and still want a different experience of it. The aim is a method that fits your health and preferences, with a safe transition if you change. Evidence about average weight effects helps that decision; it does not take the decision away from you. Modern combined pills have not shown a large average weight effect in trials. A pooled average is not an individual prediction or a diagnostic threshold. You can ask to switch without proving the pill caused the symptom. Protect against pregnancy during any change and review migraine or clot warning symptoms promptly. Do combined pills usually cause substantial weight gain? Research has not established a substantial average gain caused by combined pills. The evidence cannot exclude every individual response or small effect, so troublesome changes still deserve discussion. Is all early weight gain just water? No. Fluid changes may contribute, but it is not safe to label every increase temporary water retention without considering the pattern and other symptoms. Does the less-than-2-kg finding predict my gain? No. It was a pooled study average across several progestogen-only methods, not a prediction for an individual pill user or a threshold that diagnoses the cause. Is the contraceptive injection the same as the pill for weight? No. DMPA injections have a different evidence profile and are associated with weight gain in some users. Do not apply that finding to every hormonal method. Will a lower-estrogen pill definitely prevent bloating or weight change? No. Formulation changes may help some symptoms, but no pill guarantees a fixed weight. The choice must also consider bleeding, migraine and clotting risks. Should I reduce my pill dose myself? No. Halving, skipping or changing tablets can compromise protection. Ask for a prescribed alternative and a clear switching plan. Do I need a calorie-tracking app or metabolic blood tests? Not automatically. A brief symptom and routine history may be more useful. Tests should address a clinical concern, and detailed tracking is optional rather than a requirement. Can I wait and see whether mild symptoms settle? Often, if there are no warning signs and you are comfortable doing so. You may seek advice earlier, and persistent troublesome effects should be reviewed rather than dismissed. Can someone with migraine with aura use the combined pill? CDC guidance classifies combined hormonal contraception as unsuitable with migraine with aura. Discuss a progestogen-only or nonhormonal option; a lower estrogen dose does not remove this concern. How can I switch without a gap in protection? Ask when to start the new method, how to stop the old one and whether backup is needed. If a gap has already occurred with recent sex, seek prompt advice about emergency contraception and testing.

title: Breast calcifications: what a mammogram finding means
description: Most calcium deposits in the breast are benign. Their pattern and the imaging assessment determine whether follow-up or biopsy is needed.
body: Breast calcifications are small calcium deposits that appear as white marks on a mammogram. They are common and usually harmless. The word calcification is not a cancer diagnosis, but some patterns need a closer look. What the white marks on a mammogram mean Calcifications are tiny deposits of calcium salts within breast tissue. They show up as bright flecks or dots on a mammogram because calcium absorbs X-rays differently from surrounding tissue. Their presence describes an imaging finding; it does not, on its own, name the underlying condition. Many deposits are associated with harmless changes, and they become more common with age. Some appear alongside abnormal cells, ductal carcinoma in situ or invasive breast cancer. The useful question is what pattern the radiologist sees and what follow-up that pattern requires. You usually cannot feel individual calcifications during a breast examination, and they often produce no symptoms. Finding them on a routine screen is therefore different from noticing a new lump. Either situation can need assessment, but they should not be treated as interchangeable. Why calcifications can develop Several non-cancerous processes can leave calcium deposits. These include ageing-related changes, breast cysts, a fibroadenoma, inflammation or previous infection, and changes in fat tissue after an injury. Previous surgery and radiotherapy can also affect the appearance of breast tissue. Calcium may be visible in skin or blood-vessel walls rather than arising from the breast ducts themselves. A vascular finding is not the same as a suspicious ductal pattern, and it should not automatically be labelled cancer or used to diagnose a blocked artery. Ask whether a reported vascular finding has implications for your usual cardiovascular health review. Abnormal cells within a duct can also be associated with calcifications. Ductal carcinoma in situ, or DCIS, means abnormal cells remain within the milk ducts; invasive ductal cancer has grown beyond the duct into surrounding breast tissue. A mammogram cannot tell you everything about those cells. When necessary, tissue sampling establishes the diagnosis. These deposits are not caused simply by eating calcium-rich foods. Cutting out dairy, changing your diet to remove calcium or stopping a recommended supplement is not a treatment for a mammogram finding. Continue prescribed care and discuss any separate concern about supplements with your clinician. Macrocalcifications and microcalcifications Macrocalcifications are the larger deposits that may look like white dots or short dashes. Typical coarse deposits often reflect benign changes such as previous injury, inflammation or ageing and may not need a biopsy. Microcalcifications are much finer specks. Many are also benign, but some arrangements need closer examination. Micro does not mean cancer, and macro does not mean that every possible associated finding can be ignored. Shape, distribution, grouping and changes over time matter alongside size. Fine irregular deposits or a linear or branching arrangement may be more concerning than a typical benign pattern. A cluster can prompt further assessment, but a cluster alone is not a diagnosis. The radiologist interprets the whole image and any associated mass or tissue distortion. A simple half-millimetre dividing line is not a safe rule for interpreting your own report. Descriptions of size help classify appearances; they do not replace the radiologist’s assessment of pattern and context. Why you might be called back for more images A screening mammogram sometimes needs additional views before the finding can be classified. Magnification images can help show individual deposits and their arrangement. Being called back means more information is needed, not that cancer has already been found. Previous mammograms can be especially helpful. The team compares the actual images to see whether deposits are new, stable or changing. If your earlier examination was at another centre, provide its details so images can be requested. Stability is useful information, but its meaning depends on the pattern and the full assessment. Ultrasound or other imaging may help with associated findings, but an ultrasound cannot show every calcification and is not always a substitute for diagnostic mammography. Ask which examination is being recommended and what question it is intended to answer. Benign, probably benign and suspicious are different results A benign assessment means the appearance is not considered cancerous. Typically no treatment or special biopsy is needed for the deposits themselves. Continue the screening or surveillance schedule appropriate to your history and local programme; this is not automatically an annual scan for everyone. A probably benign assessment still needs its planned follow-up. In the BI-RADS system, category 3 means the estimated likelihood of cancer is no more than 2%. Repeat imaging is commonly recommended in 6–12 months and then at specified intervals until stability has been demonstrated, often over at least two years. Follow your report’s schedule rather than assuming every person needs a scan every six months. A suspicious assessment, such as BI-RADS 4 or 5, generally leads to a biopsy recommendation. Suspicion varies between categories and does not equal a confirmed cancer diagnosis. BI-RADS 0 means the assessment is incomplete, so additional imaging or comparison is needed. Ask for the conclusion in plain language: Is the finding benign, probably benign or suspicious? Is the next appointment routine screening, diagnostic imaging or biopsy? Who will arrange it, and when should you follow up if you hear nothing? The category and recommendation are more useful than an isolated descriptive word. Calcifications after breast surgery or radiotherapy Treatment can leave benign changes, including fat necrosis and calcification. However, a new finding in a previously treated breast still needs interpretation. Its appearance, location and relation to the treated area matter; a history of treatment does not automatically establish that a deposit is harmless. A 2015 retrospective study illustrates why context matters. Researchers reviewed six-month mammograms in 271 people after breast-conserving surgery with intraoperative radiotherapy. Five had unusual scattered round deposits. Two underwent biopsy, and the samples contained small tungsten particles rather than an ordinary new calcium deposit. The authors considered that specific postoperative appearance benign. That finding cannot justify skipping biopsy for all new calcifications after surgery or radiation. It concerned a particular procedure and appearance, and only two of the five findings were sampled. Your team should use your own treatment records and imaging pattern when deciding whether observation or tissue sampling is appropriate. What a biopsy can clarify If an area looks suspicious, a biopsy removes samples of tissue so a pathologist can examine the cells. For calcifications that are not visible on ultrasound, mammography-guided sampling, often called a stereotactic biopsy, can locate the area. Local anaesthetic is commonly used. The team may check an X-ray of the samples to confirm that the target deposits were obtained. A small marker may be left at the site for future imaging. Tell the team about possible pregnancy, medicines and allergies, and follow its preparation and aftercare instructions. Do not independently stop blood thinners. After pathology is available, the breast team checks that it explains the imaging appearance. Sometimes a benign sample does not adequately explain a suspicious finding; more sampling or removal can be recommended. Ask who will give you the result and whether imaging and pathology agree. Treatment depends on the diagnosis behind the finding Benign calcifications usually do not need to be removed or dissolved. Calcium itself does not transform into a cancer cell. When deposits accompany another condition, care is directed at that condition and at any ongoing symptoms. If a biopsy identifies DCIS, atypical cells or invasive cancer, the breast team explains the specific diagnosis and options. These are different findings with different management plans. A list of cancer treatments should never be presented as the inevitable next step for everyone whose mammogram mentions calcium. When cancer treatment is needed, surgery removes the affected area or breast tissue as appropriate, and radiotherapy treats a defined area with radiation. Chemotherapy uses medicines that act throughout the body; not everyone with breast cancer needs it. Hormone therapy is used for cancers sensitive to particular hormones. Targeted therapies act on selected features of the cancer, so suitability depends on testing. Treatment may involve one approach or a combination, according to the diagnosis, extent of disease, tumour biology, previous treatment and your circumstances. Calcifications can help reveal disease before symptoms appear, but their presence alone cannot establish the cancer stage or predict an individual outcome. Symptoms to report even after a reassuring mammogram Arrange a clinical check for a new breast or armpit lump, persistent swelling, new nipple inversion, unexplained nipple discharge or skin dimpling. Persistent itching, redness, inflammation, scaling, an unexplained bruise-like change or another new skin change also deserves attention. These symptoms have several possible causes, including benign conditions. Do not assume that a symptom comes from a previously benign calcification. Screening assesses images at a point in time; a new symptom is additional information. A clinician may examine you and request diagnostic tests even if a previous screening result was reassuring. While waiting, keep copies of the report and appointment plan, note any changes and make sure the team has a reliable way to contact you. Most calcifications are benign. Completing the recommended investigation is what allows that reassurance to be specific to your result. Calcifications are calcium deposits, not a diagnosis of cancer. Appearance and pattern matter more than size alone. Probably benign findings still need their recommended follow-up. Biopsy findings must be checked against the images. Dietary calcium restriction is not a treatment. Are breast calcifications cancer? Usually they are benign calcium deposits. Certain patterns can accompany abnormal cells or cancer, which is why the radiologist may recommend additional imaging or a biopsy. Do microcalcifications always need a biopsy? No. Many fine deposits have benign appearances. Biopsy decisions depend on the pattern and complete assessment, rather than the word micro alone. Can I feel calcifications when checking my breasts? Usually not. They are typically detected by mammography. A lump or skin change that you can feel or see should be assessed separately. What does probably benign mean? In BI-RADS category 3, the likelihood of cancer is no more than 2%. Follow-up is still important to establish stability. The report should specify when to return. Does every person need six-monthly scans for two years? No. Benign findings, probably benign findings and suspicious findings follow different pathways. Even surveillance intervals should follow the individual imaging recommendation. Can previous surgery explain the finding? It can, but it does not automatically do so. A radiologist must evaluate new deposits in the context of their appearance, location and your treatment history. Should I stop calcium supplements or avoid dairy? Calcium intake is not the cause of ordinary breast calcifications, and restricting it is not a treatment. Discuss any changes to prescribed supplements with your clinician. If a biopsy is benign, why might more tests be recommended? The sample must explain the imaging abnormality. If pathology and imaging do not agree, another sample or removal may be needed. Will I need chemotherapy if calcifications are found? The finding alone does not call for chemotherapy. Even if cancer is diagnosed, treatment depends on its type and extent; many people will not need chemotherapy.

title: Penile numbness: causes and when to get help
description: Understand reduced penile sensation, pressure and device effects, nerve conditions, assessment and symptoms needing urgent care.
body: Reduced feeling in the penis can follow pressure or device use, but it can also reflect a nerve, circulation or other medical problem. New numbness deserves attention, especially with pain, colour change, back or leg symptoms, or difficulty urinating. Describe what has changed in the sensation Penile numbness means reduced or absent feeling in part or all of the penis. It may resemble a body part falling asleep, with tingling, burning, pins and needles or an unusual dull sensation. Some people notice a cold feeling, a change during sex or difficulty recognising normal touch. Tell a clinician whether the change involves the tip, shaft, scrotum or the area between the genitals and anus, called the perineum. Note whether it is constant, intermittent or linked to a position or activity. A new colour change, especially a blue or unusually pale appearance, needs more attention than an isolated change in pleasure. Loss of touch, reduced desire, difficulty getting an erection and difficulty reaching orgasm are different symptoms, although they can overlap. Describing them separately helps the clinician choose the right assessment. You do not need to wait until the problem has seriously affected a relationship before seeking help. Check for emergency warning signs first New loss of feeling around the genitals or anus together with back pain, leg weakness or changes in bladder or bowel control can signal serious pressure on spinal nerves. Difficulty starting urination, not sensing bladder fullness or new incontinence are particularly important. Seek emergency care rather than waiting for a routine sexual-health appointment. A penis that becomes very painful, cold, blue or markedly swollen after a constriction ring or device also needs prompt attention. Remove the device if it can be removed easily and safely. If it is stuck, or the colour, pain or sensation does not promptly recover, obtain urgent medical help instead of trying stronger pulling, cutting or another device. A prolonged erection that is approaching or exceeds four hours needs emergency assessment; seek help earlier if there is severe pain or a specific emergency plan, including for sickle cell disease. Significant trauma or sudden neurological symptoms elsewhere also need urgent care. A possible cycling explanation should not override these warning signs. Cycling and prolonged sitting can put pressure on nerves A bicycle saddle can press on the perineum, affecting nerves and blood vessels involved in genital sensation and erections. Longer rides, sustained pressure and an unsuitable fit may contribute. Research in selected cycling groups supports this mechanism, but a percentage from one study cannot tell every cyclist their personal risk. Stop and get off the bicycle when numbness or tingling begins. Do not treat loss of sensation as a normal endurance milestone. Give the area a break and seek assessment if the symptom persists, repeatedly returns or occurs without cycling. A trained bike-fit specialist can review saddle design, support and riding position. A pressure-reducing or no-nose saddle may help some riders, but it requires appropriate fitting and adjustment. More padding, a wider seat or raising or tilting the saddle is not a universal solution. Regular breaks and avoiding prolonged pressure matter; treatment should not rely on simply riding through the discomfort. Vacuum pumps and constriction bands need careful use A vacuum erection device draws blood into the penis, and a band at the base may help maintain the erection. These devices can be useful for selected people with erectile dysfunction, but excessive suction or an unsuitable band can cause bruising, pain, skin injury, coldness or numbness.
