Use a medically appropriate device with a vacuum limiter and follow the clinician’s and manufacturer’s instructions. A constriction band must not remain in place longer than thirty minutes, and it should be removed sooner if symptoms occur. Thirty minutes is an upper limit, not a reason to tolerate pain or discolouration until a timer ends. Stop using a device that causes sensory loss and arrange a review before trying it again. Mild effects may settle after release, but recovery is not guaranteed simply because the pump has been switched off. Tell the clinician about bleeding disorders and blood-thinning medicines, and ask about alternative erection treatments if the device does not suit you. Nerve and neurological conditions can affect genital feeling Diabetes can damage nerves and blood vessels, sometimes affecting genital sensation, erections and bladder function. Managing blood glucose and other vascular risks can help protect health, but numbness should still be assessed rather than automatically attributed to diabetes. Multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury and other neurological problems can also change sexual sensation. The location and pattern of symptoms matter, including numbness elsewhere, weakness or urinary changes. New genital numbness alone does not establish a diagnosis of MS. Pudendal nerve problems may cause burning, tingling, pain or numbness in the genitals or perineum, sometimes worse when sitting. Similar symptoms can have other causes, so a label such as pudendal neuralgia should follow a suitable assessment. Treatment may involve reducing provoking pressure, targeted physiotherapy, medicines or specialist procedures depending on the findings. A penile plaque or curvature is a different clue Peyronie’s disease involves scar-like tissue, often called a plaque, that can change penile shape and cause curvature or pain during erections. It may coexist with erectile or other sexual difficulties, but not every sensory change is caused by a plaque. Tell the clinician about a new bend, a firm area, pain with an erection, shortening or difficulty with sex. Examination and, in selected circumstances, ultrasound may help assess the tissue and blood flow. A new finding should not be diagnosed from a photograph alone. Collagenase injections are a treatment option for selected cases of curvature, not a general cure for numbness. They require specialist selection and counselling about risks. Treating a plaque does not promise that altered sensation will return, so the clinician may need to assess a sensory problem separately. Low testosterone is not the same as losing touch sensation Testosterone influences sexual desire and other functions, including muscle and bone health. Low levels may contribute to reduced interest in sex, fewer spontaneous erections, low energy or reduced enjoyment. A person may still feel ordinary touch and pain even when desire is low. Levels can change with age, illness and other factors, but ageing alone does not diagnose testosterone deficiency. A diagnosis requires compatible symptoms and consistently low blood levels, usually confirmed with repeat morning testing. Genuine loss of touch should not simply be labelled low testosterone without considering nerves, pressure and circulation. When treatment is appropriate, formulations may include gels, injections, patches or other locally available products. Benefits and risks depend on the person; none guarantees restoration of penile sensation. External testosterone can suppress sperm production, so discuss present and future fertility plans before treatment rather than using hormones or boosters on your own. What to expect at an appointment The clinician will ask when the numbness started, whether any feeling remains, what makes it better or worse and how it affects sexual activity. Bring details of cycling, prolonged sitting, injury, surgery, devices and relevant medical conditions. Mention any new medicine or dose change and all non-prescription products. An examination may assess skin, circulation, sensation and neurological signs, with your consent. You can ask for an explanation and a chaperone. Depending on the findings, tests may include blood glucose, hormone testing when indicated or imaging to investigate a specific concern. MRI of the spine or brain is not routine for everyone with reduced penile sensation. Ultrasound also answers particular questions rather than providing a universal numbness test. Ask what the clinician is investigating, how results will change care and when persistent or worsening symptoms should be reassessed. Treatment depends on the cause and can take several forms Pressure-related symptoms may improve with rest from the provoking activity and changes that reduce compression. There is no fixed number of weeks that fits every case. If the symptom continues despite removing the pressure, the plan should be reviewed rather than repeatedly changing equipment without assessment. For diabetes, treatment includes an individual plan for glucose control, physical activity, medicines and other risk factors. For MS, a specialist assesses whether new symptoms represent a relapse or another problem. Corticosteroids are used for selected relapses; they are not an automatic treatment for every sensory symptom and should not be self-started. Medicines can affect sexual function in different ways, so a medication review is worthwhile. Timing alone does not prove causation, and the underlying condition may also matter. Do not abruptly stop a Parkinson’s medicine, antidepressant or another prescription. Ask the prescriber to assess the actual symptom and consider a safer adjustment if appropriate. Recovery and sexual comfort need an individual plan Whether sensation returns depends on the cause, the degree of nerve or tissue injury and the response to treatment. A temporary compression problem may improve after pressure is removed; a chronic neurological condition may need longer-term management. No single treatment can promise complete recovery for every cause. While sensation is reduced, avoid repeatedly testing the area with strong pressure, heat or painful stimulation. Pause activities that cause injury or discomfort and discuss practical ways to maintain comfortable intimacy if that matters to you. Reduced sensation is a health concern, not a measure of attraction or masculinity. Agree a follow-up plan and return sooner if the numbness spreads, worsens or is accompanied by colour change, urinary symptoms or weakness. Urology, neurology, physiotherapy or sexual-health support may each have a role. The aim is to identify treatable causes and protect function while being honest about uncertainty. Do not ride through genital numbness. Remove a constriction band promptly if symptoms develop. Low desire does not establish loss of nerve sensation. Testing should follow the history and examination. Recovery varies and may require specialist follow-up. Is numbness the same as low sex drive? No. Reduced touch sensation, desire, erections and orgasm are different symptoms, though they can occur together. Should I keep cycling until the numbness wears off? No. Stop and get off the bike, reduce pressure and seek assessment if symptoms persist or recur. Will a more padded saddle always solve the problem? No. Saddle design, fit and riding position matter. Get individual fitting advice rather than relying on padding or a universal angle. How long can a constriction ring stay on? No longer than thirty minutes, and less if pain, numbness, coldness or discolouration occurs. A stuck device or symptoms that do not recover needs urgent help. Does penile numbness mean I have diabetes or MS? No. These are possible contributors, but the symptom needs assessment and does not diagnose either condition. Can collagenase injections restore sensation? They are used for selected Peyronie’s curvature, not as a general treatment for numbness. Sensory symptoms may need separate evaluation. Will testosterone definitely bring the feeling back? No. It is used for appropriately diagnosed deficiency and does not guarantee sensory recovery. It can also suppress sperm production. Will everyone need an MRI? No. Imaging and blood tests depend on the history and examination and should answer a specific clinical question. Should I stop a medicine that seems related? Ask the prescriber to review the timing and symptoms. Do not abruptly stop prescribed treatment on your own. Which combination of symptoms is an emergency? New genital or anal numbness with bladder or bowel changes, back pain or leg weakness needs emergency assessment. Severe circulation or device-related symptoms also need urgent care.

title: Menopause and insomnia: finding a treatment that fits
description: How menopause symptoms can disrupt sleep, when to investigate other causes, and where CBT-I, practical habits and individual treatment fit.
body: Poor sleep during perimenopause or after menopause can leave you exhausted and worried about the next night. Hormonal changes may be part of the picture, but they are not the only explanation. A useful plan considers both menopause symptoms and the patterns that keep insomnia going. Sleep can change before periods stop completely During perimenopause, ovarian hormone levels fluctuate and menstrual patterns change. Menopause is generally recognised after 12 months without a period when there is no other explanation and hormonal contraception is not obscuring the pattern. The time afterwards is postmenopause. Sleep symptoms can begin during the transition rather than waiting for that anniversary. Trouble sleeping is common at this stage, but not everyone develops an insomnia disorder. Estimates of how many people are affected vary because studies measure different things: occasional disrupted sleep, night sweats and persistent insomnia are not identical. Your symptoms and their effect on daily life matter more than whether you fit a quoted percentage. Insomnia is about difficulty and daytime impact Insomnia can mean difficulty falling asleep, repeated waking with difficulty returning to sleep, or waking earlier than you want despite having enough opportunity to sleep. Some people lie awake for 30 minutes or more or sleep fewer than six hours, but neither number is a universal diagnostic cutoff. Sleep needs and schedules differ. You may feel unrefreshed, tired, sleepy, irritable or anxious during the day. Concentration, memory and task completion can suffer, and mistakes or accidents may become more likely. Worrying constantly about the next night can add to the problem. Headaches or stomach upset may accompany poor sleep, but should not automatically be attributed to it. Symptoms at least three nights a week for three months or longer are part of the definition of chronic insomnia. Shorter episodes still deserve help if they interfere with your life. You do not need to wait three months before asking for support. Hormones and night sweats can contribute Changes in oestrogen and progesterone can influence sleep and the body’s temperature regulation. Progesterone-related pathways may affect sleepiness, but it is too simple to describe one hormone as an on-off sleep switch or assume that a blood hormone level explains every bad night. Hot flushes and night sweats can wake you, leave bedding uncomfortable and make it difficult to settle again. You may feel a sudden wave of heat or notice a racing heartbeat. This is not adequately explained by a universal burst of adrenaline from a rapid hormone drop. Treating troublesome vasomotor symptoms may help sleep, while persistent insomnia may still need its own treatment. Look for contributors beyond menopause Work, family pressures, relationship stress, anxiety or depression can disrupt sleep. Pain, reflux, needing to urinate, thyroid problems and other health conditions may also contribute. Age can change sleep patterns, but being over 60 does not make disabling sleeplessness inevitable or untreatable. Snoring, witnessed pauses in breathing, gasping or marked daytime sleepiness can suggest sleep apnoea. An uncomfortable urge to move the legs in the evening may suggest restless legs. These conditions need assessment rather than more time in bed. Sleep-disordered breathing becomes more common after menopause. Review medicines and supplements, especially anything started or changed recently. Caffeine, nicotine, alcohol, late heavy meals, shift work and travel across time zones can also affect sleep. Do not stop a prescribed medicine abruptly; ask whether its dose, timing, interactions or an alternative could be relevant. A sleep diary can make the appointment more useful For one or two weeks, note bedtime, approximate time to fall asleep, awakenings, final waking, naps and daytime tiredness. Include night sweats, caffeine or alcohol, medicines and any events that seem related. An estimate is enough; repeatedly watching the clock can make sleep anxiety worse. Your clinician may ask about mood, breathing during sleep, pain and your menstrual history and perform an examination. Blood tests are chosen for a suspected problem, such as thyroid disease, rather than automatically being needed for every sleep complaint. An overnight sleep study is usually considered when another sleep disorder is suspected; it is not the routine next step whenever insomnia has no obvious cause. Make the bedroom comfortable, dark and quiet Aim for a room that feels comfortably cool, with bedding you can adjust if you become hot. Around 18°C is sometimes suggested as a starting point, but there is no single required temperature and colder is not always better. Your comfort, season and home conditions matter. Reduce unnecessary light from lamps, clocks and screens, and silence avoidable alerts or noise. If a clock encourages repeated checking, turn it away. You do not need to buy a sleep gadget or special product to begin. A dark, quiet environment supports sleep but may not resolve a persistent insomnia disorder by itself. Plan food, drinks and nicotine around sleep A large late meal may worsen reflux or discomfort when you lie down. Try allowing time after dinner before bed. A small snack may suit some people, but a glass of milk is not a required treatment and should fit your tolerance and dietary needs. Reduce caffeine later in the day and notice how sensitive you are to it. Nicotine is stimulating; help to stop smoking can support broader health as well as sleep. Alcohol may make you drowsy at first, but it can fragment later sleep and worsen breathing problems, so it is not a reliable sleep aid. Stay normally hydrated during the day without using water as a replacement for lost sleep. Large drinks immediately before bed may increase toilet trips. If thirst or frequent urination is excessive or new, mention it at your appointment rather than simply restricting fluids. Use a wind-down routine and a steady schedule Gentle stretching, relaxed breathing, quiet reading or a calming activity can help you transition out of the day. Yoga may suit some people if comfortable, but relaxation does not have to look a particular way. Regular daytime activity and daylight can also help support your sleep rhythm. Keep a reasonably consistent wake-up time and go to bed when sleepy. Avoid compensating for every difficult night by spending much longer in bed or sleeping late the next morning. If your natural schedule shifts earlier, discuss an achievable adjustment that still leaves enough sleep opportunity. The aim is a workable rhythm, not rigidly forcing yourself to sleep on command. Ask about cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, CBT-I, is usually the first treatment for chronic insomnia. It addresses the thoughts and habits that keep sleeplessness going, including the cycle of anxiety about sleep. It goes beyond a list of sleep-hygiene tips and can be delivered in person, remotely or through suitable digital programmes. A programme may include stimulus control, relaxation and a carefully adjusted sleep schedule. Some approaches temporarily limit time in bed to improve sleep efficiency, but do not copy a severe sleep-restriction plan without appropriate guidance, especially if you are already dangerously sleepy. Menopause-specific CBT is another option for sleep problems associated with menopause symptoms. It can be used alongside hormone therapy or when hormones are unsuitable or unwanted. Ask which approach fits your symptoms and how to access it locally. Treat menopause symptoms with an individual plan Hormone replacement therapy, HRT, can help troublesome hot flushes and night sweats and may improve sleep when those symptoms are the main driver. It is not a guaranteed cure for every insomnia problem. Choice depends on symptoms, age, medical history, preferences and the balance of benefits and risks. If you have a uterus, systemic oestrogen usually needs a progestogen to protect the uterine lining. A vaginal treatment for local dryness is a different treatment and should not be expected to resolve night sweats or insomnia. Discuss your exact symptoms rather than asking only to “balance hormones”. For some suitable people in perimenopause who also need contraception, a combined hormonal contraceptive may be an alternative. It is not a general low-dose sleeping medicine and is not taken at the same time as HRT. HRT itself does not prevent pregnancy; contraception needs a separate discussion. Antidepressants, melatonin and sleeping medicines have different roles An antidepressant may be appropriate for depression or anxiety, and selected medicines can also help vasomotor symptoms in particular circumstances. That does not mean everyone with menopause insomnia should take a low-dose antidepressant. Some medicines can worsen sleep or cause other effects, so the reason for prescribing matters. Melatonin helps signal sleep timing, but it is not a proven universal treatment for chronic insomnia or a way to restore ovarian hormones. In the UK it is prescribed mainly for short-term sleep problems in people aged 55 and over, with some specialist uses. Availability and indications differ between countries. Discuss the formulation, interactions and next-day effects before using it. Sleeping tablets or sedating over-the-counter products may sometimes be used briefly, but can cause daytime impairment, falls or dependence, depending on the product. They do not replace investigation of persistent symptoms or CBT-I. Avoid combining sedatives, alcohol and herbal sleep products without advice. Protect daytime safety and review what is working Frequent or late naps can reduce the drive to sleep at night and are not a default treatment for chronic insomnia. If you need daytime rest because of significant sleepiness, discuss timing and safety with your clinician. Do not drive or operate machinery when sleepy, and do not rely on caffeine or a glass of water to make that safe. Agree on a review date and a few useful goals, such as fewer long awakenings, less night-sweat disruption or better daytime functioning. If sleep is affecting mood, work or daily responsibilities, say so. Persistent symptoms after one approach do not mean you must accept them: the diagnosis, menopause treatment or sleep plan may need adjustment. Trouble sleeping can begin before periods stop. Six hours or 30 minutes awake is not a diagnosis by itself. Night sweats, insomnia and sleep apnoea may need different care. Frequent naps and alcohol can worsen the sleep pattern. Treatments should be reviewed against symptoms and daytime function. Do I have to wait until menopause is confirmed to ask for help? No. Sleep symptoms can begin during perimenopause, and support or treatment can be considered before periods stop completely. Does sleeping less than six hours prove I have insomnia? No. Diagnosis considers difficulty sleeping despite adequate opportunity, frequency, duration and daytime impact. A single hour count is not enough. Are all night-time awakenings caused by low oestrogen? No. Hot flushes can contribute, but stress, medicines, pain, reflux, sleep apnoea and other problems may also matter. Will everyone with insomnia need a sleep study? No. A sleep study is generally used when another sleep disorder is suspected. A history, diary and targeted assessment often guide insomnia care. Is 18°C the only correct bedroom temperature? No. It is a possible starting point, not a requirement. Aim for comfortable coolness and adjustable bedding rather than making yourself cold. Should I take frequent naps after a poor night? Not as a routine insomnia treatment. Frequent or late naps can reduce night-time sleep drive. Discuss significant daytime sleepiness and avoid driving when sleepy. Is CBT-I just advice to avoid screens? No. It is a structured treatment addressing sleep-related thoughts, behaviours and scheduling. Sleep-hygiene changes are only one part of care. Will HRT definitely cure my insomnia? No. It may help when hot flushes or night sweats disrupt sleep, but persistent insomnia may also need CBT-I or treatment of another condition. Can I use HRT and the combined pill together for sleep? No. The combined pill may be an alternative for suitable people who need contraception, but is not taken at the same time as HRT. Ask for an individual plan. Is melatonin a harmless cure for menopause sleep problems? No. It has selected uses, possible interactions and next-day effects, and is not a universal treatment for chronic insomnia. Check the indication and local product with a clinician.

title: Vulval itching and swelling: finding the cause
description: Seven possible causes of vulval irritation, why discharge alone cannot identify the problem, and how to choose gentle care and appropriate treatment.
body: Repeated itching or swelling around the vaginal opening can be uncomfortable and frustrating, particularly when it returns after treatment. Several conditions can look alike. A clear description, gentle skin care and the right examination are more useful than adding more products without knowing the cause. Itching without discharge still needs an explanation The vulva is the external genital area, including the labia around the vaginal opening. The vagina is the internal canal. People often call symptoms in either place “vaginal itching”, but identifying where you feel irritation helps guide an examination and treatment. A lack of obvious discharge does not rule out thrush or another infection. Equally, itching does not automatically mean thrush: skin irritation, eczema, a longer-term skin condition or an infestation can cause similar discomfort. If treatment keeps helping briefly and symptoms return, ask for a review rather than repeating the same product indefinitely. Contact dermatitis: a reaction to something touching the skin Sensitive vulval skin can react to lubricants, latex condoms, laundry products, scented pads, intimate sprays, wipes, soaps, bubble bath or cleansing gels. Contact dermatitis can involve direct irritation or an allergic reaction. Itching, tenderness, redness or another change in colour, swelling, a rash or hives may follow exposure. Pause a suspected nonessential product and use gentle care while arranging advice if symptoms persist. Improvement can take time and is not guaranteed within a few days. Keep a list of products and when you used them. If latex seems to be the problem, ask about a suitable latex-free condom that still provides STI protection; do not simply abandon protection. Genital herpes can begin with tingling or itching Both HSV-1 and HSV-2 can cause genital herpes. It can spread through oral, vaginal or anal sexual contact, including contact with infected skin when no sore is visible. Transmission does not require visible semen or vaginal fluid. Condoms lower risk but cannot cover every area that may shed virus. Symptoms may include tingling or burning, blisters that open into painful sores, painful urination and, during an initial episode, fever, body aches, headache or swollen glands. Some infections are mild or unrecognised. Antiviral medicines can shorten or suppress episodes but do not remove the virus from the body. Illness or stress may coincide with recurrences. Seek assessment of new sores promptly, and tell your maternity team immediately if you are pregnant and suspect herpes. Lichen sclerosus causes lasting changes in the skin Lichen sclerosus can cause pale or white itchy patches, fragile skin, soreness and small cracks around the vulva or anus. It can occur at different ages and is not a sign of poor hygiene or an infection passed through sex. Its cause is not fully understood; immune processes may be involved. A strong prescription steroid ointment is commonly used to control inflammation. The clinician should explain where, how much and how often to apply it, and how follow-up will work. Persistent symptoms may need specialist reassessment rather than an automatic switch to an immune-modifying medicine. Scarring can affect comfort and function, and a new lump, thickening or an ulcer that does not heal needs review because cancer risk is increased, although still low. Eczema can flare on vulval skin too Eczema may cause dryness, scaling, itching, soreness or a change in skin colour. It can affect the vulva even when there is little eczema elsewhere. Scratching can damage the surface and make symptoms harder to settle. A flare improving and later returning does not necessarily mean that you have picked up a new infection. Triggers differ between people. Heat, sweat, irritating fabric, fragrance, detergents, stress, illness or hormonal changes can contribute. Some people have relevant allergies, but vulval itching is not a reason to eliminate broad food groups. Pregnancy or menopause may change symptoms; dryness related to lower oestrogen is another possible explanation that needs its own assessment. Pubic lice need targeted treatment and contact care Pubic lice can cause intense itching in hair-bearing areas. You may see tiny lice or eggs attached to hairs, scratch marks or small blue-grey marks near bites. They are usually passed through close sexual contact and can occasionally spread through shared clothing, towels or bedding. Scratching may cause secondary skin irritation or infection. Use a product specifically appropriate for pubic lice as directed, with advice if you are pregnant, breastfeeding or treating a child. Do not apply these products near the eyes or inside the vagina. Wash and dry recently used clothing, towels and bedding as instructed, and ask how to handle items that cannot be washed. Recent sexual partners need notification and assessment or treatment; avoid sexual contact until treatment requirements are met. Thorough whole-house disinfection or insecticide fogging is not the solution. Persistent live lice need follow-up, not repeated unsupervised chemical applications. Fever or marked fatigue should not be dismissed as routine lice symptoms. A sexual-health service can also advise about other STI checks. Sweat and friction can keep the area irritated Moisture trapped against the skin can worsen itching, especially with close-fitting clothes or damp exercise wear. Change out of wet clothing, choose comfortable breathable underwear and avoid garments that repeatedly rub. You do not need a special deodorant to manage normal genital scent. After exercise, gently rinse or wash the external area and dry by patting rather than scrubbing. More washing is not always better: frequent soap use can damage an already irritated surface. If symptoms continue despite reducing heat and friction, consider another cause rather than assuming sweat explains everything. Shaving and waxing can cause bumps and soreness Hair removal can irritate follicles, create small cuts or lead to ingrown hairs. A shaving cream, depilatory chemical or wax can also cause a reaction. An itchy rash after hair removal may therefore be irritation, but painful blisters, spreading redness or pus should not automatically be labelled razor burn. Pause shaving or waxing while the skin heals. If you resume, work carefully on external hair-bearing skin with clean personal equipment and a product suitable for that area; do not put hair-removal chemicals on the inner labia or inside the vagina. Trimming may be more comfortable for some people, but still needs care. Do not pick, squeeze or dig out bumps. Keep home care simple and external Gently cleanse the outside with lukewarm water or an emollient soap substitute recommended for you, and pat dry. Avoid douching, scented products, intimate sprays and vigorous rubbing. A plain fragrance-free emollient may protect irritated skin if suitable for the diagnosis. Choose a bland lubricant if needed and stop if it stings; check compatibility with condoms. A clean cool damp cloth may briefly soothe itching. A comfortably warm compress may ease a minor irritated hair follicle, but avoid heat and stop if it makes symptoms worse. Loose clothing can reduce friction. Comfort measures do not treat herpes, lice or a persistent inflammatory skin condition. Do not improvise a strong baking-soda bath or use a long soak as a general cure. Oatmeal baths may be used for some eczema care, but a household mixture is not automatically suitable for genital skin. Check with a clinician before trying bath additives. Never put these mixtures inside the vagina. Treatment should match the diagnosis A clinician may recommend an antifungal for confirmed or likely thrush, an antiviral for herpes, a suitable lice medicine or a prescribed steroid for a skin disorder. Antibiotics treat particular bacterial problems; they are not a general treatment for itching. Oral antihistamines can sometimes reduce itch or help sleep, but they do not remove every underlying cause and can cause drowsiness. Hydrocortisone, stronger steroids, topical antihistamines and calamine are not interchangeable products to try on all genital symptoms. Some can irritate the skin or obscure the diagnosis. Conversely, a correctly prescribed potent steroid for lichen sclerosus is an important treatment and should not be avoided simply because the site is sensitive. Ask for clear application instructions, including pregnancy or breastfeeding precautions where relevant. Arrange an examination when symptoms persist or change Seek assessment for persistent or recurrent itching, white patches, blisters, ulcers, an unexplained lump, a change in skin texture or concern about an STI. Fever, severe pain, rapidly increasing swelling, spreading redness or difficulty passing urine needs urgent care. Breathing difficulty or swelling of the lips or tongue with an allergic reaction is an emergency. The clinician may ask about discharge, skin products, medicines, sexual contact, other skin symptoms and previous treatment. With your consent they can examine the vulva and, when needed, the vagina. Swabs or other tests may help identify infection. If the diagnosis is unclear or a patch does not respond to treatment, a small skin biopsy may be suggested. Ask for a chaperone or support person if helpful and tell the clinician if you need to pause. The vulva is external; avoid washing or treating inside the vagina without advice. Keep every proposed cause open until the symptoms are assessed. Prescribed steroids can be appropriate for diagnosed conditions. Persistent white patches, sores or lumps should be examined. Can I have thrush without noticeable discharge? Yes. Thrush can mainly irritate the vulva, but itching alone does not prove it. Other skin conditions and infections may need different treatment. Does genital herpes only come from HSV-2? No. Both HSV-1 and HSV-2 can cause it. Skin contact, including oral-genital contact, can transmit infection even without a visible sore. Are white itchy patches a reason for an appointment? Yes. Lichen sclerosus is one possible cause, but examination is needed. Persistent patches, scarring, ulcers or a new lump should not be repeatedly treated as thrush. Are strong steroid ointments always unsafe on the vulva? No. A prescribed potent steroid can be essential for conditions such as lichen sclerosus. Follow the exact site, amount and schedule instead of applying an unselected product. Must I disinfect my whole home for pubic lice? No. Use appropriate treatment and targeted care of recently used clothes, towels and bedding, with partner management. Whole-house insecticide treatment is unnecessary. Should I wash more often to stop the itching? Overwashing can worsen irritation. Gentle external cleansing and drying are preferable to frequent soap, scrubbing, scented wipes or douching. Can I use a baking-soda bath as a cure? Do not use a strong household mixture as a general genital treatment. Bath additives can irritate, and soothing the skin does not treat every cause. Ask for advice specific to the diagnosis. Should I stop eating certain foods for vulval eczema? Not routinely. Triggers vary, and broad food restriction is not a substitute for assessment. Discuss a suspected allergy before making nutritional changes. Can shaving explain every itchy bump? No. Shaving may irritate follicles or cause ingrown hairs, but infection or herpes can look similar. Stop hair removal and seek advice for blisters, pus, spreading redness or persistent symptoms. Will I definitely need a biopsy? No. History, examination and sometimes swabs may identify the cause. A biopsy can be useful when the diagnosis is uncertain, the skin has concerning changes or treatment is not working.

title: Low mood around your period: PMS, PMDD or a flare of another condition?
description: Understand the cycle, recognise PMS, PMDD and PME, track symptoms and discuss therapy, medicines, supplements and practical support.
body: Mood changes around a period can be much more than a brief bad day. The timing, severity and impact of symptoms help guide care, whether you feel better soon after bleeding starts or struggle throughout the month. You deserve support without having your experience dismissed as just hormones. Take severe distress seriously at any point in the cycle If you are thinking about suicide or harming yourself, seek urgent mental-health support or contact a crisis service now. If you might act on those thoughts, have already harmed yourself or cannot stay safe, call your local emergency number or go to an emergency department. Ask someone you trust to stay with you if possible. New hallucinations, severe confusion or possible mania also need urgent assessment. Mania can involve unusually high energy, very little need for sleep, racing thoughts or risky behaviour. Do not wait for a period to start or a diary to be complete before getting help. A recurring monthly pattern does not make a crisis less serious. Notice both the symptoms and their effect on your day Period-related distress can involve irritability, anxiety, poor concentration, tearfulness, a persistent low mood or a sense that you cannot manage ordinary demands. Headaches, cramps, breast tenderness, bloating and fatigue may occur alongside the emotional symptoms. Some people notice changes before bleeding begins and remain affected for the first few days of their period. Others feel low after it ends or throughout the month. Missing work or school, struggling with caring tasks, losing interest in relationships or repeatedly having conflicts are useful details to discuss. You do not have to prove that your experience is worse than someone else’s. Understand the cycle without forcing it into twenty-eight days Day one is the first day of menstrual bleeding. Menstruation describes the shedding of the womb lining. The follicular phase also begins on day one and continues until ovulation, so the menstrual and follicular phases overlap rather than being completely separate consecutive blocks. During the follicular phase, an ovarian follicle develops and oestrogen generally rises, helping the womb lining rebuild. Ovulation releases an egg. It does not always happen on day fourteen or exactly halfway through a cycle. The luteal phase follows ovulation, with progesterone rising to support the lining. If pregnancy does not develop, progesterone and oestrogen fall and another period begins. Cycle length and symptoms vary, and hormonal contraception can change this pattern. A calendar estimate cannot tell you precisely what your hormones or mood should be doing. Hormone sensitivity is more complex than a single low level Oestrogen and progesterone interact with brain signalling, including systems involving serotonin and dopamine. These neurotransmitters help nerve cells communicate; they are not interchangeable with the ovarian hormones. Changes in mood cannot be reduced to one predictable rise or fall in a chemical. In PMDD, sensitivity to normal cyclical hormone changes appears important. Genetic and other biological differences may contribute, but there is no routine blood or genetic test that confirms the condition. A normal hormone result does not invalidate symptoms, and a low result does not by itself explain depression. Research on hormone responses continues. It is not accurate to tell every person that ovulation causes a dopamine or serotonin drop that will resolve on a fixed day. Stress, sleep, health conditions, medicines and the wider circumstances of life may also affect how someone feels. PMS can be disruptive and still deserves treatment Premenstrual syndrome, or PMS, is a repeating pattern of physical and emotional symptoms before a period that improves after bleeding starts. It can range from manageable discomfort to symptoms that substantially interfere with daily life. Calling it PMS should not mean dismissing it as a minor inconvenience. Fatigue, disrupted sleep, cramps and mood changes can reinforce one another. A clinician will look at the timing and impact rather than assuming every episode of low mood is caused by the menstrual cycle. PMS is one explanation to consider, not a label that ends the assessment. PMDD involves a characteristic pattern and substantial impairment Premenstrual dysphoric disorder, or PMDD, includes prominent mood symptoms that usually develop in the week or two before a period, improve within a few days after it starts and become minimal or absent afterwards. Formal criteria include at least five symptoms, with at least one core mood symptom, together with significant distress or interference in daily life. Symptoms may include marked mood swings, anger or irritability, sadness or hopelessness, anxiety, reduced interest, poor concentration, low energy, appetite changes, insomnia or excessive sleep, and feeling overwhelmed. Physical symptoms can include breast tenderness, bloating, headaches and muscle or joint discomfort. Panic attacks or suicidal thoughts also require attention. The criteria help a clinician distinguish patterns; they are not a reason to withhold help if you count fewer symptoms. Nor should you wait a year untreated. An assessment can begin now, with daily records used to confirm the pattern and check for other explanations. PME means an existing condition becomes worse before a period Premenstrual exacerbation, or PME, differs from symptoms that are largely absent for the rest of the cycle. With PME, a condition such as depression or anxiety is present at other times and becomes worse before menstruation. Treatment must address the underlying condition as well as the cyclical worsening. A menstrual pattern can also be relevant to migraine, seizure disorders and asthma. Acne or bowel symptoms may change across the cycle too. If you have irritable bowel syndrome, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia or an eating disorder, tell your usual care team about any recurring change. Do not assume that every flare has the same hormonal cause or can be treated with a PMDD regimen. PME can be difficult to recognise because symptoms overlap and recall is imperfect. PMDD and another condition may also coexist. A diary and a history covering the whole month are more useful than assessing only the worst premenstrual day. Keep a daily record that is simple enough to use For at least two cycles, if feasible, note bleeding, mood, anxiety, irritability, sleep, energy, appetite, physical symptoms and effects on work or relationships. Record good days as well as difficult ones. That helps show whether there is a clear interval of improvement. A clinician may offer a validated daily rating form. Paper notes can work too; if using an app, consider its privacy arrangements. Add medication changes, illness or major stresses that might affect the pattern. You do not need to identify ovulation perfectly or produce a flawless record before seeking care. Ask for an assessment that considers more than PMS A primary-care clinician, gynaecologist or mental-health professional can review the symptoms and arrange appropriate support. Persistent depression after a period, severe anxiety, recurrent panic or symptoms that do not fit a cyclical pattern need consideration in their own right. Bring your record, medicine list and a few concrete examples of what has become difficult. Assessment may consider other conditions, including thyroid problems, depending on your history. If the concern is dismissed without a clear plan, ask for a follow-up or another opinion. Being heard should not depend on presenting your symptoms perfectly. Talking therapy can be part of effective care Cognitive behavioural therapy can help with how symptoms affect daily life, coping responses and distress. A therapist can also help identify patterns of stress or anxiety and develop a plan for difficult days. Therapy does not imply that the symptoms are invented or caused by a lack of willpower. Treatment may combine psychological and medical care. Ask what the therapy is intended to help, how progress will be assessed and what to do if symptoms worsen between sessions. Severe depression, mania, psychosis or safety concerns need an appropriate clinical assessment alongside coping strategies. Antidepressant treatment needs the right diagnosis and schedule Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs, are an established option for severe premenstrual mood symptoms. A prescriber may recommend daily use throughout the month or a defined part of the cycle. The schedule depends on the diagnosis, other symptoms and the medicine. Do not apply an intermittent PMDD schedule to treatment prescribed for ongoing depression or another condition. Discuss possible nausea, sleep changes, tiredness and sexual side effects, and agree on a review. Starting, stopping or changing a medicine should follow the prescribing plan. Mention any history of mania or hypomania, including episodes when you needed unusually little sleep and had much more energy than usual. Antidepressants used alone can destabilise bipolar disorder. Pregnancy plans and other medicines also matter when choosing treatment. Hormonal treatment is an option for selected people Some combined contraceptive pills can reduce premenstrual symptoms, particularly when contraception is also wanted. Evidence is not identical for every pill, and individual mood responses vary. A clinician will check factors such as migraine with aura, clot risk and other medicines before recommending one. Agree on how to monitor symptoms and side effects. If initial options do not help enough, specialist gynaecology and mental-health care can reassess the diagnosis and consider further treatment. Avoid repeatedly switching products on your own or assuming that a normal hormone test rules out a useful treatment discussion. Vitamins and minerals are not interchangeable mood treatments Calcium, magnesium and B vitamins are often suggested for premenstrual symptoms, but evidence, dose and safety differ. A possible benefit for one symptom does not establish that a supplement treats PMDD or an underlying depressive disorder. Review dietary intake, medical conditions and all products with a clinician or pharmacist. Excess supplemental vitamin B6 can damage nerves. Taking several products together can unintentionally increase the total dose. Do not use a high-dose B-complex product as a substitute for assessment, and do not assume that a vitamin is harmless because it is available without prescription. Check herbal products before adding them Evening primrose oil, black cohosh and St John’s wort are not equivalent to one another or to prescribed treatment. Evidence for evening primrose oil in PMS is insufficient. Black cohosh is mainly studied for menopausal symptoms, with inadequate evidence for treating premenstrual depression; liver injury has been reported with products bearing its name, although causation is uncertain. St John’s wort can reduce the effectiveness of birth-control pills and interact with many medicines. Combining it with some antidepressants or other serotonin-affecting drugs can cause serious adverse effects. Ask a pharmacist about the exact product before use, especially with pregnancy plans, breastfeeding or ongoing treatment. Do not stop prescribed care to try an herb. Use activity, sleep and relaxation as support A short walk, gentle stretching or yoga may be manageable when a full workout is not. Regular movement and a consistent sleep routine can support wellbeing, but there is no requirement to complete thirty minutes before you deserve treatment. Choose a sustainable starting point and adapt on difficult days. Slow breathing, guided imagery, progressive muscle relaxation, meditation, journalling or a comfortable massage may help you unwind. Pick what feels useful rather than treating every technique as a task. Aromatherapy is sometimes used for comfort, but it is not an established treatment for PMDD; avoid products that irritate you and do not swallow essential oils. Regular meals, rest and reducing avoidable stress can make coping easier. They cannot guarantee that depression disappears. Persistent or severe symptoms are not evidence that you have failed at self-care. Make support and follow-up specific Tell a trusted person what difficult days look like and what helps: listening without minimising, sharing a task, keeping you company or helping arrange an appointment. Agree on a safety plan with your care team if symptoms can become severe. Continue recording the pattern after starting treatment so that improvement and side effects can be reviewed. If low mood persists after the period or the first plan does not help, arrange reassessment. The aim is a workable treatment plan for your life, rather than accepting recurring distress as an unavoidable part of menstruation. PMS, PMDD and PME are related but different patterns. Symptoms after the period or all month deserve assessment too. Hormone sensitivity is not simply a low hormone level. Medicines and supplements need interaction and diagnosis checks. Supportive habits complement treatment rather than replace it. Can premenstrual symptoms continue after bleeding starts? Yes, they may take a few days to improve. Symptoms that persist throughout the cycle need assessment for other or additional conditions. Is the follicular phase after the period? It begins on the first day of bleeding and continues to ovulation, so it overlaps with menstruation. Does everyone ovulate on day fourteen? No. Timing varies with cycle length and between cycles. A fixed calendar should not be used to explain every mood change. Can a normal hormone test rule out PMDD? No. Sensitivity to normal changes appears important. Diagnosis relies on the pattern and impact of symptoms, not a routine hormone result. Must I wait a year or finish a diary before asking for help? No. Seek assessment now. Daily records can be collected while care begins, and urgent symptoms must not wait. How is PME different from PMDD? In PME, an existing condition is present at other times and worsens before a period. PMDD has a more distinct premenstrual pattern with improvement afterwards. Can I take my existing antidepressant only before my period? Do not change its schedule yourself. An intermittent regimen is suitable only for particular diagnoses and medicines under a prescribing plan. Why mention past periods of unusually high energy? They may indicate hypomania or mania and change treatment decisions. Antidepressants alone can destabilise bipolar disorder. Can St John’s wort affect contraception? Yes. It can reduce the effect of birth-control pills and interact seriously with antidepressants and other medicines. Check before using it. What if exercise and relaxation do not help enough? That is a reason to review care, not blame yourself. Psychological and medical treatments may be needed alongside everyday support.

title: Symptoms after your period: what deserves a closer look?
description: Post-menstrual syndrome is an informal label, not an explanation for every symptom. A record of timing and a targeted assessment can help.
body: A period ending does not always mean you immediately feel well again. You might notice fatigue, a headache, low mood or pain in the days afterwards. These experiences are worth discussing, but a broad label such as “post-menstrual syndrome” does not establish why they happen or which treatment will help. An informal label has limits The term post-menstrual syndrome is used online to describe symptoms after bleeding finishes. It does not have the same established diagnostic framework as PMS or PMDD, and there is no agreed symptom count, hormone test or standard treatment for it. That uncertainty does not make your symptoms less real. It means they should be assessed on their own merits rather than automatically attributed to one poorly defined syndrome. Claims about exactly how common it is, how long it lasts or whether it is more severe than PMS are not well established. PMS and PMDD usually begin before a period and improve after bleeding starts. Improvement is not necessarily immediate. Symptoms that begin only after bleeding ends, or remain throughout the month, call for a broader discussion. Record the pattern without assuming the cause For two or three cycles if practical, note the first and last day of bleeding, the days symptoms occur and their effect on daily life. Include days when you feel well so the pattern is easier to interpret. Track the main problems you want help with: for example fatigue, headache, pelvic pain, low mood or sleep disruption. Note heavy bleeding, medicine changes and hormonal contraception too. A brief record is enough; it need not become another burden. Bring the record to an appointment, but do not wait to finish it if symptoms are severe. A regular pattern is useful evidence, not proof that all the symptoms share a hormonal cause. People using this informal label describe irritability, anger, crying, anxiety, low mood, poor concentration or a sense of clumsiness. Physical complaints may include neck, back or joint aches as well as abdominal pain, headaches, pain with sex and vaginal dryness, itching or burning. Record the actual symptom and its duration rather than assuming it belongs to one syndrome. Fatigue after bleeding may need an iron assessment Heavy or prolonged periods can contribute to iron deficiency, with or without anaemia. Fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance, palpitations or shortness of breath are reasons to discuss testing, particularly when bleeding is heavy. A clinician may request a full blood count and, when appropriate, ferritin to assess iron stores. Other explanations for fatigue may also need consideration. Having a period does not automatically mean that your iron falls to a harmful level every month. If deficiency is found, treatment should address both iron replacement and the reason for blood loss. Iron tablets are not a universal remedy for post-period symptoms and can cause side effects or be harmful when taken unnecessarily. Keep them securely away from children. Pain and headaches need their own assessment Period cramps commonly occur near the start of bleeding. Persistent pelvic pain, pain during sex, or bowel or bladder symptoms should not be dismissed because a period has just ended. Endometriosis and several other conditions can cause pain at different points in the cycle. A headache diary can help distinguish migraine from other headache patterns. The usual definition of menstrual-related migraine concerns attacks around the start of bleeding; a headache after the period ends is not automatically the same diagnosis. Report a new or changing headache pattern. Sudden extremely severe headache, new weakness, difficulty speaking or a new loss of vision needs emergency assessment. A clinician can discuss treatments appropriate to the type of headache and your health history. Vulval itching, burning or unusual discharge may instead reflect irritation, infection or another local condition. These symptoms need their own review rather than being bundled into a menstrual label. Low mood should not have to follow a textbook calendar Depression and anxiety can occur at any point in the cycle. An existing condition may worsen before a period, but continuing distress afterwards still needs care. A clinician can consider both menstrual timing and your wider mental-health history. Seek support if low mood, anxiety or loss of interest affects daily life, especially when it persists. If you are thinking about suicide or self-harm, contact a crisis service or seek urgent help. If you cannot stay safe, use your local emergency service and ask a trusted person to stay with you. Therapy or medication may be appropriate for a diagnosed condition. A treatment does not need to target hormones simply because symptoms were first noticed around menstruation. Be cautious about hormone and supplement claims There is no established evidence that a universal rise in oestrogen or testosterone, failure to ovulate, or insulin resistance explains all symptoms after a period. An irregular cycle or suspected hormonal condition can be assessed separately when the history suggests it. Likewise, eating sugar has not been shown to be the single cause of this proposed syndrome. Aim for regular, varied meals rather than blaming yourself or following a restrictive “hormone-balancing” diet. Iron, magnesium, vitamin E and B-complex supplements should not be offered as an automatic package. Their usefulness depends on a specific need, and evidence from a study of depression cannot simply be applied to every post-period symptom. Review supplements with a pharmacist or clinician, including interactions and total doses across products. Excess supplemental vitamin B6 can injure nerves. Essential oils and other complementary products are not proven substitutes for assessment or treatment. If you have irregular cycles, a contraceptive implant or a diagnosed condition affecting ovulation or glucose regulation, include that in the discussion. These details can guide assessment, but they do not prove the proposed explanation that a rise in estrogen and testosterone causes a distinct post-period disorder. Foods can help meet ordinary nutritional needs: beans, lentils, meat or suitable seafood provide iron, while nuts, seeds, avocado and other varied foods contribute magnesium. A balanced pattern with fruit, vegetables, whole grains and suitable fish is reasonable. These foods are not a treatment protocol for this proposed syndrome; adjust caffeine or salty foods if they clearly worsen your own symptoms. Build a plan around the findings Regular sleep, adequate meals, manageable physical activity and practical support can improve comfort while you seek care. These habits support treatment; they do not replace it or guarantee that symptoms disappear. The plan might include treatment for heavy bleeding, iron deficiency, migraine, pelvic pain or a mood disorder. Hormonal contraception can help some specific problems, but it is not a proven universal treatment for an undefined post-menstrual syndrome. Ask what explanation is most likely, what the treatment is intended to improve and when to review it. If symptoms continue despite the first plan, ask for reassessment rather than assuming you simply have to tolerate them. Relaxation practices such as gentle yoga or massage may make stress easier to manage if you enjoy them. Cognitive behavioural therapy or antidepressants may help an identified mental-health condition, and selected hormonal contraceptives can help particular menstrual symptoms. Choices should follow the diagnosis, preferences and medical history. Know when not to wait Severe or worsening pelvic pain, fainting, heavy bleeding with weakness, or pain with a possible pregnancy needs urgent assessment. Fever with pelvic pain or unusual discharge also needs prompt medical advice. Seek emergency help for severe pain with collapse, breathing difficulty or other rapidly worsening symptoms. Timing after an apparent period does not rule out a pregnancy-related or other urgent problem. Post-menstrual syndrome is an informal description rather than a confirmed cause. Track timing and impact, including symptom-free days. Heavy bleeding and fatigue may warrant iron testing. Pain, headaches and mood symptoms may have separate explanations. Use treatment and supplements for an identified need. Does feeling unwell after my period mean I have a hormone imbalance? No. Hormones may contribute to some symptoms, but timing alone cannot identify a hormone disorder. Should everyone take iron after a period? No. Discuss symptoms, bleeding and testing. Iron is useful when indicated, but unnecessary supplementation can cause harm. Is it still worth seeking help without a recognised syndrome name? Yes. A clinician can investigate and treat the symptoms themselves, even when one label does not explain them all.

title: Black or dark brown vaginal discharge: what to check
description: Dark discharge often contains older blood, but its timing, amount and accompanying symptoms matter more than the shade.
body: Blood can darken as it takes longer to leave the uterus or vagina. A small amount mixed with discharge may look deep brown or almost black, especially near the end of a period. Colour alone, however, cannot tell you whether the cause is harmless, an infection or a pregnancy-related problem. Consider the whole pattern If a little dark discharge occurs at the end of your usual period and then stops, without pain, unpleasant odour or other new symptoms, it may simply be older menstrual blood. It does not mean you need to cleanse the vagina or “flush out” retained blood. Seek assessment for a new or persistent change, bleeding between periods or after sex, unusually heavy or prolonged bleeding, or discharge with itching, pain or an unpleasant smell. A photograph or colour chart cannot diagnose the cause. Tell the clinician about the dates, amount and duration, whether pregnancy is possible, recent childbirth, medicines and contraception. Any bleeding or blood-stained discharge after menopause needs assessment, even if it happens once or is only a small brown stain. Check whether a tampon or other item could remain inside A retained tampon, condom or another vaginal item can cause discharge, odour or irritation. A tampon cannot pass through an intact cervix into the abdomen, but it can sit high in the vagina and be difficult to reach. If a tampon is easily reachable, you can try removing it gently with clean fingers. Do not use tweezers or other tools, and do not keep trying if it hurts. Seek prompt help if you cannot remove it, are unsure whether something remains, or have pain, odour or discharge. A retained item does not always cause toxic shock syndrome, but this rare infection can progress quickly. Fever, vomiting or diarrhoea, a widespread rash, dizziness or feeling very unwell while using a tampon or menstrual cup needs urgent medical help. Remove the product if possible without delaying care. Call emergency services for collapse, confusion, breathing difficulty or rapidly worsening illness. Toxic shock can also occur in other situations, including with infected wounds; it is not diagnosed by the colour of discharge. Other possible retained items include a contraceptive cap or sponge, part of a sex toy, or a second tampon inserted before the first was removed. Local swelling, itching or difficulty urinating can accompany the discharge. Tell the clinician exactly what may remain rather than trying to retrieve it with an instrument. Infection may cause bleeding as well as discharge Some vaginal or cervical infections can cause unusual discharge, bleeding after sex or bleeding between periods. Chlamydia and gonorrhoea may have few symptoms, so a lack of pain or odour does not exclude them. Pelvic inflammatory disease can cause lower abdominal pain, pain during sex, abnormal bleeding or discharge, and sometimes fever. Seek prompt assessment if these symptoms occur, because early treatment reduces the risk of complications. Testing may include swabs or urine samples and a pregnancy test. Treatment depends on the infection; do not choose an antibiotic or antifungal because discharge looks dark. Partner treatment and avoiding sex for the recommended interval may be part of the plan. Untreated pelvic infection can contribute to chronic pelvic pain, ectopic pregnancy or fertility problems. Complete prescribed treatment and follow partner-testing advice; do not assume symptoms disappearing means a bacterial STI has been cleared. If pregnancy is possible, colour cannot provide reassurance Take a pregnancy test at an appropriate time if your period is late or pregnancy is possible. A test taken too early may be negative, so follow the instructions and repeat it when advised. Report bleeding or brown discharge in a known pregnancy to your maternity or early-pregnancy service. Light spotting can have several causes. You cannot reliably identify “implantation bleeding” by its colour, date or duration, and it should not be used to dismiss a new symptom. An ectopic pregnancy can cause light or dark bleeding rather than a heavy red flow. Get urgent assessment for bleeding with pelvic pain when pregnancy is possible, even without a positive home test. Severe or one-sided pain, shoulder-tip pain, fainting or marked dizziness needs emergency help. A missed miscarriage may have few symptoms and be found on ultrasound. Dark discharge does not confirm it, and there is no requirement that pregnancy tissue remain for four weeks before that term applies. Diagnosis may require repeat assessment when a scan is too early to be conclusive. A missed period, tiredness, nausea, breast tenderness or more frequent urination can occur in early pregnancy, but none confirms pregnancy or identifies why bleeding happened. Miscarriage is commonest in early pregnancy; cramps or weakness may accompany it, and some losses cause no obvious symptoms. Testing and follow-up matter more than guessing from a colour or a percentage. After birth, watch the amount and how you feel Postnatal discharge, called lochia, begins after birth and can continue for several weeks. It generally becomes lighter and changes from red towards brown or pink, then paler discharge. The course varies, so one exact day-by-day colour schedule is not a safety test. Contact your maternity team promptly for increasing bleeding, a bad smell, fever or worsening pelvic pain. Do not assume very dark discharge is normal simply because lochia can contain older blood. Seek urgent medical care if you soak through one or more pads in an hour, pass clots larger than an egg or pass tissue. Sudden heavy bleeding with faintness, a racing heartbeat or shortness of breath needs emergency help. Do not wait to meet a clot-size threshold if you feel unwell. Less common causes need an examination An obstruction can occasionally prevent menstrual blood from leaving normally, especially in a young person with recurring pain but no expected periods. Blood collected in the vagina is called haematocolpos. This is different from amenorrhoea, which simply means absent periods and has many possible causes. Pain, pressure or urinary difficulty with absent periods warrants assessment. A complete obstruction may prevent discharge entirely; a dark stain is not a reliable way to recognise it. Treatment depends on the anatomy and should be planned by an appropriate specialist. Cancer is one possible cause of unexplained bleeding or blood-stained discharge, but black discharge is not a specific cancer sign. Persistent bleeding after sex, bleeding after menopause or an ongoing unexplained change should be investigated. A previous normal screening result does not replace assessment of new symptoms. Obstruction can arise from a hymenal opening that did not form, a vaginal septum, or narrowing or absence of part of the cervical outflow route. A congenital missing cervix and acquired cervical scarring are different conditions. Depending on the anatomy, a procedure to create or restore an opening may be needed; it is not something to clear at home. Symptoms that can accompany cervical cancer include watery or blood-stained discharge, persistent pelvic pain and, in more advanced disease, leg swelling or problems passing urine or stool. Fatigue and unexplained weight loss also warrant review. These are not specific to cancer. If cancer is diagnosed, surgery, radiotherapy and drug treatments are selected according to its stage and other findings. Treat the cause rather than the colour An examination may be enough to identify a retained item or irritation; other situations need infection tests, ultrasound or further investigation. Ask what follow-up is needed if the initial result does not explain continuing symptoms. If miscarriage is confirmed, options may include waiting, medication or a procedure, depending on clinical circumstances and preference. Surgery does not always mean sharp curettage under general anaesthesia; suction procedures and different anaesthetic options may be available. Avoid douching, deodorants and home remedies intended to remove dark blood. Gentle external washing is enough while you seek advice. Keep track of symptoms, and seek care sooner if the amount increases or you become unwell. Very dark discharge often contains older blood, but colour is not a diagnosis. New bleeding between periods, after sex or after menopause needs review. Possible retained items should be removed safely and promptly. Pregnancy-related bleeding needs advice regardless of colour. Heavy bleeding, severe pain, fainting or systemic illness needs urgent care. Does black discharge mean a miscarriage? No. Neither miscarriage nor a healthy pregnancy can be confirmed from discharge colour. Pregnancy testing and clinical assessment may be needed. Can I wait because the blood looks old? Do not rely on that. Pain, pregnancy, postnatal symptoms, fever, heavy bleeding and bleeding after menopause change what assessment is needed. Should I wash inside the vagina to clear it? No. Internal washing can irritate the area and does not treat the underlying cause.

title: White patches on the penis: could it be vitiligo?
description: Vitiligo causes pigment loss, but other conditions can also make genital skin look pale. An examination helps distinguish them.
body: A pale patch on the penis can be worrying, particularly when it is new. Vitiligo is one possible explanation, but not every white area is vitiligo. The texture of the skin, associated symptoms and changes over time help a clinician decide what is happening. What vitiligo does to the skin Vitiligo develops when pigment-producing cells stop functioning or are lost, leaving areas with little or no melanin. The affected skin may look much lighter than surrounding skin or white. The condition can involve genital skin and other areas of the body. The patches are usually smooth rather than scarred or ulcerated. Hair within an affected area can also lose colour. Some people have only a limited area involved, while others develop more widespread patches; the course is difficult to predict. Vitiligo is not an infection and cannot be passed to a partner. Pigment loss itself does not usually interfere with erections, urination or fertility. Pain, tightness, ulcers or urinary symptoms therefore deserve assessment rather than being attributed to the colour change. Vitiligo can start at any age, often in childhood or young adulthood. Common sites include the face, neck, hands and skin folds, and it may also affect pigment around body openings or inside the mouth. Genital patches can involve different surfaces, so their location alone does not establish the diagnosis. A small focal area differs from widespread non-segmental vitiligo, which often appears on both sides of the body. Segmental vitiligo is usually limited to one area or side. These patterns help describe the condition but cannot predict exactly how it will develop. Why an examination matters Lichen sclerosus is an important alternative diagnosis. On the penis it can affect the foreskin or glans and may cause whitening, soreness, cracks, scarring or a tight foreskin. It has also been called balanitis xerotica obliterans, or BXO. Unlike uncomplicated pigment loss, lichen sclerosus may affect the urinary opening and needs treatment and follow-up. Some people have few symptoms initially, so the absence of pain does not establish vitiligo. Inflammation, a previous rash or injury, and other skin disorders can also change pigmentation. An examination may identify whether a mark is true pigment loss, inflamed tissue, scale or another kind of lesion. Do not diagnose it by matching an online photograph. Seek prompt assessment for persistent sores, bleeding, a new lump, progressive tightening or difficulty passing urine. Inability to urinate, or a retracted foreskin trapped behind a swollen glans, needs urgent medical care. Do not force a tight foreskin back. What may happen at the appointment A clinician will ask when the patch appeared, whether it is changing, and whether similar patches occur elsewhere. Mention any pain, itching, sexual-health concerns, treatments tried and family history of vitiligo or autoimmune disease. A dermatologist may examine the area with a Wood’s lamp to make pigment differences clearer. This brief diagnostic examination is different from a course of ultraviolet treatment. A biopsy is not routinely needed for a typical vitiligo patch, but may be advised if the diagnosis is uncertain or there is a concerning change. Testing for infection is considered when the symptoms or examination suggest it. Vitiligo can be associated with autoimmune conditions, especially thyroid disease. A clinician may recommend thyroid testing or other assessment according to the history and local guidance. There is no single blood test that confirms vitiligo. Mention new eye pain, light sensitivity or vision changes. Vitiligo can be associated with eye inflammation, but a visual symptom should not simply be attributed to loss of pigment; it needs its own assessment. Family history is a risk factor, not a prediction The most common form of vitiligo involves an immune response against pigment cells. Genes and other factors contribute, and having an affected relative increases the chance of developing it. This is not a simple rule that every parent passes on to a child. Many people with vitiligo have no known family history, and a family history cannot predict exactly where patches will appear or whether they will spread. Vitiligo does not automatically mean that you have another autoimmune disease. Discuss new symptoms such as unexplained fatigue or changes in weight with a clinician rather than assuming a connection. Treatment is a personal decision after diagnosis Once vitiligo is confirmed, choosing observation is reasonable if the patches do not bother you. Treatment can aim to slow progression or restore some pigment, but there is no guaranteed cure and colour may change again after treatment ends. A dermatologist may consider a topical medicine. Corticosteroids need particular care on thin genital skin because the wrong strength or prolonged unsupervised use can cause harm. Tacrolimus or pimecrolimus may be used in selected circumstances; their licensing varies, and temporary burning or irritation can occur. Small reports of successful treatment do not prove that one cream will reliably restore penile pigment. Ask about the evidence for this particular location, the chance of benefit and when to stop or review treatment. Newer prescription options are available for some forms of vitiligo, but a product’s general approval does not establish suitability for every genital surface. Treatment choice should account for the exact site, your age, medical history and local prescribing rules. Do not apply general light-therapy advice to the penis Phototherapy can help vitiligo on selected areas of the body, but genital skin requires special protection. Routine narrowband UVB guidance calls for covering male genitalia during treatment. Do not deliberately expose the penis to tanning beds, home UV lamps or extra sunlight to try to restore colour. Any exceptional consideration of a targeted procedure belongs with an experienced specialist, with a clear explanation of evidence and risks. Skin grafting and other pigment-restoring procedures are reserved for carefully selected cases of stable vitiligo and are not routine treatment for a genital patch. Circumcision should not be presented as a standard cure for vitiligo; its role in a scarring foreskin condition such as lichen sclerosus is a separate clinical question. Make room for the emotional impact A change in genital appearance can affect confidence or intimacy even when it does not impair physical function. You do not have to dismiss that concern or pursue treatment to satisfy someone else’s expectations. If helpful, explain to a partner that confirmed vitiligo is a pigment condition and is not contagious. Counselling or a reputable support group may help with anxiety or body-image concerns. Avoid bleaching agents, harsh cosmetic products and unproven remedies on genital skin. Return for review if a previously smooth patch becomes painful, thickened, ulcerated or otherwise changes. White patches need a diagnosis; vitiligo is only one possibility. Vitiligo is not contagious and usually changes colour rather than function. Lichen sclerosus can cause whitening with scarring or tightness. Genital treatments need specialist advice and realistic expectations. Do not expose genital skin to UV light as a home treatment. Can my partner catch vitiligo? No. Confirmed vitiligo is not an infection. A new undiagnosed patch still deserves assessment. Does everyone need a biopsy? No. Typical vitiligo is often diagnosed clinically. A biopsy may help when the diagnosis is uncertain or a lesion looks concerning. Is circumcision a standard treatment for penile vitiligo? No. Circumcision may be advised for certain foreskin problems, but that is different from treating pigment loss alone.

title: Why nipples and areolas can look darker
description: Explore hormonal and skin-related causes of darker areolas, the symptoms that need checking, and why colour alone cannot diagnose pregnancy or diabetes.
body: Nipple and areola colour can change through life, particularly during puberty and pregnancy. The useful questions are whether a change is new, whether it affects both sides, and whether pain, a rash, a lump or a change in skin texture accompanies it. Start with your own normal appearance The nipple is the central part of the breast, while the areola is the surrounding area of more pigmented skin. People often say “dark nipples” when they mean a change in the areola. Shape, size and colour differ widely between people, and there is no single colour that represents a healthy breast. A gradual change on both sides around a hormonal transition can have an ordinary explanation. A sudden, one-sided or persistent unexplained change deserves an examination, particularly when skin texture or other symptoms change too. Comparing your current appearance with your own usual pattern is more useful than comparing it with someone else’s. Puberty brings several breast changes During puberty, hormonal changes support breast development, including growth of glandular tissue and changes in breast fat, the nipple and areola. Areolas can become larger or darker as this happens. The two breasts may not develop at exactly the same pace. Breast appearance is not permanently fixed when puberty ends. Menstrual hormones, pregnancy, lactation, medicines and ageing can bring later changes. A change that fits development still should not be used to explain away a distinct lump, a persistent sore or another new symptom. Ask for an assessment if you are uncertain about what you are noticing. Menstrual changes and premenstrual symptoms Estrogen and progesterone fluctuate through the menstrual cycle. Breasts may feel fuller, swollen or tender before a period. Some people notice colour differences, but areola shade is not a reliable way to identify ovulation, predict the exact day of a period or confirm that hormone levels are normal. Premenstrual symptoms can include acne, fatigue, bloating, constipation or diarrhoea, headache or backache, muscle or joint aches, appetite changes and cravings. Others notice trouble concentrating, irritability, anxiety, low mood or mood swings. The timing and effect on everyday life matter more than a list of isolated symptoms. Symptoms linked to the cycle usually improve after menstruation begins. When premenstrual symptoms need support Keep a daily record across at least two or three cycles if symptoms repeatedly affect work, relationships or daily routines. A clinician can assess whether the pattern fits premenstrual syndrome, premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), or another condition that worsens before a period. Symptoms throughout the month may need a different explanation. PMDD involves substantial symptoms, especially mood symptoms, and is treatable. It is not diagnosed from nipple colour or from simply feeling emotional before a period. Seek urgent support if low mood includes thoughts of harming yourself. Even less severe recurring symptoms are worth discussing when they interfere with your comfort or routines. Hormonal contraception and pigmentation The combined contraceptive pill contains estrogen and a progestogen; progestogen-only pills have a different formulation. Hormonal contraception can be associated with pigmentation changes. Melasma, for example, commonly produces darker patches on the face and sometimes elsewhere, but every darker areola should not automatically be labelled melasma. If a change begins after a new pill or another medicine, note the timing and discuss it with the prescriber. Pigmentation may lessen when a trigger is removed, but this is not guaranteed or always immediate. Switching to a progestogen-only pill is not a proven universal solution. Plan any change with appropriate pregnancy protection rather than abruptly stopping contraception because of colour alone. Separate pill side effects from warning signs Spotting or breakthrough bleeding can occur after starting the combined pill. Headache, nausea and breast tenderness are also reported, although a symptom occurring while taking a pill is not proof that the pill caused it. Blood pressure can rise in some people, which is one reason monitoring and suitability checks matter. Persistent, troublesome or unusually heavy bleeding needs advice.
