Severe chest pain, sudden breathlessness, a painful swollen leg, a severe new headache, major visual changes, collapse or severe abdominal pain should not be treated as routine adjustment. Seek urgent medical care, and emergency help for severe or sudden symptoms. A new breast lump needs a clinical assessment too; it should not be attributed to contraception without examination. Pregnancy can darken and enlarge the areolas Pregnancy hormones change the breasts as milk-producing tissue develops. Tenderness, fullness and darker or larger areolas are common. Colostrum, the early milk, can be made during pregnancy, and some people notice leakage before birth while others do not. Neither leakage nor its absence reliably predicts later milk supply. Pregnancy can also bring melasma on the face and occasionally the neck or arms. Pigmentation may fade after birth, but not everyone returns to exactly the previous shade. Colour changes alone do not confirm pregnancy, show the baby’s sex or establish that a pregnancy is progressing normally. Use a test when pregnancy is possible A missed period can be an early clue, particularly if cycles are usually regular. Nausea with or without vomiting, fatigue, increased urination, mood changes, bloating and constipation can also occur. These overlap with other conditions and menstrual symptoms, so the combination does not replace a pregnancy test. Follow the timing instructions on a home test and repeat or seek advice if it is negative but your period remains absent and pregnancy is still possible. Arrange pregnancy care after a positive result. Light spotting is sometimes described as implantation bleeding, but appearance cannot prove its cause. Seek advice for bleeding or pain in pregnancy; severe pain, fainting or heavy bleeding needs urgent assessment. After birth and during breastfeeding Areolas may remain darker after birth whether or not you breastfeed. The suggestion that darker areolas help a newborn locate the breast is a proposed explanation, not a test of a baby’s feeding ability and not a reason to change the skin’s colour. Milk transfer is assessed through feeding behaviour, growth and other clinical signs. As milk volume increases in the early days, fullness, leaking and temporary tenderness can occur. Persistent nipple pain, damaged skin or difficulty attaching the baby needs skilled feeding support rather than an instruction simply to endure it. Colour may gradually lighten after pregnancy or weaning, or some difference may remain. A hot, painful breast is a separate issue Warmth, swelling, pain, a tender area or flu-like symptoms can indicate mastitis. Redness may be less obvious on darker skin. Do not explain these symptoms as ordinary pregnancy pigmentation. Seek feeding support and medical advice if symptoms worsen, you feel unwell or they are not improving with initial care. Breast inflammation is not always bacterial, so antibiotics are not required for every episode. Continue feeding according to your baby’s needs if able, and avoid deep massage or repeated pumping to “empty” the breast. A suspected abscess needs professional assessment and may need drainage; an ordinary painful area or narrowed duct should not be punctured or squeezed at home. Dark, thickened skin and possible diabetes Acanthosis nigricans causes darker skin that also feels thick or velvety, often at the neck, armpits or groin. Similar changes can occur elsewhere, including around the areola, but an isolated flat colour change is not enough to diagnose it. It may be associated with insulin resistance, a medicine or another cause, and some people have no related illness. Tell a clinician about increased thirst or urination, unusual hunger, unexplained weight loss, tiredness, blurred vision, recurrent infections or slow wound healing. These symptoms can occur with diabetes, but testing is needed. Irritability is nonspecific and should not be used as a diagnostic clue on its own. Treating an underlying cause may help the skin; vigorous scrubbing will not remove the condition. When to arrange a breast or skin examination Have a new persistent or unexplained change checked, particularly on one side. Mention a lump, new nipple inversion, spontaneous or blood-stained discharge, dimpling, a changing focal spot, or skin that is scaly, crusted, bleeding or not healing. Rarely, a persistent nipple-centred rash is Paget’s disease, which is associated with breast cancer. Ordinary even darkening is a different pattern, but self-diagnosis is unreliable. Avoid bleaching products, harsh acids or abrasive scrubs on nipples and areolas. During breastfeeding, products there can contact the baby’s mouth, so check suitability first. Record when the change began, one or both sides, new medicines and any pain, fever or rash. These details help the appointment; a new symptom should not wait for the next routine screening invitation. There is no single normal nipple or areola colour. Puberty, pregnancy and medicines can change pigmentation. Colour is not a reliable pregnancy, ovulation or milk-supply test. Thick velvety skin and systemic symptoms warrant assessment. New one-sided changes, rash, discharge, pain or a lump should be checked. Are the nipple and areola the same thing? No. The nipple is the central structure, and the areola is the surrounding pigmented skin. A change described as darker nipples often mainly affects the areola. Do darker nipples always mean pregnancy? No. Normal variation, hormonal changes and other factors can affect colour. Use a pregnancy test at the appropriate time if pregnancy is possible, and seek advice if uncertainty remains. Can areola colour tell me when I ovulate? No. It is not a validated marker of ovulation or a reliable method of contraception. Menstrual breast changes can occur, but colour cannot establish an exact fertile day. Could severe symptoms before my period be PMDD? Possibly, but the diagnosis depends on the pattern, symptom combination and effect on life. Keep a daily record and discuss it with a clinician. Colour changes do not diagnose PMDD. Should I stop the pill if the skin becomes darker? Discuss the timing and alternatives with your prescriber. Do not stop contraception without a plan if you want to avoid pregnancy. Changing to a different hormone formulation does not guarantee that pigmentation will disappear. Will the colour definitely return after breastfeeding? It may lighten, but lasting differences are possible. Darker areolas after birth can occur even without breastfeeding. New focal or symptomatic changes still deserve assessment. Does darker skin mean I will make more milk? No. Colour and antenatal leaking do not predict milk supply. Feeding assessment, your baby’s growth and milk-transfer signs are more useful than the shade of the areola. Does mastitis always need antibiotics? No. Inflammation is not always a bacterial infection. Worsening symptoms or feeling unwell needs assessment so a clinician can decide whether antibiotics or investigation for an abscess is needed. Does darker skin around the nipple mean diabetes? No. Acanthosis nigricans usually changes texture as well as colour, and it has several possible causes. A clinician may recommend blood tests, especially with thirst, frequent urination or other symptoms. Can I use a skin-lightening product on the area? Avoid self-treating nipples or areolas with bleaching agents, harsh acids or scrubs. First establish why the skin changed, and check any product carefully during breastfeeding because the baby may ingest it.

title: Penile pain: possible causes and when to get help
description: Pain can arise from irritation, infection, injury or a foreskin problem. Some patterns need emergency care rather than a cream or a routine appointment.
body: Pain may affect the tip, shaft or foreskin of the penis. It can occur while passing urine, during an erection, after an injury or without an obvious trigger. The location and timing help a clinician investigate, but they do not establish the cause on their own. Persistent or unexplained pain deserves an examination. Recognise an emergency Go to emergency care for a prolonged erection that is not settling and has lasted around 3 to 4 hours. Seek help sooner for severe pain, or according to an individual plan after an erection injection. With sickle cell disease, a painful erection lasting more than an hour needs emergency assessment. Do not use sex, an ice pack or an extra medicine as a reason to delay care. A foreskin pulled behind the head of the penis that becomes stuck there is paraphimosis. This can restrict blood flow even if urine still passes. Seek emergency treatment; do not repeatedly pull or squeeze it or try to cut the skin. A sudden bending injury to an erect penis, especially with a pop, rapid loss of erection, bruising or swelling, may be a penile fracture. It is a tissue tear, not a broken bone, and needs urgent hospital assessment. Inability to pass urine, severe genital injury, or rapidly worsening swelling with fever or severe illness also needs urgent care. Sudden severe testicular pain is a separate emergency even when discomfort seems to spread towards the penis. Priapism may occur without sexual desire. Causes can include sickle cell disease or other blood disorders, some antidepressants and erection medicines, recreational drugs, and injury. Mental illness itself should not simply be labelled the cause. In hospital, treatment may include numbing the area, draining trapped blood with a needle, medicines or a procedure; these are treatments for trained clinicians, not home techniques. Irritation and balanitis Balanitis means inflammation of the head of the penis. When the foreskin is inflamed as well, the term balanoposthitis may be used. Infection is one possible cause, but soaps, fragranced products, friction and skin conditions can also contribute. The area may feel sore or itchy, look swollen, or develop discharge. Recurrent episodes sometimes prompt testing for contributing conditions such as diabetes. It is not helpful to assume that every episode means poor hygiene or an STI. Treatment depends on the cause. A clinician may recommend a particular cream or medicine; an antifungal, antibiotic and steroid are not interchangeable treatments for every rash. Avoid repeatedly trying combination creams without a diagnosis. Pain when urinating or discharge Urethritis is inflammation of the tube through which urine leaves the body. Gonorrhoea, chlamydia and other infections can cause it, although irritation or injury can also be responsible. A urinary tract infection can produce overlapping symptoms. Arrange prompt assessment for burning urine, discharge or persistent irritation at the opening. In an adult with a penis, suspected UTI should be medically assessed rather than treated solely with home remedies. Fever, shaking chills, back pain or worsening illness make the need more urgent. An ordinary UTI is not the same as an STI and does not establish that a partner transmitted an infection. Urine tests and, where indicated, STI tests help distinguish causes. If an STI is diagnosed, follow treatment and partner-testing advice. Avoid sexual contact for the period specified by the clinic, including until relevant treatment is complete. Condoms reduce many risks but do not cover every area where a skin infection can spread. Sores or skin lesions from herpes, syphilis or genital warts can also be uncomfortable, although some STIs cause little or no pain. Antibiotics treat selected bacterial infections such as gonorrhoea, chlamydia and syphilis; antiviral medicines can shorten or suppress herpes episodes. The test result and diagnosis determine which treatment and partner advice apply. A urinary blockage, an enlarged prostate, immune suppression and urinary tract abnormalities can raise the chance of a UTI. Bacteria introduced during sexual activity may contribute, including after anal contact, but an ordinary UTI is not proof of a sexually transmitted infection. A tight foreskin needs age-appropriate care A foreskin that does not yet retract can be normal in a young child. Never force it back for cleaning or try to stretch it through pain. Clean the outside gently. In adults, a newly tight, scarred or painful foreskin needs assessment. Prescribed treatment may include a steroid cream and carefully explained gentle movement, or surgery in selected cases. Circumcision is not automatically required for every episode of soreness. If a foreskin retracts comfortably, gently wash and dry underneath and return it to cover the head afterwards. Stop if movement hurts or the skin tears. Painful erections and a new curve Peyronie’s disease involves scar tissue in the covering around erectile tissue. It can cause a new curve, an indentation or shortening, painful erections and difficulty with intercourse. It is different from a small lifelong curve that causes no problem. A urologist considers whether the condition is changing or stable, its effect on function, and your preferences. Observation, medicines, traction or specialist procedures may be considered in appropriate cases. Surgery is generally reserved for stable disease with significant difficulties. Do not try to straighten the penis forcibly or inject a plaque yourself. A treatment that changes curvature does not necessarily restore the previous length or solve every cause of sexual pain. Peyronie’s disease may follow repeated minor bending injuries or a more obvious injury, although no event is remembered in many cases. A tendency to unusual scar formation, connective-tissue disorders and family history may be relevant. Specialist injections into a plaque are an option for selected patients, while surgery can correct curvature in appropriate stable disease; neither is a universal way to remove all scar tissue. Persistent sores or skin changes need review Penile cancer is uncommon, and many sores have other causes. Nevertheless, a persistent growth, ulcer, unexplained bleeding or changing patch needs examination. Do not repeatedly mask it with a cream or wait for it to become painful. A clinician may use swabs, urine tests, blood tests, imaging or occasionally a biopsy according to the findings. There is no single treatment for all penile pain, and an examination should guide the next step. Risk factors for penile cancer include certain HPV infections, smoking, a scarred or tight foreskin and immune suppression. Previous PUVA treatment for psoriasis is a specific risk factor; this does not mean every psoriasis treatment carries the same risk. It is more common after age 50, but a concerning lesion needs assessment at any age. Cancer treatment may involve surgery, radiotherapy or medicines according to its type and extent. While arranging care Pause activities that provoke pain. Use lukewarm water for gentle washing, pat dry, and avoid new fragranced products or vigorous scrubbing. Do not insert objects into the urethra or use constricting devices on a sore or swollen penis. Tell the clinician about the onset, any injury, changes in erections or urine, new products, sexual exposures and medicines, including erection treatments. You can ask for a chaperone. Clear information helps the team provide appropriate care without judging you. Trauma may follow a road accident, burn, forceful bending during sex, a tight ring or another constricting device, or an object placed into the urethra. Communicate about comfortable movement and stop when it hurts. Condoms, appropriate HPV vaccination and avoiding sexual contact during active infectious lesions can reduce some risks, while cleaning only as far as the foreskin comfortably retracts protects the skin. A prolonged erection, trapped foreskin or suspected penile fracture needs emergency care. Balanitis is inflammation and is not always an infection. Urinary symptoms and discharge need assessment; a UTI and an STI are different diagnoses. Never force a child’s foreskin back. Persistent pain, a new curve or a non-healing skin change should be examined. Can penile pain be caused by soap? Yes. Irritation is possible, but persistent symptoms or swelling should be assessed rather than assumed to be an allergy. Is a trapped foreskin urgent if I can still urinate? Yes. Paraphimosis can compromise blood flow before urination stops. Does every painful or tight foreskin need circumcision? No. Age, symptoms and the cause determine whether observation, prescribed medicine or a procedure is appropriate.

title: Red spots or a rash on the penis: causes and next steps
description: Compare irritation, eczema, psoriasis and infections without self-diagnosing from colour, and understand which treatments need assessment.
body: A new spot or rash on the penis can be worrying, but many different conditions can look similar. Gentle care and a proper assessment are more useful than assuming an STI or trying several creams. New sores, persistent changes or severe symptoms should be checked. A colour chart cannot diagnose a genital rash Red spots on the penis can come from irritation, an inflammatory skin condition or an infection. Their appearance can overlap, and redness may look darker, purple or less obvious on different skin tones. Some minor irritation settles after its trigger is removed, but there is no reliable rule that a harmless rash must disappear within one or two days. Location, number of spots, itching, pain, blisters, discharge and recent exposures all help, but none is enough on its own. A new ulcer or blister, persistent rash or possible sexual exposure deserves assessment. Avoid assuming that the appearance proves an STI, poor hygiene or a partner’s behaviour. An examination and the right tests are more useful than matching a photograph. Genital herpes can cause painful blisters or ulcers Herpes can affect the penis, scrotum, nearby genital skin, buttocks or thighs. Oral and genital infection can be linked through oral sex. Both HSV-1 and HSV-2 can cause genital herpes; HSV-1 is not simply a rare exception. Some infections produce very mild or unnoticed symptoms, while others cause tingling, itching, pain and blisters that open into sores. A sore may weep or bleed when irritated, but lasting scarring is not an expected feature of every outbreak. A clinician may swab a fresh lesion to confirm the cause and virus type. Antiviral medicines such as aciclovir or valaciclovir can shorten or suppress episodes; they do not eliminate the virus from the body. Herpes can pass on even without a visible sore. Avoid sexual contact during symptoms, discuss partner protection and use barriers as advised. Condoms and suppressive treatment can reduce risk, but neither guarantees that transmission will never occur. Seek timely care for a first episode rather than waiting for every blister to resolve before testing. Syphilis can begin with a sore that is easy to miss Syphilis is caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum. An early genital sore is often painless, though appearance varies and there may be more than one. It can heal even when infection remains. Later features may include a rash elsewhere, swollen lymph nodes, headache or fever; not everyone develops the same sequence. Untreated infection can eventually damage the nervous system or other organs, sometimes causing weakness or paralysis, vision or hearing problems. A genital sore does not mean these complications are already present, but it is a reason to arrange testing promptly. A particular fever threshold is not needed before asking for help. Treatment requires the right antibiotic for the stage and circumstances. Benzathine penicillin is central to treatment; doxycycline or ceftriaxone may be used in selected situations under clinical guidance, and are not interchangeable self-treatment choices. Follow-up blood tests track response, but some tests can remain positive after successful treatment. NHS guidance advises no vaginal, anal or oral sex until two weeks after both you and your partner have finished treatment; follow the treating service’s instructions and partner-care plan. Scabies causes an itchy rash from mites in the skin Scabies spreads through close skin contact, including but not limited to sexual contact. Itching is often worse at night. Small bumps, scratch marks, dry or irritated skin and fine burrow lines can occur, sometimes with genital nodules or small blisters. The rest of the body and whether close contacts are itchy help the assessment. A clinician may recommend a treatment such as permethrin, with clear instructions on where to apply it and whether to repeat it. Crotamiton is another named option in some settings, but treatment failures are more frequent and suitability differs by age. Do not improvise the amount or apply only to visible penile spots when the plan requires broader treatment. Household and close contacts usually need coordinated treatment, even if symptoms have not yet appeared. Wash and heat-dry recently used clothes, towels and bedding as instructed, or bag items that cannot be washed for the advised interval. Avoid close skin or sexual contact until the treatment plan is completed. Persistent itching can outlast treatment, but new lesions or ongoing symptoms should be reviewed. Molluscum contagiosum needs special consideration on the genitals Molluscum is caused by a poxvirus and can spread through skin contact or shared items such as towels. It usually forms small smooth raised bumps, often with a central dip. They can become pink, itchy or inflamed, especially if scratched. Picking or shaving over them can spread the infection to more skin. Many cases elsewhere on the body clear without treatment, but CDC guidance recommends clinical assessment and usually treatment for genital lesions. Similar-looking bumps can have other causes. A clinician may consider a topical treatment, freezing, curettage with a small instrument or, in selected cases, laser treatment. The choice depends on the lesions and the risk of pain or scarring. Do not squeeze them or use a home wart-removal chemical on genital skin. Balanitis means inflammation of the head of the penis Balanitis can cause soreness, swelling, itching or red patches on the glans. There may be pain with urination, discharge or material beneath the foreskin, an unpleasant smell or difficulty retracting the foreskin. It is more common when a foreskin is present, but that does not mean every case is caused by inadequate washing. Irritants, yeast, other infections and conditions such as diabetes can contribute. Wash gently with water or a suitable emollient soap substitute and dry without rubbing. Retract an adult foreskin only as far as it moves comfortably and return it to its normal position afterwards. Do not force a child’s attached foreskin back. Treatment depends on the cause: a mild steroid such as hydrocortisone, an antifungal such as clotrimazole or an antibiotic may be appropriate in different situations. Metronidazole is used for selected bacterial causes, not every red or sore penis. Recurrent episodes need review. A retracted foreskin stuck behind a swollen glans, or inability to pass urine, needs urgent care. Contact dermatitis can follow a new product or repeated irritation Soaps, detergents, fragranced products, lubricants, condoms or other substances may irritate the skin or trigger an allergy. Contact dermatitis can produce itching, swelling, dryness, scaling or blisters. Fluid from a blister is not automatically pus; yellow discharge, increasing pain, spreading redness or fever can suggest an additional infection. Stop the suspected trigger and use gentle skin care. A cool damp cloth may ease discomfort. A lukewarm bath can be soothing, but avoid hot water; a colloidal-oatmeal product is optional and should be stopped if it irritates. You do not need to add several new products while trying to identify the cause. An oral antihistamine such as diphenhydramine may sometimes ease itching or help sleep, but it can cause drowsiness and does not remove the dermatitis trigger. Ask a pharmacist or clinician whether it is suitable rather than using it automatically. Persistent, widespread, blistering or infected-looking symptoms need assessment and sometimes a prescribed anti-inflammatory treatment. Candida thrush is different from a sexually transmitted infection Candida is a yeast that can overgrow and cause redness, burning or itching around the glans and foreskin. White material, an unpleasant smell or discomfort retracting the foreskin may occur. These signs overlap with other causes of balanitis, so a first episode or an uncertain diagnosis should be checked. Thrush is not classed as an STI and is not proof of poor hygiene. It may be triggered by irritation, antibiotics, poorly controlled diabetes or immune-system changes; sex can sometimes trigger or transmit it. Gentle washing, drying and loose comfortable underwear can reduce irritation, but do not assume hygiene alone will clear a persistent infection. Topical clotrimazole is one treatment for genital thrush; oral treatment, when appropriate, generally uses a different medicine such as fluconazole after checking suitability. Oral clotrimazole lozenges are not a substitute for genital treatment. Avoid sex if painful and ask whether an antifungal cream affects condoms or diaphragms. Repeated episodes need review rather than repeated unsupervised courses. Jock itch usually affects the groin rather than the penis Tinea cruris, or jock itch, is a dermatophyte fungal infection. It often starts in a groin fold and spreads toward the inner thigh, with itching and a scaly edge. Sweat, warm moist skin, tight clothing or fungus elsewhere on the feet or nails can contribute. It is not simply a measure of how often someone washes. The penis and scrotum are usually spared, which makes jock itch a poor automatic explanation for spots limited to the penis. A skin scraping may help when the diagnosis is uncertain. A topical antifungal such as clotrimazole may be appropriate; extensive or resistant disease needs a clinician’s plan. Keep the area dry and do not use a steroid alone to suppress a rash that could be fungal. Genital eczema needs treatment suited to sensitive skin Atopic eczema involves a vulnerable skin barrier and inflammation, influenced by inherited and environmental factors. Stress, heat, sweat, friction and contact irritants can aggravate it. Genital eczema may be itchy, dry, scaly, sore or cracked. Blistering, crusting or oozing can occur, but pus or fever should not be assumed to be ordinary eczema. Use a plain suitable emollient and avoid fragranced products. A cool compress may help. Aloe vera or a lotion marketed as natural is not automatically suitable and can itself irritate. The skin in this area absorbs topical steroids readily, so use only the strength and schedule prescribed for that site, such as an appropriate short course of hydrocortisone. A clinician may choose a non-steroid treatment such as pimecrolimus in selected cases. Mupirocin is an antibiotic for an identified bacterial problem, not routine eczema care. An injected medicine such as dupilumab is specialist treatment for selected more significant atopic disease, not the usual first step for an unexplained penile rash. If the diagnosis or response is uncertain, ask for dermatology review. Genital psoriasis can look smoother than psoriasis elsewhere Psoriasis is an immune-mediated inflammatory condition and is not contagious or an STI. On genital skin it may appear as well-defined inflamed patches with less scale than on other areas. Itching, burning, soreness, cracks or bleeding can occur. Thickened or pitted nails and stiff or swollen joints are useful additional symptoms to mention. Treatment needs to be chosen for this sensitive location. A clinician may prescribe a mild topical steroid or another local anti-inflammatory medicine. Do not transfer a strong scalp or body treatment to the genitals without checking. If symptoms remain troublesome, a dermatologist can consider the wider psoriasis picture and adjust treatment. Stronger skin treatments are not interchangeable home remedies Systemic psoriasis medicines may include a retinoid such as acitretin or a biologic such as adalimumab for selected patients. They require specialist selection and monitoring; listing them does not mean they are appropriate for isolated red spots. The best choice depends on the diagnosis, overall disease and other health factors. Direct genital phototherapy should not be copied from advice for psoriasis elsewhere. The American Academy of Dermatology warns that UV or laser treatment of this area can increase genital cancer risk. Genital skin may need shielding during treatment of other areas. Ask the dermatologist to specify exactly where any cream or light treatment is intended to be used. While waiting for assessment, reduce friction and avoid trial-and-error treatment Wash gently, pat dry, choose comfortable loose clothing and stop a recently introduced irritating product. Avoid scratching, squeezing, shaving over lesions or scrubbing the area to make it look cleaner. A short record of the onset, symptoms, exposures and products can help the appointment. Avoid sexual contact while you have unexplained sores, blisters or a possible transmissible infection, and ask the clinic when it is appropriate to resume. Do not share leftover antibiotics, strong steroid creams or mixed antifungal-steroid products. Treatments that relieve one condition can obscure or worsen another, so repeated experimentation can make diagnosis harder. Seek care for new sores, persistent changes or severe symptoms A sexual-health clinic, primary-care clinician or dermatologist can examine the skin and arrange appropriate tests. Depending on the findings, these may include a swab of a fresh sore, blood tests for syphilis, fungal testing or a biopsy of a persistent atypical lesion. Fever and fatigue are nonspecific and do not by themselves identify an STI. Arrange prompt assessment for a new ulcer, discharge, significant pain, an exposure concern or a rash that does not settle. An ongoing bleeding patch, growth or non-healing sore should not be repeatedly labelled irritation without review. Severe swelling, rapidly worsening pain, fever with marked illness, a trapped retracted foreskin or inability to urinate needs urgent care. There is no need to wait until itching or pain becomes unbearable. Genital rashes have infectious and noninfectious causes. HSV-1 and HSV-2 can both cause genital herpes. Thrush is not classified as an STI, and jock itch usually spares the penis. Genital skin needs its own eczema or psoriasis treatment plan. Persistent sores or lumps require assessment even when irritation seems plausible. Can I identify the cause from a red-spot chart? No. Appearance overlaps between conditions and varies with skin tone. History, examination and sometimes tests are needed. Can HSV-1 cause genital herpes? Yes. Both HSV-1 and HSV-2 can cause genital infection, including transmission through oral sex. Do herpes antivirals guarantee I cannot pass it on? No. Treatment and barriers can reduce risk, but transmission is still possible, including without visible sores. Must my syphilis blood test become negative before sex resumes? Not necessarily; some tests stay positive after successful treatment. Follow your clinic’s treatment and partner plan. NHS guidance advises waiting two weeks after both partners finish treatment. Should only the itchy person be treated for scabies? No. Household and close contacts usually need treatment at the same time to reduce reinfection. Can I leave genital molluscum without getting it checked? Get an assessment. Unlike many cases elsewhere on the body, genital lesions usually need treatment and confirmation of the diagnosis. Is genital thrush proof of an STI or poor hygiene? No. Candida can overgrow for several reasons, including antibiotics, irritation, diabetes or immune changes. Is a rash only on the penis probably jock itch? Not automatically. Tinea cruris usually affects the groin and inner thighs and spares the penis and scrotum. Can I use my strong psoriasis cream or UV lamp on genital skin? No. Use only a plan intended for that area. Strong products can injure sensitive skin, and direct genital phototherapy carries additional risk. What should I do if the foreskin gets stuck behind a swollen glans? Seek urgent medical care. A trapped retracted foreskin is different from ordinary irritation and should not be left to settle on its own.

title: Does the size of an ovarian cyst determine treatment?
description: How cyst type, ultrasound appearance, symptoms and life stage affect monitoring or surgery, with the limits of common size and growth figures.
body: Size matters when an ovarian cyst is assessed, but it is only one part of the decision. A measurement makes most sense alongside the scan appearance, the type of cyst suspected and how you are feeling. Read the measurement alongside the scan description An ovarian cyst is a sac on or within an ovary. Some contain clear fluid; others contain blood, thicker material or tissue. Most are benign, particularly before menopause, but the word cyst alone does not tell you which type is present. A report may give several dimensions in millimetres or centimetres. Ten millimetres equals one centimetre, so a measurement of 50 mm is 5 cm. Ask about both the largest dimension and the appearance: a thin-walled, fluid-only cyst is different from a mass with solid components. Size contributes to the decision, together with symptoms, changes over time, age, menopausal status and pregnancy or fertility plans. There is no single measurement that automatically proves a cyst is harmless, cancerous or in need of surgery. Functional cysts arise around ovulation A follicle is the small fluid-containing structure in which an egg develops. A follicular cyst can form when the follicle does not release its egg and continues to enlarge. After ovulation, the remaining structure becomes the corpus luteum; fluid or blood can collect within it and form a corpus luteum cyst. These functional cysts are related to the menstrual cycle. Many cause no symptoms and resolve over several weeks or menstrual cycles. They are not the same as dermoids, cystadenomas or endometriomas, which have different origins. A normal follicle near ovulation may measure roughly 2–3 cm. Calling every structure of that size a disease is misleading. Functional cysts are often only a few centimetres, but a larger persistent finding needs its own assessment rather than a presumed functional label. Why a list of typical sizes can mislead Ranges such as 2–5 cm or reports of functional cysts reaching 8–12 cm are not boundaries that diagnose the type. A cyst does not become functional simply because its diameter falls within a quoted range. Its appearance and whether it resolves are also informative. Unit conversions can make a large difference to how a report sounds. Two to five centimetres is about 0.8–2 inches, not two to more than three inches. Use the actual scan measurement and units rather than an approximate comparison found elsewhere. A small suspicious mass can require investigation, while a larger, clearly characterised simple cyst may sometimes be monitored. That does not mean that every simple cyst up to 10 cm can safely be left alone. Dermoid cysts contain different types of tissue An ovarian dermoid, usually a mature cystic teratoma, develops from germ cells and may contain fat, hair or other mature tissues. It is generally benign and can be found during the reproductive years. Its developmental origin does not establish that a visible ovarian cyst has necessarily been present since birth. Some dermoids remain symptom-free for a long time. Larger lesions can cause pressure or contribute to complications such as twisting of the ovary. Occasionally very large dermoids, including those exceeding 15 cm, are reported, but an extreme example is not the expected course for everyone. The scan pattern, symptoms and interval change matter more than comparing your measurement with a photograph or a dramatic case report. Dermoid growth figures need a study attached The often-quoted growth rate of about 1.8 mm a year comes from a 1997 study of small dermoids. It followed 72 people before menopause and 14 after menopause, all with cysts under 6 cm at entry. The premenopausal average was 1.77 mm per year. An average from that selected group is not a forecast for an individual cyst. A later two-case report estimated much faster growth, about 8 and 25 mm per year, after masses became visible on later imaging. Those estimates were based on intervals between scans, including earlier CT studies without a visible mass; they were not continuous measurements of a known cyst. The cases show that a benign dermoid can be considered even when apparent growth is faster. They do not make rapid growth reassuring or remove the need for review. They also do not establish an 8–25 mm yearly range that every dermoid will follow. Cystadenomas can persist and become large Cystadenomas are usually benign ovarian tumours that can contain watery or mucus-like fluid. A fluid-filled one may initially resemble a simple cyst on ultrasound, but unlike many functional cysts, it may persist and enlarge rather than disappear with subsequent cycles. Some are only a few centimetres. Rare examples can grow much larger, including around 30 cm. A measurement of 1–3 cm should not itself be described as very large, and a maximum reported size is not a threshold to wait for before seeking care. Persistent growth is a reason to revisit the assessment. Imaging can suggest the likely type, but definitive classification sometimes requires examination of removed tissue. Endometriomas are linked with endometriosis Endometriosis involves tissue similar to the uterine lining outside its usual location. When it affects an ovary, a cyst containing old, dark blood can develop. This is an endometrioma, sometimes called a chocolate cyst because of its contents. Published estimates often cited in patient information suggest that about 17–44% of people with endometriosis have an endometrioma. The denominator matters: this is not the proportion of all women with an ovarian cyst, and estimates depend on the population studied. Endometriomas vary in size and can be associated with pelvic pain, painful periods, pain during sex or difficulty conceiving. Having one does not by itself mean that pregnancy is impossible. Symptoms may involve pressure, pain or bleeding changes Many cysts are discovered incidentally. When symptoms occur, they can include one-sided lower abdominal pain, a dull ache or sharper discomfort, pelvic pressure, fullness, bloating or visible swelling. Other possible complaints include painful sex, painful or irregular periods, bleeding between periods, needing to urinate more often, or difficulty emptying the bladder or bowels. These symptoms are not unique to ovarian cysts, so an incidental cyst should not automatically be blamed for everything. Mention persistent symptoms, changes in bleeding and any possibility of pregnancy when seeking assessment. The clinician can decide whether examination, ultrasound or other testing is needed. Sudden severe symptoms need urgent assessment A cyst can rupture and cause pain or bleeding. An ovary can also twist around its supporting tissues, a condition called torsion, which can threaten its blood supply. Although these complications are uncommon, a previously reassuring scan should not delay help for new severe symptoms. Seek urgent care for sudden severe pelvic or abdominal pain, especially with nausea, vomiting or fever. Severe pain with fainting, marked weakness or rapid, shallow breathing needs emergency assessment. Do not wait for a routine repeat scan. These symptoms can have other urgent causes too. If pregnancy is possible, say so immediately; having a known cyst does not rule out a pregnancy-related emergency. Size bands are specific to the situation RCOG’s older premenopausal patient leaflet gives examples for painless simple cysts: below 5 cm often needs no treatment, 5–7 cm may be followed by ultrasound, and above 7 cm may prompt additional imaging or surgery. These examples are not a universal operation rule at 5–6 cm. After menopause, the pathway differs. RCOG’s December 2025 update says a simple cyst up to 3 cm, on one side and with a single compartment, does not require routine follow-up. That advice should not be extended to a symptomatic, complex or poorly characterised mass. Your clinician should apply the relevant current local pathway. Ask which features place your cyst in a monitoring or referral category, rather than treating one size band as a substitute for the full assessment. Monitoring and relief of discomfort Watchful waiting is an active plan: it may include a repeat scan to see whether the cyst resolves, changes or persists, together with instructions about symptoms that should prompt earlier contact. The interval depends on the type and circumstances; it is not always exactly one or two cycles. For mild discomfort after assessment, a clinician may suggest acetaminophen, also called paracetamol, or sometimes an anti-inflammatory such as ibuprofen or naproxen. Suitability depends on pregnancy, other medicines and medical history. These are pain-relief options, not cyst-dissolving treatments. Do not assume an over-the-counter anti-inflammatory is safe during pregnancy. The FDA warns against self-use of NSAIDs at around twenty weeks or later. Get individual medicine advice and do not mask escalating pain while postponing assessment. When surgery or hormonal treatment may be discussed Surgery may be considered for a persistent or enlarging cyst, significant symptoms, a complication or features concerning for cancer. Ultrasound can identify suspicious features, but it does not by itself establish the final tissue diagnosis. Many operations use laparoscopy, with small abdominal incisions. An open operation may be recommended for a very large mass or concern about malignancy. Discuss whether the plan is to remove the cyst alone, when an ovary might need removal, and the potential effect on fertility. Endometrioma surgery deserves particular discussion about ovarian reserve. ESHRE does not recommend routinely removing an endometrioma before assisted reproduction solely to improve live-birth chances; pain, access to follicles and other findings may change the decision. Hormonal contraception can sometimes reduce new functional cyst formation, but should not be promised to shrink a cyst already present. A Cochrane review of eight trials found no faster resolution with combined oral contraceptives, a distinction also retained in ASRM guidance. Treatment should match the reason it is being offered. Check whether the measurement is in millimetres or centimetres. Simple-cyst monitoring rules do not apply to every mass. Growth averages and rare giant cysts are not personal predictions. Persistent symptoms and changing scan features deserve review. Birth-control pills do not reliably make existing functional cysts resolve faster. Does a 5 cm cyst automatically need surgery? No. Symptoms, appearance, type and life stage affect the decision as well as size. Is a 2–3 cm follicle always an abnormal cyst? No. A follicle of that size can be part of ovulation; the scan needs clinical interpretation. How many inches is a 2–5 cm measurement? Approximately 0.8–2 inches. The original scan units are the clearest reference. Will every dermoid grow 1.8 mm each year? No. That figure is an average from a selected older study, not an individual forecast. Does rapid growth always mean cancer? No, but it needs assessment. A small case series of benign dermoids does not make all rapidly growing masses safe. Does the 17–44% endometrioma estimate apply to all women? No. It is a reported range among people with endometriosis and varies by study population. Can a small simple cyst after menopause be left without routine scans? In some circumstances, yes. The updated RCOG recommendation applies to a specific simple-cyst pattern; your clinician should confirm that it fits. Can ultrasound prove a mass is cancerous? It can show concerning features and guide referral, but the final diagnosis may require further assessment and tissue examination. Will the contraceptive pill shrink my current functional cyst? It has not been shown to speed resolution. Preventing new cysts is a separate possible purpose. Can I wait for my follow-up if I develop sudden severe pain? No. Seek urgent care, especially with vomiting, fever, weakness or faintness.

title: Burning nipple pain: skin irritation, feeding and other causes
description: How to distinguish common causes of burning nipple pain, get feeding support, avoid harmful home remedies and recognize changes that need medical assessment.
body: Burning nipple pain has several possible causes, and treatment works best when the cause is identified. Friction, dermatitis, feeding injury, vasospasm and inflammation can feel similar, so persistent pain should not automatically be labelled thrush. The pattern of burning helps identify the cause Burning nipple pain can come from the skin, pressure during feeding, changes in blood flow or a problem deeper in the breast. It can affect people who are breastfeeding and those who are not. The sensation alone does not tell you whether an infection is present. Notice whether one or both nipples hurt, whether the pain follows feeding or exercise, and whether there is a rash, crack, discharge or colour change. New products, medicines and changes to a feeding or pumping routine are useful clues. Many causes are treatable, but persistent pain should not be accepted as normal or left for several weeks before asking for help. Pain at every feed, worsening skin damage or a new breast change deserves assessment. Getting help early can prevent repeated injury and make feeding more comfortable. Friction, allergy and skin injury A poorly fitting bra, sports clothing or fabric rubbing during exercise can irritate the nipple. Detergents, fragrances and skin products may cause irritation or contact allergy. Cuts, bites or bruising during sexual activity, sunburn and insect bites are other possible triggers. Reduce the suspected friction or stop a newly introduced product while you arrange advice if needed. Gentle skin care and a comfortable fit are more useful than repeatedly scrubbing the area. Be cautious with aloe vera, essential oils or other remedies: a product described as natural can still irritate damaged skin. A clinician may recommend a topical steroid such as hydrocortisone for an appropriate dermatitis diagnosis, but it should not be a blanket treatment for every unexplained nipple change. Persistent one-sided symptoms, discharge or failure to improve needs another look rather than stronger and stronger creams. Using a prescribed skin treatment while breastfeeding Breastfeeding does not rule out treatment for nipple eczema or dermatitis. A clinician or pharmacist should choose the preparation and explain how much to apply, for how long and how to limit the baby’s direct contact with it. Tell them if your baby was premature or is unwell. Specialist Pharmacy Service advice favours a mild or moderate potency corticosteroid when treatment is needed directly on the nipple or areola. It advises removing the preparation with warm water before a feed and applying it again afterwards. Follow the instructions for the product and your individual situation. Wash your hands after applying medicine and avoid letting the infant touch treated skin elsewhere. Do not use another person’s prescription, a combination cream with unknown ingredients or a topical pain product near the baby’s mouth without checking its suitability. Pregnancy, attachment and pump-related pain Breast tenderness can occur early in pregnancy as well as later when the breasts enlarge. Stretching and sensitivity may contribute to discomfort, but pregnancy should not become an explanation for every new rash, lump or persistent focal pain. During breastfeeding, shallow attachment can compress the nipple and cause burning or cracks. A feed should be assessed as a whole, including positioning, milk transfer and how the nipple looks afterwards. There is no fixed fraction of the areola that every baby must cover because anatomy differs. Ask a midwife, lactation consultant or other skilled supporter to observe a feed if pain continues. If you express milk, have flange fit, suction and session length checked too. Increasing suction or simply practising through repeated painful feeds can keep the same injury going. Vasospasm can cause burning and colour changes Nipple vasospasm occurs when small blood vessels tighten and temporarily reduce blood flow. Pain may feel burning or throbbing and can occur before, during or after feeding. The nipple may turn pale, then purple, blue or red as blood flow changes. Cold can trigger symptoms, and nipple trauma may contribute. Keeping the area comfortably warm and avoiding a sudden cold exposure can help, while attachment or pump problems still need attention. Use gentle warmth rather than a hot pack that could burn sensitive skin. This is one reason that the same compress advice does not fit every problem: cooling an inflamed breast and warming a nipple affected by vasospasm have different purposes. Persistent or severe symptoms need a clinician’s assessment, including whether medicine is appropriate. Burning does not automatically mean thrush Shiny or flaky nipple skin, burning and shooting pain after feeds have often been described as signs of thrush. These symptoms overlap with dermatitis, mechanical injury and vasospasm, however. They do not prove that Candida is the cause or that it has infected tissue deep in the breast. Clinical guidance differs in how suspected nipple yeast problems are approached. The Academy of Breastfeeding Medicine finds no scientific evidence supporting the diagnosis of Candida mastitis. A clinician should assess the parent and, when relevant, the baby’s mouth rather than prescribe repeated antifungal treatment based only on pain. If an infection is diagnosed, follow the specific treatment and feeding instructions. Change damp breast pads and avoid irritating products, but do not apply yogurt to the nipple as treatment. It is not a validated remedy, and washing it off before a feed does not turn it into an evidence-based option. Engorgement and ductal narrowing need gentle care When the breasts become very full, often as milk production increases after birth or feeding patterns change, they may feel tight and painful. Swelling can flatten the nipple and make attachment difficult. Some people instead notice a more localized tender area associated with inflammation and ductal narrowing. Treating the area as a plug that must be crushed or forced out can make matters worse. Avoid deep massage, strong pressure and repeated extra pumping to empty the breast. These actions can increase tissue injury, swelling or oversupply. Turning the baby’s chin toward a lump is not a guaranteed way to resolve inflammation. Continue an appropriate feeding or expressing pattern with skilled support; if necessary, express a small amount for comfort rather than trying to empty completely. A cool compress may help swelling. Avoid excessive heat, and do not rely on a promise that every case will disappear within forty-eight hours. Mastitis can be inflammatory or bacterial Mastitis means inflammation of breast tissue; it is not always a bacterial infection from the beginning. A painful, hot or swollen area may develop, sometimes with fever, chills or flu-like illness. Redness may be less obvious on darker skin, so warmth, pain and how you feel also matter. Rest, fluids, suitable pain relief and a feeding plan may form part of care. Antibiotics are needed for some bacterial cases, rather than automatically for every sore or inflamed breast. A worsening lump or symptoms that do not respond may require assessment for an abscess or another cause. Seek advice promptly if you feel unwell or symptoms are worsening, and if suspected mastitis is not improving within twelve to twenty-four hours of supportive care. Do not stop breastfeeding suddenly without a plan. Mastitis-like symptoms in someone who is not lactating, including a man, also need assessment. Hormones and persistent nipple changes Cyclical breast pain often begins before a period and eases as it ends. Some people describe aching or heaviness; others notice burning. Hormonal medicines can also contribute. A symptom diary may help show a pattern, but discuss medicine changes with the prescriber rather than adjusting the dose yourself. A persistent nipple-centred rash, especially on one side, needs examination. Paget’s disease of the nipple is a rare condition associated with breast cancer that can resemble eczema. Scaling, crusting, bleeding, altered nipple shape or yellow or bloody discharge should not be repeatedly treated at home without a diagnosis. Most nipple pain is not cancer, and these changes do not prove Paget’s disease. They are reasons to have the area assessed. The absence of a noticeable lump or the fact that symptoms briefly improve does not remove that need. Make the next step depend on the cause Seek urgent care for severe illness, rapidly worsening breast pain or swelling, spreading skin changes, or fever with concerning breast symptoms. Arrange an examination for a new lump, bloody discharge, nipple inversion or a persistent rash. These findings deserve attention even when you are not breastfeeding. For painful feeds or cracks, ask for feeding support early. Applying a little expressed milk or changing a pad does not correct an ongoing attachment injury and is not treatment for every infection. The priority is identifying what keeps hurting the skin and whether your baby is transferring enough milk. Before leaving an appointment, ask what diagnosis is most likely, what improvement to expect and when to return if the plan is not working. A review is particularly useful after an unsuccessful cream or antifungal course. You should not have to keep cycling through remedies without an explanation for the pain. Check friction, products, attachment and pump fit. Cold-related burning may be vasospasm. Burning alone does not diagnose Candida. Avoid yogurt, deep massage and pumping repeatedly to empty. Have persistent or changing nipple symptoms examined. Is burning always an infection? No. Skin irritation, trauma, blood-vessel spasm and hormonal changes can also cause discomfort. Can a new detergent cause nipple irritation? Yes. Detergents, fragrances and other products can irritate skin or trigger contact allergy. Can prescribed nipple eczema treatment be used while breastfeeding? Often yes. A clinician should select the product and explain application, removal before feeds and infant-contact precautions. Must my baby cover a fixed amount of the areola? No. Anatomy varies; a skilled assessment of positioning, attachment and milk transfer is more useful. Why does the nipple hurt and turn white in the cold? Vasospasm is one possibility. It needs assessment, especially if pain persists or follows nipple injury. Is shooting pain after feeding always thrush? No. Several causes overlap, and burning alone does not establish a yeast infection. Should I apply yogurt to treat thrush? No. It is not a validated nipple treatment; get a diagnosis and appropriate advice. Should I massage hard and pump until the breast is empty? No. Deep massage and extra pumping can worsen inflammation or oversupply. Is every case of mastitis treated with antibiotics? No. Some cases are inflammatory; antibiotics are used when bacterial infection is suspected or diagnosed. Can a persistent nipple rash be treated indefinitely as eczema? No. Persistent or changing nipple-centred symptoms need examination, including consideration of less common causes.

title: Breast cancer in men: changes worth getting checked
description: Recognise breast, nipple and skin changes in men, understand risk factors and learn what assessment, treatment and genetic advice may involve.
body: A new chest lump, nipple discharge or persistent skin change deserves a medical check. Breast cancer in men is uncommon, and many changes have other causes, but rarity is not a reason to ignore a symptom. Here is what to notice and what the next steps may involve. Uncommon does not mean impossible Men have breast tissue and can develop breast cancer. The disease is uncommon, which can make a new chest lump easy to dismiss or uncomfortable to discuss. A breast or nipple change deserves medical assessment even if you have never thought of breast cancer as something that could affect you. For context, the American Cancer Society reports that fewer than 1% of breast cancers in the United States occur in men, with an average lifetime risk of about 1 in 755. Diagnosis is more common later in life, often between ages 60 and 70, but younger people can also be affected. These are population estimates, not a way to rule cancer in or out for an individual. Information often uses the term male breast cancer because that is how studies and services describe it. Your own assessment should consider the breast tissue you have, previous surgery, hormones, family history and symptoms, alongside respectful discussion of your gender and preferences. Nobody should be discouraged from reporting a change because of a label. Lumps and changes in the breast, armpit or collarbone area A new lump or thickened area in the breast or chest is an important reason to book an appointment. It may be near or behind the nipple. Some cancers feel firm, irregular or relatively fixed and may be painless, but no single texture, shape or degree of movement can confirm a diagnosis. A lump does not have to match every description in a checklist before it is worth checking. A painful or movable lump also needs assessment when it is new or unexplained. Do not wait for it to become larger, harder or sore before seeking advice. A swelling in the armpit or near the collarbone may involve a lymph node. There are several possible causes, and it is not necessarily a breast tumour in that location. Mention it along with any chest or nipple changes so the clinician can examine the relevant areas. Nipple and skin symptoms also matter Look out for a nipple that newly turns inward, changes shape or develops a persistent rash or sore. Fluid coming from a nipple, including clear or blood-stained discharge, should be discussed with a clinician. You do not need to squeeze the nipple to produce discharge or repeatedly test whether it is present. Other changes include dimpling or puckering, thickened or scaly skin, redness or swelling, an ulcer that does not heal, or a new difference in the size or shape of one side of the chest. Persistent pain at or around the nipple can also warrant a check. These symptoms can have non-cancerous causes. That is a reason to get a proper assessment, not to diagnose yourself from a photograph. Note when the change began and whether it is progressing; describing that clearly is more useful than deciding at home whether the skin or lump “looks like cancer”. Breast enlargement and other explanations Gynecomastia is an increase in glandular breast tissue. It can affect one side or both, and can be tender. Hormonal changes, medicines and some medical conditions can be involved. It is not the same thing as breast cancer, although a new or changing area still needs appropriate assessment. Other possible explanations for a lump or discomfort include cysts, infection or changes after an injury. A clinician may be able to identify a benign cause, but a self-examination cannot reliably distinguish all of these conditions. Enlargement on both sides does not make every new symptom harmless, and a one-sided enlargement does not automatically mean cancer. Tell the clinician about medicines, supplements and hormone treatment, but do not stop prescribed treatment on your own while trying to explain the change. Age, family history and other risk factors Risk increases with age. A close relative with breast cancer and inherited variants such as BRCA2 (and, to a lesser extent, BRCA1) can also be relevant. Changes in genes that control cell growth may be inherited or occur during life; for many people, there is no single identifiable reason why cancer developed. The source of a hormone change matters. Conditions such as Klinefelter syndrome, some testicular conditions or previous removal of the testes, and severe liver disease can affect the balance of estrogen and androgens. Previous radiation treatment to the chest and some estrogen treatments may also influence risk. Excess body weight is associated with increased risk, but it is not a diagnosis or a reason to blame someone for cancer. Gynecomastia itself should not be described as breast cancer or automatically treated as a precancerous change. Some underlying conditions can be associated with both breast enlargement and cancer risk. Having a risk factor does not make cancer inevitable, and having no known risk factor does not exclude it. A list of risks cannot tell you what a new lump is. It can help the clinician decide whether genetic advice or a longer-term screening plan is appropriate. Symptoms elsewhere in the body When breast cancer spreads, symptoms depend on the area affected. Persistent bone pain, breathlessness, unexplained weight loss, marked fatigue, yellowing of the skin or eyes, or a general feeling of being unwell can be reasons for medical assessment. These symptoms have many possible causes and are not proof of advanced breast cancer. Do not wait for general symptoms before having a breast change checked. Conversely, if you already have a cancer diagnosis, tell the team about new persistent symptoms rather than assuming they are part of treatment or ordinary ageing. Sudden severe breathing difficulty, collapse or another severe acute symptom needs emergency care. An individual outlook depends on the diagnosis, stage and treatment response. Dividing the number of annual deaths by the number of new diagnoses does not show the chance that a newly diagnosed person will die of the disease; these are different groups measured in a particular year. What happens when you have a change assessed A clinician will ask about the change, your health and family history, and may examine the chest and nearby lymph nodes. You can request a chaperone or ask about having a support person present. Being referred urgently to a breast clinic means the concern needs timely investigation; it does not mean that cancer has already been confirmed. Assessment can include a mammogram, ultrasound or a needle biopsy, depending on the findings. A biopsy examines a tissue sample and can provide information about the tumour if cancer is present. You may not need every possible test. Ask when and how results will be communicated, and who to contact if they have not arrived. If a lump changes while you are waiting, or a symptom persists after an initial reassuring assessment, tell the team. A clear follow-up plan helps prevent uncertainty from turning into a long delay. Cancer type, receptors and stage Invasive ductal carcinoma is the most common type of breast cancer in men. It begins in the ducts and has grown into surrounding tissue. Invasive lobular carcinoma starts in milk-producing lobules, which are usually sparse or absent in male breast tissue, so this type is rare. Ductal carcinoma in situ, or DCIS, means abnormal cancer cells remain inside the ducts without invading surrounding tissue. It is often called non-invasive or stage 0 breast cancer and still needs a specialist treatment discussion. Calling it simply a harmless precancer would be misleading. Many male breast cancers are sensitive to hormones. Testing the tissue for estrogen and progesterone receptors and HER2 helps guide treatment. Stage describes the extent of cancer; grade describes how abnormal the cells look. These findings are more informative for treatment planning than the outward size of a lump alone. Treatment and inherited-risk assessment Treatment is tailored to the cancer and the person. Surgery may remove the tumour or breast tissue, with assessment of lymph nodes when appropriate. Radiotherapy treats a defined area, while chemotherapy and other medicines may treat cancer cells throughout the body. Not everyone needs every treatment. For hormone receptor-positive disease, endocrine treatment such as tamoxifen may be recommended. Targeted medicines depend on tumour features and the clinical situation. The choice and sequence take account of stage, receptors, overall health, other medicines, potential benefits, side effects and your preferences. A general article cannot select a regimen for you. ASCO recommends offering genetic counselling and testing for inherited cancer-risk variants to all men diagnosed with breast cancer. Results may affect treatment or future screening and can have implications for relatives. A genetics professional can explain what a result means before family members make testing decisions. Support also matters. Ask about body-image concerns, sexual health, side effects, work or caring responsibilities, and support services that are comfortable for you. Breast cancer care should address your life as well as the tumour. Breast awareness is different from screening Know what is usual for your chest. You can notice changes while washing, dressing or looking in a mirror, including around the nipple and towards the armpit. There is no need to use force, repeatedly press a sore area or squeeze the nipples. A normal-feeling self-check cannot guarantee that no cancer is present. A fixed monthly self-examination routine is not a substitute for care, and it should not be presented as a proven screening programme for every man. Screening means testing people who do not have symptoms; investigating a new lump or discharge is diagnostic care and should not wait for a screening invitation. People with inherited risk or a personal history of breast cancer may need a specialist surveillance plan. Ask about your own risk and which checks are appropriate locally. If you notice a new or unexplained change, make the appointment even if breast cancer feels unlikely or the conversation feels awkward. Men can develop breast cancer, although it is uncommon. A lump need not be painless, fixed or irregular to deserve assessment. Gynecomastia and other benign conditions can cause changes, but self-checking cannot reliably distinguish them. Symptoms need diagnostic assessment; screening plans are a separate discussion. Treatment and inherited-risk advice are individual, and support should include the whole person. Can men get breast cancer without a family history? Yes. A family history or inherited variant can raise risk, but cancer can occur without either being known. New symptoms still need assessment. Does a painful lump mean it cannot be cancer? No. Pain does not reliably rule cancer out, and a painless lump is not automatically cancer. A clinician should assess a new or unexplained lump. Is swelling near the armpit the same as a breast tumour? Not necessarily. It may involve a lymph node or another structure and can have several causes. Mention its location and any associated chest or nipple changes at the appointment. Should I squeeze the nipple to check for discharge? No. Report discharge you have noticed, especially if spontaneous or blood-stained. Repeated squeezing is not a reliable cancer test and can irritate the area. Can gynecomastia affect only one side? Yes. It can affect one side or both. That pattern alone cannot establish the cause of a new change, so seek assessment rather than assuming it is harmless or cancerous. Do the lifetime-risk statistics tell me what my lump is? No. Population risk describes groups over time. It cannot diagnose a symptom or replace a personal assessment. Will an urgent referral mean I definitely have cancer? No. It means the symptom needs timely investigation. Examination, imaging and sometimes biopsy help determine the cause. Can men have mammograms? Yes. Mammography may be part of a breast assessment in men, alongside ultrasound or biopsy when indicated. The team chooses tests based on the findings. Does every man need a monthly self-exam and screening scan? No universal scan or formal self-examination programme fits everyone. Be aware of your usual chest appearance and feel, report changes, and discuss specialist surveillance if you have inherited risk or a previous diagnosis. Why is genetic testing discussed after a diagnosis? An inherited variant may affect treatment, future screening and advice for relatives. ASCO recommends offering counselling and germline testing to all men diagnosed with breast cancer; the genetics team explains the choices and implications.

title: Spotting or a period: what the difference can tell you
description: Compare spotting with menstrual bleeding, explore common causes and learn when testing or urgent assessment is needed.
body: A few spots of blood can be confusing, especially near the date a period is due. Amount, timing and other symptoms provide clues, but they cannot diagnose the cause. Pregnancy, contraception, hormonal changes and conditions of the cervix or uterus all need different consideration. Spotting describes the amount, not the cause A period is bleeding associated with shedding of the uterine lining during the menstrual cycle. Spotting means a much smaller amount of vaginal bleeding, perhaps marks on underwear or blood when wiping. It may happen before or after an expected period, between periods or after sex. The word describes what you notice; it does not establish where the blood came from. Spotting often needs little more than a liner, while a period usually needs a pad, tampon, cup or other period product. Product use is not a diagnostic test, however. Blood may be pink, red or brown in either situation, depending partly on how much there is and how long it has been present. A lighter color does not prove that bleeding is harmless. Compare the episode with your own usual pattern: timing, amount, duration and associated symptoms. If it is unusual or keeps returning, arrange an assessment. Do not assume that all bleeding near the expected period date is menstruation, especially when pregnancy is possible. Symptoms that help explain the pattern Bloating, breast tenderness, cramps, tiredness, mood changes and sometimes nausea can accompany a period. These symptoms overlap with other conditions and cannot reliably distinguish a period from early pregnancy or a hormonal change. Some periods begin with light spotting and become heavier, while other spotting never becomes a normal flow. Tell the clinician about missed or irregular periods, bleeding that is heavier or lasts longer than usual, pelvic pain, pain with urination or sex, itching, redness, unusual discharge or odor. Fever or feeling generally unwell is also important. Weight changes, acne or increased facial/body hair may help a clinician investigate a broader hormonal pattern, but none identifies the cause by itself. If you are not certain the blood is vaginal, say so. Blood from urine, the rectum or irritated external skin may look similar when wiping and needs a different assessment. A symptom diary can help, but you do not need several weeks of records before asking for care. Ovulation, irregular cycles and hormonal changes Some people have a small amount of bleeding around ovulation. That possibility is usually considered in the context of an otherwise predictable cycle and after other causes are assessed when appropriate. Ovulation does not always happen on day 14, and a spot of blood is not proof that an egg was released. Irregular ovulation can also cause unpredictable bleeding. The condition widely known as polycystic ovary syndrome, or PCOS, may involve infrequent periods, acne and increased hair growth. Current NHS guidance uses the name polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, or PMOS. Diagnosis involves the overall pattern and clinical testing; visible ovarian cysts are not required for everyone. Cycles may be less predictable around puberty and during the transition toward menopause. Stress, illness, medicines and other hormonal conditions may also be relevant. These possibilities help guide questions, but “hormones” should not become a catch-all explanation for persistent bleeding without assessment. Pregnancy is possible even when bleeding is light Bleeding can occur in early pregnancy and does not always mean the pregnancy is ending. Changes at the cervix, a small bleed inside the uterus or infection are among possible explanations. Miscarriage and ectopic pregnancy are also important possibilities. The amount or color alone cannot tell which explanation applies. The term “implantation bleeding” is often used for light bleeding around the expected period. You cannot confirm implantation from spotting, and using that label should not delay testing or assessment. A pregnancy test is more useful than trying to match a photograph or an exact shade of blood. Most home tests can be used from the first day of a missed period. If you do not know when the next period is due, test at least 21 days after the last unprotected sex. If the result is negative but you tested early or still think pregnancy is possible, repeat after a few days. Seek advice if a second test is negative and the period still has not arrived. Urgent symptoms need care without waiting for a positive test. Contraception can change bleeding Starting or switching hormonal contraception can cause breakthrough bleeding. Missed pills and changes in how a pill is taken can also matter. Tell the clinician which product you use, whether doses were missed and whether you recently changed the schedule. A standard monthly pill pack and a continuous-use regimen do not necessarily produce the same bleeding pattern. Both copper and hormonal intrauterine devices can cause spotting in the first months. Copper IUDs can also make periods heavier or longer, especially early on. Hormonal IUDs commonly cause irregular light bleeding for the first three to six months, followed by lighter or absent periods for many users. These expected patterns do not explain every new episode. New bleeding after a settled pattern, pain, fever, pregnancy symptoms or a change that worries you should be reviewed. The clinician may consider pregnancy, infection, device position or another cause. Do not remove an IUD yourself or change hormone doses to stop bleeding without advice; ask about options that preserve the contraceptive protection you want. Fibroids, polyps and cervical changes Fibroids are non-cancerous growths in or around the uterus. They vary in size and location and do not always cause symptoms. When they do, bleeding changes may occur alongside heavier periods, pressure or pain. A finding of fibroids does not prove that they explain every episode, and treatment depends on symptoms and individual priorities. Polyps are growths arising from the lining of the uterus or cervix. They are often benign but may cause bleeding between periods or after sex. Assessment is still important because appearance and symptoms alone cannot always determine what a growth is. Removal or sampling may be recommended in some circumstances. A sensitive cervical surface, including cervical ectropion, can bleed after contact. Pregnancy also changes the blood supply around the cervix. Vaginal dryness may make sex uncomfortable and cause bleeding. These are possible explanations for post-sex bleeding, but a new or repeated episode should be checked rather than automatically attributed to friction. Infection, irritation and injury Cervical infection, including chlamydia or gonorrhea, can cause bleeding between periods or after sex. Pelvic inflammatory disease, or PID, affects the upper reproductive tract and may cause pelvic pain, abnormal discharge and bleeding. It can result from sexually transmitted infections or from other bacteria; it is not always proof of an STI. Itching, redness or soreness may suggest vaginal or external irritation or infection, but bleeding is not enough to diagnose thrush. Antibiotics and antifungal medicines treat different problems. Repeatedly using an over-the-counter treatment without knowing the cause may delay the right care, especially if pain, odor or fever is present. Friction, an injury or non-consensual sexual contact can also cause bleeding. Stop an activity that is painful and seek assessment for an injury or persistent bleeding. If assault or coercion is involved, a sexual-assault service or clinician can offer confidential support, treatment and discussion of options. You deserve care without blame, whether or not you choose to make a report. Bleeding around and after menopause During perimenopause, ovulation and period timing may become irregular over several years. A changing cycle can explain some episodes, but frequent bleeding, bleeding after sex or a substantial change in amount should still be discussed. Do not assume age alone makes all unexpected bleeding normal. After 12 months without periods due to menopause, vaginal bleeding should be assessed even if it happens only once or consists of a little pink or brown discharge. Thinning tissues and polyps are possible causes, but changes in the uterine lining and cancer also need consideration. Tell the clinician about hormone replacement therapy, the timing of any changes and how the bleeding compares with the expected pattern for that treatment. Do not wait for bleeding to become heavy before arranging review. Most explanations are not cancer, but checking is how the cause is established. What happens during an assessment The clinician may ask about your usual cycle, last normal period, pregnancy possibility, contraception, medicines, sexual symptoms and previous bleeding episodes. An examination of the abdomen, vagina and cervix may be offered, with your consent. You can ask what the examination involves, request a chaperone and ask to stop at any time. Depending on the situation, testing can include a pregnancy test, blood tests, infection swabs and pelvic ultrasound. Some people need a closer examination of the cervix, hysteroscopy to look inside the uterus or a tissue sample. Not everyone needs every test; age, symptoms, examination findings and risk factors determine the next step. Cervical screening is not a substitute for assessing symptoms. A recent normal screening result does not explain new bleeding, and you should not wait for the next invitation if symptoms need attention. Ask when results will be available and what to do if bleeding returns before follow-up. Treatment and practical monitoring Treatment follows the cause. A diagnosed bacterial infection may need antibiotics, and a confirmed fungal infection may need an antifungal. A contraceptive adjustment, treatment for a hormonal condition or removal of a polyp may be appropriate in other cases. Fibroids do not always need intervention. There is no single medicine that suits every episode of spotting. Keep a simple record of dates, amount, period-product use, pain, discharge and any relation to sex or missed contraception. Note pregnancy-test dates and results when relevant. A tracking app can organize observations, but it cannot diagnose the cause or reliably confirm ovulation from spotting.
