Fibroids do not automatically need treatment just because they increase uterine size. Adenomyosis affects the uterine muscle wall and can cause heavy bleeding and pain. Choose treatment with a clear understanding of symptom relief, risks and future pregnancy goals. Do not delay assessment of unexplained bleeding, persistent pain or postmenopausal spotting. Is an enlarged uterus always dangerous? No. Pregnancy and benign conditions such as fibroids can enlarge the uterus. The cause and symptoms determine its significance. A clinician should assess unexplained enlargement, particularly with changing bleeding, pain or pressure. Does every fibroid that enlarges the uterus need treatment? No. Observation may be suitable if symptoms are absent or manageable and the diagnosis is reassuring. Treatment is considered for troublesome bleeding, anemia, pressure, pain or selected fertility concerns, taking your preferences into account. When should I seek urgent help? Severe or worsening pelvic pain, fainting or heavy vaginal bleeding needs emergency assessment. Pelvic pain with possible pregnancy needs urgent advice. Any postmenopausal bleeding should be checked, even a single small episode. Can an enlarged uterus affect pregnancy or fertility? Some underlying causes, including certain fibroids, can affect conception or pregnancy. Many people with fibroids conceive and have normal pregnancies. The position of the fibroid, other findings and any previous surgery help guide individual advice. Will birth-control pills shrink fibroids? They may reduce menstrual bleeding or pain but do not reliably shrink fibroids or stop their growth. Other hormone-based treatments have different purposes and limits. Ask which symptom or finding the proposed treatment is meant to improve. How is adenomyosis different from a fibroid? Adenomyosis involves lining-like tissue within the uterine muscle wall. A fibroid is a distinct benign growth from muscle tissue. Both may cause heavy bleeding, pain and enlargement, so examination and imaging help distinguish them. How long does the uterus stay enlarged after birth? It gradually contracts over the weeks after delivery and often returns close to its previous size in about six weeks. This is a general timeframe, not a reason to ignore heavy bleeding, worsening pain or other concerning recovery symptoms. Does hysterectomy mean the ovaries are removed too? Not necessarily. Hysterectomy removes the uterus; removing the ovaries is a separate decision based on the diagnosis and circumstances. Hysterectomy ends the ability to carry a pregnancy, so discuss all relevant options before deciding.

title: Endometrial cancer: symptoms, stages, treatment and risk factors
description: A full guide to endometrial cancer, including abnormal bleeding, diagnostic tests, modern staging, treatment choices, hyperplasia, inherited risk and emotional support.
body: Endometrial cancer starts in the lining of the uterus. Unusual vaginal bleeding is often its first sign, which can lead to diagnosis while the cancer is still at an early stage. Prompt assessment matters, but bleeding or pelvic pain does not automatically mean cancer. Understanding the tests and treatment choices can help you take part in decisions about your care. What endometrial cancer is The endometrium is the tissue lining the inside of the uterus. During the reproductive years, it changes in response to hormones and is shed during menstruation when pregnancy does not occur. Endometrial cancer develops when cells in this lining begin to grow without normal control. It is the most common form of uterine cancer. It is different from uterine sarcoma, which arises in muscle or supporting tissues, and from cancer that begins in the cervix. Those distinctions matter because testing, treatment and outlook can differ. Many cases can be treated successfully, especially when found early. Nevertheless, the diagnosis alone does not tell you how one person will do. The type of cancer, its extent, laboratory findings, health and response to treatment all contribute. Symptoms that should be checked The most frequent warning sign is a change in vaginal bleeding: periods that become unusually heavy or prolonged, spotting between periods, or any bleeding after menopause. Report even a small amount of postmenopausal spotting rather than waiting for it to become heavier. Other possible symptoms include watery or blood-stained discharge, pain low in the abdomen or pelvis, discomfort during sex, or painful or difficult urination. These symptoms can have other causes, including benign uterine or vaginal conditions. Changes around menopause can affect bleeding, but unexplained bleeding should not simply be attributed to the menopause without assessment. If bleeding continues or returns after an initial reassuring result, contact the clinician again. Heavy bleeding with faintness, collapse or severe pelvic pain needs emergency assessment. Otherwise, arrange a prompt appointment to establish the cause and next steps. You do not need to decide for yourself whether the symptoms sound like cancer before seeking help. Examination, ultrasound and tissue sampling The clinician will ask about your symptoms, medicines, menstrual or menopause history, previous illnesses and family history. A pelvic examination can help identify changes in the reproductive organs and other potential sources of bleeding. A transvaginal ultrasound uses a slender probe placed in the vagina to create images with sound waves. It can assess the uterine lining and look for structural changes. Ultrasound findings alone do not always settle whether cancer is present. An endometrial biopsy takes a small tissue sample, often through a thin tube passed through the cervix. A pathologist examines it in the laboratory. Hysteroscopy uses a narrow viewing instrument to inspect the uterine cavity and can guide sampling of a suspicious area. Dilation and curettage, or D&C, involves opening the cervix and obtaining tissue from inside the uterus. It may be used when another sample is insufficient or further evaluation is needed. Ask how discomfort will be managed and what to expect before consenting to a procedure. Biopsy is not reserved only for an abnormal ultrasound. ACOG’s April 2026 guidance recommends ultrasound together with tissue sampling in the initial assessment of most people with postmenopausal bleeding. The plan should reflect the person’s circumstances and shared decision-making. If cancer is confirmed, additional assessment helps determine its extent. Depending on the situation, this can involve imaging, blood tests and information obtained at surgery. Keep copies of the pathology and scan reports, particularly if requesting a second opinion. Understanding stages I to IV A stage describes how the cancer is classified at diagnosis and helps guide care. Broadly, stage I represents early disease, usually limited to the uterus; stage II includes certain more extensive local findings; stage III involves local or regional spread; and stage IV includes involvement of the bladder or bowel lining or more distant spread. Older explanations describe stage II mainly as spread into the cervix and stage III as involvement of nearby tissues, ovaries, tubes, vagina or regional lymph nodes. Those descriptions remain useful background, but they are not a complete guide to current staging. The 2023 FIGO system also incorporates features such as cancer type, invasion of small lymph or blood vessels and some molecular findings. It has selected exceptions, including some low-grade cancers involving the uterus and an ovary that can be classified as early disease. A stage cannot safely be assigned from a short checklist. Ask which staging system your team uses, the full stage and substage, and which findings led to it. Stage affects treatment and prognosis, but it is considered alongside the pathology and your health, not in isolation. Cancer type, grade and molecular findings Most endometrial cancers arise from gland-forming tissue and are called adenocarcinomas. Endometrioid carcinoma is the most common. Other groups include serous, clear-cell, mixed, undifferentiated or dedifferentiated cancers and carcinosarcoma, as well as rare forms requiring specialist classification. You may encounter the older terms type 1 and type 2. Type 1 generally referred to more common, often estrogen-related endometrioid cancers, while type 2 included more aggressive forms such as serous cancer. This two-group description is too broad to determine an individual treatment plan. Grade describes microscopic features of the tumor and is different from stage. Molecular testing can provide additional information, with groups including POLE-mutated, mismatch-repair-deficient, p53-abnormal and tumors without a specific molecular profile. These results can help estimate recurrence risk and guide treatment. Ask for an explanation in everyday language; recognizing a subtype name does not mean you should infer the outlook or choose a drug yourself. Making a treatment plan Treatment is planned with a specialist cancer team, often including a gynecologic oncologist. The recommendation depends on stage, cancer type and grade, molecular or receptor findings, other health conditions and your preferences. Ask what each treatment aims to achieve, the likely benefits, important side effects and alternatives. Some people need surgery alone, while others need several treatments. A combination is not automatically better for every diagnosis. Tell the team early if future pregnancy is important to you. Ask about fertility advice before treatment starts, because surgery, radiation and medicines can affect reproductive options. Fertility-preserving care is appropriate only for selected situations. Surgery and lymph-node assessment Surgery commonly involves a hysterectomy to remove the uterus, usually including the cervix. Removing both fallopian tubes and ovaries is called bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and is often part of the same cancer operation. The exact procedure should be explained beforehand. The team may also assess lymph nodes to help determine whether cancer has spread. This does not always mean removing every nearby node: sentinel-node mapping and biopsy can be used in suitable cases, while other findings may require a different approach. If cancer extends beyond the uterus, additional surgery may sometimes be considered. The amount of surgery depends on the location and extent of disease and whether the expected benefits justify the risks. Hysterectomy means you can no longer carry a pregnancy. Removing the ovaries before natural menopause also changes hormone production. Discuss these consequences, recovery and symptom management with the team rather than assuming that all operations have identical effects. Radiation treatment Radiation uses high-energy treatment to damage cancer cells in a defined area. External-beam radiation comes from a machine outside the body. Brachytherapy places a radiation source through an applicator close to the area being treated, often the upper vagina after surgery. One form or a combination may be recommended, commonly after surgery to reduce the risk of cancer returning locally. Less often, radiation is used before surgery to help shrink a tumor. If surgery is unsuitable because of health or other circumstances, radiation may be the main treatment. The plan depends on the actual diagnosis and treatment goal. Ask about fatigue, bowel or bladder symptoms, vaginal changes and longer-term effects, as well as how to report problems. Treatment schedules and supportive measures should come from your radiation team. Chemotherapy and newer drug treatments Chemotherapy uses medicines that affect cancer cells. It may involve one drug or a combination and is commonly delivered through a vein for endometrial cancer. The medicines and schedule depend on the treatment plan; not every cancer medicine taken by mouth is chemotherapy. It can be used when cancer has spread, has returned after earlier treatment, or when features of a newly diagnosed cancer indicate that additional treatment is appropriate. Sometimes it is combined or sequenced with radiation. Modern treatment can also include immunotherapy or targeted medicines in selected settings. Tumor testing and previous treatment can influence which options are suitable. Their availability and approved uses change, so a current specialist plan is more useful than a fixed list of drugs in a general article. Ask which side effects need an immediate call, who to contact outside office hours and whether a clinical trial is relevant. Do not change or stop prescribed cancer treatment based on general information. Hormonal treatment and preserving fertility Hormonal treatment uses hormones or medicines that alter hormone action to slow suitable cancers. It is different from hormone therapy used to relieve menopause symptoms. Progestins are one important group, but there are other approaches. It may be considered for selected advanced or recurrent cancers, particularly some lower-grade, slower-growing tumors with hormone receptors. It is not confined to stages III and IV, and it is not automatically combined with chemotherapy. A small group with carefully assessed early, low-grade endometrioid cancer may be considered for hormonal treatment that temporarily preserves the uterus. This requires specialist selection, exclusion of more extensive disease and close repeat assessment. It is not a general alternative to recommended surgery. Discuss how response will be measured, what would trigger a change in treatment and the plan after pregnancy or if the cancer does not respond. Keeping the uterus during treatment does not guarantee a future pregnancy or remove the need for cancer follow-up. Age, hormone exposure and reproductive history Risk generally increases with age and the disease is most common after menopause, although younger people can develop it. US registry information places most diagnoses between ages 45 and 74; that is a population pattern, not an age range outside which symptoms can be ignored. Longer exposure of the lining to estrogen without enough progesterone effect can increase risk. An early first period, later menopause and never having been pregnant are associated with higher risk. None means that a person will inevitably develop cancer, and pregnancy should not be pursued as cancer prevention. PCOS can increase risk, particularly when ovulation is infrequent and the lining is not regularly exposed to progesterone. It is inaccurate to assume that every person with PCOS has the same continuously high estrogen measurement. Some estrogen-producing ovarian tumors, including granulosa-cell tumors, can also stimulate the uterine lining. These are specific medical conditions requiring their own assessment. Risk factors are clues for care, not a way to diagnose cancer from personal history. Menopause therapy, tamoxifen and contraception Systemic estrogen treatment for menopause can increase endometrial cancer risk when used without adequate progestogen protection in someone who still has a uterus. Discuss the formulation and whether protection is needed with the prescriber; not all local and systemic products have the same considerations. Tamoxifen can act differently in breast and uterine tissue. It is valuable for preventing or treating certain breast cancers but can increase endometrial cancer risk. Its benefits often outweigh that risk. Report abnormal bleeding and discuss concerns rather than stopping it yourself. Oral contraceptives are associated with a lower risk of endometrial cancer. Intrauterine contraceptive use has also been associated with lower risk, but a device is not a guarantee against cancer or a substitute for investigating bleeding. Each option has benefits and possible harms beyond the endometrium. A clinician can help choose contraception or menopause care that fits your health and preferences. Do not start medication solely to reduce a statistical cancer risk without that discussion. Endometrial hyperplasia is not all the same Endometrial hyperplasia means overgrowth of the uterine lining. It is not automatically cancer, but the laboratory classification matters. Hyperplasia without atypia differs from atypical hyperplasia or endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia, often shortened to EIN, which is a precancerous condition. Abnormal bleeding is a common reason it is discovered. Some non-atypical changes may settle or respond to treatment, but a diagnosis should come with a clear follow-up plan. It is unsafe to assume that all hyperplasia will disappear on its own. Treatment can involve progestin, delivered in an appropriate oral or intrauterine form, rather than simply generic hormone replacement therapy. For EIN or atypical hyperplasia, hysterectomy is the definitive treatment; when surgery is not chosen or is unsuitable, clinicians first assess for coexisting cancer and arrange progestin treatment with close surveillance. Ask what the biopsy actually showed, how much concern there is about progression or an already present cancer, and when repeat assessment is needed. A scan reporting a thick lining is not identical to a tissue diagnosis of hyperplasia. Body weight, diabetes and metabolic health Higher body fat is associated with greater endometrial cancer risk. Fat tissue can convert other hormones into estrogen, which is one reason the relationship matters, particularly after menopause. This association does not identify the cause of cancer in an individual. Type 2 diabetes and related metabolic conditions are also associated with increased risk. Their relationships with body weight, insulin and other factors overlap. It is misleading to give everyone with diabetes or a particular BMI one fixed multiplier for their personal chance of cancer. Support with blood-glucose management, physical activity and sustainable weight-related goals can benefit overall health. Cancer is not evidence that someone failed at self-care. Continue appropriate medical assessment regardless of weight or diabetes status. Family history and Lynch syndrome Tell the clinician if close relatives have had endometrial or bowel cancer, especially at younger ages, or if the family has a known inherited cancer syndrome. Lynch syndrome involves inherited changes in DNA mismatch-repair pathways and raises the risk of several cancers, including endometrial and colorectal cancer. The level of risk differs according to the gene and family circumstances. A single lifetime figure such as 40–60% should not be applied to everyone with Lynch syndrome. Genetic counseling can clarify what a result means and whether relatives should consider testing. Risk-reducing hysterectomy and possible removal of the tubes and ovaries may be discussed after childbearing. Timing and whether to remove the ovaries require an individual discussion about the gene, age, family history, health, menopause effects and preferences; surgery is not an automatic response to any family history. A previous breast or ovarian cancer should also be mentioned because shared risk factors, inherited susceptibility or treatments may affect assessment. Prior radiation to the pelvis is another relevant part of the history. Not every cancer survivor has the same risk. Why cells become cancerous For many people, there is no single identifiable cause. Hormonal stimulation can promote growth of the endometrial lining, but a thick lining or a hormone imbalance is not by itself cancer. Changes in the genes that control cell growth, repair and survival can allow cells to multiply abnormally and form a tumor. Some susceptibility is inherited, while many changes arise in the tumor itself. Not all endometrial cancers are driven by estrogen in the same way. Researchers continue to study how these processes interact. This is why cancer type and molecular findings provide information that a list of risk factors alone cannot supply. Steps that may lower risk There is no guaranteed way to prevent endometrial cancer. Regular physical activity and support toward a sustainable, healthy weight may lower risk and have broader health benefits. The effect for a particular person cannot be promised. Have unexplained bleeding assessed and follow the treatment and monitoring plan for hyperplasia or EIN. Discuss the endometrial effects of menopause treatment and the wider benefits and risks of contraceptive options when choosing them. If Lynch syndrome is suspected or confirmed, ask for a specialist prevention and follow-up plan. Do not rely on routine cervical screening for reassurance: a Pap or HPV test is not an endometrial cancer screening test. There is no standard routine screening program for average-risk people without symptoms. Investigating bleeding is different from screening a person who feels well, and higher inherited risk requires an individualized approach. Putting survival statistics in context For context, current US SEER data estimate a lifetime uterine-cancer risk of about 3.1%, based on 2021–2023 data. The reported five-year relative survival for uterine cancer is 80.9%, using diagnoses from 2016–2022. These statistics cover a registry category broader than a single endometrial subtype. Relative survival compares survival in people with cancer with what would be expected in a comparable population. It is not a statement that treatment guarantees five years of life, nor does it mean that someone who reaches five years cannot live much longer. Outcomes are generally better when disease is found earlier, but stage, cancer biology and treatment response matter. Ask the oncology team to explain the information relevant to your diagnosis rather than applying an all-stage average to yourself. Emotional support and preparing for care Fear, sadness, uncertainty or difficulty coping can accompany diagnosis and treatment. Tell the team how you are managing emotionally as well as physically. Support can include counseling, an oncology social worker or other mental-health care. Some people find an in-person or online cancer support group helpful; others prefer individual conversations. Choose the kind of support that feels useful to you. Practical help with appointments, work, family responsibilities and communicating with loved ones can also reduce the burden. For an appointment, write down your symptoms, medicines and questions. Ask for the diagnosis, stage, treatment goal and follow-up plan in writing, and bring a trusted person if you wish. Raise concerns about pain, fertility, menopause or sexual health so they can be addressed alongside the cancer treatment. Abnormal bleeding is the most common warning sign, but symptoms alone do not diagnose cancer. Biopsy and appropriate follow-up matter, including when an ultrasound is reassuring. Stage, grade and cancer type describe different aspects of the diagnosis. Hyperplasia without atypia and EIN or atypical hyperplasia need different levels of concern and follow-up. Discuss fertility wishes before treatment and medication concerns before making changes. Population survival figures cannot predict an individual outcome; emotional and practical support are part of care. What are the main symptoms of endometrial cancer? Unexpected vaginal bleeding, including heavier or longer periods, bleeding between periods or any bleeding after menopause, is the most common sign. Watery or blood-stained discharge, pelvic pain or pain during sex can also occur. These symptoms need assessment but do not necessarily mean cancer. Is endometrial hyperplasia the same as cancer? No. It means overgrowth of the lining, but the tissue findings matter. Hyperplasia without atypia differs from EIN or atypical hyperplasia, which is precancerous and needs an appropriate treatment and surveillance plan. Generic menopause HRT is not the standard answer for hyperplasia. What causes endometrial cancer? There is often no single identifiable cause. Changes controlling cell growth and repair can lead to cancer. Prolonged estrogen stimulation contributes to some forms, while other cancers have different biology. Risk factors do not prove what caused one person’s disease. Can I lower my risk? Regular activity, supported weight and metabolic-health care, assessment of abnormal bleeding, and appropriate treatment of precancer can help. Discuss hormone or contraceptive choices with your clinician. None guarantees prevention, and inherited risk needs specialist advice. Does a normal ultrasound rule it out? Not always. Tissue sampling may still be needed. ACOG’s 2026 update recommends ultrasound plus endometrial sampling in the initial assessment of most people with postmenopausal bleeding. Persistent or returning symptoms should be reported even after reassuring initial tests. Are stage and grade the same? No. Stage classifies the extent and, in newer systems, selected additional features of the cancer. Grade describes microscopic characteristics. Molecular findings can add further information. Ask your team to explain each part of your own pathology and staging report. Does everyone need chemotherapy? No. Some people need surgery alone, while others benefit from radiation, chemotherapy or other medicines. The combination depends on the cancer’s extent and biology, the person’s health and the goals of treatment. Can fertility be preserved? Sometimes, for carefully selected early, low-grade endometrioid cancers under specialist care. Hormonal treatment with close surveillance may temporarily preserve the uterus. It is not suitable for everyone and does not guarantee pregnancy. Raise fertility wishes before starting treatment. Should I stop tamoxifen or menopause treatment? Do not stop prescribed treatment on your own. Discuss your symptoms, uterine status and individual risks with the prescriber. Tamoxifen’s breast-cancer benefits often outweigh its uterine risk, while menopause-treatment choices depend on the formulation and need for endometrial protection. What does a five-year survival figure mean? It describes outcomes in a group over a defined period, usually relative to expected survival in a comparable population. It is not an expiry date or a personal prediction. Your own outlook depends on stage, cancer biology, health and response to treatment.

title: Contraception with PCOS: options, benefits and safe use
description: PCOS does not prevent every pregnancy. Compare pills, patches, rings and hormonal IUDs, understand symptom benefits and use each method safely.
body: Irregular ovulation does not mean pregnancy is impossible. If you have polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and do not want a pregnancy, choose contraception that suits your health and preferences. Current Monash, ASRM and NHS guidance also uses the new name polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS). This guide uses PCOS alongside that name to explain pregnancy prevention, symptom treatment and the important differences between methods. Pregnancy is still possible with irregular cycles PCOS can involve infrequent or absent ovulation, irregular periods, acne and excess facial or body hair. Symptoms and fertility differ between people, and ovulation can occur unexpectedly. Do not assume that a previous fertility problem or months without periods protects against pregnancy. Bloating, cramps and pelvic pain are not specific diagnostic signs of PCOS. New or severe pain needs assessment rather than automatic attribution to the condition. Discuss pregnancy intentions and prolonged gaps in bleeding with a clinician; contraception and fertility treatment have different purposes. What hormonal contraception can and cannot do Combined hormonal contraception contains estrogen and a progestin. It mainly prevents pregnancy by suppressing ovulation, rather than making you ovulate. It can produce more predictable withdrawal bleeding or be prescribed continuously; a scheduled bleed does not show that natural ovulation has returned. Contraception can manage selected symptoms and protect the uterine lining, but does not cure PCOS or replace metabolic care. Long untreated gaps without ovulation can increase endometrial thickening risk. A plan for cycle regulation or regular progestogen is useful; needing lining protection does not mean everyone must have a monthly bleed. Combined pills: potential benefits and dose choice Combined pills can be considered for irregular cycles and excess hair when estrogen is suitable. They may also improve acne, heavy bleeding or period pain, though benefit varies and hair changes take time. They are not automatically the most effective contraceptive option; an IUD or implant may suit someone who finds daily dosing difficult. The formulation and dose should be chosen with a prescriber. The international guideline suggests considering the lowest effective estrogen dose, such as 20–30 micrograms of ethinyl estradiol or equivalent, with individual risks. A higher dose is not necessarily better for excess hair. Do not choose or change a dose yourself, or compare patch and pill doses as interchangeable. Combined pill use is associated with lower endometrial and ovarian cancer risk, but is not general cancer prevention or a guarantee against ovarian cysts. Some cancer risks, including breast and cervical cancer, may increase during use. These benefits and risks cannot simply be assigned equally to every pill, patch, ring or progestin-only method. Progestin-only pills A progestin-only pill may be an option when estrogen is unsuitable or unwanted. It prevents pregnancy through effects including cervical mucus changes and, depending on the formulation, ovulation suppression. It is not simply replacement of a universally low progesterone level and does not induce ovulation. Progestin-only contraception may help protect the endometrium, but evidence specific to PCOS is limited. Irregular bleeding or no bleeding can occur; regular monthly periods, acne improvement and reduced hair are not guaranteed. Formulations, doses and missed-pill time windows differ, so follow your own product instructions rather than a universal microgram dose. Contraceptive patches A combined patch delivers estrogen and progestin through the skin. With the usual Xulane schedule, apply a new patch each week for three weeks, then have one patch-free week. One patch is not left on for 21 days. Start the next cycle on time and follow the prescribed product regimen; do not extend the break while waiting for bleeding to finish. Patches can offer an alternative to a daily pill and may help bleeding or cramps, but PCOS-specific acne, hair and cancer benefits are less directly established than for combined pills. Skin irritation can occur. Product-specific weight or BMI restrictions and clot risks matter; Xulane is contraindicated at BMI 30 or above in its US label and may be less effective at 90 kg or above. Other products may differ. Vaginal contraceptive rings A combined vaginal ring is a flexible device placed in the vagina. The usual NuvaRing regimen is three continuous weeks in place, followed by one week without it. Insert a new ring exactly one week after removal, even if bleeding has not finished. Other ring products may be reused or have different instructions; do not assume one schedule fits all. A ring avoids daily pill taking and can help control bleeding, but it suppresses rather than restores ovulation. Discuss vaginal discomfort, discharge, headache, nausea or other symptoms and the same estrogen-related safety issues. If it comes out or replacement is late, consult the product-specific instructions and a pharmacist or clinician promptly. Side effects and safety screening Spotting, changed bleeding, breast tenderness, nausea, headache, dizziness or mood symptoms may occur. Some people report appetite, fatigue or weight changes, but these do not establish the cause, and combined pills have not been shown to cause weight gain. Many tolerate contraception well; troublesome or persistent symptoms justify review and possibly a different method. Check blood pressure and review migraine with aura, smoking, previous clots, cardiovascular or liver disease, breast cancer, recent childbirth and all medicines before an estrogen-containing method. Some conditions make combined pills, patches and rings unsuitable; avoiding oral pills does not remove estrogen risks. Progestin-only options also need individual suitability checks. Seek emergency help for sudden chest pain or breathlessness, stroke-like weakness or speech/vision changes, or a sudden unusual severe headache. A painful swollen leg needs urgent same-day assessment for a clot. Fainting or collapse, sudden severe pelvic or abdominal pain, or heavy bleeding needs immediate emergency care, especially if pregnancy is possible. Do not label new serious symptoms as routine PCOS or contraceptive side effects. Cyclic progestogen and hormonal IUDs A clinician may prescribe a short course of progesterone or a progestogen at agreed intervals to protect the uterine lining when periods are infrequent. The medicine, dose and schedule are individualized. Such intermittent treatment is not reliable contraception and does not necessarily improve acne or excess hair; ask for separate pregnancy protection if needed. A levonorgestrel-releasing hormonal IUD provides highly effective contraception and can reduce bleeding and protect the endometrium. It may cause irregular early bleeding or later very light or absent bleeding. It does not offer the same acne or hair benefits as a combined pill. A copper IUD is hormone-free contraception but does not treat PCOS symptoms or provide the same progestogen effect on the lining. Metformin and the historical recall notice Metformin is mainly considered for metabolic needs such as insulin resistance, glucose and lipid outcomes, alongside appropriate lifestyle support. It may improve cycles or ovulation in some people, but it is not a contraceptive and can make pregnancy possible if ovulation resumes. It is not a universal substitute for hormonal symptom treatment or a guaranteed fertility treatment. Use for PCOS may be off-label, meaning an approved medicine is prescribed for a use outside its licensed indication. This does not mean the medicine itself is unapproved or that evidence is irrelevant. Discuss the evidence, benefits, gastrointestinal effects, kidney suitability and possible vitamin B12 monitoring with the prescriber; do not start or stop it on your own. The source article refers to US recalls beginning in 2020 involving certain extended-release metformin products and NDMA impurities. This historical event does not mean all metformin is currently recalled. If concerned, ask a pharmacist to check the exact product and lot against current notices and arrange an alternative if necessary. Do not abruptly stop prescribed metformin because of an old report. Effectiveness depends on the method and correct use Current CDC estimates suggest about seven pregnancies per 100 users in the first year of typical pill, patch or ring use, rather than the older nine-per-100 estimate in the source. These are population estimates, not a personal guarantee. Hormonal IUD typical-use failure is below one per 100 users per year; a method that fits your routine can reduce use errors. Use reminders and know what to do after missed pills, a detached patch, an expelled ring, vomiting or interacting medicines. Instructions differ by product and timing; seek prompt advice about backup and emergency contraception after a possible gap. Do not double doses or extend a hormone-free break without the correct instructions. These hormonal methods do not protect against STIs; condoms help reduce that risk. Choosing a plan that fits your goals Discuss pregnancy plans, bleeding preferences, acne or hair concerns, medical risks, convenience, cost, access and ability to stop or remove the method. No single method is best for everyone with PCOS. If pregnancy is desired, discuss stopping contraception and appropriate fertility care instead of using contraception to stimulate ovulation. Agree on follow-up for side effects, blood pressure, prolonged unexplained bleeding or a change in health or medicines. Metabolic and emotional health support remains important alongside contraception. Keep a record of symptoms and actual dosing or change dates; an app's fertile-day prediction is not reliable pregnancy protection when cycles are irregular. PCOS can reduce ovulation frequency without preventing all pregnancies. Combined pills, patches and rings suppress ovulation; they do not induce it. Benefits, contraindications and schedules differ between methods and products. Intermittent progestogen and metformin are not reliable contraception. Follow replacement and missed-dose instructions; seek urgent care for serious warning symptoms. Are combined pills suitable with PCOS? They can help irregular cycles and excess hair when estrogen is safe, but the choice depends on your health, goals and risks. Higher doses are not automatically better, and combined pills are not fertility treatment. Can I use a progestin-only pill instead? Often it is an option when estrogen is unsuitable or unwanted, after individual review. It may protect the endometrium, but bleeding can be irregular and the acne or hair benefits of combined pills are not guaranteed. What benefits can a patch offer? It can prevent pregnancy without daily pill taking and may help bleeding or cramps. It suppresses ovulation. Follow the specific patch's weekly replacement schedule and weight/BMI restrictions rather than leaving one patch on for three weeks. What can oral contraceptives improve? Selected pills may help bleeding patterns, period pain, acne or excess hair, depending on formulation and suitability. They do not cure PCOS, restore ovulation during use or guarantee protection from all cancers or ovarian cysts. Should I wait for bleeding to end before replacing a ring? No. For the usual NuvaRing schedule, insert the next ring exactly one week after removal even if bleeding continues. Follow the instructions for your actual product and prescribed regimen. Do metformin or occasional progesterone prevent pregnancy? No. Metformin may restore ovulation in some people, and an intermittent course for lining protection is not reliable contraception. Discuss a separate contraceptive method if pregnancy is not wanted. What if I forget a dose or replacement? Check your product instructions and contact a pharmacist or clinician promptly. Backup or emergency contraception may be needed depending on the gap and recent sex. PCOS does not remove that risk. Does an old metformin recall mean I should stop it? No. The 2020 notices concerned particular extended-release products and lots. Ask a pharmacist about your current exact product and any active recall; do not stop prescribed treatment abruptly because of an old notice.

title: Semen colour changes: what they can mean and when to seek care
description: Semen appearance can vary, but colour cannot diagnose fertility or infection. Learn about yellow, red, brown or black semen and symptoms that need assessment.
body: A change in semen colour can be unsettling. Many brief changes are harmless, but visible blood, persistent changes or accompanying symptoms deserve assessment. Colour offers clues rather than a diagnosis: the same shade can have different explanations. This guide covers usual appearance, yellow or green changes, blood-related colours, dark semen, texture and when to get help. Usual appearance is not a fertility test Semen is usually whitish or greyish, with some variation in opacity and consistency. It contains sperm mixed with fluid from glands including the seminal vesicles, prostate and bulbourethral glands. Its proteins, enzymes and minerals contribute to its appearance; colour is not a direct measurement of sperm number or health. Prostatic fluid contains substances such as citrate, zinc and enzymes, alongside other salts and components. Listing these ingredients cannot explain an individual colour change. Clearer or more watery semen does not prove infertility or vitamin deficiency, and white semen does not guarantee normal fertility or freedom from infection. Yellow or green semen: several possible explanations A mild yellow tint can occur with age, medicines or small traces of urine mixing with semen in the urethra. Other explanations include inflammation, infection or jaundice. A green or pronounced yellow change, especially if persistent or accompanied by symptoms, should be discussed with a clinician rather than diagnosed from a colour chart. Small residual drops in the urethra are different from urinary retention, which means the bladder cannot empty adequately. Difficulty passing urine, a weak stream or pain needs assessment; complete inability to urinate needs immediate emergency care. Do not dismiss urinary obstruction as a normal cause of yellow semen. Inflammation, white blood cells and jaundice Prostatitis or another urinary or genital infection may cause painful or frequent urination, pelvic or perineal pain, painful ejaculation, discharge, fever or chills. These symptoms need medical assessment, and fever with urinary symptoms or marked illness needs urgent advice. Colour cannot distinguish an STI from another infection, nor show whether antibiotics are needed. Leukocytospermia means increased white blood cells in semen. It requires laboratory assessment; a yellow sample alone cannot establish it. White blood cells may indicate inflammation without proving bacterial infection. Fertility effects and treatment depend on the full findings, not colour or an isolated white-cell result. Jaundice results from bilirubin building up and can be associated with yellow semen, but the important signs are yellow skin or the whites of the eyes. These need urgent medical assessment, particularly with abdominal pain, fever or feeling unwell. Do not use semen colour as a substitute for evaluating possible liver or bile-duct disease. Food, alcohol, cannabis and other exposures Medicines, supplements and what you consume may be relevant to a colour change, so tell the clinician about them. Reports about food pigments, garlic, onions, alcohol or cannabis are not a reliable way to identify the cause from a shade. A persistent change or possible blood should not simply be attributed to a recent meal or substance use. Do not use a colour chart to decide that a particular exposure has or has not occurred. Avoid starting vitamins, detox products or antibiotics to correct the colour without an indication. If you are concerned about alcohol, cannabis, medicines or environmental exposure, discuss the actual history and appropriate testing. Pink, red, brown or orange: possible blood Pink or red streaks can represent fresh blood; reddish-brown, brown or sometimes orange-brown semen may reflect older blood. Blood in semen is called haematospermia. It often settles and is usually not due to something serious, but arrange a medical check even if you otherwise feel well. Colour alone cannot establish the bleeding site or age precisely. Possible contexts include inflammation or infection, recent prostate biopsy, surgery, cystoscopy or another urological procedure. Follow the procedure team’s advice about expected bleeding and when to contact them. Tell a clinician about urinary symptoms, blood in urine, pelvic or testicular pain, genital discharge and blood-thinning medicines; do not stop prescribed blood thinners yourself. Blood in urine needs urgent same-day medical advice, even if it happens once, is a small amount or you are unsure it is blood; do not use the routine semen-blood appointment pathway for this. Blood pressure and other medical conditions may be checked as part of assessment. Semen colour cannot diagnose high blood pressure, and headaches or nosebleeds are not a dependable way to identify it. A clinician selects blood pressure measurement, examination and tests according to your history and symptoms. Sexual activity and concerns about cancer Injury or vigorous sexual activity can sometimes precede bleeding, but that is not a reason to ignore it or guarantee it will disappear in a day or two. Holding back orgasm or stopping before ejaculation is not an established explanation that makes blood harmless. Stop activities that cause pain or injury and seek advice for visible blood. Cancer is an uncommon cause of blood in semen, but it can involve the prostate, testis or urinary tract. Persistent or recurrent bleeding, a testicular lump, blood in urine or unexplained symptoms may need further investigation. A colour cannot diagnose cancer or rule it out. Outcome depends on the specific cancer and stage; late-stage disease must not be described as routinely curable. Very dark or black semen Very dark brown or black semen may contain older blood and should be assessed, particularly if it is new, persistent or recurrent. Do not assume that its darkness identifies the cause or makes it safe. Other symptoms and the medical history matter more than a photograph or a shade comparison. Spinal cord injury and heavy-metal exposure have been described among possible contexts for dark semen, but these are uncommon explanations and colour is not an exposure test. Tell the clinician about a known injury or credible occupational or environmental exposure, such as to lead or nickel. Do not infer poisoning or a spinal disorder from semen alone. Texture changes and fertility concerns Semen can be gel-like just after ejaculation and then become more fluid. Time since ejaculation or sample collection affects how it looks. A single thick or watery sample cannot establish dehydration, hormone imbalance, nutrient deficiency or infertility. Persistent major changes, pain or other symptoms warrant discussion. A semen analysis assesses features such as volume, sperm concentration, movement and shape under standardized conditions. More than one sample may be needed, and the results are interpreted with both partners’ circumstances when relevant. Neither one colour nor one laboratory number is a simple boundary between fertile and infertile. When to seek help and what assessment may involve Book a medical review for visible blood, unexplained dark semen or a colour change that persists or repeatedly returns. A new non-bloody colour change lasting more than a week is another reason to contact a clinician; this is not a waiting period when warning signs are present. Mention genital swelling or heaviness, itching, abnormal penile discharge, pain, urinary changes, fever or systemic symptoms. Seek immediate emergency care if you cannot urinate at all. Seek urgent care for fever or chills with urinary or pelvic symptoms or marked illness. Sudden severe testicular pain requires immediate emergency care. Severe illness, confusion or major breathing difficulty also needs emergency help rather than waiting to investigate semen colour. Assessment may include a history of timing, medicines, sexual exposures and procedures, plus genital or prostate examination and selected urine, STI or blood tests. Imaging or semen testing is chosen when relevant, not automatically for every colour change. Treatment targets an identified cause; do not self-prescribe antibiotics. Keep notes of changes and follow the agreed review plan. Colour and texture cannot determine fertility, infection or cancer on their own. Arrange assessment for visible blood, unexplained dark semen or persistent or recurrent changes. Yellow or green semen has several possible explanations; white cells need laboratory assessment. Do not dismiss blood as food, sexual activity or delayed orgasm, or stop prescribed medicines yourself. Inability to urinate, fever with urinary symptoms or sudden severe testicular pain needs urgent or emergency care. What can pink, red, brown or orange semen mean? Blood is one possible explanation: fresh blood may look pink or red and older blood brownish. Arrange a medical check rather than diagnosing the cause from colour, even though many cases settle without a serious cause. Can vigorous sex or masturbation change the colour? Trauma can sometimes precede bleeding, but visible blood still deserves advice. Holding back orgasm is not an established harmless explanation, and there is no universal one- or two-day recovery guarantee. What does black semen mean? Very dark semen may contain old blood, but the cause cannot be identified by appearance. Seek assessment; mention known spinal injury or credible heavy-metal exposure rather than assuming either from colour. When should I see a clinician? Arrange review for blood in semen, unexplained dark semen or persistent or recurrent changes, and sooner with symptoms. Blood in urine needs urgent same-day advice even once, in a small amount or if uncertain. Complete inability to urinate or sudden severe testicular pain needs immediate emergency care; fever with urinary symptoms needs urgent care. Does yellow semen prove an STI or white blood cells? No. Infection is one possible cause, but age, medicines, urine traces and other conditions can contribute. Leukocytospermia requires laboratory assessment and does not itself prove bacterial infection. Does watery semen mean infertility? No. Appearance does not measure sperm quality. If fertility is a concern, clinical assessment and appropriately collected semen analyses are more useful than colour or texture. Should I take antibiotics or vitamins to restore the colour? Not without an appropriate indication. Treatment depends on the cause. Tell the clinician about medicines, supplements and exposures and follow the recommended tests and care.

title: Paratubal and paraovarian cysts: symptoms and care
description: These cysts develop beside an ovary or fallopian tube. Learn about symptoms, ultrasound, observation, surgery, fertility and when pelvic pain is an emergency.
body: A paratubal or paraovarian cyst is a sac near a fallopian tube or ovary, rather than a cyst growing within the ovary itself. Many are fluid-filled, harmless and discovered incidentally. Care depends on the actual appearance, symptoms and clinical circumstances; finding a cyst does not automatically mean that surgery is needed. What these cysts are: and are not The terms overlap: “paraovarian” means beside the ovary and “paratubal” beside the fallopian tube. They develop in nearby tissue, often within the broad ligament supporting the reproductive organs. They are not simply unattached sacs floating in the abdomen. Some contain tissue as well as fluid, which affects assessment. They can occur at different ages and range from tiny incidental findings to larger masses. Because many cause no symptoms, their frequency is difficult to measure. Unlike functional ovarian cysts associated with ovulation, they are nonfunctional: do not assume they will disappear with the next few periods. Persistence alone does not mean cancer or require an operation. Symptoms and reasons to seek assessment A small uncomplicated cyst may cause no symptoms and be found during an examination, ultrasound or unrelated surgery. A larger cyst can cause pelvic or lower abdominal discomfort, fullness, pain during sex, constipation or urinary pressure. These symptoms have other possible causes; an existing cyst does not explain every new pain. Arrange assessment for persistent or recurring pain, bloating, early fullness, bowel or urinary changes, or unusual vaginal bleeding. Do not assume bleeding comes from the cyst. Seek urgent assessment now for pelvic pain with fever, vomiting, unusual vaginal bleeding, unusual discharge, difficulty passing urine or stool, or pregnancy or possible pregnancy. How they form Some cysts arise from tissue left over from fetal development, including Müllerian (paramesonephric) or Wolffian (mesonephric) duct remnants. These ducts are involved in early reproductive-system development. Fluid can collect within nearby tissues; the precise origin of an individual cyst may only become clear after examination of removed tissue. There is no established lifestyle measure that prevents these cysts, and no reason to blame yourself for developing one. Age patterns in reported cases do not mean they occur only between 30 and 40, or that a large cyst in a younger person is necessarily dangerous. They are not an ordinary monthly ovulation follicle. Examination and ultrasound A clinician reviews the pain, menstrual history, possibility of pregnancy, previous imaging and relevant medical or family history. Examination and a pregnancy test may be appropriate. Pelvic ultrasound usually helps locate the cyst in relation to the ovary and tube, measure it and assess whether it looks simple or complex. An abdominal scan may be used; a transvaginal scan can provide more detail when suitable and accepted after explanation and consent. Discuss an alternative if it is unsuitable or you do not want it. Sometimes imaging cannot confidently distinguish a paraovarian cyst from another adnexal mass, so further specialist assessment is needed. What MRI, blood tests and laparoscopy can tell you MRI may help characterize a mass that ultrasound cannot fully assess. Blood tests are selected for the situation: a blood count can assess anaemia or infection concerns, while tumour markers may contribute to a cancer-risk assessment. Neither MRI nor a tumour-marker result alone proves or rules out cancer. Most simple paraovarian cysts are benign; concerning features need specialist review. Laparoscopy uses small abdominal cuts and a camera to inspect the pelvis, often while treating a problem. It is not a required diagnostic test for every incidental cyst. If tissue is removed, laboratory examination can establish its type. Suspected torsion is a different, urgent situation: assessment and treatment must not be delayed for repeated routine scans. Observation or surgery: an individual decision If the cyst is clearly simple, causes no symptoms and has a low risk of complications, no treatment (and sometimes no routine follow-up) may be appropriate. Other cases need planned ultrasound surveillance. Ask whether follow-up is needed, when it should happen and which symptoms should trigger earlier contact. Observation does not promise spontaneous disappearance. Surgery may be considered for troublesome symptoms, growth, uncertain or concerning imaging, or a significant complication risk. Size matters alongside appearance, age, menopausal status, health and your preferences; there is no universal “over 10 cm means surgery” rule. Smaller cysts can also need urgent treatment if they twist or bleed. Hormonal pills are not a proven way to dissolve a paraovarian cyst. Cyst removal and recovery Cystectomy means removing the cyst while aiming to preserve healthy nearby structures. Laparoscopy is keyhole surgery; laparotomy uses a larger abdominal opening and may be chosen for a very large or concerning mass or other surgical needs. These operations generally use general anaesthesia, rather than being routine procedures under local anaesthetic. Discuss the planned approach, possible changes during surgery, bleeding, infection, injury to nearby organs and anaesthetic risks. Keyhole surgery often allows a quicker recovery, but recovery varies with the operation and individual health. Follow the discharge plan and seek prompt advice for fever or offensive discharge. Severe or worsening pain, heavy bleeding, faintness or breathing difficulty require immediate emergency care. Torsion, rupture and pressure complications Torsion is twisting of the cyst and sometimes the fallopian tube, ovary or their supporting structures, potentially cutting off blood supply. Sudden severe pelvic or abdominal pain, often with nausea or vomiting, needs immediate emergency assessment, even if pain comes and goes. Normal Doppler blood flow does not by itself exclude torsion. Prompt surgery aims to untwist and preserve tissue when possible, but preservation cannot be guaranteed. A ruptured cyst can cause internal bleeding; treatment depends on the symptoms and stability, rather than every rupture requiring surgery. Rare very large cysts can compress the bladder, bowel, uterus or urinary drainage pathways. Obstructed drainage can cause hydronephrosis, swelling of the kidney from backed-up urine. Tube damage or, rarely, rupture can occur with severe complications; these are possibilities, not expected outcomes for every small cyst. Fertility and the outlook An uncomplicated small cyst usually does not interfere with ovulation or prevent pregnancy. A large mass, torsion, tubal damage, the underlying condition and the operation can affect fertility. Tell the team about future pregnancy plans before planned surgery. Early emergency treatment offers a chance to protect function; it cannot promise preservation of an ovary or tube. Sometimes removal of an ovary (oophorectomy), a tube (salpingectomy) or both is necessary. Pregnancy may remain possible with a healthy remaining ovary and functioning tube, but chances depend on the whole situation. Many people need only reassurance or monitoring. Do not replace follow-up with a promise that all cysts disappear, that every large cyst needs removal or that fertility is always unaffected. When pain is an emergency Get immediate emergency care for severe or worsening pelvic pain, sudden intense pain with nausea or vomiting, fainting or marked dizziness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty, confusion or heavy vaginal bleeding. These can signal torsion, significant bleeding or another emergency. Do not drive yourself if faint or seriously unwell. Pelvic pain with possible pregnancy needs urgent assessment even without a positive test, because ectopic pregnancy is another possible cause. Severe pain, shoulder-tip pain, faintness or heavy bleeding makes this an immediate emergency. A known cyst must not delay assessment of a new or worsening symptom; do not wait for a scheduled scan or a particular cyst size. Paratubal and paraovarian cysts develop beside the ovary or tube and are usually benign. They are nonfunctional cysts; routine disappearance over a few menstrual cycles cannot be assumed. Ultrasound guides assessment; MRI and tumour markers cannot independently diagnose cancer. Observation, follow-up or surgery depends on the full clinical picture, not a single size threshold. Sudden severe pain, fainting or heavy bleeding needs immediate emergency care; fertility preservation is an aim, not a guarantee. What causes a paratubal cyst? It can arise from nearby tissue or embryonic duct remnants, including Müllerian or Wolffian remnants. There is no established preventive lifestyle measure, and its presence is not your fault. Will it disappear by itself? Do not assume so. These are nonfunctional cysts, unlike many ovulation-related ovarian cysts. A stable simple cyst may still be harmless and need no treatment; your clinician decides whether surveillance is needed. Which symptoms can it cause? Many cause none. Larger or complicated cysts may cause pelvic pain, fullness, bowel or urinary pressure or pain during sex. Other conditions can cause the same symptoms, so new or persistent symptoms need assessment. Can MRI or a blood test confirm cancer? No single MRI or tumour-marker result establishes or excludes cancer. Clinicians combine history and imaging with selected tests and, when appropriate, specialist assessment and examination of removed tissue. Does a cyst over 10 cm always need surgery? No universal cutoff applies. Symptoms, growth, appearance, complication risk, age, health and preferences all matter. A very large cyst needs specialist assessment, while even a smaller cyst can need emergency treatment for torsion. How is it removed? Often by keyhole cystectomy, with general anaesthesia, aiming to preserve healthy structures. A larger opening may be needed in selected cases. Discuss the risks, recovery and possibility of removing a tube or ovary before planned surgery. Will my fertility be preserved? Many uncomplicated cysts do not affect fertility. Treatment aims to preserve the ovary and tube where safe, but cannot guarantee this. Pregnancy may still be possible with one healthy ovary and functioning tube; individual circumstances matter. Which complications need immediate help? Sudden severe or worsening pelvic pain, especially with vomiting, faintness, shoulder-tip pain, heavy bleeding or breathing difficulty needs immediate emergency assessment. Do not wait for a scan, a large size or every warning sign. Possible pregnancy with pelvic pain needs urgent assessment too.

title: Bilirubin blood tests: jaundice, preparation and results
description: What direct, indirect and total bilirubin mean, how blood testing works, and why newborn results need age-specific assessment and prompt follow-up.
body: A bilirubin test measures a yellow pigment made as red blood cells break down. It helps investigate jaundice and monitor treatment, but one result does not identify the cause or prove liver damage. Newborns need a different interpretation from adults. Do not postpone care for a yellow or unwell baby while arranging a routine test. When jaundice needs urgent help Get immediate emergency assessment for a jaundiced baby who is unusually sleepy or hard to wake, is not feeding, is floppy or stiff, has jerking movements, breathing difficulty, no wet nappies, or a temperature of 38°C or higher or 36°C or lower. Jaundice in the first 24 hours also needs immediate hospital assessment. Do not drive yourself with an unwell baby; arrange another driver or emergency transport. After the first day, suspected or worsening jaundice, dark urine or pale creamy/chalky stools need urgent same-day advice even if the baby seems well. New yellow skin or eyes in an older child or adult also needs urgent medical assessment. Fatigue, itching, reduced appetite, dark urine or pale stools may accompany it. Severe abdominal pain with fever, confusion or collapse needs emergency care rather than waiting for a laboratory appointment. Direct, indirect and total bilirubin Normal breakdown of haemoglobin in older red cells produces bilirubin. Unconjugated, or indirect, bilirubin travels to the liver, largely attached to albumin. The liver joins it to glucuronic acid, making conjugated bilirubin more water-soluble for excretion into bile. Bile carries it through the bile ducts to the intestine; its breakdown products leave mainly in stool. The gallbladder stores bile, but not all bile must pass through it first. Reports may list total bilirubin and a direct fraction, which broadly reflects conjugated bilirubin; indirect bilirubin is commonly calculated as total minus direct. These fractions help narrow the possibilities, not diagnose them alone. Bilirubin can rise because too much is produced, processing is altered, or bile drainage is impaired. A raised level is not automatically evidence of liver injury. Why the test is requested Testing can investigate yellow skin or eyes, suspected liver or bile-duct disease, excessive red-cell destruction called haemolysis, or a treatment response. In newborns, increased production and immature bilirubin handling commonly contribute to jaundice. That does not mean every baby has pathological haemolysis or that all jaundice is harmless. Bilirubin may be part of a wider liver panel with ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, albumin and total protein. These tests answer different questions; their pattern, symptoms, examination and previous results matter. Blood counts and other haemolysis tests, urine testing or ultrasound may be chosen. Not everyone needs every test, and a normal bilirubin result does not rule out every liver condition. What happens during sampling A trained professional usually takes a small sample from an arm vein into a collection tube. There may be a brief sting and mild aching afterwards. In newborns, a heel-prick sample is often used; a venous sample may sometimes be needed. Ask the team how they will support comfort during the procedure. A skin bilirubin meter can estimate a newborn’s level without a needle, but it does not replace blood testing in every situation. Babies in their first 24 hours or born before 35 weeks of gestation need serum testing. High or near-treatment skin readings need confirmation according to the clinical protocol. Skin colour alone cannot establish the number or its safety. Preparation: ask about food and medicines Follow the ordering clinician’s or laboratory’s instructions; there is no universal four-hour fasting rule. Older patients may be asked to fast for particular tests taken together. Clarify how long, whether water is allowed, and what to do with diabetes treatment or fluid restrictions. Do not fast a newborn for a routine bilirubin check or withhold needed feeds while waiting. Give the team a complete medicine and supplement list, including any penicillin G, phenobarbital, furosemide or theophylline you take. This is not a list of medicines to stop automatically. Furosemide is a diuretic, not a laxative. Medicines may affect results or bilirubin handling, but necessary treatment must not be stopped or altered without specific prescriber advice. Risks and care after a blood test Brief pain or a small bruise is common; faintness, a larger collection of blood under the skin called a haematoma, prolonged bleeding and infection are less common risks. Tell staff about previous fainting, bleeding problems, blood thinners and dressing allergies. Sit or lie down if lightheaded and alert the team. Press on the sampling site as directed and follow local advice about the dressing and lifting or exercise; the same timing is not needed for everyone. Keep the area clean. Seek prompt medical advice for bleeding that persists despite firm pressure, a growing painful swelling or signs of infection. Heavy uncontrolled bleeding, collapse or severe symptoms require emergency help. Prolonged bleeding needs assessment but does not by itself prove a serious blood disorder. Reading the result: age, units and trends Use the reference interval printed by the laboratory. As an adult example, MedlinePlus lists total bilirubin around 0.1–1.2 mg/dL and direct bilirubin below 0.3 mg/dL; other laboratories differ. Reports may use µmol/L instead, so numbers cannot be compared without checking units. An isolated mild abnormality needs interpretation, not an assumed diagnosis or treatment. Adult ranges and a fixed newborn cutoff such as 5.2 mg/dL do not determine neonatal safety. The team considers age in hours, gestational age, total serum bilirubin, the speed of change and risk factors such as haemolysis or illness, then uses the appropriate treatment chart. The same number can mean different things at different ages. Direct bilirubin should not be subtracted from total when applying neonatal treatment thresholds. Possible causes in older children and adults Raised bilirubin may accompany hepatitis, cirrhosis, medicine-related liver injury, Gilbert syndrome, gallstones or narrowed bile ducts. Pancreatic or gallbladder cancer is another possible cause of obstruction, but a high result is not a cancer diagnosis. Gilbert syndrome usually causes mild intermittent unconjugated elevation; it should not be guessed from a number without assessing other causes. Haemolysis can raise indirect bilirubin without primary liver disease. Causes include autoimmune conditions, inherited red-cell disorders, infections, some medicines and reactions to a blood transfusion. A transfusion reaction is a specific clinical problem, not something a bilirubin result proves. Tell the treating team immediately about symptoms during or after a transfusion; they will assess the reaction and choose tests and treatment. Newborn jaundice: different patterns and causes Physiological jaundice commonly becomes noticeable after the first day as bilirubin production and clearance adjust. Suboptimal-intake jaundice often occurs in the first week when too little milk is transferred. Breast milk jaundice is a different pattern, usually in the second or later weeks, sometimes lasting longer in an otherwise thriving baby; its exact mechanism is uncertain. Persistent jaundice still needs assessment rather than assuming breast milk is the cause. Other causes include blood-group antibody haemolysis, G6PD deficiency or other inherited red-cell/enzyme disorders, bruising, excess red cells called polycythaemia, infection and liver or bile-drainage disease. Prematurity increases vulnerability but does not itself mean polycythaemia. Sickle cell disease can cause haemolysis later in life but is not a usual explanation for jaundice in the first newborn days; symptoms generally begin months later. Maternal and infant blood groups differing does not automatically mean haemolytic disease. What to do after the result Ask who will review the result, when you will hear back, whether further tests are needed and exactly when to repeat it. Newborn follow-up may be needed within hours and must reflect the result and the baby’s condition, not a routine adult turnaround time. Prolonged neonatal jaundice, especially with pale stools or dark urine, needs assessment including the direct/conjugated fraction. Imaging is selected when liver, gallbladder or drainage disease is suspected; it does not exclude every possible cause. Treatment targets the cause and severity. Most jaundiced babies can continue breastfeeding with effective feeding support; expressed milk, donor milk or formula may be needed individually. Do not withhold necessary supplementation or interrupt breastfeeding without a clinical plan. Some babies need monitored phototherapy, rarely urgent specialist treatment such as exchange transfusion. Feeds alone are not treatment for dangerous bilirubin levels, and sunlight, water or herbal remedies are not substitutes. Keep the written follow-up plan and seek help sooner if symptoms change. A bilirubin result helps guide assessment; it does not diagnose the cause alone. Preparation depends on the ordered tests. Do not fast a newborn or stop medicines on your own. Newborn decisions require age in hours, gestation, serum results, risks and trends: not an adult range or one fixed cutoff. Follow-up, feeding support and any treatment must match the individual; urgent symptoms override a routine test appointment. When is newborn jaundice dangerous? First-day jaundice, rapid rises, haemolysis, infection or other illness need prompt assessment. A jaundiced baby who is difficult to wake, not feeding, floppy or stiff, breathing badly, has no wet nappies or a temperature at least 38°C or at most 36°C needs immediate emergency care. Do not wait for a bilirubin result. Are there three types of newborn jaundice? Physiological, suboptimal-intake and breast milk jaundice are useful patterns, not an exhaustive classification. Early low milk intake differs from later breast milk jaundice. Blood-cell, infection, liver and bile-duct causes must be considered when appropriate. What can cause an abnormal result? Excess red-cell breakdown, altered liver processing or blocked bile drainage can raise bilirubin. Examples include haemolytic disorders, hepatitis, cirrhosis, Gilbert syndrome, stones and strictures. The fractions and other findings guide further testing; one high result does not prove liver damage or cancer. What happens after testing? A clinician interprets the result, decides on further tests or imaging and sets a repeat-testing or treatment plan. Ask for the actual number, units, fractions and next contact time. Newborn follow-up may be much faster than routine adult results, and new symptoms need earlier help. Must I fast or stop medicines? Only follow specific instructions for your ordered tests and situation. There is no universal four-hour rule. Do not fast a newborn for a routine bilirubin check. Disclose all medicines and supplements, but do not stop prescribed treatment without advice. Can a skin reading replace the blood test? Sometimes it is useful for newborn screening, but babies in their first 24 hours or born before 35 weeks of gestation, and those with high or near-treatment readings, need blood testing according to the protocol. A colour estimate or home photograph cannot establish the bilirubin level. Is one bilirubin number safe for every baby? No. Age in hours, gestation, clinical condition, risks and the trend determine the assessment and treatment threshold. Use the clinician’s interpretation, not an adult reference range or a number from another baby. Should breastfeeding stop if the baby is yellow? Usually breastfeeding continues with support and assessment of effective intake. Extra expressed milk, donor milk or formula may be needed; interruption is rarely advised and needs a specific plan. Do not delay phototherapy or emergency care in favour of feeding alone.

title: Ulcerative colitis: symptoms, treatment and lifelong follow-up
description: Understand ulcerative colitis, flare warning signs, diagnosis, medicines, surgery, food choices, children’s care and individual cancer surveillance.
body: Ulcerative colitis is a long-term inflammatory bowel disease affecting the inner lining of the colon and rectum. Treatment can control inflammation and support long periods of wellbeing, but symptoms may return. A diagnosis needs medical assessment: bloody diarrhoea, pain or weight loss should not be attributed to food or stress alone. What ulcerative colitis does to the bowel Inflammation usually begins in the rectum and can extend continuously through part or all of the colon. It damages the surface lining, producing ulcers that can bleed and release mucus or pus. Inflamed bowel may empty more often and urgently; bowel noises alone do not diagnose the disease. The condition can begin at any age, often in adolescence or young adulthood, and also affects older adults. Its extent and activity differ between people and can change over time. Remission means disease activity is controlled; feeling better does not always mean all inflammation has healed. Symptoms and when to get help Common symptoms include diarrhoea, blood or mucus in stools, abdominal cramps, rectal discomfort and an urgent or persistent feeling of needing to pass stool even when the bowel is empty. Night-time bowel movements, tiredness, reduced appetite, nausea, weight loss or fever can occur. Poor intake and inflammation can contribute to malnutrition and anaemia. Arrange assessment for persistent bowel changes or suspected ulcerative colitis. Seek urgent same-day help for bloody or very severe diarrhoea, fever, a fast heartbeat, inability to pass stool or gas, or a worsening flare. Contact your existing IBD team promptly rather than waiting for a routine appointment. Severe abdominal pain, continuous or heavy rectal bleeding, large blood clots, vomiting blood or marked deterioration requires immediate emergency care. New eye pain or vision change also needs prompt assessment. Painful or swollen joints, skin changes and mouth ulcers can accompany bowel disease and should be reported. Why it happens, and who may be at risk The cause is not fully understood. Genes, altered immune responses, gut microbes and environmental factors interact; the immune system’s inflammatory activity injures the bowel. Having another immune-mediated illness may be relevant to assessment, but does not establish that you have ulcerative colitis. Family history can increase risk, although many affected people have no affected relative. Rates differ across populations, including higher reported rates in people with Ashkenazi ancestry, but any ancestry can be affected. These patterns are not a diagnosis or anyone’s fault. Studies of the acne medicine isotretinoin and IBD have produced differing observational results. An association in a study does not prove a medicine caused an individual’s illness. Discuss new bowel symptoms and medicine concerns with the prescriber; do not stop treatment or conclude causation on your own. Diagnosis and tests A clinician reviews symptoms, medicines and family history, examines you and selects tests. Stool tests look for infection, including Clostridioides difficile, and may measure faecal calprotectin as a marker of intestinal inflammation. Blood tests may assess anaemia, inflammation, hydration and nutritional status; no single blood result confirms ulcerative colitis. Colonoscopy or, in selected circumstances, a limited sigmoidoscopy allows examination of the lining and collection of biopsies. CT, ultrasound or other imaging may be useful for specific questions or complications. An upper endoscopy is not a routine substitute for examining the colon and is selected when another diagnosis, such as Crohn’s disease, is suspected. Antibody tests are not recommended to establish or exclude ulcerative colitis. Biopsy results, bowel distribution, infection testing and the clinical picture are considered together. Follow-up may combine symptoms, stool markers and endoscopic assessment rather than relying on symptoms alone. Medicines: different jobs at different stages The plan depends on disease extent, severity, previous response, other conditions and your preferences. Induction treatment settles active inflammation; maintenance treatment helps prevent relapse. Oral or rectal 5-aminosalicylates, such as mesalazine/mesalamine or sulfasalazine, are commonly used for mild-to-moderate disease. Balsalazide and olsalazine are other formulations used in some settings. Corticosteroids can help induce remission when needed, but are not maintenance treatment. Thiopurines such as azathioprine or mercaptopurine may be selected for maintenance or combination treatment, rather than as a rapid stand-alone induction treatment. Methotrexate alone is not recommended for inducing or maintaining UC remission. For moderate-to-severe disease, options include biologics such as infliximab, vedolizumab or ustekinumab, and other targeted treatments. Tofacitinib is an oral JAK-inhibitor small molecule, not a biologic or the first oral medicine ever used for UC. Other JAK inhibitors, S1P modulators and newer biologics may be options depending on local approval and individual suitability. Some treatments are used alone and others in combinations; there is no rule that every medicine must be combined. Discuss benefits, infection screening, vaccination, monitoring and medicine-specific risks. Antibiotics treat selected infections or complications, not every UC flare. Do not change doses, stop prescribed treatment or start anti-diarrhoeal or pain medicines without advice. Severe flares and hospital treatment An acute severe flare may require hospital care for blood and stool testing, close observation, intravenous fluids, electrolyte correction and treatment of anaemia, sometimes including transfusion. Intravenous steroids, prevention of blood clots and early specialist review may be needed. If initial treatment is insufficient, the team may consider rescue medicines or surgery promptly. Routine broad-spectrum antibiotics or intravenous nutrition solely to rest the bowel are not standard for everyone. Infection, nutritional needs and complications change the plan; severe symptoms should not be managed with supplements at home. Surgery: what is removed and what changes Surgery may be considered for disease not adequately controlled with medicines, unacceptable treatment effects, dysplasia or cancer, or life-threatening bleeding, perforation or toxic megacolon. It is an individual decision, sometimes an emergency, rather than an inevitable outcome for a fixed percentage of people. Removing the colon and rectum removes the bowel tissue affected by UC.
