Options include an ileostomy, which drains stool through an abdominal stoma into a bag, or an ileal pouch made from small intestine and connected to the anus. Pouch surgery is often staged and is not suitable for everyone; it does not simply join the small bowel to an unchanged rectum. Surgery can substantially improve life but has risks and long-term care needs, including possible pouch inflammation. Disease outside the bowel may persist. Limited bowel removal does not guarantee a permanent cure, and even after full removal follow-up remains important. Discuss continence, fertility, sexual wellbeing and practical stoma or pouch care before elective surgery. Supplements and “natural” treatments Boswellia, bromelain, curcumin, psyllium and probiotics are sometimes promoted for UC. Evidence, product quality and safety vary. They should not replace effective medical treatment or delay assessment. Small adjunctive studies of curcumin do not establish a cure or a universally effective product; concentrated supplements can interact with medicines. Probiotic strains and combinations are not interchangeable, and benefits cannot be assumed for any shop product. They may pose particular risks in seriously ill or immunocompromised people. Psyllium or other fibre supplements can worsen bloating or be unsuitable in some situations. Check any proposed product with the IBD team, especially for children, pregnancy or significant immune suppression. Food, fluids and nutritional support No single diet cures UC or reliably prevents every flare. A varied, balanced eating pattern supports health; a dietitian can adapt it to symptoms and nutritional needs. Claims that a low-fat diet or extra vitamin C will reliably prolong remission are not established. Choose tolerated sources of protein, carbohydrates, fruit, vegetables and healthy fats rather than imposing broad exclusions. During a flare, smaller meals, regular fluids and temporary changes in food texture or fibre may help symptoms. Fatty foods worsen diarrhoea for some, and lactose reduction may help if lactose intolerance is present. Long-term avoidance of fibre or dairy is not necessary for everyone. A food-and-symptom diary can guide discussion; expand the diet again as tolerated. Weight loss, poor intake or ongoing blood loss need nutritional assessment. Iron, vitamin D, calcium or other supplementation should address individual needs; vitamin B12 monitoring is especially relevant after ileal surgery or pouch formation. Ask before taking a multivitamin or high-dose supplement. Nutrition supports treatment but does not prove bowel inflammation is controlled. UC compared with Crohn’s disease and other colitis Ulcerative colitis generally affects the inner lining of the rectum and colon in a continuous pattern. Crohn’s disease can affect any part of the digestive tract, in patches and deeper bowel layers. Symptoms overlap, and investigations may be needed to distinguish them; sometimes IBD remains unclassified initially. Colitis simply means inflammation of the colon. Infection, impaired blood supply, medicines and other conditions can also cause it. UC itself is not contagious, although an infection causing similar symptoms can spread and needs its own care. Surgery can remove UC-affected colon and rectum; Crohn’s disease can recur elsewhere after surgery. Is there a cure? Medicines can achieve and maintain remission, but currently do not provide a permanent nonsurgical cure. This does not mean treatment cannot help or that everyone will need surgery. Removing the colon and rectum eliminates colonic UC, with important trade-offs and ongoing health needs rather than a guarantee that every symptom or extraintestinal problem disappears. Colonoscopy and cancer surveillance Colonoscopy helps diagnose disease, assess healing and detect precancerous changes. Biopsies are examined for inflammation and dysplasia. Preparation and sedation choices depend on the procedure and your circumstances: follow the endoscopy service’s instructions rather than a universal rule to avoid all solid food for several days. Cancer-surveillance timing is individual. Duration, extent, accumulated inflammation, previous dysplasia, family history and primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) affect risk. Current BSG guidance starts risk assessment around eight years after bowel symptoms begin, or from diagnosis when PSC-associated colitis is present; other local guidance may differ. There is no universal colonoscopy every two or three years for all UC. Higher-risk people need closer surveillance, while confirmed rectum-only or near-population-risk disease may follow a different plan alongside ordinary screening. Agree on your next review date, and seek care for new symptoms rather than waiting for surveillance. Ulcerative colitis in children Children can develop UC, but this does not mean one in ten children has IBD. Persistent diarrhoea or bleeding, pain, tiredness, weight loss, slow growth or delayed puberty needs assessment. Paediatric care monitors disease activity, nutrition, iron status, growth, bone health and development. Treatment is tailored to age, weight, disease severity and family circumstances. Oral and rectal mesalazine can both be appropriate; rectal therapy is not excluded simply because the patient is a child. Other medicines or surgery may be needed under specialist care. Do not copy adult doses or supplement plans. School support, vaccination review and transition to adult services also matter. Complications to monitor Complications can include anaemia, dehydration, malnutrition, weakened bones, blood clots, severe bleeding, toxic megacolon and bowel perforation. Inflammation can affect joints, skin, eyes or the liver, including PSC; kidney problems or stones can occur in some circumstances. These are possibilities, not an inevitable list for every person. Monitoring and timely treatment reduce risk. Bowel-wall thickening on a scan is not, by itself, a UC diagnosis. Discuss new joint, eye, skin or urinary symptoms. Sudden breathlessness, chest pain, fainting or severe worsening illness requires emergency assessment, including consideration of blood clots or serious complications. Can it be prevented? There is no established way to guarantee prevention of UC. After diagnosis, taking agreed maintenance medicines and attending reviews can reduce relapse and detect problems. Food choices, hydration, sleep, activity and stress support can improve wellbeing, without blaming you for flares or replacing anti-inflammatory treatment. Discuss vaccinations and medication safety with the team. Do not start smoking as a UC treatment. Avoid self-prescribed NSAID painkillers such as ibuprofen unless a clinician advises them. Any flare plan should explain whom to contact, what to monitor and when to seek urgent help. Long-term outlook and everyday life Many people have long periods of remission and lead active lives. Others need treatment changes or surgery. Agree on goals that include inflammation control, daily function, nutrition and mental wellbeing, and review progress even when symptoms improve. Planning toilet access, travel, school or work adjustments and discussing effects on relationships can help. Psychological support complements medical care; it does not imply the disease is imagined. Continue lifelong follow-up appropriate to your medicines, remaining bowel or pouch, cancer risk and other health needs. UC causes chronic inflammation of the colon and rectum; symptoms and healing need clinical assessment. Bloody or severe diarrhoea needs urgent advice; severe pain or heavy continuous bleeding needs emergency care. Induction and maintenance treatments differ, and steroids are not long-term maintenance therapy. Diet and supplements cannot promise a cure; nutritional advice and treatments must fit the individual. Surgery, children’s care and cancer surveillance require individualized specialist plans and ongoing follow-up. Why does UC cause ulcers? Inflammation damages the inner bowel lining, producing sores that may bleed or release mucus and pus. Urgency and diarrhoea can accompany this injury, but symptoms alone do not confirm UC. What symptoms should I report? Persistent diarrhoea, stool blood or mucus, cramps, rectal discomfort, urgency, night-time bowel movements, fatigue or weight loss warrant assessment. Severe pain or heavy ongoing bleeding needs emergency care; bloody or very severe diarrhoea needs urgent same-day advice. What diet is best? There is no universal cure diet. Aim for adequate, varied nutrition, adapting texture, fibre, meal size or lactose only as needed with professional advice. A low-fat diet or extra vitamin C is not proven to reliably keep everyone in remission. Can UC be cured? Medicines control disease and maintain remission rather than providing a permanent nonsurgical cure. Removing the colon and rectum removes colonic UC, but has trade-offs, and extraintestinal disease or pouch problems may still need care. Are steroids a maintenance medicine? No. They can settle a flare but are not used to maintain remission. A clinician should plan steroid reduction and a suitable maintenance strategy; do not stop or change treatment yourself. Can I replace medicines with probiotics or herbs? No. Evidence and safety vary by product, and no supplement is a universal substitute for UC treatment. Check proposed products, interactions and special risks with the IBD team. Does everyone need colonoscopy every two or three years? No. Surveillance depends on duration, extent, inflammation, PSC, family history and previous findings. Ask your team for a personal schedule and report new symptoms between tests. Is it infectious or caused by stress? UC is not contagious, and stress alone does not explain its cause. Immune, genetic, microbial and environmental factors interact. Some infections resemble or accompany flares, so testing may be necessary. Can a child use rectal mesalazine? Yes, when prescribed as part of a paediatric plan. Oral and rectal treatment may be combined; suitability and dose depend on the child. Growth, nutrition and school needs require attention alongside bowel symptoms.

title: Ovarian cysts and lower back pain: is there a connection?
description: An ovarian cyst can sometimes cause a lower-back ache. Learn other possible causes, cyst types, tests, treatment choices and warning signs needing urgent care.
body: Many ovarian cysts cause no symptoms and disappear without treatment. Some, especially larger cysts, can cause pelvic pressure or a dull lower-back ache. Back pain alone cannot identify a cyst, and finding a cyst on a scan does not prove it explains the pain. Assessment should consider both pelvic and spinal causes. How a cyst may be linked to back pain An ovarian cyst is a fluid-filled sac in or on an ovary. Functional cysts develop around ovulation and are common before menopause. Larger cysts may put pressure on nearby structures and cause lower-abdominal or pelvic discomfort that can be felt in the lower back or thighs. The ache may come and go; not everyone with a large cyst has pain. The source article refers to a selected imaging series. Such figures cannot establish how often ovarian cysts cause back pain in the general population, or whether an incidental cyst caused an individual’s symptoms. Muscle strain, disc or nerve problems and other pelvic, urinary or bowel conditions can produce similar pain. Symptoms do not confirm the cause Possible accompanying symptoms include pelvic fullness, bloating, painful or irregular periods, unusual vaginal bleeding, pain during sex, urinary frequency or difficulty emptying the bladder, and constipation or bowel pressure. Burning urination also needs assessment for other causes, including infection. These symptoms are not specific to cysts. New leg weakness, tingling or numbness should not be attributed to a cyst without assessment. Back pain with new numbness around the genitals or anus, weakness or numbness in both legs, or new difficulty urinating or loss of bladder or bowel control needs immediate emergency care. Do not wait for a planned ovarian scan. Different types of ovarian cyst Functional cysts include follicular cysts, when a follicle does not release its egg as expected, and corpus luteum cysts, when fluid collects after ovulation. Many resolve over weeks or a few cycles. A normal developing follicle is not automatically a harmful cyst, and not every ovarian cyst has the same size or course. Dermoid cysts, also called mature cystic teratomas, arise from germ cells and may contain fat, skin, hair or teeth. They are usually benign but need an individual assessment. Cystadenomas develop from ovarian surface tissue, may contain watery fluid or mucus, and can grow large. Endometriomas contain old blood and are associated with endometriosis. Endometriosis itself can cause pelvic, period-related or back pain. Cyst type, appearance, growth, symptoms and age matter together; size alone neither diagnoses the cause of pain nor determines whether surgery is necessary. How clinicians investigate the pain A clinician asks about where and when pain occurs, its relation to periods or movement, bleeding, urinary or bowel symptoms, medicines and pregnancy possibility. Examination may include the abdomen, back and, with consent when appropriate, the pelvis. A pregnancy test can be important even when a cyst is already known. Pelvic ultrasound assesses a cyst’s location, size and whether it looks simple, solid or complex. Abdominal or vaginal ultrasound is selected according to the situation and your consent. A scan can identify a cyst but cannot by itself establish that it causes back pain; other investigations may be needed. Blood tests, including CA-125, are selected rather than required for every simple cyst. CA-125 may rise in cancer but also in noncancerous conditions such as endometriosis or pelvic inflammation. Menopausal status, scan findings and the whole clinical picture guide interpretation; a result alone is not a diagnosis. Comfort measures while following a care plan If symptoms are mild and a clinician has advised observation, wrapped warmth may ease discomfort. Avoid burns. Gentle activity or stretching can help some back pain, but stop if pain worsens and do not try to exercise through severe pelvic pain. Prolonged bed rest is usually unhelpful for ordinary back pain. These measures do not shrink or cure a cyst. A clinician or pharmacist can help select pain relief. Paracetamol/acetaminophen may be considered for pelvic discomfort; it is not generally recommended alone for nonspecific back pain. Ibuprofen or naproxen may be unsuitable with pregnancy, kidney disease, previous stomach ulcers, bleeding risk or certain medicines. Do not combine NSAIDs or take them in pregnancy without professional advice; follow the product instructions. When to arrange assessment Seek assessment for persistent, recurrent, worsening or disabling pain, new pelvic symptoms, unexplained weight loss or pain that is worse at night. Fever or feeling generally unwell with back or pelvic pain needs urgent advice. New pain after injury, unusual bleeding or changes in bladder or bowel function should be discussed rather than assumed to be a familiar cyst. If pregnancy is possible, pelvic pain or unusual vaginal bleeding needs prompt medical advice, even without a positive pregnancy test. Ectopic pregnancy is one possible cause. Shoulder-tip pain needs advice immediately; sudden severe abdominal pain with dizziness or fainting needs emergency care. Monitoring and hormonal medicines Observation may be suitable for a cyst that appears benign, depending on symptoms, age, pregnancy or menopausal status, size and scan features. Some need a repeat scan and others do not. Agree on the follow-up date and what changes should prompt an earlier review; do not apply one interval to every cyst. A December 2025 RCOG update states that an asymptomatic, simple, unilateral, unilocular cyst measuring 3 cm or less after menopause does not need routine follow-up. This specific low-risk finding does not apply to every postmenopausal cyst or to unexplained symptoms. Local guidance and individual circumstances still matter. Hormonal contraception that suppresses ovulation may reduce new functional cysts in suitable people, but it does not shrink an existing cyst or treat every cyst type. Discuss contraceptive preferences, pregnancy plans, risks and alternatives; do not start hormones solely on the basis of back pain. When surgery may be appropriate Surgery may be considered for a cyst that is growing, persistent, large, concerning on imaging or causing significant symptoms. Cancer concern, torsion or bleeding changes the urgency and plan. Persistence beyond a few cycles does not automatically mean every cyst needs removal. Keyhole surgery (laparoscopy) is often possible for suitable benign-looking cysts; an open operation may be needed for a very large cyst or suspected cancer. Cystectomy removes the cyst while retaining ovarian tissue when possible; oophorectomy removes an ovary when necessary. Discuss fertility, ovarian preservation and the possibility of a different operation beforehand. Removing a cyst cannot guarantee relief if back pain has another cause. Rupture, bleeding and twisting of the ovary A ruptured cyst can cause sudden pain and sometimes internal bleeding. Some people can be observed with pain relief after assessment, while significant bleeding or instability may need hospital monitoring, intravenous fluids, transfusion or surgery. Rupture is not always harmless or always treated with an operation. Torsion means the ovary twists and its blood supply is threatened. It needs urgent gynaecological assessment and may require prompt surgery to untwist and preserve the ovary. It can occur without a large cyst, especially in younger people. Ultrasound blood flow alone cannot reliably exclude torsion; severe symptoms should not be dismissed because of one reassuring finding. Emergency signs: act on symptoms Get immediate medical help for sudden severe pelvic or abdominal pain, especially with nausea or vomiting, or pain with fever and marked illness. Fainting, major weakness, cold clammy skin or rapid breathing can signal serious bleeding or shock. Seek emergency care for severe pain with these signs rather than waiting for home treatment to work. Back pain with new saddle-area numbness, symptoms in both legs, new urinary retention or loss of bladder or bowel control requires immediate emergency assessment for a spinal problem. A serious accident or chest pain with back pain also needs emergency care. A known ovarian cyst does not rule out another emergency. Following up without assuming every pain is the cyst Many functional cysts resolve and many other cysts remain benign, but the plan should fit the actual findings. Keep the agreed appointments and ask which symptoms require urgent contact. If pain continues despite cyst improvement or treatment, reassess other causes rather than repeating an assumption. Record pain location and severity, its timing with periods or movement, bleeding, urinary or bowel changes, medicines and scan dates. Bring pregnancy or fertility concerns to the discussion. Monitoring symptoms can support a consultation, but cannot diagnose a cyst, cancer, torsion or a spinal emergency. A cyst can sometimes cause lower-back ache, but back pain or an incidental scan finding does not prove the connection. Functional, dermoid, cystadenoma and endometrioma cysts have different courses and treatment needs. Ultrasound findings, symptoms, age and pregnancy or menopausal status guide care; CA-125 alone is not a diagnosis. Observation, suitable pain relief, hormonal prevention of new functional cysts or selected surgery require an individual plan. Sudden severe pelvic pain, shock signs or new spinal nerve/bladder/bowel symptoms need immediate assessment. Can an ovarian cyst cause back pain? Yes, some cysts, especially larger ones, can cause a dull ache in the lower back or thighs. Many cause no symptoms. Back pain has many other causes, so assessment is needed rather than assuming a cyst is responsible. Which other symptoms may occur? Pelvic fullness, bloating, period changes, unusual bleeding, pain during sex, urinary frequency or bowel pressure may occur. None is specific to a cyst. New leg weakness, saddle numbness or bladder/bowel control changes require urgent assessment, with emergency care for the warning combinations described above. What cyst types can be associated with pain? Functional cysts, dermoids, cystadenomas and endometriomas can sometimes cause pain. Many functional cysts disappear; endometriosis may cause pain even apart from an endometrioma. Type and size alone cannot identify the source of every backache. What are dermoid cysts? They are usually benign germ-cell growths, also called mature cystic teratomas, which may contain fat, skin, hair or teeth. Their assessment and treatment depend on symptoms and other findings; they are not the same as an ovulation-related functional cyst. Will the contraceptive pill shrink a cyst? No. Ovulation-suppressing hormonal contraception may help prevent new functional cysts in suitable people, but does not shrink an existing cyst or treat every type. Discuss risks and pregnancy plans before choosing it. Does every cyst need repeat scans or surgery? No. Follow-up depends on symptoms and scan features as well as age and pregnancy or menopausal status. Some low-risk cysts need no routine follow-up; selected growing, concerning or symptomatic cysts may need surgery. Is a ruptured cyst always harmless? No. Some are managed with observation and pain relief after assessment, but internal bleeding can be serious. Sudden severe pain, fainting, weakness, clammy skin or rapid breathing needs immediate help. When is back pain an emergency? New numbness around the genitals or anus, symptoms in both legs, urinary retention or loss of bladder or bowel control needs immediate emergency assessment. Do not assume these symptoms are caused by a known cyst.

title: Pyosalpinx: infection in a fallopian tube
description: What pus in a fallopian tube means, when pelvic pain needs urgent care, and how antibiotics, drainage and fertility decisions fit together.
body: Pyosalpinx means a fallopian tube is swollen with pus. It can complicate pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) and needs prompt medical treatment. It does not automatically mean permanent infertility or removal of the reproductive organs. What happens in the tube? Fallopian tubes carry an egg toward the uterus; fertilization usually happens in a tube. Infection and inflammation can damage the tube and block it. Pus contains inflammatory cells, tissue debris and microbes; it is more than simply trapped white blood cells. Pyosalpinx is pus within a tube. A tubo-ovarian abscess is an infected collection involving a tube and ovary; the conditions can overlap. Hydrosalpinx is a tube distended with non-purulent fluid, a different finding. These terms cannot be diagnosed from symptoms alone. Symptoms and urgent warning signs Possible symptoms include persistent or intermittent lower abdominal pain, tenderness or a pelvic lump, fever, deep pain during sex, and pain around a period. Unusual discharge or bleeding may also occur. PID can have mild symptoms or none, so absence of fever does not rule it out. Seek urgent medical advice for suspected PID or new recurring pelvic pain. Go to emergency care for severe, sudden or worsening pain, heavy vaginal bleeding, faintness, very high fever or shivering, repeated vomiting or feeling seriously unwell. A ruptured abscess can cause sepsis. If pregnancy is possible, pelvic pain needs urgent assessment to exclude ectopic pregnancy; do not wait for a routine appointment or a home remedy. Causes: not always a sexually transmitted infection Infection may spread upward from the vagina and cervix. Chlamydia and gonorrhea are important causes of PID, but vaginal and other bacteria can also be involved. PID may follow childbirth, miscarriage or a procedure involving the cervix. A diagnosis does not prove a recent STI or infidelity. Delayed or incomplete treatment can increase complications, but illness is not a reason for blame. Genital tuberculosis is an uncommon alternative cause in appropriate clinical circumstances and needs specific testing and treatment. Pyosalpinx is not restricted to ages 20–40; there is no single frequency estimate that predicts an individual's risk. Assessment and imaging A clinician considers symptoms, pregnancy possibility, medical and sexual history, abdominal and pelvic examination, and infection tests. Pregnancy testing, swabs, urine or blood tests may be needed. A negative cervical swab does not exclude infection higher in the reproductive tract. Consent matters: ask about a chaperone and tell the clinician if an examination hurts or you want it stopped. Ultrasound often assesses a suspected collection: a gel-covered probe may be used on the abdomen or, with consent, in the vagina. MRI uses magnetic fields and radio waves to clarify selected uncertain findings; contrast may sometimes be used. You lie on a moving table in a noisy scanner and are screened for implants, pregnancy and contrast-related risks. Not everyone needs MRI. When laparoscopy is useful Laparoscopy may help when the diagnosis remains uncertain, treatment is not working, or drainage is needed. Under general anesthesia, a camera is introduced through a small abdominal cut, often near the navel; gas creates space and additional cuts allow instruments to enter. The surgeon may collect fluid or a tissue sample for laboratory testing. It is not a compulsory test for everyone with PID, nor a guarantee that the tubes will remain undamaged. Imaging and examination often guide initial care. Treatment for a suspected serious infection should not be postponed simply to obtain every possible test. Antibiotics and close follow-up Clinicians usually begin antibiotics promptly when PID is suspected, before all results return. Treatment covers several likely bacteria and is adjusted to the findings, allergies and pregnancy status. A pus-filled tube or suspected abscess warrants urgent gynecology assessment and may require hospital care, intravenous antibiotics and observation; it is not a condition to treat with leftover tablets. Complete the prescribed course, even if pain improves. Lack of improvement within 48–72 hours requires reassessment; worsening symptoms need help sooner. Recent sexual partners need assessment, testing and treatment arranged through a sexual health service, even when an STI has not been confirmed in the person with PID; the clinic will determine which partners need care under local guidance. Avoid sex until treatment is completed, symptoms have resolved and partners have been treated, and follow the clinic's testing and clearance advice. Drainage and surgery are individualized A collection may need drainage through an image-guided procedure or surgery if antibiotics are insufficient or infection is severe. Suspected rupture is an emergency. Laparoscopy can sometimes drain pus while preserving organs, but cannot promise normal fertility. The safest approach depends on the collection, tissue damage and response to treatment. Salpingectomy removes one or both tubes; bilateral salpingectomy removes both. Oophorectomy removes an ovary, and hysterectomy removes the uterus, sometimes with the cervix. These are not routine successive steps for every pyosalpinx. Extensive surgery may be necessary for severely damaged organs or uncontrolled infection. Ask which organs could be removed, why, and whether preservation is safe; share future pregnancy wishes without delaying lifesaving care. Fertility and the longer-term outlook Infection can leave scarring, reduce fertility, cause lasting pelvic pain or increase ectopic pregnancy risk. Antibiotics treat infection but do not reliably reverse established tubal damage. Outcomes depend on whether one or both tubes and other organs are affected; a diagnosis alone cannot establish that pregnancy is impossible. Early treatment offers the best chance of limiting damage. After removal or complete blockage of both tubes, conception through the tubes is not expected, but IVF may be possible if the uterus and suitable eggs are available; it is not guaranteed. Removing both ovaries affects egg supply and causes surgical menopause before natural menopause; hysterectomy prevents carrying a pregnancy. Ask for individualized fertility advice after recovery. With known tubal disease, seek advice early when planning pregnancy, and prompt assessment of pain or bleeding in a future pregnancy. Reducing the chance of another infection Condoms, STI testing based on age and exposure, and treatment of infections and partners reduce risk. Fewer new or concurrent partners, or a mutually monogamous relationship with an appropriately tested partner, can reduce STI exposure. Avoid vaginal douching. These steps cannot prevent every pelvic infection and are not a substitute for treatment. Keep follow-up appointments and ask whether repeat testing is needed; chlamydial or gonococcal PID generally warrants retesting around three months after treatment. Discuss persistent pain, emotional concerns and fertility plans. There is no home technique that reliably drains pus or restores damaged tubes. Suspected pelvic infection needs prompt assessment; severe pain or systemic illness needs emergency care. PID can involve sexually transmitted and other bacteria; a diagnosis is not proof of infidelity. Antibiotics are central; an abscess may also need hospital care, drainage or surgery. Fertility effects vary. Discuss organ preservation and future pregnancy without delaying urgent treatment. What symptoms can pyosalpinx cause? Lower abdominal pain, tenderness, fever and deep pain during sex are possible; some symptoms are mild. Severe or worsening pain, faintness, heavy bleeding or marked illness needs emergency assessment. Does it always cause infertility? No. Tubal scarring can reduce fertility, but the effect depends on the extent and location of damage. A fertility specialist can discuss recovery and options such as IVF where appropriate. What causes pus in a fallopian tube? It can complicate PID involving chlamydia, gonorrhea or other bacteria. Less common causes, including genital tuberculosis, need targeted investigation when clinically relevant. How is it treated? Prompt prescribed antibiotics, often with hospital assessment for a collection, are central. Drainage or surgery may be required; removing both tubes, ovaries or the uterus is not automatic. Is ultrasound enough to diagnose it? It can identify swollen tubes or a collection, but results must be interpreted with examination and other tests. MRI or laparoscopy is used selectively; urgent treatment need not wait for all tests. When should antibiotics start helping? Symptoms should begin improving within about 48–72 hours. Seek reassessment if they do not, and urgent help sooner if you worsen. Finish the prescribed treatment even when you feel better. Should a partner be tested? A sexual health service should assess recent partners when PID or an STI is diagnosed and arrange testing and treatment as appropriate. Partners can have no symptoms. Follow advice about avoiding sex and repeat tests. Can I prevent it with home remedies? No remedy can reliably treat a pus-filled tube. Condoms, appropriate STI testing, partner care and avoiding douching reduce some risks, but suspected infection still needs medical care.

title: Adnexal masses: symptoms, assessment and treatment
description: An adnexal mass is a finding near the uterus, often involving an ovary. Learn possible causes, warning symptoms, tests, monitoring and pregnancy care.
body: An adnexal mass is a lump or abnormal structure in the region beside the uterus, including the ovaries, fallopian tubes and nearby tissues. It may contain fluid, solid tissue or both. Many causes are benign, but the term describes a finding rather than a final diagnosis. Its appearance, symptoms, pregnancy status and stage of life guide what happens next. Symptoms and incidental findings A mass may cause no symptoms and be discovered on a scan or examination for another reason. Possible symptoms include pelvic discomfort, period changes, pain during sex, abdominal swelling, constipation, digestive discomfort, frequent urination or difficulty emptying the bladder. Symptoms depend on the cause as well as size, and none identifies the diagnosis by itself. Arrange assessment for persistent or worsening symptoms, new unexplained vaginal bleeding, or repeated bloating, early fullness or urinary changes. Tiredness, indigestion, back pain and bowel changes can have many explanations, including occasionally ovarian cancer. Bleeding within a cyst can cause pain, but internal bleeding cannot be diagnosed by looking for visible vaginal blood. When to seek urgent or emergency care Sudden severe pelvic or lower abdominal pain, especially with vomiting, needs immediate emergency assessment because ovarian twisting, cyst rupture or bleeding may be responsible. Fainting, marked dizziness, pallor, collapse or severe pain with possible pregnancy can indicate internal bleeding; seek emergency help immediately. Complete inability to pass urine also needs immediate care. If pregnancy is possible and you have pelvic pain, unusual bleeding or shoulder-tip pain, seek urgent medical advice even without a positive home test. Fever with pelvic pain or rapidly worsening swelling also needs urgent assessment. Do not wait for a planned scan or repeat test when these warning signs occur. Common benign causes Functional ovarian cysts arise with the menstrual cycle and often settle over a few weeks or months. Other causes include endometriomas associated with endometriosis, dermoid cysts and cystadenomas. Some benign tumours contain solid tissue; a solid area does not automatically mean cancer, and a fluid-filled structure is not automatically harmless. A presumed ovarian mass may instead come from a fallopian tube or another nearby structure. Benign tumours do not invade or spread like cancer, but a persistent or large benign lesion can still cause pain, pressure or twisting. The statement that most masses simply disappear applies best to selected functional cysts, not every adnexal finding. Cancer is a possibility, not a conclusion Malignant ovarian or nearby tissue growth can enlarge and spread, but many adnexal masses are not cancer. Risk is assessed from imaging features, age and menopause, symptoms, personal and family history and selected tests. Solid components or complex features warrant careful evaluation rather than a diagnosis from one word in a report. Cancer-related symptoms overlap with common benign conditions. Persistent bloating, early satiety, pelvic pain, urinary urgency or unexplained bleeding should be checked rather than dismissed. Suspicious findings may require referral to a gynaecological cancer specialist; a referral does not itself confirm cancer, and outcome cannot be promised before the diagnosis and stage are known. Ectopic pregnancy is a different urgent cause An ectopic pregnancy implants outside the uterine cavity, usually in a fallopian tube, and may appear as an adnexal finding. It cannot continue as a normal pregnancy and can rupture, causing life-threatening internal bleeding. Pain or bleeding with possible pregnancy needs prompt assessment; sudden severe pain with faintness or collapse is an emergency. A pregnancy test is important, but a single test alone does not establish where a pregnancy is located. Clinicians may use transvaginal ultrasound and serial blood hCG measurements, and occasionally surgery. Carefully monitored observation, medication or surgery are selected according to the findings; this is not a condition to watch at home without a clinical plan. How an adnexal mass is assessed Assessment includes symptoms, menstrual and pregnancy history, menopause, medicines and relevant family history. An abdominal or pelvic examination may help, but ultrasound is usually the first imaging test. Transvaginal and/or abdominal scanning describes the location, size and internal features; an examination alone cannot reliably identify every mass or exclude cancer. Selected blood tests, including pregnancy testing and sometimes CA125, can support assessment. CA125 is not a stand-alone cancer diagnosis: benign conditions and pregnancy can alter it, and results must be interpreted in context. Specialist ultrasound or MRI may clarify an indeterminate finding. Imaging risk systems support clinical judgment; routine surveillance schedules do not override acute warning symptoms. Monitoring, surgery and tissue diagnosis A small, simple, reassuring cyst without troublesome symptoms may need observation, sometimes with a repeat scan and sometimes without routine follow-up. The clinician should explain the timing and what changes need earlier review. Persistent, growing, complex or symptomatic masses may require further investigation or surgery; a solid component alone does not make an operation inevitable. Surgical choice depends on the likely cause, cancer concern, complications and fertility goals. Where appropriate, the cyst can be removed while preserving the ovary, but some situations require more extensive surgery. Removed tissue is examined in a laboratory; a malignant result may require further specialist treatment. Neither surgery nor a reassuring scan guarantees that every future symptom can be ignored. Adnexal masses during pregnancy Pregnancy scans sometimes find an ovarian cyst or other adnexal mass. Many reassuring cysts can be monitored, and some resolve as pregnancy progresses; persistent, large or complex findings need an individualized follow-up plan. Pregnancy changes how imaging and blood markers are interpreted, and MRI may help when ultrasound is insufficient. Not every mass must be removed before pregnancy or during it. Severe symptoms, twisting, bleeding or concern for malignancy may justify intervention. Timing balances maternal health, the suspected diagnosis and pregnancy stage with specialist input; urgent problems must not wait simply to prolong pregnancy. A fixed claim that 10% of all pregnancy adnexal masses are malignant is not a reliable personal estimate, and early cancer or a good outcome cannot be assumed. Outlook and useful follow-up questions The outlook depends on the actual diagnosis. Functional cysts often resolve, other benign lesions may persist, and cancer requires disease-specific care. Most cysts do not prevent pregnancy, but the underlying condition and any proposed surgery can affect fertility. Discuss ovarian preservation and future pregnancy plans before a non-emergency procedure whenever possible. Ask where the mass arises, whether it looks simple or complex, whether further tests are needed, when to repeat imaging and what symptoms require earlier help. Keep your follow-up even if symptoms improve unless the clinician changes the plan. A new or worsening symptom deserves reassessment rather than assuming an old benign label explains it. An adnexal mass describes a location and finding, not a diagnosis of cancer. Some functional cysts resolve; not every solid, complex or persistent mass behaves the same way. Ultrasound, pregnancy status and individual risks guide tests, monitoring or surgery. Sudden severe pelvic pain, collapse or signs of internal bleeding require emergency care. Pregnancy needs an individualized plan, not a fixed cancer percentage or automatic treatment delay. When does an adnexal mass need treatment? Treatment depends on symptoms, growth, scan features, life stage and the suspected cause. A reassuring simple cyst may be observed. Persistent, growing, complex or suspicious findings need further review, and acute complications require urgent care; not every solid mass automatically needs surgery. What symptoms can it cause? Some cause none. Pelvic pain, period changes, pain during sex, bloating, urinary pressure or frequency, constipation and digestive symptoms are possible. Persistent changes should be checked, while sudden severe pain, fainting or collapse needs emergency assessment. How is it diagnosed? History and examination are followed by ultrasound in most cases, with pregnancy testing and other tests as appropriate. MRI or specialist imaging can clarify uncertain findings. Neither symptoms nor a single blood marker can establish every diagnosis. What happens if the mass is small and painless? A simple, reassuring cyst may need no immediate treatment; follow-up depends on its appearance and your circumstances. Ask whether a repeat scan is needed and when. Do not assume small size makes every mass harmless or that no pain means follow-up can be skipped. Does a solid or complex mass mean cancer? No. Benign lesions may contain solid tissue or complex material, but those features need proper assessment. Cancer risk depends on the whole picture, and suspicious findings may require specialist referral or tissue examination. What if I am pregnant? Tell the team so pregnancy location, scan findings and any blood tests are interpreted appropriately. Many reassuring cysts can be monitored, but symptoms or concerning features may need intervention. Severe pain or faintness must not wait for routine pregnancy follow-up. Can BeMama tell whether my mass is benign? No. It can help organize symptoms and appointment dates, but cannot interpret a scan, exclude ectopic pregnancy or cancer, or decide whether surgery is needed. Seek clinical assessment and follow the agreed plan.

title: Diclofenac suppositories during breastfeeding
description: Learn when diclofenac may be used while breastfeeding, which health conditions and medicines need review, how to use a rectal dose and which symptoms need urgent care.
body: Diclofenac reduces pain and inflammation. Current breastfeeding guidance generally considers it an appropriate option when clinically needed, particularly for a healthy baby born at term. That does not make every product or dose suitable for everyone: the parent’s health, other medicines and the baby’s circumstances still matter. What diclofenac treats Diclofenac is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, or NSAID. Oral medicines, injections, skin preparations and rectal suppositories are available under various brands. Their doses, uses and instructions differ; do not substitute forms or combine them without checking the total dose with a clinician or pharmacist. Depending on the product and clinical situation, it may be used for inflammatory joint disease, osteoarthritis, gout, ankylosing spondylitis, back or other musculoskeletal pain, dental pain, selected migraine treatment, painful periods or pain after childbirth or surgery. A suppository is absorbed into the bloodstream: using the rectal route does not remove stomach, kidney, bleeding or cardiovascular risks. What current breastfeeding advice says NHS and Specialist Pharmacy Service advice supports diclofenac when appropriate during breastfeeding; ibuprofen and diclofenac are preferred NSAID options in SPS guidance. Milk levels appear low, although published evidence is limited. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest necessary time, with a clear reason for treatment. It is not reserved only for situations where every alternative has failed. SPS recommendations mainly apply to healthy infants born at term. LactMed’s July 2026 review notes that alternatives with more evidence may be preferred for a newborn or premature baby. Seek individual advice if the baby is premature, unwell or very young, or if several medicines are being taken. Low milk exposure is reassuring, but is not a guarantee of zero risk. Why a leaflet may give different advice Some diclofenac suppository product labels advise against breastfeeding use, whereas specialist breastfeeding guidance considers clinically appropriate use acceptable. This reflects different information and approaches to risk assessment; neither a generic online statement nor a different brand’s leaflet decides your treatment. Ask the prescriber or pharmacist to reconcile the exact product’s label with your circumstances and local guidance. Do not stop breastfeeding, discard milk, change the dose or switch medicines solely because you read conflicting advice. Agree a plan. Watch for a baby feeding less well than usual, vomiting or diarrhoea and seek advice promptly; a baby who is unusually difficult to wake or having breathing trouble needs immediate emergency assessment. Conditions that can make diclofenac unsuitable Do not use diclofenac if you are allergic to it or an ingredient, or if aspirin or another NSAID has triggered asthma, swelling or hives. Tell the prescriber about all drug allergies; an unrelated allergy does not automatically prohibit diclofenac. This suppository is contraindicated with active or recurrent gastrointestinal ulcer or bleeding, previous NSAID-related gastrointestinal bleeding or perforation, severe kidney or liver failure, or proctitis (inflammation of the rectum). Rectal bleeding needs assessment before further use. Systemic diclofenac is contraindicated in established ischaemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease, cerebrovascular disease and certain heart failure categories under UK safety advice. High blood pressure, smoking, diabetes or other cardiovascular risks need assessment. Also discuss asthma, Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis, clotting or bleeding disorders, a clot history and dehydration. Pregnancy is a separate issue from breastfeeding: do not self-start if pregnant or possibly pregnant; it is usually avoided in pregnancy and is contraindicated in the last trimester under this product label. Other medicines: bleeding, blood pressure and kidneys Give the clinician or pharmacist a complete list of prescription, non-prescription and topical medicines, vitamins, herbs and supplements. Do not add another NSAID such as ibuprofen, naproxen, ketorolac, celecoxib, indomethacin or meloxicam, or pain-relief aspirin, unless specifically advised. Check cold and pain remedies for hidden ingredients. Do not independently stop prescribed low-dose aspirin or an anticoagulant. Anticoagulants such as warfarin, heparin or enoxaparin, antiplatelet drugs, SSRI antidepressants and corticosteroids such as prednisolone or dexamethasone can increase bleeding concerns. ACE inhibitors such as captopril/enalapril, ARBs such as losartan and diuretics such as furosemide can interact with NSAIDs, affecting blood pressure, fluid balance or kidneys, particularly during dehydration. Other interactions and supplements Diclofenac can affect the handling or risks of lithium, digoxin, methotrexate and phenytoin. Ciclosporin and tacrolimus require particular kidney-risk review; other potentially kidney-affecting treatments, including tenofovir, vancomycin or aminoglycoside antibiotics, also need checking in context. Vancomycin is not an aminoglycoside. Quinolone antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin can increase seizure concerns when combined with NSAIDs. Also mention bisphosphonates such as alendronate, salicylate-containing products, glucosamine, omega-3 supplements and vitamin E. Risks and evidence differ between products and doses: this is a medication-review list, not a claim that every combination is forbidden. Other medicines may need monitoring, dose changes or an alternative; do not make those changes yourself. Using a prescribed rectal suppository Follow the instructions for your exact strength and prescription. If needed, use the toilet first; wash your hands, gently clean and dry the area and unwrap the suppository. Insert it gently into the rectum, pointed end first, as the leaflet directs; do not force it. It must not be swallowed or inserted into the vagina. Wash your hands afterwards. NHS instructions advise sitting or lying still for about 15 minutes. If a dose comes out, absorption is uncertain: do not automatically insert another, even if it happened within 30 minutes. Ask a pharmacist or prescriber what to do. Never double a missed dose; if the next is nearly due, follow advice to skip the missed one. Taking or using more than prescribed needs urgent medical or poison-service advice, even if you feel well. Side effects that need discussion Possible effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, indigestion, gas or belching, constipation, appetite change, headache, dizziness, sleepiness, rash or rectal irritation. Not everyone develops them, and not every symptom is caused by diclofenac. Discuss persistent or troublesome symptoms; do not drive or operate machinery if dizzy, sleepy or your vision is affected. For a new rash, stop diclofenac and seek prompt clinical advice before any further dose. Blistering or peeling skin, sores in the mouth or eyes, or breathing difficulty or face/throat swelling need immediate emergency care. New hearing changes or ringing in the ears, sleep or mood changes, unexplained weight loss, unusual weakness or pallor also need review. Seek urgent medical advice for markedly reduced urine, new swelling or rapid weight gain, jaundice, unusual bruising or bleeding, hives or worsening abdominal symptoms. Cloudy urine alone is not a diagnosis, but urine changes with illness or reduced output should not be ignored. Serious symptoms need urgent or emergency care Black tarry stools, rectal bleeding or severe persistent indigestion or abdominal pain need urgent assessment now; do not take another dose until a clinician advises. Vomiting blood or material like coffee grounds, fainting or loss of consciousness, or severe abdominal pain with faintness needs immediate emergency care. These are not ordinary side effects to watch at home. Chest pain, sudden shortness of breath, stroke symptoms such as one-sided weakness or difficulty speaking, or a severe allergic reaction with face/tongue/throat swelling or breathing difficulty needs immediate emergency care. Do not drive yourself. Severe illness, swelling with breathlessness or sudden major vision changes also warrants immediate assessment. After childbirth, serious symptoms may have causes other than the medicine: do not assume they are harmless drug effects. Agreeing a practical treatment plan Ask why this medicine and route were chosen, the exact strength and timing, how long to use it, whether other pain relief is appropriate and when pain should be reassessed. A persistent or worsening headache, wound pain, fever or other postnatal symptom may need examination rather than more pain medicine. Keep the medicine away from children, follow the leaflet’s storage instructions and keep an updated medicine list. Breastfeeding compatibility does not remove the need to check contraindications and interactions. A pharmacist, prescriber and, when needed, a specialist breastfeeding-medicines service can help balance effective pain relief with the parent’s and baby’s safety. Diclofenac can be appropriate during breastfeeding; it is not universally a last-resort medicine. Premature, unwell or very young babies and multiple medicines need individual assessment. Rectal diclofenac acts throughout the body and retains stomach, kidney, bleeding and heart risks. Check all medicines and supplements; do not automatically repeat an expelled suppository or double a missed dose. Bleeding, chest or breathing symptoms, fainting or loss of consciousness or a serious allergic reaction require prompt urgent or emergency care. What is a diclofenac suppository? It is a rectal form of an NSAID that reduces pain and inflammation. It enters the bloodstream and is not interchangeable with tablets, injections or skin products without checking the prescription. Can it be used while breastfeeding? Often yes, when clinically appropriate. NHS/SPS guidance is reassuring for a healthy term infant, but evidence is limited and some labels advise against use. Confirm the exact product and personal plan with a prescriber or pharmacist. What if my baby is premature or unwell? Get individual advice before treatment. LactMed notes that an alternative with more evidence may be preferable for a newborn or premature baby. Several medicines or an unwell baby also warrant specialist assessment. Which conditions or medicines need checking? Important issues include NSAID allergy, ulcers or bleeding, heart/vascular disease, kidney/liver disease, rectal inflammation, asthma, inflammatory bowel disease and possible pregnancy. Other NSAIDs, blood thinners, steroids, antidepressants, blood-pressure medicines and many other treatments need review. Should I repeat a dose that comes out? Do not automatically repeat it: some medicine may already have been absorbed. Ask a pharmacist or prescriber for advice based on the product and timing. Never double a missed dose or exceed the prescribed total. Can I stop breastfeeding to avoid any exposure? Do not stop or discard milk solely because of a general online warning. Ask for an individual plan that considers treatment needs, the exact product and the benefits of breastfeeding. What should I watch for in my baby? Contact a clinician if feeding worsens, or vomiting or diarrhoea occurs. Breathing difficulty or unusual difficulty waking needs immediate emergency assessment, whatever the suspected cause. Which symptoms in the parent are an emergency? Vomiting blood, fainting or loss of consciousness, chest pain, sudden breathlessness, stroke symptoms or face/throat swelling with breathing trouble need immediate emergency care. Black tarry stools, rectal bleeding or severe persistent abdominal symptoms need urgent assessment now. Do not take another dose while waiting for clinical advice about suspected bleeding.

title: Breast swelling and tenderness before a period
description: Learn about cyclical breast pain, hormonal changes, practical comfort measures, medicines and the breast changes that need prompt assessment.
body: Breasts can feel fuller, heavier or tender before a period and improve afterwards. This cyclical pattern is common, but it should not be used to dismiss a new lump, nipple change or persistent pain. The aim is to recognise your pattern, ease discomfort and know when to seek care. What cyclical breast discomfort feels like Cyclical breast pain, or mastalgia, commonly causes a dull ache, heaviness and tenderness in both breasts, sometimes extending towards the armpits. It may begin up to two weeks before a period and settle during or after it. Timing and severity vary; not everyone has a twenty-eight-day cycle or symptoms on fixed dates. Symptoms may occur with other premenstrual changes, and some people notice more lumpiness. Fibrocystic changes are common benign changes that can include cysts and tenderness varying with the cycle. You cannot label a new lump benign because it moves, hurts or appears before a period; have it assessed. Hormones, medicines and other explanations Breast tissue responds to hormonal changes through the menstrual cycle. This does not automatically mean an abnormal hormone level, and isolated hormone tests are usually unhelpful when breast pain is the only symptom. Cyclical symptoms often improve after menopause, but new or continuing pain can still occur. Contraception, menopausal hormone treatment and some other medicines may be associated with tenderness. Pregnancy can also cause sore breasts; symptoms alone cannot distinguish pregnancy from premenstrual changes, so use a pregnancy test when appropriate. Pain may instead come from chest-wall muscles, injury, infection or another cause, particularly if it does not follow the cycle. Breast changes that need medical attention Seek urgent clinical assessment for a red, hot or swollen breast, especially with fever or shivering. Also seek prompt urgent assessment for a new or changing lump in the breast or armpit, spontaneous or bloody nipple discharge, dimpling, a new nipple inversion or rash, or a change in breast shape. Do not wait for another period to see whether these warnings disappear. Arrange a review if pain persists, becomes focal or different, disrupts sleep or daily activities, or does not respond to simple measures. Discuss personal and family breast-cancer history. Breast pain alone is unlikely to be cancer, but that is not a diagnosis or a reason to ignore other changes. What assessment and imaging involve A clinician may ask when pain occurs, whether it affects one or both breasts, about discharge, pregnancy possibility and medicines, and may examine the breasts, armpits and chest wall. A symptom diary over two cycles can help, but do not delay assessment of warning signs to complete it. Imaging is selected for the findings, age, risk and pregnancy status; ultrasound is not governed by a universal under-thirty-five rule. Diffuse cyclical pain without suspicious findings often needs no extra diagnostic imaging beyond appropriate screening. A focal persistent symptom or lump may need ultrasound, mammography or other tests; mammography briefly compresses the breast, and a biopsy may be needed if a finding needs tissue analysis. These tests are not automatically required for every sore breast. Comfort measures at home Try a well-fitting supportive bra or sports bra, especially during activity; a soft bra at night is optional if comfortable. Avoid a tight garment that worsens pain. Regular activity, sleep and stress management can support general wellbeing and premenstrual symptoms, without guaranteeing relief of breast pain. Record the timing, location, severity and any triggers or new changes. Review progress rather than repeatedly pressing a sore area. If home care does not help or symptoms interfere with life, ask for clinical advice instead of assuming you must tolerate them until menopause. Food, caffeine and supplements Choose varied meals with vegetables, fruit, whole grains, nuts, seeds and suitable oils. Examples include spinach, carrots, bananas, avocado, oats, brown rice, peanuts or hazelnuts if safe for you. These foods support nutrition; no particular food list cures cyclical swelling. Evidence that reducing alcohol, caffeine, fat or salt specifically relieves breast pain is limited or mixed. You may discuss a practical trial of a suspected trigger without a restrictive diet. Routine vitamin E or magnesium at a fixed high dose is not an established treatment for everyone. Evidence for breast-pain supplements is weak or inconsistent, and general PMS evidence does not prove a breast-pain benefit. Supplements can cause side effects or interactions; check with a pharmacist or clinician, especially with pregnancy, kidney disease or other medicines. Do not assume a product is effective or safe because it is natural or sold without prescription. Pain medicines and safe use Paracetamol, also called acetaminophen, is a pain reliever, not a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug. Ibuprofen and naproxen are NSAIDs. A suitable simple pain reliever or topical anti-inflammatory gel may help, but follow the product instructions and pharmacist's advice rather than using several NSAIDs together. NSAIDs are not suitable for everyone, including some people with ulcers, kidney disease, particular allergies or interacting medicines. If pregnant, possibly pregnant, trying to conceive or breastfeeding, check the safest option first. Ask about gel application near the breast if feeding a baby, and avoid infant contact with treated skin. Do not start water tablets to treat ordinary cyclical swelling or continue painkillers indefinitely without review. Hormonal and specialist treatment Hormonal contraception can help some premenstrual symptoms, while breast tenderness is also reported during its use. Review benefits, risks and alternatives with your clinician rather than assuming a pill will always help. Reversible contraception does not mean giving up future pregnancy plans; discuss when you want to conceive and choose a suitable method. For severe persistent pain after assessment and simpler measures, a specialist may occasionally consider medicines such as danazol or tamoxifen. They have important adverse effects, restrictions and monitoring requirements, including pregnancy considerations; availability and licensing differ. They are not routine self-care, and the treatment plan should be individualised. Breast awareness, screening and outlook Be familiar with how your breasts normally look and feel, and report new changes. A compulsory monthly self-examination is not recommended as a substitute for screening; the American Cancer Society does not recommend routine clinical or self-exams for average-risk cancer screening. This does not remove the need for a clinical examination when symptoms occur. Screening schedules depend on local guidance, age and risk, not a single universal start age or interval. Symptoms need assessment even after a recent normal screening result. Cyclical discomfort often improves or fluctuates, but persistent problems deserve follow-up and support; there is no guaranteed cure from one supplement, food or medicine. A recurring premenstrual pattern is common, but it does not establish the cause of every breast change. New lumps, nipple or skin changes and a hot red swollen breast need prompt assessment. A supportive bra, a symptom diary and suitable pain relief may help; warning signs should not wait for two cycles. Paracetamol is not an NSAID, and supplements or water tablets are not routine cures. Imaging and screening are personalised; being breast aware does not replace clinical review or screening. Can contraception cause breast swelling? Breast tenderness is reported with hormonal contraception, while some methods help other premenstrual symptoms. Discuss persistent problems and alternatives with the prescriber; do not assume it is the cause of a new lump. When should I contact a clinician? Get urgent advice for a red hot swollen breast, fever, a new lump, spontaneous or bloody discharge, dimpling or nipple changes. Seek review for persistent or disruptive pain. Do not wait for the next period when warning signs are present. What can I try at home? A comfortable supportive bra, regular sleep and activity, a symptom diary and a suitable pain reliever may help. A soft night bra is optional. Seek assessment if these measures fail or you notice new changes. What should I eat for premenstrual swelling? Eat varied balanced meals, including vegetables, fruit, whole grains and suitable nuts or oils. No specific food cures breast swelling, and evidence for avoiding caffeine or particular foods is limited. Avoid unnecessary restrictions and ask before supplements. Does breast tenderness tell me I am pregnant? No. Pregnancy and premenstrual symptoms can overlap. Use a pregnancy test at the appropriate time and seek advice if symptoms or results are unclear. Do I need an ultrasound because I am under thirty-five? Not automatically. Examination findings, pain pattern, age, risk and pregnancy status guide imaging. Diffuse cyclical pain without suspicious findings often does not need extra imaging; a new lump or focal persistent symptom needs assessment. Are monthly self-exams enough to check for cancer? No. Know your usual appearance and feel, report changes and follow your personalised screening advice. Routine self-exams are not a replacement for screening, and a recent normal mammogram does not cancel a new symptom.

title: Perimenopausal depression: symptoms and support
description: Understand depression during the transition to menopause, how it differs from mood changes, which risks matter and what evidence says about treatment and self-care.
body: Perimenopause is the transition leading up to menopause. Period changes, hot flushes, night sweats and disrupted sleep can occur during it, and some people develop a first depressive episode or a recurrence. Depression is treatable. Persistent loss of enjoyment, distress or difficulty functioning deserves care rather than being dismissed as an unavoidable part of getting older. Is depression inevitable during perimenopause? No. Research links the menopause transition with increased vulnerability to depression, but many people do not develop it. Older studies reported different twofold or fourfold associations for different outcomes and populations; these are not a prediction of your personal risk or a single universal prevalence figure. Previous depression is particularly important to mention. Antidepressant use often identifies people with a history of depression; it does not establish that the medicine causes the problem. Childbearing history or distress about fertility may be relevant to an individual’s experience, but not having given birth does not by itself diagnose depression or mean it will occur. Symptoms to notice Symptoms can include persistent sadness, hopelessness, worthlessness or helplessness, loss of interest or pleasure, low energy, feeling slowed down, poor concentration or memory, difficulty making decisions and changes in sleep or appetite. Irritability, anxiety, mood swings or unexplained tearfulness may also occur. Not everyone has every symptom, and depression is more than occasional sadness. Hot flushes and night sweats can disturb sleep and worsen exhaustion or mood. Symptoms that persist most of the day, nearly every day, for about two weeks, or interfere with work, relationships or basic tasks, need assessment. Seek help sooner if symptoms are severe, rapidly worsening or affecting safety; the two-week description is not an instruction to wait. Hormones, sleep and life circumstances Oestrogen and other hormone fluctuations may influence systems involved in mood and sleep, including serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine pathways. Depression cannot be explained or diagnosed simply as “high oestrogen, low progesterone” or a measured shortage of one brain chemical. Biological, genetic, psychological and social factors interact. Relevant factors include personal or family depression history, severe menopause symptoms, disrupted sleep, trauma or sexual violence, isolation, low self-esteem and distress about ageing or fertility. Divorce, job loss, bereavement, caring responsibilities, inactivity and smoking can also be part of the picture. Discuss these without blame; needing support is not a personal failure, and no single factor determines the outcome. Does depression or its treatment cause earlier menopause? A 2003 observational study found an association between depression and an earlier perimenopausal transition; a subgroup with symptoms and antidepressant use had a higher measured risk. This does not prove that antidepressants caused the transition, that time to menopause was “three times shorter”, or that the final menstrual period necessarily occurred earlier. The illness and other differences between groups can affect the findings. Do not stop an effective antidepressant because of this association. If menstrual changes begin unusually early, discuss them with a clinician. Early loss of ovarian function has implications for bone and cardiovascular health, but a low mood episode does not mean that cognitive impairment, heart attack or stroke is inevitable. Individual assessment is more useful than assuming a fixed hormonal cause. Getting a proper assessment Tell a clinician when symptoms began, how they affect life, previous depression or anxiety, treatments, medicines or supplements, sleep, periods and hot flushes. Assessment should also consider physical conditions such as thyroid problems, relevant substance use, and any past periods of unusually elevated mood, reduced need for sleep or impulsive behaviour that could suggest bipolar disorder. A questionnaire or symptom diary may support the conversation but cannot make the diagnosis alone. You can ask for psychological therapy, medication review and help with menopause symptoms together. If you have experienced trauma or violence, ask for a safe, confidential discussion and support. Treatment should fit the severity, previous response, health and preferences, with a follow-up plan. Treatment: depression care and menopause care together Evidence-based talking therapies, such as cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) or interpersonal therapy, and antidepressants are established treatments for depression. The combination or order depends on severity and preference; medication is not automatically the first choice for every mild symptom. Depression should be treated even if hot flushes are also present. NICE distinguishes depressive symptoms that do not meet criteria for depression from diagnosed or suspected depression. HRT may be considered for such menopause-associated symptoms starting around the same time as other menopause symptoms; menopause-specific CBT can help selected mood, sleep and hot-flush difficulties. Suspected or diagnosed depression needs depression guidance alongside menopause care. HRT is not a universal substitute for depression treatment. What the escitalopram research actually showed Escitalopram is an SSRI antidepressant that has also been studied for hot flushes. In one 2011 eight-week placebo-controlled trial of 205 women, 55% taking escitalopram and 36% taking placebo reported at least a 50% reduction in hot-flush frequency. This describes a response in that study, not a guaranteed reduction for everyone. That trial did not compare escitalopram with HRT or show it to be three times more effective for depression. Some antidepressants can be chosen for depression and may also help hot flushes, but the indication and local recommendations matter. HRT benefits and risks depend on age, timing, personal history, preparation and route; oral and transdermal therapy do not have identical clot and stroke risks. A blanket claim that all HRT causes heart attacks or strokes is misleading. Antidepressant benefits, side effects and follow-up Antidepressants may take several weeks to help, and finding the right option can involve adjustment. Possible effects include dizziness, insomnia or sleepiness, fatigue, nausea or other stomach symptoms and sexual difficulties; effects differ between medicines and people. A trial reporting no serious events does not prove that the medicine has no serious risks. Agree when to review benefit and side effects. Report marked agitation, unusual mood elevation or worsening distress promptly. New or worsening suicidal thoughts need urgent professional help, with immediate emergency care if you cannot stay safe. Do not abruptly stop or alter antidepressants yourself; withdrawal symptoms and recurrence can occur, so changes need a prescriber-supported plan. Movement, sleep and everyday support Regular movement suited to your health, including manageable walks, can support mood, sleep and general health. Start with realistic steps and choose something tolerable or enjoyable; exercise is not a guaranteed prevention or a replacement for treatment. Regular meals, social connection and help with practical pressures can also matter. Try a consistent sleep and waking routine, a comfortable cool, dark and quiet room, and reducing stimulating screen use near bedtime. Treating hot flushes or another sleep problem may help. Gentle mindful breathing or relaxation can ease stress for some people, but there is no required 15-minute dose or promise to cure depression. If it increases distress, stop and ask about an alternative. Valerian and B vitamins: check the claims Valerian is not a proven treatment for perimenopausal depression. NCCIH finds insufficient evidence for depression and uncertain benefit for menopause symptoms or sleep. It can cause unwanted effects, interact with medicines, add to sedation with alcohol or sedatives, and has uncertain long-term safety. Tell the clinician about herbs rather than replacing established care with them. B vitamins are important nutrients, but routine high-dose supplements are not an established depression treatment. Names include B1 (thiamine), B2 (riboflavin), B3 (niacin), B5 (pantothenic acid), B6 (pyridoxine), B9 (folate) and B12 (cobalamin); niacin is not B2. Dairy or suitable fortified alternatives, leafy vegetables, beans and other varied foods contribute different nutrients. Assess a suspected deficiency individually; excessive supplemental B6 can damage nerves. When to seek help and how to prepare Arrange an appointment for persistent low mood, loss of interest, major sleep changes or difficulty managing daily life, including recurrence of past depression. Seek urgent professional support for thoughts of self-harm or suicide, rapidly worsening distress or inability to manage essential needs. You do not need to wait for menopause to be confirmed or for symptoms to become severe. If there is immediate danger, an attempt, or you feel unable to stay safe, contact local emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department now. Stay with a trusted person if possible while help is arranged. Bring a medicine list and brief notes on mood, sleep, periods and symptoms to follow-up; do not delay urgent care to complete a record. Recovery can take time and treatment can be adjusted. Depression during perimenopause is treatable and is not inevitable or your fault. Persistent low mood or loss of enjoyment differs from brief mood changes and deserves assessment. Hormone fluctuations, sleep, history and life circumstances interact; an association does not prove a medicine caused earlier menopause. Psychotherapy, antidepressants and individualized menopause care have different roles; valerian and high-dose vitamins are not proven replacements. Seek urgent help for suicidal thoughts and immediate emergency care if you cannot stay safe. What are the signs of perimenopausal depression? Persistent sadness or loss of enjoyment, hopelessness, fatigue, poor concentration, sleep or appetite changes, anxiety, irritability or tearfulness can occur. Symptoms need assessment when persistent or impairing daily life, sooner if severe or affecting safety. Do all mood swings mean depression? No. Temporary mood changes can occur during the transition, but sustained distress, loss of pleasure or impaired functioning may indicate depression or another condition. A clinician can assess the whole picture. Do antidepressants cause earlier menopause? The older observational association does not establish that. Antidepressant use can reflect the underlying depression, and an earlier transition is not the same as a proven earlier final period. Do not stop prescribed treatment because of this claim. Is HRT better than an antidepressant? There is no single answer for everyone. HRT may help selected menopause-associated depressive symptoms; diagnosed depression needs evidence-based depression care alongside menopause management. The cited escitalopram trial compared hot flushes with placebo, not depression treatment with HRT. What side effects can antidepressants cause? Depending on the medicine, dizziness, altered sleep, fatigue, stomach symptoms or sexual problems can occur. Discuss troublesome effects, unusual agitation or mood elevation. Worsening suicidal thoughts need urgent help; do not stop abruptly without a plan. How can I support myself at home? Manageable activity, regular meals, a steady sleep routine, social support and gentle relaxation can help alongside care. They do not guarantee prevention or cure. Seek help with persistent hot flushes, sleep problems or practical stresses. Does valerian or vitamin B treat this depression? Valerian has insufficient evidence, and routine high-dose B vitamins are not established treatment. Correct a diagnosed deficiency when needed with professional advice. B2 is riboflavin, not niacin; too much supplemental B6 can harm nerves. When is help urgent? Suicidal thoughts or rapidly worsening distress need urgent professional help. Immediate danger, an attempt or inability to stay safe requires local emergency services or an emergency department now. If possible, stay with someone trusted while help is arranged.

title: Prostate testing: PSA, examination and who should consider screening
description: Understand screening versus symptom assessment, PSA and rectal examination, uncertain results, MRI and biopsy, and the warning signs after a procedure.
body: There is no single prostate test that gives a complete answer. A clinician may use a history, examination, PSA blood test and sometimes imaging or a biopsy. Testing because of symptoms differs from screening someone who feels well. Before screening, discuss whether the possible benefit fits your risk, health and preferences, alongside the possibility of unnecessary investigations or treatment. What the prostate does and why it is checked The prostate is a small gland below the bladder, surrounding the beginning of the urethra. It contributes fluid to semen. Benign enlargement, inflammation and cancer are different conditions that can affect it; a change in urination does not identify which condition is present. Seek assessment for new or persistent difficulty urinating, a weak stream, frequent night-time urination or pelvic discomfort. Visible or suspected blood in urine needs urgent same-day medical advice, even once, in a small amount or if you are unsure it is blood. Complete inability to urinate or severe lower-abdominal pain needs immediate emergency care. Fever with marked illness needs urgent care; do not wait for a screening appointment. Screening is a shared decision, not an automatic annual test Screening looks for cancer before symptoms develop. It can find an important cancer earlier, but can also identify a slow-growing cancer that would never cause trouble during a person's lifetime. False alarms, biopsy complications and treatment effects on urinary, bowel or sexual function belong in the discussion. Choosing not to screen after an informed discussion is an option. Some low-risk cancers can be managed with active surveillance rather than immediate surgery or radiotherapy. Surveillance is a planned monitoring programme, not ignoring cancer, and some cancers need treatment. Overall health, likely life expectancy and willingness to undertake further tests or treatment influence whether screening makes sense. Age, family history and differing recommendations There is no worldwide age rule. ACS recommends discussing screening at 50 for average-risk men expected to live at least another 10 years, at 45 for higher risk such as Black/African American men or a father or brother diagnosed before 65, and at 40 when more than one first-degree relative was diagnosed young. These are ages to discuss a choice, not a requirement to test everyone. The current final USPSTF recommendation supports individual decisions at ages 55–69 and recommends against PSA screening from 70; its update is in progress. Other specialist and national guidelines use different risk-based starting ages and intervals. Inherited variants such as BRCA2 and a strong family history deserve individual advice, sometimes including genetic assessment. Symptom investigation should not be delayed because someone falls outside a screening age range. What a digital rectal examination can and cannot show For a DRE, a clinician gently inserts a lubricated, gloved finger into the rectum to feel the accessible surface of the prostate. You will often lie on your side with knees bent, although another position may be used. The examination is brief and may feel uncomfortable or create an urge to urinate; it is not usually painful.
