Tell the clinician about haemorrhoids, fissures, bleeding or pain, and ask them to stop if needed. The examination can provide clues about enlargement, tenderness or a suspicious area, but it cannot examine every part of the gland or rule cancer out. DRE alone is not an adequate screening strategy. It may add information during assessment, particularly with an abnormal PSA or symptoms. Ask for an explanation, privacy and a chaperone or support person if you wish. What PSA measures and why it can change PSA is a protein made by prostate cells that helps keep semen fluid. A blood sample measures the amount reaching the bloodstream. Cancer can raise PSA, but so can benign enlargement, infection or inflammation. Recent urinary retention or procedures can also affect it. A high result is a reason to interpret the whole situation, not a cancer diagnosis. There is no single PSA number that proves or excludes cancer. Some cancers occur with a relatively low PSA; that does not mean cancer generally lowers the result. Finasteride and dutasteride can lower PSA and change interpretation. Tell the clinician about all medicines and supplements rather than stopping them yourself. Preparing for the blood test and examination Follow the testing service's instructions. NHS advice is to avoid ejaculation, anal sex, cycling and vigorous exercise for 48 hours before PSA testing, and to allow time after a urinary infection has cleared. Recent catheterisation, biopsy or other urinary procedures may change timing. Report these events so the clinician can choose an appropriate date; treating urgent symptoms takes priority over obtaining an undisturbed PSA result. A PSA blood test generally does not require fasting unless another test does. Tell staff if needles make you anxious. For DRE, explain any anal or rectal problems beforehand; slow breathing and a comfortable position can help. You do not have to tolerate severe pain or continue an examination without consent. Understanding the result and planning follow-up DRE findings may be discussed immediately, while PSA needs laboratory processing. Ask when and how you will receive the result and whom to contact if it does not arrive. Keep previous values and dates if available. The interpretation may include age, prostate size, family history, medicines, infection and examination findings. A newly raised PSA is often repeated after possible temporary influences settle, with the interval chosen for the circumstances. The speed of change, sometimes called PSA velocity, should not be the sole reason for imaging or biopsy. An abnormal result does not automatically require a biopsy, and a normal PSA or DRE does not fully exclude cancer. Persistent symptoms or continuing concern still need a plan. MRI, ultrasound and deciding whether a biopsy is needed A specialist may discuss MRI, selected additional blood or urine tests and a risk assessment before deciding on biopsy. MRI can highlight areas worth sampling and may help some people avoid a biopsy; it cannot guarantee that cancer is absent. Follow-up remains important if a scan is reassuring but the overall risk stays high. Transrectal ultrasound uses a small rectal probe to show the prostate and can guide needle sampling. It is different from DRE and cannot diagnose cancer by itself. The sequence and duration of imaging and biopsy vary between services and clinical situations; a fixed ten-minute scan or automatic ultrasound-to-biopsy pathway does not apply to everyone. What happens during a prostate biopsy A biopsy collects small tissue samples for a pathologist to examine for cancer and, if found, its characteristics. Needles may pass through the skin between the scrotum and anus (transperineal) or through the rectal wall (transrectal), using imaging guidance. Ask which route, anaesthetic and infection-prevention plan are proposed, and why the result would change your care. Local anaesthetic, sedation or general anaesthetic may be used. Pressure, brief needle sensations or later soreness are possible, and the appointment can take longer than the sampling itself. Discuss blood thinners, allergies and infection symptoms in advance; change medicines only under the team's instructions. A negative biopsy can miss cancer, so it does not always end follow-up. Recovery, warning signs and the next decision Some soreness and blood in urine or semen can occur after biopsy. Expected amount and duration depend on the procedure; follow your own discharge advice about activity, drinking, sex and medicines. Ask how results will be explained and what happens if they show benign changes, uncertainty or cancer. Further monitoring, sampling or treatment depends on the full findings and your preferences. Get urgent medical help after biopsy for fever, shaking chills, worsening pain or feeling very unwell. Inability to pass urine, heavy or persistent bleeding, substantial clots, fainting or severe illness needs emergency assessment. Do not dismiss these as harmless expected bleeding. Tell the service you recently had a prostate biopsy and bring the discharge information if possible. Symptom assessment and screening are different; urinary warning signs should not wait for a routine test. Screening ages and intervals vary; discuss personal risk, likely benefit and harms rather than assuming annual testing. Neither a high PSA nor an abnormal examination alone proves cancer; normal findings do not completely rule it out. Repeat PSA, MRI, other tests and biopsy are selected according to the full clinical picture. After biopsy, fever, marked illness, heavy bleeding or inability to urinate require prompt or emergency care. Why might PSA be high without cancer? Benign enlargement, infection, inflammation and recent urinary events or procedures can raise it. The clinician considers these alongside cancer risk and may repeat the measurement; the number alone is not a diagnosis. What is the PSA blood test? It measures prostate-specific antigen, a protein made by prostate cells, in a blood sample. It can help with screening, symptom assessment or monitoring an already diagnosed prostate condition, but cannot independently confirm cancer. Why might a biopsy be recommended? Tissue sampling can clarify whether cancer is present and describe it. The decision considers PSA, examination, MRI or other tests, risk and whether the answer would change care. Not every raised PSA needs immediate biopsy. Does a prostate biopsy hurt? Anaesthesia reduces pain, but pressure or brief discomfort during sampling and soreness afterwards can occur. Ask about pain control and tell the team if it is inadequate. Severe or worsening pain, fever, heavy bleeding or retention requires medical help. Should everyone start screening at 50? No. ACS uses 50 as a discussion age for average risk and adequate life expectancy, with earlier discussions for higher risk. USPSTF and other guidelines differ. Agree a plan based on risk, health, local guidance and preferences. Can a normal PSA or rectal examination rule out cancer? No. Some cancers do not produce a clearly raised PSA or a palpable change. Persistent symptoms or important risk factors may still require review, even after reassuring initial results. Should I stop a medicine before testing? Do not stop it yourself. Give the clinician a complete list, including prostate medicines, blood thinners and supplements. They can advise about test interpretation or a specific procedure plan. Which symptoms need urgent help after biopsy? Fever, shaking chills, worsening pain or marked illness need urgent advice. Inability to urinate, heavy bleeding or substantial clots, fainting or severe illness needs emergency assessment. State that you recently had a biopsy.

title: Trachelectomy: removing the cervix and preserving pregnancy options
description: Understand simple and radical trachelectomy, who may be eligible, surgical risks, recovery, sexual health and pregnancy after cervical cancer treatment.
body: The cervix connects the womb to the vagina. Trachelectomy removes cervical tissue while retaining the womb, sometimes as treatment for a carefully selected early cervical cancer. It may preserve the possibility of carrying a pregnancy, but neither pregnancy nor freedom from recurrence is guaranteed. Decisions belong with a specialist gynaecological cancer team and should include your fertility wishes. What simple and radical trachelectomy mean A simple trachelectomy removes the cervix without the same surrounding-tissue removal as a radical operation. Radical trachelectomy also removes tissue beside the cervix and part of the upper vagina. Lymph-node assessment may be needed separately. The extent depends on the cancer findings; removing the cervix does not always mean radical surgery. The womb and usually the ovaries are retained. Hysterectomy removes the womb and prevents carrying a pregnancy; a cone biopsy removes a smaller piece of cervical tissue. These procedures have different indications and risks. Ask exactly what is proposed, what will remain and what findings could change the plan. Why it may be offered, and what HPV means The main reason discussed here is selected early cervical cancer. Persistent high-risk human papillomavirus, HPV, causes most cervical cancers. HPV is common and usually clears; CDC estimates about nine in ten infections clear within two years. A positive HPV test alone is not cancer and is not an indication to remove the cervix. Abnormal cells need their own recommended follow-up. Cervical screening depends on having a cervix, age, previous results and risk, including immune suppression, rather than assumptions about gender or partners. Smoking increases risk. Discuss HPV vaccination and local screening guidance. Early cancer may cause no symptoms; unusual vaginal bleeding, pelvic pain or pain during sex needs assessment even after a reassuring screening result. Who may be suitable for fertility-sparing treatment A specialist team reviews the biopsy, cancer type, stage, size, depth of invasion, imaging, lymph nodes and ability to obtain clear margins. Many standard candidates have a small cancer confined to the cervix, usually under or around 2 cm depending on the guideline and other findings. Size alone never establishes eligibility; some aggressive cancer types are unsuitable. Some very early, low-risk cancers can be treated with a cone biopsy or simple trachelectomy rather than a radical procedure. Others require more extensive surgery or chemoradiotherapy. Larger tumours are not routinely treated with fertility-sparing surgery. Ask about cancer control and pregnancy risks together, including the possibility of abandoning the fertility-sparing plan if nodes or margins are involved. Benefits and limits compared with hysterectomy Keeping the womb can preserve a route to pregnancy that hysterectomy cannot. Suitable patients can have effective cancer treatment, but comparisons between procedures depend on careful selection and follow-up. Broad comparisons of survival between procedures and published pregnancy percentages are not reliable personal predictions. Discuss outcomes for your particular cancer and proposed operation. A shorter admission or less blood loss in a small study does not make one operation universally better. Vaginal, open abdominal, laparoscopic and surgeon-controlled robotic approaches have different trade-offs. Smaller incisions do not automatically mean safer cancer outcomes; evidence from radical hysterectomy must not be presented as a direct trachelectomy result. Ask why the recommended route fits your situation. Preparation and what happens during surgery Before surgery, expect assessment of anaesthetic fitness, medicines, allergies and previous operations, plus imaging and pathology review as needed. Discuss fertility preservation before treatment begins and consent for possible changes. Follow your hospital's eating, drinking and medicine instructions. The operation is generally performed under general anaesthesia, with intravenous access and a urinary catheter. When indicated, the surgeon assesses pelvic lymph nodes and removes the planned cervical and surrounding tissue. The womb is joined to the remaining vaginal tissue, usually with a permanent supporting stitch, or cerclage, and an opening for menstrual blood. Removed tissue is examined. Involved nodes or margins may require a different treatment plan, including chemoradiotherapy or further surgery; this is not one automatic sequence for everyone. Risks and possible longer-term effects Risks include bleeding, infection, blood clots, anaesthetic complications and injury to the bladder, ureters, bowel or blood vessels. Temporary or persistent difficulty emptying the bladder, urine leakage, constipation, adhesions and altered sensation in the upper thighs can occur. Tell the team about continuing symptoms; do not assume they are inevitable or untreatable. Pelvic lymph-node treatment can lead to lymphocysts or lymphoedema, commonly involving the legs, lower abdomen or genital area, rather than a universal pattern of arm swelling. Periods may change or become painful; narrowing of the remaining opening can obstruct menstrual flow. Seek review for new swelling, absent periods with pain, persistent discharge or urinary problems. Hospital stay, catheter care and recovery Admission and recovery vary with the operation, complications, health and support at home. Some services describe a few nights in hospital; recovery usually takes several weeks and can take longer. A catheter may remain after discharge until the bladder empties safely. Learn its care and the removal or review plan; do not remove it yourself or accept a fixed one- or two-week timetable as universal. Use prescribed pain relief and constipation treatment, and follow wound-care and clot-prevention instructions. Increase gentle walking gradually while allowing rest. Obtain individual clearance for lifting, exercise, stairs, driving and work; driving also requires safe movement and freedom from impairing medicines. Avoid vaginal penetration, tampons and swimming until the team says healing is sufficient; around six weeks is a common instruction, not a guarantee. Sexual health and emotional recovery Pain, altered desire, tiredness, body-image concerns and anxiety can affect intimacy. You do not have to resume penetrative sex on a deadline. After healing and clinical clearance, return at your pace and seek help for pain, bleeding or persistent difficulties. Lubrication, pelvic-health care or psychosexual support may be appropriate after assessment. A small older study does not mean everyone develops sexual problems or that desire always returns at twelve months. Cancer and uncertainty about fertility can be distressing even when treatment succeeds. Ask the specialist nurse about counselling, partner support if wanted, and practical help during recovery. Pregnancy after trachelectomy Pregnancy can be possible, but scarring or a narrowed opening may make conception harder, and some people need fertility treatment. Arrange preconception advice and ask when trying is medically appropriate. Use contraception until the cancer team clears you; local waiting recommendations differ. There is no universal pregnancy-success percentage or promise that preserving the womb preserves fertility fully. Pregnancy after fertility-sparing cervical surgery needs specialist high-risk care because miscarriage, early waters breaking and premature birth are more likely. A permanent cerclage does not remove those risks. Delivery after simple or radical trachelectomy with a permanent cerclage is by caesarean section; timing and monitoring are individual. Contact the maternity team promptly with pregnancy, and urgently for bleeding, fluid loss or contractions. Warning signs after surgery Contact the surgical team urgently for fever or chills, increasing wound redness or drainage, foul-smelling discharge, worsening pain, persistent vomiting, a catheter that stops draining or new difficulty passing urine. A painful swollen leg needs urgent same-day assessment. Complete inability to urinate needs immediate emergency assessment. Do not wait for a scheduled follow-up. Get emergency help immediately for chest pain or breathlessness, coughing blood, fainting or loss of consciousness, heavy bleeding with dizziness or fainting, or sudden severe abdominal pain. These can indicate a clot, significant bleeding or another serious complication. Mild discharge can occur during healing, but increasing or troublesome bleeding should be reported rather than normalized by its colour or duration. Follow-up and the longer-term outlook Follow-up checks cancer control, healing, bladder and bowel function, lymph swelling, sexual wellbeing and pregnancy plans. The team sets examination, HPV testing and any imaging according to treatment and risk; ordinary screening schedules do not replace cancer follow-up. Report new or persistent symptoms between appointments. Ask for a written summary of the operation, pathology, stitch and ongoing plan. Trachelectomy can offer selected people meaningful pregnancy options, but additional treatment may change them. Decisions should protect cancer care while respecting your goals, with continuing support whether pregnancy happens or not. Simple and radical trachelectomy remove different amounts of tissue while retaining the womb. Eligibility depends on full cancer assessment, not tumour size or a positive HPV result alone. Keeping the womb may preserve pregnancy options but cannot guarantee fertility or cancer outcome. Recovery, catheter use, sex, work and trying for pregnancy need individual clearance. Heavy bleeding with faintness, chest or breathing symptoms, fainting or loss of consciousness or inability to urinate need emergency care. Why is the cervix removed? Selected early cervical cancer may be treated with trachelectomy while retaining the womb. A positive HPV test alone does not justify it. The specialist team determines the least extensive safe treatment. Is every trachelectomy radical? No. Simple surgery removes less surrounding tissue. A cone biopsy may suffice for some very early cancers; other findings need radical surgery or a different treatment. Ask which operation and node assessment are planned. What is the main benefit compared with hysterectomy? The womb remains, so carrying a pregnancy may still be possible. This is not a guarantee of conception, a live birth or equivalent outcomes for every cancer. What are the main disadvantages? Bleeding, infection, clots, organ or nerve injury, bladder problems, lymph swelling, painful periods or sex and fertility or pregnancy difficulties are possible. Individual risks depend on the procedure and other treatment. How long does recovery take? Usually several weeks, sometimes longer. Hospital stay, catheter removal and return to driving, work or sex vary; follow your team's instructions rather than a universal three-to-five-day admission or four-to-six-week deadline. Can I become pregnant afterwards? Some people can, naturally or with fertility treatment. Obtain cancer-team clearance and specialist pregnancy care. Miscarriage and premature birth risks are increased; a permanent cerclage requires caesarean delivery. Do I still need follow-up after the cervix is removed? Yes. Specialist cancer follow-up and any recommended HPV testing or other investigations remain important. Report new symptoms without waiting for the next appointment. Which symptoms require immediate help? Chest pain, breathlessness, coughing blood, fainting or loss of consciousness, heavy bleeding with faintness, sudden severe abdominal pain or complete inability to urinate require emergency assessment. Fever, foul discharge, worsening wounds or a painful swollen leg need urgent clinical advice.

title: No period while using contraception: causes and when to test
description: Understand lighter or absent bleeding on hormonal contraception, when to take a pregnancy test and which symptoms need urgent medical care.
body: Missing expected bleeding can feel worrying. Hormonal contraception often makes bleeding lighter or stops it, and this can be an expected effect rather than a health problem. Pregnancy is still possible, however. Your method, how you have used it and any new symptoms matter more than a calendar prediction alone. A withdrawal bleed is different from a natural period A natural period follows changes in your own menstrual cycle. Bleeding during the hormone-free days of a combined pill is usually a withdrawal bleed. It may become very light or disappear because the womb lining stays thin; blood is not building up inside you. There is no medical need for a monthly withdrawal bleed on an appropriate hormonal regimen. Absence of bleeding, sometimes called amenorrhoea, is not automatically abnormal during contraception. Having a bleed also does not reliably rule out pregnancy. Different methods have different bleeding patterns Combined pills contain estrogen and a progestin; progestin-only pills contain no estrogen. They prevent pregnancy through effects including stopping ovulation and/or thickening cervical mucus, depending on the product. Some also help heavy or painful bleeding or acne. These benefits and suitability vary. Packs and schedules differ: not every pill follows 21 active days and seven days off. Some have different placebo intervals; suitable combined pills can be prescribed with shorter, fewer or no breaks. Progestin-only pill instructions also vary. Do not copy another brand's schedule or add a break to bring on bleeding; follow your own leaflet and clinician's advice. Continuous use and contraceptive injections Extended or continuous hormonal use can mean fewer scheduled bleeds or none. Spotting is common at first and often settles, but new persistent troublesome bleeding deserves review. With injections, absent bleeding is also common and usually needs no treatment once pregnancy and other relevant causes have been considered. Injection timing depends on the product and local guidance. For DMPA, US CDC guidance schedules repeat doses every 13 weeks and allows up to 15 weeks from the last dose without extra protection. This is not a universal rule for every injection or country. Contact your service promptly if late; it can advise testing, backup protection and emergency contraception. Could you be pregnant despite contraception? No method is completely effective. Correct pill use offers very high protection, but everyday use is less reliable. CDC estimates about seven pregnancies per 100 combined-hormonal users in a year with typical use; NHS pill guidance estimates about nine. These are population estimates, not your personal chance from one episode of sex. Risk can increase with missed active pills, a late new pack, vomiting or prolonged diarrhoea, or interacting medicines. Some medicines for epilepsy, tuberculosis or HIV and St John's wort require a specific interaction check; not all antibiotics interfere. What to do after a missed pill depends on its type, timing and place in the pack. Progestin-only pills have different late-pill windows. Ask a pharmacist or sexual-health service promptly, especially if recent sex may require emergency contraception; your usual hormones can affect the choice and restart instructions. When and how to take a pregnancy test Test from the first missed natural period if you know when it is due. If hormonal contraception makes timing uncertain, test at least 21 days after the last sex without reliable contraceptive protection, including a suspected method failure. You do not need to wait for two missed bleeds. A test taken sooner may need repeating at the appropriate time. Contraceptive hormones do not stop pregnancy tests working. A correctly used positive result is usually reliable; an early negative is less conclusive. Follow the test instructions, repeat after a few days if concerned, and contact a clinician if repeat tests are negative but symptoms or uncertainty persist. A positive result needs timely pregnancy care and discussion of your options and medicines. Nausea, breast tenderness, fatigue, urinary frequency or back discomfort alone cannot confirm pregnancy. Stress, eating changes and exercise Stress, rapid weight change, inadequate energy intake and intensive exercise can disrupt natural ovulation. This is different from the planned hormonal effect of contraception, so these factors cannot explain every missing withdrawal bleed. There is no single percentage below an average weight that diagnoses the cause. Regular nourishing meals, enough rest and enjoyable activity support health. Breathing exercises, gentle yoga, walking or journalling may help with stress; they do not guarantee a bleed or exclude pregnancy. Seek compassionate professional support for restrictive eating, bingeing, purging or exercise that feels difficult to control. A clinician can assess energy needs and other causes rather than simply telling you to change your weight. When a routine review is helpful Arrange a review if absent bleeding is an unexpected change, you are unsure how to use your method, or side effects trouble you. Depending on your history, assessment may consider pregnancy, thyroid disease, polycystic ovary syndrome, breastfeeding, perimenopause or other causes. Missing three natural periods when not using a method expected to suppress them also warrants review; do not wait that long to test after possible contraceptive failure. Bring the exact product name, pack or injection dates, missed doses, medicines, test results and symptoms. Continue according to your method's instructions while seeking advice; stopping or inserting a hormone-free interval yourself can reduce protection. You can discuss a different suitable method if the bleeding pattern does not suit you. Restoring monthly bleeding is not necessarily the treatment goal. Symptoms that need urgent or emergency care Seek urgent medical advice straight away if pregnancy is possible and you have one-sided lower abdominal pain, unusual vaginal bleeding or shoulder-tip pain, even without a positive test. These symptoms can have several causes, including ectopic pregnancy; a tracking app or an early negative test cannot safely rule it out. Call local emergency services or go to an emergency department immediately for sudden severe abdominal or pelvic pain, loss of consciousness, marked dizziness or fainting, especially with possible pregnancy or heavy bleeding. Do not wait for another test or for bleeding to start. Tracking can support a conversation A record of bleeding, symptoms, pill use and injection dates can make appointments easier. It cannot tell you whether contraception worked, whether you ovulated or whether you are pregnant. Bleeding is not required every 28 days on every method. When pregnancy has been appropriately excluded and the pattern fits your method, light or absent bleeding is often harmless. Keep up recommended care and ask for a personalized plan if the pattern changes or worries you; neither lifestyle changes nor an app should replace testing or assessment when indicated. Hormonal contraception can safely reduce or stop bleeding; a withdrawal bleed is not a natural period. Use your own product's schedule. Do not add a pill break just to cause bleeding. If timing is uncertain, test at least 21 days after sex without reliable protection; do not wait for two missed bleeds. Missed-pill and late-injection advice depends on the method, so get prompt product-specific help. Possible pregnancy with pain or unusual bleeding needs urgent assessment; severe pain or fainting needs emergency care. Does no period mean I am pregnant? Not necessarily. Hormonal contraception often suppresses bleeding. If pregnancy is possible, use a correctly timed test rather than relying on bleeding or symptoms. I took every pill correctly. Should I still test? Pregnancy is less likely, but correct use does not make it impossible. Test if you have a reason to suspect pregnancy, a new unexpected bleeding change or uncertainty about protection; do not wait for another missed month. Can diet changes or stress stop periods? They can disrupt natural cycles, especially with inadequate energy intake or major weight change. They do not automatically explain absent bleeding on hormonal contraception. Consider testing and clinical review when appropriate. Is it dangerous not to bleed every month on the pill? Usually not on a suitable regimen. The lining stays thin and blood does not accumulate. A new unexplained change, troublesome symptoms or possible pregnancy still needs appropriate assessment. Should I stop the pill to make a period happen? Do not create an extra break or copy another brand's schedule. Follow the leaflet and get advice about suitable tailored regimens; an unplanned break can reduce protection. Can I test while taking hormones? Yes. Contraceptive hormones do not prevent the test detecting pregnancy. If you do not know when bleeding is due, test at least 21 days after sex without reliable protection and repeat if an earlier test was too soon. What if I missed pills or am late for an injection? Contact a pharmacist or contraceptive service promptly with the exact product and dates. You may need backup protection, testing or emergency contraception; the rules are not identical across pills or injections. When should I get emergency help? Get immediate emergency care for sudden severe abdominal or pelvic pain, fainting or loss of consciousness, particularly with possible pregnancy or heavy bleeding. One-sided pain, unusual bleeding or shoulder-tip pain with possible pregnancy needs urgent advice even without a positive test.

title: Cervical ectropion: symptoms, assessment and treatment choices
description: Learn what cervical ectropion means, why unusual bleeding needs assessment, and when observation or treatments such as cautery may help.
body: Cervical ectropion is a common, benign finding in which delicate cells from inside the cervical canal are visible on its outer surface. Many people have no symptoms and need no treatment. Bleeding or discharge should still be assessed rather than assumed to be ectropion, even if it has been diagnosed before. What ectropion means The cervix joins the womb to the vagina. Its canal contains mucus-producing glandular cells, while its outer surface usually has tougher squamous cells. When glandular cells extend onto the outside, the area can look red because the tissue is thin and blood vessels show through. The older term ‘cervical erosion’ is misleading: the cervix is not wearing away. Ectropion itself is not cancer or a precancerous change, does not cause infertility and is not in itself a sexually transmitted infection. It can nevertheless coexist with another condition. Symptoms and other possible explanations Most people notice nothing. Others have increased mucus-like discharge, spotting between periods or light bleeding during or after sex or a cervical examination. The delicate glandular cells make more mucus and bleed more easily. Pain during sex may be reported, but should not simply be attributed to ectropion. Arrange assessment for unusual bleeding, changed discharge or pain. Infection, including STIs, polyps, fibroids, vaginal dryness, contraception or an intrauterine device, pregnancy-related problems, endometriosis or, less commonly, cancer can cause overlapping symptoms. New bleeding after menopause also needs checking. Do not diagnose the cause by colour, an app or a past screening result. Hormones and contraception Ectropion is associated with estrogen and is common during adolescence, reproductive years, pregnancy and combined-pill use. Some people have it from birth; an individual cause is not always clear. It is less common after menopause. If symptoms develop with an estrogen-containing contraceptive, a clinician may discuss changing to another suitable method. Do not stop contraception without a replacement plan if you want to avoid pregnancy. Ectropion is not evidence that you caused damage or that a partner has an infection. How the cervix is assessed A clinician asks about symptoms, pregnancy possibility, contraception and screening history, then may offer a speculum examination to see the cervix. You can ask for a chaperone, adjustments, explanations or to stop. The area may bleed a little when touched. Depending on findings, tests may include pregnancy testing, infection swabs or other investigations. Cervical screening checks risk and cell changes; it is not a diagnostic test for the cause of symptoms. A recent normal result does not replace examination of persistent or unexplained bleeding. Colposcopy, a closer view using a magnifying instrument outside the body, and sometimes a small biopsy are used when indicated, not automatically for every ectropion. A suspicious-looking cervix needs prompt specialist referral. Observation is a valid option If the finding is confidently benign and symptoms are absent or acceptable, treatment may not be needed. Symptoms can settle by themselves, although the time varies. You do not have to undergo a procedure simply because an ectropion is visible. If discharge or bleeding persists and affects daily life or sexual comfort, discuss benefits, risks and alternatives after other causes have been assessed. Treatment aims to improve symptoms, not prevent cancer. Continue routine screening when eligible and return if symptoms change. Silver nitrate, freezing and heat treatment Silver nitrate treats the surface with a chemical stick and is generally used for smaller areas, usually without local anaesthetic. Cryocautery freezes the surface with a cold probe and also often needs no anaesthetic. Diathermy uses a heated probe, usually after local anaesthetic. Availability and suitability vary. These are usually short outpatient procedures using a speculum, but preparation takes longer than the treatment itself. Cramping or discomfort can occur; no method should be promised painless. Ask about pain relief that is safe for you, consent and what to expect. Tell the team if pregnancy is possible; routine ectropion cautery is generally avoided during pregnancy. Recovery depends on the procedure Most people go home when comfortable. Mild period-like cramps, light spotting and watery discharge may last days to weeks. Silver nitrate can cause dark or blackish discharge. Your team should explain what is expected for your treatment and how long it should last. Use pads during healing and follow your clinic's instructions about avoiding tampons, menstrual cups, penetrative sex and swimming. Some protocols advise up to four weeks; others depend on the treatment and when discharge settles. There is no single deadline for everyone. Ask about work, driving, pain relief and follow-up; do not push through pain or resume penetration before the advised healing period. Benefits, risks and return of symptoms Treatment often improves discharge or contact bleeding, but it may not work completely and symptoms can recur. Discuss persistent symptoms before repeating treatment, because another cause may need attention. Ectropion and its usual superficial treatments are not the same as removing cervical tissue for precancer; ask about your particular procedure and pregnancy plans. Risks include infection and bleeding; cervical narrowing is a rare risk described with cryocautery. Seek urgent same-day advice for fever, foul-smelling discharge or bleeding beyond the advised course if there are no emergency signs. Get immediate emergency care for severe or worsening abdominal or pelvic pain, heavy bleeding, fainting, loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain or difficulty breathing. Do not drive yourself to emergency care. Pregnancy bleeding still needs prompt care Ectropion is common in pregnancy and the finding itself is benign, but do not assume it explains bleeding or protects against another problem. It is not established as the most common cause of late-pregnancy bleeding. Contact your maternity or early-pregnancy service promptly for any spotting or bleeding, including without pain; tell them about unusual discharge too. If you are pregnant and bleeding with severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, dizziness, fainting, feeling acutely unwell or bleeding that rapidly soaks a pad, call local emergency services immediately. Possible pregnancy with pain and unusual bleeding also needs urgent assessment even without a positive test. Do not wait for an app prediction or a routine appointment. Living with a benign finding Once the diagnosis is assessed, reassurance and a plan matched to your symptoms are often enough. You can discuss effects on sexual comfort without pressure to tolerate pain. Ectropion does not itself prevent pregnancy, and treatment is not necessary solely to preserve fertility. Record when bleeding occurs, discharge changes, pain, contraception and any procedures to support appointments. Tracking cannot establish that symptoms are harmless, diagnose ectropion or exclude infection, pregnancy or cancer. Seek another review if symptoms persist, worsen or change, even after treatment. Ectropion is a common benign cervical finding, not erosion or a precancerous change. Unusual bleeding, discharge or pain needs assessment; screening alone cannot diagnose the cause. Observation is reasonable when symptoms are absent or acceptable; symptoms may settle naturally. Cautery options and healing instructions vary; no universal anaesthetic or four-week rule applies. Any pregnancy bleeding needs prompt advice. Heavy bleeding alone, or bleeding with severe pain, shoulder-tip pain, dizziness or faintness, needs immediate emergency care. What symptoms can ectropion cause? Often none. It may cause mucus discharge, spotting or contact bleeding after sex or examination. Pain or unusual bleeding still needs assessment for other causes. What causes it? It is associated with estrogen, pregnancy and combined-pill use, and may be present from birth. It is not proof of infection or damage. How is it diagnosed? A clinician looks at the cervix with a speculum and considers your symptoms and history. Infection or pregnancy tests, colposcopy or biopsy are chosen according to findings; not everyone needs them. Does every ectropion need treatment? No. If it is benign and not troublesome, observation is reasonable and symptoms may settle. Persistent bothersome symptoms can be treated after other causes are assessed. Does a normal smear mean bleeding can be ignored? No. Screening is not a diagnostic test for symptoms. Persistent or unexplained bleeding needs clinical assessment even after a normal screening result. Will treatment affect fertility? Ectropion does not cause infertility and usual superficial treatment is not expected to impair fertility. Discuss the exact procedure and rare risks such as narrowing with your clinician; treatment for precancer is a different situation. When should I seek urgent help? Seek same-day advice for fever, foul discharge or bleeding beyond the advised course after treatment if there are no emergency signs. Severe or worsening abdominal or pelvic pain, heavy bleeding, fainting, loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain or difficulty breathing requires immediate emergency care. In pregnancy, get prompt advice for any bleeding; heavy bleeding alone, or bleeding with severe pain, shoulder-tip pain, dizziness or faintness, needs immediate emergency help. Do not drive yourself.

title: The contraceptive implant: how it works and what to consider
description: A guide to implant effectiveness, current duration, bleeding changes, suitability, medicines and safe fitting or removal.
body: A contraceptive implant can suit someone who wants reliable pregnancy prevention without remembering a daily pill. Choosing it still involves personal preferences, a medical review and a plan for changes in bleeding. Understanding the particular product and your local instructions matters more than assuming that every implant has the same replacement date. What the implant is and how it works An implant is a small flexible rod placed just under the skin of the upper arm by a trained clinician. The commonly used etonogestrel implant is about 4 cm long. It releases a progestin, a manufactured hormone with progesterone-like effects, rather than estrogen. It mainly prevents ovulation and thickens cervical mucus, making it harder for sperm to reach an egg. It also changes the uterine lining. Describing it only as preventing implantation misses its main action; it is contraception, not a treatment to end an established pregnancy. How long it lasts: check the product and country Older information often gives three years. In January 2026, the United States FDA approved Nexplanon for up to five years, with removal by the end of year five. Current NHS information also describes five-year use. Do not apply that duration automatically to every brand or country. Ask the service to confirm your product, insertion date and current locally recommended replacement date. If your card says three years, ask whether updated guidance applies to you rather than extending use on your own. Effectiveness and protection from infections The implant is over 99% effective: fewer than one in 100 users become pregnant during a year of use. It does not depend on taking a pill correctly each day, but correct placement, replacement timing and interacting medicines still matter. No method makes pregnancy impossible. It does not protect against sexually transmitted infections, including HIV. Correct and consistent condom use reduces infection risk; vaccination, testing and HIV prevention care may also be relevant. A condom is not an absolute guarantee against every infection. Benefits, breastfeeding and return of fertility Long-lasting protection, no daily task and no interruption during sex are practical advantages. An estrogen-free method may suit some people who cannot use estrogen, although that does not make it appropriate for everyone. The implant can be used while breastfeeding under clinical guidance. The recommended timing after birth and need for extra protection depend on local guidance and circumstances; national practice guidance and product labeling can differ. Tell the service when you gave birth and how you feed your baby. Some users have lighter bleeding or less period pain, but others do not. Reduced blood loss may help someone who bleeds less; the implant is not a guaranteed treatment for anemia. Fertility can return quickly after removal, without guaranteeing an immediate pregnancy. Bleeding changes are common and can persist Periods may become lighter, absent, irregular, more frequent or prolonged. Spotting is common and heavy bleeding is uncommon. Older etonogestrel trial data describe no bleeding in about one in five users; individual patterns vary. Changes may improve, persist or change again; improvement after a few months is not guaranteed. Absent periods on the implant usually do not require treatment, but a sudden change or pregnancy symptoms may warrant a test and advice. Discuss troublesome bleeding with the service. They may check for pregnancy, infection, medicine interactions or another cause, and offer treatment or removal according to your preferences. You do not have to tolerate unacceptable bleeding until the replacement date. Who needs a careful suitability review Tell the clinician about possible pregnancy, unexplained vaginal bleeding, breast cancer or another hormone-sensitive cancer, active liver disease or liver tumors, blood clots, stroke or heart disease, and allergy to implant components. These can affect whether the product is suitable; the current US Nexplanon label lists several as contraindications. Also mention depression, diabetes, high blood pressure, abnormal cholesterol or triglycerides, gallbladder disease, seizures and allergies to local anesthetic or antiseptic. These are not all automatic exclusions, but may change monitoring, product choice or the medicine-interaction review. A BMI of 30 or above does not by itself mean an implant will fail or that you cannot use one. CDC guidance permits implant use with obesity. Discuss your individual health and the actual product rather than treating body size as an effectiveness cutoff. Other symptoms and procedure-related risks Headache, breast tenderness, acne, weight change, dizziness, nausea, abdominal or back pain and mood changes have been reported. Reports do not prove that the implant caused every symptom. Changes in sexual desire or vaginal dryness deserve discussion rather than an automatic attribution to the implant. Glucose and lipid changes may matter particularly for people with diabetes or related risks; monitoring can be appropriate. Enlarged ovarian follicles or cysts can occur and often resolve themselves, but new or severe pelvic pain needs assessment. Do not assume a painful abdomen is only a harmless cyst. Fitting and removal can cause bruising, pain, scarring or infection. Deep placement, nerve or blood-vessel injury and migration are uncommon but important risks. A trained professional should fit, locate and remove the implant; never cut it out or attempt a home procedure. Starting or switching without a protection gap The clinician first assesses whether pregnancy can reasonably be excluded. An implant can often be fitted at another point in the cycle; it is not restricted to the first five days. Under CDC guidance, insertion within those first five days needs no extra protection; later insertion usually needs condoms or avoiding pregnancy-risk intercourse for seven days. Do not stop hormonal contraception for a week before fitting as a general rule. Switching may require continuing the previous method briefly or coordinating removal of an IUD. Ask for exact instructions based on your current method, recent sex, birth or pregnancy loss. If there has been a gap, possible pregnancy or sex without adequate protection, tell the service promptly. Emergency contraception and follow-up testing may be needed; the choice and timing require advice because hormonal methods can interact with some emergency pills. Fitting and looking after the arm Fitting normally uses local anesthetic and takes only a short appointment. You and the clinician should be able to feel the rod afterward. Get the product details, date, replacement plan and advice on checking it without repeatedly pressing the area. Follow the service’s wound instructions. For Nexplanon, the US patient information describes keeping the pressure bandage for 24 hours and the smaller dressing clean and dry for three to five days. Your clinician may give instructions suited to the actual procedure. If the implant cannot be felt, seems to have moved, becomes exposed, or the arm develops increasing pain, redness, swelling, discharge, numbness or weakness, contact the service promptly. Use additional pregnancy protection until its presence and effectiveness are confirmed if it cannot be located. Do not probe for it yourself. Medicines can change the protection Give the prescriber a complete list of medicines and herbal products. Some enzyme-inducing medicines, including certain seizure medicines, rifampicin-type antibiotics and some HIV treatments, and St John’s wort can reduce protection. Not every medicine in those groups interacts in the same way. A pharmacist or clinician can advise on another contraceptive method or additional non-hormonal protection, including how long it is needed after an interacting medicine stops. Do not stop necessary treatment yourself or assume that adding another hormonal pill solves the interaction. Removal, warning signs and your next plan You can request removal at any time, including for side effects or a wish to conceive. A trained clinician removes it; a deeply placed or non-palpable implant may need imaging and specialist care. Arrange replacement or another method immediately if you want continued pregnancy prevention. Seek urgent same-day assessment if pregnancy is possible and you have lower abdominal pain or unusual vaginal bleeding, even without a positive test. Ectopic pregnancy must be considered. Severe or worsening pelvic or abdominal pain, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, heavy vaginal bleeding or breathing difficulty, needs immediate emergency help. Do not drive yourself. Get emergency help for sudden breathlessness, chest pain, coughing blood, stroke-like symptoms or a severe allergic reaction. These symptoms are not expected adjustment effects. Most users will not have a serious complication, but a new concerning symptom should not be dismissed just because an implant is present. Check the exact product and local replacement date; five-year Nexplanon guidance is current in the US and NHS. Bleeding can change in several directions and may stay troublesome; ask about options. Do not stop your existing contraception before switching without a coordinated plan. Review interacting medicines, and do not use BMI alone as a failure cutoff. Only a trained professional should fit, locate or remove an implant. What is a contraceptive implant? It is a small hormone-releasing rod placed beneath the upper-arm skin by a trained clinician. It mainly suppresses ovulation and thickens cervical mucus. Does every implant need replacing after three years? No. Current US Nexplanon labeling and NHS information describe five years. Other products or local instructions may differ; confirm your own replacement date with the service. What are its main advantages? It is highly effective, long acting and does not require a daily pill or interruption during sex. It is estrogen free, can be used while breastfeeding with suitable advice, and is removable when you want. Who should discuss another option? People with possible pregnancy, unexplained bleeding, relevant cancers, liver or vascular conditions, or component allergies need a clinical suitability review. Do not decide from a checklist alone. Will my periods stop? They might, but they may instead become lighter, irregular or prolonged. Your pattern cannot be predicted reliably. Ask for help if changes are unacceptable. Can I use it if my BMI is over 30? Obesity alone is not a reason to assume implant failure or exclude use. Review the actual product, health conditions and medicines with your clinician. Should I stop the pill before the appointment? Do not create a gap yourself. The switching plan may involve continuing your current method briefly and using extra protection. Get instructions for your particular situation. Can I get pregnant immediately after removal? Fertility can return quickly, even before a first period. Pregnancy is not guaranteed. Arrange contraception immediately after removal if pregnancy is not wanted.

title: Depression around menopause: symptoms and treatment choices
description: Recognise depression during and after the menopause transition, understand the limits of HRT, and discuss talking therapy, antidepressants and support tailored to you.
body: Mood can change around menopause, but persistent depression deserves its own assessment and treatment. Hormonal changes, sleep problems, previous depression and life pressures can interact. You do not have to wait for your periods to stop, or assume that hormones alone explain how you feel, before asking for help. Menopause, perimenopause and mood are not the same thing Perimenopause is the transition leading to menopause. Periods may become more or less frequent, heavier or lighter. Natural menopause is usually recognised after 12 months without a period, when another cause does not explain it; hormonal contraception can obscure this pattern. The transition often begins in the forties but timing varies. Some people experience mood swings, anxiety or low mood, while others develop a depressive disorder. Depression is not inevitable, a character weakness or simply an expected part of ageing. It can start before, during or after menopause, and needs attention even when hot flushes are absent. Hormones, sleep and life pressures can interact Changing reproductive hormones can affect brain systems involved in mood, including serotonin signalling, but depression is not explained by a single falling hormone or a simple shortage of a happiness chemical. Biological, psychological and social factors contribute. Hormone-sensitive periods, including menstrual changes, pregnancy and the postpartum period, can be vulnerable times for some people, not everyone. Night sweats and insomnia can worsen tiredness, irritability and mood; depression can also disturb sleep. There is no universal tenfold risk from poor sleep. Caring for ageing parents, work demands, health concerns, relationship changes or children leaving home may add pressure. A previous depressive episode is a reason to plan support and watch for returning symptoms, not a certainty of relapse. Recognise symptoms and seek an assessment Possible symptoms include persistent sadness, hopelessness or irritability, losing interest or pleasure, low energy and motivation, changes in appetite in either direction, sleeping too little or too much, and trouble concentrating, remembering or making decisions. Thoughts about death, suicide or self-harm always deserve prompt attention. Not everyone has every symptom. Arrange a clinical appointment if mood affects work, study, relationships or everyday activities, or symptoms persist most days for about two weeks. Seek help sooner if severe or worsening. Discuss periods, sleep, hot flushes, previous mental health problems, medicines, alcohol and life stresses. Assessment considers duration, impact, safety and other possible causes; a symptom checklist or hormone result alone cannot diagnose depression. Talking therapy and antidepressants: a personal plan Psychological treatment such as cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) can help with depression. Menopause-specific CBT can also help some menopause-related low mood, hot-flush distress or sleep problems. These uses overlap but are not identical. For less severe depression, supported self-help or psychological approaches may be appropriate; antidepressants are not automatically the first option unless they are your informed preference. For more severe or recurrent depression, antidepressants, individual therapy or a combination may be considered. CBT plus medication can be useful, but it is not invariably the best choice for everyone. Antidepressants are not reserved only for people who decline HRT. Agree on expected benefits, side effects, interactions, early follow-up and a relapse plan. Do not start, change or abruptly stop medication without the prescriber’s advice. Where hormone replacement therapy fits HRT treats menopause symptoms and may be considered for depressive symptoms that began alongside other menopause symptoms but do not meet criteria for depression. If depression is suspected or diagnosed, use depression care alongside appropriate menopause management. HRT is not a default substitute for depression treatment or a guaranteed antidepressant. Systemic oestrogen may be given as a patch, gel, spray or tablet. People who have a uterus usually also need progestogen to protect its lining; the regimen depends on menstrual stage and history. HRT can be used after menopause when appropriate: being postmenopausal is not itself a prohibition. Discuss personal benefits, risks and review arrangements rather than copying another person’s prescription. HRT and the combined contraceptive pill have different risks Smoking, blood pressure, clotting history, cancer history and liver disease need a careful review. Smoking is a reason for risk assessment and stopping support, not an automatic rule that every HRT form is forbidden. Uncontrolled high blood pressure should be treated before HRT; controlled blood pressure does not automatically exclude it. Previous clots require individualized, often specialist advice; tablets and skin-delivered HRT have different clot risks. A patch does not remove every risk or make self-prescribing safe. A combined contraceptive pill may suit selected people during perimenopause who also need contraception, but it is different from HRT and is not a general depression treatment. Smoking at age 35 or older, hypertension and a history of clots can make combined hormonal contraception unsuitable. HRT itself does not prevent pregnancy. Discuss a safe contraceptive and symptom-management plan rather than switching or combining hormones yourself. Daily support and recovery after menopause Regular meals, enjoyable activity, a manageable sleep routine and practical or social support can help wellbeing alongside treatment. Reducing caffeine if it worsens sleep or flushes, limiting alcohol and getting help to stop smoking may be useful. These steps are not a test of willpower or a replacement for care when depression is significant. Discuss supplements or herbal products before using them because interactions and uncertain safety matter. Some symptoms improve as the transition settles, but depression may persist or recur after menopause. Recovery cannot be predicted simply from the final period or hormone stability. Keep follow-up appointments, review response and side effects, and agree what to do if symptoms return. You can ask for changes to a plan that is not helping; effective treatment sometimes takes adjustment. When help is urgent Seek urgent professional help for suicidal or self-harm thoughts, even without a plan. If you may act on them, cannot stay safe, or have already seriously harmed yourself or taken an overdose, contact local emergency services or go to an emergency department immediately. Tell a trusted person and ask them to stay with you while help is arranged. Do not wait for a routine menopause appointment. New or worsening agitation, marked mood changes or suicidal thoughts after starting or changing treatment need prompt contact with the treating team; immediate danger requires emergency help. A clinician can arrange more support and review treatment. Asking about safety is a normal part of care, and depression remains treatable even when symptoms are severe. Depression around menopause is treatable and is not inevitable or your fault. Persistent symptoms, functional difficulties or returning depression need assessment; safety concerns need help sooner. CBT, antidepressants and menopause treatment have different roles and should be chosen with you. HRT is not a universal depression treatment, and its risks differ from those of the combined contraceptive pill. What is the main cause of depression around menopause? There is no single cause. Hormonal changes can interact with sleep, previous depression, health and life pressures; a simple serotonin-deficiency explanation is inadequate. Which symptoms should I mention? Persistent low mood or irritability, loss of enjoyment, changes in appetite or sleep, low energy, concentration or decision difficulties, and thoughts of death or self-harm. Explain how these affect daily life. What is the best treatment? It depends on severity, history, risks and preferences. Talking therapy, antidepressants or both may help; appropriate menopause symptom treatment can be considered alongside depression care. When should I see a clinician? When symptoms affect daily activities or persist most days for about two weeks, and sooner if severe or worsening. Suicidal thoughts need urgent help; immediate danger or inability to stay safe needs emergency care. Can I use HRT after menopause? Sometimes, after an individual benefits-and-risks review. Postmenopause alone is not a ban, but HRT is not automatically the treatment for diagnosed depression. Does high blood pressure rule out every hormone treatment? No. Uncontrolled pressure needs treatment before HRT, while controlled pressure may allow an individualized plan. The combined contraceptive pill has different restrictions; never choose by this distinction alone. Will depression end when periods stop? Not necessarily. Some symptoms improve, but depression can persist or recur and may need ongoing treatment and relapse prevention. Should I stop an antidepressant if I start HRT? Do not stop or change it yourself. Review both treatments with the prescriber, including benefits, side effects, interactions and any gradual stopping plan.

title: Vaginal microbes: symptoms, infections and probiotic limits
description: Understand the vaginal microbiome, BV, yeast, trichomoniasis and urinary infections. Learn why symptoms need assessment, what probiotics cannot promise and when care is urgent.
body: The vagina naturally contains a community of microorganisms, often called its microbiome or flora. A change in discharge, odour, itching or urinary comfort can have several explanations. “An imbalance” is not a complete diagnosis, and buying a probiotic does not establish the cause or replace appropriate treatment. What is a healthy vaginal microbiome? Many people of reproductive age have vaginal communities rich in Lactobacillus species, which produce lactic acid and help maintain an acidic environment. Communities differ between individuals and across life stages; there is no fixed count of 50 species or single bacterial recipe that proves health for everyone. Having fewer lactobacilli in a report is not, by itself, a reason to treat an otherwise well person. Hormones, menstrual bleeding, pregnancy, menopause, medicines and sexual exposures can influence the local environment. Douching can disturb it. New or multiple partners and not using condoms are associated with BV, but symptoms do not prove poor hygiene or infidelity. Do not stop prescribed contraception because you assume every hormone method causes BV; risks differ by condition and method. Symptoms overlap: testing matters Fishy or different odour, altered discharge, itching, burning, soreness and pain with sex or urination may occur with different conditions. BV, candidiasis and trichomoniasis need different treatment; irritants, skin conditions and low-estrogen changes can also cause discomfort. Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted infection, not simply a consequence of lacking “good bacteria.” Assessment may involve your symptoms, medicines, pregnancy possibility, sexual history, a consensual examination and a vaginal swab, microscopy or a molecular test. Urinary symptoms may need a separate urine assessment. Neither discharge colour, a home pH reading nor a commercial microbiome score diagnoses every cause. Tell the clinician about products already used, and ask about appropriate STI testing. Bacterial vaginosis, or BV BV involves a change toward a mixed community of BV-associated bacteria. It may cause thin white or grey discharge and a fishy odour, while many people have no symptoms. Vaginal pH is often above 4.5, but pH alone is not diagnostic; clinicians use combined findings or validated tests. Burning or itching should not automatically be attributed to BV. Symptomatic BV is usually treated with a prescribed antibiotic, such as metronidazole or clindamycin, by a suitable oral or vaginal regimen. Pregnancy symptoms should be assessed and treated with an appropriate option. Recurrence is common and deserves reassessment rather than endless self-treatment. Ask about other STIs and whether a planned treatment affects condoms; some clindamycin creams weaken latex or rubber barriers. BV partner advice has changed Older CDC 2021 guidance does not recommend routine partner treatment based on earlier trials. New evidence led ACOG in October 2025 to advise considering concurrent oral and topical treatment of male partners for adults with recurrent symptomatic BV; shared decisions are advised in some other situations, including same-sex partners and a first symptomatic episode. February 2026 New York State guidance supports offering treatment to ongoing partners of people with symptomatic BV. These are updated approaches with differences in scope, not a universal instruction to treat every past partner. If BV keeps returning, ask your clinician or sexual-health service about current local partner guidance. The partner needs their own assessment and prescription; do not share medicines or apply vaginal products to a partner without instructions. Discuss avoiding sex until both courses finish, or the appropriate protection if sex occurs, including possible condom weakening by creams. Sharing BV-associated bacteria does not establish exposure to an outside partner. Yeast infection, or candidiasis Candida albicans causes many yeast infections, but other species occur. Symptoms can include marked itching, irritation, vulval redness or swelling, soreness, a rash, thick white or sometimes watery discharge, and burning with sex or urine touching inflamed skin. None is specific to yeast. Candida can be present without symptoms and does not always need treatment. Its overgrowth is not explained by a simple rule that lactobacilli are missing. Antibiotics, pregnancy, poorly controlled diabetes, immune suppression and some higher-estrogen exposures can contribute; many uncomplicated cases have no obvious trigger. Treatment may use a suitable local azole cream or vaginal preparation, or oral medicine in selected nonpregnant people. Severe, recurrent or persistent symptoms need testing and a tailored plan, sometimes for another yeast species. During pregnancy CDC recommends a topical azole for 7 days; oral fluconazole should not be used. Ask before self-treating, and return if symptoms persist after an over-the-counter course or recur within two months. Trichomoniasis is an STI Trichomonas vaginalis is a parasite transmitted through sexual contact. It may cause itching, burning, redness, soreness, urinary discomfort and changed clear, white, yellow or green discharge with an unusual smell, but it can be symptomless. Testing is needed; neither probiotics nor a yeast treatment cures it. A prescribed oral nitroimidazole is used, commonly metronidazole; vaginal metronidazole gel does not adequately treat trichomoniasis. Current partners should be evaluated and treated even without symptoms. Avoid sex until you and partners have completed treatment and symptoms have resolved; discuss other STI tests. CDC recommends retesting sexually active women around three months after treatment because reinfection is common. Symptomatic pregnant patients should be tested and treated at any stage; tinidazole should be avoided during pregnancy. Pregnancy, breastfeeding, allergies and other medicines affect the prescription. Urinary infection is a separate possibility A UTI usually starts when bacteria enter the urinary tract through the urethra, often from the bowel. The urethra lies near the vagina, but a UTI is not automatically a vaginal infection or proof of a microbiome imbalance. Burning, urgency, frequent small amounts and lower abdominal discomfort may occur. Cloudy or strong-smelling urine alone does not prove infection; colour changes can have several causes. A shorter urethra increases susceptibility. Sex, spermicide use, some diaphragm use, menopause, pregnancy, urinary blockage or poor emptying, immune suppression or diabetes, a catheter and recent urinary procedures can matter. Tell the clinician your relevant history rather than blaming cleanliness or partner number. A urine test or culture may help in selected circumstances; treatment depends on pregnancy, health, likely bacteria and local resistance. Some lower UTIs can be managed differently, while kidney or severe infection may need hospital and intravenous antibiotics. What probiotics can and cannot do Probiotics are live microorganisms intended to provide a health benefit when given in appropriate amounts. They may be bacteria or yeasts, found in certain foods or supplements. A benefit for one digestive problem or one studied strain does not prove benefit for the vagina. A product labelled Lactobacillus acidophilus is not a demonstrated cure for every infection. CDC guidance does not support available probiotic products as an established adjunct or replacement treatment for BV, and finds no substantial evidence for treating candidiasis with probiotics. Research into specific preparations continues, but it does not validate every shop product or guarantee restoration after antibiotics. Probiotics do not treat trichomoniasis or an acute UTI. Discuss supplements first, especially with serious illness or immune suppression; do not delay prescribed care. Gentle care and follow-up Wash the external vulval skin gently with water or a recommended bland emollient; do not scrub or wash inside the vagina. Avoid douches, perfumed washes, sprays and unprescribed products. Do not insert food or yogurt, essential oils or homemade mixtures. Comfortable clothing and avoiding irritants may help comfort but do not replace treatment of a diagnosed infection. Complete prescribed courses and follow method-specific instructions. Contact the service if symptoms do not settle or return, rather than repeatedly using leftover antibiotics, antifungals or a “flora reset.” Tell the clinician if pregnant or breastfeeding. Keep a record of symptoms, treatments, test results and recurrences so assessment can distinguish persistent infection, reinfection and noninfectious causes. When to seek prompt or emergency care Seek urgent same-day assessment for fever or chills, back or side pain under the ribs, worsening pelvic or lower abdominal pain, vomiting, suspected UTI in pregnancy or with diabetes or immune suppression, or visible or suspected urine blood even once, in a small amount or if uncertain. These may signal kidney infection or another condition. Pregnant patients should discuss new unusual discharge, itching, soreness or painful urination with maternity care promptly; any vaginal bleeding needs immediate maternity advice. Severe abdominal or pelvic pain, fainting or loss of consciousness, confusion, unusual drowsiness, breathing difficulty or severe illness require emergency care now, especially if pregnancy is possible. Do not wait for a probiotic or a scheduled swab to work. New symptoms after sexual exposure, a first suspected infection or recurrent symptoms also deserve clinical assessment rather than a diagnosis from odour alone. The vaginal microbiome varies; one bacterial count or pH result does not define health or diagnose infection. BV, yeast, trichomoniasis and UTIs overlap in symptoms but need different assessment and treatment. Newer BV partner-treatment guidance differs from older CDC advice; ask about your situation and local recommendations. Probiotics do not replace proven treatment or guarantee a restored vaginal microbiome. Pregnancy, fever, flank pain, urine blood or severe illness change how urgently to seek help. What is a probiotic? A live microorganism given in an appropriate amount for a health benefit. Benefits are strain- and condition-specific; a gut benefit does not prove that a supplement treats vaginal symptoms. Is BV the same as any vaginal imbalance? No. BV is a particular change in vaginal bacterial communities, often with thin discharge or fishy odour, but it can be symptomless. Yeast, an STI and irritation can resemble it; assessment establishes the likely cause. What can a yeast infection feel like? Itching, soreness, irritation, redness, a rash, altered white or watery discharge and burning with sex or urination may occur. These are not specific to yeast. Pregnancy, recurrence or failed treatment needs clinical advice. What symptoms can a UTI cause? Burning, urgency, frequent small amounts and lower abdominal pain can occur. Cloudiness or smell alone is not proof. Fever, flank pain, pregnancy or suspected urine blood requires urgent same-day advice; confusion or severe illness needs emergency care. Should my partner be treated for recurrent BV? Possibly. ACOG 2025 and New York State 2026 guidance support discussing concurrent treatment of ongoing partners in defined situations, while older CDC guidance differs. Ask the clinician; do not share medicines. Recurrent BV does not prove infidelity. Can probiotics replace an antibiotic or antifungal? No. Available products are not established substitutes or guaranteed additions for BV or yeast, and do not treat trichomoniasis or an acute UTI. Research on a specific strain cannot be applied to every product. What changes during pregnancy? Ask about new symptoms rather than self-treating. Symptomatic BV or trichomoniasis needs appropriate assessment and treatment. Yeast treatment uses a topical azole for 7 days under current CDC advice, not oral fluconazole; tinidazole should be avoided in pregnancy. Does trichomoniasis need partner care and retesting? Yes. Current partners need assessment and treatment even without symptoms; avoid sex until treatment is complete for everyone and symptoms have resolved. Sexually active women should be retested around three months; discuss other STI tests.

title: Vaginal odor: causes, testing and when to get help
description: Understand changing vaginal odor, fishy discharge, urinary symptoms, treatment and gentle external care, with warning signs that need prompt help.
body: A vagina does not need to be odorless. A new strong or fishy smell can have several causes, and smell alone cannot identify an infection. You deserve comfortable, confidential care without shame or blame about cleanliness or sex. Normal variation and changes worth checking Discharge is often clear or white, and its amount and texture vary with the menstrual cycle, pregnancy and contraception. Menstrual blood and sweat around the external genital skin (the vulva and groin) can change the smell. Sweat comes from this surrounding skin, rather than from the vagina itself. Arrange a clinical or sexual-health appointment for a new persistent or strong unpleasant odor, a change in discharge, itching, redness, burning, pain with urination or sex, or bleeding between periods or after sex. Gray-white, yellow-green or curd-like discharge can guide testing but cannot establish the cause. A fishy smell after exercise is not proof of infection, and a new odor should not simply be attributed to genetics. Bacterial vaginosis and odor after sex Bacterial vaginosis (BV) is a change in the balance of vaginal bacteria. Thin gray-white discharge and a fishy odor, often more noticeable after sex, are common; many people have no symptoms. BV does not usually cause marked itching or soreness, so these symptoms may indicate another or an additional problem. BV can occur without sexual activity. A new partner, exchange of bacteria during sex and douching can influence risk; hormonal stages can also change the vaginal environment. BV is not evidence of poor hygiene or infidelity. Post-sex odor does not prove that sex has worsened an infection: seek assessment, and avoid sex if painful or while awaiting advice about a possible STI. Vaginitis, thrush and trichomoniasis Vaginitis means vaginal inflammation and can have infectious or noninfectious causes, including irritation. Thrush is a yeast infection that more often causes itching, redness, soreness and thick white discharge than a fishy smell. Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted parasitic infection that can cause unpleasant-smelling yellow-green discharge, irritation or urinary discomfort; it can also cause no symptoms. These conditions require different treatments. A person can have more than one problem, and irritation or hormonal changes may resemble infection. Do not assume that every odor is BV, that all vaginitis is bacterial, or that an antifungal will treat an STI. Urine odor is a separate clue An odor noticed in the toilet or underwear may come from urine. A urinary tract infection affects the urethra, bladder or kidneys, rather than directly causing vaginal discharge. Burning, needing to urinate more often or urgently, and cloudy urine support the need for urinary assessment. Strong-smelling urine alone can also reflect concentrated urine, foods, medicines or supplements. Drink enough to avoid dehydration, following any medical fluid restriction. Some people find coffee or alcohol irritate bladder symptoms, but avoiding them or drinking extra water does not cure an infection. A clinician decides whether urine testing and antibiotics are needed; take prescribed treatment as directed. Seek same-day advice for visible or suspected urine blood, even once, a small amount or uncertain blood, or for fever, flank/back pain under the ribs, pregnancy with urinary symptoms, or rapid deterioration. Suspected UTI in someone with diabetes or a weakened immune system also needs urgent same-day advice. Periods and a retained tampon Menstrual blood may alter odor. However, a forgotten tampon can cause a strong unpleasant smell or discharge and needs removal. A tampon cannot travel through the cervix into the abdomen. If it will not come out easily, you are unsure one remains, or it has been retained beyond the recommended time, contact a clinician or sexual-health service promptly; do not force removal or use tools. Rarely, tampon use is associated with toxic shock syndrome. If you suspect toxic shock, fever, a rapidly developing rough rash, vomiting or diarrhea, dizziness or feeling very unwell warrants immediate medical assessment; you do not need to have all these symptoms. Confusion, fainting or loss of consciousness, or difficulty breathing needs emergency care. Remove a tampon or cup if you can do so easily, but do not delay help to remove it. How the cause is diagnosed A clinician asks about the odor, discharge, itching, pain, menstrual timing, pregnancy possibility, products and medicines, and sexual history without judgment. With your consent, an examination may check for inflammation or a retained tampon and collect a vaginal swab. You can request a chaperone and ask to pause or stop the examination. Depending on symptoms, tests may include microscopy or molecular tests for BV, yeast or trichomoniasis, other STI tests and a urine sample. Vaginal pH is one part of assessment, not a diagnosis by itself. Neither a positive test for a single commonly present bacterium nor a home odor/pH check automatically means antibiotics are required. Treatment and partner care depend on the diagnosis Symptomatic BV is usually treated with a prescribed antibiotic such as oral or vaginal metronidazole or vaginal clindamycin. Recurrence is common and needs reassessment, rather than repeated self-treatment. Partner advice is changing: ACOG's 2025 update supports considering concurrent treatment of an ongoing male partner for recurrent symptomatic BV, and NYSDOH's 2026 guidance supports offering ongoing-partner treatment for symptomatic BV. Discuss your situation and local guidance with the clinic; assessment and shared decisions for partners with vaginas differ. Do not share antibiotics or assume every partner needs the same regimen. Thrush treatments can include topical azoles such as miconazole or tioconazole, but first-time, severe, persistent or soon-recurring symptoms need assessment. During pregnancy, ask the clinician: CDC recommends a seven-day topical azole course rather than oral fluconazole. Trichomoniasis needs an appropriate oral antiprotozoal medicine, not a thrush cream or metronidazole vaginal gel. Current partners need treatment; avoid sex until everyone has completed treatment and symptoms have resolved, and follow retesting advice. A retained tampon needs removal, not odor masking.
