Gentle care, exercise and protection Wash only the outside gently with warm water; a little mild unperfumed soap may be tolerated, but stop products that irritate. Do not wash inside the vagina or douche. Avoid scented deodorants, wipes, harsh soaps and other irritating chemicals. Pat the external skin dry, change damp exercise clothes and choose comfortable, breathable underwear. These measures support comfort; they do not treat BV, thrush or an STI. There is no general reason to ban non-latex condoms to prevent odor. Appropriate latex or synthetic non-latex condoms can reduce STI exposure; choose a suitable product if latex irritates. Some vaginal antifungal or clindamycin products weaken latex/rubber barriers, so check the medicine and condom instructions and ask the pharmacist about protection during and after treatment. Follow diagnosis-specific advice about sex rather than relying on washing after sex. Food, probiotics and follow-up Foods such as asparagus, broccoli, garlic, onion and some fish are sometimes blamed for odor. Foods such as asparagus and garlic can affect urine odor, but eliminating this list is not an established treatment for fishy vaginal discharge. Maintain a balanced diet rather than restricting nutritious foods to correct an assumed infection. Commercial probiotics are not an established replacement for BV or thrush treatment; evidence is insufficient to recommend them as a reliable cure or routine adjunct. Ask about supplements and possible interactions if you want to try one. Return if symptoms persist, recur or change, and tell the clinician if you are pregnant. Do not wait several days if pain, fever or other warning signs appear. When odor needs urgent care Seek urgent same-day assessment for pelvic/lower abdominal pain with unusual discharge, fever or suspected infection, including pain in pregnancy or possible pregnancy. For any vaginal bleeding during pregnancy, contact your maternity team immediately, even without pain. Severe or worsening pelvic pain, pain that hurts with movement or touch, sudden intense pain, heavy bleeding, shoulder-tip pain with possible pregnancy, fainting or loss of consciousness each needs immediate emergency care. These symptoms can indicate conditions beyond a simple vaginal infection. After a recent birth, miscarriage or procedure, tell the maternity or clinical team promptly about new foul-smelling discharge, fever or pelvic pain. Breathing difficulty, confusion or rapidly becoming very unwell needs emergency care. An app, odor description or home test cannot rule out a serious infection or another urgent cause. Odor varies naturally; a new persistent fishy or unpleasant smell needs assessment rather than shame or self-diagnosis. BV, yeast, trichomoniasis, urine odor and a retained tampon have different causes and treatments. Use gentle external care; avoid douching, odor-masking products and unproven dietary or probiotic cures. Partner care follows the diagnosis and current local advice. Pain, fever, pregnancy-related symptoms or feeling very unwell can make assessment urgent. What does a strong fishy vaginal smell mean? BV is one possibility, but trichomoniasis, a retained tampon or odor from nearby urine or skin can be confused with it. Smell alone cannot identify the cause; changes in discharge, pain and itching help the clinician choose tests. Is a fishy smell after sex normal? BV odor can be more noticeable after sex, but a new or persistent strong smell deserves assessment. It does not prove poor hygiene, infidelity or worsening infection. Avoid painful sex and follow the clinic's STI and treatment advice. Does fishy-smelling urine mean a vaginal infection? No. Urine odor may come from food, concentrated urine or a urinary infection. Burning, urgency, frequency or cloudy urine needs urinary assessment. Suspected blood in urine (even once or uncertain) requires same-day advice. Can a pH test diagnose the cause? No. A clinician considers symptoms and history, sometimes an examination, swabs and urine or STI tests. Vaginal pH is only one clue and does not identify every infection or justify antibiotics by itself. Should my partner be treated for BV? Ask the clinic, especially for recurrent symptomatic BV. Newer guidance supports treatment of some ongoing partners to reduce recurrence, with recommendations differing by setting and partner anatomy. This is different from trichomoniasis, for which current partners need treatment; do not share medicines. Will washing, avoiding certain foods or probiotics cure the smell? These do not reliably treat an infection. Gently wash the external vulva, never inside the vagina; avoid douches and scented products. Diet changes may alter urine odor, but food restrictions and commercial probiotics do not replace diagnosis-specific treatment. What if I may have forgotten a tampon? Seek prompt help if it cannot be removed easily or you are unsure it remains; do not use tools. Fever, rash, vomiting, diarrhea or feeling rapidly unwell needs immediate assessment. Confusion, fainting or loss of consciousness or breathing difficulty needs emergency care. When should I seek urgent help rather than book routinely? Get same-day advice for pelvic pain with unusual discharge or fever, urinary red flags, or pain in possible pregnancy. Contact your maternity team immediately for any vaginal bleeding during pregnancy, even without pain. Severe or worsening pelvic pain, pain with movement or touch, heavy bleeding, shoulder-tip pain with possible pregnancy, fainting or loss of consciousness, confusion or breathing trouble needs immediate emergency care. Do not wait for an app result or for odor to settle.

title: Vulvovaginitis: causes and care in children and adults
description: Understand vulval and vaginal irritation, infections, childhood symptoms, appropriate tests and treatment, gentle care and warning signs that need prompt help.
body: Vulvovaginitis describes inflammation or irritation involving the vulva and vagina; it is not the name of one infection. The vulva is the external genital area, including the labia and clitoris, rather than only the vaginal opening. Causes and suitable care differ with age, symptoms and circumstances. Possible causes: infection is not the only explanation Bacteria, yeast and some sexually transmitted infections can cause symptoms, but so can friction, trapped moisture, soap or other irritants, allergy and skin disorders such as eczema or lichen sclerosus. Lower estrogen before puberty, after menopause or during breastfeeding can affect tissue sensitivity. Do not assume all inflammation is bacterial or apply one prevalence estimate to every age group. Consider recent medicines, antibiotics, period products, detergents, perfumed sprays, lubricants or spermicides, tight clothing and wet swimwear. A product may irritate one person without being universally harmful; an ingredient list alone does not diagnose an allergy or infection. Gentle care helps reduce irritation without blaming the person’s cleanliness. Bacterial and yeast conditions Bacterial vaginosis involves a change in a mixed vaginal bacterial community, including Gardnerella and other organisms, not simply one dangerous bacterium multiplying. Thin grey or white discharge and a fishy smell can occur, but symptoms overlap. Some other bacteria can cause a targeted infection, particularly in children; a positive culture must be interpreted with symptoms and examination. Candida can cause marked itching, soreness, redness and thick white or sometimes different discharge. Antibiotics can contribute, but symptoms are not proof of yeast and Candida may be present without causing illness. Thrush is unusual between infancy and puberty, so do not automatically give a child an antifungal. Persistent or recurrent adult symptoms may need testing rather than repeated over-the-counter courses. Sexually transmitted infections, viruses and parasites Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted parasitic infection and may cause irritation, urinary discomfort and changed discharge, or no symptoms. Chlamydia and gonorrhoea can cause cervicitis and discharge needing different treatment. Herpes may cause painful blisters or ulcers; HPV often has no symptoms or may cause warts, rather than being a usual explanation for general vaginitis. A new sore, growth or suspected STI deserves assessment. Pinworms can produce troublesome night-time vulval or anal itching in children. Scabies affects skin, while pubic lice live on body hair; they are not ordinary organisms living inside the vagina. Each needs appropriate assessment and treatment, sometimes involving household or sexual contacts. Ask about age, pregnancy and breastfeeding before using an antiparasitic; do not put skin-infestation products inside the vagina. Why childhood vulvovaginitis is different Before puberty, delicate lower-estrogen tissues can be easily irritated. Mild nonspecific vulvovaginitis often improves with simple measures and is not automatically an infection needing medicine. Symptoms may recur and often become less frequent as a child grows; puberty does not guarantee that every symptom disappears. Teach relaxed toileting and gentle front-to-back wiping, change damp clothing and avoid irritants without shaming the child. A clinician may recommend a suitable barrier product. Steroid cream is sometimes considered for particular severe irritation or a diagnosed skin condition, and antibiotics for a supported bacterial cause; neither is an automatic treatment for every child. Persistent night itch, constipation or recurrent symptoms also deserves attention. Recognising symptoms and concerning changes Symptoms may include itching, burning, soreness, redness or swelling of the labia and surrounding perineal skin, altered discharge or odour, painful urination and discomfort with sex. Dry, cracked or patchy skin may point toward a skin disorder or hormonal change. Not everyone has every symptom, and discharge colour alone cannot choose the right medicine. A child with blood-stained or offensive discharge, bleeding, significant pain or persistent symptoms needs medical review; a foreign body or other cause may need specialist assessment. Do not try to remove something from inside the child’s vagina yourself. If there is a disclosure, injury or concern about abuse, seek appropriate urgent paediatric and safeguarding support; symptoms alone do not establish abuse. Assessment and testing should fit the person The clinician may ask about timing, discharge, pain, medicines, products, urination, periods, puberty and relevant sexual exposures. An adult examination or swab is discussed with consent; you can ask to stop. Microscopy, culture or molecular tests may help distinguish infections, and urine testing may be needed for urinary symptoms. History or appearance alone can be misleading. Most mild childhood cases need no tests. Prepubertal children should not have routine internal vaginal examinations or internal swabs. If indicated, a trained clinician can assess externally and take a sample at the entrance for profuse or offensive discharge. Specialist advice is appropriate if the cause is unclear or a foreign body is suspected. A vulval skin biopsy is occasionally used for an uncertain or persistent skin abnormality, not a routine way to identify a vaginal organism. Treatment is directed at the cause Treatment may involve an appropriate antibiotic for a diagnosed bacterial condition or STI, an antifungal for confirmed or likely yeast, or an antiviral for herpes. Oral and local treatments are not interchangeable for every cause. Skin disorders may need prescribed steroid treatment, while low-estrogen symptoms may respond to a suitable moisturiser, lubricant or individualized local hormone treatment. An antihistamine may sometimes ease itch, but does not cure an infection. Ask a clinician or pharmacist before selecting treatment, especially for a child, pregnancy, severe symptoms, recurrence or a first episode. In pregnancy, CDC recommends a topical azole for seven days for candidiasis, not oral fluconazole. Trichomoniasis needs prescribed oral treatment; vaginal metronidazole gel is not sufficient. Complete the prescribed course and follow its specific directions, including medicine interactions and effects on condoms. Gentle care and the limits of home remedies Wash the external vulval skin gently with water or a recommended bland emollient and pat dry; do not scrub, over-wash or douche inside the vagina. Avoid perfumed washes, bubble baths, deodorants and products that make symptoms worse. Loose comfortable underwear, changing wet clothes and a clean cool damp cloth against the outside can ease irritation. Do not apply ice directly to skin. A short plain lukewarm bath may be soothing if comfortable, but avoid hot or prolonged soaking. Tea-tree oil, essential oils and salt mixtures are not established infection cures and may irritate; do not insert them or food. Use a barrier or other cream only as recommended for that area. Home care supports comfort and does not replace appropriate treatment or justify waiting a week with concerning symptoms. Sex, partner care and avoiding reinfection If an STI is possible, avoid sex until assessed. For trichomoniasis and certain other STIs, current partners may need treatment even without symptoms; follow infection-specific advice and avoid sex until everyone’s treatment is complete and symptoms have resolved. Sexually active women treated for trichomoniasis should usually be retested around three months. Herpes can be managed, but treatment does not eliminate the virus or all future transmission risk. Yeast is not usually acquired through sex, and partners do not automatically need treatment. BV is associated with sexual activity and sharing associated bacteria; newer 2025–2026 guidance supports discussion of concurrent treatment for ongoing partners in defined situations, differing from older routine-partner advice. Ask about current local recommendations rather than sharing medicines or assuming every cause needs the same partner treatment. Symptoms or recurrence do not prove infidelity. Recovery and review Many causes improve with appropriate care, but the time varies and recurrence is possible. If symptoms fail to improve as expected, change, recur soon after treatment or keep returning, contact the service rather than repeating leftover medicines. Do not wait a fixed week when symptoms are worsening. A new lump, ulcer or persistent skin change also warrants examination. Record symptom changes, products used, treatment and test results to help reassessment. Diabetes, immune suppression, pregnancy and medication effects may change the plan. Some persistent pain reflects a skin or pain condition rather than continuing infection, and a specialist may help. There is no guarantee that a shop antifungal or hygiene change will settle every episode. When to seek urgent or emergency help Seek urgent same-day assessment for fever or chills with symptoms, worsening pelvic or lower abdominal pain, pain in the back or side under the ribs, significant swelling, suspected urinary infection in a child or pregnancy, or visible or suspected blood in urine. Promptly report childhood vaginal bleeding, offensive discharge or significant pain. During pregnancy, discuss new or worsening genital or urinary symptoms with the maternity team; any vaginal bleeding during pregnancy needs immediate advice. Sudden severe abdominal or pelvic pain, fainting or collapse, confusion, unusual drowsiness, breathing difficulty or severe illness requires immediate emergency care, particularly if pregnancy is possible. These signs may have a cause beyond local irritation, including ectopic pregnancy or serious infection. Do not wait for a cream, home remedy or routine appointment to help. Vulvovaginitis describes irritation or inflammation; infection is only one possible cause. Children and adults need age-appropriate assessment; childhood irritation is not automatically thrush or a bacterial infection. Tests and treatment should match the suspected cause, with consent and no routine internal examination or swabs in prepubertal children. Gentle external care may help comfort; oils, douching and unselected medicines can worsen problems. Fever, worsening pelvic pain, urinary warnings or severe illness need prompt or emergency care. What causes vulvovaginitis? Possible causes include irritation, moisture, allergy, skin disease, hormonal changes, bacteria, yeast, STIs and certain parasites. Symptoms overlap, so do not assume one infection from discharge or itch alone. How is it treated in children and teenagers? Mild childhood irritation often improves with gentle external care and avoiding irritants. A clinician considers specific causes if symptoms are severe, persistent or recurrent. Antibiotics, steroids and antifungals are not automatic; thrush is uncommon before puberty. Adolescents may need a different assessment according to puberty and relevant exposures. What symptoms can it cause? Itch, soreness, swelling, redness, altered or smelly discharge and discomfort with urination or sex may occur. Blood-stained or offensive discharge in a child, fever or worsening pain needs review. Severe pain with collapse or marked illness needs emergency care. Which home measures are reasonable? Gentle external washing, drying without rubbing, comfortable clothing and avoiding irritants can help. A cool damp cloth or brief plain lukewarm bath may soothe. Do not douche or insert tea-tree oil, salt mixtures, food or other remedies; they are not proven cures. Do not delay assessment of concerning symptoms. Does a child need an internal examination or vaginal swab? Not routinely. Most mild cases need no tests, and prepubertal children should not undergo routine internal examinations or internal swabs. A trained clinician can assess externally and, if appropriate, sample at the entrance or arrange specialist care. Can I use a yeast medicine I used before? Past thrush does not prove the current cause. Ask first for pregnancy, a child, new or severe symptoms, recurrence or treatment failure. During pregnancy, current CDC advice uses a topical azole for seven days and avoids oral fluconazole. Persistent symptoms after an over-the-counter course need review. Does every partner need treatment? No. It depends on the cause. Current partners need assessment and treatment for trichomoniasis, even without symptoms; yeast does not routinely require partner treatment. For recurrent or symptomatic BV, newer guidance supports discussion of ongoing-partner treatment in defined settings. Follow current local advice and do not share medicines. When should I seek urgent help? Fever, worsening pelvic pain, flank pain, significant swelling, urinary infection suspected in a child or pregnancy, or urine blood needs same-day advice. Childhood bleeding or offensive discharge needs prompt assessment. Sudden severe pain, fainting, confusion, breathing difficulty or severe illness needs emergency care now.

title: Back pain with vaginal discharge: causes and warning signs
description: Back pain and vaginal discharge can have separate or related causes. Learn about eight possibilities, appropriate testing, treatment and urgent warning signs.
body: Back pain is common, and vaginal discharge is often normal. Having both together does not prove that a vaginal infection is causing the back pain. New or unusual discharge, pelvic or urinary symptoms, pregnancy possibility and the pattern of pain help determine how quickly you need assessment. Two symptoms do not always share one cause Back pain can be brief or persistent and feel aching, sharp or tingling; muscle strain and other back conditions are common. Normal discharge is usually clear or white and changes with the menstrual cycle, hormonal contraception and pregnancy. A dried mark on underwear is not, by itself, a diagnosis. Seek assessment for discharge that is new or different for you, particularly with strong odor, itching, burning, redness, irritation, painful sex or urination, or bleeding outside your usual period. Thick curd-like, green or yellow discharge may guide testing, but color and consistency cannot identify the cause alone. Normal white discharge does not automatically need treatment. 1–2. Urinary infection and urethritis A urinary tract infection affects the urethra, bladder or kidneys and is usually bacterial. Burning, frequency, urgency and cloudy urine are clues. Back or side pain under the ribs, fever or vomiting can indicate a kidney infection and need urgent assessment. A UTI does not directly explain vaginal discharge; another condition may coexist. Urethritis is inflammation of the tube carrying urine out of the body. It can cause painful urination and genital discharge; sexually transmitted infections such as chlamydia or gonorrhea are possible causes, alongside irritation. Associated cervical infection may produce vaginal discharge. Do not assume uncomplicated urethritis explains substantial back or pelvic pain; seek evaluation for spread or another cause. 3–4. Pelvic inflammatory disease and vaginitis Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is an infection of the upper reproductive tract, such as the uterus and fallopian tubes. Lower abdominal/pelvic pain, painful sex, abnormal discharge or bleeding can occur; symptoms may be mild and fever can be absent. STI organisms or other vaginal bacteria can be involved. Prompt treatment helps reduce complications; do not wait a week to see if it settles. Vaginitis means vaginal inflammation, from infections such as yeast or trichomoniasis or noninfectious irritation and hormonal changes. BV is a bacterial imbalance that can also change discharge. Uncomplicated thrush or BV should not be assumed to cause back pain. If pain accompanies discharge, assess both rather than choosing a cream from the discharge's appearance. 5–6. Pregnancy and ectopic pregnancy Pregnancy can increase normal thin, clear or milky discharge and contribute to backache. These symptoms cannot confirm pregnancy; a test and clinical assessment may be needed. New unpleasant odor, itching, pain or abnormal discharge should be discussed with the maternity team. A gush or ongoing watery trickle may be leaking amniotic fluid, rather than ordinary discharge: contact maternity care immediately, especially before 37 weeks with unusual backache, cramps or contractions. An ectopic pregnancy implants outside the uterine cavity, usually in a fallopian tube. Possible pregnancy with one-sided lower abdominal pain, unusual bleeding or shoulder-tip pain needs urgent assessment, even without a positive test. Sudden severe pain, marked dizziness, fainting or collapse requires immediate emergency care. Do not use the color of blood/discharge or a negative early home test to rule it out. 7–8. Cervical disease and reactive arthritis Cervical cancer is one possible cause of persistent unusual discharge, bleeding after sex/between periods/after menopause, painful sex or pelvic/lower back pain. These symptoms commonly have other causes and do not mean you have cancer, but need examination. Do not wait for the next routine cervical screening appointment to discuss new symptoms. Reactive arthritis is inflammation of joints after an infection, often a gut infection or STI. It can affect the spine as well as other joints and occur with urinary/genital symptoms or sore red eyes. It is not simply infection inside the joint. A suddenly hot swollen joint, fever with joint pain, or painful red eyes/visual change needs urgent assessment; treatment of active infection and joint inflammation are different decisions. When to seek urgent or emergency help Get same-day urgent advice for pelvic pain with unusual discharge, fever/shivering, suspected kidney infection, pregnancy with urinary symptoms, or visible/suspected blood in urine: even once, a little or uncertain. Contact your maternity team immediately for any bleeding during pregnancy. Call maternity care immediately for suspected waters breaking, reduced fetal movements or possible preterm labor. New symptoms do not need to last a week before you seek help. Use emergency care for severe or worsening pelvic pain, sudden intense abdominal pain, heavy bleeding, fainting/collapse, confusion or breathing difficulty. With back pain, new numbness around the genitals/anus, weakness or numbness in both legs, or new difficulty passing urine or loss of bladder/bowel control also needs immediate emergency assessment. These can signal a spinal emergency, not a vaginal infection. What assessment may involve Tell the clinician when each symptom began, pain location and severity, discharge changes, period dates, pregnancy possibility, fever, urinary symptoms, sexual contacts, recent procedures and medicines. Testing may include pregnancy and urine tests, vaginal/cervical swabs or STI tests. With your consent, a pelvic examination can help assess inflammation, tenderness or cervical changes; ask for a chaperone or to pause/stop. Ultrasound, blood tests or specialist referral depend on the findings. Suspected PID may need treatment before every test result is available. Persistent cervical symptoms and joint/eye findings need their own assessment. A urine infection result or a yeast diagnosis does not automatically account for every symptom. Treatment depends on the cause Yeast infection may need an antifungal cream, vaginal preparation or, when appropriate, tablets; first-time, severe, persistent or recurring symptoms need advice. In pregnancy, CDC recommends seven days of topical azole rather than oral fluconazole. Symptomatic BV can be treated with prescribed metronidazole or another appropriate antibiotic. PID, urinary/kidney infection and STIs require their own regimens; a yeast cream or vaginal BV gel cannot treat all of them. Use prescribed medicines for the recommended course, unless the prescriber changes the plan; seek help for worsening symptoms or significant reactions. Alcohol advice for metronidazole differs: NHS advises avoiding alcohol with tablets/liquid/suppositories and for 48 hours afterward, while CDC's BV guideline finds insufficient evidence for the presumed interaction. Follow your product instructions and prescriber's/pharmacist's advice rather than treating one universal rule as settled. Partner testing/treatment and when sex can resume follow the diagnosis and current clinic advice. Comfort measures while arranging care For external irritation, a cool clean cloth for a short period may help; never apply ice directly or put it inside the vagina, and stop if uncomfortable. Avoid sex that hurts or worsens irritation; when an STI is possible, wait for clinical advice. Do not repeatedly use over-the-counter antifungals for unexplained back pain and discharge, or let temporary symptom relief postpone assessment. Ask a pharmacist or clinician which pain medicine suits you. Paracetamol/acetaminophen is usually the first choice in pregnancy, within recommended use; it is not a treatment for the underlying cause. Do not start ibuprofen if pregnant or possibly pregnant without professional advice, and avoid it in suspected kidney infection unless a clinician advises it. For assessed uncomplicated muscular back pain, gentle activity and a wrapped heat/cold pack may help; prolonged bed rest is usually unhelpful. Reducing irritation and infection risk Wipe front to back after using the toilet, gently wash the external vulva with water and dry it, and choose clean comfortable cotton underwear. Avoid vaginal douching, scented tampons, deodorants and irritating cleansers. Drink enough fluid according to your health needs and eat a balanced diet; neither excessive water nor a special diet treats pelvic or vaginal infection. Use appropriate condoms/barriers to reduce STI exposure and follow testing and partner-care advice. Some vaginal medicines weaken latex/rubber barriers, so check the instructions. These steps can reduce some risks but cannot prevent every cause of back pain or discharge. Return if symptoms persist, recur or change; get help sooner for any warning sign. Back pain and discharge can be unrelated; neither symptom alone identifies the cause. All eight possibilities need context: urinary infection, urethritis, PID, vaginitis, pregnancy, ectopic pregnancy, cervical disease and reactive arthritis. Pain with unusual discharge, fever, urinary red flags or pregnancy symptoms may need prompt assessment; neurological back-pain signs can be an emergency. Treatment and partner care follow the diagnosis. External comfort care and pain relief do not replace assessment or cure an infection. What causes back pain and vaginal discharge together? They may have one cause or two separate causes. Normal discharge can coexist with muscular back pain; urinary, pelvic, vaginal or cervical conditions and pregnancy also need consideration. A UTI or thrush should not automatically be assumed to explain both. When should I book an appointment? Arrange assessment for new or unusual discharge, itching, burning, irritation, strong odor, painful sex/urination or bleeding outside your normal period, especially with back or pelvic pain. You do not need to wait a week. Normal white discharge alone is not evidence of infection. How are these symptoms treated? The clinician treats the cause: antifungal for confirmed yeast when appropriate, antibiotics for relevant bacterial infections, or pregnancy, cervical or joint care as indicated. Different infections need different medicines; finish the prescribed course unless advised otherwise, and return for worsening or persistent symptoms. What can I do at home? Gentle external washing, a brief cool cloth and avoiding painful sex may ease irritation. Ask about suitable pain relief, especially with pregnancy possibility or kidney symptoms. Do not insert ice, self-treat repeatedly or let comfort measures delay urgent assessment. Could watery discharge and backache mean labor? In pregnancy, a gush or trickle of fluid can be the waters breaking. Contact maternity care immediately, particularly before 37 weeks with unusual backache, cramps or contractions, or with reduced fetal movement. Do not wait to confirm it at home. Do these symptoms mean cervical cancer? Usually there are other explanations, but persistent changed discharge, bleeding after sex/between periods/after menopause or pelvic/back pain needs checking. Symptoms are assessed separately from routine cervical screening; do not wait for screening to seek care. Can I take ibuprofen or drink alcohol with metronidazole? Ask your clinician/pharmacist and follow your product instructions. Ibuprofen is not suitable for everyone, particularly in pregnancy or suspected kidney infection. NHS and CDC differ on metronidazole-alcohol advice; discuss the exact formulation rather than relying on a blanket rule. Which symptoms need emergency care? Severe pelvic/abdominal pain, heavy bleeding, fainting/collapse, confusion or breathing difficulty need emergency help. With back pain, new saddle-area numbness, both-leg weakness/numbness, or new bladder/bowel dysfunction also needs immediate emergency assessment.

title: A tilted uterus or cervix: fertility, symptoms and pregnancy
description: Understand a retroverted uterus, how cervical position differs, possible pain and fertility concerns, the rare trapped pregnant uterus and when to seek urgent help.
body: A uterus that tilts backward is a common anatomical variation and often causes no symptoms. Hearing “tilted cervix” does not, by itself, diagnose a problem or mean that pregnancy will be difficult. The important questions are what position was actually seen, whether symptoms are present and whether another condition needs attention. The cervix, uterine tilt and prolapse are different The cervix is the lower part of the uterus opening into the vagina. The uterine body may lean forward, backward or more upright; retroversion describes a backward direction, while retroflexion describes additional bending between the body and cervix. Uterine size varies with age, pregnancy and other factors, so a fixed four-centimetre length is not a useful universal description. A cervix pointing toward the back is not automatically proof of a retroverted uterus: with retroversion the cervix commonly points more forward as the uterine body points back. “Tilted cervix” is an imprecise description worth clarifying. Prolapse is a different condition in which organs descend or bulge into the vagina; a backward tilt alone does not diagnose prolapse. Why a uterus may tilt backward Many people naturally have this position as part of development. Pregnancy and childbirth can change supporting tissues, and position can vary over time. A tilt does not mean that someone caused damage or failed to exercise enough. Acquired changes may occur with pelvic adhesions after surgery or inflammation, endometriosis or a pelvic mass such as a fibroid. A fibroid can alter shape or position without every fibroid being scar tissue. Adhesions or an underlying condition may pull or fix the uterus; ordinary retroversion does not automatically create adhesions. Symptoms need context Most people have no symptoms and learn the position incidentally. Some report painful periods, discomfort with deeper penetration, difficulty using a tampon or urinary concerns. Those symptoms have several possible causes and should not all be attributed to uterine angle. For example, endometriosis, pelvic-floor problems, infection, a bladder condition or prolapse may need assessment. A 2025 review found no clear significant association with several common bladder dysfunction diagnoses in the studies it reviewed, despite reports of rare retention. New urinary leakage, difficult emptying or a vaginal bulge should be assessed on its own merits. How position is assessed A clinician may discuss symptoms and history and offer a pelvic examination with consent. They may feel the position of the uterus and cervix; ultrasound can help clarify it and look for other causes. Internal or abdominal ultrasound is selected according to the question and circumstances. MRI may help in selected complex cases, rather than being needed for every tilted uterus. Ask what was found and why a test is recommended. Follow the scanning service’s preparation instructions; bladder preparation differs between scan types. You can ask for a chaperone, discuss alternatives and ask to stop an internal examination or scan. A result showing retroversion alone does not establish the cause of pain or infertility. Does it affect fertility? An otherwise ordinary retroverted uterus generally does not prevent conception. It should not be assumed that the cervical angle blocks sperm from reaching an egg, and surgery is not a routine fertility treatment just because of the tilt. If conception is difficult, assess other possible factors, including ovulation, sperm, tubal disease, endometriosis or relevant fibroids. ASRM advises evaluation after about 12 months of trying under age 35, six months from age 35, and sooner over 40 or with a known risk or concerning history. Relevant contributing partners should be evaluated as appropriate; do not delay care by focusing only on the uterine angle. What usually happens during pregnancy? The enlarging uterus usually rises out of the pelvis as pregnancy progresses, and an initial backward tilt usually does not interfere with pregnancy or vaginal birth. Ordinary retroversion alone is not a reason to predict miscarriage or require a caesarean. Your maternity team considers the whole pregnancy, including symptoms and other conditions. If problems develop, do not assume they are harmless because a tilt was previously described as normal. New pain, bleeding or urinary difficulty during pregnancy needs appropriate advice. The rare exception: an incarcerated pregnant uterus In uterine incarceration, the enlarging pregnant uterus remains trapped low in the pelvis instead of moving upward normally. This is different from ordinary retroversion and is not another word for adhesions. Adhesions, fibroids, endometriosis, previous surgery or structural factors can contribute, but it can occur without an identified risk factor. Published frequency estimates and outcomes come largely from limited reports and case series, so a single number is not a reliable personal prediction. Some cases have few symptoms; others cause pressure or urinary difficulty. Persistent incarceration can complicate pregnancy or delivery, making timely recognition and specialist planning important. Symptoms and complications that need attention Possible signs include persistent pelvic pain, pressure toward the low back or rectum, worsening constipation, difficult urination, incomplete emptying or leakage. Complete inability to urinate or severe abdominal pain requires immediate emergency care; do not wait for a routine appointment, even if there is some leakage. Pregnancy with new urinary difficulty or pelvic pain needs prompt maternity assessment. Untreated obstruction can affect the bladder or kidneys. Reported pregnancy complications include miscarriage, preterm birth, abnormal fetal position and injuries or bleeding around delivery; serious uterine complications are also described. These are possible complications of the rare trapped uterus, not expected outcomes for everyone with an ordinary tilt. Sudden severe or worsening pain, fainting, heavy vaginal bleeding, breathing difficulty or confusion also needs immediate emergency care. Specialist diagnosis and treatment of incarceration The team may use examination and ultrasound to identify the displaced uterus and cervix; MRI can clarify complex anatomy or assist procedure and birth planning. Management depends on symptoms, gestation, bladder function and anatomy. Clinicians may drain an obstructed bladder with a catheter and select close observation, supervised positioning, a carefully planned reduction procedure or surgery. Some reported cases resolve during monitored observation, but that does not make waiting at home safe with retention or severe symptoms. Manual repositioning and procedures have risks, and no single gestational-week rule determines every plan. Do not try to move the uterus yourself or follow online knee-to-chest routines as treatment. Follow-up imaging and a delivery plan are individualized; success and an uncomplicated outcome cannot be guaranteed. Pain during sex deserves support Deeper penetration can be uncomfortable for some people, but pain is not proof that uterine tilt is the only cause. Talk with a trusted partner about comfort, stop painful penetration and consider gentler depth or another comfortable position. There is no obligation to continue an activity that hurts. Seek assessment for repeated pain, bleeding or associated symptoms. The clinician may look for endometriosis, infection, dryness or pelvic-floor pain and discuss treatment. Support and physiotherapy may help when appropriate, but the plan should fit the cause; repeated tightening exercises are not a universal answer. Feeling isolated is a reason to seek support, not to dismiss the pain. Painful periods and the limits of one study The source mentions a study of 181 patients with pelvic pain. The original paper appeared online in 2013 and in a 2014 journal issue. It linked certain uterine flexion angles with menstrual-pain intensity in that selected group; uterine version itself was not associated with pain intensity. This does not prove that menstrual blood is blocked or that all retroverted uteri cause painful periods. For familiar uncomplicated cramps, protected warmth and gentle activity may help. Ask a pharmacist or clinician about suitable pain relief, especially if pregnancy is possible, other medicines are used or health conditions limit options. Period pain that changes, disrupts life or comes with unusual bleeding, sex pain or bowel or bladder symptoms needs assessment. Age or childbirth does not guarantee that the pain will disappear. Tampons, cups and discs If inserting or wearing a menstrual product hurts, do not force it. A different comfortable posture or product may help, but pain may relate to muscle tension, irritation or another condition rather than the uterine position. Follow the product’s instructions for placement, wear time and removal. Pads are a reasonable alternative while symptoms are assessed. A menstrual disc sits in the vagina and is not a treatment that repositions the uterus; it is not guaranteed to be easier than a cup or tampon. Persistent insertion pain or difficulty removing a product deserves advice rather than repeated painful attempts. When treatment of an ordinary tilt is considered An incidental symptom-free retroverted uterus generally needs no treatment. When symptoms are troublesome, the priority is to identify and treat contributing conditions and discuss comfort measures. Pelvic-health physiotherapy can be individualized; exercises are not a proven permanent correction for everyone. Do not attempt manual repositioning yourself. A fitted support pessary, a plastic or silicone vaginal device rather than a medicinal suppository, may be considered in selected symptomatic situations, particularly with support problems. It needs appropriate fitting and review and can cause discomfort or discharge. Surgery to reposition or suspend the uterus is also selective, with risks and uncertain benefit for pain; randomized evidence is limited. Ask about alternatives, follow-up, fertility plans and expected benefit rather than assuming a normal tilt requires a device or operation. A retroverted uterus is usually an anatomical variation; cervical direction, uterine bending and prolapse are different descriptions. Ordinary retroversion usually does not prevent conception or vaginal birth. Pain or urinary symptoms deserve assessment for other causes rather than automatic attribution to tilt. Rare pregnancy incarceration is a distinct condition requiring individualized specialist assessment and planning. Complete inability to urinate or severe abdominal pain requires immediate emergency care; do not try to reposition the uterus at home. Does a tilted uterus make pregnancy difficult? Ordinary retroversion generally does not prevent conception. If trying is taking longer than expected, assess other fertility factors and use age- and risk-appropriate referral rather than assuming the angle blocks sperm. What symptoms can it cause? Many people have none. Some report period or sex pain, tampon difficulty or urinary concerns, but these can have other causes. Leakage or incomplete emptying needs its own assessment; complete inability to urinate needs immediate emergency care. Can it make sex painful? Some people experience discomfort with deeper penetration, but pain can also come from endometriosis, dryness, infection or pelvic-floor conditions. Stop what hurts, discuss comfort and seek assessment for recurrent pain or bleeding. How is a tilted uterus treated? Usually no treatment is needed without symptoms. Treat underlying causes first; individualized physiotherapy, a fitted support pessary or surgery are considered only in selected cases. Exercises or repositioning are not a guaranteed cure, and home manual repositioning is unsafe. Is a posterior cervix the same as a retroverted uterus? No. A cervical direction alone does not establish the direction of the uterine body. In retroversion the body points backward and the cervix often points more forward. Ask what the examination or scan actually showed; prolapse is a separate descent condition. What is uterine incarceration in pregnancy? A rare situation where the enlarging uterus remains trapped low in the pelvis. It can occur with or without known adhesions or risk factors. Urinary difficulty, pressure or pain needs maternity assessment, and complete inability to urinate or severe abdominal pain needs immediate emergency care. Should I use knee-to-chest exercises to correct it? Do not use an online routine as treatment for suspected incarceration or try to reposition the uterus. Specialists may choose supervised positioning among other options after assessing the situation. Ordinary tilt does not require correction, and lasting benefit of exercises is uncertain. Does the period-pain study prove blood cannot drain? No. It found an association between flexion angles and pain in a selected group of 181 patients, not proof of blocked menstrual flow or a universal cause of pain. Troublesome or changing pain should be assessed.

title: Cushing syndrome and Cushing disease: symptoms, tests and care
description: Understand prolonged cortisol excess, the difference between Cushing syndrome and disease, steroid safety, diagnostic tests, treatment and recovery.
body: Cushing syndrome means prolonged exposure to excessive glucocorticoid effects, from steroid medicines or cortisol produced within the body. Cushing disease is the specific form caused by an ACTH-producing pituitary tumour. Both need careful clinical assessment; a change in appearance, ordinary stress or a single cortisol result cannot establish the diagnosis. Recognising symptoms and complications Changes can develop gradually: more fat around the trunk, face, neck or upper back; relatively thin limbs; wide purple stretch marks; easy bruising, fragile skin, slow wound healing or acne. Weakness around the shoulders and hips may make climbing stairs or rising from a chair difficult. Fatigue, headache, irritability, anxiety, depression and difficulty concentrating can occur, but these symptoms also have other causes. Excess glucocorticoid effects can contribute to high blood pressure, high blood glucose with thirst or frequent urination, repeated infections, bone loss and fractures, muscle loss and blood clots. Seek an appointment for progressive or combined symptoms, particularly during steroid treatment. Weight gain, diabetes or hypertension alone does not mean Cushing syndrome, and routine screening of everyone with these common conditions is not recommended. Children, sexual health and pregnancy In children, weight gain accompanied by slowing height growth is an important warning pattern; blood pressure and other symptoms also need assessment. Adults may notice reduced sexual desire. Some women develop increased facial or body hair and irregular or absent periods; men may have erectile difficulties and reduced fertility. These changes deserve assessment without assuming that they identify a single hormonal disorder. Cushing syndrome can disrupt fertility, but pregnancy may still occur. Active disease increases pregnancy risks, so discuss disease control, contraception and medicines with an endocrinologist before trying to conceive. If already pregnant, contact the endocrine and maternity teams promptly for specialist planning. Neither future fertility nor a pregnancy outcome can be guaranteed, and ordinary pregnancy-related cortisol changes need specialist interpretation. Defer trying to conceive while Cushing syndrome is active, until the disease is controlled and your specialist advises that you can proceed. Cortisol, ACTH and the different causes The adrenal glands normally make cortisol, which helps regulate metabolism, blood pressure, glucose, inflammation and the response to illness. ACTH from the pituitary stimulates adrenal cortisol production; ACTH is not converted into cortisol. A usually non-cancerous pituitary tumour making excess ACTH causes Cushing disease. Other adrenal tumours or nodular disorders may produce cortisol independently; some adrenal tumours are cancerous. Tumours outside the pituitary, sometimes in the lungs or pancreas, can produce ACTH: this is ectopic ACTH production and has nothing to do with ectopic pregnancy. Most Cushing cases are not inherited, although selected endocrine tumour syndromes warrant genetic advice. Exercise or everyday stress does not by itself establish pathological Cushing syndrome. Severe illness, depression, heavy alcohol use and other conditions can alter cortisol regulation or mimic test abnormalities and must be considered during assessment. Steroid medicines: review every route, never stop abruptly Prescribed glucocorticoids, especially substantial exposure over time, are the most common cause. Tell the clinician about tablets, injections, inhalers, nasal sprays, skin preparations and every other medicine or supplement. Risk depends on the preparation, dose, duration, combinations and drug interactions; inhaled or topical treatment is not automatically risk-free. These medicines may still be essential for asthma, inflammation or transplant care. Do not stop, reduce or switch a prescribed steroid on your own. The prescriber weighs control of the original illness against adverse effects and decides whether and how to taper. Steroid exposure can suppress the body's own cortisol production, so abrupt withdrawal can cause dangerous adrenal insufficiency. Ask whether you need a steroid emergency card, an illness or surgery dosing plan and training in any prescribed emergency injection. How clinicians confirm cortisol excess Assessment starts with symptoms, examination, growth or weight history and a full medicine review. For suspected cortisol overproduction, selected tests include late-night salivary cortisol, cortisol in urine collected over 24 hours, and a low-dose dexamethasone suppression test. Sampling or testing often needs repetition or a complementary test. These are different tests with specific instructions, not interchangeable home checks. A random single blood cortisol or ACTH measurement cannot establish the diagnosis. Sleep patterns, pregnancy, oestrogen treatment, kidney function, other medicines and illness can affect which tests are suitable and how results are interpreted. Cyclical disease may require assessment at different times. An endocrinologist considers false-positive and false-negative results; do not take dexamethasone or change medicines to prepare for a test unless instructed. Finding the source and choosing treatment Once excess cortisol is confirmed, ACTH and other targeted tests help distinguish pituitary, adrenal and ectopic causes. Pituitary MRI, adrenal or other body imaging, and occasionally specialist blood sampling from veins draining the pituitary may follow. A scan alone cannot prove that an incidental tumour caused Cushing syndrome, and a small pituitary tumour may not appear on routine imaging. Treatment depends on the cause, severity and individual circumstances. For a suitable cortisol- or ACTH-producing tumour, expert surgery is often the first approach; selected patients need radiation, medicines, further surgery or combined care. Removing both adrenal glands is an option in particular situations and requires lifelong adrenal hormone replacement. Blood pressure, diabetes, infections, bone health, clot risk and mental health also need care. Medicines require specialist selection and monitoring Depending on local approval and the clinical situation, medicines may reduce adrenal cortisol synthesis, reduce pituitary ACTH or block cortisol's effects. Options include metyrapone, ketoconazole or levoketoconazole, osilodrostat and selected pituitary-directed treatment such as pasireotide. Mitotane has a particular role in selected adrenal disease, including adrenal cancer. These are not interchangeable treatments; monitoring may include cortisol, potassium, liver tests, glucose and heart rhythm, depending on the medicine. Mifepristone blocks glucocorticoid receptors rather than lowering cortisol production. Its Cushing indication applies to selected adults with cortisol-related glucose problems when surgery has failed or is unsuitable, according to the product and jurisdiction. It is contraindicated in pregnancy and interferes with hormonal contraception; specialist pregnancy testing and suitable non-hormonal contraception are essential. Cortisol levels alone cannot monitor its effect or exclude adrenal insufficiency. Do not substitute brands, select a drug or adjust a dose yourself. For Korlym, use suitable non-hormonal contraception throughout treatment and for one month after stopping; contact your prescriber immediately if pregnancy is suspected or confirmed. Food, activity and emotional support No diet, supplement or stress remedy cures a cortisol-producing tumour or replaces endocrine treatment. A dietitian can help plan adequate nutrition, protein and energy, with vegetables, fruit, whole grains and suitable protein foods. Glucose and blood-pressure management may call for individual changes to carbohydrate choices and sodium intake. Discuss calcium and vitamin D needs and bone protection rather than starting universal supplement doses or a crash diet. Heavy alcohol use can affect health and cortisol assessment; seek support if reducing it is difficult or dependence is possible. Build activity gradually with advice about muscle weakness and fracture risk, and consider rehabilitation. Anxiety, depression, body changes and sexual difficulties can continue during recovery; psychological support and patient groups may help. Symptoms are not a failure of willpower, and relaxation alone is not treatment. Recovery, follow-up and emergency planning Improvement may take months or longer and differs by cause, complications and treatment. Remission does not guarantee that disease will never return; follow the team's long-term testing plan. Cortisol replacement may be needed after successful treatment until normal production recovers, sometimes permanently. Never stop replacement because you feel better: ask about testing, sick-day instructions, medical identification and any emergency injection training. Seek immediate emergency care for possible adrenal crisis, especially if at risk of low cortisol and vomiting prevents you keeping down replacement medicine, or if there is collapse, confusion, severe weakness or severe abdominal pain. Follow your prescribed emergency plan, including an injection if supplied and you are trained, while arranging emergency help; do not wait for tests. Sudden breathlessness, chest pain or collapse also needs emergency care; a new painful swollen leg or signs of significant infection need urgent assessment. Cushing disease is one pituitary cause of the broader Cushing syndrome. Review all steroid routes and interactions with the prescriber; do not stop treatment abruptly. Diagnosis requires appropriately selected and interpreted tests, with imaging used to investigate the cause. Treatment and recovery are individual, with long-term follow-up and a plan for possible low cortisol. Can corticosteroid medicines cause Cushing syndrome? Yes. Risk depends on exposure and interactions, including medicines given through routes other than tablets. Review treatment with the prescriber; never reduce or stop it yourself. How is Cushing syndrome diagnosed? A clinician reviews symptoms, examination and all medicines, then chooses appropriate cortisol tests when needed. Repeated or complementary testing may be necessary. One random result or a scan alone is not diagnostic. What is the difference between syndrome and disease? Cushing syndrome describes prolonged excessive glucocorticoid effects. Cushing disease is the form caused by excess ACTH from a pituitary tumour; adrenal, ectopic and medicine-related causes are different. Can someone with Cushing syndrome become pregnant? Yes, although fertility may be reduced. Active disease makes pregnancy higher risk. Plan with endocrine and maternity specialists before conception, or contact them promptly if already pregnant; medicine and contraception advice is individual. Defer trying to conceive while Cushing syndrome is active, until the disease is controlled and your specialist advises that you can proceed. What diet is best? No diet cures the condition. Individual advice addresses adequate nutrition, glucose, blood pressure and bone health. Avoid extreme restriction and unreviewed supplements; ask about calcium, vitamin D and safe activity. Will Cushing syndrome get better? Treatment can bring remission or control, but results and recovery time vary. Some symptoms and complications persist, recurrence is possible and ongoing follow-up matters. Replacement hormones may be temporary or lifelong. Can stress or one high cortisol result prove Cushing syndrome? No. Cortisol changes with timing, illness, medicines and other factors. Everyday stress is not equivalent to the syndrome; an endocrinologist interprets the overall clinical and test pattern. When is low cortisol an emergency? If you are at risk of adrenal insufficiency, vomiting that prevents replacement dosing, collapse, confusion or severe weakness can signal adrenal crisis. Seek immediate emergency care and follow your prescribed emergency plan without waiting for tests.

title: Menstrual odor: normal changes and when to seek care
description: Learn which period odors can be normal, when fishy or foul odor needs assessment, and how to use menstrual products safely without irritating washes.
body: Periods have a smell, and a mild familiar odor is not a sign that you are unclean. Blood, uterine lining, vaginal bacteria and sweat can all contribute. A new, strong or persistent odor deserves attention, especially with pain, unusual discharge or illness; smell alone cannot identify the cause. What can be normal during a period? Menstrual fluid contains blood and shed uterine lining, mixed with vaginal secretions. It may smell mildly metallic or like blood, and the scent can vary through a period or between cycles. Menstruation is not a visible discharge of unfertilized eggs. Normal vaginal bacteria and changing acidity also influence odor. There is no requirement to have no genital scent. Whether someone else notices a smell is not a reliable test of health. Compare a change with your usual pattern, but do not rely on smell to diagnose infection or to rule it out. Persistent concerns are a reasonable reason to ask for care without embarrassment. A strong or rotten smell needs context Blood left in a used product can develop a stronger smell. Changing the product may help, but a new persistent foul or rotten smell should not automatically be dismissed as normal menstrual tissue. Unusual discharge, soreness or pelvic pain can suggest a problem needing assessment, including a retained tampon or infection. If you think a tampon may be forgotten, remove it promptly if it comes out easily with clean hands. Do not use tools, pull forcefully or insert another tampon. If you cannot remove it easily, are unsure one remains or think part is still inside, arrange prompt medical help. Do not wait for the period to end or for the smell to disappear. Fishy odor and bacterial vaginosis A fishy smell, sometimes with thin grey-white discharge, can occur with bacterial vaginosis (BV), an imbalance in vaginal bacteria. BV is not a fungal infection. Odor alone does not confirm it, and BV often causes no itching or soreness. Burning, itching, irritation or a different discharge can indicate another or an additional problem, so testing may be needed. BV may become more noticeable around a period or after sex; menstruation is not its only cause. It can occur without sexual activity and is not proof of poor hygiene or infidelity. A clinician may examine and sample discharge to distinguish BV from sexually transmitted and other infections. Prescribed antibiotics can help, but recurrence is common; persistent or recurrent symptoms need review rather than a promise of permanent odor removal. Sweaty, salty or onion-like changes A sweaty, musky, salty or onion-like smell may come from the groin and external skin rather than from inside the vagina. Heat, activity, moisture and normal skin bacteria can contribute even with regular washing. These descriptions do not by themselves diagnose infection or establish that someone has neglected hygiene. Change damp clothing and choose comfortable, breathable underwear if helpful. Cotton and other suitable fabrics may reduce trapped moisture, but they do not cure BV or another infection. Seek assessment if an unusual smell persists, worsens or comes with discharge, itching, burning or pain rather than trying to mask it. Different products have different care instructions Wash your hands before and after changing menstrual products. For tampons, FDA advice is to change every 4–8 hours, never exceed 8 hours and use the lowest absorbency needed for your flow. Use them only during menstruation and remove the final tampon when the period ends. Lighter bleeding is not a reason to leave one in longer; use another suitable product if needed. Pads and period underwear collect blood outside the body; cups collect it inside. Change pads when wet or soiled and regularly according to the instructions and your flow. Follow the specific cup or disc emptying limits and cleaning instructions, and the washing and drying instructions for reusable products. Do not apply one wear time to every product. Pain, irritation or unusual symptoms warrant stopping the troublesome product and seeking advice. Gentle care without deodorizing the vagina Gently wash the outside genital skin, the vulva, with warm water; a mild unperfumed soap may be used if tolerated. Routine bathing and changing products can improve comfort, but repeated scrubbing or internal washing is unnecessary. The vagina cleans itself; do not douche or insert antiseptics, scented wipes, sprays or deodorants to eliminate its natural scent. Scented tampons, pads or washes can irritate some people; choose unscented options if irritation occurs. A fragrance-free routine does not guarantee an absence of odor or replace treatment. Do not self-treat a fishy smell as thrush or use leftover antibiotics. The right approach depends on the cause, not on trying to achieve a perfume-like smell. When to book care and what assessment may involve Arrange assessment for a new persistent fishy or foul odor, yellow or green discharge, itching, urinary burning, bleeding between periods or after sex, or bleeding or cramps different from your usual pattern. A primary care clinician or sexual health clinic can help; not every concern requires a gynecologist first. Possible pregnancy should be mentioned because bleeding is not always a period. Seek urgent same-day advice for pelvic or lower abdominal pain with unusual discharge, fever or possible pregnancy. Evaluation may include symptom and product history, an examination with consent, swabs or a pregnancy test. Conditions such as PID need early treatment. You can ask questions, request a chaperone and stop an examination. Do not delay because you feel ashamed of a smell. Warning signs that need immediate help With a retained tampon or other vaginal object, fever of 38°C or higher, rash, dizziness, confusion, breathing difficulty, muscle aches or diarrhea need emergency assessment. Sudden fever, vomiting, diarrhea, rash or feeling faint during or shortly after tampon or cup use can signal rare but life-threatening toxic shock syndrome. Seek immediate medical help; remove the product if easily possible, but do not delay help or wait for every symptom. An odor is not required. Get immediate emergency care for severe or worsening pelvic pain, sudden intense abdominal pain, pelvic pain with heavy bleeding, fainting, confusion, breathing difficulty or feeling severely unwell. If pregnancy is possible, pain with bleeding needs urgent advice even without a positive test; severe pain, shoulder-tip pain with bleeding or fainting are emergency warning signs. An app prediction that it is your period must not delay care. Mild familiar menstrual odor, including a metallic smell, can be normal and is not a cleanliness judgment. New persistent fishy or rotten odor needs assessment; smell alone cannot diagnose BV, an STI or a retained tampon. Follow each product’s instructions. Tampons must never stay in longer than 8 hours; other products have their own care requirements. Avoid internal washing and deodorants. Urgent illness, retained-product warning signs or severe pain need prompt or emergency care. Is a rotten smell during a period normal? A used product can smell stronger, but a new persistent rotten smell should not receive blanket reassurance. Consider a forgotten tampon and seek assessment if the smell persists or comes with unusual discharge, pain or illness. A retained product should be removed promptly and safely. Is a fishy smell just part of menstruation? It can occur with BV or other conditions and should not be diagnosed by smell alone. BV is a bacterial imbalance, not a fungal infection or proof of poor hygiene. A clinician can check the cause and prescribe treatment when needed. How can I reduce menstrual odor safely? Change products as directed, gently wash the external vulva and change damp clothes if needed. Avoid douching, fragrances and internal antiseptics. Breathable underwear may help comfort but does not treat infection. Persistent odor needs assessment rather than masking. When should I see a clinician? Book care for a new persistent odor or unusual discharge, itching, urinary burning or abnormal bleeding. Pelvic pain with discharge, fever or possible pregnancy needs urgent same-day advice. Severe pain, heavy bleeding with pelvic pain, fainting or severe illness needs immediate emergency care. How long can I leave a tampon in? FDA advice is to change it every 4–8 hours and never exceed 8 hours. Choose the lowest absorbency needed, follow the label and use only during a period. Lighter flow does not justify longer use. Pads, cups and reusable products have different instructions. What if I cannot find or remove a tampon? If it comes out easily with clean hands, remove it promptly. Do not use tools or force. If you are unsure whether one remains, cannot remove it easily or suspect a piece remains, get prompt medical help. Fever or systemic symptoms with a retained object need emergency assessment. Does a sweaty or onion-like smell mean I am dirty? No. External sweat, moisture and normal skin bacteria can produce these smells despite regular washing. Gentle care may improve comfort. Persistent changes or additional symptoms should be assessed without blame. Can toxic shock syndrome happen without a bad smell? Yes. Odor is not required. Sudden fever, rash, vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness or feeling faint during or shortly after tampon or cup use need immediate medical help. Remove the product if easy, but do not delay care or wait for every symptom.

title: Anal fistulotomy: what it treats, alternatives and recovery
description: Learn how anal fistulotomy differs from fistulectomy, why sphincter muscles matter, other treatment options, wound care and when to seek help.
body: A fistulotomy opens an anal fistula tract so it can heal from its base. It can work well for a suitable simple fistula, but is not the right operation for every fistula. The tract's relationship to the muscles that control bowel movements, any infection and the underlying cause guide treatment and recovery. What is a fistula, and which type is discussed here? A fistula is an abnormal connection between body surfaces or organs. An anal fistula usually connects the inside of the anal canal to skin near the anus, often after an abscess. It may cause repeated pain, swelling, irritation and drainage of pus or blood. Symptoms can temporarily improve as it drains, without the tract having healed. Fistulas can also involve bowel, bladder, urethra, vagina or blood vessels. For example, vesicovaginal and urethrovaginal fistulas connect the urinary tract to the vagina, while rectovaginal or colovaginal fistulas involve bowel and vagina. These are different conditions with different investigations and treatments. This article concerns anal fistulotomy; its advice must not be applied to every urinary, vaginal, intestinal or vascular fistula. Fistulotomy and fistulectomy are different operations In fistulotomy, the surgeon lays open the tract along its length, leaving a wound that heals from the bottom upwards. Fistulectomy instead removes the tract. Ask which procedure is proposed and why; the names are not interchangeable. The goal is to treat the fistula while preserving bowel control, not simply to remove as much tissue as possible. A low, simple tract involving little sphincter muscle may be suitable for fistulotomy when bowel-control function is appropriate. A high or branching tract, previous operations, existing leakage or other risk factors can change that choice. Cutting too much sphincter muscle can impair control of gas or stool. Discuss your existing bowel function and any relevant childbirth injury or other pelvic surgery with the colorectal surgeon. Assessment before deciding on treatment The clinician asks about symptoms, previous abscesses or operations, bowel control, medicines and conditions such as Crohn's disease, then examines the area. Examination of the anal canal with a small instrument or examination under anaesthesia may help define the tract. Sometimes the final plan depends on what is found during that examination; agree in advance what procedures you consent to. MRI or specialised ultrasound is useful in selected complex or recurrent cases. CT may help assess a deep infection; bowel endoscopy or other targeted investigations depend on suspected underlying disease. Not everyone needs every scan, contrast study, scope or probe. An abscess needs timely assessment and usually drainage; antibiotics alone do not reliably treat a typical anal abscess or close an ordinary anal fistula. Alternatives and Crohn's-related fistulas If laying open the tract risks bowel-control muscles, options may include a loose draining seton, staged treatment, LIFT (ligation of the intersphincteric fistula tract) or an advancement flap. A loose seton is a loop that keeps the tract draining; it often controls infection while another treatment is planned rather than curing the fistula on its own. Do not cut, tighten or replace it yourself. Laser, endoscopic techniques, plugs or glue may be discussed in selected settings, but their effectiveness and long-term evidence differ; being less invasive does not guarantee a better result. Crohn's-related fistulas need coordinated gastroenterology and colorectal care, often combining drainage or a seton with medicines such as biologic therapy. Having Crohn's does not automatically mean surgery is unnecessary, and fistulotomy is not automatically suitable either. Preparing for surgery and going home Anal fistula surgery is commonly performed under general anaesthesia, although the anaesthetic and setting are individual. Many people go home that day; complex disease, infection or other health needs may require admission. There is no universal one-hour operation or guaranteed same-day discharge. Follow the team's exact eating, drinking, bowel-preparation and medicine instructions; do not choose fasting times or stop medicines yourself. Arrange transport and an adult to stay with you for the period required after anaesthesia, often at least 24 hours. Before discharge, ask for written wound-care and medicine instructions, supplies, follow-up arrangements and a number for problems outside normal hours. Nausea, pain and temporary urinary difficulties can occur; tell staff before leaving if symptoms are not controlled or you cannot pass urine. Wound care, pain and bowel movements An open healing wound may be sore and have some discharge or a small amount of blood, especially with bowel movements. Follow the nurse's instructions for gentle cleaning, drying and changing any external pad or dressing. Plain warm water may help comfort; avoid irritating perfumed products, soap or additives on the healing wound unless your team specifically advises otherwise. Packing, dressing removal and any technique to keep the wound healing from its base must be prescribed and demonstrated for your particular wound; do not insert gauze, fingers or other objects on your own. Take pain relief only as directed and ask about constipation, particularly with opioid medicines. Fluids, suitable fibre and a prescribed stool-softening medicine may help, with adjustments for your bowel condition. Do not strain or ignore the urge to open your bowels. Activity, healing and recurrence Rest after anaesthesia and gradually resume comfortable activity according to your discharge plan. Return to work, lifting, exercise, swimming, driving and sexual activity depends on the wound, operation, symptoms and type of activity. Do not drive while impaired by anaesthesia or sedating medicines, or before you can safely control the car and meet the team's and insurer's requirements. Ask specifically about pressure or penetration near the wound. Healing often takes several weeks and sometimes longer; a fixed three-to-twelve-week deadline does not fit everyone. More than one procedure may be needed. Recurrence, a new abscess, infection, bleeding or changes in bowel control can occur despite appropriate care. A permanent success rate such as 92–97% cannot be promised to every patient. Report persistent or returning drainage, a reopening wound or new leakage, and keep the agreed follow-up. Questions to ask and symptoms needing help Ask: what type of tract do I have and how much sphincter is involved? What alternatives protect bowel control? Could the plan change during examination? Which anaesthetic, fasting and medicine instructions apply? Who manages dressings or packing, how is pain and constipation treated, and when can I resume each activity? Bring someone you trust or take notes if that helps; support needs and treatment preferences matter. Seek urgent same-day assessment for fever or chills, increasing pain, new swelling or redness, worsening discharge, or bleeding that continues. These may indicate infection or an abscess, even if the surface opening seems closed. Seek immediate emergency care for heavy or uncontrolled bleeding, fainting or collapse, confusion, breathing difficulty, or acute inability to pass urine. Do not squeeze or drain a swelling yourself or wait for an app update if seriously unwell. Anal fistulotomy opens a tract; fistulectomy removes it, and other fistula types need different care. Protecting bowel-control muscles is central to choosing between fistulotomy and alternatives. Hospital stay, dressings, packing and recovery instructions are individual; do not manipulate a wound or seton without instruction. Recurrence is possible, and fever, worsening pain, significant bleeding or inability to urinate require timely help. What is a fistula? It is an abnormal connection. An anal fistula usually links the anal canal to nearby skin, often following an abscess. Urinary, vaginal, bowel and vascular fistulas are different and are not all treated by anal fistulotomy. Will I stay in hospital after fistulotomy? Many operations are day cases, but complex fistulas, infection or other health needs may require an overnight or longer stay. Ask about your anaesthetic and discharge criteria; neither operation length nor discharge time is guaranteed. How can I recognise infection? Increasing pain, swelling, redness, fever or chills, and worsening discharge need urgent same-day assessment. Confusion, collapse or breathing difficulty means immediate emergency care. Do not try to drain a swelling yourself. Can the fistula come back? Yes. Recurrence or another abscess can happen even after healing, and further treatment may be needed. Results depend on the tract, cause, procedure and bowel-control risks; no single permanent success percentage applies to everyone. Is fistulotomy the only treatment? No. Depending on anatomy and cause, a seton, LIFT, flap or another selected approach may be appropriate. Crohn's-related fistulas often need combined medical and surgical care. Discuss benefits, uncertainties and continence risks. Must I pack the wound myself? Not automatically. Follow your own surgical plan for dressings, packing or any wound manipulation, with training or nursing help if required. Do not insert anything or cut or adjust a seton on your own. When can I return to normal activities? Timing depends on your operation, symptoms and wound. Ask separately about work, lifting, driving, swimming and sex. Follow anaesthetic and medicine restrictions and seek advice if healing is not progressing rather than relying on a fixed deadline.

title: Vaginal odor: seven descriptions and what changes mean
description: Explore sour, metallic, sweet, chemical, sweaty, fishy and rotten odors, why smell and pH cannot diagnose infection, and when to seek assessment.
body: A healthy vagina has a natural scent; it does not need to smell like flowers. Odor can reflect vaginal secretions, external sweat, menstrual blood or urine on the skin. Mild temporary changes can be normal, but not every change is beneficial or something to ignore. Odor descriptions are clues, not diagnoses. Scent, bacteria and acidity Vaginal bacteria, including lactobacilli in many people, help maintain an acidic environment. A mildly tangy or sour scent can be familiar and normal. Comparing it with fermented foods is only a description, not a test of healthy bacteria or a reason to put food inside the vagina. Acidity varies with hormones, menstrual blood, semen and life stage. A single pH range is not a universal rule for every person. A home pH result or smell cannot confirm BV, thrush or an STI; even a normal pH does not exclude every infection. Clinical assessment considers symptoms and, when needed, examination and testing. Metallic or copper-like odor Blood can produce a metallic smell, often around menstruation as blood and uterine lining pass through the vagina. A temporary change after sex may also involve semen or a small amount of blood, but the scent does not reveal why bleeding occurred. Dryness or friction can cause discomfort, and a suitable lubricant may help. Nevertheless, bleeding after sex or between periods should be checked rather than automatically attributed to vigorous sex or a small scratch. Persistent unusual odor, itching or discharge also needs review. Any bleeding after menopause should be assessed, even if it is slight. Sweet or earthy odor Some people describe a mild scent as sweet, bittersweet or earthy. Normal bacterial and hormonal variation can influence it. These words do not prove a disease, but they also cannot guarantee that a new persistent change is harmless. Distinguish vaginal scent from the smell of urine on underwear. Sweet-smelling urine has a different range of possible causes and should not be assumed to be normal vaginal bacteria. Ask for advice for a persistent change or accompanying symptoms rather than diagnosing yourself by a comparison with food. Chemical or ammonia-like odor Urine on external skin or clothing can contribute to an ammonia-like smell, especially if it is concentrated. Urea is a waste compound excreted in urine, not a type of ammonia. An odor alone cannot establish dehydration, a urinary infection or a vaginal diagnosis. Gentle external care and drinking normally may help if concentrated urine or residue is involved; follow any prescribed fluid restriction. Burning or frequent urination needs advice. Urinary symptoms with fever, pain in the back under the ribs or possible pregnancy need urgent same-day assessment. A chemical or fishy description can also overlap with vaginal conditions, so persistent symptoms warrant testing rather than bleach-like cleansing.
