Sweaty, musky or smoky-earthy odor The groin has sweat glands, and sweat interacting with normal skin bacteria can create a stronger smell. Heat, exercise and stress may contribute. A smoky, skunky or earthy comparison is subjective; it does not prove a particular chemical process, infection or exposure to a substance. External sweat is not the same as an infection inside the vagina, and a smell is not a judgment of cleanliness. Change damp clothes and use comfortable breathable underwear if helpful. Persistent odor or accompanying itching, burning, discharge or pain needs assessment; extra scrubbing or fragrance is not a treatment. Fishy odor: BV and trichomoniasis Amines produced in some bacterial environments can contribute to a fishy smell. BV is an imbalance of vaginal bacteria and may cause thin grey-white discharge and fishy odor, often without itching. Trichomoniasis is an STI caused by a parasite; it may cause irritation, urinary discomfort or thin discharge of different colors, and many people have no symptoms. A stronger smell does not prove trichomoniasis, distinguish it from BV or reveal seriousness. Testing guides treatment. BV can recur after prescribed antibiotics. Trichomoniasis needs appropriate oral treatment and concurrent treatment of sexual partners to reduce reinfection; avoid sex until everyone has completed treatment and follow the clinic’s advice about symptoms and repeat testing. Do not treat a fishy smell as thrush or use someone else’s medication. Rotten odor and a forgotten tampon A forgotten tampon or another vaginal object can cause a strong rotten smell, unusual discharge or discomfort. It should be removed promptly. If a tampon comes out easily with clean hands, you may remove it; do not use tools, force removal or insert another tampon. Seek prompt medical help if removal is difficult, you are unsure one remains or suspect a fragment. Removal is not automatically risk-free, and a retained object should not be left for days while waiting for odor to settle. With a retained object, fever of 38°C or higher, rash, dizziness, confusion, breathing difficulty, muscle aches or diarrhea require emergency assessment. Possible toxic shock needs immediate medical help; remove the product only if easy and do not delay help or wait for every symptom or a bad smell. Changes after sex and during menopause Semen is less acidic than the usual vaginal environment and can temporarily change acidity and scent after sex. This can be normal if brief and otherwise symptom-free, but a persistent fishy or foul smell, painful sex, unusual discharge or bleeding needs assessment. A temporary change does not prove or exclude an STI. Lower estrogen around menopause can change vaginal tissue, fluid, bacteria and acidity. Dryness, soreness or pain can be treated after assessment; there is no need to accept discomfort as inevitable. New persistent odor or bleeding must not simply be blamed on hormones. Daily odor changes are neither necessary nor automatically a sign of better health. Care without trying to erase natural scent The vagina cleans itself. Gently wash the external vulva with warm water; a mild unscented cleanser may be suitable if tolerated. Avoid douching, internal deodorants, perfumed sprays and irritating wipes. These can disturb the environment or irritate skin; it is inaccurate to assume every marketed product has identical approval status or that every use inevitably causes BV. Use menstrual products according to their own instructions. FDA tampon advice is change every 4–8 hours, never more than 8, using the lowest absorbency needed and only during menstruation. Pads, cups and reusable products have different requirements. Fragrance, probiotics or pH products are not substitutes for diagnosing persistent symptoms; ask before trying internal remedies. When to seek routine, urgent or emergency care Book assessment for a new persistent unpleasant odor, itching or burning, pain with sex, thick curd-like or otherwise unusual discharge, or bleeding unrelated to your period. You do not need an unbearable smell or every symptom before asking. An examination, swabs, urine or pregnancy testing may be offered with consent. A primary care or sexual health service can help. Seek urgent same-day advice for pelvic or lower abdominal pain with unusual discharge, fever or possible pregnancy. Possible pregnancy with pain and bleeding needs urgent help even without a positive test. Severe or worsening pain, heavy bleeding with pelvic pain, shoulder-tip pain with bleeding, fainting, confusion, breathing difficulty or severe illness need immediate emergency care. Retained-object warning signs also require emergency assessment; do not wait for a tracker result. A natural mild scent is expected; there is no need for a floral smell or for daily odor changes. Seven odor descriptions are not seven diagnoses. Smell intensity or pH alone cannot identify or exclude infection. Bleeding after sex, between periods or after menopause needs assessment, even if dryness seems a possible cause. A retained tampon needs prompt safe removal; illness or severe pain can require emergency care. Avoid internal washing and masking symptoms. Can odor change normally after sex? Yes, semen can temporarily change acidity and scent. A brief change without other symptoms can be normal. Persistent fishy or foul odor, painful sex, unusual discharge or bleeding needs assessment; smell cannot rule out an STI. When should I ask a clinician about vaginal odor? Ask about a new persistent odor, itching, burning, pain with sex, unusual discharge or bleeding outside your period. Pelvic pain with discharge, fever or possible pregnancy needs urgent same-day advice. Severe pain, fainting, heavy bleeding with pelvic pain or severe illness needs immediate emergency care. Why can the vagina smell tangy or sour? Lactobacilli and normal acidity can contribute to a mild familiar sour scent. It is a description, not proof of healthy bacteria. A new persistent change or other symptoms should be assessed; neither a home pH result nor smell diagnoses infection. Why can there be a copper-like smell? Blood, commonly menstrual blood, can smell metallic. Odor does not determine the cause of bleeding. Bleeding after sex, between periods or after menopause should be checked rather than assumed to be a harmless scratch. Does the strongest fishy smell mean trichomoniasis? No. Smell strength cannot distinguish trichomoniasis from BV or another cause. Trichomoniasis may cause no symptoms and requires testing. It is treatable, but partner treatment and follow-up matter because reinfection is possible. Is an ammonia-like smell always dehydration? No. Concentrated urine or residue can contribute, but odor does not diagnose dehydration, a UTI or vaginal infection. Urea is different from ammonia. Urinary burning or frequency needs advice; fever, back pain under the ribs or possible pregnancy with urinary symptoms requires urgent same-day assessment. Can I remove a forgotten tampon myself? Only if it comes out easily with clean hands. Do not use tools or force. Seek prompt help if uncertain or unable to remove it easily. Fever of 38°C or higher or systemic symptoms with a retained object need emergency assessment; easy removal must not delay medical help. Should I use washes to keep odor changing or eliminate it? No. A mild natural scent is expected, and daily changes are not required. Clean the external vulva gently, avoid douching or deodorants inside and follow product instructions. Persistent unusual odor needs assessment rather than masking or self-directed pH treatment.

title: Swollen labia: causes, treatment and when to seek help
description: Learn what can cause swollen labia, how infections differ from irritation or cysts, which comfort measures may help and when assessment is urgent.
body: The labia are the outer and inner folds of the vulva, around the vaginal opening; the vagina is the internal canal. Their size, shape and symmetry vary naturally. A new change in swelling, especially with pain, itching, discharge or a lump, needs attention to its cause rather than treatment based on appearance alone. Normal variation and symptoms to notice One labium may normally be larger than the other. Temporary changes can also occur with arousal or pregnancy-related blood flow. These do not explain every new swelling. Notice whether the change affects one side or both, appeared suddenly, follows a product or activity, or keeps returning. Associated symptoms can include itching, burning, soreness, changed vaginal discharge or smell, a lump, pain when walking or sitting, painful sex or stinging when urine touches irritated skin. None identifies a particular infection by itself. A persistent sore, bleeding skin or a changing patch or lump also deserves examination. Yeast infection is one possible cause Candida overgrowth can cause vulval redness, itching, soreness, swelling and sometimes thick discharge. Recent antibiotics, pregnancy, poorly controlled diabetes or reduced immunity can increase the likelihood, but many people have no obvious trigger. These symptoms overlap with other conditions, so having had thrush before does not make self-diagnosis reliable. Confirmed yeast infection is treated with an appropriate antifungal; severe, recurrent or persistent symptoms may need testing and a different plan. In pregnancy, current CDC guidance recommends a topical azole for seven days and advises against oral fluconazole. Check treatment with your maternity clinician or pharmacist. An asymptomatic partner does not routinely need treatment for uncomplicated thrush; a partner with symptoms should be assessed. Bacterial vaginosis is not a fungal infection Bacterial vaginosis, or BV, is a change in the balance of vaginal bacteria, not yeast overgrowth. It may cause thin discharge and a fishy smell, or no symptoms. Marked swelling or pain should not automatically be labelled BV; another cause or more than one condition may be present. BV is not proof of poor hygiene or infidelity. Symptomatic BV is treated with clinician-selected antibiotics, not antifungal cream. Recurrence is common. Partner advice has changed with newer evidence: 2025–2026 guidance supports discussing concurrent treatment of ongoing partners, especially with recurrent symptomatic BV, while evidence and recommendations differ by situation. Ask the sexual-health clinician about the appropriate plan for you and your partners; do not share medicines or assume partners never need care. Trichomoniasis and other sexually transmitted infections Trichomoniasis is caused by a parasite transmitted through sexual contact. It can cause vulval irritation, altered discharge, odour or painful urination, but many people have few or no symptoms. Testing distinguishes it from yeast or BV; colour or smell cannot do that. Other infections, including genital herpes, can also cause vulval symptoms and need their own assessment. Trichomoniasis requires an effective prescribed medicine and treatment of current sexual partners, even when they have no symptoms. Avoid sex until everyone has completed treatment and symptoms have resolved. Testing for other STIs is advised; women treated for trichomoniasis are generally retested at about three months because reinfection is common. Ask for individual pregnancy and follow-up advice rather than using leftover tablets or a vaginal antifungal. Contact irritation, allergy and friction Perfumed soaps, detergents, wipes, deodorants, some pads, latex, spermicides or a lubricant can irritate sensitive vulval skin or trigger an allergy. A product previously tolerated can still become a problem. Stop a suspected irritant and tell the clinician what you have used. Dermatitis and other skin conditions may need specific treatment; do not start steroid cream for unexplained swelling without advice. Sexual activity with insufficient lubrication can cause friction and soreness. Stop if it hurts; consent and comfort take priority. When symptoms have settled and no treatment restriction applies, a suitable unperfumed lubricant may reduce friction. Check compatibility with condoms and any medicine, since some oils and creams weaken latex. If latex or spermicide seems responsible, ask about suitable alternatives that retain the protection you need. A one-sided lump may be a Bartholin cyst or abscess Bartholin glands lie near either side of the vaginal opening. A blocked duct can form a small, painless cyst; infection may produce a very painful abscess, swelling, pus or fever. A growing painful lump, hot or red swelling, or feeling unwell needs urgent same-day assessment. Do not squeeze, puncture or drain it yourself. Have any new vulval lump examined. A new Bartholin-area mass at age 40 or older, or after menopause, needs particular attention; the clinician may recommend a biopsy to rule out uncommon malignancy. A small confirmed cyst may need observation and gentle warm-water comfort measures. A symptomatic cyst or abscess may require a drainage procedure, a catheter or another treatment, sometimes with antibiotics; removal of the gland is not automatic. How the cause is assessed and treated A clinician asks about onset, pain, discharge, products, medicines, previous episodes, medical conditions, sexual exposure and possible pregnancy, then examines with your consent. You can request a chaperone and ask to pause. Vaginal or skin samples, urine tests or STI tests may be selected according to the findings; not everyone needs every test. A biopsy is a targeted investigation when a lesion looks concerning, a diagnosis remains unclear or symptoms fail to respond; it is not the routine test for every infection. Treatment follows the cause: antifungal for yeast, appropriate antibiotics for BV or trichomoniasis, removal of irritants and selected prescribed skin treatment, or cyst care. Reassessment matters if symptoms persist, worsen or recur rather than repeatedly treating presumed thrush. Gentle comfort measures and remedies to avoid Gently rinse the external vulva with lukewarm water and pat dry; avoid scrubbing, repeated washing, vaginal douching and scented products. Comfortable loose clothing and breathable underwear may reduce rubbing. A cool pack wrapped in a soft cloth can briefly soothe external irritation; do not place ice directly on skin or insert a pack into the vagina. For a diagnosed uncomplicated cyst, warm rather than hot water may help comfort, without delaying care for an abscess. Pain relief should suit your health, pregnancy status and other medicines; ask a pharmacist or clinician if unsure. Yogurt and probiotic products are not proven substitutes for treatment of yeast or BV. Do not insert garlic, thyme preparations, tea tree oil, coconut oil or oregano oil, or assume a natural product is safe: they can irritate or cause allergy and do not reliably treat the cause. Avoid multiple over-the-counter creams that may worsen symptoms or obscure the diagnosis. Recovery, follow-up and urgent symptoms Many causes are treatable, but recovery depends on the diagnosis and swelling can recur. Arrange assessment for a new lump, persistent or recurrent swelling, unusual discharge or smell, sores, skin changes or pain. In pregnancy, contact your maternity clinician about new concerning genital symptoms before self-treatment. Keep the recommended follow-up and ask what to do if the first treatment does not help. Seek urgent same-day care for a rapidly enlarging painful lump, fever, spreading redness, pus, or pelvic pain with unusual discharge or possible pregnancy. Seek immediate emergency care for sudden severe pelvic or abdominal pain, fainting or collapse, heavy bleeding, confusion, breathing difficulty or acute inability to urinate. Swelling with throat or tongue symptoms or breathing difficulty may be a serious allergic reaction. Do not wait for a home remedy or an app entry to confirm the cause. Labial size varies normally, but new swelling with symptoms needs its cause assessed. Yeast, bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis are different conditions with different treatment and partner advice. Avoid irritants, painful friction, douching and unproven inserted remedies; comfort measures do not replace diagnosis. A painful growing lump or fever needs same-day care; severe pain, collapse, breathing problems or inability to urinate needs immediate help. What symptoms can accompany swollen labia? Itching, burning, soreness, altered discharge or smell, a lump and pain when walking, sitting, urinating or having sex may occur. No single symptom proves a particular infection. Persistent sores, bleeding skin or changing patches also need examination. What can cause the swelling? Possible causes include yeast infection, bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, contact irritation or allergy, a Bartholin cyst or abscess, and friction. BV involves bacterial imbalance, not fungus. Other skin disorders or infections can look similar. Can allergy cause swollen labia? Yes. Latex, spermicides, scented products or other contact substances can cause irritation or allergy. Stop the suspected trigger and seek assessment if symptoms persist. Throat or tongue swelling, breathing difficulty or collapse needs immediate emergency care. How is the cause diagnosed? History and examination guide selected swabs, urine or STI tests. Biopsy is considered for particular concerning, unclear or persistent lesions rather than every case. Tell the clinician about products, medicines, sexual exposure and possible pregnancy. Is swelling on one side always a Bartholin cyst? No. A cyst is one possibility, but any new lump should be examined. A rapidly growing painful lump, pus or fever needs same-day care. A new Bartholin-area mass at age 40 or older or after menopause may need biopsy. Do not drain it yourself. Can I use a yeast treatment during pregnancy? Ask your maternity clinician or pharmacist to confirm the cause and treatment. For pregnancy-related yeast infection, CDC recommends a topical azole for seven days and advises against oral fluconazole. Swelling alone does not confirm thrush. Does my partner need treatment? For trichomoniasis, current sexual partners need treatment and sex should wait until treatment is completed and symptoms have resolved. Uncomplicated thrush does not routinely require treatment of an asymptomatic partner. Newer BV guidance supports discussing concurrent care for ongoing partners, especially with recurrent symptoms; a clinician should choose the plan. Will yogurt, herbs or a cold pack cure it? A wrapped cool pack may soothe external irritation, but does not treat the underlying cause. Yogurt, probiotics and inserted herbal or essential-oil products are not reliable cures and may irritate. Persistent, worsening or urgent symptoms need clinical care.

title: How to use a vaginal pessary medicine safely
description: Preparation, gentle insertion, leakage, wetting, storage and periods: follow the instructions for your exact vaginal medicine, not one rule for every product.
body: A vaginal pessary or suppository is a medicine placed inside the vagina; it is different from a reusable support pessary for prolapse. Products vary in how they dissolve or release medicine, how much is absorbed and how they are inserted. They are not all faster than oral medicine or intended to act throughout the body. Your own pack leaflet and clinician’s instructions take priority. First identify the medicine and the route Check the medicine name, strength, prescribed dose, timing, expiry date and the words indicating vaginal use. Do not swallow a vaginal product or interchange vaginal and rectal routes. Antifungal, hormone and other vaginal medicines have different purposes and precautions; similar appearance does not make them interchangeable. Ask a pharmacist to demonstrate using the supplied instructions if anything is unclear. Tell the prescriber about pregnancy or possible pregnancy, allergies, other medicines and unexplained symptoms. Do not assume a medicine is suitable in pregnancy because it goes into the vagina. If helping someone else, obtain their consent, protect privacy and follow professional advice rather than forcing insertion. Prepare hands, supplies and the external skin Have the correct medicine, its leaflet and any specified applicator ready on a clean surface. A clean towel and an unscented pad or liner may be useful. Wash and dry your hands before handling the medicine, then open the wrapper when ready; avoid touching it to unclean surfaces. If washing is needed, gently clean the external vulval skin with warm water; mild unperfumed soap may be tolerated outside, but stop products that irritate. Do not put soap, cleansing fluid or water inside the vagina or douche. The vagina does not need internal washing before a dose; perfumed wipes, deodorants and repeated scrubbing can irritate. Insert gently using the method for that product Some products use a prefilled applicator, others need loading into one, and some are inserted with a clean finger. Follow the exact leaflet for assembly and loading. During pregnancy, certain products such as clotrimazole pessaries should be inserted without an applicator; this is not a rule to transfer to every vaginal medicine. Confirm your own instructions with the maternity team or pharmacist. Choose the advised comfortable position, often lying with knees bent or standing with knees gently bent and feet apart. If an applicator is appropriate, guide it only as far as comfortably instructed; do not force it or aim for an arbitrary depth. Release the medicine as directed, usually by pressing the plunger to its stop, then withdraw the applicator. Stop and ask for help if insertion causes pain, resistance or bleeding. After insertion and applicator care Wash your hands afterwards. Dispose of wrappers and a single-use applicator as instructed, safely away from children; do not flush it. A disposable applicator must not be reused or shared. A medicine’s applicator design may differ from another pack, even for a similar treatment. Only clean and reuse an applicator if its manufacturer explicitly permits this. Follow the specified disassembly, washing, rinsing, drying and storage steps. Do not invent a boiling, disinfectant or sterilizing method. If a device is damaged, incomplete or the directions are unclear, ask a pharmacist before the next dose. Leakage, residue and bedtime use Some leakage or residue is common with particular products, and a pad or liner may protect clothing. Bedtime may reduce leakage for some medicines, but prescribed timing and frequency still apply; not every dose can simply be moved to bedtime. Residue alone does not necessarily mean the treatment failed. An intact tablet or large undissolved pieces coming out is different from expected residue. Ask a pharmacist whether the dose may have been ineffective; do not automatically insert another or double the next dose. A new offensive smell, worsening pain, bleeding or unusual discharge should not be dismissed as harmless medicine leakage. Should a pessary be wetted before insertion? There is no universal instruction to dip vaginal medicines in water. Use water only if the specific product leaflet or clinician says to. For example, the Fluomizin tablet instructions allow a drop of water for a very dry vagina; this does not authorize soaking other products or adding oil, soap or a lubricant. If dryness makes insertion difficult or tablets repeatedly remain intact, ask for advice about the medicine and a suitable method. Do not force insertion, break or crush the dose, or add a vaginal moisturizer or another medicine without checking compatibility. Persistent dryness or pain may itself need assessment. Storage and keeping the medicine intact Read the labelled storage conditions and keep the medicine in its original packaging, away from children and pets. Protect it from unsuitable heat and moisture as directed. Refrigeration is not a general requirement: some products have a temperature limit, while others need no special storage conditions. Do not freeze or refrigerate a product merely because it is called a suppository. Ask a pharmacist what to do if it has softened, crumbled, leaked from packaging or been stored incorrectly. Check expiry and packaging integrity; do not improvise repairs or combine broken fragments to guess a dose. Periods, tampons and completing treatment Whether to use a medicine during menstruation depends on the product. Current clotrimazole guidance says not to use pessaries during a period; Fluomizin instructions advise pausing and resuming afterwards. Other prescribed vaginal treatments may differ. If bleeding begins during a course, ask how to handle the schedule rather than following a blanket continue-or-stop rule. Tampons may absorb medicine and reduce effectiveness; many vaginal treatments advise a pad or liner instead and prohibit other intravaginal products. Check instructions about menstrual cups, intercourse, condoms and diaphragms too: some medicines affect latex protection. Follow the prescribed course and any planned pauses; do not shorten, extend or repeat treatment or double a missed dose without the appropriate instructions. When to get further help Ask for advice if you cannot use the product comfortably, symptoms persist beyond its stated review point or keep returning, or you are unsure about a dose. New unexplained bleeding, sores, urinary pain or a changed discharge needs clinical assessment rather than another assumed thrush treatment. Fever, chills or worsening pelvic pain warrants prompt same-day advice; severe pelvic or abdominal pain, heavy bleeding, fainting or collapse needs immediate emergency assessment, especially if pregnancy is possible. Sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, tongue or throat, difficulty breathing or swallowing, or collapse after a medicine can be a serious allergic reaction: get immediate emergency help and do not take another dose while awaiting urgent advice. Do not wait for the course to finish. Bring the pack or a list of medicines when seeking help; careful technique cannot guarantee painless use or exclude another cause of symptoms. Read the instructions for the exact medicine, route and applicator; vaginal products are not interchangeable. Wash hands and clean only the external skin as needed; never wash or soap inside the vagina. Insert gently without forcing; pregnancy may change the applicator method for a particular product. Leakage, wetting, storage, period use and applicator reuse all depend on the product; do not automatically redose. Persistent symptoms need review; severe pain, heavy bleeding, collapse or signs of a serious allergy need immediate help. Is leakage after a vaginal pessary normal? Some residue or leakage is expected with certain products and a liner may help. Follow the medicine’s timing instructions. An intact tablet or large undissolved pieces, worsening symptoms, offensive discharge or bleeding needs advice; do not automatically use another dose. Can I wet a pessary to make insertion easier? Only when its own instructions permit it. Some tablets have a specific water instruction for marked dryness, while others do not. Do not routinely soak medicines or add oil, soap or another product; ask if dryness or pain makes use difficult. How do I stop the medicine breaking or melting before use? Follow the storage label and keep the original packaging intact. Refrigeration is not suitable or necessary for every product. Ask a pharmacist about a damaged or incorrectly stored dose rather than crushing it, repairing it or guessing a replacement amount. Can I use a vaginal pessary during my period? It depends on the medicine. Some current product instructions say to avoid use during menstruation or pause and resume; other treatments differ. Ask about your exact course if bleeding starts. Do not use an older generic instruction as permission for every product. Can I use a tampon at the same time? Many vaginal medicines say not to, because tampons can absorb medicine; a pad or liner may be recommended. Check guidance for cups and other intravaginal products too, and whether the medicine affects condoms or diaphragms. Follow the product-specific advice. Does every vaginal medicine need an applicator? No. Some use a supplied applicator, some a prefilled device and some a clean finger. Pregnancy changes instructions for certain products, including clotrimazole. Ask rather than changing the device or applying one medicine’s method to another. Should I wash inside my vagina first? No. Wash and dry your hands, and gently clean the external vulval skin if needed. Do not douche or put soap or cleansing water inside the vagina. Follow applicator-cleaning instructions separately; cleaning a device does not mean washing inside your body. When should I seek urgent help? Fever, chills or worsening pelvic pain needs prompt same-day advice. Severe pelvic or abdominal pain, heavy bleeding, fainting or collapse needs immediate emergency care, especially with possible pregnancy. Sudden airway or mouth swelling, trouble breathing or swallowing, or collapse after medicine also needs immediate emergency help; do not wait for another dose or completion of the course.

title: Period-related weight changes: bloating, fluid and when to seek help
description: Weight and bloating can change around a period. Learn about fluid, appetite, bowel symptoms, magnesium uncertainty and safer treatment choices without weight blame.
body: Feeling puffy, having tighter clothes or seeing a temporary scale change around your period does not automatically mean you have gained body fat. Fluid, bowel contents and appetite can contribute, but there is no single number of kilograms that is normal for everyone. Notice your own pattern and seek help for persistent, marked or distressing changes rather than assuming every change is menstrual. How much change is normal? Some people notice bloating or weight changes before or during bleeding, while others do not. These symptoms often ease after a period begins or ends, but timing varies. Having a symptom does not necessarily mean you have clinically significant premenstrual syndrome, or PMS; the recurring pattern and effect on daily life matter. Universal claims that everyone gains 1.5–3 kg, or that 90% have PMS and 92% retain fluid, are not reliable personal rules. In a 2023 observational study of 42 adults, average weight during menstruation was about 0.45 kg higher than in the comparison phase, mainly alongside increased extracellular water. This small study is an example, not a personal target, safe upper limit or prediction for every body. Temporary water changes and a sustained trend are different; do not assume that a large or continuing change will disappear after bleeding. Hormonal changes and fluid retention Estrogen and progesterone change across the cycle and influence fluid regulation. Sensitivity to normal hormonal changes may contribute to PMS, but its exact cause is not fully understood. Puffiness in the breasts, abdomen, hands or feet can accompany a cycle-related pattern; a higher scale reading from fluid is not the same as new body fat. The sequence is more complicated than all hormones rising together a week before a period or a single fall explaining every symptom. Swelling can also reflect medicines or thyroid, kidney, liver or heart conditions. Persistent, worsening, unusually extensive or one-sided swelling deserves assessment instead of a hormonal assumption. Bloating, cramps and bowel symptoms Bloating is a full or swollen abdominal feeling and may occur without a major weight change. Gas, constipation and fluid can contribute; diarrhea or nausea may also accompany periods. Prostaglandins made in the uterine lining promote uterine contractions and cramps. These symptoms do not establish a new increase in fat, and they do not follow one mandatory five-day or whole-period timetable. Mild familiar symptoms can be managed, but severe or worsening pain, persistent bowel changes, blood in stool or continuing bloating need review. Conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome or endometriosis can overlap with menstrual symptoms. Do not label every episode of diarrhea, constipation or abdominal pain normal solely because you are bleeding. Appetite, sweet cravings and metabolism Appetite and food preferences can change around a period. Hormones and neurotransmitter pathways, including serotonin, may be involved, but a craving does not measure serotonin or prove that sugar is needed as treatment. Nor does one hormone level make everyone overeat. Research on cycle-related energy use varies and does not justify a fixed extra-calorie rule for everyone. Changes in eating over time can affect weight, but a brief scale rise cannot reveal how much is food, fluid or bowel contents. Avoid shame, skipping meals or compensatory restriction. Regular balanced meals and satisfying snacks, such as fruit with a protein-containing food, can support intake; persistent loss of control, distress or restrictive eating deserves professional support. Magnesium: a nutrient, not a craving diagnosis The chain ‘a period lowers magnesium, causing dehydration that feels like hunger and makes you eat sweets and gain weight’ is not established. A sweet craving, thirst or bloating cannot diagnose magnesium deficiency. Magnesium supports muscle and nerve function and is found in foods such as legumes, nuts, seeds, whole grains and leafy vegetables. Some small studies have explored magnesium for premenstrual symptoms, but evidence is limited and it is not a routine cure for fluid retention, cravings or mood symptoms. Discuss supplements with a clinician or pharmacist, especially with kidney disease or other medicines. Supplements can cause diarrhea and cramps and interact with medicines; more is not necessarily better. Do not take a supplement just to force a lower scale reading. Movement, fatigue and other PMS symptoms Cramps, fatigue, poor sleep or discomfort can make activity harder. Adjust activity to how you feel: a gentle walk, stretching or other enjoyable movement may help, and regular activity across the month can support wellbeing. You do not need a compulsory 30-minute session despite pain, and resting when needed is not a failure or proof that you are gaining fat. Other possible symptoms include breast tenderness, headache or backache, acne, constipation or diarrhea, sleep problems, anxiety, tearfulness, irritability, mood swings, poor concentration and changed sexual interest. They vary between people and months. Severe emotional symptoms that disrupt work or relationships may indicate PMDD or another condition and deserve assessment, not dismissal as ordinary moodiness. Daily habits for comfort, not forced weight loss Drink regularly and enough for your needs; do not deliberately dehydrate yourself or force excessive water to ‘flush’ weight away. If a clinician has given you a fluid limit for a medical condition, follow that plan. Avoiding excess salt may help some fluid symptoms. Check foods you regularly eat rather than banning all prepared foods or whole food groups. Smaller, regular meals may be more comfortable. If fizzy drinks, lots of caffeine or particular foods reliably worsen bloating, try a measured change and keep nutritional variety. There is no universal two-week ban on all sugar, caffeine or gas-producing foods. Support sleep and stress management. Movement is for comfort and health, not sweating out fluid; replace fluids lost through activity rather than aiming for dehydration. Medicines and treatment choices Treatment depends on the cause and on which symptoms affect your life. A clinician may discuss appropriate pain relief, cognitive behavioral therapy, an SSRI or a suitable hormonal option for PMS or PMDD. Benefits, risks, contraception needs, pregnancy possibility and other conditions matter. Do not abruptly stop prescribed medicines or assume one treatment works for everyone. A prescription diuretic may help selected people with troublesome fluid symptoms, but ‘water tablets’ are not a routine weight-loss or self-treatment plan. Spironolactone, for example, can affect potassium and kidney function, interact with medicines such as NSAIDs, and is not usually recommended in pregnancy. Assessment and individualized monitoring are needed; do not borrow tablets, use detox products or change a prescribed dose to reduce menstrual weight. Tracking and arranging an assessment Record bleeding dates, bloating, bowel symptoms, appetite, sleep, mood and their effect on daily life for at least two cycles. Note whether symptoms settle and whether there is a symptom-free interval. If weight measurements are useful and not distressing, compare similar conditions and cycle stages; weighing is optional and should not become compulsive. A diary supports assessment but does not diagnose PMS or exclude other illness. Book a review if symptoms disrupt daily life, do not improve with self-care, become new or different, or persist outside the usual cycle pattern. Continuing abdominal swelling, unexplained weight change, reduced appetite, bleeding between periods or worsening pain also deserve assessment. A clinician can consider medicines and other causes and decide which examinations or tests are appropriate; not everyone needs a hormone panel or magnesium test. Symptoms that should not wait for the next period Get urgent same-day advice for sudden, painful, red or hot swelling, unexplained swelling in one leg, or bloating with fever, vomiting, significant abdominal pain or inability to pass stool or gas. Complete inability to urinate needs immediate emergency care. Possible pregnancy with pelvic pain or unusual bleeding needs urgent assessment even without a positive test; severe sudden pain, shoulder-tip pain with bleeding, fainting or collapse needs emergency help. Swelling with breathlessness, chest pain, coughing blood, faintness or confusion needs emergency help. So do sudden severe abdominal pain, vomiting blood or severe breathing difficulty. Suicidal thoughts or a mental health crisis require immediate urgent help; if there is immediate danger or you cannot stay safe, use emergency services. Do not wait for bleeding to end or for a tracking pattern to improve before seeking care. Temporary fluid and bowel changes can affect weight around a period; no kilogram range is a universal normal limit. Cravings and bloating do not diagnose a hormone or magnesium deficiency and are not a reason for weight blame. Balanced meals, regular hydration, sleep and tolerable movement may help; do not force water loss or self-prescribe diuretics or supplements. Track symptoms over two cycles and seek assessment for persistent or disruptive changes, with immediate help for emergency symptoms. Why can my weight rise around a period? Fluid shifts, bloating, bowel contents and appetite changes may contribute. A short-term scale rise is not automatically new body fat. Timing and amount vary; marked, persistent or unusual changes need assessment rather than a universal normal-weight rule. Why do I want sweets or feel hungrier before bleeding? Preferences and appetite may change with the cycle, but no single hormone or serotonin level explains everyone’s experience. A craving is not a deficiency test or a need for sugar therapy. Eat regular balanced meals and seek support for distress or loss of control. How are period-related weight and bloating symptoms treated? Start with comfortable, balanced habits and assessment if symptoms persist or disrupt life. Treatment targets the cause; options may include pain relief, psychological or hormonal care. A prescribed diuretic is only for selected circumstances with safety review, not routine weight loss. Do not self-start water tablets or supplements. Can I prevent these changes? Regular tolerable activity, balanced meals, adequate fluids, sleep and reducing excess salt or personally identified bloating triggers may help. They cannot guarantee no symptoms. Do not force water intake, sweat out weight or adopt a universal two-week food ban. Keep a diary and ask for help if needed. Does magnesium cure fluid retention or sweet cravings? No reliable cure is established. Evidence for premenstrual supplements is limited; a craving does not diagnose low magnesium. Food sources can support a balanced diet. Discuss any supplement’s risks and interactions, particularly with kidney disease, rather than taking high doses or using it to lower weight. When should I get medical help? Persistent bloating, swelling, unexplained weight change, worsening pain or disruptive mood symptoms need review. Sudden or one-sided painful swelling or bloating with fever or vomiting needs same-day advice. Complete urinary retention, severe sudden pain, fainting, chest pain or breathing difficulty needs emergency help. Possible pregnancy with pain or unusual bleeding needs urgent assessment, and suicidal thoughts need immediate urgent help rather than waiting for a cycle to end.

title: Alexander disease: symptoms, diagnosis and care across the lifespan
description: Understand GFAP-related Alexander disease, age-related symptoms, genetic diagnosis, supportive care and the limits of the new US-approved treatment.
body: Alexander disease is a rare genetic condition affecting the brain and spinal cord. It can begin in infancy, childhood or adulthood, and its effects vary considerably. Assessment by a specialist team matters: a large head, feeding difficulty or a walking problem alone does not identify this disease. Treatment information has also changed. In September 2026, the US FDA approved the first medicine specifically for Alexander disease, while coordinated symptom care remains essential. What changes in Alexander disease? Alexander disease involves astrocytes, cells that help support other cells in the nervous system. A disease-causing change in the GFAP gene can lead to an abnormal build-up of proteins, including deposits called Rosenthal fibres. This disrupts the environment needed for healthy nerve function. It is classed among the leukodystrophies, disorders affecting the brain’s white matter and myelin, the insulating material around nerve fibres. However, it is not simply a general loss-of-myelin diagnosis: the GFAP-related astrocyte disorder and its particular clinical and imaging patterns matter. Published descriptions of about 500 reported cases are historical figures, not a reliable current count or a person’s risk. Symptoms form a spectrum Possible problems include muscle stiffness or spasms, delayed development or loss of acquired skills, seizures, feeding difficulties, poor growth, speech changes and impaired movement or coordination. Some people have an enlarged head or brain, and some develop hydrocephalus, an accumulation of fluid that can increase pressure. These are related assessment questions, not interchangeable diagnoses. Swallowing difficulty, an ineffective cough, sleep-related breathing problems and other changes in automatic body functions can also be important. Not everyone has every feature. Symptoms overlap with many other neurological conditions, so a list cannot establish Alexander disease or explain a new symptom without examination. In babies and younger children Early presentations may involve seizures, stiffness in the limbs, head enlargement and difficulties with development, feeding or growth. A rare neonatal presentation starts within the first month and can be severe. A clinician follows the child’s progress and head growth over time rather than interpreting one head measurement in isolation. Earlier onset is often associated with substantial needs, but age does not provide an individual timetable. Arrange assessment for loss of skills, new movement problems or feeding changes. The care plan should address comfort, nutrition, communication and development alongside investigations and disease-specific treatment discussions. In older children, adults and people over 65 Later presentations may be dominated by changes in speech or voice, swallowing, balance and coordination. Brainstem and spinal-cord involvement can contribute to stiffness, autonomic symptoms or sleep-related breathing problems. Head size and intellectual abilities may be relatively preserved, so an ordinary head size does not exclude the disease. Late-onset disease is not invariably mild. Some people progress slowly and others have considerable disability; symptoms can be mistaken for other neurological disorders. Diagnosis during life is possible even in older adults and does not depend on an autopsy. Terms such as infantile, juvenile, adult or type I/type II describe patterns, not rigid boundaries or guaranteed outcomes. GFAP changes and inheritance Alexander disease usually results from a new, or de novo, disease-causing GFAP variant. This means a person may be the first affected family member. It does not mean the condition is non-genetic, and it does not imply that a parent caused it through something they did during pregnancy. The inheritance pattern is autosomal dominant: one disease-causing copy can be enough. A person with such a variant can pass it to a child. Genetic counselling interprets the exact result, considers testing relatives and discusses future pregnancies. A negative parental blood test does not always make recurrence impossible, because a variant may be present in only some parental cells. Family-specific advice is more useful than a blanket reassurance. How specialists establish the diagnosis Assessment combines the person’s history, neurological examination, brain imaging and molecular testing. MRI can show patterns that suggest Alexander disease; the relevant pattern varies with age and may involve the brainstem or upper spinal cord as well as white matter. The specialist also considers other leukodystrophies, inflammatory conditions and structural causes that could explain the findings. A laboratory can use a blood sample for GFAP testing, a gene panel or broader sequencing, depending on the clinical question. This is not an ordinary blood count. A pathogenic or likely pathogenic result must fit the clinical assessment; a variant of uncertain significance is not by itself confirmation or exclusion. An inconclusive result may need expert review rather than assuming that no disorder is present. The September 2026 treatment update On 3 September 2026, the FDA approved Zanvastro, the brand name for zilganersen, for children and adults with Alexander disease in the United States. It is an antisense medicine designed to reduce production of GFAP protein. Older statements that there is no approved disease-specific treatment are therefore no longer accurate for the US. This approval is not a cure claim and does not establish access in every country. A specialist must discuss local authorization, availability, suitability and realistic goals. Treatment is administered by trained healthcare professionals into the fluid around the spinal cord through a lumbar puncture; it is not a medicine to obtain or inject independently. What the evidence does and does not show The approval study found a benefit in walking-speed change over 61 weeks in a selected subgroup aged five or older, with smaller amounts of motor-function evidence in younger children. This does not mean every person improves, that lost abilities return, or that a particular lifespan has been established. The label includes children under two, but direct data in that age group are limited; people aged 65 and over were not studied. The prescribing information describes risks including aseptic meningitis and lumbar-puncture-related effects, with vomiting, back pain, cough and headache among reported adverse reactions. Human pregnancy and breastfeeding data are lacking. Discuss these issues and the monitoring plan with the treating team. The NCT04849741 registry checked for this article lists the study as active but not recruiting; a continuing study is not automatically an open enrolment offer. Supportive care remains central A coordinated plan may involve neurology, genetics, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy. Seizure treatment, positioning, mobility aids, communication support and educational adjustments depend on the person’s needs. Care should be reviewed as abilities and priorities change rather than waiting for a crisis. Discuss pain, stiffness, sleep, breathing, fatigue and the practical work of daily care. Antibiotics are used for an infection when clinically appropriate, not automatically for every illness or as treatment for the GFAP change. Do not stop existing medicines or substitute supplements because a new disease-specific medicine is available. Feeding, swallowing and respiratory assessment Swallowing difficulties can make eating tiring or unsafe and contribute to poor nutrition, dehydration or chest infections. A swallowing specialist and dietitian can assess food and drink consistency, equipment and whether tube feeding is needed. Do not make major texture changes or force food or fluids without the individualized plan. Seek urgent assessment for trouble swallowing, coughing or choking with meals, food feeling stuck, repeated regurgitation, a wet-sounding voice, breathlessness after eating or repeated chest infections. In babies, distressed feeding or back arching also needs assessment. Report an ineffective cough or sleep breathing pauses to the team; emergency breathing signs need immediate action, not a routine appointment. Hydrocephalus and shunt care When hydrocephalus is confirmed, a neurosurgeon may recommend a shunt to drain fluid or another selected procedure. This addresses the fluid-pressure problem; it does not remove the underlying genetic disease. New headaches, vomiting, unusual sleepiness, vision or walking changes, or an infant’s tense soft spot or feeding changes need medical assessment. A person with a shunt needs a written plan for possible blockage or infection. Contact the care team immediately for redness or tenderness along the shunt, fever, headache, vomiting, neck stiffness, abdominal pain with an abdominal shunt, or unusual irritability or sleepiness in a baby. Shunt obstruction can require emergency surgery. Do not assume that deterioration is simply the expected course of Alexander disease. Outlook and conversations about the future Alexander disease can be progressive and life-limiting, but its course varies widely. Statements that every infant dies within a year or cannot live beyond six years are not appropriate predictions for an individual child. Later onset may be slower, but it also does not guarantee a mild course or normal lifespan. Ask the team which findings are relevant to this person, what changes to watch for and how treatment goals will be measured. New treatment evidence does not yet settle every long-term question. Palliative care can support comfort, symptoms and family decisions alongside active treatment; discussing it does not mean abandoning care. Family support and useful appointment questions Bring the genetic report, MRI reports, a medicine list and a brief timeline of development or new symptoms. Ask who coordinates the plan, how to reach the team between visits, what to do during a seizure or feeding problem, and whether relatives need counselling. Older children and adults should be included in decisions in a way that fits their communication needs. Rare-disease services and patient organizations can help families find information, connect with others and discuss practical support. GARD lists Alexander-disease and leukodystrophy organizations, but a listing does not guarantee a service, treatment place or financial help. Ask the clinical team to check research opportunities and their current recruitment status. Seizures: know the emergency plan Call emergency services for a first seizure, a seizure lasting longer than usual, or one exceeding five minutes when the usual duration is unknown. Also call if the person does not regain full consciousness, has repeated seizures without recovery, is seriously injured, or has trouble breathing afterwards. A known seizure disorder should have an individualized rescue plan; only give rescue medicine as instructed and trained. Protect the person from nearby hazards, cushion the head, time the episode and stay with them. After convulsions stop, place them on their side when safe. Do not put objects or fingers in the mouth, and do not offer food or drink until recovery. Record what happened for the team without delaying emergency care. Breathing and sudden deterioration Get emergency help for an adult with severe breathing difficulty, a tight or heavy chest, pain spreading to the arms, back, neck or jaw, very pale, blue or grey lips or skin, or sudden confusion. In a child, breathing difficulty, those colour changes, sudden confusion, or being floppy or abnormally unresponsive are independent emergency signs. New or worsening adult breathlessness also needs prompt assessment even when it is not severe. Possible meningitis needs emergency assessment, including after intrathecal treatment; do not decide at home whether it is drug-related or infectious. In adults and children aged five or older, warning alternatives include a very high or low temperature or feeling hot, cold or shivery, a very painful headache, confusion or unclear speech, a stiff neck with light intolerance, a non-fading rash or a first seizure. Do not wait for a rash or every sign. Do not drive yourself: arrange another driver or an ambulance. Urgent changes in babies and young children For possible meningitis in a child under five, get emergency help for a very high temperature, including 38°C or more under three months or 39°C or more at three to six months; a temperature below 36°C, coldness or shivering; an unusual weak, high-pitched or continuous cry; a non-fading rash; or not responding normally, not feeding, floppiness, difficulty waking or more sleepiness than usual. Concern about meningitis is itself reason to seek immediate assessment. A familiar diagnosis should not make new illness seem routine. Use the child’s care plan and tell emergency staff about Alexander disease, medicines, recent spinal treatment and any shunt. If the child seems seriously unwell, do not wait for several signs, the next appointment or an app record before seeking help. Alexander disease is a GFAP-related disorder with presentations from infancy into late adulthood. Newly arising variants are common, but inherited disease and family counselling still matter. Diagnosis combines clinical assessment, MRI and meaningful genetic-result interpretation. September 2026 US approval of zilganersen changes treatment options, without establishing a cure or worldwide access. Individualized supportive care, realistic prognosis discussions and a clear emergency plan remain essential. What symptoms can Alexander disease cause? Symptoms vary with age and the individual. They can include developmental delay or loss of skills, seizures, stiffness, feeding problems, enlarged head size, speech or swallowing difficulty, poor coordination and sleep or breathing problems. None of these alone confirms the diagnosis. What causes it, and can it be inherited? Disease-causing GFAP changes affect supporting cells in the nervous system. Many arise newly, but the condition has an autosomal-dominant inheritance pattern and can be passed on. A genetics team should explain the exact result and family-specific testing and recurrence questions. Does a blood test alone diagnose Alexander disease? A blood sample may be used for molecular genetic testing, but diagnosis brings together symptoms, examination, MRI and interpretation of the result. A routine blood test does not diagnose it, and a variant of uncertain significance is not a definite answer. Is treatment available now? Yes. The US FDA approved zilganersen, sold as Zanvastro, in September 2026 for children and adults. Access elsewhere must be checked locally. It is specialist intrathecal treatment with benefits and risks, not a proven cure, and supportive care remains necessary. Can an adult have Alexander disease with a normal-sized head? Yes. Later disease may mainly affect swallowing, speech, balance, movement or automatic body functions. Normal head size does not rule it out, and diagnosis can be made during life even in older adults. Specialist assessment distinguishes other causes. Does the diagnosis predict a fixed lifespan? No. Alexander disease can be serious and life-limiting, but age alone cannot provide a deadline. Individual findings and changes over time inform discussion; neither later onset nor a new treatment guarantees a particular outcome. Does everyone need a feeding tube or a shunt? No. Feeding support depends on swallowing safety, nutrition and the person’s needs. A shunt is considered for a confirmed fluid-pressure problem, not for every person with Alexander disease. These decisions require the relevant specialist team. When should we seek urgent help? Call emergency services for a first or prolonged seizure, seizures without full recovery, serious injury or breathing trouble after a seizure; follow the specific thresholds and plan above. Emergency breathing, colour, consciousness or possible meningitis signs also need immediate help. Seek urgent assessment for swallowing changes and immediate team advice for possible shunt trouble. Do not wait for several signs or drive yourself in an emergency.

title: Vaginal air: common causes and when to seek care
description: Air leaving the vagina is often ordinary, including during sex or movement. Understand pelvic-floor concerns, six fistula types, warning signs and individualized care.
body: Air can enter the vagina and later escape with a brief sound or bubbling sensation. Often called vaginal wind or queefing, this is usually trapped air rather than intestinal gas. It is not a sign of poor hygiene or something to feel ashamed about. Persistent troublesome air or accompanying pain, unusual discharge or leakage deserves attention; sound alone does not diagnose a fistula. How ordinary vaginal air happens Penetration and changes of sexual position can move air into and out of the vagina. It may escape during movement, withdrawal or orgasm. Exercise, stretching and ordinary changes of position can also release trapped air; it does not have to happen during sex to be harmless. Tampon insertion or removal and a pelvic examination can introduce air too. Brief, painless air without unusual leakage or other symptoms usually needs no treatment. A change that worries you, happens frequently or affects daily life can still be discussed with a clinician. Oral sex and deliberate air blowing Oral sexual activity can be a trigger, but deliberately blowing or forcing air into the vagina should be avoided. Rare case reports describe air entering the bloodstream, an air embolism, particularly during pregnancy or the early period after birth. This is different from ordinary trapped air escaping. Do not use a pump, nozzle or forced blowing to test or clear vaginal air. Stop activity that hurts, communicate about comfort and consent, and follow any pregnancy or postoperative restrictions. Sudden chest pain, breathing difficulty, fainting or collapse during or after such activity needs immediate emergency help. Pelvic-floor changes need individual assessment The pelvic floor supports the bladder, bowel and reproductive organs. Changes after childbirth or menopause, weakness or coordination problems may be associated with vaginal air, but the noise alone does not prove muscle damage, looseness or a particular diagnosis. A pelvic-health professional can assess associated urinary leakage, a bulge, bowel symptoms or sexual pain. Some people benefit from strengthening, while tight or overactive muscles may first need relaxation and coordination work. Repeated Kegels, tightening products or surgery are not universal treatments for vaginal sounds. What a vaginal fistula means A fistula is an abnormal connection between the vagina and another organ. It is a less common explanation for vaginal gas. It may develop after a difficult birth or obstetric injury, pelvic surgery, trauma, infection, pelvic cancer or radiation; inflammatory bowel disease and diverticulitis are other possible contexts. Crohn’s disease is an important bowel-related cause; fistulas can also occur with other bowel conditions, including less often ulcerative colitis. A fistula is not itself a sexually transmitted infection. Its cause and the organs involved need professional assessment rather than assumptions based on a sound. Three urinary connections A vesicovaginal fistula connects the bladder and vagina. A ureterovaginal fistula connects a ureter (the tube carrying urine from a kidney to the bladder) to the vagina. A urethrovaginal fistula connects the urethra, which carries urine from the bladder out of the body, and the vagina. These urinary types can cause urine to leak through the vagina, sometimes continuously. They do not all cause gas or stool leakage. Ordinary urinary incontinence has other possible causes, so examination is needed to establish where fluid is coming from. Three bowel connections A rectovaginal fistula joins the rectum, the final part of the large bowel, to the vagina. A colovaginal fistula joins the colon to the vagina. An enterovaginal fistula connects the small intestine to the vagina. Bowel connections may allow gas or stool to pass through the vagina. Birth injuries, bowel inflammation, surgery, cancer, radiation or diverticular disease can contribute, depending on the type. Stool in urine is not a general defining symptom of a vaginal fistula; report it promptly because it may indicate a different abnormal connection or other problem. Symptoms that need review and urgent help Seek prompt assessment for urine or stool leaking from the vagina, recurrent urinary or vaginal infections, unusual or foul-smelling discharge, irritation around the vagina or anus, painful sex or persistent troublesome air. Diarrhoea, nausea or abdominal discomfort can accompany an illness but do not identify a fistula by themselves. New leakage after birth or a pelvic procedure needs prompt contact with the treating team. Pelvic pain with fever or chills, vomiting, difficulty passing urine or stool, unusual bleeding or possible pregnancy needs urgent same-day advice. Get immediate emergency care if abdominal or pelvic pain is severe, worsening or hurts when you move or touch the area, or if pelvic pain comes with dizziness or fainting, shoulder-tip pain, heavy bleeding, breathing difficulty or sudden confusion. Collapse also needs immediate emergency help. Do not wait for a routine appointment or try to exercise the symptoms away. How clinicians investigate Explain the timing, relationship to movement or sex, odour, pain, fluid or stool leakage, urinary and bowel symptoms, births, operations and relevant illnesses. Examination is explained and performed with consent; you can request a chaperone and ask to pause. A clinician may identify a fistula on examination or arrange specialist review. Tests are selected for the suspected connection and may include urine or blood tests, a medical dye test, cystoscopy to look inside the bladder, bowel endoscopy or imaging such as ultrasound, CT or MRI where appropriate. Not everyone needs all tests. Do not put dye or instruments inside yourself to try to locate a fistula. Treatment and practical comfort Ordinary painless air usually needs reassurance rather than medicine or surgery. If a movement or position bothers you, try a comfortable alternative without giving up all activity. Avoid douching, deodorants or internal tightening products; use gentle external hygiene and seek help for pain or skin irritation. A confirmed fistula needs a specialist plan based on its location, size, cause and tissue health. Selected small urinary fistulas may heal with medically supervised bladder drainage or ureteral stenting; infection or bowel inflammation needs appropriate treatment. Many fistulas need surgical repair, sometimes after inflammation settles. Neither observation nor surgery is right for every case, and home exercises cannot close an abnormal tract. Recovery, outlook and wellbeing Repair often helps, but healing is not guaranteed and some fistulas recur or need more than one procedure. Follow the team’s catheter, wound, bowel-care and follow-up instructions. After repair, resume vaginal penetration, tampons or other insertion only when cleared; timing is individual. Untreated leakage can irritate skin, contribute to infection and affect relationships, mood and confidence. Ask for practical continence and emotional support as well as treatment. You deserve respectful care without blame. Agree what changes to report and when to seek urgent help; occasional ordinary vaginal air does not automatically require surgery. Brief painless vaginal air can occur during sex, exercise or everyday movement and is not caused by poor hygiene. Do not deliberately blow or force air into the vagina; sudden chest pain, breathing difficulty or collapse needs emergency help. Pelvic-floor treatment depends on assessment; strengthening is not appropriate for every person. Urinary fistulas usually leak urine; bowel fistulas may pass gas or stool through the vagina. Six types are defined by their connected organs. Persistent pain, unusual discharge or vaginal urine or stool leakage deserves assessment; treatment and recovery are individualized. Can oral sex cause vaginal air? It can be a trigger, but never deliberately blow air into the vagina. Rare air-embolism reports, especially during pregnancy or soon after birth, are different from ordinary air escaping. Sudden chest pain, breathlessness, fainting or collapse needs immediate emergency care. Can sexual activity cause the sound? Yes. Movement and position changes can introduce air, which can escape on withdrawal, movement or orgasm. Painless air alone is usually ordinary. Stop painful activity and seek review if there is unusual discharge, fluid or stool leakage or other concerning symptoms. How can I prevent it? It cannot always be prevented and ordinary air often needs no treatment. A comfortable change of position may help if you wish. Do not force air, douche or use tightening products; ask for individualized pelvic-floor advice instead of assuming everyone needs Kegels. When should I see a clinician? Arrange assessment for frequent bothersome air, pain during sex, unusual odour or discharge, recurrent infections or vaginal urine or stool leakage. New leakage after birth or surgery needs prompt contact. Fever with pelvic pain needs same-day advice; severe pain, heavy bleeding, fainting or breathing difficulty needs immediate emergency help. Does air outside sex mean a fistula? No. Exercise, stretching and everyday movements can also release trapped air. A fistula is one possible cause, especially with urine or stool leakage or other symptoms, but timing or sound alone cannot diagnose it. Does a fistula always need an operation? Many need repair, but selected small urinary fistulas may heal with clinician-supervised drainage or a stent and treatment of the cause. The type, tissue health and symptoms determine the plan. Do not wait for it to close without assessment or attempt a home procedure. Will pelvic-floor exercises cure vaginal air? There is no universal cure. An assessment may identify weakness needing strengthening or overactivity needing relaxation first. Fistulas and other illnesses require their own treatment. Avoid repeated squeezing or painful exercises without advice.

title: Changes in penis size: causes and care
description: Separate ordinary variation from persistent shortening, buried appearance, changes after prostate surgery and Peyronie’s disease. Learn when assessment and treatment may help.
body: The penis can look different depending on temperature, erection firmness and how much of its base is visible. A lasting change is different from a brief change when relaxed. There is no universal two-centimetre rule for what is normal or safe. Size does not define worth or sexual satisfaction, but pain, curvature or erection problems can affect sex and deserve respectful care. Ordinary variation or a persistent change? A relaxed penis changes with temperature and other circumstances; comparing a cold, relaxed appearance with an erection does not establish shortening. Reduced erection firmness can also change apparent size. The visible part may differ from the length of the underlying shaft. Arrange review for a new persistent change, a lump, pain, curvature, difficulty with erections or problems passing urine. Avoid repeated forceful measuring or comparison with online images. A clinician can assess the change in a consistent way and discuss what matters to you. Age, circulation and scarring With age, conditions affecting blood vessels, nerves or hormone levels can alter erections and the way the penis looks or functions. This does not mean that every older person inevitably loses a set amount of length or that one mechanism explains every change. Injury and abnormal scar tissue can also change shape or restrict stretching. Not every episode of sex or exercise causes such damage. A new change should not simply be labelled ageing; new testicular changes or a lump also warrant assessment rather than assuming they are normal. Body tissue and a buried appearance More tissue around the pubic area can cover part of a normally sized shaft, making the visible penis look shorter. Adult acquired buried penis can involve surrounding skin, inflammation and scarring as well as body fat; it is not necessarily true shortening of the erectile tissue. Tell a clinician about difficulty cleaning, urine trapping, irritated skin, recurrent infections or sexual difficulties. Individual weight and health support may help, and some people need specialist treatment. Avoid blame or promises that weight loss alone will fix every case; do not postpone assessment until your weight changes. Changes after prostate surgery Some people notice shortening or altered erections after radical prostatectomy, the removal of the prostate for cancer; others do not. Nerve and blood-flow changes and tissue responses may contribute. The outcome varies with the operation, previous erections, age and other health factors, rather than a single proven groin-muscle explanation. Discuss possible sexual and size changes before surgery and report concerns during recovery. Some changes may improve over time, but a return to the previous length within six to twelve months is not guaranteed. Do not simply wait a year without a follow-up plan or delay care for pain, swelling or other new symptoms. What Peyronie’s disease can do Peyronie’s disease involves scar-like plaque in the tissue surrounding the erectile chambers. It can cause a new bend, narrowing, an hourglass shape, shortening, painful erections or erectile dysfunction. Severity varies: not everyone has a severe curve or finds intercourse impossible. Seek assessment for a new lump, painful erection or changing curvature. Examination and sometimes ultrasound help assess plaque and blood flow; an ultrasound scan does not itself dissolve scar or cure a curve. Treatment may help pain, function or shape, but cannot promise restoration of all lost length. Urgent symptoms are different from gradual change Sudden injury with severe pain, a pop or crack, rapid bruising or swelling or immediate loss of erection can indicate a penile fracture and needs immediate emergency assessment. Do not try to bend it straight or wait for all of these signs. Complete inability to pass urine also requires immediate emergency care. An erection lasting more than three to four hours needs immediate hospital care; seek help sooner for severe pain or according to your own treatment plan. With sickle cell disease, a painful erection lasting over one hour is an emergency. Fever with increasing genital pain or swelling needs urgent same-day advice, or emergency care if severely unwell. Erection treatment and postoperative rehabilitation Your team may offer treatment such as sildenafil or tadalafil, a medically suitable vacuum erection device or other options after prostate treatment. These can help assisted erections and sexual activity. Evidence does not establish one best rehabilitation routine or guarantee spontaneous erections or restored length for everyone. Use medicines and devices only after a safety review and instruction. PDE5 medicines such as sildenafil or tadalafil must not be combined with nitrates or recreational nitrite products called poppers; dangerous blood-pressure falls can result. Do not stop prescribed heart medicines to take an erection drug. Tell the team all medicines and follow the operation-specific timing. Selecting treatment for Peyronie’s disease Treatment depends on symptoms, erection quality, the active or stable phase and your goals. Options include observation, pain treatment, selected traction or vacuum devices, specialist injections and, for suitable stable disease causing functional difficulty, surgery. Device evidence has limitations. Shockwave treatment may ease pain in selected cases but is not recommended to correct curvature. In the US, collagenase clostridium histolyticum (XIAFLEX) is approved for selected adults with a palpable plaque and curvature of at least 30 degrees; plaque involving the urethra is a contraindication. Availability and local criteria differ. It requires trained specialist care and can cause penile rupture, severe bruising or serious allergy. Follow the prescribed modelling, activity and follow-up instructions; do not obtain or inject it yourself. Discuss treatment trade-offs and daily health Operations to straighten a penis have different risks. Plication can shorten the longer side; grafting may restore some length in selected people but can affect sensation or erections. An implant may be considered for appropriate erectile dysfunction. No operation is a universal enlargement treatment; discuss realistic length, function and complication goals before consenting. Regular suitable activity, nutritious food, stopping smoking, avoiding heavy drinking and managing vascular or metabolic illnesses can support erection health. They are not guaranteed length-restoration methods. Avoid unregulated enlargement pills, hormones, injections, forced stretching or a self-designed pump routine; adult testosterone is not a treatment to enlarge a normal penis. A realistic and supportive outlook The course depends on the cause. Postoperative changes may improve, while persistent scar-related shortening may need targeted treatment; it is inaccurate to say that every Peyronie’s change is untreatable. Treatment aims include comfortable function, confidence and relief of distress, not an ideal size or guaranteed return to the past. Enjoyable intimacy can take many forms, but a promise that size changes never affect sexual life dismisses real pain or erection difficulties. Discuss comfort and preferences with a partner if you wish and ask for sexual-health or psychological support. Agree follow-up and urgent warning signs; you deserve care without shame. A relaxed appearance, erection firmness and a buried shaft can differ from true persistent shortening. Age, surrounding tissue, prostate treatment and Peyronie’s disease are different contexts that need individual assessment. Do not assume recovery within six to twelve months or a guaranteed rehabilitation routine. Never combine erection medicines with nitrates or poppers; devices and injections need professional instruction. Acute injury, inability to urinate or a prolonged erection can be emergencies; new persistent changes deserve respectful review. Does ageing always shorten the penis? No fixed amount is inevitable. Blood-vessel, nerve or hormone-related health changes can affect erections and appearance, while scarring can alter shape. New persistent shortening, pain, a lump or testicular change deserves assessment rather than being dismissed as ageing. Can body fat make the penis appear smaller? Yes. Tissue around the base can hide part of a normally sized shaft. Buried penis may also involve skin inflammation or scarring and cause urinary, hygiene or sexual problems. Individual health support may help, but weight loss is not a guaranteed complete treatment and should not delay review. How can I protect erection health? Suitable activity, balanced nutrition, not smoking, limiting heavy alcohol use and managing other conditions can help. They do not guarantee preventing every size change. Ask about new erection problems and avoid unregulated enlargement products or forced exercises. What if it looks shorter after prostate removal? Contact your surgical or sexual-health team for assessment and a recovery plan. Some changes improve, but previous length is not guaranteed within six to twelve months. Medicines or devices may assist erections when suitable; one routine is not proven to restore length or spontaneous erections for everyone. Is every curve Peyronie’s disease? No. A longstanding slight curve may be ordinary. New curvature, plaque, pain, narrowing or erection difficulty needs assessment. Ultrasound can assist diagnosis; it is not a treatment that removes scar. Can lost length from Peyronie’s be treated? Some treatments can improve function, shape or selected length changes, but full restoration is not guaranteed. Choices depend on disease phase and erections; surgery can also shorten the penis or cause other complications. Discuss benefits, risks and your priorities with a urologist. Is collagenase suitable for anyone wanting enlargement? No. US XIAFLEX has a specific adult Peyronie’s indication involving a palpable plaque and at least 30-degree curvature, with contraindications and serious injury risks. Access and criteria vary by country. It is not a home injection or general enlargement medicine. Which symptoms need emergency help? Get immediate emergency assessment for sudden severe injury with swelling or bruising, complete inability to urinate or an erection lasting more than three to four hours. Sickle cell disease with painful erection over one hour is an emergency; severe pain can warrant help sooner. Do not try to straighten an injured penis or wait for routine follow-up.

title: Penile cancer: symptoms, stages, treatment and support
description: Learn which penile changes need assessment, how biopsy and staging guide treatment, and what organ preservation, follow-up and support can involve.
body: Penile cancer is an uncommon cancer of the skin or tissues of the penis. Most cases are squamous cell cancers. A new lump, sore or skin change often has another explanation, but needs assessment rather than a diagnosis from its appearance. Earlier assessment can give more treatment options. Changes to get checked Arrange a medical appointment promptly for a new or persistent lump, ulcer, rash, skin thickening, colour change or bleeding on the penis. Changes often affect the glans or foreskin but can occur elsewhere. Unusual or unpleasant-smelling discharge, itching, burning, difficulty retracting the foreskin or a groin lump also deserve review. Do not wait four weeks before asking about a concerning change. These symptoms can come from inflammation, infection or other conditions as well as cancer.
