A referral to a specialist does not confirm cancer. If you cannot pass urine at all, seek immediate emergency care; this can be dangerous regardless of its cause. Embarrassment should not prevent care: you can ask about privacy, a chaperone and how an examination will be done. Risk factors without blame Anyone with a penis can develop penile cancer, although it is more common at older ages. Some cancers are associated with HPV, while others are not. Smoking, a tight foreskin called phimosis, long-term inflammation and some conditions or treatments that reduce immunity can increase risk. Having a risk factor does not mean you will develop cancer, and its absence does not exclude it. Phimosis and smegma are not sexually transmitted infections. Smegma is a collection of shed skin cells and oils; it is not itself a proven cancer-causing substance. Having a foreskin, HPV or cancer is not evidence of poor character or a partner's infidelity. Ask about gentle hygiene, treatment for painful or tight foreskin, stopping smoking and HPV vaccination according to local eligibility. Condoms reduce some HPV exposure but cannot prevent every infection. Examination, biopsy and selected tests A clinician examines the penis and both groins. A biopsy removes a sample for laboratory examination and is central to confirming the diagnosis and identifying the cancer's features. Ask about pain relief, the procedure and when results will arrive. MRI or ultrasound may help assess depth when this affects treatment; CT, PET/CT or lymph-node sampling may be needed in selected circumstances. Cystoscopy looks inside the urethra and bladder; it is not a routine test for spread throughout the body. Normal scans or no palpable groin lumps cannot exclude microscopic lymph-node disease. Depending on the tumour's risk, the specialist may discuss a sentinel-node biopsy, other node surgery or surveillance. Enlarged groin nodes can also reflect infection, so the team uses examination and appropriate sampling rather than assuming every lump is metastatic cancer. What the stage describes The TNM system describes the primary tumour (T), regional lymph nodes (N) and distant spread (M). The following is a simplified stage-group guide; grade and microscopic features matter. Stage 0 includes carcinoma in situ, called penile intraepithelial neoplasia (PeIN), or a non-invasive verrucous tumour, without nodal or distant spread. Stage I is T1a: invasion into tissue beneath the surface with lower-risk microscopic features, N0 M0. It is not simply surface-only disease. Stage II has no nodal or distant spread: IIA includes higher-risk T1b invasion or T2 invasion into the corpus spongiosum; IIB involves the corpora cavernosa (T3). Stages IIIA and IIIB combine a T1–T3 tumour with N1 or N2 regional nodal disease respectively, without distant spread. Stage IV includes invasion into other adjacent structures (T4), N3 regional disease or distant metastasis. Stage IV does not always mean distant spread. Why groin-node assessment matters Clinical and pathological nodal categories differ. On pathology, N1 means one or two involved groin nodes on one side; N2 means three or more on one side or involved nodes on both sides. Pelvic-node involvement or cancer extending outside a node is N3. You cannot assign these categories by counting lumps yourself. Ask whether the stage is based on examination and scans or on tissue examined after surgery. Nodal assessment and treatment are a separate part of the care plan, even when the penile lesion is small. Decisions balance the risk of hidden spread against the complications of node procedures. Specialist experience matters in this uncommon cancer. Ask what tests are recommended, what uncertainty remains and whether review by a specialist multidisciplinary team or a second opinion would help. Treating superficial disease Non-invasive disease has not grown into deeper tissue; invasive disease has, but is not automatically present in lymph nodes or distant organs. For selected PeIN or superficial lesions, options can include prescribed topical 5-fluorouracil or imiquimod, local excision, circumcision for suitable foreskin lesions, glans resurfacing or laser treatment. The choice requires an appropriate diagnosis and discussion of recurrence and side effects. Topical chemotherapy is different from chemotherapy that circulates through the body. Do not use cancer creams, wart treatments or freezing products on an undiagnosed lesion. Cryotherapy is described among possible treatments, but evidence in PeIN is limited and it is not a standard solution for every lesion. Treatment response needs review; persistent or recurrent changes can require biopsy or a different approach. Surgery can sometimes preserve the penis Selected localised invasive cancers can be treated with organ-preserving surgery, such as wide local excision or removal of part or all of the glans with reconstruction. Removing cancer with adequate margins must be balanced with urinary and sexual function and the risk of recurrence. Invasion alone does not mean that everyone needs removal of the entire penis. Partial penectomy removes part of the penis; total penectomy may be needed when a large or advanced tumour cannot be adequately treated with a smaller operation. Urination may then be redirected through an opening in the perineum. Reconstruction can be discussed but is individual and cannot guarantee previous appearance, sensation or sexual function. Ask about wound care, activity, pain, urinary changes and when to seek help. Radiotherapy and treatment for more advanced cancer External-beam radiotherapy or brachytherapy, which places a radiation source close to the tumour, can be options for selected localised cancers. Radiotherapy can also be used in other treatment settings or to relieve symptoms. Possible effects include skin changes, scarring and urinary or sexual problems; discuss these alongside surgical options rather than assuming one approach is always less harmful. Cancer involving nodes or more extensive disease may need a combination of node surgery, systemic chemotherapy and sometimes radiotherapy. Chemotherapy can be given before or after surgery in selected circumstances. For advanced cancer, the specialist can explain current systemic options, clinical trials and whether a treatment aims to cure, control disease or ease symptoms. Palliative care can help manage pain and support wellbeing alongside cancer treatment. Follow-up and outlook are individual Keep the follow-up plan agreed with your team. It depends on the original tumour, lymph-node findings and treatment; there is no universal appointment interval for everyone. Follow-up can include examination of the penis and groins, selected scans or biopsies, and support with treatment effects. Report a new lesion, groin lump or other concerning change between visits rather than waiting for the next appointment. Early localised disease is often treatable, but recovery cannot be guaranteed. Outlook depends particularly on nodal involvement, as well as tumour features, overall health and response to treatment. A population five-year survival figure is not a personal prediction or a limit on lifespan. Ask your specialist to explain your own results and the benefits and uncertainties of the proposed plan. Support for daily life and relationships Cancer and its treatment can affect body image, intimacy, erections, urination, fertility concerns and emotional wellbeing. Ask a specialist nurse or clinician about psychosexual support, counselling, rehabilitation and practical or financial assistance. With your consent, a trusted person can join appointments; peer groups may help, but you decide what to share. Intimacy and personal worth are not defined by one body part or performance. BeMama can help organise questions, appointments and symptoms to discuss with your team. It cannot assess a lesion, confirm a biopsy result, assign a stage, select cancer treatment or predict survival. A photograph or app record must not delay examination. If recording intimate information, consider your privacy and the service's settings; bring the information you choose to share to a clinician. New penile sores, lumps or skin changes need prompt examination; appearance alone cannot diagnose cancer. Biopsy and risk-based assessment of the tumour and lymph nodes guide staging and treatment. Some invasive cancers can receive organ-preserving treatment; treatment and follow-up are individual. Urinary, sexual and emotional support matter, and BeMama cannot replace specialist assessment. What may be the first sign? A lump, ulcer or change on the glans or foreskin can be an early sign, but cancer has no single diagnostic appearance. Rash, thickened or discoloured skin, bleeding or unusual discharge also need assessment. Ask promptly about a concerning change rather than waiting for it to become painful or large. Who is more at risk? Risk rises with age and can be associated with HPV, smoking, phimosis, chronic inflammation or reduced immunity. Not all cancers are HPV-related. A foreskin or a risk factor does not establish the diagnosis, and phimosis and smegma are not STIs. Risk discussions should support care, not blame. How is penile cancer diagnosed? Examination and a biopsy are central. Further imaging or lymph-node tests depend on the findings and risk. A cystoscopy is not a routine whole-body staging test, and normal scans do not rule out microscopic nodal spread. Ask when and how you will receive results. Is stage I only on the surface? No. Stage 0 includes surface-confined in-situ disease. Stage I describes T1a invasion beneath the surface with lower-risk microscopic features and no regional nodes or distant spread. The specialist should explain the exact TNM and grade rather than relying on a simplified label. Does invasive cancer always require total penectomy? No. Selected localised invasive tumours can receive organ-preserving surgery or other suitable treatments. Partial or total penectomy is needed in some situations to control cancer adequately. Discuss margins, recurrence, follow-up, urinary and sexual effects, and reconstruction with the specialist team. Are cancer creams the same as systemic chemotherapy? No. Prescribed topical 5-fluorouracil or imiquimod can treat selected superficial disease after diagnosis. Systemic treatment is used in different circumstances, including some nodal or advanced cancers. Do not self-treat an unexplained genital lesion with creams or freezing products. Do survival statistics tell me how long I will live? No. They describe groups treated in particular periods, not an individual's lifespan. Stage, lymph nodes, tumour biology, health and treatment response affect outlook. Ask your team what the findings mean for you, including uncertainty and available support. When should I seek help before my next appointment? Report new penile or groin changes promptly and follow the team's instructions for treatment complications. Complete inability to pass urine requires immediate emergency care. BeMama can keep questions and dates, but cannot decide whether a lesion, stage or treatment is safe.

title: Sex after vasectomy: healing, comfort and semen-test clearance
description: When to resume sex or masturbation, what pain means, why backup contraception is essential, and how vasectomy usually affects erections, desire and ejaculation.
body: Vasectomy blocks the vas deferens, the ducts that carry sperm from the testicles into the ejaculate. It is intended as permanent contraception, but it does not work immediately. Healing enough for sexual activity and receiving clearance to rely on vasectomy are separate milestones. Follow your surgical team’s recovery and semen-testing instructions rather than a fixed day or ejaculation count. Allow the surgical area to heal Techniques and wounds differ; not everyone has two incisions or the same stitches. Sex or masturbation too early may strain a healing wound, worsen pain or bleeding and increase the risk of wound problems. Do not try to speed sperm clearance by ejaculating during the initial recovery restriction. CDC advises avoiding ejaculation for about a week, while NHS patient advice gives a minimum period of two to seven days. Follow the period your own team specifies, and wait longer if pain, swelling or an unhealed wound remains. A calendar date alone is not permission to push through symptoms; ask the team if unsure. Restart gently, without a pain guarantee Mild soreness, bruising and swelling can occur after surgery. Early erections or ejaculations may be uncomfortable, and there can be a small amount of blood in semen. These should improve rather than steadily worsen. A blood collection in the scrotum, called a haematoma, is a possible complication, not a symptom to assume is harmless for weeks. Once your team’s restrictions have passed and you are healing comfortably, restart gently and stop if activity hurts or pulls on the wound. Use backup contraception until formal clearance. Supportive underwear, prescribed wound care and suitable pain relief can help; ask about medicine suitability rather than increasing doses or taking leftover antibiotics. Avoid heavy lifting or sport for the period advised. When pain or swelling needs urgent care Contact the surgical team or obtain urgent same-day assessment if pain or swelling suddenly worsens, does not begin improving after a few days, or there is fever, blood/pus/fluid from the wound or an enlarging scrotal lump. Do not wait a month to report these signs, and do not drain a swelling yourself. Get immediate emergency care for sudden severe testicle pain; testicle pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain; or new or unexplained testicle pain lasting more than an hour or continuing at rest. Do not assume surgery explains these signs. Severe illness, fainting or loss of consciousness, or uncontrolled bleeding also needs immediate emergency care. Do not drive yourself; arrange another driver or an ambulance. This differs from expected mild postoperative soreness that is steadily improving. Persistent or recurrent pain with sex, ejaculation or everyday activities deserves review even without an emergency sign. You can still cause a pregnancy before clearance Sperm may remain beyond the blocked ducts and can still appear in semen after surgery. Twenty ejaculations, three months, normal-looking semen or a healed wound cannot confirm that contraception is effective. CDC specifically notes that ejaculation count is not a reliable indicator of clearance. Continue an effective agreed contraceptive method until the clinician confirms success from the required post-vasectomy semen analysis. Options may include condoms or an existing suitable pill, injection or other method; a partner should not start or stop medication without their own advice. If sex occurs without effective contraception before clearance, seek prompt emergency-contraception advice rather than assuming the operation protected you. Follow the laboratory’s semen-test protocol The 2026 AUA guideline allows the first semen sample as early as eight weeks; CDC’s 2024 recommendation uses eight to sixteen weeks, and many services schedule around twelve weeks or later. Your service chooses timing, collection, transport and repeat-testing requirements. Keep using contraception if testing is delayed or the result is unclear. Under the AUA protocol, clearance may follow one properly assessed uncentrifuged sample showing no sperm, or at most 100,000 rare non-motile sperm per millilitre when examined within two hours. For a sample examined after two hours, that guideline requires no sperm for clearance because movement cannot be reliably judged. These are clinician/laboratory criteria, not permission to interpret a home result or another service’s report yourself. Abnormal results and rare later failure If sperm remain, your clinician decides whether repeat samples, continued contraception or further treatment is needed. AUA recommends discussing repeat vasectomy when motile sperm persist at six months; larger persistent counts of non-motile sperm require shared decisions. An early positive sample does not automatically mean immediate repeat surgery. Even after confirmed success, pregnancy risk is very low rather than zero; counselling commonly cites about one in 2,000 after appropriate clearance. This is a post-clearance estimate, not the risk before testing or a yearly guarantee. Rare reconnection can occur. A suspected pregnancy after clearance needs prompt pregnancy assessment and contact with the vasectomy service. Desire and erections usually remain intact Vasectomy does not remove the testicles or interrupt testosterone production. It is not designed to impair libido or the structures responsible for erections. Many people have unchanged sexual enjoyment, and some feel less anxious once contraceptive success is confirmed; an increase in desire or confidence is not guaranteed. Pain, worry, relationship circumstances, medicines or unrelated health problems can affect sex. New or persistent erection or desire difficulties deserve a respectful assessment instead of being dismissed because the procedure usually preserves function. Discuss concerns with the clinician and partner if you wish; there is no requirement to resume before you feel ready. Ejaculation, orgasm and ongoing pain Ejaculation continues: most seminal fluid comes from glands, so removing sperm from its transport route usually causes no noticeable change in semen amount. Semen appearance cannot show whether sperm are present. Orgasm is generally preserved, but it is not possible to promise identical sensations or pain-free sex for every person. Early discomfort should settle; persistent or recurrent scrotal or ejaculation pain may reflect infection, a sperm granuloma, nerve-related pain or other causes. Post-vasectomy pain syndrome is one possible longer-term problem, not a diagnosis to make yourself. Individual treatment can include appropriate pain medicines and sometimes specialist procedures; do not wait a fixed month if pain concerns you or worsens. Pregnancy prevention and STI prevention differ Vasectomy does not prevent sexually transmitted infections, including HIV. Correct, consistent use of suitable external or internal condoms reduces some infection risks, but cannot eliminate all risks, especially from uncovered skin. Barrier use may still be appropriate after pregnancy-prevention clearance. Condoms are not the only part of prevention: individual testing, treatment, appropriate vaccination and, for eligible people, prescribed HIV PrEP may be relevant. PrEP does not prevent pregnancy or other STIs. Ask a sexual-health professional about your situation rather than treating either vasectomy or a negative semen test as infection protection. Healing for sex and clearance for contraception are different; follow your team’s instructions for both. Do not use an ejaculation count or elapsed months instead of the prescribed semen test and explicit clinical clearance. Stop if sex hurts; worsening swelling, fever or wound discharge needs urgent review, and sudden severe testicle pain needs immediate emergency care. Desire, erections and ejaculation are usually preserved, but ongoing symptoms deserve assessment and no outcome is guaranteed. Vasectomy is intended to be permanent and does not prevent STIs; after clearance a small pregnancy risk remains. When can I have sex or masturbate again? Follow your surgeon’s initial restriction, commonly around a week, and wait until healing is comfortable. NHS and CDC wording differs, so use your own instructions. Stop for pain or wound pulling. You still need effective contraception until the required semen test is reviewed and the clinician clears you. Can sex still cause pregnancy after vasectomy? Yes, particularly before semen-test clearance. Sperm may remain for weeks or months. Twenty ejaculations or three months alone cannot prove success. Continue agreed contraception until explicit clinical clearance, and seek prompt emergency-contraception advice after inadequately protected sex before clearance. Does vasectomy change sexual desire? It does not interrupt testosterone production and usually does not reduce desire. Less pregnancy anxiety may help some people after clearance, but increased libido is not promised. Pain, mood, medicines and other factors can affect desire; new or persistent concerns deserve assessment. Will I still be able to get an erection? Vasectomy usually preserves erections and long-term sexual function. Early discomfort can affect readiness. A new or ongoing erection problem should be evaluated, not dismissed or assumed to be permanent surgical damage. Do not force painful activity. Will ejaculation or orgasm feel different? You still ejaculate, and semen volume usually changes little because sperm form only a small part. Orgasm is generally preserved, but identical sensation is not guaranteed. Early discomfort should improve; persistent, recurrent or worsening pain needs review sooner than an arbitrary one-month wait. Does any sperm in a sample mean the operation failed? Not necessarily. The clinician considers timing, movement, concentration and the laboratory method. AUA allows certain rare non-motile sperm results under specific collection and assessment conditions, whereas delayed samples need no sperm for clearance. Other services have their own protocol. Keep using contraception until your clinician gives explicit clearance. Which symptoms need urgent help? Worsening pain or swelling, fever, wound discharge or a growing lump needs urgent same-day assessment. Get immediate emergency care for sudden severe testicle pain; testicle pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain; or new or unexplained testicle pain lasting more than an hour or continuing at rest. Do not assume surgery explains these signs. Severe illness, fainting or loss of consciousness, or uncontrolled bleeding also needs immediate emergency care. Do not drive yourself; arrange another driver or an ambulance. Do not wait to finish sex or for a routine appointment. Can I stop condoms after clearance? You may rely on vasectomy for pregnancy prevention when your clinician confirms the required test criteria, with a small remaining failure risk. This does not provide STI protection. Condoms and other appropriate prevention may still be needed; discuss your circumstances with a sexual-health professional.

title: Hirsutism in women: causes, tests and hair removal options
description: Understand coarse facial and body hair, hormonal causes, warning signs, and the benefits and limits of medicines, laser and electrolysis.
body: Unwanted facial or body hair can take time, money and confidence to manage. You deserve support whether you want treatment or prefer to leave the hair alone. Hirsutism describes coarse, usually dark hair in an androgen-sensitive pattern in women; it does not mean that every unwanted hair reflects a hormone disorder. A useful plan combines checking the cause with choosing care that fits your skin, health and priorities. What hirsutism means Hair on the upper lip, chin, chest, lower abdomen or back may become thicker and more visible with hirsutism. Fine, soft facial hair is different. Estimates suggest hirsutism affects about 5–10% of women, although definitions and normal hair patterns vary with family background and ancestry. The amount of hair alone does not measure how distressing it feels. Hypertrichosis is excess hair growth that is not limited to this androgen-sensitive pattern; it may be local or widespread. Virilization means additional changes such as a deepening voice or increased muscle bulk. Hirsutism can occur without virilization, so these terms should not be used interchangeably. Hormones, ovarian conditions and less common causes Everyone produces androgens, including testosterone. Hirsutism may reflect higher levels or hair follicles that respond more strongly to ordinary levels. A common cause is the condition traditionally called polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), now called polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) in current NHS and international resources. It can involve irregular periods, acne and difficulty becoming pregnant. Hair growth alone does not establish this diagnosis, and the condition is not simply caused by ovarian cysts. Fatigue, mood changes or sleep problems can accompany an ovarian hormone condition but also have many other explanations. Pelvic pain and headaches need assessment on their own merits. Do not diagnose yourself from a symptom checklist. Less commonly, adrenal or ovarian disorders contribute, including nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia, Cushing syndrome and androgen-producing tumours. Adrenal glands sit above the kidneys and make several hormones. Enzyme differences affect hormone production in congenital adrenal hyperplasia; excess cortisol occurs in Cushing syndrome. Blood-pressure changes, unusual bruising, muscle weakness or changes in body fat may guide testing, but these disorders do not all share one symptom pattern. Tumours are uncommon. Medicines and hair growth without an identified cause Testosterone and anabolic steroids can cause androgen-related hair changes. Minoxidil and ciclosporin can instead produce hypertrichosis. Bring a list of prescribed medicines, supplements and non-prescribed hormones to your appointment. Do not stop a necessary medicine yourself; the prescriber can assess alternatives or ways to manage the effect. Sometimes periods and measured androgen levels are normal and no clear cause is identified: this may be called idiopathic hirsutism. That label does not make the hair or distress imaginary. Treatment can still be discussed. When to seek care and what testing involves Arrange a medical appointment for coarse hair that bothers you, particularly with irregular periods, acne or difficulty conceiving. Ask for an urgent appointment if thick hair appears suddenly or progresses rapidly, your voice deepens, or your muscles become noticeably larger. These changes need assessment rather than a trial of cosmetic treatment first. Assessment usually starts with the timing and pattern of growth, menstrual and family history, medicines and an examination. A clinician may use a hair-growth score and check androgen levels when hirsutism is more widespread or other signs suggest a hormonal problem. A few local unwanted hairs with regular periods do not automatically require hormone tests. Other blood tests are chosen for the findings, such as testing for an adrenal enzyme disorder or checking blood glucose when metabolic risk is relevant. Ultrasound or other imaging is used selectively; everyone with facial hair does not need an ovarian or adrenal scan. Tell the clinician about hair you have already removed so its extent is not underestimated. Medicines and supportive lifestyle care Treatment aims to reduce growth and manage any underlying condition. Balanced eating, movement and support for metabolic health may help when PMOS/PCOS or insulin resistance is present. For some people, weight management modestly improves hair growth, but it is not a guaranteed cure or a prerequisite for receiving care. For someone not trying to conceive, a combined contraceptive pill may be an initial medicine if medically suitable. An antiandrogen may be considered when needed. These medicines do not simply shrink ovarian cysts: they reduce androgen production or effects. The choice depends on health risks, other medicines and pregnancy plans. Antiandrogens can harm a developing fetus. Reliable contraception is needed when pregnancy is possible; tell your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding. Do not start, share or adjust these medicines yourself. Because hair grows in cycles, oral treatment usually needs at least six months before judging its effect or changing the plan, unless side effects require earlier review. Prescription eflornithine cream slows facial hair growth rather than removing existing hair. Improvement may appear after about eight weeks; ongoing treatment is needed to maintain the benefit, and skin irritation can occur. Its product information advises an alternative during pregnancy or pregnancy planning and says it should not be used while breastfeeding. Availability varies; discuss suitability with a clinician. Shaving, waxing and depilatory products Shaving, threading, plucking and waxing can remove visible hair without treating its hormonal cause. Shaving does not make hair grow thicker, although the cut end may feel blunt. These methods need repeating; frequency depends on the area and your preference. Depilatory creams and bleaching products may help but can irritate or burn skin. Follow the label, use products intended for the area, and test a small patch as directed. Avoid damaged or inflamed skin. Choose the method you can tolerate, rather than assuming a painful or expensive option must work better. Laser and electrolysis: longer-lasting results and limits Laser uses light absorbed by pigment to damage hair follicles and usually works best on darker hair. Several sessions are needed because hairs are at different growth stages. Many people have substantial reduction for months or years, but regrowth and maintenance treatments are common, especially on the face when a hormonal driver remains. A promise of permanent clearance after a fixed number of sessions is unrealistic. Electrolysis treats individual follicles with a fine probe and electric current. It can permanently destroy successfully treated follicles and can be useful for pale hair that laser does not target well. Treating an area takes repeated visits; new hair or incompletely treated follicles can still require further care. Both options can be uncomfortable, costly and time-consuming. Choose a qualified practitioner experienced with your skin tone and the proposed device. Laser can cause burns, pigment changes or scarring if used poorly; appropriate settings and cooling matter, especially for darker skin. Facial laser treatment can occasionally increase hair growth, with a greater reported risk in Mediterranean and Middle Eastern women. Discuss electrolysis or other alternatives and follow the provider’s eye-protection, sun and aftercare instructions. Making a sustainable plan There is no single best method for everyone. Consider the cause, hair colour, skin sensitivity, treatment area, cost, pregnancy plans and whether you want temporary removal or longer reduction. Medicines and direct hair removal can be combined under professional guidance; treating a hormone disorder may reduce regrowth but does not instantly remove existing hair. Hirsutism often needs ongoing management. Review the plan if growth changes, treatment irritates your skin or expectations are not being met. Emotional support, counselling or trusted friends may help if hair affects body image or relationships. You can request treatment even when a clinician describes the amount of hair as mild. Coarse hair in an androgen-sensitive pattern differs from fine hair and from hypertrichosis. Sudden or rapidly worsening growth, a deeper voice or increased muscle bulk needs urgent medical assessment. Testing and treatment should follow your symptoms, health risks and pregnancy plans. Oral medicines take months; antiandrogens require pregnancy precautions. Laser reduces hair over time, while electrolysis treats individual follicles; neither guarantees every hair will disappear forever. Does excess hair always mean PCOS or PMOS? No. Follicle sensitivity, family patterns, medicines and other conditions can contribute. PMOS/PCOS is common, but diagnosis needs a clinical assessment. Can weight loss remove the hair? It may modestly improve androgen-related growth for some people with metabolic or ovarian hormone problems. It is not a reliable way to remove existing hair, and care should not depend on losing weight. When might hormonal medicine help? It may be appropriate for bothersome hirsutism, especially with an underlying hormonal condition. A clinician should assess contraindications and fertility plans before recommending it. How long does treatment take? Oral medicines usually need at least six months for a fair assessment. Hair removal works on a different timescale, and long-term maintenance depends on the cause and method. What is the best hair removal method? The best fit depends on hair and skin colour, location, comfort, cost and desired duration. Laser suits pigmented hair better; electrolysis can treat pale hairs. Both need multiple visits. Will shaving make the hair thicker? No. Regrowth can feel stubbly because the hair has a cut end, but shaving does not increase its thickness. Which changes need prompt assessment? Sudden or rapidly increasing coarse hair, a deepening voice or increased muscle bulk warrants an urgent appointment. Do not wait for a cosmetic treatment to work. What if I am planning pregnancy? Tell your prescriber before treatment. Antiandrogens can harm a fetus and require pregnancy precautions. Eflornithine product guidance recommends an alternative during pregnancy or pregnancy planning and no use while breastfeeding.

title: Changed vaginal odour: gentle care and when to get checked
description: Learn what can change vaginal odour, safe external care, products to avoid, when testing matters and which symptoms need urgent or emergency help.
body: A vagina has a natural scent, and it does not need to smell like perfume or have no smell at all. A new, strong or persistent change deserves attention, especially with discharge, itching or pain. The useful question is what has changed and whether treatment is needed, rather than how to cover the smell. Extra washing and fragranced products can make irritation worse. Natural scent and changes that deserve attention Normal vaginal fluid helps keep the vagina moist and clean. Its amount and texture can change with the menstrual cycle, pregnancy, contraception and sexual activity. Sweat from the surrounding skin, menstrual blood and semen can also temporarily affect the scent. There is no single approved smell that everyone should aim for. A pronounced new or persistent smell, particularly with changed discharge, burning, soreness, urinary pain, sores or bleeding, should be assessed. Discharge is not abnormal just because it exists, and clear or white discharge does not rule out every problem. Smell or colour alone cannot identify an infection, establish an STI or measure fertility. When to seek care promptly or immediately Arrange a clinician or sexual health assessment for a persistent or worsening change, troublesome itching, burning, unusual discharge or bleeding after sex. Do not spend a week trying home products before seeking help. Pelvic pain with abnormal discharge or possible pregnancy needs urgent assessment. Pelvic or abdominal pain that is severe or worsening, or pelvic pain that hurts with movement or touch, heavy bleeding, fainting, confusion or breathing difficulty requires immediate emergency care. Do not drive yourself to emergency care; ask someone to drive you or call an ambulance. In pregnancy, contact your maternity team about an unusual smell or discharge; any bleeding or suspected leaking waters needs immediate contact with your maternity team rather than a home smell test. After birth, loss or another recent procedure, bad-smelling discharge, fever or worsening lower abdominal pain needs urgent clinical advice now. If very unwell, faint, confused, breathless or bleeding heavily, seek emergency care. A retained tampon with fever, rash, dizziness or other systemic illness also needs emergency assessment. Possible causes: not all odours are yeast Bacterial vaginosis (BV) is a change in the vaginal bacterial balance and can cause a fishy smell with thin discharge, often more noticeable after sex. It is not a fungal infection and is not classified as a conventional STI, although sexual exchange can contribute to recurrence. Trichomoniasis is an STI that can cause odorous discharge; chlamydia, gonorrhoea and other conditions may cause discharge or associated pain and bleeding. Tests, not scent descriptions, distinguish them. Thrush often causes itching and soreness with thick discharge and usually no strong smell. Skin irritation, a retained tampon or other object can also cause symptoms. If a tampon is forgotten or cannot be removed easily, seek prompt help; do not use tweezers or another instrument, and do not keep probing. A broken or fragile object needs urgent professional removal. Odour alone does not mean infertility; some untreated infections can affect reproductive health, which is a reason for appropriate testing rather than alarm. Gentle washing means external care The vulva is the outside skin and folds around the vaginal opening; the vagina is the internal canal. Wash the external area gently with lukewarm water and your hands, and pat dry. If a mild fragrance-free cleanser is comfortable, keep it external; sensitive or sore skin may do better with a clinician-recommended soap substitute. Do not scrub with a rough cloth or loofah, wash repeatedly or put soap inside the vagina. Avoid douching, including rinsing inside with plain water. Avoid perfumed soap, scented wipes, deodorants and antiseptic washes. The vagina does not need flushing to remove semen or restore cleanliness after sex. Persistent irritation may need examination for a skin condition, not more cleaning. A product that stings should be stopped and discussed with a clinician or pharmacist. Underwear, moisture and sex Choose comfortable, breathable underwear, such as cotton, and clothing that does not rub. Change damp exercise clothes or underwear and wash with a product that does not irritate your skin. These steps can improve comfort, but cotton is not a guaranteed infection treatment and synthetic fabric does not automatically cause disease. The vagina does not need extra oxygen from special clothing to function. Gentle external washing when needed is enough; there is no requirement to wash internally before or after intercourse. Barrier protection reduces STI risk, but does not prevent every cause of odour. Avoid sex that is painful, and follow infection-specific advice on abstinence and partner treatment. Some prescribed vaginal creams and oil-based products weaken latex barriers, so check the medicine and condom instructions rather than assuming protection is unchanged. Perfume, essential oils and pH products Do not use perfume or genital deodorant even outside the vaginal canal: the vulvar skin is sensitive and fragrances may irritate it. Diluting an essential oil does not make it a proven or reliably safe genital treatment. Avoid tea tree oil, other essential oils, herbal mixtures or food inserted into the vagina to remove odour. Masking the smell can delay finding the cause. A home pH result cannot tell BV from every other cause, and a normal result cannot exclude every infection. Over-the-counter products advertised to rebalance pH are not a universal first treatment. Do not start boric acid, antiseptics or repeated antifungals simply because of a smell. A clinician may prescribe a specific product for a confirmed condition, but that differs from routine self-treatment, especially in pregnancy. Food, fluids and probiotics A varied diet and enough fluids support general health, but no food or drink is established as a way to cure vaginal odour or reset vaginal pH. Drinking extra water to make yourself sweat is not a treatment. Yoghurt can be part of your diet if tolerated; it is not a vaginal medicine. Do not insert yoghurt or other foods. Probiotic supplements and fermented foods are not substitutes for testing or prescribed BV or thrush treatment; results from a particular researched product do not establish that every shop product works. In pregnancy follow food-safety guidance, including avoiding unpasteurised milk and yoghurt. Do not use raw dairy or an unregulated fermented drink as an odour remedy. A balanced diet cannot guarantee that BV or another condition will not recur. What an appointment and treatment may involve Tell the clinician when the change began, whether there is pain, itch, bleeding or urinary symptoms, any recent products or medicines, possible pregnancy, tampon use and relevant sexual exposures. With your consent, an examination and vaginal swab or urine tests may be offered. A pH measurement can be one part of assessment; a cervical screening test is not a substitute for testing these symptoms. You can ask for a chaperone and ask to stop an examination. Treatment follows the cause: antibiotics for diagnosed BV or an STI, antifungals for confirmed or appropriately assessed thrush, removal of a retained object, or a skin-care plan for irritation. Do not share leftover medicines or assume all discharge needs an antifungal. Pregnancy changes the choice: for vaginal thrush, CDC guidance recommends a seven-day topical azole course rather than oral fluconazole. Complete the prescribed course and return if symptoms persist or recur. Recurrence, partners and realistic prevention Recurring BV is common and deserves reassessment, not blame or escalating cleansing. Clinicians may discuss longer treatment and triggers. Partner guidance has changed: ACOG's October 2025 update supports considering concurrent treatment for male partners of adults with recurrent symptomatic BV, and shared decisions for first episodes or same-sex partners. Ask your service about current local guidance; do not copy an antibiotic regimen or treat everyone automatically. For an STI such as trichomoniasis, current partners need clinical treatment and sex should wait until treatment is completed and symptoms have resolved; repeat testing is usually recommended for sexually active women around three months later. Uncomplicated thrush does not routinely require treatment of an asymptomatic partner. Gentle external care and following product instructions may reduce irritation, but cannot guarantee no recurrence. BeMama can help record changes and questions; it cannot diagnose the cause or rule out an emergency. Natural scent varies. A new strong or persistent change with other symptoms needs assessment, not perfume or repeated washing. Wash gently outside only; avoid douching, deodorants, essential oils and routine pH remedies. Foods, probiotics and cotton underwear are not infection cures. Treatment depends on the actual cause and pregnancy status. Pelvic pain, pregnancy or postpartum warning signs, a retained tampon with systemic symptoms, or severe illness changes the urgency; do not wait for home remedies or an app. What should I eat to prevent vaginal odour? No food is proven to prevent or cure all vaginal odour. A varied diet and ordinary hydration support health; yoghurt and probiotics do not replace appropriate testing or treatment. Do not insert foods into the vagina. During pregnancy follow food-safety advice and avoid unpasteurised milk or yoghurt. How can I reduce irritation and unwanted odour? Use gentle external care, avoid fragranced products and douching, wear comfortable underwear and change damp clothes. These measures support comfort, not guaranteed infection prevention. Seek assessment for persistent or changed odour, particularly with discharge, pain, itching or bleeding. Is a little itching normal? Brief irritation can happen, but persistent, recurrent or troublesome itching should be assessed. It may reflect a skin condition, irritation or infection, and does not automatically mean thrush. Do not keep adding scented products or repeating antifungals without advice. Which products should I avoid around the vagina? Avoid scented soap and wipes, deodorants, perfume, antiseptic washes, rough scrubbing and essential oils on genital skin. Do not wash inside the vagina or insert food or unprescribed pH treatments. For sore skin, ask about an appropriate fragrance-free soap substitute. Does a fishy smell prove BV or an STI? No. It can suggest BV, but a clinician must consider other causes and tests. BV is bacterial imbalance, not thrush; sexual activity can contribute without proving infidelity. An odour alone cannot establish an STI or infertility. Do I need to treat my partner? It depends on the diagnosis. STI partners often need treatment, while asymptomatic partners do not routinely need treatment for uncomplicated thrush. For recurrent symptomatic BV, newer guidance supports discussing concurrent partner treatment in selected circumstances. Let a clinician plan it; do not share medicines. Should I wait a week for home care to work? No fixed waiting week is appropriate. Arrange assessment for persistent or worsening symptoms, and seek urgent care for pelvic pain, pregnancy or postpartum warning signs. Pelvic or abdominal pain that is severe or worsening, or pelvic pain that hurts with movement or touch, heavy bleeding, fainting, confusion or breathing difficulty needs immediate emergency help. Do not drive yourself to emergency care; ask someone to drive you or call an ambulance. What if I might have forgotten a tampon? Have it removed promptly. If it does not come out easily or you are unsure, contact a clinician rather than using instruments or repeated probing. A retained object with fever, rash, dizziness, confusion, breathing difficulty or other systemic illness needs emergency assessment.

title: Vulvar bumps: causes, skin care and when to get help
description: A new genital bump may involve irritation, a hair follicle, a cyst or infection. Learn why location and examination matter, which care is safe and when assessment is urgent.
body: A bump described as a vaginal pimple is often on the external vulva, rather than inside the vaginal canal. Many causes are treatable, but appearance alone cannot confirm acne or prove that a lump is harmless. New, painful, persistent or changing genital bumps deserve assessment without embarrassment. Start with the location, not a diagnosis The vulva includes the external folds of skin around the vaginal opening. Hair follicles are present on hair-bearing outer skin, not inside the vaginal canal. A spot around a hair, a lump near the opening and a deeper vaginal lump can have different causes. A photo or the word pimple cannot reliably distinguish them. Note when it began, whether there is pain, itching, blistering, discharge or bleeding, and any change in size or number. A clinician may ask about skin products, hair removal, medicines and sexual contact, then examine with your consent. Selected swabs, STI tests or a biopsy may be appropriate; not every lump needs every test. Contact dermatitis: irritation or allergy Soaps, fragranced bubble baths, wipes, deodorants, lotions, powders, laundry products, scented menstrual products, spermicides, condoms, lubricants or topical medicines can irritate skin or trigger allergy. Sweat, rubbing, urine, semen or persistent moisture can also aggravate sensitive skin. Dermatitis more often causes itching, burning, raw skin or a rash than a true acne lesion. Avoid a suspected nonessential irritant and discuss a simpler care routine. Do not stop prescribed treatment or abandon contraception without asking about an appropriate alternative. Deliberately trying suspected allergens again on the vulva is unsafe; a dermatologist can arrange patch testing when needed. Treatment for diagnosed eczema or itching is selected for the site and severity, rather than choosing random creams or antihistamines for every bump. Folliculitis, ingrown hairs and shaving injury Hair removal or friction can damage follicles on the outer vulva, causing inflamed bumps or allowing infection. An ingrown hair bends back into the skin and can look like a spot. Shaving can also leave cuts, razor burn or blisters; these are not proof that every genital bump is an infected hair. Pause shaving, waxing or plucking on affected skin and avoid picking or tight rubbing clothing. Some mild follicle problems settle, but enlarging, persistent or painful bumps may need examination and selected treatment. A gentle warm compress may ease a diagnosed superficial problem; avoid heat that burns, squeezing or using it to delay assessment of a worsening lump. Recurrent deep lumps may be hidradenitis suppurativa Hidradenitis suppurativa, or HS, is a long-term inflammatory condition involving blocked hair follicles. It can cause recurrent painful nodules, abscesses, scars and channels that drain fluid in the groin and other skin folds. It is not simply a sweat-gland infection, ordinary acne or evidence of poor hygiene, and it is not contagious. Early recognition helps a clinician plan care. Depending on severity, treatment may include medicines to reduce inflammation, antibiotics for selected purposes, specialist immune treatments or procedures. Some people have long-lasting disease while symptoms improve with care; no universal cure or fixed recovery time can be promised. Ask for support with pain, dressings and emotional impact. Molluscum requires particular care around the genitals Molluscum contagiosum is a viral skin infection causing small, firm bumps, sometimes with a central dip. It can spread by skin contact or shared items and, in adults, through sexual contact. Scratching or shaving over lesions can spread them to other areas. Other conditions can look similar, so do not diagnose it from a dimple alone. Many ordinary cases eventually clear without treatment, but current CDC advice recommends prompt professional assessment and usually treatment for genital lesions. The choice depends on location, age, immune health and pregnancy. Do not scrape out the centre, squeeze fluid or apply internet treatments or ordinary wart removers to genital skin. Avoid sharing towels and follow advice to reduce contact transmission. Cysts and skin tags can resemble spots A Bartholin cyst commonly forms as a lump on one side near the vaginal opening. It may be painless, but an abscess can become very painful, hot and swollen, with pus or fever. Have a new lump checked; rapid growth or worsening pain needs urgent assessment. Care may include observation, comfort measures, medicines or a drainage procedure selected by the clinician, not home lancing. A new Bartholin-area mass in someone over forty may need additional assessment, including a selected biopsy, to exclude a less common cause. Skin tags are usually harmless soft growths, but a changing, painful or bleeding growth should be reviewed rather than assumed to be a tag. Do not cut, tie off or burn genital growths yourself; removal can cause bleeding, infection or scarring. Herpes and genital warts need the right diagnosis Herpes can cause painful blisters or ulcers around the vulva, vagina or anus, although symptoms may be mild or atypical. A fresh lesion may be tested to identify HSV. Antivirals can treat symptoms and reduce recurrences or transmission risk but do not eradicate the latent virus. A first episode needs prompt clinical care; tell maternity care promptly about possible herpes during pregnancy. HPV-related warts may occur singly or in groups and can resemble other growths. Clinicians choose treatment according to the site and circumstances; treating visible warts does not cure HPV, and recurrence is possible. Do not use a hand-or-foot wart product on the genitals. Sexual-health advice, relevant testing and partner discussion help; condoms reduce some risks without covering every affected area, and HPV vaccination prevents selected infections rather than treating an existing wart. Do not pop a bump, and do not wait on warning signs Squeezing, puncturing or cutting a genital lump can spread infection, injure delicate tissue and worsen pain. If it opens by itself, keep the area gently clean and dry and seek advice for continuing pain, pus, bleeding or worsening swelling. Professional drainage, when indicated, is different from forcing a boil to empty at home. Seek urgent same-day care for a lump becoming larger and more painful over hours or days, pus, fever, spreading redness or warmth, or feeling unwell. Get immediate emergency care for severe illness, confusion, breathing difficulty, skin that is unusually pale or blue/grey or blotchy, fainting or loss of consciousness, inability to wake, or complete inability to pass urine. Do not drive yourself; ask someone to drive you or call an ambulance. Do not wait for a temperature threshold or for every sign to appear. Gentle care and hair-removal choices Wash the external area gently with lukewarm water and pat dry; do not wash inside the vagina, scrub or douche. Avoid fragranced baths, sprays, wipes and unnecessary products. Comfortable breathable underwear, including cotton, and looser clothing can reduce rubbing; change damp clothing. Ask about suitable menstrual products if they seem to irritate, rather than repeatedly testing a known trigger. Pubic hair removal is optional, not a cleanliness requirement. Avoid shaving inflamed or infected skin and do not share razors. If you later resume shaving, use a clean razor, work gently in the direction of hair growth and stop if irritated. Trimming also can injure skin, so use care and avoid cutting close to an active lesion. Do not start strong acne acids, steroids, antibiotics or antifungals without an appropriate diagnosis and instructions for this area. Outlook and follow-up depend on the cause Minor irritation or some follicle bumps may settle after the trigger is removed; molluscum, HS, warts and other conditions follow different courses. There is no reliable promise that every lump will disappear within a few weeks. Review symptoms that persist, recur, worsen or do not respond to the chosen treatment. A persistent lump, ulcer, bleeding, lasting itch, thickened skin or a new colour change needs examination. These changes often have noncancerous causes, but should not be dismissed as acne. Ask about follow-up, expected response, ways to prevent recurrence and who to contact if symptoms change. The condition is not a reason for shame or blame. A vulvar spot is not automatically acne; hair-bearing external skin and the internal vagina are different. Irritation, follicle problems, HS, molluscum, cysts and STIs need different assessment and treatment. Never squeeze, puncture or remove a genital lump yourself, or deliberately re-test suspected allergens on sensitive skin. Rapidly worsening painful swelling, pus or fever needs urgent same-day care; severe illness or inability to urinate needs emergency care. Use gentle external care and seek review for a persistent lump, ulcer, bleeding or skin change. What helps prevent irritation and bumps? Reduce friction and avoid a known irritant, fragranced products and douching. Choose comfortable breathable underwear, change damp clothing and wash externally with lukewarm water. Prevention depends on the cause and cannot guarantee that all cysts or infections are avoided. What could look like a pimple? Folliculitis, an ingrown hair, dermatitis, HS, molluscum, a Bartholin cyst, herpes, a wart or a skin tag may look like a bump. Other conditions, including uncommon serious causes, are possible. Location, symptoms, examination and selected testing distinguish them. How are these bumps treated? Treatment follows diagnosis: avoiding an irritant, selected skin medicine, treatment of infection, specialist HS care or a procedure may be appropriate. Some lesions can be observed. Antibiotics, antihistamines, antifungals or wart remedies are not universal treatments, particularly on genital skin or during pregnancy. Is popping or draining a lump safe? No. It can cause infection, bleeding or injury. Do not cut, puncture, squeeze or force out a hair or a core. Rapidly growing painful swelling, pus or fever needs urgent assessment; severe illness, impaired consciousness or inability to urinate requires immediate emergency care. Can shaving cause a bump? Yes, it can injure follicles or cause ingrown hairs and razor irritation on outer hair-bearing skin. Pause hair removal on affected areas. A new genital lump still needs assessment when painful, persistent or uncertain; shaving history does not exclude another diagnosis. Does every genital bump mean an STI? No. Irritation, follicle problems and cysts are among the non-STI causes. Some viral bumps or sores are transmissible, so new lesions and possible exposure deserve sexual-health assessment without blame. Appearance alone cannot establish when or from whom an infection was acquired. Can I identify an allergy by trying products again? Do not deliberately reapply a suspected allergen to the vulva. Discuss triggers and safer alternatives; clinician-supervised patch testing can help when allergic contact dermatitis is suspected. Ask before changing prescribed medicines or contraception. When should I seek urgent help? Get urgent same-day care for a rapidly enlarging painful lump, pus, fever, spreading redness or feeling unwell. Get immediate emergency care for severe illness, confusion, breathing difficulty, skin that is unusually pale or blue/grey or blotchy, fainting or loss of consciousness, inability to wake, or complete inability to pass urine. Do not drive yourself; ask someone to drive you or call an ambulance. Persistent ulcers, bleeding or other skin changes also need examination; do not assume every lump is harmless.

title: Vulvar discomfort after exercise: irritation, infections and pelvic floor care
description: Understand itching, soreness, discharge or pressure after exercise, how infections and pelvic floor problems differ, and when to get medical advice.
body: Exercise can support mood, sleep and long-term health, but genital discomfort deserves attention. “Sports vagina” is an informal expression, not a diagnosis. Friction, moisture or pressure may irritate the external vulva; persistent pain, changed discharge or a vaginal bulge needs assessment rather than being accepted as a normal cost of exercise. What “sports vagina” actually means The vulva is the external genital area around the vaginal opening; the vagina is the internal canal. Sweat comes from skin glands in the groin and outer genital area, not from the vaginal canal. Normal vaginal discharge is different from sweat. Heat, damp clothes, rubbing and pressure can worsen sensitive skin without proving an infection. Discomfort may vary with the activity, intensity, duration and frequency of exercise. Cycling or a stationary-bike saddle can put direct pressure on the vulva and vestibule, the tissue around the vaginal opening. Tight or rubbing clothing may also matter. Neither exercising nor having a natural genital scent means that you are unclean. Symptoms and when to seek care Itching, redness, burning, soreness, irritation, changed discharge or a new strong odor can have several causes. Pain when urinating or having sex, sores, a bulge or persistent pressure also needs attention. Arrange an assessment for first-time, recurrent, persistent, unusual or troublesome symptoms, or symptoms after a new sexual partner. Do not diagnose yeast or BV from appearance or smell alone. Seek urgent same-day advice for pelvic pain with fever, shivering, unusual discharge, urinary difficulty or possible pregnancy. Severe or worsening pelvic pain, pelvic pain that hurts with movement or touch, feeling faint, dizzy or lightheaded, fainting or loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty, heavy bleeding or sudden confusion needs immediate emergency care. Contact your maternity team immediately for any bleeding during pregnancy. Stop exercising and seek care when these warning signs occur. Do not drive yourself to emergency care; ask someone to drive you or call an ambulance. Yeast infection is one possibility, not an exercise diagnosis Candida overgrowth can cause intense itching, redness, soreness, thick white clumpy discharge, painful sex or external burning when urine touches irritated skin. These symptoms are not specific to yeast. Many uncomplicated infections have no identifiable trigger; a sweaty workout does not establish that Candida caused the symptoms. Examination and selected vaginal tests help distinguish causes. Confirmed or clinically suspected yeast infection may need an appropriate vaginal antifungal or, in selected nonpregnant cases, oral treatment. In pregnancy, CDC recommends topical azoles for seven days and advises against oral fluconazole; check treatment with your clinician, pharmacist or midwife. Persistent symptoms after over-the-counter treatment or recurrence within two months needs reassessment. Yogurt or probiotics should not be relied on to prevent or treat infection; probiotics are not an established treatment. Routine partner treatment is not recommended for uncomplicated thrush, although a symptomatic partner needs advice. Bacterial vaginosis and other infections BV is a change in the vaginal bacterial community, distinct from a yeast infection. Thin grayish discharge or a fishy smell may occur, but many people have no symptoms, and odor alone cannot diagnose it. Warmth or sweating does not demonstrate that exercise caused BV. STIs, skin irritation and hormonal dryness can also cause symptoms; testing is chosen according to the history and examination. Symptomatic BV generally needs clinician-selected treatment such as metronidazole or clindamycin, with pregnancy and medication circumstances considered. Return if symptoms persist or recur. Current 2025–2026 guidance supports discussing treatment of ongoing partners in selected situations, particularly recurrent symptomatic BV; advice varies with anatomy and local guidance, so do not share medicines or assume every partner needs the same treatment. BV does not prove infidelity. Follow the clinic’s advice about sex, STI testing and medicine or condom compatibility. Vestibulodynia: persistent pain at the vaginal entrance Vestibulodynia is localized vulvar pain around the vaginal entrance within the broader condition vulvodynia: pain lasting at least three months without a clearly identified cause after assessment. Skin may look normal. This does not make the pain imaginary. Exercise does not by itself establish this diagnosis, but saddle pressure, touch or rubbing can provoke pain in someone affected. Do not wait three months to ask about new pain. Care is individualized and may combine gentle skin care, changes to pressure-provoking activities, pelvic health physiotherapy and selected medicines. A clinician may recommend a suitable external barrier or prescribe a local anesthetic such as lidocaine. Do not start numbing products to push through painful exercise; they can irritate skin or mask a problem. Reduce or stop the activity that worsens pain while an assessment and tolerable return plan are arranged. Pelvic organ prolapse and pelvic floor muscles Prolapse occurs when weakened or damaged pelvic supporting muscles, ligaments and connective tissue allow the bladder, uterus, bowel or vaginal top to bulge into the vagina. Heaviness, dragging, a visible or felt bulge, urinary leakage or incomplete emptying, bowel difficulty and sexual discomfort may occur. A bulge needs examination; symptoms cannot establish its type or severity at home. Pelvic floor training can help selected prolapse symptoms, preferably with a specialist physiotherapist. Not every painful pelvic floor needs more Kegels: overactive muscles may need relaxation and coordination before strengthening. Heavy lifting, skipping, trampolining, running, high-impact aerobics or strenuous abdominal work may worsen symptoms. Adapt load and impact with your team rather than repeatedly testing through pain or assuming a permanent ban on all activity. Pessaries or other treatments may be appropriate depending on the findings. Change damp clothing and clean gently Change out of sweaty exercise clothes or wet swimwear promptly. A shower or gentle external rinse can remove sweat; pat dry rather than rubbing. Clean the vulva, not inside the vagina. Avoid douching, scrubbing, antiseptics, scented washes, deodorants and wipes. Repeated washing can aggravate irritation, so more washing is not automatically better. For sensitive or already irritated skin, ask whether water alone or a suitable fragrance-free soap substitute is preferable. Avoid leaving cleanser or detergent residue, and stop a newly introduced product that irritates you. Persistent symptoms need assessment rather than repeated washing, perfume to cover odor or another unconfirmed antifungal course. Choose clothing and skin protection that suit you Choose comfortable, breathable clothing that does not rub, with cotton underwear or a cotton-lined gusset when comfortable. Change fit or fabric if seams, tight leggings or damp material worsen symptoms; no particular outfit guarantees prevention of infection. Do not use talc or fragranced genital products to control sweat. A thin layer of a simple fragrance-free emollient, such as petroleum jelly, may help selected external friction irritation if recommended and tolerated. It is not a universal treatment for discharge, infection or persistent pain. Do not put ordinary barrier ointments inside the vagina. Vitamin A+D or multi-ingredient creams are not automatically suitable, and some can cause allergy. Oil-based products can damage latex condoms; check compatibility and follow medicine-specific instructions. Adapt the workout while keeping movement manageable Notice whether symptoms follow saddle pressure, running impact, jumping, heavy lifting, abdominal strain or particular clothing. Temporarily choose a comfortable alternative, reduce load or duration, and take breaks. Walking or another tolerable lower-impact activity may suit you; cycling may be reasonable for some prolapse plans yet still aggravate vulvar pressure pain. The cause and your symptoms guide the choice. Return gradually with professional advice when pain, prolapse, pregnancy, postpartum recovery or recent treatment affects the plan. A pelvic health physiotherapist can assess strength, relaxation and technique. Do not use pain relief as permission to continue an activity that clearly worsens symptoms, and do not let self-care postpone assessment of persistent or changing symptoms. Support the rest of your exercise routine Maintain normal hydration before, during and after exercise, adjusted to conditions and any medical fluid restriction; forcing excessive water is not an infection treatment. Eat varied balanced meals, including suitable protein sources, whole grains, fruit, vegetables and healthy fats. Prioritize sleep, realistic goals, gradual aerobic and strength activity, and a supportive exercise companion if helpful. These habits support general health without guaranteeing freedom from vulvar symptoms. Journaling, relaxation or meditation can help manage stress, but stress does not make pain unreal or replace investigation. Avoid applying aromatherapy oils or other scented products to genital skin. Record symptoms, activities and products to discuss at your appointment. You deserve a workable exercise plan and effective care, rather than blame for clothing, hygiene or an infection. “Sports vagina” is not a diagnosis; external friction or sweat is different from vaginal discharge and infection. Persistent itching, changed discharge, pain or a bulge needs assessment; do not repeatedly self-treat presumed thrush. Gentle external care, prompt clothing changes and an adapted workout may reduce irritation; do not douche or numb pain to exercise through it. Pelvic floor care is individual: some people need strengthening, others relaxation, and urgent warning signs override exercise plans. What is “sports vagina”? It is an informal label for genital discomfort associated with exercise, not an official medical diagnosis. Sweat is from outer genital and groin skin; the vaginal canal produces discharge, not sweat. Friction, pressure, skin conditions or infection may require different care. What symptoms can occur after exercise? Itching, redness, burning, soreness, irritation, changed discharge or odor can occur. Pressure, a bulge, painful urination or pain during sex also deserves attention. Symptoms alone cannot identify the cause; first-time, persistent, recurrent or troublesome symptoms should be assessed. How is an infection after exercise treated? First establish whether there is an infection and which kind. Yeast may need an antifungal; symptomatic BV or an STI needs appropriate clinician-selected treatment. Pregnancy changes medicine choices. Probiotics or yogurt do not replace evaluation or prescribed treatment, and repeat symptoms need reassessment. How can I reduce burning after a workout? Change damp clothes, gently rinse only the outside and pat dry. Try less rubbing or pressure and comfortable breathable clothing. Avoid douching, perfume and scrubbing. If burning persists, returns or accompanies changed discharge, sores or pain, arrange assessment rather than washing more. Can I use lidocaine and keep cycling? Do not self-start a numbing product to push through pain. Lidocaine may be part of an individually prescribed vulvar pain plan, but saddle pressure can still aggravate the problem. Reduce the provoking activity and discuss diagnosis, skin tolerance and alternatives with your clinician. Should everyone do more Kegels? No. Pelvic floor strengthening may help some prolapse or leakage, but tight, overactive muscles can need relaxation before strength training. A pelvic health physiotherapist can assess the problem and tailor exercise rather than prescribe the same routine for every pain or bulge. Does my partner need treatment? It depends on the diagnosis. Routine partner treatment is not recommended for uncomplicated thrush, but symptoms in a partner need advice. STIs need diagnosis-specific partner care. Newer guidance supports discussing ongoing-partner treatment for selected BV cases, especially recurrent symptoms; follow local clinical advice rather than share medicines. When is this more than minor exercise irritation? Severe or worsening pelvic pain, pelvic pain that hurts with movement or touch, feeling faint, dizzy or lightheaded, fainting or loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty, heavy bleeding or sudden confusion needs emergency care immediately. Pelvic pain with fever, unusual discharge, urinary difficulty or possible pregnancy needs urgent same-day advice. Any bleeding in pregnancy warrants immediate contact with the maternity team. Do not drive yourself to emergency care; ask someone to drive you or call an ambulance.

title: Vaginal anatomy, size and body changes: what is usual?
description: Vaginal length and vulvar appearance vary. Learn about arousal, childbirth, pelvic floor care, skin colour, hair removal, cleaning and changes that need assessment.
body: The vagina is an adaptable internal canal; the vulva is the external genital area. Neither has one ideal appearance or measurement. Understanding their differences can reduce worry, while new pain, bleeding, a lump or a persistent change still deserves care rather than being dismissed as normal variation. The vaginal canal has variable dimensions The vagina extends from its opening to the cervix, the lower part of the uterus. It is not an endless open space. Its walls, folds and surrounding support can change shape; a single length cannot describe every person or every situation. Research measurements depend on position, technique and whether the tissues are relaxed or distended. Small MRI studies demonstrate variation rather than a universal normal-length test. Comparing your body with a hand, a partner’s penis or an online range cannot diagnose a problem; there is no need to measure internally at home. Arousal can change shape, but pain is not an arousal test During sexual arousal, blood flow to genital tissues increases, lubrication may develop and vaginal shape or length can change. Small imaging studies have observed these changes, but they do not establish an identical response or required depth for everyone. Deep penetration may feel uncomfortable for several reasons. Pain is not proof that someone is insufficiently aroused or doing sex incorrectly: dryness, pelvic floor tension, infection, endometriosis, injury and other conditions may contribute. Stop painful penetration, communicate and seek assessment for frequent or severe pain. Consent and comfort matter more than achieving a particular depth. Childbirth stretches tissues; recovery is individual During vaginal birth, the vaginal canal and opening stretch to allow passage of the baby. Afterwards, soreness, swelling, dryness, healing tears or a different sensation can occur. Hormonal changes, including during breastfeeding, may affect lubrication. Some changes improve with healing, but not every symptom should be assumed harmless. There is no promise that everyone returns to a previous size or feeling within days or six months. Recovery depends on injury, pelvic support, hormones and other factors. Ask for help when pain, a wound concern, leakage or a dragging sensation bothers you; you do not have to wait for a routine postnatal appointment. Do not rush or endure painful sex. Elasticity and pelvic support can change over time Vaginal tissue is elastic, but saying it can never change permanently is misleading. Pregnancy and childbirth, ageing, hormonal changes and pelvic surgery can affect tissues or support. These changes do not determine personal worth, sexual desirability or whether someone has had sex. A feeling of looseness, heaviness or a bulge may involve pelvic floor function or prolapse rather than a simple length problem. Urinary or bowel leakage and difficulty emptying also deserve discussion. A clinician can examine with consent and explain suitable physiotherapy, other treatments or observation; not everyone needs surgery or a tightening procedure. Pelvic floor care includes relaxation as well as strength The pelvic floor supports the bladder, uterus and bowel and helps continence. Childbirth, surgery, age, persistent coughing, constipation and pressure on the pelvic floor can contribute to weakness. Correctly taught strengthening may help selected people with leakage or support symptoms. More Kegels are not the answer to every symptom. Overactive or painful muscles may need relaxation and coordination work with a pelvic health physiotherapist. Seek advice if exercises hurt or worsen symptoms; avoid repeatedly stopping urine as an exercise. A personalized plan considers both contraction and full release, rather than promising that squeezing changes every vagina. The clitoris also responds to arousal The clitoris includes a visible glans near the top of the vulva and structures extending inside the body. A hood partly covers the visible portion. Increased blood flow during arousal can produce swelling and altered sensation in clitoral and nearby tissues. The size and visibility of these changes differ. There is no rule that the clitoris must retract in one particular way or enlarge by a set amount. Its response is not a reliable test of desire, consent or pleasure. New persistent pain, swelling or an unusual change should be assessed rather than compared with another person’s anatomy. Labia and external appearance are not identical The labia, clitoral hood and other external structures vary in size and shape. The inner labia may extend beyond the outer labia, and the two sides may be uneven. These differences can be usual anatomy; symmetry and a particular appearance are not requirements for health. Become familiar with what is usual for you without repeated measuring or checking. Appearance alone cannot establish sexual history or explain every symptom. If tissue causes persistent rubbing, pain, trouble using a menstrual product or another functional concern, discuss it with a clinician rather than assuming cosmetic change is necessary. Skin colour varies, and a new change needs context Vulvar skin can be lighter or darker than skin elsewhere, and natural shades differ between people. Blood-flow changes can temporarily alter colour during arousal. A stable familiar colour without symptoms is different from a new patch, a painful swelling or a changing mole. Purple colour alone does not diagnose yeast infection or lichen simplex. Persistent new colour change, thickening, itching, an ulcer, bleeding or a lump needs examination; many causes are noncancerous, but should not be guessed from colour. Assessment and any selected tests identify the cause, not a photograph or a colour chart. Pubic hair removal is optional There is no medical or hygiene requirement to shave or wax pubic hair. Grooming is a personal choice. Shaving, waxing and depilatory chemicals can cause cuts, irritation, burns or ingrown hairs; removing hair does not make the vagina healthier. If you choose to groom, use care, clean suitable equipment and stop when skin is irritated. Avoid shaving an active painful or inflamed area and do not share razors. Trimming can reduce close-skin injury but still requires care. Do not apply unsuitable depilatories or harsh products to genital tissue, and seek review for a persistent painful bump. Clean the outside gently; do not douche Normal vaginal fluid helps maintain the internal environment and carries away shed cells. The vagina does not need internal rinsing, deodorizing or scrubbing. Douching can disrupt its microbial balance and irritate tissue; trying to remove every trace of scent is unnecessary. Gently wash external skin with lukewarm water and pat dry. Avoid perfume, scented wipes, sprays and harsh washes; use a mild unperfumed product only if tolerated on external skin. For dryness, ask about a suitable vaginal moisturizer or lubricant rather than inserting ordinary body lotion. Persistent symptoms need cause-directed advice, not escalating cleansing. A usual scent differs from a persistent new odour Some genital scent is normal, and discharge or scent may vary through the menstrual cycle. Sweat, menstrual blood, sexual activity and products can affect what you notice. A particular food or supplement is not a reliable explanation for a new persistent vaginal odour, and scent alone cannot diagnose infection. Seek advice for a lasting new strong odour or a change in discharge, especially with itch, soreness, urinary symptoms or bleeding between periods or after sex. Clinicians may examine and select tests for infection or another cause, including a retained product when relevant. Do not mask the change with perfume, douche or self-prescribe antibiotics. Know which changes need urgent help Arrange assessment for persistent pain, a lump, an ulcer, skin change or unexplained bleeding, including any bleeding after menopause. Get urgent same-day advice for pelvic pain with unusual vaginal discharge or bleeding, fever or shivering, urinary difficulty or possible pregnancy. Contact maternity care immediately for any vaginal bleeding during pregnancy. Seek prompt advice for other new concerning genital symptoms during pregnancy. Get immediate emergency care for severe or worsening pelvic or abdominal pain, pain there with movement or touch, faintness, dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty, heavy vaginal bleeding or new confusion. Do not wait for a particular pad count or a positive pregnancy test. An examination should be explained and agreed with you; you can ask for a chaperone and ask the clinician to stop.
