Do not drive yourself to emergency care; ask someone to take you or call an ambulance. Vaginal dimensions and vulvar appearance vary; there is no single ideal length, shape or colour. Painful sex is not proof of inadequate arousal; stop painful penetration and seek care when pain is frequent or severe. Recovery after birth and later-life changes are individual; pelvic floor treatment may involve relaxation as well as strengthening. Hair removal is optional. Gentle external care is enough; avoid douching and fragranced products. Persistent changes need assessment; severe pelvic pain, heavy bleeding or fainting require immediate emergency care. Does the clitoris become larger during arousal? Increased blood flow can cause swelling and altered sensation in the clitoris and nearby tissues. The response varies, and there is no required amount of enlargement or retraction. Appearance does not establish consent or how much pleasure someone feels. Do all vulvas and vaginas look the same? No. Labial size, symmetry, the clitoral hood and internal dimensions vary. An inner labium extending beyond an outer one can be usual. New persistent pain, swelling or another change still deserves assessment rather than comparison with a single ideal. Why can genital skin be darker than other skin? Natural pigmentation varies, and blood flow may temporarily alter colour during arousal. A familiar stable shade is different from a new persistent patch or symptomatic change. Purple colour is not proof of yeast infection or lichen simplex; new thickening, itching, bleeding, a lump or an ulcer should be checked. Can vaginal scent vary during the month? Yes, some scent and cycle-related change can be usual. A persistent new strong odour or changed discharge, especially with soreness, itching, urinary symptoms or unusual bleeding, needs advice. Do not assume food is the cause or use perfume and douching to cover it. Is there one normal vaginal length? No single measurement captures every person or situation. Research methods and tissue state affect the result. The vagina can change shape, but a size comparison cannot diagnose health or guarantee comfort. Do not measure internally or push through pain to test capacity. Will everything return to the same state six months after birth? There is no universal deadline or guarantee. Healing, hormonal changes, tears and pelvic support differ. Ask for help for pain, leakage, heaviness or other concerns, and do not endure painful sex or delay assessment until a scheduled check. Should everyone do more Kegels? No. Strengthening may help appropriately assessed weakness, while painful or overactive muscles may need relaxation and coordination. A pelvic health physiotherapist can tailor the plan. Stop exercises that hurt and seek advice; do not repeatedly practise by stopping urine flow. When is a genital or pelvic change urgent? Pelvic pain with fever, unusual discharge or bleeding, urinary difficulty or possible pregnancy needs urgent same-day advice. Get immediate emergency care for severe or worsening pelvic or abdominal pain, pain there with movement or touch, faintness, dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty, heavy vaginal bleeding or new confusion. Persistent lumps, ulcers and skin changes need examination even without an emergency. Contact maternity care immediately for any vaginal bleeding during pregnancy. Do not drive yourself to emergency care; ask someone to take you or call an ambulance.

title: Vaginal pain after sex: causes, relief and when to seek care
description: Understand vulval and vaginal soreness after sex, possible infections and pelvic causes, safer comfort measures, and warning signs that need urgent help.
body: Pain after sex deserves attention, whether it is a brief burning feeling at the entrance or a deeper pelvic ache. You do not need to push through pain to satisfy a partner or prove that nothing is wrong. Dryness or friction may explain an isolated episode, but recurring, severe or unexplained symptoms need assessment. The location, timing and accompanying symptoms help guide care; they cannot reliably diagnose the cause on their own. Where the pain is and when it needs urgent help The vagina is the muscular canal between its opening and the cervix. The vulva is the external genital area, including the labia, clitoris and openings of the vagina and urethra. Pain described as vaginal may actually come from the vulval skin, bladder, pelvic muscles or deeper reproductive organs. Tell a clinician whether it is at the entrance, on one side or deep inside, and whether it begins during penetration or afterward. Seek emergency care for pelvic pain that is severe or worsening, pain with fainting or marked dizziness, shoulder-tip pain, heavy vaginal bleeding or difficulty breathing. If pregnancy is possible, pelvic pain needs urgent assessment because an ectopic pregnancy is one potential cause. Do not assume that pain following sex is only friction. Seek prompt medical advice for pelvic pain with fever or shivering, unusual discharge or bleeding, painful urination or vomiting. A rapidly enlarging, very painful vulval lump also needs urgent assessment. Repeated or persistent pain, bleeding after sex or symptoms that interfere with daily life should be checked even without emergency signs. Dryness, friction, swelling and product irritation Inadequate lubrication, prolonged penetration or vigorous pressure can irritate the vulva or vaginal entrance and sometimes cause small surface injuries. Fingers and sex toys can also create friction; technique, cleanliness and product compatibility matter. Take time for arousal if you want sexual activity, use enough compatible lubricant, and stop when something hurts. Dryness is not a personal failure or a measure of attraction. Blood flow during arousal can temporarily make the labia fuller. Painful swelling that persists, a new lump or swelling with burning, discharge or urinary symptoms needs assessment. Do not rely on a fixed number of hours or days to decide that severe symptoms are harmless. Latex, spermicides, fragranced washes, lubricants or other products may irritate the skin or cause allergy. Stop a suspected irritant and avoid douching or scented genital products. A suitable non-latex condom may be an option for latex allergy; choose a product labelled for pregnancy and STI protection. Sudden swelling with breathing difficulty is an emergency. Infections, vaginitis and a Bartholin’s cyst Vaginitis means inflammation in or around the vagina and has several causes; it is not simply an imbalance of bacteria. Thrush can cause itching, soreness, redness and sometimes thick discharge. Sexually transmitted infections such as chlamydia, gonorrhoea or genital herpes can also cause pain, sores or discharge, and some infections have few obvious symptoms. A urinary tract infection more often causes burning or urgency when urinating and may cause lower abdominal discomfort. Symptoms overlap, so do not assume every sore vagina is thrush. A clinician or sexual health clinic may recommend swabs, urine tests or STI testing according to symptoms and exposure. For a diagnosed STI, partner testing or treatment and advice about when to resume sex depend on the infection. Routine partner treatment is not needed for uncomplicated thrush. A blocked Bartholin’s gland duct can cause a lump on one side near the vaginal opening. It may hurt with sitting, walking or sex; an infected abscess can become very painful and cause fever. Have any new vulval lump checked. Do not squeeze, puncture or try to drain it yourself. Hormonal changes, medicines and pelvic conditions Lower estrogen around menopause can make vaginal tissues drier and more sensitive. Pregnancy, breastfeeding and some medicines, including certain hormonal contraceptives or antidepressants, can also contribute to dryness. This does not mean all contraception causes thinning or that you should stop treatment yourself. Ask the prescriber about symptoms and suitable alternatives. Endometriosis involves tissue similar to the uterine lining growing elsewhere and can cause deep pain during or after sex, often alongside troublesome periods. Fibroids are non-cancerous growths in or around the uterus; some cause pressure, heavy periods or discomfort during sex, while others cause no symptoms. The location of pain alone cannot confirm either condition. Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is infection of the upper reproductive tract, including the womb, tubes and ovaries. Chlamydia and gonorrhoea can cause it, but other bacteria can too. Deep pain, unusual discharge, bleeding between periods or after sex, and fever may occur. Suspected PID needs prompt assessment and treatment to reduce complications. Vulvodynia, vaginismus and tense pelvic muscles Vulvodynia is vulval pain lasting at least three months without a specific identifiable cause after other causes are considered. It may burn, sting or throb, even when the skin looks normal. Touch, clothing or penetration may trigger it. You do not need to wait three months before seeking help for pain. Vaginismus involves involuntary tightening around the vaginal entrance when penetration is attempted. It can make sex, tampon use or examination painful or difficult; it is not something you are choosing. Overactive or tender pelvic floor muscles can also contribute to pain. Do not assume the muscles need strengthening: repeated squeezing exercises may be unsuitable if relaxation is the problem. A pelvic health physiotherapist can assess and guide a tailored approach. Comfort measures that avoid further irritation Pause painful penetration and choose activities that feel comfortable, if you want them. Tell your partner what hurts and what helps; consent remains essential throughout. For external burning, a cool pack wrapped in a soft cloth may help briefly. Keep it off bare skin, never put it inside the vagina and stop if it makes symptoms worse. This is comfort care, not treatment for infection or deep pelvic pain. A water-based or silicone-based lubricant may reduce friction. Check the condom and toy instructions for compatibility; oil-based products can weaken latex condoms, and some lubricants are unsuitable for particular toy materials. Avoid a product that stings, and do not use a numbing product to force painful sex. Vaginal moisturizers intended for that purpose may help ongoing dryness, rather than only providing lubrication during sex. Wash the external area gently and avoid perfumed soaps, deodorants and internal washing. Choose comfortable clothing while sore. Do not repeatedly try antifungal creams, antibiotics or other treatments without a diagnosis when symptoms are new, different or recurring; the wrong treatment can delay appropriate care. What an assessment and treatment may involve A clinician may ask about onset, location, bleeding, discharge, urinary symptoms, periods, pregnancy possibility, medicines, sexual exposure and past procedures or childbirth. You may be offered a gentle examination, infection tests, a pregnancy test or selected imaging. Ask for explanations, a chaperone or adjustments; you can ask to pause or stop an examination. Treatment follows the cause. Bacterial infections may need antibiotics, thrush antifungal treatment, and genital herpes antiviral treatment; antibiotics do not treat every genital infection. Follow the specific course and partner advice given. Menopause-related dryness may improve with moisturizers or prescribed vaginal estrogen when suitable, rather than requiring systemic hormone therapy for everyone. Endometriosis or fibroid care may include medicines or selected procedures depending on symptoms and fertility plans. A symptomatic or infected Bartholin’s cyst may need drainage or another procedure; removal of the gland is not the automatic first step. Pelvic physiotherapy, guided relaxation, vaginal trainers or specialist pain care may help muscle-related pain and vulvodynia. These should be individualized, not forced through pain. Emotional support and follow-up Pain can lead to worry about sex, and anxiety can make it harder to relax. Psychosexual therapy or counselling may help alongside medical care; recommending it does not mean the pain is imagined or that its physical causes should be ignored. Share only what feels safe, and seek support if there is pressure, coercion or a past painful experience. Note when pain occurs, what it feels like, products used and other symptoms to help the appointment. Seek review if symptoms return, fail to improve with the recommended treatment or change. Even pain that settles quickly is worth discussing when it repeatedly limits comfort or enjoyment. Vaginal, vulval, urinary and deep pelvic pain can have different causes. Severe pelvic pain, fainting, shoulder-tip pain or heavy bleeding needs emergency care; possible pregnancy with pelvic pain needs urgent assessment. Dryness and irritation may improve with gentler activity and a compatible lubricant, but persistent or recurrent pain needs evaluation. Infections require the right diagnosis and treatment; partner advice differs by infection. Pelvic muscle and chronic vulval pain care may include physiotherapy and emotional support without dismissing physical symptoms. Is pain after sex something I have to accept? No. Stop activities that hurt and arrange assessment for recurring, persistent or severe pain. You deserve comfortable, consensual sexual experiences. Can lubrication help every cause? It can reduce friction from dryness, but does not treat infections, an abscess, endometriosis or other deep pelvic conditions. Persistent symptoms need assessment. What if my labia swell after sex? Temporary fullness can accompany arousal. Painful or persistent swelling, a new lump, urinary symptoms or unusual discharge should be checked; rapidly worsening pain or fever needs urgent advice. Should I treat both partners for an infection? It depends on the diagnosis. Some STIs require partner evaluation and treatment, while routine partner treatment is not recommended for uncomplicated thrush. Follow the clinic’s specific advice. Will Kegel exercises fix the pain? Not always. Tight or overactive muscles may need relaxation and tailored physiotherapy rather than extra squeezing. Ask for pelvic health assessment before choosing exercises. Do I need hormone therapy or surgery? Many people do not. Treatment depends on the cause, symptoms and preferences; vaginal estrogen or a procedure is considered only when appropriate. When should I seek urgent help? Emergency signs include severe or worsening pelvic pain, fainting, shoulder-tip pain, heavy bleeding or breathing difficulty. Pelvic pain with possible pregnancy, fever, unusual discharge or urinary symptoms needs urgent medical advice. Can therapy help without implying the pain is psychological? Yes. Counselling or psychosexual therapy can support confidence, communication and recovery alongside examination and treatment of physical contributors.

title: Vaginal cysts: symptoms, assessment and treatment
description: Learn how vaginal-wall and Bartholin cysts differ, when a lump needs examination, and how observation, drainage or removal and follow-up are chosen.
body: A new lump inside the vagina or near its opening can be worrying. Many cysts are benign and cause little trouble, but you cannot identify every lump by touch or appearance. The useful first step is a clinician's examination, especially if a lump is changing, painful or new after menopause. Treatment depends on its exact location and cause rather than a single rule for all vaginal cysts. A cyst is not the same as every vaginal lump A vaginal cyst is a closed sac within or beneath the vaginal lining, often containing fluid or other material. The vagina is the internal canal; the vulva is the external genital area. A cyst on the vaginal wall differs anatomically from a Bartholin gland cyst near the vaginal entrance, although both may be described casually as a vaginal lump. Neither is an ovarian cyst. Other conditions, including a prolapse, a urethral diverticulum, a benign solid growth or, less commonly, cancer can resemble a cyst. An itchy, sore or swollen area is not enough to diagnose one. Most diagnosed vaginal cysts are benign, but that is a reason for proportionate assessment, not a reason to ignore an unexplained lump. Inclusion cysts and Gartner duct cysts Inclusion cysts can form when tissue becomes trapped after a vaginal injury, repair of a childbirth tear or surgery. A previous procedure is useful history to tell the clinician, but not every person with a cyst has had an injury and a scar alone does not establish the diagnosis. Gartner duct cysts develop from remnants of a duct present during fetal development, usually along a side wall of the vagina. They are not simply a leftover organ in the cervix. Other developmental cysts can occur too. Location and examination help distinguish these from a nearby urinary-tract problem; the name cannot reliably be decided at home. Bartholin cysts and abscesses are a related but separate problem The Bartholin glands lie near either side of the vaginal opening. If a duct becomes blocked, gland fluid can collect and form a usually one-sided cyst. A small cyst may be painless. If infection produces an abscess, pain, tenderness, heat, swelling, pus or fever can develop. A blocked duct does not necessarily mean an STI or poor hygiene. A lump that becomes larger and more painful over hours or days, feels hot and tender, produces pus or is accompanied by fever or feeling unwell needs urgent same-day assessment. Do not wait several days to see whether a bath works. Seek immediate emergency help if you cannot pass urine, have confusion, breathing difficulty, fainting or severe rapidly worsening illness. For emergency care, do not drive yourself; ask someone to drive you or call an ambulance. Symptoms and finding a cyst without symptoms Many vaginal-wall cysts cause no symptoms and are found during an examination done for another reason. Others cause a noticeable lump, pressure, discomfort with penetration or tampon insertion, or urinary symptoms. Growth or infection may increase pain; itching is nonspecific and may have a different cause. Arrange a clinical appointment for any new lump in or around the vagina, even if it is painless. Mention bleeding, unusual discharge, urinary changes, previous childbirth injury or surgery, and whether it has grown. You do not need repeated internal self-examinations or to insert a tampon to test it. Stop an activity that hurts, including sex, while arranging advice. What examination, tests or biopsy may involve A clinician asks about symptoms and history, then examines the vulva and, if appropriate, the vagina with your consent. You may ask for a chaperone and to pause or stop. Appearance and location often provide the main information. Swabs for infection or STI testing are selected for the symptoms and sexual history; routine tests for every asymptomatic cyst are not required. Ultrasound may help when the diagnosis or anatomy is unclear or when planning surgery; MRI can be considered if more detail is needed. CT is not an automatic next step. A suspicious, solid, fixed, persistent or changing lesion may need biopsy. A new Bartholin-region lump at age 40 or older, or after menopause, deserves particular assessment and discussion of biopsy to exclude a rare cancer; this does not mean the lump is cancer or that every vaginal cyst needs biopsy. Observation, drainage or removal A small, stable, asymptomatic vaginal cyst can often be observed after diagnosis, with follow-up examinations agreed with the clinician. Increasing size, pain, difficult intercourse or tampon use, urinary symptoms, infection or concern about the diagnosis may change the plan. A symptomatic vaginal-wall cyst may be opened surgically to maintain drainage or removed; choices depend on its type, location and nearby structures. An abscess may need professional drainage, with antibiotics when indicated; antibiotics alone are not a reliable answer for every abscess. For a Bartholin cyst or abscess, a Word catheter can maintain a drainage opening, or marsupialisation can stitch an opening in place. These procedures differ from simply puncturing a lump. Gland removal is usually reserved for selected recurrent or suspicious cases. Discuss alternatives, anaesthesia, benefits and risks rather than assuming all cysts require the same operation. Comfort measures are not home drainage For a diagnosed uncomplicated Bartholin cyst, a comfortably warm shallow bath may ease mild discomfort. This is a comfort measure, not a cure for every vaginal-wall cyst and not a reason to delay assessment of an abscess. Ask which pain relief is suitable, particularly during pregnancy or breastfeeding or if you have other conditions or medicines. Do not squeeze, puncture, cut or try to drain a lump, or insert foods, essential oils or unprescribed products. Gentle external washing and drying may support comfort; internal douching does not prevent cysts. If a cyst opens by itself, keep the area clean and seek advice for persistent pain, fever, worsening swelling or discharge. Condoms reduce the risk of some STIs but cannot prevent every cyst, developmental remnant or childbirth-related inclusion cyst. Recovery, complications and recurrence Many cysts remain small and harmless, while some enlarge, become infected or press on nearby structures. Procedures can cause bleeding, infection, pain or scarring, and a cyst or abscess can recur. Removal is not a guarantee that it will never return. The chance of recurrence and the appropriate follow-up depend on the diagnosis and procedure. Follow your own wound, catheter and activity instructions after treatment, including when to resume penetration, tampons, swimming and exercise. Do not manipulate or remove a catheter yourself. Contact the team for increasing pain, swelling, redness, pus, bad-smelling discharge, fever or wound opening. Heavy bleeding, inability to urinate or severe systemic illness needs immediate assessment; use emergency services for fainting, confusion or breathing difficulty. Ask how and when you will receive biopsy or culture results and who to contact if symptoms return. For emergency care, do not drive yourself; ask someone to drive you or call an ambulance. A practical plan for your appointment Record when you first noticed the lump, its symptoms, any change, urinary problems and relevant pregnancy, birth or surgery history. Ask what diagnosis is most likely, whether a test would change care, what observation means, and which symptoms should bring you back sooner. You can discuss discomfort and sexual concerns without being expected to continue painful penetration. BeMama can help organise symptom notes and questions for the appointment. It cannot identify the lump, distinguish a cyst from a tumour or urinary problem, decide whether biopsy or drainage is needed, or exclude an urgent infection. A record or image in an app should not delay an examination or emergency help. Vaginal-wall cysts, Bartholin cysts and ovarian cysts are different; a new lump needs examination rather than self-diagnosis. Small diagnosed symptom-free cysts may be observed. Tests, biopsy and procedures are chosen for symptoms, location and concerning findings. Rapid growth with increasing pain, pus, fever or feeling unwell needs same-day help. Inability to urinate or severe systemic illness needs immediate care. Do not squeeze or drain a lump yourself. Follow individual aftercare and results plans, because recurrence is possible even after treatment. What symptoms can a vaginal cyst cause? Many have no symptoms. A lump, pressure, pain with penetration or tampon insertion, or urinary symptoms may occur. Itching or swelling alone does not prove a cyst. Have any new lump examined; rapidly increasing pain, pus, fever or illness needs urgent same-day care. What complications can occur? A cyst may grow, become painful, get infected or press on nearby structures. Treatment can cause bleeding, infection or scarring, and recurrence is possible. Seek prompt advice for worsening symptoms and immediate emergency help for inability to urinate, confusion, breathing difficulty or fainting. For emergency care, do not drive yourself; ask someone to drive you or call an ambulance. How are vaginal cysts treated? After diagnosis, a stable symptom-free cyst may need observation only. Symptomatic or concerning cysts may need surgery; an abscess may require drainage with antibiotics when indicated. Bartholin treatments include a Word catheter or marsupialisation in selected cases. No single treatment or permanent-cure guarantee applies to all cysts. How can a cyst be found if there are no obvious symptoms? A clinician may notice it during an examination for another reason. Some cysts relate to previous birth injury or surgery, others to developmental remnants or blocked ducts. Do not repeatedly probe yourself to search for one. A warm bath can ease mild discomfort from a diagnosed uncomplicated Bartholin cyst, but does not diagnose or cure all vaginal cysts. Does every lump need imaging or biopsy? No. Examination often guides the diagnosis. Ultrasound, MRI, infection tests or biopsy are used when findings or symptoms justify them. A new Bartholin-area lump from age 40 or after menopause should be assessed carefully, with biopsy considered to exclude a rare cancer; age alone does not diagnose cancer. Can I prevent cysts or drain one at home? There is no guaranteed prevention for every type. Condoms reduce some STI risks but do not prevent all blocked ducts, developmental cysts or inclusion cysts. Never squeeze, puncture or drain a lump yourself, and do not douche or insert remedies. Seek advice rather than waiting on a home treatment when pain or swelling worsens. What should I ask after a procedure? Ask about wound and catheter care, suitable pain relief, activity and sex restrictions, warning signs, results and follow-up. Do not remove a catheter yourself. Increasing pain, pus, bad smell or fever needs urgent advice; heavy bleeding, inability to pass urine or severe illness needs immediate care.

title: Can swallowing semen cause pregnancy? Risks and next steps
description: Swallowing semen does not cause pregnancy. Understand direct semen exposure, oral STI risks, withdrawal, condoms, emergency contraception and pregnancy testing.
body: Swallowed semen goes into the digestive tract, which has no route to the uterus or fallopian tubes. Oral sex and kissing do not cause pregnancy. A different question arises if fresh semen actually reaches the vulva or vagina, or if vaginal sex occurs during the same encounter. Assess what happened without treating every imagined chain of contact as an exposure. Swallowing, kissing and direct genital exposure are different Pregnancy requires sperm to fertilize an egg and an embryo to implant, normally in the uterus. Swallowing semen cannot achieve this: sperm do not travel from the stomach into the reproductive tract. Whether semen is swallowed or spat out does not change pregnancy risk from oral sex. Kissing after oral sex does not itself create a pregnancy route. Do not interpret an imagined sequence involving lips, saliva and later contact as equivalent to semen deposited directly on the genital area. Fresh wet semen actually placed on the vulva, near the vaginal opening or inside the vagina is a separate exposure that may allow sperm to enter. Pregnancy can also occur through assisted conception; vaginal intercourse is not the only possible route. Oral sex can transmit infections Oral sex can pass infections including gonorrhoea, chlamydia, syphilis, herpes and HPV. Infection may involve the mouth, throat, genitals or rectum and may have no symptoms. Oral contact with the anus can also spread hepatitis and intestinal infections. No pregnancy risk does not mean no STI risk. HIV risk from oral sex is extremely low compared with vaginal or anal intercourse, but that comparison does not apply equally to every STI. Condoms or dental dams reduce oral exposure. Discuss the actual activities with a sexual health clinician so testing can include the relevant sites. Seek immediate advice after a concerning potential HIV exposure: PEP must start within 72 hours when indicated. CDC does not routinely recommend PEP for oral-genital contact alone, but clinicians assess exceptional factors such as blood exposure or injury. Withdrawal and pre-ejaculate do not provide reliable protection Pulling the penis out before ejaculation can fail because timing is difficult and pre-ejaculate may contain sperm. It is not possible to tell by appearance whether a particular release contains sperm. Ejaculating near the vaginal opening can also expose the vulva even without ejaculation inside. Withdrawal alone is less dependable than established contraceptive methods and is not recommended by the NHS. Annual failure estimates describe repeated use over a year, not a one-in-five chance from every act. If avoiding pregnancy matters, choose a suitable regular method; a condom can add STI protection. Do not assume withdrawal protects against infections. Fingers, toys and anal sex: consider actual semen transfer Fingering alone does not cause pregnancy. Fresh wet semen on a finger or toy that touches the vulva or enters the vagina can, however, create a pregnancy exposure. This is less common than pregnancy from vaginal intercourse, but a precise percentage cannot be assigned to an individual event. Wash semen off hands before genital contact and clean toys according to their instructions. There is no internal passage from the anus into the vagina through which sperm normally travel. Anal sex itself does not cause pregnancy, but semen can leak or be wiped onto the vulva afterwards. Use a new condom before changing from anal to vaginal contact, and clean toys appropriately; washing alone is not a substitute for changing the condom. Avoid transferring anal bacteria to the vagina. Condoms work best when used throughout contact Use a new suitable condom from before genital contact until the end of each act. Check the expiry date and intact packet, open carefully and follow the product instructions. For an external condom, leave space at the tip, roll to the base and hold the base while withdrawing. Use compatible lubricant: oil damages latex, while water-based or silicone-based products are generally suitable for latex. Do not use two external condoms, two internal condoms or an internal and external condom together; friction can cause failure. A condom can be used with another contraceptive method, such as an appropriate pill or IUD. CDC US typical-use estimates are about 13 pregnancies per 100 external-condom users and 21 per 100 internal-condom users over a year. These are annual population estimates, vary between guidance sources and do not predict the risk from one encounter. Condoms reduce STI risk but cannot eliminate every infection. The first time, a period and a calendar do not guarantee safety Pregnancy can occur with the first episode of vaginal sex. The hymen is not a contraceptive barrier or a reliable record of sexual history. Ejaculation is not required for every exposure because pre-ejaculate may contain sperm. Standing, changing position or having vaginal sex in water does not prevent pregnancy; shared pool water alone is not a pregnancy route. The fertile window is usually described as the five days before ovulation plus ovulation day. Sperm can remain viable for up to about five days in the reproductive tract, while the egg has a much shorter lifespan. Ovulation does not always occur on day 14. Short or irregular cycles and variable ovulation mean bleeding days or an app prediction cannot rule out pregnancy risk. Proper fertility-awareness contraception needs instruction and method-specific precautions; a calendar guess is insufficient. Ask promptly about emergency contraception After unprotected vaginal sex, condom failure or direct fresh-semen genital exposure, contact a pharmacist or sexual health service as soon as possible. Swallowing semen alone does not require emergency contraception. The copper IUD is the most effective emergency option and is usually inserted within five days of the first unprotected act; a clinician may assess later insertion when it is still within five days of estimated ovulation. Pill timing depends on the medicine and local guidance. UK NHS advice gives levonorgestrel a 72-hour limit and ulipristal 120 hours. CDC guidance allows emergency pills within five days, but levonorgestrel becomes less effective later and ulipristal performs better on days three to five. Do not delay while choosing or assume every pill has the same window. These methods prevent pregnancy; they do not end an established pregnancy or treat an STI. Weight, medicines and restarting contraception need a plan Higher body weight or BMI can reduce oral emergency-contraception effectiveness, especially levonorgestrel; this is a reason to discuss options promptly, not to withhold help. The copper IUD avoids this oral-weight concern. Tell the clinician about medicines, supplements, breastfeeding, health conditions and every unprotected encounter so they can choose an appropriate method and check interactions. After ulipristal, CDC usually advises waiting at least five days before starting or restarting hormonal contraception, then condoms or avoiding sex for seven days after restarting. After levonorgestrel, regular contraception can usually start immediately, with seven days of backup under CDC advice. Follow the clinician’s instructions for your actual method and local protocol. Emergency pills do not protect later unprotected sex; ask again if a new exposure occurs. Test at a useful time, rather than diagnosing from symptoms Breast tenderness, tiredness, headache, mood changes, cramps, nausea, food aversions and bleeding cannot confirm or exclude pregnancy. Most home tests are reliable from the first day of a missed period. If the next period date is uncertain, test at least 21 days after the last unprotected sex that could cause pregnancy. Follow the kit instructions; hormonal contraception does not stop the test working. A positive result needs appropriate follow-up and a confidential discussion of care or available options. A negative test taken too early may be misleading: repeat after a few days if pregnancy still seems possible, and seek advice if a second test is negative but the period has not arrived. Do not wait for a test or a scheduled appointment when urgent symptoms occur. Know when to seek urgent care Get urgent medical advice for possible pregnancy with new one-sided lower abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding or shoulder-tip pain, even without a positive test. Pregnancy-related bleeding can be mistaken for a period. Seek prompt sexual health assessment after known STI exposure or new sores, unusual discharge or urinary pain; testing may be appropriate even without symptoms. Get immediate emergency care for severe or worsening abdominal or pelvic pain, or pain there with movement or touch, fainting, loss of consciousness, marked dizziness or heavy bleeding, particularly when pregnancy is possible. Pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or new confusion is also an emergency. Do not drive yourself; ask someone to take you or call an ambulance. An ectopic pregnancy can cause internal bleeding without obvious vaginal bleeding. After sexual assault or a potentially significant HIV exposure, seek urgent specialist care immediately so time-sensitive treatments and support can be assessed. Do not douche or insert home remedies to try to prevent pregnancy or infection. Swallowing semen and kissing do not cause pregnancy; direct fresh semen reaching the vulva or vagina is a different exposure. Oral sex can transmit STIs, even when pregnancy is impossible; barriers and site-appropriate testing can help. Withdrawal, a first sexual encounter, a period, standing or water do not provide dependable pregnancy prevention. Use one condom correctly throughout each act; annual failure percentages are not per-act probabilities. After a real pregnancy exposure, ask about emergency contraception promptly and test at the appropriate time. Severe pain, fainting or heavy bleeding need immediate emergency care. Can I get pregnant by swallowing semen or kissing afterwards? No. The digestive tract is not a route to the uterus or fallopian tubes, and kissing does not create one. If fresh semen actually reaches the vulva or vagina, assess that separate exposure rather than the swallowing or kissing itself. Is oral sex safer than vaginal or anal sex? Oral sex does not cause pregnancy, and HIV transmission risk is extremely low compared with vaginal or anal sex. Other STIs can still spread through oral contact, sometimes without symptoms. Condoms or dental dams and tests at the relevant sites reduce risk; no single comparison describes every infection. Can pregnancy happen if a partner pulls out in time? Yes. Timing can fail, pre-ejaculate may contain sperm and semen near the vaginal opening can enter the vagina. Withdrawal does not protect against STIs and is less reliable than established contraception. A yearly failure estimate is not the chance from one act. What if a finger or toy had semen on it? Fingering without semen does not cause pregnancy. Fresh wet semen transferred to the vulva or into the vagina can create a risk, although this is less common than vaginal intercourse and cannot be given a precise personal percentage. Wash hands and clean toys before genital contact; ask promptly about emergency contraception after an actual exposure. Can anal sex cause pregnancy? There is no normal internal route from the anus to the vagina. Pregnancy may become possible if semen leaks or is transferred onto the vulva. Use a new condom when changing from anal to vaginal contact and clean toys appropriately to reduce bacterial transfer as well. Can I use two condoms or rely on a period? Do not double condoms or combine an internal and external condom, because friction can cause failure. One condom can be combined with a suitable different contraceptive method. Bleeding days and a predicted ovulation date do not guarantee safety; cycles vary and sperm can survive for several days. How soon should I ask for emergency contraception? As soon as possible after a pregnancy-risk exposure. Copper IUD and pill eligibility depend on timing, medicines and individual factors. UK levonorgestrel advice uses 72 hours and ulipristal 120 hours; CDC allows pills within five days with reduced late levonorgestrel effectiveness. Swallowing semen alone is not an indication. Follow the specific restart and backup plan after the selected pill. When should I test or seek urgent help? Test from the first missed period, or at least 21 days after the last unprotected sex if the period date is uncertain. Repeat an early negative result if needed. Possible pregnancy with one-sided pain, bleeding or shoulder-tip pain needs urgent advice. Get immediate emergency care for severe or worsening abdominal or pelvic pain, or pain there with movement or touch, fainting, loss of consciousness, marked dizziness or heavy bleeding, particularly when pregnancy is possible. Pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or new confusion is also an emergency. Do not drive yourself; ask someone to take you or call an ambulance. Do not wait for a positive test or obvious vaginal bleeding.

title: Prostatitis: infection, pelvic pain and treatment
description: Understand the four prostatitis types, symptoms, appropriate tests and treatment, and when urinary problems need urgent or emergency care.
body: The prostate is a small gland below the bladder, surrounding the urethra and contributing fluid to semen. Prostatitis describes inflammation or related prostate-area symptoms. Some cases are bacterial infections; many persistent pelvic pain cases are not. The type matters because antibiotics do not treat every cause. Four types, with different causes Acute bacterial prostatitis starts suddenly and can make you very unwell. Chronic bacterial prostatitis involves persistent or recurrent bacterial infection, often with repeated urinary infections. Chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CP/CPPS) involves ongoing pelvic pain without a demonstrated bacterial cause. Asymptomatic inflammatory prostatitis is found incidentally without symptoms and often needs no treatment. Bacteria may reach the prostate from the urinary tract; catheter use, urinary procedures, obstruction or previous urinary infection can contribute. Some infections are sexually transmitted. In CP/CPPS, muscle tension, nerve sensitivity and immune or other pain mechanisms may interact; a previous infection does not prove continuing infection. Symptoms and when to get help Possible symptoms include burning, frequency, urgency, night-time urination, a weak stream or difficulty starting, and pain in the lower abdomen, back, groin, penis, testicles or between the scrotum and anus. Ejaculation may hurt. Acute infection can also cause fever, chills, nausea, vomiting and body aches. Cloudiness or odor alone cannot diagnose infection. Seek same-day assessment for new painful urinary symptoms, particularly with fever or feeling ill, and for visible or suspected blood in urine even once, in a small amount or when uncertain. Complete inability to urinate needs immediate emergency care. Confusion, severe breathing difficulty, blue/pale/blotchy skin, fainting or rapidly worsening severe illness also need emergency help. Do not wait several days. Seek immediate emergency help if you are breathing very fast, have slurred or incoherent speech, have a rash that does not fade when pressed, or think you may have sepsis. You do not need to have every sign. Persistent and recurring pelvic pain Chronic bacterial infection may produce milder symptoms that return, including recurrent urinary infections, pain and painful ejaculation. CP/CPPS can affect the same areas, with symptoms fluctuating and affecting sleep, work, sexual function and wellbeing. The chronic label commonly describes symptoms lasting at least three months; it is not a reason to delay assessment. Pain is real even when cultures show no infection. A clinician should consider other urinary, genital, bowel or musculoskeletal causes and assess pelvic floor tenderness, stress and the impact on daily life. Several mechanisms can coexist, so one treatment may not address everything. How clinicians investigate Assessment starts with symptoms, previous infections or procedures, medicines, supplements and sexual history. With explanation and consent, examination may include the abdomen, genitals, groin nodes and a gentle rectal examination of the prostate. A rectal examination alone cannot exclude cancer. Do not massage the prostate during suspected acute bacterial prostatitis: it can spread bacteria into the blood. For suspected acute infection, a midstream urine culture is important, ideally before antibiotics without delaying necessary treatment in severe illness. Blood tests or cultures may be needed if unwell; STI testing is selected according to risk. In non-acute cases, a specialist may use urine samples before and after prostate massage to localize bacteria. This is not a home procedure. Other tests and PSA Ultrasound or other imaging may be used for a suspected abscess, obstruction or another diagnosis. Cystoscopy and urine-flow or bladder-function tests are selective, not routine for everyone. Semen testing alone is not the usual diagnostic approach; a prostate biopsy is not a routine prostatitis test and should not be performed during untreated bacterial infection. Inflammation can raise PSA, so it is not a useful test for diagnosing active prostatitis and does not itself diagnose cancer. Testing or repeat testing should be timed after infection has settled, according to the individual situation. A persistently raised result needs appropriate assessment, not automatic longer antibiotics or a biopsy solely because a fixed one-to-three-month interval has passed. Treating bacterial prostatitis Bacterial prostatitis needs a prescribed antibiotic chosen for the organism, local resistance, previous treatment, allergies and ability to reach the prostate. NICE advises reviewing acute treatment after 14 days, with another 14 days if needed; EAU describes a total of two to four weeks for acute infection and commonly four to six weeks for chronic bacterial infection. These are clinical frameworks, not personal prescriptions or a universal six-month course. Severe infection may require hospital care, intravenous antibiotics and fluids. Retention needs clinical drainage, and an abscess may need a procedure. Take treatment as prescribed and attend review. If acute symptoms are not starting to improve within 48 hours, seek urgent reassessment; get help sooner for worsening or severe illness. Recurrence needs a review of cultures, resistance, obstruction or other causes rather than repeatedly using leftover antibiotics. Antibiotics are not every pelvic pain treatment AUA 2025 guidance discourages empirical prolonged antibiotics for CP/CPPS without evidence of infection. EAU allows a selected initial course in some previously untreated primary prostate pain cases, but emphasizes avoiding unnecessary antibiotics and changing approach after failure. Your clinician should explain the rationale; repeatedly treating negative-culture pain as infection can delay useful care. Treatment usually combines options matched to symptoms. Alpha blockers such as silodosin can relax muscles and help selected urinary symptoms; they are not antibiotics and do not shrink the prostate. Anti-inflammatory pain medicines such as ibuprofen or aspirin are not antibiotics either. Suitability, interactions, stomach or kidney problems and other risks need review; do not start a drug combination yourself. Other medicines need careful selection Muscle relaxants such as cyclobenzaprine, benzodiazepines such as clonazepam, and medicines targeting nerve pain are not antibiotics. Some are considered for selected symptoms, but benefits are uncertain or limited and side effects matter. Benzodiazepines can cause sedation, dependence and dangerous withdrawal; do not start or suddenly stop them without a prescribing plan. Glycosaminoglycan-related products, including chondroitin, are also not antibiotics. Evidence and indications vary, and treatments studied for bladder pain must not automatically be applied to prostate pain. Supplements can interact with medicines. Prostate surgery is not a routine cure for CP/CPPS; procedures are reserved for a clear indication such as an abscess or obstruction. Physical and psychological support A pelvic health physiotherapist can assess overactive or tender muscles and offer relaxation, selected manual techniques or biofeedback. Biofeedback helps you recognize muscle activity; it is not a guaranteed cure. Repeated strengthening exercises or Kegels may worsen an overactive pelvic floor, so follow an individual assessment rather than assuming everyone should strengthen. Warm baths or protected gentle heat may ease discomfort; avoid burns and prostate self-massage. Acupuncture may help selected people. Relaxation, paced breathing, stress-management skills or cognitive behavioral therapy can support pain coping alongside medical care. These approaches do not mean the pain is imagined, and no single complementary treatment reliably cures every case. Daily habits, sex and follow-up Drink enough to avoid dehydration without forcing large volumes or assuming water clears infection. Caffeine, alcohol, spicy or acidic foods may trigger symptoms in some people; a symptom diary can guide personal adjustments rather than a universal restrictive diet. Seek support for persistent pain, mood changes or sexual difficulties. Prostatitis is not automatically contagious, but an STI can cause related infection. If an STI is suspected or confirmed, follow sexual-health advice about testing, partner assessment and treatment; avoid sex until the advised treatment period is complete, symptoms have resolved and partners are treated. Otherwise adapt sexual activity if painful. Persistent symptoms or blood in semen still merit assessment; do not assume they are always harmless. Complications and outlook Acute bacterial prostatitis can cause urinary retention, an abscess, bacteria in the bloodstream and sepsis, which can be fatal without timely treatment. Chronic conditions may cause ongoing urinary problems, painful ejaculation, sexual difficulties and pelvic pain. Early assessment and a clear follow-up plan matter, even if symptoms seem mild. Bacterial infection often improves with appropriate treatment, but recurrence needs investigation. CP/CPPS may require several coordinated treatments and ongoing adjustment, without a guaranteed cure date. Prostatitis is not prostate cancer; overlapping symptoms or an abnormal PSA still need assessment, and an earlier prostatitis diagnosis does not rule out another condition. Prostatitis includes bacterial infections and persistent pelvic pain without demonstrated infection; treatment depends on the type. Complete inability to urinate or sepsis signs need emergency care; new painful urinary symptoms and blood in urine need same-day advice. Antibiotic choice and duration are individualized. Silodosin, pain medicines, muscle relaxants and chondroitin are not antibiotics. Chronic pain care may combine medicines, specialist pelvic therapy and coping support; avoid repeated unnecessary antibiotics, prostate self-massage and automatic Kegels. What causes prostatitis? Bacterial forms may follow a urinary infection or urinary procedure, and some related infections are sexually transmitted. Many chronic pelvic pain cases have no demonstrated bacterial cause; muscle, nerve, immune and other pain mechanisms may contribute. What symptoms should I watch for? Burning, urinary frequency or difficulty, pelvic or genital pain and painful ejaculation are possible. Fever, chills, vomiting or feeling very ill suggest urgent assessment. Complete inability to urinate, severe breathing difficulty, confusion or fainting needs immediate emergency care. Seek immediate emergency help if you are breathing very fast, have slurred or incoherent speech, have a rash that does not fade when pressed, or think you may have sepsis. You do not need to have every sign. How is it diagnosed? History, examination and appropriate urine testing are central; blood or STI tests depend on the situation. Imaging and specialist tests are selective. PSA, semen testing or biopsy are not routine ways to diagnose prostatitis. Prostate massage is unsafe during acute bacterial infection. How long do antibiotics take? Duration depends on the bacterial diagnosis, response and medicine. Acute treatment is commonly two to four weeks with review; chronic bacterial treatment is often four to six weeks. Do not choose a course yourself or assume every prostatitis case needs antibiotics for months. Are silodosin or clonazepam antibiotics? No. Silodosin is an alpha blocker; clonazepam is a benzodiazepine. Anti-inflammatory drugs, cyclobenzaprine, nerve-pain medicines and chondroitin are not antibiotics either. They have different uses and risks; clonazepam must not be stopped abruptly without professional advice. Should I do Kegels or massage the prostate? Not automatically. An overactive pelvic floor may need relaxation rather than strengthening. A trained physiotherapist can assess this. Do not massage your prostate yourself; massage during acute bacterial prostatitis can spread infection. Does prostatitis mean cancer or an STI? No, but symptoms can overlap with other conditions. PSA can rise with inflammation and needs individual follow-up. If an STI is suspected or found, sexual-health testing, partner care and the advised period without sex are important; not all prostatitis is sexually transmitted. What if treatment is not helping? For acute infection, seek urgent reassessment if symptoms are not starting to improve within 48 hours, and sooner if worsening. Recurring infection or persistent pain needs a review of the diagnosis and treatment plan. Complete retention or sepsis signs need immediate emergency help.

title: Oral sex and HIV: exposure, testing and prevention
description: Understand the very low HIV risk from oral sex, when urgent PEP assessment is appropriate, how test windows differ and why other STIs still matter.
body: Oral sex carries little to no HIV risk, much lower than unprotected anal or vaginal intercourse. Swallowing semen does not provide a reliable way to calculate an individual risk. If there may have been a significant exposure within the past 72 hours, contact urgent care or a sexual health service now for assessment; do not wait for symptoms or a test to turn positive. What oral exposure means HIV can be present in semen and pre-ejaculate. Transmission requires an appropriate route into susceptible tissue; simply having a fluid in the mouth does not establish that infection occurred. The person’s viral load, effective prevention and the actual contact matter more than assumptions about appearance or health. Mouth sores, bleeding gums, injury or blood exposure can matter to an individual assessment, but there is no sound calculation that turns fluid volume, swallowing, spitting, holding semen in the mouth or the number of oral encounters into a personal percentage. Do not rely on a small amount, quick spitting or a healthy-looking mouth as a guarantee. Viral load and undetectable equals untransmittable A person with HIV who takes effective antiretroviral treatment and maintains an undetectable viral load does not transmit HIV through sex: undetectable equals untransmittable, or U=U. This depends on sustained suppression and ongoing treatment and monitoring, not a single old result or simply saying that medicine was started. HIV treatment supports long-term health but is not a cure. U=U does not prevent other STIs or pregnancy. Do not assume that the sexual-transmission statement means zero risk from sharing injection equipment or that pregnancy, birth and breastfeeding need no specialist prevention plan. PEP is urgent treatment after a qualifying exposure Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is HIV medicine for someone without HIV after a potentially significant exposure. It should start as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours and no later than 72 hours, and is normally taken for 28 days. Assessment and the first dose must not be delayed while waiting for laboratory results. The 2025 CDC guidance does not routinely recommend PEP for oral-genital contact alone, regardless of the partner’s HIV status. Blood, significant trauma, damaged mucosa or a source with high viraemia can justify an individual decision. Unprotected anal or vaginal exposure, shared injection equipment, a broken condom and current PrEP use require their own assessment; none should be judged solely by the word “oral”. PrEP protects against HIV before exposure; it differs from PEP Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is prescribed before potential HIV exposures for people without HIV. Pills or injections, eligibility, time to protection and follow-up differ by product and situation. HIV testing is required before starting and during use; correct adherence is essential. Do not borrow tablets or assume a newly started regimen already provides full protection. PEP is an emergency course, not a substitute for ongoing prevention. Repeated exposures may warrant a clinician-guided transition from PEP to PrEP, with testing and no avoidable prevention gap. Neither medicine prevents all other STIs or pregnancy, and no individual is promised a fixed “99%” outcome after an exposure. Testing has a window period No HIV test can exclude an infection immediately after exposure. Typical CDC windows are 10–33 days for a nucleic acid test, 18–45 days for a laboratory antigen/antibody test using venous blood, 18–90 days for a rapid finger-stick antigen/antibody test, and 23–90 days for antibody tests. These are test-specific ranges, not instructions to wait before seeking care. An early negative result may need repeating. PEP or PrEP can affect detection, so tell the clinician what you took, including recent long-acting injections, and follow the prescribed schedule. US 2025 PEP guidance uses laboratory antigen/antibody testing plus diagnostic nucleic acid testing during follow-up, commonly at 4–6 and 12 weeks after exposure. A home or oral-fluid test alone is not a substitute for this plan. A positive screening result needs confirmation and prompt linkage to treatment. Symptoms do not diagnose HIV or another STI Some people develop a flu-like illness a few weeks after acquiring HIV; others have no symptoms. Fever, chills, fatigue, sore throat, muscle aches, night sweats or swollen glands have many causes. Do not use their presence or absence to decide whether HIV was acquired, and do not wait for them before requesting time-sensitive PEP assessment. Other STIs may cause genital, anal or oral sores, blisters, bumps, rash or itching; unusual vaginal, penile or anal discharge; bleeding between periods or after sex; or urinary burning or frequency. Many cause no symptoms. Seek sexual health assessment and mention the sites exposed, because throat, genital or rectal sampling may be needed. Severe illness, breathing difficulty, fainting or loss of consciousness needs immediate emergency care. Barriers, oral health and respectful communication Use an appropriate new condom for penile oral sex and a dental dam or suitable barrier for oral contact with the vulva or anus. Latex or suitable synthetic condoms reduce HIV transmission; natural-membrane condoms do not provide reliable HIV protection. Follow the product instructions and use compatible lubricant, usually water- or silicone-based with latex. Barriers reduce but do not eliminate every skin-contact STI. Maintain ordinary gentle oral care; do not treat brushing, rinsing, spitting or swallowing as a way to undo an exposure. Discuss testing, prevention and viral-load information respectfully and without pressure. HIV status cannot be inferred from appearance, identity or symptoms. A clinic can support confidential assessment and partner notification where appropriate; partners need individual advice about their own actual exposures. Anal, vaginal and injection exposures are different Without effective prevention, receptive anal intercourse carries a greater HIV risk than oral sex, and vaginal intercourse can also transmit HIV. An intact correctly used condom and sustained undetectable viral load change the assessment. A condom that slips or breaks needs advice based on the contact, timing and other prevention, rather than an automatic conclusion that infection occurred. Sharing needles, syringes or other drug-injection equipment, including preparation equipment, can transmit HIV. Use sterile equipment and available harm-reduction services. Alcohol or other substances can affect decisions and adherence; seek support without shame. HIV is not spread through ordinary casual contact, sharing food or unbroken-skin contact. HIV types and acquiring a different strain HIV-1 and HIV-2 are different types. HIV-2 is less common globally, but can still cause serious untreated disease; having both types is possible. Appropriate testing and specialist interpretation matter because treatment choices can differ. A type cannot be identified from symptoms or the kind of sexual contact. The established U=U evidence comes from HIV-1 studies. NIH notes that direct data on HIV-2 treatment as prevention are lacking; effective treatment likely reduces sexual transmission, so HIV-2 viral-load results and prevention need specialist interpretation. This evidence limitation does not change the established HIV-1 U=U message. A person who already has HIV can acquire a different strain, called superinfection. This may complicate treatment, especially with drug resistance. It does not mean every new contact causes a second infection or that the risk can be quantified from swallowed semen. Continue prescribed treatment and discuss prevention, viral suppression and other STI screening with the care team. Pregnancy, birth and infant care HIV can pass during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding, but early diagnosis, effective maternal treatment and a coordinated prevention plan greatly reduce transmission. HIV testing is recommended early in each pregnancy, with additional testing when indicated. Delivery and infant-feeding plans depend on viral load, treatment, resources and local guidance; do not stop HIV medicines yourself. An infant exposed during pregnancy or birth needs prompt specialist assessment and preventive medicines, preferably started within six hours of birth. The medicines and duration are tailored to the infant’s risk, gestational age and other factors; there is no universal four-to-six-week course for every baby. Continued feeding-related exposure also requires an individual plan and follow-up. When to contact a service Contact urgent care or a sexual health service immediately if a potentially significant exposure occurred within 72 hours; the earlier the assessment, the better. Even after that window, request testing and prevention advice rather than assuming there is nothing useful to do. Pregnancy or breastfeeding should be mentioned promptly and does not justify delaying assessment. Arrange review for STI symptoms, a partner’s diagnosis, uncertainty about a test window, a missed prevention dose or anxiety that persists despite advice. Discuss medicines, contraception and mental health support as needed. A recent exposure is not an HIV diagnosis, and an HIV diagnosis is not the same as AIDS. Effective treatment allows many people to live long, healthy lives. Oral sex has little to no HIV risk, but can transmit other STIs. Fluid amount, swallowing or spitting cannot provide a personal guarantee. U=U prevents sexual HIV transmission when viral suppression is sustained on effective treatment; it does not prevent other STIs or replace pregnancy and infant care. PEP is time-sensitive after a qualifying exposure: seek assessment immediately within 72 hours. Oral contact alone does not routinely require it. PrEP is ongoing prevention, PEP is post-exposure treatment and ART treats HIV. Testing, adherence and clinician follow-up matter for each. Test windows differ, and PEP or PrEP changes follow-up needs. Symptoms, an early negative test or a photograph of a laboratory kit cannot diagnose or exclude HIV. Can swallowing a small amount of semen cause HIV? Oral exposure has little to no HIV risk, and amount alone does not establish a personal risk. There is no safe-volume threshold or reliable swallowing-versus-spitting calculation. Blood, injury, viral load, prevention and any other contact guide clinical assessment. Does oral sex always require PEP? No. CDC guidance does not routinely recommend PEP for oral-genital contact alone. Significant blood, trauma, damaged tissue or high viraemia may change an individual decision. If there may have been a significant exposure within 72 hours, seek assessment now rather than deciding from a checklist yourself. Are PrEP and PEP the same medicine plan? No. PrEP is prescribed before potential exposures for ongoing prevention; PEP is an urgent, usually 28-day course after a qualifying exposure. Neither is a do-it-yourself substitute for HIV testing, adherence or clinical follow-up, and neither prevents every other STI. When will an HIV test be conclusive? It depends on the test, exposure timing and any PrEP or PEP. A laboratory antigen/antibody test usually detects infection within 18–45 days without antiretroviral-related changes, while other tests have different windows. Follow the clinician’s repeat-testing plan; do not wait for the window to end before requesting PEP assessment. Can symptoms or an undetectable result answer every concern? Symptoms cannot diagnose HIV or exclude it. Sustained undetectable viral load on effective treatment prevents sexual HIV transmission, but one old result does not prove continuing suppression. Other STI testing and pregnancy-related care may still be needed. Are anal or vaginal sex and needle sharing comparable to oral sex? No. Anal and vaginal intercourse and shared injection equipment have different transmission routes and assessments. Anal exposure, especially receptive intercourse without effective prevention, carries more HIV risk than oral contact. Seek advice about the actual event and prevention used. Can someone with HIV acquire another type or strain? Yes. HIV-1/HIV-2 coinfection and acquisition of a different strain are possible. A resistant strain may complicate treatment. This is not a diagnosis from symptoms or semen amount; specialist testing, prescribed treatment and individualized prevention are needed. Can HIV pass to a baby, and must every baby take medicine for six weeks? Transmission can occur during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding, but coordinated treatment and prevention greatly reduce it. Exposed newborns need prompt specialist care and medicines, preferably within six hours of birth. The regimen and duration depend on risk; six weeks is not a universal rule. Delivery, feeding and follow-up are individualized.

title: Blood from the penis: urine, semen and when to seek help
description: Understand possible causes of blood in urine or semen, urgent warning signs and why assessment matters even after exercise or a recent procedure.
body: Blood noticed at the penis may be mixed with urine, appear in semen or come from an external wound. Those situations can have different causes and levels of urgency. Many causes are treatable, but a symptom alone cannot tell you whether antibiotics, another treatment or urgent care is needed. Get visible blood in urine assessed promptly, even if it happens once, is painless or looks like only a small amount. Identify what you have noticed without self-diagnosing Blood in urine is called hematuria. It may look pink, red or dark brown, or be found only on a urine test. It can come from the kidneys, ureters, bladder or urethra rather than the penis itself. Cloudiness, odor, burning, difficulty passing urine and pain in the side or back are useful details, but do not establish the cause. Blood in semen is called hematospermia and may look red or brown. It can accompany painful ejaculation, urinary symptoms or pelvic discomfort. It often clears without serious disease, but still deserves a clinical check. Discharge, sores or bleeding on the skin are different findings; tell the clinician exactly where the blood appears and when it began. When care is urgent Arrange urgent medical advice for visible or suspected blood in urine, even once or without other symptoms. Blood that disappears still needs attention. Seek urgent care for inability to urinate, clots that obstruct flow, severe side or abdominal pain, fever or chills with urinary symptoms, vomiting or marked illness. Get emergency help for sudden severe testicular pain, a significant penile injury with a snap, rapid swelling, deformity or blood at the urethral opening, heavy uncontrolled bleeding, fainting, confusion or severe breathing difficulty. These can signal torsion, major injury, significant blood loss or serious infection. Blood in semen without these signs generally needs an appointment rather than an emergency visit; use the more urgent pathway when urine is also bloody. Enlarged prostate and prostatitis The prostate lies below the bladder, surrounds the urethra and contributes fluid to semen. Benign prostate enlargement can cause poor flow, frequency or incomplete emptying, and can be associated with bleeding. It is non-cancerous, but a previous enlargement diagnosis does not explain every new episode or exclude cancer. Alpha blockers relax outlet muscles; they do not shrink the gland. Finasteride or dutasteride may reduce an appropriately enlarged gland over time. Prostatitis means inflammation of the prostate, not necessarily bacterial infection. It can cause urinary, pelvic or ejaculation pain and sometimes fever. Bacterial prostatitis needs prescribed antibiotics, while nonbacterial chronic pelvic pain needs a different, individualized approach. Fever, worsening illness or retention requires prompt care; urine tests and sometimes other investigations help guide treatment. Urinary infection and kidney infection A urinary infection can involve the urethra, bladder or kidneys. Burning, frequency, urgency and cloudy or strong-smelling urine may occur with blood. These features overlap with other conditions, so assessment and urine testing are important. Antibiotic choice and duration depend on the infection, test results and the person's circumstances; a short course is not a universal answer to bleeding. Kidney infection can cause fever, chills, side or back pain, nausea or vomiting and urinary symptoms. It can develop from a lower urinary infection, but does not always mean someone left a bladder infection untreated. It may lead to sepsis or kidney damage if not treated. Prompt antibiotics are usually needed; severe illness may require hospital treatment. Kidney stones Stones are hard deposits that can irritate the urinary tract and cause visible or microscopic blood. Small stones may cause little discomfort; a moving or obstructing stone can cause severe pain in the side, back, abdomen or groin, sometimes with nausea. Pain with fever or inability to urinate needs urgent assessment rather than waiting for a stone to pass. Urine tests and imaging may help identify a stone and obstruction. Some can pass with a clinician's plan for pain control, suitable fluid intake and sometimes medicine; others require shock-wave treatment or removal through a thin instrument, sometimes with a laser. Do not force large amounts of fluid or assume every stone is safe to manage at home, especially with kidney or heart conditions. Sexually transmitted infections, epididymitis and orchitis Sexually transmitted infections such as gonorrhea or chlamydia may cause urethral inflammation, discharge or painful urination and can be associated with blood in semen. Herpes may cause sores and local bleeding; visible blood is not a reliable way to identify which infection is present. Explain relevant vaginal, anal or oral sexual contact so the service can select suitable tests. Antibiotics treat appropriate bacterial infections; herpes management may use antivirals. Follow advice on sex and partner testing or treatment. Epididymitis is inflammation of the sperm-carrying tube behind a testicle. Pain and swelling may accompany urinary symptoms or semen changes; bacterial causes can include an STI or urinary infection. Orchitis is inflammation of the testicle itself and can be viral, including mumps, or bacterial. Treatment depends on the cause; antibiotics do not treat a virus. Supportive care may include suitable pain relief and scrotal support. Significant inflammation can affect fertility, and sudden severe pain must be assessed as a possible torsion rather than assumed to be infection. Prostate and bladder cancer need appropriate assessment Cancer is one possible cause, not the explanation for every episode. Early prostate cancer often has no symptoms; urinary or sexual changes, blood, ejaculation pain or pelvic/rectal discomfort are not specific to cancer. PSA can help guide assessment, but benign enlargement or inflammation can also raise it. Examination, imaging and sometimes biopsy may be needed; PSA alone neither diagnoses nor excludes cancer. Prostate cancer treatment depends on risk, stage, health and preferences. Active surveillance involves planned tests for selected cancers; watchful waiting has a different, symptom-focused aim. Neither is suitable for every cancer. Surgery, radiation and drug treatments are other options. Discuss effects such as leakage, erectile problems and fertility rather than assuming surgery or observation is always best. Bladder cancer can cause blood that comes and goes, sometimes initially without pain. Similar bleeding also occurs with non-cancerous conditions, so color and intermittent timing cannot distinguish them. Depending on stage and other factors, treatment may include removal through the urethra, medicines placed in the bladder, removal of part or all of the bladder, chemotherapy, radiation, immunotherapy or other medicines. If the bladder is removed, urinary diversion is planned; this is not simply an automatic replacement with an artificial bladder. Bleeding after tests, treatment or vasectomy A prostate biopsy or another urinary procedure can cause temporary blood in urine or semen. Expected amount and duration differ by procedure. Follow the actual discharge instructions and contact the service for increasing bleeding, clots, fever, worsening pain or difficulty urinating. Do not dismiss these signs as normal just because some discoloration was expected. Prostate brachytherapy delivers radiation close to the tumor using permanent seeds or a temporary source. Urinary irritation, blood in urine, bowel or rectal symptoms and sexual effects can occur. Tell the cancer team about bleeding, including blood from the rectum; obtain urgent help for retention or significant bleeding. Discuss benefits, risks and aftercare before treatment. Vasectomy blocks the tubes carrying sperm; it does not stop semen production or provide immediate pregnancy protection. Early soreness, swelling or a little blood in semen can occur, but symptoms do not have to disappear within a fixed few days. Follow aftercare, report worsening pain, swelling, fever or persistent concerning bleeding, and keep using contraception until the service confirms success after the required semen testing. Injury and strenuous exercise An accident, sport or forceful sexual activity can injure the penis or urinary tract. Blood at the opening, urine or semen after trauma needs medical advice; significant injury, rapid swelling, severe pain, a snapping sound or inability to urinate needs emergency assessment. A small superficial skin cut is different from an internal injury, but do not attempt to treat a suspected urethral injury yourself. Strenuous exercise can be associated with temporary blood in urine, but the mechanism is not always clear and it is not safe to assume dehydration or red-cell breakdown explains it. Do not wait a promised 72 hours before seeking advice about visible blood. Pause strenuous activity and arrange assessment; persistent or repeated blood may require further investigation even if it followed a workout. Assessment and a treatment plan Describe whether the blood was in urine, semen or on the skin, its timing, whether it recurs and any pain, fever, discharge, injury, recent procedure or exercise. Bring a medicine list, including blood thinners; do not stop prescribed treatment yourself. Depending on the findings, assessment may include examination, urine and infection tests, blood tests, imaging, cystoscopy or prostate investigations. Not everyone needs every test. Treatment targets the cause. Antibiotics can help a bacterial infection, but do not cure stones, every form of inflammation, an injury or cancer. Ask when results will arrive, who will review them and what changes should prompt urgent care. A reassuring initial result does not replace follow-up if bleeding persists or returns. Visible blood in urine needs prompt assessment, even once or without pain. Blood in semen often resolves, but should still be checked. Retention, severe pain, significant injury or systemic illness increases urgency. Antibiotics are for appropriate infections, not a universal treatment for bleeding. Exercise or a recent procedure does not automatically make new bleeding harmless. Can an injury cause bleeding from the penis? Yes. External or internal trauma can cause bleeding. Significant injury, blood at the urethral opening, rapid swelling, severe pain or inability to urinate needs emergency assessment. Can a sexually transmitted infection cause it? Some can cause inflammation, discharge or bleeding. Testing identifies the cause; bacterial and viral infections need different management, with advice about partners and sex. Can there be blood in semen after vasectomy? Yes, early blood or discomfort can occur. Follow the service's aftercare and report worsening or concerning symptoms. Vasectomy is not effective immediately; continue contraception until testing confirms success. Can strenuous exercise cause blood in urine? It can be associated, but that does not prove the cause is harmless. Visible blood needs prompt medical advice rather than waiting 72 hours or assuming dehydration. Does blood mean cancer? No. Infection, stones, procedures and other causes are possible. Cancer is also a reason to assess unexplained blood; symptoms, color or a PSA result alone cannot settle the diagnosis. Is blood in semen the same as blood in urine? No. They may come from different sites and have different urgency. Mention both if present. Visible blood in urine warrants urgent advice even when blood in semen might otherwise be reviewed routinely. Will antibiotics stop it? Only if an appropriate bacterial infection is the cause. Do not take leftover antibiotics or delay assessment while trying them. What if the blood goes away? Still arrange the recommended assessment, especially for visible urine blood. Tell the service if bleeding returns, persists or comes with new symptoms.

title: Swallowing semen: nutrition claims, infections and allergy
description: What semen contains, why it is not a protein supplement or proven mood treatment, and what matters for oral STI exposure, rare allergy and consent.
body: Whether to swallow semen is a personal choice that requires freely given consent. It is not necessary for a partner's pleasure, your nutrition or a healthy pregnancy. Semen contains substances that support sperm, but swallowing it has no established role as a nutritional treatment, antidepressant or way to prevent pre-eclampsia. Oral infection exposure and rare allergic reactions deserve more attention than claimed benefits. Semen is more than sperm Sperm are microscopic reproductive cells carrying genetic material. Semen is the ejaculatory fluid that may contain them, mixed mainly with secretions from the seminal vesicles and prostate. It is often whitish-grey and initially thicker, but appearance varies; not all semen contains sperm. The fluid contains water, proteins, sugars such as fructose and glucose, citrate, and small amounts of substances including calcium, magnesium, potassium, sodium and zinc. Other chemical constituents include chloride, lactate and urea. Their role in a reproductive fluid does not make semen a food supplement, and a single fixed percentage for every component would be misleading. Protein, calories and digestion Semen contains protein and energy-containing compounds, but the small and variable amount of ejaculate is not a meaningful way to meet nutritional needs. Claims of a fixed protein fraction, a universal teaspoon-sized ejaculation or exactly five to seven calories should not be treated as a nutritional prescription. Swallowed fluid enters the digestive tract; that does not erase contact already made with the mouth and throat.
