It is therefore misleading to call swallowing universally harmless because digestion occurs. Persistent nausea, pain or other symptoms deserve assessment rather than assuming either poisoning or an allergy from the act alone. Taste and smell vary, without a reliable food recipe People describe semen as salty, bitter or slightly sweet, and perception differs. Lists promising that pineapple, celery, herbs or spices will improve flavour, or that garlic, vegetables, dairy or coffee will spoil it, are not a reliable basis for prescribing a diet. Do not stop useful medicines or take supplements to meet a partner's taste preference. Semen is usually mildly alkaline; some people describe a bleach-like smell, but smell cannot measure pH, fertility or infection. Sweat, urine and genital hygiene can also affect the overall smell noticed during sex. A new persistent unpleasant smell, pain, discharge or blood needs clinical advice rather than being explained away as food or judged by tasting. Use gentle external hygiene, not bleach, perfume or disinfectant on genital tissue. Mood and stress claims are not a treatment A frequently quoted 2002 study compared condom use with depression scores in sexually active college women. Condom use was an indirect measure of exposure in the reproductive tract; it was not a trial of swallowing semen. An association cannot establish that semen caused a mood change. A later 2014 study did not replicate the proposed antidepressant effect. Finding hormones, signalling molecules or antioxidants in semen does not show that swallowing delivers an effective antidepressant or anti-stress dose. Effects on sperm within the fluid are different from benefits to the person swallowing it. Do not replace mental-health care, stop prescribed treatment or give up condoms on this basis; seek support for persistent low mood or anxiety. It is not a proven way to prevent pre-eclampsia Older research explored semen exposure and immune tolerance in pregnancy. A 2003 case-control study concerned duration of cohabitation and barrier use, not a prescribed swallowing treatment. A 2013 case-control study found no association between oral seminal-fluid exposure and reduced pre-eclampsia risk. These studies cannot justify recommending oral sex or abandoning barriers for pregnancy protection. Attend antenatal appointments and discuss your individual risk with the maternity team. For selected higher-risk pregnancies, clinicians may recommend preventive medicines such as low-dose aspirin; do not start it or calcium supplements yourself. During pregnancy or the weeks after birth, severe persistent headache, visual changes, pain beneath the ribs, sudden swelling or feeling very unwell requires immediate maternity advice. Oral sex can transmit infections Gonorrhoea and chlamydia can affect the throat after oral sex; syphilis, herpes and HPV are also relevant. Infection can occur through contact before swallowing, and some infections spread without ejaculation. Spitting afterwards is not a reliable way to undo exposure. Many oral infections cause no symptoms, so appearance, smell and a partner feeling well cannot establish safety. CDC describes HIV risk from oral sex as little to none, much lower than from vaginal or anal sex; that does not apply equally to other STIs. Discuss the actual contact and any other exposures with a sexual-health service for site-specific tests and timing. HIV PEP is not routinely needed for every oral encounter; if a clinician considers an exposure potentially substantial risk, seek assessment immediately and no later than 72 hours, without waiting for symptoms. Reducing infection exposure Talk without blame about recent testing, any exposures since testing and symptoms. An old or very early negative test is not a certificate that every infection is absent. A service may recommend a throat swab as well as other tests according to the activities; follow its testing, treatment and partner-care advice. For oral contact with a penis, an appropriate condom can reduce exposure; dental dams or suitable barriers are options for oral contact with a vulva or anus. Barriers reduce but do not eliminate every infection risk. Use a suitable non-latex option if latex allergy is suspected, and stop if contact is painful or irritating. Neither swallowing nor spitting replaces a barrier or appropriate testing. Rare seminal-plasma allergy needs proper assessment A rare allergy to proteins in seminal plasma can affect the lips, mouth, skin or other contact areas and can sometimes cause a whole-body reaction. Burning, pain, itching, redness, swelling or hives are possible; symptoms may begin soon after exposure, but there is no exact 20-to-30-minute rule or reliable population count to apply to everyone. Trouble breathing, throat or tongue swelling, a hoarse voice with breathing difficulty, fainting or loss of consciousness can signal anaphylaxis: call emergency services immediately. Use prescribed adrenaline according to your action plan; do not wait for an antihistamine to work. Avoid further exposure until assessed. Infection, irritation, latex or lubricant reactions can resemble semen allergy, so do not diagnose yourself or attempt desensitisation at home. Swallow, spit or decline: the choice is yours You may decline oral sex or semen contact, change your mind, spit or swallow without owing a partner an explanation about supposed health benefits. Agree beforehand about ejaculation and boundaries; comfort and consent matter more than completing a particular act. A partner's status should be discussed respectfully, without assuming infection or judging fidelity. Swallowing semen does not itself cause pregnancy: the digestive and reproductive tracts are separate. Fresh sperm-containing fluid reaching the vaginal opening or entering the vagina during the same encounter is a different exposure and may warrant contraception advice. If you feel pressured or unsafe, seek confidential support; persistent symptoms after contact should be assessed rather than tolerated to please someone. Semen contains proteins and other compounds, but is not a useful nutritional supplement or established mood treatment. Old observational findings do not justify swallowing semen to prevent pre-eclampsia or giving up barriers. Oral STIs can be symptomless; contact occurs before any decision to swallow or spit. Breathing difficulty, throat swelling or fainting after exposure needs immediate emergency care; consent remains essential. What is in semen? It may contain sperm plus glandular fluid with water, proteins, sugars, citrate and small amounts of minerals and other compounds such as chloride, lactate and urea. Composition varies. These reproductive-fluid constituents do not make it a nutritional treatment. What does semen taste like? Descriptions include salty, bitter or slightly sweet, with individual variation. There is no reliable food recipe that guarantees a preferred taste. Taste is not a test for infection, fertility or safety, and no one needs to taste it. What does semen smell like? Some describe a mild bleach-like smell, but individual perception and surrounding sweat or urine can affect what is noticed. Smell alone cannot diagnose pH or infection. A persistent new unpleasant change, especially with pain, discharge or blood, warrants clinical advice. Is swallowing semen harmless? Not universally. Oral exposure can transmit some STIs, often without symptoms, and rare seminal-plasma allergy can cause serious reactions. Digestion does not undo mouth or throat contact. You can decline without sacrificing a proven health benefit. Can swallowing improve mood or reduce stress? There is no established treatment benefit. The often quoted 2002 study concerned condom use and depression scores, not a swallowing trial; a later study failed to replicate its proposed effect. Hormones or antioxidants in a fluid do not establish an effective treatment dose. Does it prevent pre-eclampsia? No reliable evidence supports recommending swallowing for prevention. Older observational associations are not proof of benefit, and a 2013 study found no reduced risk with oral exposure. Follow antenatal risk assessment and prescribed prevention, not semen exposure. Could symptoms mean semen allergy? Burning, itching, redness, swelling or hives after contact can have several causes. Seek assessment and avoid further suspected exposure. Breathing difficulty, throat or tongue swelling, fainting or loss of consciousness needs emergency services immediately; use prescribed adrenaline as directed. Is spitting safer than swallowing, and can either cause pregnancy? Spitting does not reliably undo infection exposure that already occurred in the mouth or throat. Neither swallowing nor spitting itself causes pregnancy. Semen reaching the vaginal opening or vagina during the encounter is a separate pregnancy-risk question. You may choose either or decline contact.

title: Cephalosporin antibiotics: uses, generations and safe treatment
description: Understand how cephalosporins differ, when they treat bacterial infections, allergy assessment, side effects and pregnancy or breastfeeding decisions.
body: Cephalosporins are prescription antibiotics in the beta-lactam family. They can treat selected bacterial infections, but the right medicine depends on the infection, bacterial susceptibility and the person receiving it. A later generation is not automatically better, and penicillin allergy or breastfeeding does not create the same rule for every cephalosporin. What cephalosporins treat and how they work These medicines interfere with bacterial cell-wall construction. Gram-positive bacteria have a thicker peptidoglycan wall; Gram-negative bacteria have a thinner layer and an additional outer membrane. These differences help explain antibiotic spectra, but laboratory susceptibility and local resistance still matter. Cephalosporins do not treat viruses, including colds and flu; many coughs, sore throats and ear infections do not need an antibiotic. Depending on the particular drug, uses include skin and soft-tissue infections, urinary infections, selected bacterial throat, ear, sinus and lung infections, meningitis, bloodstream infections, gonorrhoea or prevention around surgery. Some are oral; others are intravenous or intramuscular, depending on the formulation. Severe illness may need hospital treatment, but an injection is not automatically better for every infection. First and second generations First-generation examples include cefalexin, cefadroxil, cefradine and injectable cefazolin. They commonly cover susceptible streptococci and methicillin-sensitive staphylococci, with some Gram-negative activity. Cefazolin is also used for selected surgical infection prevention. These examples do not make every medicine suitable for every skin, ear or urinary infection. Second-generation examples include cefuroxime, cefaclor and cefprozil. Their spectra differ, often extending coverage of some Gram-negative organisms. A clinician may select cefuroxime for particular bacterial respiratory, urinary or skin infections. Ordinary viral bronchitis is not a reason to prescribe it, and second-generation drugs are not a universal treatment for gonorrhoea, meningitis or sepsis. Third-generation medicines and important exceptions Examples include oral cefixime, cefpodoxime and ceftibuten, and injectable ceftriaxone, cefotaxime and ceftazidime. Selected agents treat serious infections, including some cases of meningitis, pneumonia or bloodstream infection. They are not interchangeable: for gonorrhoea, CDC guidance prefers ceftriaxone; cefixime is a limited alternative when ceftriaxone is unavailable, while oral cefuroxime and cefpodoxime are not recommended. Ceftazidime can treat susceptible Pseudomonas infections, but not every third-generation cephalosporin has that activity. A positive culture, infection site and local resistance guide selection. Hot-tub folliculitis is a different situation: it usually settles without antibiotics, so its association with Pseudomonas does not justify routine ceftazidime treatment. Fourth generation and newer anti-MRSA options Cefepime is a fourth-generation medicine used for selected serious infections, including pneumonia, complicated urinary infection and suspected bacterial infection with fever in a person with low neutrophils. Additional antibiotics may be needed for organisms outside its spectrum. Kidney function affects dosing; confusion, hallucinations, jerking movements or seizures during treatment need immediate medical assessment because neurotoxicity can occur, particularly with renal impairment. Ceftaroline is often described as a fifth-generation cephalosporin. Ceftaroline and ceftobiprole are newer cephalosporins with activity against some resistant staphylococci, including MRSA. Ceftaroline has specific skin-infection and community-acquired-pneumonia indications. FDA approved ceftobiprole in April 2024 for defined bloodstream, skin and pneumonia settings, with age and infection restrictions. Neither is a universal treatment for resistant bacteria, and availability and approved uses vary by country. Penicillin allergy needs an individual assessment Tell the prescriber the exact medicine, symptoms, timing and treatment of any previous reaction, including anaphylaxis, blistering rash or organ injury. Cross-reactions depend substantially on chemical side chains rather than simply sharing the beta-lactam name. A penicillin-allergy label does not automatically exclude every cephalosporin; cefazolin, for example, has a distinct side-chain pattern. This does not mean choosing or testing a substitute at home. Specialist guidance distinguishes unverified mild reactions, anaphylaxis and severe delayed reactions. Product labels can impose stricter contraindications, which the treating team must consider. A past severe skin reaction or organ injury needs particular specialist care; do not deliberately re-expose yourself or use another person’s antibiotic. Digestive effects and C. diff diarrhoea Nausea, vomiting, loose stools, thrush and sometimes dizziness or injection-site discomfort can occur, depending on the drug. Ask about troublesome effects. Simple meals and fluids may help when tolerated, but food instructions are product-specific; for example, cefuroxime axetil tablets are taken after food. Do not assume that all cephalosporins should be taken on an empty stomach. Antibiotics can disturb gut bacteria and allow Clostridioides difficile infection during or after treatment, even without a long course. New diarrhoea warrants advice; severe or persistent watery diarrhoea, blood or mucus, fever, abdominal pain or dehydration needs urgent assessment. Do not self-treat suspected antibiotic-associated colitis with medicines that slow the bowel. Probiotics do not guarantee prevention or replace assessment; discuss supplements first if immunity is weakened. Pregnancy and breastfeeding A bacterial infection that needs treatment should be treated during pregnancy. Data for commonly used cephalosporins are generally reassuring, but the drug, infection and available evidence determine the benefit–risk decision; this is not a class-wide guarantee of zero risk. BUMPS does not recommend extra birth-defect monitoring solely because of cephalosporin exposure. Newer agents may have less pregnancy information. Breastfeeding is not automatically prohibited. Cefalexin is generally compatible with breastfeeding, with low milk levels; other medicines require their own assessment. Watch the baby for poor feeding, diarrhoea, thrush or rash and seek advice if these occur. Premature, unwell or especially vulnerable infants need individualized professional guidance. Do not automatically stop breastfeeding or an essential antibiotic without discussing the plan. Kidneys, other medicines and contraception Report kidney disease, previous C. diff, pregnancy or breastfeeding and all prescription, non-prescription, herbal and vitamin products. Some cephalosporins need renal dose adjustment. Warfarin or similar anticoagulants may require monitoring, while probenecid, kidney-harming medicines or acid-reducing drugs can interact with particular products. The pharmacist should check the exact combination rather than assuming one rule for the entire class. Cephalosporins do not automatically make hormonal contraception ineffective. However, vomiting or severe diarrhoea can reduce absorption of an oral contraceptive; follow that pill’s instructions and ask about additional protection. Mention antibiotic treatment before blood or urine tests because some products interfere with particular laboratory methods. Avoid driving if dizzy, confused or otherwise impaired. Following the prescription and reviewing progress Take the prescribed dose, spacing and duration, using the correct formulation and any food or storage instructions. Do not borrow, share or save antibiotics for a future illness. Follow the leaflet or pharmacist’s advice after a missed dose; do not double a dose to make up for it. A culture result or clinical reassessment may lead the clinician to shorten, stop or change treatment. Do not stop merely because you feel better, and do not keep taking a medicine through a serious reaction just to finish a course. A new rash needs prompt advice before further doses; blistering, peeling or mouth/eye sores need immediate emergency assessment. Worsening infection or lack of expected improvement needs review, following the condition-specific timeframe rather than waiting for the pack to run out. When to seek urgent or emergency help Stop taking the suspected medicine and call emergency services for swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, breathing difficulty, fainting or loss of consciousness, or rapidly worsening allergic symptoms. Blistering or peeling skin, mouth/eye sores, a seizure, severe new confusion or inability to wake also need immediate emergency help. Do not drive yourself. Tell emergency staff which medicine was taken. Seek urgent same-day advice for severe diarrhoea, blood or mucus in stools, fever with abdominal pain, dehydration, jaundice, unexplained bruising or a worsening infection. Severe abdominal pain with marked illness, faintness, confusion or very little urine warrants emergency assessment. A new rash should be assessed before another dose; do not dismiss it as an ordinary side effect or wait for several warning signs together. Abdominal pain that starts suddenly and is severe also needs immediate emergency care on its own; do not wait for another warning sign. Cephalosporins treat selected bacterial infections, not viruses; drug and route depend on the infection and susceptibility. Generation numbers describe broad differences, not a ranking of strength or a list of interchangeable prescriptions. Penicillin allergy requires reaction-history and side-chain assessment; do not test an alternative yourself. Pregnancy and breastfeeding decisions are drug-specific. A blanket breastfeeding ban is incorrect. Follow the current treatment plan, but act immediately on serious allergy, skin, neurological or diarrhoeal warnings. What is the difference between first and second generations? First-generation drugs often cover susceptible streptococci and methicillin-sensitive staphylococci. Some second-generation drugs extend selected Gram-negative coverage. Individual spectra and approved uses differ; later does not automatically mean better. Can I take a cephalosporin if I have penicillin allergy? Sometimes, after a clinician reviews the exact reaction, side-chain relationships and the specific product label. Anaphylaxis or a severe delayed skin or organ reaction requires special care. Do not take a test dose or choose a substitute yourself. What side effects can occur? Digestive upset, diarrhoea, thrush or dizziness can occur. A new rash needs advice before further doses. Breathing difficulty, swelling, fainting, blistering skin, mouth/eye sores, seizures or severe confusion need emergency help. Are all cephalosporins safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding? There is no universal zero-risk rule. Commonly used options have reassuring pregnancy data, and cefalexin is generally compatible with breastfeeding. The exact drug and infant’s health matter; premature or unwell babies need individual advice. Does a higher generation work against every resistant infection? No. Ceftazidime has selected Pseudomonas activity, while newer anti-MRSA medicines have specific indications. No generation treats all bacteria, and resistance, infection site and local guidance determine the choice. Should I take probiotics for antibiotic diarrhoea? They do not guarantee prevention or treatment and should not delay assessment. Discuss them first if you have an existing illness or weakened immunity. Severe or persistent diarrhoea, fever, pain, blood or dehydration needs prompt medical advice. Should I finish the course even if I develop a reaction? Follow the current prescription and do not stop simply because you feel better. However, serious reactions require immediate action, not continued dosing. Seek advice before another dose for a new rash; the clinician may appropriately change or stop treatment. When is immediate emergency care needed? Call emergency services for breathing difficulty, lip/tongue/throat swelling, fainting or loss of consciousness, blistering or peeling skin or mouth/eye sores, seizures, severe confusion or inability to wake. Severe abdominal illness or dehydration with faintness, confusion or very little urine also needs emergency assessment. Abdominal pain that starts suddenly and is severe also needs immediate emergency care on its own; do not wait for another warning sign.

title: Benign prostate enlargement: symptoms, tests and treatment
description: How an enlarged prostate can affect urination, when to seek urgent help, and how assessment, medicines and procedures are chosen.
body: Getting up repeatedly at night, waiting for urine to start or feeling that the bladder has not emptied can disrupt everyday life. Benign prostate enlargement is one possible explanation, especially later in life, but urinary symptoms deserve assessment rather than a diagnosis made from age alone. Treatment depends on the cause, how much symptoms bother you and whether complications are present. What BPH means and why it happens The prostate is a small gland below the bladder. It surrounds the urethra, the tube that carries urine out, and contributes fluid to semen. Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) means non-cancerous growth of prostate tissue. Enlargement can narrow the urethra and make the bladder work harder to empty. BPH becomes more common with age, particularly after 50, although it can affect anyone with a prostate. Its exact cause is not fully understood; age-related hormonal changes and family history are relevant. Body size, activity and other health conditions may also be associated with risk. Prostate size does not reliably predict symptom severity. A large gland may cause little trouble, while a smaller enlargement can obstruct flow. Neither an unusual testicular finding nor a general statement about hormones proves that someone has BPH; mention previous testicular or prostate surgery during the assessment. Surgery on the testicles is not a prevention strategy for ordinary urinary symptoms. Symptoms and signs that need prompt attention Possible symptoms include difficulty starting, a weak or interrupted stream, straining, dribbling afterward, urgency, frequent urination, waking at night and feeling incompletely emptied. Leakage can occur too. Symptoms may develop gradually, but they do not inevitably worsen in everyone. Arrange an assessment for persistent or bothersome urinary changes. Pain when urinating or visible blood needs prompt medical advice; do not assume either is simply BPH. Similar symptoms can arise from infection, prostatitis, bladder problems, medicines or cancer. Seek urgent care if you cannot pass urine at all, particularly with a painful swollen lower abdomen. Fever or chills with painful frequent urination, severe urinary or abdominal pain, or marked illness also requires urgent assessment. Do not wait two months for home measures to work when a warning sign is present. BPH and prostate cancer are different conditions BPH is not prostate cancer and does not itself increase the risk of prostate cancer. However, the two can occur together. Early prostate cancer often has no symptoms, and later symptoms can overlap with other prostate or urinary problems. Symptoms alone cannot reliably distinguish them. A PSA blood test may help guide assessment, but it does not diagnose or exclude cancer by itself. BPH and inflammation can raise PSA, while finasteride or dutasteride can lower it. Discuss what a result means in your circumstances and whether further tests are needed. Choosing screening without symptoms is a separate discussion about potential benefits and harms. What an assessment may involve The clinician asks about your symptoms, their effect on sleep and daily life, infections, medical and family history, previous procedures and all medicines or supplements. A short bladder diary of drinking, urine amounts and timing can help. Examination may include the abdomen and a finger examination through the rectum to assess the prostate. A urine sample can check for blood or infection. Depending on the findings, the clinician may discuss PSA testing, kidney function, a urine-flow test and an ultrasound measurement of urine left after emptying. Not everyone needs every test. Specialist tests can include cystoscopy, using a thin camera to inspect the urethra and bladder, or urodynamic testing to study bladder pressure and function. These are selected for a reason, not routine requirements for everyone. Review decongestants, antihistamines, antidepressants, sedatives and diuretics with a pharmacist or prescriber; do not stop or change prescribed doses yourself. Monitoring and practical ways to ease symptoms Mild symptoms without complications may be managed with agreed monitoring and lifestyle changes. Keep follow-up appointments and seek review sooner if symptoms change. Monitoring is an active plan, rather than ignoring persistent difficulty. Reduce caffeine or alcohol if they worsen urgency, and adjust drinking before bedtime or outings while staying adequately hydrated during the day. Do not severely restrict fluids. Relax rather than strain, allow time to empty and try again after a brief pause if advised. Regular movement, managing constipation and maintaining a suitable weight can also help. Use a toileting plan suited to your symptoms; repeatedly forcing urination without an urge or holding through pain is not a universal solution. Bladder training or pelvic-floor exercises may help selected symptoms with appropriate instruction. Managing stress and keeping comfortable may ease symptoms for some people, but neither warmth nor exercise removes an obstruction. No food or herbal product is an established cure; saw palmetto alone has shown little or no benefit in good-quality studies. Medicines: different roles and important cautions Alpha blockers, such as tamsulosin, alfuzosin or doxazosin, relax muscles around the prostate and bladder outlet. They may improve flow without shrinking the gland. Dizziness or low blood pressure and changes in ejaculation are possible; suitability and the choice of drug require a review. Finasteride and dutasteride reduce the formation of dihydrotestosterone (DHT), rather than hormones made by the prostate itself. They can shrink a suitably enlarged gland over time and may be combined with an alpha blocker. Benefits take time; sexual side effects and changes in PSA interpretation need discussion. Selected people may be offered other medicines for bladder symptoms or a PDE5 inhibitor, depending on local guidance and their health. Antibiotics do not treat non-infected prostate enlargement. They may be prescribed for a diagnosed bacterial urinary infection or bacterial prostatitis, which can coexist with urinary symptoms. They do not treat every form of prostatitis. Avoid self-treatment with leftover antibiotics or changing any prostate medicine without advice. Procedures are chosen individually A procedure may be considered when symptoms remain unacceptable despite other treatment, medicines are unsuitable or complications occur. The decision considers prostate size and shape, health, anesthesia, the desired effect on urination, sexual function, recovery and the chance of needing further treatment. Options for selected patients include water-vapor therapy, often called Rezūm, and a prostatic urethral lift, often called UroLift. Steam treats excess tissue; a lift uses small implants to hold tissue away from the urethra rather than removing the prostate. Some procedures may better preserve ejaculation, but no option guarantees preserved sexual function, the same symptom relief as TURP or lower overall cost in every setting. Older lists may include needle ablation (TUNA), microwave therapy (TUMT), hot-water thermotherapy (WIT) or high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU). These should not be presented as interchangeable current choices; availability and recommendations vary, and NICE does not recommend several older techniques as alternatives to its standard operations. Ask which currently recommended procedure fits your anatomy and priorities. Surgery, recovery and possible complications TURP removes obstructing tissue through the urethra. Other approaches include laser treatment such as HoLEP, or a transurethral incision (TUIP) that widens the outlet with cuts rather than removing a large amount of tissue. A simple prostatectomy removes the enlarged inner portion and may be considered for a very large gland; it is different from removing the whole prostate for cancer. Repeated retention, recurrent infections or bleeding, bladder stones and obstruction affecting kidney function may make an operation necessary. Leakage alone does not automatically determine the operation or hospital admission. Some procedures are day cases; others need a hospital stay. There is no universal ten-day admission, and a catheter may be needed during recovery. Discuss bleeding, infection, scarring, temporary or persistent urinary difficulties, leakage and sexual or fertility effects, including semen passing backward into the bladder during ejaculation. Recovery and risks differ by procedure and person. Symptoms can recur and further treatment may be needed, so follow the surgeon's aftercare and review plan. Complications and a continuing care plan Untreated significant obstruction can lead to retained urine, infections, bladder stones, bleeding and damage to the bladder or kidneys. Not every enlarged prostate causes these problems, and treatment should be proportionate to your symptoms and findings. Record changes in flow, night-time urination, pain, leakage and medicines, then review whether the agreed plan is helping. Pads or other continence products can support daily life; a catheter may be needed if the bladder cannot empty. New blood, pain, fever or inability to urinate needs medical attention rather than reassurance from a previous BPH diagnosis. Urinary symptoms need assessment; an enlarged prostate is one possible cause. BPH is non-cancerous, but a BPH diagnosis does not exclude a separate cancer. Inability to urinate, fever with urinary pain or visible blood needs prompt help. Medicines, monitoring and procedures have different benefits and risks. Do not stop prescribed medicines or use antibiotics or supplements as a self-directed cure. How is an enlarged prostate treated? Depending on symptoms and complications, options include monitoring, practical changes, medicines and a procedure or surgery. A clinician helps choose the approach with you. When are antibiotics needed? For a diagnosed bacterial infection such as bacterial prostatitis or a urinary infection, not for non-infected BPH itself. Other forms of prostatitis do not automatically need antibiotics. What complications can occur? Significant obstruction can cause retained urine, infections, stones, bleeding and bladder or kidney damage. Many people do not develop these complications; follow-up helps identify changes. How does BPH differ from prostate cancer? BPH is benign tissue growth and is not a cancer risk factor itself. Cancer can coexist, and symptoms can overlap; early cancer often has none. Examination and appropriate tests are needed when indicated. Does a high PSA prove cancer? No. BPH, infection and other factors can raise PSA. Some medicines lower it. A clinician interprets the result with your history and other findings and may recommend further assessment. Can I try home measures before seeing a clinician? Practical changes can help mild symptoms within an agreed plan. Persistent symptoms deserve review, and blood, pain, fever or inability to urinate should not be left for a prolonged home trial. Are less invasive procedures always as effective as TURP? No. Relief, recovery, sexual effects and retreatment differ. Prostate anatomy and your priorities help determine which option is suitable; no procedure is best for everyone. Will treatment affect sex or fertility? Some medicines and procedures can affect erections, desire or ejaculation. Backward ejaculation can affect fertility. Discuss what matters to you before choosing treatment rather than assuming every option has the same effects.

title: STI symptoms in men: what to notice and when to get tested
description: Understand symptoms and silent infections in chlamydia, gonorrhea, hepatitis, herpes, HPV and syphilis, plus testing, vaccines, partner care and urgent warning signs.
body: Sexually transmitted infections can cause discharge, burning, sores or other symptoms, but many cause none. Symptoms overlap with nonsexual conditions, and appearance cannot identify an infection reliably. Testing and appropriate care protect your health and your partners without blame or assumptions about when an infection began. Symptoms are a reason to seek care, not a diagnosis Arrange a sexual-health or medical assessment for penile discharge, burning when urinating, genital or mouth sores, new growths, rectal pain, discharge or bleeding, or a partner’s diagnosis. Tell the clinician about oral, anal and vaginal contact so testing includes the relevant sites. Do not wait for visible symptoms after a known exposure. Seek emergency care immediately for sudden severe testicle pain, testicle pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or pain lasting over an hour or continuing at rest: torsion can threaten the testicle. New testicular swelling needs urgent assessment too. Do not assume pain is an STI or wait for a routine test to exclude an emergency. Chlamydia Chlamydia is a bacterial infection transmitted through vaginal, anal or oral sex. It often causes no symptoms; when symptoms occur they may take weeks. Men may notice burning during urination, penile discharge or, less commonly, testicular pain or swelling. Rectal infection can cause pain, discharge or bleeding, or be silent. Urine or site-appropriate swab tests help diagnose it. Prescribed antibiotics can cure the infection, but do not reverse damage already present and do not prevent reinfection. Complete treatment, follow the clinic’s advice about partners and when sex can resume, and arrange repeat testing, commonly around three months after treatment. Gonorrhea Gonorrhea is another bacterial infection that can affect the urethra, rectum or throat. Symptoms can include burning urination, white, yellow or green penile discharge, and sometimes painful or swollen testicles. Rectal infection can cause itching, soreness, discharge, bleeding or painful bowel movements; infections at any site may be unrecognized. Discharge colour does not distinguish gonorrhea from other causes. Testing may require urine plus throat or rectal swabs according to exposure. Treatment must account for antibiotic resistance. Rare spread to blood or joints can be serious: fever with a painful swollen joint or rash needs urgent assessment. Follow prescribed treatment, partner care and repeat-testing advice; persistent symptoms need reassessment. Hepatitis A is caused by HAV, not HIV Hepatitis A is a liver infection caused by the hepatitis A virus, HAV. It spreads when tiny amounts of infected stool reach the mouth, including through contaminated food or water and some sexual practices, particularly oral–anal contact. Contaminated raw shellfish can be a food-related source. It is not limited to sexual transmission. Symptoms can include tiredness, fever, poor appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, dark urine, pale stools and yellow eyes or skin. Most people recover with supportive care, but serious liver illness can occur. Vaccination and careful handwashing with soap and water are important; barriers alone cannot guarantee prevention. Seek prompt advice after an exposure because vaccine, sometimes with immune globulin, may help within two weeks. Hepatitis B and silent liver infection Hepatitis B is caused by HBV and spreads through infected blood, semen and certain other body fluids, including during sex. Infection may be acute or become chronic. Many people feel well while liver damage develops, so lack of genital symptoms or a flu-like illness cannot establish whether infection is present. Possible symptoms include poor appetite, fatigue, fever, aches or joint pain, nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, dark urine, pale stools and jaundice. Blood testing and follow-up assess infection and liver health. Acute and chronic care differ; selected chronic infections need antiviral treatment and ongoing monitoring. Vaccination prevents infection. New jaundice needs medical assessment, and recent exposure warrants prompt advice about prevention. Herpes: HSV is different from HPV Genital herpes can be caused by HSV-1 or HSV-2. HSV-1 often affects the mouth, but either type can cause genital infection; oral sex can transmit oral HSV to the genitals. Many people have mild or unnoticed symptoms and can pass the virus without visible sores. Tingling, itching or burning may precede painful blisters or ulcers around the genitals, anus or mouth. A first recognized outbreak can include fever, body aches, tender groin glands and feeling unwell; recurrent outbreaks can be milder. Timing or appearance cannot reliably identify who transmitted it. A fresh sore can be swabbed, while blood tests have limits and are not routine screening for everyone. Antiviral treatment can shorten or suppress outbreaks but does not eradicate HSV. Avoid sexual contact during sores or warning symptoms, and discuss ongoing prevention with the clinician. HPV: warts and cancer risk are different issues Human papillomavirus is a large group of viruses spread through intimate skin contact, including vaginal, anal and oral sex. Most infections cause no symptoms and many clear without harm. Some types cause genital warts: flat or raised bumps, sometimes in clusters resembling cauliflower. Persistent high-risk types can cause penile, anal or throat cancers; wart-causing types are different from cancer-causing types. New genital, mouth or throat lumps, sores or persistent changes need assessment rather than a diagnosis from a photograph. There is no routine test that establishes a man’s overall “HPV status” or screens the mouth and throat for HPV. Clinicians can assess visible lesions and relevant cancer concerns. Treating warts does not guarantee that the virus is gone, and a late diagnosis does not prove a recent transmission. HPV vaccines: products and ages matter Gardasil 9 targets nine HPV types: 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52 and 58. It includes wart-associated and cancer-associated types. Cervarix targets types 16 and 18; it does not provide the same 6/11 wart coverage. Vaccines prevent new infections and related disease, not an existing infection or current warts. Available products and national schedules differ. In the United States, CDC recommends routine HPV vaccination at 11–12 years, starting as early as 9, and catch-up through 26 if not adequately vaccinated. Some adults aged 27–45 may benefit after an individual discussion; it is not routinely recommended for everyone in this range. FDA licensing through age 45 does not mean approval above 45. Ask about your local schedule, earlier doses and immune status rather than choosing a course yourself. Syphilis can change stages without being cured Syphilis is bacterial and spreads through contact with an infectious sore during oral, vaginal or anal sex. Primary infection may cause one or more sores on the penis, anus or mouth, often firm and painless but not always, with nearby swollen glands. A sore can heal without treatment while infection remains. Secondary infection may cause a rash, including palms or soles, fever, sore throat, headache, fatigue and swollen glands. Latent syphilis has no visible symptoms but remains in the body. Untreated infection can later damage the heart, blood vessels and other organs. Brain, nerve, eye or ear involvement can occur at any stage, not only late disease. New vision or hearing changes, eye pain or neurological symptoms need urgent assessment. Appropriate antibiotics can cure infection but may not undo damage; follow-up blood tests and partner care remain necessary. Testing and HIV prevention after an exposure No single urine or blood test checks every STI. The clinician chooses tests and sampling sites from symptoms, exposures, vaccination and local recommendations. Blood tests may assess HIV, syphilis or hepatitis; urine and swabs assess other infections. A test taken too early can be negative despite infection, so ask about the window period and repeat testing. HIV self-test positives need confirmatory testing. For a recent possible HIV exposure, seek assessment immediately for post-exposure prophylaxis, or PEP: it must start within 72 hours, and sooner is better. Do not wait for symptoms or a test window. Discuss PrEP for ongoing HIV risk; it does not prevent other STIs. Prompt HIV diagnosis and treatment improve health; maintaining an undetectable viral load prevents sexual transmission. Testing frequency depends on individual risk and local guidance, not symptoms alone. Reducing risk without assuming complete protection Use condoms correctly for vaginal or anal sex and appropriate barriers for oral contact. They reduce risk but cannot cover every area that transmits herpes, HPV or syphilis. Avoid contact with sores and, for herpes, prodromal tingling or burning. Avoid fecal–oral contact and wash hands after toileting or handling materials exposed to stool and before food preparation. Reducing partners or a mutually monogamous relationship with an appropriately tested uninfected partner can reduce exposure. Vaccination can prevent hepatitis A, hepatitis B and selected HPV types, but not every STI. Avoiding sexual contact prevents sexual exposure, not all nonsexual transmission of hepatitis. Discuss prevention without stigma: having no symptoms, one partner or a previous negative result is not a lifetime guarantee. Treatment, partners and follow-up If an infection is diagnosed, follow its specific treatment and partner-notification plan. A clinic can help partners obtain assessment and treatment where appropriate, including when they have no symptoms. Do not share antibiotics, use leftovers or assume every partner needs identical medicine. Ask exactly how long to avoid sex, whether symptoms must resolve and which follow-up tests are needed. Seek review for persistent or returning symptoms. New jaundice, severe illness or fever with joint swelling needs urgent medical advice; new eye, hearing or neurological changes also need urgent assessment. If a partner is pregnant, their maternity team should know promptly about relevant exposure or diagnosis. Keep vaccination and testing records, but never let an app reminder delay time-sensitive exposure care or emergency assessment. Many STIs are silent, and similar symptoms can have different causes; testing must match exposure sites. HAV, HBV, HIV, HSV and HPV are distinct viruses with different prevention and treatment. Vaccines and barriers reduce specific risks; they do not provide complete protection against every infection. Possible recent HIV exposure needs immediate PEP assessment; emergency testicle pain must not wait for STI testing. What symptoms can hepatitis B cause in men? Often none. Possible symptoms include fatigue, poor appetite, fever, aches, nausea or vomiting, abdominal discomfort, dark urine, pale stools and jaundice. Blood testing is needed; feeling well does not exclude chronic liver infection. What are common HPV symptoms in men? Most infections cause no symptoms. Some types cause genital warts, including flat or raised bumps or clusters. HPV is different from herpes: painful blisters and tingling are not a reliable HPV diagnosis. New genital, mouth or throat changes need assessment. Can vaccines prevent STIs? Vaccines can prevent hepatitis A, hepatitis B and selected HPV types, but not every STI. They are not treatment for an existing infection. Ask about local recommendations and your vaccination history; HPV products and eligible ages differ. Do condoms prevent all STIs? Correct use reduces risk but does not eliminate it, particularly for infections spread from uncovered skin or sores. Oral barriers can also reduce exposure. Vaccination, appropriate testing and partner care remain important. Can I have an STI with no symptoms? Yes, and it may still spread or cause complications. Ask about testing after a partner’s diagnosis or relevant exposure. The right tests and repeat timing depend on the infection, contact sites and test window periods. How quickly should I seek care after possible HIV exposure? Immediately. PEP must start within 72 hours and works best when started sooner. Do not wait for symptoms or a test result. A clinician determines whether it is appropriate and arranges follow-up; PrEP may suit ongoing risk. Do sores healing or treatment mean I cannot get infected again? No. A syphilis sore can heal while infection remains. Treatment of a bacterial STI does not prevent reinfection; HSV can recur and HPV may persist. Follow the specific partner, sexual-contact and repeat-testing plan. When is testicular pain an emergency? Get emergency care immediately for sudden severe pain, pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or pain lasting over an hour or continuing at rest. Torsion needs rapid treatment. Do not wait for STI testing; new swelling or worrying discomfort also needs urgent assessment.

title: Ajwain while breastfeeding: milk-supply claims and safety
description: Ajwain is a familiar spice, but medicinal use during breastfeeding has uncertain benefits and safety. Learn what milk-supply concerns need instead.
body: Ajwain, also called carom or ajowan, is used in food and traditional remedies. A small amount seasoning a meal is different from drinking concentrated preparations or taking an extract. There is no established evidence that ajwain reliably increases breast milk, enriches it or is safe at a medicinal dose for a breastfeeding parent and baby. Low milk supply deserves skilled feeding assessment rather than a herbal promise. What ajwain is The accepted botanical name is Trachyspermum ammi, a member of the Apiaceae family. It is a branching annual with finely divided leaves and small white or pink-tinged flowers in umbrella-like clusters. The tiny ridged dry fruits are commonly called seeds and used as an aromatic spice. Common names can be confusing: ajwain is not interchangeable with cumin, fennel or ordinary caraway. Its aroma is associated with compounds including thymol, but composition varies between plants and preparations. The photograph shows a culinary spice, not a medicine or a guide to identifying wild plants. Growers’ descriptions of height, soil or appearance do not establish safety during breastfeeding; use clearly labelled food rather than foraging from a picture. Food, nutrients and concentrated products Ajwain fruits contain plant nutrients and aromatic constituents, but a pinch of spice is a small serving. Claims that it supplies abundant vitamins, minerals, protein, fibre or antioxidants should not be treated as evidence that a usual serving meets nutritional needs. An old study analysing several traditional supplementary foods, including an ajwain recipe, measured food composition and digestibility; it did not prove that ajwain itself increases milk production. A varied diet supports the breastfeeding parent’s health. Ajwain is not a replacement for meals, treatment of a nutrient deficiency or recommended parent and infant supplements. Seeds in food, strong tea, distilled herbal water, capsules, extracts and essential oil can deliver different amounts of constituents. A recipe or a product described as natural does not provide a proven medicinal dose. Traditional benefits are not established treatments Ajwain has been promoted for indigestion, gas, reflux or ulcers, diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting, intestinal worms and other infections; coughs, colds, throat or sinus symptoms and asthma; and urinary symptoms, kidney or bladder stones and increased urination. Other claims involve blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol and heart protection, pain, muscle spasm, back or joint symptoms, gout, headaches, seizures, relaxation, dental problems and liver health. These claims do not establish effective treatment in breastfeeding people. Further claims include energy, sexual function, sperm quality or male fertility, withdrawal from dependence, menstrual timing or pain, heavy bleeding and supposed uterine cleansing. Laboratory antioxidant, antimicrobial or anti-inflammatory effects do not prove that swallowing ajwain treats these conditions. Plant-oil assays and rat ulcer or isolated-thymol diabetes experiments are not clinical trials of a breastfeeding parent and infant. Do not replace prescribed care or delay assessment of infection, asthma, seizures, bleeding or other illness. Does it increase breast milk? Ajwain is sometimes called a galactagogue, a substance intended to increase milk. Reliable evidence of a clinically useful ajwain effect, a suitable dose and infant safety is lacking. Long traditional use, a nutritious recipe or a laboratory result cannot show that a baby receives more milk. It should not be advertised as improving milk quality or guaranteeing a supply increase. Milk production depends on several factors, including effective and regular milk removal. A clinician or lactation specialist can assess an observed feed, attachment, swallowing, feeding frequency, weight and age-appropriate nappies, alongside parent and baby health. Hormone or medicine treatment, if appropriate, needs individual evaluation; do not borrow a prescription or assume another galactagogue is suitable. Culinary use is different from herbal treatment An occasional ordinary food exposure is not, by itself, a reason to stop breastfeeding or discard milk. This does not establish the safety of repeated large quantities, concentrated tea, distillates, supplements or essential oil. There is no verified ajwain medicinal breastfeeding dose or universal waiting period after taking it. Ask a pharmacist or clinician before using a remedy, especially with a newborn, premature or unwell baby. Give the product name, full ingredient list, preparation, amount and timing, and mention all medicines and supplements. Mixed products and extraction methods vary; labels, purity and contaminants can create additional uncertainty. Do not give ajwain remedies or essential oil directly to an infant, add them to expressed milk, or apply them where a baby could lick them. Keep concentrated products out of children’s reach. Side-effect lists need careful interpretation It is not established that ajwain inevitably causes jaundice, thyroid or liver damage, ulcers, mouth inflammation, headaches or dizziness in a breastfeeding parent or baby. Nor is there a reliable rule that using it for more than seven days dries up milk. A symptom occurring after a product may be important without proving that ajwain caused it; product mixtures, dose, contamination, medicines and other illness need consideration. Stop a nonessential herbal product and seek advice if new rash, mouth irritation, persistent vomiting, abdominal pain or unusual drowsiness develops; seek emergency care for severe features described below. Do not test a suspected allergy by taking it again. Yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, persistent symptoms or a marked supply change need medical assessment rather than treatment with another herb. Do not stop prescribed medicines without advice. What to do about suspected low supply Ask a midwife, paediatric clinician or qualified lactation professional to observe a whole feed and review growth, milk transfer and nappies. A baby seeming unsettled, breasts feeling softer or a small pump yield alone does not diagnose low supply. Feeding problems, illness, some medicines, previous breast surgery and other parent or infant factors may need targeted care. Use a practical feeding and expression plan agreed with the team. If supplemental milk is needed, make sure the baby receives enough nutrition; do not abruptly remove prescribed top-ups to try an herb. Any changes should include a plan to protect milk production and check the baby’s weight and hydration. Appropriate treatment can help many families, but no food or medicine guarantees a particular result. When the baby needs urgent help Seek prompt same-day assessment for feeding that is worsening, fewer wet nappies than expected for age, poor weight gain, repeated vomiting, or suspected new or worsening jaundice. Jaundice needs assessment, not ajwain water or sunlight treatment. A baby with jaundice needs immediate emergency care if any one of these applies: under 24 hours old; sleepier than usual or difficult to wake; not feeding; floppy, stiff, jerking or twitching; temperature 38°C or higher or 36°C or lower, or feeling hot or cold or shivering; no wet nappies; or breathing difficulty or very fast breathing. Do not wait for all these signs. Any baby with breathing difficulty or very fast breathing, blue or grey lips or tongue, a seizure, loss of consciousness or who is not responding normally needs emergency help now. Do not wait to see whether stopping a herb is enough. Follow emergency-service instructions and do not drive yourself when emergency transport is needed. Keep the product packaging available so the team knows what exposure occurred. After a concerning exposure If an infant swallows essential oil or another potentially harmful concentrated product, contact emergency services or a poison service immediately; do not wait for symptoms. If you are unsure whether an exposure is harmful, get urgent poison or medical advice. Keep the container and do not induce vomiting. A small amount of spice in a normal meal is a different situation and should not be treated automatically as poisoning. The breastfeeding parent needs immediate emergency care for breathing difficulty, swelling of the lips or tongue, fainting or loss of consciousness, or a seizure. Severe abdominal pain, vomiting blood or black tar-like stools also need emergency assessment. Persistent vomiting, jaundice or other new concerning symptoms warrant prompt medical advice. Ask for individual guidance about feeding after a significant exposure rather than using a guessed pause or milk-discard schedule. Ajwain’s milk-boosting benefit and medicinal breastfeeding dose are not established. A culinary pinch and a concentrated remedy are different exposures. Traditional, laboratory and animal findings do not prove parent or infant benefit. Low supply needs feeding, growth and health assessment, with adequate infant nutrition. Poor feeding, jaundice or severe symptoms should not wait for a herbal remedy. What is ajwain? Ajwain or carom is Trachyspermum ammi. Its small aromatic dry fruits are called seeds and used as a spice. It is not interchangeable with cumin, fennel or ordinary caraway, and a photograph should not be used to identify plants for eating. Does ajwain increase or enrich breast milk? A reliable clinical benefit has not been established. Traditional use and nutritional analysis of a recipe do not prove increased milk transfer to a baby. Get feeding and growth assessed rather than relying on a milk-boosting claim. Is a little ajwain in a meal the same as ajwain tea or oil? No. Ordinary food seasoning and concentrated or repeated medicinal use are different. An occasional food exposure alone is not a reason to stop breastfeeding, but it does not establish the safety of tea, distillate, capsules, extracts or essential oil. Is there a safe medicinal breastfeeding dose? No verified ajwain dose or universal waiting period has been established for breastfeeding. Discuss the exact product and exposure with a clinician or pharmacist, especially for a newborn, premature or unwell baby. Do not give remedies or essential oil directly to the infant. Does ajwain dry up milk after seven days? That fixed timeline is not supported by reliable evidence. A supply change should prompt assessment of milk removal, feeding, medicines and parent and baby health, not an automatic diagnosis of herbal toxicity. Can it treat stomach problems, infections or other illnesses? Traditional claims cover many conditions, but laboratory or animal findings do not prove clinical effectiveness during breastfeeding. Do not use ajwain instead of treatment for asthma, infection, seizures, bleeding, diabetes or another diagnosed illness. What helps if I think my baby is not getting enough milk? Arrange an observed feed and review of weight, milk transfer and age-appropriate nappies. Follow an individual feeding and expression plan. Keep any needed supplemental nutrition until the care team guides changes; do not remove it abruptly to try an herb. Which signs need emergency help? Any baby with breathing difficulty or very fast breathing, blue or grey lips or tongue, a seizure, loss of consciousness or who is not responding normally needs emergency help now. A baby with jaundice needs immediate emergency care if any one of these applies: under 24 hours old; sleepier than usual or difficult to wake; not feeding; floppy, stiff, jerking or twitching; temperature 38°C or higher or 36°C or lower, or feeling hot or cold or shivering; no wet nappies; or breathing difficulty or very fast breathing. Do not wait for all these signs. Potentially harmful oil ingestion needs immediate poison or emergency advice.

title: Testicular ultrasound: preparation, the scan and results
description: Learn what a scrotal ultrasound shows, how to prepare, what happens during the scan and which testicular pain symptoms need immediate emergency care.
body: A testicular, or scrotal, ultrasound uses sound waves to examine the testes and nearby tissues. It can help investigate a lump, swelling, pain or injury. It supports a clinical assessment; it cannot answer every fertility question or safely replace urgent care when testicular torsion is possible. What the scan examines The testes sit in the scrotum below the penis and produce sperm and testosterone. The epididymis stores and matures sperm. The spermatic cord runs between the abdomen and each testis and contains blood vessels, nerves and the vas deferens; it does not attach the testis to the penis. The vas deferens carries sperm onward from the epididymis towards the ejaculatory ducts and urethra. Doppler ultrasound assesses blood flow, not the movement of sperm. Blood-vessel findings alone do not establish sperm transport, sperm quality or the ability to conceive. Why a clinician may request it Ultrasound can locate a lump inside or outside a testis, distinguish a fluid-filled cyst from a solid lesion, and assess pain, swelling, injury or inflammation. It can show fluid around a testis (hydrocele), an epididymal cyst such as a spermatocele, or enlarged veins (varicocele). A solid lesion is not automatically confirmed cancer. Imaging is selected for the clinical question. It is not routinely required in the initial male infertility assessment, which includes history, examination and semen testing, with parallel partner assessment. For a child with an undescended testis, specialist assessment should not wait for a routine scan: ultrasound cannot reliably find or exclude a testis in the abdomen. Pain that must not wait for routine imaging Seek immediate emergency care for sudden severe testicular pain; testicular pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain; or pain lasting over an hour or continuing at rest. Do not wait an hour if another emergency feature is already present. These symptoms can indicate torsion, where twisting of the spermatic cord threatens the testis’s blood supply. Doppler can help an emergency team, but preserved blood flow does not always exclude early, partial or intermittent torsion. Strong clinical concern needs urgent specialist action without waiting for a routine scan or report. A new lump, swelling, change in size, shape or feel, or a worrying ache also needs timely medical assessment, even without severe pain. How ultrasound creates the images A transducer sends high-frequency sound waves through gel on the scrotal skin and receives returning echoes. A computer turns the echoes into images. The examiner compares the tissues and both testes, taking measurements and saved images; real-time views show movement. Doppler adds information about the direction and pattern of blood flow. A radiologist or suitably qualified practitioner interprets these findings with symptoms and examination. Ultrasound may identify an abnormality without determining its exact tissue type; additional tests or specialist review may still be needed. Preparation and appointment length An isolated scrotal ultrasound usually needs no fasting, special diet or full bladder. Follow your own appointment instructions, especially if another examination is combined with it. Wear clothing that is easy to remove, tell the team about medicines and support needs, and do not stop prescribed medicines yourself. It is commonly an outpatient examination in a hospital or clinic, and routine sedation is usually unnecessary. Timing varies: one NHS testes leaflet describes about 5–20 minutes, sometimes longer; another service may book 20–30 minutes. Allow for the whole appointment and ask the department about its arrangements. What happens during the examination The practitioner explains the scan and seeks your agreement. You have privacy to lower clothing or change, with a cover for areas not being examined. You usually lie on your back with the legs slightly apart; a towel may support the scrotum and the penis is kept clear. Ask about a chaperone, communication support or preferences before the appointment. Water-based gel, which may feel cool or warm, helps the probe contact the skin. The practitioner moves it over both sides, applying gentle pressure and asking you to stay still or adjust position. Tell them if pressure hurts or you need a pause; you can ask to stop. A sensitive or injured area can be uncomfortable. Safety and care afterwards Diagnostic ultrasound uses no ionizing radiation and is generally considered very safe. This does not guarantee that the examination will be painless or entirely without risk. Cambridge University Hospitals notes a very low infection risk associated with gel; remove it thoroughly and follow the department’s cleaning advice. After a routine external scan, you can normally dress, eat and resume usual activities without a recovery period. This does not override restrictions or treatment for the condition being investigated. New or worsening symptoms still need clinical advice; emergency pain should never wait for the scheduled results. Understanding the report and next steps The report goes to the referring clinician. Ask who will explain it, when to expect it and whom to contact if it does not arrive. Findings may suggest infection or inflammation, a benign cyst, hydrocele, spermatocele, varicocele, injury, torsion or a suspicious mass; the next step depends on the whole assessment. A suspicious mass needs prompt specialist evaluation and sometimes further tests; the scan alone does not confirm every cancer diagnosis. A normal scan is not a complete fertility assessment or a guarantee that persistent symptoms are harmless. Attend the recommended follow-up and seek reassessment if symptoms change. Ultrasound examines structure and Doppler blood flow; it does not directly measure sperm transport or fertility. Sudden severe pain, pain with nausea/vomiting/abdominal pain, or pain over an hour or at rest needs immediate emergency care. Routine preparation is usually minimal, but follow the actual appointment instructions and keep prescribed medicines unchanged unless advised. Ask about comfort, a chaperone, the report and follow-up; a normal scan does not settle every symptom. What are the risks? There is no ionizing radiation and the test is generally very safe. Pressure may hurt over a tender area, and a very low gel-related infection risk is described by one NHS service. Tell the practitioner about discomfort and follow cleaning advice. How long does it take? Duration varies with the examination and service. Some scans take about 5–20 minutes, others are booked for 20–30 minutes or longer. Ask about the total appointment time rather than treating one estimate as a guarantee. Do I need to fast or fill my bladder? Usually not for an isolated scrotal scan. Follow your appointment letter if another scan is included or special instructions apply. Do not independently stop medicines. How is the scan performed? You usually lie on your back with a cover, the scrotum exposed and sometimes supported by a towel. Gel is applied and a probe is moved over both testes. Routine sedation is usually unnecessary; ask for a pause or stop if needed. Does normal blood flow rule out torsion? No. Early, partial or intermittent torsion can still show blood flow. Emergency symptoms and clinical concern require urgent assessment without waiting for routine imaging or a reassuring report. Does a solid lump mean cancer? Not necessarily, but a suspicious testicular mass needs prompt specialist assessment. Ultrasound helps characterize and locate it; additional investigation may be needed to establish the diagnosis. Can the scan prove fertility or find every undescended testis? No. Fertility assessment requires clinical context and semen testing, often with partner assessment. Routine ultrasound is not required before referral for a child’s undescended testis and cannot reliably exclude an abdominal testis. Which symptoms need immediate emergency care? Sudden severe testicular pain; pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain; or pain lasting over an hour or continuing at rest needs immediate emergency care. Do not wait an hour when another emergency feature is present or wait for a routine scan.

title: Metabolic syndrome: risk factors, diagnosis and care
description: Learn how the five metabolic syndrome risk factors are assessed, what they mean for long-term health and why treatment and aspirin advice must be individualized.
body: Metabolic syndrome describes a cluster of blood pressure, blood sugar, blood-fat and waist measurements associated with higher cardiovascular and diabetes risk. It often causes no obvious symptoms. Recognizing the pattern offers a chance to act early, without treating a body shape or one abnormal result as a diagnosis. A cluster of risks, not a prediction of your future A commonly used adult definition requires at least three of five components: increased waist circumference, high triglycerides, low HDL cholesterol, raised blood pressure and raised fasting glucose. One or two components still deserve attention even when the syndrome criteria are not met. The combination increases the chance of type 2 diabetes, heart disease and stroke, but these outcomes are not inevitable. This adult risk cluster is different from inherited metabolic diseases diagnosed in babies. Prevalence varies with population and definition; a single percentage does not describe everyone. Why the risks can occur together Abdominal fat and insulin resistance are important contributors. Insulin resistance means cells respond less effectively to insulin; it can exist before glucose rises. High blood glucose is a related finding, not another name for insulin resistance. Risk also reflects age, family history, physical inactivity, sleep, smoking, some medicines and social circumstances that affect access to food and care. Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), formerly polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), can be associated with metabolic risk. None of these factors alone proves the diagnosis or makes it a personal failing. The five measurements clinicians assess Common adult criteria include triglycerides of at least 150 mg/dL (1.7 mmol/L); HDL below 40 mg/dL in men or 50 mg/dL in women; systolic pressure at least 130 OR diastolic at least 85 mmHg; and fasting glucose at least 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L). Specific treatment for the corresponding abnormality can also count, even when the current number is controlled. Waist thresholds depend on the population and clinical definition. Values around 102 cm for men and 88 cm for women are used in some settings; lower thresholds apply to some populations. These are not universal targets, pregnancy waist measurements are not interpreted in this way, and adult thresholds should not be applied to children. How an assessment works A clinician reviews history, medicines and family risks, measures the waist and blood pressure correctly, and arranges appropriate glucose and lipid tests. Blood pressure may need repeated readings. Follow fasting instructions for tests; a single home measurement or online checklist cannot establish every component or diagnose diabetes. Assessment also considers overall cardiovascular risk and kidney health rather than just counting components. The broader cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) framework in 2026 guidance connects these systems; metabolic syndrome remains one part of that assessment. Your team may check kidney blood tests and urine albumin and assess other conditions according to your situation. Possible complications and what the label does not mean The risk pattern is associated with atherosclerosis, heart attack, stroke, peripheral artery disease, kidney problems and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), previously often called nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. Association does not mean everyone will develop each condition or already has organ damage. If diabetes develops, persistently high glucose can contribute to eye, nerve, kidney and foot damage; severe foot complications can sometimes lead to amputation. These are risks to prevent and monitor, not automatic consequences of metabolic syndrome. Follow-up and appropriate treatment can reduce risk. Food, movement and practical support Aim for sustainable meals with vegetables, fruit, whole grains and appropriate protein, while limiting excess salt, saturated fat and added sugars. Build activity gradually; many adults work towards at least 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly, adapted to ability and medical advice. Support for stopping smoking, sleep and stress also matters. If weight reduction is appropriate, even a modest change may improve some measurements; agree realistic goals rather than applying one percentage to everyone. Do not pursue weight-loss dieting during pregnancy. Pregnancy, breastfeeding, illness, disability and eating-disorder history call for tailored nutrition and activity plans. Dietetic and practical support can make changes more manageable. Medicines and the important aspirin distinction Treatment may include medicines for blood pressure, cholesterol or triglycerides and glucose, alongside everyday changes. Some people with diabetes, kidney disease or higher cardiovascular risk benefit from medicines with heart or kidney protection; selected patients may discuss obesity medicines or metabolic surgery. Choice depends on diagnoses, risk, contraindications and reproductive plans, not the syndrome label alone. Do not start aspirin simply because you have metabolic syndrome. For prevention of a first cardiovascular event, a clinician balances potential benefit against bleeding risk; it is not routinely recommended for everyone. Aspirin prescribed after a cardiovascular event or for an obstetric reason has a different purpose. Do not stop prescribed aspirin or other medicines without discussing your individual indication. Outlook, prevention and warning signs Measurements and overall risk can improve, and some people no longer meet the syndrome definition after treatment. This does not guarantee a permanent cure or remove the need for follow-up. Agree when to repeat pressure, glucose and lipid checks, review kidney health and medicines, and seek support for barriers to care. Call emergency services for possible heart attack symptoms such as chest pressure or unexplained breathlessness, or stroke signs such as sudden face drooping, arm weakness, speech difficulty, balance or vision change: even if they resolve. Fainting with these symptoms or loss of consciousness also needs emergency assessment. Do not wait for a routine metabolic review or an app result. Metabolic syndrome commonly means at least three of five adult risk components; fewer components still matter. Insulin resistance and raised blood glucose are related but distinct. Waist thresholds and test interpretation require clinical context, not a universal body-shape rule. Sustainable changes and individualized medicines can reduce risk; aspirin is not a routine self-treatment. Heart attack or stroke warning signs require emergency help, even if symptoms improve. How is metabolic syndrome diagnosed? A clinician assesses waist, blood pressure, triglycerides, HDL and fasting glucose, including relevant treatment history. At least three components meet a common adult definition; thresholds and repeat testing depend on context. What complications are possible? Risks include type 2 diabetes, heart and vascular disease, stroke, kidney problems and fatty liver disease. Diabetes can add eye, nerve and foot risks, but none is an inevitable outcome for every person. How is it treated? A plan combines sustainable food and activity changes, smoking cessation and sleep support and, when indicated, medicines for individual risks. Weight goals and treatment must fit your health and reproductive circumstances. Can it be prevented? Healthy habits, support and regular assessment can lower the likelihood or delay progression, but prevention is not guaranteed. Family history and other factors also matter. Does raised glucose mean insulin resistance? Not necessarily. Insulin resistance concerns the response to insulin; glucose can remain normal for a time. Raised glucose needs appropriate interpretation and may require testing for prediabetes or diabetes. Should I take aspirin? Do not self-start it for metabolic syndrome. Prevention of a first event requires an individual benefit–bleeding-risk discussion. Continue prescribed aspirin until you have discussed its specific indication with your clinician. Should I lose weight while pregnant? Do not try weight-loss dieting during pregnancy. Ask your maternity team for nutrition, activity, monitoring and medication advice suited to you. When do symptoms need emergency care? Possible heart attack or stroke symptoms, fainting with these symptoms or loss of consciousness need immediate emergency assessment. Stroke signs still require help if they disappear; do not wait for routine testing.

title: Semen for skin and hair: evidence, myths and safer care
description: Understand why semen is not an established acne, anti-ageing or hair treatment, how laboratory ingredient studies differ, and what to do after a reaction or eye exposure.
body: Semen is not an established skin-care or hair-growth treatment. Testimonials and before-and-after photographs cannot show that it treats acne or wrinkles. Research on an isolated chemical does not prove that applying the whole fluid works, and contact can cause irritation, allergy or an infection exposure depending on the route. Does semen treat acne? There is no established clinical evidence supporting semen as an acne treatment. Antioxidant or anti-inflammatory activity of a substance in a laboratory does not show that semen clears blocked pores, inflammatory spots or cysts on a person's face. It is not a substitute for an acne treatment plan. Benzoyl peroxide, salicylic acid and other appropriate topical treatments have defined uses. Painful, deep, scarring or persistent acne deserves professional assessment; selected prescription or hormonal treatments may help. Facials, light treatments and chemical peels are not interchangeable proven cures for everyone, and combining harsh products can worsen irritation. Ageing claims confuse a compound with the whole fluid Spermine and spermidine are related polyamines, not another name for semen. A 2009 Nature Cell Biology paper studied spermidine and cellular ageing processes in organisms and human immune cells. It did not inject semen into facial skin or demonstrate wrinkle reduction from a semen facial. A laboratory finding cannot establish a safe cosmetic treatment. For everyday care, gentle cleansing, a suitable moisturizer and sun protection are more useful starting points. Glycerin or hyaluronic acid can be moisturizer ingredients. Vitamin C or retinoid products may suit selected concerns, but stronger products are not automatically better and can irritate. Broad-spectrum, water-resistant SPF 30 or higher, shade and clothing help protect exposed skin. Protein and zinc do not make semen a skin supplement Semen contains proteins and minerals, but their presence does not establish a useful skin dose, absorption or benefit. Cosmetic peptides are selected ingredients in formulated products; finding proteins in a body fluid does not make the fluid equivalent. Exact nutrient percentages vary and do not justify applying or consuming semen for skin health. Meet nutritional needs through varied food: beans, lentils, chickpeas, tofu, nuts, whole grains and other appropriate protein sources can contribute. Zinc supports normal body functions and wound healing, but extra zinc is not a universal acne or anti-ageing prescription. Excess supplements can cause harm, including copper deficiency and medicine interactions; ask a clinician or pharmacist before adding them. Urea creams are different from semen Urea is naturally present in the skin and is also made synthetically for moisturizers. Depending on formulation and concentration it can retain moisture and soften thick, dry skin. This is evidence for a specific preparation used appropriately, not proof that the small, variable amount in semen provides the same result. Choose a product for the condition and body area, with professional advice when needed. Urea can sting and irritate, and products should not go into eyes or onto infected, bleeding or severely inflamed skin unless specifically advised. Neither a natural origin nor a shared ingredient makes a fluid a suitable moisturizer.
