How to assess salon and commercial claims A salon service, a synthetic ingredient or an impressive marketing percentage does not prove that semen improves skin. A cream may contain ordinary moisturizers, oils, vitamins or purified compounds that are distinct from whole semen. Any benefit must be assessed for the complete formulation, not assigned to a suggestive ingredient name. Look for the actual ingredient list, safety instructions and human studies relevant to the product and intended outcome. Old stories about named salons, salmon-derived ingredients or discontinued brands do not establish current availability or effectiveness. Do not reproduce an animal-semen facial or hair treatment at home; a commercial setting does not remove allergy or infection concerns. Irritation, seminal-plasma allergy and eczema differ Contact can cause burning, redness, itching or swelling. Seminal-plasma hypersensitivity is a rare allergy to proteins in seminal fluid; it is not simply another name for atopic eczema, and not every rash after sex is semen allergy. Lubricants, latex, other products and infections can cause similar symptoms. Avoid re-exposure and arrange assessment rather than testing the suspected trigger yourself. Breathing difficulty, tongue or throat swelling, marked faintness, fainting or loss of consciousness after exposure may mean anaphylaxis. Use a prescribed adrenaline/epinephrine auto-injector if available and call emergency services immediately; do not wait for a rash or take an antihistamine instead of emergency treatment. Allergy testing and any desensitization belong in specialist care, not a home experiment. Infection risk depends on the contact Semen from someone with an infection can expose the eyes, mouth or damaged skin to pathogens. HIV does not pass through intact skin; exposure assessment depends on the fluid, route, source and treatment status. Gonorrhea or chlamydia can affect the eyes. Herpes can spread through infected skin or sore contact, including without visible sores, so it should not be explained only as a semen-borne infection. After a potentially significant HIV exposure to an eye, other mucous membrane or broken skin, seek emergency or urgent specialist assessment immediately, even without symptoms. PEP, when indicated, should begin as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours and no later than 72 hours; do not use that limit as a waiting period. Clinicians decide whether PEP and other testing or follow-up are appropriate. Even after that window, seek advice about testing and care. What to do after eye or skin contact If semen enters an eye, rinse promptly with plenty of clean, non-hot water using a gentle flow; do not rub it or add soap, disinfectant or cosmetic products. Remove contact lenses if easily possible and do not reinsert them while symptoms remain. Rinsing does not replace infection-exposure assessment or guarantee prevention. Get immediate emergency eye care for sight changes, severe pain, light sensitivity or pus; seek prompt clinical advice for redness, burning or other persistent symptoms after exposure. Gently wash exposed skin and stop irritating products. Do not scrub, apply bleach or repeatedly challenge a suspected allergy. Tell the clinician the contact time and route so time-sensitive care is considered. Hair claims and a safer longer-term plan A 2011 PLOS ONE study exposed cultured human scalp follicles and cells to isolated spermidine. It was not a trial of rubbing semen on people's heads and does not demonstrate that semen prevents hair loss or conditions hair safely. Protein-rich salon mixtures or animal-semen anecdotes cannot separate effects of other ingredients or establish benefit. For persistent hair loss or skin concerns, seek a diagnosis and a plan suited to your skin, medicines and reproductive circumstances. Tell the prescriber if pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding. Oral isotretinoin must not be used in pregnancy; avoid topical retinoids in pregnancy and discuss pregnancy planning before use. Other acne products, procedures and supplements also need individualized review rather than replacing semen with an indiscriminate strong-product routine. Semen is not an established acne, wrinkle or hair-growth treatment. Isolated spermidine research is not evidence for applying whole semen. Formulated moisturizers, sun protection and tailored acne care are safer starting points. Breathing trouble, throat swelling, fainting or loss of consciousness after contact need immediate emergency care. Rinse eye exposure promptly and seek time-sensitive assessment when infection exposure is possible; do not wait for symptoms. Can semen clear acne? There is no established clinical evidence for that use. Choose an appropriate acne regimen and get advice for deep, painful or scarring acne. Does the ageing study prove a semen facial works? No. The research involved isolated spermidine and laboratory ageing processes, not a clinical trial of semen applied to facial skin. Does the urea in semen moisturize like a cream? That has not been established. Urea creams have particular concentrations and formulations; the presence of urea in semen does not make it an equivalent product. What could happen if semen touches skin? It may cause irritation or an allergic reaction. Infection risk depends on the organism and route; intact-skin contact is not an HIV transmission route. Breathing trouble, throat swelling, fainting or loss of consciousness needs emergency care. What if semen gets into an eye? Rinse with plenty of clean water, do not rub or add disinfectant, and seek prompt exposure advice. Sight changes, severe pain, light sensitivity or pus need emergency eye care. Should I wait 72 hours before asking about HIV PEP? No. Seek assessment immediately. When indicated, PEP starts as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours and no later than 72 hours; that is a treatment window, not a waiting instruction. Can semen make hair grow? The cited hair study tested isolated spermidine in cultured follicles and cells. It did not prove semen application works on a person's scalp. Can I use any acne medicine during pregnancy? No. Oral isotretinoin must not be used in pregnancy and topical retinoids should be avoided. Discuss all products, pregnancy plans and breastfeeding with a clinician to choose suitable care.

title: Ejaculation frequency: what the prostate-cancer studies mean
description: There is no required weekly ejaculation count. Understand the “21 per month” research, its limits, abstinence, sperm production and when to seek care.
body: There is no medically required number of ejaculations per day, week or month, and no single minimum interval suits everyone. The often-quoted “21 per month” comes from research on prostate-cancer risk, not a prescription. Comfort, choice, consent and any symptoms matter more than reaching a quota. A change that causes distress or pain deserves assessment rather than an instruction to ejaculate more. Where did “21 times a month” come from? A 2016 study followed 31,925 men in a US health-professional cohort. In 1992 they reported their usual ejaculation frequency at ages 20–29 and 40–49 and during the previous year; researchers then followed prostate-cancer diagnoses through 2010. Frequency was not measured anew in both 1992 and 2010. The questionnaire did not ask whether ejaculation occurred during partnered sex, masturbation or sleep. Men reporting at least 21 ejaculations monthly had a lower rate of prostate-cancer diagnosis than those reporting 4–7, especially for low-risk disease. This was an observational association, not a trial assigning a frequency. Recall, differences between participants and cancer detection can affect results. It does not prove that increasing your count prevents aggressive cancer or death, or that fewer ejaculations are dangerous. What do the earlier studies add? The 2004 report from the same cohort was not simply negative: some highest-frequency comparisons were associated with lower total prostate-cancer risk, while many other comparisons were not. The 2016 analysis added follow-up to related evidence; these are not two independent experiments proving a treatment effect. A 2003 Australian case-control study compared men with prostate cancer with age-matched controls, rather than enrolling only men who already had cancer. Recalled earlier frequency showed an association in some comparisons, but case-control studies also have recall and selection limitations. Current EAU guidance describes frequency as an association and finds no conclusive basis for specific preventive measures. Do not use a monthly quota to replace discussion of symptoms, family history or appropriate prostate assessment. Erection, orgasm and ejaculation are different An erection is penile firmness, orgasm is the experience of sexual climax, and ejaculation is the movement and release of semen. They often occur together but can occur separately: for example, orgasm may happen with little or no semen. A new, persistent change may relate to medicines, surgery or a health condition and merits a clinical review if troublesome. Some people feel pleasure, relaxation or sleepiness after sexual activity or orgasm. Dopamine and oxytocin are involved in sexual responses, but that does not establish a required ejaculation count or a treatment for depression. Claims that ejaculation reliably boosts immunity, treats migraine or reduces death from heart disease are not established reasons to prescribe it. Seek care for those conditions on their own merits. Does the way ejaculation happens change the benefits? The prostate-cancer cohort did not distinguish partnered sex, masturbation and nocturnal emissions, so it cannot show that one method protects better. There is no proven universal health advantage of making yourself ejaculate through one particular method. Choose activities freely, with consent and attention to comfort. Solo activity without exchanging fluids avoids pregnancy, but shared toys and sexual contact can carry infection risks; use appropriate cleaning and protection. Repeated or rough friction may cause soreness or irritation. Stop painful activity and allow recovery; persistent symptoms need assessment. A count alone does not diagnose compulsive behaviour, but loss of control that disrupts work, relationships or daily life is a reason to seek support. Can you run out of sperm? Testicles normally continue producing sperm after puberty, but the rate varies between people and with health. There is no universal production rate of 1,500 sperm every second. Several ejaculations close together can temporarily change semen volume or sperm numbers; this is not evidence that a lifetime supply has been used up. Semen is a mixture of sperm and glandular fluids. Its appearance or amount cannot reliably establish fertility. If trying to conceive is difficult, a clinician may assess semen and both partners’ reproductive health rather than judging the number of ejaculations alone. Follow the laboratory’s own abstinence and collection instructions before a semen test. Is there a medical reason to avoid ejaculation? You can choose not to ejaculate if that is comfortable for you. Abstinence does not automatically cause disease, and there is no need to force ejaculation to remove a toxic buildup. Equally, retention is not a proven long-term way to preserve energy, balance testosterone or improve health. Neither a fixed maximum nor a fixed minimum is a general medical rule. A clinician may recommend temporary limits after a procedure, an injury or during treatment; follow the instructions for your situation. Choosing abstinence is different from suddenly being unable to ejaculate despite wanting to, or developing pain or a distressing change. Do not stop prescribed medicines or use hormones or supplements yourself to alter frequency. What happens to unused sperm? The body can break down and absorb sperm that are not ejaculated. Some people have nocturnal emissions, or “wet dreams”; these may happen after puberty and in adulthood. They are not required to keep the reproductive system healthy, and their absence does not by itself mean something is wrong. Frequency is not a reliable measure of testosterone, sexual desire or overall fertility. Desire can vary with sleep, stress, relationships, medicines and health. A persistent unwanted change, erectile difficulty or orgasm without the usual semen should be discussed with a clinician when it causes concern, particularly if fertility is a goal. Trying to conceive is a separate timing question For couples trying to conceive through vaginal intercourse, ASRM advises that intercourse every 1–2 days in the six-day fertile window ending on ovulation gives the highest pregnancy rates; 2–3 times weekly is nearly as effective. Daily ejaculation does not automatically reduce fertility. There is no need to save up sperm by avoiding comfortable, consensual intercourse. This is flexible advice, not a target to impose on either partner. Ejaculation away from the vagina does not create the same chance of conception as sperm entering the reproductive tract at the relevant time. Fertility problems, assisted treatment and laboratory samples may require individual instructions; neither “21 per month” nor abstinence alone is a fertility treatment. Which changes need medical help? Arrange medical assessment for blood in semen, persistent painful ejaculation, a troublesome change in ejaculation or erection, or behaviour that feels out of control. Blood in semen is often not serious, but it should still be checked. Suspected blood in urine needs urgent same-day assessment even if it happens once, is slight or you are unsure it is blood. Get emergency care now for sudden severe testicle pain, testicle pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or pain lasting over an hour or continuing at rest. An erection lasting more than 3–4 hours needs emergency care; with sickle cell disease, a painful erection lasting over an hour does too. Do not drive yourself, wait to reach an ejaculation target or try sex or masturbation to resolve a prolonged erection. No daily, weekly or monthly ejaculation quota is medically required. The “21 per month” finding is an association, not proof of cancer prevention. Erection, orgasm and ejaculation are related but different processes. Unused sperm can be absorbed; abstinence is not automatically harmful or beneficial. Comfort, consent, fertility goals and new symptoms guide individual decisions. How many ejaculations per week are normal? There is no single normal or required number. Frequency varies, and a comfortable choice without pain, pressure or disruption is more useful than a quota. A distressing new change deserves assessment. Must I ejaculate 21 times monthly to avoid prostate cancer? No. That category came from observational research, which cannot prove that raising frequency prevents cancer or death. It does not identify a safe minimum or replace appropriate prostate care. Did the 2004 and 2016 studies disagree completely? No. The 2004 analysis also found lower total risk in some highest-frequency comparisons, although many comparisons were not significant. The later report added follow-up in the same cohort, rather than being an independent treatment trial. Does ejaculation improve sleep, immunity, migraine or heart health? Some people feel relaxed or sleepy after orgasm. That does not establish ejaculation as treatment for insomnia, immune problems, migraine, depression or heart disease, or show a required frequency for benefit. Should I limit ejaculation to protect sperm or testosterone? There is no universal limit or proven long-term testosterone benefit from retention. Sperm production continues, unused sperm can be absorbed and short-term semen changes do not mean permanent depletion. Follow individual advice after procedures or before laboratory tests. Is choosing not to ejaculate unhealthy? Not automatically. Choosing abstinence can be comfortable and does not require a remedy. It is different from a new inability to ejaculate, pain or unwanted sexual changes; discuss those with a clinician and do not stop prescribed medicines yourself. What happens if sperm are not released? The body can absorb unused sperm, and nocturnal emissions may occur in adolescents or adults. Neither having nor lacking wet dreams by itself establishes fertility, testosterone status or a health problem. When should I get urgent or emergency help? Suspected blood in urine needs urgent same-day assessment even once or in a small amount. Sudden severe testicle pain, pain with nausea/vomiting/abdominal pain or lasting over an hour or at rest needs emergency care. So does an erection over 3–4 hours, or a painful erection over an hour with sickle cell disease. Blood in semen or persistent painful ejaculation also needs medical assessment, without assuming it is cancer.

title: Penile fracture: emergency signs, treatment and recovery
description: A sudden injury to an erect penis can tear its fibrous covering. Learn the emergency signs, tests, surgical treatment and why recovery advice must be individual.
body: Penile fracture is a medical emergency, despite there being no bone in the penis. Sudden bending can tear the tissue that supports an erection and sometimes injure the urinary tube. Rapid assessment and treatment offer the best chance of avoiding lasting problems. This article explains what to recognize and what hospital care may involve; it should never delay urgent help. Suspected penile fracture needs emergency care A penile fracture is an urgent injury to the erect penis. If it bends suddenly and you develop pain, swelling, bruising or a rapid loss of erection, go to an emergency department immediately. Do not wait for a routine appointment, a photograph review or symptoms to settle. Stop sexual activity. Do not bend, massage or try to straighten the injured penis, and do not test whether another erection is possible. Embarrassment should not delay care. Even if the injury happened earlier and you have not yet sought help, get assessed; a delay does not make treatment pointless. What tears if there is no bone? The penis has no bone. Its paired erectile chambers, the corpora cavernosa, fill with blood during erection. A strong fibrous covering called the tunica albuginea surrounds them; a penile fracture is a tear in this covering, often with injury to the underlying erectile tissue. The urethra, the tube carrying urine out of the body, may be injured as well. That is why treatment considers both erections and urination. An ordinary bruise and a true fracture can look similar from the outside and need professional assessment to distinguish them. Warning signs and possible urethral injury A cracking or popping sound, immediate loss of erection, pain and rapidly developing swelling or dark bruising are typical warning signs. The penis may bend or look misshapen. Not everyone has every feature, so the absence of a sound does not safely rule out injury. Tell the emergency team about blood at the urinary opening, blood in the urine, pain when urinating or difficulty passing urine. These can indicate a urethral injury. Inability to urinate is especially important; do not put anything into the urethra or attempt a catheter yourself. Other injuries, such as a torn superficial vein or ligament, can also cause bruising. You cannot reliably decide at home which injury it is or whether an operation is needed. A reduction in pain does not establish that the deeper tissues are intact. How the injury happens The usual mechanism is a sudden forceful bend or impact while the penis is erect. It can happen during intercourse if the penis slips out and strikes the partner’s body, during vigorous masturbation, when rolling onto an erection, or after another accident or blow. No sexual position makes injury impossible. Different studies report different circumstances; a simple ranking of positions cannot predict an individual injury. Focus on avoiding sudden bending and uncontrolled force rather than blaming either partner. Examination, imaging and urine tests The clinician asks when and how the injury happened and examines swelling, bruising and deformity. A clear history and examination can be enough to identify a fracture. Ultrasound may help in an uncertain case, with MRI used selectively when doubt remains and it is available. Imaging should not delay necessary surgery when the diagnosis is clear. Cavernosography uses injected contrast to image the erectile chambers. It is a specialized option mentioned in trauma guidance, not a routine test that every patient needs. The treating team selects investigations according to the findings and local expertise. A urine sample can show blood, but it is not the same as imaging the urethra. If urethral injury is suspected, a retrograde urethrogram uses contrast introduced through the urinary opening and X-rays; a flexible camera examination may also be used, including during surgery. Explain urinary symptoms so the team can choose the appropriate assessment. Why prompt surgical repair is usually recommended For a confirmed fracture, urological guidance recommends prompt surgery to close the torn tunica with stitches and repair associated injuries when necessary. The aim is to preserve comfortable erections and urinary function and reduce later curvature or scarring. A superficial injury without a tunical tear may have a different treatment plan after assessment. This does not mean that rest, ice or painkillers are a safe substitute for emergency evaluation of a suspected fracture. The surgeon will explain the procedure, anaesthetic, possible catheter and individual risks. Recovery and follow-up Hospital stay and healing time depend on the injury, the repair and whether the urethra was involved. Some people go home relatively soon, while others need a longer stay or a catheter. Follow the team’s instructions for dressings, prescribed medicines, activity and catheter care; do not remove a catheter yourself. Follow-up checks wound healing, urination and sexual function. Additional scans or urethral tests are selected when needed, rather than promised for everyone. Contact the service for increasing pain, fever, wound redness or discharge, significant bleeding or urinary problems; inability to pass urine needs urgent care. When can sexual activity resume? Wait for the surgical team’s clearance before intercourse or masturbation. Advice depends on healing and the extent of repair. BAUS patient information advises avoiding all sexual activity for six weeks; a generic one-month date is not permission to restart in your own case. An erection occurring during recovery does not prove that the repair is ready for sexual activity. Ask what to do about painful erections and when to return to exercise, work and sex. Do not use medicines or devices to test the repair without the treating team’s advice. Longer-term outlook and reducing future injury Prompt treatment generally improves the outlook, but no success percentage guarantees an individual result. Curvature, painful erections, scar tissue, erection difficulties or urinary narrowing can occur after the injury or repair. Report persistent or new problems at follow-up; further care may help. Use adequate compatible lubricant and controlled movements, and pause to guide the penis if it slips out or you change position. Avoid deliberate bending, forceful manipulation or pressing an erection into restrictive clothing. These precautions reduce avoidable force but cannot guarantee prevention. An injury can affect confidence and relationships as well as the body. Ask for support if worry or distress persists. Be honest with clinicians about what happened; the purpose is appropriate treatment, not judgment. Go to an emergency department immediately for a suspected penile fracture. A missing popping sound or improving pain does not safely exclude serious injury. Report blood at the urinary opening, blood in urine or trouble urinating. Clinicians choose imaging and urethral tests; clear fractures usually need prompt repair. Resume sex only with individualized surgical advice and attend follow-up. What should I do if I think I have a penile fracture? Stop sexual activity and go to an emergency department immediately. Do not wait for bruising to worsen, try to straighten the penis or test another erection. Seek assessment even if you delayed initially. Does a penile fracture mean a bone has broken? No. The penis has no bone. The injury is a tear in the strong covering of the erectile chambers, and the underlying tissue or urethra may also be injured. Do I need every symptom to seek help? No. A pop, sudden loss of erection, pain, swelling or bruising after bending are warning signs, but not every person has all of them. Tell clinicians about urinary symptoms or bleeding. Is a urine test the same as a retrograde urethrogram? No. A urine sample checks for findings such as blood. A retrograde urethrogram is a contrast X-ray examination of the urethra. The team decides whether it or a camera examination is needed. Can a true fracture heal with ice alone? Do not rely on home treatment. Confirmed fractures usually need prompt surgical repair. Other bruising injuries may be managed differently only after assessment. Can I have sex a month after surgery? Do not use one month as automatic clearance. Follow the surgeon’s plan; BAUS patient guidance advises six weeks without intercourse or masturbation, and some injuries may need a different recovery period. Does surgery guarantee normal erections? No. Prompt repair improves the outlook, but curvature, pain, erection or urinary problems can still occur. Follow-up is important, and ongoing symptoms should be discussed.

title: Hawthorn while breastfeeding: fruit, supplements and uncertain safety
description: Hawthorn is not a proven milk booster. Learn how fruit differs from extracts, what breastfeeding evidence is missing and when feeding or reaction symptoms need help.
body: Hawthorn fruit and hawthorn herbal products are not interchangeable. There is no reliable evidence that hawthorn improves milk supply or milk quality, and its safety for a breastfed baby has not been established. Before using it as a remedy, review the actual product with a pharmacist or clinician and seek feeding support if supply is a concern. What is hawthorn? Hawthorn refers to Crataegus plants in the rose family, also known by names such as may tree or shan zha. These often thorny, deciduous shrubs or small trees have spring flower clusters and small apple-like fruits that ripen later in the year. Leaves, fruit colours, height and the number of hard stones vary by species; common hawthorn has lobed leaves, pale flowers and red fruit with one stone. Hedgerow use and a long food history do not make every wild berry edible or identify a product. Do not rely on a photograph or common name for foraging, and do not eat the hard seeds. Fruit eaten as food is a different exposure from concentrated leaf, flower, fruit or root preparations; a botanical description cannot establish breastfeeding safety. Antioxidants and traditional claims are not clinical proof Hawthorn contains flavonoids and other polyphenols. Antioxidant activity in a laboratory does not prove treatment benefits. Traditional claims include improved mood or depression, relief of grief, cognition, eyesight, seizures, headaches, energy, fatigue, detox, metabolism and fat burning. These are not established breastfeeding treatments, and there is no evidence that hawthorn causes weight loss. Other claims concern hair growth, bones, blood sugar, blood fats, bile and digestion of heavy meals, intestinal infections, worms or dysentery, tuberculosis, skin aging or eczema, and kidney stones. Do not substitute hawthorn for assessment or effective treatment of these conditions. A plant compound or traditional use is not proof of a safe medicine. Heart claims need particular caution Hawthorn is promoted as a heart tonic for rhythm, contraction strength, circulation, stress tolerance, clot prevention and chronic heart failure. Human heart-failure studies have conflicting results, and evidence is insufficient for many other heart claims. Possible effects on vessels or heart cells do not establish that a fruit or supplement prevents clots or treats an arrhythmia. Some European leaf-and-flower products have traditional-use recognition for mild nervous cardiac complaints after serious illness has been excluded, or mild stress and sleep symptoms. This is not approval as a breastfeeding remedy. The final EMA monograph is from 2016; the 2025 revision is a draft. Do not replace prescribed cardiac treatment or self-treat chest symptoms. Does hawthorn increase milk or improve its quality? No valid clinical trial establishes hawthorn as a milk booster. LactMed describes an old, very small study reporting changes in milk volume and fat, but it lacked adequate controls and blinding. It cannot establish a dependable benefit, a dose, or better infant nourishment. Traditional claims about richer or more plentiful milk are not sufficient evidence. There are no useful published measurements of hawthorn components in human milk or breastfed infants, and infant safety data are lacking. A rise in a hormone or laboratory antioxidant finding would not by itself prove improved milk transfer or infant growth. Do not give hawthorn tea, drops or supplements directly to a baby. Is the fruit safer than a supplement? Ordinary fruit, strong tea, tinctures, capsules and extracts differ in plant part, concentration and other ingredients. Studies of one standardized extract cannot establish the safety of another product. Food use also does not supply a proven breastfeeding-safe amount; avoid interpreting “in moderation” as a validated dose. The NHS advises against herbal medicines during breastfeeding because there is not enough evidence to guarantee safety. The EMA leaf-and-flower monograph also does not recommend use during lactation because data are insufficient. If you want to eat hawthorn fruit or have already used a product, discuss the actual exposure individually rather than assuming either certain harm or certain safety. Possible side effects and medicine interactions Adult reports include dizziness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and other abdominal discomfort; headache, fatigue or rash may occur. Confusion, sleep changes, nosebleeds, marked low blood pressure, palpitations and an irregular heartbeat are sometimes attributed to hawthorn, but these are not all predictable effects of ordinary fruit. Toxicity or overdose can involve low blood pressure and rhythm problems; breastfeeding-specific rates are unknown. Ask a pharmacist to check heart medicines, digoxin, blood-pressure treatment, blood thinners and diabetes medicines alongside every supplement. Some proposed interactions come from laboratory findings and their clinical importance is uncertain; not every combination is proven harmful. Mention upcoming surgery and unusual bleeding. Do not stop necessary prescribed medicines or change doses yourself to accommodate hawthorn. Product quality: a specific root-supplement warning In its September 2026 update, the FDA warned that certain products sold for weight loss, including some labelled tejocote or Mexican hawthorn root, contained toxic yellow oleander. This can cause serious gastrointestinal, neurological and heart problems, including death. The warning concerns particular adulterated products, not evidence that all ordinary hawthorn fruit contains oleander. Check the actual product against official safety alerts. Do not use a product named in the warning; if you took one, stop using it and contact a clinician immediately, even if use was not recent. Severe symptoms need emergency care. Keep the packaging; a label, “natural” claim or online sale cannot guarantee identity or quality. If you have already consumed hawthorn Record whether it was fruit, tea, extract or a mixed product, the amount and dates, ingredients, medicines and any symptoms. Give the clinician your baby’s age, prematurity or jaundice history and feeding pattern. Pause further unsupervised medicinal use while obtaining advice; one exposure alone does not prove that your baby has been harmed. There is no evidence-based universal waiting period, milk-discard schedule or automatic reason to wean after hawthorn. A clinician can assess the product and whether any temporary feeding plan is needed. Do not induce vomiting, try a home detox or stop necessary prescribed treatment. Suspected poisoning or known harmful ingestion needs immediate emergency care; if you are unsure whether a product is harmful, obtain urgent poison-service or medical advice. If poisoning is suspected, do not eat or drink anything while waiting for medical help. For emergency care, do not drive yourself; ask another person to drive or call an ambulance. Low supply concerns need a feeding assessment Ask a trained breastfeeding professional to observe a feed and assess latch, swallowing, effective milk removal, age-appropriate wet nappies and weight gain. Maternal or infant illness, medicines and feeding difficulties may need treatment. A balanced varied diet supports health, but no special fruit is required to make good-quality milk. Agree a practical feeding or expressing plan and follow-up for both you and your baby. If additional milk is needed, use an individualized supplementation plan rather than delaying it for a herbal trial. Poor feeding, fewer wet nappies or unusual drowsiness needs prompt assessment; do not wait for a supplement to work. Symptoms that must not wait Seek emergency care for persistent palpitations that do not settle, or palpitations with chest pain, breathlessness or feeling faint; fainting or loss of consciousness and severe breathing difficulty also need emergency help. If concerning palpitations have stopped, arrange urgent medical assessment. Swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, difficulty breathing or swallowing, or faintness after a possible allergic reaction needs emergency help; a rash is not required. For emergency care, do not drive yourself; ask another person to drive or call an ambulance. For a baby, breathing difficulty, blue, grey or unusually pale skin, a seizure, being difficult to wake or unresponsive, or no urine for 12 hours needs immediate emergency care. Poor feeding or dehydration signs need urgent assessment even without all these signs. Do not assume a symptom is caused by hawthorn or delay help while checking an app or product label. For emergency care, do not drive yourself; ask another person to drive or call an ambulance. Hawthorn has no reliable milk-supply or milk-quality benefit, and infant safety has not been established. Fruit and concentrated herbal preparations differ; no breastfeeding-safe hawthorn dose is proven. Review the actual product and medicines with a clinician or pharmacist; do not stop necessary prescribed treatment yourself. Feeding concerns and warning symptoms need assessed care, not a herbal trial. Are the traditional benefits proven? Claims about mood, heart health, digestion, infections, skin, metabolism and other conditions are not all established. Heart-failure studies are mixed and laboratory antioxidant activity does not prove clinical benefit. Do not use hawthorn instead of effective treatment. Does hawthorn increase milk supply or improve milk quality? No valid trial establishes either benefit. A very small old uncontrolled study cannot show that hawthorn reliably increases milk, improves infant nourishment or supplies a useful dose. Feeding assessment is the first step for a supply concern. Is eating hawthorn while breastfeeding safe? Safety for a breastfed baby is not established. Ordinary fruit differs from medicinal extracts, but “moderation” is not a proven safe dose. Ask about the actual product and exposure; NHS advice recommends avoiding herbal medicines during breastfeeding. What side effects are possible? Adult reports include dizziness and digestive symptoms; toxicity can involve low blood pressure or an irregular heartbeat. Many other attributed symptoms and breastfeeding-specific risks remain uncertain. New symptoms need assessment, and severe reactions need emergency care. Should I stop breastfeeding after one exposure? One exposure does not prove harm or automatically require weaning. Keep the label and discuss the amount, preparation, timing, baby’s age and health, and medicines with a clinician. There is no universal milk-discard or waiting schedule; any temporary feeding plan must be individualized. Can hawthorn interact with medicines? Possible interactions concern cardiac medicines, digoxin, blood-pressure treatment, blood thinners and diabetes medicines, but some evidence is theoretical or limited. A pharmacist should review your full list and surgery plans. Do not change necessary prescribed treatment yourself. What if I used a tejocote-root weight-loss product? Check current FDA alerts for the exact product. Certain products contained toxic yellow oleander. Stop a named product and contact a clinician immediately even if use was not recent; severe symptoms need emergency care. This warning does not mean all hawthorn fruit is adulterated. When do feeding or reaction symptoms need help? Poor feeding, fewer wet nappies or unusual drowsiness needs prompt assessment. A baby with breathing difficulty, blue/grey or unusually pale skin, a seizure, difficulty waking or no urine for 12 hours needs immediate emergency care. Severe allergy signs, persistent palpitations or palpitations with chest pain, breathlessness or faintness, and fainting or loss of consciousness need emergency care; do not wait for every sign. For emergency care, do not drive yourself; ask another person to drive or call an ambulance.

title: Semen and sperm: the difference, production and test results
description: Understand semen fluid and sperm cells, where they come from, pre-ejaculate, survival and why a count or appearance cannot prove fertility.
body: Semen and sperm are closely connected, but they are not the same. Understanding the distinction makes questions about ejaculation, pregnancy prevention and semen testing easier to discuss without relying on appearance or fixed numerical rules. Semen is fluid; sperm are cells Semen is the mixture of fluid released during ejaculation. Sperm are microscopic reproductive cells that may be carried in it. These words describe different things, even though they are often used interchangeably in everyday conversation. Most of the visible ejaculate comes from glands, not from the sperm cells themselves. Semen can contain very few sperm or none; a white appearance or an apparently usual amount cannot show whether someone is fertile. An orgasm with little or no visible fluid also does not reveal its cause without assessment. What seminal fluid contains and does The seminal vesicles and prostate provide much of the fluid, with contributions from other glands. The mixture includes water and substances such as sugars and proteins. For example, fructose from the seminal vesicles can provide energy for sperm. The presence of nutrients does not make semen a nutritional treatment. Fluid helps carry sperm out through the urethra, and each sperm has a tail that enables its own movement. Movement through the female reproductive tract also depends on its environment and transport mechanisms, not simply on the amount of semen. Where sperm and semen come from Sperm develop in the seminiferous tubules inside the testes and undergo further maturation in the epididymis, a coiled structure beside each testis. During ejaculation, they travel through the vas deferens and mix with glandular secretions before leaving through the urethra. Testes also produce testosterone through different cells. The seminal vesicles lie behind the bladder. The prostate lies below the bladder and surrounds part of the urethra. The bulbourethral glands contribute lubricating secretions during arousal. This shared route does not mean urine and semen are the same fluid. Sperm are too small to identify by eye A sperm cell has a head carrying genetic material, a midpiece and a long tail. The head is much smaller than the whole cell, which includes that tail. Microscopy is needed to see and assess these cells. Looking at semen, including its thickness, color or apparent amount, cannot count sperm or assess their movement and shape. A laboratory semen analysis measures several features together. Home observation is not a substitute for that assessment. Why the amount of semen varies Ejaculate volume varies between people and between samples. The interval since ejaculation, collection completeness, age, health and some medicines can affect the result. A teaspoon is not a required amount, and there is no universal early-thirties peak that determines an individual’s fertility. Volume and sperm concentration are different measurements. More fluid does not automatically mean more sperm or a better chance of pregnancy. Follow the laboratory’s collection instructions, including its requested interval without ejaculation; tell the laboratory if part of the sample was missed. Do not stop prescribed medicines to change a result. Concentration, total count and reference values Concentration means sperm per milliliter; total count means the number in the whole ejaculate. The EAU table based on WHO’s 2021 reference data lists lower fifth-centile values of 16 million sperm/mL, 39 million per ejaculate and 1.4 mL volume. These describe a reference population, not an average or a pass/fail fertility test. Someone below a reference value may conceive, and someone above it may still have difficulty. No single count proves fertility or infertility. Clinicians consider movement, shape, history and the other partner’s reproductive health. A finding of no sperm is called azoospermia and needs proper investigation; an unexpected result may require a repeat sample, with timing chosen by the clinic. Pre-ejaculate can carry sperm Pre-ejaculatory fluid appears during arousal before ejaculation. Although the secreting glands do not manufacture sperm, samples can contain them, including moving sperm. A small 2011 volunteer study demonstrated this but cannot tell an individual their chance of pregnancy. It is unsafe to assume that sperm can only be left over from a previous ejaculation. Urinating after an earlier ejaculation does not guarantee sperm-free pre-ejaculate. Withdrawal is not a reliable way to rule out pregnancy. Put a condom on before genital contact and use it correctly throughout sex if that is your chosen protection; condoms also reduce STI transmission. After possible unprotected exposure, seek emergency-contraception advice promptly rather than trying saliva or water. How long sperm may survive In favorable conditions in the female reproductive tract, sperm can remain capable of fertilization for up to about five days. This helps explain why the fertile window includes days before ovulation. It does not mean all sperm survive five days in the vagina or that an app can identify a guaranteed safe day. Outside the body, conditions such as drying and temperature matter, so there is no dependable universal countdown in minutes. Wet semen reaching the vulva or vagina, including on fingers or toys, can pose a pregnancy risk. Washing, saliva, a bath or having sex in water is not contraception after genital exposure; seek timely advice if worried. Production and maturation take time Making and maturing sperm takes more than 70 days, often described as roughly two to three months. This is an approximate biological process, not a promise that every person produces an entirely new, healthy supply exactly 74 days after a change. Illness and medicines can affect later samples. Sperm production is ongoing in many people after puberty, but ejaculation does not switch it off or permanently use up a fixed lifetime supply. When trying to conceive, regular intercourse is generally more useful than prolonged abstinence to save sperm. Use the clinic’s specific collection instructions when preparing a test. Age and health can affect production Many people continue to produce sperm into later life, but production is not guaranteed to continue unchanged until death. Hormonal problems, testicular disease or injury, some cancer treatments, genetic conditions and other factors can reduce or stop it. Age-related changes vary; there is no universal switch at age 50. Smoking, recreational drugs and some medicines may affect reproductive health. External testosterone and anabolic steroids can suppress sperm production and are not a fertility treatment. Discuss the exact products and your reproductive plans with a clinician; do not abruptly stop prescribed treatment or assume supplements can repair a low count. When to request assessment For pregnancy planning, seek assessment after a year of regular unprotected sex, or earlier when there is a known risk or concern. ASRM advises earlier evaluation after six months when the partner providing eggs is 35 or older. Both partners may need assessment. Repeated little or no ejaculate, painful ejaculation or possible infection also warrant clinical advice. A new testicular lump or swelling needs urgent clinician assessment. Blood in semen should be checked at an appointment. Sudden severe testicular pain, testicular pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or pain lasting more than an hour or continuing at rest needs immediate emergency assessment. Do not wait for a routine semen test or assume it is harmless because the amount of semen looks usual. Do not drive yourself; ask someone to take you or call an ambulance. Semen is mainly glandular fluid; sperm are microscopic cells that may be carried in it. A usual-looking amount cannot show sperm count, movement or fertility. Reference values are not a pass/fail test. Pre-ejaculate can contain sperm. Urinating, withdrawal, saliva and water do not guarantee pregnancy prevention. Sperm development takes roughly months; health, treatment and age can affect production. Discuss concerns rather than self-treating. Does pre-ejaculate contain sperm? It can, including moving sperm. The amount varies and cannot be judged by looking. Urinating after an earlier ejaculation does not guarantee it is sperm-free; use appropriate contraception from the start of genital contact. How many sperm are released during ejaculation? The total depends on concentration and volume. A laboratory measures both, along with movement and shape. The WHO2021-based lower reference values are 16 million/mL and 39 million per ejaculate; neither is a personal fertility guarantee or a diagnostic cutoff by itself. How long does making sperm take? Development and maturation take more than 70 days, roughly two to three months. It is an approximate process rather than an exact 74-day reset, and illness or medicines can affect later samples. Does the body ever stop producing sperm? It may. Many people continue later in life, but disease, hormonal changes, treatments and other factors can reduce or stop production. There is no guarantee of unchanged lifelong production or one age at which it always stops. Can semen contain no sperm? Yes. Semen is largely glandular fluid, so sperm may be absent despite a visible ejaculate. Confirmed azoospermia requires clinical investigation; appearance cannot diagnose it. Can sperm survive five days outside the body? The often-quoted five days refers to favorable conditions within the female reproductive tract, not a dry surface or a universal time in the vagina. Outside-body conditions vary. Wet semen reaching the vulva or vagina can still pose a pregnancy risk; ask promptly about emergency contraception after possible exposure. Does a larger amount mean better fertility? No. Volume is different from concentration, total count, movement and shape. A clinician interprets these together with both partners’ history. Follow collection instructions and report a missed portion rather than judging fertility by a teaspoon estimate. When is testicular pain an emergency? Seek immediate emergency assessment for sudden severe testicular pain, pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or pain lasting more than an hour or continuing at rest. Do not wait for a routine scan or semen analysis. Do not drive yourself; ask someone to take you or call an ambulance.

title: Everyday penile health: gentle hygiene, optional grooming and prevention
description: Build a simple penile-care routine, compare optional grooming methods and understand vaccines, STI testing, sexual function and warning signs that need care.
body: Penile health includes comfortable skin, urination and sexual function as well as preventing infection. You do not need a hairless body, a particular penis size or performance supplements to be healthy. A gentle routine and an individual prevention plan are more useful than repeated scrubbing, food promises or trying to diagnose every change yourself. A broad view of health and normal variation Erections depend on blood vessels, nerves, hormones and psychological wellbeing. Diabetes, cardiovascular disease, some neurological conditions, depression, stress and medicines can affect function. Age-related changes are variable; persistent difficulty should not automatically be dismissed as inevitable ageing or blamed on anxiety. Describe a new change to a clinician and do not stop prescribed treatment yourself. Penises vary in size and shape, and a slight lifelong curve may be normal. A new curve, hard area, pain or difficulty with erections deserves assessment. Neither appearance nor the amount of semen alone measures fertility. Sexual activity or abstinence can be a personal choice; there is no required frequency for penile maintenance, and nobody owes a partner sex. Keep washing simple and comfortable Wash the penis and surrounding groin gently each day with warm water; a mild, fragrance-free cleanser may suit healthy outer skin, but avoid products that irritate. If the skin is inflamed, ask about water or a suitable emollient soap substitute. Clean the shaft, testicles and skin folds without scrubbing, rinse and pat dry. Avoid deodorant, talc, disinfectant and inserting products into the urethral opening. An adult foreskin should only move as far as comfortable: gently clean underneath if it retracts, then bring it forward to cover the head again. Never force a child's attached foreskin back. Change damp underwear and sweaty clothes. Washing gives you a chance to notice a persistent sore or lump, but a normal-looking penis does not exclude infection; washing after sex does not prevent an STI or pregnancy. Trimming or shaving is an optional choice Pubic hair does not have to be removed for cleanliness. If you prefer it shorter, use a clean personal trimmer with a suitable guard, good lighting and a stable position where you can see the skin. Keep blades or scissor tips away from delicate folds and do not share tools. Stop if the skin catches, hurts or bleeds; postpone grooming over a rash, sore or broken skin. A close shave can cause cuts, razor irritation or ingrown hairs. If you shave external hair-bearing skin, use a clean razor, a suitable shaving product and gentle strokes in the direction of growth rather than repeated scraping. A fragrance-free moisturiser may help the outer shaved skin. Do not routinely add hydrocortisone or another steroid to genital skin; ask for advice about persistent irritation rather than treating every bump as an ingrown hair. Waxing, threading and chemical removers need caution Waxing pulls hair out and can cause pain, irritation or burns; threading also pulls hair out and is not an established risk-free genital method. Ask a qualified practitioner about suitability, skin conditions and medicines such as isotretinoin or topical retinoids. A salon should use hygienic equipment and a fresh applicator for each dip into wax. Avoid DIY treatment of delicate penile or scrotal skin, especially when sore or damaged. Depilatory creams dissolve hair but can irritate or burn. A product labelled for legs or even a bikini line is not automatically suitable for the penis, scrotum or mucosal skin. Respect its exact permitted areas, patch-test and timing instructions; do not apply an unsuitable product to test whether it is safe. Rinse off immediately if burning or stinging occurs and seek advice for a burn, blistering or persistent pain. Trimming or leaving hair alone are reasonable alternatives. Use barriers and testing as complementary prevention Condoms used correctly for vaginal, anal or oral sex reduce many STI risks, but do not cover every area where HPV, herpes or syphilis can spread. Use a new condom for each act and before sexual contact; use water- or silicone-based lubricant with latex and stop when movement hurts. Never deliberately bend an erect penis or force intercourse. Cleaning, grooming or a partner's appearance cannot substitute for prevention. Many STIs cause no symptoms. Discuss testing with new partners and ask a sexual-health service which urine, blood or site-specific swabs and repeat tests fit your exposures. Window periods differ: a negative result only addresses the infections, sites and timing tested, not a permanent 'STI-free' status. Seek assessment now for discharge, sores or urinary pain rather than waiting for a window period. Follow diagnosis-specific treatment, partner care and advice about when sex can resume; do not share antibiotics. Vaccination, PrEP and time-sensitive exposure care Ask about HPV vaccination and other vaccines relevant to your circumstances. Current CDC guidance recommends routine HPV vaccination at 11–12 years, starting from 9, catch-up through 26, and an individual discussion for some unvaccinated adults aged 27–45. Local schedules may differ. HPV vaccination prevents new infections; it does not treat an existing infection or eliminate the need for other prevention. PrEP is prescribed medicine for people without HIV who want protection before possible exposure; options and monitoring are individual. HIV testing is needed before starting and during follow-up. PrEP does not prevent other STIs or pregnancy, and it is not the same as HIV treatment. After a possible HIV exposure, seek urgent assessment for PEP immediately: it must start within 72 hours and works best as early as possible. Do not wait for symptoms or take a partner's pills. Support general health without performance guarantees Regular activity, balanced food, smoking cessation, realistic weight management and limiting alcohol can support cardiovascular and sexual health. Sleep and help for stress also matter. Hydration needs vary with health and activity; forcing two litres daily is not a treatment for erectile dysfunction. No particular serving of spinach, chilli, avocado, tomato, carrot or flavonoid-rich food guarantees higher testosterone, erections or fertility. Small studies or associations do not establish a cure for everyone. Pelvic-floor rehabilitation may help selected problems, but strengthening is not a universal penile-health routine: pain or overactive muscles may need relaxation and professional assessment. Avoid unsupervised high-repetition exercises or repeatedly stopping urine flow as exercise. Persistent erection or libido concerns merit review of medicines, sleep and underlying conditions; testosterone requires an appropriate diagnosis and can suppress sperm production, particularly important when trying to conceive. Foreskin and circumcision questions are individual A tight foreskin that cannot comfortably retract is phimosis; a retracted foreskin stuck behind the head is paraphimosis, an emergency. Painful tightness or recurrent inflammation needs assessment, not forceful stretching or an automatic assumption that circumcision is necessary. Circumcision removes the foreskin and may be an option for selected medical problems after discussion of alternatives, healing, bleeding, infection and sensory changes. Circumcision does not make someone immune to balanitis or STIs. Evidence supports partial reduction of certain infections in particular circumstances, including acquisition of HIV by men during heterosexual sex; this must not be generalized to all exposures or partners. It does not replace condoms, vaccination, testing or PrEP. People with or without a foreskin can keep comfortable skin with appropriate gentle care; do not judge hygiene or sexual health by circumcision status. Notice changes without diagnosing them by colour or smell Urine colour can change with fluid intake, food, medicines or illness; pink, red or dark-brown urine may be blood rather than simple dehydration. Suspected blood needs urgent same-day advice even once, in a small amount or when uncertain. Burning, new frequency or urgency, foul-smelling discharge, blood in semen or pain on ejaculation should be assessed. Suspected UTI in an adult with a penis needs prompt same-day clinical advice, especially with fever or feeling unwell. Odour, itching, swelling or pain can reflect irritation, skin disease or infection; none alone establishes an STI, yeast infection, cancer or infertility. A persistent ulcer, growth, bleeding patch, new lump or new loss of sensation needs examination. Bring the timing, exposures, products, medicines and any injury history. Routine check-ups and tests depend on age and risks rather than a universal yearly genital examination; new symptoms should not wait for a screening appointment. Know the emergencies and ask for confidential help Go to emergency care for a foreskin trapped behind the head, inability to pass urine, suspected penile fracture after bending trauma, or severe genital injury. A pop with rapid loss of erection, swelling or bruising can be a fracture of the tissue covering, not a bone injury. Do not wait for all these signs or for ice or pain medicine to work. Sudden severe testicular pain, pain with nausea or abdominal pain, or persistent testicular pain at rest also requires emergency assessment. An erection lasting around 3–4 hours needs emergency care; seek help sooner for severe pain or according to an individual injection-treatment plan. With sickle cell disease, a painful erection lasting more than an hour is an emergency. Rapidly worsening genital pain or swelling with severe illness, confusion, fainting or loss of consciousness also needs emergency help. You can ask for a private appointment or chaperone; care should be respectful and based on the problem, not blame or assumptions about identity. With a suspected UTI, confusion, drowsiness or difficulty speaking requires immediate emergency care even without other signs of severe illness. Do not drive yourself. Gentle washing and comfortable foreskin movement are enough; always return a retracted foreskin and never force a child's foreskin. Hair removal is optional, and trimming, shaving, waxing, threading and creams have different injury risks. Combine appropriate barriers, vaccination, testing and HIV prevention; a negative test is not a permanent guarantee. Healthy habits support wellbeing but no food, fixed water target, hormone booster or universal exercise guarantees sexual function or fertility. Persistent changes need assessment; trapped foreskin, urinary retention, suspected fracture, testicular emergencies and prolonged erections need immediate care. Is waxing or threading pubic hair harmful? It can cause pain, skin injury, irritation or burns with hot wax. It is optional. Ask about suitability and hygienic technique, avoid damaged or delicate genital skin, and consider trimming or keeping the hair instead. Can I use a chemical hair remover on the penis? Do not assume a leg or bikini-line product is genital-safe. Follow the exact permitted areas and instructions; avoid the penis, scrotum or mucosal skin when not expressly suitable. Rinse immediately if it burns and seek advice for injury. Is penile odour always an infection? No. Sweat and trapped material can contribute, but a persistent new smell with soreness, discharge or urinary symptoms needs assessment. Do not mask it with deodorant or diagnose the cause by smell. Can a penis fracture without a bone? Yes. Forceful bending of an erection can tear the tissue covering. Suspected fracture needs immediate hospital care, even if some classic signs are absent; do not try to straighten it or wait for swelling to settle. Do I need to shave or have sex to keep it healthy? No. Hair removal and sexual activity are personal choices, not maintenance requirements. Comfortable hygiene, consent and appropriate prevention matter more than a cosmetic or performance standard. Does a normal appearance or negative STI test guarantee safety? No. Infections may be symptomless, and a test depends on the infection, site and timing. Discuss testing windows and repeat tests with a service and seek assessment for symptoms now. Do circumcised people still need condoms and testing? Yes. Partial protection against certain infections in particular circumstances is not immunity. Circumcision does not replace other prevention or rule out inflammation. Which foods or exercises guarantee better erections or fertility? None can guarantee this. General health habits may help, but persistent concerns need assessment. Pelvic-floor exercises should fit the problem, and testosterone can reduce sperm production. Can dark urine simply be dehydration? Sometimes, but colour alone cannot establish the cause. Possible blood, including pink, red or dark-brown urine, needs urgent same-day advice even if it happens once or is uncertain. Which changes need emergency care? Trapped foreskin, inability to urinate, suspected fracture, severe genital injury, sudden severe or concerning persistent testicular pain, or an erection lasting around 3–4 hours need emergency care. Seek help earlier for severe pain; with sickle cell disease a painful erection over an hour is an emergency. Severe illness with confusion, fainting or loss of consciousness also needs immediate help. With a suspected UTI, confusion, drowsiness or difficulty speaking requires immediate emergency care even without other signs of severe illness. Do not drive yourself.

title: Headaches around menopause: migraine changes and HRT choices
description: Why migraine can change during perimenopause, how HRT choices differ from contraception, and when headaches need assessment rather than a hormone explanation.
body: Headaches can change around menopause, but hormones are not the only possible cause. Migraine often becomes less predictable during the transition and may improve gradually after natural menopause; improvement is not guaranteed. A new or different headache deserves assessment, with treatment based on the headache pattern and your menopause symptoms. Perimenopause and menopause are different stages Perimenopause is the transition when ovarian hormone levels fluctuate and periods often change. Menopause is usually identified after 12 months without a period when hormonal contraception is not affecting bleeding. It commonly occurs between 45 and 55, but can happen earlier. A clinician interprets symptoms and medical history; missed periods alone do not always establish menopause. Hot flushes, night sweats, sleep or mood changes and vaginal dryness may accompany the transition. Hair thinning and weight changes can also occur, but are not specific to menopause. Symptoms can continue afterwards. In otherwise healthy people aged 45 or over with a typical pattern, routine hormone tests are usually unnecessary. Why migraine can worsen before periods stop Rapidly changing estrogen levels can trigger migraine in susceptible people; perimenopausal migraine is not simply a sign of too little estrogen. Irregular cycles, disturbed sleep and stress may also complicate the pattern. Someone whose attacks were linked to periods may notice more frequent or less predictable attacks. After natural menopause, hormonal triggers often settle and migraine without aura may gradually improve. It does not necessarily improve immediately, and some people continue to have attacks or become worse. Migraine with aura may be less likely to improve. New headaches should not automatically be attributed to the transition. Recognise the headache pattern and keep a diary Migraine can cause throbbing pain, nausea and sensitivity to light or sound, with or without aura. Aura can involve temporary visual, sensory or speech symptoms. A history of migraine does not make every new neurological symptom harmless; new weakness, speech difficulty or loss of vision needs emergency assessment. Record headache days, duration, severity, associated symptoms, periods, sleep and every medicine used. Note HRT starts or changes and possible food or drink associations. A diary supports diagnosis and treatment review, but do not wait weeks to complete one before seeking help for warning signs. HRT treats menopause symptoms, with variable migraine effects Systemic hormone replacement therapy can treat troublesome hot flushes and related menopause symptoms. It is not a guaranteed migraine treatment: headaches can improve, stay the same or worsen. Conventional HRT adds hormones and does not reliably suppress ovarian cycling; this matters particularly during early perimenopause. Ask your prescriber to review the timing, preparation and dose if attacks or aura change. Hormonal cycle control and HRT have different purposes and are not interchangeable. HRT does not provide contraception. The plan depends on symptoms, stage of transition, bleeding pattern, medical risks and your preferences. Discuss route, dose and aura with the prescriber For someone with migraine who needs HRT, estrogen through the skin (patch, gel or spray) is generally preferred for steadier levels, using the lowest dose that controls menopause symptoms. This does not mean patches eliminate every adverse effect or are suitable for everyone. If you have a uterus, appropriate progestogen is normally needed to protect its lining. Migraine aura alone does not rule out HRT, although combined estrogen-containing hormonal contraception has different restrictions. New or worsening aura still needs assessment. Discuss personal clot, stroke and cancer risks and medicines before choosing treatment; do not change hormones yourself. NICE recommends review at about three months and then annually, or earlier for problems. Treat migraine itself, not only the hormones A clinician can agree an attack-treatment plan and, if attacks are frequent or disabling, prevention. Options may include suitable pain relief, migraine-specific medicines and treatment for nausea; preventive choices depend on health conditions, interactions and preferences. A pharmacist can check whether an over-the-counter product is appropriate. Frequent use of acute headache medicines can itself make headaches more frequent. Record how many days you take them and seek a review rather than repeatedly increasing doses. If pregnancy remains possible, tell the prescriber because some preventive medicines need strict pregnancy precautions. Do not abruptly stop prescribed treatment without advice. Food, sleep and activity: look for your own pattern Regular meals, adequate fluids and a consistent sleep routine can help. Alcohol, caffeine, chocolate or cheeses are sometimes suspected triggers, but dairy and other food groups do not need automatic elimination. A diary may reveal an individual association; change one thing at a time while keeping a balanced diet. Walking, swimming or other enjoyable activity can be built up gradually according to health and tolerance. There is no single exercise schedule that guarantees relief. Stress-management approaches can be useful alongside care. A new headache triggered by exercise needs medical advice rather than simply pushing through it. Acupuncture is an option to discuss, not an energy-pathway cure Acupuncture involves inserting fine needles. Research suggests it can help some people, although specific needling effects and nonspecific effects both contribute. This does not establish a proven energy-channel explanation or a menopause-specific cure. NICE considers a course for migraine prevention when certain standard preventive options have failed or are unsuitable. Discuss whether it fits your plan and use a suitably qualified practitioner with sterile needles. It should not delay diagnosis or replace emergency care. Check supplements carefully, especially butterbur Riboflavin (vitamin B2), magnesium and coenzyme Q10 have been studied for migraine, with varying and often limited evidence. Vitamin D studies also do not establish a universal menopause-headache remedy. Treat a documented deficiency or other nutritional need individually; do not assume several supplements together work better. Butterbur is a Petasites plant, not culinary butter. It has important liver-toxicity concerns, including reports involving products labelled free of harmful pyrrolizidine alkaloids; do not start it yourself. Magnesium can cause diarrhoea and interact with medicines, and Q10 can interact with warfarin. Review products and doses with a clinician or pharmacist rather than assuming “natural” means safe. When to seek assessment urgently Arrange a review for new, substantially changed, worsening or difficult-to-control headaches, especially a new pattern in later life. Seek urgent same-day advice for headache with jaw pain when chewing, scalp tenderness or new eye problems; temporal arteritis needs rapid assessment. A migraine lasting over 72 hours or aura over an hour also needs urgent advice. Use emergency care for a sudden extremely painful headache, new weakness or difficulty speaking, new blurred or double vision, loss of vision, a seizure, fainting or loss of consciousness, confusion or drowsiness, or headache with signs of meningitis such as fever and stiff neck. Recent head injury is another emergency reason. Do not assume these are menopause or familiar aura, and do not drive yourself. Hormonal fluctuation can worsen perimenopausal migraine; improvement after menopause is variable. HRT and contraception differ; route, dose, aura and personal risks need an individual review. Use a headache diary and a tailored migraine plan without blanket food bans or unsupervised supplements. New patterns and warning symptoms need assessment; emergency signs must not wait for hormone treatment. Does migraine always get worse during menopause? No. Attacks may become less predictable during perimenopause, then gradually improve after natural menopause, particularly migraine without aura. Some people still have troublesome attacks. A new or changed headache should not automatically be labelled hormonal. Can HRT cure menopause headaches? HRT treats menopause symptoms and may improve or worsen migraine. It is not a guaranteed headache cure or reliable suppression of ovarian cycles. Review new attacks or aura with the prescriber and agree whether the preparation, dose or another approach needs adjustment. Can I use HRT if I have aura? Aura alone does not contraindicate HRT. A prescriber still assesses individual risks, usually preferring low-dose transdermal estrogen when HRT is needed. Combined hormonal contraception follows different rules. New weakness, speech difficulty or loss of vision requires emergency assessment, not an assumed aura diagnosis. How are headaches treated? Treatment combines an appropriate diagnosis, an attack plan and prevention when needed, alongside regular meals, sleep and activity. Choices depend on headache type, frequency, medicines and health risks. Frequent acute medicine use needs review because it can worsen the pattern. Should I cut out cheese, chocolate or dairy? Not automatically. Track possible individual associations without removing many foods at once. Keep regular balanced meals and discuss a consistent pattern; suspected triggers are not universal causes. Which supplements should I take? There is no universal supplement plan for headaches around menopause. B2, magnesium, Q10 and vitamin D need individual consideration, with uncertain benefit and possible interactions. Butterbur is a plant with liver-safety concerns, not butter, and should not be started without professional review. What if headaches do not settle after my final period? Persistent migraine is possible; menopause does not guarantee a cure. Review the diagnosis, medicines, HRT, sleep and other health factors instead of waiting indefinitely. Seek earlier assessment if the pattern changes or affects daily life. Which symptoms need urgent or emergency help? Jaw pain while chewing, scalp tenderness or new eye symptoms with headache need same-day advice. Sudden extreme headache, new weakness or speech problems, new blurred or double vision, loss of vision, seizure, fainting or loss of consciousness, confusion or meningitis signs need emergency care. Do not drive yourself.

title: IUD removal: planning the appointment, procedure and aftercare
description: When to remove or replace a copper or hormonal IUD, contraception before removal, comfort options, missing threads, recovery and warning signs.
body: A copper or hormonal intrauterine device can be removed when you want to stop using it, plan pregnancy or change contraception. A trained clinician should remove it and help plan what happens next. Many routine removals are brief, but pain, device position and pregnancy risk vary; a difficult removal deserves assessment rather than force. Check your device, purpose and replacement date Copper devices contain no contraceptive hormone; hormonal devices release a progestogen, usually levonorgestrel. Their main contraceptive actions occur before fertilisation, including effects on sperm and, for hormonal devices, cervical mucus. Levonorgestrel is a synthetic progestogen, and hormonal devices also thin the uterine lining. Duration depends on the exact product, country, age at insertion and reason for use. For example, US Paragard is labelled for up to 10 years of contraception, while US Mirena is labelled for 8 years of contraception but 5 years for heavy menstrual bleeding. Other devices have different limits; protection of the uterine lining during hormone replacement therapy may have a different timetable too. Check your insertion record and local advice. There is no universal need to remove every device one year early. Reasons to discuss removal or a change of method You may request removal before the planned replacement date because you want pregnancy, prefer another method or no longer want an IUD. New or troublesome bleeding, cramps or other symptoms should be discussed; you do not have to tolerate unwanted effects to keep contraception. Assessment can also identify a cause unrelated to the device. A partly expelled device, suspected perforation or pregnancy needs clinical review, not pulling on the threads yourself. New severe headaches also deserve medical assessment rather than assuming removal alone solves them. Sudden face or arm weakness, speech difficulty or loss of vision needs emergency help, even if it resolves. Do not wait for a routine removal visit. Infection or pregnancy needs an individual plan A sexually transmitted infection or pelvic inflammatory disease does not automatically mean immediate IUD removal. PID requires treatment and close follow-up, generally reassessment within 48–72 hours; lack of improvement can change the plan. If you want it removed, the clinician normally starts antibiotics first. Do not stop antibiotics or remove the device yourself. If pregnancy occurs with an IUD, contact a clinician promptly to check the pregnancy location and device position and exclude ectopic pregnancy. Leaving an IUD in an ongoing pregnancy increases miscarriage, infection and preterm-birth risks. Removal can reduce these risks when threads are visible or safely reachable, but cannot guarantee a normal outcome. If threads are not accessible, imaging and specialist advice guide care; blind attempts are inappropriate. Plan contraception before the appointment If you do not want pregnancy, use condoms or avoid sex that could cause pregnancy for the seven days before removal. Plan this even for a replacement appointment because insertion of the new device may not be possible. Tell the service about recent sex, condom failure, an overdue device or possible displacement before attending; the plan may need emergency contraception, a later removal or follow-up testing. A pregnancy test taken immediately after recent sex cannot rule out a very early pregnancy. The clinician may advise a test 21 days after the last pregnancy-risk sex and tailor temporary contraception. Tell them if you want to conceive instead. Bring the device record if available, medication and allergy details, and information about symptoms or previous difficult procedures; preparation is more than simply booking a visit. Discuss comfort, consent and support Some people feel only brief cramping; others experience more pain or distress. Removal is often easier than insertion, but mild pain cannot be promised and speculum discomfort is not the only possible cause. Discuss previous pain, anxiety or trauma, the examination steps, a chaperone or support person and how to pause or stop. Your consent remains important throughout. Ask which pain relief is suitable for you rather than taking a fixed combination for everyone. Paracetamol or ibuprofen may be suggested when appropriate; allergies, pregnancy possibility, kidney or stomach problems and other medicines can affect the choice. Complex removal may need local anaesthetic or another planned approach. Follow clinic-specific food, medicine and travel instructions, especially if sedation or hospital care is planned. What happens during a routine removal? You are positioned for a vaginal examination and a speculum allows the clinician to see the cervix. When threads are accessible, they gently draw the device out using appropriate instruments; the flexible arms usually fold as it passes through the cervix. This describes clinician care, not a home technique. Do not pull threads or insert tools yourself. The clinician checks that the removed device is intact and is the expected type. Routine removal may take only a few minutes, although consultation and recovery add time. Pain, bleeding or a faint feeling can occur; tell the team immediately. There is no guarantee of zero cervical trauma or that every device will slide out easily. Missing threads or a difficult removal changes the approach Threads may have retracted while the IUD is correctly positioned, but missing threads can also reflect expulsion, pregnancy or perforation. Until checked, use alternative contraception and ask promptly whether emergency contraception is needed. A clinician excludes pregnancy and locates the device, usually with ultrasound and sometimes further imaging, before attempting appropriate removal. Resistance, embedment in the uterine wall or a broken device calls for a careful plan rather than stronger pulling. A trained specialist may use ultrasound guidance, cervical preparation or dilation, anaesthesia or hysteroscopy, which uses a small camera to view the uterus. Occasionally a different surgical approach is needed. Ask about benefits, uncertainties and alternatives; not every case needs the same procedure. Can a new IUD be fitted at the same visit?
