Often yes, if pregnancy can reasonably be excluded and the new device is suitable. Choice depends on infection status, bleeding needing investigation, uterine anatomy and the product. Fibroids are not all equivalent: distortion of the uterine cavity matters. A clinician may recommend treating a condition first or using another method temporarily. Before leaving, confirm the device name, insertion date, next review or replacement date and exactly when protection starts. Copper and hormonal devices and switches from other methods do not all have the same backup requirements. Use the agreed temporary contraception when needed; do not assume a planned replacement guarantees uninterrupted protection if fitting is delayed or unsuccessful. Recovery and symptoms after removal Mild period-like cramps and some light bleeding or spotting can occur for a few days. Recovery after a complex procedure may differ. Use pain relief only as suitable and follow your individual aftercare instructions; rest or arrange help with travel if you feel unwell. Persistent or increasing bleeding or pain should be reviewed rather than automatically called normal for weeks. Your previous bleeding pattern may return after hormonal contraception stops, but the timing varies and underlying causes of irregular or heavy periods may still be present. Ask when and how to resume usual activities after your procedure. Seek advice if recovery differs from the expected plan; removal does not prove that every later symptom is caused by or cured by the device. Fertility can return immediately Pregnancy is possible as soon as either type of device is removed, even before the first period. After uncomplicated removal, there is no routine requirement to wait one month before trying to conceive. Discuss preconception care, medicines and any separate condition that might require a different plan. Immediate return of fertility is not a promise of immediate pregnancy. If you do not want pregnancy, agree your next method before removal and follow its start and backup instructions. Continue condoms for STI risk reduction when needed; an IUD does not protect against STIs. If sex occurs without the planned protection, contact a pharmacist or sexual-health service promptly about emergency contraception instead of waiting for bleeding. When to seek urgent or emergency care Seek urgent same-day advice for fever or chills, offensive vaginal discharge, persistent troublesome bleeding or pelvic pain with unusual bleeding or discharge. Possible pregnancy with new lower abdominal pain or unusual bleeding needs prompt assessment even without a positive pregnancy test. Shoulder-tip pain with possible pregnancy needs immediate medical advice. Do not wait for the next scheduled check. Seek emergency care now for severe or worsening abdominal or pelvic pain, pain that hurts with movement or touch, heavy vaginal bleeding, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or confusion. Fainting or loss of consciousness is also an emergency. Do not drive yourself. A serious symptom after removal should not be dismissed as ordinary cramps or treated by trying to remove any remaining material at home. Use the exact product and purpose to check replacement timing; a blanket one-year-early rule is inappropriate. Arrange trained removal and plan contraception for the seven days beforehand if pregnancy is not wanted. Discuss pain relief and consent; missing threads or resistance needs assessment, sometimes specialist removal. Pregnancy can occur immediately after removal; replacement and method-switch protection must be confirmed. Fever, offensive discharge or unexpected recovery needs advice; severe pain, heavy bleeding or fainting needs emergency care. Can I have another IUD fitted immediately? Often, if pregnancy can be excluded and the device is suitable. Infection, unexplained bleeding or uterine-cavity problems may change the plan. Confirm any backup contraception and prepare for the possibility that fitting cannot be completed that day. What side effects can happen after removal? Brief cramps and light bleeding or spotting can occur. Pain and recovery vary, particularly after a complex procedure. Do not assume worsening pain, substantial bleeding, fever or offensive discharge is normal. Ask about suitable pain relief and follow the specific aftercare plan. Can I become pregnant straight away? Yes, pregnancy is possible immediately, including before the first period. There is no routine one-month delay after uncomplicated removal. Fertility also depends on age and other factors; immediate return does not guarantee conception. Arrange another method beforehand if pregnancy is not wanted. Which symptoms mean I should contact a clinician? Seek same-day advice for fever or chills, offensive discharge, troublesome persistent bleeding or pelvic pain with unusual discharge or bleeding. Severe or worsening abdominal/pelvic pain, pain with movement or touch, heavy bleeding, fainting or loss of consciousness, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or confusion needs emergency care. Do not drive yourself. Why use condoms or avoid pregnancy-risk sex beforehand? Sex in the days before removal can lead to pregnancy after contraceptive protection ends. Use condoms or avoid sex that could cause pregnancy for seven days before removal, including planned replacement. Tell the service about any recent risk; a very early negative test is not enough to exclude pregnancy. Must an IUD be removed for every pelvic infection? No. PID needs prompt treatment and close follow-up; clinicians usually reassess in 48–72 hours and consider removal if improvement is inadequate. If you choose removal, it is generally done after antibiotics start. Do not remove it yourself or delay treatment. What if the clinician cannot see the threads? The device may still be correctly placed, but pregnancy, expulsion or perforation must be considered. Use backup contraception and ask about emergency contraception. Location is checked, usually by ultrasound, before trained removal attempts; specialist techniques or hysteroscopy may be needed. Can I remove the device myself to avoid an appointment? Arrange removal with a trained clinician. Do not pull on threads or insert a hook or other tool: incomplete removal, pain, injury and an unplanned pregnancy are possible. If access is difficult, ask a sexual-health or contraception service for a removal appointment and advice about bridging contraception.

title: Nausea around menopause: possible causes, medicine review and when to seek help
description: Nausea should not automatically be blamed on menopause. Learn about other causes, HRT and antidepressant side effects, practical relief and urgent warning signs.
body: Feeling sick can occur around the menopause transition, but timing alone does not establish a hormonal cause. Nausea may accompany a migraine, another illness or a medicine change, and pregnancy remains possible during perimenopause. Persistent or recurrent symptoms deserve assessment rather than being accepted as a normal part of ageing. There are practical comfort measures and treatments, but the right approach depends on the cause. Nausea does not diagnose menopause Perimenopause is the transition in which periods and other symptoms may change before the final menstrual period. Menopause is generally recognised after twelve months without a period when hormonal contraception or another explanation does not account for the change. It commonly occurs between 45 and 55, but can happen earlier, including after certain treatments. Age or nausea alone is not a diagnostic test. Changes in ovarian hormones are involved in menopause, but a new episode of nausea cannot simply be labelled low oestrogen. There is no reliable figure here for how often nausea is caused by menopause itself. If you feel sick repeatedly, throughout the day or enough to disrupt eating and daily activities, seek advice; persistent nausea is not something you must endure because you are approaching menopause. Look at the whole pattern and other possible causes Hot flushes can involve sudden heat or cold in the face, neck and chest, sweating, palpitations, anxiety or dizziness. Night sweats may disturb sleep. Some people feel unwell at the same time, while migraine can cause nausea in its own right. Headache, fatigue, chills or a racing heart need to be considered in context rather than all being attributed to a flush. A symptom diary may show a pattern, but does not prove the cause. Other possibilities include a stomach infection or food poisoning, reflux, inner-ear or balance problems, anxiety, alcohol and medicines. Pregnancy is still possible during perimenopause, and HRT is not contraception. If pregnancy could have occurred, follow a test's instructions: most tests work from the first missed period, or at least 21 days after the last unprotected sex if the next period's date is uncertain. A negative test taken too early is less reliable; repeat as advised, and do not wait for a positive test before seeking help for warning signs. HRT benefits and risks depend on the person and preparation Hormone replacement therapy can relieve appropriate menopausal symptoms such as hot flushes and night sweats, but it is not a general treatment for unexplained nausea. Oestrogen comes in several forms, including tablets, patches, gel and spray. People with a womb usually also need a progestogen to protect the womb lining; after hysterectomy, oestrogen alone may be appropriate. The regimen also depends on periods and medical history. Not every preparation is the same oestrogen-plus-progestin tablet. Discuss benefits and risks in relation to age, symptoms, history, hormone type, route and duration. Blood-clot, stroke and breast-cancer risks do not apply identically to every formulation; oral and skin-delivered treatments differ. Many people have no side effects or only mild ones. Nausea, breast tenderness, headache, bloating, mood changes or spotting are not all life-threatening reactions, but troublesome symptoms and unexpected bleeding need review. Regulated body-identical medicines are different from unregulated compounded products marketed as natural. Review nausea after starting or changing HRT Both oestrogen and progestogen can cause nausea. Note when it began relative to starting treatment, changing the dose or using a different preparation, and check the leaflets for both medicines. For an oral oestrogen product, taking it with food may help if consistent with its instructions. A prescriber may adjust the dose, route or product after assessing you; do not make those changes yourself or assume the medicine is the only possible cause. Some early side effects improve as the body adjusts, and a routine HRT review is often planned around three months. That is not a requirement to wait three months with persistent, severe or disruptive nausea. General nausea that does not improve within a few days or keeps returning warrants a clinical review; oestrogen-specific NHS advice also recommends contacting the prescriber when nausea lasts more than a week, sooner if troublesome or accompanied by warning signs. Report new or heavier bleeding, or bleeding after established menopause, instead of dismissing it as a harmless hormone effect. Use food and drink for comfort, not a hormonal cure Try small, more frequent meals and regular sips of a drink you tolerate. Fresh air and avoiding strong cooking smells may help. Rich, greasy, very hot or spicy foods can worsen nausea for some people; caffeine, alcohol or hot drinks may also trigger flushes. Notice your own response rather than banning many foods or following a rigid hot-versus-cold food theory. Eat enough and ask for help if nausea is limiting nutrition or weight is falling. Drink for adequate hydration rather than forcing large amounts of water, and follow any fluid restrictions for another condition. Plant-oestrogen foods may be part of ordinary nutrition, but neither a specific food nor a supplement is a proven cure for unexplained nausea. Concentrated isoflavones and other herbal products have uncertain effects, quality and interactions; discuss them with a clinician or pharmacist, especially if you take other medicines. Natural does not guarantee safe. Reduce discomfort from flushes and support sleep Light layers that can be removed, a cooler bedroom, a fan or cool drink may make flushes more manageable. Choose comfortable, breathable clothing rather than treating cotton as a required medical treatment. If hot weather worsens symptoms, seek a cooler, well-ventilated space and adapt activities. These steps can improve comfort without guaranteeing that nausea will resolve or proving that a flush caused it. Support regular sleep, manageable physical activity and relaxation that suits you. If you exercise outdoors, choose a comfortable temperature and adjust to your health and symptoms rather than pushing through illness. Seek smoking-cessation support if needed and consider reducing personal triggers such as alcohol or caffeine. Stress support is useful without implying that symptoms are your fault. If symptoms remain disruptive, you can discuss treatment without first completing a compulsory lifestyle trial. Nonhormonal medicines and contraception need separate decisions Menopause-specific cognitive behavioural therapy may help with hot flushes, sleep or associated distress. Prescription nonhormonal options are available when appropriate. Some SSRIs or SNRIs are used for diagnosed mood conditions or selected menopause symptoms, but NICE does not routinely recommend them as first-line treatment for hot flushes alone. They are not general anti-nausea medicines, and nausea can itself be a side effect. Tell the prescriber about new symptoms; do not abruptly stop an antidepressant, share medicine or choose a dose yourself. A contraceptive method may sometimes also help suitable people manage perimenopausal symptoms, but a low-dose pill is not an automatic remedy for nausea. Age, migraine history, smoking, clot risk and other factors affect the choice. Contraception and HRT serve different purposes; HRT does not prevent pregnancy. Discuss a coordinated plan with the clinician rather than combining or switching hormones on your own. Treatment for nausea itself, including an anti-sickness medicine if needed, should follow assessment of its cause. Arrange assessment and prepare a useful symptom history Seek a review if nausea is not improving within a few days, returns often, lasts throughout the day or interferes with meals, sleep, work or usual activities. Do not wait months. Mention persistent bloating, early fullness, unexplained weight loss, changes in bowel habits, pelvic discomfort, urinary symptoms or new bleeding. These have several possible causes and should not automatically be labelled menopause. A clinician may examine you and select tests according to the history rather than order the same hormone panel for everyone. Bring a timeline of periods, possible pregnancy exposure, flushes, headaches, vomiting and food or drink triggers, plus all medicines, doses, recent changes, supplements and relevant conditions. Ask what other causes need checking, whether a medicine may contribute, what relief is suitable and when to return if it persists. Follow-up should respond to the symptoms and findings. An initially reassuring assessment does not mean continuing or worsening symptoms should be ignored. Recognise symptoms that need urgent or emergency care Get urgent same-day advice for repeated vomiting with inability to keep fluids down, dehydration, or pain, redness or swelling in one leg while using hormones. Seek immediate emergency help for chest tightness or heaviness, pain spreading to the arm, back, neck or jaw, breathlessness, new difficulty speaking, one-sided weakness or facial drooping. Vomiting blood or material like coffee grounds, green vomit, a sudden severe headache, confusion, fainting or loss of consciousness also needs emergency assessment. Do not assume these are ordinary HRT effects or a hot flush. Severe or worsening abdominal or pelvic pain, pain worsened by movement or touch, or pelvic pain with shoulder-tip pain, dizziness, faintness, breathing difficulty or heavy vaginal bleeding needs immediate emergency care. Possible pregnancy with pelvic pain needs urgent assessment even without a positive test; do not wait for diet or a hormone adjustment. New bleeding after established menopause needs clinical checking even once or in a small amount. If symptoms are an emergency, use emergency services rather than waiting for a routine menopause appointment. Nausea around menopause is not proof of low oestrogen or a symptom that must be tolerated without assessment. Consider other causes and possible pregnancy during perimenopause; HRT is not contraception. HRT and antidepressants can cause nausea, but their benefits, risks and changes require an individual prescriber review. Small meals, tolerable drinks, cooling and personal trigger adjustments may help comfort; no food or supplement is a guaranteed cure. Persistent or recurrent nausea needs review, while chest, neurological, bleeding, severe pain or loss-of-consciousness warning signs may need emergency care. What can cause nausea around menopause? The timing does not identify one cause. Migraine, infection, reflux, balance problems, anxiety, pregnancy and medicines are among the possibilities. Symptoms may occur with flushes, but persistent nausea should not automatically be called hormonal or normal. Does HRT treat menopause-related nausea? HRT can help appropriate menopausal symptoms, but it is not a general remedy for unexplained nausea and can itself cause it. A clinician should assess the cause and discuss individual benefits, risks, route and regimen rather than promise a cure. Which foods should I avoid? Adjust foods or drinks that actually worsen your symptoms, such as rich or spicy meals, strong smells, alcohol, caffeine or hot drinks. Avoid a very restrictive diet or assuming traditional hot foods are medically harmful. Try small meals and regular tolerable sips; seek help if eating becomes difficult. When should I see a clinician? If nausea persists beyond a few days, keeps coming back, lasts throughout the day or disrupts normal activities, arrange a review rather than waiting three months. Inability to keep fluids down or dehydration needs urgent advice; chest symptoms, neurological changes, blood or green vomit, loss of consciousness or severe or worsening abdominal or pelvic pain need emergency care. Could I still be pregnant during perimenopause? Yes. HRT does not prevent pregnancy. Most urine tests can be used from a missed period, or at least 21 days after unprotected sex if timing is uncertain. Follow the instructions and repeat an early negative as advised; possible pregnancy with pain or other warning signs needs assessment without waiting for a positive result. Are all HRT side effects dangerous? No. Many people have no side effects or mild, temporary ones. Nausea, breast tenderness or headache is different from a clot, stroke or serious allergic reaction. Report troublesome symptoms and bleeding, and get urgent or emergency help for the warning signs rather than self-diagnosing. Must I wait until the three-month HRT review? No. That routine review checks how treatment is working, but persistent, severe or disruptive nausea should be discussed earlier. Contact the prescriber for oestrogen-related nausea lasting over a week, sooner for concerns or warning signs; unexplained nausea that persists or recurs also needs review. Should I stop an SSRI or use a contraceptive pill instead? Do not abruptly stop an antidepressant or switch or combine hormones yourself. SSRIs can cause nausea and have specific uses; contraceptive choice depends on your health and reproductive needs. Ask the prescriber to review the symptoms, medicines and suitable alternatives.

title: Painful ejaculation: possible causes, assessment and care
description: Pain during ejaculation or orgasm deserves attention. Explore infection, treatment effects and pelvic pain, with practical questions and urgent warning signs.
body: Pain during or after ejaculation can range from mild discomfort to severe pain in the penis, scrotum or perineum, the area between the scrotum and anus. Terms such as dysorgasmia or orgasmalgia describe pain linked to orgasm, which can also happen without semen being released. Pain can affect confidence, intimacy and daily life. It deserves assessment without embarrassment or an assumption about the cause. When to arrange care and when it is urgent Contact a clinician for new, repeated or persistent pain with ejaculation or orgasm, particularly with burning urine, discharge, blood in urine or semen, a changed urine stream or a new lump. Primary care or a sexual-health service can begin the assessment and arrange urology referral when needed. Tell a cancer-treatment or surgical team about symptoms after their treatment. Get urgent same-day advice for visible or suspected blood in urine, even once, in a small amount or if you are unsure it is blood. Seek urgent same-day advice for fever or shaking chills with urinary or pelvic pain, rapidly worsening symptoms or feeling very unwell. Inability to pass urine, sudden severe testicular pain, severe lower-abdominal pain, confusion or serious breathing difficulty needs emergency care. Do not wait for a routine sexual-health appointment if these occur. Prostatitis and infection are not the same in every case The prostate contributes fluid to semen. Prostatitis describes inflammation involving the prostate and sometimes nearby tissues. Bacterial infection is one cause; chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome can occur without an identified bacterial infection. Painful ejaculation, urinary burning or frequency, lower-abdominal discomfort and erection difficulties can overlap, so symptoms alone do not establish the type. Previous urinary infection, urinary procedures or a catheter, enlarged-prostate obstruction, diabetes, reduced immunity and sexual exposures can be relevant to the history. They are not a checklist that proves prostatitis or blame for an infection. Acute bacterial illness may need prompt antibiotics or hospital care; chronic pelvic pain often requires a different approach. Surgery, radiotherapy and changes in orgasm Prostate surgery or hernia repair can be associated with pain during sexual activity, sometimes through scarring, nerve effects or other postoperative problems. Radical prostatectomy removes the whole prostate and seminal vesicles, rather than only part of the gland. Ejaculation of semen normally stops afterwards, but orgasm can still occur and can sometimes be painful. Report painful dry orgasms as well as pain when semen is released. Pelvic radiotherapy can affect sexual function and cause discomfort. Some effects improve during recovery; others develop later or persist. Do not assume all radiation effects are temporary or that new pain is an unavoidable effect to tolerate. The treating team can assess infection, scarring or other problems and discuss appropriate rehabilitation. Cysts, stones and blockage of the ejaculatory ducts An obstruction in the ducts carrying semen, sometimes related to a cyst or stone, is one possible cause of pain or blood in semen. It can also affect fertility, but pain does not by itself mean obstruction or infertility. Low semen volume, fertility concerns and previous procedures may help determine whether specialist tests are appropriate. A urologist may consider targeted imaging and semen testing when the history warrants it. A procedure to open an obstructed duct or a fertility treatment is an option in selected cases, not a mandatory operation for every cyst or painful ejaculation. Discuss the evidence, risks, alternatives and whether treatment is intended to address pain, fertility or both. Medicines, including antidepressants Antidepressants can affect desire, erection, ejaculation or orgasm; painful ejaculation has also been reported. SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclic or tetracyclic medicines and monoamine oxidase inhibitors have different side-effect profiles. A symptom beginning after a medicine or dose change is useful information, but does not prove that the drug is responsible. Do not suddenly stop an antidepressant or change its dose yourself. Withdrawal and relapse can cause harm. Tell the prescriber about timing, other medicines and the effect on sexual life. They may review the diagnosis, adjust treatment or discuss alternatives, balancing mental-health benefit and side effects; finding a suitable plan may take time. Pudendal nerve and pelvic-floor pain The pudendal nerve supplies areas of the pelvis and genitals. Irritation or injury may cause burning, shooting pain, tingling or numbness, sometimes worse with sitting or sexual activity. Pelvic injury, surgery, diabetes or neurological conditions such as multiple sclerosis may be relevant, but they do not prove a pudendal diagnosis; other causes need consideration. A pelvic-health physiotherapist may assess muscle tenderness and coordination and use an individual plan, including relaxation when muscles are overactive. Repeated strengthening or Kegel exercises are not suitable for every painful pelvic floor. Specialist options can include nerve-pain medicines, selected injections or nerve blocks, and occasionally surgery for confirmed compression after other care fails. None guarantees relief. Sexually transmitted infections and partner care Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted infection that can cause genital or urinary irritation and may be associated with ejaculation discomfort. Other infections can cause urethritis or prostatitis too. Symptoms may be absent, and pain cannot identify the organism. Give an honest exposure history and ask which tests, including other STI tests, are appropriate. Confirmed trichomoniasis needs an effective prescribed oral antimicrobial; not every antibiotic works, and a topical product is not a substitute. Current partners need concurrent treatment to prevent reinfection. Avoid sex until both you and partners have completed treatment and symptoms have resolved. Follow the service’s advice about follow-up and retesting; do not share leftover medicines. Cancer concerns without assuming a cancer diagnosis Prostate cancer often has no symptoms early on. Urinary changes, erection difficulties or blood in urine or semen can have many causes, and painful ejaculation alone does not diagnose cancer. Tell the clinician about persistent symptoms, age, family history and previous cancer treatment so they can decide which investigation is useful. If cancer is diagnosed, treatment depends on its risk, stage, spread, general health and personal priorities. Options can include surgery, radiotherapy, hormone therapy and selected chemotherapy, targeted or immune treatments. For suitable low-risk disease, active surveillance involves planned tests and follow-up, not minimal attention. No single cancer treatment is prescribed just because ejaculation hurts. Stress, relationships and a respectful assessment Stress, anxiety and relationship difficulties can influence pain, muscle tension and sexual experience. Pain occurring with a partner but not during masturbation is useful context, but it does not prove a psychological cause or exclude a physical problem. Sometimes no single cause is found despite appropriate assessment. Psychosexual counselling or psychological support may help with distress and coping alongside medical or pelvic-pain care. It should not replace examination of concerning symptoms or imply that the pain is imagined. You can ask for an explanation of a proposed examination, consent to it and request appropriate support or a chaperone. What the appointment and tests may involve Prepare to describe when pain began, whether it happens during or after orgasm, how long it lasts and whether semen is released. Note other genital or urinary symptoms, medicines and dose changes, surgery or radiotherapy, sexual exposures, diabetes, neurological illness and family history. A focused examination may include the abdomen and genitals and, when appropriate, a rectal examination of the prostate. Urine testing or culture, STI tests and selected blood, semen or imaging tests may be useful. PSA testing requires an individual discussion: prostate inflammation can raise it, and a result alone does not diagnose cancer. Not everyone needs a PSA test, rectal examination or scan. Persistent symptoms after treatment deserve reassessment rather than repeating the same treatment indefinitely. Treatment, comfort and talking with a partner Care follows the cause. Bacterial prostatitis may need a clinician-selected antibiotic course; severe infection may require intravenous treatment. Anti-inflammatory pain relief is suitable only for some people. Postoperative pain, obstruction, nerve pain and chronic pelvic pain need different plans, and underlying diabetes or neurological disease should also be managed. Do not self-prescribe antibiotics, steroid injections or a procedure. Avoid pushing through painful sexual activity. Choose a calm, unhurried time to explain what hurts, how it affects you and what assessment you are arranging; listen to your partner’s concerns without treating pain as rejection. Agree on comfortable forms of intimacy without pressure. Record symptoms and review progress with the clinician. Many causes can be treated or managed, but timing and outcome vary and improvement cannot be guaranteed. Pain with ejaculation or orgasm is a symptom with several possible causes, including painful dry orgasm after prostate surgery. Fever with pelvic or urinary pain needs prompt advice; inability to urinate or sudden severe testicular pain needs emergency care. Antibiotics, surgery and pelvic-floor exercises are not universal treatments. Do not stop antidepressants or other necessary medicines without prescriber advice. Assessment and open, pressure-free communication can support care; symptoms do not prove cancer or a psychological cause. What problems can painful ejaculation cause? Pain can affect sexual confidence, relationships and quality of life. Some underlying conditions need treatment, but pain does not automatically mean a dangerous illness or infertility. Assessment helps identify the next step. Can surgery cause pain even without semen? Yes. After radical prostatectomy the whole prostate and seminal vesicles are removed, so semen is no longer ejaculated. Orgasm can still happen and can be painful; tell the surgical team about a painful dry orgasm. Does it mean prostate cancer? No. Prostate cancer is one possible context, but infection, pelvic pain, treatment effects and other causes are possible. Persistent symptoms or blood need review; a symptom or PSA result alone does not diagnose cancer. When should I contact a clinician? Arrange assessment for new, recurring or persistent pain, especially with urinary changes, discharge or blood. Fever with urinary or pelvic pain requires prompt same-day advice. Inability to urinate, sudden severe testicular pain or severe systemic illness needs emergency care. Should I stop my antidepressant? No, not on your own. Report the pain and its timing to the prescriber. They can assess possible causes and discuss a gradual, supervised change if appropriate; abrupt stopping can cause withdrawal or relapse. Should I strengthen my pelvic floor? Not automatically. Painful muscles may be overactive and need relaxation or coordination work rather than repeated tightening. A trained pelvic-health therapist can assess which approach suits you. Does pain only with a partner prove it is emotional? No. Differences between situations are helpful history, but do not establish a psychological cause. Medical assessment and appropriate psychological or relationship support can be combined. How are partners managed for trichomoniasis? Current partners need concurrent treatment. Avoid sex until all have completed treatment and symptoms have resolved, and follow local advice about other STI testing and follow-up. Pain alone cannot diagnose trichomoniasis.

title: HPV in men: cancer risk, testing limits and prevention
description: Most HPV causes no symptoms. Learn how warts differ from high-risk infection, when men need assessment or selected anal screening, and what vaccination can do.
body: Human papillomavirus, or HPV, is common in men and often causes no noticeable symptoms. Most infections are controlled without causing serious disease, but persistent high-risk HPV can contribute to certain cancers. The useful plan combines vaccination and realistic prevention with attention to symptoms and any screening recommended for your individual risk. HPV is common and often invisible HPV is a large group of related viruses, with more than 200 types; some affect genital skin or the mouth and throat. Many sexually active people encounter HPV without knowing it. Having no visible wart does not prove that you have never had HPV or cannot pass it on. Most infections become undetectable within a year or two as the immune system controls them. Some persist or become detectable again. This is not an individual timetable for permanent clearance or a date when transmission is impossible. A diagnosis does not mean cancer is inevitable. Wart-causing types and cancer-causing types differ Low-risk types, especially HPV6 and HPV11, commonly cause genital warts. Persistent infection with certain high-risk types, including HPV16 and HPV18, can cause precancerous cell changes and cancer. High-risk infection can be silent; it is not simply a more painful or more obvious wart. More than one type can be present. In men, relevant cancer sites include the penis, anus and oropharynx: the back of the throat, including the tonsils and base of the tongue. HPV also causes cervical, vaginal and vulval cancers in people with those organs. A typical wart does not usually turn into one of these cancers, and not every cancer at these sites is caused by HPV. Genital or anal changes need a diagnosis Warts can appear on the penis, scrotal skin, around the anus or inside the anal canal. They may be flat, raised or clustered and may be painless or cause irritation. A new lump is not automatically a wart; other skin conditions and some more serious lesions can look similar. Arrange assessment for a new growth, a sore that does not heal, unexplained genital or anal bleeding, discharge or persistent pain or itching. Do not diagnose cancer yourself or assume a familiar wart explains every change. An examination and sometimes a biopsy can clarify an unusual, bleeding, ulcerated or treatment-resistant lesion. Mouth and throat symptoms are a separate question HPV can affect the mouth and throat, including occasional low-risk warts, while persistent high-risk infection can contribute to oropharyngeal cancer. A throat symptom is not proof of HPV, and an oral wart is not the same as cancer. Do not try to identify a throat lesion from a photograph. A persistent sore throat, a new mouth or neck lump, an unexplained persistent mouth lesion, ear pain or trouble swallowing deserves clinical or dental assessment. Many causes are not cancer. Trouble swallowing needs urgent advice; inability to swallow, drooling, noisy or difficult breathing, or severe symptoms worsening quickly need immediate emergency care. Transmission does not establish blame HPV can pass through vaginal, anal or oral sex and intimate genital skin contact without penetration. Someone without symptoms can transmit it. Partners often share HPV, but the timing of a wart or diagnosis cannot show who acquired it first, when it happened or whether someone was unfaithful. If warts are diagnosed, discuss them with current partners and follow clinic advice about contact during treatment and healing. Partners can seek assessment for symptoms and appropriate other STI tests; routine partner HPV testing is not a useful way to reconstruct transmission. There is no fixed wart-free waiting period that guarantees no remaining risk. Risk depends on the person and the site HIV, transplant-related immune suppression and other causes of reduced immunity can make HPV-related disease more persistent and change follow-up. Smoking also matters. Men who have sex with men have higher anal-cancer rates in some populations, especially with HIV; this is a clinical risk context, not a judgement about identity, and anyone can acquire HPV. Circumcision status alone does not predict whether infection will persist or cancer will develop. Some studies show lower penile HPV rates after circumcision, but protection is incomplete and evidence differs by population and body site. It is not an HPV treatment or a substitute for vaccination and other prevention. Discuss immune conditions, medicines, smoking and prior lesions privately with your clinician. There is no routine whole-body HPV status test A blood test, routine STI panel or a single genital or mouth swab cannot establish a man’s HPV status at every site or predict which infection will progress. HPV tests used in cervical screening are not a general test for male partners, and routine screening for penile or oropharyngeal cancer is not established for the general public. Symptoms still need examination and site-specific investigation. A clinician may biopsy a suspicious lesion or arrange specialist assessment; testing a diagnosed tumour for HPV is a different purpose from screening someone without symptoms. A negative sample from one site does not rule out disease elsewhere or replace review of a changing lesion. Selected people may need anal screening Anal screening is not the same as a universal HPV test. For people with HIV, current US NIH guidance recommends annual anal-symptom assessment and age- and risk-based pathways: screening starts at 35 for men who have sex with men and for transgender women with HIV, and at 45 for other people with HIV. Symptoms require assessment regardless of whether a screening age has been reached. International anal-neoplasia guidance also addresses other higher-risk groups, including men who have sex with men without HIV from age 45 and solid-organ recipients from ten years after transplant. Local recommendations and services vary. Screening may involve anal cytology and selected HPV testing linked to high-resolution anoscopy and biopsy when indicated. Ask what applies to you and whether the necessary follow-up is available; do not order a stand-alone test as proof of safety. Treat the condition, not an assumed virus-clearing cure There is no standard antiviral or oral medicine that reliably eradicates an otherwise silent HPV infection. Diagnosed external warts may be observed or treated with suitable prescribed topical medicines or clinic procedures. Internal or suspicious lesions need site-specific care. Do not apply ordinary hand-wart products, household acids or genital creams inside the mouth or anus. Precancer and cancer need their own specialist plan, which can include local treatment, surgery or other cancer therapies depending on the diagnosis and stage. Earlier detection may improve treatment options, but does not guarantee a cure. Ask about results, follow-up and what changes should prompt an earlier visit rather than relying on an immune-boosting product. Vaccination and barriers reduce risk HPV vaccination prevents new infection with covered types; it does not treat existing infection, warts or cancer. Prior exposure does not necessarily mean you have encountered every vaccine type. Check your actual vaccine record and local eligibility. In the US, catch-up is recommended through 26 if not adequately vaccinated; ages 27–45 involve shared decision-making for selected adults, not a routine recommendation for everyone. Dose requirements depend on the local programme, age at the first dose and immune health. Correct, consistent condom use lowers exposure but does not cover all skin that can carry HPV. Avoid sexual contact involving visible warts or treated skin as your clinic advises. Stopping smoking supports health; no barrier, supplement or wart treatment promises zero transmission risk. Make an assessment and follow-up plan A sexual-health or primary-care appointment can review symptoms, exposure concerns, vaccination and immune health without requiring you to prove when HPV was acquired. Ask which examinations or other STI tests are relevant, how results will arrive and whether selected anal screening or specialist review is appropriate. People with a cervix should continue their own recommended cervical screening. Seek urgent advice for swallowing difficulty, serious illness or concerning new symptoms, especially with reduced immunity. Use emergency care for breathing difficulty, inability to swallow, non-stop or heavy rectal bleeding, or fainting or loss of consciousness with significant bleeding or severe illness. Do not drive yourself or wait for an HPV test, app assessment or routine screening appointment. No wart does not mean no HPV; most infections are controlled, but individual clearance cannot be dated. Typical warts and persistent high-risk HPV have different implications; symptoms need assessment rather than a photograph diagnosis. General male HPV-status testing differs from selected anal-screening pathways and tests of a suspicious lesion. Vaccination prevents covered new infections, not existing disease; agree prevention and follow-up with a professional. What is an oral wart? Some low-risk HPV types can cause mouth or throat warts, but not every lump is HPV and a wart is not the same as cancer. Persistent lesions, throat symptoms or a neck lump need assessment. Breathing difficulty or inability to swallow needs immediate emergency care. How do men get HPV? It can pass during vaginal, anal or oral sex and intimate genital contact without penetration, including when no symptoms are present. A diagnosis cannot establish when it was acquired or prove infidelity. What should I do if I think I have HPV? Arrange an assessment for a new genital, anal, mouth or throat change. A clinician can examine it, choose tests or biopsy when needed and review vaccination and relevant screening. Do not use a home wart remedy or wait for a whole-body HPV result. Can HPV in men be cured with medicine? No standard medicine reliably clears silent HPV itself. Warts, precancer and cancer can be treated according to the diagnosis; removing a wart does not prove the virus is gone. Early assessment helps, without guaranteeing a cancer cure. Does a genital wart mean cancer? Usually not: typical warts involve low-risk types, different from the main cancer-causing types. Other HPV types can coexist, and an unusual or bleeding growth still needs assessment. Should all men have an HPV or anal test? No universal test establishes HPV status at every site. Selected higher-risk people may need an anal-screening pathway with appropriate follow-up, particularly people with HIV under age- and risk-specific guidance. Symptoms need assessment at any age; ask what applies locally. Am I too old to benefit from vaccination? Eligibility and benefit depend on age, prior doses, exposure and local guidance. US catch-up extends through 26; selected adults 27–45 can discuss vaccination. It prevents covered new infections rather than treating an existing one, and dose schedules should follow your service’s advice. When is urgent or emergency help needed? Get urgent advice for trouble swallowing or significant illness, especially with reduced immunity. Breathing difficulty, inability to swallow, non-stop or heavy rectal bleeding, or fainting or loss of consciousness with significant bleeding or severe illness needs emergency help. Do not wait for a test or screening visit.

title: Masturbation worries and erectile dysfunction: assessment and treatment
description: Repeated erection difficulties deserve assessment. Understand masturbation and pornography research, mixed causes, treatment choices and important medicine warnings.
body: Difficulty getting or keeping an erection can be upsetting, especially if you have been told that masturbation damaged your body. Ordinary masturbation is not an established cause of permanent erectile dysfunction (ED), and frequency alone does not diagnose a problem. Persistent difficulties deserve their own medical assessment. The useful next step is to explore health, medicines, stress and sexual circumstances, then choose treatment that fits your needs rather than blame one habit. Separate erection symptoms from masturbation myths ED means difficulty attaining or maintaining an erection firm enough for wanted sexual activity. An occasional difficulty with tiredness, stress or too much alcohol is different from a repeated pattern. Having erections during masturbation or on waking can be useful information, but does not by itself prove that a problem is entirely psychological or exclude a health condition. Tell the clinician when it happens and what has changed. Masturbation does not cause blindness, and a familiar sexual habit is not an explanation for a new visual symptom. Rough pressure or friction can still cause soreness or injury: stop painful activity and seek care for significant injury. A person's account of masturbation, depression or relationship breakdown cannot establish that the habit caused ED. You can choose whether to masturbate without needing to prove sexual health through abstinence or a frequency target. What pornography research can and cannot show Studies of pornography and erections have produced differing findings and often rely on self-reported habits and symptoms. In a study of 3,586 men published in its journal issue in 2023, pornography frequency was not associated with ED severity after accounting for other factors; masturbation frequency had weak or inconsistent associations. Anxiety or depression, relevant medical illness, low desire and relationship dissatisfaction were more consistent factors. This is observational evidence, not proof of cause or a guarantee for every individual. Concerns about compulsive use, expectations or differences between solo and partnered arousal are still worth discussing if they bother you. A therapist can help explore the situation without assuming that pornography inevitably damages nerves or that stopping it guarantees recovery. Communication and psychosexual treatment may help selected couples, but improvement in a relationship study does not identify masturbation as the cause. A partner's involvement is optional and requires consent; therapy should reduce pressure, not create a performance test. Look for physical and psychological contributors together Erections involve blood vessels, nerves, hormones and the brain. Diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, heart or vascular disease, obesity, low testosterone or thyroid problems, and neurological conditions such as multiple sclerosis or Parkinson's disease can contribute. Pelvic surgery or injury and some medicines can also affect function. Low blood pressure or dizziness needs its own review, especially before ED treatment; it is not a diagnosis made from an erection symptom. Stress at home or work, anxiety, depression, low sexual interest and relationship difficulties can interact with physical factors. Smoking, excess alcohol and recreational drugs can add to the problem. More than one contributor is common. ED can be a reason to assess cardiovascular and metabolic health, but it does not mean everyone with ED has heart disease. Do not stop an antidepressant, blood-pressure medicine or another prescription on your own. Prepare for an assessment rather than ordering every test Book an appointment when erection problems keep happening or are causing distress. Bring a list of medicines, supplements and recreational substances, and describe onset, morning or solo erections, desire, ejaculation, orgasm, pain and any curvature. A clinician can discuss your health and emotional wellbeing and perform an appropriate examination, including blood pressure and relevant genital, vascular, hormonal or neurological findings. Blood glucose or HbA1c, lipids and an early-morning testosterone measurement may be part of the assessment; additional tests depend on the findings. An unexpected low testosterone result usually needs appropriate confirmation and interpretation, not an automatic prescription. Penile blood-flow ultrasound, overnight erection testing or an injection test is for selected circumstances, not a universal checklist. Discuss fertility plans before hormone treatment: external testosterone can suppress sperm production and is not a treatment for someone trying to become a father. Support health and reduce sexual pressure alongside treatment Stopping smoking, limiting excess alcohol, regular activity suited to your health, a varied eating pattern and management of diabetes or cardiovascular risk can help overall health and sometimes erections. These steps can accompany clinical treatment; you do not need to complete a fixed daily exercise quota or wait through a lifestyle trial before asking for help. Ask for support that fits your physical abilities and circumstances rather than a food or supplement promised to cure ED. Counselling, psychosexual therapy or cognitive behavioural therapy can help when anxiety, low mood, distress or relationship patterns are involved, including alongside medicine. Relaxation or meditation may help with stress but does not replace care for depression or an underlying illness. Agree on comfortable, consensual intimacy that does not require penetration or an erection every time. Follow-up should consider satisfaction, side effects and goals, rather than simply whether one treatment produced firmness. Oral medicines require an individual safety check Sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil and avanafil are PDE5 inhibitors that can support penile blood flow when there is sexual stimulation; they do not automatically create desire. Choice, timing and instructions differ between products. Headache, flushing, indigestion, a blocked nose or dizziness can occur. If treatment seems ineffective, ask the prescriber to review use and suitability rather than increasing doses, combining products or borrowing someone else's medicine. Do not combine PDE5 inhibitors with nitrates such as GTN, nitric-oxide donors such as poppers, nicorandil or riociguat: dangerous blood-pressure lowering can occur. Tell the clinician about all medicines and heart, blood-pressure, eye, kidney or liver conditions; controlled high blood pressure is not automatically the same as a contraindication. Unstable cardiac illness may make sexual activity and treatment unsafe until assessed. Avoid unverified online or herbal sexual-enhancement products, and do not stop necessary heart medicine to make an ED drug possible. Vacuum devices are a medical option, not an enlargement promise A vacuum erection device uses a cylinder and pump to draw blood into the penis; a constriction ring can help maintain the erection. It can be an option when tablets are unsuitable, ineffective or unwanted. Ask a qualified service about an appropriate device, training and your health history rather than improvising equipment or assuming temporary fullness means permanent growth. Bruising, coldness, numbness, discomfort or restricted ejaculation can occur. A constriction ring must not remain in place longer than 30 minutes, and should be removed promptly when finished, following the device instructions. Blood-thinning treatment or a bleeding disorder can make a device unsuitable and needs specialist review first. Stop if it hurts, and seek urgent medical help if a ring cannot be removed or the penis develops marked pain or abnormal discolouration; do not apply more suction. Injections and urethral medicine need training A clinician may offer a medicine such as alprostadil injected into erectile tissue, or an appropriate preparation placed in the urethra. These are different from oral tablets and can be options within an individualized plan. The team should teach correct use, select the preparation and explain follow-up and what to do if an erection does not settle. This article is not an injection or insertion instruction sheet. Possible harms include penile or urethral pain, bleeding, scarring and a prolonged erection; suitability depends on the product and health history. Do not use another person's supply, improvise a mixture, repeat a dose because you are disappointed, or combine treatments without the specialist's plan. Know the urgent contact instructions before using the medicine. A painful or unexpectedly prolonged erection warrants prompt advice, with emergency assessment by the prolonged-erection threshold, not further sexual stimulation. Surgery is selective and does not guarantee a cure A penile prosthesis may be considered when other choices are unsuitable or have not worked, or after a fully informed discussion of preferences. Inflatable and malleable devices work differently. Ask about realistic function, infection, mechanical failure, possible repeat surgery and the recovery plan. An implant is not a promise of restored natural erections, libido or fertility, and its benefits and harms should be discussed with an experienced team. Arterial reconstruction is reserved for carefully selected cases, such as a younger person with a defined arterial injury after pelvic or perineal trauma. Its aim is to improve blood supply, not block penile arteries to prevent blood leaving. Operations tying off veins for veno-occlusive ED are not recommended routinely because long-term results are poor. Most people with ED do not need surgery; choosing among counselling, medicines, devices and procedures depends on the cause, safety and personal priorities. Recognise urgent symptoms and arrange useful follow-up An erection lasting around three to four hours needs immediate emergency care to prevent tissue damage; seek help sooner for pain or according to your injection team's earlier instructions. With sickle cell disease, a painful erection lasting more than one hour needs immediate emergency assessment. Do not try to end a prolonged erection with sex or masturbation. Sudden loss or reduction of vision or hearing after an ED medicine needs immediate medical help and no further dose until advised. Call emergency services for persistent squeezing or spreading chest pain, chest pain with breathlessness, sweating or faintness, loss of consciousness, or sudden throat or tongue swelling and breathing difficulty. If chest pain follows an ED medicine, tell the team exactly what you took and when; do not self-treat it with GTN or another nitrate. For recurring ED without emergency signs, agree on a review of benefit, adverse effects and underlying health. There is no universal annual visit or guaranteed treatment schedule that suits everyone. Ordinary masturbation is not an established cause of permanent ED; assess repeated symptoms rather than assume blame. Pornography research is mixed and largely observational; neither a correlation nor a personal account proves causation. Assess medical, medication, emotional and relationship factors together, including cardiovascular health when appropriate. Tablets, devices used after training, injections, urethral medicine and selected surgery have different benefits and risks; do not combine or self-prescribe treatments. Prolonged erections, sudden sensory loss, chest-pain warning signs or loss of consciousness need urgent or emergency care as appropriate. What can I do to reduce the chance of erection problems? Stopping smoking, limiting excess alcohol, activity and food choices suited to your health, and treating relevant medical conditions may help. Manage stress and seek review when problems recur; a fixed 30-minute daily rule or a yearly check alone cannot guarantee prevention. Does masturbation cause blindness? No. A new eye symptom needs its own assessment. Sudden visual loss or a sudden visual change after an ED medicine needs immediate medical care, rather than being blamed on masturbation. What causes ED? Blood-vessel, nerve, hormone, medication and psychological factors can contribute together. Diabetes, cardiovascular risks, neurological illness, stress or depression are among the possibilities. An appointment helps distinguish contributors rather than diagnosing from one symptom. Can pornography cause ED? Research has differing findings and important limitations. Frequency alone has not established a causal explanation for every case, and observational associations cannot prove cause. Discuss distress, loss of control or changes in partnered arousal respectfully, while assessing other medical and psychological factors. Can I take sildenafil with heart medicines? Some combinations are dangerous. PDE5 inhibitors must not be combined with nitrates, poppers, nicorandil or riociguat. Have the complete medicine list and cardiovascular history checked; do not stop a necessary heart medicine to take an ED drug. What if tablets do not work? Ask the prescriber to review correct use, the diagnosis and suitability. Depending on your preferences and health, options include counselling, a vacuum device used after training, injection or intraurethral medicine, and selected surgery. Do not simply add doses or buy unverified products. Does vascular surgery block arteries to hold an erection? No. Selected arterial reconstruction aims to restore blood supply after a specific injury or blockage. Venous ligation for ED is not routinely recommended because long-term results are poor. These are specialist decisions, not an inevitable next step. When is an erection problem an emergency? A prolonged erection around three to four hours needs immediate emergency assessment, sooner with pain or according to an earlier treatment plan; a painful erection over one hour with sickle cell disease is an emergency. Chest-pain warning signs, loss of consciousness or a serious allergic reaction need emergency services. Sudden vision or hearing changes after medicine need immediate medical help. Tell the team which ED drug you took and when, and do not take a nitrate for chest pain after it.

title: Watery semen: appearance, normal changes and when to get checked
description: Semen normally becomes thinner after ejaculation. Learn why watery appearance cannot measure fertility, what testing checks and which changes need care.
body: Semen can look thicker at one moment and more watery later. That change can be normal, and looking at it cannot tell you how many sperm it contains or whether pregnancy is possible. A persistent new pattern, other symptoms or difficulty conceiving deserves assessment rather than a home diagnosis or a product to make semen thicker. Semen normally becomes more fluid Semen is the ejaculated fluid containing sperm and secretions from reproductive glands, including the seminal vesicles and prostate. Sperm are microscopic cells, not the whole fluid. Semen often initially forms a gel and then becomes thinner through a process called liquefaction. A sample seen later may therefore look more watery than it did just after ejaculation. The WHO laboratory manual describes normal complete liquefaction within about 15–30 minutes at room temperature; delayed or incomplete liquefaction is recorded by the laboratory. This is a testing observation, not a home fertility test or an instruction to heat or chemically alter semen. Thickness, transparency and amount vary and need context. Watery appearance does not diagnose a low sperm count Sperm concentration, total sperm number, movement and shape cannot be judged reliably by eye. Thin or clearer semen does not prove infertility, and thick white semen does not guarantee healthy sperm, conception or absence of infection. A persistent appearance change can be discussed without assuming it is either dangerous or meaningless. A low sperm concentration is called oligozoospermia. Current WHO-based reference data use a lower fifth percentile of about 16 million sperm per millilitre, rather than treating an older 15-million figure as a rigid fertility boundary. These reference values describe a population, not a pass-or-fail test: results below them do not automatically prevent conception, and results above them do not guarantee it. If testing finds a problem, the cause needs investigation Reduced sperm production or delivery can have several explanations, including a clinically important varicocele, some reproductive-tract infections, testicular injury or tumours, endocrine disorders and obstruction. Hypothalamic, pituitary and testicular signals have different roles. Retrograde ejaculation can alter the amount released because fluid goes back into the bladder. None of these can be identified from watery appearance alone. Immune factors, including antisperm antibodies, can matter in selected circumstances, but antibody testing is not recommended routinely in the initial infertility assessment. The clinician selects further tests from the history, examination and semen results. A new testicular lump needs prompt assessment; do not assume a visible vein or a fluid change proves the explanation or requires surgery. Frequent ejaculation is not a fertility injury A shorter interval between ejaculations can change the amount and composition of the next sample. It does not follow that masturbation makes semen unhealthy or permanently depletes sperm. There is no universal number of recovery hours after which semen becomes normal, nor a required thickness that shows the body has recovered. ASRM guidance notes that frequent ejaculation does not necessarily reduce fertility and advises against routinely restricting intercourse when trying to conceive. Prolonged abstinence is not a treatment for watery semen. Instructions before a laboratory sample serve a different purpose: follow that laboratory’s collection and abstinence instructions so the result can be interpreted properly. Zinc is a nutrient, not an appearance-based treatment Zinc is needed for normal body function, but watery semen does not diagnose zinc deficiency or antisperm antibodies. A balanced diet and treatment of a demonstrated deficiency are different from taking a fertility supplement. Claims that zinc sulphate reliably counters antibodies or restores fertility are not a reason to self-treat. In a large trial of couples seeking infertility treatment, a folic-acid-and-zinc combination did not significantly improve semen quality or live-birth rates. That does not establish that food zinc or treatment of a deficiency is useless, but it limits a general supplement promise. Excess zinc can cause stomach symptoms and copper deficiency and can interact with medicines, including some antibiotics. Discuss the actual product before taking it. Colour changes need context as well as consistency Pink, red or brown semen can contain blood. It often has a non-serious explanation, including inflammation, infection or a recent procedure, but should be checked rather than automatically attributed to the prostate or dismissed because it may resolve. Describe any pain, urinary changes, procedures or medicines to the clinician. Yellow or greenish semen does not by itself prove urine contamination, excess white blood cells or prostatitis. White cells require laboratory identification and can reflect inflammation without a bacterial infection. New persistent colour change, unpleasant smell, pain or discharge should be assessed. Fluid appearing outside ejaculation may be urethral discharge and needs its own assessment, including STI testing when appropriate. What a semen analysis can and cannot tell you A laboratory can assess volume, liquefaction and viscosity, and sometimes acidity, alongside sperm concentration and total number, movement and shape. These answer different questions. The report may also distinguish white blood cells from immature germ cells; simply seeing round cells does not identify an infection. Results vary between samples. An abnormal result often needs repeating, with timing set by the service and circumstances; NHS patient guidance commonly describes a repeat around three months, while specialist pathways can differ. Tell the team about fever or illness, medicines, supplements and any collection problem. A normal result is not a complete fertility guarantee, and a single low measurement is not a verdict of permanent infertility. When to arrange a routine assessment Arrange an appointment for a persistent new change in ejaculated fluid, blood in semen, painful ejaculation, unexplained discharge or a concern that continues. You do not have to wait until conception has been attempted to discuss symptoms. A clinician can review timing, sexual and medical history and perform an examination before deciding which tests are useful. If pregnancy is the concern, assessment should consider both partners. Many guidelines use a year of regular unprotected intercourse as a starting point, with earlier evaluation for an older egg-producing partner or a known reproductive problem; exact age and referral rules vary locally. An abnormal semen result, testicular problem or other concerning history can justify earlier help rather than waiting for a fixed deadline. Treatment follows a diagnosis, not a thickness target Normal variation or liquefaction does not need a medicine to thicken semen. Confirmed infections may need clinician-selected antibiotics and partner care when relevant. Hormonal treatment is appropriate only for particular diagnoses; testosterone or anabolic steroids can suppress sperm production and should not be used as fertility boosters. Do not stop a prescribed medicine abruptly because the fluid looks different. A clinical varicocele with abnormal semen findings may be considered for treatment in selected infertility care, but not every vein or scan finding needs repair and surgery does not guarantee a pregnancy. If a significant sperm problem is confirmed, options may include specialist treatment or assisted reproduction according to both partners’ circumstances. A lower count does not automatically mean natural conception is impossible. Support health without promises or blame Stopping smoking, reducing heavy alcohol use, regular manageable activity and support for a healthy weight can help general health and may improve some semen measures. They cannot guarantee a thicker sample or a baby, and a fertility difficulty is not proof that someone caused it through lifestyle. Discuss workplace chemical exposure and recreational or performance-enhancing drugs honestly with the team. Avoid repeated visual checking, forced abstinence, unprescribed hormones and products promising stronger or thicker semen. Keep a brief record of when the change occurs and associated symptoms, and follow up actual test results. Contraception and STI prevention are still needed when relevant: watery or clear fluid is not a contraceptive sign. Symptoms that take priority over fertility testing Seek urgent same-day advice for fever or significant illness with urinary, pelvic or scrotal symptoms, or suspected blood in urine even if it happened once, is only a little or you are unsure. A new testicular lump, swelling or worrying persistent discomfort also needs prompt assessment. Blood only in semen usually starts with a routine clinical appointment, unless other warning symptoms change the urgency. Use immediate emergency care for sudden severe testicular pain; testicular pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain; pain persisting at rest; complete inability to urinate; or severe abdominal pain, confusion, severe breathing difficulty, fainting or loss of consciousness with serious illness. Do not wait for a semen sample, a change in colour or an app assessment. Do not drive yourself when emergency help is needed. Semen normally liquefies; watery appearance alone does not measure sperm count or fertility. Persistent changes and other symptoms deserve assessment, while semen results need clinical context and sometimes repetition. Do not use zinc, hormones, antibiotics or prolonged abstinence as a home thickness treatment. Urgent urinary or testicular warning symptoms take priority over fertility appointments and tracking. What causes watery semen? Normal liquefaction and sample-to-sample variation can change appearance. A low count or other reproductive problem is one possibility if testing finds it, but cannot be diagnosed by looking at the fluid. A persistent new change or fertility concern can be assessed. Does yellow semen mean infection? Not by colour alone. Persistent yellow or greenish change, pain, unusual smell, discharge or urinary symptoms needs assessment. White blood cells and organisms require appropriate testing; do not choose an antibiotic from the colour. What does pink or brown semen mean? It may contain blood, which often has a non-serious cause but should be checked. Do not assume the exact source from its colour. Suspected blood in urine needs urgent same-day advice even once or in a small amount, unlike an otherwise uncomplicated semen-blood appointment. Can frequent masturbation make semen watery? A short interval can change the next sample’s amount and composition, but does not prove damage or infertility. No fixed recovery-hour rule applies, and prolonged abstinence is not a fertility treatment. Follow separate laboratory instructions if providing a sample. Can someone with watery semen cause a pregnancy? Yes, appearance does not establish sperm count or make pregnancy impossible. Use contraception when pregnancy is not wanted. A semen analysis can assess sperm measures, but cannot guarantee or exclude conception by itself. Should I take zinc or have an antibody test? Not simply because semen looks thin. Deficiency and selected immune problems need their own assessment; routine antisperm antibody testing is not part of the initial infertility work-up. Supplements have uncertain fertility benefits and can cause harm or interactions. Will I need antibiotics, hormones or surgery? Only an identified problem and the whole clinical assessment can guide treatment. Normal liquefaction needs none of these. Do not self-prescribe, use testosterone for fertility or assume every varicocele needs an operation. When should I seek urgent or emergency help? Ask for same-day help for fever with urinary, pelvic or scrotal symptoms or suspected blood in urine. Sudden severe testicular pain, pain with vomiting or abdominal pain or persisting at rest, complete inability to urinate, severe abdominal pain, or serious illness with confusion, breathing difficulty, fainting or loss of consciousness needs immediate emergency care. Do not wait for fertility testing.

title: Hypogonadism: ovarian and testicular hormone deficiency
description: Understand primary and central hypogonadism, symptoms, targeted tests, hormone treatment and fertility care for ovarian or testicular hormone deficiency.
body: Hypogonadism means that the ovaries or testes are not producing enough sex hormones for a person’s age and circumstances. The problem may lie in these glands or in the brain signals controlling them. It can affect puberty, periods, sexual function, bones and fertility, but symptoms alone cannot establish the diagnosis. Treatment depends on the cause, other health conditions and whether pregnancy is wanted. Primary and central hypogonadism are different In primary hypogonadism, the ovaries or testes cannot respond adequately to signals from the pituitary gland. Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinising hormone (LH) are often raised as the brain tries to stimulate them. In central, or secondary, hypogonadism, the hypothalamus or pituitary does not provide an appropriate signal, so FSH and LH may be low or inappropriately normal despite low sex hormones. Sex hormones contribute to breast and genital development, body hair, bone and muscle health, periods and sperm production. Interpretation differs in childhood, puberty, reproductive life, pregnancy, breastfeeding and menopause. A normal age-related change or one low testosterone result is not automatically a disease or a reason to prescribe hormones. Premature ovarian insufficiency (POI), occurring before age 40, requires assessment distinct from usual menopause. Causes include gland damage and disrupted brain signals Primary causes include genetic conditions such as Turner or Klinefelter syndrome, undescended testes, damage after mumps orchitis, gonadal surgery, radiation or some cancer treatments, and autoimmune disease. Iron overload can affect the glands or their controlling system. Associated autoimmune conditions, including adrenal disease, may guide selected investigations; they do not mean every person has all these disorders. Kidney or liver illness can also disturb reproductive hormones through several mechanisms. Central causes include congenital conditions such as Kallmann syndrome, pituitary tumours or other pituitary disease, head injury, brain surgery or radiation, and selected infiltrative, inflammatory or infectious diseases, including sarcoidosis, histiocytosis, tuberculosis or HIV-related illness. Obesity, inadequate energy intake, rapid weight loss, severe illness, opioids, glucocorticoids or anabolic steroid use can suppress signalling. Several factors may coexist; do not stop a prescribed medicine abruptly to test a theory. Symptoms depend on age and which hormones are low In children or teenagers, puberty may start late, progress slowly or stop; breast, genital or testicular development may be affected. With ovarian hormone deficiency, periods may become irregular or stop, hot flushes may occur and sexual desire can change. Milk-like breast discharge outside expected pregnancy or breastfeeding can suggest raised prolactin and deserves assessment; it is not a universal sign of ovarian failure. With testicular hormone deficiency, possible features include reduced desire, erectile difficulty, fewer spontaneous erections, reduced body hair or muscle, breast enlargement, hot flushes, low bone density or fertility problems. Fatigue and concentration difficulties are nonspecific and have many other causes. These symptoms cannot show whether the problem is primary or central, and genital size alone is not a diagnosis. Tests must fit the clinical situation A clinician reviews growth and puberty, menstrual or sexual symptoms, medicines, illnesses, nutrition and fertility plans, and offers an appropriate, consented examination. For suspected adult male testosterone deficiency, diagnosis usually requires relevant symptoms and consistently low, accurate early-morning fasting testosterone measurements on two separate occasions. Illness, sleep patterns and medicines can affect results; repeat testing and interpretation may be needed. For absent periods or suspected ovarian insufficiency, assessment starts by excluding pregnancy when possible and considering breastfeeding, menopause, hormonal contraception and other causes. FSH, LH and estradiol help distinguish ovarian from central patterns. Timing and repeat tests depend on the question: POI assessment does not require FSH on a particular cycle day. Contraceptive hormones can obscure the picture; arrange a testing plan rather than stopping them yourself. Additional blood tests and scans are selective Depending on the findings, tests may include prolactin, thyroid function, iron studies or other pituitary hormones. Suspected pituitary disease also requires attention to cortisol and other potentially important deficiencies. Genetic or autoimmune testing, a bone-density assessment or semen analysis may be appropriate for particular patients. There is no single mandatory panel for everyone, and a semen test assesses a different question from a testosterone result. Pituitary MRI is considered for relevant hormone patterns, raised prolactin, headaches, visual problems or other pituitary concerns; CT may be used when appropriate. Pelvic ultrasound can investigate anatomy or another cause of menstrual symptoms, but it does not by itself diagnose every hormonal disorder. Finding ovarian cysts, for example, does not alone establish polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), formerly called polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Ovarian hormone treatment protects more than periods When indicated, estrogen replacement can help symptoms and protect health affected by deficiency. If the uterus is present, a suitable progestogen is normally added to protect the uterine lining; after hysterectomy the plan can differ, with exceptions requiring specialist advice. Formulation, route, bleeding pattern and personal risks matter. In POI, replacement is generally recommended until the usual menopause age unless contraindicated, followed by an individual review. It is not automatically lifelong and is not contraception. Low sexual desire needs a broader assessment of discomfort, relationships, mood, medicines and health. Testosterone is not an automatic prescription for a low desire score or hormone result; selected patients with a diagnosed distressing desire disorder may discuss specialist, usually transdermal treatment and its uncertain long-term safety. Puberty induction and treatment of central ovarian deficiency require individual specialist plans, rather than an adult regimen applied to every child or patient. Testosterone treatment needs confirmation and monitoring Testosterone replacement may be appropriate for confirmed testicular or central testosterone deficiency when benefits outweigh risks. Available products can include gels, patches, injections, implants or other regulated formulations, depending on country and indication. A buccal product is a specific gum-applied system, not an ordinary dissolving lozenge. Products are not interchangeable, and external testosterone is unsuitable when current fertility is the goal because it can suppress sperm production. Before and during treatment, clinicians assess blood count and haematocrit, blood pressure, relevant prostate risks, symptoms and other health conditions. Testosterone can raise blood pressure and red-cell concentration; clotting, fluid retention, sleep-apnoea and other risks require individual review. FDA removed the cardiovascular-outcomes boxed warning in 2025 while adding class-wide blood-pressure warnings; this does not mean treatment is risk-free or recommended simply for ageing. Gel users must follow product instructions to prevent transfer to children or other people. Fertility treatment follows a different pathway Tell the team about pregnancy goals before starting hormone treatment. In selected central disorders, carefully monitored gonadotropin injections, such as hCG and FSH, or pulsatile GnRH can support sperm production or ovulation. These are specialist treatments with different indications; FSH is not an ordinary tablet prescribed for every irregular cycle, and GnRH does not treat every kind of gonadal failure. Ovulation treatment needs monitoring for excessive ovarian response and multiple pregnancy. POI can involve intermittent ovarian activity, so it does not always mean pregnancy is impossible, but no treatment reliably restores natural conception for everyone. Fertility counselling may include donor eggs or other appropriate options. Hormone replacement alone is not a fertility treatment or reliable contraception.
