Examination and diagnosis The clinician asks about puberty, periods, pain, tampon use, urinary or bowel symptoms, relevant surgery and known kidney or reproductive findings. Tell them about possible pregnancy when relevant. An external examination and, where needed, an internal examination help distinguish the level of a blockage and identify the cervix or cervices. Examination should be explained, consented and appropriate to age and comfort. Discuss privacy, a chaperone or support person, and any need to pause or stop. A specialist may arrange examination under anesthesia when needed rather than forcing a painful office examination. History, examination and imaging are interpreted together; a home check or one symptom is not a diagnosis. Ultrasound, selected MRI and associated anatomy Pelvic ultrasound is usually the first imaging test for cyclical pain with absent periods or persistent menstrual pain. An abdominal scan is often used first in adolescents. Expert three-dimensional ultrasound may clarify anatomy; MRI is useful when findings are uncertain or a transverse or more complex obstruction is suspected, including planning around the septum's height and thickness. Assessment may map the uterus, cervix and both vaginal channels, retained blood and nearby structures. Kidney imaging is particularly important with a one-sided obstructed reproductive anomaly or a known kidney difference. The necessary tests depend on the findings; neither every septum nor every patient needs the same set of scans. Imaging before puberty can be harder to interpret. When treatment is needed An asymptomatic, non-obstructing septum may be observed after assessment. Treatment is considered for blocked menstrual flow, troublesome tampon use or penetration, or a potential birth obstruction. Decisions should reflect symptoms, anatomy, personal goals and any associated condition; infertility or pregnancy problems should not automatically be attributed to the vaginal septum alone. A stable outflow obstruction often needs carefully planned specialist treatment rather than immediate surgery without adequate mapping. Complete inability to urinate, severe pain or suspected infection requires urgent assessment and may accelerate treatment. Clinician-prescribed menstrual suppression can sometimes support a planned interval before surgery. Simple puncture and drainage is not a substitute for definitive specialist care. Surgery and recovery are individualized Surgery removes the partition when appropriate. A longitudinal septum and a low thin transverse septum are not the same operation as a high thick or complex transverse septum. Reconstructive work, a graft or a stent may be needed in selected cases. The surgeon must protect nearby bladder, bowel, urethra and cervix; ask about experience, alternatives, anesthesia and procedure-specific risks. Recovery and return to school, work, exercise, tampons and sexual activity vary. Follow the written plan; insert nothing until cleared, apart from specifically prescribed postoperative care. A transverse repair may require supervised dilation or a stent to prevent scar narrowing, and the patient needs preparation and support. Do not start a dilator regimen yourself. Attend follow-up even if the first period improves. Outlook, sexual comfort and future pregnancy Restoring menstrual drainage can relieve symptoms, but no operation guarantees painless sex, a particular blood flow or fertility. Scar narrowing or renewed obstruction can require further treatment, and endometriosis or another cause of pain may persist. A small older observational study documented varied long-term outcomes; its figures are not personal predictions. Emotional support is part of care, and penetration is always a choice. Before trying for pregnancy, discuss any uterine or cervical anomaly, previous repair and ongoing symptoms. Pregnancy and birth planning depend on the complete anatomy, not the septum label alone; neither infertility nor a caesarean birth is inevitable. A septum can interfere with labour, so tell the maternity team. Any vaginal bleeding in pregnancy needs prompt maternity or early-pregnancy advice rather than assuming the partition caused it. When to seek urgent help Seek immediate medical care if you cannot pass urine. Obtain urgent same-day advice for pelvic pain with fever, unusual or foul-smelling discharge, vomiting, difficulty urinating or possible pregnancy, including after surgery. Follow any stricter postoperative instructions. Recurrent pain or poor menstrual drainage also needs review rather than being accepted as normal. Get emergency assessment for severe or worsening abdominal or pelvic pain, pain when moving or touching the area, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty, heavy vaginal bleeding or new confusion. During pregnancy, heavy bleeding alone or bleeding with severe pain, shoulder pain or faintness also needs emergency care. Do not drive yourself to emergency care; ask someone to drive you or call an ambulance. A congenital vaginal partition can be longitudinal or transverse; location, thickness and obstruction matter. Normal visible periods do not exclude a blocked channel on the other side. Tampon leakage or penetration pain needs assessment and does not diagnose a septum by itself. Some non-obstructing septa need no operation; complex repairs require specialist planning and follow-up. Unable to urinate or emergency pain and associated warning signs need immediate care; do not drive yourself. What does a longitudinal vaginal septum look like? It is a lengthwise internal tissue partition creating two side-by-side vaginal channels, sometimes of unequal size. It may occur alone or alongside uterine or cervical differences. External appearance does not reliably show the complete anatomy. Can tampon leakage mean I have a septum? It can happen if blood leaves through a second channel, but leakage has other causes. Repeated insertion or removal difficulty, pain or unusual flow deserves clinician assessment. Do not use repeated or forced tampon insertion as a diagnostic test. Can I have a transverse septum and still menstruate? Yes, if it has an opening. Flow may drain slowly or periods may last longer; some people have few symptoms. Complete obstruction can cause retained blood and cyclical pain without visible periods. Bleeding from an open side also does not exclude an obstructed half-vagina. How is a vaginal septum diagnosed? A clinician combines the history, a consented age-appropriate examination and imaging. Ultrasound often comes first; selected MRI helps clarify uncertain or complex anatomy and surgical planning. Associated uterine, cervical or kidney findings may need assessment. Does every vaginal septum need surgery? No. A symptom-free, non-obstructing septum may be monitored. Blocked drainage or troublesome symptoms may justify removal. The timing and operation depend on type, height, thickness and associated anatomy; not every repair is a simple procedure with quick recovery. Will removal cure pain and infertility? It may improve drainage and reduce mechanical discomfort, but does not guarantee pain relief or fertility. Scar narrowing, endometriosis or associated uterine or cervical conditions may affect symptoms or reproduction. Follow-up and individual pregnancy planning remain important. Can I use dilators or resume sex after surgery? Only follow the specific postoperative plan and clearance. Some transverse repairs need supervised dilation or a stent; this is not a universal regimen. Avoid unapproved vaginal insertion and stop painful penetration. Ask the team about healing, warning signs and support. Which symptoms need immediate care? Inability to pass urine needs immediate medical care. Seek emergency assessment for severe or worsening pelvic pain, pain with movement or touch, or pain with faintness, dizziness, loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty, heavy bleeding or new confusion. Pregnancy bleeding needs prompt maternity advice; heavy bleeding or bleeding with severe pain, shoulder pain or faintness is an emergency. Do not drive yourself; ask someone to drive or call an ambulance.

title: Bone grafting: choices, surgery and recovery
description: Understand why bone grafts are used, own-bone and donor options, surgical risks, preparation, healing and symptoms that need prompt medical help.
body: A bone graft supports repair when bone is missing or needs help joining. It may be one part of fracture repair, fusion or reconstruction, rather than a separate operation. Knowing why it is proposed, which material will be used and what recovery involves helps you make an informed decision with the surgical team. What a bone graft does Bone tissue or a suitable substitute is placed in or around an area that needs to heal. It can provide a framework for new bone; some materials also supply bone-forming cells or growth signals. The surrounding blood supply and a stable repair matter too. Graft material alone does not reliably hold an unstable fracture in position. This is different from a bone-marrow or blood stem-cell transplant. Here the aim is structural bone healing. Grafts may be used in the limbs, pelvis, spine or other sites. Dental grafting has its own procedure and aftercare, so instructions for an arm or leg should not be applied to the mouth. Why grafting may be recommended Examples include a complicated fracture with bone loss, a fracture that has failed to unite, a planned fusion joining bones, or reconstruction after damaged bone is removed. A graft may also help restore bone around a replacement joint or another implant. Infection, tumour treatment or loss of blood supply can change the reconstruction plan. Not every fracture, painful joint or delayed recovery needs a graft. The team considers the underlying problem, imaging, stability, infection and general health, and discusses alternatives. In selected nonunions, a brace or bone stimulator may be appropriate; other situations need fixation, grafting or a combination. Ask what the graft is expected to add in your case. Using your own bone: autograft An autograft comes from your body. Bone removed during the main operation can sometimes be reused, avoiding a separate harvest incision. Otherwise a small amount may be taken from a suitable donor site, often the rim of the pelvis; the site and quantity depend on the procedure. Your own bone can provide cells, growth signals and a scaffold. However, harvesting may cause pain, bleeding, infection or injury at a second site, and the available amount is limited. Ask whether you will have one wound or two, how both will be cared for and whether donor-site discomfort will affect walking or everyday activities. Donor bone and substitute materials An allograft comes from another person, commonly a deceased donor, and is supplied through a tissue service. Conventional processed donor bone mainly acts as a scaffold and avoids harvesting your own bone. Materials vary: some products contain living cells, so it is inaccurate to say that every allograft is nonliving or has identical properties. Screening and processing reduce infection risks but cannot make transmission impossible. Synthetic substitutes, demineralized bone and other products may be used alone or in combinations for selected purposes. A product advertised as containing stem cells is not automatically better or proven for every use. Discuss the actual material, evidence, alternatives and specific risks; no single graft is best for everyone. Risks and the chance of healing Possible problems include bleeding, infection, anaesthetic complications, blood clots, nerve injury, stiffness and persistent pain. Donor-site problems add to the risks when your bone is harvested. The graft may not incorporate or the bones may still fail to unite, sometimes requiring further treatment. A low rejection risk does not mean a guarantee of healing. The operation, graft type, blood supply and stability influence the outcome. Smoking, diabetes, infection and poor nutrition can make healing harder. Ask which risks apply to you, how they will be reduced and what the next options would be if healing stalls. There is no useful universal success percentage for all bone-grafting procedures. Preparing for the operation Give the team a complete list of prescriptions, nonprescription medicines, supplements and herbal products. Mention allergies, earlier anaesthetic problems, possible pregnancy, diabetes, recent fever or infection, and smoking or nicotine use. Imaging and other tests are selected for the procedure. Do not stop blood thinners or other prescribed medicines on your own. Follow your own fasting and medicine instructions rather than a blanket midnight rule. Ask about the anaesthetic plan, expected hospital stay and help after discharge. Arrange transport, an adult to support you after general anaesthesia, and practical help with children, stairs or mobility restrictions. The team should explain any crutches, brace or equipment before you need them. What happens during surgery Anaesthesia is chosen for the operation and your health; general anaesthesia is common for major grafting. The surgeon exposes the area needing repair, prepares it and places the selected graft. If your own bone is needed, it may be collected locally or through another incision. The exact sequence depends on the underlying problem. Plates, screws, rods, pins or an external frame may provide stability when required. Other repairs can take place during the same operation. The wounds are closed, and a dressing, splint, brace or cast may be used. An educational model cannot show every technique or tell you which fixation or graft is right for you. Recovery has more than one timetable Wound healing, feeling comfortable and the bone becoming solid are different milestones. Bone incorporation or union often takes months and may take longer in complex reconstruction. Returning home or having stitches removed does not mean the graft can take full load. A fixed two-week, three-month or one-year promise is unreliable without knowing the operation. Follow the written limits on weight bearing, lifting, movement, work, driving and sport. Physiotherapy helps rebuild function when appropriate; moving other joints or exercising unaffected muscles must still fit the surgical plan. Follow-up examination and imaging help guide progression. Do not test the graft by loading it early because pain has improved. Wound care, comfort and clot prevention Keep dressings and any cast protected as instructed, and ask when showering is safe. Use the agreed pain-relief plan. Check before adding ibuprofen, naproxen or other anti-inflammatory medicines, because their suitability depends on the operation and your health. If cooling or elevation is advised, protect the skin and follow site-specific instructions. Ice and elevation are not a substitute for blood-clot prevention. Depending on your risk, the plan may include prescribed anticoagulants, compression and permitted movement. Take any prescribed course for its intended duration and ask before changing it. Avoid prolonged immobility when safe movement is allowed, but do not break weight-bearing restrictions to follow generic walking advice. Supporting healing without promises A varied diet with adequate energy, protein, calcium and vitamins supports recovery. Tell the team about poor appetite, weight loss or difficulty getting enough food. Treat identified deficiencies with advice; extra-large supplement doses have not been shown to make an otherwise well-nourished person's fracture heal faster. Stopping smoking is important for bone and wound healing. Ask for a supported quit plan as early as possible and disclose vaping or other nicotine use. Surgical services differ in their advice about nicotine replacement, so discuss suitable cessation treatment with the surgeon and prescribing clinician rather than abandoning prescribed support unaided. Good preparation improves the conditions for healing but cannot guarantee success. Symptoms that should not wait Contact the surgical team promptly for increasing wound redness, heat or swelling, pus or substantial drainage, fever or chills, or pain that is worsening rather than settling. New loss of feeling or weakness needs urgent assessment. New one-sided calf or leg pain or swelling may signal a clot and also needs urgent medical help; do not assume it is ordinary postoperative soreness. Coughing blood also needs urgent medical assessment. Seek emergency care for sudden severe limb pain, especially with numbness, weakness or a very tight cast. New breathlessness, chest pain or collapse can signal a serious complication and require emergency help. Do not drive yourself with emergency symptoms or wait for the next review. Keep your discharge contact details and follow-up appointments available. A graft supports bone repair; blood supply and stability also matter. Own bone, donor bone and substitutes have different benefits and limitations. Preparation, medicines, loading and rehabilitation need an individual surgical plan. Bone healing can take months; less pain does not prove the graft is ready for full load. Act promptly on wound, nerve or clot warning signs and seek emergency care for severe sudden symptoms. What are the risks of a bone graft? Risks include infection, bleeding, clots, nerve injury, anaesthetic problems and failure to heal. Harvesting your own bone adds donor-site risks. The procedure and your health determine the balance; ask for an individual explanation. How can I help recovery? Follow loading, wound, medicine and rehabilitation instructions, attend reviews, eat adequately and seek help to stop smoking. Cooling or elevation may relieve symptoms if advised, but they do not replace clot prevention or assessment of worsening symptoms. How long does healing take? It depends on the defect, procedure, graft and health of the surrounding bone. Skin recovery and bone union have different timelines; union often takes months. The team uses examination and imaging to decide when activity can increase. Does smoking affect a bone graft? Yes. Smoking increases the chance of poor bone and wound healing. Discuss a quit plan, vaping and nicotine products with the surgical team; do not stop prescribed cessation treatment without advice. Is donor bone always free of living cells or infection risk? No. Conventional processed grafts differ from products that retain living cells. Screening and processing reduce risks, but infection transmission is not impossible. Ask which product is planned and what alternatives exist. Will bone have to be taken from my hip? Not always. Local bone may be reused, a different harvest site selected, or donor or substitute material used. The amount needed and the operation determine the options. Ask about any additional wound and donor-site pain. Is this the same as a bone-marrow transplant? No. Bone grafting aims to repair structural bone. Bone-marrow or blood stem-cell transplantation is a different treatment. Confirm the name and purpose of your planned procedure. When do I need urgent help? Worsening wound symptoms, fever, new numbness or weakness, one-sided leg swelling or coughing blood need prompt medical assessment. Sudden severe limb pain, breathlessness, chest pain or collapse needs emergency care.

title: Bone marrow oedema: understanding the finding, its causes and treatment
description: What marrow oedema on an MRI means, how doctors investigate it in adults and children, and why treatment and recovery depend on the cause.
body: Reading “bone marrow oedema” on a scan report can sound alarming. It describes an abnormal signal within a bone, often related to injury or inflammation, rather than a complete diagnosis. The useful next question is what caused it and whether the bone needs protection or specific treatment. In a child with a painful limb or limp, symptoms and examination remain important even after a scan. What the words mean Marrow is tissue inside bones that contains fat and blood-forming cells. Oedema means swelling associated with fluid, but the MRI term is broader than a pocket of water that needs draining. The signal can reflect inflammation, bleeding or microscopic injury, depending on the condition. A radiologist interprets its location and pattern alongside the rest of the images. A marrow lesion is an area of change; the word does not by itself mean cancer, a fracture or permanent damage. Some findings accompany pain, while others are incidental. The size of a bright area alone cannot tell you how strong the bone is, what caused the pain or whether an operation is needed. Symptoms that deserve prompt assessment Pain, tenderness, swelling, reduced movement or difficulty using a limb may lead to imaging. In a child, sudden inability to walk or bear weight needs urgent assessment. Fever with bone or joint pain, a hot swollen joint, severe pain or a child who appears unwell also needs urgent care. A serious infection can occur without fever; do not wait for every sign to appear. Persistent or recurrent pain, pain waking a child at night, an unexplained lump, weight loss or unusual tiredness should be assessed promptly. These signs have several possible causes and do not diagnose cancer. Do not label them growing pains or wait weeks for an MRI appointment if the child is deteriorating. If your child is severely unwell, use emergency care. Injury and joint disease are possible causes A blow or joint injury can bruise the bone beneath its surface. Repeated loading, such as a rapid increase in running or jumping, can cause a stress reaction and sometimes a stress fracture. Weakened bone can also be injured during ordinary activity. The history, examination and other imaging features help distinguish these situations; oedema alone does not prove a fracture. Osteoarthritis, inflammatory arthritis and inflammation near tendon or ligament attachments can also produce marrow changes. A painful joint may have several abnormalities, so the oedema is not always the main problem. Continuing to exercise through focal bone pain can worsen a stress injury; arrange assessment instead of using pain relief to push through. Other causes need different treatment Bone or joint infection, impaired blood supply such as osteonecrosis, and some tumours can be associated with marrow abnormalities. Cancer treatment, including radiotherapy, may also alter marrow signals. Tell the clinician about previous illnesses, treatment and medicines, but do not assume a new finding is harmless treatment change or stop prescribed medicines yourself. Bone marrow oedema syndrome is a term used for a different, often temporary painful condition after other causes have been considered. It is not a label for every report mentioning oedema. Infection, fracture, inflammatory disease and blood-supply problems need their own assessment; apparent similarity on one image does not mean the same recovery or treatment. How the cause is investigated The clinician asks where and when pain started, about injuries or training changes, fever, other joints, medical conditions and medicines. Examination assesses tenderness, movement and limb use. In children, pain can be referred from a nearby joint, and age changes the likely causes. Bring the complete report and available images, rather than only one phrase or screenshot. MRI is particularly useful for seeing marrow and surrounding structures. A normal early X-ray does not exclude all stress injuries or bone infection, but X-rays can reveal fractures, joint changes or other important abnormalities. CT can clarify selected bone damage or fracture details. These tests are complementary; it is inaccurate to say X-rays and CT have no role. Ultrasound, blood tests and biopsy Ultrasound is useful for joint fluid and soft tissues, but it generally cannot look through bone to assess the marrow inside it. Its usefulness around infant cartilage does not make it the routine test for marrow oedema. MRI choice, contrast or sedation depends on the clinical question and the child; tell the team about implants, other conditions and any possible pregnancy. Blood tests may help investigate infection, inflammation or another suspected cause, but no single normal result rules everything out. A biopsy is reserved for a specific unresolved concern, for example distinguishing a tumour from infection. Most oedema findings do not automatically require tissue sampling. Ask what question each proposed test would answer and how the result could change care. Treatment starts with the underlying problem An injury may need reduced loading, a support or crutches and a staged return to activity. Physiotherapy can help restore movement and strength when it is appropriate for the diagnosis. Do not assume either complete bed rest or unrestricted exercise is right for everyone; ask how much walking, play and sport are safe for the particular bone. Infection may need prompt antibiotics and sometimes drainage or surgery. Inflammatory disease, a tumour or osteonecrosis needs condition-specific specialist care. Rest and painkillers are not substitutes. If the expected improvement does not occur, the team may need to reconsider the diagnosis rather than repeatedly prescribing the same rehabilitation plan. Use pain medicines with a clear plan Paracetamol or an anti-inflammatory such as ibuprofen may help some people, but they do not establish the cause or repair every lesion. Discuss other medicines, kidney or stomach problems, bleeding risks and pregnancy or breastfeeding before choosing an NSAID. Do not combine different NSAIDs or take someone else’s prescription. For a child, use an age-appropriate product and the advised dose for their weight and product strength, measured with the supplied device. Ask a pharmacist or clinician if uncertain; avoid ibuprofen when dehydrated and check relevant health restrictions. Do not give aspirin to a child unless specifically prescribed. Increasing pain or a need for more medicine should prompt reassessment. When an operation may be considered Surgery is not routine treatment for the words “marrow oedema”. A fracture needing stabilisation, a joint infection, a tumour or selected osteonecrosis may require a procedure for that diagnosis. In some early osteonecrosis cases, core decompression creates channels in bone to reduce pressure and support its blood supply. It is not simply draining a fluid-filled cavity. Bone grafts or a person’s own marrow cells may be used with selected procedures, but they do not guarantee normal marrow regeneration or a pain-free result. Ask about the exact diagnosis, stage, alternatives, evidence, complications and rehabilitation. Do not treat a promise of stem-cell repair as proof that the procedure is appropriate for an adult or child. Follow recovery rather than a fixed deadline Recovery varies with the cause, site and severity. Some injury-related changes settle over weeks or months; other conditions need longer treatment. Pain can improve before the MRI signal disappears. Repeat MRI is not automatically needed just to prove that an uncomplicated bone bruise has vanished, but persistent symptoms or a different diagnosis may justify further imaging. Agree on a review date, safe loading and return-to-school or sport advice, and the changes that should bring review forward. Ask: what is the working diagnosis, what remains uncertain, and what would change the plan? Keep a record of symptoms, activity and medicines. Reassurance should come from a clinical explanation and follow-up, not a promise that every marrow finding disappears with rest. Marrow oedema is an imaging finding; its cause determines what it means. MRI, examination and selected other tests work together; ultrasound is not a routine marrow test. A child unable to bear weight or with severe pain or illness needs urgent assessment. Loading, medicines and rehabilitation need an individual plan; surgery is for selected diagnoses. Recovery and repeat imaging depend on symptoms and the underlying condition. What is bone marrow oedema? It is a marrow signal change on MRI that can accompany injury, inflammation and other conditions. It is not a complete diagnosis, a simple drainable water pocket or automatic evidence of cancer. How is it diagnosed in children? A clinician combines the symptoms and examination with imaging when needed. MRI shows marrow changes; X-rays, ultrasound for joint fluid and selected blood tests answer other questions. Not every limp needs MRI, and urgent symptoms should not wait for a routine scan. Who can develop it? People with injury or repeated loading, arthritis, infection or other bone conditions may develop it. Some changes occur without symptoms. Age, history and the complete imaging pattern matter more than a single risk-factor list. What treatment is needed? The cause guides treatment: protected loading and rehabilitation for some injuries, specific medicines for infection or inflammatory disease, and selected procedures for other diagnoses. Pain relief alone does not treat every cause. Does it mean cancer? No. Many causes are not cancer, but the phrase alone cannot exclude cancer either. The clinician and radiologist assess the whole picture and arrange further tests if a particular concern remains. Will I need a biopsy or decompression? Not routinely. Biopsy answers a specific diagnostic question; decompression is an option for selected conditions such as early osteonecrosis. Neither follows automatically from an oedema finding. Can my child keep playing sport? Ask for advice on safe loading and activities for the diagnosis. Avoid painful impact exercise while awaiting assessment. Sudden inability to walk or bear weight, severe pain, fever with limb pain or an unwell child needs urgent care. How long does recovery take? There is no single timetable. Symptoms and MRI can improve at different speeds. Agree on a review plan and seek earlier reassessment if pain worsens, function declines or new symptoms appear.

title: Cleaning your home for COVID-19: effective routines without unsafe disinfection
description: Know what to clean, when disinfection helps, how product labels and contact time matter, and how to protect skin, electronics and laundry.
body: A home does not have to be sterile to be cared for well. Regular cleaning removes dirt and many germs; extra disinfection can be useful when someone is ill or has weakened immunity. For COVID-19, a manageable surface routine belongs alongside cleaner air and hand hygiene, rather than endless spraying of everything that enters the house. Put surface risk in perspective SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19, spreads through respiratory particles released by an infected person, including during breathing and talking. Contaminated hands and surfaces can also contribute, but surface transmission is not the main route. Cleaning a table cannot remove virus-containing particles that people are sharing in poorly ventilated air. Bring in outdoor air safely and use appropriate air filtration where feasible; follow current respiratory precautions when someone is ill. The often repeated two-to-three-day survival figure comes from an early laboratory experiment on plastic and stainless steel. Conditions, the amount of virus and transfer from a surface to a person all matter. Detecting infectious virus in an experiment does not mean a household object remains equally dangerous for three days, nor that a fixed waiting period makes every item safe. Use sensible cleaning and hygiene rather than a countdown. Which areas of the home need attention? Prioritise surfaces people touch often: door and cupboard handles, switches, taps, counters, tables, shared phones, remote controls and keyboards. Include frequently handled car controls if relevant, using the vehicle manufacturer's care advice. Clean these regularly and when dirty; clean less-touched areas as needed. A bag on a table or an outing does not automatically mean that every object needs chemical disinfection. When someone is sick, add appropriate disinfection after cleaning, especially for shared high-touch surfaces. Extra precautions can also be appropriate for a household member with weakened immunity; agree any specific needs with their care team. Keep food preparation and infant-feeding equipment hygiene suited to their particular task. A general surface disinfectant is not automatically suitable for food, toys that go in a mouth, or feeding items. Cleaning, sanitising and disinfecting are different Cleaning uses a suitable detergent or soap, water and physical wiping or scrubbing to remove dirt and many germs. Sanitising lowers germs to levels considered acceptable for a particular public-health use. Disinfecting inactivates or kills specified germs when a suitable product is used correctly. These words are not interchangeable, and none means that a home will stay free of every germ. Remove visible dirt before disinfection and follow the product's cleaning instructions. Dirt can prevent a disinfectant from working properly. SARS-CoV-2 has a lipid-containing outer envelope that cleaning agents can disrupt, as well as being physically removed during cleaning. Ordinary cleaning is useful; there is no need for antibacterial soap merely because the concern is a virus. A surface that looks clean is not proof of disinfection, but routine cleaning alone is enough in many everyday situations. Choose the product by its label, not its smell For disinfection, check that the product is authorised for the intended use where you live, the relevant organism, the surface material and the setting. In the United States, EPA's List N helps identify products expected to work against SARS-CoV-2 when their directions are followed. Match the EPA registration number, rather than relying on a familiar brand name. List inclusion is not a promise that a product suits every surface or is harmless. Some EPA emerging-virus claims are supported by reviewed evidence against viruses that are harder to inactivate. This is a regulatory route for eligible products, not permission to treat any cleaner advertised against another virus as a coronavirus disinfectant. A claim such as 'kills 99.9%' describes particular test conditions and uses; it cannot guarantee your personal protection. If the label is unclear or unreadable, ask the manufacturer or choose a suitable clearly labelled product. Use a simple, safe cleaning sequence Read the directions before starting, keep children and pets away, ventilate the area and wear the gloves or eye protection the label specifies. Clean first, then use the disinfectant only where needed and as directed. Keep the treated surface wet for its stated contact time; wiping it dry immediately may prevent it from working. Follow any rinsing requirement, particularly on food-contact surfaces, and wait until the item is ready for use as directed. A ready-to-use product does not need extra chemicals added. If dilution is required, follow the actual label exactly; stronger is not necessarily better. Do not mix cleaning products, including bleach with ammonia, acids such as vinegar, or another cleaner. Keep products in their original labelled containers with caps closed and stored securely away from children and pets. Wash your hands after removing cleaning gloves. Reduce chemical exposure as well as germs Cleaning and disinfecting products can irritate skin, eyes or airways, and some can trigger asthma. Hazards depend on ingredients, concentration, how a product is used and the exposure. It is misleading to describe every household cleaner as causing cancer, or to assume that a strong smell proves either effectiveness or safety. Bleach and ammonia are not interchangeable descriptions of one type of volatile chemical; mixing products can create dangerous fumes. Use only the amount and method allowed on the label. Do not spray a person, apply a surface disinfectant to hands or pets, inhale it deliberately, swallow it or put it into food. Do not improvise room fogging or spray clothes while wearing them. If a product causes symptoms, stop the exposure and obtain appropriate advice; someone with asthma or persistent irritation may need another person to clean or a different suitable product. Clean your hands without substituting surface products Wash with soap and running water for at least 20 seconds, including fingers, fingertips and the backs of the hands, then dry with a clean towel. Use comfortable lukewarm water rather than very hot water. Important times include after coughing or sneezing, after the toilet, before food preparation or eating, and after handling dirty laundry or cleaning materials. Gloves do not replace handwashing. If soap and water are unavailable, use a hand sanitiser containing at least 60% alcohol, cover the hands and rub until dry. Wash instead when hands are visibly dirty, greasy or contaminated with chemicals. Do not substitute surface alcohol or disinfectant for a product intended for hands. Supervise children and store sanitiser safely; it can poison someone who swallows it. Both ethanol and isopropanol products can irritate, so do not assume one is always gentler for everyone. Protect dry or cracked skin Keep necessary hand hygiene while supporting the skin barrier. Choose a soap your skin tolerates and apply a fragrance-free cream or ointment after washing, while the skin is still slightly damp. Let hand sanitiser dry before moisturising. Repeated wet work, detergents, fragrances and some glove materials can cause irritant or allergic hand dermatitis. Persistent painful cracking, bleeding or a rash deserves clinical advice rather than repeated use of a product that stings. For cleaning, choose protective gloves suitable for the product and any known allergy. Cotton liners or cotton-lined protective gloves can help with prolonged wet work, but cotton alone is not chemical protection. Keep the inside clean and dry, dry your hands before putting gloves on, and change damp liners. Avoid leaving sweaty gloves on unnecessarily. A clinician can help if eczema or a glove allergy makes routine care difficult. Follow the device maker's instructions for electronics Phones, keyboards and remote controls need material-specific care. Turn off and disconnect a device when its instructions require it; use the recommended cloth and avoid liquid entering openings. Do not spray a cleaner directly onto electronics or immerse them. A wipeable cover can make regular cleaning easier if suitable for the device. Seventy-percent isopropyl alcohol is not a universal screen-cleaning rule. For example, Apple permits certain alcohol wipes on specified hard, nonporous surfaces but has important product and material exceptions. Coatings, leather, fabric and specialist displays can need different care. Check the exact model's guidance before using alcohol or a disinfectant, and do not assume that a product safe for a kitchen counter is safe for a touchscreen. Laundry and soft furnishings need ordinary care Wash clothes, towels, bedding and washable cloth toys with detergent at the temperature recommended for the item, and dry them fully. Use the warmest appropriate setting where the care instructions allow it, rather than the hottest setting regardless of material. CDC says a sick person's dirty laundry can be washed with other people's items. Wash hands after handling it and clean the laundry basket as appropriate. For rugs, upholstery and other soft surfaces, use the care method and product intended for the material; launder or vacuum where appropriate. Do not soak them in a hard-surface disinfectant or assume that alcohol spray replaces washing. A manageable routine that respects materials is more useful than repeatedly applying chemicals to every coat, bag or parcel. If a cleaning product causes harm If someone may have swallowed, breathed in or been splashed with a harmful product, seek immediate emergency medical assessment; do not wait for symptoms. If you are unsure whether an exposure is harmful, contact a poison-information service or urgent medical service immediately. After fumes, move to fresh air if you can do so without further exposure. Follow the product's first-aid directions and professional advice for skin or eye contact; do not try to neutralise it with another chemical. Breathing difficulty, a seizure, fainting or loss of consciousness, or inability to wake requires emergency help now. Do not drive yourself; ask someone to take you or call an ambulance. Do not induce vomiting or give anything to eat or drink while waiting for medical advice about suspected poisoning. Keep the product name or packaging available if safe, without returning to a dangerous area to retrieve it. Regular cleaning usually suffices; add appropriate disinfection when illness or weakened immunity makes it useful. Prioritise high-touch surfaces while keeping cleaner air and hand hygiene in the plan. Use the actual product label for material, dilution, wet contact time, protection and rinsing; never mix cleaners. Protect hands with appropriate skin care and gloves, and follow device and laundry care instructions. Get immediate advice for possible poisoning; emergency symptoms must not wait for a cleaning task to finish. How can I reduce coronavirus on surfaces at home? Clean regularly with a suitable soap or detergent and water, especially high-touch areas. Add a locally authorised disinfectant when someone is ill or has weakened immunity, following the label. Surface care complements cleaner air and hand hygiene. Which places should I clean first? Shared handles, switches, taps, tables, counters, phones and controls are sensible priorities. Use material-appropriate methods; there is no need to disinfect every object merely because it came from outside. Does the virus staying alive for three days mean everything is dangerous? No. That familiar figure came from early controlled laboratory conditions. It does not measure the chance of infection from your belongings or justify a fixed waiting rule for every object. Does every disinfectant need the same contact time? No. Read the actual label and keep the surface wet for that product's specified time. Follow its precleaning, dilution, material and rinsing instructions; an immediate wipe-off may not disinfect. Can I use 70% alcohol on every phone or screen? No. Follow the exact device manufacturer's instructions. Some specified hard surfaces tolerate approved alcohol wipes, while coatings and other materials may not. Avoid direct spraying, openings and immersion. Should I stop washing if my hands become dry? Keep necessary hygiene and use tolerable soap, lukewarm water and a fragrance-free cream or ointment. Let sanitiser dry before moisturising. Ask a clinician about persistent painful cracks, bleeding or a rash. Must a sick person's laundry be washed separately on maximum heat? Not routinely. Use detergent, the recommended temperature and complete drying. CDC permits washing their laundry with other people's items. Follow any specific instructions for a particular infection or care situation. What should I do after a possible cleaning-product poisoning? Seek immediate emergency assessment for a possible harmful exposure; if unsure it was harmful, obtain poison-service or urgent medical advice immediately. Breathing difficulty, seizure, fainting or loss of consciousness, or inability to wake is an emergency. Do not drive yourself, induce vomiting, or give food or drink while awaiting medical advice.

title: Cleaner indoor air: ventilation, filters and masks for respiratory viruses
description: Practical ways to improve indoor air at home, school and work, choose compatible filters and portable cleaners, and use masks without assuming zero risk.
body: Respiratory viruses, including the virus that causes COVID-19, can spread through particles people release while breathing, talking or coughing. Cleaner air reduces exposure, but a cool room, open window or air-cleaner label cannot prove that infection is impossible. Start with the room, its occupants and the equipment you can safely use. Understand what cleaner air can do Infectious particles can accumulate in shared indoor air, particularly in crowded or poorly ventilated spaces. Bringing in outdoor air dilutes them; filtration removes particles from air that passes through a filter. Neither measure instantly removes a fresh plume from someone nearby. Laboratory or classroom simulations depend on their airflow, room layout and assumptions. A result from one model is not a universal percentage of viruses removed, and particle capture is not the same as a measured reduction in infections. Layer cleaner air with other appropriate precautions. Bring in outdoor air when it is safe Open windows or suitable doors to improve air exchange; openings on different sides can help. Even a partial opening may be useful. In uncomfortable weather, shorter openings may be more practical, but there is no single opening duration that makes every room safe. Consider outdoor smoke or pollution, extreme temperatures, asthma triggers, security and falls before opening windows. Keep children away from unsafe openings. Do not prop open fire doors or interfere with building safety systems. When outdoor air is unsafe, prioritize suitable filtration and ask about safer ventilation options. Direct airflow thoughtfully A safely positioned fan at an open window can help move indoor air outside. Avoid directing a strong stream from one person toward another. Keep fans stable and protect children from blades, cords and accessible controls; follow the manufacturer's placement instructions. Fans that only move the same indoor air do not supply outdoor air. Room mixing can help distribute cleaner air, but poorly arranged flows or barriers can leave stagnant areas. Ask building staff to assess outlets and layout rather than declaring every supply vent or doorway an infection hotspot. Cooling is not necessarily ventilation Many wall, window and split air conditioners mainly recirculate indoor air. Cooling or dehumidifying the room does not necessarily bring in fresh air. Other heating, ventilation and air-conditioning systems combine outdoor air and recirculation: check what your actual system does. Recirculated air can still be useful when it passes through effective, compatible filtration. Ask the building operator about outdoor-air supply, filter performance and operating hours. Do not modify dampers, ducts or controls yourself; extra outdoor air and longer operation affect energy use, humidity and comfort. Upgrade central filters only if the system supports them CDC recommends MERV 13 filtration, or the highest efficiency the system can accommodate without harming performance. MERV describes tested particle-capture efficiency; it is not a promise of protection for everyone in the room. Ask an HVAC professional about compatibility rather than choosing only the highest number. A filter that is too restrictive can reduce airflow and strain operation. Correct dimensions, a good seal and timely replacement matter. Follow service instructions and keep air intakes and outlets clear. Most ordinary central systems cannot simply accept a HEPA filter as a direct replacement. What HEPA means for small particles HEPA filters capture particles; they are not simple sieves that let everything smaller than a stated size pass through. The often-quoted 0.3 micrometre figure describes a difficult test size, not the smallest particle captured. Smaller and larger particles can be collected efficiently too. Viruses usually travel in respiratory particles rather than as isolated virus-sized objects. However, a filter's laboratory efficiency describes air passing through it, not every breath someone takes in a room. Airflow, leaks, placement and operating time still determine how much useful cleaning occurs. Choose and position a portable cleaner Look for a mechanical particle-filtering unit with a clean air delivery rate, or CADR, suitable for the room. Consider floor area, ceiling height and the speed you will actually tolerate. Smoke CADR is useful for fine-particle comparisons; a large advertised room area may assume conditions unlike yours. Follow placement instructions, leave air inlets and outlets unobstructed and run the unit while the space is used. A suitable location near activity can help, but do not blow air from an ill person directly across others. One small unit will not necessarily clean several rooms or an entire open-plan building. Work with building and budget limits A windowless room is not automatically unventilated: it may receive outdoor air mechanically. Ask who maintains the system and whether it works for the current occupancy. If ventilation is inadequate, consider another space, fewer people, shorter visits or added suitable filtration while the problem is addressed. Compare running costs, replacement filters, noise and maintenance as well as purchase price. Simple safe changes may help without replacing a whole system. Schools and workplaces need a responsible person, a service schedule and professional advice for equipment changes; published example prices are not local quotations. Use air-change targets and monitors with care CDC offers roughly five or more clean-air changes per hour, where possible, as a practical workplace guide. Outdoor ventilation and effective filtered-air delivery can contribute. It is not a universal household pass/fail threshold: room volume, occupancy, activity and vulnerability affect what is appropriate. Carbon-dioxide readings can help investigate outdoor-air ventilation, but do not detect viruses or prove a room infection-free. Particle filters do not remove the carbon dioxide people exhale. A reassuring reading cannot replace assessment of crowding, close contact or whether the equipment is operating correctly. Use fresh-air settings in vehicles When sharing a car, open windows if conditions and road safety allow, and use the setting that draws in outdoor air rather than continuous recirculation. Check the vehicle manual or controls if the symbols are unclear. Protect children from unsafe window access. Outdoor pollution, severe weather or other hazards can limit window opening; use a practical combination of ventilation and other precautions. Air conditioning alone does not establish that the cabin has good air exchange. Keep journeys and the number of occupants reasonable, especially when someone may be infectious. Masks add protection that airflow cannot guarantee A well-fitting mask can reduce particles released into the air and particles breathed in. Choose the most protective type you can comfortably wear correctly, covering nose and mouth. Well-fitting respirators such as N95 or KN95 generally provide better wearer protection than loose medical masks or cloth masks. Fit and material both matter; softness or a tight weave alone does not establish a cloth mask's performance. Gaps allow leakage. A community fit check is not the same as occupational fit testing. A face shield alone does not replace a mask, even in a well-ventilated room. Adapt the plan for children and household illness Do not put a mask on a child under two. For older children, consider their ability to tolerate, put on and remove it safely, with appropriate supervision and local advice. Keep cleaner-air measures accessible for people who cannot safely use a mask rather than relying on masking alone. If someone is unwell, avoid unnecessary close indoor contact and improve air in their room and shared areas when safe. Do not deliberately blow their room air into the rest of the home. Families with a pregnant person, young child or other vulnerable member may want extra layers and tailored clinical advice. Treat ultraviolet and other devices cautiously Professionally designed germicidal ultraviolet systems can supplement ventilation in some buildings. Design, installation and maintenance determine performance and safe exposure. This is a specialist building decision, not a recommendation to aim a household UV lamp at people or attempt a homemade air-disinfection system. Avoid air cleaners that intentionally generate ozone. Be cautious with ionization or chemical air-treatment claims; ask for evidence of performance and safety in the actual setting. A device's registration or a dramatic laboratory claim does not establish that it safely prevents household infection. Make a plan people can keep using Identify the rooms used most, who may be at greater risk, how outdoor air enters and who checks filters or equipment. Choose changes that can run safely and consistently. Reassess when seasons, occupancy or room layout change rather than treating the initial purchase as the whole solution. Cleaner air complements staying away from others when ill, appropriate vaccination and other current local prevention advice. It does not guarantee protection or replace care for someone who is sick. Ask a building professional about ventilation faults and a healthcare professional about individual illness or vulnerability. Outdoor ventilation and particle filtration do different, complementary jobs. Check the actual system; cool or recirculated air is not automatically fresh air. Match filters and portable cleaners to equipment, room size and practical use. Well-fitting masks add protection; face shields alone do not replace them. Use safe, sustainable layers rather than a promise of zero infection risk. Does opening a window guarantee a safe room? No. It can improve air exchange, but the effect depends on conditions, openings and occupants. Balance it with pollution, weather, security and child safety, and use other appropriate precautions. Does air conditioning bring in fresh air? Not always. Many wall or split units recirculate room air; some larger systems add outdoor air. Ask what your actual system provides and how it is maintained. Are viruses too small for HEPA filters? That is not a useful conclusion from virus size alone. HEPA captures very small particles, including respiratory particles carrying viruses. Its test efficiency is not a guarantee for every person in a room. Can I put HEPA into any heating or cooling system? No. Many central systems cannot handle its airflow resistance. Use the highest compatible filter advised for the system, or a suitably sized portable unit with its own fan. Where should a portable cleaner go? Follow its instructions, keep airflow unobstructed and choose a location serving the occupied area without blowing air directly from one person to another. Account for room size, ceiling height, noise and the speed you actually use. How can I improve air in a shared car? Use outdoor-air mode and open windows when safe. Do not assume cooling alone ventilates the cabin. Consider pollution, weather, passenger vulnerability and other protective measures. Is a cloth mask or face shield enough? Cloth masks generally offer less protection than well-fitting medical masks or respirators. Fit still matters with every type. A face shield alone is not a mask replacement, and children under two should not wear masks. Do five air changes or a low CO2 reading prove there is no risk? No. Air-change guidance is contextual, and CO2 is a ventilation clue rather than a virus detector. Neither proves that a room is infection-free or removes the need for other precautions.

title: Period-like cramps without bleeding: possible causes and next steps
description: How to assess cramps when a period has not started, including pregnancy, ovarian, bladder and bowel causes and signs that need prompt care.
body: Cramps that feel like a period do not necessarily come from the uterus. Start with the timing, pregnancy possibility and accompanying symptoms, then choose the appropriate level of care rather than trying to name the cause from pain alone. First separate the missing bleed from the pain A predicted period date is an estimate. A later ovulation, stress, changes in energy intake, contraception or another health condition can change bleeding, while a separate bowel or bladder problem causes discomfort. Irritability, breast tenderness or cramps cannot reliably distinguish an approaching period from pregnancy. Record the last normal bleed, usual cycle pattern, contraception, medicines and when pain began. Note its location and whether eating, passing stool, urinating or sex changes it. A recurring pattern is useful information, but does not rule out a new problem. Check pregnancy at a useful time If pregnancy is possible, use a home test from the first day of a missed period. If the due date is unknown, test at least 21 days after the last unprotected sex. Follow the kit instructions; hormonal contraception does not prevent a test from working. Repeat a negative test after a few days if pregnancy remains possible, and seek advice after a second negative if bleeding has still not started. Cramps cannot establish that implantation has occurred. Do not wait for another test when pain or other symptoms need urgent assessment. Ovulation pain can resemble a cramp Some people feel a brief ache or sharp twinge on one side around ovulation, often about two weeks before the next period. It may last minutes to one or two days. This is approximate timing, not a way to prove that an egg was released or to predict the next bleed precisely. A new, severe, recurring or persistent pain should not automatically be called ovulation pain. Cysts, infection and ectopic pregnancy can feel similar. Once a mild familiar cause has been assessed, warmth or suitable pain relief may help; seek medicine advice if pregnancy is possible. Ovarian cysts can cause pressure or sudden pain Many ovarian cysts cause no symptoms and settle naturally. A larger cyst may cause pelvic pressure, bloating, pain during sex, altered bleeding or a frequent need to urinate. Finding a cyst does not prove it explains every symptom, and most cysts are not cancer. Rupture or twisting that affects the ovarian blood supply can cause sudden pain, sometimes with nausea or vomiting. Follow the urgent and emergency advice below rather than waiting for a planned scan. Ultrasound findings, symptoms and life stage guide monitoring or treatment. Perimenopause changes timing, but does not explain every pain During the menopause transition, periods may become irregular alongside hot flushes, night sweats, sleep problems, mood changes or vaginal and urinary symptoms. Weight changes and longer-term bone health may also need discussion. One missed period, breast tenderness or nausea cannot diagnose this transition. Pregnancy remains possible during perimenopause, and hormonal contraception can obscure the bleeding pattern. Ask about contraception and symptom care rather than assuming fertility has ended. Persistent pelvic pain needs its own assessment; any bleeding after established menopause also needs review. Possible pregnancy with pain needs attention An ectopic pregnancy develops outside the uterine cavity. It may cause one-sided lower pain, unusual bleeding, shoulder-tip pain or discomfort with urination or bowel movements, but early symptoms may be absent. No vaginal bleeding and no positive home test do not make concerning pain safe. Seek urgent advice for pelvic pain when you are or might be pregnant. Severe or worsening pain, faintness, dizziness, actual fainting or shoulder-tip pain calls for emergency help. Internal bleeding may occur without visible bleeding; do not drive yourself or wait for every warning sign. Endometriosis can hurt between periods Endometriosis can cause pelvic or back pain outside bleeding days, as well as painful periods, pain during or after sex and pain with bowel movements or urination. Fatigue and difficulty conceiving may also occur. The pattern overlaps with other conditions, so symptoms alone do not confirm it. Describe the effect on sleep, work and daily life. Assessment may include examination, imaging and sometimes laparoscopy, with pain treatment, hormonal options or surgery chosen individually. Tell the clinician if you are trying to conceive, because that changes treatment choices. Pelvic infection may be mild Pelvic inflammatory disease affects the upper reproductive tract. Chlamydia and gonorrhoea are important causes, but infections that are not sexually transmitted can also contribute. Lower pain, unusual discharge, bleeding between periods, pain during sex or burning urination deserve assessment even without a high fever. Diagnosis uses the history, examination and relevant tests; no single symptom identifies PID. Prompt antibiotic treatment can prevent further harm but cannot undo existing scarring. Complete prescribed treatment and follow partner testing, treatment and advice about when sex can resume. Notice whether bladder filling changes the pain Bladder pain syndrome, also called interstitial cystitis, can cause lower-abdominal pressure, frequent small urinations and an urge to urinate even when the bladder is empty. Discomfort may increase as it fills and ease after emptying. This pattern is a clue, not a diagnosis. A clinician checks for urinary infection and other causes before diagnosing a long-term bladder condition. Urine tests and sometimes further investigations help. Blood in urine or pain with fever or feeling hot, cold or shivery needs urgent advice; do not assume it is a familiar flare. Appendicitis does not always follow the textbook pattern Appendicitis often begins near the navel and moves to the lower right, with worsening pain, nausea, loss of appetite or fever. Pain can be in another place or develop differently, particularly during pregnancy. Not having the usual location does not exclude it. Seek urgent assessment for pain that worsens, does not go away or moves to the lower right; severe pain needs emergency care. Brief improvement can occur if the appendix bursts and does not prove recovery. Hospital tests and treatment are needed when appendicitis is suspected. IBS and inflammatory bowel disease are different IBS can cause recurring cramps, bloating, diarrhoea or constipation, sometimes worse after meals and better after passing stool. It can be felt as pelvic discomfort. Bowel symptoms may coexist with menstrual symptoms, but relief after a bowel movement does not prove IBS or explain why a period is late. Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis are inflammatory bowel diseases, distinct from IBS. Persistent diarrhoea, blood or mucus in stool, fatigue or unintended weight loss needs assessment. Report a new pattern rather than repeatedly treating it as period pain; significant bleeding or severe pain changes the urgency. Indigestion usually has an upper-digestive pattern Fullness, belching, nausea or burning after meals may suggest indigestion or reflux. These sensations can be confused with general abdominal discomfort, but they are not a satisfactory explanation for new lower-pelvic cramps. A meal-related pattern does not exclude another cause. Seek review for repeated symptoms, difficulty swallowing, unexplained weight loss or repeated vomiting. A pharmacist can advise on suitable treatment, especially if pregnancy is possible. Do not use indigestion medicine to delay assessment of chest pain, bleeding or severe abdominal pain. Persistent bloating or early fullness deserves a review Ovarian cancer is a less common explanation, and these symptoms often have other causes. However, frequent or persistent bloating, pelvic pain, early fullness, reduced appetite or increased urinary urgency should be checked. Symptoms are not confined to advanced disease. Book an assessment and return if symptoms persist or become more frequent despite previous reassurance. Mention relevant family history. Examination, selected blood tests and ultrasound may be appropriate; neither a symptom list nor a single abnormal blood result establishes cancer. Choose the urgency from the symptoms Get emergency help for severe or worsening pelvic pain, pain that hurts with movement or touch, faintness, dizziness, fainting, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty, heavy vaginal bleeding or sudden confusion. With abdominal pain, blood, green material or coffee-ground material in vomit, heavy rectal bleeding or black sticky stool, inability to urinate or to pass stool or gas, or a rash that does not fade under pressure also needs emergency help. A squeezing chest pain, pain spreading to an arm, neck or jaw, or pale, blue or grey lips or skin is also an emergency. Do not drive yourself; ask someone to drive you or call an ambulance; these are alternatives, not a requirement to have them together. Seek urgent medical advice for pelvic pain with possible pregnancy, fever or feeling hot, cold or shivery, nausea or vomiting, diarrhoea, unusual vaginal discharge or bleeding, urinary pain or frequency, difficulty passing urine or stool, or blood in urine or stool. Yellow skin or eyes also needs urgent assessment. Sudden increased breathlessness, or chest pain with nausea, vomiting or a racing, slow or irregular heartbeat, needs urgent advice unless an emergency pattern above is present. Do not wait for a period to arrive. Leave with an assessment and follow-up plan For recurring or persistent milder symptoms, arrange a medical review. Bring your cycle and symptom record, test dates, medicine list and relevant bowel or urinary changes. Examination, a pregnancy or urine test, blood or stool tests and imaging are selected according to the findings, rather than ordered as a universal panel. Ask what can safely relieve discomfort and when to return if the cause remains uncertain. Do not take unprescribed antibiotics, hormones or herbs to force bleeding. Three consecutive missed periods warrant review even without pain, but concerning symptoms justify earlier care. Period-like pain does not identify the organ or prove pregnancy. Use a correctly timed pregnancy test without delaying urgent care. Bladder and bowel patterns matter alongside the menstrual calendar. Persistent or changed symptoms deserve a cause-specific assessment. Act on one relevant emergency sign; do not wait for several. Can IBS feel like period cramps? Yes. IBS can cause pelvic cramps with bowel changes, but that does not explain every pain or a late period. Blood in stool, weight loss or a new pattern needs assessment. Can indigestion explain it? Indigestion usually causes fullness, burning or nausea after meals. New lower-pelvic pain should not automatically be attributed to it. Can ovulation feel like a period is starting? A short one-sided ache can occur around ovulation. Its timing is approximate, and severe, persistent or recurring pain needs assessment for other causes. Can an ovarian cyst cause these symptoms? Yes, some cause pressure, bloating, altered bleeding or pain. Many cause no symptoms. Sudden pain or pain with nausea or vomiting needs prompt assessment. Do cramps without bleeding mean implantation? No. Symptoms cannot confirm implantation or pregnancy. Test at the appropriate time, and seek urgent advice for pain if pregnancy is possible. Could it be perimenopause? Cycle changes and hot flushes or sleep changes may fit, but one missed period does not diagnose it. Pregnancy and separate causes of pain still need consideration. What if pain is worse when my bladder is full? Tell the clinician. Bladder pain syndrome is one possibility, but infection and other causes must be checked. Fever, chills or blood in urine needs urgent advice. Should I wait until bleeding starts? No. Severe or worsening pain, pelvic pain with movement or touch, fainting or faintness, dizziness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty, heavy bleeding or sudden confusion needs emergency care. Do not drive yourself; ask someone to drive you or call an ambulance. Other concerning or persistent symptoms need assessment rather than waiting for a period.

title: Sonohysterography: preparing for a saline ultrasound of the uterus
description: What saline sonohysterography can show, how the appointment works, pain and safety planning, and how it differs from HSG and other fertility tests.
body: Saline infusion sonohysterography, also called SIS or SHG, uses fluid and vaginal ultrasound to examine the inside of the uterus. Understanding the question it is meant to answer helps you decide how to prepare, what support to request and what the result can change. What the saline scan examines A thin catheter passes through the cervix and introduces sterile saline into the uterine cavity. The fluid gently separates its walls, making the lining and structures projecting into the cavity easier to see with ultrasound. This scan does not use X-rays. Ordinary SIS primarily examines the cavity. It is not automatically a complete test of both fallopian tubes, a tissue biopsy or proof that implantation will occur. Ask which exact test is booked: similar names can describe different procedures. Why a clinician might recommend it SIS can help investigate abnormal bleeding, a suspected polyp, a fibroid that projects into the cavity, scar tissue or an unusual uterine shape. It may also clarify a lining that was difficult to assess on an ordinary scan, including in selected people with infertility or recurrent pregnancy loss. Whether it is useful before IVF depends on your history, previous imaging and the treatment plan; it is not a compulsory test for everyone. Pain or bleeding may have causes outside the cavity, so a normal SIS does not end every investigation. Bleeding after menopause still needs appropriate assessment. What a finding can and cannot tell you The scan can outline a possible polyp, submucosal fibroid or adhesion and help plan further assessment. Three-dimensional imaging or MRI may be needed to clarify certain congenital shapes. A scan finding must be interpreted with symptoms and other results. Imaging cannot establish the microscopic diagnosis of a lining abnormality or reliably replace a biopsy when tissue is needed. A reassuring cavity image does not guarantee fertility, exclude every cause of bleeding or prove that a visible lesion is harmless. What usually happens at the appointment The clinician commonly starts with vaginal ultrasound. The probe is then removed, a speculum allows access to the cervix, and a thin catheter is positioned after cleaning. With the speculum removed and the ultrasound probe reinserted, saline is introduced slowly while images are taken. The order, equipment and duration can vary; some visits take around half an hour, with the infusion itself shorter. Ask the team to explain each step before it happens. You can request a pause or ask to stop; this is a clinical procedure, not something to attempt at home. Timing and reasons to contact the clinic first For people with cycles, SIS is often arranged after the period and before ovulation, ideally early in the cycle. A fixed calendar day cannot exclude pregnancy, especially with short or irregular cycles. Follow the clinic’s instructions about sex, contraception and pregnancy testing, and report any possibility of pregnancy. SIS should not proceed in pregnancy or possible pregnancy, with active pelvic infection, or with an intrauterine device still in place under the AIUM procedure guidance. Tell the clinic about an IUD, fever, unusual discharge or new pain; do not remove an IUD yourself. Active bleeding can obscure the view, and services differ about rescheduling it. Preparation should match your own appointment Ask whether your bladder should be empty and whether you may eat normally; do not copy bowel preparation or bladder instructions from a different tubal test. Tell the team about medicines, allergies to latex or cleaning products, previous pelvic infection and difficult examinations. Do not stop prescribed medicines without advice. Discuss pain relief in advance, including whether a usual pain medicine is suitable for you. Pregnancy possibility, kidney or stomach problems and other medicines can affect that choice. Antibiotics are not routinely needed for everyone; a history of pelvic infection or other individual risks may change the plan. Do not self-start them. Pain deserves an individual plan Pressure or period-like cramping can occur with the catheter and fluid. Some people find the examination quite painful; others have little discomfort. Prior painful examinations, vaginismus or trauma are reasons to plan support, not reasons to blame anxiety or dismiss pain. Online experiences cannot predict yours. Ask about a slower examination, positioning, a support person where permitted and available pain-control options. Local anaesthetic may be discussed, but evidence and availability vary, and sedation is not a standard promise. Agree on a clear signal to pause or stop. If the test cannot be tolerated, discuss another approach. Risks and an incomplete test Brief cramping, light spotting and fluid leakage are common after-effects. Pelvic infection is uncommon, and injury or perforation is very rare, but a guarantee of no harm would be misleading. Cervical manipulation can also cause a faint or dizzy feeling; tell the team immediately. A narrow cervix, scarring, fluid leakage or a cavity that does not expand adequately can prevent a clear result. An incomplete scan does not mean the uterus is normal or abnormal. The clinician may recommend another appointment, a different imaging method or hysteroscopy according to the question. SIS, HyCoSy and HSG answer different questions HyCoSy uses ultrasound with an appropriate contrast medium to assess passage through the tubes. HSG uses X-rays and contrast to examine the cavity and tubes. Ordinary saline appearing in the pelvis may show that at least one tube is open, but cannot reliably tell whether both are open. Some services combine cavity imaging with tubal contrast ultrasound when both are needed. That does not mean every SIS can be combined with an X-ray HSG using one catheter. Ask which investigation will change your care, whether contrast is involved and what its specific risks and preparation are. When hysteroscopy or a biopsy may be next Hysteroscopy uses a camera to inspect the cavity and can sometimes allow a biopsy or treatment of a lesion. A lining biopsy samples tissue for laboratory analysis. These procedures have their own discomfort, preparation and consent discussions; they are not interchangeable with a saline scan. Depending on symptoms and the initial finding, further vaginal ultrasound, three-dimensional imaging or MRI may be more appropriate. Ask why another test is needed and what happens if you defer it. A normal SIS should not be used to dismiss ongoing bleeding or other persistent symptoms. Aftercare and prompt medical advice Some saline or blood-tinged fluid may leak afterwards, with mild cramps or spotting. A pad can help. Follow your service’s advice about activity, sex and vaginal products, because instructions vary. Before leaving, obtain a contact number and know when and how results will be discussed. Contact the service promptly for persistent or increasing pain, fever or chills, unusual discharge or bleeding that is more than expected. Pelvic pain with difficulty passing urine or stool, blood in urine or stool, painful or frequent urination, vomiting or feeling sick also needs urgent advice. Tell the clinician if pregnancy is possible. When to seek emergency help Seek emergency assessment for pelvic pain that is severe, worsening or painful with movement or touch; or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, actual fainting, shoulder-tip pain, difficulty breathing, heavy vaginal bleeding or sudden confusion. These are alternatives: you do not need several signs together. Do not drive yourself; ask someone to take you or call an ambulance. Do not wait for the clinic to reopen or for a pregnancy test if emergency signs are present. Possible pregnancy with pelvic pain needs urgent assessment even without bleeding or a positive home test. Costs, results and the next decision Ask for an itemized estimate covering the scan, contrast if used, clinician fees and any separate biopsy or follow-up. Coverage depends on the service, insurer and indication; a fertility-related test may be covered differently from a bleeding investigation. Obtain confirmation rather than assuming a universal price or reimbursement. Ask who will interpret the report, when you will receive it and whether the result changes treatment. Write down any remaining questions about bleeding, fertility or pain. The useful outcome is an agreed next step, including follow-up when symptoms continue despite a reassuring image. SIS outlines the uterine cavity; it does not automatically assess both tubes or collect tissue. Confirm pregnancy precautions, infection checks and your own clinic’s preparation instructions. Discuss pain and consent beforehand; a pause or alternative approach may be needed. Know the difference between expected mild after-effects and symptoms needing urgent care. Agree on costs, how results arrive and what further assessment could be necessary. Is sonohysterography completely painless? No. Pressure and cramps vary, and some people have significant pain. Discuss previous difficult examinations, support and suitable pain relief, and agree how to pause or stop. Does every person starting IVF need SIS? No. The decision depends on previous imaging, symptoms and the fertility plan. Ask what uncertainty the test will resolve and whether it would change treatment. Does SIS show whether both tubes are open? Ordinary saline SIS does not reliably distinguish one open tube from two. HyCoSy or HSG may be chosen when tubal passage needs assessment. Can it diagnose cancer or replace a biopsy? It can show an abnormality that needs investigation, but it does not provide a microscopic tissue diagnosis. A biopsy or hysteroscopy may still be needed. When should it be postponed? Contact the clinic for possible pregnancy, pelvic infection symptoms, an IUD in place or new unexplained pain. Active bleeding may affect visibility and scheduling. Follow the clinic’s assessment rather than deciding from a calendar day alone. Can SIS and HSG be done with one catheter? A combined appointment is not guaranteed. Some services combine SIS with tubal contrast ultrasound, while X-ray HSG is a different procedure. Confirm exactly what is planned and why. What is expected afterwards? Mild cramps, light spotting and fluid leakage can occur. Follow local aftercare instructions; persistent or increasing pain, fever, chills, unusual discharge or unexpected bleeding needs prompt clinical advice. Which symptoms need emergency help? Severe or worsening pelvic pain, pain with movement or touch, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, actual fainting, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty, heavy bleeding or sudden confusion needs emergency assessment. Do not drive yourself; ask another driver or call an ambulance. Possible pregnancy with pelvic pain also needs urgent advice.

title: Women’s health screening: building a plan at every age
description: Choose appropriate breast, cervical, bone, skin, heart, diabetes, HIV, bowel and eye checks using your history, local programme and a clear follow-up plan.
body: A “complete checkup” is not one universal collection of tests. Useful screening depends on your age, risks, previous results and local health programme.
