Whether you are planning pregnancy, approaching menopause or looking after your health later in life, the aim is to choose checks that can help you and understand what happens next: not to order everything at once. Start with your history, not a universal test package A useful preventive visit considers your age, the organs you have, previous results, medicines, personal and family history, and whether you are pregnant or planning pregnancy. Screening looks for a condition or risk before symptoms appear. Tests for a new symptom, monitoring of an established illness and follow-up of an abnormal result have different purposes and schedules. Bring previous screening dates and reports, operations, diagnoses, family cancer or fracture history, and a medicine list. Ask which checks are due now and why. An annual preventive visit can help coordinate care; it does not mean that every blood test, scan, pelvic examination or cancer test should be repeated annually. Preconception care is one part of a plan that continues through later life. Weigh benefits, limits and the next step Suitable screening can find treatable risks, detect some cancers earlier or identify changes that can be treated before cancer develops. No test guarantees prevention or rules out all illness. A false positive can lead to extra tests and worry; a false negative can miss a problem. Some screening also finds disease that would never have caused harm, leading to unnecessary treatment. Before agreeing, ask what a result would change, what discomfort or complications are possible, and who will arrange follow-up. Recommendations differ between countries and organisations because tests, evidence, resources and judgments about benefit and harm differ. The US and England examples below are labelled examples, not one worldwide timetable. Personal high-risk or previous-abnormal-result pathways may override routine invitations. Breast changes and screening examinations are different Be familiar with what is usual for your breasts and seek assessment for a new lump, nipple or skin change rather than waiting for screening. A clinician may examine a breast because of symptoms or individual risk. That is different from scheduling a clinical breast examination as an automatic screening test for every healthy woman. The American Cancer Society does not recommend routine clinical breast examinations for average-risk screening at any age. A normal examination is not a substitute for a mammogram when one is indicated. Tell your clinician about previous breast cancer, relevant inherited gene changes, a strong family history or earlier chest radiation; these may require a specialist surveillance plan. Mammography: use a named programme and your risk Mammography uses low-dose X-rays to look for breast changes. For average-risk women, the US Preventive Services Task Force recommends screening every two years from 40 through 74. The American Cancer Society offers annual screening as an option at 40–44, recommends it annually at 45–54, and allows every two years or annually from 55 while health and life expectancy support it. These are different recommendations, not appointments to combine. Mammography can miss cancer and can lead to additional imaging or biopsy when no cancer is present. Discuss discomfort, radiation and overdiagnosis as well as benefit. High-risk people may need MRI alongside mammography and an earlier start. Dense breasts alone do not create a universal instruction for extra ultrasound or MRI; the USPSTF finds the evidence insufficient to recommend for or against supplemental screening on that basis. Older-age decisions also need individual discussion. Cervical screening: HPV and cell tests have specific intervals Cervical screening checks a sample from the cervix for high-risk HPV, abnormal cells, or both, depending on the programme and age. HPV is common; a positive screening result does not itself mean cancer. Finding and treating important cell changes can reduce cancer risk. Screening is not a test for every gynaecological cancer and does not replace assessment of symptoms. In England, routine invitations generally cover ages 25–64 every five years, with earlier follow-up when results or history require it. US guidance uses different starting ages and test-dependent intervals, so use your own service’s schedule. Ask specifically about previous abnormal results, treatment, immune suppression, whether a hysterectomy removed the cervix, or being older without adequate prior screening. Bleeding after sex, between periods or after menopause, or unusual discharge needs assessment without waiting for the next screen. HPV vaccination and STI testing are separate decisions HPV vaccination helps prevent new infections; it does not treat an existing infection or replace cervical screening. In the US, routine vaccination is at 11–12 years and can start at 9; catch-up is recommended through 26, while some adults 27–45 may benefit after an individual discussion. Products and programmes vary by country. Tell the service if you are pregnant: remaining doses are usually delayed, but an inadvertently given dose is not a reason for alarm. A cervical screening sample is not a complete STI check. CDC guidance recommends annual chlamydia and gonorrhoea testing for sexually active women under 25, and for older women with risk factors such as a new or multiple partners. Pregnancy has its own recommended infection tests. Discuss symptoms, exposure sites and partner history privately so the service can select the right urine, swab or blood tests; not everyone needs the same annual panel. Bone density: assess fracture risk as well as age Osteoporosis can weaken bones without pain before a fracture. A central DXA scan measures bone mineral density, usually at the hip and spine, and is interpreted with fracture risk. The USPSTF recommends screening women aged 65 or over, and postmenopausal women under 65 who have increased fracture risk after clinical risk assessment. A scan is not automatically needed by every younger person. An earlier low-trauma fracture, low body weight, early menopause, family history, eating problems, kidney or inflammatory disease, and medicines such as long-term steroids deserve discussion. A previous fragility fracture or a disease or medicine causing bone loss is a separate clinical pathway, not a reason to wait until 65. Results should lead to an appropriate prevention or treatment plan, not an assumption that calcium supplements alone solve the problem. Skin checks: act on changes, not a blanket annual rule Risk assessment considers UV exposure, skin characteristics, previous skin cancer and family history; skin cancer can occur in any skin colour. For asymptomatic people at average risk, the USPSTF finds insufficient evidence to establish the benefit–harm balance of routine clinician skin screening. That does not mean suspicious lesions should be ignored or that people with an important history should have no follow-up. Arrange assessment of a mole changing in shape, border, colour or size, a mole that hurts, itches, bleeds or crusts, or a new unusual mark that persists. An unexplained dark area under a nail also needs checking. Small lesions can matter; do not use a size cut-off or phone photograph to rule out cancer. A specialist may examine the skin closely and remove a suspicious lesion for laboratory testing, called an excision biopsy. Blood pressure: repeat and confirm appropriately Blood pressure is written with the systolic pressure first and the diastolic second: 120/80 mmHg is in that order, not reversed. A properly sized cuff, a validated device and correct resting technique matter. One high clinic measurement does not usually establish chronic hypertension; a clinician may confirm it with home readings or an ambulatory monitor. Symptoms, pregnancy or very high readings can require a different response. As a US example, the USPSTF recommends adult screening from 18, with annual checks for people 40 or over or at increased risk. For low-risk adults 18–39 with a previous normal result, every three to five years may be reasonable. Definitions and treatment thresholds differ between programmes and measurement settings. Ask what your own result means and what follow-up is needed rather than applying a single online “normal” label. Cholesterol: consider the whole cardiovascular picture A lipid blood test may report total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol and triglycerides. LDL can contribute to arterial plaque, while HDL and the other values help interpret the overall picture; no single number determines treatment for everyone. Age, blood pressure, smoking, diabetes, kidney disease and family history can change the risk discussion and testing frequency. CDC advice gives every four to six years as an example for many healthy adults, with more frequent testing for higher-risk people. Most routine cholesterol tests do not require fasting, although a service may request it for a particular test or result. Follow the actual instructions rather than fasting automatically. Appropriate food, activity and smoking-cessation support, and sometimes medicine, are considered together; tell the prescriber about pregnancy plans before changing treatment yourself. Diabetes screening: risk and pregnancy change the plan A US USPSTF recommendation covers asymptomatic, nonpregnant adults aged 35–70 with overweight or obesity. Other risks can justify earlier testing, including a history of gestational diabetes or a strong family history. A normal result may be repeated after about three years in that programme, but the right interval depends on risk and results. Neither age 35 nor a normal past test is a reason to ignore symptoms. Possible tests include fasting plasma glucose, HbA1c and an oral glucose tolerance test. Pregnancy uses a separate gestational-diabetes pathway with its own timing and interpretation; do not substitute a routine adult screening schedule for antenatal care. If a test indicates increased diabetes risk, ask about effective support for suitable activity, nutrition and other risk reduction, and when to check again. Understand glucose tests without diagnosing yourself HbA1c reflects average blood glucose over roughly the previous three months; it does not measure blood pressure and usually requires no fasting. A fasting plasma glucose test generally requires at least eight hours without food. An oral glucose tolerance test measures glucose after a specified drink and timed blood samples. Follow the service’s preparation instructions, particularly if you take medicines. For nonpregnant adults, fasting plasma glucose of 100–125 mg/dL is in the prediabetes range and 126 mg/dL or higher is in the diabetes range. These values are not interchangeable with mmol/L or a home meter reading; diagnosis usually needs a confirming test and clinical interpretation. Pregnancy uses different criteria, and anaemia or some haemoglobin conditions can make HbA1c less reliable. Ask which test and units were used rather than treating a highlighted number as a complete diagnosis. HIV testing: the test type and timing matter CDC advice includes at least one HIV test for people aged 13–64, repeat testing when risk continues, and testing during each pregnancy. A laboratory antigen–antibody test using blood from a vein can usually detect infection 18–45 days after exposure; other tests have different windows. A negative result too early may need repeating, and medicines used for prevention can change the follow-up plan. A positive screening result requires confirmation. HIV is not the same as AIDS, and effective treatment can protect health and greatly reduce transmission risk, including through appropriate pregnancy care. Condoms, selected pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) and exposure-specific advice remain relevant. After a possible substantial-risk exposure, seek urgent medical advice immediately about post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP): it should start as soon as possible and no later than 72 hours when indicated. Do not wait for symptoms or the next routine screening date. Colorectal screening: several methods, with follow-up Screening can detect some bowel cancers early and identify polyps that can be removed before they become cancer. The USPSTF recommends average-risk screening at 45–75, with individual decisions at 76–85. Examples include a yearly stool FIT test or a colonoscopy every ten years after an appropriate negative examination. Previous polyps, cancer, inflammatory bowel disease or inherited risk change the plan; these routine intervals are not for everyone. A positive stool screen needs colonoscopy follow-up to obtain the screening benefit; repeating a stool test to avoid that discussion is not a substitute. Colonoscopy requires preparation and may involve sedation, and it can allow polyp removal. Bleeding and bowel perforation are uncommon but important harms to discuss. Screening lowers risk rather than guaranteeing prevention. New bowel symptoms require assessment through the appropriate clinical pathway, even after a recent normal screen. Glaucoma and eye checks: pressure alone is not enough Glaucoma damages the optic nerve and may progress without obvious early symptoms. It can occur even when eye pressure is within the usual range. An eye professional considers the optic nerve, visual function and other findings, not just a pressure reading. Discuss family history, age, ancestry, eye injury, long-term steroid use and medical conditions such as diabetes; never stop a prescribed steroid independently. The USPSTF finds insufficient evidence for population primary-care screening for open-angle glaucoma in asymptomatic adults aged 40 or over. That is a different question from regular comprehensive sight checks: NHS advice generally recommends sight tests at least every two years, with shorter intervals when advised. Use an individual eye-care plan rather than universal age bands copied from a checklist, and have new eye symptoms assessed promptly. Include mental health in preventive care A preventive visit is also a place to discuss mood, anxiety, sleep and how you are coping. The USPSTF recommends adult depression screening, including during pregnancy, after birth and in older adulthood, when positive results can be followed by assessment and appropriate care. A questionnaire result is not itself a diagnosis, and normal blood tests do not rule out depression. Seek help when low mood persists, you lose interest in usual activities or coping becomes difficult; you do not have to wait for a routine screening invitation. If you need urgent mental health support, contact an urgent clinical or crisis service. If someone’s life is at risk or you cannot keep yourself or someone else safe, get emergency help immediately. An evidence gap about population suicide screening does not lessen the importance of actual danger. Leave with an achievable plan and a results contact Ask for a written list of what is due, which programme or risk factor supports it, how to prepare and when results should arrive. Mention possible pregnancy, previous difficult examinations, accessibility needs and anything that would make attendance hard. You can ask what will happen during an examination and discuss support or alternatives before consenting. Do not silently repeat a test because an old report is missing; ask whether the record can be obtained. Agree who will explain each result and what to do if no result arrives. A normal result does not cancel a future symptom; an abnormal screen often needs another step rather than an immediate diagnosis. Ask about costs and help arranging follow-up if these are barriers. Keep future dates alongside any referral or monitoring plan so age-based screening does not displace care already needed for an illness. Symptoms should not wait for the next screening round Arrange assessment for a new breast lump or nipple or skin change, unusual vaginal bleeding or discharge, a changing mole, or new bowel symptoms. Eye pain, a red painful eye, light sensitivity, blurred or double vision, flashing lights or a moving dark shadow need urgent assessment. These are reasons for clinical care, not reasons to book a routine screening test and wait. Get emergency help if you suddenly cannot see from one or both eyes, or have sudden severe eye pain. Sudden glaucoma-type symptoms (such as a red or tender eye, coloured halos, blurred sight, intense eye pain, headache or nausea and vomiting) also need emergency assessment; do not wait for all symptoms together or try to confirm the diagnosis yourself. Do not drive yourself to emergency care: ask someone to take you or call an ambulance. Immediate danger to your own or another person’s safety also needs emergency help. Preventive visits coordinate care; they do not make every blood test, scan or examination an annual requirement. Use your own country’s programme and personal risk assessment. Average-risk schedules do not cover every previous abnormal result or high-risk condition. Cervical screening, HPV vaccination, STI testing and HIV testing have different purposes and timing. Blood pressure, cholesterol, glucose and bone results need interpretation and a follow-up plan; a number alone is not the whole diagnosis. New symptoms need assessment even after normal screening. Sudden vision loss or severe eye pain and immediate safety danger need emergency care. Which tests belong in a complete women’s checkup? There is no fixed package for everyone. Review the screening that fits your age, organs, medical and family history, previous results and local programme. Breast, cervical, bone, skin, blood-pressure, lipid, diabetes, HIV, bowel and eye checks may have different indications. A preventive appointment can coordinate them without ordering all of them. Can cervical screening or the HPV vaccine completely prevent cervical cancer? They reduce risk but do not provide a guarantee. Vaccination prevents new infections rather than treating existing ones, and appropriate screening is still needed. Follow up an abnormal result. Unusual bleeding or discharge needs assessment even when a previous screen was normal. When should I ask for a bone-density scan? The USPSTF recommends screening women from 65 and younger postmenopausal women at increased fracture risk after assessment. A previous low-trauma fracture, relevant disease or long-term steroid treatment can need a separate pathway earlier. Age alone does not decide every person’s need for DXA. Which mole changes need checking? Seek assessment for a change in size, shape, border or colour, or a mole that becomes painful, itchy, bleeding or crusted. A persistent unusual new mark or unexplained dark nail area also needs checking. Small size does not rule out melanoma; a specialist decides whether examination or biopsy is needed. Who is at higher risk of glaucoma? Family history, age, ancestry, eye injury, long-term steroid use and some eye or medical conditions can increase risk. A pressure-only test cannot rule it out, and normal-range pressure does not exclude it. Ask an eye professional about a complete examination and your follow-up interval. Do all these blood tests require fasting? No. HbA1c usually does not, and most routine cholesterol tests do not. Fasting plasma glucose and some other tests do require preparation. Follow the specific laboratory instructions and ask about your medicines rather than fasting or withholding treatment on your own. Does an abnormal screen mean I have cancer or another disease? Not necessarily. Screening identifies people who may need more assessment. Ask what confirmation or follow-up is needed and how quickly. A positive stool screen, for example, needs the recommended colonoscopy discussion; a normal screen also cannot explain away a new symptom. Why do mammogram ages differ between guidelines? Organisations can weigh the benefits and harms differently. The USPSTF and American Cancer Society have different US average-risk schedules, and national programmes also vary. Choose a plan with your clinician using one relevant programme and your history; do not combine all schedules or apply an average-risk rule to a high-risk condition. Can I use a routine adult diabetes test schedule during pregnancy? Pregnancy has its own gestational-diabetes testing pathway and thresholds. Tell the service you are pregnant or may be pregnant and follow the antenatal plan. HbA1c measures glucose, not blood pressure, and is not an automatic substitute for the required pregnancy test. When should I seek care rather than wait for screening? New lumps, unusual bleeding or discharge, changing skin lesions and new bowel symptoms need clinical assessment. New painful or disturbed vision needs urgent advice; sudden inability to see or sudden severe eye pain needs emergency care. Sudden glaucoma-type eye symptoms also require emergency assessment without waiting for a full set of signs. Do not drive yourself to emergency care. Get immediate help if you cannot keep yourself or another person safe.

title: BeMama: Pregnancy Guidance and Baby Tracking
description: Meet BeMama: pregnancy guidance, a baby tracker for feeding and sleep, and free website tools for planning and everyday care.
body: BeMama brings pregnancy guidance and baby care records into one app. Follow your current stage in Daily Journey, record everyday care in a baby profile, or use the free calculators and checklists on this website. Start with the part that helps with today’s question. During pregnancy: follow your week Set up a pregnancy journey with the date requested in the app. Daily Journey organizes content around your stage, while pregnancy tools show estimated week, trimester and due date. These dates are estimates; use the dating information your maternity team gives you for clinical care. See how to set up your pregnancy tracker: https://bemamas.com/about-bemama/daily-journey/ After birth: keep everyday care records together The baby tracker has separate entries for nursing, bottle feeds, sleep, solids and diaper changes. Choose the baby profile before adding an entry. Record the time and relevant details, then use Reports to review the day or week. A record can help you remember what happened and prepare questions. It does not measure milk transfer during breastfeeding, decide how much your baby needs, or diagnose a sleep or growth problem. Guidance, community and AI-assisted support The app also includes Q&A and community spaces. Read personal experiences as experiences, and take medical questions to a qualified professional. AI-assisted explanations are educational and can be wrong; they are not a diagnosis or an emergency service. Read about feature access before choosing a subscription: https://bemamas.com/about-bemama/premium/ Free tools on the website Use the ovulation and due date calculators for estimates, make a hospital bag or newborn checklist, or keep a growth log. Checklists support your own tasks and notes, progress tracking, printing and a downloadable backup. The public tools do not require an app account. Browse the current tools and their individual instructions: https://bemamas.com/tools/ Choose where to start Open the app at https://app.bemamas.com/ or use the Android and iOS download links on this website. The website’s public tools are a separate place to work: their saved records do not automatically appear in your app account. For setup, tracking and backup steps, start here: https://bemamas.com/about-bemama/getting-started/ Continue with these practical guides Daily Journey organizes pregnancy and parenting content around your selected stage. Baby profiles support feeding, sleep and diaper records with report views. Free website calculators and checklists work without an app account. Website tool records and app account records are separate. Use records and estimates to support conversations with your care team. Is BeMama a pregnancy app or a baby tracker? It supports both: stage-based Daily Journey guidance during pregnancy and baby profiles with feeding, sleep and diaper tracking after birth. The public website also has free tools and educational guides. Can I try a tool without an account? Yes. Open the public tools at https://bemamas.com/tools/ and choose a calculator or checklist. App account features have a separate sign-in flow. Does BeMama replace medical care? No. It provides education, estimates and records. It does not diagnose, prescribe or provide emergency care.

title: Pregnancy Tracker App: BeMama Daily Journey
description: Use BeMama’s pregnancy tracker app to follow your week, set up Daily Journey and understand pregnancy date estimates and feature access.
body: Looking for a pregnancy tracker app that explains what to do with your dates? BeMama’s Daily Journey brings stage-based content together with pregnancy progress estimates. Start with the right journey and date, review your current week, and update your details when your situation changes. 1. Set up your pregnancy journey Open BeMama, create an account or sign in, then set up Daily Journey. Choose Pregnant from the stage options. The other options cover planning, baby care and child growth. Enter the date requested by the pregnancy setup form and check it before saving. Pregnancy dating uses the first day of the last menstrual period in the app’s calculator. Do not enter a due date into a field asking for a last-period date. If your clinician gives you different dating, follow their advice rather than a calculator estimate. 2. Follow your pregnancy week by week Open Daily Journey for content matched to your selected stage. The pregnancy tools show estimated week and day, trimester, due date and days remaining. Together, these help you understand where you are in the pregnancy calendar. Use a topic you read as a prompt for your next appointment. BeMama’s week-by-week guidance is general education; it cannot confirm fetal development or replace appointments and tests. 3. Keep the journey up to date Use the journey setup or edit controls when your stage or dates change. After birth, set up the baby stage with the child’s birth date so the baby care experience uses the appropriate age. A change of stage is something you control. Check the active journey before reading a daily plan or recording information, especially when you have more than one profile. Need a date estimate without signing in? The free website calculator accepts either a last-period date or a known due date and shows pregnancy progress with a timeline: https://bemamas.com/tools/due-date-calculator/ Keep appointment dates and questions in the separate website calendar, with a calendar-file download: https://bemamas.com/tools/appointment-symptom-calendar/ Website calculator and calendar entries are separate from your app account. Save a backup where the tool offers one; the website does not automatically sync these records to Daily Journey. Free access and optional features Daily Journey remains available without an active Premium subscription in the current app. Some tools, AI features and other account capabilities have separate access requirements. Check the feature and subscription screen in your app for what is available to your account. Review the free and Premium explanation: https://bemamas.com/about-bemama/premium/ Download the pregnancy app Use BeMama on the web at https://app.bemamas.com/, on Android at https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.bemama.client.bemama_client, or on iOS at https://apps.apple.com/us/app/bemama/id6783137312. After birth, learn how the feeding, sleep and diaper tracker works: https://bemamas.com/about-bemama/tools/ Choose the pregnancy stage and enter the date requested by the setup form. Follow pregnancy week by week with Daily Journey and the pregnancy progress tools. Update your stage and dates when your circumstances change. The website due date calculator also works without an app account. Pregnancy calculations are estimates, not confirmation of development or clinical dating. How do I track my pregnancy in BeMama? Set up a Pregnant journey, check your last-period date and open Daily Journey. The pregnancy tools show estimated week and day, trimester and due date. Confirm clinical dating with your maternity team. Is BeMama a free pregnancy tracker app? Daily Journey is available without an active Premium subscription in the current app. Other features have their own access requirements. The public website’s due date calculator is free and does not need an account. Does the pregnancy calendar schedule my appointments? Pregnancy progress shows estimated dates. It does not book appointments. Use the separate website appointment calendar to organize dates you have arranged, and check them with your care team. Can I use BeMama after my baby is born? Yes. Set up the baby stage with the birth date, then use the baby profile for nursing, bottle, sleep and diaper entries. Review the selected profile before saving records.

title: Q&A and Community: Ask, Learn, and Connect
description: How BeMama’s Q&A and community spaces work: ask questions, browse related discussions, and find supportive, moderated connection with others on the same journey.
body: Some questions need an article. Others need a person who has been there. BeMama’s Q&A and community spaces exist for the second kind: a place to ask, browse what others have asked, and feel a little less alone at three in the morning. Ask your question, find related answers In BeMama you can post a question and browse discussions related to it. Often someone has wondered the same thing: whether that is a strange pregnancy symptom, a sleep-routine struggle, or how to feel about a slow month of trying to conceive. Browsing related threads before or after asking often surfaces perspectives you had not considered, and it means your question joins a living library that helps the next person too. Supportive, moderated spaces BeMama’s community spaces are moderated. Content and behavior that harass, shame, mislead, or endanger others can be reported, reviewed, and acted on: because a support space only works when it stays safe. Moderation is not about silencing disagreement; it is about keeping the room kind. Different choices and different experiences are welcome. Cruelty and dangerous misinformation are not. Why peer support matters in motherhood Research and lived experience agree: feeling connected to people who understand your situation reduces stress and isolation, especially during pregnancy and the early months with a baby. A clinician can explain what is typical; a peer can tell you what it actually felt like. Peer support does not replace professional care: it complements it. Hearing "that happened to me too, and here is what helped" is a different kind of medicine, and sometimes exactly the kind you need. Community guidelines keep it kind BeMama’s guidelines ask members to be respectful, avoid sharing other people’s private information, and keep medical claims humble: sharing experience rather than issuing instructions. Urgent symptoms and emergencies do not belong in community threads. For anything urgent, BeMama consistently points members to qualified local care or emergency services, because a forum is never the right first responder. A quieter kind of internet Unlike open social media, BeMama’s spaces are built for one purpose: supporting people through planning, pregnancy, and parenting. No viral outrage, no algorithmic doom: just people at similar stages helping each other through. You choose how much to share. Reading quietly is participation too, and many members start that way before posting their first question. Find a group and take part safely Open Community, use group search and review the group information before joining. Search public groups by a topic that matters to you, then use Join where it is available. Read recent posts and the group rules before writing a question. Include useful context without posting a child’s full name, address or private health documents. Use the group or member menu to report a concern, with a short description of what happened. Review membership and privacy before posting. Group access and posting permissions can vary. Topic search is not a promise of nearby-parent matching, an active due-date club or professional medical advice. Post questions and browse related discussions from people at your stage. Spaces are moderated, with reporting and review to keep them safe. Peer support reduces isolation and complements (never replaces) professional care. Community guidelines keep conversations kind, respectful, and privacy-aware. Urgent concerns always belong with local care or emergency services, not a forum. Do I have to post to benefit from the community? Not at all. Many members browse existing questions and discussions quietly. Reading others’ experiences is often valuable on its own, and you can post whenever you feel ready. What happens if someone is unkind or shares bad information? You can report the content or account. Moderators may review it and respond (from hiding content to limiting or closing accounts) to keep the space safe and supportive. Can I ask medical questions in the community? You can ask about experiences and general topics, but community answers are peer perspectives, not medical advice. For diagnosis, treatment, or anything urgent, contact a qualified healthcare provider.

title: Baby Tracker: Feeding, Sleep and Diaper Logs
description: Learn how BeMama’s baby tracker records nursing, bottle feeds, sleep and diapers, with report views and separate free website care tools.
body: BeMama’s baby tracker helps you record what happened, when it happened and which baby the entry belongs to. Use nursing and bottle feeding logs alongside sleep and diaper records, then review your entries in Reports. Here is how those app workflows differ from the free care tools on this website. Start with the right baby profile Sign in to the app and set up the baby journey with your child’s birth date. Open the baby tracking area and check the selected profile. Choose the type of entry you want to record; baby and older-child stages have different available actions. Enter only the details you want to keep. Check the time and profile before saving, and use the entry’s edit controls if you need to correct a mistake. Breastfeeding tracker: record a nursing session Choose Nursing, select the starting side, then choose Timer for a session happening now or Manual for one that has already finished. For a manual entry, check the start and end time before saving. When using a timer, stop it when the session ends. A nursing log records timing and side. Duration does not tell you how much milk your baby transferred, so the tracker cannot tell you whether a feed was sufficient. Bottle feeding tracker: record milk type and amount Choose Bottle and enter the feed time. Select breast milk or formula, choose mL or oz, and record the amount before saving. Check the unit when reviewing entries or changing devices. Use the feeding tracker to remember amounts you recorded. It does not recommend a target intake or tell you how to prepare formula; follow the product instructions and your clinician’s advice. Baby sleep tracker: save a sleep period Choose Sleep to record a sleep period using the available start and end controls. For a running sleep timer, end it when your baby wakes. Review completed entries to see the timing of naps and overnight sleep. The log depends on your entries. It does not automatically detect sleep, promise a next-nap time, or assess whether your baby is sleeping safely. Diaper change tracker: record the change Choose the diaper entry, select the relevant type and save the time. Together with nursing and bottle records, this gives you a feeding and diaper tracker in the same baby profile. Review the entries when you need to recall a day’s care or prepare questions for an appointment. A diaper count alone cannot confirm hydration or rule out illness. Review your day, week and recorded patterns Open Reports for the selected child. Day, Week, List and Summary organize the records differently. The current CSV download covers that child’s latest 30 calendar days through today; check the saved file’s dates rather than assuming it follows the visible report filters. Empty periods can mean nothing was logged, rather than no feeding or sleep happened. Report totals describe the entries you saved. They are not a diagnosis, a growth assessment or proof that a routine is working. AI-assisted analysis and some advanced features have separate access requirements. See https://bemamas.com/about-bemama/premium/ Free website tools: calculators, checklists and a growth log The public tools at https://bemamas.com/tools/ work without an app account. They include ovulation and due date estimates, an appointment and symptom calendar, preparation checklists, a baby-name shortlist and a growth log. Checklist tools let you add tasks and notes, filter the list, mark tasks done or not needed, review progress, and print or download a backup. The growth log plots your measurements and offers a WHO weight-for-age reference view for supported ages; it does not calculate an individual percentile. These website tools save on the current device when you save your work. They do not automatically synchronize with the app. Clearing browser storage can remove saved work, so download backups you want to keep. Read about account data and retention separately: https://bemamas.com/privacy/ Shared care, both parents and twins Keep a separate profile for each child, including twins. Check the selected name before starting a timer, adding a feed or opening Reports. At handover, compare the last saved event and any running timer so the next caregiver does not record the same activity twice. Use separate caregiver accounts and confirm access to the intended child before relying on shared records. Access and management options depend on your account and app version; contact BeMama support if you cannot find them. Do not share your password. A record of who added an event helps explain a handover, but does not replace a conversation. Where caregiver sharing is available, the profile owner invites a caregiver by email. The recipient must sign in with that same verified email to accept; invitations expire after seven days. Accepted caregivers have editor access. The owner controls pending invitations and caregiver removal. Confirm access on both accounts before handing over care. Offline records and syncing between devices Read the status on each care-history entry: Waiting to sync means the change is still local; Syncing means it is being sent; Synced confirms synchronization. Sync failed or Needs review calls for checking the entry rather than assuming it reached another device. If a record is missing on another phone, first compare the account, child and event time. Reconnect the original phone and check its status. Keep the original local data until the issue is resolved; reinstalling is not a recovery step. If it still fails, send support the app version and error text, without private care notes. Pumping tracker: total or left and right Open the child’s care screen and choose Pumping. Under amount style, choose Total or Left / right, then select mL or oz. Use Timer for a session in progress or Manual for one you have finished. Check the start time and amount before saving. For example, a left entry of 40 mL and a right entry of 30 mL describe one 70 mL pumping session. These are sample records, not a supply target. Do not also log the same session as a separate total. Open its care-history entry to correct it. A later bottle feed is a different event. Read reports and export a useful care record In Reports, confirm the child’s name in the heading. With multiple children, use the child-switch icon. Choose Day, Week, List or Summary for the question you want to answer, and check the dates and activity selection. Standard summaries and extended 90/365-day comparisons have different access requirements. For CSV, use the download icon in Reports. The current app first tries to synchronize, then exports the selected child’s latest 30 calendar days through today. The on-screen date or activity filter does not redefine that export window. Choose a file destination and inspect the dates in the saved CSV before sharing it. Example: two logged bottles of 60 mL and 90 mL total 150 mL of recorded bottle feeds. If another feed was not logged, that total is incomplete. Nursing duration is not milk volume. A blank period is missing information, not proof that nothing happened. Growth records: read the measurements first Choose Growth in the child’s care screen. Set the measurement date and units, then enter only the measurements you have: weight, length/height or head circumference. Leave unknown measurements blank. Save the entry and check it in care history; correct the original entry if its date or unit is wrong. The screenshot shows measurement entry, not a clinical growth assessment. Read the child, date and unit together before comparing points. Basic care logging, the app’s separate Premium tools and the free browser growth log are different workflows. Continue with these practical guides Choose the baby profile before recording a feed, sleep period or diaper change. Nursing entries record timing and starting side; bottle entries record milk type, amount and unit. Reports show saved records by day, week, list and summary, with a CSV download. Missing entries are missing data, not evidence that no care happened. Website tools and app tracking are separate; keep backups of records you need. Can BeMama track newborn feeding and diapers together? Yes. A baby profile has nursing, bottle and diaper entries. Save each event with its time, then open Reports to review the records for that baby. Can I use the app to track feedings when I breastfeed and bottle feed? Yes. Use Nursing for sessions at the breast and Bottle for expressed milk or formula. Nursing time and bottle volume describe different things and should not be treated as equivalent intake measurements. Does the baby sleep tracker predict the next nap? This workflow records sleep entries and displays recorded patterns. It does not promise a next-nap prediction or a personalized sleep plan. Will my website growth log appear in the app? No. Website tools keep their own device-local records. Use the tool’s backup controls and enter information separately in the app if you want it there. Is every tracking feature free? Feature access can differ by account and platform. Daily Journey and the public website tools do not require an active Premium subscription, but check the app’s feature and subscription screens for advanced tools and AI access. Why is a CSV different from the report I am viewing? The export currently uses the selected child and a rolling 30-day window. The screen can show a different range or activity selection. Compare the dates and entries before drawing conclusions. Can I fix a pumping entry without adding another session? Yes. Open the saved entry in care history and edit it. Check the amount style, unit and time. Re-entering the same session as a new event can inflate recorded totals.

The table separates those tasks; your account’s purchase screen confirms the offer available to you. Daily Journey does not require an active Premium subscription. Check the included features and billing details on the current purchase screen. Website tool records and app account records are separate. Will Daily Journey stop when my trial ends? In the current app, Daily Journey remains available without an active Premium subscription. Other capabilities can change with your account access. Do I need Premium for the website calculators and checklists? No. The public website tools work without an app account or Premium subscription. title: How AI-Assisted Support Works in BeMama
description: How BeMama’s clearly labeled AI-assisted support works, its firm limits (no diagnosis, prescriptions, or emergency use) and how to use it well alongside your care team.
body: BeMama includes AI-assisted support for general education: and it is always clearly labeled, so you know exactly when you are reading an AI-generated answer. This page explains what that support does, what it deliberately does not do, and how to get the most from it. Clearly labeled, always When AI-assisted features generate a response in BeMama, that response is labeled as AI-assisted. You will never have to guess whether an answer came from an AI system. This matters because AI answers deserve a particular kind of reading: helpful for background and orientation, but never treated as a clinical verdict. The label is your reminder. What AI-assisted support is for The AI-assisted features exist for general education: explaining a term your provider used, giving an overview of a topic, helping you understand what is commonly considered typical at your stage, or helping you organize your thoughts. Used this way, it is like a patient, always-available explainer: good for building background understanding before and after the conversations that really matter. The limits are firm BeMama’s AI-assisted support does not diagnose conditions, does not prescribe or dose medications, and must not be used in emergencies. These are hard boundaries, not fine print. AI-generated content can also simply be wrong: incomplete, outdated, biased, or a poor fit for your specific situation. That is inherent to the technology, which is exactly why its role in BeMama is limited to general education. If you have urgent symptoms or a safety concern, skip the app entirely and contact qualified local care or emergency services. Humans stay in charge of medical decisions Every medical decision in your journey belongs with you and qualified clinicians: people who can examine you, know your history, and take responsibility for your care. AI-assisted support in BeMama is built to sit firmly below that level. Think of the hierarchy simply: AI for background education, BeMama’s human community for shared experience, and your clinicians for actual medical judgment. How to use it well The best use of AI-assisted support is preparation. Ask it to explain a concept before an appointment, use it to understand the vocabulary around a topic, and let it help you draft a list of questions for your provider. Then bring those questions to a real appointment. Members who use AI-assisted support this way tend to have more focused, confident conversations with their care team: which is the outcome we actually want. AI-generated answers in BeMama are always clearly labeled. AI-assisted support is for general education only. It does not diagnose, prescribe, dose medication, or handle emergencies. Medical decisions stay with you and qualified clinicians. Use it to build background understanding and prepare questions for your provider. How do I know when an answer is AI-generated? AI-assisted responses are clearly labeled in the app. You never have to guess whether you are reading AI-generated content or something else. Can the AI tell me what is wrong with me or my baby? No. AI-assisted support does not diagnose. It can offer general educational context, but figuring out what is happening in your specific case is work for a qualified healthcare provider. What should I do in an emergency? Do not use the app. Contact local emergency services or qualified urgent care immediately. BeMama’s AI-assisted support is not built for emergencies and must never be used as one.

title: Your Privacy and Data Safety on BeMama
description: A plain-language overview of how BeMama treats sensitive motherhood data: what it is used for, the deletion and export request paths, and where to read the full policy.
body: The information you share on a motherhood journey (cycles, pregnancies, symptoms, your child’s details) is among the most personal data there is. This page explains, in plain language, how BeMama approaches that responsibility. The full privacy policy on the website is always the complete and authoritative version. Sensitive data, treated with care BeMama is designed around the understanding that planning, pregnancy, fertility, baby, child, and wellbeing information is sensitive. That understanding shapes how the app is built and how your information is handled. The guiding principle is simple: your information exists to serve you inside the app, not to be scattered around. We aim to describe our practices honestly and in plain language rather than burying them in legal fog. What your data is actually used for Your information is used to provide the features you ask for: personalizing your Daily Journey to your stage, remembering what you track, running your account, and making Q&A and community spaces work. It is also used for safety and moderation (for example, reviewing reported content to keep community spaces safe) and for practical operations like troubleshooting problems and responding to your support or privacy requests. You can request deletion or export BeMama provides paths to request deletion of your data and to request an export of it. If you decide to leave, or simply want a copy of your information, those routes exist and are described in the privacy policy. Requests can be sent through the support channels listed on the website, and the privacy policy explains what to expect from the process. Your choices in everyday use You control a lot day to day: what you choose to enter, what you post publicly versus keep to yourself, and which device permissions (like notifications, camera, or microphone) you allow. Permissions are requested only for features that need them. A good habit anywhere on the internet applies here too: keep urgent medical details and other people’s private information out of public community posts. Read the full policy: really This page is a friendly summary, not the fine print. The full privacy policy on the BeMama website describes what is collected, how it is used and shared, retention basics, and your request paths in detail: and it controls if anything here differs. We wrote it to be readable. If something in it is unclear, you can ask through the support channels on the site, and we would genuinely rather answer the question than leave you unsure. Motherhood data is sensitive, and BeMama is designed around that responsibility. Your data is used to personalize your journey, run features, and support safety and moderation. Deletion and export request paths exist and are described in the privacy policy. You control what you share, what you post publicly, and which device permissions you grant. The full privacy policy on the website is the complete, authoritative version. What is my data used for? Mainly to provide what you ask for (personalizing your Daily Journey, powering tools and community features, and running your account) plus safety, moderation, and troubleshooting. The privacy policy has the full detail. Can I delete my data or get a copy of it? Yes. BeMama provides paths to request deletion and export of your data. The privacy policy and the support channels on the website explain how to make these requests. Where do I find the complete privacy details? On the privacy policy page of the BeMama website. It is written in plain language and is the authoritative description of BeMama’s data practices.

title: Cycle Tracker App: Periods, Symptoms and BBT
description: Use BeMama to record periods, symptoms and basal body temperature, read your cycle calendar and understand the limits of ovulation estimates.
body: Keep your own observations together when you are planning a pregnancy. BeMama’s cycle records help you remember dates and prepare questions; a predicted fertile window cannot confirm ovulation. 1. Select your planning journey Choose the person and planning journey before logging. Keep the first day of your period and subsequent bleeding observations separate from a predicted date. If a date was entered incorrectly, correct the record instead of creating a duplicate. 2. Record symptoms and temperature Use the relevant log for symptoms, temperature and test observations. For a basal body temperature record, include the reading and any context such as disrupted sleep or illness. A single reading is not a fertility conclusion. Keep units consistent when comparing records. 3. Read the cycle calendar The calendar puts recorded days and estimated timing in context. Check which dates are observations and which are predictions, especially with irregular cycles. The screenshot shows the calendar view, not a guarantee of fertile days. 4. Use records for a conversation Review dates and patterns with your healthcare professional when you have concerns. Do not use BeMama to avoid pregnancy. The public ovulation calculator is a separate educational tool; its inputs do not become app records. Continue with these practical guides What should I record if I do not know my last period date? Keep the uncertainty in your notes and use dates you actually know. Do not enter a guessed date as a confirmed observation. Discuss dating questions with your healthcare professional. Does one temperature rise confirm ovulation? No. An isolated reading is not confirmation. Keep the measurement and its context, including illness or interrupted sleep, for a discussion with your clinician.
